### Series title page

## Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library

Containing all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprint of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, collated with one another and with several manuscripts, and corrected with the greatest care; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by the discovery of all works completed after the extensive editions issued during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of some importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the material treated; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes:

The first is an index of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance.

The second is an index of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers commented on the individual texts of each book of Scripture, and in which places of their works they did so.

This is the most accurate edition, and easily preferable to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and especially this collection itself: a single, methodical, chronological work bringing together six hundred fragments and short works previously scattered here and there, but assembled for the first time in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

## SECOND SERIES

In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Prepared by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of the Complete Courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

Patrology was issued in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin. The Latin edition sells for 1,200 francs; the Greek-Latin edition for 1,800 francs. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are presented in it only in Latin translation.

# In the year of the Lord 966

## Flodoard, canon of Rheims

[Col. 0009]

# Historical Notice on Flodoard

*(In Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, volume VII, page 325.)*

[Col. 0009A] Learned men, following Sigebert, include Flodoard, a priest of Rheims and the chief ornament of the tenth century, among the monks; among them are Guillelmus Marlotus in his *Metropolis of Rheims* and Natalis Alexander in his *History of the Tenth Century*. Flodoard, whom Sigebert himself calls Flawaldus, a man who can never be praised sufficiently—and I do not know whether any writer of those times was his equal—was born in the town of Sparnacum on the Marne, commonly called Epernay, in the year 894, since, according to his own *Chronicle*, he was seventy years old in 963.

The archive of the Church of Rheims was entrusted to his care, together with the crypt or chapel of Saint Peter, as appears from his *History*, book II, chapter 19, where he speaks of Ebo in these words:

> “He built the archive of the church in most secure buildings, together with a crypt dedicated in honor of Saint Peter and all the apostles, [Col. 0009B] martyrs, confessors, and virgins, where, by God’s favor, we seem to serve God, with fitting workmanship.”

In the same place he calls Gundacrus, whom I think was a canon of Rheims, his foster-father. His mother’s uncle was named Flawardus; he had two sons in the monastery of Saint Basolus, one of them Tetbertus, who, he says, “died among us some time ago as a priest.”

Having gone to Rome with Archbishop Artaldus, for some reason unknown to me, around the year 936, he was received with great honor by Pope Leo VII. Thus he himself sings at the end of his metrical book on the Roman pontiffs, where he speaks of Leo VII:

> As I visited the holy thresholds of heavenly Peter,  
> he joyfully received me, kindly admitted my requests,  
> favored me piously, and attended to me modestly.  
>
> Speaking welcome words, he refreshed me with banquets  
> for body and soul alike; he blessed me and bestowed kisses;  
> then, doubling the gift of his holy favor, he dismissed me,  
> rejoicing and laden with gifts, in an honorable embrace.

[Col. 0009C] In the year 940, when Hugh, son of Heribert, Count of Vermandois, was placed over the Church of Rheims in Artaldus’s position, Flodoard, disapproving of the act, used a pilgrimage to the shrine of Saint Martin as a pretext, but was detained by Heribert. Flodoard himself relates the matter in nearly the same words both in his *Chronicle* under that year and in the *History of Rheims*. His words should be cited, so that it may be evident that the same man was the author of both works.

Thus he writes in the *Chronicle*:

> “Finally, as I was arranging to visit the tomb of Saint Martin for the sake of prayer, I was detained by Count Heribert, after certain persons secretly accused me before him of wishing to depart for the purpose of harming him or his son. He had me held under guard, taking from me the possessions that I held from the bishopric, together with the church that I governed at Culmisciacum (Cormicy), and thus I was detained for five full months.”

The same account appears in book IV, chapter 28, of the *History*:

> “He also took from me the church of the village of Culmisciacum, together with the benefice land that I then held. Finally, as I was arranging to visit the tomb of Saint Martin for the sake of prayer, I was detained by him, after certain persons secretly accusing me before him that I wished to depart for the purpose of harming him or his son; and because I refused to entrust myself to this man whom they had chosen, not knowing whether it pleased God that he should be our bishop. Thus, for five full months, at the command of the count, I was held under guard, partly at liberty, among our brothers—that is, the canons of Rheims.”

[Col. 0010B] He then adds what followed: namely, that once released from custody, “on the very day of the conception and passion of our Lord Jesus Christ,” he proceeded with his chosen bishop to the city of Soissons, where Hugh’s ordination was confirmed in an assembly of bishops.

> “There,” he says, “Hugh, then the prince, taking me by the hand, entrusted me for good treatment to this Hugh, his nephew. He gave me the church of Saint Mary situated at Colridum (Coroy); he also returned the land that his father had taken from me and added another piece in the aforesaid village.”

From this it is clear that before the year 940 Flodoard had been entrusted with the care of the church of Culmisciacum; and consequently he was a priest before the pontificate of Agapetus, who began to sit in 946. The reason for noting this here will become clear below. In the year 941 Flodoard “was first recalled from exile at Hugh’s command.”

He also took part in the synod of Verdun in 947, as is inferred from his statement after the synod: “We remained with Robert of Trier”—that is, Artoldus and he himself. The same words are found in both places, in the *Chronicle* under the aforesaid year and in the *History*, book IV, chapter 35.

Nothing further is read about him until the year 962, when Archbishop Hugh was reduced to the ranks and Odalricus was substituted in his place. The *Chronicle* says:

> “We elected as bishop of Rheims Odalricus, an illustrious cleric, son of a certain Count Hugh,” etc.

Finally, in the following year:

> “Odalricus, Archbishop of Rheims, summoned the leading men of France who had occupied certain possessions of the Church of Rheims.”

[Col. 0010D] Flodoard adds:

> “But I, broken by age and worn down by illness, renounced my office of prelacy before that same bishop; and he, freeing me from this yoke, imposed it, through the election of my brothers, upon my nephew Flodoardus in the seventieth year of my age.”

Thus far Flodoard speaks about himself.

What that prelacy was which he renounced is very obscure. By this name, no doubt, is meant not the simple title of canon, but either the provostship of the Church of Rheims—for I remember reading that provosts, at least of monasteries, were sometimes called prelates—or an abbatial dignity.

For many arguments and indications prove that Flodoard was an abbot, indeed even a monk. First, this is stated precisely in a letter of Adelgagus, or Adelagius, Archbishop of Bremen and legate of the Apostolic See, to Flodoard. In it he consoles him because, having been elected to the see of the Church of Noyon, he was compelled to yield to Fulcherius. The letter’s inscription reads:

> “To Flodoard, Father of Rheims: a word of peace.”

Perhaps it should be read, “to the priest of Rheims.” In this letter, which appears wholly sincere and genuine, Adelgagus, who wrote it in the year 951, on the day before the Kalends of October, testifies that Flodoard, “having laid down his benefice, withdrew into solitude and the retreat of a monastery.”

Whether the Church of Noyon was then without a pastor is not sufficiently clear from Flodoard’s *Chronicle*. In it, the ordination of Bishop Rodulfus is placed in the year 950; then, without mention of his death, it says that in 954 “Fulcarius, dean of the monastery of Saint Medard of Noyon, was ordained bishop at Rheims.”

If the date in the aforementioned letter is free from error, it must be said that Rodulfus died in the year following his ordination, 951; then, in choosing his successor, the votes were divided, some favoring Flodoard and others Fulcarius or Fulcherius, who ultimately prevailed.

Nor should anyone say that the Flodoard mentioned in the aforesaid letter was another man, since the time, place, and every other circumstance agree. Certainly Sigebert, his contemporary, calls Flawaldus of Rheims, who wrote the deeds of the bishops of Rheims, a monk in chapter 131 of his work on ecclesiastical writers.

The same is asserted in an old epitaph written in French verse and reported by Bulaeus, as are Flodoard’s homeland and abbatial dignity. Here is the epitaph:

> If you wish to know the bishops of Rheims,  
> > Read the chronicle of wise Flodoard.  
> > And he died in the time of Bishop Odalricus,  
> > Having been born at Epernay by lineage.  
> > He lived a chaste cleric, a good monk, a better abbot,  
> > And from Agapetus the Roman he was “aubé.”  
> > Through his history you will learn many new things,  
> > And in it you will draw up all antiquity.

Bulaeus rendered it as follows:

> “If you wish to know the archbishops of Rheims, read the chronicle of learned Flodoard. He died in the time of Bishop Odalricus, having come from Sparnacum. He lived as a chaste cleric, a good monk, and a better abbot. He was made a priest by Pope Agapetus. From his *History* you will learn many new things, and in it you will draw up the whole of antiquity.”

This is altogether elegant, but I do not think that the word *aubé*, which occurs in the sixth verse, means that Flodoard was made a priest by Agapetus, who began to occupy the see in 946. For before the year 940, according to the statements in section 9, Flodoard was rector of the church of Culmisciacum and therefore a priest.

*Aubé* is undoubtedly the same as the Latin *albatus*, “clad in white.” But what this word means here I do not understand. Whatever the case may be, these verses, which were written not long after those times, show that Flodoard, the author of the *History of Rheims*, was a monk and an abbot. This is attested not only by Sigebert but also by Adelgagus’s letter, which must shortly be reproduced in full.

One objection can be raised against this letter: it says that Flodoard had already laid down his benefice before the year 951, whereas the final passage of the *Chronicle* cited above makes clear that he did not renounce his prelacy until the year 964.

It may be answered that by “benefice” Adelgagus meant the charge of the church of Culmisciacum and the title that Flodoard held in the Church of Rheims; whereas by “prelacy” is meant the abbatial dignity which Odalricus, “through the election of the brothers”—that is, the monks—conferred upon Flodoard’s nephew and namesake.

“But whose monastery,” you ask, “if he was ever a monk and abbot?” Marlotus, following the common opinion, writes that he assumed the monastic habit at Saint Remigius; Colvenerius likewise says that he was abbot there.

I fear that neither statement is true. For in the careful catalogue we possess both of the abbots of that illustrious monastery and of the monks who lived under each abbot, no Flodoard is found. Indeed, after the restoration of regular discipline there, Hincmarus was the first abbot, beginning in the year 945 and remaining for twenty-two years; this calculation excludes Flodoard.

Others assign his withdrawal to the monastery of Saint Basolus, where they say he was later made abbot. This is supported by the fact that he had two relatives there, his maternal uncle’s sons, as he himself says in book II, chapter 3.

But the following stands in the way: according to the *Chronicle*, in the year 952 Archbishop Artoldus “restored the monks in the monastery of Saint Basolus, expelling the clerics who served there and entrusting it to the abbots Hincmarus and Rotmarus.”

Yet before the year 951 Flodoard was already a monk, according to Adelgagus’s letter—provided, that is, that no error has entered into the dates. Therefore he was not at Saint Basolus, but rather among the monks of Altivilla, where Rotmarus was abbot. Among the monks of that period at Altivilla I find one named Flodoldus. Is this Flodoard? Certainly this is the only conjecture left to us, since the monks were restored at Saint Theodoricus only later, as we shall see below.

Moreover, that Rotmarus was abbot of the monastery of Altivilla, and that the care of restoring monastic discipline at Saint Basolus was entrusted to him together with Hincmarus, is established by the aforementioned catalogue of the monks of Altivilla, which [Col. 0013A] we possess from a very ancient Remigian manuscript, where the abbots Rotmarus and Rodulfus are listed.

Hence it may be conjectured that, with the support of Abbot Hincmarus, Rotmarus entrusted the care of the monastery of Saint Basolus to Flodoard, his monk. But this carries us too far.

The appendix to Flodoard’s *Chronicle* shows that he died in the year 966, in these words:

> “In that same year, namely 966, a man of venerable life and a priest of the Church of Rheims named Flodoard, venerable for the honor of holiness, angelic in the splendor of chastity, heavenly in the radiance of wisdom, and abundantly filled with the insignia of the remaining virtues, an outstanding author of the preceding book and of others, leaving the exile of his earthly pilgrimage on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, as we believe, attained the rights of the heavenly city.”

[Col. 0013B] Flodoard is praised on that very day in the necrology of the Church of Rheims, according to Sirmond, but without the addition of any title or rank. Another Flodoard must therefore be considered the priest and canon who is recorded in the necrologies of the Church of Rheims and of Saint Remigius on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June.

In a manuscript of the Discalced Carmelite Fathers at Paris, the following epitaph is appended to fourteen books of verse written by the same man, apparently by Flodoard himself:

> Here lies Flodoard, a priest unworthy of his rank,  
> awaiting the return of the heavenly Judge.  
> Trusting that the Merciful One will grant him pardon,  
> though he be beset by countless sins.  
>
> Whoever reads this inscription, mindful of his own future lot,  
> pray to the Lord for him who lies in the earth.  
> Christ, graciously spare your servant Flodoard,  
> and at the judgment grant pardon to your servant.

As for his writings, the *History of Rheims* cannot be praised sufficiently. He extracted and composed it in four books from the ancient archives of that church, the acts of councils, the deeds of martyrs and other saints, letters of the pontiffs, and other records. He dedicated this history to an R. prelate—that is, as Sirmond interprets it, to Rodulfus of Laon.

His *Chronicle* is unquestionably also of great importance. It was first published under his name by Pithoeus, who unjustly doubted whether the same man was its author, as we have clearly established above by mutual comparison. Concerning it, the following is read in the Angevin *Chronicle*, volume I of Labbe’s *Bibliotheca*, page 285:

> “In the year 917, the beginning of Flodoard’s *Chronicle*”; and: “In the year 965, the end of Flodoard’s *Chronicle*.”

The *Chronicle* as printed is defective by two years.

Henricus Bunderius, a Dominican of Ghent, who lived in the year 1555, lists other short works of Flodoard in his catalogue of Belgian manuscripts, in these words:

> “Flodoard the priest wrote, in verse, fifteen books *On the Italian Triumphs of Martyrs and Confessors*, preserved in manuscript at Trier in the cathedral; three manuscript books *On the Triumphs of Christ and the Saints of Palestine*, also there; and, third, two manuscript books *On the Triumphs of Christ and the Deeds of Antioch*, in verse, likewise there.”

The first work consists not of fifteen but only fourteen books, extant in the very ancient manuscript that I have already mentioned and that now belongs to the Discalced Carmelite Fathers. From these books we have published several passages concerning the Roman pontiffs.

In them are preserved in full the acts of our holy father Benedict and of Saint Columbanus and other saints whom Gregory the Great also mentions in his *Dialogues*. We give below this metrical life of Columbanus and the poem on Saint Benedict.

Browerus, in his *Trier Annals*, cites from a Trier manuscript a fragment concerning Pope Leo VII, namely the same passage that we presented above.

Finally, Flodoard also sang in verse certain miracles of blessed Mary, which he discusses in book III, chapter 6, of his *History*.

Bishop Ratherius of Verona held him in such high esteem that he entrusted his works to Flodoard for correction. Folcuinus testifies to this in chapter 20 of the *Chronicle of Lobbes*, where he says that a letter written by Ratherius to Flodoard of Rheims was preserved in his own time in the archives of the monastery of Lobbes.

It remains for us to reproduce here the letter addressed to Flodoard by Adelgagus, first published by Colvenerius and later by others, including Binius in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*.

> “Adelgagus, by divine mercy servant of the Church of Bremen, to Flodoard, Father of Rheims: a word of peace.
>
> “You formerly laid down your benefice in order to carry with you into solitude and the retreat of a monastery your spirit, contemptuous of worldly glory, intending by your vow not to depart before the end. Why then do you now grieve that you are not permitted to leave that place and ascend to the episcopate, which Fulcherius has seized? Do you stand, and yet do you not stand?
>
> “You promised God stability, so that, if you should ever act otherwise, you would know that you must be condemned by the One whom you mocked; and yet now you waver? Be firm in the way of God, and from morning until night forget the things that belong to honor and dignity.
>
> “You prayed: [Note: Formula of the Benedictine profession.] ‘Receive me, Lord, according to your word, and I shall live.’ The word of God is this: ‘Anyone among you who does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple.’ Those who flee from them will be saved, and they will be in the mountains like doves of the valleys.
>
> “God saw in you the desire for good work; he granted you the opportunity to practice it and heard your prayers. Do not doubt that he would bring you help to complete it.
>
> “But you say: ‘God lends a talent to one who wishes to trade with it; blessed are those who make a profit.’ Do you not know that the higher a person has been raised, the nearer he is to falling? Do you not know that the rank of honor is an incitement to pride and material for empty glory?
>
> “Beware of flattering yourself; beware of desiring to perform your righteousness before men, so that you may be seen by them. Make yourself fit for the kingdom of God; trade, and gain profit beyond the appointed prize of your calling in Christ Jesus.
>
> “Those who say that you are suited to a higher dignity are deceiving you, brother, and, with the devil as their adviser, are attempting to scatter the path of your steps.
>
> “I confess that whoever desires to be a bishop in order to benefit rather than to rule, to endure contradictions rather than honors, labors rather than pleasures, and work rather than wealth, desires a good work. But examine your inner spirit in all things, and learn that Christ did not glorify himself in order to become a pontiff.
>
> “We have indeed undertaken the episcopal office, but we do not fulfill the work of the office. Danger lies hidden in the desire for preeminence. I shudder to drink what the saint said, what the saint wrote back:
>
> “‘I would now be among the number of the condemned if I had been among the number of bishops.’
>
> “Receive these words from one who is yours, and cast your thought upon the Lord: your patience will not perish forever. Those who hate you will become desolate; suddenly they will fail and perish because of their iniquities. The Lord will be known as one who executes judgments, and the sinner will be caught in the works of his hands.
>
> “Pray for me.
>
> “Written on the day before the Kalends of October, in the year 951.”

Thus far the letter. Bulaeus thinks that the year 955 should be substituted for 951, so that the date may agree with the year 954, in which Fulcarius is recorded by Flodoard as having been ordained. Jacobus Vassor retains the earlier year in his *History of the Church of Noyon*.

For the rest, I hope no one will take offense that I have discussed Flodoard’s monastic life at length, without pronouncing on it as decisively as other authors have, for whom the matter is of no concern. Indeed, the learned Natalis Alexander, after reproducing Adelgagus’s letter, says:

> “From this letter it is clear that Flodoard was a monk.”

I should therefore rightly be accused of neglecting the dignity of our order if I did not at least bring forward whatever arguments may in some way claim so great a man for us, leaving the final judgment to fair-minded readers.

[Col. 0015]

# Second Notice

## Compiled from the books of the *History of the Church of Rheims* and elsewhere by Georgius Colvenerius

*(From volume XVII of the Lyon edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, page 500.)*

[Col. 0015B] To begin with his name, we think the author’s full name was Flodohardus, or Flodoardus, from which, by syncope, arose Flohardus and Floardus. The latter form is found in nearly all our copies, and this is likewise the form read by Joannes Savaro in his notes on Sidonius Apollinaris.

Sigebert calls him Flawaldus; Trithemius calls him Flavaldus. Petrus Pithoeus, in the twelve authors published together, Papirius Massonus, and, following them, the most illustrious Cardinal Caesar Baronius call him Frodoardus.

But he uses *l*, not *r*, in the first syllable, because in book II, chapter 3, of this *History* he mentions Flawardi—or, as another copy reads, Flavardi—the maternal uncle of his mother, and in his *Chronicle*, under the year 963, his nephew Flodoardus, as the more correct Divionense copy reads.

Hence the aforementioned Pithoeus, in the *Glossary of the Capitularies of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious*, which he later enlarged and published, consistently calls him Flodoardus; so does Josias Simlerus in the preface, or dedicatory letter, to the *Cosmography of Aethicus*. We shall follow them.

His homeland was Sparnacum, a town situated not far from Rheims. He lived under the archbishops of Rheims Haeriveus, Seulfus, Artoldus, and Odalricus. That he composed this work under Artoldus is evident from book III, chapter 6.

He lived under the Frankish kings Charles the Simple, Louis from Overseas, and Lothair, son of that same Louis, whom Artoldus consecrated king of the Franks in 954.

That he was a priest and canon of the Church of Rheims is attested by the Rheims and Igniac manuscripts, which adorn him with these titles; indeed, all our handwritten copies conclude with the words:

> “Here ends Floardus, or Flohardus, priest and canon of Rheims.”

Likewise Josias calls him a priest, and Joannes Filesacus, a Parisian theologian, calls him a canon of Rheims in his *Complaint of the Ancient Gallican Church*. Joannes Molanus does the same in *The Saints of Belgium* under the fifth day of August.

[Col. 0016B] He was also at some time rector or pastor of the village of Culmisciacum, as he himself testifies in book IV, chapter 28.

But that he later changed his way of life, abandoned his canonry, submitted himself to the monastic rule, and subsequently became an abbot, is certain from the documents contained in the letter of Adelgagus, Archbishop of Bremen, which you will find below.

The same follows from what he writes about himself in his *Chronicle* under the year 963:

> “But I, broken by age and worn down by illness, renounced my office of prelacy before that same bishop”—namely Odalricus, the successor of Artoldus—“and he, freeing me from this yoke, imposed it, through the election of my brothers, upon my nephew Flodoardus in the seventieth year of my age.”

Thus it stands there.

The Gallic verses found in a very ancient manuscript, which we placed at the beginning, confirm the same thing. Their interpretation is as follows:

> “If you wish to know the bishops of Rheims, read the chronicle of the learned Flodoard. He died in the time of Bishop Odalricus, having come from Sparnacum. He lived as a chaste cleric, a good monk, and a better abbot; he was made a priest by Pope Agapetus. From his history you will learn many new things, and in it you will draw up all antiquity.”

Finally, this is also proved by the testimony of Cardinal Domenico Grimani, which we have placed below.

Flodoard was a monk and abbot of the Order of Saint Benedict at Rheims, in the monastery of Saint Remigius. Therefore Trithemius is not mistaken, nor does he unjustly claim him for his order, when, following Sigebert, he says in book II, chapter 68, of *On Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, and in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, that Flodoard was a Benedictine monk of Rheims.

Conrad Gesner likewise follows them in his *Bibliotheca*, as does Arnoldus Wion in book II, chapter 67, of *The Tree of Life*. Wion, however, is mistaken about Flodoard’s date by nearly a hundred years, writing that he flourished in the year 870.

Antonius Possevinus is also mistaken in his *Sacred Apparatus*, where he distinguishes Flavaldus from Flodoardus and Frodoardus as though they were different authors, attributing the *Chronicle*—which we shall discuss below—only to Frodoardus, and this *History of the Bishops of Rheims* to Flodoardus. He corrects the matter somewhat in the appendix.

Likewise the aforementioned Wion, in his additions to *The Tree of Life*, page 909, incorrectly distinguishes Flodoardus from Flavaldus.

Papirius Massonus is further mistaken in his *Catalogue of Authors Used in His Annals*, when he calls Flodoard a bishop of Rheims. Baronius followed him in the year 933, unless there is an error in Baronius and the reading should be “Archbishop of Rheims,” referring the statement to Artaldus. For in the year 948 he calls Flodoard a priest of the Church of Rheims, as Papirius himself does in book II, in his treatment of Charles the Simple; thus he seems to have called him a pontiff inadvertently.

[Col. 0017B] It is nevertheless true that, after the death of Rodulfus, Flodoard was elected bishop of Noyon and Tournai by both chapters, of Noyon and Tournai, on 20 July 950.

He was not, however, confirmed, because Louis from Overseas, king of the Franks, craftily, secretly, and by an extraordinary procedure intruded and installed in the sees of both churches an impure monk and simoniacal cleric, Fulcherus, the illegitimate son of Kent, the king’s chief cook.

When Adelgagus learned of this—or, as Albert Krantzius calls him in his *Metropolis*, Adaldagus, Archbishop of Bremen and legate of the Apostolic See—he burst out in these words:

> “The Lord will be known as one who executes judgments.”

He then sent him the consolatory letter reproduced above in the notice from Mabillon.

The following accounts of Fulcherus by Jacobus Meyerus and Antonius Demochares in their lists of the bishops of Tournai agree with these manuscripts:

> “44. Fulcharus or Fulcherus, a monk of Saint Medard of Soissons, buried in the church of Saint Eligius outside the walls of the city of Noyon, concerning whom Meyerus writes under the year 955. Fulcherus, a bastard believed to be the son of Kent, King Louis’s chief cook, obtained the bishopric of Noyon by evil arts, made everything worse, and administered it for eighteen months in all. He was consumed by the disease of lice and phthiriasis—a great example of the punishment of ambition and simony, if only we descendants feared God.”

Flodoard was, moreover, a man outstandingly adorned with learning and character, as the testimonies that we shall append below demonstrate. In historical matters he was distinguished by varied reading, great diligence, and tireless labor.

Hence, in the preface to this *History*, he says that “this work was collected from every source”: namely, from sacred and secular writers, the deeds of martyrs and the lives of other saints, the acts of councils, and the letters of the pontiffs, especially those of the bishops of Rheims, which he drew from the archives of his own Church.

Indeed, the most learned annalists of our age, Baronius and Papirius Massonus, commend him for these very things, and greatly embellished their *Annals* from his writings.

Baronius mentions him very frequently in volume X, from the year 845 through the year 962. Unfortunately, however, when citing material from the mutilated and defective French copy that he had translated into Latin, he himself admits this under the year 845. There he recounts the diploma of Charles the Bald by which he ordered all the possessions of the bishopric of Rheims to be restored to Hincmarus; the diploma is found in book III, chapter 4.

Concerning this Pithoeus reasonably says in the aforementioned *Glossary*, under the entry *Beneficiario jure* (“by right of a beneficiary”):

> “I would not wish a man of extensive reading to have reported this same diploma from a French interpretation, in words alien to its meaning.”

From the year 865 onward, Baronius begins to cite Flodoard’s actual Latin words, but from a single copy, and one frequently incorrect and corrupted, as may be seen under the same year and also under 871, 877, 892, 893, and elsewhere.

Nevertheless, he mentions Flodoard with due praise, as under the year 933, calling him an accurate writer of that period. Baronius places such confidence in him that under the year 954 he uses him to refute all the others for falsehood.

How great Flodoard’s authority was, we learn from the fact that he was sometimes employed on embassies and public affairs. Thus, in book I, chapter 20, he writes that he was sent by Bishop Artaldus concerning certain affairs of the Church of Rheims to King Otto and Duke Conrad.

And now let us come to his writings. The author’s prologue demonstrates that this work consists of four books, in which he calls the work of his labor fourfold. Therefore Trithemius, and those who follow him, are wrong to count only three. Besides these four books of the *History of the Church of Reims*, or, as others call it, *On the Deeds of the Bishops of Reims*, he inserts much additional material concerning the saints and monasteries of that same city and diocese.

He also wrote a most exact *Chronicle* of his own age, from the year of the Lord 919 to 966, [Col. 0018C] which Petrus Pithoeus published among the twelve contemporary writers of the *Annals and History of the Franks*. The work was printed in octavo at Paris in 1588 and at Frankfurt in 1594. Nevertheless, in his preface Pithoeus himself doubts whether it belongs to the same author. He says:

> “Now concerning Frodoard’s *Chronicle*—whether he was Flavaldus or Floardus, a priest of the Church of Reims, who wrote the Lives of his archbishops from Blessed Remigius to Artaldus in a wholly different style—it seemed appropriate to add this warning: the material concerning the bishops of Verdun, as well as certain other passages enclosed in quotation marks, are from one of the three manuscripts, which we called the Dijon manuscript, although it seems rather to have been copied at Verdun. Whoever that writer was, he will certainly dispel many of the shadows obscuring the history of his own age for us,” and so forth.

Concerning this matter, Sirmondus says in his preface that Pithoeus was not without reason in doubting it, adducing also this argument: in the old calendar of Saint Mary of Reims, his death is recorded in these words: “16 Kalends of June: Flodoard, priest and canon”; whereas the appendix to the *Chronicle* states that the author of the *Chronicle* died on the fifth Kalends of April.

But it must be understood that in the Churches an anniversary commemorating someone’s death is not necessarily celebrated on the same day on which he departed this life, as customary practice everywhere testifies. This occurs because of various impediments, especially around Easter, at which time he died. Accordingly, Papirius, in Book II of his *Annals of the Franks*, under Charles the Simple, not only admits that the author of both works was the same person, but this is also demonstrated most clearly by what appears in the same *Chronicle* under the year 940, when compared with what is found in Book IV, chapter 28, of the *History of Reims*. In both places the author recounts the same event concerning himself: his detention in custody by Count Heribert and the seizure of the church which he governed at Colmisciacum.

Pithoeus would certainly never have written this if he had likewise read this history, which does not begin with Blessed Remigius—who was the fifteenth archbishop of the see of Reims—but with Blessed Sixtus, the first bishop of that see, and with the earliest fathers and founders of the faith. Nor is the style so different that, even when the same event is reported, the author does not use nearly the same words. Let the material in Book IV, chapters 15 through 35, be compared with this *Chronicle*.

Whether he wrote one work before the other is not certainly known. The *Chronicle* seems to be later, because this history ends with the acts of Artoldus, reaching only to the year 948, whereas the *Chronicle* proceeds further, to 966.

As for what Trithemius says—that in addition to the deeds of the bishops of Reims, Flodoard also wrote, in one book, the Lives of many saints—since he nowhere mentions any such work, it may perhaps be not another work but this very one, as Sigebertus implies, in which he treats of the life and miracles of many saints.

Moreover, Flodoard was competent not only in prose but also in verse. He wrote in verse the miracles performed in his own time in the church of Blessed Mary, built by Hincmar, as he himself testifies in Book III, chapter 6. That he wrote several works on the Lives of the saints in verse is testified by Joannes Bunderius of Ghent, of the Order of Preachers, who was living in the year 1550, in an index of manuscript books existing in Belgium. He writes:

> “Flodoard the priest wrote, in verse, fifteen manuscript books *On the Triumphs of the Italian Martyrs and Confessors*, at Trier in the high church. Three manuscript books, also in verse, *On the Triumphs of Christ and the Saints of Palestine*, are held there. Third, two manuscript books, in verse, *On the Triumphs of Christ and the Deeds at Antioch*, are held there as well.”

If these writings still exist, may the people of Trier publish them for the public benefit of the Church.

I have no certain knowledge of his other works. He died full of days, in the seventy-third year of his age, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 966, on the fifth Kalends of April—that is, on 28 March—not on 5 April, as Nicolaus Chesneau and Possevinus inadvertently recorded. For this is what we read in the supplement to his *Chronicle*:

> “In that year”—namely, 966—“a man venerable in life, a priest of the Church of Reims named Flodoard, venerable for the honor of his holiness, angelic in the splendor of his chastity, heavenly in the radiance of his wisdom, and abundantly filled with the marks of the remaining virtues, an outstanding composer of the preceding book and of other books, relinquishing the exile of his earthly pilgrimage on the fifth Kalends of April, obtained, as we believe, the rights of citizenship.”

[Col. 0019]

## BIBLIOGRAPHICAL NOTICE

*(From Fabricius,* Bibliotheca medii et infimae Latinitatis*.)*

[Col. 0019C]

Flodoard, or Frodoard; called Flauvaldus by Sigebertus and Trithemius; of the Benedictine order of Culmiciacum (Cormicy); priest and canon of Saint Remigius at Reims; died in the year 966, on 28 March, at the age of seventy-three. His writings are as follows:

**Annals, or Chronicle of his own age**, from the year 919 to 966, in P. Pithoeus’s *Twelve Contemporary Writers*, Paris 1588 and Frankfurt 1594, octavo, pages 109–198, with a brief appendix extending to the year 978, pages 198–201; and with a continuation from 977 to 990, taken from the *Chronicles* of William of Nangis, monk of Saint-Denis, pages 207–214.

Although Pithoeus does not dare to attribute this *Chronicle* to Flodoard with certainty, he nevertheless does not deny that it sheds extraordinary light upon those times. It was reprinted under Flodoard’s name, and more accurately corrected from the Thuane Codex, in André du Chesne’s, or Quercetanus’s, *Writers on the Affairs of the Franks*, volume II, p. 590.

Jacques Le Long testifies in the *Bibliotheca Historica of France*, nos. 3746 and 6870, that a new and improved edition of this *Chronicle* and of all Flodoard’s works had long been in preparation by D. de Targny of Noyon, treasurer of the Church of Reims and royal librarian.

The more complete Cottonian manuscript should be consulted, together with the continuation by Reginald, archdeacon of Angers, extending to the year 1277. See the catalogue of the Cottonian manuscript library, no. 69.

**History of the Church of Reims**, or, as Sigebertus calls it in chapter 132, **Deeds of the Bishops of Reims**, in four books, extending to the year 948. Nicolaus Chesneau, or Querculus, dean of Reims, had published a French translation, though with many omissions throughout, at Reims in 1580, in quarto. Jacobus Sirmondus was the first to publish all four books complete in Latin, Paris 1611, octavo, together with an appendix by an anonymous canon of Reims, composed around the year 1140, who had abridged Flodoard, and with other short works concerning the same Church.

After Sirmondus came Georgius Colvenerius, who states that he collated his edition with the Latin manuscript from which Chesneau had prepared his French translation. In addition to scholia and explanations of obscure words, he added an appendix by Sonacius concerning the synodal statutes of the Church of Reims, together with a catalogue of the archbishops of Reims. Douai 1617, octavo.

Colvenerius’s edition was reproduced by the *Bibliothecae Patrum*, Paris 1639, and by the latest Lyon edition, volume XV, p. 500.

**On the Roman Pontiffs from Blessed Peter to Leo VII**, a heroic poem in fifteen books. Papebrochius notes in the *Acta Sanctorum*, volume VII, May, p. 773, that it is a paraphrase of the work of Anastasius on the Lives of the Pontiffs, except that encomia of various saints are interspersed throughout.

Mabillon published a substantial portion of this work—from Gregory II, in the year 715, to Leo VII, in the year 935—from a manuscript of the Discalced Carmelites, in *Saeculum Benedictinum* III, part II, p. 596. From the encomia of the saints interspersed in it, Mabillon likewise published a considerable number, as the distinguished Cave had already noted: those of Saint Columbanus the abbot, *Saeculum* II, p. 30; of Saint Attala, p. 127; of Saint Bertulfus, abbot of Bobbio; and, from Book XIII, the eighth poem, on Saint Benedict and his miracles, in the supplement to the first *Saeculum*, at the end of the second *Saeculum*, p. [Col. 0021A] 1095.

Papebrochius borrowed from Mabillon the poem by Flodoard on Pope Paschal, which he presents in the *Acta Sanctorum*, appendix to 14 May, volume VII, p. 773.

It should not be doubted that this is the same work which Joannes Bonderius testified was preserved at Trier, in the high church, when he wrote to Miraeus, Sigebertus, and Vossius in 1555, in the *Index of Manuscripts in Belgium*: *On the Triumphs of the Italian Martyrs and Confessors*, fifteen books written in verse.

This is clear from Theodoric Ruinart’s observation concerning the manuscript of the Carmelites at Saint-Germain, which I shall append below. Before doing so, however, I note that, according to Bonderius, the same library at Trier also preserved three books *On the Triumphs of Christ and the Saints of Palestine* and two books *On the Triumphs of Christ and the Deeds at Antioch*, likewise in epic verse, but distinct from the earlier work.

In Book III of the *History of the Church*, chapter 6, Flodoard, reporting the miracles believed to have occurred in the basilica of Blessed Mary at Reims, says:

> “Many of these events, which took place before our own time, are unknown to us. Nevertheless, since we were present and saw those which we relate, or learned of them from persons who had seen them, we judged it inappropriate to pass over them here in silence as well, although we once committed them to verse.”

But let us hear Ruinart explaining, in his own language—which is familiar today to most learned people—what he observed in that manuscript.

> “I examined this manuscript, whose beginning is torn away; the work begins with the end of the first chapter of the third book. It speaks there of the martyrs who suffered under the persecution of Valerian.
>
> “The fourth book begins with Pope Saint Felix and treats of the persecutions of Aurelian, Claudius, Numerian, and Diocletian. It speaks of the popes according to the times in which they lived.
>
> “The fifth and sixth books are not found in it, although it seems that nothing is missing there.
>
> “The seventh treats only of the persecution of Diocletian.
>
> [Col. 0021C] “The eighth is entitled *On the Persecution of Maximian*. It begins with the history of Saint Marcellus and of all the martyrs who appear in his spurious Acts; then it speaks of the holy martyrs who are venerated in the cities of Italy. Chapter 15 concerns Saint Afra of Augsburg. Chapter 16 concerns Saint Eusebius, pope.
>
> “The ninth book speaks of Saint Valentine, a martyr at Rome; then of the martyrs of the surrounding region and of the Acts of Saint Sylvester, of Gallicanus, of Saints John and Paul, and of several other martyrs whom people place at Rome under Julian the Apostate.
>
> “The tenth book begins with Saint Julius, pope, and ends with Vitalian and Adeodatus. It mixes in several other saints, as in chapter 2. It speaks of Eusebius, whom it calls *praesul* and who is said to have suffered at Rome under Constantius, together with Orosius and others; of Saint Eusebius of Vercelli; of Victorinus the Rhetorician; and of Saint Denis of Milan. It mentions the translation of the latter, carried out by Saint Basil, who sent his body to Saint Ambrose. I possess Saint Basil’s letter addressed to Saint Ambrose, from an ancient manuscript, in which this translation is mentioned.
>
> “In chapter 3, where it treats of Saint Damasus, pope, it speaks of Saint Jerome. In chapter 8 it speaks of the schism of Laurentius, of Paschasius the deacon . . . In chapter 19 it treats of Hormisdas, pope; the peace of the East; Saint Germanus of Capua; the restoration of Africa; Saint Remigius; the conversion of Clovis; the crown which he sent to Rome; and the consular garments which he received from the emperor. In chapter 10 it treats of Saint John, pope; Symmachus; and Boethius, whom Theodoric had killed. In chapter [Col. 0022B] 12 it treats of Cassiodorus and of what Belisarius did against the Goths in Italy and Africa. Finally, it treats at considerable length of Saint Gregory and of what occurred in his monastery.
>
> “The eleventh book contains the history of the popes from Agatho to Christopher. In chapter 5 it speaks at length of Saint Boniface of Germany, whom it calls a teacher and martyr. In chapter 6 it treats of Carloman, a Frankish prince who became a religious. In chapter 7 it treats of Pope Stephen II, his journey into France, his miraculous healing at the abbey of Saint-Denis, and so forth.
>
> “The twelfth book contains the history from Leo IV to Leo VII. In chapter 1 it speaks of Hincmar’s two pallia and of the establishment of the octave of the feast of the Assumption of Our Lady. In chapter 2 it treats of John, bishop of Ravenna. In chapter 3 it treats of Hincmar and Charles the Bald. In chapter 4 it treats of Fulk, archbishop of Reims, and of several commissions which the popes entrusted to him. In chapter 5 it treats of the translation of Saint Calixtus, pope, to Reims, which he calls *urbem nostram*, ‘our city.’ It treats at length of the actions of Formosus, to whom it says that Charles, king of France, asked that he send him blessed bread, *panem benedictum*.
>
> “The thirteenth book concerns the saints whom Saint Gregory treats in his *Dialogues*, and other female saints of Italy.
>
> “The fourteenth book concerns the patron saints, martyrs, and others of the cities of Italy.
>
> “It ends with Saint Columbanus and his disciples.
>
> “At the end there is an epitaph of Flodoard himself.
>
> “This manuscript is scarcely less ancient than Flodoard.”

[Col. 0021]

## TESTIMONIES AND ELOGIES OF FLODOARD

[Col. 0021D]

### I. Sigebertus of Gembloux, in Book *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 132

Flavaldus, a monk of Reims, wrote the *Deeds of the Bishops of Reims*. He begins his narrative with the founding of the city itself, which, because of the character of its citizens—who were hard-hearted in war—first took for itself the name *Cordurus*. Later, the soldiers of Remus, fleeing from the face of Romulus, his brother, took refuge there and named it Remus, after the name of their prince Remus.

This writer deserves to be counted among writers because, departing from his principal work, he made known to readers the Lives or passions of the holy martyrs and confessors resting in churches adjacent or subordinate to the Church of Reims.

[Col. 0022D]

### II. Joannes Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

Flavaldus, a monk of Reims and of the Order of Saint Benedict, learned in the divine Scriptures and exceptionally well educated in secular literature, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, wrote works worthy of serious reading, through whose study he transmitted his name with glory to posterity.

Among them is said to be a distinguished work beginning with the founding of the city of Reims, which, according to the account, the soldiers of Remus, slain and driven into exile by Romulus, his brother, built in memory of their lord and thus named. It extends to his own times and intersperses much material concerning holy martyrs and other events and deeds. He wished to give the volume the title *Deeds of the Bishops of Reims*, in three books.

He also wrote, in one book, the Lives of many saints. It is further said that he wrote many other works which have not come to my attention.

### III. Cardinal Dominicus Grimanus of Saint Mark, in the *Dario* addressed to Desiderius Erasmus, canon regular of Saint Augustine, printed at Basel in 1508 by Michael Furter and Joannes Scotus, folio 32, note 13

When I was staying at Reims, the most illustrious Lord Robert Briconet, archbishop and chancellor of France, offered me a manuscript register containing four books of the *History of the Church of Reims*, by Flodoard, formerly its canon and subsequently a monk.

The change of status, and the fact that he became a monk from a canon, indicates the man’s piety. He wrote learnedly and carefully. For I compared much of that register with the copies preserved here in the Vatican and found it faithfully transcribed: it is free from the rust of the old corrupters and from the harshness of modern authors.

If the miserable poverty of our age did not prefer profit for life to the study of history, and did not consult avarice more than knowledge of antiquity, the author would be worthy of the press.

### IV. Guillelmus Eysengrein, in the *Catalogue of Witnesses to the Truth of the Orthodox Mother Church*

Flavaldus, a monk of the Benedictine profession at Reims, a man learned in both sacred and secular writings, a perfect historian and a profound theologian, brought the *Deeds of the Bishops of Reims*—from the founding of the city of Reims, which, according to the account, the soldiers of Remus, slain and driven into exile by Romulus, Remus’s brother, built in memory of their lord—down to his own times in three volumes, in which he recounts the histories of many holy martyrs.

### V. Papirius Massonus, Book II of the *Annals of the Franks*, under **CHARLES THE GREAT**

Frodoard flourished under Charles the Simple and Louis, and transmitted to posterity the carefully written Lives of the bishops of Reims. We saw several copies of this work at Paris.

### VI. The same author, under **CHARLES THE SIMPLE**

In the following year—that is, 920—great disturbances arose in Gaul. We shall speak of these and of other public affairs from the *Chronicles* of that same Frodoard—whom others call Flodoard—the priest of the Church of Reims.

For, in addition to the Lives of the bishops of Reims, this author wrote a chronicle from the year 919 to the year 966, in which he departed this life on the fifth Kalends of April, in the seventy-sixth year [this should read seventy-third] of his age. From this point onward we shall follow this writer in our accounts of Charles, Robert, Rudolf, Louis, and Lothair, setting aside Widukind and other writers of lesser diligence and reliability.

# HISTORY OF THE CHURCH OF REIMS

[Col. 0023]

## THE FOUR BOOKS OF FLODOARD, CANON OF REIMS, ON THE HISTORY OF THE CHURCH OF REIMS

Published through the work and effort of Georgius Colvenerius, Doctor of Sacred Theology, royal and ordinary professor, provost of the collegiate church of Saint Peter, and chancellor of the University of Douai; enriched with extensive scholia and notes.

*(Bibliotheca Patrum, volume XVII.) (C)*

## PREFACE TO THE READER

[Col. 0023C]

Kind reader, receive briefly an account of what we have done in this edition of the author.

The work was collated in all with seven copies. Three of them had been collated with one another by the late Nicolaus Chesneau, dean and canon of Saint Symphorianus in the city of Reims. He translated this history—or, more accurately, a substantial part of this history—into French and published it in that language, printed at Reims in 1581 by Joannes Foygni.

Thomas Witus, licentiate in both laws, brought me the Latin manuscript copy of this dean, from which he had translated into French. It had been given to him by the Reverend Lord Antonio Beauchesne, canon and succentor of the Church of Reims, who had been the executor of the aforesaid Lord Chesneau’s will. [Col. 0023D] We designate this copy by the letter *c*.

It was also collated with the copy of the monastery of Saint Remigius, which we designate by the letter *r*; with the copy of the metropolitan church of Blessed Mary; and with a third copy, which is not designated by a particular name but which I believe belonged to Igny.

The second of these differed from the copy later sent to me, about which more below. For he often notes in the margin that the copy of Blessed Mary reads differently from the one in our possession. For example, in Book I, chapter 20, he says that the metropolitan manuscript reads *beside the river Saram*, whereas the copy we possessed reads *Faram*. In Book III, chapter 4, he notes that it reads *Abbess Algardis*, as does the copy of Saint Remigius, whereas our copy has *Adalgardis*. In the same book, chapter 7, he says that the copy of Saint Mary and Saint Remigius reads *with palms*, whereas another copy has *with psalms*, as our copy of Blessed Mary also reads.

I therefore had this copy of Lord Chesneau transcribed at my own expense and subsequently reread it carefully. When I discovered that several things were missing in certain places, I began seeking other copies from which these gaps could be filled.

Then, opportunely through the efforts of the aforesaid Lord Witus, two other complete copies were sent from Reims. One came from the archives of the metropolitan church of Blessed Mary. It was written by hand on ancient parchment, and we designate it by the letter *m*. The other was copied recently, in the year 1596, on paper, from the same old copy by Lord Georgius Montgerard, prior of the monastery of Saint Martin at Épernay, with some words corrected in certain places and others altered.

We designate it by the letter *s*. We generally cite both together as *ms*, since they should be regarded as one copy, inasmuch as the later was taken from the earlier. We nevertheless count them as two because corrections or alterations were made in many places.

After receiving these complete copies, I discovered that the copy of the aforesaid Lord Chesneau was easily missing a quarter of the work. Accordingly, after transcribing each of the places that were lacking, I supplemented my copy in its entirety through renewed labor, collated it completely with the two complete copies mentioned above, reread it, and afterward punctuated it as accurately as possible.

In addition, for greater clarity, I reviewed everything against the French copy and usually noted in the margin the proper names that were more obscure in the vernacular. I had no doubt that this would be agreeable to the reader.

Of all the copies, the one from the monastery of Saint Remigius appeared the most correct. From it the copy of the metropolitan church—which was otherwise sufficiently accurate—had to be supplemented in many places, not merely with words but even with complete sentences that had been omitted.

I knew that more copies written by hand existed in Paris and elsewhere. Papirius Massonus mentions in Book II of his *Annals* that he had seen several copies at Paris. But because purer waters are ordinarily drawn from the source itself, I judged that these should rather be sought from the archives of Reims. For them I give great thanks to the treasurers and archivists of the aforesaid metropolitan church, who placed them at my disposal for two years.

After these labors had been completed, the work appeared without any notes or scholia, at Paris in 1611, under the care and direction of the Reverend Father Jacobus Sirmondus, priest of the Society of Jesus. When I obtained that copy, I reread everything with it from beginning to end. Just as I removed a considerable number of errors with its assistance, so I discovered that many remained in it, and that sometimes entire lines were missing. We designate this copy by the letter *I*.

For the rest, we have changed nothing or placed nothing in the text that was not found in the copies or in the originals of passages cited from elsewhere, unless we expressly indicated it in the margin or in the scholia, or unless it was certain that the reading was an error and a copyist’s slip, one letter having been written for another.

Where the reading differed and it was not certain which was correct, we retained the more probable reading in the text and generally relegated the other to the margin.

[Col. 0026A]

We have likewise changed nothing in the orthography except spellings judged unusual and corrupt, such as *dompnus*, *dampnatio*, *sompnus*, *contempnet*, *solempnitas*, *ebdomas*, *parrochus*, *parrochia*, *carta*, *summittere*, *Nicholaus*, *Nichasius*, *subiciens*, *adiciens*, *exenium*, and similar forms.

In other cases we preferred to retain the spelling customary in that period, for the sake of antiquity, such as *Karolus*, *Karlomannus*, *Pippinus*, *Theodulfus*, and *Rodulfus*.

We added in the margin all the passages of Scripture that are cited, and generally also those to which the text refers. Likewise, we added passages cited from other authors, all of which we compared with the originals and often corrected from them. Some, however, could not be found.

By this method certain passages were corrected which otherwise could scarcely have been emended, since the author’s copies had been corrupted in many places and, through age, escaped the eyes of readers.

[Col. 0026B]

The material contained in Book III—which is entirely concerned with the deeds and writings of Hincmar—I compared with the short works and letters of that same Hincmar, published both by the Reverend Father Joannes Busaeus and by Joannes Cordesius, canon of the Church of Limoges.

In addition, the work was collated with the volumes of the Councils and the letters of the Roman pontiffs wherever councils are discussed. It was also compared with the ecclesiastical *Annals* of Caesar Baronius and with the principal historians of Gaul and Belgium: Gregory of Tours, Aimoins, Sigebertus, Christianus Massaeus, Jacobus Meyerius, Papirius Massonus, and others.

From these authors, a reliable indication of the date of each event has generally been added in the margin or in the scholia placed after the end of the work.

[Col. 0026C]

We judged these scholia entirely necessary, first because the author’s diction is frequently obscure for the reason that he weaves long periods, which become complicated through the variety and multitude of the matters he gathers and inserts; and also because he sometimes uses words that were very common in that age but have since fallen into disuse.

We have collected these in a separate index. Finally, we believe that we have brought considerable light to the author through these scholia because we have explained whatever might be called into doubt, confirmed most of the author’s statements by the testimony of others, and indicated where further material concerning the matter under discussion could be sought.

Finally, we added a catalogue of all the archbishops of Reims, listing not only their names but also, as accurately as possible, the period of their tenure and death, together with their principal deeds.

If, however, amid such antiquity, the scarcity of writings, and the diversity of opinions, we have not everywhere reached our goal, the fair-minded reader will grant pardon and correct us candidly.

In preparing this catalogue we received much assistance from the material which Claudius Despretz of Arras, Lord of Queant, a highly learned doctor of both laws, kindly supplied to us, drawn from various antiquities of places in France, partly manuscripts and partly printed sources.

He also supplied us with the synodal statutes by Lord Sonnacius, Adelagius’s letter to Flodoard, and several other testimonies concerning the same man.

We were further assisted by a catalogue, written in a different hand at the end of the copy belonging to the metropolitan church of Blessed Mary at Reims. Although it contains only bare names up to the fifty-fourth archbishop, it is fuller in what follows.

[Col. 0028A]

## THE AUTHOR’S PROLOGUE TO BISHOP R.

[Col. 0027]

[Col. 0027A]

To the venerable lord, and one greatly beloved in the love of Christ, the distinguished prelate R., Flodoard, servant of such great kindness, sends every joy of the holy virtues in Christ.

Urged by the very frequent goads of your admonitions, at last, having shaken off the sluggish torpor of my laziness and set aside the occupations of various cares, I submit anew to the diligence of your fervent study the fourfold work of my labor, gathered from every quarter and arranged by chapters, as you have deigned to command: namely, the book of the histories of our Church of Reims.

Nor should the holiness of your high estate be at all surprised by this reminder of our service, since we have been hindered by various occupations, constrained also by the icy cold of winter, and further restricted by a shortage of scribes.

Nor is it surprising that I, the least of men, spend time correcting my little works, since some of the ancient writers are said to have lingered more over revising their books than over composing them.

Yet I do not think that I have completely removed all errors. If any faults of the scribe should be found, they can be purged by the discernment of your industry. For I do not regard myself as so perfect a scrutinizer, down to the last detail, that I would be unwilling to endure finding a more diligent corrector in the removal of faults.

Therefore, because your holiness’s affection toward our littleness seems to have overflowed abundantly, I have judged this fruit of our study worthy of being entrusted to the protection of your patronage, so that what has been spoken by us in the darkness of humility may be spoken forth in the light by the height of your industry.

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 0027]

## CHAPTER ONE: On the Founding of the City of Reims

[Col. 0027C]

As we prepare to disclose the foundations of our faith and to recall the fathers of our Church, it may not seem particularly relevant to investigate the founders or builders of our walls, since they are shown to have contributed nothing to our eternal salvation, but rather to have left behind, carved in stone, the traces of their error.

Regarding the founder of our city, or the author of its name, the common opinion is not in every respect approved by us. It maintains that Remus, the brother of Romulus, founded this city and gave it its name. Yet, since the city of Rome was founded by the twin founders Romulus and Remus, we accept from reliable writers that Remus was killed by his brother’s soldiers.

Nor do we find that he first withdrew from his brother, since the two, born at one birth, raised among shepherds, and devoted to banditry, are reported to have founded a city. After a quarrel arose and Remus his brother was killed, Romulus is said to have given the city its name from his own.

To use the words of Livy (*Decade I*, Book I):

> “When control of Alba had been entrusted to Numitor, Romulus and Remus were seized by a desire to found a city in the places where they had been exposed and everywhere brought up, and where there remained a multitude of Albans and Latins. The shepherds also joined them, all of whom could readily create the hope that little Alba and little Lavinium would be insignificant beside the city that was to be founded.
>
> “Then an ancestral evil intervened in these plans: the desire for kingship. From it arose a shameful contest, beginning with a sufficiently mild dispute. Since they were twins, and respect for age could not establish a distinction between them, they decided that the gods under whose protection those places stood should choose through auguries who would give his name to the new city and who would rule the city once founded.
>
> “Romulus chose the Palatine and Remus the Aventine for the taking of auspices. It is said that the augury first came to Remus: six vultures. The omen had already been announced when a double number appeared to Romulus. The multitude had hailed each of them as king at the time prescribed for that purpose, but they based their claim to kingship on the number of birds.
>
> “Then, after they came to blows in dispute, the quarrel turned from anger to murder. In the ensuing crowd Remus was struck down. The more common story is that Remus, to mock his brother, leapt over the new walls. Thereupon the angry Romulus killed him, adding these words as a reproach: ‘So shall it be hereafter with anyone else who leaps over my walls.’ Thus Romulus alone gained the power, and the city, once founded, was called by the name of its founder.”

So Livy.

It therefore seems more probable that our city was founded by the soldiers of Remus, exiles from their homeland, or that the people of Reims were established by them. Both our walls, marked by Roman auspices, and the higher Gate of Mars, called, according to the opinion of the ancients, after the name of the propagator of the Roman race, have preserved the ancient name even to our own times.

We can also see its arch marked with the story of the she-wolf offering her teats to the little Remus and Romulus as they emerge on the right. The middle arch, carved according to the Roman arrangement, opens with a design representing the twelve months. The third, which is on the left, is formed with the auspice of swans or geese.

Sailors indeed say that a swan gives a favorable omen, as Aemilius says:

> “The swan is always the happiest bird among omens.”

Sailors desire this bird because it does not sink into the waves. Geese likewise keep watch at night, as they demonstrate by their continual cries. Finally, the Roman Capitol is also said to have been saved from the enemy by a goose.

Nevertheless, it is not surprising that the founding or origin of our city is not openly revealed, since, as Isidore testifies (*Etymologies*, Book XV, chapter 1), disagreement commonly arises even concerning the founding of Rome herself, mistress of peoples and of the world, so that her origin cannot be carefully ascertained.

For Sallust says (*Concerning the Conspiracy of Catiline*):

> “The city of Rome, as I have received the account, was founded and first inhabited by Trojans who, under the leadership of Aeneas, were wandering without fixed settlements.”

Others say that it was founded by Evander, according to Virgil (*Aeneid* VIII):

> “Then King Evander, founder of the Roman citadel.”

Eutropius likewise speaks as follows in his historical work:

> “Romulus, while he was engaged in banditry among shepherds, at the age of eighteen, established a small city on the Palatine Hill. He called the founded community Rome, after his own name. After him Tullus Hostilius enlarged it by adding the Caelian Hill. From that time onward, the other rulers, each in different periods, became its founders or enlargers.”

The former name of our city, *Durocortorum*, is asserted by Caesar’s *History*, in which Book VI reads:

> “After devastating the regions, Caesar led the army back to Durocortorum of the Remi and, having summoned an assembly of Gaul to that place, began an inquiry concerning the conspiracy of the Senones and Carnutes.”

Aethicus likewise records in his *Cosmography*:

> “From Mediolanum through the Cottian Alps to Vienna: 409 miles. From there to Durocortorum: 333 miles, which make 221 leagues. Likewise, from Durocortorum to Divodorum: 62 miles. By another route, from Durocortorum to Divodorum: 88 miles. From Durocortorum to Trier: 99 leagues. From Bagacum of the Nervii to Durocortorum of the Remi: 53 miles.”

## CHAPTER TWO: On the Friendship of the Romans and the Remi
It is therefore established that the people of Reims were joined to the Roman people by the most steadfast friendship in ancient times. The books of the aforementioned *History of Julius Caesar* attest this very point—Book II, at the beginning—where we read:

> “When Caesar himself, arriving unexpectedly and more quickly than anyone supposed, had reached the territory of the Belgae, the Remi, who among the Belgae are nearest to Gaul, sent to him as envoys Iccius and Andebrogius, the foremost men of their state. Offering themselves and all that they possessed into the protection and friendship of the Roman people, they bound themselves by an oath without reservation, declaring themselves ready both to give hostages, to carry out orders, to receive him into their towns, and to assist him with grain and other supplies. All the other Belgae were under arms, and the Germans who inhabit the banks of the Rhine had joined themselves to them. Their collective fury was so great that they could not even be deterred from joining the others by the Suessiones, their brothers and close kinsmen, who use the same legal rights and the same laws, and share one magistrate with them.”

Again, in the same work:

> “After Caesar saw that all the forces of the Belgae, gathered into one place, were coming toward him and were no longer far away—and learned this from the scouts whom he had sent and from the Remi—he hastened to lead his army across the river Axona (the Aisne), which lies at the farthest limits of the territory of the Remi, and there established his camp. This both fortified one side of the camp with the riverbanks and made everything behind it secure from the enemy; it also made it possible for supplies to be brought to him without danger from the Remi and the other states. There was a bridge over the river. He stationed a garrison there and left the legate Quintus Titurius Sabinus with six cohorts on the opposite bank. He ordered the camp to be fortified with a rampart twelve feet high and a ditch eighteen feet wide.

> “The Belgae began attacking with great force the Remian town called Bibrax, which lay eighteen miles from the route [Original: eight]. The assault by the Gauls and Belgae was with difficulty held off that day. When, after surrounding the entire circuit of the walls with a multitude of men, they began casting stones against the wall from every side, and the defenders had been stripped from it, they advanced under a testudo toward the gates and undermined the wall, which at that time was easily done [manuscript: ‘by an approach’]. For such a multitude was hurling stones and missiles that no one could remain standing on the wall.

> “When night brought an end to the assault, Iccius the Remian, a man of the highest nobility and influence among his people, who at that time was in command of the town and was one of those who had come to Caesar as envoys concerning peace, sent a messenger to him, saying that unless aid were sent, he could not hold out any longer. In the middle of the night Caesar, using the same leaders who had come from Iccius as messengers, sent Numidian and Cretan archers and Balearic slingers to assist the townspeople. With their arrival, the Remi gained fresh zeal for defending the town in the hope of defense, while the enemy, for the same reason, lost hope of taking it. Thus, after lingering for a short time around the town and ravaging the fields of the Remi, burning all the villages and buildings to which they could gain access, they marched with all their forces toward Caesar’s camp and pitched their camp less than two miles away.”

And shortly afterward:

> “The enemy immediately proceeded from that place toward the river Axona, which was shown to lie behind our camp as well. Having found fords there, they attempted to lead part of their forces across, intending, if they could, to storm the fortress commanded by the legate Quintus Titurius and cut down the bridge [Original: ‘cut through it’]. If they could not do this, they would ravage the fields of the Remi, which were of great use to us in conducting the war and supported our supplies.

> “When Caesar was informed by Titurius, he led across the bridge all his cavalry, the light-armed Numidians, slingers, and archers, and hastened toward them. A fierce battle was fought at that place. Our men attacked the enemy, who were impeded in the river, and killed a great number of them. When the rest tried with the utmost boldness to cross over the bodies of their comrades, they drove them back by a multitude of missiles and by their courage; they killed the first men who had crossed after surrounding them with cavalry.”

Again, in Book III of the same *History*:

> “Caesar sent the legate Labienus with cavalry against the Treveri, who are nearest to the Rhine. He instructed him to approach the Remi and the other Belgae and keep them to their duty.”

Again, in Book V:

> “Caesar, of course, brought about such a change in everyone’s disposition that, apart from the Haedui and the Remi—whom Caesar always held in the highest honor, the former because of their ancient and perpetual loyalty toward the Roman people, the latter because of their recent services in the Gallic war—there was scarcely any state that was not viewed with suspicion by us.”

Again, in Book VI:

> “The Carnutes sent envoys and hostages, relying upon the intercession of the Remi, whose clients they were. They gave the same response as the Senones, when hostages were demanded.”

It is also established that the Remi had held the leading position among their neighboring peoples from ancient times. It is likewise recorded that they had obtained this same position among the Romans, and that both their legal standing and their honor had been increased, as is stated in the previously mentioned history, in Book VI:

> “The Sequani had relinquished the leadership; the Remi had succeeded to their place.”

For the Remi had always, and in every war, preserved their loyalty to the Romans. In Book VII also, when nearly all the peoples of Gaul are said to have conspired against the Romans and to have held a council at Bibracte, they absolutely refused to attend, because they followed the friendship of the Romans.

It is also reported that, in times of need, they supported the Roman forces, as in Book V of this history:

> “In that year, since grain had been produced in smaller quantities because of the droughts, he”—namely Caesar—“was compelled, unlike in earlier years, to place the army in winter quarters and distribute the legions among several states. Of these, he assigned one to be led into the territory of the Morini under the legate Gaius Fabius; another to the Nervii under Quintus Cicero; a third to the Essui under Lucius Roscius; and he ordered the fourth to winter among the Remi with Titus Labienus on the border of the Treveri.”

Again, in Book VII:

> “He stationed Gaius Fabius and Lucius Minucius with two legions among the Remi.”

Moreover, Orosius, in Book VI, confirms that the Remi fought almost to annihilation for the safety of the Romans. He refers to the battle in which the Bellovaci, after the army of the other Gauls who had taken up arms against the Romans had been defeated, renewed the conflict, and states that a large body of Remi, who had come to the aid of the Romans, was slaughtered.

Finally, Lucan in Book I testifies that the Remi were brave in battle and excellent javelin-throwers; he also records that they set out at Caesar’s invitation for the civil wars in which, after Pompey had been defeated, Caesar obtained, as is said, sole rule over the entire world. He writes in these verses:

> He who holds the fields of the Nemetes  
> and the banks of the Satyr, where, along the curved shore,  
> the Tarbellic sea gently admitted is enclosed,  
> moves his standards, and rejoices when the Santonian enemy has been removed.  
>   
> And the Biturix [manuscript J: “Bitures”], and the Axones, light in their long weapons,  
> and Leucus, excellent in the cast arm, and the Remus.  
>   
> The finest people, with the Sequana’s bridles bent in a circle,  
> and the Belga, a pliant driver of the beaked chariot.  
>   
> **Lucan, *On the Civil War*, Book I**

## CHAPTER III. On the first bishops of this city

It is established that the people of Reims were held in such great esteem not only among the pagans of that time, but also among the first propagators of the Church of God and the fathers in Christ through the Gospel. The bishops of the first see of our province were always honored to such a degree that the most blessed prince of the Church of Christ, the apostle Peter, judged that the blessed Sixtus, whom he had ordained archbishop, should be sent to our city, assigning him suitable and necessary companions in that same province with the assistance of suffragan bishops: namely, Saint Sinicius, first bishop of the see of Soissons and afterward our own prelate, and the blessed Memmius, ruler of the city of Châlons.

Saint Sixtus, the first bishop of Reims, is also said to have founded the church of Soissons and to have appointed the blessed Sinicius there as his fellow worker and assistant. After the death of that same Saint Sixtus, he is said to have ordained his nephew, Saint Divitianus, as bishop of Soissons. Since the newly established church of Reims, still like a nursing infant, was perhaps tenderly nurturing its offspring and not yet strong enough to bear the episcopal burden, Sinicius assumed the archiepiscopal see at Reims, compelled by that necessity. There, laboring faithfully for the salvation of souls and fighting the good fight, he deserved to share a partnership with his predecessor both in heaven and on earth, receiving a tomb in the same temple and sepulchre as the blessed Sixtus.

Afterward, through their merits, the basilica—their dwelling—was illumined by conspicuous miracles, enriched with numerous gifts, endowed with fields, houses, and vineyards, and likewise adorned by the ministries of clerics. Sometimes twelve clerics, sometimes ten, as is found to have been the case in the time of Bishop Sonnatius, formed a congregation there. This continued until recent times, when, because iniquity abounded and charity grew cold, the company of those serving God there began to decline, and the place itself became the title of a single presbyter [variant: presbytery].

For this reason, their bones were recently transferred from there and are preserved buried in the church of the blessed Remigius, behind the altar of Saint Peter, their teacher. Nor is it only from the city of Rome that our Church is known to have received them as fathers or founders: it is also shown to have been crowned with martyrs and sanctified by their blood and triumphs, at the very time of the persecution under Nero.

## CHAPTER IV. On the first martyrs of this city

The blessed Timothy, arriving at this city of Reims from the regions of the East, did not fear to preach publicly the truth of Jesus Christ the Lord. Therefore he was seized by the governor Lampadius, who at that time ruled this people, and was brought before him because he was persuading people to accept the purpose of the new law. Harassed by the threats of rulers and the severity of the laws, and tested also by promises of wealth, he did not fear to return to the wicked trafficker in heavenly grace the response that he had once learned from the prince of the Church:

> “May your riches be with you for your destruction, and you will go with them into eternal fire” (Acts VIII, 20).
