“My Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, will himself judge you.”

Then the governor, filled with anger, ordered him to be tortured. While he steadfastly confessed Christ amid the torments, he added, among other things, that those whom the governor thought he was killing for Christ’s name would themselves judge him with punishment.

The governor said: “So you will be my judge? I will kill you; and who will rescue you from my hands?”

Saint Timothy replied: “My Lord, in whom I believe, can free me; but against you he will inflict the torments you deserve.”

Again, when he had been ordered to be tortured through many punishments, he said to the judge: “The greater the torments you inflict upon me, the greater the refreshment the Lord, in whom I believe, will grant.”

When he was being beaten by the attendants, he cried out in a loud voice:

> “Look, Lord, and see what the devil is inflicting upon your servant. Do not abandon me, lest people say, ‘Where is his God?’”

Finally, the governor ordered his wounds to be sprinkled with quicklime and vinegar. Saint Timothy said:

> “I give you thanks, Lord Jesus Christ, who grant me endurance so that I can bear these things. What has happened in my body is as though I had been anointed with oil.”

One of those beating him, named Apollinaris, saw two angels standing at his side and saying to him:

> “Take courage, Timothy. We have been sent to you to show you the Lord Jesus Christ, for whose name you are suffering punishment, so that you may see what is taking place in heaven. Lift up your head and look.”

When Saint Timothy looked, he saw the heavens opened and Jesus at the right hand of the Father, holding a crown made of precious stones and saying to him:

> “Timothy, this crown that you see has been prepared for you. On the approaching third day you will receive it from my hands.”

The angels said to him, “Take courage, Timothy,” and went up into heaven.

When Apollinaris had seen these things, he fell at Timothy’s feet and said to him:

> “Lord Timothy, pray for me. For I will most willingly be tortured for Christ’s name, because I saw men of extraordinary brightness speaking with you while they told you the great things of that God who reigns in heaven.”

Then, when the governor saw that he had been confounded, he said:

> “Let Apollinaris be brought forward. Bring me boiling lead and pour it into his mouth, so that he will not speak such words.”

When the boiling lead had been brought and poured into his mouth, it became cold like ice. When the great multitude saw this miracle, it believed in the Lord Jesus Christ.

Then the governor, filled with anger and confusion, said:

> “Take them to prison until I consider by what punishment they should be killed.”

As they were being led away, a very large crowd followed them, weeping and saying:

> “O unjust judgment that has fallen upon this city!”

They were brought into prison, and many people were around them, desiring consolation from Saint Timothy. That same night a certain presbyter named Maurus arrived and baptized a multitude of people in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

When Apollinaris was being baptized, he saw the heavens opened and heard an angel saying to him:

> “Blessed are you, Apollinaris, because you have believed; blessed are all who have been immersed in the water in which you were purified. Whoever is baptized here tonight will be received into paradise tomorrow.”

All who were present there heard this statement. Bending their knees, they said:

> “Spare us, Lord our God, and grant your mercy to those who love your name.”

The next day the governor ordered them to be brought before his tribunal. When they were standing there, the governor said to them:

> “Most foolish men, what has deceived you, that you believe in a crucified man who suffered many things under Pontius Pilate and is finally said to have been crucified?”

They replied:

> “This night we saw an angel of God speaking with the saints whom you hold in prison. The angels themselves told us that today they would go into paradise and receive crowns that your eyes will not deserve to see.”

The governor, filled with anger, ordered them all to be beheaded [manuscript J: “each one”]. As the saints were being led outside the city, they marked themselves with the sign of Christ, and thus they were martyred, confessing the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

All those who were beheaded were fifty men, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September.

The next day the governor went out, sat upon the tribunal, and ordered Saint Timothy and Apollinaris to be brought before him. When they were standing there, the governor said to them:

> “Most wretched of men, submit to the commands of the emperors and worship those whom they worship.”

Timothy and Apollinaris said:

> “We do not worship demons, but only the Lord Jesus Christ, who is the living and true God. Him we ought to confess. Therefore do not suppose that by your arts you can separate us from the love and kingdom of God. Know this: at the hour when you think we are being put to death, we are being brought to life, just as those whom you killed yesterday are alive in heaven.”

They added:

> “Jesus Christ will truly strike you with a most grievous affliction.”

The governor became angry and said:

> “If I do not kill these men, many others will come to this new sect.”

Thus he pronounced sentence against them, ordering them to be killed by the sword. They were led with great confidence outside the city, along the road called Caesarea, to a place called Buxitus. There he had them martyred on the tenth day before the Kalends of September, and they were crowned by angels. A voice was heard saying:

> “Come, Timothy and Apollinaris, my beloved, and I will show you how many wonders you have deserved because of the souls that you offered for my name. And know what I am going to do to the governor Lampadius.”

Immediately a fiery spear descended from heaven in the sight of many people, entered his right shoulder, and, when he was seized by a demon, he ended his life.

The bodies of the saints were buried by Christians on the ninth day before the Kalends of September. A certain distinguished man named Eusebius, who himself had believed through their preaching, built a basilica for them, in which they displayed many signs and cures. They restored sight to the blind and walking to the lame, and those who were tormented by demons were healed in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

The archbishop Lord Tilpin, moving their bodies from the old tomb, honorably adorned their sepulchre with silver and gold. Finally, the altar that stands in front of their tomb is said to have been dedicated to the relics and honor of Saint Maurus, who, having been beheaded for Christ at the same time as those mentioned above, deserved to shine in their company. His bones are preserved deposited in the church of the blessed Celsinus. His head is venerated, carefully enclosed in a reliquary beneath the city, within the basilica of the blessed Mother of God Mary, beside the altar.

That same church of the aforementioned martyrs is also said to be distinguished by the relics of many saints. On its right side, the bodies of Saints Silvanus and Silvianus [J: Silvinianus] are said to be preserved; on the left, those of Saint Tonantius and Saint Jovinus.

It is also found that the blessed Remigius ordered a tomb to be prepared for him in that same basilica of the saints. After setting down the contents of his testament, he added:

> “After composing—or rather, sealing—my testament, it came to my mind that I should assign there a silver vessel weighing six pounds to the basilica of the lords and martyrs Timothy and Apollinaris, so that from it the future seat of my bones might be fashioned.”

In his same testament he also ordered twelve solidi to be given for constructing the roof or chamber of that basilica.

Various people enriched the same church with various endowments. Lord Gondebertus, a most distinguished man, together with his wife Bertha, gave it a villa situated in the district of Vontinse, called Perthas.

It is found that sometimes twenty, sometimes twelve clerics formed a congregation there, as occurred in the time of King Theodoric, when numerous gifts of estates are recorded as having been given to the same basilica. Until quite recent times, when, as religious observance declined, it was reduced to the title of a single presbyter, it remained distinguished by a community of men serving God.

Other churches in various places also shine, adorned by the honor of these saints. For, since they once glittered with many miracles, lovers of Christ strove to cultivate and protect their possessions through memorials to them.

One of these devotees, as Bishop Gregory of Tours relates in his Book of Miracles, eagerly sought their relics after a basilica had been built in their honor. The local bishop honorably sent them through a presbyter. While that presbyter was making the journey, a certain woman met him, greeted him, and earnestly and insistently begged him to give her some portion of these relics.

For a long time he delayed, wavering, but at last, overcome by the woman’s persistence, he gave the petitioner a portion of the sacred ashes. After mounting his horse and attempting to continue the journey entrusted to him, he was utterly unable to make it advance, despite striking its flanks repeatedly. Moreover, he himself was so weighed down and oppressed that he could scarcely lift his head.

At last, realizing that he was being detained by the power of the martyrs, he was moved to repentance. He took back what he had improperly presumed to give, returning the portion of the sacred ashes that he had removed; then, freed, he was released to continue on his appointed way.

At the village of Duodeciacum as well, a beautiful basilica of the holy martyrs was built in their honor. It is said to shine with the brilliance of great miracles and to gleam with the desirable grace of healings.

Finally, King Otto, with the consent of Archbishop Artald [Note: Otto I, also called the Great], had the bones of the blessed Timothy transferred to Saxony and founded a monastery of monks in his honor. During this translation many miracles are said to have been displayed. For, as Anno, then abbot and now bishop, reported to me—the person by whom those sacred relics were transferred—in addition to many other cures, twelve people among the lame and blind were healed.

The blessed Apollinaris also, after his bones had been transferred to the monastery of Orbacum [Orbay or Orbé], is observed to flourish there with various distinguished signs of grace.

## CHAPTER V. On the successors of the aforementioned prelates

As the frequent storms of persecution thundered and our Church’s ship was tossed and oppressed by various waves, scarcely able to raise its head, it is not easy to determine how long this see remained without a worthy ruler. Thus, after the aforementioned fathers of our faith, the blessed Sixtus and Sinicius, we find only one bishop, Amantius, up to the reign of Constantine. Under Constantine, Betausius is found, who, together with his deacon Primogenitus, is recorded as the first from this Belgic province to have attended the first synod of Arles, as reported by Bishop Marinus to the most blessed Pope Sylvester, during the consulships of Volusianus and Anianus.

After him came Aper, then Maternianus. Archbishop Lord Hincmar records in a letter sent to King Louis beyond the Rhine concerning the relics of these and other saints that he had dispatched Maternianus’s bones to him.

After this Donatianus became bishop. His relics, carried to the coastal regions of the bishopric of Noyon or Tournai, are reported to have been adorned by the varied splendor of miracles.

He was followed by the blessed Viventius, as eminent in the merits of his illustrious life as he was distinguished in the lofty order of the episcopate. His sacred remains, carried across the river Meuse by our bishop Lord Ebo, were deposited with due honor for preservation in a church constructed at Braquis, with a company of clerical attendants assigned there. There also, it is said, he once displayed many distinguished miracles, restoring walking to the lame and sight to the blind. Severus succeeded him.

## CHAPTER VI. On Saint Nicasius

After the prelates mentioned above, the blessed Nicasius follows in the dignity of the episcopate. He was a man of great charity and great steadfastness, a most vigorous ruler of the holy Church entrusted to him during the Vandal persecution in Gaul; in peace, its ennobler and adornment, but in danger, its guide and protector. He instructed the people through devout teachings and examples, and raised the beauty of the celibate bride of Christ, the Church, through buildings and ornaments.

He is said to have founded, after receiving a divine revelation, the basilica of this holy see in honor of the perpetual Virgin, Mary the Mother of God, and to have consecrated it with his own blood. The episcopal chair is said to have existed in ancient times in the church called “at the Apostles.”

This blessed bishop, instructed by an angelic warning, is taught to have foreknown long beforehand the destruction that was to come, and, by reproving the ruinous security of prosperity, to have foretold the approaching vengeance of divine chastisement.

Anxious, he carried on the shoulders of charity the burden of the sins of the flock entrusted to him, ready to die for all, so that he might turn away from the people the anger of God’s indignation, or at least, in the very act of vengeance, appease heavenly mercy through a spirit of humility and a contrite heart, so that the sword—though temporal, not eternal—might not reach even to the soul.

But because the seed of God’s word, sown among the thorns of riches, is choked, and those who prosper and glory in the vanity of the world do not admit the counsels of salvation into the ear of their heart so as to bear fruit; indeed, entangled in perishable occupations and pursuing not the true rewards of life but the deadly wages of sin and death, they were unable to pursue worthy and genuine goods because they did not perfectly hate evil.

Moreover, they neglected devout religion, set aside the commandments of God, served vanities, clung to the vices of desire, stirred up schismatic scandals, and, alas, did not fear to offend God in all these things.

And behold, suddenly, during those times of prosperity, the hostility of savage nations was aroused. A multitude of Vandals hastened forward with fierce purpose to avenge God’s anger for the offense against him throughout various provinces. They overthrew the fortifications of many cities and killed parents of both sexes together with their children. They appeared to desire no other glory of rank and no other temporal gain so eagerly as to drain and shed human blood, and above all to thirst for the destruction of Christians.

In the midst of this storm there shone gloriously in Gaul among the bishops Saint Nicasius, the prelate of Reims; the most blessed Anianus, bishop of Orléans; Saint Lupus of Troyes; the blessed Servatius, bishop of Tongeren; and several others distinguished by their virtues. By their merits and prayers they strove for a long time to delay this anger of God, so that, after extinguishing the heresies and depraved practices of the people, they might recall them through repentance to the Catholic religion and the true worship of God, and turn the sword of such persecution and divine judgment away from the necks of the Church.

But, alas for the impiety! As it is written, “When the wicked man has come into the depths of sins, he despises” (Prov. XVIII, 3). They did not obey their salutary instructions in any way.

The most blessed bishop Nicasius, however, through persistent efforts, continual teaching, and prayers, urged the people of God toward repentance or endurance and toward the triumph of martyrdom. Those whom careless prosperity had driven into the pit of offense might, through devout endurance of adversity, make it the cause not of condemnation and judgment but of purification and salvation.

Meanwhile, the armies of the Vandals encamped around the city of Reims. After devastating the entire region, they devoted themselves with the greatest zeal to slaughtering the Christians who lived there. They sought to kill them as enemies of their gods and opponents of pagan customs, and to wipe them completely from the earth.

Thus the blessed Nicasius, following Christ’s example and ready to lay down his life for his brothers, chose and firmly resolved not to abandon the flock entrusted to him. He determined either to live together with them or to endure together with them whatever the master of the household might wish them to suffer, lest by fleeing he should appear to abandon the ministry of Christ, without whom people can neither live nor become Christians.

Therefore, according to the judgment of blessed Augustine (Epistle 80), he found a greater fruit of charity than the man who, fleeing not for the sake of his brothers but for his own sake, was captured and did not deny Christ, and so received martyrdom.

For the most holy bishop feared more that, if he abandoned them, the living stones might be extinguished than that, while he remained among them, the stones and timbers of earthly buildings might be burned. He feared more that the members of Christ’s body, deprived of spiritual nourishment, might perish than that the members of his own body might be tormented under the enemy’s assault.

He was prepared for either outcome, so that, if this cup could not pass away, the will of him who cannot will anything evil might be done (Matt. XXVI, 42). He did not seek his own interests, but imitated him who said:

> “I do not seek what is useful for me, but what is useful for many, so that they may be saved” (I Cor. X, 33).

And lest he should harm the people more by fleeing through his example than benefit them by fulfilling his office through remaining, he agreed to flee under no circumstances.

He feared not temporal death—which will come at some time even if it is avoided—but eternal death, which can come if it is not avoided and can fail to come if it is avoided. He did not please himself, nor did he judge his own person, endowed as it was with exceptional grace, more worthy of escape amid such dangers, lest the ministry that was especially necessary and obligatory in those dangers be withdrawn from the Church.

He did not flee like a hired servant who sees the wolf coming and abandons the sheep, but, like the good shepherd, he was fully ready to offer his life for the flock entrusted to him (John X, 11–12). The best course of action that he could find was to pour out persistent prayers to the Lord for himself and his people.

At last, when the fighters had been exhausted by continual attacks, watches, and hunger, while the enemies raged all around and violently battered the city in war, the whole city, struck by the excessive weariness of terror, rushed to the most holy Nicasius, who was prostrate in prayer. Fearing the future victory of the pagans, they sought from him, as children from a father, the help of consolation.

They asked what counsel he judged most useful: whether they should surrender themselves to the servitude of the nations or fight to the death for the safety of the city.

The blessed Nicasius, foreseeing by heavenly revelation that the city of Reims was to be overthrown, consoled them and prayed unceasingly for the Lord’s mercy, so that this tribulation of temporal death might benefit those who persevered in the true confession of faith—not toward judgment but toward pardon.

He taught them to fight for the salvation of their souls not with visible weapons but with upright conduct, not by reliance on bodily strength but through the exercise of spiritual virtues. He demonstrated that this heavenly indignation had been aroused by the just judgment of God because of the crimes of sinners.

He proclaimed that the sure counsel of salvation was to turn their minds, moved by repentance, toward the divine scourges, accepting these things not unwillingly or despairingly like children of iniquity, but patiently and gently like children of piety, destined to receive the promised rewards of the heavenly kingdom.

He urged them, in the hope of eternal salvation, to endure the present tribulation with the utmost devotion and willingly to offer themselves to this momentary death, so that they might deserve to escape the punishment of everlasting condemnation due to their sins, and so that their present death might become not a punishment but a perpetual remedy for their souls.

He also admonished them to pray for their enemies, so that at last they might repent of their wickedness, and those who then appeared to be ministers of impiety might at some time become worshipers of piety and followers of truth.

Declaring that he himself was ready, as befits a good shepherd, to lay down his life for the sheep (John X, 11), he was prepared to despise the present life so that they might deserve to receive forgiveness of their sins and eternal salvation together with him.

His own sister, the blessed Eutropia, also stood there, a most sacred virgin of Christ. Because she was fortified by chastity, she always followed the most holy bishop by imitating and adhering to him, so that her purity of mind might be preserved by the Lord, free from spiritual wickedness, and the integrity of her body might remain protected and undefiled by carnal pleasures.

Thus both of them encouraged the people of God with pious exhortations, as far as they could, toward the crown of martyrdom, and commended the contest of their victory to the Lord through their prayers.

Finally, on the day of the invasion, by the decree and judgment of God, when the blessed bishop Nicasius perceived the furious attack of the pagans approaching, strengthened by the power of the Holy Spirit and accompanied by his noble sister, he is said to have gone to meet them with hymns and spiritual songs at the door of the basilica of the holy Mother of God Mary, which, as we have mentioned, he had founded at the summit of this city.

While devoted to divine psalmody, he sang a verse of David to the Lord in a devout voice, saying:

> “My soul has clung to the pavement” (Psalm CXVIII, 25).

Immediately afterward, as the sword pursued him, his neck was struck, but the word of devotion did not cease from his mouth. As his head fell to the ground, he completed, as is reported, the sentence of immortality:

> “Give me life according to your word” (ibid.) [manuscript adds: “Lord”].

Saint Eutropia, seeing the impiety around her somewhat abated and her beauty seemingly preserved for the contests of the pagans, sprang upon the very slayer of the priest. Rebuking him with a great cry and challenging him to the battle of her martyrdom, she struck the face of the sacrilegious man with a slap; and, by the power of the divine majesty, she is said to have torn out his eyes and cast them upon the ground. She was soon slaughtered by the sword of the frenzied men and, having shed her sacred blood, deserved to attain the palm of victory with her brother, the bishop of Christ, and the other holy triumphators.

There were, indeed, some—both from the clergy and from the lay assembly—who followed and accompanied this steadfastness. By sharing in the endurance of the present, they strove to obtain, together with this most blessed Father, a share in eternal blessedness. Among them, the deacon Florentius and blessed Jocundus are reported to have been especially renowned; their heads are preserved buried at Reims behind the altar of Saint Mary, the holy Mother of God.

After the slaughter had been completed and the Barbarians, astonished by the virgin’s steadfastness and by the sudden punishment of the profane observer, had been cleansed by the sacred blood, a terrible horror seized them all, as though they saw heavenly armies fighting and avenging so great a crime, while the basilica itself resounded with a dreadful roar. The terrified bands of Vandals therefore abandoned their spoils wherever they lay and, fearing divine vengeance, fled irretrievably in various directions, anxiously deserting the city they had invaded.

While the city thus remained deserted for a long time, the Christians who had fled to the mountain fortifications were fearful of pagan incursions, while the pagans feared the heavenly horrors they had experienced there. Under divine and angelic protection alone, the bodies of the holy martyrs were preserved in that place. At night, heavenly lights could be seen from a distance, and some heard songs, while the most pleasing sounds of the stars resounded sweetly with the choruses of the heavenly powers.

Strengthened, therefore, by the revelation of heavenly victory, the fellow citizens who, by divine providence, had remained behind to bury the bodies of the saints eventually returned to the city with vows of prayer. Where the funerals of the saints were being adorned, they inhaled an immeasurable fragrance of sweetness; mingling joy with lamentation, they magnified the Lord with tearful praises. Preparing themselves to bury the sacred relics, they reverently placed them in suitable locations around the city.

But the sacred remains of the most blessed bishop Nicasius and of his sister were solemnly and magnificently placed in the cemetery of Saint Agricola, in a church once founded and richly adorned by Jovinus, a most Christian master of the Roman army, long before that time. This makes it apparent that, by the prompting of divine providence, it had been prepared more for the honor of their commemoration than for the dignity of its original foundation.

[Note: [Col. 0039] This is today the church of Saint Nicasius, as it is called below, chapter 12.]

The aforementioned Jovinus entitled this basilica with the following verses, adorned with golden beauty:

> Jovinus happily assumed the devout  
> Belts of military service, advanced to the height  
> Of the summit of valor; twice appointed through his merits  
> Master of cavalry and infantry,  
> He raised an everlasting name from age to age.  
>   
> Yet by weighty piety he surpassed such praises  
> And dedicated illustrious triumphs to religion,  
> So that he might surpass in honor the renown  
> That fame bestowed upon his deeds,  
> And by his achievements hope for perpetual life.  
>   
> Conscious here of the salvation flowing from the holy fountain,  
> He gladly prepares a living dwelling-place  
> For mortal limbs, and, as a happy settler, adorns  
> A lodging for the body, providing that the members  
> To be restored to life may be saved.  
>   
> Almighty Christ, venerable and terrible Judge,  
> Merciful, patient, faithful hope of those who pray,  
> Does not charge his servants with noble and exceptional deeds.  
> May the rewards of faith and piety prevail beyond what is just.

[Col. 0041A] After the bodies of these holy martyrs had been deposited there, the same church is known to have been adorned with innumerable signs of miracles, so that through their merits and prayers a multitude of sick people might receive there the joy of recovery, and so that the people, by their examples, might learn to hasten toward heavenly [C., devout] sublimity.

Blessed Jerome recalls this barbarian persecution in a letter (Epistle 11) written to a certain noble young widow, Aggerunchia, exhorting her to persevere in widowhood. Among other things, he writes as follows:

> “Innumerable and most savage nations have occupied all the Gauls. Whatever land lies between the Alps and the Pyrenees, enclosed by the Ocean and the Rhine, has been devastated by the Quadi, Vandals, Sarmatians, Alans, Gepids, Heruli, Saxons, Burgundians, Alamanni, and—O lamentable commonwealth!—Pannonian enemies. For indeed, Assur came with them (Ps. 82:9). Mainz, once a noble city, was captured and destroyed, and many thousands of people were slaughtered in the church. The people of Worms were wiped out by a long siege. The mighty city of Reims, Amiens, Arras, and the Morini, the furthest of men—  
>   
> [Note: This half-line is Virgilian, from Aeneid 9:  
>   
> *The Morini, the furthest of men, and the two-horned Rhine.*]  
>   
> —as well as Tournai, the Nemetes, and Strasbourg have been transferred into Germany. The provinces of Aquitaine, the Nine Peoples, Lyon, and Narbonne have, except for a few cities, been entirely ravaged; and even those few are devastated from outside by the sword and within by famine,” etc.

Finally, blessed Remigius is said to have had the custom of staying in the aforementioned basilica, so that through the merits of the holy martyrs he might be near them in body as he always was in spirit. A small chapel beside the altar is still shown, where, withdrawn from the crowds, he customarily devoted himself in secret to the Lord and most devoutly offered to the supreme Observer the sacrifices of a most blessed contemplation.

He was engaged in these duties when, having learned of the city’s fire, he hurried forward while invoking the divinity. Sustained by the saints’ intercession, he left behind, on the church’s stone steps, the imprints of his feet.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Miracles of This Church

This building is said to have been illuminated at various times by many kinds of glory. But we have learned from our own elders, who were present, of one event that occurred almost in our own days, and we have judged it worthy of being made known.

The solemn feast of the aforementioned martyrs was being celebrated in winter, as was customary on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of January [December 14]. For the vigil of this celebration, the brothers rose earlier than usual and found the keepers of the church asleep and the doors carefully barred.

After knocking for a long while and receiving no answer from within, they went to the presbyter’s house, repeatedly striking the door and beating upon the roof with stones. When they were unable to rouse anyone who would open the church door for them, they returned to it and found it standing open of its own accord. They saw all the lights burning, but no one inside who might have caused it.

After praying, they gave thanks to Christ and began the nocturnal praises. When a large part of these had already passed, the presbyter was awakened by their voices. Astonished at what had happened with his companions, he hurried up in amazement to sing the hymns with the others.

In the end they could discover no agency responsible either for lighting the lamps or for opening the doors, except that of the supreme giver of divine gifts, who never ceases to extend the honor of his saints through the continual splendor of their miracles.

A certain bishop of the Noviomagian people obtained some relics of this blessed bishop and carried them to his own city. They are reported to have been glorified by many notable miracles both at Noviomagus and at the fortress of Tournai, where they are said still to be preserved.

Later, Archbishop Fulco transported the rest of the body of this martyr, together with the body of his blessed sister Eutropia, within the walls of Reims, and buried them with due reverence behind the altar of Saint Mary, the holy Mother of God, where we now venerate them, beside the remains of blessed Pope Callistus.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Saint Oriculus and His Sisters

During the same persecution of the Vandals or Huns, a certain servant of God named Oriculus devoted himself to God with his sisters Oricola [ms. i: Oricula] and Basilica in this same bishopric of Reims, in the district of Dulcum, in the village of Sinduno, in a church he had built. He is also said to have been killed there by the Barbarians together with his aforementioned sisters.

It is reported that, after he had been beheaded, he himself washed his head in a certain spring. It is also said that with his own finger he traced the sign of the cross in a rock using his blood—a sign that is still said to be clearly visible—and that, carrying his own head in his hands, he sought the tomb he had built for himself [ms. i: had founded]. Many miracles are reported to have been displayed there.

Once there was a peasant living in that place who received a revelation in a dream commanding him to cover the spring in which, as we have said, the saint of God had washed his head. After being warned twice, he delayed carrying this out and fell into an illness in which he lay sick for an entire year.

Afterward, when he made vows and promises to fulfill the command, he recovered. He surrounded the spring with wooden boards and covered it. Many who drink from this spring are cured of various illnesses.

The presbyter of that place, named Betto, ordered a bath to be prepared for himself from the well which, it is said, this holy martyr had brought forth beneath the church. After bathing in it, he became so weak that he is known to have lain ill until the end of the year and never afterward to have fully regained his strength.

The bodies of these saints, once long ago placed in a single sarcophagus, were raised from the earth in the time of Archbishop Seulf. The ground first opened of its own accord, and the little coffin in which they lay was miraculously lifted upward by itself.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Successors of Blessed Nicasius

After the aforementioned departure of the Vandals, Baruc [ms. Baructius] is said to have succeeded blessed Nicasius in the episcopal see. Barucius is reported to have been followed by Barnabas; then came Bennadius, whose name, however, is found written as Bennagius in his will, inscribed in his own hand, as it is read there.

By the authority of this will, he himself made the Church of Reims heir to his property together with the son of his brother, whom he records that he had received at the sacred font under the promise of everlasting grace.

Among other things, he assigns to his Church as heir a silver vessel that, as he recalls, had been granted to him by his predecessor, Bishop Barnabas of holy memory. He declares that he had reserved it for the adornment of the Church, although he could have sold it for his own uses.

He assigns twenty solidi for the repair of the same Church, together with small fields and woods; eight solidi for the presbyters of that church; four solidi for the deacons; twenty solidi for captives; two solidi for the subdeacons; one solidus for the lectors; one solidus for the doorkeepers and exorcists; and three solidi for the nuns and those entered on the register.

Further addressing his Church as his heir, he directs it to regard as placed in its care whatever had been piously devoted for his own refreshment to presbyters, deacons, the various orders of clergy, captives, and the poor.

## CHAPTER X. On Saint Remigius

After the aforementioned Bennadius, the most blessed Remigius succeeded him and arose as a brilliant light for the nations, to instruct them in the faith.

Divine mercy chose him, as our poet Fortunatus also asserts at the beginning of his Life of Saint Remigius, not only before he was born but even before he was conceived. So great was this choice that, while a certain monk named Montanus was resting in a very light sleep, he was prompted by a third admonition [Or.: *fuerit*, “would have been”] to announce truthfully to his blessed mother Ciliniа that she would conceive a male child and to indicate his name and future merit.

This Montanus, leading a solitary life in seclusion, constantly devoted himself to fasts, vigils, and prayers, and made himself acceptable to the divinity through the distinction of his other virtues as well. While he was praying tirelessly to the heavenly mercy of Christ for the peace of his holy Church, which was suffering various afflictions throughout the provinces of Gaul, he once allowed his limbs, compelled by the weakness of the flesh, to be restored by sleep.

Suddenly, by divine grace, he seemed to be present among angelic choirs and assemblies of holy souls. He appeared to hear a most renowned conversation, hearing them discuss the humiliation and restoration of the Gallican Church and consider that the time had now come to have mercy on it.

Meanwhile he heard a voice sounding most sweetly from higher and more secret places:

> “The Lord looked forth from his high and holy place; from heaven he gazed upon the earth, to hear the groaning of the prisoners, to release the children of the slain, so that his name might be proclaimed among the nations, in gathering peoples and kings together, that they might serve him” (Ps. 101:20–23).

He also heard that Cilinia, conceiving in her womb, would give birth to a son named Remigius, to whom the people destined for salvation would be entrusted.

Having received such consolation, this venerable man, after the third divine admonition concerning these matters, announced to Cilinia the oracle of the heavenly vision.

This blessed mother, once in the flower of her youth, had borne from her only husband Aemilius a son, Principius, later the holy bishop of the city of Soissons and father of blessed Lupus, Principius’ successor.

Blessed Cilinia, now advanced in age, wondered how she could bear an old woman’s child or nurse offspring. Both her husband and she had already passed many years, were exhausted and barren in body, and had neither hope of producing another child nor desire for offspring.

But blessed Montanus, so that the merits of his patience might increase, had for a time been deprived of the light of his bodily eyes. To confirm the truth of what he had said, he declared that his eyes were to be anointed with her milk and that he would then recover the light he had lost through the nourishment of the child.

The parents therefore rejoiced at such great consolation, and the future bishop of Christ was conceived. Brought forth happily with the assistance of grace, he received the name Remigius from the sacred font.

During his nursing, the joy previously promised to the prophet was truthfully fulfilled: when the eyes of blessed Montanus were touched with the milk of the child’s mother, the light he had once lost was restored.

This child, proclaimed by praises before he was born, was born in the district of Laon, shining with the noble blood of parents who were already elderly and had long been sterile. He was made wondrous in his birth, having been magnificently destined to become wondrous in his deeds.

By divine command he was fittingly given the name Remigius, since he was to steer the Church of God, and especially the Church of Reims, with the oars of teaching through the sea of this storm-tossed life, and to lead it to the harbor of eternal salvation through merits and prayers.

Some ancient writings, however, record that he was called “Remedy” (*Remedium*). Considering his merits and deeds, we would rightly believe this unless more carefully corrected accounts made us recognize that, by divine oracle, he ought to be called Remigius.

The following is also said to have been read in verses composed by him and engraved at his command on a vessel dedicated by him to God:

> From this vessel may the people draw life from the sacred blood  
> Which Christ, eternal, shed from the wound inflicted upon him:  
> Remigius the priest returns his vows to the Lord.

This vessel survived until recent times, when, after being melted down, it was given long ago to the Northmen as a ransom for Christians.

The nurse of this most blessed Remigius is said to have been blessed Balsamia, who is remembered as the mother of Saint Celsinus. Celsinus himself is said to have been a close disciple of blessed Remigius; he later became renowned for miracles and is still considered especially distinguished in the petitions of the sick. His blessed mother herself also rests in the same church.

Given by his parents to school to be instructed in letters, blessed Remigius soon became more eminent in learning than his contemporaries and even than those older than he. Surpassing all his fellow students in maturity of character and the charity of goodwill, he sought to avoid the crowds of the people and serve the Lord alone in seclusion. He attained this goal and, as a pious young man growing in the practices of holy conduct and in seclusion, served Christ at Laon.

## CHAPTER XI. On His Ordination to the Bishopric of Reims

When he had entered his twenty-second year, the aforementioned venerable Archbishop Bennadius died. In this city of Reims, by the unanimous wishes of all, Remigius is recognized as having been not so much elected to the height of the episcopate as carried off to it.

A gathering of the people took place: persons of different sexes, conditions, ranks, and ages acclaimed with one and the same voice that he was truly worthy of God and ought to be placed over the people.

The most holy young man, weighed down by these difficulties, since no opportunity for flight was open to him anywhere and he could in no way persuade the people to abandon the course they had begun, began to complain publicly of the weakness of his age and to proclaim that ecclesiastical law did not admit one of that age to so great a dignity.

But when the multitude of the people continued to acclaim him irrevocably, and the man of God was held by great steadfastness, Almighty God was pleased to reveal by unmistakable signs the judgment he deigned to hold concerning him.

For it is reported that the light of a heavenly ray suddenly descended upon his holy head, and that together with this light a liquid of divine anointing was poured from heaven upon his head, so that his entire head seemed to be moistened by the infusion of that sacred nectar.

All doubt having therefore been set aside, he was consecrated with episcopal blessing by the unanimous agreement of the province of Reims.

He immediately appeared wonderfully devoted and most capable of carrying out this office: generous in almsgiving, diligent in vigils, attentive in prayers, lavish in kindness, perfect in charity, eminent in teaching, and most holy in conduct.

The sincerity of his most pure mind was displayed by the cheerful openness of his pious face, and the goodness of his most merciful heart was shown by the tranquillity of his speech.

He fulfilled the duties of eternal salvation no less by his deeds than he taught them by his preaching. Revered in appearance, venerable in his bearing, fearsome in severity, and worthy of embrace in kindness, he tempered the discipline of strictness with a mixture of gentleness.

The austerity of his face seemed to threaten, but the serenity of his heart offered consolation. Thus, toward the devout he appeared as Peter in his countenance, while against offenders he seemed Paul in spirit. Through the diversity of graces brought together in one, he was an imitator of the former’s piety and of the latter’s authority.

He neglected repose, fled pleasure, sought labor, endured abasement, could not endure honor, was poor in money, rich in conscience, humble in regard to merits, and proud in opposition to vices.

As it is recorded that others praised him before us—Hincmar, in his book On His Life—he cultivated in himself such diverse virtues of grace that scarcely so few possessed the individual ones as he fulfilled them all.

Always engaged in the exercise of holy work, always moved by compunction, he had no more ardent care among all things than either to speak of God in reading and conversation or to speak with God in prayer. Thus, with his body weakened by continual fasts, he fought against the persecuting enemy, triumphing through perpetual martyrdom.

Amid all this, the most blessed man also strove, as others are reported to have long before praised him—Hincmar in the same work and Fortunatus—to flee the boasting of virtues, in which lofty grace could not remain hidden.

He stood out to everyone’s amazement like a city situated upon the summit of a mountain. Nor did the Lord wish to conceal beneath a bushel this lamp, which he had set high upon a lampstand (Matt. 5:14–15), assigning it to burn with the fire of divine charity and to provide the bright lights of his Church’s resplendent virtues.

## CHAPTER XII. On the Various Miracles Performed by Him and on His Teaching

[Col. 0046B]

At the innocence of his holiness, not only rational beings but even irrational creatures were accustomed to grow gentle. Thus, when it sometimes happened that he held a private meal among his household and took pleasure in the cheerfulness of his friends, sparrows would descend to him without fear, gather the remains of the meal from his hand, and depart satiated while others approached to be fed. He did not make this known out of a desire to boast of his merits; rather, the Lord had arranged it with a definite benefit for those dining, so that through this and the many other miracles frequently witnessed through this servant of Christ, they might devote themselves more fervently to the service of the Lord.

This most blessed man, when at a certain time he was making his customary rounds of the parishes with pastoral vigilance, so that as a faithful servant of Christ he might recognize whether anything was being done negligently in divine worship, came to a village called Calmiciacum out of devotion to this duty.

There, when a certain blind man had asked him for the help of mercy, the man began to be tormented by bodily suffering from the demonic affliction by which he had long been held captive.

Then Saint Remigius, in the prayer to which he always devoted himself with holy purpose before God, prostrated himself bodily. Immediately he restored the blind man’s former sight and also drove away the plague of the unclean spirit, bringing threefold healing: comforting the needy with food, giving sight to the blind, and restoring the captive to freedom.

At another time, while traveling through a parish out of episcopal concern, he was asked by a certain cousin of his named Celsa, consecrated to God, to visit her estate called Celtum (Gaulish: Cernay). There, while the blessed man customarily offered his hostess the cups of life through spiritual conversation, Celsa’s servant announced to his mistress that there was not enough wine.

When the holy Remigius learned of this, he consoled her with a cheerful face. After offering gentle words of comfort, he ordered the rooms of the same house to be shown to him.

First inspecting the other areas deliberately, he finally came to the wine cellar. Having it opened for him, he carefully searched to see whether any wine might have remained in any of the vessels.

When a vessel was pointed out to him in which a very small amount of wine had been left—specifically, so that it might be preserved—he ordered the door to be closed and commanded the cellarer to remain where he was.

He himself went to the other end of the vessel, which was of considerable size, and marked it with the sign of Christ’s cross. Then, kneeling beside the wall, he directed a prayer devoutly toward heaven.

Meanwhile, astonishing to relate, wine began to pour out through the upper opening and flow abundantly across the floor. The cellarer cried out at the sight, struck with amazement. But the holy man immediately restrained him and forbade him to make it public.

Yet because so brilliant a deed could not be concealed, when his cousin learned what had happened, she gave that estate to him and to his Church to possess perpetually and confirmed it by lawful right.

A nearly similar miracle is said to have been performed by the same lord Remigius with the liquid of oil.

When a certain sick member of a respectable household, though not yet baptized, asked Saint Remigius to visit him, declared that he believed himself already near his final breath, and requested baptism, the blessed bishop asked the local presbyter for oil and chrism. Discovering that both had been entirely exhausted from the ampoules, he placed the nearly empty ampoules upon the altar and prostrated himself in prayer.

When he rose from prayer, he found the vessels full. He anointed the sick man with the oil divinely supplied, baptized him according to ecclesiastical custom, and anointed him with the chrism granted from heaven. Restored to health, the man was given both salvation of soul and bodily wellbeing.

[Col. 0047C] Finally, the enemy of the human race, never ceasing to display the wickedness of his malignity, set fire to the city of Reims by sending forth sudden masses of flame. Through cruel devastation, the fire had already consumed nearly a third of the city, while the victorious flame was licking what remained.

When the blessed bishop received news of this, he turned to the usual refuge of prayer. In the basilica of blessed Nicasius the martyr, where he had been accustomed to stay at that time, he prostrated himself and sought the aid of Christ.

Rising from prayer, he lifted his eyes to heaven and cried out with a groan:

> “God, my God, attend to my voice!”

Then, descending rapidly by the steps laid with stones before the church, he went toward the city. On those stones the imprints of his feet can still be seen, as though pressed into soft mud, in memory of the divine miracle.

Hurrying swiftly, he confronted the flames. As soon as he stretched out his right hand toward the fire and made the sign of the cross while invoking the name of Christ, the entire conflagration, its strength broken and turned back upon itself, began to yield and flee as though from the presence of the man of God.

Blessed Remigius pursued it and placed himself between the fire and the things that still appeared untouched, making the sign of holiness. Sustained by the protection of divine power, he drove the whole monstrous mass of flames fleeing before him through the open gate and closed that same gate.

He forbade anyone ever to open it, threatening punishment against whoever should presume to violate this prohibition.

After several years, however, a certain citizen named Fersinctus, who lived beside that gate, broke through the wall with which the gate had been blocked, intending to remove the rubble of his house through it. But such vengeance is said to have immediately followed his audacity that, when disaster overtook the house, neither animal nor human being remained there.

A certain girl, born in the city of Toulouse of illustrious parentage, had been held captive since infancy by the possession of an evil spirit. Her parents loved her with tender affection and brought her with great devotion to the tomb of the holy apostle Peter.

At that time the venerable Benedict shone in those same regions by his power and radiated with many virtues. When the girl’s parents learned of his reputation, they made every effort to bring her to him.

He labored for her purification with many fasts and prayers. But when he was unable to drive the venom of the dreadful serpent from her, he could extract only this reply from the ancient enemy, under adjuration by the divine name: the demon could never be expelled from that dwelling by anyone’s prayers except those of this most blessed bishop Remigius.

Then her parents, supported by the words both of blessed Benedict and of Alaric, king of the Goths, and, as is reported, relying upon letters from them addressed to blessed Remigius, came to the same holy bishop with their possessed daughter. They begged to witness his power in cleansing their child, a power they had already learned through the confession of the thief himself.

The most blessed Remigius, however, resisted with prolonged reluctance, asserting that he was unworthy and opposing their request with his customary humility. He was overcome by the prayers of the supplicating people, so that he poured forth a prayer for her and sympathized with her parents’ tears.

Armed with the merits of holiness, he commanded by the authority of his word that the wicked robber depart by the way he had entered and release the servant of Christ.

And so, with excessive vomiting and foul stench, the demon departed through the mouth by which it had entered.

But shortly afterward, when the bishop had gone away and the girl, exhausted by excessive suffering, tottered, deprived of the warmth of life, she lost her vital breath.

The crowd of supplicants therefore returned to the physician with renewed prayers. Blessed Remigius accused himself rather of having committed a crime than of having granted a remedy of health; he claimed to be guilty of homicide rather than to have conferred healing.

He therefore returned to the basilica of Saint John, where the girl’s lifeless body lay, at the people’s insistence. There he prostrated himself in prayer with tears upon the pavements of the saints and urged the others to do likewise.

Then, rising after pouring out a rain of tears, he raised the dead girl whom he had previously cleansed from possession. She immediately took the bishop’s hand, rose in perfect health, and happily returned to her own home.

The works of this most blessed father testify to the brilliance of his teaching, holiness, and wisdom, for wisdom is undoubtedly recognized as true when it is approved by the display of works, like a tree by its fruits.

The Frankish people, converted through him to the faith of Christ and consecrated by the sanctification of baptism, bears witness to this. His various deeds and teachings, performed and proclaimed with the greatest prudence, bear witness to it. Various persons of his time bear witness as well.

Among these, it has pleased me to insert a letter addressed to this most blessed bishop by Sidonius, bishop of Clermont, a most learned man, renowned alike in birth, religion, and speech (Sidonius Apollinaris, Book 9, Letter 7):

> **Sidonius to Remigius, lord pope, greetings.**
>
> A certain man traveling from Clermont to Belgica—I know the person, not the reason, and it is irrelevant—after arriving at Reims, extracted from your secretary, or bookseller, by price or perhaps by the favor of office, whether willingly or unwillingly, a very abundant bundle of your declamations.
>
> When he returned to us, exceedingly proud—for he had acquired so many volumes—he brought in as a gift whatever he had carried away, although you were prepared to sell it, as was not unjust, since he was a citizen.
>
> It immediately became my concern, and because we were rightly eager to read them, to possess many of them and copy them all. By unanimous agreement it was declared that few people now could dictate anything similar.
>
> Indeed, rare or nonexistent is the person who, when preparing to write, has an equal arrangement of subjects, placement of letters, and composition of syllables.
>
> In addition, there is aptness in the examples, fidelity in the testimonies, precision in the epithets, urbanity in the figures, strength in the arguments, weight in the thoughts, a flowing stream in the words, and thunder in the clausulae.
>
> The structure is strong and firm, and the connections of the conjunctions are fastened by cuts so artfully made that they cannot be undone.
>
> Yet it is no less fluid and smooth [i.e. gentle], rounded in every way, so that it gracefully releases the reader’s tongue unhindered. It does not allow the tongue, after encountering rough joints, to roll about the chamber of the palate and stammer.
>
> In short, the whole discourse is entirely fluid and pliable, like crystal or onyx slabs beneath a nail that does not strike them with force—provided that nothing, caught in fissured obstacles, delays it by a tenacious construction [Orig. i: *fractura*, “break”].
>
> What more can I say? At present there is no speech of any living person that your skill could not, though with effort, pass beyond and surpass.
>
> Hence, lord pope, I almost suspect that, because of your overflowing and ineffable eloquence—forgive me for saying so—you are proud.
>
> But although you shine in goodness, both of conscience and of speech arranged with the greatest order, we are nevertheless not people whom you should shun, since we praise well-written works even though we do not write things worthy of praise.
>
> Therefore, in the future, cease to avoid our judgments, which contain nothing biting and threaten no rebuke.
>
> Otherwise, if you delay enriching our sterility with your eloquent conversations, we shall lie in wait for the markets of the winged creatures, and, while we wink and provide accomplices, the clever hand of burglars will plunder your book chests of its own accord.
>
> Then, once robbed, you will begin in vain to stir yourself if now, when asked, you do not stir yourself out of duty.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the Conversion of the Franks
Whose prudence, and how holy his zeal, our gracious Father and pastor possessed, and how faithfully and wisely he excelled in distributing the money of his Lord, is demonstrated by the conversion, already mentioned, of the Franks from idols to the true God through him. At that time they had crossed the Rhine and were plundering the Gallic provinces, and had already occupied Agrippina, that is, Cologne, as well as certain other cities of Gaul. But after their king Clovis defeated and killed Syagrius, a Roman commander who then governed Gaul, he began to rule over almost the whole of Gaul.

When the fame of the deeds of the most blessed Remigius became known—namely, that he shone through the power of holiness and wisdom and was renowned for the display of miracles—Clovis revered him and, although a pagan, nevertheless loved him. Once, as he was passing near the city of Reims, some vessels belonging to the Church of Reims are said to have been taken by certain soldiers of his army. Among them was a large silver ewer, elegantly fashioned, for the recovery of which blessed Remigius is said to have sent envoys to him, asking that he might at least deserve to receive it back.

But when they came to the place where the booty was to be divided—[Note: The place of division was the city of Soissons]—the king asked his soldiers not to refuse to give him that ewer. Although most of them agreed, a certain Frank struck the ewer with a battle-axe and loudly declared that nothing should be taken from it by the king except what fell to him by lot. The others were astonished at this act of audacity. The king, patiently bearing the insult for the moment, seized the vessel and, with the support of many, returned it to the church’s envoy, while concealing his anger in his heart.

When a year had passed, he ordered the entire equipment of his army to appear, as usual, in the field, so that he might inspect the polish of the weapons according to custom. They were accustomed to call this assembly, after Mars, the “March” assembly. As the king properly inspected the drawn-up ranks, he came to the man who had earlier struck the ewer. Disdaining his weapons, he finally threw his francisca to the ground. When the soldier bent down to retrieve it, the king drove his battle-axe into his head—the same axe with which he had previously struck the vessel—while bitterly rebuking him and recalling his presumption. When he had thus been killed, great fear at this vengeance by the king seized the hearts of the other Franks.

After Clovis had subjected Thuringia to himself and extended his kingdom and dominion, he also took as his wife Rothildis, daughter of Chilperic, the brother of Gundobad, king of the Burgundians. She was a Christian, and although her husband opposed it, she had the sons she bore him consecrated through baptism; she also tried to lead her husband to faith in Christ. But the woman could not bend the barbarian’s mind toward belief.

Meanwhile war broke out between the Franks and the Alemanni. As the Franks were falling in immense slaughter, the king was advised by his counselor Aurelianus to believe in Christ, confess him as the King of kings and God of heaven and earth, and invoke him, since he could grant him victory according to his will. When he had done this, devoutly sought Christ’s aid, and vowed that he would become a Christian if he were permitted to experience Christ’s power in gaining victory, immediately after this promise the Alemanni were put to flight. When they learned that their king had been killed, they submitted themselves to Clovis’s dominion.

He placed them under tribute and returned victorious to his own country, bringing great joy to the queen because he had obtained victory through the invocation of Christ’s name. Then the queen summoned blessed Remigius and begged him to show the king the way of salvation. The holy priest instructed him in the teaching of saving life and urged him to approach the sacrament of baptism.

The king replied that he would go and exhort his people concerning these matters. He sought to address his army, urging them to abandon the gods who could not help them and to embrace the worship of him who had bestowed on them so splendid a victory. The multitude cried out that, with divine grace going before them, they would abandon mortal gods and believe in Christ, who had been their protection.

This was reported to holy Remigius. Filled with great joy, he hastened to instruct the king and the people how they ought to renounce the devil, his works, and his pomp, and believe in the true God. Since the solemnity of Easter was approaching, he imposed on them a fast according to the custom of the faithful.

On the day of the Lord’s Passion, that is, the day before they were to receive the grace of baptism, after the nocturnal hymns and prayers, the bishop went to the king’s chamber so that, once the king had been freed from worldly cares, he might more freely entrust to him the sacred mysteries of the word. Admitted respectfully by the chamberlains, the king sprang up and eagerly came to meet him. Together they entered the oratory of the most blessed chief of the apostles, Peter, which happened to adjoin the king’s chamber.

When seats had been arranged, the bishop, king, and queen sat down. Some clergy were admitted, along with certain of the king’s officials and household members. As the venerable Father filled the king with saving admonitions, the Lord also deigned, in order to strengthen the saving teaching of his faithful servant, visibly to show himself always present with the faithful gathered in his name, as he had promised (Matthew 18:20).

Suddenly a light so abundant filled the whole church that it seemed to surpass the brightness of the sun. Immediately a voice accompanied the light, saying: “Peace be with you; I am he; do not be afraid” (Luke 24:36). “Remain in my love” (John 15:9). After these words the light that had come departed, but an ineffable fragrance of sweetness remained in the same building. So that it might clearly be recognized that the author of the light, peace, and holy sweetness had arrived there, the blessed bishop also appeared to draw from that same light a considerable radiance upon his face.

The king and queen therefore prostrated themselves at the feet of the gracious priest. With great fear they asked to hear his consolation, prepared to carry out in deed whatever the patron’s mouth should reveal. They delighted in the words they had heard, inwardly illuminated by the light they had seen, although outwardly terrified by the brightness of the light.

The holy Father, filled with the splendor of heavenly wisdom, instructed them according to the customary manner of the heavenly vision. At its coming, it indeed terrifies the hearts of mortals, but with the consolation that follows it soothes the preceding fear. Thus, to those to whom it appeared among the fathers, it first brought dread, but afterward poured out the caresses of joy through the grace of mercy.

The most blessed man Remigius, likewise irradiated both outwardly—after the example of the ancient lawgiver, by the illumination of his face—and, much more, inwardly, by the illumination of divine radiance, is said through a prophetic spirit to have foretold what would happen to them and to their descendants. He foretold, namely, how their posterity would nobly extend the kingdom, exalt the Church of Christ, attain Roman dignity or dominion, and gain victories against the assaults of other peoples, provided that they did not degenerate from what was good, abandon the way of salvation, and fall into the snares of destructive vices by pursuing crimes that offend God—vices by which kingdoms are customarily overturned and transferred from one nation to another (Ecclesiasticus 10:8).

Finally, a road was prepared from the king’s house to the baptistery; curtains and hangings were suspended, the streets on either side were paved, the church was arranged, and the baptistery was sprinkled with balsam and other perfumes. The Lord supplied the people with such abundant grace that they rejoiced as though they were being refreshed by the fragrances of paradise.

Thus, with the holy Gospels going before, together with crosses, litanies, hymns, and spiritual songs, the supreme pontiff held the king’s hand and proceeded from the palace to the baptistery, followed by the queen and the people. As they went, the king is said to have asked the bishop whether this was the kingdom of God that he had promised him. “This,” replied the bishop, “is not that kingdom, but the beginning of the way by which one reaches it.”

When they arrived at the prepared place of the baptistery, a cleric carrying the chrism was intercepted by the people and was completely prevented from reaching the font. When the font had finally been sanctified, the chrism was lacking by divine ordinance. The holy pontiff, raising his eyes to heaven, is said to have prayed silently with tears.

And suddenly a white dove, like snow, flew down, carrying in its beak a small vessel filled with the chrism of the heavenly gift. When those present had been sprinkled with the miraculous nectar of its fragrance, they were filled with an inestimable sweetness surpassing all the delights they had previously experienced. The holy bishop took the vessel, sprinkled the font with the chrism, and immediately the appearance of the dove vanished.

When the king had witnessed the miracle of so great a grace, he rejoiced and at once renounced the pomp and works of the devil. He asked the venerable pontiff to baptize him. As he entered the fountain of enduring life, the blessed bishop proclaimed in eloquent speech:

“Bend your neck gently, Sicamber. Adore what you have burned; burn what you have adored.”

After the confession of the orthodox faith, he was immersed three times in the name of the divine, undivided Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. He was received by that same holy pontiff and consecrated, marked with the sacred anointing.

The king’s sisters, Albofledis and Landehildis, were baptized, together with three thousand men from the Frankish army, besides the women and children. On that day we may believe that great joy was celebrated in heaven among the holy angels, and that no small gladness was granted on earth to the faithful.

A large part of the Frankish army, however, had not yet been converted to the faith of Christ. With a certain prince named Raganarius, it remained in unbelief for some time beyond the River Somme, until, by the arrangement of heavenly grace, when the aforesaid king Ludovicus had won glorious victories, that same Raganarius—a follower of crimes and disgraceful practices—was bound and handed over by the Franks and killed. Then the whole Frankish people were converted and baptized into the faith of Christ through blessed Remigius.

## CHAPTER XIV  
### The possessions that King Ludovicus and the Franks bestowed upon him

The king and the nobles of the Franks therefore bestowed many possessions on blessed Remigius in various provinces. From these he endowed both the Church of Reims and several other churches of France [reading: detavit, “endowed”; ms. j: ditavit, “enriched”]. He also gave a considerable portion of these properties to the church of Saint Mary at Laon, the fortified place of the diocese of Reims where he had been raised. There he ordained as bishop Genebaudus, a man noble by birth and learned in both sacred and secular letters, who, after leaving his wife, had—so the tradition relates—embraced the religious life; she was a niece of Saint Remigius. He also subjected the parish of the county of Laon to that fortress.

Genebaudus, placing too much confidence in his former life and in the eminence of his rank, unwisely allowed the wife whom he had abandoned to visit him frequently, supposedly in order to instruct her. But, as the divine words testify, “The waters wear away stones, the earth is consumed by the flood, and the rock [printed variant: rupis; reading: rupes] is removed from its place” (Job 14:19). So it happened to him: the woman’s frequent visits and pleasant conversations softened the bishop’s hard and vigorous heart against lust and, as though removing a rock from the place of holiness, transferred it into the mire of wantonness.

Driven by diabolical persuasion, he broke out into the flames of lust, joined himself again to his former companion, and fathered a son by her. Since he had been conceived, as it were, in banditry, he ordered that the boy be called Latro, “Robber.” Because the fault was unknown to many—and because suspicion might otherwise arise if the woman withdrew from her customary visits to the bishop—she began to frequent the bishop’s house as before. Thus, while the guilt remained concealed from human beings and the passion of both man and woman was kept secret, the bishop, whose heart had first been pierced by compunction against sin, was drawn back into guilt.

As though he had forgotten what he had lamented, he repeated the crime he had bewailed. When he learned that a daughter had been born from the disgraceful affair, he ordered that she be given the name Vulpecula, “Little Vixen,” as having been born from a mother crafty in deceit.

When the Lord, who had looked upon blessed Peter, once again looked upon him also (Luke 22:61), Genebaudus was moved to compunction in mind and asked that holy Remigius go [variant: ut eat, “that he go”] to Laon. When the bishop had been received with due reverence, after they had entered the privacy of the chamber, Genebaudus broke into a great wail, tried to remove his stole, and, guilty, prostrated himself at the feet of his holy patron.

When the saint carefully investigated the cause of such grief, the sinner, impeded by tears and sobs, could scarcely recount in order what he had done. Seeing him contrite and almost despairing, the man of God sought to console him gently. He declared that he grieved not so much over the crime committed as because Genebaudus seemed to distrust the Lord’s goodness, for whom nothing he wills is impossible; the Lord despises no sinner who returns to him, and even shed his blood for sinners.

The kind and prudent man therefore tried by various examples to raise the fallen man, explaining that it would be easy before God to obtain pardon for this guilt if he earnestly sought to offer God fruits worthy of repentance. At last, having encouraged him by suitable exhortations, he imposed penance upon him. He built a small dwelling, illuminated by little windows and provided with an oratory—these are still said to remain beside the church of Saint Julian—and enclosed the penitent bishop within it.

For seven years he governed Genebaudus’s diocese, customarily celebrating one Sunday at Reims and the next at Laon. How strictly that man subjected himself to contrition and self-restraint in his confinement, and how worthy were the fruits of repentance that he produced there, divine clemency later revealed.

In the seventh year, while the penitent was spending the vigil of the Lord’s Supper in prayer and lamenting that, although he had advanced so far that he reconciled penitents to the Lord, on that day he himself could not—because of his crimes—deserve to stand in the church even among the penitents, an angel of the Lord came to him around midnight with a great light. He was lying prostrate in the oratory, and the angel is said to have addressed him as follows:

“Genebaudus, the prayers of your Father Remigius for you have been heard. The Lord has accepted your penance, and your sin has been forgiven. Rise, go out from here, perform the ministry of your episcopal office, and reconcile penitents to the Lord for their crimes.”

Genebaudus, struck with extreme terror, could not answer. Then the angel of the Lord encouraged him not to fear, but rather to rejoice in the mercy the Lord had granted him.

At last strengthened, he is said to have replied that he could not go out because his lord and Father Remigius had the key of the door with him and had also sealed it with his own seal. The angel answered him:

“To remove your doubt that I have been sent by the Lord, just as heaven is open to you, so this door will also be open.”

Immediately the door was opened, with its seal and bolt unharmed. Then Genebaudus prostrated himself in the form of a cross upon the threshold and is said to have declared:

“Even if the Lord Jesus Christ himself should deign to come to me, a sinner, I will not go out from here unless he comes who established me in this confinement in his name.”

At these words the angel immediately departed from him.

Meanwhile blessed Remigius was spending the night in prayer in the crypt beneath the church of Saint Mary at Reims. The bishop Heriveus later consecrated that crypt in honor of the same most blessed Remigius. There, at that time, the holy man, wearied by vigils and seemingly asleep, was carried away in ecstasy. He saw an angel standing beside him, who related to him all that had happened and commanded him to go as quickly as possible to Laon, restore Genebaudus to the see that had been given to him, and persuade him, in his presence, to perform his episcopal ministry.

At once the blessed man, without hesitation, went with great speed to Laon. When he arrived, he found Genebaudus lying on the threshold, the door unsealed and unbolted. With outstretched arms and tears of joy, he praised the Lord’s clemency, raised him up, restored him to his see and priestly office, and returned joyfully to Reims.

Afterward Genebaudus spent all the days of his life in holiness, relying on the grace of God, and publicly proclaimed what the Lord had done for him. Thus Genebaudus died in peace and was numbered among God’s saints. He had served as bishop for so long that his son Latro succeeded him, himself later becoming a bishop and a saint.

King Ludovicus finally established his seat in the city of Soissons and delighted in the presence and conversation of Saint Remigius. But since this holy man possessed no other estates in the vicinity of that city except a small one that had been given to Saint Nicasius, the king—at the queen’s suggestion and at the request of the inhabitants of the region, who were burdened by many requisitions of hospitality and wished to pay to the Church of Reims what they owed the king—proposed to Saint Remigius that he should give him everything he could encircle while the king rested at midday.

Blessed Remigius therefore set out along boundaries that are still clearly visible and left signs of his route. In the course of this survey, a certain man who possessed a mill drove the holy man back, so that he would not include it within the boundaries. The man of God addressed him gently:

“Friend, do not regard it as a hardship that we should possess this mill together.”

But when the man rejected him, the mill wheel immediately began to turn in the opposite direction. The man who had rejected him began to shout after Saint Remigius:

“Servant of God, come back, and let us possess the mill together.”

The holy man replied:

“Neither for me nor for you.”

Immediately such a great depth was formed in that place, as the earth withdrew beneath it, that no mill could ever afterward be maintained there.

Some others also drove him back, preventing him from including a certain small wood within his boundaries. He declared that never again should a leaf from that wood, although it was adjacent, fly across those boundaries, nor should a branch from it fall toward the same borders. This is said to have been observed by God’s will for as long as the wood continued to exist.

Proceeding from there, he came to a village called Caviniacum [Chavignon]. As he sought to include it within his boundaries, the inhabitants of the same village prevented him. Then, with a gentle expression, now rejected and now drawing near again, he left signs along his route that remain visible to this day. Finally, after being rejected, he is said to have told them:

“Always labor, and suffer poverty.”

The power of this sentence, which still remains, shows that it continues to be fulfilled.

When the king rose from his midday sleep, he gave by royal authority to Saint Remigius all the things that the blessed man had enclosed within the circuit of his survey. Among these were Juliacus and Codiciacus [Juilly and Cocy], the principal estates, which the Church of Reims still possesses by undisturbed right.

Finally, a certain exceedingly powerful man named Eulogius was convicted before King Ludovicus of a crime against royal majesty and fled to blessed Remigius for intercession. The holy man obtained for him both his life and possession of his property. As though in return for this favor, Eulogius offered his own estate, Sparnacum [Épernay], to his beneficent patron as a possession.

But the blessed bishop, refusing to accept a temporal reward for the service of his intercession, wisely exhorted the aforesaid man. Eulogius, crushed by shame because he had deserved to be granted life through pardon contrary to the dignity of his birth, did not wish to remain in secular dress. Remigius therefore said to him:

“If you wish to be perfect, sell all that you possess, give it to the poor, and follow Christ” (Matthew 19:21).

Accordingly, the price was assessed, and Remigius is said to have given Eulogius five thousand pounds of silver from the treasures of the Church, purchasing the estate itself for the Church’s possession.

He thus left a good example for all bishops and other priests: when they intercede for those who flee to the Church’s embrace or to the protection of God’s servants, or when they perform any good deed for them, they should not do so for temporal recompense, nor desire to receive transitory things. Rather, according to the Lord’s command, “Freely you have received; freely give” (Matthew 10:8), they should strive to bestow freely what they have received.

## CHAPTER XV  
### The victories of Ludovicus through the aid of Saint Remigius, and the end of that king

King Ludovicus therefore led an army against Gundobad and his brother Godegisil [A.D. 501, Sigeb.]. After receiving a blessing from blessed Remigius, who foretold victory for him, he received from him this instruction: he was to fight against his enemies for as long as the blessed wine that the man of God had given him continued to suffice for his daily use.

The Burgundians, preparing to fight against him under the aforesaid leaders, came to the River Ouche near the fortress of Dijon. When they engaged in a fierce battle, the Burgundians were put to flight. Gundobad, shutting himself within the fortress of Avignon, obtained peace from Ludovicus through his counselor Aredius, after giving many treasures.
