Ludovicus, having gained possession of enormous booty with the Frankish army, returned to his own country.

Likewise, after establishing at Paris a basilica in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul—today Saint Geneviève—and after a synod had been held at Orléans on the advice of his holy patron Remigius, he proceeded against King Alaric the Arian. Receiving a blessing from blessed Remigius, he was made confident of obtaining victory.

The holy man, as he had done earlier, also gave him a vessel commonly called a flask, filled with wine blessed by him. He gave the same instruction as before: the king was to proceed to war only so long as this wine from the flask did not fail him and those to whom he wished to distribute it.

The king drank from it, as did many of his men, yet the vessel of wine did not diminish. When he engaged the Goths in battle, he put them to flight and, with blessed Remigius assisting him, emerged victorious. In that battle two Goths struck him in the sides with spears, but, protected by the merits of his patron, he could not be wounded.

After subduing many cities to his dominion, he proceeded as far as Toulouse. Having taken Alaric’s treasures, he passed through the city of Angoulême, before whose walls—at the sight of the king himself—they collapsed. After killing the Goths who were inside, he returned to his own country with glorious victory; the wine in the flask did not fail until he had returned home [A.D. 509, Sigeb.].

Finally, at the exhortation of Saint Remigius, King Ludovicus sent royal insignia—that is, a golden crown set with precious gems—as a gift to the blessed apostle Peter. He also received from the Emperor Anastasius letters [ms. i: codicellos] sent to him concerning the consulship, together with a golden crown and a purple tunic, and is recorded from that time to have been called consul.

Hormisdas, pontiff of the Roman See, also entrusted his own authority in the kingdom of Ludovicus to Saint Remigius in letters addressed to him.

After this, King Ludovicus died in peace [A.D. 514, Sigeb., Baronius, Haraeus] and was buried in the basilica of the holy apostle Peter that he had built at Paris. At the very moment when he gave up his spirit, blessed Remigius, who was at Reims, learned through the revelation of the Holy Spirit that he had died and made this known to those standing around him.

## CHAPTER XVI  
### The synod at which he converted a heretic

The bishops of Gaul once gathered for a synod on account of the faith and asked blessed Remigius to come to the same council, since he was exceedingly learned in the divine words and highly practiced in ecclesiastical teachings.

An Arian bishop, a very sharp disputant who trusted in dialectical propositions and conclusions and was consequently extremely conceited, attended the assembly. When Saint Remigius entered the council and all the assembled brothers reverently rose for him, except for the heretic, that proud man disdained to stand.

But as soon as blessed Remigius passed before him, the heretic lost the power of speech, his mouth being obstructed. Everyone waited for him to speak after Saint Remigius had addressed them, but he could not utter even a single word. At last he prostrated himself before the blessed man’s feet and begged forgiveness by gestures.

Saint Remigius said to him:

“In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, the true Son of the living God: if this is what you rightly believe about him, speak; and believe and confess concerning him as the Catholic Church believes.”

At his words the heretic, previously proud but now made humble and Catholic, confessed the orthodox faith concerning the divine and inseparable Trinity and concerning the incarnation of Christ in Catholic terms, and promised that he would remain in the faith of that confession.

Thus, since the soul had been lost through unbelief and the bodily voice had justly been condemned because of pride, the venerable pontiff, by divine power, restored health both to the soul and to the body. He plainly showed to all priests who were present or would learn of these things how they ought to act toward those who think wrongly about Christ—who deigned to become near and a brother to us through his humanity—and toward those who sin against him or against the Church and rebel, as well as toward those who afterward recognize their error and repent.

## CHAPTER XVII  
### The abatement of the fire, and his death and burial

As Saint Remigius grew old, and the Spirit of God revealed to him that famine would follow the abundance then present, he ordered several heaps to be made from the harvests of the episcopal estates, so that they might later benefit the people suffering from hunger. Several such heaps were made at an estate called Celtus.

The men of that estate, however, were seditious and rebellious. One day, having become drunk, they began saying to one another:

“What does that Jubilaeus”—for so they called the holy man because of the length of his life—“intend to do with these heaps of grain that he has gathered? Does he intend to build a city out of them? For, just as towers are arranged around the walls of a city, so these heaps can be seen set out around the estate.”

At last, persuaded by the devil, they encouraged one another and set fire to the heaps. When this had been reported to the blessed bishop, who at that time happened to be staying in a nearby estate called Basilica Cortis [Bazancourt], he immediately mounted his horse and hastened to Celtus to restrain so great an act of presumption.

When he arrived and found the grain burning, he began to warm himself at the fire, saying:

“A fire is always a good hearth, if it does not prevail over it.”

Nevertheless, he added:

“Let all who have done this, and all who are born from their stock, become heavy men, and let the women be punished by an affliction of the throat.”

This is also known to have been fulfilled.

Indeed, until the time of Charlemagne, who exterminated such men from Celtus because they had killed the church’s vicedominus in that estate, the perpetrators of the murder having been killed, those who consented having been scattered through various provinces and condemned to perpetual exile, and who caused the same estate to be restored from the other estates of the bishopric, the men and women of this lineage remained punished, as the holy man’s sentence had declared.

The man of God acted suitably, for he had foreseen that their descendants would be rebellious and seditious. He therefore decreed that such vengeance should punish not only the presumptuous offenders but also their descendants.

After these events, and many other great works of virtue that the Lord deigned to perform through this faithful servant, hearing his groans and sighs—for he was accustomed to say, “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Psalm 41:3); “I shall be satisfied when his glory is revealed” (Psalm 16:8)—the Lord, in loving consolation, revealed to him that the day of his death was approaching.

Relying on this revelation, he drew up his testament, hastening to reach that inheritance of which the Prophet says: “When he gives sleep to his beloved, this is the inheritance of the Lord” (Psalm 127:3, 4). Thus this holy man of God, abandoning an earthly inheritance, received an eternal one.

After making his testament and properly arranging all his affairs, because the true farmer cleanses every fruitful branch of the true vine so that it may bear more fruit (John 15:2), he was deprived for a time of the light of his bodily eyes, so that he might more attentively contemplate with the eyes of his mind the heavenly things toward which he longed with his whole desire.

He strove throughout the trial of his testing always to give thanks, devoting himself day and night to the praises and hymns of God, faithfully reflecting that those who patiently and humbly receive chastisements are afterward received in exaltation into rest.

The Lord, wishing to show in him a pledge of eternal glory, restored his sight before he died. For this reason, as he had done when he lost it, he blessed the name of the Lord.

Not long afterward, knowing that the day of his departure had arrived, he took leave through the celebration of Mass and participation in holy communion, and gave peace to his sons. After he had served the Lord as a most faithful and prudent servant for seventy-four years in the episcopate, in the ninety-sixth year of his age, on the Ides of January [manuscript *i*: “the ninth day before the Ides”], having completed the course of his holy contest, preserving the faith, rich in the fruit of many good works and in the gain of souls, his soul entered heaven, as he had long desired, and left his body to the earth.

He received a white robe, that is, the everlasting blessedness of the soul, and was destined at the resurrection to receive another: namely, the immortality of the blessed glory of a resurrected body. He would possess a share and fellowship with the chief members of Christ in the heavenly kingdom, as testified by the apostolic grace bestowed upon him: the Frankish people converted through him to the faith of Christ; the palm of martyrdom; the long endurance of patience in the longevity of his life; the glory of confession; the preaching of the orthodox faith; and the splendid manifestation of great works both during his bodily life and after his death.

When his most holy funeral procession was being carried to the burial prepared in the church of the holy martyrs Timothy and Apollinaris, the bier became so heavy in the middle of the street that it could not be moved at all, no matter how strenuously the people exerted themselves.

All were astonished and asked God’s mercy to deign to show in what place he wished the body of his saint to be buried. They directed the bier toward the basilica of the aforesaid martyrs, but they could not move it. They proposed taking it to the church of Saint Nicasius, but the coffin could not be lifted. They decided to go to the church of Saints Sixtus and Sinicius, but even then it could not be moved.

At last, compelled by necessity—for there was a small church remaining in honor of the blessed martyr Christopher, and no publicly known saint’s body was kept there, although the cemetery of ancient Reims was said to extend around the church’s atria—they asked that the Lord declare whether he had decided that this most sacred pledge should be placed in that little church.

In response to these prayers, they lifted the coffin with such ease that they felt no burden as they carried it. The limbs of this most reverend Father were buried in that little church, by divine providence, in the place where the altar of the blessed virgin Geneviève now stands.

Afterward, where the bier is known to have become heavy, many miracles are said to have been displayed. A cross also stands there, placed at that time and affixed to a column inscribed with these words:

> When he had passed from this world to the heavenly homeland,  
>   
> The great blessed bishop Remigius was brought here  
>   
> Worthily by the holy people, to be buried in body  
>   
> [Col. 0060A] In the church of the martyr Timothy.  
>   
> Here he remained for a time; nor could he be moved,  
>   
> Until the Lord revealed where he was to be placed:  
>   
> Where now, with Christ’s favor, he excels in miracles,  
>   
> Granting fitting benefits to those devoted to God:  
>   
> Sight to the blind, walking to the lame, and healing to the sick.  
>   
> Therefore, with abundant prayers, let us beseech the Lord  
>   
> That through his holy prayers we may deserve to obtain  
>   
> Forgiveness of sins and the joys of heaven.  
>   
> Holy Remigius, precious confessor of the Lord,  
>   
> Have mercy also on your servant Adeloldus.

## CHAPTER XVIII  
### The testament composed by him

“In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Glory to God. Amen.

“[Col. 0060B] I, Remigius, bishop of the city of Reims, having obtained the priesthood, have drawn up my testament according to praetorian law, and have ordered it to have the force of a codicil if anything should appear to be lacking in its legal validity. Whenever I, Remigius the bishop, shall have departed from this light, you shall be my heir, holy and venerable Catholic Church of the city of Reims; and you, Lupus, son of my brother and bishop, whom I have always loved with exceptional affection; and you, my nephew Agricola, priest, who have pleased me by your service from childhood: you shall be my heirs in all my property that came to me by my share before my death, except what I shall have given, bequeathed, ordered to be given, or wished any one of you to possess as a special bequest.

“[Col. 0060C] You, my holy heir, the Church of Reims, shall possess the tenant-farmers whom I have in the territory of Portus, whether from my paternal and maternal property, or whom I exchanged with my brother, Bishop Principius of holy memory, or whom I possess as gifts: Dagaredus, Profuturus, Prudentius, Temnaicus, Maurilio, Baudoleifus, Provinciolus; the female tenant-farmers Naviatena, Lauta, and Suffronia; and also the slave Amorinus, together with all those whom I shall leave intestate—you shall claim them under your ownership.

“Likewise, the estates and fields that I possess on Portus soil—namely Tudiniacum and Balatonium [manuscript: Balatonum], or Plerinacum and Vaculiacum, and whatever I have possessed on that same Portus soil by any title—you shall reclaim in their entirety, with all their fields, meadows, pastures, and woods, by the authority of this testament.

“[Col. 0060D] In the same way, my most holy heir, whatever has been bestowed upon you by my relatives and friends, on whatever soil or in whatever territory, just as I shall have assigned it among the parishes, monasteries, martyria, deaconries, hospices, and all the institutions living under your authority, my successors in the future, mindful of their office, shall preserve my arrangement without disturbance and without any opposition, just as I have preserved that of my predecessors.

“Among these are Celtus (*quam*; Briss.: *quem*), whom Celsa, my cousin, delivered to you through my hand, and the estate of Huldriciaca, which Count Hulderic gave to that place where my holy brothers and fellow bishops of your diocese shall have chosen to lay my bones: let these serve for its coverings. Let that place be a possession specially belonging to my successors, the bishops of Reims; and let a village from my own property at Portus, and . . . tenant-farmers likewise from the episcopal estate in the territory of Reims, serve for the support of those who serve God there.

“[Col. 0061A] Let the estate Blandibaccius in Portus, which I bought from my co-heirs Benedictus and Hilarius with money paid from the church treasury, and Albiniacus from the episcopal estate, be assigned jointly for the support of the clergy of the Church of Reims.

“Let Berna, from the episcopal estate, which used to belong specially to my predecessors, together with the two estates that Ludovicus, whom I received from the sacred baptismal font, gave me out of affection for my name—called Piscofesheim in his own language (*vocatis*; corrected: *vocatas*)—or together with Coslo and Gleni, and all the woods, meadows, and pastures that I bought through various agents in the Vosges, within, around, and beyond it, both across and this side of the Rhine, on payment of a price, provide pitch annually. Let it also distribute annually to all regular establishments founded either by me or by my predecessors, or to be founded in the future by my episcopal successors, according to the needs of the places, for the making of wine vessels.

“[Col. 0061B] As for Crusciniacum [elsewhere: Cruciniatum] and Faram, the estates that the most holy virgin of Christ, Genovefa, deserved to obtain from the most Christian king Ludovicus, for the convenience of her journey whenever she frequently visited the Church of Reims, and assigned for the support of those serving God there: just as she arranged, so I confirm it. Let Crusciniacus be assigned to the services and repairs of the principal church of my future episcopal successor. I order Faram likewise to serve that bishop and the repairs of the church where I shall lie forever.

“[Col. 0061C] Sparnacus [manuscript: Spernacus], an estate that I bought from Eulogius for five thousand pounds of silver, is seen to belong to you, my most holy heir, and not to my other heirs (chapter 14). For when that same man was held liable on a charge of treason against the royal majesty and could not clear himself, I secured the estate for you—not only so that he would not be killed, by paying the aforesaid price from your treasuries, but also so that his money would not be confiscated. Therefore, by a generous decree, I have confirmed that the aforesaid Sparnacus shall serve you forever, both for the restoration of the treasury and for the support of your bishop.

“Duodeciacus, as it was confirmed to you by Clodovaldus, a boy of most noble character, shall serve you, my heir, forever.

“The estates that the lord and illustrious-memory king Ludovicus, whom I received from the sacred baptismal font while he was still a pagan and ignorant of God, delivered to me as personal property, I assigned to poorer establishments, lest, while he was still an unbeliever, he should perhaps think that I was greedy for earthly things and seeking from him not the salvation of his soul but rather his external goods.

“[Col. 0061D] Marveling at this, both as a believer and before he came to the faith, he kindly and generously allowed me to intercede for all who suffered need.

“And because he recognized that, among all the bishops of Gaul, I labored above all for the faith and for the calling together of the Franks, God gave me such favor in his sight, and divine power—which through the Holy Spirit caused me, a sinner, to perform many signs for the salvation of the aforesaid Frankish people—that he not only restored to all the churches of the Frankish kingdom what had been taken away, but also, from his own property and out of free generosity, enriched very many churches.

“[Col. 0062A] I was unwilling to attach even as much ground as a footstep from his kingdom to the Church of Reims until I had obtained that he fulfill this obligation toward all the churches. Nor, after his baptism, did I seek anything except Codiciacum and Juliacum. The most holy and like-minded boy Clodovaldus, already mentioned, and the inhabitants of that place, burdened by numerous gifts that they owed to the king for my church, compelled me to ask for these by their earnest entreaties. The most devout king, receiving this gratefully, gave them with the greatest willingness; and, by episcopal authority, I have confirmed them for your use, my most holy heir, according to the command of that most devout donor.

“[Col. 0062B] I order that the properties that the often-mentioned and most devout prince granted you in Septimania and Aquitania, and those that a certain Benedictus granted you in Provence—I restored his daughter, sent to me by Alaric, from the bondage of diabolical deceit and even from the underworld through the grace of the Holy Spirit by the laying-on of my sinful hands—shall continually serve the use of your light and of the place where my body shall lie, together with the estates in Austrasia or Thuringia.

“To my future episcopal successor I leave one white Easter cloak, two dove-colored coverings, and three curtains, which are for the doors on feast days—of the dining room, cell, and kitchen.

“Of the silver vessel weighing thirty pounds, and another weighing one hundred and eight pounds, I have distributed them between you, my heir, and your diocesan Church of Laon, having made patens and chalices for the sacred ministry, as I desired, with God’s approval.

“[Col. 0062C] Of that golden vessel weighing ten pounds, which the often-mentioned lord and illustrious-memory king Ludovicus, whom, as I said, I received from the sacred baptismal font, graciously deigned to give me so that I might do with it whatever I wished, I order that a small tower and an illustrated chalice be made for you, my heir, the aforesaid Church. I also wish the inscriptions that I myself dictated at Laon on silver to be written on this as well.

“I shall do this myself if I have sufficient time in life. But if I shall have closed my final day [Briss.: *sin* before *ante*], you, Lupus, son of my brother and bishop, mindful of your office, shall complete the aforesaid objects.

“To my fellow priests and deacons who are at Reims I leave twenty-five solidi, to be divided equally among them in common. They shall likewise possess jointly the vine-plant above my vineyard situated in the suburb, together with Melanius the vine-grower, whom I give in the place of the ecclesiastical man Albovicius, so that Albovicius may enjoy the fullest liberty.

“[Col. 0062D] I order twelve solidi to be given to the subdeacons, and eight solidi to the lectors, doorkeepers, and juniors.

“To the twelve poor people registered in the hospice, waiting for alms before the church doors, two solidi shall be supplied for their refreshment; to them I previously ordered the estate Corcellum to serve.

“To three other poor people, where the brothers must wash their feet daily, and for whom I established Balatoforum [Relatoforum], which is called a hospice, for this ministry, one solidus shall be given.

“To the forty widows waiting for support in the church portico, who were being supplied with stipends from the tithes of the estates Calmisciacum, Tessiacum, and Novavilla, I add the following from the estate of Huldriciaca mentioned above: let stipends be brought to them forever, and I order that three solidi and four denarii be given.

“[Col. 0063A] To the Church of Saint Victor at the Suessionian Gate, two solidi.

“To the Church of Saint Martin at the Collatitian Gate, two solidi.

“To the Church of Saint Hilary at the Mars Gate, two solidi.

“To the Church of the holy martyrs Crispinus and Crispinianus at the Treveran Gate, two solidi.

“To the Church of Saint Peter within the city, which is called the Lord’s Estate, two solidi.

“To the church that I built in honor of all the Martyrs above the crypt of Reims, when, through the help of God’s power, I rescued almost the whole city from the fire of the devil, two solidi.

“To the church that I built within the city, through the same sign of God’s power, in honor of Saint Martin and all the confessors, two solidi.

“To the deaconry within the city called ‘At the Apostles,’ two solidi.

“To the titular church of Saint Maurice on the Caesarian Road, two solidi.

“[Col. 0063B] To the Jovinian church [manuscript: Jovian church], of the title of blessed Agricola, where that most Christian man Jovinus himself and the holy martyr Nicasius rest with many martyrs of their company in Christ, and where also five confessors, the immediate predecessors of Lord Nicasius, are buried together with the most holy virgin and martyr Eutropia, three solidi.

“To that same church I have added, from my own property, what had belonged to Jovinus in the territory of Soissons, together with the Church of Saint Michael and its previous possessions.

“To the Church of the holy martyrs Timothy and Apollinaris, where, if it should seem right to my brothers and sons, the bishops of our diocese, I have determined, with the Lord’s permission, to lay my bones, four solidi.

“[Col. 0063C] To the Church of Saint John, where the power of Christ, when I prayed, raised the daughter of Benedictus, two solidi.

“To the Church of Saint Sixtus, where he rests with his three successors, three solidi; to it I have also added, from my own property, Plebeias above the Matrona.

“To the Church of Saint Martin situated on the same territory of the holy Church of Reims, two solidi.

“To the Church of Saint Christopher, two solidi.

“To the Church of Saint Germanus, which I myself built on Reims territory, two solidi.

“To the Church of the holy martyrs Cosmas and Damian, situated on the territory of the aforesaid mother church, two solidi.

“To the hospice of Saint Mary, which is called a hospital, where twelve poor people await alms, one solidus shall be given.

“[Col. 0063D] Finally, I order that this hospice remain wherever it shall please my brothers and sons to lay my bones; and so that for a long time, day and night [manuscript: *die*, ‘by day’], they may pray to the Lord for my sins and crimes, from my own hereditary property, in addition to the possessions that my predecessors gave to the Lord for their support, I add the estate Soladrona, the estate of Saint Stephen, and whatever came to me by inheritance in the estate of Herimundus. As for what I bought there for a price, I assigned it long ago to the Church of Saint Quintinus the martyr.

“From the aforesaid Vaculiacum I order Fruminius, Dagaleifus, Dagaredus, Ductio, Baudowicus, Udulfus, and Vinofeifa to be free.

“Temnaredus, who was born of a free mother, shall enjoy the status of freedom.

“But you, Lupus, son of my brother and bishop, shall claim under your ownership Nifastes and his mother Nucia.

“I also assign to you the vineyard that Aeneas the vine-grower cultivates; I order Aeneas and his younger son Monulfus to enjoy freedom.

“[Col. 0064A] You shall assign to your right Melloficus the swineherd and his wife Paschasida, Vernivianus with his sons, except Widragasius, to whom I have granted freedom.

“I order my slave from Cesurnicum to be yours.

“You shall reclaim for yourself the portion of the fields held by my brother Bishop Principius, together with the woods, meadows, and pastures.

“I leave to you Viteredus, my slave whom Mellowicus held. I transfer to your right and ownership Teneursolus, Capalinus, and his wife Theodorosena.

“Let Theodonima also be free by my order.

“You shall retain Edoneifa, who was joined to your man, and her family.

“I order the wife of Aregildus and her family to be free.

“You shall reclaim my portion of the meadow that I have at Laon near you, situated toward the imitation of the mountains—those little meadows called Jovia—which I held.

“[Col. 0064B] I have assigned Labrinacum to you, where I laid the bones of my mother, with the boundaries specified.

“To you, my nephew Agricola the priest, who spent your childhood within my household walls, I deliver and transfer Merumvastus the slave, his wife Meratena, and their son named Mercovicus.

“I order his brother Medovicus to be free.

“I leave Amantius and his wife to you. I order their daughter Dasounda to be free.

“I assign Alaricus the slave to your portion; his wife, whom I redeemed and freed, I commend to you to be defended as a free woman.

“You shall claim under your ownership Bebrimodus and his wife Moria. Their son Monacharius shall rejoice in the benefit of freedom.

“[Col. 0064C] You shall reclaim Mellaricus and his wife Placidia under your ownership. Their son Medaridus shall be a freedman.

“I give you the vineyard that Mellaricus made at Laon, together with Britobaudes, my slave, and also Gibericus.

“I leave you the vineyard that Bebrimodus cultivates on this condition: on feast days and on all Sundays, my offering shall be made from it at the sacred altars, and annual banquets shall be provided for the priests and deacons of Reims.

“To my nephew Praetextatus I assign Moderatus, Totticio, Marcovicus, and Innocentius the slave, whom I received from Profuturus, my hereditary tenant; four of the larger spoons; a small dish; the lamp that the tribune Friaredus gave me; and a figured silver bowl.

“To his little son Parovius, a small dish, three spoons, and a chasuble whose fringes I exchanged.

“[Col. 0064D] I transfer to Remigius three spoons bearing my name, and his own tablecloth, which I have for ordinary use. I also give him the *hichinaculum* [an item of uncertain identification] about which I spoke to Godebodus.

“To my blessed daughter Hilaria the deaconess I assign the female slave named Noca; I give her a trained vine adjoining her vineyard, which Catusius cultivates. I also transfer my portion of Talpusciacum in return for the services that she continually renders me.

“To my nephew Aetius I assign the portion of Cesurnicum that came to me by lot in the division, together with all the rights that I held and possessed.

“I also transfer the boy Ambrosius to his right and ownership.

“[Col. 0065A] I order Vitalis the tenant-farmer to be free, and his household to belong to my nephew Agathimerus. To him I give the vineyard that I planted at Vindonissa and established through my labor, on the condition that from his share, on every feast day and Sunday, an offering be presented to the sacred altars in remembrance of me, and that, with the Lord’s permission, annual banquets be provided for the priests and deacons of Laon.

“I give to the Church of Laon, from the estates that the aforesaid king Ludovicus of holy memory gave me, two estates, including Anisiacum [the second is not named in the supplied text], and eighteen solidi, which the priests and deacons shall distribute among themselves in equal shares.

“Let the Church of Laon reclaim in its entirety my portion of Secium, and Lauscita, which my dearest daughter and sister, and, as I believe, most holy virgin of Christ, Genovefa, fully assigned to you for distribution to the poor of Christ.

“[Col. 0065B] To your holiness, Lupus, son of my brother and bishop, I commend, from the aforesaid estates, the following persons, whom I order to be free: Catusius and his wife Auliatena, Nonnio, who cultivates my vineyard, Sonnoveifa, whom I redeemed from captivity and who was born of good parents, and her son Leutiberedus, Mellaridus and Mellatena, Vasantes, Cocus, Caesaria, Dagarasena, Baudorosena, the granddaughter of Leo, and Marcoeifus, the son of Totnonus. All these, Lupus, son of my brother and bishop, you shall defend as free persons by priestly authority.

“To you, the heir of my church, I give Flavianus and his wife Sparagildis. I have established their little daughter Flavarasena as free.

“The priests and deacons of Reims shall possess Fedamia, the wife of Melanius, and their little daughter.

“[Col. 0065C] I order Crispiciolus the tenant-farmer to be free, and his household to belong to my nephew Aetius. The tenant-estate Passiacum shall come to both of them, that is, to Aetius and Agathimerus.

“To my great-niece Praetextata I give Modorosena.

“To Profuturus I deliver the boy Leudocharius.

“I order Leudonera to be given to Profutura.

“To the subdeacons, lectors, doorkeepers, and juniors of Laon I leave four solidi.

“One solidus shall be given to the poor registered in the hospice for their refreshment.

“I assign from the gift of the aforesaid prince Salvonaria above the Mora, and ten solidi to the Church of Soissons, in remembrance of my name.

“For my heirs I have assigned Sablonaria above the Matrona.

“To the Church of Châlons, from the gift of the aforesaid son of mine, Gellonos above the Matrona, and ten solidi.

“[Col. 0065D] To the Church of Saint Memmius, Fascinarias from the gifts of the aforesaid prince, and eight solidi.

“To the Church of Mouzon, five solidi.

“To the Church of Verdun, a field beside the millworks that are established there.

“To the Catarigensian Church (*ecclesia Catarigensis*), four solidi; the same number shall be paid to the Church of Portus in remembrance of my name.

“To the Church of Arras, to which, with the Lord’s approval, I consecrated my dearest brother Bishop Vedastus, I assigned from the gift of the aforesaid prince two estates for the support of the clergy, namely Orcos and Sabucetum. I order that twenty solidi also be given to them in remembrance of my name.

“Because of the familiar services of the archdeacon Ursus, I give him at home a fine woven chasuble and another fuller one, two delicate cloaks, the carpet that I have on my bed, and the best tunic that I shall leave at the time of my passing.

“[Col. 0066A] My heirs, Bishop Lupus and Priest Agricola, you shall divide my pigs equally between you.

“Friaredus, whom I bought for fourteen solidi so that he would not be killed, shall have two of the pigs allotted to him and shall give twelve for making the chamber of the basilica of the lords and martyrs Timothy and Apollinaris.

“This is how I give, how I bequeath, how I testify. Let all the rest of you be disinherited—be disinherited.”

“This testament of mine is free from fraud and shall remain so. If any erasure or scraping is found in it, it was made in my presence while it was being reread and corrected by me.

“Nor shall my two earlier testaments obstruct, oppose, or in any way harm this one—the first, which I made fourteen years ago, and the second, which I made seven years ago—for everything contained in them is known to have been inserted here in the presence of my brothers, with what was lacking added, and also with what the Lord later deigned to grant me appended.

“[Col. 0066B] But this present testament, which I have drawn up, is to be preserved [manuscript reading: *conservatum*, ‘preserved’] unshaken and undefiled by my brothers who are my successors, namely the bishops of Reims; and it is also to be defended and protected everywhere and against all persons by the kings of the Franks, my dearest sons, whom, through baptism, by the gift of Jesus Christ and with the cooperation of the grace of the Holy Spirit, I consecrated to the Lord. Let it always possess inviolable and perpetual firmness in every respect.

“And if anyone in the clerical order, from a priest down to one who has merely received the tonsure, should presume to contradict or oppose it, and, after being corrected by my successor, should neglect to make satisfaction, let him be deposed from his rank after three bishops from the neighboring places of the diocese of Reims have been summoned.

“[Col. 0066C] But if—which I neither wish nor desire, nor even hope for—any bishop who succeeds me in this seat of Reims, driven by accursed greed, should presume to divert elsewhere, alter, exchange, or under any pretext grant to lay uses for the sake of profit the aforesaid properties, which I, with the authority of my Lord Jesus Christ, ordered for his honor and for the consolation of his poor; or should favor or consent to their being given by anyone else, then, after all the bishops of the diocese of Reims, together with the priests and deacons, and also very many of my dearest sons, the devout Franks, have been summoned, let him pay the penalty of his guilt by deprivation of his episcopate; and he shall by no means deserve in this world to recover the rank he has lost.

“[Col. 0066D] But whoever, in lay attire, should despise what we have established and, favoring himself, presume under any pretext to abuse or usurp what has been assigned to the poor of the Church, let the alienator, petitioner, giver, receiver, and invader alike be separated from the Catholic Church by the bond of an equal and perpetual condemnation, until, by God’s mercy, they may deserve forgiveness through an amendment worthy of satisfaction.

“But if anyone chooses to persist in this on the occasion of any gift, let all hope of restoration in the present or future be utterly removed from him by my successor, the bishop of Reims.

“[Col. 0067A] Only with regard to the royal line—which, for the honor of the holy Church and the defense of the poor, I chose together with all my brothers and fellow bishops of Germany, Gaul, and Neustria, establishing it to reign perpetually at the height of royal majesty; which I baptized, received from the sacred font, marked with the gift of the sevenfold Spirit, and, after its consecration as king through the anointing of that same sacred chrism, appointed—I decree the following.

“If that royal line, so often consecrated to the Lord through my blessing, should ever wish to repay good with evil and become an invader, destroyer, or ravager of God’s churches, oppressive or hostile to them, let it first be warned after the bishops of the diocese of Reims have been summoned. Then let the aforesaid Church of Reims (*Remensi*; corrected: *Remensis*) be convened again, with its sister, the Church of Trier, joined to it [corrected reading: *conveniat*, ‘let it convene’].

“[Col. 0067B] Third, after only three or four archbishops of Gaul have been summoned, let that prince, whoever he may be, be warned, so that, if he previously refuses to make satisfaction, the matter may be deferred until the seventh warning, with the long-suffering of paternal kindness.

“Finally, if, after setting aside all the blessings mentioned above [perhaps: ‘warnings’ (*monitionibus*)], he does not lay aside the spirit of incorrigible obstinacy and, unwilling to submit to God in every respect, refuses to share in the blessings of the Church, let the sentence of separation from the body of Christ be delivered against him by all. It is known to have been sung long ago by the prophet and king David, under the dictation of the same Holy Spirit who is in the bishops:

“‘[Col. 0067C] For he persecuted,’ he says, ‘the poor man and the beggar and the brokenhearted, and did not remember to show mercy; he loved the curse, and it shall come upon him; and he did not desire blessing, and it shall be far from him’ (Psalm 108 [109]:17–18).

“Let everything that the Church customarily sings, in the person of Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, and of wicked bishops, be sung against him in each of the churches, because the Lord said: ‘As long as you did it for one of the least of mine, you did it for me’ (Matthew 25:40); and ‘as long as you did not do it for these, neither did you do it for me’ (ibid., 45). Therefore, what is proved concerning the head must without doubt be understood concerning the members.

“Only one word there shall be changed by substitution: ‘Let his days be few, and let another take his office’ (Psalm 108 [109]:8).

“[Col. 0067D] If my successors, the archbishops of Reims, should neglect to carry this out as I have ordered, may they find in themselves, corrupted by curses, whatever ought to have been cut away from princes, so that ‘their days may be few, and another may take their episcopate.’

“[Col. 0068A] But if my Lord Jesus Christ should deign to hear the voice of my prayer, which I pour out daily before the divine majesty especially for that line, so that, just as it received it from me, it may persevere in the ordering of the kingdom and in the governance of the holy Church of God, then let many blessings be added by the same Holy Spirit upon its head, more illustrious than the blessings that the Holy Spirit poured through my sinful hand upon its head. And from it may kings and emperors proceed who, in the present and in the future, according to the Lord’s will, confirmed and strengthened by his power in judgment and justice, may continually be able to possess and enlarge the kingdom for the increase of his holy Church; and in the house of David—that is, in the heavenly Jerusalem—may they deserve to be exalted and reign with the Lord forever. Amen.

“Completed at Reims, on the day and in the consulship stated above, with the subscribing witnesses present and intervening.

“I, Remigius the bishop, reread, signed, subscribed, and, with God’s help, completed my testament in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

“+ Vedastus, bishop, whom my father Remigius cursed, I have cursed, and whom he blessed, I have blessed; I was also present and subscribed.

“+ Genebaudus, bishop, whom my father Remigius cursed, I have cursed, and whom he blessed, I have blessed; I was also present and subscribed.

“[Col. 0068B] + Medardus, bishop, whom my father Remigius cursed, I have cursed, and whom he blessed, I have blessed; I was also present and subscribed.

“+ Lupus, bishop, whom my father Remigius cursed, I have cursed, and whom he blessed, I have blessed; I was also present and subscribed.

“+ Benedictus, bishop, whom my father Remigius cursed, I have cursed, and whom he blessed, I have blessed; I was also present and subscribed.

“+ Eulogius, bishop, whom my father Remigius cursed, I have cursed, and whom he blessed, I have blessed; I was also present and subscribed.

“+ Agricola, priest, whom my father Remigius cursed, I have cursed, and whom he blessed, I have blessed; I was also present and subscribed.

“+ Theodonius, priest, whom my father Remigius cursed, I have cursed, and whom he blessed, I have blessed; I was also present and subscribed.

“[Col. 0068C] + Celsinus, priest, whom my father Remigius cursed, I have cursed, and whom he blessed, I have blessed; I was also present and subscribed.

“Pappolus, *vir clarissimus* (V. C., ‘most distinguished man’), was present and subscribed.

“Eulodius, *vir clarissimus* (V. C., ‘most distinguished man’), was present and subscribed.

“Eusebius, *vir clarissimus* (V. C., ‘most distinguished man’), was present and subscribed.

“Rusticolus, *vir clarissimus* (V. C., ‘most distinguished man’), was present and signed.

“Eutropius, *vir clarissimus* (V. C., ‘most distinguished man’), was present and signed.

“Daweus, *vir clarissimus* (V. C., ‘most distinguished man’), was present and signed.

“After the testament had been drawn up—or rather, signed—it occurred to my mind that I should assign to the basilica of the lords and martyrs Timothy and Apollinaris a silver serving dish weighing six pounds, so that from it the future seat of my bones might be fashioned.”

## CHAPTER XIX  
### On the Remedy for the Bubonic Plague and Other Things Bestowed through Him

[Col. 0068D]

After the death of this most blessed Father, “when the bubonic plague,” as Gregory of Tours recounts (*On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 79), “was devastating the people of First Germania, and everyone was terrified by hearing of this calamity, the people of Reims hurried to the tomb of the saint, demanding a fitting remedy for the crisis. Having lit candles and many lamps, they kept vigil throughout the entire night with hymns and heavenly psalms.

“When morning came, they examined in their deliberation what might still be lacking in their prayer. For, with God revealing it, they discovered how, after the prayer already offered, they might fortify the defenses of the city with an even greater protection.

“Accordingly, they arranged a cloth taken from the blessed man’s tomb in the form of a bier; with candles lit upon crosses and candle-bearers, they raised their voices in song and went around the city with its districts, passing no lodging that they did not encompass in this procession.

“[Col. 0069A] After not many days, the plague mentioned above attacked the borders of this city. Yet when it came as far as the place to which the blessed relic had advanced, as though it recognized an appointed boundary, it did not dare enter; indeed, by the repulsion of this power, it abandoned even those places that it had invaded at the beginning.”

Many miracles were afterward divinely displayed at his tomb, but through negligence they have not been committed to writing.

## CHAPTER XX  
### On the Translation of His Body and Certain Miracles Performed Again

[Col. 0069B]

After the body of the most blessed Remigius had been buried in the basilica mentioned above, and many astonishing miracles were being performed there by the Lord’s grace, the church itself was enlarged and exalted, and a crypt was made behind the altar into which the venerable relic might be transferred.

They uncovered the coffin from the earth in order to lower it, once prepared, into the crypt, but they could not move it at all. When night came, after many lights had been lit, sleep overcame all those keeping vigil around midnight. When they awoke, the sarcophagus was found to have been carried away with its sacred treasure and conveyed into the prepared dwelling—not by human hands, but by angelic ones.

Everyone was filled with such sweetness of fragrance that no human tongue can express it. [Col. 0069C] This delightful pleasantness remained in the church throughout that entire day and also on the following one.

On the day of his translation, namely the Kalends of October, relics were taken from his hair, his chasuble, and his tunic amid divine praises; and his entire body, although dried, was found wrapped in a red cloth.

This venerable Father, both during his bodily life and after his death, just as he bestowed the grace of healing upon the sick, so he very often appeared as an avenger against invaders and presumptuous offenders.

Regarding him, the aforementioned Bishop Gregory was eager to report the following, and it has seemed worthwhile to insert it here in his own words (Gregory of Tours, cited above):

“For there was not far from the basilica”—that is, the basilica of Saint Remigius—“a farm on fertile soil—such places the inhabitants call *olcae*—and it had been given to the saint’s basilica. One of the citizens invaded it, showing contempt for the man who had bestowed it upon the holy place.

“[Col. 0069D] Although he was repeatedly summoned by the bishop and the abbot of the place to restore what he had unjustly seized, he disregarded the words he heard and stubbornly defended what he had taken.

“Finally, not devotion but the lawsuit caused him to hurry to the city and approach the saint’s basilica. There he was again reproved by the abbot for his seizure of the field, but he gave no reasonable reply.

“When his business was concluded, he mounted his horse and prepared to return home. But the injury done to the priest obstructed his efforts. For, wounded by blood [manuscript: ‘satiated’], he collapsed to the ground; the tongue that had spoken of taking the field was bound; the eyes that had coveted it were closed; the hands that had seized it were contracted.

“[Col. 0070A] Then, stammering and scarcely able to form words, he said: ‘Carry me to the saint’s basilica, and throw upon his tomb however much gold I have upon me [variant: with me]; for I sinned by taking away his property.’

“But when the donor of the field saw this man being carried with his gifts, he said: ‘Do not accept, I beg you, holy man of God, his gifts, since you were never accustomed to accept gifts greedily. Do not, I beseech you, be his helper—he who, inflamed by desire for your possessions, proved himself their wicked possessor.’

“The saint did not delay in hearing the voice of his poor man. For although that man had given gifts, the saint of the Lord showed that he had not accepted them: when the invader returned home, he lost his spirit, and the church recovered its property.”

In the time of Chilperic, king of the Franks, Moderamnus, bishop of the church of Rennes, is said to have lived. He was born of noble lineage. Having obtained permission from the aforementioned king to visit the threshold of Saint Peter, he turned aside to the monastery of blessed Remigius, situated in the suburb of the city of Reims. There he was generously received by the brothers of that place, and obtained from Bernehard, guardian of the sacred things, relics from the stole, hair shirt, and shroud of Saint Remigius.

Having gratefully received these, he happily continued the journey he had begun. As he passed through Italy, he spent one night encamped on Mount Bardonum and hung the aforesaid relics on a holly branch. When he rose at dawn and resumed the journey he had begun, he forgot them—and, as is believed, by divine providence—the sacred tokens remained there.

After the bishop had proceeded some distance farther, he remembered the relics he had left behind and immediately sent his cleric, named Vulfadus, to retrieve them. When he reached them, he was unable by any means to touch them, since, whenever he attempted to do so, they were raised aloft by a marvelous sign.

When the bishop heard of this miracle, he turned back and pitched his tent in the same place. Yet that night he was entirely unable to recover the relics he had left behind. Only when morning came, while celebrating Mass in the monastery called Bercetum, built there in honor of Saint Abundius the martyr, did he vow that he would leave part of the gifts mentioned above there. Thus, recovering what had been taken from him, and having reverently fulfilled his vow, he resumed the journey he had begun.

Luitbrandus [Luidbrandus], the energetic king of the Italians, then met him. Having already learned by report of the power of the sacred relics, and moved by love for blessed Remigius, he granted to the aforementioned bishop Moderamnus that same monastery—namely Bercetum—with all its dependencies and its entire abbey, said to contain eight hundred manses [C., eight], and, in the presence of his faithful men, legally invested him in it according to custom and drew up a charter for him.

On his return from the city of Rome, the aforementioned bishop went to the venerable tomb of blessed Remigius. Just as the king who has already been mentioned had handed over this land to him, so he in turn bestowed it upon Saint Remigius. Having thus safely returned to his own episcopal seat, he had a successor ordained for himself. Then, bidding farewell to his sons, he returned to the monastery of Bercetum and lived there until the day of his death, conducting himself moderately and honorably as a servant of God. That place, too, later became renowned and illustrious through several miracles.

At length, in the course of time, King Pippin, father of Charlemagne, attempted to take a villa of the bishopric of Laon called Anisiacus, as though under a rent, just as he had taken certain others. He entered it, and while he slept, Saint Remigius appeared to him and said:

“What are you doing here? Why have you entered this villa, which a man more devoted to me than you gave me, and which I gave to my mistress, the church of the Mother of God?”.

He scourged him quite severely, so that bruises afterward appeared on his body. When blessed Remigius disappeared, Pippin rose and, seized by a violent fever, withdrew from that villa as quickly as possible. He suffered from that fever for a considerable time.

From then onward, no prince of the kingdom remained there until modern times. Nor did one remain at Codiciacum or Juliacum, except King Louis of Germany, who, when he seized the kingdom of his brother Charles, stayed at Juliacum and from there shamefully fled the next day before that same brother, barely escaping.

This blessed Father also bought a large part of a forest in the Vosges woodland, paying the required price. He is said to have established certain little estates there, called Cosla and Gleni. He transferred to them inhabitants from a neighboring villa of the bishopric called Berna, which had formerly been given to him by the Franks, and arranged for them to remain there. He also instituted that they should annually supply pitch to the religious houses of the church of Reims.

He assigned them a payment, which is received today from their successors, and from which they also discharge their own obligation. He determined the boundaries of this purchase of his in a circuit in such a way that the determination itself might be evident to all who saw it, and that the boundaries marked out by him might continue to be named and assigned by his name alone.

In marking these boundaries, he is said to have thrown a stone by his own hand into the hollow of a certain tree. Anyone who wishes to handle it can put his hand into the cavity and roll the stone about, but cannot in any way remove it from that hollow.

Some time later, a certain man, envious of the blessed man’s praises, tried to pull the stone out of the wood by hand. Unable to accomplish this, he attempted to enlarge the hole with an axe. But when he raised the iron to strike the tree, his right hand—which he had rashly lifted—immediately dried up. He himself also lost the light of his eyes. Thus the man who had wished to extinguish the fame of this holy Father unwillingly increased the honor of his praise.

Two brothers, guardians of the royal forest, invaded part of the forest purchased through the efforts of this nourishing patron of ours. They maintained that it belonged to the royal fisc rather than to the jurisdiction of Saint Remigius.

Once, while they were arguing about this with inhabitants subject to the authority of the church of Reims, one of them went to his pigs, which he had sent to pasture in that same forest, and found a wolf among them. He mounted his horse and quickly pursued it, attempting to strike it. But when the frightened horse collided headfirst with a certain tree, the man’s brains poured onto the ground, and he died.

His brother, proceeding to another part of the forest, came to a certain stone and said: “Let it be known to all that this forest belongs to the emperor as far as this stone.” When he struck the stone with the double-edged axe he was carrying in his hand, fragments of the rock sprang from it into his eyes, and he was made blind. Thus each of them received the reward of his presumption and of his lie.

A certain nobleman from the territory of Nevers, having obtained relics of blessed Remigius, built an oratory on his own property in honor of the saint. There the Lord deigned to display several signs in order to reveal the merits of this beloved servant of his.

After Emperor Louis had died, and the Aquitanians had been freed from the yoke of a ruler, they were stirred by their customary restlessness. Each began, as he could, to assert himself, attack others, and rage through the neighboring districts. Every poor person therefore tried to place his possessions in churches for safekeeping.

Trusting in the reputation of the miracles performed there, many eagerly stored their belongings in that same oratory. When robbers heard that the oratory was filled with the possessions of so many people, they attempted to seize them by force.

One of them tried to break the lock of the door. As soon as he struck the door with his foot, his foot remained attached to it, and the presumptuous man fell backward onto the ground. When the others saw this, they fled.

The wretched man himself, compelled by pain, began to express his anguish with the loudest cries and, amid bitterest tears, to make this declaration: if God, through the merits of Saint Remigius, released his foot from that bond, he would never again take anything from that church or any other church, nor, as far as he was able, consent in any way that anything be taken.

He also gave that same church his horse with its saddle, and whatever else he could. After his confession, tears, and vow, his foot was released from the door to which it had adhered. Nevertheless, he remained lame in that foot thereafter. His leg and thigh rotted, and he died.

When the three brothers Lothair, Louis, and Charles divided the kingdom of the Franks among themselves after their father’s death, Charles distributed the villas of the bishopric of Reims, which the priest Fulco held, among his soldiers. Among these he gave the villa of Juliacum to a certain Ricuinus.

His wife, named Berta [c. i, Beuta], was lying in the bedchamber of that villa when Saint Remigius came to her in a dream and said:

“This is not your place for lying down. The person who is to possess this villa and lie in this bedchamber must be of another merit and office. Rise as quickly as possible and leave this place.”

She paid little attention to this, thinking that she had seen an empty vision. Again the saint of the Lord appeared to her and said:

“Why have you not left this place, as I commanded you? Take care that I do not find you here again.”

As before, she regarded this as nothing. For a third time the most blessed bishop came to her and said:

“Have I not already commanded you once and twice to leave this place? But since you have scorned to go, you will leave through the removal of others.”

He struck her with the staff he held in his hand. Immediately she was overcome throughout her body by an enormous swelling. She told her husband and several others what she had seen, and after being cruelly tormented for several days, she died.

Her husband had her body carried to the church of Saint Remigius and buried there. That this nourishing Father received her funeral into his church should not greatly surprise anyone who considers properly the purpose with which saints customarily exercise vengeance upon wrongdoers: namely, that if they repent, they may receive here what they deserve, lest afterward they be consigned to eternal punishments.

Thus we read in the Book of Kings about the prophet who disobeyed the word of the Lord and was struck by a lion and killed; after the punishment had been inflicted, his body remained untouched by the beast (1 Kings 13).

But in taking care to warn the woman mentioned above three times, and in refusing to strike her when he visited her the first or second time—although, as one joined to God, he knew that she would be punished—what other example did he set before us than one of patience? We should not, then, be quick to pronounce judgment upon anyone, since we are separated from God in various ways, even while we prove that we patiently await the one whom we trust to be joined to God and to judge together with him.

In our own time, a certain tenant of a villa belonging to the bishop of Reims, called Plumbea Fontana, lived beside a royal fisc-villa called Rosetum. Because of the oppression of the fiscal officials, he could not peacefully retain either his harvest, his meadow, or any other property. He often asked the royal officials to administer justice to him, but could not obtain it.

At last he found a saving plan. He baked bread and cooked meat, took beer as seemed appropriate in small vessels, placed all these things on a vehicle commonly called a benna, yoked oxen to it, and hurried to the basilica of Saint Remigius, carrying a candle in his hand.

When he arrived, he fed the matricularii with the provisions he had brought, placed the candle at the tomb of the saint, and sought his help against those who oppressed him. He also gathered dust from the floor of the church, tied it up in a cloth, placed it in the aforementioned benna, and spread a linen cloth over it, as is customarily done over the body of a dead person. Then he began to return home.

If any of those he met asked what he was carrying in the cart, he answered that he was carrying Saint Remigius. Everyone marveled at his words and deeds, considering him insane.

When he reached his meadow, he found shepherds from Rosetum grazing animals of various kinds there. But as he invoked Saint Remigius and asked him to bring assistance, the oxen, goats, and she-goats began attacking one another with their horns; pigs fought with pigs; rams collided with rams; and the shepherds struck one another with sticks and fists.

A great tumult arose. The shepherds cried out, and the animals, each making the sound proper to its kind, began fleeing noisily toward Rosetum, as though a multitude of pursuers were driving them with whips.

When the fiscal officials saw this, they were terrified and, fearing that the dangers of death threatened them, at last came to their senses and ceased afflicting the poor man of Saint Remigius.

But because he lived beside the river Serre in a muddy place and suffered great disturbance from snakes in his dwellings, he took the dust that he had brought with him after gathering it from the church floor and scattered it throughout his dwellings. Afterward no snake appeared in those places.

It is also reported that a snake is never ordinarily found in any of the courtyards or cemeteries surrounding the church of blessed Remigius; and if one is brought there in any way, it cannot live there at all.

In the time of Lord Hincmar, a certain Blitgarius obtained from the custodian of the church a mansus belonging to the church in the villa of Tenoilus, paying a price for it. He drove out the servants of Saint Remigius with whips, while they cried out that Saint Remigius would bring them help.

Blitgarius mocked them, saying: “Now it will be clear how Saint Remigius will help you. See how he comes to your assistance.”

Immediately, while he was speaking, he groaned with a tremendous cry, swelled up with a marvelous distension, and, dying, burst open in the middle.

By this vengeance we are warned to fear divine retribution, not to treat the church’s household cruelly, and to take the greatest care to avoid blasphemy against God and his saints.

In former days, a certain Warnerius, count of the district of Worms, invaded the possessions of Saint Remigius mentioned above, situated in the Vosges, and distributed them among his men.

Blessed Remigius then came to Heriger, bishop of Mainz, appearing to him in a dream and ordering him to go to King Conrad and urge him to command his subjects to release the land under their control.

When Heriger awoke, although he was astonished by the vision, he nevertheless failed to inform the king. After several days Saint Remigius appeared to him again and reproached him for not having fulfilled his command, once more warning him not to delay announcing the order to the king.

As before, Heriger considered the vision empty and neglected to carry out the command. For a third time the saint came to him, now with a scourge, rebuked his obstinacy, seized him by the arm, and seemed to drag him from his bed. He beat him severely with the scourge he held, then released him humbled.

No longer daring to disregard the command, Heriger immediately went to the king, requested a private audience, removed his clothing, showed his bruised body, and faithfully explained in order what had been said and done.

It happened that on that same day the envoy of our lord bishop Heriveus, named Tendoinus, had arrived with gifts before the king, sent by his own lord to recover those possessions. He was waiting outside for the hour when he might be presented to the king.

When the king, astonished by what had happened, ordered an inquiry as to whether anyone among his people happened to be from our region, Tendoinus was found to be waiting outside for this very matter. The king was informed, and at his command Tendoinus was brought before him. The matter that had been disclosed was revealed to him.

Giving thanks, he declared that he had been sent for those very possessions, received them when the king restored them, and, with the king’s approval, entrusted them to the aforementioned bishop Heriger to be guarded faithfully for Saint Remigius.

Afterward, while our lord bishop Heriveus lived, he received annually, without opposition, the due rent from those possessions.

Lord Bishop Artaldus had formerly entrusted these same possessions to Duke Conrad, who had assigned them to one of his men, a certain Ragenbaldus. Ragenbaldus oppressed the tenants of those possessions severely.

They often cried out to Saint Remigius because of their oppression, coming to Reims and seeking the protection of their patron. On this matter we recently spoke with King Otto and the aforementioned duke, when we were sent to the same king at Aachen. But we were unable to obtain that Ragenbaldus’s plundering of those possessions should cease.

It happened this year [i.e., this very year] that, on a certain Saturday, when he had gathered those tenants to perform some work and ordered the priest not to ring the evening bells until nearly nightfall but to continue pressing on with the work, he was struck by an unseen striker.

When he asked who had struck him, and everyone denied having seen anything, he was driven mad, lost his senses, and, gravely tormented, breathed his last.

When Duke Conrad learned of this, he was exceedingly frightened. He came to Saint Remigius and restored those possessions to him. The aforementioned bishop Artaldus had assigned them to Abbot Hincmar and the other monks for the provision of food.

At Vulfiniacus Rivu, in the district of Laon, there is an oratory dedicated in honor of Saint Remigius. When King Rudolf was pursuing Count Heribert, who held the bishopric of Reims, entrusted to him by the king, the inhabitants of that villa tried to hide their possessions because of enemy raids.

When the aforementioned king came to besiege the city of Reims and camped at Culmisiacum, his army occupied the neighboring villas. One of the soldiers who had his camp in the aforementioned villa, Vulfiniacus Rivu, seized wine that had been stored in the church out of fear. Setting up what was virtually a tavern in that same church, he began selling it to his companions.

While he was doing this, he was suddenly struck by illness and lost his senses. His mouth was twisted almost as far as his ear, and after being tormented for a long time, he ended his life in suffering.

When the others saw this, they thereafter showed the sacred place the reverence due to it and refrained from such presumption.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the second or repeated translation, or return, of his body to the city

Lord Archbishop Hincmar transferred the venerable relic of this most blessed Father of ours [in the year 852, on the Kalends of October], after enlarging his church and preparing a crypt through work of greater scale and beauty, in the presence and with the assistance of the bishops of this diocese of Reims. He placed the relic intact, together with the cloth in which it had previously been found wrapped, into a silver casket.

The shroud that had been over his head, together with part of the aforesaid cloth, was placed in a little ivory shrine and remains preserved at Reims, in the church of blessed Mary, Mother of God.

When his most sacred body was transferred from the stone sarcophagus into the aforementioned casket, a certain Rado, then a subdeacon of the church of Soissons, who had come there with his bishop Rothad, had been afflicted by toothache for an entire year, so severely that it was feared he would lose his reason from the excess of pain. He placed the afflicted cheek against the spot where the sacred relic had lain, and immediately he was freed from the illness. Thereafter he was granted freedom from pain of this kind.

On that same day, two men afflicted by illness are reported to have received healing in the district of the Ribuarian country [Bruières in the Laonnois], in an oratory dedicated to the memory of this blessed patron of ours.

In the basilica where his body rests, continual wonders do not cease to occur: the sick who come are healed, perjurers are seized by a demon, the possessed are freed, the blind receive sight, and the lame are raised up. Thus it is shown that he lives gloriously with Christ in heaven who, through so many signs of miracles, is proved to live on earth wherever his bodily remains are kept.

On the casket in which his body was then deposited, these verses composed by Lord Hincmar are read, engraved:

> Here Hincmar, servant of the Lord, placed the sacred limbs  
> > Of gentle Remigius, moved by devout love.  
> He was holy before he was created in the world by his mother,  
> > And great, so called by the heavenly voice of God.  
> Having happily completed twenty-two years,  
> > By God’s allotment he assumed the pontifical dignity.  
> For sixty years and twice seven he remained  
> > The honor of this city, its bishop, and the love of the world.  
>
> Giving life back to the dead and light also to the blind,  
> > While living he performed very many wondrous deeds.  
> For, devout in spirit and overflowing in speech, he subdued savage hearts,  
> > Anointing the royal scepters of the Sicambrian people.  
> When he had completed ninety-six years,  
> > The splendid light left our darkness.  
> When the month of January had reached its full Ides,  
> > The veteran soldier received his fitting rewards.  
>
> That same Hincmar, the first priest in this see after thirty [predecessors],  
> > Held his place and rank.  
> The sixteenth beneath this radiant lamp,  
> > He rendered dear offices to Remigius at Reims.  
> For seven years and five months he carried out  
> > The care of a shepherd, performing these things worthy of remembrance.  
>
> In the eight-hundred and fifty-second year  
> > From that year in which God was born human from a virgin;  
> When Charles the Third was arranging the affairs of the kingdom,  
> > And October gave the first day,  
> And the year touched three hundred and eight,  
> > This righteous man of the Lord sought the stars of heaven.  
> There had been three hundred and forty-three years  
> > Since, rejoicing, he washed the Franks in the torrent of life.  
>
> May he be placed in the heavenly seat through his prayers,  
> > The true lover whom he honored on earth. Amen.

Afterward, because the merits of sinners demanded it, it happened that in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 882, under King Carloman, while the aforementioned Lord Archbishop Hincmar was laboring to arrange it, the venerable relic of the body of this most sacred father and lord of ours, Remigius, was transferred—because of the incursions of the pagans—to his villa mentioned above, called Sparnacum. At that time the city of Reims had no wall enclosing it.

Through the protection of the relic, safety was provided, as is shown, for the entire district to which this precious gift was carried, against the persuasion of the barbarians and the attacks of robbers.

After the death of Bishop Hincmar [he died in the aforesaid year 882, as recorded at the end of Book III], this desirable treasure of the sacred members was taken to the monastery of Orbais. There, too, through the intercession of this most blessed patron of ours, every advantage of the air was granted to the inhabitants living all around, together with an unusual fertility of the earth.

After the death of the aforementioned Bishop Hincmar, when Fulco had assumed the episcopal dignity, he resolved in the first year of his episcopate to return the bones of this blessed Father of ours [in the year 883]. When he undertook this, and had already arrived with his fellow bishops and many clergy at the place where the precious relic was kept, the sky being perfectly clear but the drought exceedingly severe, such a great rain suddenly poured down that it seemed to have abundantly watered the entire surface of the earth.

On the following day, while they proceeded to return the sacred gift, everything became bright, everything cheerful, everything pleasant and beautiful to behold. As they advanced prosperously, with people streaming together from every direction, they came to the village of Calmisiacum, in which this exceptional Father is known to have displayed several great miracles while he was still clothed in the flesh.

There they placed the venerable limbs in a church dedicated in his name and refreshed their weary bodies with the night’s rest. After this assistance of repose, when the sun was already illuminating the earth with its radiance, voices rang out everywhere blessing and praising God, because he was restoring to them bodily their own shepherd, patron, and protector—one whom they trusted always to have as an intercessor before the divine mercy and as a constant advocate.

Meanwhile, after the aforementioned bishop had duly celebrated the mysteries of the heavenly sacraments, he climbed the rising slopes of the mountain with praises, surrounded on every side by throngs of people accompanying him.

When he had poured out prayer to the Lord for the people’s offenses and for the appeasement of divine anger, and they had proceeded a little farther, Christ—who had chosen to magnify this most blessed Father of ours on earth, whom he had chosen to glorify with the angels in heaven—resolved to reveal to the assembled multitude how great his merit was before him.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the many healings subsequently bestowed

A blind woman named Doda then approached, leaning on the hand of one who guided her steps. As soon as she drew near, she obtained the restoration of her sight in the presence of everyone.

When the bishop heard this, he celebrated a hymn of praise to God with the people, filled with great joy. They had not yet finished the odes that filled heaven with rejoicing when, behold, a certain man who had been unable to walk for many days came forward, joyfully walking in complete health.

They proceeded a little farther with praises, and a certain woman who had received the use of her hands followed. The accompanying crowds therefore doubled and tripled their thanksgiving.

Those nearby, shaken by the magnitude of the miracles, decided for a while to withdraw from the sublimity of such great holiness. Yet the answering voice of those who praised had not ceased from their mouths when a boy named Grimoldus, deprived of light for a long time, with his mouth also miserably twisted from its proper position and disfigured by an unsightly deformity, was brought forward by his parents. He regained the sight he had lost long before and, through the miraculous aid of this most holy Father, was restored to his natural appearance.

After an interval of about an hour, another boy, whose body had been contracted, was happily raised upright through the intercession of the same patron.

The devout company, wholly unable to echo the songs of David with melodies sufficient for the occasion, was deeply moved in heart. Amid voices of praise, joy drew abundant tears from their faces, and they formed sighs and sobs in place of songs.

The excessive crowding of the people who came running together, wishing to kiss the casket carrying the sacred gift, began to impede the bearers’ steps through its great pressure. The report of the miracles being performed spread ever more widely. Both the healthy and those worn down by various misfortunes hastened eagerly, wishing to behold the great deeds that the omnipotent Lord had decided to multiply in glorifying his saint.

Everyone considered it a great loss—or rather counted it a sin—not merely not to proceed, but even to arrive last.

As the citizens hurried out to meet them and saw the welcome gift being carried, they prostrated themselves and kissed the ground. When they looked up and saw the place where the bearer of the precious jewel of the divine diadem was being carried, they shed many tears amid extraordinary joy, begging that they should no longer be judged worthy to suffer the absence of this same Father, but might deserve to rejoice in his perpetual presence.

Meanwhile, the most blessed Father, favoring the devotion of his children with splendid signs of approval, continued to gladden his people through divine wonders of many kinds.

While the clergy and priests resounded with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, the people too echoed with immense cries of jubilation, so that they might proclaim the wondrous God in his saints with hearts made still more joyful. The multitude of the sick was plainly seen to recover its former health, as many were raised up from various diseases. Indeed, heavenly miracles were disclosed at almost every moment, so that the intervals of time and place could scarcely be considered sufficient to enumerate them.

Then a certain woman named Hosanna wonderfully obtained the restoration of her sight with the swift joy of those who rejoiced. Shortly afterward, a certain lame man received the use of his legs as a blessed gift.

A certain Deodata, when the doors of her ears were opened, obtained hearing. A certain man named Teuto received the desirable gift of illumination. Likewise, a certain woman rejoiced happily in the same benefit.

Ausoldus [j, Ansol.] likewise obtained the sight which he ardently desired, enjoying it, as he believed with a faithful heart, through the most merciful intercession of this Father.

A certain Gerbertus was healed of paralysis, his bodily dissolution being cured. Another man also rejoiced after receiving the benefit of the same gift.

As everyone eagerly strove to run out to meet the relic through the zeal of pious devotion, bringing not only the intention of a benevolent heart but also offerings of temporal goods according to each person’s ability, a poor woman hurried from the city to meet it, carrying in her hand a wax candle that had never been lit.

Wonderful to relate, suddenly, by a divine sign from heaven, the candle in the bearer’s hand was kindled. She carried it along the entire road, confessing God’s miracle, and it did not lose the benefit of the heavenly light until the relic of the miraculous Father had been carried to its appointed station and the bishop had celebrated the solemn Masses there.

Then the woman handed the candle, still burning with its miraculous light, to the custodian of the basilica. Because of his joy at what had happened through heavenly grace, he ordered all the lamps that could be seen burning throughout the church to be extinguished, and then relit them with this light given by God. He decreed that part of the candle, the witness of the miracle granted from heaven, should be preserved.

A woman named Rotgardus [ms., Totgardis], from the district of Castricius, who lacked the ability to walk, rejoiced in the gift of her former health. She had been brought in a wagon and was afterward able to return home on her own feet.

Moreover, a certain woman brought with her a little daughter of about six years, named Vulfid. One day, while the girl was playing with her peers, a passing woman happened to strike her on the head. Injured by the blow, she seemed to have the back of her head bent backward and fixed in that position, unable to incline her head in any other direction. She could take no nourishment except liquids and had spent nearly an entire year under such hardship.

Her mother, loving her tenderly and anxious for the recovery of her health, tried to bring her out to meet the sacred procession. Since she could not approach closely because of the density of the crowd, she arranged to get somewhat ahead of the people.

Then, prostrating herself on the road along which the procession was to pass, she directed devout prayers to the Lord with strong faith, together with her daughter. She had not yet ceased praying when her daughter began to cry out.

The mother rose to comfort her with maternal caresses and, looking at her, saw that her head had returned from its bent position to the proper line of its natural alignment. Filled with immense joy and confident in her child’s recovery, she examined the site of the injury and saw it wet with blood. The nerves, long contracted, had been stretched out as though they were cords.

Having received the blessing of mercy that she had sought, she returned home happily, giving thanks.

With this glorious manifestation and the wonder at the deeds performed, the crowded company, seized by a vow of thanksgiving, strove with all its ardor to complete the journey, hastening along with songs and hymns.

The bishop had gone ahead, but then returned and, accompanied by the choirs of the clergy, took the most precious treasure upon his own shoulders. In this way he carried it with great glory and jubilation to the house of the most blessed Father himself.

When they reached the church, everything that seemed appropriate was properly arranged. As the spiritual sacrifice had already begun, a certain woman from the district of Troyes, afflicted by convulsions of all her limbs, came and fell on the pavement before the altar.
