After being miserably tormented there for a long time, she rose through the mercy of this most merciful consoler, restored to health.

Questioned about the cause of such a terrible calamity, she confessed that she had committed the murder of her own mother.

When the solemn Masses had been completed according to custom, everyone returned home, intending to come back early the next day in order to carry the protection of this treasure into the city.

When morning had come, and everyone was eagerly hastening to the appointed place, a certain woman named Erluidis, living not far from the city, prepared to go out to witness so great a procession, so that she might deserve to receive the gift of the health she desired.

She had already been oppressed by illness for five years. Her right side was almost dead and nearly useless. Nevertheless, she tried as best she could to approach and make her way toward the casket of this sacred gift so that she might see it.

When, through such effort, she had traversed almost half the distance, she could go no farther and collapsed, exhausted by severe exertion. She thought about returning home, but could not accomplish this in any way.

After she had lain there for some time, wavering in this indecision, she finally renewed her attempt and tried to see whether she could come a little closer.

Immediately, through the mercy of divine compassion, strength was added to her sickly efforts. When her powers had been restored together with her health, she hurried forward freely and swiftly, rejoicing with immense delight. She began to approach by an agile stride the place toward which, in her illness, she had been struggling.

She carried in her hand a staff, the support of her infirmity, and completed the journey intended—not because she still needed its assistance, but in order to display it as testimony to the health granted her.

When she reached the place she had desired, she offered devout thanks in praise to her intercessor. Then, laying down the staff that she had carried, the support of her former misfortune, she cheerfully resumed the journey she had made, now no longer needing such aid, and joyfully reported the help of divine consolation that she had obtained.

The bishop arrived, surrounded by a multitude of clergy and nobles. After the sacrifice of salvation had been offered, he dressed in white garments and, with choirs of those singing psalms, led the most welcome treasure to the walls of the city.

As they happily advanced and gratefully proceeded toward the appointed place, almighty God deigned to pour out abundantly the fountain of his kindness and generosity in glorifying this beloved servant of his. The tongue of anyone could scarcely express what was accomplished on this journey in the intervals of almost moment-by-moment hours.

For on that day the Lord performed such a multitude of great miracles that four men and nine women deserved to receive their sight, while two men received the use of their legs.

Amid the wonder of this splendid thanksgiving, they arrived at the city, at the church of the Mother of God, with the greatest rejoicing.

Thus this lamp, shining and burning eternally, was set upon the step of the altar. As the bishop approached to consecrate the life-giving gift of the mystery, who possessed a breast so hard, a heart so stony, that he would not utter groans, beat his breast, and shed tears on seeing such astonishing gifts of divine graces?

Who, indeed, could enumerate the abundance of wonders poured out from heaven on that day? Truly no one could adequately explain in words how many sick were healed, how many wavering were raised upright, and how many were freed there on that very day from various afflictions.

[Cols. 0081B–0081C]

After the sacred rites of the mysteries had been completed, they departed, each hastening to return to his own home. But as they were leaving, an ominous terror began to arise: exceedingly dark clouds gathered, terrifying, and shut the sky in with savage darkness; flashes of lightning appeared, thunderclaps resounded, and hail began to beat upon the ground with no little force. Struck by this terror, many turned back, entreating the mercy of the Most High, that through the intercession of this most blessed father they might deserve to be rescued from the dangers threatening them. In a wondrous manner, the disturbance that had inspired terror began to change: the darkness of the clouds grew thinner [or, according to the manuscript, “to grow brighter”], the lightning ceased, the thunder was subdued, and the whole storm began to calm and disperse. The storm, transformed from something savage into the desired rain, abundantly drenched the surface of the earth, which had been scorched and parched by the excessive heat of the sun, and beneficially refreshed it with welcome moisture. Thus it was clearly perceived that an agitation provoked by indignation for a time had been changed into an aid to salvation. Finally, through the consolation of this most kindly father, the corruption of the dreadful plague appears to have been driven from all our borders. The air became wholesome, the rain fell suitably, and even the fear of the hostile power that had spread throughout the kingdom gradually turned, through the tranquillity of peace, into hope of security.

[Cols. 0081C–0082A]

On this same day, namely the day when the sacred body was brought into the city, when the sun’s fiery wheel was already hastening to plunge into the Ocean, a certain deaf-and-mute man named Nivolus, from a village called Dominica situated on the slope of the mountain of Rheims, and whose hands as well as feet had been weak for nine years, made his way with whatever effort he could muster throughout the entire day. From the light of the rising dawn he crawled for nearly five thousand paces, scarcely reaching the threshold of the building containing the tomb at about the tenth hour.

When he arrived and discovered that the sacred body was not there, and saw that the doors of the church had been carefully closed and secured with bolts, he fell face-down upon the ground. With a kind of presumptuous importunity, he began secretly to strike upon the ears of the saint with his cries, complaining in a very loud voice that he had been wearied by such labor and had not even been permitted to see the little shrine bearing the sacred relics, although he by no means doubted that its lofty power could come to his aid. While he silently turned such thoughts over in his mind, the force of healing gradually began to creep through all his limbs, and at the same time he was amazed to recover all the powers of his senses that he had formerly possessed.

When news of this action reached the ears of many through the reports of those who announced it, everyone rushed out eagerly and joyfully beheld the marvelous works of God. They led the man in triumph to the place of the venerable tomb, rang the bells, and resounded with joyful voices in praises of God. Moved by the fame of this miracle, very many people went to the church, wishing to see the mighty works of God. When they saw the signs of divine power, just as they had heard, they raised their hands gratefully toward heaven and blessed the Lord. This miracle of divine kindness is recognized as having greatly strengthened those who complained that they had been physically abandoned by so great a patron. Yet by this proof of the piety shown toward them, he demonstrated that he was not spiritually absent from them.

[Cols. 0082A–0082D]

In the church of the blessed Mother of God, where the venerable relic of this father was being kept, several sick people were meanwhile cured of various ailments. A certain Natalis of Burdenacum, a woman named Teutberga, and another woman named Gonthildis were granted the recovery of their sight through the patronage of this father. Another woman also recovered, in the same church, the sight she had lost in one eye.

Moreover, a certain girl surnamed Flotgildis, from a village called Caucella situated beside the stream of the Libra, about four years old, slipped and fell, injuring both her knees. She became so lame that she was entirely unable either to take a step or to stand upon her feet. Her parents, although poor, were nevertheless concerned for her health and arranged for her to be carried to various churches of the saints. But after she had been afflicted by the severity of this illness for nearly twelve years and could find no remedy for her suffering, she learned from reports about the sacred body and the miracles of its works. With whatever strength she could muster, she began to crawl toward it. She refused to be placed in a cart, but insisted on making the journey by being dragged along as best she could.

When she reached the church where she had heard that the precious gift of salvation was present, she poured out prayers and begged the Lord’s mercy for her deliverance. She is also said to have moistened the pavement with her own tears. After she had done this for three days, while she again persisted in prayer, divine grace came upon her. Scarcely able to bear the force of the healing, she began to cry out loudly and utter bitter lamentations. Then, when the knots of her tendons had been loosened and every contraction of her knees had been relaxed, she lay exhausted for nearly an hour as though dead.

But he who had granted the aid of release also added strength and vigor. Soon, as though awakening from a deep sleep, she sensed that the heavenly benefit had come upon her. She sought the little shrine of the holy relic, and had no doubt that the healing had come to her through its power. Thereafter she gave thanks there, deciding to remain in that place and persisting in frequent prayers. She celebrated the vigils owed to her healer and offered daily offerings of the salutary sacrifice.

[Cols. 0082D–0083B]

At Rheims, in the aforesaid church of the Mother of God, that most sacred body of our blessed patron Remigius remained while the aforementioned bishop, Lord Fulco, exercised the episcopal office—that is, until the episcopate of the venerable Archbishop Heriveus. When the persecution of the Northmen had ceased and peace had been recovered through God’s mercy alone, Heriveus decided to return the same heavenly gift to the city walls, to the saint’s own place of burial.

As he hastened to carry this out after summoning certain nobles of the kingdom, the Lord did not delay in adding to the saint’s glorification by recalling his bones to their proper resting place. For it happened that, while a great throng of the assembling people surrounded them, after they had gone out from the city, a certain lame man named Abraham, whose knees and hamstrings were contracted through the drying up of his tendons, was dragging himself along the ground by clinging to little stools, as best he could. When, approaching the city, he had begun to direct his journey toward the holy basilica, he was touched by divine power. The stiffness of his joints was loosened, and he began to be extended toward the remedies of healing. We saw him remain healthy for many years afterward, walking upright and rejoicing in the prosperity granted to him.

At the place where this gift of healing occurred, a column marked with a cross was later erected; it preserves the memorial of this glorification. Moreover, both before and afterward, the church of his tomb was frequently adorned with many illustrious miracles, which have by no means been comprehended in writing, for they are of many kinds.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the disciples of the same blessed Remigius

[Cols. 0083B–0084C]

In the time of this most blessed father of ours there were in this city illustrious men, acceptable to God for their virtues, both from the clergy and from the lay order, since they served such a venerable and most holy father. The most distinguished among them appears to have been his nephew Agricola, a venerable presbyter, who, as he himself testifies, had pleased him by his service from childhood and had lived within his household. Remigius appointed him heir, together with the Church of Rheims and his nephew Lupus, the blessed bishop, in all his property except what he had specially given or ordered to be given to each of them.

He also assigned and handed over to him certain slaves together with vineyards, expressly charging him to ensure that an offering be made at his sacred altars on feast days and every Sunday, and that annual banquets be provided for the presbyters and deacons of Rheims.

There was another nephew of his named Etius, to whom he gave that portion of Cesurnicum which had fallen to him by lot in the division, together with all the rights he had held and possessed there. He also designated and transferred to his ownership the boy Ambrosius, together with certain households.

There was also Agathimerus, likewise his nephew. To him Remigius assigned certain households and gave the vineyard that the same most blessed father had planted at Vindonissa and established through his own labor, on the condition that an offering be made at the sacred altars for his commemoration on all feast days and Sundays, and that annual banquets be prepared for the presbyters and deacons of Laon.

Declaring that he had made use of the familiar services of his archdeacon Ursus, he gave him a certain fine chasuble and another fuller one, two delicate cloaks, the carpet that he had on his bed, and the best tunic he would leave behind at the time of his death.

There were also other reputable men from the clergy at Rheims at that time, both presbyters and deacons. He showed them worthy of his gift, bestowed presents upon them, and assigned them a vineyard to possess jointly with the vinedresser, adding certain other slaves to them as well.

There was also Hilaria the deaconess. The same most holy father blessed her and called her his daughter. He assigned her a female servant, gave her a vineyard-measure adjoining his own vineyard, and transferred to her his portion of Talpusciacum in return for the services that, as he testifies, she continually rendered him.

There was also Remigia, to whom he gave three spoons bearing the name of the most blessed father himself, together with certain other small gifts.

Several distinguished laymen also stood out. Pappolus, Eulodius, Eusebius, Rusticolus, Eutropius, and Dauveus took part in the private affairs of the blessed man and, subscribing to his testament, added their own names.

The distinguished man Attolus also shone forth. As is read in his epitaph, out of love and devotion to Saint Remigius he built twelve hospices from his own resources. He was buried with his son and daughter behind the altar in the church of the blessed martyr Julian, and the following inscription, placed upon the pinnacle of the church, declares the title of his burial:

> Let no one here remain unaware of what the earth holds,  
> lest anyone wishing to learn should go away disappointed.  
> For beneath it stand three stone monuments,  
> in which the bodies of the blessed have been laid.  
> Here lies father Attolus, buried with son and daughter;  
> they now await the coming day of the Lord.  
> His son, certainly, is remembered as Elanus;  
> his daughter is called Eufrasia.  
> They pleased God by words and deeds, the Most High,  
> and now together their limbs occupy the tomb.  
> He built twice six hospices from his own resources,  
> rightly sustaining the poor in wealth.  
> Thus he carried his own estate up to heaven,  
> where he received what he had given in compassion.  
> He did all this out of love and devotion to the holy Remigius,  
> for whose sake he himself holds the radiant heaven.

I also think this must be the church about which Gregory of Tours reports (*Book II of the Miracles*, concerning the Passion and Miracles of Saint Julian, chapter 32): a certain man in the suburb of the city of Rheims, in the province of Belgica Secunda, zealously built a basilica in honor of this blessed martyr. After completing the building, he earnestly and devoutly sought out and obtained the martyr’s relics. Then, returning by road while singing psalms, as he entered the countryside of Rheims with them, a certain man was freed from demonic possession when the relics of this holy martyr were brought near him.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On Saint Theoderic

[Cols. 0084D–0089D]

In the time of the most blessed Remigius there also lived the blessed man Theoderic, the pious disciple of that gracious master. He was not born of exalted blood, although the master had resolved to ennoble him gloriously among the generation of the righteous. Born in the region of Rheims, in a village said to be called Alamannorum Corte, he was the offspring of a robber father, produced in horror like a rose among thorns.

To demonstrate the purity of his chastity, it is said that the well in which the cloths of his infancy were washed was not polluted by the casting in of filth or by the contamination of any uncleanness, although its mouth has, in the customary way, remained open from that time.

The blessed Theoderic was commendably raised until the age of puberty. Then, according to the customary course of human development and compelled by the insistence of his parents, he began to have a bride in name only, as one who did not intend to have her as a wife. Secretly inflamed by love of heavenly things, he strove to become a hidden worshiper of God.

For this angelic way of life he soon had a physician by whom he could be healed, a patron by whom he could be assisted, and a teacher by whom he could be instructed: namely, the most blessed father Remigius, his spiritual leader. Enlightened by the example of this most devoted teacher and burning with the desire for virtue, he grew eagerly toward perfection.

Love of the marriage bond grew bitter, while love of chastity grew sweet; one desire was restrained by another desire, and the heat of the flesh was overcome by the heat of the spirit. The lover of purity renounced the world and entered into a covenant with God. War was declared against the enemy on behalf of continence, and a place was sought for single combat.

The blessed Theoderic addressed his bride, urged her toward the eternal love of the heavenly Bridegroom, and promised her perpetual honor in exchange for virginity. But the bride, wasting away under the love of carnal desire, rejected the bridegroom’s saving counsels and answered with a bitter heart, seeing herself despised.

When the servant of God perceived that his exhortation had no place in the bride’s heart, he left the dissenting woman and went directly to the city of Rheims. There he sought an abbess devoted to the celibate life, named Susanna.

The sober man approached the sober woman, the chaste man the chaste woman, the virgin the virgin. She presided over the community of girls under the protection of the blessed Remigius: a woman of manly courage, a heroine of profound counsel, and a counsellor of lofty intelligence.

The holy Theoderic withdrew into the exceedingly gentle embrace of this most pious mother, prostrated himself upon the ground before the feet of his spiritual mother, and revealed to her alone the secrets of his heart known only to God. Tears burst forth, he was shaken by groaning and convulsed with sobs, and he earnestly begged that a salutary counsel, together with the support of prayers, be offered to him.

The tenderest compassion of the kindly mother was stirred by the devout young man’s sorrowful contrition. She sympathized with him as he wept, consoled him as he mourned, gladdened him in his sorrow, and entreated the Lord in his mercy to grant him the fulfillment of his desire.

Accordingly, the most devoted common father of both was consulted by both of them together on this matter: Saint Remigius, under whose instruction the blessed Theoderic had already made great progress.

A message was finally sent to the bride. The father showed her that an eternal reward was reserved for those who persevered in virginity, and he made clear that virginity is pleasing to and a friend of angelic purity. At last the bride consented to the most prudent father’s words—indeed, she embraced them—words sweetened by the sweetness of the heavenly life. She promised that, if she were found worthy, she would cling to Christ and remain undefiled, preserving her chastity.

Then the bridegroom, rejoicing in the beauty of chastity, embraced the bride whom he saw rescued from the will of the seducer and from the pleasure of the flesh, and already devoted to her Creator under the honor of integrity.

The virgin Susanna and the virgin Theoderic were sent to seek a place in which they might live. There is a little forest situated on a mountain, three miles from the city. The venerable father Remigius, who was always ardently devoted to divine things, decided that a monastery should be built there. Under the pious direction of a leader whose progress he recognized through his example of virtue, he wished to gather there a company of brothers who would serve as soldiers of Christ.

When they had climbed to the summit of the wooded mountain and were considering the site of the monastery, looking around with their eyes, suddenly a winged messenger was sent down from the lofty heavens. Through it, a place on earth was revealed to the blessed Theoderic, who was destined to ascend to heaven.

For a mystical bird, an eagle, circling as it ranged about and flying around as it circled, cut through the air and marked out, as far as it could, a place broad enough for the monastery. To show more clearly what the Lord willed, it hovered for nearly an hour over the place where the church was to be built. And lest unbelievers think that this had happened by chance, the same eagle was seen, to the amazement of many, flying around the monastery on the very day of the Nativity of the Lord for four successive years.

But what works of virtue and what remarkable miracles the soldier of Christ Theoderic performed there cannot be recounted individually by human speech.

After some time had passed, when he assumed the honor and burden of the priesthood, wishing to fulfill the office of a priest, he began to preach the precepts of salvation to everyone. In particular, the loving concern of his dearest father stirred the heart of his devoted offspring. “A wise son makes his father glad” (Proverbs 10:1), and he regenerates in heaven the one who begot him on earth. From a man of slippery ways he made a monk; from a robber, a most generous giver; from a servant of the devil, a freedman of Christ.

By now holy opinion of him was spreading among the peoples, person by person. And lest he remain hidden like a lamp covered under a bushel, but shine for everyone in the house of God, just as he was exalted in merits, so he began to shine forth conspicuously through brilliant miracles.

For his most blessed reputation had reached the palace of the king of the Franks. Their king at that time was Theoderic, son of Clovis. One of his eyes had been afflicted by a sudden and exceedingly painful disease, so that no physician could restore it to its former health by medicines of any kind. The tearful illness of one eye had provoked the tears of many among the people.

Various outcomes of the disaster troubled the king’s mind. On one side fear urged him on—the fear of losing his sight; on the other, shame at the deformity that threatened him. For if the king appeared with one eye, it would be a great disgrace among the people: either, while reigning, he would bear the reproach of an ugly disfigurement, or perhaps, together with the loss of his sight, he would also lose his kingdom.

One course of action therefore remained for the king: where human medicine failed, divine help was to be sought. He sent for the venerable Theoderic, and when the holy man came, he disclosed to him the disease of his wretched eye. He revealed the suffering he endured and forestalled the dangers he feared by means of prayers.

But the man of God, knowing that the power of the deed belonged to divine activity and not to human weakness, prostrated his body upon the ground, raised his spirit above the heavens, and committed himself wholly to prayer. At last, when he had finished praying, he rose, lifted his face toward the stars, invoked the name of the holy Trinity, poured a little consecrated oil onto the tip of his thumb, and, making the sign of the saving cross upon the diseased eye, restored its sight in an instant together with its health.

The joyful king magnified the King of kings; the people were filled with celebrated rejoicing; the entire senate exulted with immense joy. Theoderic, the servant of God, was praised, and God, wondrous in his saints, was glorified by all.

The king summoned the leading men of the people. They congratulated him on the greatness of the miracle: the king had so quickly experienced the power of the spiritual remedy, and no trace of a scar, darkness, or even a blemish of glaucoma remained in the restored eye.

With what honors the king would have exalted Christ’s servant, if he had wished, and with what gifts or dignities he would have rewarded him, had the man himself, who despised dignities, permitted it! For what is dearer in the body than the eye?

But he rejected human praise and worldly reward, and preferred to give freely what he had freely received. As a man of great humility, concerned lest he should bear the same name as the king, he asked that henceforth he not be called Theoderic but Theodorius.

Then the king, amazed at the humility of such pure simplicity, kissed the venerable hands, devoutly requested the priest’s blessing, and ordered that he be escorted honorably back to his monastery. How many crowds of weak and afflicted people you would then have seen flocking to him, all receiving without delay the healings they sought!

This magnificent herald of the Lord is also said to have restored the king’s daughter to life by the breath of life. The king had sent to Saint Remigius on behalf of the sick girl, asking him to come to him and lay his hand upon his ailing daughter together with his prayers.

But the pious bishop, as is said, was held back by some bodily illness. He therefore entrusted the requested task, as a father to his son, to the blessed Theoderic, whom he had piously and chastely raised and instructed in spiritual teachings, and whom he saw filled with the grace of healings.

Wishing diligently to fulfill his master’s command, Theoderic hurried along the road to the king’s palace, confident that divine mercy would be present to him. There he received from messengers the news that the girl had died, and they advised him not to tire himself but to return to his own cell.

He nevertheless did not cease obeying his teacher’s command. He reached the palace and found the parents weighed down with grief and the members of the court overcome with mourning. The holy man of God himself was moved by their tears. He ordered most of them to withdraw and sat down with a few people beside the bier.

He raised his heart and eyes, together with his hands, toward heaven. His face covered with tears, he poured forth in the chamber devout prayers of the mind to God, full of compunction. When he perceived in spirit that he had been heard, he approached the lifeless body and anointed the passages of the senses with holy oil by touching them with his thumb.

In a wondrous manner, the dead limbs were restored to their living functions. The eyes received light; when he touched the chest, a voice burst forth; and the girl declared that she had been restored to health through the prayers of the blessed Theoderic.

Her parents ran up in amazement and joy at the miracle. The entire palace exulted, and the household rejoiced in celebration. The saint was venerated by both the king and the nobles, and glorified by all the members of the court. The common people proclaimed his praises.

The king therefore, wishing to exalt by his generosity not only his disciple, the holy Theoderic, but also Blessed Remigius, bestowed upon the reverend father Remigius the estate called Venderam [Vendier], situated on the river Marne; and by an authoritative decree he gave Gaugiacum, in the region of Rheims, to Saint Theoderic.

After some time, while Charles, son of the Emperor Louis, was governing the scepter of the Frankish kingdom, one of the courtiers named Angilrannus, unaware of this transfer, asked the king to give Venderam to him.

When the king had agreed, Lord Hincmar, the bishop who occupied the see of the Church of Rheims, heard of it. He sent Charles a royal charter found in the archive of this church, containing the record of the grant, and endeavored to warn him not to seize the Church’s property contrary to canon law.

In that charter it is clearly read that King Theoderic, after obtaining through Saint Theoderic’s prayers the resurrection of his daughter, not only favored the servant of God by granting him the aforementioned estate, but also offered the estate of Venderam as a benefaction to his master, the outstanding Remigius, to whom the Lord had granted such grace that he possessed such a disciple—one who, by the gift of the Holy Spirit, could raise the dead just as his master could.

When Charles recognized from the very records of the charters that these things had indeed taken place, he abandoned his attempt to seize the estate and permitted the Church to use its property freely.

It is reported that, at the suggestion of this blessed man, Saint Remigius transformed a group of prostitutes, whom he is said to have kept outside the city in brothels until that time, by demolishing the brothels, into a community of forty widows. He established the expenses necessary for their daily sustenance and decreed that the number of widows should remain permanently—as it still does.

For when Saint Remigius was visiting the monastery of Saint Theoderic and passing beside the brothels while singing psalms together with this beloved disciple, the voice of Saint Theoderic stuck in his throat. The same thing happened again, as is related, when they were returning, in the same place and at the same verse.

The most holy father was astonished and asked why his diligent disciple had stumbled, contrary to his custom, in the praises of God. He learned that the blessed man grieved over the loss of the souls who were being ruined, and that in the neighborhood of so holy a father such great profits of foul shame were accruing to the devil.

Thus the most pious father was persuaded, at the suggestion of his chaste disciple, to overturn the devil’s hiding places and lead the souls who had been deceived—and those who deceived others—into the chastity of Christ.

Many other works of virtue are also known to have been performed by this faithful servant of God. Restoring sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, and walking to the lame; loosening dry and contracted hands; freeing those possessed by demons; he destroyed a thousand deceits by which Satan sought to inflict harm, opposing them with divine medicine.

And truly happy is the shepherd of Christ’s flock to whom it was granted to bring salvation both to bodies and to souls!

He persevered in the service of God until the end, and demonstrated by the clearest examples what he had taught with his mouth. After many works of virtue and distinguished miracles, having brought the good contest to victory and completed his course happily, with holy spirits coming to meet him and angels joyfully receiving him, he departed to Christ in glory on the day of the Kalends of July.

When the aforementioned King Theoderic heard of his most precious death, he hurried to the monastery with a great multitude. Remembering the benefit he had received, and not forgetting the service he owed, he strove to carry the body of the most blessed abbot to the tomb upon his own shoulders.

Nor is it surprising that the king of human beings placed his limbs in the tomb, since the King of angels received his soul with joy in heaven.

At his venerable tomb divine power continues, to this very day, graciously to work salvation in many forms.

Through the negligence or infrequency of writers, many miracles are known to have been left unrecorded in silence. Nevertheless, we have decided to insert one that we recently learned had occurred.

One Saturday, as the eve of the Lord’s Day was drawing near, a poor woman named Gillaidis [manuscript: Gistaidis], from the household of Saint Dionysius at the estate of Upper Corte, was turning a mill by hand. The handle of the mill clung to her right hand so firmly that no one could pull it away.

At last she was forced to cut the mill handle away from both sides of her hand, unwilling to carry with her the evidence of that wretched mishap. Concerned for her salvation, and since the limbs of Blessed Dionysius were then being kept at Rheims because of the attacks of the pagans, she hastened swiftly to approach the relics of that holy martyr, her lord.

When she arrived, she fell upon the ground with great fear and reverence and begged for deliverance from the misery of such disgrace. After she had spent both that day and the night there, without abandoning hope of receiving a remedy, a man appeared to her in a dream, dressed in clerical clothing and wearing a white garment. His face was pleasant, his hair very white, and his expression somewhat thin. He said to her:

> Rise from here and go to Saint Theoderic, for the second day from now, Monday, is the feast that is to be celebrated in his honor. See that you do not appear empty-handed in his house. Take wax, according to what your means presently allow, and go in this way to his church; through his intercession you will obtain what you are asking.

She immediately awoke, astonished at the vision. She prayed that what she had seen might be confirmed according to the will of God, and joyfully hastened to carry out the command.

She therefore came to the saint’s church on the day of the venerable solemnity, namely the feast of the blessed Theoderic. Three weeks had passed since the misfortune had happened to her.

Then she prostrated herself with tears before his tomb and poured forth prayers for her healing. Remaining there in prayer throughout the night, she humbly and confidently [manuscript: faithfully] sought pardon for her sins.

While she was still lying before the tomb of the blessed confessor of Christ, by the command of divine grace and through the intercession of the saint, the woman’s hand gradually began to separate from the wood and to open without any painful injury. Then the entire hand opened out, and the wood slipped onto the pavement more quickly than words can say, as though it had never appeared to be attached.

Many who were present, seeing this miracle of heavenly mercy, glorified God, wondrous in his saints.

## CHAPTER XXV. On Saint Theodulf

[Cols. 0089D–0091C]

The third rector of the same monastery after the blessed Theoderic was Saint Theodulf. He is said to have shone through his conspicuous kinship with courtiers and through the dignity of venerable monks and priests. Yet he considered the pomp of nobility worthless, chose to serve God in holiness, abandoned the crooked byways, and sought the road of the straight path, following those footsteps by which, passing through the swollen waves of the world, he might hasten toward heavenly things.

After entering the monastery of Blessed Theoderic, he consigned the glory of this age to oblivion, despised the dignity of his birth through humility, and subjected himself to the service of the lowest condition. He dug the soil with a mattock and cut the back of the earth with the plowshare, striving to fulfill in deeds the words of the psalmist:

> “For you shall eat the labors of your hands;  
> blessed are you, and it shall be well with you”  
> (Psalm 127:2).

He devoted himself to this daily work for twenty-two years. With two young oxen assigned to him for the task, he endured with unconquered strength the hard and varied labors imposed by the seasons.

What is especially memorable is that those same oxen did not fail either through age or weariness. What other farmers could scarcely accomplish with four, six, or eight oxen, he completed tirelessly with two. Whenever he paused briefly from the plow, he hastened again to apply himself to the mattock.

It is also exceedingly astonishing that, although he was devoted to such harsh service and did not flag, he is said, on returning from the fields, often to spend one entire night—and frequently two—keeping vigil in hymns and psalms of praise.

One day, when he had stopped working the land at the time for interrupting his labor and was returning home, he happened to encounter some task requiring the repair of a plow as he was going back to the monastery. He stuck the shaft of his goad into the ground and, forgetting it—or rather, as divine providence arranged it—reached the house toward which he was heading.

Wondrous to relate, during the night the thorny shaft took root in the earth. In the morning, when the blessed man returned to his accustomed work and wished to take it up again, he found it swelling with leaves.

It grew for a very long time, accumulating strength and rising aloft, and became an object of wonder to many. At last, while someone was traveling along the road who was destined to be punished, he cut it down; and when the light of his eyes was taken from him together with the cutting, he fell into continual darkness.

After this, the faithful hung Theodulf’s plow in the church of the village of Colubrosa. It remained there until, when the enemy so impelled it, a devouring flame burned down the basilica.

Whenever anyone suffering from toothache cut off a small piece of it and caused a little blood to flow from the place of pain, he deserved immediately to receive the desired remedy of healing through the merits of the blessed Theodulf.

These benefits are known not only by report but also by the testimony of many who saw them, and they were proclaimed with complete certainty after health had been restored.

When the abbot who had presided over Blessed Theodulf—the third, as stated above—had died, this venerable man was appointed abbot in the place of blessed memory, Lord Theoderic, with the bishop’s approval and at the request of the community of monks.

After attaining the honor of leadership, he applied almost no rest to his limbs, as though he were an inexperienced novice newly assigned to labor. Just as he had proved tireless in the work of his hands, so by disciplining himself, sparing himself nothing, he devoted himself entirely and doubly to divine ministries.

For he built a basilica in honor of Saint Hilary, in order to double the course of his labor. When the signal was given, he assembled with the brothers and performed the praises of the hymns. But, as though he had accomplished nothing before, he again offered the prescribed prayers in the church, so that a double crown of merit might be his. Although he wished to obtain his reward by doing such things in secret, the divinity did not allow the works of its worshipper to remain unseen.

One day it happened that a pig, walking near the well where the animals of that place were watered, fell into it. The monks gathered around on every side, but no one could rescue the animal from the depths, especially since the well is said to have been one hundred feet deep.

The man of God arrived. When he learned what had happened, he began to worry that the water might be polluted if the animal died there. Raising his eyes toward heaven and fixing his mind upon the Lord in prayer, he devoutly sought Christ’s aid. Suddenly, with water overflowing the mouth of the well, the animal arrived unharmed at his feet.

Everyone who saw this was filled with intense amazement and gave thanks to God, who had bestowed such a great grace of his kindness upon his faithful servant.

On another day, while the same man of God was traveling from the monastery toward a certain place, he found a farmer plowing the public road along which he was accustomed to pass.

He said to him: “It is not good, O man, for a road to be cut by a plow, since travelers ought to tread it with an unhindered foot.”

When the holy man was returning along the same road, he again encountered the farmer plowing the road as he had begun to do.

“Did I not tell you,” he said, “that you must not plow this road?”

Then, approaching him, he touched the peasant’s head with his holy hand and said: “By this head, man, I charge you never again to plow this road.”

When he withdrew his hand, the entire part of the man’s head that the man of God had touched [manuscript: “that one”] appeared white, shining like wool.

There is no doubt that the man of God did not intend the hair to fall out, but rather that the signs of this deed might be preserved through successive generations, so that no one would dare to do something similar to what the holy man of God Theodulf had commanded not to be done.

For as long as the farmer’s line continued, the sign that the father had received from the holy man was borne by his descendants in the same manner.

A certain man finally came to the man of God with an eye [Col. 0091D] struck by a twig and deprived of sight. He was given no relief from his suffering, nor was there any hope of recovering his vision. Blessed Theodulf led him to the sacred altars and instructed him to kiss them. The man touched the holy coverings with his mouth, while the servant of Christ devoted himself to prayer. The saint rose from the pavement, and no trace of pain remained in the young man’s eye. As was fitting, he gave thanks to the man of God for the cure and returned home rejoicing, having received the remedy he had sought.

A certain envoy of the Austrasians, named Offo (that is, of the upper Franks), came from the eastern regions while he was being sent to the ruler of that kingdom at the time. For the sake of prayer, he appears to have entered the monastery of the man of God [Col. 0092A]. Saint Theodulf, however, his body exhausted by labors and vigils, was perhaps resting tired in bed. The envoy, moved by the bitterness of his spirit because the abbot of the place had not come out to meet him, agitated by resentment, gave utterance to words that were unbecoming. As he departed indignantly, so that anger might be added to anger, his very powerful horse was reported by a boy to be dead. Grinding his teeth inwardly and heaping fury upon fury, he thus suffered a double anguish in his mind: resentment, namely, and loss.

When the holy man learned of this through a messenger after his sleep, he did not delay to go out and console the man. Following his customary manner, he tried by gentle speech to calm his savage temper. He invited him to prayer, urged him to place his hope in God, and warned him not to be greatly troubled by what had happened [Col. 0092B]. As they proceeded to the basilica of Christ’s confessor Hilary, when they came to the place where the sign of the cross is worshiped, after offering the customary prayer on the road, he turned his face gently toward the aforementioned envoy and said:

“Do not be afraid, because you will find your horse sound before the monastery gates. If you had departed as enraged as you began, you would have left us the corpse of a dead horse.”

The envoy paid no attention to this, especially since he had seen the horse dead and its whole body swollen. But his servant ran up and affirmed that matters were exactly as Christ’s priest Theodulf had indicated. Thus, when the miracle of divine power had been demonstrated, he laid aside his mental fury and gave thanks to the Lord, declaring that he had learned by the true evidence of his own eyes what he had earlier heard from the report of certain people about the servant of the Lord [Col. 0092C].

The holy man of God said: “Do not attribute this to my merits, since I am a sinful man. Rather, give thanks to God and do not cease to venerate the merits of the saints, who can bestow assistance upon you in all things.”

After instructing the man with such admonitions, he gave him his blessing and allowed him to depart. From this it is plainly evident that, together with the power of miracles, he also possessed the spirit of prophecy, since he foretold that the animal he had left dead was alive.

Nor are we at all sufficient to enumerate all the distinguished signs of his virtues. How many people, held by various illnesses, received complete health through his intercession, only he knows who granted that these things should occur. Among the other blessings that Christ [Col. 0092D] granted to this servant of his, this is proclaimed as memorable and remarkable: although he lived to the age of ninety, distinguished by his white hair, pleasant in appearance, temperate in conduct, full of charity, generous in almsgiving, and glorious in his contempt for the world, he was afflicted neither by the pain of fevers, nor by bodily weariness, nor by any accident of changing circumstances; he was disturbed by no mental distress and never ceased from prayer or from the practice of God’s works for as long as his blessed soul gave life to his body.

When divine mercy wished to reward the faithful servant, weakened by old age, for his labors with the refreshment of rest and the reward of his merit, it allowed him to burn somewhat with the heat of fever. One day he entered the basilica while the solemn rites of Matins were being celebrated. Applying himself fervently to prayer, he strove to commend to God the soul that he already knew would soon be released from its bodily prison [Col. 0093A]. When the darkness of night had been driven away and the dawn was shining red, he returned to his cell accompanied by certain monks. He was cheerful because of the visitation granted to him by the saints and because of the revelation by which he rejoiced that the hour of his departure had been disclosed to him.

When he recognized that he had reached that hour, he made peace with the brothers, raised his eyes and hands toward heaven, and joyfully returned to his Creator the holy soul rescued from the shipwrecks of the world. Christ received it amid the rejoicing of the heavenly court.

This monastery of the blessed fathers now has clerics in place of monks. One of them [Col. 0093B], recently, Otbertus by name, before Gaul was handed over to be torn apart by the swords of the Hungarians, was brought to his final extremity. While he endured the struggles of demons contending over him and trying to carry him off to destruction, he finally saw himself rescued through the merits of his gracious patron, the lord Theoderic. He also saw the demons, through the invocation of the name of Christ and of his saints, withdraw from him with great noise and indignation.

He also saw a certain brother named Bertricus, who had died not long before, repeatedly visiting him and consoling him, while warning him not to wish to remain any longer here in the world, but rather to rejoice in going to him as quickly as possible, so that he might see what he had never been able even to imagine. For if he delayed longer in the world, he would never have seen as great an evil as he was soon going to see [Col. 0093C].

The truth of his words was confirmed by what followed. For this man, touched by a slight bodily pain, hurried to the church and commended his departure to the Lord in prayer. He summoned the brothers and made them repeat the Mass, which they had celebrated somewhat more hastily than was proper. He told them what he had seen and asked them, for the sake of charity, to take food and drink in his presence. He urged them to devote themselves more earnestly to God’s service and to sing the psalmody with devotion. Then, as though already secure and cheerful, he departed.

After his death, the people of the Hungarians entered Gaul and devastated almost everything with slaughter, fires, and plunder [Col. 0094A]. They burned the monastery itself and overthrew nearly all the neighboring villages with their surrounding ruins. We now see plainly how true were the things that he had heard by revelation.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Concerning the spring that recently arose in the monastery of these saints

In a small wood adjoining this monastery, a spring recently arose. A certain man suffering from fever happened to come to it and saw an old man in clerical dress standing above the spring, leaning over it and holding a golden staff in his hand. When the old man seemed to rise from the spring with the sound of the approaching man’s movement, the latter was so shaken with fear that he fell stunned to the ground and was completely unable to see [Col. 0094B].

But after recovering himself a little, he rose and saw the great brightness by which the old man had departed toward the monastery. Thus cured of his illness, he went away rejoicing. At that time several blind people were given sight in this place, the lame were made to stand, the mute spoke, and the deaf recovered their hearing.

Recently, after Hugh had been ordained bishop of Reims, a certain paralytic woman named Magenildis, who lay in the city at the doors of the church of Saint Mary, was warned by a vision and asked to be carried there. As soon as she had been drenched with the water of this spring, she recovered her health.

Another woman, Adelwidis by name, whose arms were withered, departed in good health as soon as she had been washed with the same water. A certain blind man from the castle of Mosomus (Mousom), coming there at that time, had scarcely entered the church of Saint Theoderic when he was judged worthy to receive his sight [Col. 0094C].

A certain poor woman from the same place washed her eyes in this spring and recovered the sight that she had lost for more than sixteen years. A certain Fulbertus, whose arm was withered and useless to him, poured this water over himself and recovered both his health and the use of his arm. At that time also a certain blind man named Amalricus received his sight there as soon as he had washed himself in this spring. Many other miracles are now attested to have shone forth there, and various remedies have been granted for various illnesses.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0093]

## CHAPTER I. Concerning the successors of blessed Remigius

[Col. 0093D]

Romanus is traditionally said to have succeeded blessed Remigius; Flavius succeeded Romanus; after them came Mapinius, to whom certain estates are found to have been transferred from royal authority, to be possessed thereafter by the Church of Reims. During his time, Queen Suavegotta is also found to have assigned to the Church of Reims, by the document of her will, a third part of the estate of Virisiacus [Verzy].

That same bishop granted that portion of the estate to Teudechildis, the aforementioned queen’s daughter, by a precarious grant of usufruct, with the rights of the Church preserved. This was provided expressly so that after her death it should be restored to the dominion of the Church of Reims without any prejudice, in the condition in which she had improved it. This Queen Teudechildis later transferred certain estates to the Church of Reims by the authority of her will, during the time of the lord Egidius [Col. 0094D].

## CHAPTER II. Concerning Bishop Egidius

Bishop Egidius is recorded as having followed Mapinius in the episcopate [Col. 0095A]. He is also found to have enlarged the bishopric, purchasing fields and a number of slaves. Some documents of these purchases still survive, such as the one recording that he bought two fields from Obolenus beside the River Rotumna [j. c., Rotona, Retourne] for a stated price. One of these is said to contain a thousand modii of seed, while the other is recorded as containing four hundred.

He also acquired a certain estate from a man named Bertulfus, together with an adjoining field containing one hundred modii. He is likewise found to have purchased part of a certain forest from a man named Charibodus. Moreover, he obtained from the royal majesty a privilege of immunity for his church, so that it should be and remain entirely exempt from every fiscal obligation or exaction, and so that everything given to the church should possess permanent security.

King Childebertus [Col. 0095B] is also found, in documents that still survive, to have transferred to him and to his church for their possession a certain estate situated in the Vosges, near the River Saroa. The Italian Fortunatus, who at that time was renowned throughout Gaul for his poetry, took care to commend both the life and preaching of this bishop in the following verses (Book III, Poems 18):

> O Egidius, venerable summit of distinguished deeds,  
>   
> By whose merits the dignity of rank has grown in honor,  
>   
> I am withdrawn by my talent, compelled by ready love,  
>   
> And gladly encouraged to reveal a little in your praises.  
>   
> For I seem guilty of so great a charge  
>   
> If I alone remain silent about whatever resounds everywhere.  
>   
> Yet although I cannot confess it in worthy speech,  
>   
> Forgive me for having wished to speak according to my desire.  
>   
> The fame of your deeds has gone forth throughout the world [or: into the world],  
>   
> And by your own merits you shine as a star throughout the earth.  
>   
> You shine more brightly than Lucifer with serene countenance.  
>   
> He shines with his rays; you with your piety. [Col. 0095C]  
>   
> No wolf by its snares carries anything off from the flock you tend,  
>   
> While you, a holy shepherd, keep watch over the flock.  
>   
> With eloquent speech you pour forth heavenly doctrines,  
>   
> And under your guidance the house of the Church has grown.  
>   
> By the zeal of the pontiff you are regarded as the correction of the people;  
>   
> You are present as the path of light, lest darkness cause harm.  
>   
> You restore the spirits of all by the sweetness of your word;  
>   
> You satisfy them with feasts and feed the flocks with your mouth.  
>   
> The commandments are fulfilled; we are not fed by bread alone.  
>   
> We receive the delights that your words convey.  
>   
> As the body rejoices when gentler food is prepared for it,  
>   
> So souls rejoice when your tongue gives voice.  
>   
> That heresy falls, with you a strong soldier of Christ;  
>   
> You win for the King who [variant: because] gave you weapons.  
>   
> You clear the fields of thorns with your cultivating speech,  
>   
> And everywhere a harvest cleansed for God rises.  
>   
> Whoever comes as an exile, sorrowful, weary, and needy,  
>   
> Receives his homeland here, as you restore him.  
>   
> You remove what has caused grief, turning groans into joys;  
>   
> Removing exile, you return homes through love.  
>   
> The poor man has earned food, and the naked man has also earned clothing. [Col. 0095D]  
>   
> Here everyone always finds whatever good he desires.  
>   
> You grant one common counsel to all alike.  
>   
> You are the father of the people and rightly govern so many devoted ones.  
>   
> May this life of yours endure long, with the Lord granting it,  
>   
> And may the future shine with a brighter day.

Gregory of Tours also kindly relates that he was once received by this bishop (Book II of the *Miracles*, chapter 17), when a certain Siggo, referendary of King Sigebert, recovered the hearing of his deaf ear in the sacristy of the church at Reims through the power of blessed Martin, whose relics Gregory then had with him.

That same Gregory, however, in his *History of the Frankish People* (Book VI, chapter 3), relates concerning this bishop that he was sent, together with other envoys, from Childebert, son of King Sigebert, to Chilperic, King Childebert’s uncle [Col. 0096A]. In that embassy, he says, it was determined that, after the kingdom of King Guntram, Chilperic’s brother, had been taken away, they should join peace to themselves. After this pact had been confirmed, the envoys returned to Childebert with great gifts (ibid., chapter 31).

He also relates that after a son had been born to Chilperic and Chilperic himself had seized Paris, when Childebert’s envoys came to him, this bishop was the first among them. After submitting their petition, they openly urged that the peace which Chilperic had made with the aforementioned Childebert should be preserved, but said that Childebert could not have peace with Chilperic’s brother Guntram because Guntram had seized part of Marseille after their father’s death and, retaining his fugitives, refused to return them to him.

Chilperic added that this same brother of his was guilty in many respects, and that through his collusion the father of this Childebert had been killed. Moved by this, the envoys also requested that due vengeance be inflicted upon him more swiftly. Since the matter had been confirmed by oath, they departed after giving and receiving hostages [Col. 0096B].

Because of these embassies, King Guntram was always hostile to this archbishop. Therefore, when he later made peace with Childebert, he urged him in no way to trust or retain this bishop, accusing him of the crime of perjury. Later, when a certain prisoner was being tortured—one who had been sent by Queen Fredegund to strike King Childebert—he confessed that this bishop had been an accomplice in a plot by certain people to kill that same King Childebert (Gregory, Book X, chapter 13).

Without delay the bishop was seized and brought to the city of Metz, although he was extremely exhausted by a prolonged illness. While he was being held under guard there, the king ordered bishops to be summoned for his examination and commanded them to be present at the city of Verdun at the beginning of the eighth month [August].

Then, rebuked privately by certain priests for ordering a man to be dragged from the city without a hearing and thrust into custody (the word *clam* is absent from the manuscript and from Gregory), he allowed him to return to his own city. He sent letters to all the bishops of his kingdom, ordering them to be present in the aforementioned city in the middle of the ninth month to examine him.

Finally, when they had assembled, they were brought as far as the city of Metz, and Bishop Egidius was also present there. The king then declared him to be his enemy and a traitor to religion, and sent Duke Ennodius to prosecute the case.

His first charge was this:

> “Tell me, bishop, what possessed you, after abandoning the king in whose city you enjoyed the dignity of the episcopate, to submit yourself to the royal friendship of Chilperic, who is known always to have been an enemy of our lord the king, who killed his father, condemned his mother to exile, and seized his kingdom? In those cities which, as we have said, he subjugated by an unjust act of usurpation, how did you deserve to receive estates belonging to the royal fisc from that same man?”

He replied:

> “I cannot deny that I was a friend of King Chilperic, but this friendship did not arise against the interests of King Childebert. As for the estates [Col. 0097A] you mention, I acquired them through charters of that king.”

When he produced those documents publicly, the king denied that he had granted them. Otto, who had then been referendary and whose purported subscription appeared on them, was summoned for questioning; he denied having signed them. Thus the bishop is said first to have been exposed as a deceiver.

After this, letters were produced containing many insults against Brunechildis, letters that had been written to Chilperic. Likewise, letters from Chilperic to the bishop were brought forward. Among other things, they contained the following statement: “If the root of any matter is not cut out [manuscript: excised], the stalk that has risen from the earth does not wither.” It was therefore entirely clear that these writings had been composed so that, after Brunechildis had been overcome, her son might be crushed.

Several other matters were also brought against the same bishop [Col. 0097B], concerning both agreements between the kings and the disturbance of the country. Some he denied; some he could not deny. While the dispute was being prolonged, Abbot Epiphanius of the basilica of Saint Remigius also appeared. He said that the bishop had accepted two thousand gold pieces and many kinds of goods to preserve King Chilperic’s friendship. Together with the envoys who had been sent with the bishop to the aforementioned king, the abbot disclosed how an agreement had been made concerning the destruction of the region and of King Guntram, and he related the whole matter in its proper order.

When the bishops heard this and saw a priest of the Lord involved in such great evils, they requested a period of three days for deliberation—namely, so that the bishop might perhaps find some means by which he could excuse himself from the charges brought against him.

But when the third day dawned [Col. 0097C], they assembled in the church and questioned the bishop, asking him to declare whether he had any defense. Confounded, he said:

> “Do not delay in pronouncing judgment upon the guilty man. For I know that I am guilty of a capital crime against majesty, since I have always acted against the interests of this king and his mother. I know that many conflicts were undertaken on my advice, by which various places in Gaul were devastated.”

When the bishops heard this and lamented the disgrace of their brother, they secured his life but removed him from the priestly order after reading the canonical statutes. He was immediately taken to the city of Argentoratum, now called Strasbourg, and condemned to exile.

In his place, Romulfus, son of Duke Lupus and already invested with the dignity of a priest, was appointed bishop [Col. 0097D]. Epiphanius was removed from the office of abbot, which he had held over the basilica of Saint Remigius. For many weights of gold and silver were found in the register of this bishop. Whatever had come from that campaign of iniquity was conveyed to the royal treasury; whatever was found to have come from taxes or from the remaining property of the Church was left there.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning Saint Basolus

During the time of this Egidius, the holy servant of the Lord Basolus, born of noble lineage in the territory of Limoges, in the region of Armorica, came from the parts of Aquitaine to the city of Reims, earnestly seeking the protection of the most blessed Remigius. As he approached, an angel of the Lord is said to have appeared as his companion on the journey [Col. 0098A], and it is established that the angel went before him as he entered the city to which he had been directed.

The aforementioned Bishop Egidius received him with the greatest dignity. Once he learned of the pilgrim’s desire and was asked to grant him a dwelling for a more secluded way of life, he most willingly allowed him to find, wherever he wished, a suitable place within the bishopric of Reims. At last, by the arrangement of heavenly grace, he found a fitting place for himself in the village of Viriziacus, at the foot of the mountain of Reims, which the wood called Rigetium, beginning there, shades.

At that time a monastery stood there, containing twelve monks. He was kindly received by the brothers and is said to have been entrusted by the abbot with instruction in letters. Before long his learning shone so brightly that he surpassed his peers and companions in the light of wisdom [Col. 0098B]. No concern was more dear to him than either speaking about God in reading or conversation, or speaking with God in prayer. He despised transitory things and longed for eternal ones; he distributed his allowance of food to the poor, reserving only a little for himself to sustain the weakness of his body.

As he rose to the summit of virtue, he desired a solitary life. He chose the height of the neighboring mountain as a more secluded dwelling and built there a cell with an oratory, where he could devote himself more freely to heavenly contemplation. In this enclosed dwelling he is said to have served God for forty years and to have fought manfully against the temptations of the ancient serpent, devoting himself without interruption to fasts, almsgiving, vigils, prayers, and readings, and flooding those who came to him with the light of holy teaching [Col. 0098C].

While he was striving in this life-giving way of conduct, it pleased heavenly goodness to display the power of its soldier through evident signs. For while he was praying, the Lord brought forth water for him from a rock at the summit of the mountain. It is said to spring up beneath the saint’s tomb and to pour itself through the foundations of the church as though from a vessel. It is sweet to drink and healthful for those who drink it. From this spring many sick people obtain remedies for their illnesses by drinking, bathing, or washing their heads.

At a certain time, a boy named Annegiselus, who had been deprived of the light of his eyes from earliest childhood, was keeping watch before the doors of the saint’s cell. In the twelfth year of his blindness, heavenly power descended through the prayer of the man of God, and he was endowed with the gift of sight [Col. 0098D]. When the monks learned of this miracle of divine radiance, they glorified God with great acts of thanksgiving for the glorification of his faithful servant.

It also happened that a certain hunter named Attila was pursuing a boar in the woodland adjoining the saint’s cell. The animal reached the saint’s very presence and, as though believing that he would set it free, laid aside its wildness and fell at his feet. The dogs, forgetting their natural skill, ceased to pursue it.

From that time, by custom—or rather, by the power of Christ, to the honor of his beloved servant—the practice is still maintained that whenever any driven game enters the raised enclosure surrounding his wood, it is pursued no further with the eagerness of dogs, nor is it attacked by the boldness of hunters [Col. 0099A].

Another miracle of no little importance is also reported to have been granted by the Lord through the merits of this blessed confessor. A certain man named Ragenulfus had been hanged by his adversaries. When, in the utmost peril of death, he raised his eyes toward heaven and invoked blessed Basolus in a tearful voice, he immediately deserved to be freed from terrible death when the noose broke.

After many distinguished works of compassion had been performed through him during his life, he foresaw through the Spirit that the time of his vocation was approaching. He sent for his nephew, named Balsemius, summoning him from the region of Limoges to come to him. He informed him that after his death he was to lead his life in the aforementioned dwelling of religious discipline, according to what had been revealed to him by the Lord.

The nephew obeyed these saving instructions [Col. 0099B] like a good son, desiring to attain the heavenly inheritance, and remained in that dwelling until the day of his own death. Blessed Father Basolus died on the sixth day before the Kalends of December and was gathered to the citizens above. Many distinguished miracles were later displayed at his tomb, but because of negligence and their frequent occurrence, they were not committed to writing.

In the course of time, after the death of the holy man, a certain man of noble birth but savage in the pride of his spirit came there. After praying, he took the staff of this blessed Father and placed it upon his own foot. Since he was tall in body, he mockingly said:

> “Behold, this staff shows how small Basolus must have been in stature.” [Col. 0099C]

Without delay, the same foot upon which the saint’s staff had been placed withered. When it had putrefied, the man, struck by divine vengeance, died in great agony. His body was prepared to be carried for burial to the monastery of this holy man of God, but the bier, weighed down, could not be moved in any way. It was proposed that he be carried to the cemetery of Saint Remigius, but even then it could not be moved. At last, compelled by necessity, they carried him into the territory of Châlons, where finally he was permitted to have a grave.

Not long before our own time, namely during the period of the lord Archbishop Ebbo, a religious man named Benedictus was appointed abbot of this abbey by his authority. He governed [Col. 0099D] the household of Saint Basolus with moderation, serving the Lord in simplicity, adorned the church with various gifts, and, after a considerable span of life, was called to the Lord by divine command.

His brother in the flesh, named Speruus [manuscript: Spernus, and below], was appointed abbot in the same place. Unlike his brother in character and burning with the torches of a dreadful greed, he was once sitting drunk and began to say that his brother had known how to gain nothing good from that abbey. He ordered the stewards of the estates to bring the peasants before him the next day, intending to torture them with various punishments so that he might extort their resources from them.

When the inhabitants of the estates heard of the punishments being threatened against them, they all tearfully [manuscript: suppliantly] sought the aid of Saint Basolus [Col. 0100A], praying that they not be handed over to such a cruel butcher for dismemberment. They spent the night mourning and groaning and did not cease to implore the consolation of Saint Basolus.

The saint of the Lord did not refuse to hear the complaints of his people. For when morning came, Speruus was found dead. When his servants attempted to remove him from the bed, his middle burst open, and such a stench filled the place that no one could remain there. Thus the household of Saint Basolus was defended and rescued from the punishments it feared.

My maternal uncle, named Flavuardus [manuscript: Flavardus], had two sons serving God in the monastery of this holy man. We saw the younger of them, named Tetbertus, overflowing even beyond his strength in charity; he died some time ago as a priest among us. He used to tell us the following story about his father. A certain Ratoldus [variant: Rautnoldus], a priest and the third brother, had until recently remained as a witness to the matter [Col. 0100B].

The aforementioned man used to come once a year to the monastery and provide for the brothers from his resources. Once, when he was coming as usual, robbers attacked him on the road. They took the horse on which he was riding, together with everything else that caught their fancy, as well as the money he was carrying to distribute to the servants of God and also his wife’s ornaments.

After they had gone on for a short distance, rejoicing over their spoil, his wife, who had been present with him, groaned over the injury and began to call upon Saint Basolus in plaintive words, saying:

> “We will come no more to serve him or his servants if, when we are thus cast aside, he does not provide protection for us.”

After these words of lamentation, the robbers’ horses, which were carrying them swiftly away with the plunder, suddenly became fixed in place and could not be made to move forward in any way. A kind of darkness also covered the robbers, so that they did not know where to turn [Col. 0100C].

At last the brigands came to their senses. They agreed among themselves that such things had happened to them because of the wrong they had inflicted upon the innocent. After taking counsel, they returned to those whom they had unjustly deprived of their possessions. They restored everything to them and begged them to seek pardon for their crimes.

Thus, having received consolation through the patronage of the lord Basolus, they let the robbers go and proceeded more devoutly to the monastery they had intended to visit. They gave thanks to God and to his confessor for the benefits granted to them, eagerly served the servants of God, honored them with money [Col. 0100D], and thereafter, each year, carried out with greater readiness what they had begun.

When, recently, these regions of Gaul were handed over to be torn apart by the swords of the Hungarians, because our sins impelled it, certain barbarians entered the monastery of Saint Basolus. Since the clerics had already fled to the city with the relics of their patron, they found the monastery’s dwellings almost empty of people. Establishing their camp there, they began to return to the place with plunder gathered from every direction.

One of them saw gilded metal gleaming on the little tower of the church and, greedy for gold and money, climbed onto the roof of the basilica. As he tried to dismantle the little tower, he suddenly slipped and fell to the ground, dying with his limbs broken [Col. 0101A].

Another of them attempted to climb upon the altar of that church, consecrated in honor of blessed Martin. When he placed his hand upon the horn of the altar, his hand adhered so firmly to the marble that afterward it could not be torn away from it by any means [FLODOARD, *Chronicle*, year 937]. Since his companions did not wish to leave him there, they cut away with double-headed axes the portion of stone around his hand and led him away, unwillingly carrying with him the piece of marble that remained attached to his hand.

Even as the captives who returned relate, he carried that stone all the way to his own land, his arm already withered, proclaiming that this had happened through the power of Basolus.

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning Bishop Romulfus

[Col. 0101B]

After Egidius, Romulfus governed the bishopric of Reims. He was a man noble by birth and the brother of John, who at that time was a duke. Their father, Lupus, left them many possessions to be divided equally between them. They obtained a royal command that this division should be carried out with equal right.

He excelled in many patrimonies, especially beyond the Loire and in the district of Poitiers. From the greater part of these, by the document of his will, he made the Church of Reims his heir. He left some possessions to his brothers or nephews, assigned some to the foundation (*matricula*) of Saint Martial, and some to the basilica of Saint Remigius.

He gave the estate of Lautiniacum on the River Caltaio to the monastery of nuns constructed at Reims in honor of Saint Peter. He records that he had purchased this estate for a stated price [Col. 0101C]. In addition, by his will he assigned certain gifts to various churches, both to the bishopric of Reims and to those of Soissons, Tours, and several others.

He granted freedom to the greater part of his household. A copy of this will is still preserved in the archive of the Church of Reims, together with the authority of King Childebert. The same king was petitioned by the aforementioned bishop through Sonnatius, a venerable deacon, and resolved to confirm the will. The purpose was that, if anyone among the bishop’s heirs should unjustly presume to seize the lands, vineyards, and slaves that the bishop had assigned principally to the Church of Reims or to the other holy places mentioned, the priests of those places should have full power to recover them by every means [Col. 0101D].

He also exchanged with King Childebert certain estates situated in the territory of Metz, whose principal one is Ortivallis [variant: Orcivallis], which the lord Egidius is said to have purchased from a certain Vincentius, in return for other estates located in the district of Reims, namely Marciliana and Arbidogilo [perhaps Margilly and Ardeuil].

He is also found to have purchased property and slaves that had been placed in the bishopric for the enlargement of the church. Finally, he built an oratory in the atrium of Saint Remigius under the patronage of blessed Germanus. He is also found to have recovered at the royal court certain properties seized by others, through the action of the aforementioned Sonnatius, archdeacon; documents of royal authority concerning these recoveries still survive.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning Bishop Sonnatius

[Col. 0102A]

Sonnatius followed Romulfus in the episcopate. He is found to have celebrated a synod with forty or more other bishops of Gaul. Saint Arnulfus, bishop of Metz, is also found to have taken part, together with Theodoricus of Lyon, Sindulfus of Vienne, Sulpitius of Bourges, Medegiselus of Tours, Seconus of Elusa, Leontius of Saintes, Modoaldus of Trier, Chunebertus of Cologne, Richerius of Sens, Donatus of Besançon, Auspicius of Autun, Modoaldus of Langres, Ragnebertus of Bayeux, Childoaldus of Avranches, Bertegisellus of Chartres, Palladius of Auxerre, Gondoaldus of Meaux, Leudebertus of Paris, Chainoalgus of Laon, Godo of Verdun, Ansaricus of Soissons, Claudius of Riez, Berthoaldus of Cambrai, Agomarus of Senlis, Caesarius of Clermont, Verus of Rodez, Agricola of Gévaudan, Lupoaldus of Mainz, Willegiselus of Toulouse, Constantius of Albi, Nammatius of Angoulême, Rusticus of Cahors, Audericus of Auch, Emmo of Aire, Felix of Châlons, Hadoindus [manuscript, corrected: Chadoindus] of Le Mans, Magnebodus of Angers, John of Poitiers, and Leobardus [variant: Loutbardus] of Nantes.

At this synod many useful provisions are recorded as having been established:

1. Concerning how the property of the Church should be administered, and concerning those things obtained from the Church by a precarious grant, so that, through the passage of time, they should not be usurped by anyone as his own property and thereby defrauded from the Church [Col. 0102C].

2. Concerning clerics: if any, out of a spirit of rebellion, bind themselves by oaths or by a written conspiracy and, through a crafty accusation, lay a plot against their bishop, then, if they refuse to amend after being admonished, they are to be entirely deprived of their proper rank.

3. That the chapters of the canons enacted at Paris in a general synod, convened through the efforts of King Lothair in the basilica of Saint Peter, are to be preserved with complete force.

4. That if anyone in Gaul is still suspected of being a heretic, the pastors of the churches are to investigate them; and if they are truly found to be so, they are to be recalled to the Catholic faith.

5. That no one is to be excommunicated rashly. If an excommunicated person believes that he has been condemned unjustly, he is to have permission to appeal at the next synod [Col. 0102D]. If he has been condemned unjustly, he is to be absolved; but if justly, he is to fulfill the period of penance imposed upon him.

6. If any judge of whatever rank presumes to subject a cleric to public proceedings, or, for any reason whatsoever, presumes to constrain him or inflict insults or injuries upon him without the knowledge and permission of the bishop, he is to be deprived of communion. The bishop, however, must not delay in correcting negligence concerning the established conditions of clerics.

7. Those who are subject to the public census are not to dare to join themselves to the religious life without the permission of the ruler or the judge.

8. If anyone removes a fugitive from a church without the oath by which he is required to swear that he will leave secure from torture and mutilation [c., “from avoided torture”] [Col. 0103A], under whatever pretext, let him be deprived of communion.

9. Likewise, if anyone violates an oath that has been sworn, let him be deprived of communion.
