But the man who is freed from death through the benefit of the holy Church shall not receive permission to depart until he promises that he will undertake penance for his crime and fulfill whatever is canonically imposed upon him.

10. Concerning incestuous unions: if anyone, within the degree prescribed by the canons, joins himself in an incestuous relationship to persons with whom divine regulations forbid him to unite, unless they demonstrate their penance by separation, let them be deprived of communion, and let them have neither military service at the palace nor permission to conduct legal actions. And when the aforesaid incestuous persons have united, the bishops or priests in whose diocese or district this has occurred shall announce the crime to the king or to the judges, so that, once it has been reported, they may separate themselves from their communion and cohabitation, and their property may pass to their proper relatives—on the condition that, before they are separated, they may not come into their own property by any device, whether through relatives, purchase, or royal authority, unless they acknowledge penance through separation from the aforesaid crime.

11. If anyone voluntarily commits homicide, not resisting violence but perpetrating the act by force and in an assault, no communion is to be maintained with him at all; nevertheless, if he performs penance, communion as viaticum shall not be denied him at the hour of death [Col. 0103C].

12. Clerics, and likewise laymen, who presume to retain offerings of their parents, whether donated or left by testament, or who think that what they themselves have donated to churches or monasteries may be taken away, shall, as the holy synod previously decreed, be excluded from the churches as “murderers of the poor” until they make restitution [Concil. Paris. III, c. 1].

13. Christians are not to be sold to Jews or pagans. If any Christian, compelled by necessity, chooses to sell his Christian slaves, he shall sell them only to Christians. For if he sells them to pagans or Jews, let him be deprived of communion, and let the sale have no legal validity. If Jews presume to summon Christian slaves to Judaism or afflict them with severe tortures [Col. 0103D], the slaves themselves shall be restored to the authority of the fisc. Jews, however, shall not be admitted to any public office. Jewish insults against Christians are to be utterly rejected.

14. Likewise, if a cleric departing from one city wishes to go to other cities or travel to other provinces, he shall be commended by letters from his bishop. If he has departed without letters, he is not to be received in any way if this is evident.

15. Likewise, a bishop shall not presume either to sell slaves or property belonging to the rights of the Church, or to alienate them after his death by any contracts whatsoever, since the poor live from them.

16. Likewise, concerning those who are found to imitate auguries or pagan rites [Col. 0104A], or who eat superstitious foods with pagans: it has pleased us that they be admonished kindly and urged to return from their former errors. If they neglect this and associate with idolaters or those who offer sacrifices, let them fulfill an appropriate period of penance.

17. Likewise, servile persons are not to be admitted as accusers. Whoever undertakes the role of accuser, if he has not proved one charge, shall not be admitted to bring another accusation.

18. Likewise, if anyone established in any rank or office, or supported by authority, when a bishop has died, dares to seize property of any condition placed in the Church’s houses or fields before the opening of the testament or the hearing of the case, or presumes to break the Church’s barriers [Col. 0104B] and touch or search the furnishings placed inside the Church’s house, let him be utterly excluded from the communion of Christians.

19. Likewise, if anyone wishes to force a free man or freedman into servitude—or has perhaps already done so—and, when warned by the bishop, neglects to withdraw from harassing him or refuses to make amends, let it be decreed that he be separated as one guilty of calumny.

20. Likewise, clerics of any rank shall not go to court, whether for their own cases or for ecclesiastical cases, in any other way, nor dare to plead cases except those which they have been entirely permitted to conduct with the permission and counsel of the bishop.

21. Likewise, no layman is to be placed over the parishes as archpriest [Col. 0104C]; rather, the cleric who ought to be senior among them is to be appointed.

22. Likewise, bishops who have been established in the highest priesthood shall count among the Church’s possessions whatever is left or donated to them by outsiders—whether together with the Church or separately—not as their own property but as property left to the Church, because the donor is shown to offer it for the remedy of his soul, not for the advantage of the priest. For it is just that, just as the priest has what has been left to the Church, so the Church should have what the priest has left behind [i., “what is left to the priest”]. Certainly, whatever is perhaps left by a trust either in the priest’s name or in the Church’s name, for the subsequent benefit of someone else, the Church may not retain by counting it among its own possessions [Col. 0104D].

23. Likewise, if any bishop seizes, by any device or crafty greed, property presently possessed by another church, or presumes to usurp it without a hearing and restore it to his own authority or that of his Church, let him, since he cannot be deprived of communion as a “murderer of the poor,” be removed from office.

24. Likewise, if any bishop presumes to break sacred vessels or furnishings for any reason whatsoever—except in the event of pressing necessity for the redemption of captives—he shall cease from the Church’s office.

25. Likewise, no one, whether acting through royal authority, supported by any power, or acting on his own temerity, may dare to abduct or drag away widows who have asked to be consecrated to the Lord, or girls consecrated to the Lord [Col. 0105A]. If either party consents, let both be deprived of communion.

26. Judges who disregard the statutes established by the authority and royal edict concerning the canons, or who violate or despise that royal edict made at Paris, shall, it has pleased us, be deprived of communion.

27. Likewise, when a bishop dies, no one else is to be substituted in his place except a native of that locality, whom the universal vote of the whole people has chosen and the will of the comprovincial bishops has approved. Whoever presumes to act otherwise shall be cast out of the see which he invaded rather than received. We decree that the ordainers shall abstain for three years from the administration of their see’s office.

[Col. 0105B] Moreover, the aforesaid lord bishop Sonnatius is credibly reported to have properly ordered the Church’s property, also enlarging the episcopal estate with lands and slaves bought for a price; some records of these purchases are still found. Certain properties which some wicked men had seized he duly recovered and restored to the Church through the royal majesty, both personally and through his agents, with the priest Marcus, his legate, also conducting the cases. He also organized the colonists of certain episcopal estates after their services had been commuted. He obtained royal charters confirming the immunity of ecclesiastical property, as well as the security of certain transfers. He is also found to have exchanged certain property with Queen Brunhild, according to the convenience of both parties.

[Col. 0105C] He also drew up a testament of his property, in which he bestowed many gifts upon various churches. He made the basilica of blessed Remigius especially his heir, choosing to be buried there; and he assigned there a gilded silver serving vessel. He also assigned twelve spoons, a silver salt-cellar, and his portion of a certain estate with slaves, vineyards, meadows, and the other appurtenances, as well as some other things which he remembered having purchased for a price.

To the basilica of Saints Timothy and Apollinaris he assigned certain houses, both near that church and within the city. To the basilica of Saint Martin, whom he calls his personal patron, he gave the entire estate called Mutationis, which he had purchased, just as it had been possessed by him [Col. 0105D]; in addition, he gave gold with which a chalice was to be made there.

To the basilica of Saint Julian, five gold solidi for its recovery. To the basilica of Saint Nicasius, likewise five solidi. To the basilica of Saint John, five solidi. To the basilica of Saint Sixtus, likewise three gold solidi. To the basilica of Saint Maurice, three solidi. To the basilica of Saint Medard, three solidi. To the nunnery, a vineyard situated at Germaniacum (Germiny), together with certain vessels useful to that basilica.

To the basilica called “at the Apostles,” three gold solidi, with other small gifts from which a chalice was to be made. To the basilica of Saint Peter in the city, three gold solidi. To the basilica of Saint Theodoric, his portion of the estate of Germaniacum, with slaves, vineyards, and the other appurtenances [Col. 0106A]; also silver for making or ornamenting the tomb of lord Theodulf.

To the basilica of Saint Vitus, a certain silver vessel for making a chalice, and fifteen gold solidi. To the basilica of the holy martyrs Rufinus and Valerius, fifteen gold solidi. To the basilica of the holy martyrs Crispinus and Crispinianus, fifteen gold solidi. He also bestowed various gifts upon the matricula of the holy Church of Rheims.

He assigned various gifts also to the other matriculae and congregations. To certain persons among his heirs he left estates on the condition that, after their deaths, they should return to the holy places he had designated. He granted freedom to a number of slaves and enriched them by adding personal property. This testament of the man of God is found confirmed by a page of royal charter [Col. 0106B].

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning Bishop Leudegiselus, Angelbert, and Lando

After this blessed man, Leudegiselus, the brother of Bishop Attila, governed the episcopal estate during the reign of King Dagobert. He also enlarged it with purchased property, namely woods, meadows, and lands. He exchanged certain possessions with Abbo, bishop of Troyes, according to the convenience of both parties, and other possessions with various other persons. He also arranged certain properties of the Church with properly appointed colonists.

Angelbert followed him. He too is found to have enlarged the episcopal estate with purchased property. He was succeeded by Lando, a most illustrious man and possessor of many estates [Col. 0106C]. Some of these he joined to the Church, while others he distributed among his relatives.

He also recovered by legal process before the royal majesty the property which the Church of Rheims had possessed beyond the Loire and which a certain Felix, abbot of the church of the holy martyr Julian, was improperly retaining. For this matter his predecessor, Bishop Angelbert, is found to have previously disputed with Gallus, bishop of Clermont, before the king.

Therefore Bishop Lando duly made the Church of Rheims heir to his property by the page of his testament, and whatever he gave to other persons or churches he assigned to be administered for that same Church or by his successor. He assigned various gifts to the basilicas of various saints.

To the basilica of Saint Remigius, where he chose that he should be buried, he gave estates and gifts. To the basilica of Saint Gaugericus and Saint Quintinus, various gifts of silver. Likewise, to the basilicas and matriculae at Rheims: namely, of Saints Timothy and Apollinaris; of Saint Martin; of Saint Nicasius; of Saint Genevieve; and to the monastery of Saints Theodoric and Theodulf.

Likewise, to the basilica of Saint Germanus and its matricula; of Saint Julian; of Saints Cosmas and Damian; of Saint Peter at the Court; of Saint Peter at the Nunnery; to the basilica of Saint Symphorian, which is called “at the Apostles”; of Saint Medard; of Saints Crispinus and Crispinianus; of Saint Victor; of Saint Maurice; and of Saint Basolus, he bestowed various gifts.

He also assigned to the Church of Laon his portion of a certain estate [Col. 0106D], and to the basilica of Saint Genevieve established there he gave the estate of Appia (the village of Eppes), with everything belonging to it [Col. 0107A]. He also placed upon the altar of Saint Mary’s Church at Rheims a golden tower which he had had made in fulfillment of his vow, together with three patens and a golden armlet. This took place during the reign of King Sigebert.

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning Saint Nivardus

After those mentioned above, the blessed Nivo, also called Nivardus—for he is found to have been called by both names—was chosen for the episcopal dignity. He is said previously to have lived at the king’s court, being a most illustrious man.

Once established in the episcopate, he is found to have enlarged the Church’s property by purchasing estates and houses in various places, as well as slaves. He also arranged certain episcopal estates with properly organized colonies [Col. 0107B]. He is found to have exchanged some property with Attila, bishop of Laon, according to the convenience of both parties.

He also exchanged with the brothers Bavo and Theoderamnus a certain place on the river Marne, from the property of the Church of Rheims, where he built a monastery called Altumvillare (Hautvillers). This was at the request of Abbot Berecarius, who had asked him to give him a place where he could live with his brother-monks under the Rule of the Fathers Saint Benedict and Saint Columbanus; and the same bishop endeavored to do this, as is related below.

He also exchanged certain property with some other persons, as seemed appropriate. Under the protection of a privilege, he gave to the monastery of Saint Basolus a church at Viriziacum, built in honor of Saint Mary [Col. 0107C], with everything belonging to it, together with a small estate called Wasciacus. He also established an immunity for the monks serving God there under Abbot Petrus, so that no ecclesiastical judge would presume to harass them improperly in anything, but that they might be permitted to live peacefully under the holy Rule and serve God.

He also obtained from King Childebert (Childebert III) a charter of immunity for the Church of Rheims concerning tolls and certain taxes. King Louis likewise granted, under the name of his Church, certain properties at Malliacum on the river Vidula, which he had recovered after expelling certain of his unfaithful men, by a charter of his authority.

During his time, the illustrious Grimoald gave his estates Calmiciacum and Victuriacum (Mally, Veeste) to Saint Remigius [Col. 0107D], for the remedy of his soul.

When this blessed Nivardus, with the common consent of the entire council of the bishops of Gaul, at the command of the Roman pontiff, with the king’s favor, had rebuilt the church of the monastery on the bank of the river Marne at a place called Villare—formerly established there but destroyed by barbarians—and this church, after he had built it from the foundations, had collapsed, he is said to have rebuilt it again in another place, where it again fell.

One day, coming from the estate of Sparnacum with the aforesaid Abbot Berecarius accompanying him, he thought that, after crossing the river, he ought to rest for a little while. Reclining his head in the lap of Berecarius, who was sitting, he fell asleep and saw a vision: a dove seemed to circle around a place in the forest and, after circling, settle in a certain beech tree. He saw the same dove do this a third time and then rise toward the heavens [Note: [Col. 0107D] The same account is related at greater length in the Life of Saint Bercharius.].

He is said to have received this vision in sleep, while the aforesaid Berecarius received it while awake. Struck by what he had seen, the abbot began to shed tears. When the blessed bishop awoke from sleep, he found that his face was wet from Berecarius’s tears. He asked him why he was weeping and learned that he had wept because of the collapse of his work.

When they had told each other what they had seen, the bishop is said to have related the vision also to a certain servant of God named Bavo, whose property it was. Bavo had an oratory there in honor of the holy Cross and lived there [Col. 0108B]. After learning of the bishop’s vision and his intention, Bavo offered him that same property, as well as part of the property of one of his brothers, named Baldinus.

He reported, however, the case of another brother, named Theoderamnus: he was engaged in a conflict against Count Reolus, who later became bishop of Rheims, on behalf of his own sons, whom Reolus had killed in revenge for his own sons, whom Theoderamnus had put to death by hanging because of the brigandage they practiced.

Therefore Lord Nivardus reconciled Theoderamnus with Reolus, whose wife was Nivardus’s niece, the daughter of Childeric; and so Theoderamnus, together with his other brothers, gave that same property to Saint Nivardus in exchange for property received from him.

Immediately the bishop ordered the forest to be cut down and built there a church in honor of Saint Peter [Col. 0108C] and all the Apostles. Where he had seen the dove settle, he established an altar, and, gathering servants of God, organized a monastery. There the aforesaid Theoderamnus became a monk.

Reolus also asked that his son Gedeon, born of the niece of Saint Nivardus, be made a monk there, and he donated part of his property to the same monastery. After establishing the monastery, the blessed Nivardus transferred to that place whatever possessions he appeared to have had before the episcopate. He also exhorted the blessed Reolus and urged him to assume the religious habit.

At the request of the aforesaid Abbot Berecarius, he also granted the monastery a privilege: namely, that while he lived, the bishop himself should preserve the monastery under his jurisdiction and authority; and that after his death, the bishop of Rheims should govern the monastery and defend the same monks against every adversity. The monks themselves, however, were to have the power to elect their own superior regularly, as is contained in the wording of the privilege.

After this, he is said to have died in the little church of Saint Mary which he had built in the same monastery. He was carried to the Church of Saint Remigius at Rheims and buried there.

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the Translation of Saint Helena to the Same Monastery

It is established that the body of blessed Queen Helena was brought from the city of Rome to the aforesaid monastery of this holy man [Col. 0109A]. A certain priest of the parish of Rheims, named Tergisus, had traveled to Rome. Remaining unexpectedly in a church during the night, he carefully endeavored to steal the body and carry it away with him.

When he had already reached the second stopping-place, in a forest adjoining the city of Sutrium, one of his companions, wishing to lift the holy relics onto a little donkey, was completely unable to move them. Bewildered, he reported this to his master. The latter hurried over, seized the treasure in fear, and placed it upon the animal without any apparent weight, although he himself was weaker and had been repelled by the force required.

The same minister confessed that he had been polluted by a nocturnal emission.

When they came to the very swift river Taram and did not dare to enter it because of the strength of its current [Col. 0109B], the animal bearing the sacred gift descended into the river of its own accord. The other donkey, carrying the priest, followed it. Although it seemed almost submerged by the waves, it nevertheless crossed the river, while it was proved that the sides of the bearer of the holy relics had not been touched by the waves.

Likewise, while they were crossing certain ridges of the Alps, a girl accompanying the party fell headlong, driven forward by the slope. As she rolled miserably down the declivities, the companions of the blessed queen cried out and sought her protection. Suddenly the girl, having fallen, became caught on the steep side of the mountain. Thus, by means of the lowered straps, she was drawn back unharmed to the heights, having suffered no injury, as it seemed to her.

When some people had learned of these miracles, they served more devoutly in attending to this burden. Among them, a certain man leaped down from his horse, placed the blessed relics upon it [Col. 0109C], and, entering a narrow path on the descent of the mountain, lifted the burden onto his own shoulders.

But suddenly, when his foot slipped, he fell headlong, yet he did not abandon the sacred gifts, which were tightly held in his arms. Immediately, while the following crowd repeated the queen’s name in prayers, the horse that had carried the sacred relics, disregarding its own fall, embraced the falling man with its forelegs and held him for so long, God sustaining it, until the inhabitants living below had raked the ice with iron and both man and horse had been drawn back onto the path with ropes.

When they came to the district of Langres, to a village called Osismus, they brought the holy relics to the church of Saint Winebald. There a little woman whose knees were contracted and who crawled on them touched the reliquary of the relics and, her sinews being restored to their proper functions, was returned to perfect health [Col. 0109D].

After traveling for one day, a certain man whose limbs had been entirely crippled for six years sent a cloth of the blessed queen together with a sword as a gift. Before his wife, who had brought these little offerings, returned to him, the sick man recovered the functions of all his limbs.

When this was heard, a little girl blind from her mother’s womb was brought here to the holy protection. As soon as she touched the bier of the blessed Lady, her blindness was driven away and she received her sight. When they entered the estate of Averga, a mute woman, deprived also of the use of her hands, came forward to meet them; immediately, after recovering the functions of her limbs, she obtained the healing she desired.

[Col. 0110A] Next, when this venerable gift had been placed in the church of the estate of Falesia, a certain lunatic entered the same basilica. Though he had most recently been tormented, when all sought the merits of the most blessed woman, he returned fully freed and endowed with complete health.

In the same estate, a certain man, worn down by disease, had spent fifteen years in bed. His flesh had become so rotten that twenty-three bones are said to have fallen from his body. When he was carried to the divine healer, he was raised by divine power and, to the amazement of the people, restored healthy.

A certain girl named Bava, drawn along on her knees, crawled because both her knees had been contracted from her mother’s womb. When her legs had been strengthened here, she departed walking upright; afterward she remained at Rheims in the holy religious life.

A woman also came who, weakened by paralysis, had completely lost the use of her tongue [Col. 0110B], while the loosened sinews of her right hand hung uselessly. A little cloth brought as an offering touched the case containing the sacred body, and the woman fully recovered the functions of her former health.

A certain man deaf from birth brought a ram and entered the church, where he stood for the celebration of Mass. When the reading of the Gospel was reached, he began to perceive with his ear the unfamiliar words of life. After it had been read, he confessed that he had never before heard the Gospel.

A certain father arrived with his nursing infant, whom the force of illness was already driving toward death. The father made a vow for the life of his child and returned. He found the boy, who for five days had refused the nourishment of his mother’s breast, safe and suckling milk.

A certain paralytic from the territory of Trier was brought there. Previously, he had seven times gained strength in all his limbs and just as many times, because the desires of the flesh pressed upon him, been miserably crippled again. After he confessed his sins—something he had not done for twenty years—he obtained health that thereafter remained.

A certain woman was also brought who had been crippled by disease on her right side. She obtained complete healing and returned home sound. Likewise, a blind woman was brought in the morning; at the third hour, she returned with both eyes illuminated.

Finally, when the most sacred relic had been brought to the aforesaid monastery of Altumvillare, some people doubted whether it was truly Helena, mother of Constantine Augustus and discoverer of the life-giving wood. Christ graciously confirmed this by a sign involving water, after being entreated with a three-day fast [Col. 0110D].

Three brothers were also sent from the same monastery to Rome to investigate the certainty of this blessed queen’s translation. When they returned, they brought to this monastery both the confirmation of this truth and a doubled joy: namely, the body of the blessed priest Polycarp, companion of Saint Sebastian.

As the birthday of this blessed queen was approaching, the monks’ fishermen were fishing at night in the river Marne. Having labored almost the entire night in vain and grown weary, they finally began to call upon Saint Helena to relieve their fatigue. Then, casting the net in the name of God and of the saint herself, they rejoiced, enriched by two pike.

But soon [Col. 0111A] one of them, returning to his mother, interrupted their joy with a certain sorrow. While they were complaining again and becoming disturbed as they called upon the lady once more, a fish caught in the net miraculously leaped from below, seized the net’s upper rope with a very strong bite, and, clinging to the rope, hung there until the astonished fisherman finally received it gratefully.

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning the Translation of Saint Sindulf to the Same Monastery

The bones of blessed Sindulf were translated to this monastery. They had been placed in an estate called Alsontia, where the same holy man had served God in the priestly office and where he had become renowned after his death through many miracles.

When his relics had been brought to the estate called Spida [Col. 0111B], a certain blind woman rejoiced at receiving her former sight. When they were already approaching the gates of the city of Rheims, with a multitude of people hurrying out to meet them, a mute and weak girl came forward. When she prostrated herself on the ground, she deserved to be healed of both afflictions.

A little woman was brought there whose hands and knees were contracted. As soon as she had been placed on the ground, she rejoiced at being restored to health. But when, overcome by vanity, she began to boast that her husband would receive her whether he wished to or not—the husband who had abandoned her because of this illness—she fell back again into the misery from which she had been freed.

When the limbs of the blessed man had been placed in the church before the altar of Saint Mary, a girl came crawling on contracted knees. She was raised by the saint’s power and, through his merits, stood there healed [Col. 0111C].

A woman who had been blind for seven years was also brought there. As soon as she touched the doors of the church, she deserved to receive her sight.

After the sacramental rites of Mass had been celebrated, the body of the blessed man was carried from there to the basilica of Saint Remigius. On the following day it was taken to the monastery of Avennacum. As the nuns came out to meet it, a man who had been lame for two years arrived. When he prostrated himself on the ground, he rose and began to set down his steps as before.

A woman who was contracted and whose limbs were weakened was also brought. Without delay, she rejoiced at being restored to health.

Then this venerable gift was carried to the monastery of Altumvillare. There a little girl who had been blind from the first year of her birth was brought. As soon as she reached the monastery gate, she began to see the light.

Two brothers, advanced in age, who had been deprived of sight for less than a year, entered the oratory together. When they devoted themselves to prayer, blood began to flow from their eyes in place of tears [Col. 0111D]. Soon, having received their sight, they rejoiced to see the tomb of their healer.

A woman consecrated to God had made a vow with her companions to go to the place where the relic lay. Having turned back halfway through the journey while the others continued, she became rigid in her knees and arms as soon as she reached the place of her own cell. Later she was carried in a cart to the aforesaid monastery. After remaining there for some time in this illness, she finally rejoiced that her former health had been restored to her.

## CHAPTER X. Concerning Saint Reolus, Bishop

After Saint Nivardus, the aforesaid lord Reolus (Saint Rieul) obtained this episcopal estate [Col. 0112A]. He is found to have enlarged it with both inherited and purchased property.

At the command of lord Nivardus, he is found to have conducted and won cases before the royal majesty concerning ecclesiastical property and the legal rights of colonists.

Once the blessed Reolus had been established in the episcopate, he had a major dispute concerning the property of the aforementioned Saint Bishop Nivardus with Gundebertus, a nobleman of the king and the full brother of lord Nivardus. Gundebertus maintained that the estates of his brother Nivo, both from their paternal and maternal inheritance, which Nivo had left when he died, belonged to him by lawful right.

Lord Reolus and his agents, however, asserted that lord Nivardus had transferred all his property, for the remedy of his soul, to the holy places through his instruments [Col. 0112B]: namely, to the Church of Saint Mary, to Saint Remigius, and to the monastery of Altumvillare, as well as to Viriziacum, where lord Basolus rests bodily. Lord Nivo himself had built or rebuilt these monasteries by his labor.

Likewise, at Rheims, he had transferred property to the nunnery, where Boba appeared to preside as abbess; and to Saints Rufinus and Valerius, as well as to the other holy places.

While this dispute was being waged between the two parties, peaceable persons eventually brought them back to agreement, so that they returned to peace under these terms: Gundebertus would receive into his own authority the property beyond the Loire which had belonged to their mother Emma, without any claim being made by Bishop Reolus or his agents.

All the remaining property which lord Nivo of blessed memory had assigned to the holy places through his instruments [Col. 0112C] would be possessed in full and perpetually by those same holy places, with God’s help, without any claim by Gundebertus or his heirs. A written agreement concerning this settlement, confirmed by the assignment of both parties, is still preserved among us.

While he was bishop, he purchased a portion of the estate of Diciacum; likewise, a mansus and fields in the estate of Bersiniacum [ms., Hersiniacum]; likewise, more than four mansus within the city of Rheims from various persons, as well as some other property; likewise, a portion of the estate called Mons Allonis.

He also purchased portions of the estates of Rosiciacum and Popiciacum, and some other things. During his time the illustrious Waratus transferred to the Churches of Saint Mary and Saint Remigius at Rheims various properties, both estates and slaves [Col. 0112D]: the mountain of Cruciniacum (Cruny), the estate of Curba (Courville), together with Acciniacum, in the district of Tardenois (Arcini in Tardenois).

Finally, this blessed bishop Reolus is found to have exchanged certain Church property with some persons, according to the convenience of the parties and with their freedom secured.

He had a daughter consecrated to God in the monastery which Ebroinus built at Soissons. She lived there under the holy Rule; her name was Odila. He had fathered her in a legitimate marriage before entering the clerical state. He transferred to her certain estates, both in the district of Rheims and in that of Beauvais, as well as in the regions beyond the Loire, under the condition that those properties should, after her death, benefit the same monastery forever.

[Col. 0113A] This venerable bishop built the monastery of Orbais in a place which he obtained as a gift from King Theuderic, with the king’s permission and also with the support of Ebroinus, mayor of the palace.

The same lord Reolus obtained from the monastery of Rasbacum six monks who would maintain the governance of the holy Rule there and teach it to others. From among them he appointed one named Landemarus [i., Leudomarus] abbot of that place; he governed the same monastery for as long as he lived.

Although he was expelled by a certain Odo, he was later restored by King Childebert. After his death, Archbishop Rigobert received and governed the monastery.

The Hungarians recently attempted to seize and slaughter a monk of this monastery named Hucboldus [Col. 0113B] [Note: [Col. 0113D] The same author relates this in his Chronicle under the year 937.]. But they were entirely unable to cut him with iron. For, as the same author relates—and some captives who saw it and have now returned also testify—when the barbarians attacked him naked from every side with arrows, the arrows rebounded from his body as though struck from diamond; no sign of a blow appeared on his skin. Even when he was struck with a sword with all their force, he nevertheless remained unharmed.

Therefore, saying that he was a god, they reverently took him with them until he was ransomed by a certain bishop and, having been released, returned.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning Saint Rigobertus

Blessed Rigobertus succeeded the aforesaid lord Reolus in the episcopate. He was, it is reported, also related to him by blood. He was born in the region of the Ripuarians (the region of Ribemont) of noble lineage: his father, named Constantinus, came from that same district [Col. 0113C], while his mother originated from the territory of Porcensis.

He was a man instructed in pious conduct and adorned with the marks of virtue. Finding some parts of the episcopal estate in ruins, he repaired them. He restored the canonical religious life to the clergy, established sufficient provisions for them, and granted them certain estates. He also established a common treasury for their use.

To this treasury he assigned the following estates: the court of Gerniacum (Gernicourt), Musceium, Roceium, Wilfiniacum, Rivus, and Curcellas. He also assigned the Church of Saint Hilary, together with the suburb belonging to it, so that from it sufficient refreshment might be prepared for them each year on the anniversary of his passing; whatever remained would be distributed among them collectively.

He also assigned servants and their colonies to the necessary services of the canons [Col. 0113D], and determined that these poor of Christ should become heirs to his property. The total of these possessions amounts to forty or more mansus.

He also properly organized certain estates of the episcopal estate, listing their colonies and services.

The bishop also acquired some properties with which he enlarged the episcopal estate, purchasing certain of them for a price: for example, the estate called Cartobra, in the Tardonian district, from Gomnoaldus, for which he is said to have given five hundred gold solidi; and, in the estate called Turba, two manses from various persons. Likewise, a portion of the estate called Campaniaca, on the river Vidula, from Hosomo [manuscript: Hosonio], [Col. 0114A] for which he is found to have given 140 gold solidi. Likewise, from a certain female cousin of his, named Gilsinda, a portion of the estate of Bracancium [Briquenay], on the river Rotumna, with its slaves, buildings, and everything belonging to that possession. Likewise, from the same Gilsinda, a certain part of the estate of Bobiliniacum, above the river Suippia [Boul-sur-Suippe], with houses, slaves, meadows, fields, and the other things belonging to that possession; for these properties he is recorded to have given one hundred gold solidi. He is also found to have purchased certain properties beyond the Loire, paying a considerable weight of gold. He is likewise found to have exchanged certain properties with various persons, according to the convenience of the parties.

Finally, from King Dagobert [Dagobert II] he obtained a charter of immunity for his church, representing to that king how this church, under the preceding Frankish kings, from the time of the lord Remigius and King Clovis—whom Remigius himself baptized—had always been entirely free from every burden of public exactions. [Col. 0114B] The aforesaid king, intending to confirm or renew this privilege, decreed, with the counsel of his nobles, in the form established by his royal predecessors, that all the properties of that holy church of God—whether in Champagne, within the city, or in its suburbs; in Austrasia, Neustria, or Burgundy; in the region of Marseille; in the Rhône valley, the Gévaudan, Auvergne, Touraine, Poitou, Limousin; or wherever within his kingdoms the church of Reims or the basilica of the most blessed Remigius appeared to possess estates or men—might remain forever under complete immunity. [Col. 0114C]

Likewise, no public judge was to dare enter those lands to establish lodgings, or presume in any way to exact judicial payments or hospitality there. Rather, whatever had been granted by his royal predecessors to the church of Reims or the basilica of Saint Remigius, that same church was to be able to preserve throughout all days. He also diligently sought and obtained from the king’s son, as well as from the other kings of his time, charters confirming the immunity and remission of tolls belonging to his church. Likewise, a charter of King Theuderic, specifically concerning the estate of Calmiciacum, which Grimoaldus, an illustrious man, had bestowed upon the church of Reims. [Col. 0114D] The records of these royal charters are [Col. 0114D] still preserved in the archive of this holy church of Reims.

This venerable bishop is said to have been a very close friend of Pippin, mayor of the royal palace. He frequently used to send him blessed loaves (eulogiae) as a benediction. Once, when he had come to speak with him, the prince began asking what he might offer that would please this holy Father. At that time the bishop was staying at the estate of Gerniacum. When Pippin learned that this estate, which had been offered to him, was pleasing to the blessed bishop, he presented it to him, telling him to take as much land around it as he wished, or as much as he could encircle while Pippin rested at midday.

Blessed Rigobert, therefore, following the example of the most blessed Remigius, proceeded along boundaries that were clearly visible and ordered markers to be placed at intervals along his route, so that the boundary might be distinguished from the fields. [Col. 0115A] When he returned, Pippin rose from sleep and granted him the entire area enclosed by his circuit. As a memorable indication of this journey, the grass there is seen to be greener at every season than in the surrounding places.

There is also another miracle of no little significance, which unquestionably was granted by the Lord to those same properties because of Rigobert’s merits. For after they had come under his dominion, it is said that no storm ever damaged them, nor did hail fall upon them. Even when hail appeared to be falling in neighboring places, it did not presume to reach their boundaries.

Finally, he obtained these properties and the others he is seen to have acquired without seeking them out of worldly greed. In everything he consulted the interests of his church and made it his heir. [Col. 0115B] He also made other churches beneficiaries of his properties, as we learn from various documentary charters.

During his episcopate, a certain abbot named Ado gave to the church of Saint Mary of Reims his properties situated in the district of Laon, in the village called Rausidus [c. i: Raosidus], together with their appurtenances—namely, houses, tenants, fields, vineyards, meadows, woods, fishponds, waters and watercourses, and all their dependencies. Likewise, he gave to the matricula of Saint Remigius certain properties situated in the Tardonian district, in the estate of Corneciacum.

Various persons in different places also entrusted their properties to the church of Reims under this most blessed Father, for the remedy of their souls: Beroaldus [manuscript: Heroaldus] and Sairebertus gave houses, arable land, slaves, vineyards, and woods at Mount Betelini and at Taxovaria; Gairefredus and Austreberta gave, in the district of Laon, in the estate of Warocius, manses with their adjoining lands, vineyards, and slaves; Abbo gave his properties situated in the Porcian district, in the estate of Augusta; Landemarus gave, at Camarciacum in the district of Reims, manses with buildings, slaves, fields, vineyards, woods, meadows, and other appurtenances; Rodemarus gave his properties situated in the village of Castricum; and Austrebertus gave his in the same estate. Copies of these grants are still preserved in our possession. [Col. 0115C]

## CHAPTER XII  
### On his expulsion from the city of Reims

[Col. 0115D] [Annals 717; Sigebert 7, 8.]

At length, when a conflict arose between King Chilperic and Charles, the son of the aforementioned Pippin, and between them and Ragenfrid, the mayor of the palace, this Charles, while passing near the city of Reims, is said to have called out to blessed Rigobert, who was stationed above the city gate, ordering him to have that gate opened so that he might go to the church of the holy Mother of God to pray.

When Charles repeatedly pressed him with this demand, the man of God is said to have replied that he would not open it to him until he knew what outcome the dispute that had begun would have, lest he betray the city entrusted to him to be plundered by one who had plundered the property of several other cities. Charles is said to have angrily threatened him, declaring that, if he returned victorious and at peace, the man of God would no longer remain safe in that same city.

The blessed servant of the Lord is said to have customarily stayed above the gate called Basilicaris, either because it was supplied with basilicas arranged around it or because it provided access for those going to the basilicas situated in the village of Saint Remigius. With the windows of his upper room open, he used to contemplate the shrines of Saint Remigius and the other saints in order to pray. [Col. 0116A]

He had also built an oratory above the same gate in honor of Saint Michael the Archangel. From there he had made a practice of descending to the neighboring church of Saint Peter out of love of prayer. This oratory remained there for a considerable time, until the Emperor Louis gave that monastery of Saint Peter to his daughter Alpais. Her husband, a man named Bego, ordered the aforesaid oratory to be demolished, because one day he had struck his head violently against the lintel of its small doorway. He was tall in stature and had walked with his neck erect, without stooping to enter. He also alleged that, because of its height, the oratory obstructed the window of the church. [Col. 0116B]

Yet as soon as the oratory began to be demolished, Bego was immediately seized by a demon while he was in the district of Laon, far from the city of Reims. Moreover, through the road by this gate, dust and winds were constantly carried, so that darkness seemed to be brought upon the city; and no one could easily walk along that road. The oratory has since been repaired and restored, and it is venerated in the aforementioned honor of Saint Michael.

After the aforementioned Charles had gained supreme power through war, he removed this man of God, Rigobert, his own patron, who, as is reported, had received him from the holy baptismal font, from the episcopate, and gave the episcopal see to a certain Milo, a cleric known only by his tonsure, who had accompanied him on campaign [manuscript: who had proceeded with him to war]. [Col. 0116C]

This Charles was born from illicit intercourse with a serving woman, as is read of him in the royal annals. More audacious than the kings who had preceded him, he gave not only this episcopate but also other bishoprics of the Frankish kingdom to laymen and counts, allowing bishops no authority over the property of the churches.

But the evil that he perpetrated against this holy man and against other churches of Christ, the Lord returned upon his own head by a just judgment. The writings of the Fathers report that Saint Eucherius—whose body is buried in the monastery of Saint Trudo and who had once been bishop of Orléans—while engaged in prayer and directing his mind toward heavenly things, was carried away into the other life. Among the other things that the Lord revealed to him, he saw this Charles being tormented in the lowest hell. [Col. 0116D]

When Eucherius asked about this, his guiding angel replied that, by the judgment of the saints who will judge with the Lord at the future tribunal, Charles had been assigned to everlasting punishments because he had taken away their possessions. When blessed Eucherius returned to this world, he took care to report these things to Saint Boniface, who at that time had been sent by the apostolic see to Gaul to restore canonical rights, and to Fulrad, abbot of the monastery of Saint Denis and chief chaplain of King Pippin. He gave this as confirmation, so that, if they approached Charles’s tomb and did not find his body there, they would know that what he had reported concerning him was true. [Col. 0117A]

When they came to the place where the body of that Charles [Charles Martel] had been buried and opened his tomb, a serpent was suddenly seen to emerge. The tomb was found to be completely empty within and so blackened as if it had been burned by flames.

Concerning the aforesaid Milo, Pope Zacharias of Rome wrote the following to the recently mentioned Saint Boniface, among the other instructions he sent him (Zacharias, Letter 12):

> “Concerning Milo and others like him, who do great harm to the churches of God, preach to them at every opportunity, in season and out of season, so that they may withdraw from such wicked conduct, in accordance with the Apostle’s words (2 Tim. 4). If they heed your admonitions, they will save their souls; but if not, they themselves will perish, wrapped up in their sins. You, however, who preach rightly, will not lose your reward.” [Col. 0117B]

For the rest, Saint Rigobert of the Lord, obeying the Lord’s commands—which order those under persecution to flee from city to city— withdrew to Gascony. While living there in exile and visiting, with holy fervor, the memorials of many saints, he entered a certain basilica. While he remained intent upon prayer, the bells were rung as usual, but the two bells that were struck there were found to produce no sound.

Then the priest and the others standing around carefully investigated who he was and from where he had come. He declared himself to be a cleric who had come from Francia. They questioned him further about this strange occurrence: why, when struck in their customary manner, the bells did not resound. He then disclosed that two bells had been secretly stolen from one of his churches, and he supposed that these might be the same ones. [Col. 0117C]

When the bells were shown to him and he asserted that they had belonged to him, he was asked, as a test, to strike them. At his stroke they resounded loudly, proving that he had spoken the truth. While everyone was astonished at this event, his bells were returned to him, and he was deemed worthy alike of admiration and veneration. They were later brought back to Francia and restored to the estate of Gerniacum.

The aforementioned Milo—who had received the bishopric of Reims from Charles—is said to have encountered this man of God while serving as an ambassador among the Gascons in that region. He urged him to return to Francia and promised that his episcopal see would be restored to him.

When Rigobert returned, Milo asked him to hand over to him as his own property the possessions that he had already assigned to the church. Since Rigobert would not agree to this in any way, and Milo changed his mind about his promise, the man of God asked only that the altar of the holy Mother of God be granted to him, so that he might be permitted to celebrate Mass there. [Col. 0117D]

After finally obtaining this, he lived for a considerable time at the estate of Gerniacum, conducting his life in humility, frugality, vigils, prayers, almsgiving, and the practice of other good works. It was his custom to visit the city of Reims frequently and, as he had wished, to celebrate Mass at the altar of blessed Mary. Then he would proceed through the church of Saint Mauritius to Saint Remigius for the sake of prayer. From there he would visit the monastery of Saint Theoderic and return through the church of Saint Cyricus [Quiricus], at Culmiciacum, to Saint Peter at the estate of Gerniacum. [Col. 0118A]

## CHAPTER XIII  
### On the miracles displayed during his life

It happened once, then, that when he had come to Culmiciacum to pray at Saint Cyricus, he spoke with the steward of the church of Reims, who was present. When he was invited to dinner, he refused, since he was going to celebrate Mass at Saint Peter.

Meanwhile, a certain woman brought a goose to the vicedominus. He offered it to the bishop and asked him to order that it be received and carried away with him. A servant of the man of God took it and carried it, but suddenly it escaped from his hands and flew away, depriving the boy of any hope of catching it again.

When the holy Father saw the boy extremely distressed, he consoled him gently, as the very mild man he was. He taught him that one should neither weep nor become troubled over the loss of temporal possessions, but should always hope in the Lord, who gives generously to all (James 1). [Col. 0118B]

And behold, after some time, the bird flew back of its own accord, descended to the ground before the holy bishop, and proceeded ahead of him like a guide. It never strayed from the path until it reached the estate of Gerniacum, where they were going. The man of God would not allow it to be killed and kept it as a guide along the journey. For it is said to have been accustomed to run ahead of him whenever he went to the city or returned from it.

Adrian, pontiff of the apostolic see, also mentions this blessed bishop in a letter addressed to Tilpin, later bishop of Reims. In it he makes a complaint concerning him, writing as follows:

> “Your Fraternity has reported to us that, when discord arose among the Franks, the archbishop of Reims, named Rigobert, was removed and expelled from his see contrary to the canons, without any crime, without any judgment of the bishops, and without any consent or inquiry by the apostolic see. This occurred solely because he had previously refused to join the party (Latin *parte*; original reading *partem*) of the man who later took that part of the kingdom into his own power—the part in which the city of Reims lies, namely, in the kingdom of Austrasia. That episcopate, together with another episcopate and other churches, was given, or rather usurped contrary to God and his authority, by secular powers to a certain Milo, a cleric known only by his tonsure and ignorant of ecclesiastical order. [Col. 0118C]
>
> “Other episcopates of that same diocese of Reims were divided in various ways; some remained, for the most part, without bishops; bishops and clerics sometimes received ordination from other metropolitans; they had unauthorized places of refuge and did not submit to being judged or disciplined by their own bishops; and clerics, priests, monks, and nuns lived without ecclesiastical law, according to their own will and license,” and so forth. [Col. 0118D]

## CHAPTER XIV  
### On his death and burial

Finally, this blessed bishop Rigobert, distinguished by excellent deeds and great virtues, spent many years in this way of life. Having bravely completed the warfare of the present life, he died on the day before the Nones of January.

He was reverently buried by priests in the aforementioned estate where he used to live, in the church of Saint Peter, on the southern side of the altar. After his holy burial, he shone there through many miracles, plainly revealing how great was his merit before God. These miracles, however, were not recorded because of negligence or the scarcity of writers. [Col. 0119A]

Three lame men from that same place are remembered by its inhabitants as having been healed there. The signs of their restored health—namely, their walking sticks and stools—were kept for a long time in the same church, until his blessed relics were transferred from there.

A certain blind woman named Ansildis [probably Ausisdis], an inhabitant of that place, also received there the former light of her eyes through the merits of his intercession.

A boy who was devoted to his studies under the priest of the place once began to leap playfully over his tomb, showing no honor to God or to his saint who was buried there. But so that the merit of the buried man might be revealed and such presumption restrained, the boy’s foot immediately began to hurt. Soon he became lame and lost the use of one foot. [Col. 0119B]

When the priest learned of this, he arranged for a railing to be made around the tomb, so that no ignorant person might suffer something similar. In the same basilica, after Rigobert’s burial, voices of such sweetness are reported to have been heard repeatedly that they were proved to be nothing other than angelic voices.

A light of such brilliance also shone there in the middle of the nights that it seemed to surpass the radiance of the sun. Once, with an immense brightness, it penetrated the priest’s nearby dwelling. When he saw this, such fear seized the priest that thereafter he showed this place greater reverence than he had previously been accustomed to show. [Col. 0119C]

Many sick people suffering from various illnesses are healed at this man of God’s tomb. Certain fever sufferers, coming with faith, offer a candle as a votive gift and take up dust scraped from the tomb. They mix it with water, drink it, and obtain health through the merits of this saint. Those afflicted with toothache kiss this tomb with the veneration owed to it and likewise deserve to be healed.

## CHAPTER XV  
### On the translation of his body

While this illustrious confessor of the Lord shone in that place, glorified by many signs, Hincmar, bishop of Reims, transferred him from there and carried him to the monastery of Saint Theoderic, placing him beside the tomb of that blessed man. [Col. 0119D]

While he was venerated there for several years, the Lord deigned to perform many more miracles through him. Many who were afflicted with fevers or tormented by toothache came there in faith, sought his assistance, and rejoiced to receive divine healing.

Among them was a certain woman named Audinga, from a nearby estate called Colmelecta. Worn down by fevers, she is said to have conducted the following experiment privately in the hope of recovering her health. She had three candles made of equal size. She assigned one to Saint Theoderic, another to Saint Theodulf, and the third to Saint Rigobert. Lighting them all at once, she decided to see which would outlast the others in burning.

When this had been done, and the candle bearing the name of blessed Rigobert continued burning longer than the others, the woman regarded this as pleasing to God and resolved to make her vow to that saint. Immediately she prepared another candle, dedicated solely to the veneration of this gracious man. She came to the appointed place, offered her little gift, and, after praying before the relics of the saint of God that she had sought, fell asleep. When she awoke, she found that she had recovered the health she desired. [Col. 0120A]

Nine years later, the bones of this blessed bishop were carried to the city of Reims and placed in the basilica dedicated to Saint Denis, where the burial place of the canons of Reims was then located.

At that time there was a certain blind woman in an estate called the Court of the Alamanni [Aumencourt]. While sleeping, she heard in a dream a voice saying to her: “What are you doing here? Why are you lying here? Tomorrow Bishop Hincmar and the canons of Reims will transfer Saint Rigobert. Go to him, and he will help you.” [Col. 0120B]

At daybreak she rose and hastened there, carrying a candle with her. As soon as she approached the little shrine containing the blessed relic, she deserved to receive again the light she had once lost.

A certain deaf man also came on the very day of this translation. When he touched the little shrine carrying the sacred body, he immediately recovered his hearing. He too reported that he had been summoned in the following manner.

At night, while he was resting in an inn, an unknown person lightly (Latin *leviter*; manuscript I: *leniter*, “gently”) struck him on the side and awakened him. After waking him, the person called him. He felt the one touching him but, being deaf, did not hear the caller. Those who were staying with him in the house, however, heard a voice urging him to go as quickly as possible to Saint Rigobert, although they saw no one. He went immediately and found the salvation he had long desired. [Col. 0120C]

Because the aforementioned church was later being demolished on account of the need to construct the city wall in response to the attacks of the pagans, Bishop Fulco brought the venerable limbs of this blessed Father into the city and placed them in the middle of the church of the blessed Mother of God, Mary, behind the altar of the holy Cross. There, too, many who approached with faith found the healing they desired.

About this same time, a monk of the monastery of the most blessed Remigius named Sigloardus was seized by a very severe fever and appeared also to have become incapable of rational thought. One night, when he had gone to bed without having eaten and was unable in any way to rest, being tormented on every side, he called upon blessed Rigobert, crying out for him to bring assistance. He immediately recovered the health he desired. [Col. 0120D]

After some time, the relics of this holy man were carried to the Vermandian district, to an estate called Nemincum, which Count Odalricus had at that time bestowed upon the church of Reims and which Bishop Fulco had assigned for the sustenance of the canons. A nearby priest named Signinus lived there and was tormented by severe toothache.

When he heard that these precious relics had been brought there, but was prevented by his illness from going in person, he took care to send a candle there. Although absent in body, he did not cease to implore Saint Rigobert of the Lord with prayers and tears, so that through his intercession he might deserve to receive healing.

As soon as his little offering reached the saint’s shrine, he deserved to feel that the heavenly physician was present to him, having recovered his health. He immediately set out for the place of the sacred healer, poured himself out in tears before his memorial, gave thanks, and declared how many benefits the Lord had granted him through the invocation of this Father. [Col. 0121A]

Not long afterward, the sacred relics were brought back to the city of Reims. The church of Saint Denis outside the city wall was rebuilt through the efforts and at the expense of the canons of Reims, and the relics were honorably installed there together with those of blessed Theodulf.

## CHAPTER XVI  
### On Abel, his successor

Abel is found to have followed blessed Rigobert in the episcopal succession, although some report that he was only a chorepiscopus. Nevertheless, we find from various testimonies that he was a bishop, especially in the letters of Pope Zacharias addressed to Saint Boniface (Zacharias, Letter 85, volume III of the Councils). [Col. 0121B]

In one of these letters Zacharias mentions that the aforementioned blessed Boniface had indicated in his letters, among other things, that he had ordained three bishops in the respective metropolitan cities: Grimo in the city called Rouen; Abel, the second, in the city called Reims; and Hartbertus, the third, in the city called Sens:

> “He was also with us,” he says, “and brought us your letter, as well as writings from Karlomannus and Pippin, through which you requested that we send the three pallia to the three metropolitan bishops named above. We have granted this for the reunification and restoration of the churches of God.” [Col. 0121C]

Likewise, in another letter of his to the same man (Zacharias, Letter 9, elsewhere numbered 4):

> “As for the metropolitan bishops, namely Grimo, whom we now know, Abel, and Haribertus, whom you established in each metropolitan see throughout the provinces, we confirm these through your testimony and send them pallia for their firm stability and for the increase of the church of God, so that it may advance in a better condition.
>
> “For [manuscript I: *etiam*, “also”], we have sent them instructions concerning what the custom of the pallium is and how those who are granted permission to use the pallium ought to profess their faith, so that they may know what (Latin *quod*; manuscript I: *quid*) the use of the pallium entails and may preach to the people entrusted to them the way of salvation. Thus ecclesiastical discipline may be preserved unimpaired in their churches and remain unshaken; and the priesthood within them may be undefiled, as it was formerly, but clean and acceptable to God, insofar as the human condition [manuscript: *conditio*] permits.
>
> “In this way no one may be found deviating from the sacred canons, and their pure sacrifice may be offered by them, so that God may be pleased with their gifts and they may be able to present to the people of God, purified in mind from every stain, the sincere service of the Christian religion.” [Col. 0121D]

Certain charters of this bishop are also found, bearing his name as their title.

Pope Adrian also mentions him in the aforementioned letter to Tilpin, archbishop, adding after the matters already stated above as follows (Adrian I, in the passage cited above, chapter 13):

> “The archbishop of blessed memory, Boniface, legate of the holy Roman Church, and the aforementioned most beloved Fulradus, archpriest of Francia, labored greatly during the time of our predecessors Zacharias and Stephen [Stephen II], the successor of that man, so that our predecessor of blessed memory, the lord Zacharias, might send the pallium to the archbishop of Reims, named Abel, at the request of the aforementioned Boniface. Abel had been appointed by him, but was not permitted to remain there; rather, he was expelled contrary to God’s will, and the church of Reims remained without a bishop for a long time and for many years. The property of the church was taken away from that episcopate and divided among laymen, as happened with other bishoprics, but especially with the metropolitan city of Reims. [Col. 0122A]”

## CHAPTER XVII  
### On Bishop Tilpin

Tilpin followed those mentioned above in the episcopal succession. He had been taken from the monastery of Saint Denis, and it is found that the great Charles obtained the pallium for him from Pope Adrian, as is revealed by a letter of that pope addressed to Tilpin himself, which begins as follows:

> “ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and most holy brother TILPIN, archbishop of the church of Reims [Note: [Col. 0121D] It is not extant among his letters.]. [Col. 0122B]
>
> “Because we well remember that, at the request of our spiritual son and glorious king of the Franks, Charles, and with our most beloved abbot Fulradus, archpriest of Francia, giving you a good testimonial concerning your holiness and learning, we sent you the pallium according to custom, together with a privilege, so that the metropolitan church of Reims might remain in its established condition; and [manuscript I omits *et*] we remember this.” [Col. 0122C]

After several further matters, when he was speaking about the property taken from the church of Reims, he says:

> “Your Fraternity has already recovered a large part of those properties through our glorious son Charles, and previously through his brother Carlomannus. You also possess, in part, an order of affairs correctly arranged both with respect to the bishops and in other matters according to canonical and apostolic authority. Therefore you asked us to grant you and your church a privilege by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of the holy Roman see and of ourselves, so that what you already possess in completed form may continue to endure, and what is not yet complete may, with the help of God and the Apostle Saint Peter, be brought to completion through our authority. [Col. 0122D]
>
> “For this reason, with ardent spirit and divine assistance, supported by apostolic authority, we establish not only the old provisions according to the sacred canons and the decrees of this apostolic holy see, but also grant you new provisions in response to your good zeal. By the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, to whom God and our Savior Jesus Christ gave the power of binding and loosing human sins in heaven and on earth (Matt. 16; John 21), we confirm and strengthen these provisions.
>
> “We confirm that the church of Reims shall remain a metropolitan church, as it was in ancient times, and the first see of its diocese; and that you, who by God’s cooperation have been ordained in that see, shall be the primate of that diocese, together with all the cities that from ancient times were subject to the metropolitan church of Reims. This shall also be confirmed forever to you and your successors. [Col. 0123A]
>
> “We also forbid anyone, according to the tradition of the holy canons, after your summons from this world, to transfer or appoint there a bishop brought from another episcopate. Nor may anyone remove your parishes, churches, or cities, or ever divide the diocese of Reims, but it shall remain intact as it was in ancient times, as the sacred canons, the authority of our predecessors, and our own authority have established.
>
> “No one shall ever presume or be able to remove you, or a bishop and primate of Reims in future times, from that episcopate without canonical judgment; nor, in that judgment (Latin *illo*; manuscript I: *ullo*, “any”), without the consent of the Roman pontiff, if the person under judgment appeals to this holy Roman see, which is recognized as the head of the entire world. [Col. 0123B]
>
> “Remaining solely subject to the Roman pontiff, strive and endeavor, with the Lord’s help and supported by the authority of blessed Peter and of ourselves from this holy see, to govern the diocese and parish of Reims entrusted to you according to the holy canons and the commands of this holy see, so that you may be able to hear with his elect that desirable voice of our Lord Jesus Christ: ‘Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your lord’ (Matt. 25). [Col. 0123C]
>
> “You have also brought to our attention that certain persons from that same diocese of Reims were receiving ordinations from other bishops and had unauthorized refuges. We prohibit this in every respect. Rather, as sacred authority teaches, in the summoning and holding of provincial synods, in ordinations, and in judgments, the church of Reims and the archbishop established in it shall possess such authority as the sacred canons and the constitutions of this holy Church teach.
>
> “No one, at any time, shall presume to inflict upon you or the church of Reims any division or violence concerning the property lawfully belonging to it, as was done previously. For if—which we do not believe—anyone should attempt to act against this command of ours with rash audacity, unless he corrects himself quickly, and especially after admonition, let him know that he is bound by the bond of anathema under God’s eternal judgment. But if anyone observes the apostolic commands and attains the standard of right and orthodox faith, let him receive the grace of blessing. [Col. 0123D]
>
> “We command that these matters defined by us in this document of confirmation be preserved in your church forever for the sake of their confirmation.
>
> “We also enjoin upon your Fraternity that, since certain matters concerning the ordination of a bishop named Lul of the holy church of Mainz have reached us, you are to take with you Viomagus and Possessor, bishops, as well as the envoys of our glorious spiritual son Charles, king of the Franks, and diligently investigate everything concerning his ordination. Examine his faith and teaching, his conduct and morals, and his life. If he proves suitable and worthy to govern the episcopal chair, let him send to us, through his envoys and with your letters and testimony—or those of the other bishops whom we have ordered to be with you—a written and subscribed Catholic and orthodox confession of faith. Then we may send him the pallium according to custom, judge his ordination valid, and have him established as archbishop in that holy church of Mainz. Farewell.” [Col. 0124A]

That bishop recovered for the Church, in various places, properties that had been seized, obtaining them through the royal authority itself and, through the Church’s representatives, before various judges according to law, and restored them to ecclesiastical right. In particular, through a certain Achabbus, who labored diligently both in Francia and beyond the Loire to recover the Church’s property, he restored to the Church, after legally vindicating them, many estates as well as slaves. This bishop is also found to have increased the Church’s possessions through properties and slaves purchased from certain persons for a price; and, after arranging colonies, he organized the rights of certain villages. He also supplied this Church with books of the sacred Scriptures, some of which we still use.

Finally, he is reported to have established monks in the monastery of Saint Remigius and to have trained them in the monastic life, although that same monastery is said previously to have housed canons, from the time of Abbot Gibehard, who is found to have gathered that congregation out of love for God and Saint Remigius and to have maintained it up to this time.

Finally, in the very first year of King Karlomannus’s reign, he obtained from Karlomannus, the son of Pippin, a privilege of immunity for the church of Rheims, modeled on the immunities that his predecessors, the kings, had granted to this church. He also took care to show him the documents of these privileges, so that no public judge would dare enter the lands of this church to provide lodging, administer any judicial proceedings, or demand any hospitality there at all. Whatever his predecessors had granted to that church, it was to be able to retain perpetually as an established grant.

Afterward he also obtained from the same king another privilege remitting all tolls; another concerning the bridge of Baison; another concerning the burned charters, which had been destroyed by fire through negligence at that time, so that the property and resources of the Church that it possessed at that time would remain confirmed to that same Church, without diminution, by the king’s authority; another concerning the soldiers residing in the village of Juviniacum on the land of Saint Mary and Saint Remigius, to whom he granted and remitted every military levy that they owed. He obtained yet another concerning those who resided at Cruciniana, at Curba village, or anywhere in the district of Tardenois within the land of the church of Rheims.

The same King Karlomannus, during this bishop’s pontificate, also gave by charter, for the place of his burial and for the remedy of his soul, the village of Novilliacum, situated in the district of Urtinum, with all its appurtenances and dependencies, in complete integrity, to the basilica or monastery of Saint Remigius, where he is also known to have received burial.

His brother, the emperor Charles the Great, obtained for this bishop Tilpinus the pallium from Pope Hadrian through his legates and letters, as is contained in the letters of that same pope addressed to that king concerning this request of his. This bishop also obtained from that king a privilege of immunity for the church of Rheims, according to the exemplars of the preceding kings’ privileges; another privilege concerning the soldiers of the district of Tardenois, according to the cession made by his brother, King Karlomannus; another concerning the burned charters; and another confirming the gift of his aforementioned brother the king, by which that king donated the villages of Novilliacum and Bebriacum to the basilica of Saint Remigius.

Moreover, during this bishop’s episcopate, many people transferred their possessions to the church of Rheims, both to Saint Mary and to Saint Remigius.

This bishop died in the forty-seventh year of his episcopate. His body was buried at the feet of Saint Remigius, where it is seen to bear this inscription:

> Here in this earth rests Tilpinus, bishop of honor,  
> For whom Christ was life both in living and in dying.  
> Holy martyr Dionysius sent him  
> As a watchful shepherd and a father  
> To the people of Rheims.  
> Feeding them for more than forty years,  
> He departed stripped of the garment of old age.  
> When the month of September had reached its fourth day before the Nones,  
> At the time when he died, death remains life for him.  
> And because place and rank had joined these two, Hincmar  
> Made this tomb for him and composed its inscription.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning Bishop Vulfarius

Vulfarius followed Tilpinus. Before his episcopate, the aforementioned great emperor Charles had appointed him as a royal envoy over all Campania to settle lawful judgments. He was assigned to the following districts: Dolomensis, Vongensis, Castriciensis, Stadonensis, Catalaunensis, Otmunensis [otherwise Ormunensis], Laudunensis, Vadensis, Portianus, Tardenois, and Suessionensis. Like certain other wise and God-fearing abbots who had been delegated throughout Gaul and Germany by the aforementioned emperor, he was charged to investigate carefully how bishops, abbots, counts, and abbesses conducted themselves in each district; what agreement and friendship they maintained with one another; whether they had good and suitable stewards and advocates; and, wherever necessary, inquire into and carry out both the royal justice and the justice of the churches of God, of widows and orphans, and of all other people. They were also to strive to correct whatever required correction, as far as they could do so better; and whatever they could not correct themselves, they were to bring before the emperor and faithfully report all these matters to that prince.

Thus the aforementioned illustrious man Vulfarius, while sitting with certain counts in the public judicial sessions to determine the judgments entrusted to him, and although he had already been summoned to the episcopate but had not yet been ordained, is found to have recovered certain properties and several slaves or tenant-farmers for the church of Rheims and to have legally vindicated them through the Church’s advocates. After he had been ordained bishop, he is likewise found to have acquired still more for the Church—property and tenant-farmers—both before the royal authority and before tenant-farmers and public judges, not only through the Church’s representatives but also when acting in person. The great emperor Charles is shown to have trusted him greatly by the fact that he entrusted to his keeping fifteen illustrious Saxon hostages whom Vulfarius had brought from Saxony.

He is found to have held a synod in the year 814 from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the church of Noyon, during the reign of Louis, the son of Charles. His fellow bishops Hildoardus, Ermeno, Jesse, Ragumbertus, Grimboldus, Rothardus, Wendilmarus, and Ostroaldus were assembled with him, as were the chorepiscopi Waltarius and Spernus, and the abbots Adalbardus, Nantarius, Fulradus, Erichus, Hildericus, Remigius, Ebo, and Sigbaldus, together with the rest of the clergy, priests, and deacons. The counts Gunthardus, Rotfridus, Gislebertus, and Otnerus were also summoned.

When all these men were seated, a dispute was heard between the bishops Wendilmarus and Rothardus concerning the boundaries of their dioceses. It was requested and determined that the following places beyond the River Oise, in the district of Noyon, should belong to the parish of the church of Noyon: Varina, Urbscampus, Trapiacus, Jerusalem, Harbaudianisva, or the church of Saint Leodegarius, together with the remaining villages belonging to these churches. All the other places beyond the aforesaid river, in the aforesaid district, were to belong to the parish of the church of Soissons.

The bishops, chorepiscopi, abbots, priests, and deacons written above investigated these matters most carefully and agreed to them, as did the portion of the church of Noyon—clergy and laity—and likewise the portion of the church of Soissons, clergy and laity. With one mind and one consent they resolved to confirm them.

Nor was it only in his own diocese. We also find that Amalarius, archbishop of the city of Trier, together with his fellow bishop Adalmarus and Herilandus, was summoned by command of the great emperor Charles by that same metropolitan Vulfarius to the episcopal ordination of a certain Frotharius, a priest of the aforesaid church of Trier, and obeyed him.

During the episcopate of this Bishop Vulfarius, a council of many Fathers is also found to have been assembled at Rheims by the emperor Charles the Great. Forty-three chapters are read as having been established there, dealing with the basis of the faith, the honor of the Church of God, the administration of its rulers and ministers, fidelity to the king, and the welfare of the entire kingdom.

He also properly assigned certain estates of the church of Rheims to colonies, after distributing and describing them. He exchanged some of the Church’s property and slaves, together with certain persons, as the needs of the parties required. From the treasures of Saint Mary and Saint Remigius he likewise exchanged [or lent] certain things, with the testimony of illustrious men, both clerical and lay, and had ecclesiastical ornaments or vessels made from them, as seemed appropriate to him.
