Finally, in one of his letters he states that he received permission from the emperor to travel to Rome for the sake of prayer at Saint Peter’s; but whether he went, we do not know for certain.

The revenues of certain estates of the Church, commendably distributed as alms for the salvation of his body and soul, are recorded in several descriptions made at that time. Among them are Termidum, Grand Meadow, Vindicum, Furvilla [manuscript: Furnilla], Gramadum [Graviagum], Pidum, Cadevellum, and the Court of Magnaldus. In the distribution of alms there were 1,975 modii of grain [variant: 1,167]. Of animals, both large and small, there were 168 head. Likewise, among the estates of Fagus, or Boleticum, and certain others, there were 1,052 modii of grain, 64 modii of wine, 5 modii of salt, together with various animals and other assorted goods expended. Provision was also made for whatever would suffice for the brothers of the monastery of Orbais. From this it may be understood that, in the larger places as well, many more things were then being dispersed.

He also obtained from the emperor Louis a privilege of immunity for the church of Rheims and the monastery of Saint Remigius, according to the privilege granted by Charles Augustus, his father.

## CHAPTER XIX. Concerning Bishop Ebo

Ebo succeeded him. He was an energetic man, educated in the liberal disciplines, a native of the region beyond the Rhine and a German, and, as is said, the foster-brother and fellow student of the emperor Louis. He took care to furnish the Church with many advantages, especially with craftsmen whom he gathered from various places, giving them homes and rewarding them with benefits.

He restored to ecclesiastical right certain slaves or tenant-farmers who had deserted the Church, after they had been legally vindicated and recovered before public judges, both by himself and through Radulphus, the steward and advocate of the Church. He also exchanged certain properties and slaves of the Church with various persons for the parties’ mutual advantage. He obtained temporary privileges concerning these exchanges. From the emperor Louis he also secured letters to Count Robert for the defense of ecclesiastical property, which certain people were attempting to seize. He organized several colonies of the Church, assigning tenants and their services through capable men.

He constructed the Church’s archive in extremely secure buildings, together with a crypt dedicated in honor of Saint Peter and all the apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins, where, by God’s favor, we appear to serve Him. It was built with fitting workmanship, and there the relics of many apostles and other saints are preserved. Several manifestations are known to have been displayed there.

I myself saw a slave belonging to my foster-father Gundacrus, who lived in sight of that church, so terrified by a dreadful vision, as though of an armed man, when he rashly approached to urinate near the window of this crypt, that he was thought to have lost his senses. They also say that a certain Rohingus, a deacon of this place, was restrained from a similar presumption by an identical vision. Henceforth it was carefully ordained and prohibited that anyone should dare attempt such a thing.

The pinnacle of this church appears to display the following inscription, adorned also with figures or images of Pope Stephen and the emperor Louis:

> When Louis Caesar was made emperor, with Stephen crowning him,  
> In this place, with the great pope present, and Ebo then bishop,  
> He renewed all the foundations of this place;  
> The bishop subjected the city’s rights to himself and increased everything.

The following epitaph is preserved for Ebo’s mother:

> If you ask about the beginnings of my life,  
> Know that they belonged to the dawn of Charles’s reign.  
> My final day passed while Louis was triumphing.  
> The Rhine, the German stream, washed my earliest years;  
> Then the Gallic Loire nurtured my second age.  
> The Seine fostered my youth; the foul Vidula—filth-fouled [the sense is elliptical].  
> The bishop of this city was my only-born son.  
> He took me as his companion in his labors,  
> Eager to restore a place close to ruin.  
> We spent nearly ten years together here.  
> Ebo was the ruler; I, Himiltrudis, his humble mother.  
> Together we raised the foundations of the holy see.  
> While the bishop was carrying out the labor owed to God,  
> I, weary, was seeking rest. Behold, beneath this tomb  
> The fifth day before the Kalends of September carried me away.  
> Traveler, always beware of excesses.  
> I confess that I was not of service as I ought to have been, while I was able.  
> Say, “Forgiveness instead of vengeance; grant it, O God, to sinners.”

At the urging of this bishop, Halitgarius, bishop of Cambrai, composed six books, *On Remedies for Sins*, and on the order and judgments of penance. The following letter of Ebo to him survives:

> To the most reverend brother and son in Christ, Bishop Halitgarius, Ebo, an unworthy bishop, sends greetings.
>
> I do not doubt that your Charity knows how greatly we are constrained by concern for ecclesiastical discipline, by the many necessities of our subjects, and, in addition, by the worldly oppressions by which we are daily harassed. Therefore, as I told you, I have been quite unable to extract from the sayings of the Fathers and the judgments of the canons a Penitential for the use of our fellow priests, because when the mind is divided among many things, it becomes less capable of attending to each one.
>
> This is what greatly troubles me in the present matter: the judgments concerning penitents in the little books of our priests are so confused, so diverse, and so mutually contradictory, and are supported by the authority of no one, that they can scarcely be distinguished because of their disagreement. As a result, our priests are entirely unable to assist those who come seeking the remedy of penance, both because of the confusion of the books and because of their own slowness of understanding.
>
> Therefore, dearest brother, do not refuse yourself to us—you who have always flourished with ardent spirit in divine disciplines and with diligent care in meditation upon the Scriptures, in the most perfect leisure. Take up, I beg you, without a word of excuse, the burden of this task, imposed upon you by me but to be lightened by the Lord, whose burden is light (Matthew 11).
>
> Do not fear or dread the size of this work. Approach it confidently, for the one who said, “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Psalm 80:11), will be with you. You know very well that small things suffice for the small, and that a poor crowd cannot approach the table of the great.
>
> Do not withhold from us the knowledge of your devotion. Do not place the lamp that has been kindled in you beneath a bushel; set it instead upon a lofty lampstand, so that it may shine for all your brothers who are in the house of God (Matthew 5:3). Bring forth for us, like a learned scribe (Matthew 13:52), what you have received from the Lord.
>
> His grace will be with you on the journey of this labor—the grace of the one who added himself as a third companion on the road to the two disciples who were traveling, and opened their understanding so that they might comprehend the holy Scriptures (Luke 24:32).
>
> May the Paraclete Spirit cause your breast to shine with every teaching of truth and with perfect knowledge of charity, dearest brother. Farewell.

To this, Halitgarius replied as follows:

> To the lord and venerable Father in Christ, Archbishop Ebo, Halitgarius, the least of Christ’s servants, sends greetings.
>
> After I received the letters sent by Your Blessedness, in which you deigned to exhort me not to submit the sharpness of my mind to sluggish and idle leisure, but to devote myself vigilantly each day to the knowledge and meditation of sacred Scripture, and, moreover, to gather into a single volume a Penitential from the judgments of the holy Fathers and the canons, this command seemed harsh to me, very difficult, and fearful: that I should undertake a burden which I know was abandoned by prudent men.
>
> I resisted your will greatly—not with the insolent stubbornness of an impudent man, but warned by my own weakness. For, troubled by this concern, I considered it necessary to suspend myself for a time from the rashness of writing, since I had weighed the difficulty of the task imposed. Yet I neither wished nor ought entirely to resist the authority of the one imposing it. I was certain that the dignity of your command would assist my weakness far more than the difficulty of my ignorance would burden me.
>
> Farewell.

This Bishop Ebo received at Rheims the aforementioned Pope Stephen together with King Louis, after that king had defeated and subdued with an army the Slavs living in the East. The aforementioned Pope Stephen, who had succeeded Leo, sent his legates to that prince and informed him that he would gladly see him wherever it pleased him.

When the king heard this, he was filled with great joy and ordered his men to go out to meet the supreme pontiff and prepare suitable services for him. After them the king himself also went. They met one another in the great field of Rheims, and each dismounted from his horse. The prince prostrated himself three times on the ground before the feet of so great a pontiff. They greeted one another magnificently, embraced, and kissed one another peacefully, and proceeded to the church. After they had prayed there for a long time, the pontiff rose and, with his choir, proclaimed royal praises for the king in a loud voice.

Afterward the pontiff honored him with great and numerous honors, and likewise Queen Hirmingard, and then their nobles and ministers. On the following Sunday, in the church, before the solemn celebration of Mass, in the presence of the clergy and all the people, he consecrated and anointed him emperor, placing upon his head a golden crown of extraordinary beauty adorned with the most precious gems, which he had brought with him. He named the queen Augusta and placed a golden crown upon her head.

As long as the apostolic pope remained there, they conferred daily concerning the defense of the holy Church of God. But after the emperor had bestowed upon him the greatest gifts—far more than he had received from him—he dismissed him to return to Rome with his legates, commanding them to provide him with honorable service everywhere along the journey.

Since the aforementioned Bishop Ebo desired to repair the building of the church of Saint Mary, the holy Mother of God, which had almost collapsed through prolonged decay, and in which Pope Stephen II is found to have once bestowed apostolic privileges upon King Pippin, and Leo III upon the great emperor Charles, as is mentioned in the letter of the emperor Lothair addressed to Leo IV in commendation of Archbishop Hincmar (below, Book III, chapter 10), he asked the aforesaid emperor Louis to grant him the city wall for the purpose of renewing and enlarging that basilica.

That prince, enjoying the most tranquil peace and supported by the most glorious power of the empire, fearing no barbarian incursions, did not refuse. Rather, out of love for God and in honor of His blessed Mother, he granted the request most graciously and ordered it to be carried out by a written record of his command, issuing the following decree of his privilege:

> In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the ordering of divine providence, emperor Augustus.
>
> If, with religious generosity, we remit to venerable places what our predecessors, kings or emperors, had required from them for the uses of the commonwealth, so that it may be expended for the advantages and necessities of those holy places, and if we lend a favorable ear to the most salutary suggestions and petitions of our faithful concerning this same matter, we provide most wisely both for our soul and for the king and kingdom. For nothing belonging to the commonwealth is seen to be diminished when anything from that same commonwealth is granted through pious acts to religious places, to the needs of the churches of God, or to the benefit of God’s servants.
>
> Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of God, present and future, and especially to our successors in the height of authority in which, by the Lord’s will, we have been established, and to those who are thereafter established by the Lord of lords: that the venerable Archbishop Ebo of the church of Rheims, bishop of the most reverend see of Saint Remigius, the most glorious pontiff and our special patron, has made known to our Clemency that the holy mother church of the aforesaid metropolitan city, consecrated in honor of holy Mary, ever virgin and Mother of God, has been worn down by the old age of time.
>
> In that church, by God’s authorship and with Saint Remigius as cooperator [manuscript: cooperating], our Frankish people, together with our namesake king of that people, was deemed worthy to be washed in the baptism of the sacred font and illuminated by the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. That most noble king himself was also found worthy, by God’s mercy, to be anointed for royal power. There, too, by divine favor, we were crowned by the hands of the lord Stephen, Roman supreme pontiff, to the title and authority of the empire.
>
> Desiring to renew that church for the sake of so many benefits bestowed upon us there by God, and seeing the inconvenience of the place for carrying out this work, we grant for this purpose, and for all other structures that must be built for the necessities of the servants of God dwelling there, the entire wall of the city with its gates, and all the labor with all the expenses that customarily had been performed and paid at our royal palace of Aachen from the property and resources of that church and of the bishopric of Rheims.
>
> We grant this as our alms and for the remedy of the soul of our lord and father, and of the other predecessors who had held that bishopric for some time to their own peril and had expended its property and resources for their own uses against ecclesiastical regulations; as a result, less benefit than ought to have accrued had come from them to the holy places established in that bishopric.
>
> We also wish the vassals and all our faithful who possess anything from the property of that bishopric to serve this work, as was established by our lord and father of good memory and as was decreed by our lord and grandfather of pious memory, Pippin: they are to pay tithes and ninths to that holy church from the property they possess from it.
>
> We also grant that all the public roads running around that church, which may obstruct the construction of cloisters and dwellings for the servants of God, may be transferred and altered. And if anything belonging to our treasury is held there, we likewise perpetually grant it through this privilege of our authority, so that no judge, count, envoy, or anyone exercising judicial power may ever presume to inflict upon that aforesaid holy church of God at Rheims any disturbance or impediment of accusation.
>
> We beseech our successors, mindful of their salvation—both present and eternal—and mindful also of the benefits conferred upon us, our people, and our predecessors in that holy place through Blessed Remigius and by the merits of Saint Mary, to preserve for all time, inviolate, whatever we have often granted to that aforesaid holy place for the love of God, His holy Mother, and our blessed protector Remigius, just as they will wish their own good deeds to be preserved by their successors.
>
> And so that this authority of our grant may possess more fully the strength of permanence in future times, we have decreed that it be undersigned by the impression of our ring.

He also granted to the church of Rheims, at the request of that bishop, a certain slave craftsman of his named Rumaldus, so that he might use the talent granted to him by the Lord and make progress according to his abilities throughout the days of his life. He confirmed this cession by a written record and the sealing of his ring.

He also gave that pontiff another privilege concerning the relocation of public roads in order to construct certain enclosures in places near the city, and concerning various advantages for the Church; he marked it as well with his ring.

Moreover, concerning the restoration to that holy see of estates that had once been taken from it, he issued, together with his son, the emperor Caesar Lothair, the following authority of a privilege:

> In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis and Lothair, by the ordering of divine providence, emperors Augustus.
>
> If, through the gift of our generosity, we confer some benefit upon places dedicated to God and relieve ecclesiastical necessities through our assistance, we clearly believe that this will profit us both in passing through mortal life in time and in happily attaining eternal life.
>
> Therefore we wish it to be known to all our faithful, present and future, that, out of reverence for the Christian faith and for the salvation of our souls, we had the holy church of Rheims—where our predecessors, the kings of the Franks, received the faith and the grace of holy baptism, and where we also received the imperial insignia through the laying on of the hand of the lord Pope Stephen—built from its foundations, and we decreed that it be consecrated in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ, Savior of the world, and likewise in honor of that holy and undefiled Mother, Mary.
>
> Thus, pierced by divine inspiration and inflamed by love of the heavenly homeland, we ordered certain estates that had once been taken from that holy see to be restored with devoted intent. These are: in the suburbs of that holy church, the church of Saint Sixtus, and likewise the church of Saint Martin, with their dependencies; outside the city, in the same parish, the baptismal church at the castle of Vonc, and likewise the baptismal church of Saint John in the same parish, with their dependencies, and Bretiniacum; also the estate of Sparnacum with its dependencies; and, in the estate called Lucida [Lude], as well as at Proviliacum [Prouilly], in the same district of Rheims.
>
> In the district of Dulcomensis, the estate called Cavera [variant: Canera], and likewise the estate called Verna in the district of Vertudum.
>
> And if thereafter we should decide in our time that anything more is to be added to the property of the aforesaid holy church, we establish through this privilege of our authority that not only what has been restored but also what is to be restored, whatever the rulers and ministers of the aforementioned church choose concerning those properties or within them, they shall perpetually possess, arrange, and administer as they see most advantageous. Without anyone’s unjust opposition, they shall order, dispose of, and do whatever they judge to be suitable and beneficial to the aforesaid church.
>
> And so that this confirmation of our authority may always possess firmer strength in all things in present and future times, we have signed it with our own hands and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our ring.

That bishop also obtained from the same emperor Louis a privilege of immunity for the church of Rheims, according to the ancient exemplars of the former kings. He obtained another privilege concerning the bridge of Bansion and the tolls or public exactions; another concerning the burned charters, according to the authority of the emperor Charles; and from Pippin, king of the Aquitanians, a privilege of immunity concerning the property of the church of Rheims situated in the district of Auvergne.

Concerning the estate of Sparnacum, he is also found to have received a separate privilege from Louis, and afterward another privilege separately from Lothair, his son.

This Bishop Ebo, with the counsel of the emperor Louis and the authority of Pope Paschal of Rome, traveled as far as the territory of the Danes for the sake of preaching and baptized many of them who came to the faith.

Finally, when a conflict arose between the father and the son—namely, between the emperor Louis and Lothair—he took the son’s side and, together with the other bishops, rebuked the emperor Louis for certain alleged faults, when his sons seized him and Lothair brought his father with him to the palace at Compiègne. There he afflicted him together with the bishops and certain other nobles [manuscript: leading men], who ordered him to go into a monastery and remain there for all the days of his life.

He refused this and did not consent to their will. Then all the bishops who were present are said to have harassed him, reproaching him for his sins, taking the sword from his thigh, and clothing him in sackcloth.

While Bishop Ebo was therefore frequently staying at the palace, the following vision concerning him was revealed in the monastery of Saint Remigius.

There was a certain monk named Raduinus, a Lombard by birth, who had once been abbot of the monastery on Mount Bardon in Italy, a place renowned for the memory of the most blessed Remigius. It had been dedicated through the efforts of Moderamnus, bishop of Rennes.

While the aforementioned Raduinus was performing the duties of his monastic profession in that monastery, he was led by love of the merits of the blessed Remigius to seek the threshold of his tomb. Living a religious life with the brothers of that place, he strove worthily to prepare himself for the heavenly warfare.

On a certain day—the feast of the sacred Assumption of the holy Mother of God—after the office of Matins had been completed and the other brothers had gone to rest, he alone remained in the choir for the sake of prayer, while the custodians of the church were sleeping.

When, fatigued by the continuation of the psalms, he began to fall asleep as slumber overtook him, he saw the most blessed Mother of God proceed from the place of the holy bishop’s tomb, shining with immense light. The evangelist John and the holy Remigius himself clung to her sides, and they seemed to approach him together by measured steps.

The glorious Virgin placed her hand gently upon his head and said:

“Brother Raduinus, what are you doing here?”

When he immediately fell forward to kiss her feet, she added:

“Where is Ebo, archbishop of Rheims, now living?”

He replied: “At the king’s command he is carrying out affairs of the palace.”

“And why,” she said, “does he wear away the thresholds of the palace so assiduously? He will certainly not become richer in the power of holiness by doing so. For the time will come—indeed, it will come very quickly—when he will not prosper in such matters.”

When he dared answer nothing to this, she continued to address him:

“What dispute among your kings is being debated by men?”

He replied: “Lady, Mother of the Savior of the world, your incorruptible holiness knows this better.”

She said: “Those who have been seduced by a desire for such great evil are now raging with empty audacity.”

For it was then the time when the emperor Louis was being mistreated by the insults of his sons.

“Behold,” she said, clasping the hand of Saint Remigius, “to him belongs the authority, handed down by Christ, over the enduring empire of the Franks. Just as this people received from his teaching the grace of conversion from unbelief, so too it always possesses the inviolable gift of establishing for them a king or emperor.”

When the most blessed Mother of God had said this, the aforementioned brother suddenly awoke.

## CHAPTER XX. Concerning the Deposition of Ebo

Therefore, after Louis had been restored to his kingdom and honor by his son of the same name, Ebo was deposed from the episcopate because of this action, on account of his disloyalty to the emperor.

For this same reason, he is reported previously to have deposed Jesse, bishop of Amiens, but is now said to have restored him to his former rank.

Concerning Ebo’s deposition, Pope Nicholas later inquired of the bishops of Gaul, and especially of the province of Belgica, and among other matters received the following in their replies.

Ebo, bishop of Reims, having received from Lothair the abbey of Saint Vedast for the betrayal of his father, became an instigator of false accusations. Having likewise falsely accused that same emperor, Ebo caused him to be expelled from the threshold of the church by his accomplices and committed to public penance, where he had him kept (in the year 834), until, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 834, Lothair, terrified by the assembly of his brothers and of many of the emperor-father’s faithful, fled and abandoned his father, who was still excluded from entering the church.

Along with him, among others, certain bishops who had supported him in his father’s adversity left their sees contrary to the sacred canons and departed with him: Jesse of Amiens, Herebold of Auxerre, Agobard of Lyon, and Bartholomew, bishop of Narbonne. After Lothair’s departure, the bishops who had been present reconciled the emperor in the church of Saint Denis and restored him to ecclesiastical communion.

When Ebo heard this, he entrusted to certain of his familiars a full complement of his men and assigned them a definite meeting place, telling them where and when they should return to him. It is also added that Ebo, taking with him as much of the church’s property as he could then carry in silver and gold, fled from Reims by night with certain Normans who knew the routes and harbors of the sea and of the rivers flowing into it, and with a few other members of his household. No one attacked or pursued him. He abandoned not only his own diocese but also the region of Belgica, and set out for the Normans, to whom he had been sent as preacher by Pope Paschal [Paschal I] and by his successor Eugenius [Eugenius II], as we learn from letters which those prelates sent to him concerning this matter.

When the men with whom he had devised this plan revealed it, the emperor could no longer remain unaware of it. Therefore he had Ebo recalled through the bishops Rothad of Soissons and Erchenrad [al., Arkenrad] of Paris, and ordered that the necessities of life be supplied to him and to the clerics and laymen who were with him in the monastery of Saint Boniface, and that they await a synod.

Hildemannus, bishop of Beauvais, was likewise accused of intending, like the aforementioned bishops, to flee to Lothair. He was detained in the monastery of Saint Vedast and awaited the synod.

When they came to it in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 835, all the bishops who had assembled individually issued, by common deliberation and consent, written statements concerning the emperor’s restoration and signed them with their own hands. Ebo too joined them—truly still remaining in his episcopal status—and issued a document written in his own hand with an addition by the archbishop. In that document he declared that whatever had been done to dishonor the emperor had been done unjustly.

A little later the account continues:

“After the written statements had been delivered, the bishops came with the emperor, together with very many of his faithful and the chief men of the kingdom, to the city of Metz. In the basilica of blessed Stephen, the things that had been unanimously determined concerning the emperor’s restoration were publicly reread by Bishop Drogo.

“After this announcement, Ebo, bishop of Reims, who had been, as it were, the standard-bearer of that faction, ascended the same place where Drogo had stood. In the presence of all, he declared that the same Augustus had been deposed unjustly, and that everything perpetrated against him had been contrived wickedly and contrary to the course of all authority; he had therefore been restored deservedly and justly to his own imperial throne.

“Thus, while all were singing praises to God and carrying out what had to be done there, they returned to the palace at Thionville, the estate of Theodonis. There, in the presence of the synod, Hildemannus duly cleared himself of the charge brought against him and satisfied the synod, and through it the emperor.

“Ebo, however, was accused in that same synod, with the emperor present, of having falsely charged him and, on the basis of those same false accusations, having driven him from the kingdom after attacking him, taking away his weapons, and, although he had neither confessed nor been convicted, excluding him contrary to ecclesiastical regulations from access to the church and from the fellowship of Christians—just as Ebo himself had confirmed in writing with his subscription and had declared in words before everyone.

“And since there were also other crimes for which he was to be accused after this accusation, crimes of which he had previously been accused before the emperor and had not been canonically cleared—as the bishops’ letter to Pope Sergius also demonstrates—and for some of which he had been expelled from the emperor’s council, crimes which, once the truth had been revealed, he could not deny, he requested seclusion, so that he might conduct his case in the synod of bishops without the emperor’s presence.

“Having obtained this, he summoned certain bishops to himself. No one compelled him; rather, of his own accord, following their counsel and that of the African Council, he dictated and caused to be written in his presence a document of his deposition, and signed it with his own hand. He did this so that his shame might be spared, and so that, on account of the church’s reproach and the insolent attacks of secular persons, the priestly dignity might not be polluted if he were publicly found to have confessed or been convicted of the matters of which he had been accused and was still to be accused.

“According to ecclesiastical tradition, he then voluntarily presented that document to the synod as his abdication, having attested it by his own written and spoken confession, without anyone asking or demanding it of him. As those who were present could then see, he voluntarily removed himself from the priesthood, seeking a remedy through penance, as is contained in the same document of his declaration and subscription, in these words.”

> “I, Ebo, an unworthy bishop, recognizing my frailty and the weight of my sins, appointed as judges of my offenses the witnesses of my confession—namely, Archbishop Aiulfus and Bishops Badaradus and Modoinus. I made a full confession to them, seeking a remedy through penance and the salvation of my soul, so that I might withdraw from the office and ministry of the episcopate, of which I recognize myself to be unworthy, and might render myself alien on account of my offenses, in which I have confessed to them privately that I sinned.
>
> “This is to be done in such a way that they may be witnesses to another’s succeeding me and being consecrated in my place, one who may worthily preside over and benefit the church over which I have hitherto presided unworthily. And so that thereafter I may have no authority under the canons to make any claim or appeal, I have confirmed this by subscribing with my own hand. I, Ebo, formerly a bishop, have subscribed. +”

And so that he might legally fulfill everything according to the laws by which the Church is governed, together with those whom, according to the canons of the province of Africa (canon 63), he had chosen as his judges, he also summoned three other bishops to bear witness to his profession. For the Apostle says: “Do not accept an accusation against a presbyter except on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (1 Tim. 5:19), and the Lord says that “at the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established” (Matt. 18:16). This was also so that another might succeed him once he had relinquished the priesthood.

These three were Bishop Theoderic, Achardus, a bishop of his own diocese, and Archbishop Nothon. Thus Ebo himself made his declaration, and six bishops bore witness to it, as we have said; he presented the document to the synod, and all the bishops who were present at the synod said to him individually and one by one: “According to your declaration and subscription, cease from the ministry.”

Before everyone, Bishop Jonas dictated on behalf of all to the notary Helias—who had written Ebo’s document, to which Ebo himself subscribed, in accordance with the fifty-ninth chapter and likewise the seventy-fourth chapter of the African Council—this record, together with the aforesaid document, to be preserved for future generations. The same Helias wrote what follows:

> “This declaration of Ebo was made and confirmed by the subscription of his own hand in a synodal assembly generally convened at Thionville, in the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 835, and also in the twenty-first year of the reign of the glorious Caesar Louis.”

A little later:

> “After his condemnation, the synod gave the document presented to it by Ebo to the presbyter Fulco, who succeeded that same Ebo in receiving the bishopric of Reims, together with the synodal record. It is preserved in the archive of the church of Reims, and we have learned that a copy of it was sent to Pope Leo of holy memory, and so forth.”

After this deposition, Ebo is said to have lived in the regions of Cisalpine Gaul until the death of Emperor Louis, which occurred in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 840. When that emperor had died, Lothair came from Italy into Gaul. Ebo met him at the city of Worms, and after several days Lothair restored to him by imperial edict the see and diocese of Reims.

A copy of that edict is as follows:

> “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, the eternal God, Lothair, by divine providence ordering it, Augustus emperor.
>
> “Because confession of sins is no less necessary in adversity than in prosperity, and God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart (Ps. 50:19), we do not doubt that there is joy among the angels in heaven over one sinner doing penance (Luke 15:7). We mortals on earth likewise do not despise those for whom we know, by divine testimony, that the angels rejoice in heaven.
>
> “Divine kindness has taught us that those who accuse and rebuke themselves for their transgressions are not condemned but restored by God. He not only rescued the adulterous woman from legal condemnation (John 8:11), but also did not condemn the humbled publican who accused himself; rather, by justifying him, he exalted him (Luke 18:14). He did not say, ‘Everyone who humbles himself will be condemned,’ but rather, ‘will be exalted’ (ibid.).
>
> “Therefore, at the request of the sons of your church, and in the presence of the prelates who stand by and decree this, we restore to you, Ebo, the see and diocese of the city of Reims, which you lost when you were carried away on account of our cause. Thus, clothed again in the former pallium of holy apostolic generosity, after humbly completing your satisfaction and receiving it from our solemn generosity, you may exercise concord and the favor of divine service with us.
>
> “I, Bishop Drogo, have assented; Archbishop Otgarius; Archbishop Hecti; Archbishop Amaluvinus; Archbishop Audax; Bishop Joseph; Bishop Adalulfus; Bishop David; Bishop Rodingus; Bishop Giselbertus; Bishop Flotharius; Bishop Badaradus; Bishop Hagano; Bishop Hartgarius; Bishop Ado; Bishop Samuel; Bishop Rambertus; Bishop Haiminus; Ratoldus, a presbyter called to the episcopate; Amalricus, called to the episcopate; together with many other presbyters and deacons publicly standing in attendance.
>
> “Issued at the public palace of Engilenheim, in the month of June, on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, while Lord Lothair Caesar was reigning and ruling, in the first year of his return, having succeeded his father in Gaul, in the third indiction.”

The synod held at Soissons, however, opposed this restoration, asserting that one condemned by itself and by thirty-four bishops could not be restored by a smaller number.

Ebo carried the king’s edict with him and circulated it among the bishops and among many persons of different professions and ranks. He also had it publicly read in the church of Reims.

Thus, at the time when Lothair expelled Charles from the kingdom and drove him beyond the Seine, Ebo recovered the see of Reims six years after his deposition and began to exercise the episcopal ministry. Celebrating ordinations, he ordained certain clerics, and held this bishopric for approximately a year, until Charles, having regained his strength, returned to Belgica.

When Ebo heard this, he abandoned the see of Reims, went to Lothair, and remained in his personal service until he went to Rome together with Drogo, bishop of Metz. There he asked Pope Sergius [Sergius II] to reconcile him and grant him the pallium. That pope granted him communion only and refused to give him the pallium.

When Ebo returned from Rome, he held the abbey of Saint Columbanus in Italy as a gift from the emperor Lothair, until he refused to carry out the embassy to Greece entrusted to him by that emperor. Consequently, after the property given to him by the emperor had been taken away, he moved to Louis, king of Germany. From him he obtained a certain bishopric in the region of Saxony, where thereafter he carried out the episcopal ministry.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0137]

## CHAPTER ONE. On the election and ordination of Hincmar

[Col. 0137D]

Finally, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 845, Charles [the Bald] convened a synod of the bishops of his kingdom at the city of Beauvais in the province of Reims. Among the other affairs of the Church and kingdom, he began to discuss with those bishops the desolation of the church of Reims. Since Fulco the presbyter had held it for a long time, and Nothon had succeeded him there, it appeared to have remained without a shepherd for so long a period.

The bishops, recounting Ebo’s deposition as they had seen or heard it, and recalling the authority of the holy Fathers concerning such matters, decided by common agreement—necessity compelling and authority urging—that at last a bishop should be ordained in that church after a decade had passed since Ebo’s deposition.

Accordingly, with the consent of the clergy and people of that metropolitan church, and of the bishops of the same province, with the approval of Wenilo, archbishop of the church of Sens, and of Ercamrad, bishop of Paris, and with the consent of his abbot and the brothers of the monastery of Saint Denis, where he lived, and with the support of King Charles, Hincmar was elected.

The decree was completed, ratified by the hands of those who had elected him, and he was ordained bishop of the church of Reims.

This Hincmar, having from childhood been raised in monastic discipline and instructed in literary studies at the monastery of Saint Denis under Abbot Hilduin, had thereafter been brought to the palace of Emperor Louis because of the nobility both of his family and of his understanding, and had gained the emperor’s intimate acquaintance. There, as far as he could, he worked with the emperor and the aforementioned abbot under the authority of the bishops so that the monastic order in that monastery, which had long been declining through the pleasure-seeking faction of certain men, might be restored.

And so that he might fulfill by his actions what he urged in speech, he too submitted himself to religious discipline with the others, chastising his body and subjecting it to spiritual servitude.

In the course of time, when the aforementioned Abbot Hilduin, Emperor Louis’s archchaplain, incurred the displeasure of that Augustus together with other leading men of the kingdom to such a degree that his abbeys were taken from him and he was sent into exile in Saxony, Hincmar, with the permission of his own bishop and the blessing of the brothers, followed him into exile.

Because of his closer [al., earlier] acquaintance with the emperor, the Lord bestowed on him such favor with the emperor and the nobles that he was able to advocate for his former teacher until Hilduin was recalled from exile and restored to the governance of two abbeys.

Then, when Pope Gregory [Gregory IV] came into the regions of Gaul and the kingdom of the Franks defected from the aforementioned emperor, Hincmar’s abbot wished to lead him into his service against loyalty to the emperor; but he was entirely unable to compel him to do so.

After the emperor had been restored, Hincmar worked as far as he could to benefit his abbot. Thereafter he lived in the monastery without reproach, as guardian of the sacred relics and of the church of the holy martyrs, until, summoned to royal service, he assumed responsibility for the monasteries of Saint Mary, the holy Mother of God, and Saint Germanus, by royal and episcopal authority and at the command of his abbot Louis the deacon.

By royal generosity he also received possession of certain property and serfs, which, after he had been consecrated bishop, he transferred by testament to the monastery of Saint Denis, where he had served Christ.

## CHAPTER TWO. On the reopening of the case concerning Ebo’s deposition

[Col. 0139D]

When a year had passed after Hincmar’s ordination, Emperor Lothair, provoked against him because of the conflict over the kingdom that he was waging against his brother Charles, whose service the same prelate faithfully supported, demanded letters from Pope Sergius [Sergius II] for the reopening of the judgment concerning Ebo’s deposition.

Therefore that pope sent a letter to King Charles and ordered him to send Bishop Guntbold of Rouen, together with the other bishops of his kingdom whom Guntbold himself should choose for this purpose, to meet the pope’s legates at Trier and investigate this complaint; he also ordered him to have Bishop Hincmar come to that synod.

He likewise instructed Guntbold by letter that, after Easter Day, when he had sent his envoys into the emperor’s service, Guntbold himself should go with the bishops to the aforementioned place to settle this case.

He also sent Hincmar a letter ordering him to come to the same council.

When Pope Sergius’s legates did not come at the agreed time, Guntbold, with the approval [i.e., support] of King Charles, held a synod with the bishops. On the authority of the aforementioned pope, he summoned Ebo to it by letters and legates.

Ebo, however, is said neither to have come nor to have sent a representative in his place or canonical letters.

Nevertheless, Guntbold and the other bishops who had then assembled at Paris (in the year 847)—namely, Wenilo, metropolitan of the church of Sens, with his diocesan bishops; Lantrannus [al., Lanfrannus] of Tours with his suffragans; and Hincmar in particular with all the fellow bishops of the diocese of Reims—sent their letters to Ebo and placed the diocese of Reims under interdict.

They forbade him thereafter to solicit anyone from that diocese, either in writing or by word or through any messenger, until, according to the command of Pope Sergius, he should appear before them and receive from them, in a general assembly, a judgment of settlement in accordance with the canonical and apostolic statutes.

After this he sent no further protest or claim concerning the see of Reims or his rank, either to any synod or to the apostolic see.

After the bishops had reported his deeds to Pope Leo [Leo IV], and after the royal letters had additionally confirmed that Hincmar’s ordination—when he also sent the account of his faith to Rome—was valid, together with the granting of the pallium, Ebo is said to have survived in the body for approximately five years, that is, until the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 851.

## CHAPTER THREE. On the vision of the same Bernold

Afterward the following revelation was shown to a certain man of the parish of Reims named Bernold. Overcome by illness, he came almost to the point of death, so that for four days he could take neither food nor drink, nor could he speak.

On the fourth day, at the ninth hour, he lay as if lifeless, so that no breath seemed to remain in him. Only at intervals, when someone placed a hand at his mouth or upon his chest, could that person scarcely perceive that the man still had a spirit. His face nevertheless appeared intensely flushed, and he lay in this condition until midnight.

Then he opened his eyes with vigor, addressed his wife and those standing around him, and ordered them to run as quickly as possible and urgently ask his presbyter to come to him.

When the presbyter had been summoned, before he entered the house the sick man said that they should place a chair there, because the presbyter was already about to enter.

After the presbyter came in and had poured out a prayer for him, Bernold told him to sit beside him and listen to what he was going to say, so that, if Bernold himself could not survive to announce it to him, the presbyter might at least report it.

Then he began to weep bitterly and said amid sobs:

> “Taken from this world and brought into another, I came to a certain place and found forty-one bishops. Among them I recognized Ebo, Pardulus, and Aeneas, ragged, blackened, and filthy like the others, as if they had been burned. At intervals they trembled horribly in extreme cold, with weeping and gnashing of teeth; at other times they were tormented by excessive heat.
>
> “Bishop Ebo called me by name and said: ‘Because permission will be given you to return to your body, I and these fellow brothers of ours beg you to help us.’
>
> “I replied: ‘How can I help you?’
>
> “He said: ‘Go to our men, clerics and laymen, to whom we have done favors, and tell them to give alms and offer prayers for us, and to obtain that sacred offerings be presented for us.’
>
> “I said that I did not know where their men were.
>
> “He replied: ‘We will give you a guide to lead you to them.’
>
> “They gave me a guide, who went ahead of me and led me to a great palace, where there was a multitude of their men, and those men were speaking among themselves about those bishops. I told them what I had been ordered to say on behalf of the bishops.
>
> “From there I returned with my guide and came back to the place where the bishops were. It was as if the things they had requested had already been done for them: I found them cheerful in appearance, as though newly shaved and bathed, dressed in white, wrapped in stoles, and shod with sandals.
>
> “The aforementioned Bishop Ebo said to me: ‘Do you see how much your mission has helped us? Until now, as you saw, we had an excessively harsh guardian and a burdensome custody; but now we have Lord Ambrose as our guardian and a gentle [i.e., lenient] custody.’”

And other things that he saw and reported were written down by Bishop Hincmar.

## CHAPTER FOUR. On the restoration of the church’s property carried out by King Charles

After Hincmar had been ordained archbishop of the church of Reims, as has been related, King Charles restored to that holy church the property from the same bishopric which he had permitted his palace officials to appropriate.

Concerning this restoration he issued the following authority in his decree:

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Charles, king by the grace of God.
>
> “If we strengthen by our decrees the things that were rightly handed down, established, and confirmed by our predecessors or through the devotion of the faithful; and if by our royal authority we correct and improve those things that have been corrupted by whatever necessity, we provide for our salvation and exercise the royal ministry entrusted to us by the Lord.
>
> “Therefore let the diligence of all God’s faithful and of our own people, present and future, know that the property from the bishopric of Reims which, while that holy see was vacant through lack of a shepherd, we entrusted to our faithful for a time—although under great necessity and entirely unwillingly, so that they might receive from our service some temporary support—now that Hincmar has been elected and ordained archbishop in that holy see through the gift of the Holy Spirit and by God’s and our arrangement, we presently restore in full, by this decree of our authority, whatever of it we granted as a benefice to our faithful.
>
> “This includes Sparnacum and Juliacum, and whatever Richuinus held from that bishopric, or whatever Count Odo held from it; also the estate of Culmiciacum, with the chapel which the presbyter Rabanus held; as well as what Pardulus, and Adalgardis [possibly Algardis], the abbess, and Rotbertus, Amalbertus the cleric, Altmarus, John the physician, and likewise Rabanus, little Pumilio, Ratboldus [ms., Ratholdus], Goderamnus, Herenboldus, and Donatus, or Gilbuinus held; and also everything that both clerics and laymen who had for some time been under our lordship possessed, and whom we have now entrusted to the aforesaid bishop.
>
> “To bring everything to a conclusion: whatever from that bishopric, when we received it from the hand of Fulco, we granted to anyone as a benefice, by this authority of our confirmation, having examined before our assembly of faithful persons—both of ecclesiastical and lay rank—the testament of Saint Remigius, we presently return and restore in full to the holy house of Saint Mary and Saint Remigius and to Hincmar, the archbishop.
>
> “Thus, with all other written instruments annulled, let him receive these properties by this authority of ours without any opposition, so that, just as the property of the Church ought to be administered for the benefit of the Church of God, both he and his successors may administer it.
>
> “We promise by this authority that we will never again do anything of this kind against that house of God, and we beseech the almighty Lord, the Son of that Virgin, that none of our successors may attempt to do so. So that this authority may be regarded as more secure in future times and may serve as a record against the adversaries of that holy church, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and decreed that it be strengthened by the impression of our ring.
>
> “Given on the Kalends of October, in the sixth year of the reign of Charles, the most glorious king, in the eighth indiction. Issued in the county of Anjou, at the estate of Avegio.”

Concerning the other properties that were not then returned, he is later found to have issued the following decree:

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Charles, king by the grace of God.
>
> “We wish it to be known to all counts, abbots, abbesses, royal envoys, vassals, and all the faithful of the holy Church of God and of our own realm, present and future, that Hincmar, the religious and greatly beloved and venerable bishop of the holy church of Reims, coming before the majesty of our highness, made known to our gentleness that from the property of holy Mary, the Mother of God, and of the holy and precious confessor of Christ, Remigius—which appears to have been withdrawn from that holy church through the gifts of our royal ancestors, through the imprudence or concession of the rulers of that church, or through the schemes of any malicious persons—the ninths and tenths are not paid to the aforesaid church as justice requires.
>
> “He therefore requested the dignity of our magnificence that, for the love of God and of his holy Mother, as well as of our precious patron Remigius, we should order a decree of our authority to be issued to him.
>
> “Yielding to and freely and peacefully complying with his agreeable and necessary petitions, we ordered this decree of our great authority to be made for him.
>
> “By it we expressly command that whoever among God Almighty’s faithful or among our own people is known to possess anything from the property of holy Mary, the Mother of God, or of the holy confessor of Christ Remigius, belonging to the church of Reims, or from the bishopric of the most religious and beloved Hincmar, the venerable archbishop—whether through a grant conceded by our generosity, through the acquisition or machination of any of those mentioned above, or through their intercession, or who is seen to hold or possess anything whatsoever from the aforesaid property—shall, in the presence of our envoys, re-pledge the ninth and the tenth to the envoy of the church of Saint Mary or of Saint Remigius of Reims, or to Hincmar, the venerable archbishop, and shall diligently ensure that every year he pays them to the same aforesaid and mentioned church, without opposition arising from any pretext.
>
> “Whoever presumes to act against this decree of our authority concerning this matter shall know that, according to the capitularies of our grandfather of worthy memory and of our father of pious memory, he will make restitution and lose those same properties without obtaining anyone’s intercession (Book I, chapter 163; Book II, chapter 21; Book IV, chapter 40).
>
> “And so that this authority of our decree may retain inviolable strength and may be believed more truly and certainly by all the faithful of the holy Church of God and by our own people, present and future, we ordered it to be sealed below with our ring.
>
> “Given on the fourth day before the Nones of September, in the eighth year of the reign of Charles, the most glorious king, in the tenth indiction. Issued in the monastery of Saint Quentin.”

He also granted the same holy see an authority of immunity according to the examples of his royal predecessors.

He likewise confirmed, by the following authority, the concession of his father Louis concerning the royal levy (above, Book II, chapter 19), which had been assigned to laborers and to the city wall for the restoration of that holy church:

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Charles, king by the grace of God.
>
> “If we graciously grant assent to the petitions of our faithful, especially of the Lord’s priests, and above all in matters that can provide for ecclesiastical interests, we believe that this brings us an increase of eternal reward.
>
> “Therefore let the diligence of all God’s faithful and of our own people, present and future, know that the venerable Hincmar, archbishop of the city of Reims, presented to our serene presence a decree of Lord Louis, emperor of pious memory and our father. He had decreed that, as an increase of his alms, the labor, the laborers, and every levy that in the time of our grandfather, Lord Charles the emperor, was exacted from that house of God and brought to the palace called Aachen, should in future times, until the end of the world, contribute to the building and restoration of that church of God for the benefit of the aforesaid holy church as an act of his almsgiving. He also decreed that those payments or expenses should never at any time be exacted for that place or for any other, but that, through his indulgent remission, they should benefit that same place.
>
> “Judging these good deeds to be valid, by this decree of our authority we determine that whatever our aforesaid lord and father granted in his decree concerning the levy or the laborers mentioned above, and also concerning the city wall itself or the roads contributing to the usefulness of the canons’ cloister, shall remain permanently granted, confirmed, and established by our perpetual indulgence, concession, and authority.
>
> “And so that this authority of our confirmation and concession may be known with greater certainty in future times and remain unshaken, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.
>
> “Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, in the tenth year of the reign of Charles, the glorious king, in the thirteenth indiction. Issued at Vermeria, in the royal palace, successfully, in the name of God. Amen.”

## CHAPTER FIVE. On the restoration of the church of Reims carried out by Hincmar himself

Having exercised these authorities of royal benevolence and been confirmed in the episcopal see, the aforementioned Hincmar, archbishop, completed with splendid magnificence the temple of blessed Mary, the Mother of God, which Ebo had begun to renew from its foundations, now enjoying royal peace and favor.

Moreover, he covered the altar of holy Mary, the Mother of God, with gold and adorned it with precious stones. He inscribed it with these verses:

> This altar, dedicated to the honor of the Lord’s Mother,  
> Its devoted worshiper, Bishop Hincmar, adorned.  
> The priest who served this see with sacred gifts,  
> After eight times a hundred years had been completed,  
> With forty-five years together running beneath them,  
> When the young Charles ruled the kingdom’s diadems,  
> The city’s people asked him to be their shepherd.

And on the image of the Mother of God on that altar:

> The Virgin Mary holds the man, the king, and God,  
> Born from her own womb through the Holy Spirit.

He covered the roof of the temple with sheets of lead, adorned the temple itself with painted ceilings, illuminated it with glass windows, and paved its floors with marble. He covered a large cross with gems and gold. He also prepared other crosses of both gold and silver.

He made a large chalice with a paten and a spoon from gold and illuminated it with the brilliance of precious stones. That chalice was later given to the Normans for the redemption and salvation of the fatherland; the paten is still preserved there.

He also had a little book written concerning the birth of holy Mary, the Mother of God, as well as blessed Jerome’s sermon on the Assumption of that Lady, and fortified them with ivory tablets covered in gold.

He also ordered a certain reliquary to be made—that is, a larger chest, which is usually carried by two clerics—and covered it with figured and gilded silver. In it he placed relics of many saints for the protection of the entire city.

In addition, he prepared other altar vessels, both of gold and of silver. He had a Gospel book written in letters of gold and silver, fortified it with golden tablets, and adorned it with precious gems. He also marked it with these verses:

> Holy Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary,  
> I, Hincmar, your bishop, bring these gifts to you.  
> These pious works were taught us by Christ Jesus,  
> Born from your womb, O chaste maiden.

He also adorned with ivory and silver the book of the sacraments and the lectionary that he had ordered to be written.

He covered the candlesticks with silver, adorned the temple with various lamps and crowns, and covered it with various ornaments of pallia, curtains, and carpets. He also procured sacred altar vestments for the ministers.

Finally, after summoning many bishops and after King Charles had come to this city, he solemnly dedicated the basilica in honor of the incomparable and perpetual Virgin, Mary, Mother of God, just as it had been consecrated in ancient times, and, with the cooperation of his fellow bishops, consecrated it under the invocation of the all-powerful, life-giving Trinity.

## CHAPTER SIX. On the miracles later revealed in the same church
In this church, therefore, many miracles were accomplished at various times by God’s power in honor of Mary, the ineffable Mother of Christ. Of the many that occurred before our own age, most are unknown to us. [Col. 0145C] Nevertheless, we considered it inappropriate to pass over in silence here those that we ourselves saw while present, or learned about from people who had seen them, although we once set them down in verse.

A certain woman, a citizen of this city, named Altrudis, was raising an only daughter, a little child who, while still at her mother’s breast, became blind. When the mother had struggled in vain with various remedies for her, and no treatment could help her, she resolved to turn to the supreme physician. She judged that she could ask mercy more fittingly through no saint than through the Mother of the very one whose servant she herself was. Preparing offerings of candles, both for herself and for her daughter, she went to this church to ask the clemency of the Queen of Heaven. Fixing lights to the candelabra and prostrating herself upon the pavement, [Col. 0145D] she poured out her suppliant heart in prayers. Not presuming that she herself was sufficient, she humbly asked the ministers of the altar to assist her petition with their prayers. Because she had asked devoutly and faithfully, she was worthy to obtain what she prayed for, and she secured sight for her child. We later saw her giving thanks to God and to his most holy Mother, together with the sacred ministers who had assisted her, when she presented her daughter to us healthy and clearly seeing.

A certain cleric of our congregation, noble by birth, named Hugh, was so tormented by an excessive toothache that, because of the severity of his illness, he could neither sleep nor take food. When an elder questioned him and he explained the distress of his suffering, the elder gave him this advice: he should prostrate himself before the altar of the Mother of God [Col. 0146A] and, with his heart, beseech her mercy concerning his affliction. Then, rising from prayer and kissing the altar, he should lay his cheek upon the bare marble itself, where he was suffering; trusting that he would be healed, he should return home, have himself covered with his clothing, and give himself over to sleep.

After carrying this out in order, he fell asleep. It was the season of the solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity, and after celebrating the evening office the brothers were sitting in the upper chamber, where they customarily gathered for warmth. The brother mentioned above dreamed that he was standing there before the steps of the upper chamber, while the blessed Mother of God stood above, before the entrance to her house. On the left, on the lowest step, he saw an evil spirit standing in the guise of a certain surgeon. Without doubting who the lady was whom he beheld, and casting aside fear of the dreadful enemy, he climbed up to her. Falling at her feet, he was received by her hand, so that, holding his chin, the most holy lady touched the cheek that was troubling him. [Col. 0146B]

She raised him up, gently comforted him, and explained that he had not found her in the church because she was standing there to guard the brothers. “That evil one whom you see standing nearby,” she said, “is thinking of coming up here and wants to disturb our brothers.” She ordered him to return and to trust in the healing granted to him. He again prostrated himself at her feet and was raised up by her, kissing only the purple garment with which she was clothed. Immediately awakened, he ordered that food be given him. [Col. 0146C] When his attendants heard this, they thought he had become insane, since he was asking so eagerly for food, and they began to worry. But he insisted that he had been healed by the blessed Mother of God and that he was suffering neither illness nor madness. Thus he was restored to health with great speed, and afterward he often affirmed confidently that he would never again suffer such a thing, since so great a lady had restored him to health. This indeed happened: for the rest of the many years that he lived, he never again experienced such an illness.

Hugh’s fellow cleric and deacon, named Ebrard, was afflicted by the burning heats of a panting fever. [Col. 0146D] Troubled by the anguish of his sickness, he sat wearily in the crypt consecrated in honor of Saint Remigius beneath the seat of this church, while the mysteries of the Mass were being celebrated there. Exhausted by the force of the fevers, sleep overcame him, as commonly happens to those suffering from fever. And behold, he saw the blessed Mother of God standing beside him. She placed her hand upon his head, passed over him, and then seemed to enter behind the altar. At once he opened his eyes and rose; when the mysteries had ended, he answered “Amen” already healed and energetically joined in the completion of the offices. His head was so anointed at the touch of the miraculous lady that it seemed as though it had been rubbed with oil at that very hour. We too were amazed at this, for we saw him that same day cheerful and eating with us.

Finally, at different times we saw [manuscript: “we learned of”] three lame men, with contracted knees, who were entirely unable to set their feet to walking, raised upright in this church. [Col. 0147A] One lived under the episcopate of Lord Heriveus, the bishop. He had been carried there by the hands of others but returned on his own feet. Another, under Bishop Seulf, was named Maganerus. A Briton by nationality, lame in both knees and clinging to crutches, he had been supported among us by the alms of the devout and had already remained there for nearly a year.

While we were celebrating the nocturnal praises on the solemnity of All Saints, the tendons of his knees were suddenly stretched out while he lay in the midst of the people, so violently that even the straps by which his legs were fastened to his hips broke. The skin at his knees also split, and blood flowed from them. He rose and, to the amazement of the people, thereafter walked on his own feet. [Note: [Col. 0147D] He reports the same event in the Chronicle, under the year 934.]

[Col. 0147B] The third was under the pontificate of our lord Bishop Artold. While he was celebrating the sacred Mass, on the solemn day of that most holy Virgin—the day on which the archangel Gabriel was sent to her from the stars to announce to her the wondrous birth destined for the ages—the lame man, poor and miserable, was dragging himself over the marble pavement. Suddenly freed, he was stretched out, measuring the earth with his body; then at last he rose to his feet and, walking in a new manner, increased the joy of the rejoicing people. He still lives among us, supported by the bishop’s charity.

[Col. 0147C] There was also a fourth, a certain peasant named Gerlaius [variant: Gerlanis], from the household of this church. Coming to this city to pray, he entered the basilica of the blessed Mother of God Mary. While he was pouring out his prayers there, he suddenly became rigid with numbness; his tendons contracted, and nearly all his limbs were bound. Thus constricted, he promised that he would remain there and serve, insofar as he was able, if he were released. At last, after a month, he was freed from these bonds and assigned to ecclesiastical service. For five years he served unharmed, partly in this church and partly in the basilica of Saint Denis outside the city walls.

After that period of time, on the same solemnity—namely, the Hypapante of the Savior—he entered this church. While he was engaged in prayer, his limbs became so rigid that he seemed to have stuck to the pavement, and he could not lift either his mouth or any limb from it. When those standing nearby raised him up, both his legs and both his hands contracted. He was freed again on the fifteenth day and, not long afterward, was taken from human affairs.

[Col. 0147D] But who could recount how many sick people here receive the gracious gift of healing almost every day? How many fever sufferers? How many possessed persons are saved? Who could even declare the plagues driven away here from those who have been liberated? But it will be enough to have recalled at least a few of innumerable events.

## CHAPTER VII. The vision of a certain priest named Gerhard

A certain priest from the Porcian district, named Gerhard, had once fallen into an illness so severe that he was thought to have been poisoned. During this illness he was consoled by several visits from saints, namely from the blessed apostle Peter, who twice commanded him to take care to restore the church that he governed; in visions, Peter also rebuked him for having so often sought physicians for the sake of his health. Later he saw Saint Remigius [Col. 0148A] standing beside him, revealing his own identity to him and promising him remedies for this illness.

Soon afterward he came to the city of Reims. While visiting the basilicas of the blessed Mother of God and of Saint Remigius for the sake of prayer, he spent the night in a village. He saw himself led by Saint Remigius into a certain most splendid church. There he saw the most blessed Virgin Mary hastening toward it, with Saint Remigius and Saint Martin accompanying her at either side.

In the church itself, a multitude of the Levitical order and of priestly rank awaited her. Deacons dressed in dalmatics were standing there, some with palms and some without them. A very large company of other saints also appeared to be present. The priest himself recognized no one’s face in particular [Col. 0148B] except that of the blessed Peter, who had already been revealed to him earlier.

When the blessed Mother of God reached the church mentioned above, where this brother saw that her arrival was being awaited, she began to ask who he was and what he was seeking. Saint Remigius answered him: “He is my servant, lady, seeking from your goodness remedies for his health.” What she herself replied, however, he could not hear, as he later reported. A certain curtain appeared to be hanging there. When she entered beyond it, a light brighter than the sun came from her into his eyes, so that, because of the greatness of its radiance, he could not look directly at it.

[Col. 0148C] After several days, Saint Martin appeared to him. He testified that he had been sent to him by Saint Remigius and stated that life had been granted to him and healing bestowed. Yet afterward a certain doubt remained in his mind concerning the person of the blessed Mother of God, because he had not heard her name revealed in the vision. He prayed constantly that the Lord might deign to show him whether she whom he had seen was truly the Virgin Mary, Mother of God.

After nearly six months, it happened that, while he was resting at night, he was suddenly oppressed by such a serious illness that he despaired of being able to live any longer. In great distress, with relics of the blessed Mary hanging above him, he began to pour out this prayer:

“O blessed Mother of God, whose relics hang here above me: if, as we believe, these remains suspended over me truly come from you; and if the vision I recently saw truly came from you; if you are that lady whom Saint Martin and kindly Remigius [Col. 0148D] accompanied as you went to that wondrous church, where the most glorious assembly of saints awaited you and joyfully received you while I looked on, help me, your unworthy servant. Obtain life and strength for me long enough to celebrate the mysteries of the Mass to the Lord and to become worthy to receive the life-giving gifts of Christ’s body. And you, blessed bishops of Christ, whom I saw accompanying her, help me with her, you who deigned to console me with your most holy address.”

Meanwhile, amid his anguish and prayers, scarcely had a light sleep come upon him when suddenly the most blessed Queen appeared to him to be seen, under the same face and in the same clothing in which he had formerly beheld her. She was leaning against the same columns against which she had previously seemed to lean [Col. 0149A], and she shone with the brightest light. Trembling at so great a radiance and daring to say nothing, he appeared to remain stupefied with his eyes lowered to the ground.

Saint Remigius addressed him: “Why did you summon us here? Do you not see that our Lady, the Mother of God, is ready to comfort you? Why do you delay approaching her in doubt?” At these words the trembling departed, his spirit was lifted, and, raising his eyes, he recovered his strength. He saw himself fall before the feet of the most blessed Lady.

She deigned to raise him with her hand, placed the sign of the cross upon his forehead, and continued in these words: “Do not fear, and do not despair. Trust in the Lord, because you will receive from him the gift of salvation. Order the bell to be rung so that you may celebrate the sacred mysteries and give thanks to God, praising him who heals you after your sufferings.”

After saying this [Col. 0149B], she withdrew from his sight, accompanied by her attendants. The same brother immediately rose happily, having received health, and hurried to fulfill her commands. He became so healthy and vigorous that he could never have been more vigorous. When we learned these things from the same priest as he recounted them, we considered it fitting to record them as well.

## CHAPTER VIII. Certain other miracles

This illustrious Queen of Heaven, just as she is accustomed to help those who humbly seek her with their hearts, sometimes inflicts punishments as vengeance upon presumptuous or contemptuous people. We believe that this too is done piously, so that in the present life those who offend may receive fitting blows and not be tormented by heavier punishments in the future.

[Col. 0149C] What I am about to relate I did not see myself, but I often heard it recounted by many of the Fathers. A certain cleric of our congregation, named Bernard, was custodian of this church. Some frivolous persons asked him—as he later showed in writing—to give them certain relics of the saints. One day, while he was alone in the church with a certain boy, he seized a small box containing relics of the saints and, with rash audacity, presumed to open it.

After doing so, he was shaken by overwhelming fear, and the whole place was filled with a thick mist and surrounded by such terror that he thought he would not live any longer. Thus, having lost his voice, both he and the boy who was with him were unable to speak further or to say anything about what they had seen.

[Col. 0149D] Another custodian of this church, as he himself told us, once wished to rest in the church after the morning praises. He seized the church’s carpets, spread them out as a bed, and gave himself over to sleep there. And behold, a certain matron appeared to him in the guise of an old woman, seeming to carry some herbs with her.

At first she began to address him with gentle words. But when she saw the sacred carpets beneath him, she attacked him with these words, frightening him also by changing her expression:

“And you have dared to violate the sacred ornaments of the holy Lady, the Mother of God, and arrogantly trample them under your feet? Have you not feared so great a lady? For now I will spare you; nevertheless, never again presume to do such a thing.”

She gave him the example of a certain man [Col. 0150A] who used to make his bed for himself in this way, and whom we knew to have once been afflicted by misfortunes and to have died even upon the poorest bed.

So terrified, he rose, confessed his own fault, returned the carpets to the benches, and praised the Lord and his Mother for this correction. He did not recognize the lady who had visited him; nevertheless, we believe that she had been sent by blessed Mary.

We also know certain devout people who had been promised by their parents to Christ in this church and to serve his Mother. When their parents later wished to change this vow, they were compelled by illness in their children to fulfill their promise.

Some time ago, after Easter, farmers living near the city came to this city according to their customary practice, seeking the help of this miraculous [Col. 0150B] lady and bringing their vows. But the inhabitants of a certain village neglected to seek her customary protection. When the time for harvesting their crops was approaching, their fields were so battered by hail in the storm that nearly all their crops perished. Their vineyards too, with their shoots scorched and broken, lost the fruit of their grapes.

But in the territories of those who had fortified themselves with the aid of this most holy Lady, the hail did not dare even to touch them, much less enter them. From then on, both these people and all the others living nearby, coming every year more promptly and willingly to this city of Reims to seek the patronage of the same Lady, of Saint Remigius, and of the other saints, made this their custom.

## CHAPTER IX. The second translation of the body of Saint Remigius

[Col. 0150C]

The aforementioned Bishop Hincmar built a crypt of splendid workmanship at the feet of Saint Remigius. As stated above (Book I, chapter 21), he transferred the body of that most blessed patron from the site of the earlier crypt, together with his tomb, in the presence of the bishops of the diocese of Reims whom he had gathered. Before his tomb he produced a remarkable work in gold and adorned it with gems. He made there a window through which the saint’s tomb could be seen, and around that little window he placed these verses:

> Great Remigius, Hincmar your bishop, led by love of you,  
> Built this tomb for you,  
> That, O holy one, the Lord may grant me rest through your prayer  
> And through your worthy merits, O my revered one.

He adorned the Gospel book with letters of gold and protected it with golden walls distinguished by the brilliance of gems; he also gave it a title in verses overlaid with gold. He further covered a large cross with gold and decorated it with gems. He likewise presented there a sacramentary beneath ivory covers marked with silver, and a lectionary book for the Mass, furnished with equal beauty. He also assigned other books and various ornaments to that venerable place.

As for the body of that most blessed Remigius, he did not dare to take anything from it, as he himself also testifies in his letter to King Louis beyond the Rhine, who had asked him for such a gift. But this bishop considered it a very great act of presumption [Col. 0151A] to break apart the body that the Lord had preserved intact for so long.

## CHAPTER X. The reception of the pallium for daily use from the bishop of the Roman see, and the ecclesiastical possessions granted under him

This venerable Bishop Hincmar, on account of the respect owed to his holiness and wisdom, through the intervention of Emperor Lothar received from Pope Leo IV a pallium for daily use [variant: accepted], although he had already received another pallium from him, to be used properly on the solemnities assigned to him. [Variant: recepit, “received.”] In a letter then sent to Hincmar, that same pope testified that he had never granted, and would never afterward grant, such daily use of the pallium to any archbishop.

The aforementioned bishop wrote to that same Pope Leo six times—as he himself states in one of his letters to him—or seven times, sending his writings to him. In this letter he inquired about those whom chorepiscopal presumption dared to ordain, or to whom it presumed to confer the Holy Spirit by confirmation. He also wrote that secular power often offended in this matter: namely, whenever an episcopal see became vacant, the ministry owed to bishops was carried out by a chorepiscopus alone, and the property and resources of the church were spent for secular purposes, as had already happened twice in our own church.

He also wrote about those whom Lord Ebo had ordained after his deposition. In another letter he wrote about a certain Fulcric, a vassal of Emperor Lothar, about whom he had also previously informed him. Several churches throughout this kingdom suffered great hindrance because of him: after abandoning his wife, and after being excommunicated by Hincmar for that reason, he had nevertheless presumed to take another wife.
