In the same letter he wrote about the privileges of the church of Reims, which it had possessed from the beginning, from the time when sees began to have privileges. Since the bishop of Reims had always been first among the primates and one of the foremost primates of Gaul, and had no superior except the apostolic bishop, he asked that the privileges granted and preserved for so long by Hincmar’s predecessors might be preserved and increased.

From Emperor Lothar he also obtained an imperial order concerning certain properties situated in these places—Meuravallis, Termedo, and Roserolis—which, during the time of Emperor Charles, had been taken away from the church of Reims on some occasion and subjected to public use. Emperor Lothar restored them by his authority to the possession of Saint Mary and Saint Remigius.

This Emperor Lothar is also found to have honorably commended Bishop Hincmar to Pope Leo before several bishops and envoys. When the bishop was planning to go to Rome, the emperor sent a letter ahead on his behalf, urging the pope to receive him decently and affectionately and to grant him willingly and generously whatever he requested.

He sent another letter concerning the synodal decisions about those ordained by Ebo after his deposition, asking that they be confirmed by the apostolic see, and concerning certain privileges to be granted to Hincmar and to the see of Reims. He also explained that, because Hincmar wished to travel to Rome, both he and his brother Charles, king of the Franks, would retain him, since he was then very necessary to them for calming the disturbances that had arisen.

In that letter he recalled that at this see of Reims the predecessors of that pope—Saint Sixtus, its first bishop and a disciple of the apostles, Stephen I, and Leo III—had conferred apostolic offices: Stephen upon Pippin and Leo upon Charlemagne. Another Stephen, Stephen V, had crowned Louis Augustus with the imperial diadem at the same see.

To secure what he was requesting for the aforementioned bishop, Lothar sent Peter, bishop of Spoleto, as executor, personally instructed with commands concerning this matter. He also notified another Peter, bishop of Arezzo, by letter, and sent certain other faithful men, both his own and those of the aforementioned pope, to carry this out.

The aforementioned Bishop Hincmar wrote to Emperor Lothar concerning Fulcric, his vassal whom he had excommunicated, explaining how he ought to come to penance. He sent another letter containing Fulcric’s offenses and explaining how he had reasonably excommunicated him, because Fulcric had refused to come to penance. He sent yet another letter in which he greatly praised the emperor, rejoicing in his humility, because he had obeyed Hincmar’s admonitions concerning the excommunicated man; Hincmar absolved the emperor when he humbly asked for this, because of the participation he had had with Fulcric.

He also wrote after that emperor had recovered from his illness. In that letter he admonished him, sufficiently in an episcopal manner, though briefly, concerning the salvation of his soul. He wrote several other things to him as well.

From his own king Charles, Bishop Hincmar obtained again a cell constructed in honor of Saint Martin in the town of Vongo [Col. 0152C], together with everything lawfully belonging to that cell, and received it into the possession of the church of Reims by the king’s own authoritative order.

At Hincmar’s request, King Charles gave certain properties to the church of Saint Remigius, or to the monks serving God there: namely, in the district of Pertinse [variant: Portinse], two manses in the estate of Baildronis; two manses on Dodelinus Mountain; and two manses in the estate of Waldo, together with the dependants and everything legally belonging to those properties.

Hincmar also obtained from Charles an order concerning the road [Col. 0152D] that obstructed the enlargement of the cloister of the canons of the holy church of Reims, since he had also increased the number of those canons.

He further labored to have restored to the church certain properties that had long before been taken from the bishopric by this king: namely, the estate of Noviliacum, which Karlomannus had given to the church of Saint Remigius for the remedy of his soul, together with both the estate itself and the properties and dependants belonging to it that various people held as gifts from the king.

He likewise had restored certain properties [Col. 0153A] situated at Culmiciacum and Bairacum; other properties lying along the river Rotomna and in several other places; and he obtained from King Louis beyond the Rhine a written order for the restoration of certain properties formerly bequeathed to Saint Remigius. These included, in the district of Worms, Scavenheim [variant: Stadenheim] with everything belonging to it, and Cossa and Gleni in the Vosges forest.

In Thuringia and Austria he also obtained properties in a place called Schonerunstat and at Helisleba, with everything belonging there. He is also found to have recovered various properties, rights of the church, and dependants, vindicated according to law through advocates.

He exchanged certain properties of the bishopric—lands and dependants—with various persons, for the growth of the church and as circumstances required. He also took care to obtain royal orders concerning many of these exchanges.

For the canons of this church of Reims [Col. 0153B] he established a hospice for the reception of pilgrims and the poor, assigning suitable properties for this purpose, with the consent of the co-bishops of the diocese of Reims and with their signatures. The condition was that at no time should any bishop or any other person presume to grant these properties to anyone as a benefice, or remove them in any way for other uses, nor should anyone receive any rent or payment from them. Everything that could justly be acquired from these properties was to be spent for the use of the poor and the canons, according to the arrangement described in the privilege and confirmed by the other bishops.

Concerning this arrangement he also obtained from King Charles an order of royal authority, which was issued and confirmed. He further had nearly all the properties and estates of the bishopric [Col. 0153C] recorded with properly organized tenant settlements.

## CHAPTER XI. The provincial synod held at the city of Soissons

This honorable Bishop Hincmar, in the seventh year of his episcopate (853), held a provincial synod at the city of Soissons, in the monastery of Saint Medard, in the church consecrated in honor of the Holy Trinity. Present were Wenilo, archbishop of Sens; Amalric of Tours; Bishop Theodoric of Cambrai; Rothad of Soissons; Lupus of Châlons; Immo of Noyon; Erpuinus of Senlis; Ermenfrid of Beauvais; Pardulus of Laon; Hilmerad of Amiens; Hubert of Meaux; Agius of Orléans; Prudentius of Troyes; Hermann of Nevers; Jona [Col. 0153D] of Autun; Godelsald of Chalon; Dodo of Angers; Guntbert of Évreux; Hildebrand of Sées; and Rigbold, chorepiscopus of Reims.

Presbyters and abbots were also present: Dodo, abbot of the monastery of Saint Sabinus; Lupus, abbot of the monastery called Ferrières; Bernard, abbot of the monastery of Saint Benedict called Fleury; Odo of the monastery called Corbie; Heriacus of the monastery of Corbion; Bavo of the monastery of Orbais; and very many other priests and abbots, with deacons and clergy of the other ranks standing by. The glorious King Charles also sat in the midst. There certain necessary matters concerning the Church of God were discussed.

At this synod certain [Col. 0154A] canons and monks of the church of Reims arrived: namely, Radoldus, Gislodus, Vulfadus [manuscript: Volfadus], and Fredebertus from the canons of that mother church; Sigimundus from the monastery of Saint Theodoric; and from the monks of the monastery of Saint Remigius, Nortvinus, Heinradus, Mauringus, Antheus, Tetlandus, Hairohaldus, Radulfus, and Wicpertus. They declared that they had been suspended by their archbishop from the exercise of ecclesiastical orders, to which they had formerly been promoted by Ebo.

Concerning this complaint, the aforementioned Bishop Hincmar chose as judges Wenilo and Amalric, the archbishops named above, and also Pardulus, bishop of Laon, who in this judgment retained the place of his metropolitan authority. The complainants accepted these judges and added Prudentius, bishop of the city of Troyes.

[Col. 0154B] The appointed judges ruled that, if Archbishop Ebo had ordained these brothers canonically while remaining in his proper status, they ought to minister. If he had been unjustly deposed and canonically restored, and had ordained them after his canonical restoration, then they ought likewise to minister without any question.

The ordainers of Hincmar were therefore questioned, so that they might state what they knew concerning Ebo’s deposition and Hincmar’s ordination. Then Bishop Theodoric of Cambrai rose and presented before the prince and the synod a document containing the procedure of Ebo’s deposition.

The question was then examined [Col. 0154C] of how a bishop who had been deprived of office ought to be restored. Since Ebo had not been canonically restored, and since he had also been condemned by the apostolic see, with Pope Sergius confirming his deposition, it was determined that he was to remain only in lay communion.

The authority concerning the manner in which a metropolitan ought to be ordained was then read aloud. Also read were the canonical letters of Erchamradus, bishop of the church of Paris, confirmed by the hands of himself, his archbishop, and his co-bishops, which he had granted to Hincmar at the request of the church, clergy, and people of Reims. A canonical decree, strengthened by the hands of the clergy and nobles of Reims, was also produced, showing how they had requested that Hincmar be ordained their bishop. It was thereby demonstrated that Hincmar had been canonically ordained archbishop in the presence or with the consent of all the co-bishops of the diocese of Reims.

After this, Hincmar himself rose and presented before the prince and the synod [Col. 0154D] the canonical letters that the sacred canons command an ordained man to receive from his ordainers, bearing the date and the name of the consul. He also presented a letter of the province of Reims, subscribed by the hands of nearly all the bishops of Gaul, which had been sent to the apostolic see for confirmation of his ordination.

He further displayed the sacred diploma marked by the hands of the venerable prince and endorsed with his seal, confirming his ordination to that same holy and apostolic Roman Church. Thus it was judged and confirmed that Hincmar had been canonically ordained bishop.

Next, the question was examined [Col. 0155A] of what should be decided concerning those whom Ebo had presumed to ordain after his deposition, without legitimate restoration. Then Bishop Immo of Noyon rose and presented a roll containing canonical and apostolic authority, stating that those whom Ebo had appeared to ordain into ecclesiastical orders could not have received from him what he himself did not possess, and so forth.

It was therefore decreed that whatever Ebo had done in ecclesiastical ordinations after his deposition should, according to the tradition of the apostolic see, be considered invalid, except for holy baptism, which is complete when performed in the name of the Holy Trinity. Those whom he had ordained were to remain deprived of ecclesiastical orders.

Then one of the aforementioned brothers, named Fredebertus, read a written complaint. It stated that they had allowed themselves to be ordained by Ebo because they had seen the suffragan bishops of the church of Reims—namely Rothad, Lupus, Simeon, and Erpuinus—come to the metropolitan church of Reims with letters from Emperor Lothar and restore Ebo.

They further produced letters apparently written in the name of Bishop Theodoric, Rothad, Lupus, Immo, and the other bishops of this diocese, confirmed by their hands. [Col. 0155B] Yet when these letters were read out by those same bishops [variant: read; perhaps rejected], they were proven false. Because the clerics had presumed to attribute such things to the bishops, they were ordered to be deprived of communion.

When these matters had been concluded, by the decree of the judges and with the consent of the prince, Archbishop Hincmar received back his place of primacy.

A question was then raised [Col. 0155C] concerning a certain priest and abbot of the monastery of Altivillare, named Halduinus. He had apparently been ordained deacon by Ebo and had afterward been consecrated priest by Lupus, bishop of Châlons.

Bishop Lupus rose and presented a volume containing the circumstances. He had been ordered by royal letters from King Charles that, because the metropolitan church of Reims was without a shepherd, he should, as far as he was able, provide assistance in the preparation of chrism and in other ecclesiastical matters. Accordingly, when the royal letter had been brought to him by the archdeacon of the church of Reims, together with other fellow ministers, both canons and monks, ordering him to ordain Halduinus a priest and consecrate him abbot of the monastery of Altivillare, he had ordained him according to the wish of the aforementioned prince and of those who presented him.

The synod therefore judged that no condemnation [Col. 0155D] attached to that bishop on account of Halduinus’s ordination. But because Halduinus had leapt into the priesthood without passing through the rank of deacon, he ought to be sent back into the degradation that was due to him.

The synod then inquired about those who had communicated with Ebo after his deposition. After the authority concerning how they ought to be healed had been read, it was found in the canonical regulations that, after making satisfaction, receiving pardon, and being granted sacred communion with a blessing through their own bishop, they could, with the work of our Lord Jesus Christ, be purified and healed. This was also carried out by the venerable Archbishop Hincmar.

When these matters had been completed, the gracious Prince Charles asked Archbishop Hincmar [Col. 0156A] and the other bishops that, since the aforementioned brothers could not retain ecclesiastical orders, they might at least be permitted to receive communion through the indulgence of the synod. The priestly mercy readily agreed and mercifully granted pardon to those brothers.

Thus all these matters were inserted into the acts, read aloud before the synod, judged valid, and confirmed by the signatures of the aforementioned bishops and of the others who had been present.

This synodal action was sent by Hincmar to the Apostolic See and confirmed by Pope Benedict, successor of Leo (Leo IV). Benedict (Benedict III), too, granted, by the authority of blessed Peter and of that Apostolic See itself, a privilege to our bishop Hincmar (letter 1), decreeing that no one subject to the regulations of this diocese, despising him, should dare or be able with impunity to seek or await judgments elsewhere. But Lord Nicholas (Nicholas I), successor of that same Benedict, is found to have reconsidered and censured the previously mentioned proceedings of the synod, at the request of the aforesaid deposed men (letter 46), especially because the subjects’ mere obedience had been reckoned as guilt, while those who had not rashly resisted the judgment of their prelate but had humbly submitted their necks were punished with the utmost severity, and those who had sought mercy had not, as he asserts, obtained a just judgment.

He also explains how Lord Hincmar had sent Pope Leo supplicatory letters more than once concerning these proceedings of the council, asking that, by approving the same council, he confirm it with apostolic authority. Leo had firmly declined to do this, because the statutes of that synod ought to have been sent by some of the bishops who had taken part in it, so that every doubt might be uprooted completely—especially since representatives of the Apostolic See had not been present there. And because those whom Hincmar asserted had been deposed by the authority of the synod had appealed to the Apostolic See in their own letters, and wished to be heard once again in the presence of that See, the same pope had also ordered Bishop Hincmar to appear with them at the council to which he himself had sent his own legate, namely Peter, bishop of Spoleto, as his representative, specifically to renew the judgment in his place. Since Lord Hincmar did not present himself at that hearing, and the desired outcome had thereby been frustrated, Pope Leo was taken from this life.

When the apostolic man Benedict succeeded him, he was deceived in this matter, and at the very beginning of his consecration was persuaded to confirm that council; yet he could not be persuaded to deviate from the course of a just determination. Rather, through the privilege granted to him, he confirmed the council’s decree in such a way that he reserved the supreme authority of decision to the Apostolic See. Thus he decreed that the matters requested should remain unshaken if everything were in fact as Hincmar had reported concerning that synod, and so that no question might ever arise from it in the future. But since it was shown that the facts had not been entirely as they had been represented, he rightly declares that what had not simply been obtained against the deposed men was rendered void.

Therefore, in the first place, he instructed Lord Hincmar (Nicholas I, letter 47) to make every effort, with a merciful disposition, to call back the aforementioned men—namely Wulfad and his colleagues—and to discuss their restoration fraternally with him, striving to complete the matter mercifully. Otherwise, Hincmar was to appear with them at the council together with those bishops to whom the pope himself had also written for this very purpose (Nicholas I, letters 46, 47), so that, when all had assembled together, they might examine the case of those clerics and, with God before their eyes, determine it without any dispute arising. If, however, any dispute should arise between the parties, they were to come together to the Apostolic See to receive its special judgment, with representatives of both sides acting in place of the parties.

But after this judgment had been completed with the help of God’s grace, he states that he had received letters from all the bishops who had taken part in it—letters worthy of being embraced with affection—which most clearly indicated that the frequently mentioned clerics had been declared worthy of receiving their ranks by the unanimous voice of the entire council. There, as was found in the letters of those same bishops, no dispute had arisen; no difference, as had been supposed, had occurred among the various defenders; no accuser and no condemner had been found. Rather, one and the same opinion and determination concerning their restoration had become clear, and those innocent men had been approved in every respect by the unanimous consent of all.

The aforesaid Pope Nicholas also censured this council (letter 46), because they had not carried out everything solemnly, according to what he himself had determined, by laying open to the Apostolic See, in a complete report, the sequence of the proceedings. He said that they ought to have informed him unanimously, fully, and faithfully in writing of everything concerning Ebo’s deposition, his appeal [Nicholas: banishment], the promotion of these clerics, Ebo’s renewed rejection and migration to another church, and whatever else had been discussed there. They were also to preserve it, inserted into the records, for fuller knowledge and certainty on his part.

He therefore ordered that everything written on this matter, whether issued by the Apostolic See or by their own people, and whatever Bishop Hincmar and the deposed clerics had suggested and reported to the Apostolic See, should be compiled into a single volume in the order in which the documents had been sent, and dispatched with the greatest care to the Apostolic See, while copies were retained for themselves. If anything of this kind should happen again in the future, on account of which he ordered that an assembly of priests be held in those regions, they were to consign this matter, among the rest, to no one’s oblivion; after all other business, they were to attend to it most diligently, in the manner of their predecessors, and so forth.

Finally, the bishops of the aforementioned council, obedient to the commands of the Apostolic See, gathered together the sequence of events concerning Ebo’s deposition, restoration, and renewed rejection, and sent it to the venerable pope, prefacing it with the following letter:

“To the most reverend and most holy Lord Father and Pope Nicholas, we, the bishops who last year, by the grace of God and by your decree, assembled at the city of Soissons with the others who at that time were unable to attend.

“We send to Your Most Holy Paternity and pre-eminent authority the sequence of the events concerning the deposition of Ebo, formerly archbishop of Reims, and also concerning his restoration, as well as the promotion of Brother Wulfad and his colleagues, and the renewed rejection of the aforementioned Ebo and his migration to another church. You ordered us to investigate these matters and report them back to you. Since none of us, except Brother Rothad, took part in these events in the episcopal order, we have briefly compiled the account from the records of kings and bishops who were present and left written accounts to their successors.

“We did not previously consider it necessary to gather these matters and send them to Your Authority, because, as we suggested to you in writing through Egilo, the venerable archbishop, we had no record of any deposition of Ebo and at that time did not consider it necessary to obtain one. In restoring those brothers, we were not disputing or issuing differing decisions, but were of one and the same mind according to the tradition of our predecessors, which we took care to report to your discernment. Since those men had not been made liable through insolence, but had been rendered blameless through obedience in their attainment of the sacred ranks, we would have hastened, without contradiction, to restore them to their offices, according to the most sincere understanding of your decision, had not the privileges of the Holy Roman See, produced by our revered fellow bishop Hincmar, been accorded the reverence due to them. Those privileges laid down certain provisions concerning the men in question.

“Their authority, complete and entire, as became clear and as was just, had been reserved to the judgment of the Apostolic See. Our same fellow brother and fellow priest showed us the authentic documents of these privileges, with their seals intact and their writings uncorrupted—not to harm the aforementioned brothers, nor to offer any contradiction, but to render, as was fitting, the reverence due to the Apostolic See. This he did together with the records of the bishops, whose proceedings you told us you had reread and from which you had discovered how the aforesaid clerics had been degraded.

“He did not subscribe to those proceedings, because he himself had not deposed the same brothers by his judgment, as both he and we have written to you, as the proceedings themselves demonstrate, and as we have already suggested to Your Most Holy Paternity. In the conduct of this matter, while we were disputing and examining certain points but not bringing them to a conclusion, we carried the case to the point at which their restoration alone was assigned to your magisterial eminence, their reformation entrusted to it, and their reintegration attributed to it. Therefore, afterward, our unanimity did not incline in either direction, even if certain men, for whatever reason and without our knowledge, turned aside from it.

“Thus, as best we could, we have made a concise compilation of the proceedings and of the bishops concerning Ebo’s case, and, as you commanded, we send it to Your Authority.”

After describing the sequence of these proceedings, they added:

“Here, as Your Authority commanded, we send to you what we have learned from the writings of those who have preceded us to the Lord, and from the truthful reports of those who were present, concerning the deposition of Ebo, formerly archbishop of Reims, which occurred approximately thirty-three years ago, and afterward concerning his restoration, as well as the promotion of Brother Wulfad and his colleagues, the renewed rejection of the aforesaid Ebo, and his migration to another church.

“These matters are also contained, for the most part, in the records of the bishops of the provinces of Belgium, Gaul, Neustria, and Aquitaine, which were sent to Pope Sergius and to Pope Leo together with their letter, as well as in the letters subsequently sent by Emperor Lothar and King Charles. We believe these are preserved in the Roman archive. We send them to Your Authority.

“We have also gathered into this volume, in the order in which they were sent or returned, according to your command, the documents which we reread as having been sent from Your Authority and returned to Your Holiness. If any others concerning this affair were sent either by us or to us, we have not read them.

“We also send below what our brother and fellow priest Hincmar gave us to send to Your Authority, according to your command (Nicholas, letter 56), saying among other things:

“‘Everything written concerning this matter, whether previously issued by us or now by you, and whatever Archbishop Hincmar and the deposed clerics have suggested and reported concerning it to the Apostolic See, is to be compiled into one volume in the order in which it was sent and, with copies of the documents retained by you, is to be sent with the greatest care to the Apostolic See, as is appropriate.’ To these instructions we append the following, and so forth.”

## Chapter XII  
### The vacancy of the see of Cambrai and the union of Baldwin with Judith, the king’s daughter

There is also the matter of the vacancy of the see of Cambrai and the improper union of Count Baldwin and Judith. This Judith, the daughter of King Charles, had previously been joined in marriage to King Æthelwulf of the English, also called Æthelbald, and had been distinguished by the dignity and blessing of a queen. After his death, she sold the possessions she had held in the kingdom of the English and returned to her father. It was determined that she should remain under royal protection; but she followed Count Baldwin, who had enticed her, with the consent of her brother Louis.

Therefore King Charles, consulting the bishops and the other leading men of his kingdom, had a canonical judgment pronounced by the bishops against the aforesaid Baldwin and Judith, after the judgment of secular law and according to the decrees of blessed Gregory. The aforesaid prelate is also found to have sent the Apostolic See writings of the following kind concerning the deposition of Rothad, bishop of the city of Soissons, whom he had removed from episcopal ministry by the judgment of the bishops; concerning the mention of Ebo’s name; and concerning the condemnation of a certain heretic named Gottschalk:

“To the uniquely and singularly beloved Lord, Father of Fathers, and to the most reverend Pope Nicholas, honored with supreme veneration: Hincmar by name, undeservedly bishop of Reims and servant of the people of God.

“In the letter of Your Holiness sent through Bishop Odo to the bishops in King Lothar’s realm, for the prejudice of the Church of Cambrai, I reread your authority asking whose neglect had caused that Church to remain without a shepherd for more than ten months. Therefore, lest I be censured by your apostolate as negligent, I report to Your Authority (Nicholas, letters 63, 64, 65) that, after letters had been sent to Lothar, to the bishops of his kingdom, and to Hilduin, who had irregularly occupied that Church, the prejudice has continued until now, even before you sent those letters.

“I repeatedly admonished King Lothar, through envoys and letters, as far as I was able, and continued to do so until he replied to me in a royal letter that Hilduin had sent his own envoy to Your Authority and that he ought not to make any other arrangement concerning the aforesaid Church than the one he had made, until he received your reply concerning it.

“Last October, in the month that has just passed, on the fifth day before the Kalends of November, Baldwin also sent me, through two of his men, a letter from Your Authority. It contained instructions that I should read the same letter to my fellow bishops of the province and that we should receive Judith to be presented before the eyes of her father and mother, provided that we understood that our most excellent king, as he had promised in writing and through his envoys to report to Your Apostolate, truly intended to fulfill what he had pledged concerning her. If we could discover that their minds were set on delaying this, we were under no circumstances to receive her. Otherwise—that is, if we acted differently—we would be unable to enjoy your grace and communion.

“I reverently received the letter of Your Authority, as was proper, and reread it to my fellow bishops. Concerning the aforesaid Judith, we jointly intervened with her father and mother, as far as we could, in accordance with your instructions, and endeavored to present her before their paternal and maternal eyes.

“Afterward, since it had seemed right to us according to the sacred rules as we understand them—for we do not think that what we see bound by the bond of anathema under the sacred rules can be absolved without worthy fruits of repentance—we wished them first to make satisfaction to the Church whom they had injured, and only then to ensure that what the laws of the world prescribed was carried out according to ecclesiastical tradition.

“But because they wished to regard your letters, which prescribed nothing concerning this matter and indeed indicated that no delay was to be made in their union, as sufficient for themselves, they ought not to have been compelled, without your authority—the authority to which they had appealed—unless they submitted themselves in some other way. From another letter of Your Holiness I reported to them that you had not dissolved the ecclesiastical laws, but had sent petitions on behalf of one who could be punished according to secular laws, so that he might have a place for repentance concerning what he had committed against the divine laws.

“In this way our Savior, who wishes all human beings to be saved and wills that no one perish (1 Timothy 2), interceded at the cross with the Father, by priestly right, for his persecutors (Luke 23). This he effectively obtained for those who believed after his Passion and, being pierced with remorse, performed penance; with the Father he grants all things.

“Following his example, you, as the vicar of the apostles, and as supreme pontiff of the Catholic and Apostolic Church, to whose thresholds they had fled, asked that what had been committed against the human king and the laws of the world be forgiven, so that, through repentance, they might have time to erase what had been committed against the King of heaven and earth and against the laws of the heavenly kingdom.

“On the other side, the worldly-minded—and even some of those who had previously opposed such a union—protected themselves with this defense, as it seemed to them, but in truth stripped themselves of salvation. They refused to depart from the words of this latest letter of yours, which, they said, demonstrated that their union ought to take place without delay.

“When I said to them that I ought not to abandon what I understood from the ecclesiastical rules for the sake of any earthly power—especially since our lord king Charles, your son, was acting with me, indeed with God—some men, as though offering me advice, gave me the following counsel. I will use not my own words but theirs; your gentleness, as an example and teacher of God’s discipline, being mild, humble in heart, and patient, will bear with them calmly.

“They said that, since it was not secular but ecclesiastical authority that commanded me in this matter, I should withdraw somewhat from the conspiracy of those resisting, lest some rival should suggest to Your Holiness that I had acted in contempt of your holy apostolate and of the Apostolic See, and thereby stir up your gentle disposition toward me and obtain some excommunication—just as had been done in Rothad’s case, although it did not reach me except insofar as Bishop Odo and afterward Luido [ms.: Lando] reported it, before we were able to send Your Authority the sequence of the proceedings; or lest you should learn through your envoys how the matter had been conducted.

“This was especially so because your letter of authority says: ‘If we acted otherwise than is written in it, we would be unable to enjoy your grace and communion.’

“I replied that you had inserted this in your letter so that that woman would not be deceived by us, not so that she would fail to make satisfaction to the Church. They answered: ‘Why do you wish to understand your letter otherwise than you chose to compose it, when from those previously sent to me I can clearly understand its meaning?’

“Therefore, remembering your earlier letters sent by you to the bishops of the kingdom of your son, our lord Charles, and also considering what your kindness had recently instructed me in the letter sent through Luido—for these matters were being discussed at Auxerre after Luido’s arrival—I avoided contention in this case by dissembling between the fear produced by your earlier letters and the hope displayed by your later and milder letter. I also concealed my concession, as though postponing it to another time, awaiting your disposition of the present case, so that from Rothad I might learn how I ought henceforth to act in such matters.

“Thus, while we did not prohibit them from ecclesiastical ministry, but merely withdrew our presence from this affair as far as we could, Baldwin and Judith endeavored to carry out the rights of the secular laws which they had chosen. Our lord king, your son, did not wish to be present at this betrothal and union; but, sending officers of the public administration, and in accordance with his promise to you, he permitted them to be joined to one another in marital union according to the laws of the world, and granted honors to Baldwin solely at your request.”

## Chapter XIII  
### The case of Rothad, bishop of Soissons, who was deposed

“Finally, concerning the letter of Your Authority (Nicholas, letter 32), to which you sent me in obedience to hear it, addressed through Bishop Odo to all the bishops of the kingdom of our lord, the glorious King Charles, concerning Rothad: as Your Holiness commanded in the letters sent to my lowliness, I assembled with them. Together with those venerable bishops, as far as depended on me, I immediately took care—before the synod was dissolved—to fulfill your command concerning Rothad, lest any delay in carrying out your instruction, or an invasion by the pagans, or any other cause, should intervene. This will be fully made known to Your Holiness by the envoys of our lord king and by ours, as well as by the letters.

“But because, when a circumstance arose which the envoys themselves will report to you, they were unable to go with Rothad into your presence as soon as we had given our letters and appointed our representatives, they were delayed longer than we wished. Meanwhile Luido, the envoy of our lord king, returning from Your Holiness, brought your apostolic letters to our lord king, your son, in the city of Auxerre on the day before the Kalends of December.

“His son and namesake, Charles, had offended his father’s disposition in certain matters and, because of this, through the suggestion of some men, had delayed coming somewhat into his presence. The king therefore asked his envoys to send my small self, together with certain other faithful men, to lead him to his feet, so that through our intervention he might be able to find his father more conciliatory. Our lord king had ordered my humble person to come there into his service.

“As soon as I arrived, he gave me your letters to read. In them, although Your Sublimity, by your condescension, treated my humility kindly, without any claim to merit, and although you graciously deigned to praise the writings of your wisdom above my ignorance—though not without some cauterizing incision—I seem nevertheless to see that my verbosity is becoming burdensome to you.

“Therefore may Your Holiness graciously accept what blessed Augustine did not hesitate boldly to say to the Lord of lords concerning his own verbosity, when he wished to make himself excusable before him. Among other things he wrote: ‘To speak at length is not excessive, provided that it is necessary.’

“On this account, most holy lord and most reverend Father, bear calmly with a little of my foolishness, and also support me (2 Corinthians 11), if I continue to write something about Rothad’s case, which is already sufficiently known to you, as though repeating it. Since it pleases you—who are pleased by every good thing—we are sending our representatives to you, not as accusers to engage in conflict, but as men accused by Rothad and by our neighbors, who either do not fully and truthfully know the case or do not wish to know it, in order humbly to report to Your Supreme Authority that we judged Rothad—not in contempt of the Apostolic See, to which he appealed according to the Sardican canons (4, 6), but as one who had appealed to the judgment of the chosen bishops concerning specific charges—according to the Carthaginian and African canons (African Council, chapters 63, 88, 89, 94) and the decrees of blessed Gregory.

“Far be it from us to value so lightly the privilege of the pontiff of the first and supreme see, that we should bring before Your Supreme Authority, to burden it, controversies and disputes of both higher and lower order, which the Nicene canons (chapter 5), the other canons of the sacred councils, and the decrees of Innocent (letter 2, chapter 5) and of other pontiffs of the Holy Roman See command to be settled in provincial synods by metropolitans.

“But if a case should arise concerning bishops for which we do not possess certain and explicit judgments in the sacred rules, and which for that reason cannot be determined in a provincial or comprovincial examination, we must have recourse concerning it to the divine oracle, that is, to the Apostolic See.

“Likewise, if, in a major case, a provincial bishop has not appealed to the judgment of the chosen bishops, and that bishop has been judged in some case—that is, deposed from his rank in a comprovincial synod—and thinks that he has a good case, and the deposed man appeals and flees to the bishop of the Roman Church, wishing to be heard, then, if he judges it right that the examination be renewed, those who examined the case after the episcopal judgment must write to that supreme pontiff, and the examination will be renewed according to his disposition, in accordance with chapter 7 of the Council of Sardica.

“But in the case of a metropolitan established by the sacred rules, who by ancient custom receives the pallium from the Apostolic See—as Leo writes to Anastasius (letter 84, chapter 1), as the Council of Nicaea also indicates (chapter 7), and as the other pontiffs of the Roman See demonstrate in their decrees from the sacred canons—the judgment of that pontiff of the See must be awaited even before the trial.

“For he is the one who, according to the prophet Ezekiel, dwells in the treasury that faces the southern way and keeps watch in the guardianship of the temple (Ezekiel 40). We metropolitans, by comparison with him, are those who serve in the ministry of the altar which is before the face of the temple, where the flesh is burned; we labor to settle the disputes of carnal persons in provincial synods, and concerning greater matters and the cases of greater men we take care to report, after judgment, to the examination of the pontiff of the supreme See. We have men under his authority as fellow soldiers under ours, and we say to one, ‘Go,’ and he goes, and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes (Matthew 8).

“For, as Leo says (chapter 11), ‘Even among the most blessed apostles, although they were alike in honor, there was a certain distinction of authority; and although the election of all was equal, to one nevertheless was given the pre-eminence over the others. From this pattern, too, arose the distinction among bishops, and provision was made by a great ordering that none should claim everything for himself, but that in each province there should be one whose judgment held first place among the brethren, and through whom the care of the universal Church might flow to the see of blessed Peter, so that nothing anywhere might be separated from its head. Therefore, whoever knows that he has been placed over certain persons ought not to resent having someone placed over him; but the obedience he demands, he too should render.’

“Rothad strove more to demand this obedience from his subjects than to render it to the sacred rules, although even the holy angels in heaven are read to obey those superior to them. Therefore he reached the point at which he deserved to be deposed.

“For many years I took care, through benefits bestowed, admonitions, and entreaties, through myself, through my fellow bishops, and through everyone familiar with him whom I could enlist, to admonish him to obey the sacred rules. Many times I also tried to impress threats upon him through metropolitan letters and by the authority of the Apostolic See, and I endeavored to show him from the reading of Catholic writers how gravely he was giving offense.

“To this he replied that I knew how to do nothing else except show him my little books all day long. For this reason I was rebuked by many people, and very frequently, for knowingly carrying for so long, against the will of God and sacred authority, a man who was incorrigible and useless to the sacred ministry.

“Although he very often strove, as though deliberately, to provoke the king, his fellow bishops, his neighbors, and even me—much more often than the rest—to anger, though he could not succeed, I knew that it is extremely dangerous for a priest to give expression to disturbed and impetuous anger, to pronounce a hasty judgment, and to heighten the cruelty of persecutions. Therefore I bore him for a long time—along with the dissimilarities of conduct, the obstinacies of the disobedient, and the darts of malicious tongues—not without fear for the danger to the souls entrusted to him.

“When I ought no longer to bear with him, I brought him before the counsel of many bishops, so that at least he might hear them. He preferred not to hear their counsel but to demand a judgment against me. To answer his request, so that he might at least be ashamed and withdraw from the folly he had begun, I bound myself to judgment, as I have already reported more fully to Your Holiness in other letters, and as necessity compels me to repeat for the satisfaction of Your Authority: you should know that I did nothing against him with an inimical spirit, but out of divine zeal, as far as I can discern in my conscience.

“These things are also known to our lord king, to the bishops of his kingdom, and to very many ecclesiastical and secular men.

“After his deposition, I obtained the agreement of our lord king and the bishops that he should receive a very good abbey. All of us were to support him from our own resources as we would a father, so that he, who had always lived in luxury, would not be broken, provided only that he did not strive to be seditious and troublesome to the Church over which he had presided.

“At first he agreed to this. But, as certain men who claim to know the matter say, some bishops of King Lothar’s realm, driven by bitter zeal against us because we had not followed their counsels concerning Waldrada, and also, as some say, certain men from Germany, at the persuasion of their king Louis—because I had not acted toward him as Rothad had acted in the expulsion of his brother from the kingdom—persuaded Rothad not to give up stirring up sedition, and promised to obtain from you that he should be restored.

“Now, as you commanded, we have obtained from our lord king, your son, that he be brought into your presence and submitted to your disposition, trusting that God will deign to inspire your heart with what will be more pleasing to him in this matter.

“Concerning this, Your most gracious condescension deigned to write to me, your servant, through Luido, instructing me, once the full college of the brethren had joined me, to rely on your apostolic judgment and endeavor to restore him properly to his former office, according to the procedure described there.

“Let Your Most Reverend, most loving, sweetest Paternity know that I was unable to do this for the reasons contained below. Rothad had already been entrusted, together with the letters to be brought to Your Authority, to those who were to lead him into your presence, and it was not possible for me to summon the full college of the brethren. As I wrote above, I was far removed from our diocese, serving your son, our king.

“Furthermore, he could not be restored canonically without the judgment of those who had taken part in his deposition and to whom you had written concerning it. The bishops of other provinces could not be assembled through my convocation, since they were occupied with many matters. Moreover, the fellow bishops of the province of Reims had hastened from the very synod at which we heard the letter of Your Holiness to return to their sees, because they had to resist the Northmen.

“The few bishops who were with me in the service of your son, our king, reread with them your expression of kindness concerning Rothad. They replied that they did not know that he possessed such a life, understanding, or zeal for the sacred ministry as would enable them to dare to involve themselves in this matter. This was especially so since the man who had previously retained some reverence concerning his deposition, and who had always been disobedient both to the sacred rules and to royal dignity and to metropolitan privilege, was now raging even more unrestrainedly, to the harmful example of many and the scandal of many well-disposed people, living more carelessly and more perniciously, serving his own desires when he ought to have lived in freedom.”

«Concerning what your graciousness wrote, weighing not the beastly but the human disposition of the man: “Perhaps he will recognize his offense and of his own accord choose to persevere in the judgment by which he was judged.” But if he does so, action must be taken with King Charles—your most beloved son, that is—so that by his generosity he may graciously bestow upon him suitable benefits, sufficient for him and his people to be supported and for him to live honorably. Let your Excellency know that he is not a man of such moderation. For from what he began he could never be recalled.

This too I, a servant of your dominion, pondered in my heart; and, conferring with your most faithful son, my lord the glorious king, I considered it worthy to write to your most wise authority on this matter. That is: although, relying upon letters of your authority sent through Luidon to my insignificance—letters you mentioned in the epistle which you sent to your son, our lord the king, and which I reread to him—I might have obtained from him an order to his envoys, who had undertaken to lead Rothad into your presence, that they should wait before beginning the journey to Rome until a suitable time arrived for summoning the bishops of our regions, there was no reason for it to become known to others why Rothad’s dispatch was being delayed before your letter of authority had been read to the bishops:

[Col. 0166A] it could have happened that those who, by divine mercy, his kindness, and their devotion of love, esteem me, and think me to be something when I am nothing, learning that this had occurred because of my intervention, would have taken offense at me, as though I were causing your recommendation to be despised or neglected—although within the time appointed by you in the letter sent through Bishop Odo, I had hastened, as far as I could, to obey your command.

And if the bishops who know Rothad’s negligence and his long-standing uselessness in the sacred ministry, and who know that I know these things together with them, were ever to assemble and I were to speak with them about his restoration, they would all hiss me away and judge me utterly insane. Even if we were to promise Rothad that we would obtain benefits for him, so that he would entrust himself to us—which he will not do with his salvation in view—they would respond in the same way. For nearly everyone in these provinces knows that, according to the Carthaginian and African canons (63, 88, 89, 94) and the decrees of blessed Gregory, he submitted himself to the judgment of the electors.

More than five hundred men of various orders were present when the golden chalice set with gems was taken from the innkeeper and the tavern-keeper by the king’s agent, recovered from the pledge Rothad had given, and brought to the synod. They also know that silver crowns were reclaimed from the Jew to whom he had given them; that ecclesiastical property which he had concealed and secretly entrusted elsewhere was recovered from there and restored to the Church; and [they know of] silver vessels, of no small weight, which had long hung in the churches.

[Col. 0166B] He also gave away at his own pleasure other things which his predecessors and forebears, and other faithful people, had offered to that Church for the remedy of their souls, without the consent of the metropolitan and co-bishops, and without the approval of the steward, priests, or deacons of his church. Yet blessed Gregory repeatedly writes in his letters, on the basis of the sacred canons, that whatever a bishop acquires after his episcopal ordination belongs entirely to the Church in which he was ordained. Hence it is clear that he himself ought not to distribute such things without the steward and the knowledge of the clergy.

All the inhabitants and people of the city who came with the king and the bishops to the synod—and who, as though truly running to a spectacle, saw him come as far as the door of the synod and then return from there like a madman—know how, despising the king’s and his brothers’ kindness, he withdrew harder than stone, though both king and bishops were weeping, after being judged on definite charges for which the sacred canons have prescribed explicit judgments.

[Col. 0166C] They would therefore think that we, who judged him according to the sacred canons as we understood them, and who afterward, as those canons command, arranged through our co-bishop who had taken part in that judgment for our judgment concerning him to be reported, and who now have endeavored to send him, with our letters and representatives, to the Apostolic See—as you commanded—the See which confirms that the ancestral canons must be observed and demonstrates through its own observance that they are confirmed and must be observed, would doubt the justice and equity of your authority.

And therefore, if we were to promise him an allowance so that he would entrust himself to us, they would rightly mark us as insane. Even if it could happen—which we do not believe would happen through that first and holy See and through your supreme apostolate—that, once you had examined such a man, you were to name him restored to his order, we would thereafter have no danger of conscience concerning the souls entrusted to us by you.

Since everyone in these regions knows how negligent he has been toward the sacred canons and how contemptuous of them, how long and with what patience and kindness he was tolerated, and how unwillingly he was judged—because he refused to correct himself according to the sacred rules as we understood them—we could feel no shame at his restoration if it were carried out by the power of your supreme pontificate.

For all of us, old and young, know that our Churches are subject to the Roman Church, and that we bishops are subject in the primacy of blessed Peter to the Roman pontiff. Therefore, while the faith which has always flourished in that Church remains unharmed, and, with the Lord’s cooperation, will flourish, we must obey your apostolic authority.

[Col. 0166D] For it is written to us, together with all others, that Jesus was subject to his parents (Luke II). It is likewise written to us: “Obey your leaders and submit to them” (Hebrews XIII), and, “Do nothing out of rivalry or empty glory” (Philippians II). And, “If anyone wishes to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor the Church of God” (I Corinthians XI).

Therefore, after speaking with your most faithful son, my lord the glorious king, I repeated to him what I have often emphasized, and what he most willingly accepted and desires to fulfill: that, just as “the earth is the Lord’s and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it” (Psalm XXIII), so the kingdom is his, and he gives it to whomever he wishes (Matthew XVI). In the same way, he founded his Church upon the foundation of the apostolic rock (John XX), and both before his Passion and after his Resurrection entrusted it, with special care and singular privilege, to blessed Peter and, in him, to his vicars.

Whoever honors Peter’s see and the pontiff of that see honors him who said: “Whoever receives anyone whom I send receives me” (John XIII). And he will be honored by him who says: “Those who honor me I will honor, and those who despise me will be held in dishonor” (1 Kings II).

[Col. 0167A] Since many know the nature of Rothad’s complaint, while some speak of it otherwise, and since everyone generally knows that your authority has commanded him to be sent with our representatives to your judgment, it is right and just that whenever a Roman pontiff commands any bishop to come to him at Rome, that bishop should strive to come—unless illness, some grave necessity, or impossibility prevents him, as the sacred canons prescribe. Much more, then, should one whom the pontiff judges must be brought into his presence because he cries out to him in any manner concerning such a complaint come to him.

Whoever sees or hears that the king and bishops readily obey and honor the supreme pontiff of the Apostolic See will obey their own superiors all the more readily and humbly. For, as blessed Gregory says: “Just as the members subject to a head languishing are vigorous in vain, so, when the head is crowned—that is, honored and adorned—with glory and honor, its subject members will shine with its honor and beauty.”

And Rothad could not have been satisfied in any better way than by going into your presence, where the signatures of so many bishops—who do not wish to lie either to God or to you—and the arguments of so many representatives of those bishops would have shown him that he by no means had a good case.

«Therefore he ought to attribute to himself, and not to you, the fact that he has wearied himself and many others without a good cause. Your most discerning piety, which knows that compassion is owed to one’s neighbor and rectitude to faults, sufficiently warned him of this in your apostolic letters.

Among his other slothfulnesses [i.e. *socordias*], he is recognized as possessing such hardness that, although so many times, for so many years and in such important matters, without any regard for fear or love of God and without any human shame, he resisted the sacred canons, the decrees of the Roman pontiffs of the holy See, the privilege of his metropolitan see, and synodal judgments, and although he was tolerated for so many years and by so many people, he scorned to turn back from his foolishness.

Though repeatedly entreated by the king and bishops, he could not be brought to subscribe that henceforth he would obey the sacred canons and the decrees of the Roman pontiffs of the holy See, and, according to them, the privilege of his metropolitan see—for without observing these no one among us can be a bishop—and thus enjoy fraternal peace in every respect.

[Col. 0167B] Later, of his own accord, in the document of his profession by which he appealed to the judgment of the electors, he sent these claims to the synod, shamelessly asserting that he had observed them, although everyone knew this to be false. Thus he appealed to the judgment while refusing to subscribe to the rules which he was to observe if he were not to be judged.

As those who heard it from him later told us, he refused to subscribe for this reason—which we too understood: lest he be defeated. But if the king and bishops remained in our judgment, he would go to Rome before being defeated; and when he arrived there, he would subscribe to these matters through your command, once he had been absolved by you against our will.

He did not understand—indeed, he was unable to understand, for his wickedness had blinded him—that your authority wisely understood why the Lord, speaking from heaven to Paul when Paul said, “What do you command me to do, Lord?” (Acts IX), did not explain everything that had to be done, but directed him to Ananias, from whom he was to hear and receive what he had to do.

[Col. 0167C] So too, after the angel announced to Cornelius that he had been heard, he sent him to Peter’s teaching and obedience (Acts X). Although, so to speak, he had been baptized before baptism by the Holy Spirit, blessed Peter commanded him to be baptized with the baptism of the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit, in whom the hearts of believers are purified by faith (Acts XI).

When a question was therefore raised against him even by his subordinates, though faithful men, as to why he had entered among the Gentiles, that same prince of the apostles—filled with the grace of the highest gifts and supported by the power of innumerable miracles—answered the complaint not by authority but by reason. He set out the matter in order with the gentleness with which, when the aforesaid Cornelius wished to worship him, he said in humility: “See that you do not do this. For I myself am also a man, just as you are” (Acts X).

For if, as Gregory says, he had asserted something of his authority in the complaint of the faithful, he certainly would not have been a teacher of gentleness. Thus he appeased them by a humble explanation, and humbly gave a reason in the matter of his rebuke. He also brought forward witnesses, saying: “These six brothers also came with me” (Acts XI).

[Col. 0167D] Following his humble authority, most gentle power, and most upright preaching—“not lording it over the clergy, but becoming an example to the flock” (1 Peter V)—Blessed Gelasius says in his decrees (epistle 9) to all bishops, concerning ecclesiastical institutions:

“Since we desire that nothing be rashly permitted to us contrary to the reverence due to salutary rules; and although the Apostolic See, by the Lord’s favor, strives with pious and devoted purpose to uphold all those things which have been established by the ancestral canons, it is exceedingly unworthy that any bishop, or anyone of the ranks that follow, should reject this observance, which he sees the See of Blessed Peter both follow and teach. It is also altogether fitting that the body of the whole Church should agree with itself in this observance, which it sees flourishing there where the Lord placed the primacy of the whole Church” (Galatians I).

Concerning Barnabas and Saul he likewise says truthfully that Paul the Apostle was not from men, nor through a man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father. After they had for a long time enjoyed the company of the apostles, the Holy Spirit said—not to the apostles themselves, but, according to the faith of sacred history, to the prophets and teachers who were ministering to the Lord in Antioch: “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work of the ministry to which I have taken them” (Acts XIII).

Then, after fasting and praying and laying hands upon them, they sent them away. Sent by the Holy Spirit, they departed, called apostles. In the following year—that is, the fourteenth after the Lord’s Passion—although he who worked through Peter for the apostleship to the circumcision also worked through Paul among the Gentiles, nevertheless, according to the agreement of James, Cephas, and John, Paul, together with Barnabas, received the teaching of the Gentiles.

[Col. 0168A] Paul himself also wrote to the Corinthians, when their leaders were negligent, concerning the incestuous man: “When you are assembled, and my spirit is present, deliver such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord” (1 Corinthians V).

The leaders of the Corinthians delivered him to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, and Paul, after learning of his deed, did so by his authority together with them. Once his repentance was known, they restored him, and Paul did so by his authority together with them, saying: “If you have forgiven anything, I forgive it also. For if I have forgiven anything, I have forgiven it for your sake in the person of Christ” (2 Corinthians II).

Hence blessed Gregory says (Moralia, book XXXIII, chapter 8, elsewhere 11): “I do not dissent from your good action. Let what you have done be mine.” If we should dare to ask him, as it were, “Why do you so cautiously join yourself to your disciples? Why do you so carefully conform either yourself to their actions or them to yours?” he answers: “So that we may not be deceived by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his thoughts”—that is, lest he turn what the mind begins well into an end of malice.

And Innocent (epistle XXVII, to the letter of Macedonius): “This apostolic kindness toward the Corinthians was declared so that, when a judgment is reached and withdrawn under one spirit, good men may always follow it impartially.”

«Leo too, drawing upon the Apostle (epistle 84, chapter 11), says:

“Let no one seek what is his own, but what belongs to another; and let each person please his neighbor for good, unto edification” (1 Corinthians X). For the firm structure of our unity cannot exist unless the bond of charity binds us into inseparable solidity. For just as in one body we have many members, but all the members do not have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another (1 Corinthians XII).

The connection of the whole body produces one health and one beauty. This connection of the whole body requires unanimity, but it especially demands harmony among priests. Although their order is general, their dignity is not common to all.”

These matters, preserving their higher meaning, were carried out concerning those mentioned above and taught by those already mentioned, so that it might be understood how inferiors ought to obey their superiors, superiors provide for their inferiors, and the order arranged by God be maintained by everyone and in everything.

[Col. 0168B] Hence the supreme Pastor of the Church teaches: “If anyone ministers, let him do so as from the strength which God supplies, so that God may be honored in all things” (1 Peter IV). He entrusted his affairs to his servants, and to each according to his own ability (Matthew XXV). It is likewise written concerning the Holy Spirit that he distributes gifts to each as he wills (1 Corinthians XII).

Accordingly, following the Council of Sardica (chapter 7), the supreme pontiff of the first and holy Roman See, when a provincial bishop who has been deposed appeals and flees to him with his complaint for a renewed examination, does not immediately restore him by the singularity of his privilege and authority. Rather, he either sends him back to the province where the case occurred, and where, according to the Carthaginian canons (the Council of Carthage, or Africa, cited above) and the provisions of Roman law, the case can be carefully investigated, since it is not difficult to produce witnesses and discover the truth; or he deigns to write to neighboring bishops, or sends one from his side who, possessing his authority and being present with the bishops, may judge and carefully investigate and decide the case; or he deigns to believe that the bishops are sufficient to bring the matter to an end.

And Innocent (epistle 2, chapter 3): “If any disputes or contentions arise among clerics, whether of higher or lower order, he commands that the quarrel be settled by assembling the bishops of that province according to the Council of Nicaea” (Nicene Synod, chapter 5).

[Col. 0168C] Boniface too writes concerning Maximus that he should be compelled to come to the province and present himself there before the established judgment; and whatever the bishops of the province should decide concerning him, once it had been reported to him, should be confirmed by his authority. Thus, as he writes to Hilary (epistle 3, canon 6), each province should always await the arrangement of its metropolitan in all matters, as it is written in the Nicene Council (canon 5): “Just as at Alexandria, since the bishop of the city of Rome also has a similar custom, so likewise at Antioch and in the other provinces, let the privileges of the Churches be preserved.”

“Therefore it was rightly agreed” (ibid., canon 5) “that councils should be held twice each year in every province, so that, when all the bishops of the province are assembled together, such questions might be examined.”

«I say these things not, God forbid, to prejudice in any respect the power of the supreme Apostolic See and of your holy apostolate, which I am ready, as is right, to obey in all things.

[Col. 0168D] Rather, I think I am rendering obedience to your supreme authority when I humbly lay before the wisdom of your teaching what I think, either for proof or for correction. I endeavor to make Rothad’s character known to you, lest, through my negligence, the things I know about him remain hidden from you, so that your true authority may more certainly decree whatever seems good to you concerning him.

If you now decide that he is to remain under your judicial disposition, we know the kindness, moderation, and piety of your son, our lord Charles: whatever you command that aforesaid son of yours concerning him, and whatever he can reasonably fulfill, he will obey without any objection.

Our co-bishops too will provide him most abundantly from the revenues of their Churches. As for my insignificance, just as I have never wished to seek repayment for the evil he inflicted upon me through his contempt and insults, so whatever kindness I can show, I will endeavor to provide most willingly and even more abundantly than I have ever done.

[Col. 0169A] But if, without any satisfaction for his long-standing contempt of the sacred canons, the decrees of the Apostolic See, the privilege of his metropolitan see, and the synodal judgments—which he has neither wished to obey nor to profess or subscribe that he would henceforth obey—and without a profession or subscription of his correction and obedience before his brothers, whose canonical admonitions he had repeatedly despised, although this is read in several passages of the letters of Leo and Gregory; and if, to pass over those matters which, out of reverence for the priesthood and to avoid secular reproach, following the African Council, we did not even permit to be brought forward for nomination at the synod; if, then, after those charges for which he had been judged by the bishops to whose judgment he had appealed had been disregarded and dismissed without any correction, although they had been sent to your authority under a pledge of faith and according to the explicit decrees of the sacred canons and the Apostolic See—Celestine saying (epistle 3), “For what worthy thing will be preserved by us if the norm of decretal constitutions is broken, and license is granted to peoples according to the pleasure of certain persons?”—if then it should please your authority to restore him, I will bear it with an even mind, as is fitting for the regular judgment of the pontiff of the first See, the mother and teacher of all Churches, and the father and teacher of all bishops.

[Col. 0169B] Yet I believe that your most diligent discernment will take into account the contempt and obstinacy of subjects toward their superiors, and the freedom to sin against the sacred canons with impunity, which from this example may, as some think, acquire harmful force in our regions.

This is especially so since it is well known to your most wise authority that the Council of Sardica demonstrates in its seventh chapter how the execution of the restoration—or the continuation in deposition—of a bishop who has been deposed and appeals to the Apostolic See ought to be carried out by that See without prejudice to those who judged him. Innocent, Boniface, and especially Leo in the decrees cited above, and Gregory still more clearly in his letters, demonstrate the same thing, following the decrees of the Council of Carthage—indeed of the Apostolic See, which presided over that council through its representatives (Third Council of Carthage, canon 10):

[Col. 0169C] “Namely, if an appeal has been made from any ecclesiastical judges to other ecclesiastical judges where there is greater authority, this should not harm those whose sentence has been dissolved, unless they can be convicted either of having judged with an inimical spirit or of having been corrupted by some greed or favor.”

Hence our conscience bears witness to us, and it is recognized as having become known to all who were present, that we preferred to preserve him rather than judge him, if we had not feared being condemned together with him for neglecting the sacred canons by the judgment of those through whom, under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, they were promulgated, together with the man whom we were unable to correct.

Therefore, corrupted by no hostile spirit, no greed, and no favor, we carried out against him the canonical judgments, mourning his incorrigible slothfulness and irreversible obstinacy. We did not dare suspend those judgments any longer.

[Col. 0169D] Your supreme authority in deciding will also attend to the Apostle’s teaching: “The sins of some people are manifest, going before them to judgment; but those of others follow after” (1 Timothy V). As blessed Ambrose explains this (On the Apology of David, book I, chapter 6), it is as though they were placed in a balance and examined in judgment, to determine whether good works, weighed more heavily, precede and show that evil deeds are to be mercifully overlooked as minor, or whether evil deeds, weighed more heavily, precede, so that they deserve the judgment of condemnation and choke out the few good works.

[Col. 0170A] We too, according to our limited ability, weighed in Rothad not only uselessness but also harmfulness, together with his deeds. Like a barren fig tree occupying rational soil uselessly for too long, and even after many seasons and many admonitions failing to receive, as it were, baskets of fertilizer placed around it, but remaining sterile, we judged that it should be cut down, not without anguish of heart.

Since these things are so, I have no doubt that your moderation will not overlook what immediately follows in that chapter of the aforesaid Council of Carthage (Third Council of Carthage, canon 10, and African canon 89): “Certainly, if judges have been chosen by agreement of the parties, an appeal may not be made even from a smaller number than has been established.”

That established number, demonstrated in the preceding twelfth chapter, and the agreement of the parties having been sought, is clearly shown to have been complete in Rothad’s trial.

[Col. 0170B] If, for whatever perhaps more reasonable cause, still unknown to us, it should please your supreme authority to oppose their judgment—and many things hidden from us do not escape you—since it is my duty to entrust myself to you by obeying you, not to examine your judgments, I will endure it. If, in the regular restoration you decree for him, some action is to be taken—which your authority will arrange, including how he, as usual, once victorious and having obtained his wish, is thereafter to behave as a bishop—I will not resist.

I will regard it as a great blessing if at last I can breathe freely after the long and many troubles which I have endured from him and on his behalf, and if I never again have to labor uselessly against his disturbances.

Moreover, ecclesiastical persons are not the only ones who despise and regard our judgments as worthless; secular people do so much more, saying these things and bringing forward what must not be attributed to your authority, lest I in any way stir the sweetness of your disposition—a thing I most earnestly desire to avoid.

[Col. 0170C] If any people in our province, whose complaint could reach you after his restoration, commit certain serious offenses—as some matters are being committed more frequently in these regions than in former times—I will strive to warn them, lest God condemn me for silence, and I will rejoice if they wish to correct themselves. If not, I will appeal to your judgment on their behalf.

If they wish to go, your holy wisdom will endeavor to decide what it sees to be best in the matter. If they do not wish to go, they will do what they judge useful for themselves.

Would that the sentence of Saint Ambrose might free me from divine condemnation in this matter, when he says: “If someone lacks the power which he knows would enable him to reject the guilty, or is unable to prove the charge, he is free from blame.”

Thus, I think, because I am occupied with many matters, constrained by the length of the journey and by my obligations, and unable to report everything to the Apostolic See before the complaint of insolent persons reaches you, being weighed down by illness and—thanks be to God—already near the end, I may take precautions so that your holy disposition is not moved against me by anyone, and so that some excommunication is not threatened against me.

[Col. 0170D] Although I know, according to the Apostle’s Gospel, that the Lord will repay each person according to his works (2 Corinthians V), with their conscience bearing witness to them (Romans II), and with their thoughts accusing or even defending one another on the day when he will judge the secrets of human beings; and although, as Leo says, “If anything is fulfilled through our service, that is, the priestly ministry, in good order and with a joyful disposition, let us not doubt that it has been given to us by the Holy Spirit; and whatever is otherwise cannot be valid,” I will strive by every means, insofar as he grants it—he from whom every good gift and every perfect gift comes (James I)—to ensure that the last day, whose time is uncertain and which may come suddenly, does not find me, God forbid, in any way expelled from communion with the Apostolic See.

[Col. 0171A] For it will come, although later than necessary, since I, a great sinner, am held for a long time confined in the grievous prison of the body, afflicted in many ways under the providence of the all-provident Lord. For there will come a time and a person in the Church of Reims when, and in whom, the privilege bestowed and preserved for it by apostolic authority according to ancient custom will be maintained.

That Church has never had a primate except the Roman pontiff, except for the time when, after its pontiff had been expelled without any fault of his own through the violence of the tyrant Milo, and the see was vacant of a pastor in the time of Prince Charles, it was entrusted for a while to Boniface, the legate of the Apostolic See, as was also the Church of Trier.

Between the Churches of Reims and Trier—for these are the only two provinces that the region of Belgica contains—there has always been this distinction, as we find in ecclesiastical records and have discovered to have been maintained by the most ancient custom: the bishop who had previously been ordained in the metropolitan church of either of these Churches was regarded as senior according to the sacred rules, not by locality but by the dignity of his rank.

[Col. 0171B] It will be necessary for me to conduct myself in such a way that I do not henceforth receive so many letters from your authority threatening excommunications and containing rebukes—letters which we read are to be sent by apostolic men only rarely and under great necessity—as I have frequently received in these times, deserving them because of my sins.

If it should please your holiness, you will not need to take action against me in the future, unless your apostolic command finds me disobedient in some matter against the sacred rules, God forbid, through contempt.

For whoever understands why the Lord praised the faith of the centurion in the Gospel (or something similar), when he said, “Say the word and my servant will be healed” (Matthew VIII), understands how effective the word of a bishop is—or rather, as in Paul, Christ speaking in him (2 Corinthians XIII)—and understands how much more effective is the word of the pontiff of the Apostolic See and how greatly his command must be obeyed, even without the addition of any adjuration.

We bishops are debtors to the wise and the foolish alike: we must impress this upon those who know it and make it known to those who do not. If, from now on, the words of wicked men prevail against us, as they boast and proclaim, it will not be necessary to labor greatly over the provincial synods in which we have hitherto labored; for each person will have his own law and his own hope.

[Col. 0171C] I gratefully received, with due reverence, what your sublimity wrote to our humility: first, that you had been moved to investigate Rothad’s case by the care with which you are bound to all your brothers. I understood from this that we, however unworthy as metropolitans, must be counted among the number of your brothers.

Therefore, just as your discretion must take care that subject bishops are not irregularly condemned by metropolitans, so it must likewise take care that metropolitans are not irregularly despised by subject bishops.

Second, you wrote with complete clarity that Rothad is known to have appealed to the Apostolic See, and that you did not wish to appear to tolerate calmly, during your days, any diminution of the privileges of your Church. This too must rightly be accepted and most carefully preserved by us and by all.

I have wished, and still wish, to preserve it as far as I am able, and, with the Lord’s favor, I will remain in this devotion, knowing that the privilege of the metropolitan see of Reims—to which divine graciousness has appointed me to serve—remains within the supreme privilege of the holy Roman See.
