It is also the privilege of the Roman See, if by its authority it causes the privilege of a see subject to it to endure and takes care to confirm it.

[Col. 0171D] Concerning the third matter which you brought forward, I did not presume to write anything else except that Rothad’s case differs in almost every respect from the cases about which you wrote.

Concerning what your apostolic kindness finally deigned to write to my unworthiness—that I should consider these matters with you, approve what you decide concerning Rothad, and not suppose that you had acted in any way to my injury—I return immense thanks to your holy apostolate with all the devotion of my heart, with every supplication and due submissive humility, replying with complete sincerity of mind: just as you deigned to write to me, so I believe in every respect.

And because, as is fitting, you possess the privilege of your supreme pontificate vindicated—and none of us had opposed your command that Rothad be brought into your presence—I desire, and trust that I shall, see what you have deigned to pardon.

For I ask nothing other than what I have shown above: what the sacred rule commands me to request and you to grant. Namely, that compassion be shown to Rothad by your authority in such a way that ecclesiastical vigor is not dissolved; and that ecclesiastical vigor be preserved in such a way that due mercy and necessary sufficiency are not denied him.

[Col. 0172A] Thus, neither should others be provoked by his example to transgress, nor should those to whom, in these regions farther removed from the Apostolic See, the moderation of ecclesiastical discipline has been entrusted see here—God forbid—a source from which they may grow lukewarm through negligence or laxity, or claim that they can take occasion to transgress the boundaries established by the fathers (Proverbs XXII). We believe that, as we have understood them, we have preserved those boundaries until now.

You will see what will be best in the deed itself; and in your judgment we must see what God wills. For divine judgments cannot be unjust, since they will be pronounced by justice speaking from the solidity of confession of the apostolic rock, against which the gates of hell—that is, evil suggestions or actions—will not prevail (Matthew XVI).

The letter which your authority commanded me, with an adjuration, to send to Rothad was sent by our lord the king, your son, through his abbot to Rothad as soon as he came to him.»
«Rodulfus as well, the uncle of that son of yours, our lord the king, returned from Ludovicus, king of Germany, on the third day before the Ides of the past month of December. When, very late in the evening, we were hurrying from our king’s court to our lodgings [Col. 0176B] on the River Loire, near the boundary of the kingdom of Aquitaine, he sent me one of his men, named Rodulfus, instructing me that the aforesaid King Ludovicus had entrusted a certain man of Rothadus, together with letters from Your Holiness, to his protection and keeping, so that he might bring him with those same bishops into the presence of our lord King Karolus without inflicting any harm upon him.

For that man has been accused before our lord the king of having stolen property and treasure belonging to the Church and, after committing perjury in the matter, having fled and gone to King Ludovicus. Therefore the same Rodulfus asked me to assist him with our lord the king in this matter, so that, since he had received the aforesaid man under his protection, no harm might come to him. I replied that he should keep the man with him, so that in the meantime he might suffer no harm, until I returned to the court, and that I would endeavor to assist him in the matter as far as I could. But I saw that man neither then nor afterward, nor did I hear where he had gone with the letters.

I have therefore taken pains to write this to Your Holiness so that, if any of our ill-wishers should, as is their custom, wish to suggest anything sinister to you concerning this matter, you may know what is true about it and may not change your disposition toward me.

«Finally, the account which I rendered before the chosen judges, before whose judgment I had been summoned by Rothadus through a petition of appeal, the venerable bishops themselves are sending to Your Authority. As for the proceedings compiled by Rothadus after his excommunication at the provincial synod, which we have heard reached you through our neighbors in order to discredit us, the bishops of the province of Reims have taken care to inform Your Holiness, through our common envoys, of what they know.

«Likewise, after a few matters concerning the promotion of that lord Hincmarus to the episcopate—which we have already partly noted above and have not thought it necessary to repeat here—finally, after the aforesaid Ebo had died, our Church, and also our diocese, according to the custom it has held from ancient times—even concerning those who did not remain in the episcopate in the same Church until death—began, as an act of piety, to recite his name among the bishops in the catalogue during the sacred mysteries, and continues to do so to this day.

I did not presume to forbid this without the authority of the Apostolic See, lest I scandalize the devout, as though I begrudged the salvation of a brother, and especially of a soul resting in the Lord—a soul resting in the Lord: for he had not been anathematized for straying from the soundness of the Catholic faith, but, goaded by his own conscience, had first condemned himself and afterward had been condemned by a synod and also by the Apostolic See. The blessed Pope Coelestinus says (Epistle 1, chapter 12): “For it is impious that religious souls should suffer such things; and since they are our members, we too ought to be chastened by their affliction.”

Now, however, in the letters of Your Holiness which the deacon Engelwinus brought to us, we find that Teotgaudus and Guntarius are not to be admitted into the catalogue of bishops. And since the Council of Antioch [understand: “established” or “commanded”]—as we have stated above, and as you yourself know better—concerning one who, after condemnation, presumes to exercise episcopal ministry according to the preceding custom—which there is no doubt Ebo did—may Your Apostolic Authority deign to write back to me whether I may permit that same Ebo to be named among the bishops in the sacred diptychs in our church, or whether I ought to forbid his name from henceforth being mentioned in the catalogue of bishops. Thus, supported by your authority, I may show without ambiguity what must be observed concerning this matter in our Church, in accordance with your decision (Council of Antioch I, canon 4).»

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning a certain schismatic, Gothescalcus

Moreover, Luido told me that you had discussed with him the condemnation and confinement of Gothescalcus. Since I had already heard from others that certain words had reached Your Holiness, I sent to Your Authority, through Bishop Odo, a written statement setting out some passages from the words and opinions of Catholics, explaining how I understand the matter against the opinion of that pestilent man; but I deserved to receive no reply concerning it. Nevertheless, when certain bishops—who had no concern whatever with him, since, as they themselves clearly showed, neither charity moved them to this nor authority compelled them—sought an account from me, they summoned me, by a layman [Col. 0177C], to the little council recently held at Metz, which, as I understand, you forbade to be called a synod. They summoned me irregularly, four days before it was to assemble (in the year 863), although I was more than eighty miles away from that city and Gothescalcus himself more than one hundred miles distant, and although I had received no prior notice whatever.

I therefore briefly bring this matter to Your Holiness’s attention because, before I reached the episcopal order, Gothescalcus was, as his abbot and the monks among whom he had lived testify, a monk in habit but savage in mind, in the monastery of the metropolitan Church of Reims, in the diocese of Soissons, called Orbais [j, Orbacus]. Unable to endure quiet, delighted by novelty of expression, and singular among his fellows in harmful fickleness, he selected for himself certain propositions from all the perversities which he had learned were then held in these regions, so that through the novelty of his expressions he might become known. He sought thereby to corrupt the understanding of the simple and devout, to usurp for himself the name of teacher, and to draw disciples after him; and to obtain improperly—for he could not obtain it legitimately—a position of leadership over those who, with itching ears (I Tim. IV), strive to heap up teachers for themselves according to their own desires, by means of a pretended religious life and doctrine.

Although he had been ordained a priest contrary to the rules by the chorepiscopus of Reims who then held office, he irregularly left the monastery, traveled through many regions, and, as a most destructive sower, scattered deadly seeds. At last, when a synod was held in Mainz (in the year 848), he presented to Archbishop Rabanus a written statement of his error. He was condemned by all the bishops of Germany and sent with synodal letters to the metropolitan Church of Reims, over which, by the Lord’s authority, I already presided.

Afterward he was heard by the bishops of the Belgian province of Reims and of the provinces of Gaul and was found to be a heretic. Because he refused to repent of his perversity, he was, lest he harm others when he was unwilling to benefit himself, by the judgment of the bishops of those provinces, confined in a monastery within our diocese. Rothadus, whose diocese he belonged to, did not know how to resist him; and we feared that this man, who loved novelties, might learn to think perversely, since he had refused to learn and teach what was right. Moreover, lest Gothescalcus, living a common life with others, make them share in his error, he was committed to monastic custody, in accordance with the Apostle’s teaching: “Avoid a heretical person after the first and second admonition” (Tit. III), knowing that such a person is corrupted and condemned by his own judgment.

As Pope Leo says concerning Eutyches (Epistle 13), when he saw that the opinion of his folly displeased Catholic ears, he ought to have recalled himself from his position and not stirred up the bishops of the Church in such a way as to deserve to receive a sentence of condemnation. If he chooses to remain in his opinion, no one will be able to release him from that condemnation.

If he had wished to repent of that condemnation and return to the Catholic understanding, I was and always have been ready—since the venerable bishops so judged—to receive him into the communion of the Catholic Church, just as I order that the necessities of the body be supplied to him. But if Your Catholic Wisdom wishes to know what he appears to say against the Catholic faith from the ancient Predestinarian heresy—which first arose in Africa and afterward in Gaul at the same time as the Nestorian heresy, and which, in the time of Pope Coelestinus, was refuted by that pope’s authority and through the efforts of Saint Prosper—we shall briefly set out for you, in a number of propositions small in number but not in weight, a few of the many points.

He says what the ancient Predestinarians also said: that just as God predestined some to eternal life, so he predestined others to eternal death.

He says what the ancient Predestinarians also said: that God does not wish all human beings to be saved, but only those who are saved; and that all are saved whom he himself wishes to save. Consequently, whoever is not saved is altogether outside his will to be saved. For if not all whom God wishes to be saved are saved, he has not done everything that he wished; and if he wishes what he cannot accomplish, he is not omnipotent but weak. Yet he is omnipotent who has done everything that he wished, as Scripture says: “Everything that the Lord willed he did in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the deeps” (Psalm CXXXIV). And again: “All things are placed in your will, O Lord, and there is no one who can resist your will” (Esther XIII): “If you have decreed to save us, we shall immediately be delivered.”

He says what the ancient Predestinarians also said: that our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ was not crucified and died for the redemption of the whole world—that is, for the salvation and redemption of all human beings—but only for those who are saved.

With a tradition differing in form but with the same error, he says what the ancient Predestinarians also said when explaining the Apostle Peter’s statement, “denying the Lord who bought them” (II Peter II): “He bought them,” he says, “through the sacrament of baptism; nevertheless, he did not undergo the cross for them, nor endure death, nor shed his blood.” That the reception of baptism is called redemption, however, the teacher of the nations openly declares: “Do not grieve,” he says, “the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (Ephesians IV).

But that redemption which is proper and particular to all the elect alone—the redemption which their gracious Redeemer bestowed upon them by being crucified—he redeemed, delivered, and cleansed from sins all the elect alike: those born in the past, those born in the present, and those yet to be born; the living and the dead. They, precisely they, are the world for which the Lord suffered, as he himself said: “The bread that I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John VI, 52).

And elsewhere that same Gothescalcus writes: “Far be it from me even to dream of such a thing, much less to whisper it even once: that the ancient serpent could ever carry away to perish with him eternally any of those for whose redemption so precious a blood was poured out to God the Father of our Lord God, his Son. Amen.”

And again, speaking to God: “It is therefore plainly and clearly evident that none of those redeemed by the blood of your cross is lost to you.”

What the ancient Predestinarians did not say, this man says all the more boldly and therefore all the more destructively: that the deity of the Holy Trinity is threefold.

There are also other things which he and many others in these regions say, and which appear to us contrary to sound faith. When Your Authority learns of them through someone other than me, you may perhaps attend to them more carefully and hasten to teach what must be held concerning them. For there will soon be need of this. Although their hearts boil with the madness of a perverse opinion, nevertheless, during the reign of our orthodox king, they do not dare openly to express the wrong ideas they hold.

Thus we clearly see fulfilled what is written: “Gathering the waters of the sea as into a wineskin” [manuscript: “wineskin”] (Psalm XXXII). The water of the sea has been gathered as into a wineskin, because the bitter knowledge of the heretics compresses within the breast whatever today in this kingdom of your son, our lord Karolus, holds a perverse opinion, and does not dare to speak openly.

They also secretly gnaw at my insignificance with a dog’s tooth. With the Lord’s help I shall easily be able to bear this, because little time remains to me; and if, by God’s permission, they receive power to afflict me bodily among the sons of the Church, with divine grace assisting me they will exercise my patience. Even if they oppose me merely by holding evil opinions, they will exercise whatever small measure of knowledge I possess; and, so that even enemies may be loved according to the Lord’s command (Matthew V, 44), they will exercise benevolence.

If Your Authority writes to me that I should release the aforesaid Gothescalcus from custody and grant him permission either to come to you, so that through you you may examine his teaching, or to go to anyone whom you designate by name, I shall in no way resist your commands. For, as you yourself know better, just as no one can be regularly ordained absolutely, so a monk, or anyone subject to a rule, cannot be released from his place according to the sacred rules unless he is entrusted, with his own consent, to a specific person of whom he is known to be the charge, and sent to a definite place. I ask only that I have Your Authority, lest I seem, through my presumption, to disregard the judgment of so many bishops.

I do not take pleasure in the confinement which that pertinaciously obstinate man justly endures, however slight its hardship may be; rather, I grieve over the perfidy from which he cannot be recalled. If Your Authority judges that he should be entrusted to someone, it will also provide in the letter of entrustment that the person to whom he is entrusted be Catholic and possess ecclesiastical seriousness, vigor, and knowledge of Scripture. For he is able to recite by heart, throughout the entire day without any pause for breath, not only Scriptures violently twisted to his own meaning but also mutilated statements of Catholics.

Thus he was accustomed to lead into his opinion not only the uneducated, filling them with admiration for himself, but also the half-learned and the unwary, and those who possess zeal for God but not according to knowledge (Romans X, 2). He seeks to appear not only the teacher of his own teachers but also pays close attention to whether he can entrap those who speak with him in conversation. If he cannot prevail by truth, he will strive invincibly to assert on oath that those speaking with him said things which perhaps they had not said, so that he himself may appear truthful and those who contradict him may be proved liars and teachers against his doctrine.

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning the books composed by that same prelate Hincmarus

He also wrote to the aforesaid Pope Nicolaus, setting forth the content of his faith and his defense against the error of the aforementioned Gothescalcus—a defense which he endeavored to ground in the Catholic faith. He wrote many other works as well.

He also compiled a book from the statements of orthodox Fathers for the sons of his Church, demonstrating that the deity of the divine Trinity ought not to be called threefold, since the supreme Trinity is one, in order to refute the previously mentioned blasphemies of Gothescalcus. He also wrote one book to King Karolus on this same matter.

He likewise wrote for that same King Karolus an excellent work in verse on the grace and predestination of God; on the sacraments of Christ’s body and blood; on the vision of God; on the origin of the soul; and also on faith in the Holy Trinity. He called this work *Solomon’s Dish* (*Ferculum Salomonis*).

He also collected and composed a huge volume containing several books on the predestination of God and free will, against certain of his critics and against Ratramnus, a monk of Corbie, and addressed it to the same King Karolus. He prefixed to it the following letter:

«To the glorious lord King KAROLUS (the Bald), HINCMARUS, in name but not in merit bishop of Reims and servant of the people of God, together with my fellow bishops, venerable lords and brothers, devoted intercessors for your salvation and prosperity.

[Col. 0181B] «We give thanks to God, who has kindled your heart with love for himself, and has enflamed you with knowledge of the truth and with understanding and diligence in orthodox faith; who has also divinely bestowed upon you prudence and understanding in the writings inspired by him; and who, through your meditation upon them and your exertion in them, advances the devotion of your study day by day, insofar as public affairs permit you, for the benefit of his holy Church.

Moreover, we have gone through the synodal propositions of our venerable fellow priests, namely those of the three provinces, as they are contained there and will be found written below. You delivered them to our humility to be read and examined, in accordance with the example of preceding kings, for the sake of learning the truth, just as Scripture commands: “Ask the priests concerning my law” (Haggai II, 12), for we also read that there is a law of faith.

In these propositions, although our names are not mentioned, we find ourselves reproached, as though non-Catholics, by the designation of their effects, and despised without regard for brotherhood. We also find that the propositions which, because of the necessity made known to you and to be explained below, we extracted from the opinions and words of Catholic Fathers have been rejected and abominated as useless, indeed harmful.

Those who composed these propositions did not wish to insert them into their own writings as we had extracted them, lest they be read by those into whose hands their propositions might come. Instead, they touched upon certain matters contained in the propositions extracted by us, but in another sense and with other words, in order to portray those propositions as abominable. Others they suppressed, and referred to them in such a way as though we had held opinions contrary to the teaching of the holy Fathers at the African and Arausican synods.

Concerning one proposition in particular—namely, that God wills all human beings to be saved (I Timothy II, 4), although not all are saved—they remained entirely silent. We shall demonstrate this more expressly later, when the Lord says: “Behold, I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms, to uproot and destroy, to disperse and demolish, to build and to plant” (Jeremiah I, 10).

For if they trusted in the conscience of a correct understanding, they ought first to have placed before their readers, in their entirety, the things they were striving to destroy—the things which they had received complete and in which matters requiring uprooting and dispersal were found—and then, having destroyed and dispersed them by authority, they ought rationally and orderly to have planted their own positions and raised them up by building them on high.

Concerning another proposition, as though some mockery could exist in the sacred mysteries, they wrote in such a way that readers might understand it to have been said by us, although we made no mention of it. We shall explain in its proper place why we said nothing about it and in whose writings we found it after writing the propositions.

They also inserted in those same writings certain sixteen propositions, as though they ought to be charged to us, although we had neither heard nor seen anything of them before the venerable Ebo, bishop of Grenoble, brought them to you at the palace of Vermeria as having been sent by your brother of blessed memory, Lotharius.

We found no author of those propositions recorded, nor, although we searched greatly, were we able to discover one. Therefore we thought that they had been compiled through someone’s envy in order to disgrace another’s reputation, as we often read has happened.

To mention a few examples from many: there was the letter of propositions which the venerable Bishop Ibas denied at a synod to be his; and there was what certain rivals, while blessed Augustine was still alive, composed from his words, which he cleverly and Catholicly rejected when it came to his attention.

After his death, certain envious persons also took care to collect propositions from his writings, including matters such as those now at issue, so that they might succeed, through hostility toward his person, in cheapening his orthodox and most useful teaching and in turning devout readers away from reading and loving him, and from necessary severity.

Saint Prosper showed, in a Catholic and prudent style, through a commission from the Holy Roman See by Pope Coelestinus, that these lies of his rivals were false and had been rashly brought forward, and he most clearly demonstrated that the teaching of that man—already mentioned and still to be mentioned—was orthodox.

It is therefore possible that these propositions, which were brought or sent to you in the name of our fellow brothers by others rather than by them, were not written in this way to disparage us, but that, at the devil’s instigation, they were composed among the other evils that are now increasing in this world, in order to introduce discord among the priests of the Lord. The devil intensely fears and envies the charity which he sees us preserving among earthly human beings on earth, the charity which he, as an angelic spirit unwilling to preserve it, lost in heaven.

For how could it be that our brothers would judge us so angrily and with such contemptuous disregard, when they continually keep before their eyes and daily practice the Lord’s rule concerning how each person ought to admonish his brother (Matthew XVIII, 33)? For they know that it is written: “Before you inquire, do not blame anyone; and when you have inquired, correct justly” (Ecclesiasticus XI, 7).

«Saint Augustine accepted most graciously the writings of heretics and of those who criticized him whenever he found something praiseworthy in them, and he labored to interpret many passages according to their correct meanings; but he never attempted to bend anything from a correct meaning toward a perverse one.

How, then, could our brothers have acted in such a way before questioning us about the matter, according to the evangelical rule, either by word of mouth or in their writings? They ought either to have taught us if we wished to learn, or, if we held a perverse opinion and refused to return to the path of truth and faith, to have admonished us fraternally and repeatedly; they ought to have presented to us the divine authorities [alternative: “of divine authority”] and the writings of the holy Fathers; and they ought to have invited us with gentleness and mildness to meet together, knowing that a bishop ought to come to a synod of fellow priests either to learn or to teach.

Through the kindness of some among them, we received letters from certain of them in a fraternal spirit, and we sent our replies to them; yet we neither saw, heard, understood, sensed, nor were able to perceive anything of this sort from their side.

If they did write such things—if, perhaps, they did write them in order to display their wisdom by contrasting it with our folly, and to seek praise more from boasting than from our good qualities; if they preferred to make what we had said well, supposing that we had said anything good, their own through charity; and if, whenever they found that we had said something otherwise, they preferred to publish it rather than correct us fraternally—we marvel at such great and such distinguished men, archbishops and leaders among the bishops, and especially at Ebo (Ebo, nephew of Ebo of Reims, archbishop), who, as we have heard, is a religious man.

For he was raised from almost the very cradle under religious discipline and the regular habit in the monastery of the Church of Reims, where Saint Remigius rests. In that religious place he spent his life until, by Lord Ebo his uncle, then archbishop of Reims, he was consecrated there as a deacon and, by episcopal decree, appointed abbot of the monks to maintain and govern the regular order.

We say that he was so formed in humility and desired and wished to hold the place of humility that the following words are written for him and for everyone: “If the spirit of one who has authority rises up against you, do not leave your place” (Ecclesiastes X, 2). The spirit of one who has authority is the spirit of pride; our place, however, is humility. The truly fortified place and tower of strength commands us to learn this from him who says: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matthew XI, 29).

We have heard, and firmly believe, that this religious man wished earnestly to hold humility as a secure place against the aforementioned spirit of arrogance and boasting. For this reason we do not believe that these propositions were composed by him, since, leaving aside the names of the other fellow priests, they appear to express only the name of Ebo together with those of the archbishops, boastfully, as some think. It also seems especially in this matter as though he himself had contributed to it, as though the intention were that he should appear greater than the others and more learned in his judgment, even among the archbishops.

«We certainly do not find this concerning Saint Augustine, who surpassed others in knowledge, labor, and vigilance at the African councils. For Saint Augustine himself not only did not place himself above his fellow bishops, seeking private glory, nor permit himself to be placed above them; rather, he subjected himself to others, although he had labored more than they. Anyone who wishes to read the letters written to Saint Pope Innocentius and to other prelates of the Apostolic See (Augustine, Epistles 90, 92, 95) will be able to find this.

Nor do we read anything different concerning any bishop at any council, unless perhaps an apostolic letter, for an evident reason, decreed that a particular fellow bishop should be designated by name for a certain matter together with his archbishop, as we read concerning the bishop of Autun in the letters of blessed Gregory.

How much less would this religious and prudent man have wished to exalt himself in such a matter, or have permitted himself to be preferred while the other fellow bishops were despised and passed over?

Moreover, our brothers and fellow priests ought not to have ignored Solomon’s admonitory saying if they had secretly received anything sinister from us, either by hearing or in writing, and then, moved by some fickleness of our own—for which we are not conscious—had rashly broadcast it publicly into disputes and quarrels.

For he says: “What your eyes have seen, do not bring out hastily in a quarrel, lest afterward, when you have dishonored your friend, you be unable to correct it” (Proverbs XXV, 8).

Yet we know that there are some who, while striving to understand more than they ought to understand (Romans XII, 3), recoil from the peace of their neighbors, despising them as dull and foolish. Therefore Truth itself admonishes us, saying: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark IX, 49), so that whoever strives to possess the salt of wisdom must necessarily take care never to depart from the peace of concord.

Therefore Paul admonishes us terribly, saying: “Pursue peace with all, and holiness, without which no one shall see God” (Hebrews XII, 14).

Above all, we must preserve and pursue that peace—that is, follow it perfectly—we who must sacrifice to God daily, and who are specially commanded, as though by the testimony of Truth, that if we offer our gift at the altar and there remember that our brother has something against us, we should leave our gift there before the altar, go first to be reconciled to our brother, and then return and offer our gift (Matthew V, 23–24).

Behold: our leader and teacher does not wish to receive a sacrifice from those who are at odds; he refuses to accept a burnt offering. Here, therefore, we must consider how great an evil discord is, since it prevents even that by which guilt is released.

We do not, however, hold anything against our brothers if they wrote such things against us before bringing them to a meeting; rather, it must be believed that, if they had written them, they would have sent them to us, against whom they had written them.

But how can we reply to them when we do not know whether they wrote them? Nevertheless, lest Your Lordship remain without our reply, we shall endeavor, without fear, to answer the disparagement directed against us in heart, word, and writing—addressing you, from whose hand we received these materials.

«First, we shall send the things which are said to have been written by those same brothers of ours at the synod, although it appears from what follows that other things had previously been written here. But since these are known to have been composed to disparage us and against the propositions extracted by us, we judged it appropriate to place first those which, although greater in reputation rather than in authority—for some are not truthful—nevertheless deserved, because of their synodal heading, to be treated as significant.

Next we shall set out those which we received from many people and through the hands of others concerning several of these matters. For that reason, as we have said, we arranged to re-extract those four propositions from the opinions and words of the Catholic Fathers, on the condition that from the writings of each individual we should set down, as necessity required, certain passages from the individual opinions contained in the propositions extracted by us.

After this we shall endeavor to set down the propositions extracted by us from the opinions and words of the Fathers, just as we extracted them. If we are able to demonstrate that our understanding expressed in these propositions agrees with the divine and authoritative Scriptures, with the faith of the Catholic and Apostolic Church and of the Holy Roman See, and with the opinions of the orthodox Fathers who presided over that same holy mother Church and whom the Apostolic See of Rome has given us in the canon to receive (Distinction XV, canon “Sancta Romana”), we shall earnestly strive to act truthfully, humbly, and devoutly.

For we neither wish to accept nor to put forward the opinions of others as pledges for our Catholic understanding, since it is clear that that understanding is true and Catholic which the mother of all Churches, the universal Church, has judged worthy of approval.

Even if some have been called teachers, we neither accept nor put forward their opinions to prove the sincerity of the faith, unless the Catholic mother Church herself has decreed their opinions to be credible.

If, however, some have emerged who occupied a teaching chair after the canon of the sacred Scriptures and of the Catholic teachers had been written by that same holy See and given to all the faithful, and who understood and taught otherwise than those whom the Catholic mother Church has received, embraced, and nourished in her orthodox bosom, we neither ought nor need to produce or accept their opinions as authorities. For in these things and through these things we possess enough for salvation.

If any have taught, or presumed to teach as dogma, that something else must be held on the basis of a more mature and sounder instruction than theirs, we regard as wholly contrary to faith and salvation whatever is demonstrably different from their salutary teaching.

We also embrace with equal reverence the opinions of those who, by divine favor, flourished in the Church in Catholic understanding, doctrine, and holiness of life after the canon itself had been written by blessed Gelasius, and who, in faithful adherence to those orthodox Fathers recorded in that canon, wrote and taught nothing discordant or different from Catholic doctrine.

Thus we embrace the opinions of the venerable Bede the priest, instructed in the Catholic faith by disciples of Saint Pope Gregory and by Saint Theodore the archbishop, learned in both languages, Greek and Latin, who was sent by the Holy Roman Church to the Angles, after the disciples of blessed Gregory, for their instruction; and likewise those of Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia, of venerable memory, and of Alcuin, a religious and learned man.

The Roman Apostolic See not only most graciously accepted their faith and doctrine but also praised them highly, as we find in the writings of that holy See, which our Church received from that mother of Churches in the time of Charles, emperor of divine memory, when a synod was held concerning the known infidelity of Felix and its proceedings were sent to the Roman Church, as to the summit of the Churches. Anyone who reads the writings of these men understands how worthy they are of praise and acceptance.

Finally, if we cannot demonstrate that the propositions we have extracted agree with the opinions of such men as we have mentioned, we are prepared to yield our understanding to more learned and Catholic men, to submit ourselves, and without contention to subject ourselves to their doctrine.

And because we received from the archive of your brother Lotharius, of blessed memory, a booklet without the author’s name, in which, one by one and in their several places, the propositions extracted by us were set out and, with the approval of whoever he may have been, criticized and condemned, when we undertake, if we can, to confirm our propositions from the sayings of the Catholic Fathers, we shall also set out his criticisms and endeavor, as the Lord grants, to refute them.

Only then shall we set out the fifth proposition of our fellow brothers, concerning which they directed against us, as though silently and obliquely, a reproach which we found in the writings of Gothescalcus after we had extracted the four propositions so often mentioned. With the Lord’s inspiration, we shall state what we think concerning it.

Finally, we shall append those nineteen propositions for which our fellow brothers, through no fault of ours, decided to feed us in this particular matter on Scottish porridge, and we shall show from the opinions of Catholic brothers what we think concerning those same propositions.»

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning the matters he wrote to King Karolus

He also published another distinguished volume for the same king, against the aforesaid Gothescalcus and the other Predestinarians. Concerning it he writes the following letter to him:

To the glorious lord King KAROLUS, HINCMARUS, in name but not in merit bishop of Reims and servant of the people of God, together with my fellow bishops, venerable lords and brothers, devoted intercessors for your salvation and prosperity.

[Col. 0186D]

“Recently, after the month of June had passed, in the seventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 859, you gave us certain chapters, as you told our Humility, which had been presented to Your Highness by Remigius, the most reverend archbishop of Lyon. You ordered us, at a suitable time, to give you our response concerning them, asking whether we agreed unanimously and with one voice in their meaning, or whether, because they seemed to you in certain respects to dissent from the venerable, time-honored faith of the Fathers, our opinion—which you believed did not deviate from the Catholic path—differed from theirs in any way. In this we were to follow both the command of the Lord and the Christian custom of your predecessors.

“For it is established both by divine laws and by the ancient custom of former rulers that whenever something new arises concerning the Catholic faith or divine religion, it should be referred by imperial authority to the deliberation of the bishops; and whatever they decide, on the authority of the sacred Scriptures, the teaching of orthodox teachers, canonical authority, and the decrees of the Roman pontiffs—the vicars of Christ our God and prelates of his holy Church—is to be believed, followed, held, and preached: believed by all in the heart for righteousness, confessed by the mouth for salvation (Rom. 10:10), followed for vocation, held for the crown, and preached for gain.

“These chapters were indeed read out at a gathering of bishops held in the territory of Toul, in a village called Saponarias, two days before they were presented to you. The synod was led and the chapters were submitted by Lord Remigius, archbishop of Lyon. As he said, and as is contained in the heading of those chapters, in this same year, on the Kalends, he and his comprovincial bishops likewise issued them there from written replies, and in the suburb of the city of Langres, for the instruction of the Christian people. On the following day certain other chapters were left for later discussion. Concerning these matters, as it seemed to some of the brethren, the opinions of certain men were disturbed.

“For, to speak truthfully, when the chapters presented to the synod by Archbishop Remigius, as we have said, had been read out, and we recalled the traditions of Catholic teachers, our consciences were shaken not a little. Therefore some of our number, inflamed by zeal for the Christian faith, wished to make certain suggestions to the synod; but our agitation was temperately settled by that venerable archbishop Remigius of Lyon, who earnestly urged that, if the opinions of any of us were troubled by dissent from any point in the chapters that had been produced, each of us should take care to bring the books of Catholic teachers to the next synod; and that, according to what we might commonly find to be better and more consistent with Catholic and apostolic teaching, we should thereafter all hold it unanimously.

“From his devotion, and from that of the co-bishops of his diocese—whose Catholic mind and teaching, even before his ordination, we have recognized, as you also know—we have gathered, insofar as we dare to entrust our humble understanding to it, that those chapters were not issued by them—still less, let us not say, through them.

“Therefore, although some wished to mark them with a gentle hiss because of what Saint Celestine says in rebuking the Gallican bishops (Celestine, Letter 1, chap. 1):

> ‘What hope is there,’ he says, ‘where, while the teachers are silent, those speak who, if this is so, were not their disciples? I fear that silence may amount to connivance. I fear that they themselves may speak more boldly if they permit others to speak in such a manner. In such matters silence is not free from suspicion, because the truth would come forward if falsehood were displeasing. The matter rightly concerns us if we favor error by our silence.’

“We, nevertheless—many of us knowing their faith, teaching, and prudence—repeatedly set before those who knew these matters less well in their case the judgment praised by Saint Augustine concerning Saint Cyprian’s dissent over baptism, a judgment set forth repeatedly in the second book *On Baptism*:

> ‘For how,’ he says (Augustine, Book 2 *On Baptism*, chap. 4), ‘could this matter, enveloped in such thick clouds of controversy, have been brought to the clear illumination and confirmation of a plenary council, unless it had first been examined for a long time throughout the regions of the world, by many discussions and conferences among bishops on both sides? This is what the health of peace accomplishes: when matters that are more obscure are investigated for a long time and, because of the difficulty of discovering the truth, give rise to differing opinions in fraternal debate, the bond of unity remains until the truth is reached and made clear, lest an incurable wound of error remain in a severed part’ (ibid., chap. 5). ‘And therefore something is often revealed less fully to the more learned, so that their patient and humble charity—in which the greater fruit lies—may be proved; or so that it may be shown how they preserve unity while holding different opinions concerning obscure matters, or how they accept the truth when they learn that what has been declared is contrary to what they had thought.’

“For those same venerable, Catholic, and learned men knew that this pestilential teaching had again arisen in many regions and provinces. Therefore they were unwilling to impose silence on error in their provinces as readily as they perhaps could have done, until the question, having come to the knowledge of many, might be brought to rest by the judgment of many. For, as Saint Celestine says in his letter addressed to Nestorius (Celestine, Letter 6):

> ‘All ought to know what is being undertaken whenever the concern of all is being considered—so that, when the deliberation concerning all has been settled in the proposition of one, the resolution may be conveyed from all to all.’

“These same chapters, as you can easily recall, were given to us three years ago in a village belonging to the bishopric of Rouen called Melpsa, when we were staying on guard against the Norman invasion, under the title of having supposedly been written at the synod of Valence, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 855, under the emperor Lothair. You gave them to us so that, from the teaching of orthodox authorities, we might respond in a Catholic manner to those points that seemed so to us, together with whatever writings of others had reached your knowledge from this side.

“We received some of those writings, but we did not wish to publish them, being anxious to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Eph. 4:3), until we could speak familiarly with those who had sent them to you and, with the Lord’s cooperation, recall them from this wrongful intention to the unity of the Catholic faith, if in any way we could. But partly hindered by our occupations, and partly because our fraternal exhortations were heeded less than was necessary, we were unable to recall from their intention those whom we had determined to bring back.

“Therefore, since, as the Apostle says, ‘the sins of some people are manifest’ (1 Tim. 5:24), and what is otherwise hidden cannot remain concealed, the dissent of certain men grew so greatly that this discord reached your knowledge. Before you entrusted these matters to us for examination, out of zeal for the faith and love of unanimity, you had four chapters collected by episcopal decision from the sayings of the Catholic Fathers and required them to be confirmed by the hands of each individual.

“Afterward, however, the folly of some of those who had subscribed to those chapters, and of others as well, increased to such an extent that it became necessary—both because of the urgency of your command and because of our obedience in carrying it out—for us to answer in writing their writings and propositions, which we have mentioned above. Among these we also responded, according to the capacity of our small intellect, though with some hesitation, to the chapters that you recently gave us.

“For we did not believe that our brothers and fellow bishops could have written such things against us in violation of ecclesiastical rules, especially since they knew that the institutions of the Lord and the laws promulgated by the Holy Spirit had prescribed that, if we contradicted the faith in the chapters so often mentioned, they ought to compel us, and then, by synodal judgment, expel us and our opinions from their communion (Matt. 28:19–20).

“Now, however, since we are certain what response we owe concerning the frequently mentioned questions, reserving the resolution of the reports against those persons concerning whom, by your lordship’s authority, we were ordered to render an account in the ministry imposed upon us, we shall endeavor to respond simply to these chapters alone, insofar as we are able, while maintaining peace with everyone (Rom. 12:18), on the authority of the holy Scriptures and the judgments of the Catholic Fathers.

“Thus anyone who has neither been able nor wished to read all those writings may here find brief responses, suitable for the present, to the chapters. Snatching occasional hours from the many distractions of our occupations—we have no leisure for study—we have endeavored to commit these responses to sheets in hurried language, just as we receive them from the judgments of the holy Fathers, lest through sluggishness or disobedience we should be marked as lacking Christian devotion toward you.

“For in the reports mentioned above, provoked by the manifold assertions of many people and by manifold and repeated discussions, we have labored to respond in three books, in a disjointed style, though—as we know and confess—not without weariness to the reader, yet with a Catholic meaning.

“Nevertheless, we think that we satisfy the kindly reader chiefly in this respect: we have always set down each individual judgment separately and endeavored to respond individually to the objections and arguments resisting the faith. We trust that, for this alone, we may win the goodwill of every devoted reader, because when each one has considered our labor according to his own judgment, he will hold us excused in his own mind.

“Whoever composed these chapters, to whom we are now compelled to respond as though to something new, will reveal himself when necessity forces him to come into the light of truth. For the one who practices works of darkness—for among such works the Apostle also counts heresies (Gal. 6:1)—hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works be exposed. But everyone who does what is good—for among good works the Apostle also counts faith—comes to the light, so that his works may be revealed, because they have been done in God (John 3:21).

“Yet whoever he may be, if he comes to the light and consents to the truth from his heart, he may become a son of light. But if he stubbornly contradicts the truth, he himself will impose upon himself the name of heretic through his unbelief and the folly of his contention. For something is not immediately heretical merely because, through ignorance, it is judged different from the faith; it becomes heretical when it is maintained with stubborn contention.”

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning the synod of six provinces of Gaul held at Troyes

Finally, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 867, a synod of the provinces of Reims, Rouen, Tours, Sens, Bordeaux, and Bourges assembled at Troyes on the eighth day before the Kalends of November. There, as often happens, certain bishops, favoring Vulfadus through the favor of King Charles, began to contrive something against Hincmar in opposition to the truth and the sacred authority of the canons.

But Hincmar, opposing their efforts with reason and authority, prevailed through the judgment of the majority. By common agreement, the bishops who had assembled sent to Pope Nicholas, through Actardus, the venerable bishop of Nantes, a letter setting forth the order of the events under discussion.

The contents of that letter were the same as those of the letter of Hincmar, bishop of Reims, which he had sent to Rome through his clerics in the preceding month of July, disguised as pilgrims in order to avoid the ambushes of his opponents. Actardus undertook to carry the letter produced at the aforesaid synod and sealed with the seals of the archbishops who had assembled. With certain bishops he returned to Charles, just as Charles himself had ordered.

But Charles, forgetful of the loyalty and labors that the aforementioned Hincmar had repeatedly undertaken over many years for his honor and for the preservation of his kingdom, demanded that Actardus hand the same letter over to him. Breaking the archbishops’ seals, he reread the acts of the synod; and because Hincmar had not been refuted at that synod as Charles had wished, he had another letter dictated in his own name to Pope Nicholas, in opposition to Hincmar. He sealed it with a seal bearing his own name and sent it to Rome through Actardus himself, together with the synodal letter.

The aforementioned clerics of Hincmar, arriving in Rome in August, found Pope Nicholas already very ill and laboring intensely in the dispute that he was carrying on against the Greek emperors Michael and Basil, as well as against the Eastern bishops. Therefore they remained there until October.

Pope Nicholas, however, gratefully receiving what Hincmar had written to him, replied that he had been satisfied concerning everything. [Note: This letter of Nicholas to Hincmar is not extant.]

He also sent another letter to Hincmar and to the other archbishops and bishops established in the kingdom of Charles. In it he reported that the aforementioned Greek emperors, together with the Eastern bishops, were accusing the holy Roman Church—and indeed the whole Church that uses the Latin language—because we fast on Saturdays; because we say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son; because we prohibit priests from taking wives; because we prevent those same priests from anointing the foreheads of the baptized with chrism, while the Greeks themselves say that we Latins make chrism from the water of a Latin river; and because they reproach us Latins for not abstaining, according to their custom, from eating meat for eight weeks before Easter and from eating cheese and eggs for seven weeks.

They also said that at Easter, following the custom of the Jews, we bless and offer a lamb upon the altar together with the Lord’s body. They were angry with us also because our clerics shave their beards, and they said that among us a deacon is ordained bishop without having first received the office of presbyter.

Concerning all these matters, he ordered replies to be sent from each province by the metropolitans together with their fellow bishops. At the end of his letter he addressed Hincmar in these words:

> “Your Charity, Hincmar, when it has read this letter, must take the greatest care that it be promptly conveyed also to the other archbishops who are established in the kingdom of our son, the glorious King Charles. You must see to it that each of them, in his own diocese, together with his suffragans—wherever they may be established in any kingdom—properly examine these matters and take care to report to us what they discover. Do not neglect to summon them, so that in all that the scope of this present letter contains, you may be there both its energetic executor and, before us, a truthful and prudent reporter through the sequence of your written account.”

Hincmar received this letter and reread it to King Charles, who was staying at the palace of Corbeny, together with many bishops. He also endeavored to send it through the other archbishops, as he had been instructed.

Pope Nicholas died on the Ides of the immediately preceding month of December (see the year 11 of Louis II). Pope Adrian succeeded him in the pontificate, by election of the clergy and with the consent of the emperor Louis. When Actardus came to Rome with the letters written above, he found Adrian already ordained in the apostolic see.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Again concerning the aforementioned King Charles

The aforementioned Lord Hincmar wrote for the same King Charles a small book collected from the sacred Scriptures and the sayings of the Catholic Fathers, arranged in three parts: concerning the person of the king and royal ministry in the affairs of the commonwealth; concerning the proper distinction to be made in mercy; and concerning the punishment of particular persons. He concluded it in thirty-three chapters.

He also wrote to the aforementioned king a very useful instruction (Book 7, Letter 126) concerning the avoidance of vices and the practice of virtues, sending him at the same time the letter of Saint Gregory to Reccared, king of the Visigoths.

He likewise wrote to the same king a collection of numerous authorities concerning churches and chapels, against the disposition of Prudentius, bishop of Troyes. He also wrote for the king’s instruction concerning the twelve abuses of the saints, collecting in it sayings of the Fathers and the constitutions of former kings.

He further reminded him of the promise that he had made, in word and writing, to the leading men and bishops before he was consecrated king.

He also wrote many letters to that king, who sought the archbishop’s advice on many matters and arranged many things prudently at his suggestion.

When his son Karlomannus, a cleric, rose up against him, while the king himself had set out for Vienne against Count Gerard, who had revolted from him, the king sent his letters to our prelate, ordering him to summon the bishops of the kingdom and the laymen loyal to him. The bishops were to prohibit Karlomannus, according to their ministry, from doing any harm in that kingdom, while the laymen were to resist him so that he could not do so.

Concerning this matter Hincmar wrote to Counts Engilrannus, Gossinus, and Adelelmus, asking them—or rather giving them counsel—about what they ought to do in the matter. He had also already sent supplicatory letters to the king on behalf of Karlomannus and was working for peace between him and his father, although he suffered many evils and acts of plunder from Karlomannus and his accomplices.

He approached Karlomannus’ conference together with other faithful men of the king, gave him hostages, and received from him a promise that peace would be made in the kingdom and that Karlomannus’ men would remain peacefully in the kingdom. Karlomannus himself was to remain peacefully with a few men in the villages of Saint Medard until the king’s envoys arrived; then Karlomannus was to go with the king’s faithful men to his father, make an agreement with him, or return safely to his own people.

After receiving the king’s envoys, I sent letters to Karlomannus asking him to come to the conference with him, where he would hear what the king commanded. Hincmar also summoned the king’s faithful men so that they could establish peace there according to the king’s command and strive to carry it out. This was indeed done at that time.

But afterward the king had his same son and his followers excommunicated by the bishops of the entire kingdom because of the evils that he refused to abandon; moreover, after having him captured, he ordered him to be deprived of his sight.

King Charles also used to command Lord Hincmar not only concerning ecclesiastical matters, but also concerning the summoning of the people to war, requiring him to carry this out. Hincmar, having received the king’s command, was accustomed to summon both bishops and counts.

Concerning this King Charles, the following vision is reported in the vision of the revived Bernoldus, of which we have already related something above [chap. 3].

Bernoldus came to a certain dark place, toward which light shone from another nearby place that was exceedingly bright, beautifully flowering, and fragrant. There he saw this King Charles lying in mud formed from the pus of his own corruption and being eaten by worms, which had already consumed almost all his flesh, so that nothing appeared on his body except nerves and bones.

Calling Bernoldus by name, he said: “Why do you not help me?”

He replied: “Lord, how can I help you?”

The king said: “Take that stone which is beside you and place it beneath my head.”

When this had been done, he said to him: “Go to Bishop Hincmar and tell him that because I did not heed the good counsels of him and my other faithful men, I am suffering what you see as punishment for my sins. Tell him that I have always trusted in him, that he might help me to be freed from this punishment, and ask on my behalf all those who were faithful to me to help me. For if they undertake a struggle for this purpose, I shall soon be freed from this punishment.”

When Bernoldus asked him what place it was from which that light shone, he heard that it was the rest of the saints. As he tried to approach more closely, he saw such brightness, felt such sweetness, and perceived such beauty [j, sweetness] that no human tongue can express it.

He also saw there a multitude of people of different orders rejoicing in white garments, and certain shining seats, on which none of those for whom they had been prepared yet sat.

On that journey he entered a certain church, in which he seemed to find Bishop Hincmar prepared to celebrate Mass with clerics dressed for the service. He told him what Charles had commanded.

Immediately returning to the place where he had seen the same king lying, he found him in a bright place, healthy in body and clothed in royal garments. The king said to him: “Do you see how your messenger helped me?”—and so forth.

Lord Hincmar described this vision after it had been reported to him, explaining it in the places where this seemed necessary, and caused it to become known to many. Both personally and through other royal officials who were also subject to him, he labored piously and faithfully for the absolution of the king’s soul and the attainment of rest.

That same prelate very often offered the king advice concerning many matters necessary to him. Among other things, he wrote to him concerning the election of the bishop of Beauvais after the death of Hildemannus, the prelate of that city. In this letter he sought to restrain the king from the Simoniac heresy, asserting that it would be much more acceptable to him to abandon that bishopric according to worldly considerations than, contrary to canonical institution, to bless a bishop—or rather to curse himself with an eternal curse.

He also wrote concerning the cell or monastery of Flaviacum, which the same king had given him while Hincmar was serving him before becoming a bishop, and which the king had confirmed by a written grant so that Hincmar might hold it during his lifetime. Hincmar had rebuilt it after it had been destroyed by an invader and had restored religious observance there as far as he could; afterward the same king attempted unjustly to take it away from his possession.

He wrote concerning a certain fugitive who had joined himself to a nun, advising the king to have him arrested and, by his royal power, separate him from this crime, since the adulterer had refused to obey episcopal judgment.

He wrote concerning the case of Bishop Rothadus [manuscript: Rothardus], whom the king had summoned concerning his own cases and ordered to send an advocate to answer against a certain man of Rothadus concerning a benefice belonging to Rothadus, over which a dispute existed between them. For this matter Hincmar reproved the king subtly and diligently, striving to recall him from this intention by introducing sacred authorities.

He wrote concerning his own mission, which he carried out before Emperor Lothair and Louis beyond the Rhine, the brothers of Charles, to arrange a peace pact among the three brothers.

He wrote another letter concerning the same matter, in which he instructed King Charles how he ought to act toward his brothers, and also concerning their reception or rejection in the matter under discussion.

He wrote concerning the case of his brother, Emperor Lothair, explaining how he was being treated at Rome and when he would come to these regions. He also instructed the king concerning how he ought to conduct himself both before God and before human beings. For this reason he also admonished the queen to exhort the king earnestly to an honorable manner of life appropriate to a king.

He wrote concerning military arrangements for lifting the siege of the city of Beauvais. In this letter he took care to indicate how he should administer the Church entrusted to him: ecclesiastical affairs through the heads of monasteries and archpriests; the care of the villages and the management of the household, royal services, and guests; and the complaints of those crying out or making appeals through the most faithful laymen.

He wrote concerning the journey to Upper Francia, how it should be arranged, and how this kingdom should be left in an orderly condition.

He wrote concerning the synod that the king ordered to be summoned within the parish of Reims, explaining for what reasons the synod ought to be convened, as well as concerning certain other useful matters.

He wrote concerning the case of the deceased Abbot Hilduin; concerning the case of Count Gerard; concerning the case of Louis, king of Germany and brother of the same Charles; concerning the case of Lothair, king of Italy and nephew of Charles; concerning the construction of the bridge that the king was building at Pîtres on the Seine with Hincmar and certain other faithful men; and concerning the case of his nephew Hincmar, bishop of Laon. He wrote many letters on behalf of the latter and labored greatly for him before the same king.

He wrote concerning his own illness and the reception of certain pilgrim monks; concerning the possessions of Saint Remigius situated in the province of Vienne or Aix; concerning the ordinations of certain bishops and several churches; concerning the king’s journey to Italy after the death of his nephew, the emperor Louis, explaining how he should arrange that journey and how he should leave this kingdom in an orderly condition; concerning the questions of a certain Mancion; concerning the village of Noviliacum and the property belonging to it; concerning letters from Louis, the king and brother of Charles, which Louis had sent him concerning a vision in which his father had appeared to him. Hincmar sent Charles a copy of those letters together with a copy of the letter he had addressed to Louis concerning this matter.

He wrote concerning the case of the deceased Waltarius, a man of great distinction, and concerning an image of the Savior; concerning the case of the people of Laon and the appointment of a bishop for them after the deposition of Hincmar; concerning the same matter; concerning the passion of Saint Dionysius, dictated in Greek by Methodius of Constantinople and written in Latin by Anastasius, librarian of the Roman see; and concerning the life or deeds of Blessed Sanctinus, including what he had found in them concerning the commemoration of Saint Dionysius.

He wrote concerning the villages of Saint Remigius in the Vosges, explaining how they had been held up to that time. He also sent the same king various other letters concerning various matters.

## CHAPTER XIX. What he wrote to Louis, the son of the same Charles

He wrote to Louis (Louis the Stammerer), the king and son of this Charles, whom Hincmar had anointed and consecrated, concerning the levy imposed upon the Normans [uncertain]; concerning arrangements for the welfare of the kingdom, and concerning following the ordering and counsel of his father, the emperor; and, after the death of that emperor, concerning the establishment of the foundations of his kingdom. He proposed to him the examples of his predecessors and instructed him through chapters concerning the just governance of the kingdom, the honor of the holy Church of God, and other matters necessary to him and to the kingdom.

He wrote concerning the correction of certain presumptuous men, the moderation of corrective discipline, and other useful matters; concerning the need not to contrive anything against the canonical rules, nor to command any bishop anywhere to do so, lest he incur divine judgment; and concerning how, at the king’s command, he had admonished Hugh, the son of King Lothair, regarding the evil deeds he was committing and the sending of his men to the king with hostile equipment.

He also wrote to the sons of that deceased king, Louis and Karlomannus, concerning obtaining a canonical election for the church of Tournai or Noyon after the death of Bishop Ragenelinus. [Note: Louis the Stammerer died in 870, on 10 April.] He wrote concerning the election already held, which they had resented as having been arranged by the same archbishop in an unworthy manner.

He wrote concerning the same election, explaining how he had consented to their election when they were chosen to rule the kingdom, what instructions he had received from them concerning that election, what the royal ministry is, what the episcopal ministry is, what sort of person should be elected or ordained bishop, what sort of person should not be ordained and in what manner, and urging them to take care to learn the divine authorities.

He wrote concerning the same matter, demonstrating through sacred authorities how gravely those men sinned against God who caused that ordination to be delayed for so long. He also wrote concerning the objections raised against him by Gossinus regarding the consent of their father, King Louis: why he had not compelled him to take back his rejected wife Ansgardis; why he had not forbidden him to retain Adelaide; concerning the letters of King Louis sent to him on behalf of the advancement of his sons; and concerning the improper commands that these kings had sent to Hincmar.

He wrote to Louis alone concerning the advice he had requested from him: what kind of counsel is useful to a king, how he ought to administer judgment and justice, what good observance of these matters provides, and what evils their neglect commonly brings, and so forth.

He wrote to the young King Karlomannus and to the bishops an admonition, arranged in chapters, concerning the administration of the royal ministry, and another admonition to the same king, likewise arranged in chapters.

## CHAPTER XX. Concerning what he wrote to Louis, the brother of the same Charles
To King Louis of Germany, brother of the aforementioned King Charles, he is also found to have written several letters, at the request of that king, concerning certain questions about which he had been questioned by him on behalf of a certain Fulcric, giving him a fitting account of why he had excommunicated him, though he had absolved him on condition that he undertake penance; likewise, concerning the protection and defense of the properties of the Church of Reims situated in Thuringia; likewise, concerning the invasion of his brother’s kingdom, dissuading him from this by worthy and most useful admonitions, lest he undertake it to his own condemnation; likewise, on this same matter he wrote another letter to the same king together with the other bishops of this kingdom, full of episcopal moderation; likewise, once and a second time, he wrote to him personally concerning what he had ordered to be done by him on his arrival at Reims, telling him that he should not come as he was planning, nor at such a time, because it would be inappropriate and untimely for his soul; likewise, to the same king, concerning how he was working to establish peace between him and his brother Charles, giving him thanks for the sons of the Church of Reims, who were being well treated in his kingdom, and asking that they be allowed to retain securely the properties they possessed there; likewise, concerning the metal that he sent him for making a sign, adding an admonition about preserving peace and charity and following the will of God, as he commanded him; likewise, concerning the properties of the Church of Reims located in Thuringia; likewise, concerning the relics of the saints of the Church of Reims, which he was sending him, as he had requested, and concerning the book of the life and miracles of Saint Remigius; likewise, concerning the properties of Saint Remigius located in Thuringia; likewise, concerning the passions of the saints and the properties of his own men which they possessed in that king’s realm, so that they might suffer no prejudice on account of them; likewise, together with Remigius of Lyon, Arduic of Besançon, Erard of Tours, Ado of Vienne, and Egilo, archbishops of Sens, he wrote to the same King Louis on behalf of Bertulf, archbishop of Trier, showing that what he had learned had been done concerning this metropolitan church—that is, the Church of Trier—was reprehensible and dangerous: namely, that he had allowed it to be invaded, divided, and despoiled by a certain monk of that same church who had usurped it. He demonstrated that although royal power rules the human race through its dignity, it nevertheless humbly submits its neck to the prelates of divine matters, seeks from them the causes of its salvation, and recognizes that, in receiving the heavenly sacraments and in arranging them as is fitting, it ought, in the order of religion, to be subject rather than to rule. Thus, amid these matters, he said that he depended upon their judgment, but did not wish them to be reduced to his own will.

“Therefore,” he says, “just as a serious danger threatens bishops if they remain silent about what accords with divine worship, so also royal power—God forbid—is in no small peril if, when it ought to obey, it refuses what is announced to it by priests through the divine voice. For the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘Whoever is from God hears the words of God’ (John 8). But if someone less devoted has suggested to you that, in that same metropolitan church, we caused a metropolitan bishop to be ordained in contempt of you or against your loyalty, know rather that we ordained him there according to the sacred canons, with the unanimous consent of us all. For, as it is written: ‘Just as God is not confined by the narrowness of a place, so his word is not bound’ (2 Timothy 2), our Redeemer and Savior commending what the centurion had said in this sense: ‘Speak the word, and my child will be healed’ (Matthew 8)—that is, what you say here will be done there. He still speaks to us today, through his disciples, although we are unworthy: ‘The Spirit of your Father speaks in you’ (Matthew 10), the Spirit ‘who fills the whole world’ (Wisdom 1).

“We beg you, do not believe one who gives wicked counsel. For you should know with certainty that we did not ordain a bishop in that same metropolitan church in contempt of you or against your loyalty. Rather, considering—as you also know better than we do—how long and in how many ways that Church had been desolated and left destitute, and how many things contrary to God’s will had grown up not only in that diocese but throughout the entire province belonging to it, we canonically ordained a bishop, since the suffragan bishops can do nothing canonically without a primate and could find no proper canonical arrangement for matters pertaining to their own dioceses there. If the suffragans of that metropolitan church had been sufficiently numerous, they could and should, according to the divine laws, have ordained a bishop themselves in due form; for a bishop is to be canonically ordained by no fewer than three.

“He continues by bringing forward the authorities of the holy Fathers, by which they had supported their action. Then he adds:

“‘And because there were not so many suffragan bishops in that province that they could regularly ordain a metropolitan, and because the Churches of Reims and Trier are regarded, both by authority and by ancient custom, as neighboring and sister churches of the same province, on the condition that whichever of them first had a bishop ordained should also be regarded as first in the synod, and that they should support and strengthen one another by mutual counsel and assistance, the bishops of the province of Trier sought from the primate of the province of Reims the assistance necessary for their ordination, according to the sacred canons. The Sardican canons state this as follows (Council of Sardica, canon 5, elsewhere 6): if it should happen that in a province in which there had formerly been many bishops only one bishop should remain, and the people should assemble and summon bishops from a neighboring province, they must first approach the bishop who resides in that province, show him that the people are asking for a ruler, and declare that it is just that they themselves should come and ordain a bishop with him. But if, when summoned by letter, he keeps silent, dissembles, and sends no reply, the people must be satisfied by having bishops come from the neighboring province and ordain a bishop.

“‘From this it is properly inferred that if the province of Trier had only one bishop, or none at all, the bishops of the province of Reims, at the request of the clergy and people of the Church of Trier, ought to ordain a bishop. To that Church, all whose names your glorious self read written at the beginning of this letter, we, with one accord and consent, ordained our brother and fellow priest Bertulf, as we have already stated, as bishop in due canonical form. We can demonstrate this from the sacred regulations and from the records of his ordination, and, if necessary, we shall demonstrate it.

“‘Therefore we defend, and shall defend forever, his ordination and the administration of the ecclesiastical properties and resources, just as the sacred canons prescribe, as well as our own canonical order. For if he is not a bishop, neither should we be called bishops. And if anyone wishes to say anything malicious against his ordination, let him come forward and say it. Let him nevertheless remember his own communion: either he will not share in the ecclesiastical and episcopal order, or we will not share in the episcopal ministry.

“‘Accordingly, using the words of blessed Leo when he once addressed the emperor Theodosius (Leo, Letter 24), we address you, most Christian, venerable, and dearly beloved king, together with our fellow priests. We fulfill the reverence due to your clemency through the service of sincere love, and we desire that you please God in all things. For you, we and the Churches entrusted to us offer prayers to him. We beseech you, before the inseparable Trinity of the one Godhead—which is injured by such an act, since it is itself the guardian and author of your kingdom—and before Christ’s holy angels, to order and preserve the Church of Trier, together with its bishop, in the same condition, immunity, and privilege in which your ancestors and predecessors preserved it, and also in which your brother and nephew Lothair, father and son, preserved it canonically. Thus may you gain merit from this before God and before blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, in whose honor that church was consecrated, and may you acquire us as further debtors to you in our prayers and in the other duties of our service.

“‘For unless, out of reverence for you, we were postponing this matter, we would already have brought upon the invader of that church the judgment pronounced on earth by the sacred canons—judgment which the 630 bishops at the great Council of Chalcedon decreed in such a case (according to canons 7 and 18), which they threaten against him from heaven, and which divine judgment will bring upon him for eternal condemnation unless he performs worthy penance.’”

He adds further material from the authorities of the sacred canons. After this he adds:

“Therefore, your religious lordship, who is most dear to us, should know with complete certainty that as long as this brother of ours, Bertulf, whom we ordained bishop in the Church of Trier, lives in this mortal body, no other bishop will be ordained in that same Church—unless he himself, God forbid, contrary to the sacred regulations, is deposed by those same sacred regulations. Nor will that presumptuous and apostate monk Walto, from a monastery in the diocese of Trier, ever be bishop in the Church of Trier, which he has so ruinously usurped and injured, since the judgment of the Holy Spirit has already been pronounced against him. And if, as we have said, we were not postponing this out of reverence for you, we would decree not only, according to the sacred canons, that he should never and nowhere presume to approach the ecclesiastical ranks, but also, placing him under anathema, that he should be confined in prison according to the sacred regulations. If he persists in his obstinacy, we shall decree this in every way, without any reconsideration.

“But we earnestly beseech the Lord, through whom kings reign (Proverbs 8), and from whom and through whom the sacred episcopate first began, to make you immune and exempt from the penalties threatened by the sacred canons. We implore his clemency to grant you both the will and the ability to carry out, according to his good pleasure, what he has commanded (Philippians 2), so that you may deserve to receive the eternal joys that he promises to those who love him.”
