He also replied to a letter that the same king had sent him, asking that he, and anyone else he could, offer prayers for the king’s father, who had appeared to him in a vision, begging him to rescue him from the punishments in which he was being held. Accordingly, he wrote back to him a very useful letter about the manner and character of prayer, full of authorities. He also wrote on behalf of the properties of Saint Remigius situated in the Vosges, and on many other matters.

He also wrote to the king’s son, who had the same name as his father, on behalf of the estate of Deduciacum, explaining how Saint Clodoald had given it to Saint Remigius, and how Charles, son of King Pippin, had obtained the same estate from Archbishop Tilpin on lease, on the condition that the bishop of Reims retain the chapels belonging to it, together with the ninths and tenths, while the king would give twelve pounds of silver for the church’s lamps; and that both this king and his successors had paid this rent, and that he himself had also received the same rent from that king’s father from the aforesaid estate. He also wrote concerning the estate of Noviliacum: how it had been given by Karlomann to Saint Remigius and what had later been done with it. Likewise, to the same man, concerning seeking and observing the counsel of divine Scripture, and concerning thoughtless counselors and other matters; he explained how the kingdom was being governed and warned him not to presume to invade it. He wrote on behalf of preserving the city of Reims and sparing the holy places if he should come. He explained how the bishops had acted toward Louis, son of Charles, when they consecrated him king, since this king had heard a different account. He also wrote about the two wives of that Louis, son of Charles, explaining how the matter had been handled, and on other matters.

He also wrote to King Pippin of Aquitaine concerning his Church’s properties situated in the districts of Auvergne, Limoges, and Poitiers. On their behalf he also obtained letters from King Charles to the same Pippin, and entrusted those properties to the protection of Frigidolon, a distinguished man.

He also wrote to Charles, son of Louis from across the Rhine, praising the benevolence of the faith that he preserved toward the sons of his cousin Louis—Karlomann [Charles the Fat] and Louis—and begging him, for the honor of God’s Church and for the condition and defense of this kingdom, to appoint prudent and just tutors for the aforementioned royal boys. These men were to teach them to honor God’s servants, keep God’s commandments, govern themselves, and manage the reins of the kingdom properly. He also wrote on behalf of his faithful Sigebert.

To King Lothair, son of the emperor Lothair, he wrote concerning the estate of Deduciacum, which his father had restored to the Church of Reims, warning him not to hand over to anyone, at his own peril, the properties belonging to it as possessions—as he heard that he was doing—or to free the estate’s tenants. If he had done anything of this kind, he urged him to make amends. He also wrote concerning the estate’s ill-managed administration and the rent, which Lothair confessed that he was retaining at the peril of his soul. Hincmar explained that Saint Clodoald had given the estate to Saint Remigius and admonished him not to do anything by which he might incur the condemnation of his soul. He also wrote on behalf of granting the Church of Cambrai permission to elect a bishop, and concerning the benefit of the soul and his royal honor. In this letter he recalled how his father, Lothair Augustus, had entrusted himself and his soul to him.

## CHAPTER XXI. Concerning what he wrote to various archbishops and bishops

He also sent many highly useful writings to various bishops and archbishops.

To Hecti, archbishop of Trier, he wrote about the beginnings of his ordination, offering himself as a companion and servant in the ecclesiastical affairs of his fatherhood; likewise, concerning the same matter, asking to be instructed by him and treated as a son, and also explaining his journey, on which he was planning to travel to Rome; likewise, concerning Gondric, whom Hecti had excommunicated, and Fulcric, whom Hincmar had excommunicated and who seemed to have found refuge in the bishopric of Trier.

To Archbishop Guntbald [Gunt. of Rouen] he wrote on behalf of a certain priest, concerning the preservation of ecclesiastical rights; likewise, concerning what had been done at a synod.

To Amolo of Lyon he wrote about the hearing he had held with the king and the leading men of the kingdom, and concerning the status of the Jews in this kingdom; likewise, concerning the synod summoned by the three kings, and concerning Ebo, his predecessor, and several others. In this letter he indicates that he regarded Amolo as a most dear and like-minded father. He also wrote concerning King Lothair and certain other matters, calling himself his son of affection.

He wrote to Amolo about the life or conduct, preaching, arrest, and condemnation of Gothescalc, setting forth the truth of the matter.

To Hrabanus, bishop of Mainz, he wrote concerning the reception and examination of that same Gothescalc, whom the same bishop had expelled from his diocese because of the seeds of heresy that he was spreading and had sent to Hincmar, together with certain of his associates [i.e., his own]. Likewise, he wrote about the same matter, asking what he had done with Gothescalc after receiving him and what madness he had found in him, and requesting more reasonable counsel about what should be done against him. He also wrote concerning his doctrine and heresy, what he had done to him after he had been proved a heretic at the synod and could not be corrected, and what he himself thought about his doctrine and condemnation. He sent Hrabanus writings against Gothescalc for examination, asking also how various Fathers’ statements concerning the faith of the Trinity and predestination should be understood. In this letter he asserts that blessed Hrabanus was at that time the only one remaining of the discipleship of blessed Alcuin.

To Archbishop Landramnus he wrote about the advice he had sought from him concerning a convent of nuns that the king was ordering to be given to an unsuitable person. He usefully admonished him about what he should do, urging him to exercise more fervently the care of the ministry entrusted to him.

To Teutgaud of Trier he wrote concerning the primacy which Teutgaud had written should be accorded by Hincmar to the see of Trier, explaining that the see of Reims had never granted such primacy to that see, and so forth. He also wrote a second and third time concerning the case of the excommunicated Fulcric.

He wrote on behalf of the properties of the Church of Trier situated in Aquitaine. Hincmar himself had worked diligently with a certain Arnold of Aquitaine, who held them, so that he would restore them to the Church of Trier, and he indicates that he had obtained this result.

To Amalric [Amal. of Tours], a devout archbishop, he wrote in sympathy with his tribulations, consoling his patience and rejoicing with him in his holiness. He indicates that he had chosen him as the dearest among the dear. He sent him certain costly ornaments, namely, a green-patterned chasuble, the only one he possessed, and other small gifts together with one hundred solidi. He also wrote to him on behalf of the properties of the Church of Reims situated in Aquitaine, which the king ordered to be restored to it and which Hincmar confidently entrusted to Amalric for administration.

To Archbishop Rothland he wrote on behalf of the properties of Saint Remigius situated in the province, and on behalf of a certain priest who had been excommunicated at a synod, in whose place another had been ordained.

To Rodulf of Bourges he wrote concerning the properties of the Church of Reims situated in the district of Limoges; likewise, concerning certain excommunicated persons.

To Guntarius of Cologne he wrote asking him to intercede with King Lothair and work for the canonical election of a bishop of Cambrai after the death of the venerable bishop Theodoric. He wrote a second and third time concerning the same matter, affirming that a bishop should be ordained there during his lifetime only in due canonical form.

To Luitbert [c. j., Luidbert] of Mainz he wrote concerning the properties of Saint Remigius situated in the Vosges [Vosge], explaining how a certain Gibero had lost his senses while invading those properties and, after being tormented without interruption for a full month, had ended his life in the greatest pain and danger. He often wrote on behalf of protecting those properties and defending or governing their dependents.

He also wrote concerning the conversation he had had at Troyes with Pope John, and what good things he had discussed with him about Luitbert, urging him to receive the pope’s letter and envoy kindly and to make an effort to come to him. He also wrote concerning a certain transgressing priest.

The same venerable Hincmar also wrote to Lothair, king of Italy, who, having abandoned his own wife, had joined himself to a certain woman. Hincmar gave him advice and admonished him to remove her entirely from his presence. He explained that he had received letters and commands from Lord Pope Adrian [Adrian II] on this matter (Letter 13), and took care to urge the king to preserve the pope’s instructions in this case.

He also wrote another letter concerning men unwilling to accept peace, explaining what should be done about them and praising the fact that he had already exercised the royal ministry against certain such men.

He also wrote an *Apologeticus* against his detractors, who slandered him with various attacks of defamation—namely, before Pope John [John VIII], claiming that he did not wish to accept the authority of the decrees of the bishops of the Roman See. To these charges he had replied both at the Synod of Troyes [synod of Troyes, 878] and afterward in this *Apologeticus*. He refuted these revilers and explained that he accepted and followed the decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs that had been received and approved by holy councils, discerning the manner in which they ought to be followed [*rest.*, in place of *atque*]. He also explained how the deposition and restoration of Hincmar of Laon had been handled.

He wrote about another matter for which certain people had slandered him before the same pope, as though he had said that the pope himself was not of greater dignity than Hincmar. He also wrote concerning the ordination of Hedenulf in Hincmar’s place in the bishopric of Laon and the pope’s confirmation of that ordination, as well as concerning Karlomann and several other matters in which the truth rendered him excusable.

Although he could have replied to certain people who slandered him, he asserts that he did not wish to do so, lest he seem to have returned insult for insult [manuscript: “added faults to faults”]. He considered it more glorious to escape from them by silence than to overcome them by replying, lest he be thought to have sought his own glory.

He also wrote certain letters to Pope Adrian, whom he recalls had sent him some writings. To Adrian, sending his own letter through Actard, bishop of Nantes—a letter full of praise—he delegated Actard to act in his place in these regions concerning the affair of Lothair, so that what Pope Nicholas had decreed in that matter might be preserved.

He also replied to certain capitularies concerning the privileges of the see that Pope John had sent to the bishops of the kingdom of the Franks in seven chapters, since that pope had tried to establish Ansegisus, bishop of Sens, as primate, so that he might exercise apostolic authority throughout Gaul and Germany [French: *fungeretur*, “might exercise”; manuscript: *frueretur*, “might enjoy”]. This venerable prelate Hincmar effectively opposed that attempt.

Finally, the same Lord Hincmar wrote many letters to various bishops.

To Remigius, archbishop, he wrote on behalf of the properties of Saint Remigius situated in the Cisalpine province, asking him to receive them under his protection; likewise, concerning the ordination of Isaac, bishop of Langres; likewise, concerning the synodal regulation established because of invaders of ecclesiastical properties [Remigius of Lyon], and on other matters; likewise, concerning the case of the aforementioned King Lothair, and he sent him several writings concerning the properties mentioned above.

He also wrote to the same Remigius and to the other bishops who, by the authority of Lord Pope Nicholas, had been ordered to come to a synod at Soissons, concerning the case of Vulsad and his associates.

To Archbishop Ado of Vienne he wrote, among other things, concerning the letter of blessed Avitus written to Saint Remigius, which a certain monk, Rotfrid, had told him he had read in Ado’s possession. He added that, if Ado could find anything further concerning Saint Remigius, he would send it to him as something more precious and desirable than gold and topaz (Psalm 118:127).

To Herard, bishop of Tours, he wrote concerning certain apostates returning to the Church and concerning the reception of other penitents. He also wrote about several other matters, as to a most dear friend who, coming to our prelate, had entrusted himself to him in brotherly affection. Hincmar asked him to speak to the royal lord on behalf of his Church wherever he could.

As his death was approaching, Herard himself dictated letters to Hincmar and gave them to the man who was to announce Herard’s death to Lord Hincmar, so that he might deliver those letters to him. Envoys of the Church of Tours, relying on this confidence, came to the same Lord Hincmar after the death of their archbishop. They brought him the petition of the clergy and people, asking him to plead their case before the royal majesty so that the king might grant them a canonical election. The same prelate carried this out most readily.

He also informed the king about a certain cleric who was putting himself forward and whom the king was not to receive. He explained that the bishops of that province, together with the clergy and people of that Church, invited by the authority of the Apostolic See, wished Actard to be given to them as bishop. Actard had been baptized, raised, and ordained in that same church, although he had been appointed bishop of another city; driven out by the attacks of the pagans, he had been honored by the Apostolic See with the pallium, so that, even if an opportunity should arise from the metropolitan church, he might be incardinated there (Adrian, Letters 11 and 12).

He further gave the king advice about what should meanwhile be ordered for the clergy and the laity, and what he should do concerning the properties that he held by royal benefice. He explained which of the properties he had left behind might please the king and asked him to indicate this.

He also wrote concerning certain books of Saint Augustine that he had asked Bertulf to send back to him, and concerning the objections of the Greeks, about which Pope Nicholas had given him instructions, as well as on several other matters.

To Bertulf, archbishop of Trier, he wrote instructing him about ordering and governing his diocese or parish, and so forth. At Bertulf’s request he also sent Wiliebert, bishop of Châlons, to the ordination of Arnold, bishop of Toul, because Bertulf was confined by illness and the number of bishops prescribed by the sacred canons was not present for the ordination of the prelate.

Previously, at the command of King Charles, he had sent Bishop Hincmar of Laon, Hodo of Beauvais, and John of Cambrai to Bertulf’s ordination, at the request of the bishops Adventius and Arnulf of that same diocese of Trier. He instructed them, by canonical and apostolic authority, how the matter ought properly to be conducted, so that they would depart from the sacred regulations in nothing, whether through negligence or presumption.

He also wrote to the aforementioned Bertulf concerning certain chapels belonging to the estate of Duodeciacum, which someone from the diocese of Trier was usurping through the influence of a certain priest, and asked that justice be done for him in this matter.

Likewise, he wrote concerning letters that he was sending to King Louis from across the Rhine, asking Bertulf to have them read again to the king and queen and to send Hincmar by letter what he heard from them about the matter. He also asked him to have the letters that he had sent to Bishop Arno read aloud to him, and to admonish the king, queen, and people concerning their salvation and the peace of God’s holy Church.

To John of Rouen he replied to his question about a certain cleric who had been promoted to govern a church but could not properly be ordained because of his age.

To Rothstan of Arles, who had written to him concerning the persecution of his church and a powerful woman who was usurping ecclesiastical properties, he wrote back explaining what should be done about these matters.

To Adelold of Tours, who had asked permission to build and consecrate an oratory on an estate belonging to his church, given by royal gift and situated in the diocese of Reims, called Turris, he replied granting the request on the condition that, because of this, the ancient church of the estate or its priest should suffer no loss of its privilege.

He sent letters to Leo, bishop and custodian of the library of the Roman Church, concerning the reception of his embassy, asking him to obtain from Pope Leo that he kindly receive Hincmar’s request and reply to him as a father concerning the matters contained in the letters Hincmar had sent.

He also wrote to Gregory, nomenclator and *apocrisiarius* of the same Roman Church, asking him to deign to keep Hincmar among his faithful friends. He likewise asked him to request that his petition be made acceptable to the Apostolic Lord, sending him small gifts of blessing.

To Formosus, a devout bishop of the same see [Note: “He later became Roman pontiff”], he wrote praising the form of holiness and learning that he had heard he possessed, seeking his friendship and asking him to pray for him. He promised to offer reciprocal correction and sent him certain gifts, so that Formosus might remember him in his prayers. After Formosus had sent him a letter expressing his affection for Hincmar, Hincmar wrote that he had great confidence in him.

He also wrote to Gauderic, bishop of the aforementioned Church, asking him to receive Hincmar into the embrace of his affection and to deign to implore the Lord and the holy apostles on his behalf.

To John, a bishop of the aforementioned see, he wrote nearly the same things. He also asked him to send him the canons of Pope Martin and the Gospel of the Nazarenes for transcription, and he sent him certain gifts.

To Vulfad, archbishop of Bourges, he wrote concerning those who thoughtlessly killed their wives, setting out the opinion of Paulinus that he had asked to have sent to him. He also wrote concerning other matters.

To Frotarius of Bordeaux, who had recited this verse to him:

> “Reims [sends] a horse to us, Bordeaux [sends] a mule to you.”

he later sent this in reply:

Reims sent a horse; Bordeaux, no mule. He also wrote certain other things to the same man; likewise concerning the regular election of an abbess for the monastery of Saint Radegund, etc.; likewise concerning the ordination of Fulcricus; likewise to Wenilo of Rouen, concerning the workers and the work that he was carrying out at Pistas on the Seine; likewise concerning the case of the bishops Rothadus and Odo.

To Drogo, bishop of Metz and brother of the emperor Louis, he wrote in order to obtain his friendship; likewise, reporting his thanks [Col. 0204D] for the concern that he appeared to have for the Church of Reims, and also asking, concerning a certain brother of this church who served as a minister, that he might so enjoy his services that this church could make use of his necessary assistance, and certain other matters.

To Rothadus of Soissons, whom he often summoned because he delayed or neglected to come to the synod, he wrote concerning certain accused persons of the diocese of Soissons, whether they should be purged or subjected to penance; likewise concerning the ordination of certain ministers of the churches; likewise concerning receiving and bringing to judgment Gottschalk, whom the lord Rabanus had sent back to the diocese of Reims. He had departed from the diocese of Soissons, namely from the monastery of Orbais; [Col. 0205A] likewise concerning the ordination of the monastery of Saint Medard and the restoration of the rule there; likewise concerning certain monks who had fled from the monastery of Altvillar; likewise concerning Godoldus, who complained that he was being deprived of communion unjustly, on whose behalf he also sent him letters a third time; likewise concerning certain priests who had complained in the synod that he had unjustly deprived them of the affairs of the church, and because he had handled the synod’s mandates irrationally, he threatened him with canonical punishment unless he corrected himself; likewise concerning the ordination of Hincmar after the death of Pardulus, bishop of Laon; likewise concerning restoring the priest Adeloldus in accordance with the synod’s sentence, on whose behalf he had sent him letters, which the other utterly disregarded; likewise concerning the mandates of King Louis and a guarantee sought from him which was not compatible with the priesthood; [Col. 0205B] likewise concerning a cleric whom he was to send to be ordained to govern a church situated in the village of Turre; likewise concerning the diocese over which there was a dispute between him and Erpuinus, bishop of Senlis; likewise, together with the other bishops of the diocese of Reims, concerning the innovations of the Greeks, which they were attempting to establish contrary to canonical rules. On these matters Pope Adrian had sent letters both to him and to the other archbishops of this kingdom. In addition, he sent him letters very frequently concerning various other affairs.

To Immo, bishop of Noyon, he wrote concerning the provincial synod summoned by the king at Paris, and concerning the ordination of Irminfridus after the death of Hildemannus, bishop of Beauvais; likewise concerning the ordination of Pardulus after the death [Col. 0205C] of Simeon, bishop of Laon; likewise concerning giving counsel and assistance to Theoderic, bishop of Cambrai, regarding a certain disobedient man who did not fear God and did not respect ecclesiastical ministry; likewise concerning a certain priest, for whom he urged that the canonical law be granted; likewise concerning a certain woman whom he complained that the other had excommunicated unjustly; likewise concerning holding an episcopal conference.

To Erpuinus of Senlis, concerning a certain man whom, as he had learned, the other had excommunicated irrationally, he explained the matter, ordering him to come to meet him and deliberate with him what should more correctly be done about it; likewise concerning a certain priest unjustly deprived of ecclesiastical goods; likewise concerning a certain cleric who had complained that he was suffering prejudice at his hands; likewise concerning Pope Adrian’s mandates about the aforementioned priest; [Col. 0205D] likewise concerning regularly carrying out the king’s command.

To Lupus of Châlons, concerning the holding of a synod; likewise concerning a certain man who had been deceived by trickery into keeping his own infant for catechization; likewise concerning what the synod had decreed about this matter. In a letter that he wrote to King Charles after Lupus’s death, seeking a regular election for the Church of Châlons, he also bears witness to his good life.

Writing to Prudentius of Troyes, he asked why he was withholding his presence from him, indicating that he wished to seek his counsel about the condition and restraint of Gottschalk. He informed him of what had been done or judged concerning Gottschalk in the synod, by whose judgment he was keeping him confined; and because he had attempted in many ways to convert him, [Col. 0206A] he asked about Gottschalk’s character and pride, and whether he ought to admit him at the Lord’s Supper or at Easter to hear the sacred office or receive communion. He also asked what Prudentius thought of the sentence of the prophet Ezekiel: “On whatever day the righteous man falls, all his righteousnesses shall be delivered over to oblivion; and on whatever day the sinner is converted, all his iniquities shall be delivered over to oblivion” (Ezek. XVIII). He also wrote concerning the custom of celebrating the Lord’s Supper.

Likewise, concerning the churches of the see of Reims situated in Prudentius’s diocese, which he was treating otherwise than episcopal equity permitted, so that they might discuss together these and other matters that he had heard about him, exhorting them to instruct one another and commend one another mutually to the Lord. It is also found that he wrote a book on this matter.

To Pardulus, [Col. 0206B] bishop of Laon, he wrote concerning the death of his predecessor, Lord Ebo, so that priestly kindness should be shown to him with wishes full of charity. Likewise concerning the unsuitable reconciliation of Luidus, since he had not been able to be deflected from carrying it out by the flatteries or reproaches of foolish men; strengthening him in episcopal rectitude by testimonies from the divine Scriptures, so that he might walk along the path of authority, and indicating what he should do concerning the aforementioned Luidus; likewise concerning the same matter; likewise concerning the recognition, humiliation, and absolution of Fulcricus; likewise concerning the absolution of a certain person, asking his advice; likewise concerning a fast commanded by the queen; likewise concerning the illness and humiliation of Rothadus of Soissons, and concerning the counsel he had given him, asking Pardulus to strengthen Rothadus in it and prudently exhort him to obey; [Col. 0206C] likewise concerning gold that he was sending him, to be offered by him to the queen for making a certain ornament of the Mother of God; likewise concerning a little work, the *Ferculum Salomonis* (“Solomon’s Dish”), which he himself had composed and read to him, asking what he thought of it (above, chap. 15).

Likewise concerning the Church of Thérouanne, vacant through the absence of a pastor, asking him to discuss with the king how the election itself might properly be conducted, and concerning books of Saint Ambrose on the faith to be sent to him.

To Irminfridus of Beauvais, concerning the canonical consecration of a pastor for the Church of Amiens after the death of Bishop Ragenarius; likewise concerning prudently steering the ship of the Church, which was being shaken amid the internal wars of this shipwrecked age.

To Bishop Ebo, a son of the Church of Reims, concerning a certain brother who had fled from this [Col. 0206D] church and was staying with him, asking him to take care to send him back as quickly as possible; likewise concerning the ordination of Isaac to the bishopric of Langres, asking him to exhort Archbishop Remigius to carry out the same ordination.

To Theoderic of Cambrai, concerning a certain Hecton, a vassal of King Lothair, upon whom they had jointly imposed penance, but who claimed that he had been absolved by the aforementioned Theoderic; and concerning a certain priest whom that same Theoderic had excommunicated, on whose behalf the Roman pope had sent letters to Lord Hincmar, which Hincmar was sending to that same Theoderic. Likewise concerning the absolution of the aforementioned Hecton [ms. Hetton]; likewise concerning the possessions of the Church of Reims, which Bishop Theoderic was asking to be assigned to him by lease; [Col. 0207A] likewise concerning the ordination of Hunfridus to the bishopric of Thérouanne; likewise concerning the ordination of Ercamra after the death of Lupus, bishop of Châlons; likewise concerning the arrival of Louis from across the Rhine, because he had come to Reims, and what he had done and what he had commanded him; likewise concerning Baldwin, who had abducted Judith, the widow and daughter of King Charles, so that he might know that Hincmar had placed him under anathema and announce this throughout his diocese; likewise concerning a certain man who had been persuaded by the father of a certain girl to take the woman into concubinage.

To Folcuinus of Thérouanne, concerning a certain priest ordained in his diocese, who complained that he was suffering injustice from Bishop Immo; and he also asked that relics of the saints resting in the diocese of Thérouanne be sent to him, because he was preparing an altar of the Mother of God, to be consecrated by Folcuinus at the consecration of the church of God, and to be honored with relics from his diocese. To Bishop Rainnerus, concerning a certain priest whom Nothus, archbishop of Arles, had reported to him by letter as canonically rejected and excommunicated by the synod, with another priest appointed in his place.

To Bishop Agio (Agio of Orléans), concerning the possessions of the Church of Reims lying in Aquitaine.

To Abbo of Auxerre, concerning the deceased Bishop Heribald, who, appearing to a certain brother, admonished him about almsgiving, prayers, and offerings to be made for him.

To Aeneas of Paris, concerning Rothadus of Soissons, about whom certain unsuitable matters had been debated before the king, and the king was sending that same Aeneas together with Immo of Noyon to investigate them.

To Almaricus [j. Almericus], bishop of the Church of Cumae, concerning Egilbert, a deacon and monk of the monastery of Saint Remigius, whom, at the bishop’s request, he entrusted to him for ordination and governance.

## CHAPTER XXII. What instruments for life, or rebukes, he wrote to his nephew Hincmar.

To his nephew Hincmar, bishop of Laon, at the beginning of his ordination, he wrote instructing and teaching him how, in accordance with canonical authority, he ought to administer the Church entrusted to him. Likewise, he admonished him to take care not to foster conspiracies among his subjects; and, if they should arise, that they be immediately cut down by the moderation of reason, or that, if necessary, he should take care to report them to him, and he instructed him when he ought to celebrate a synod.

He labored greatly on his behalf and wrote much to him, rebuking and chastising him for the levity of his character and actions, and admonishing him to return to his own heart and strive to pray to God with complete attention, so that God might look upon him and grant him to understand and correct his perversity. For he seemed to himself excessively wise and obstinate in disputes, and he attempted to bend ecclesiastical laws toward the intention of his own will, thinking that he understood them better than his elders.

He labored so greatly over this that he says he even incurred the displeasure of his own elder, the king; yet he endured seeing Hincmar, before many people, rejecting his petition and humility with an impudent face, an erect neck, trembling lips, and inflamed words.

He rebuked him because he was never prepared to acknowledge himself guilty of any fault, but always to defend himself; he rebuked him also for his dress, gait, laughter, oaths, impatient speech, impulsive anger, and many other things. Likewise, because, contrary to the course of the holy Scriptures, he had exceeded the bounds in governing his own diocese on account of his alleged injury [the text is corrupt], he admonished him to strive to correct these matters and reminded him what kind of person he ought to show himself to be according to the Apostle’s words to Timothy.

Likewise concerning a certain sacrilege, and concerning a man whom Hincmar had excommunicated for crimes, because he had given him ecclesiastical property as the reward of shameful profit; likewise, concerning a certain cleric of his named Hadulfus, whom Hincmar had excommunicated, asking him to deal with him; likewise concerning Pope Adrian’s letter to certain bishops, which Hincmar was to deliver; [Col. 0208B] likewise concerning the disposition of certain ecclesiastical goods in his diocese, asking him to await the provincial synod in this matter; likewise concerning the excommunication of Karlomannus, on account of which Hincmar refused to obey him. He often admonished him to lay aside the contumacy of his mind and incline himself to obey him, as he had already professed before many witnesses in the synod and had confirmed by his signature; likewise concerning the deacon Bertharius [j. Bercharius], whom he was unjustly keeping in custody because he had appealed to the judgment of the metropolitan and provincial synod.

For this reason, explaining to him that he ought not to act against him in such a way, he commanded him, by the authority of the sacred canons and his own authority, to permit that same deacon—and any other clerics detained by him who might be invoking regular judgment—to come freely to his own judgment and that of the other bishops, and to present himself to that same judgment.

Likewise, he summoned him to the synod at which Pope Adrian’s mandates were to be discussed. He also wrote much else to him; finally, he wrote a lengthy account, recalling in it and bringing before the eyes of his mind how he had raised him, an orphan, with tender affection under religious discipline, instructed him in letters, and advanced him through each ecclesiastical rank up to the summit of the episcopate.

“Now,” he says, “evil is repaid to me for good, and you hate me without cause (Ps. XXXIV), because I do not favor your fruitless works. How long shall I endure you, afflicted by many injuries from you? (John XV.) For from the very day of your ordination I have been so burdened by your words and writings, your disordered actions and frequent movements, by your lacerations and blows, that I am weary of my life, because, by the duty of my office, I am so bound to your insolence that I cannot avoid admonishing you—not only after a first and second correction, according to the Apostle (Titus III), but not even after very many admonitions, privately and before our common associates, and also before the king, the bishops, and many others, in words and in writing.

“And although I wish that wings might be given me like a dove’s, so that I might fly away and rest far from you in some solitude (Ps. XLV), I cannot escape anywhere without being afflicted by reports about you: whether by your obstinate presence, which persists in contumacy; by the harsh speech of your messengers; by the disparagements and useless trifles—or rather, tragedies—of your writings; or by such things as do not suit a bishop. And at last I thought that you had become ashamed of carrying out such things, when behold, on the Ides of November of the fourth indiction, you sent me a very long scroll filled with lies, irrationalities, and reproaches against truth and authority.

“And I wonder why, having become so shameless that, as the Lord complains concerning Judaea, you do not know how to blush (Jer. VI and VIII), you are not disgusted to write such and so many things—unless it is because you are not devoted to useful matters and are occupied with nothing necessary. And, to say nothing of other matters—for if I wished to review them in order, daylight would fail before the page ran out of material to read—I shall recall to you some matters that I can neither can nor ought to pass over in silence.

“Namely, as soon as you flew out of the nest of your paternal education, having become a bishop, you deserted me and those who had raised you, and sought and acquired secular friendships and familiarities. Then, abandoning and acquiring others and still others, you rose to such a position not only among your peers but also among those entrusted to you that, contrary to the sacred Antiochene rule which commands that you should do nothing apart from me (Council of Antioch I, canon 9), and contrary to the ancient rule established by our Fathers, you obtained in the palace of the lord king the administration of possessions—except only those things that pertained to your diocese and its subject estates—without the knowledge of me or our co-bishops.

“I prohibited that administration to you before the same lord king and the others who were present, on the basis of the sacred rules, and for some time you abstained from that administration. Afterwards, however, through outside—that is, secular—powers, contrary to the canons of Sardica (Council of Sardica, canon 15), you obtained the same administration together with an abbey in a third province beyond the province of Reims, without my knowledge.

“Whenever you pleased, you went to that abbey without my permission, and you remained there for as long as you pleased, contrary to the decrees of Pope Hilary, who says (Hilary, Letter 8): ‘We could not pass over that matter which must be guarded with more diligent care: that no bishops should dare to proceed to any province without the letters of their metropolitans. This must likewise be observed in every kind of clerical office throughout the individual churches.’

“And thus Zosimus earlier (Zosimus, Letters 5 and 9), and Saint Gregory afterwards (Gregory, Book IV, Letter 51), decreed. For this reason, although summoned once and twice by canonical letters to the ordination of a bishop in the Church of Cambrai, a church in our province left without a pastor, for which the apostolic see, at my urging, labored greatly, you neither came yourself nor sent me a representative in your place or letters expressing your consent, as the sacred rules prescribe.

“Therefore Pope Symmachus promulgated from the sacred rules to Eonius (Symmachus, Letter 11, to Caesarius) that, if any bishop, summoned to the metropolitan pontiff according to the canonical definition, should refuse to obey, he should know that ecclesiastical discipline would cut him down—which we do not desire. Moreover, when I called you to account for this, you offered neither satisfaction nor even a humble reply to me and our co-bishops.

“After these things, in keeping with your customary instability and inconstancy, you rose so irrationally and contumaciously against the lord king that he removed both the palatine administration and the abbey itself from you, and, provoked by you, proposed to impose harsher measures upon you. Therefore, by my writings and words on your behalf, I reconciled him to you.

“After that, as many know, you rose against him again and, despising his commands that you come to him, provoked him to such anger—as everyone in these regions knows—that, compelled by circumstances, he attacked you through his faithful men as though you were unfaithful.

“Yet you hurled an unprecedented excommunication against my parishioners and those of many other archbishops and bishops, and even against the king himself, without my knowledge and contrary to the sacred rules. In doing so, you scandalized many and brought the greatest scandal not only upon the Church but also upon the king and the kingdom, although the law forbade that, when passing through another’s field, one should put in the sickle, but permitted one to crush the ears with the hand and eat them (Deut. XXIII, 25).

“‘You cannot,’ says blessed Gregory, ‘put the sickle of judgment into that harvest, because it appears to have been entrusted to another; but by the effect of a good work strip the Lord’s grain of the chaff of its vices, and by admonishing and persuading, as though commanding, convert it into the body of the Church’ (Gregory, Reply 9 to Augustine’s Questions).

“After this presumption, bringing our fellow bishops together with me, I reconciled you both with him and with the bishops whose parishioners you had excommunicated, and I persuaded them not to rise against you with a synodal sentence. I also caused those whom you had excommunicated, although not without labor and with the assistance of the lord king, to cease their opposition to you.

“But you, adding worse things to those that came before, again provoked the lord king so greatly—as it would take me a long time to recount, and many know—that, for the sake of chastising you, he ordered you to be detained for a time, without my will and without my consent.

“You, however, on account of the injury you claimed to suffer, without consulting me and without the consent of the co-bishops of the province of Reims, as the petition presented to me by the clerics of the Church of Laon demonstrates, excommunicated the priests and fellow ministers of the church and diocese entrusted to you. You decreed that no one in that diocese should celebrate the offices of the Mass, baptize any child—even one placed in imminent danger of death—assist anyone to penance, or provide communion as viaticum to anyone at the point of death; nor should anyone offer the service of humanity to the dead in burial, until either you yourself came to them or they received a response about this from the apostolic see.

“When I heard this, I confess, I was struck with extreme horror. Therefore, with metropolitan concern, I sent letters to you, warning and exhorting you to dissolve as quickly as possible such a destructive excommunication and bond of impiety, undertaken at the peril of yourself and many others.

“I also sent to the ministers of the Church of Laon, fearing the immense destruction of many, the most certain and irrefragable definitions of evangelical truth, apostolic authority, the sacred canons, and the apostolic see, so that, according to those same definitions—which cannot be shaken in any respect—they themselves might also act against that dangerous and irregular excommunication and obtain sufficient remedy.

“But because you were unwilling to obey my admonition, I sent you letters about it again, and also to the clerics of the diocese of Laon; yet even then I was unable to induce you to obedience.

“After this, seeking inventions by which you might free yourself from metropolitan subjection, you collected a booklet from writings of the ancient Fathers, issued before the sacred canons of the Council of Nicaea and of other saints. Into it you inserted opinions discordant with one another and contrary to evangelical, apostolic, canonical, and apostolic-see authority. You subscribed that same booklet without the knowledge and consent of the metropolitan and of the co-bishops of the province of Reims, and you caused it to be subscribed by the clerics of your church and by the parish priests, wishing to display yourself as stripped of subjection to your metropolis and to annul the privilege of the metropolitan see.

“You acted as though I could not, by canonical authority and without your consent or a synodal assembly in your diocese, dissolve the bonds of your impiety, although we possess, concerning certain and manifest matters that are in no way doubtful or obscure to us, definitive sentences promulgated by the holy Fathers which cannot be overturned by any reasoning. Accordingly, I ought not to await synodal deliberation or the counsel or consent of the co-bishops of our province; nor ought I depart from the rules established in advance, as Saint Leo says (Leo, Letter 84, chapter 2), through negligence or presumption; nor ought I trouble the apostolic see about this, as the blessed pontiffs of that holy see—Innocent, Zosimus, Celestine, Leo, Hilary, Gelasius, Gregory, and many other rulers of the same holy see—show in their decrees,” and so forth.

Likewise, after citing authorities of Pope Gelasius:

“After your subscription and that of your followers to the aforementioned monstrous booklet, monstrously compiled by you, in letters whose copy I possess, I admonished you again to strive to correct what you had done irrationally and contrary to reason and authority in your diocese; but you did not obey my admonition.

“Then, from the aforementioned letters of the pontiffs of the Roman see written before the Council of Nicaea, you compiled a booklet, entitled in the name of the lord King Charles with little verses (versiculi). Through the venerable former archbishop Wanilo, at the villa of Gundulf, before the bishops who were present, you sent it to me. I replied to you in writing; I possess a copy of that reply. I admonished you to place your faith in the sacred canons and in the decrees of the apostolic see promulgated from those same sacred canons and from the apostolic see, and to render them their due obedience.

“Then, at Attigny in the diocese of Reims, before the bishops, I gave you a booklet containing ecclesiastical authorities in fifty-five chapters (Symmachus, at Attigny, A.D. 870), against the things you had collected in your aforementioned two booklets. I admonished you to restrain yourself from such and similar criticisms, [Col. 0212A] and, submitting yourself to the sacred rules, to strive, according to the Apostle, to pursue peace and holiness (Heb. XII).

“You, however, offered no satisfaction for my admonition. Rather, at that same synod you presented a very long scroll woven together against truth, authority, and reason, and brought forward at the same synod that aforementioned monstrous booklet, subscribed by you and your followers. I received it there and have kept it to this day.

“And when I saw that, after so many admonitions, I could accomplish nothing with you, I presented a written memorandum at a synod of bishops from ten provinces (the synod of Douzy, A.D. 871), asking those same venerable bishops for advice about what I could do against your persistent contumacy. I also had read aloud before them the measures I had sent to you and to your diocese against the bonds of your impiety.

“Therefore, by the authorities of the sacred assembly of those same bishops, because you had presumed to carry out so many and such grave excommunications unjustly and irregularly, and because you had been accused by the lord king of not observing the oaths you had sworn to him over the sacred objects; and also because you had invaded property belonging to him contrary to divine and human laws; and because, having been accused by the Norman in the synod, you had expelled him from possessions granted to him by Lord Charles through your grant and consent, without royal authority, with an armed military force and a crowd of common people gathered together with swords and clubs—first his wife, who was there without any protection, and afterwards the man himself—contrary to the laws and rules, and had taken away everything of his that he had there; [Col. 0212C] and also because you had been accused by your own men of taking away their benefices contrary to divine and human laws, you gave to the king and to me at the same synod a booklet of your profession of regular obedience, which I possess.

“You cannot deny this, because you received its copy from my hand at that same synod, as I shall demonstrate in the course of my account. [Note: [Col. 0211D] It is extant in Aimon, book V, chapter 24.] But, being a man double-minded and unstable in all your ways (James I), on the following day you immediately sent me through Harduicus, the venerable bishop of Besançon, a brief for you to profess and subscribe, which read as follows:

“‘And I, Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, will preserve for you, Hincmar, co-bishop of the Church of Laon, your due privilege, as the sacred canons command; and in whatever ecclesiastical matters you may have need, I shall provide you, according to the sacred rules, with the assistance due to you by right, through archiepiscopal authority.’

“This proposal proceeded not merely from a humble mind, but not even from a sound one. For it appears unjust and irrational that an archbishop who does not deviate from the sacred canons should satisfy a suffragan bishop ordained by him, through a booklet of profession and subscription, as you had requested.

“For just as, according to Scripture, the lesser is blessed by the greater (Heb. VII), so entirely is the lesser judged, bound, or released by the greater, as is also demonstrated in the decrees of Gelasius (Gelasius, Letters 4 and 13). Thus the answer given to you here is just and reasonable, in the words of James: ‘You asked and did not receive, because you asked wrongly’ (James IV).

“Moreover, in what you proposed should be subscribed by me—that I should preserve for you, as the sacred canons commanded, your due privilege—you asked for what you wanted, but did not know what you said. For, as Saint Jerome says: ‘The privileges of individuals cannot be made into a common law’ (Jerome, on chapter I of Jonah).

“And the sacred canons did not grant provincial bishops and their churches or sees privileges—that is, private laws or private rights—in general, because what everyone possesses generally cannot be a special right or a private law of dignity. But they granted privileges to metropolitan bishops and metropolitan sees,” and so forth, followed by material from the sacred canons and the decrees of Pope Leo.

[Col. 0213B] After this he adds:

“Therefore, when you sent me such a document to profess and subscribe, you ought to have known what almost no one in these regions is ignorant of: that the municipality of Laon, in which you were ordained bishop, from its beginning—after it was founded, as the histories report, by the praetor Marcobrius—never had a name or place among the provincial sees of the province of Reims, whether in paganism or in Christianity, until Saint Remigius, the fifteenth archbishop of Reims, for certain circumstances and particular reasons, first ordained a bishop there and assigned to that municipality, which had been sufficiently and more than sufficiently enriched from the possessions of the metropolitan see of Reims, the very county in which it is situated, namely, a portion of the diocese of Reims.

“But it was always a municipality of the province of Reims, just as today there are other municipalities in the diocese of Reims that remain in their place and name under subjection.

“Therefore, what you ought to have asked was not that a privilege but that municipal status be preserved for you. For, as our Fathers and the teachers of the Church transmit, the Apostle Paul does not call himself a citizen but a municipal inhabitant, saying: ‘I am indeed a Jewish man from Tarsus in Cilicia, a municipal inhabitant of no obscure city’ (Acts XXI).

“The Apostle was born in the town of Giscala in Galilee. When it was captured by the Romans, he migrated with his parents to Tarsus in Cilicia. From there, because of his devotion to the law, he was sent to Jerusalem and instructed by Gamaliel, a most learned man, as he himself later recalls (Acts XXII). Therefore he calls himself not a citizen but a municipal inhabitant, from municipium, that is, from the territory of the same city in which he was raised.

“Municipium is so called because it renders only munera, that is, due tributes or services. For the liberal and most famous causes, and those that proceed from the prince, pertain to the dignity of cities.

“Nor is it surprising that he calls you Tharsian and not Giscalian, since the Lord himself, born at Bethlehem, was called not Bethlehemite but Nazarene, after the place in which he was raised.

“And so you, born in the diocese of Reims, raised in the metropolitan city of Reims, and ordained in the municipality of Laon, ought to have recognized yourself not as a citizen or civic bishop but as a municipal—that is, tributary or service-rendering—bishop, if only in respect of spiritual gifts; and, except insofar as you were ordained by several bishops, almost as a substitute bishop, whom the Greeks call a chorepiscopus.

“Accordingly, what ought to be ascribed to you is not a privilege but municipal status. You ought not to have rebelled against the privilege of your metropolis; and you would not have done so if in spirit you had been a Paul—that is, little and humble.

“Therefore it is to be feared that in this too you imitate the son of perdition, who opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called God or worshiped (II Thess. II). As far as depended on you, you handed over to him those whom you had excommunicated irregularly, as I said above—not so that their spirit might be saved, according to the Apostle (I Cor. V), but so that, insofar as your fury and indignation could prevail, they might perish on the day of the Lord.

“Against these bonds of impiety, as has often been said and must always be said, since they were regularly dissolved contrary to your wish, you rose up against me.”

Likewise, after authorities concerning the unlawful excommunication:

“As for the oaths you gave to the king, I do not need to write anything to you, since almost everyone knows what the Lord says about perjury—if indeed you committed it—in the Law (Deut. V), in the prophets (Zech. V; Mal. III), in the Gospel (Matt. V), through the apostles (James V), and through the teachers and masters of the Church.

“And because, as it is said in the decrees of the apostolic see, ‘we do not wish to aggravate what has been done, lest we be compelled to judge what is just,’ since what was held against you in the synod was not established in judicial order but was remitted through royal clemency, I have omitted placing a regular judgment here, in order to refer you back to your own conscience.

“But your seizure of the king’s property was shown most clearly, because it was never legally proved that those possessions had belonged to the rights of the Church of Laon, nor was it shown that they had been possessed by that church through its own donation or concession, or through anyone else’s.

“Therefore legal inquiry was made concerning your man Teduinus, to whom you had granted the seized possessions as a benefice.

“The Norman’s complaint against you was also shown to be true and required no witnesses, because what you had done there against the laws and rules was so manifest to everyone in these regions that the deed could not be concealed or excused by any evasion.

“For it is well known to many, and you confess this in writings that you sent to the lord king and to me, that, at the entreaty of Rodulfus and Conradus, after the lord king had for a long time withdrawn those possessions from the Church of Laon and restored them to that church by his own authority, you granted those same possessions as a benefice to the lord king himself, without the knowledge and consent of me, our co-bishops, and your fellow ministers, so that he might grant them as a benefice to that same Norman.”

Likewise, after citing certain authorities:

“And this act of yours, so irrationally done, you dissolved even more irrationally: with an armed military force and a mixed multitude of common people carrying weapons and clubs, amid the greatest tumult, as those who saw and heard the deed report, you violently and without royal authority, word, or letter expelled that same Norman, who retained those possessions granted to him by you and held them through the king’s benefice.

“After expelling him, you invaded them, entered upon them, and took possession of them, although there are laws and rules, and although the king bears the sword for the punishment of evildoers (Rom. XIII), and although there are bishops and canons for judging the crimes of sacrilegious persons.

“If that Norman had been an invader of ecclesiastical possessions, he should have been punished by the sword—that is, by royal vengeance—if he were proved sacrilegious, and he should have been judged by episcopal and canonical judgment.

“There are also judges and laws, by whose judgment, if anything had perhaps been done unjustly to you or to the Church entrusted to you, it could have been corrected legally and regularly.”

[Col. 0215B] Again, after citing certain decrees, especially those of blessed Gregory:

“Finally, because your men appealed to the king, alleging that you had unjustly and irrationally taken away from them their benefices, which they had retained under your predecessors, after I had given the king and you a memorandum at the synod concerning your regular obedience, in accordance with the sacred canons and the decrees of the Roman pontiffs of the holy see promulgated from those same sacred canons, you requested from me chosen episcopal judges, and accepted the three whom I designated to you according to the African council (African Council, canons 63, 88, 89, 94), namely Actard, Ragenelinus, and John. At the judgment of these men and of the God-fearing bishops, in the presence of the lord king, as you requested, it was decreed concerning some of them that they should recover their benefices, which they had irrationally lost. The case of certain others, however, because definite reasons intervened, was left undecided until another hearing, when it was to be decided; and before that decision you fled and contemptuously refused to await the regular judgment, contrary to the sacred canons and without any necessity or reason.”

Again, after citing various passages from the canons:

“And, as I said, after you had carelessly and dishonorably fled from the judgment of the chosen judges and withdrawn, you irrationally composed and sent me, through your deacon Ermenold, on 2 July, in the third indiction, a little memorandum subscribed by your own hand and wholly contrary to your aforesaid profession. It runs as follows [Note: [Col. 0215D] It appears at the end of the work of 55 Chapters]:

“‘To the most reverend Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, Hincmar, by God’s mercy bishop of the holy Church of Laon, sends due devotion in Christ.

[Col. 0215D] “‘You know that I have twice been summoned by the universal pope of the holy Roman Church, our father and teacher Adrian (Adrian II), and that you yourselves reproached me in the memorandum which you gave me at the palace of Attigny, in the presence of the archbishops and bishops who were present, because I declined to come to that same see when summoned so many times. If, through the error of the scribe, *detractem* was written instead of *detrectem*—for *detrectem* means “I evade” or “I delay,” whereas *detractem* may properly be understood to mean “I handle at length”—the word was not marked with an interlinear correction.

“‘Therefore I now beg you, for the love of almighty God and in reverence for Saint Peter, [Col. 0216A] as I also begged you at that same synod convened by you at Attigny—something which I was unable to obtain—and as I have now earnestly implored for a full year, especially at the synod formerly held at the palace of Verberie (Synod of Verberie, A.D. 870), where I pleaded and entreated: now also I beg and again implore, as I have done until now, that by your archiepiscopal authority you obtain from the clemency of our lord, the most glorious king Charles (Charles the Bald), permission for me to obey, as is expedient for everyone, the commands of the lord and universal pope Adrian and the ecclesiastical ordinances, since he has the right to judge concerning the whole Church. Specifically, may I be deemed worthy, as I vowed, to enter the thresholds of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, since I have moreover been summoned there by him.

[Col. 0216B] “‘Otherwise, know that from this point onward I cannot canonically obey you as an archbishop, as a co-bishop ought to obey, because, as blessed Pope Gelasius decrees (Gelasius, Letter 4), “They do not know what they are saying who set the decrees of the bishops of the holy Roman Church against them as though they were canons; to oppose these decrees is to rise up against the canons themselves.” This venerable and holy Pope Gelasius solemnly decreed that all decretal letters are to be received with reverence. Anyone who does not obey them does not receive them with reverence, even if he bows his head reverently to the volume; rather, extending his hands against them, he rejects them, as one who does not foresee that he himself will be judged by them—an act that cannot be done without danger. For, whether we wish it or not, we shall either obey them or be struck down by their judgment, and no one of them can any of us repudiate.

“‘As for the archbishops Remigius and Harduicus, concerning whom you sent me instructions through your deacon Teutland, this does not prejudice the privilege of the holy Roman Church; rather, what that same holy see wished and decided to entrust to them concerning me, it entrusted to them. You, for your part, do what belongs to you. Farewell in the Lord Jesus Christ. I, Hincmar, bishop of the holy Church of Laon, have willingly subscribed.’

“Concerning this memorandum I delayed replying to you, thinking that you would retract it and repent of your contumacy. But you did not desist, as I omit for the sake of brevity. After this you sent your letters to the lord king through your cleric Bertharius, excusing yourself on the grounds that you could not come to him as he had instructed you, because, being feverish, you could not bear exposure even to the sun; but asking him to grant you permission to go to Rome, in accordance with the vow you made when you previously had a fever, so that, coming to the threshold of the holy apostles as you had vowed, you might there be freed from that fever.

[Col. 0216D] “The lord king, however, through that same cleric, sent you this reply in the presence of the bishops and his other faithful men who were present: it was strange and untrue that you should say you could not come to him while you were able to go to Rome. You should come to him, and if he could ascertain that you wished to go there for a reasonable cause, he would not deny you permission.

“But you refused to come to him until, around the Kalends of September in the third indiction, he returned to Silvacum from a meeting with his brother Louis. When you came to meet him there, you said nothing to him—nor to me, either personally or through your messengers or letters—about permission for you to go to Rome. Moreover, when the apostolic envoys were at Reims, you spoke with the king and me every day for seven days, and said nothing about this.

“As for your claim that you requested permission to go to Rome at the synod at Verberie and afterward at Attigny, and that you were unable to obtain it, all the bishops who were present at those synods know perfectly well that, when you were reproved for your insolence, fearing regular judgment or the king’s correction, you requested permission to go to Rome. But whenever you saw that both the king and the bishops were favorably disposed toward you, you said nothing about that permission, just as you do now—until once again you commit some novelty, as is your custom, which I always fearfully await; then, when questioned, you bring out your usual song.

“Your petition to the lord king, when you came to him, was as follows. As many, indeed almost everyone, in these provinces are said to know, and as is evident, adding one grave matter to another, and as the judgments of the sacred canons themselves demonstrate, by certain contrivances devised by you, I do not know how, a royal order was elicited: concerning those matters for which you had requested chosen judges according to the sacred canons, not only should the complaint of those whose case had been left for decision at another hearing be reopened, but also matters which, as I said, had been decided in the presence of the lord king by the sentence of the chosen judges should be reopened by secular judges—without the knowledge of the metropolitan and without canonical or episcopal judgment.

[Col. 0217C] “These secular judges were Helmigarius, toll collector of the royal market, and Flotharius and Ursio, administrators of the royal estates. This was contrary to the canons, which permit appeals from ecclesiastical judges to ecclesiastical judges of greater authority, not from greater judges to lesser ones, nor from ecclesiastical judges to secular judges, nor to judges not chosen by agreement of the parties.

“Through these secular judges, whom you requested, some matters already decided were reopened and altered, while others that were still to be decided were decided, by an invented process of deliberation—as is said by those who were present at that hearing—on the basis of unnecessary and inappropriate oaths. You brought these matters before the judges themselves, with the very accusers whom you had accepted against the chosen judges, as you had requested, so that the person whose case had been legally and regularly decided, namely that he should possess his benefice, which he had lost contrary to reason and equity, might by the same contrivance surrender it; and so that those to whom it had been adjudged that, since you had evaded the judgment of the chosen judges after requesting it, they should retain their benefices until a legal decision, might abandon those benefices, while you might vindicate what you had begun.

“For just as it is not lawful for you, whether in an accusation involving a criminal or a civil case, to abandon ecclesiastical judgment and submit yourself to public judgment, so also it is not lawful for you, having set aside or despised ecclesiastical judgment, to flee to secular courts, or to drag anyone—even a layperson—to them, or to follow that person to his own forum if the layperson has consented to undergo ecclesiastical judgment, as the law of Valentinian, which the Church approves, demonstrates.” [Col. 0218A]

Again, after the authorities cited:

“And let it not escape your consideration why the lord king assented to your petition: why, after you had accepted from him, in his presence, chosen episcopal judges according to the sacred canons, he should have consented, without the metropolitan’s knowledge and without ecclesiastical judgment, to accept secular judges to reopen matters already decided, or to decide matters concerning which you had received judges.

“For I know, and am certain, that he knows the canonical judgment in this matter. I am amazed and grieved that you did not wish to see this, or, blinded by arrogance under God’s judgment, were unable to see it. Therefore apply, according to the counsel of the Apocalypse of John, salve to your eyes so that you may see (Apoc. III), and may cast from the eye of your mind—that is, from your understanding—the cataract of arrogance.

“Consider whether perhaps the lord king, whom you have so often provoked, knowing the divine judgments and utterances, in granting your requests has thought of the divine sentences against those who are stiff-necked and stubborn of heart: ‘Let the one who does harm continue to do harm’ (Ezek. II), and ‘Let the one who is filthy continue to be filthy’ (Apoc. XXII), so that ‘they may always fill up their sins’ (I Thess. II); and: ‘He gave them over to the desires of their hearts; they shall go on in their own devices’ (Ps. LXXX); and: ‘Are these things not stored up with me, sealed in my treasuries? Vengeance is mine, and I will repay them in due time, so that their foot may slip; the day of their destruction is near, and the appointed times hasten’ (Deut. XXXII).

[Col. 0218C] “And although you are found guilty of so many transgressions, you do not cease provoking me, so that I may write concerning your promised memorandum of profession and subscription, to which, as I said, I have until now delayed replying, and also concerning your other professions and subscriptions, whether provoked or otherwise. Thus, when more people read the histories of your professions and subscriptions—if there are still some who do not know them—they may come to recognize their care, caution, and usefulness.

“I shall first reply to you concerning the memorandum you subscribed, in which you write that, as a support to you, I was reproved by you, and you show me to be reprehensible. But I disregard your reproof, by which, as though under a certain veil of excuse, you plainly strive, in your customary manner, to reprove me for a scribal error: either because I did not know the distinction between the words *detrectem* [I evade]—which I used in the writings I gave you—and *detractem* [I draw out or discuss at length], or because I did not know how to correct the scribe’s error in them, or neglected to amend it, and because you wished to display your learning through my reproof, like Ham, the son of Noah (Gen. IX).

[Col. 0218D] “You wished to display this not only in the distinction between those words, but also in another word which I found repeated in your inventions for the display of yourself. And while you wished thereby to show my ignorance, you strove to reveal your own folly before the learned.

“As for me, I care nothing about saying anything. For it is a very small matter to me to be judged by you (I Cor. IV), or to be reproved without charity by your learning. But lest you boast before those who eagerly collect rumors with you, as though you had rendered me mute and speechless, and as though you alone in our times had entered into the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, I shall here, for the sake of brevity, pass over the matter. When I have time, I shall show what the authorities on the rules of grammar, the teachers of orthography, and the interpreters of sacred Scripture think and say about it.” [Col. 0219A]

The same author, after some intervening material:

“But there are also other matters from the sacred canons and the decrees of the apostolic see which it would have been lengthy for me to set down here. You can reread them in the work of 55 chapters which I gave you for your admonition, correction, and instruction, apart from the letters mentioned above which I sent you to rebuke your rashness against evangelical truth, apostolic and canonical authority, and the decrees of the apostolic see, in your own destruction and that of many others, as was confirmed at a synod of many bishops.

“But apart from the other letters and writings which I sent or gave you to restrain your insolence and to admonish and instruct your devotion, so that you might act according to the Lord’s saying: ‘What does the Lord your God require of you, except that you fear the Lord your God, do his will, and obey his command?’ (Deut. X), revolve these matters, brother, with attentive intention of heart, and reflect upon what you said: ‘From the time when you sent me those letters, I was to know that you could not canonically obey me, as a co-bishop ought to obey an archbishop.’

“Recall before your eyes what you professed before the bishops of ten provinces and subscribed with your own hand: namely, that, in accordance with the privilege of the metropolitan of the province of the Church of Reims, and according to the sacred canons and the decrees of the apostolic see promulgated from the sacred canons, you professed and subscribed that you would obey, insofar as you knew and were able.

“Tell me, brother, when and where, or in what matters, did I ever ask or try to force you to obey me in anything contrary to this? I have never sought what is yours, but, according to the Apostle, you yourself (II Cor. XII). As for injuries done to me—that is, to my person—I can easily, thanks be to God, forgive them, just as I devoutly pray daily for the Lord’s omnipotence on your behalf.

“But I cannot and ought not patiently endure the injuries against the divine ordinance which your insolence seeks to inflict: that you should not be canonically subject to the metropolitan privilege, injuries which rebound upon the one who instituted the canons through his Holy Spirit, from whom they are read and believed to have been promulgated. I shall strive against this as much as I can.

[Col. 0219D] “For just as the care and primacy of the whole holy Catholic Church have been divinely conferred upon the pontiff of the holy Roman see, so also the care of the province entrusted to each metropolitan and primate is known to have been committed to him through the sacred canons, established by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world,” and so forth.

Finally, many further passages concerning the professions and subscriptions of the same Hincmar and his corrections follow, continuing to the end of the work.

Another work begins as follows:

“HINCMAR, bishop of Reims, to Hincmar, bishop of Laon.

[Col. 0220A] “‘A man worn down by various scourges from various sources says: “Those who eat me do not sleep” (Job XXX), as though he were saying, “They do not rest.” And you, brother, do not cease wearing me down with the scourges of your tongue and poisoning me by provoking me to anger with your venomous writings.

“‘But he who guarded his servant from murmuring can also guard me, a sinner and a frail man who trusts in him, from rancor and malice against your false accusations. After adding much else to the sorrow of my wounds (Ps. LXVIII), you say: “As I find in your perverse writings, I detract from the authority of the apostolic see.”

“‘No one of sound judgment has ever believed you, or will believe you, for the very writings which I have so often sent to the apostolic see, and those which I have often sent to you in reply, will convict you, both in this world and at the future judgment. You will never be able to prove, anywhere or at any time, that what you say about me is true: that by those for whom it was right to contend even to death for the privileges of the apostolic see, which are Christ’s, I am declared and taught to be rejected in the matters which that same see has established.”

“‘But you are shown to oppose its privilege, since, according to the sacred canons of the holy councils set out above and approved by that first see and by the whole Catholic Church—as truly established by the Spirit of God, consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, and promulgated according to the decrees of that holy see from those same sacred canons—you have refused to obey the metropolitan privilege, although admonished once, twice, and three times.

“‘You were to loosen the bonds of wickedness (Isa. LVIII) which, to your destruction and that of many others, you have fatally bound against evangelical truth, apostolic and prophetic authority, the canons of the holy Fathers, and the decrees of that revered see. Moreover, against the sacred rules, you perniciously subscribed and caused to be subscribed a memorandum against the metropolitan privilege.

“‘Therefore, when summoned at the synod by the bishops of ten provinces (the Synod of Douzy), you presented a memorandum of profession concerning your future obedience, subscribed with your own hand, which I possess. Against this you subscribed again.

“‘For I both reverently receive and declare that decretal letters of the apostolic see, issued at various times by the pontiffs of that see for the consolation or consultation of various Fathers, are to be received with reverence. I profess that the sacred canons of the holy councils, together with the decrees of the apostolic see promulgated from those same sacred canons, are to be received, guarded, and observed, as I demonstrated above.

[Col. 0220D] “‘As for your claim that you hear people speaking against the judgment of the lord Pope Nicholas: if you are speaking about me, you are lying. For I did not oppose what he judged concerning Rothad or Vulfad; rather, I took care to obey as he commanded.

“‘As for what you say about Rothad—that you did not consent to his deposition—your own subscriptions convict you. I did nothing concerning it which you did not do with me; I judged nothing which you did not judge; I subscribed nothing which you did not subscribe. For I possess those very subscriptions in your own hand.’”

[Col. 0221A] Near the end of this work:

“As for the other matters which, in the writing given to me at Attigny, you falsely and reproachfully attribute to me, I do not care to answer you. But know that I have not forgotten what is written in the prophet Isaiah (Isa. XXXVII): Saint Hezekiah, pressed by distress, spread out before the Lord in the temple the blasphemous letters sent to him, cried out to him, and was heard.

“I shall spread out my hands to the Lord with the blasphemous and exceedingly proud writings which you sent me, praying that, when he knows and when he wishes, and as he knows and as he wishes, he may convert you to love of true peace, charity, and the obedience that is owed [perhaps: ‘direction’], and free me from lying lips and a deceitful tongue (Ps. CXIX).

“And through the merits of my blessed and glorious Lady Mary, Mother of God, and through the prayers of Saint Remigius, whose privilege you disparage, may my helper hear me in times of need and in tribulation (Ps. IX).

“And because blessed Jerome says concerning those whose office you have freely undertaken against me: ‘Let my dogs hear’ (Jerome, preface to Job), you who have grown from being a nephew into a brother, and from there have advanced so far that you have grown into my dog, accept, as the occasion of your perverse and contumacious memorandum demands, this lengthy reply.

“When I have time, I shall write more briefly concerning your other perverse and disorderly writings, in which you have written some things falsely, some reprehensibly in reproving me, and some with feigned humility but genuine pride. In that writing, since I read that the Lord said, ‘I will no longer be angry with you’ (Ezek. XVI), I shall, insofar as it remains possible for me, put an end to writing to you about such controversies.

“As for your statement that people say about me, ‘What sort of uncle is he, to write such things to his nephew?’ let those same people also say about you: ‘What sort of nephew is he, one who, having been adopted by his uncle as he then was, and having become what he now is in spiritual and temporal honor, demands such things from his unwilling uncle, lest, being judged by others as he is portrayed by his nephew, he cause the name of the Lord to be blasphemed (Rom. II) and his ministry to be reviled (II Cor. VI)?’

[Col. 0221C] “He followed the Apostle, who wrote against those who blasphemed him and labored to have him despised by others. The excellent teacher acted so that, when his character was recognized, the life and speech of those who preached evil might be cheapened by his preaching; if he had hidden himself, he would have commended them, and if he had not shown himself, he would have given error an opportunity.

“Those same people also say about you: ‘What sort of nephew is he, who plots such things against his uncle, foster-father, and ordainer, and does as much evil as he can, and desires to do more than he can, as you will plainly see on the day of the great judgment, unless beforehand you recognize this and amend through worthy fruits of repentance?’

“You weary me greatly, and rightly so; yet the weariness should not be charged to you, because my fatigue is consoled by what, as I wrote to you, blessed Gregory says: ‘Even if an Ethiopian enters the bath black and leaves the bath black, the bath attendant nevertheless does not lose the coin for his bath.’

[Col. 0221D] “I fear concerning my Alexander what Paul said concerning his: ‘Alexander the coppersmith showed me many evils; the Lord will repay him’ (II Tim. IV).”

CAPUT XXIII. What he wrote to Altfrid, bishop of Transrhenania, and to certain other bishops.
