He wrote to Altfrid, bishop of Transrhenania, concerning certain possessions of Saint Remigius located in Thuringia, which he had entrusted to him so that he might send their revenues to him at the proper time. In accordance with the disposition of blessed Remigius, he forbade anyone to presume to oppress their tenants with his own service. He also wrote that he had granted those same possessions as a benefice to one of his own men, asking Altfrid to strive to provide that man with assistance in whatever he might need.

He wrote to Adventius, bishop of Metz, concerning a certain question of faith about which Adventius had asked him; concerning the journey which Adventius was to begin in order to go to Rome; concerning his own arrival at the synod announced by the king to deal with the aforementioned question; concerning the son of his niece, whom he entrusted to him; and concerning what Adventius had sent him word about Hincmar, bishop of Laon, briefly explaining what good he had done toward him and what wrongs the other had committed against him.

He also wrote to Adventius, when Adventius asked his advice about what he ought to do when Charles came into the kingdom of his elder brother Louis, explaining what he himself had done when Louis had invaded Charles’s kingdom and what Adventius ought then to do.

He wrote concerning the acceleration of the ordination of Berard, elected and summoned as bishop of the Church of Verdun; concerning the excommunication of Carloman, which he sent to him, explaining how he ought to handle it; concerning the envoys of Adventius whom he had sent to Rome on behalf of the case of Bertulf, archbishop of Trier, wondering why Adventius had not informed him, since those envoys had reported back to him; concerning the letters of King Louis which Adventius had sent him; and asking that Adventius either send or give him the letters which Hincmar himself was sending to Louis.

He wrote concerning the letters of Adventius which Adventius had sent him, informing him of the arrival of his envoys bearing the pallium from the apostolic see for Archbishop Bertulf, and exhorting him to work for concord between the kings. From this it is evident that Adventius had always worked and ought to continue working for that cause.

He also wrote concerning the mule which Adventius had asked to have sent to him, explaining that the lord Hincmar did not possess such an animal and was not accustomed to ride; and concerning several other matters.

He wrote concerning the proper discernment in excommunication, since Adventius had reported that he had excommunicated certain evildoers belonging to the Church of Metz, namely the men of Count Walter and of Lambertius, asking him to preserve apostolic discipline and episcopal patience in such a matter.

He wrote concerning the order in which metropolitan and diocesan bishops ought to be consecrated.

To Ercamraus, bishop of Châlons, he wrote concerning certain matters which he did not gladly hear about him, admonishing and instructing him how he ought to act and urging him to attend carefully to the apostolic admonitions.

He also wrote on behalf of certain inhabitants of a village whom Ercamraus had irrationally removed from all consolation through the divine ministry because of a homicide not committed by them. He explained how, in this act, Ercamraus had preserved neither charity nor the moderation of discernment.

He wrote concerning the absolution of a certain man whom Ercamraus had excommunicated and on whose behalf Guntarius, bishop of Cologne, had sent him letters of petition, which Ercamraus had refused to receive. Hincmar showed what sort of bishop he ought to present himself as toward the guilty and what sort toward those who acknowledged their fault.

To Hilmerad, bishop of Amiens, he wrote on behalf of a certain monk who had killed a priest and a monk in the monastery of Saint-Riquier. Concerning this matter, the lord Pope Nicholas had sent the lord Hincmar letters setting out the form of the penance.

He also wrote concerning letters of Pope Adrian [Note: [Col. 0223] These letters of Nicholas I and Adrian to Hincmar are not extant] which Adrian had sent him on behalf of a certain priest, warning him to obey the apostolic commands.

He wrote concerning a certain priest who had appealed to him because, after wresting weapons from the hands of a drunken man who wished to kill him, throwing them away, and fleeing, the bishop had taken both the priest’s church and his possessions from him. Hincmar rebuked the bishop for acting against the authority of the sacred canons toward that priest, instructing him what should be done and what, according to canonical authority, ought to be observed in the matter.

He also rebuked him for resting in the torpor of negligence and following the counsels of wicked men, although he appeared, both because of his age and because of bodily weakness, to be pressed toward the end of his life. Hincmar showed him, from the admonitions of the sacred Scriptures, for what transgressions he was found guilty.

He wrote on behalf of another priest, commanding and forbidding by metropolitan authority that no prejudice be inflicted upon him, but instructing him to take care to meet Hincmar at the synod convened on the appointed day.

Again, concerning this same matter, he explained that if the priest did not appear at the synod according to the pope’s command, whatever the synod judged concerning him was to be carried out against him.

To Isaac, bishop of Langres, he wrote on behalf of a certain royal soldier whom Isaac had excommunicated, urging him to act more mildly toward him because of the pressing necessity caused by the attacks of the pagans. He explained how he himself usually acted in such cases involving excommunicated persons, and that the anathema lasts no longer than the person continues in sin.

He also wrote on behalf of Isaac’s nephews, who had been raised with the lord Hincmar, and concerning several other matters.

To Bishop Hungarius he wrote concerning the excommunication of Baldwin, who had abducted Judith, the king’s widowed daughter, and taken her as his wife; for this reason Baldwin had also been excommunicated by the bishops of that kingdom.

He urges Hungarius to warn Roric, the Norman recently converted to the faith of Christ, not to receive Baldwin or offer him protection. He also urges him to strive to make worthy amends through penance for the fact that, as Hincmar had heard, one hundred [that is, “if the rest”] Normans, on Baldwin’s advice, had plundered that kingdom after his conversion.

To Fulcric, bishop of Troyes and a foster-son of the Church of Reims, he gave thanks for certain letters of Augustine which Fulcric had sent him. He also wrote concerning the book of Didymus, which Fulcric had requested be sent to him, and concerning the churches of the monastery of Orbais, warning him not to presume to act perversely against his mother, namely the Church of Reims, or against his patron Saint Remigius.

To Odo, bishop of Beauvais, whom he often calls his dearest son, he wrote many things with confidence [manuscript reading: “faithfully”].

He wrote concerning a letter of Pope Adrian which Odo had sent him about the appeal of a certain priest from the diocese of Amiens, asking Odo to undertake the matter so that Bishop Hilmerad might obey the pope’s commands. He also explained how the priest had prudently brought the written documents from Rome and ought to handle them.

He wrote concerning certain royal men who were at odds with one another, asking Odo to urge them to make peace and to tell them that, unless they did so, they were to be excommunicated by the lord Hincmar.

He wrote concerning a synod which the king had ordered to be held at an unsuitable time, asking Odo’s advice about what he ought to do. He also asked Odo to send him word about what the king had replied concerning those men whom Hincmar had indicated he would excommunicate, and concerning other necessary matters.

He also wrote concerning certain writings, questions of the Greeks, homilies of blessed Peter, and other matters; and concerning responses to the objections of the Greeks, which Odo had collected, written out, and sent to the lord Hincmar.

For these things he gives thanks to God, because he found that both he and Odo had been filled from one spirit. He indicates that they ought to discuss together what he thinks about these matters. He also asks that Odo always be excused before the king, since at that time Odo had been unable to go into the king’s service because he was detained by various illnesses.

He recalls as well the matter of the men who were at odds, concerning whom he had already instructed Odo to urge them to return to peace. He praises Odo for having acted diligently and episcopally, loving God and his brother, concerning what Odo had reported to him in his letters. He asks him to admonish the king and to perform his ministry in that matter, and asks that Odo write back to him concerning certain matters between Odo and the king.

He also informs Odo of certain matters which he was to communicate privately to Bishop John concerning the synod which, although the king had ordered it, was not then to be held, and explaining why it ought not then to be convened.

He adds matters concerning certain writings which he was returning to Odo, or which he requested Odo to send him.

He wrote concerning the ordination of Willebert, to whom the king had given the bishopric of Châlons, warning that in his ordination Odo should not depart from the proper order. He explained that the people of Châlons had acted irrationally after the death of their bishop, driven by their own necessity, and that they had sent their letters to the king concerning the election of the aforementioned Willebert, but had not sent their decree to the archbishop, as they ought to have done, so that the archbishop might canonically do what needed to be done.

He explained how they ought properly to have acted in the matter. Since they had not done so, he set out what he thought should be done more cautiously, and instructed Odo to attend prudently to the matter so that a regular election might take place. Finally, he asked Odo to arrange it as seemed best according to Odo’s own prudence.

He wrote concerning the case of Odo’s diocese, which was being disputed between Odo and Rothad, bishop of Soissons, and also concerning the priest who had brought the pope’s letter from Rome. He asked Odo to admonish the king and moderate his spirit, so that he might not do anything against the Lord in the Church of God. Hincmar insists that he says this not merely for the sake of his nephew Hincmar, but as much for the king himself, his elder, so that the king might not sin in such a way and thereby perish eternally.

He wrote concerning the correction of his letter which he had previously sent to Odo and which had been corrupted by an unskilled scribe, and concerning the matters alleged against Hincmar, his scandalizer.

He wrote concerning the letters which he was sending to the king on behalf of that same Hincmar, asking Odo to deliver them to the king and report how the king received them and whether he assented to them. He also asked Odo to send him word about other matters which he ought to know.

He wrote concerning the case of Bishop Erpuinus, who was unable to come to the appointed synod, asking Odo to strive to pursue his case between Erpuinus and his accusers; and, if he could not carry this out fully, to urge Erpuinus and his accusers to go to the synod to be held at Pîtres.

He wrote concerning letters sent to him by Odo, in which he had learned that certain monks were rising up against sacred authority, and concerning the privileges of the monastery of Corbie.

He wrote concerning his own journey to the king.

He gave thanks to God for the sweetness of satisfaction and correction which he found in Odo’s letters, namely, the great kindness of Odo’s acknowledgment concerning the matters for which Hincmar had reproved him.

He wrote concerning the election of the bishop of Soissons after the death of Rothad; concerning a synodal assembly to discuss the response to the letter of Pope Adrian; concerning the king’s letters ordering the bishops of the kingdom to be summoned by the lord Hincmar, so that they might restrain the king’s son Carloman from persisting in the presumption which he was accused of exercising against his father; concerning the ordination of Ansegis, a monk of the diocese of Reims, to the bishopric of Sens; and concerning a little book of the history of the birth of Saint Mary and the homily of blessed Jerome on the Assumption of that Mother of God, which a certain monk of the monastery of Corbie argued ought not to be accepted.

To this the same lord Hincmar replies that he possesses the aforementioned history for reading, not for presenting it as an authority. He asserts, however, that the same homily was composed catholically by Saint Jerome, as its style, the care of its meaning and interpretation, and other certain indications demonstrate; trustworthy persons also attest this, through whom it was brought from the eastern regions at a definite time and reached our lands. He adds concerning Odo’s own booklet against the objections of the Greeks that he had noted certain matters in it which ought to be reconsidered and corrected; likewise, concerning the ordination of Hedenulf, in accordance with the command of Pope John, to the episcopate of Laon, which had long been vacant through the absence of a shepherd; likewise, concerning the paschal lunar reckoning and the reading which Abbot Adalard composed on that subject; likewise, on the same matter, giving thanks to God for Odo’s diligence, by which he endeavored to investigate the mystical observance of the paschal solemnity, and so forth; likewise, concerning his journey to the council of Pope John, urging him also to hasten to come to it; likewise, concerning the investigation, undertaken by Odo himself and the aforementioned Hedenulf, of the lawsuit involving the monastery of Auriniac, concerning the administration of Abbess Ricoara, who had usurped that monastery contrary to the laws. He warns him to suggest to the king that he should not act in this matter in such a way as to entangle himself in the sins of others. He likewise speaks of his journey—not into the presence of an earthly king, but to the judgment of the eternal King, toward which, he indicates, he is already hastening through continual illnesses; likewise, concerning the ordination of Hetilo, whom the people of Noyon had chosen to be ordained their bishop; and several other writings are also found to have been sent to the same man.

To Hildegarius, bishop of Meaux, he writes concerning certain members of his parish who had committed homicides in the parish of Reims, exhorting him to strive to save them by whatever counsel and assistance he could, promising that he would help so that they might come to peace.

He also writes to the same man a certain booklet, *On the Judgment of Cold Water*.

To John, bishop of Cambrai, who was asking that letters of recommendation be given to him as he traveled to Rome, to be offered in the name of Lord Hincmar to Pope Adrian, he replies that, if he wished to go to Rome in order to render service to Caesar in such a way that this service would not be contrary to the service owed to God, he would gladly grant him canonical letters; but if he wished to go on behalf of the case of King Lothair, which had long been debated between him and his wife, then, since he was unable to give letters of recommendation in this matter, he dared not—and indeed ought not—give letters that would expose him to reproach, especially since Lord Adrian had recently sent him a letter of his authority through Actard, bishop of Nantes (ADRIAN II, letter 13), in which he indicated that he was following the contests which the Apostolic See, through his predecessors Benedict and Nicholas, had conducted in this case. He warned him not to consent in any way to the weakening of what had been done concerning this affair, and explained how Waldrada had been excommunicated. He also adds that he could not give him letters of dismissal without the counsel of his fellow bishops, especially concerning an uncertain matter; likewise, concerning the death of King Lothair, exhorting him to come without delay to King Charles (Charles the Bald); likewise, concerning a certain priest of the Cambrai parish who had castrated himself after being repeatedly warned against doing so during a visitation, while he did not know what the sacred canons prescribed in such a case. He gives counsel and warns that the manner in which it had been done should be carefully investigated, and that meanwhile, by indulgence, the same priest should remain in his order until it could be established at a provincial synod what should be observed in the matter—something that would be found neither contrary to the Gospel precepts nor opposed to the decrees of the saints; likewise, giving thanks for the benefits which he had often received from him, and asking him to look for Saint Augustine’s discourse *On the Fall of a Monk and a Widow*, and to send it to him for copying, or have it copied, and bring it to the next synod. He also asks that Bede’s exposition on Solomon’s Proverbs be brought to that same synod. He further informs him that the Roman pope had sent certain instructions to King Charles and to the bishops of his kingdom, which had to be discussed at the synod; therefore the king had also sent letters to the metropolitans of his kingdom, ordering them to summon their fellow bishops to the same synod; likewise, concerning a tenth part which he had been informed had been taken from the ancient royal chapel and added to an altar which he had newly consecrated: because this was contrary to the regulations, he advises that it be corrected, if it had been done; likewise, concerning a certain priest who had lodged a complaint before the see of Reims, alleging that he was suffering prejudice from that same bishop, who had forbidden him, together with his property, also the exercise of his priestly office, although he had neither confessed voluntarily nor been canonically convicted, on account of a riot and homicide that had been committed in his presence, where he had taken up arms in self-defense and wounded a man, though not the man who had been killed. In these letters he shows, from sacred authority, what discretion must be exercised in such a case and which chapters of the sacred canons must be applied.

He also writes several other things to the same man.

To Ragelinus of Noyon, concerning a certain priest who had brought him letters from Pope Adrian [Note: [Col. 0227D] This letter of Adrian does not survive.], he gives instructions that, if that bishop delayed correcting what had unjustly been done against the same priest, Lord Hincmar should, after a first and second warning, strike Ragelinus with canonical authority until satisfaction was given. He therefore warns him by letter to obey the pope’s commands, and explains why such instructions commonly came from the Apostolic See to him or to certain other bishops: namely, because in judging their subjects they did not follow the regular path of discernment, and because they neglected to have recourse to metropolitan authority by asking questions and obeying; likewise, concerning the visitation of the Church of Thérouanne after the death of Bishop Hunfrid, in accordance with the king’s arrangement; likewise, concerning a certain Rothad, a friend of that bishop, who complained that he had lost through fraud the property which he had entrusted to his faith. He gives advice about what he should do in the matter, so that it would not reach a synodal judgment.

To Villebert [manuscript: Guilobert], bishop of Châlons, he replies to his inquiries concerning Count Gangulf, advising him to act gently, in accordance with the apostolic command, regarding those things which he either denied having done against him or admitted in part, so that in this he might fulfill the law of Christ, namely charity [Col. 0227D] (Gal. 6), and might bring him, as far as possible, to satisfaction and affection. He urges the same count with every available effort and allows his kindness toward him to become evident. For it was fitting that he should commend the beginnings of his priesthood by devotion and affection. Likewise, concerning a certain transgressing priest, he advises him to act regarding the priest’s absolution according to the instructions of blessed Gregory, in accordance with the prophetic judgment concerning the confession of the penitent and the apostolic judgment concerning judgment and mercy. The aforementioned count, who had indicated that he now fully acknowledged his fault, he should receive kindly, following the kindness of the father who joyfully received the prodigal son (Luke 15); and he should admit the viscount as a mediator of peace between them all the more kindly insofar as he recognized him as a son of God on account of the truth of the Gospel; likewise, concerning two salt vessels which the king was sending to Saint Stephen, and a golden cross with relics of the saints which the queen was assigning to the altar of that same saint; likewise, concerning the investigation, according to the king’s command, of the case being disputed between Bishops Odo and Rothad; likewise, concerning the ordination of Arnold, bishop of Toul, that he should go to meet Adventius and Berard, who were making the same request, namely, that the ordination be celebrated in the district of Metz, in accordance with the king’s command; likewise, with Odo, that they should speak together in the king’s presence about convening a provincial synod; likewise, in response to his consultation whether he could, under the pressure of necessity, appoint a monk as archdeacon; [Col. 0228B] likewise, concerning one of his men who had been excommunicated by him. Because he had heard that the man had been bound irrationally, he advises that he be carefully absolved; likewise, concerning the synod of Pope John [John VIII], sent by the emperor Charles to Lord Hincmar, which the same Villebert had copied. He orders him to transmit it to the neighboring bishops Berard and Arnold, and so forth.

He also writes certain other things to the same man.

To Hildebold of Soissons, concerning a certain church over which a dispute had arisen between him and Odo, bishop of Beauvais, and which the king was ordering to be destroyed; likewise, concerning the ordination of ministers of the monastery of Orbais, and certain brothers who had irrationally left that monastery and were later received back; likewise, concerning certain priests from the monastery of Saint Crispin, about whom Lord Pope John had written to Lord Hincmar and concerning whom it had been determined that they should not go outside the monastery’s enclosure, and that the same penalty should be tempered toward them paternally; likewise, concerning the ordination of Hadebert to the episcopate of the Church of Senlis; likewise, concerning letters of Pope John brought by a priest accused of a crime, which he says clearly diverged from the sacred canons and the decrees of the holy Fathers, and accordingly gives useful advice about how one should act; likewise, asking that he travel with him into the presence of Pope John, who had come to Troyes to settle certain cases; likewise, concerning the settlement of the kings, the sons of Louis, about which the bishops, abbots, and counts who were with them had sent him instructions to direct a letter and his envoy to them. This he did, instructing this bishop, as he traveled to them, to follow with prayers and petitions whatever they might discover by God’s inspiration; likewise, with Bishops Walter, Gislebert, and Angelin, that they should come together with him to carry out the command of the aforementioned Pope John between Hedenulf and Hincmar, bishops of Laon, with observance of the sacred canons; likewise, an exhortation to the same Hildebold, who was suffering from bodily illness. In accordance with the request contained in his letter of confession, he absolves him by reconciling him, although he was physically absent; and he writes several other things to him.

To Atulf [i.e., Octulf, and below], bishop of Troyes, concerning relics of the saints which he had reported finding, after miraculous signs had been displayed, he writes about how he should arrange them, and concerning the church of Saint Peter, which he was planning to rebuild, about how he should proceed; also concerning his illness or recovery, and so forth; likewise, concerning the estates of Boleticum and Fagum, which refused to give the tithes owed to the priests, advising what should be done; likewise, concerning the instructions of Pope John about Hincmar of Laon, which the pope himself had directed to the same Atulf, and what he ought to observe.

To Walo, bishop of Metz, in response to the letters which he had sent him asking for instruction in pastoral life, for a confederation of fraternal unanimity, and concerning his sudden advancement, and requesting that he send him words of encouragement; likewise, concerning a certain priest to whom Lord Hincmar had entrusted certain properties of the Church of Reims situated in the Vosges, who had mismanaged them, and some of whose properties had come under the authority of the Church of Metz; likewise, concerning the advice he had requested from him about a dispute over certain properties between the Church of Metz and the Church of Trier, and concerning the pallium which he had obtained from the Roman See, on account of which his archbishop refused to receive the pope’s letters; likewise, concerning the ordination of the bishop of Verdun, whom he had discovered had been advanced contrary to the regulations after Berard’s death. He instructs this letter with sacred ordinances and demonstrates from divine authorities how a bishop ought, or ought not, to be ordained, along with several other matters.

To Hedenulf, whom he had ordained bishop of Laon after Hincmar, concerning certain deacons whom he was sending to him to be advanced to the priesthood; likewise, concerning an orphan whose inheritance that bishop was bringing forward on his behalf, and certain other matters.

To Bishop Arnold, concerning certain men who had committed homicide in the parish of Reims and were unable to obtain peace, but wished to do penance, which they could not perform in that parish; he writes about what ought to be observed concerning them; likewise, concerning the advice which he had requested about the arrival of Louis from beyond the Rhine, and what Lord Hincmar himself had sent back in reply to that king when the king ordered him to come to him.

To Bishop Franco, concerning letters of admonition which, by the king’s command, he was sending to Hugh, the nephew of the emperor Lothair, asking that Franco also send an envoy of his own with Hincmar’s envoy, one who could lead Hugh safely there and bring him back; likewise, concerning Evrard, whom he calls their common son, and whom he implores Franco to support before King Louis of the Transrhenine kingdom and the queen, and so forth.

To Berno of Châlons, concerning envoys of the Church of Noyon who had come to him after the death of their bishop Rainelin, he asks that Berno lead them into the presence of the kings, read Lord Hincmar’s letters to those kings, and make them understand them, and that for this cause he strive to intercede both with the kings and with the members of the palace, according to his office; likewise, concerning the election of a shepherd for the aforementioned Church of Noyon or the Church of Tournai, and because he had sent Bishop Adalberno and that Church the form of visitation or election, he warns him to ask the kings and Abbot Hugh that letters from the kings concerning this matter be sent to him as soon as possible, since that Church could not remain for long without a shepherd without suffering harm; likewise, concerning the same matter and several others.

To Adalberno, concerning the visitation of the aforementioned Church of Tournai, he asks that he diligently perform his visitation of it and frequently reread and inculcate the form of election to the clergy and people, lest through ignorance they depart from that form in any respect; likewise, concerning the election of a shepherd for that Church, and because many were working not to enter through the door (John 10), without fearing or being ashamed to become thieves and robbers; and because he was to be sent into the presence of the kings, he says that when he had gone there he should speak with him, so that together they might consider how he should act in this matter thereafter; [Col. 0230B] and so forth; likewise, concerning the complaint and protest of a certain priest of his parish, he explains how bishops ought to organize and govern the churches of rural parishes. He warns him to read frequently blessed Gregory’s homily from the Gospel, *Jesus Appointed*, concerning the seventy-two others. He also instructs him to reread frequently the *Pastoral Rule* of that same blessed Gregory (GREGORY, *Homily 17 on the Gospels*), together with the sacred canons, and vigorously to carry out what is read there as needing to be followed, while carefully avoiding what is found to be forbidden [i.e., “the rules, etc., which he should reread, so that he may vigorously carry out what is read there as needing to be followed, and carefully avoid what is found to be forbidden”].

To Hetilo [otherwise Hedit.] of Noyon, that he should strive, through prayers and whatever assistance he could provide, for the aid and fidelity of the kings, indicating that he was surrounded by great distress from the barbarians and that, after everything else had been plundered, such a ransom was being demanded for the city that he could not pay it; likewise, because King Louis of Germany had ordered him to go and meet him, which he would nevertheless be unable to do because he was confined by illness, he orders this bishop, both personally and through those entrusted to him, to persist in prayers for the peace and defense of the Church, and, if he could accomplish anything useful against the pagans, to act with the leading men of the kingdom as far as he was able.

He also writes concerning the monasteries that had been burned, saying that he grieved over what the bishop had reported and greatly feared for those that had not yet been burned.

To Bishop Sigemund, concerning the reconciliation of penitents and other matters pertaining to the sacred ministry, on which he indicates that he had instructed Bishop Hildegarius. Likewise, concerning the kind protection and treatment of subjects, reminding him that God had made him a spiritual physician from a bodily one; likewise, in response to his question about what knowledge he himself required from the priests of his parish.

To the bishops assembling at the synod of Soissons [Note: [Col. 0229D] This synod is absent from the volume of the Councils.], by order of King Louis of the Transrhenine kingdom, he sends a certain priest as his representative and excuses himself on account of the impossibility caused by his illness. He declares that he assents to whatever they might decree, with the Lord’s favor, according to canonical institution and episcopal ministry, justly and reasonably, with equity as their guide; but whatever might oppose the sacred canons or deviate from the path of right faith, equity, and justice, he would in no way approve, nor would he agree that his representative should approve it, even under compulsion.

To the bishops of the diocese of the Church of Sens, concerning the election of Ansegis, a monk of the diocese of Reims, to the episcopate of Sens, he gives his consent to his ordination.

Also to the bishops and leading men of the whole kingdom, he sends admonition and exhortation that they preserve inviolate faith toward their king Charles when that king went to Rome; likewise, to bishops, abbots, counts, and the other faithful of God who were assembling for a certain gathering which he himself, hindered by bodily illness, had been unable to attend. He gives thanks to God for certain leading men of the kingdom who had been somewhat at odds with the bishops but who, at that time, through God’s grace, had been joined to a pleasing unanimity. By these letters, and through an ecclesiastical fellow minister whom he sent, he indicates that he rejoices with them over their good endeavors and arrangements. He advises them, according to the wisdom given them by God and in obedience to the divine commands, to set aside private interests, illegitimate desires, and harmful disputes, and first to seek and carry out what concerns the salvation, peace, and benefit of the community. He adds sacred authorities concerning the garment of Christ, which is the Church of God, and urges them to arm themselves with all their strength, rise up in zeal for justice, break the yoke of the burden of their mother Church and the rod of her taskmaster (Isaiah 9), and loosen the bonds from the necks of her children (Isaiah 52). If any are oppressed, they should extend a helping hand; if any have perhaps been led astray by desire or favor, they should strive to restore them to the unanimity of the Lord’s flock. They should embrace the counsel of blessed Gregory and the other holy Fathers. He too will pursue, with prayers and services, insofar as the Lord grants, whatever they decree for securing the peace of God’s people and justice. He also adds sacred authorities concerning the canonical advancement or election of a bishop.

## CHAPTER XXIV. What he wrote and sent to certain abbots

He is also found to have sent various writings, for the benefit of each person, to many different individuals, both clerics and laymen, including respectable women. He spared no one through flattery, but endeavored to suggest to each person what was useful according to the circumstances.

He sent letters to his abbot Louis concerning the recovery of the body of Saint Deodatus, which a certain Giso, driven by greed for the saint’s possessions, had secretly caused to be transferred from the diocese of Reims to the parish of Paris, without consulting the bishop in whose episcopal residence it lay. In these letters he asserts that he spares no one—neither another person, nor himself, nor even his own blood—in opposition to the divine laws. He also did not cease to admonish the abbot again by letter, who was indignant over this matter, exhorting and warning him to endeavor to satisfy the ecclesiastical regulations; likewise, concerning a certain nephew of his whom he had entrusted to him, and concerning property handed over by the king, through the arrangement of Lord Hincmar himself, to the monks of Saint Denis.

To Abbot Hilduin, concerning a letter from King Charles and his envoy, who was to be brought with letters to the emperor Lothair. In these letters he openly states that he is offering certain advice concerning the emperor’s salvation, so that he might correct what Hincmar identifies to him as needing correction, and concerning the payment of the census from the estate of Dudecia.

Likewise, together with the synod of bishops held at Quierzy [Note: [Col. 0231D] It was held in the year 855, under Benedict III.], he writes to Hilduin, archchaplain of King Charles, also concerning the Church of Langres, which Wlfadus, a fosterling of the Church of Reims, had occupied contrary to canonical decrees. Accordingly, that same synod had suggested to the king that he appoint another person to govern the aforementioned Church, and the king had ordered the bishops to seek someone who could benefit that Church in the episcopal ministry. Their votes had converged on Isaac, a disciple of Hilduin. They implore Hilduin’s consent in this matter and his intercession for Isaac before the king.

To Abbot Brunuard, concerning the properties of Saint Remigius and the tenants of the Church of Reims established in Thuringia; to Abbot Adalard, concerning the friendship between them and how a true friend ought to be; to Abbot Grunold, concerning his faithful Sigebert, asking him to receive the latter’s properties, which lay in the kingdom of Louis, as entrusted to his authority and protection, and to advise King Louis not to involve himself any further, believing the counsel of wicked men, in actions such as those he had then undertaken against his brother Charles. From this, he says, such disgrace had befallen him as would not have occurred had he been willing to heed the exhortations of Lord Hincmar.

To Transulf [i.e., Transulf] of Corbie and the brothers subject to him, concerning a certain brother who had presumptuously left the monastery. The same pontiff had ordered him, after the king had received him back into favor, to return quickly to the monastery. The king had asked that he give instructions that the man be received peacefully in the monastery until the king and the same archbishop could, at a suitable time, determine the manner of his conduct; likewise, to the same men, giving thanks for the kindness they had shown him, declaring that he placed the greatest confidence in their prayers and was devoted to them, and sending them admonitions and exhortations for their salvation: each of those who had undertaken to steer the ship of the Lord’s governance among them should strive to guide it with tireless care against the assaults of rising storms, and, when persecution by the pagans threatened, should not depart from a good purpose, wherever it might be necessary to withdraw, and so forth; likewise, to Hilduin, that he should strive before the king to secure the granting of a canonical election for the Church of Thérouanne, since he too would endeavor to do this as far as he could.

To Abbot Adalgarius, giving thanks for the prayers which he and the brothers entrusted to him had offered to God for Hincmar, and for the blessing of the abbot’s gifts. He also recalls the properties of the Church of Reims situated in Thuringia, which he had entrusted to a certain Amalric; but Amalric had abused them and consequently received divine judgment. The abbot was asking that these properties be granted to him subject to a census. Lord Hincmar, however, refusing to do this without the counsel of his clerics, instructs him to receive them provisionally for safekeeping, to endeavor to send him an inventory of them; afterward Hincmar would report to him what he had judged more reasonably with the counsel of the Church’s ministers.

Likewise, concerning the same matter, after the inventory had been sent to him, he indicates that he had also sent letters to King Louis concerning those properties, at the abbot’s request. He informed the king that he had entrusted the properties to the abbot and asked him to provide assistance so that the abbot might be able to administer them peacefully. He also writes to a certain Poppo, restraining him from disturbing these properties, and orders the household settled on them by letter to obey the same abbot in everything.

To Anastasius, venerable abbot and librarian of the holy Roman Church, giving thanks for the most holy blessings which he had sent to him through Bishop Actard; he also sends that abbot his own blessings of gifts. He entrusts to him certain little works completed through his own labor; likewise, concerning the benefits bestowed on him by Anastasius, and asking him to make Hincmar’s request acceptable to the lord pope, and concerning the remembrance of the blessing which he was sending him (on this, above, chapter 21).

To Gregory, nomenclator and apocrisiarius of the same Roman Church, he asserts that the aforementioned Anastasius had informed him by letter of many marks of Gregory’s goodness and had sincerely assured him that he could place great confidence in Gregory’s friendship. He therefore asks that Gregory deign to count him among his faithful friends.

To Abbot Guntarius, concerning a certain irreligious monk whom he had allowed to leave the monastery irreverently, according to his own whim. Hincmar therefore strongly reproves him, showing from the authority of the Rule that he ought not to have dismissed him in this way. He advises that the monk be sought and apprehended with the king’s envoy, returned to the monastery, and shut up in the strictest custody; that his faults be recorded; and that this record, together with a letter from his own bishop, be sent to Hincmar, so that he might decide concerning him, with the counsel of his fellow bishops, according to the sacred rules.

To Gozlinus, concerning his nephew Bernard, who was said to be plotting a revolt against the king, he exhorts him to strive to recall Bernard from this intention, and warns Gozlinus himself not to turn aside from the right path on account of any carnal affection. He also warns his brother Gozfrid that both of them, remembering their parents, should not degenerate from the sincerity of faith; likewise, asking why he did not send an envoy or letters to him as he had been accustomed to do, and exhorting him to strive to do so frequently for the sake of mutual love and consolation; likewise, explaining how the same Gozlinus had become an enemy to him from being a beloved son, while he still calls him a dear son and declares that he bears the injuries inflicted on him by Gozlinus not only patiently but willingly.

He asks him to remember that the Church of Reims had regenerated him in Christ, raised and taught him as a tonsured cleric under religious discipline, redeemed him from captivity among the pagans, advanced him through the ecclesiastical grades as far as the diaconate, and, through the concessions of kings, appointed him abbot of many monasteries. He then explains how, lifted up by power against these benefits, Gozlinus had stirred up the rebellion that was wickedly raging in that Church or in that kingdom, what similar actions he had committed, and how many evils threatened him. He implores him to remember these things, hear the voice of the Lord calling him back, and have mercy on his own soul (Ecclesiasticus 30), so that he might attain salvation; likewise, giving thanks to God for his correction and praying that God confirm what He had worked in him (Psalm 67), and grant him both the will and the ability to accomplish what is pleasing to Him according to His good will (Philippians 2), along with several other matters.

To Abbot Grunharius [manuscript: Grimharius], concerning the properties of Saint Mary and Saint Remigius situated in the district of Auvergne, which he had forbidden Count Bernard to possess; he instructs this abbot to inventory them and bring the inventory to him.

To Adalgarius, the bishop-elect, concerning the properties of the Church of Reims situated in the regions of Aquitaine, which Bernard, count of Toulouse, had seized and, because he could not obtain them by payment, had ruined through plunder, until God exercised His judgment in the matter. Lord Hincmar had entrusted these properties to Bishop Agilmar, to whom, by the king’s order, he had also given a booklet concerning incestuous persons and usurpers of ecclesiastical property. He sends to this man the instructions that had also been given to that bishop concerning the same properties and urges him, after sharing counsel with Agilmar, to work on behalf of those properties. He names certain districts in which they lay, namely Auvergne, Nigrum-Mont, Limoges, and Poitiers. In other districts, whose names he does not recall, he asks that the matter be investigated and recorded, and that the inventory itself be sent to him.

To Lambert, whom he remembers as his uniquely beloved and deeply cherished son, he gives admonition and exhortation about how he should act toward those among whom he lived and who appeared likely to elect him to the episcopate of Metz. He especially warns him to guard against the plague of the Simoniac heresy in every respect. “For,” he says, “he will not be able to advance in the ecclesiastical order who is promoted so that he may become a heretic.” He also advises him to read the pastoral rule of Saint Gregory quickly and store it in his mind, and according to that same rule to direct and correct himself inwardly and outwardly along the path by which one reaches the episcopate and by which, in the episcopate, one advances toward eternal life.

He indicates that he was sending letters on his behalf to his friends, both bishops and counts of the kingdom of Lothair, bearing witness that Lambert would not deviate from their counsels and salutary exhortations, and asks him not to make him a liar before those friends concerning these matters.

To Abbot Hugh, concerning the election of a bishop of Noyon after the death of Ragenelin, he asks him to urge Kings Louis and Karlomann [Note: [Col. 0233D] These were the sons of Louis the Stammerer and grandsons of Charles the Bald.] to preserve in this matter the will of God and the custom of their predecessors. He also informs him of the death of his nephew Hincmar, bishop of Laon, asking him to strive to implore the Lord’s mercy for the remedy of his soul through his subjects and household [manuscript: “let them strive”].

Likewise, he asks him to appoint suitable tutors for the aforementioned kings, since they had a counselor who was much too young. He also writes concerning what the same kings had ordered him to do for the protection of the parish of Tournai [i.e., “for protecting the parish of Tournai”], what he had done about these matters, what they had later sent back to him, and what he had written in reply when they refused to give their consent to the canonical election of the aforementioned Church of Noyon. He says that he had done nothing else in the matter except what he had been accustomed to do in such affairs for thirty-five years. He also reports what had later been communicated to him on behalf of the kings or of Hugh himself through the cleric Warinus, and what letters the aforementioned kings had afterward sent to Hugh.

He adds the authorities promulgated by the sacred canons concerning canonical election, showing that bishops are not to be ordered to be elected from the palace but from each individual Church, and that, concerning the ordination of a bishop, the recommendation should not come from the king or the members of the palace, but that there should first be the election of the clergy and people, then the metropolitan’s judgment in the election, afterward the consent of the earthly prince, and then the laying on of hands by the bishops. He asserts with certainty that he had no particular candidate in mind, except that each person should approach this office according to sacred authority and should know and do what the spiritual ministry requires, and so forth.

Likewise, he sends him a copy of the letter which he had sent to King Charles, son of Louis of the Transrhenine kingdom, concerning the still-underage kings Louis and Karlomann. He urges Hugh, if he can obtain it, to arrange that this Charles—since he had no son—adopt one of these young kings as his son and have him raised under the authority of a good and energetic guardian, so that he might establish him as his heir either wholly or in part. He also asks that Hugh privately obtain from Charles that Charles take upon himself the entire responsibility for these boys and this kingdom, and that he himself arrange whatever should be administered in the royal service.

He further advises that Hugh, if the writings Hincmar was sending to Charles were useful and reasonable, should pursue them with his wise counsel and prudent care; but if anything in them seemed otherwise than it ought to be, he should wisely alter it, or, if necessary, strive to add or obtain something.

Likewise, concerning the instructions and exhortations of King Louis of Germany: first, that he should order the bishops of the diocese of Reims to go to meet that king at Attigny; second, that he should send him advice about how to govern this kingdom—namely, what response should be given to the king’s envoys—and, if Louis himself arrived and asked to be consecrated king, what should be done and how it should be done in that matter, and so forth.

He also writes several other things to the same abbot.

## CHAPTER XXV. What he wrote to priests or to certain monasteries
Gautsuinus, a priest, and the other brothers serving God and Saint Denis: he writes concerning a certain house formerly granted to him by them, and partly purchased from the same [Col. 0236A], which one of them, secretly taking it from him, had usurped. He expresses his astonishment if the brothers had indeed forbidden this to be done by one who, as far as he remembered, had never been useless to them, but, as had then seemed fitting to them, had remained among them useful and necessary in many ways, and had obtained and re-obtained no small benefits for them. He says this not because that house, or its little garden, is precious to him to retain without their charity, and so forth.

Likewise, to Wiligiso, together with the other monks of that monastery, concerning what he had heard: that they were demanding payment from a certain priest for a tithe. He says that he feels the greatest shame on account of the other people who would hear of this. He demonstrates to them from divine authority, and then from the promulgation of the canons, how great a danger this is. He continues:

“Far be it, brothers, that other ecclesiastical and religious men should hear that the monks of the monastery of Saint Denis are trying to sell a tithe, so that with its price they may purchase hell. Much more, then, let it be far from them that laymen should hear of it—something that no one even entangled in public sins dares to do in my parish. For if anyone from another monastery, rather than from ours, should attempt this, how much more boldly would he presume to do it? I would excommunicate him from my parish and exclude him from all communion,” and so forth.

Likewise, to the same monks, concerning the visitation of divine mercy, by which, he says, he had been reminded that his days had declined like a shadow and that he had withered like hay (Psalm 101). He sends to their service a very small blessing, namely two hundred solidi in pure coin, and asks them continually to remember him in their sacred prayers before their common patron, the most blessed Dionysius. He also petitions them on behalf of Haimo, his faithful servant, who was almost at the point of death, and whom he calls his beloved son.

To Fulcramnus [i.e. Fulcrannus], the provost, and the brothers of the monastery of Corbie: he writes concerning the election of an abbot granted to them by the king, concerning the royal letters on the same matter, and concerning the arrival of the lord Hincmar among them. Since they had consulted him, he instructs them how they should proceed in this election according to the teaching of the blessed Father Benedict: in all things they should follow the Rule as their mistress, and no one should rashly depart from it, since they would have to give an account for everything before the tribunal of our Lord Jesus Christ.

To Magenardus, the provost (concerning him above, chapter 23), and to the brothers living in the monastery of Saint Richarius [Col. 0236D]: concerning the letters that the apostolic pope had sent to King Charles and to Hincmar himself about a man who had killed a monk and a priest. In those letters the pope had set out the terms of the penance imposed. Hincmar urges them to take care to obey the divine commands in the matters prescribed by those letters.

To the monks of the monastery of Saint Medard: concerning Hainoaldus, a monk who had sought pardon from the king for his offenses. On the king’s word, he instructs them either to receive Hainoaldus among them so that he may live according to the Rule, or, in accordance with his request, to provide him with letters of dismissal to a definite place and permit him, absolved, to depart in peace.

To Sigebodus, a priest and provost of the monastery of nuns of the Church of Lyon [Col. 0237A]: concerning the question he had asked him—how he ought to proceed with the investigation entrusted to him at the monastery of nuns at Oriniac concerning the abbess and the provost of that monastery. Hincmar had replied to the questioner that matters of this kind should be answered not orally but in writing. Accordingly, in his reply he also shows what has been written about such matters in the laws approved by the Catholic Church and in ecclesiastical rules. He further orders that the monastery’s privilege be brought to him, and that accusations against the abbess and the provost concerning definite matters be reported to him by reliable persons, so that, according to the sacred rules, with the advice of his fellow bishops and of the visitor of the bishopric of Laon—for at that time there was no bishop there—he may, with the Lord’s inspiration, decide the matter [i.e. “let it be decided”].

To certain deans of the parish of Soissons [Col. 0237B]: concerning a certain priest who, having suffered prejudice, was unable to obtain justice and judgment from his own bishop, Rothadus. For this reason the lord Hincmar himself had warned that prelate that, if illness prevented him from coming to the synod, he should send his representatives—namely, fellow ministers of the Church entrusted to him—so that the matter might be determined canonically. Through these letters Hincmar warns the same deans, and by metropolitan authority commands them, to admonish the priests of their deanery to come to the announced assembly, and to come there themselves with them. If they failed to do so, they should know that they would receive a synodal sentence at the next synod.

To a certain priest named Sigebert: concerning his bishop Heidilo [Col. 0237C]. Hincmar grieved that he had heard such things about the bishop as would not be appropriate to say even about a good layman, and that he was being blamed for having ordained such a bishop. He asserts that, concerning a man whom he had not previously known, he had trusted the faith and testimony of Sigebert himself. He orders Sigebert to come to him, so that he may tell him in person what he has heard about the bishop; if the reports were true, they would consider together how to correct them, and if they were not true, how to demonstrate that they were lies.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Letters to Certain Distinguished Men

To the most illustrious Eberard, one of the leading men of Emperor Lothar: writing to regain the favor of an intimacy which Eberard had formerly freely offered him, he rejoices at the good reports of him received from reliable persons, especially through Bishop Amolo, whom he calls his most sincere and dearest father. He sends him his letters also by a certain most faithful messenger. Praising likewise the devotion of Eberard’s sincerity toward God, his reverence for sacred authority, the unanimity of princes, his zeal for ecclesiastical peace, and the duty of religion, he exhorts him, as an office of charity, to advance, as he has begun, ever better and better. For, as Job testifies, human nature never remains in the same state (Job 14); and in this world, whatever power a man possesses, he sails against the current of a river. Therefore, by sailing manfully he will seek the heights, or, with his hands slackened, he will fall back to the depths [Col. 0238A]. Above all, he should strive to please God; then to provide for the peace of the Church; and then not merely to suggest, but even to press, good things upon princes. He should devote himself to obtaining due privileges for ecclesiastical men and holy places; secure peace and unanimity for the Christian people; rejoice with those who act well; resist those who act badly; and diligently guard himself by living soberly, justly, and piously (Titus 2), together with other exhortations that are highly necessary. After this he also sets forth certain needs, both of monasteries and of others, on whose behalf he had written to the emperor, matters within his parish requiring correction by imperial authority; and other matters concerning the welfare of the soul and the preservation of spiritual counsel.

To a certain Fulcric [Col. 0238B] (the same man as above, chapter 20), a magnate of the aforesaid emperor, who had unlawfully put away his lawful wife and had moreover taken another: summoning him to a synod, he sets out the form of the excommunication already pronounced against him and to be confirmed in a provincial synod. Likewise, after Fulcric appeared to have undertaken penance for this deed, but repeated his former courses and returned to his vomit, he pronounces a public sentence of excommunication and takes pains to notify every person among Christ’s faithful who might hear of it, especially the bishops in whose parishes he appeared to reside or visit.

To a certain Wlfing, an official of the same Emperor Lothar: recalling the familiarity which he had once sought from him [Col. 0238C], and the affection which Wlfing had promised him, he asks him to inform the emperor concerning a letter which the emperor’s brother, King Charles (Charles the Bald), was sending to him, so that, having received it, the emperor may examine it privately and read it in secret. He asks him also to have sent to him the rent from the estate of Duciacum for the preceding year together with that of the present year, so that he might make some ornament in Wlfing’s memory at the tomb of Saint Remigius, which he was adorning and where he was arranging to transfer the saint’s body into a newly prepared crypt. Likewise, concerning the recovery of the aforesaid rent of six pounds from the estate of Duciacum: lest perhaps the emperor be told that he is reclaiming this rent through greed, though he had never diverted it to his own use. Rather, he wishes to avoid the danger that, through his silence during his lifetime, the rent itself might perish [Col. 0238D], the estate be turned into an allod, and the church’s slaves be divided among male and female slaves—as was already happening with many properties and dependants of this church, and even with that estate itself. He strives also to prevent his lord from incurring danger in this matter, or himself from sharing in that danger. He declares that, if greed were troubling him in this matter, he would reclaim the twelve pounds which the grandfather and father of this king paid from it, and so forth.

He further adds some matters about the aforementioned Fulcric, who, returning from Rome, boasted that he was bringing letters of the pope granting his absolution, both to the kings and to this archbishop. He warns Wlfing to advise the king not to be deceived in this affair, but to guard prudently against every danger [Col. 0239A]; he should have the letters brought before himself and the bishops, and they should follow whatever is found preferable in the matter. Meanwhile, what was done reasonably and canonically ought not to be despised.

To his faithful friend Nantarius, concerning the administration of the property of Saint Remigius in the district of Worms: he reports that certain persons had asked him to lend them the tenants of those properties for various works, while others asked that he allow their hunters to stay on the properties for some time. He confesses that he had granted neither request and would not grant either, because his predecessors had not dared to do this, since Saint Remigius, under a great curse and threat, had forbidden it (Saint Remigius, in his testament), and so forth.

To Count Immo, concerning the possessions of this church situated in the kingdom of Aquitaine: that he should assist their steward, to whom they were entrusted.

To the most noble Count Gerard, concerning Isaac, bishop-elect of the see of Langres: that by Gerard’s exhortation Isaac might be ordained bishop, because Wlfadus, who had occupied that church, could not canonically be ordained. Likewise, concerning what Gerard had informed him by letter: namely, that Charles, king of France, wished to seize for himself the kingdom of his lord Charles, king of Cisalpine Gaul. Lord Hincmar asserts that this is by no means so. Concerning the property of Saint Remigius located in Provence, for which Gerard had heard that Hincmar had lodged a complaint with the king, he entirely denies having done so; nor, whenever necessary, had he sent a representation concerning those properties [Col. 0239C] to anyone other than Gerard himself and his faithful men. Concerning also what this count had written that he had heard, namely that this King Charles wished to usurp the monasteries which Gerard had handed over to the blessed apostle Peter: and that, if Gerard’s property in this kingdom were taken from him, he, although unwillingly, would seize property of this kingdom held in that other kingdom. The bishop replies that no one should, at his own peril, usurp the property of the Church at his own will; he fears lest before God he be judged worthy that the church entrusted to him should suffer this during his episcopate. Yet if anyone should dare it, it would grieve that person more than Hincmar himself, as he shows the danger to the aggressor from divine authorities. He adds, concerning Gerard’s warning that, because of his sacred office, he should recall the king from such excesses, that he had not previously perceived such things to be within the king’s disposition; it was not his place to rebuke his lord upon idle suspicions, and therefore he had not warned him. But now, having both a definite case and a definite person, he will strive with due devotion and fidelity to admonish his lordship.

Likewise, concerning the aforesaid property of Saint Remigius, about which Gerard had written to this archbishop that he grieved because it was being devastated by many people, and several of its devastators said that they occupied it by permission of King Charles and of Lord Hincmar. Hincmar informs Gerard that, from the time he entrusted the property to him, he delegated it to no other person’s administration, except that he had charged a certain Hildoard, his fosterling, to assist the chief officer of the estate [Col. 0240A] in whatever was necessary, but under the protection and guardianship of the aforesaid Count Gerard. He adds what he thinks should be done about the other usurpers of the property. He would not dare grant that property as a benefice to any man, his own or another’s, because Saint Remigius had terrifyingly forbidden this in his testament. But the count, who for love of the holy Mother of God and Saint Remigius had undertaken its protection, should, as he had begun well, take care henceforth to act manfully. For in the church of Rheims, in ten monasteries of canons, monks, and nuns, more than five hundred continual intercessors pray in psalms, spiritual songs, and sacred offerings for his present and everlasting salvation, and so forth [Col. 0240B].

Likewise, concerning the same property, almost the same matters. Likewise, he sends, for the ordering and administration of that property with the count’s help [read: counsel], a monk and priest of the monastery of Saint Remigius named Rotfrid.

To the illustrious Count Rodulf, concerning the illness of his wife, and concerning reports that the count was sowing certain discordant things between the king and some of his subjects: Lord Hincmar declares that, since he considered himself very free of such conduct, he takes it ill to be so regarded; and that messages concerning those who were with the king were arriving which were inappropriate. He could therefore write nothing to the count or send a message through another until they could speak together and mutually confer about what, from what they saw, better served the advantage and honor of their lord [Col. 0240C]. He urges him to go to the king as quickly as possible, and, by staying with him, to strive as much as he can that he may guard himself before God in heart and deed, and set a guard upon his mouth even against those who were thought his friends (Psalm 111 [probably 141]). He writes also concerning the assembly of the king’s faithful men, the direction of the king’s mind, and the division of this kingdom; the killing of the Bretons Herispoë, Salomon, and Almarchus; the queen’s journey to the king, as the count had instructed him; and because he greatly feared for the king. Likewise, concerning the improper disturbance between the count and the king which he had learned from the count’s letters, he says that he had become quite sad. He will strive, insofar as he can, to deal with the king about the matters reported to him; and, if the count sends him whatever he discovers, he will take care to send him word in return [Col. 0240D]. He adds what had happened to his own men whom he had had with him beyond the Loire, and admonishes and strengthens him in the Lord not to be lightly stirred by such things, by which men who do not know how to fear God are stirred; rather, he should strive, as he has begun well, to preserve his good name to the end. Since he now knows the king’s mind well, although the king may be troubled by some disturbance, as soon as the count has spoken with him and made his devotion known to him, as is fitting and right, he will have him favorably disposed. He admonishes him, in accordance with the Apostle, to put away all indignation with all malice (Ephesians 4). If he does so, because the king is his nephew he will show him a more affectionate disposition; because the king is his lord [Col. 0241A], he will show him a more humble disposition toward him, and so forth.

To a certain nobleman Uvelf: he gives many thanks because Uvelf had kept such friendship toward him that he refused to receive Hincmar’s man without his consent. That man had left him without cause and had departed irreverently without leave, which none of his other men had yet done. He explains how he had received and generously maintained him, and had done him many good services, and how this man, sent to Hincmar between his lord and the king, had acted improperly. He asks Uvelf not to receive him at all until he has spoken with Hincmar and knows whether the man has a just claim against him. He adds that he repeats this not because he harbors any hatred against the man, but lest Uvelf, by receiving him against justice, sin against God and offend Hincmar, his friend—especially since, with their friendship preserved, he may have him with Hincmar’s permission [Col. 0241B].

To Count Folco of the king’s palace, concerning a priest of the parish of Soissons who, abandoning the ecclesiastical court, had appealed to a civil judgment against his accuser, who had promised to prove the charges brought against that priest. He instructs the count not to involve himself in this case until Hincmar has considered whether that may reasonably be done, because the determination of a priest’s and the Church’s case belongs to bishops and a synod, not to the disposition of the mallus or civil judges, and so forth.

To the illustrious Count Maio, giving thanks for the kindness and concern which he took care to show to Lord Theoderic, the holy bishop of Cambrai [Col. 0241C], and to his church: he asks that, should that servant of God pass to their common Lord in their lifetime, Maio should strive before Emperor Lothar to obtain permission for the clergy and people of that church to elect a successor.

Concerning also the procurement of peace between the kings, about which Maio had written him, he replies that he had always desired it and had taken care, as far as he could, to urge that it remain inviolate between them; and that, with God’s help, he will strive for it as far as he is able.

To Roric the Northman, converted to the faith of Christ: that he should advance in God’s will and in observance of His commands, as Hincmar had heard from many that he wished and did; and that no one should persuade him to furnish either counsel or assistance to pagans against Christians. For it will profit him nothing to have received Christian baptism if he has devised perverse or hostile actions against Christians, whether himself or through any others; and Hincmar goes on to explain episcopally how great is the danger in such plotting [Col. 0241D]. He further warns him by no means to receive Baldwin, anathematized by episcopal authority, through the Spirit of God by whom the holy canons were established, because he had abducted the king’s daughter as wife; nor to permit him to have any aid or refuge with him, lest both Roric and his men become entangled in Baldwin’s sins and excommunication and be condemned. Rather, he should take care to conduct himself so that the prayers of the saints may avail him.

To the illustrious man Luitard, concerning reports about him that concerned the peril of his soul, especially concerning a priest whom he had driven from a church contrary to the laws and had replaced with another: he powerfully and episcopally admonishes him to refrain from such presumptions. If he does not, Hincmar will do to him what the sacred laws prescribe, and will have it announced to bishops throughout all kingdoms, as far as the pope of Rome, that he is excommunicated [Col. 0242A]. He declares that the foreign priest whom Luitard had placed in that church is excommunicated from the whole parish of Rheims. Likewise, calling him his beloved son, and saying that he calls him so in order that he may make himself such that he may rightly remain in Hincmar’s love, as a bishop likewise desires. But because he hears that Luitard is not conducting himself as he ought toward the church of Rheims, from which he had many benefits, and, by harassing its servants, does not allow them to live in peace, he commands him, by the authority of God, Saint Mary, Saint Remigius, and his own episcopal authority, and also by the king’s ban, whose envoy the bishop was, that neither he nor his men cause any hindrance to men of the church of Rheims, whether by any contrivance or with his consent. If he wishes to seek anything reasonable against the authority of the church of Rheims, he must seek it through the law. If he acts otherwise, he will suffer what is right in the matter, both through episcopal authority and through the king’s missaticum. He also excommunicates a certain deacon of his who opposed the servants of Saint Remigius, and so forth.

To Count Theodulf [read: Theudulf] [Col. 0242C], concerning an usurpation of ecclesiastical ministry: after a certain priest died, he had taken what that priest had directed to be given in alms for himself, and had moreover usurped what had properly been left to that church.

He makes clear how great a crime of sacrilege the count committed, how he acted against human laws, what ought to be done, and how, according to the sacred canons and imperial capitularies, churches are under the authority and administration of bishops. He commands him, according to sacred authorities and royal commands, immediately to restore to the church whatever he had received from that church’s resources and to return it to the priests to whom the goods had been entrusted. Then he is to come to Hincmar to receive a remedy, that he may be healed. He grants him seven days after receiving the letter, so that on the eighth day he may come to him, either to give due account if the matter is not so, or to make fitting satisfaction if it is so. If he does not do this, Hincmar will send a copy of the letter to the king, that he may perform his office in the matter, and afterwards the bishop himself will carry out his own duty. And because he had heard that the count was preparing to sell that church for a stated price, he added:

> “Therefore know this: if any cleric gives you even one denarius for that church, or for any other in my parish, either personally or through an intermediary, he shall not be ordained in it by me. But if you wish to have a priest there, send me a cleric who is fit for sacred ministry [Col. 0243A], and I will examine him and give him the church, and then ordain him, if that cleric gives me satisfaction that he has given no payment for it. If you will not do this, I will arrange that the people there have the office until I ordain a priest there. If you cause him any hindrance contrary to divine and human laws, and it is proved, the priest shall remain there, and you and all who have agreed with you shall be separated from all Christendom until satisfaction is made. Beloved son, I give you this command and admonish you thus because I desire you safe and honored, and wish to have you among the sons of the Church in the place of a son. If you compel me, as the Lord says in the Gospel, to treat you as a heathen and a publican (Matthew 18), you must reckon it not to me but to yourself. After I dictated this letter, I was told that you expelled from that matricula the matricularii appointed by my officer, and sent Bovarius [read: Bonarius] there; and that you received one ass as a price for that matricula. If this is so, you have not only acted criminally, because, contrary to all laws, you, a layman, have usurped ecclesiastical ministry and, like Judas the traitor, sold almsgiving—that is, mercy for the poor—and thereby God, who is the mercy of the wretched. But you have also acted most shamefully in this: from the begging by which beggars ought to live, you, a count and honored counsellor of the king, received an ass as payment. All who hear this can judge how justly and rightly you act in other matters for love and fear of God and reverence for your office [Col. 0243C], when without any shame you seek shameful gain from such misery.”

To the illustrious man Anselm, concerning a priest whom he had accused before him but who had not come to the appointed hearing: Hincmar reports that this priest canonically cleared himself of the charge before Anselm’s representatives, in the presence of many clergy and laymen; nevertheless, he had not sent several priests, who were witnesses of his oath, because he had not been obliged to do so. He exhorts and warns Anselm to expel from his heart all resentment toward the aforesaid priest, showing how great an evil it is to retain hatred in one’s heart. By the authority of God and His saints, he also forbids him to inflict any prejudice or plot upon that priest; if he does, Hincmar will perform his office in the matter [Col. 0243D]. He asks him also to render justice to God and to himself concerning Anselm’s men who had dared to inflict injuries upon certain priests, witnesses of the aforesaid priest; for if he does not, Hincmar will perform his office concerning them as well.

To his kinsman Count Bernard of Toulouse, concerning the possessions of the church of Rheims in Aquitaine, which Bernard requested should be granted to him in precaria: the bishop denies that he will do this, because he does not dare, on account of Saint Remigius’s testament, which had wholly forbidden it. Therefore he writes also to another Count Bernard of Rouen [read: Rodonensis], asking him to speak to this Bernard, so that he may not grant those possessions as benefices to his men, as Hincmar had heard he had done; and concerning an inquiry into those possessions, should the king order it, to be conducted through him [Col. 0244A]. Likewise, to the aforesaid Bernard of Toulouse concerning the same possessions: he adjures him by God almighty, the Lord Jesus Christ, by His Mother, and by Saint Remigius, to presume nothing in the matter, to cause no hindrance to the dependants living on them, and not to harass Count Bernard of Auvergne, to whom Hincmar had entrusted their defense. If he does so, Hincmar will separate him from the thresholds of holy Church and from the communion of the faithful, with the full body of bishops of Aquitaine and of other kingdoms. Likewise, admonishing him concerning the same matter, he urges him to gain the friendship of Saint Mary and Saint Remigius through the aforesaid possessions, showing from sacred authorities how dangerous it is unjustly to retain sacred property; and he should beware lest he deserve ecclesiastical judgment for it in this world and eternal perdition in the next. Likewise, because he was causing prejudice and no small loss to the church of Rheims, Hincmar shows that he stands condemned by the sacred canons, by the judgment of the saints, and by Hincmar and the other bishops whose ecclesiastical property he was usurping [Col. 0244B]. He reports that an embassy had been sent because of this injury and was then to be sent again with the emperor to the pope of Rome, so that, by papal authority, a synod might be assembled and strike him and the other invaders of ecclesiastical property with a sentence of condemnation. Therefore, in accordance with evangelical authority, he first admonishes him by episcopal authority (Matthew 18), and through Christ’s cross and blood forbids him to presume upon the property of the church of Rheims, or to permit anyone to presume upon it except in defense against those who invade that property [Col. 0244C].

He writes to Counts Engelramn, Goslin, and Adalelm (above, chapter 18), sending with his own letters a copy of the king’s letter, in which it was ordered that bishops and the king’s lay faithful should be summoned to prevent or resist Karlomann, the king’s son, a deacon, who had risen against his father. Asking what they should do under this royal command, he states that Karlomann was not of his province, since he had been ordained by Hildegarius, bishop of Meaux, and that under the canons he could not make any disposition concerning him. Nor did a bishop have power to summon bishops from another province; moreover, there was then no time to summon even the suffragans of his own see, since Christmas Day was at hand [Col. 0244D]. Even if the bishops should meet and interdict Karlomann from their parishes, he does not think that Karlomann would desist from what he had begun unless another power opposed him. He urges rational consideration of what should be done in this affair under the king’s command, lest a greater evil arise. He indicates how they should meet and summon others, and advises that Karlomann should not provoke God, his father, the bishops of this kingdom, and the people to anger against him, lest both he and those who followed him perish in soul and body. The bishop and these counts should send to the king, in order to make him as placable toward Karlomann as they can [Col. 0245A]; otherwise, if they think differently, they should send word to Hincmar, and so forth.

Likewise, to the same men concerning the same affair: he says that their counsel seemed good to him, because they had not stirred up the people before speaking together and considering whether they could find some good course with Karlomann, since he believes Karlomann ought to obey his and their counsel, and so forth.
