Likewise, to Karlomann, Goslin, and Conrad, concerning the king’s command that the bishop, with the other faithful men of the king, should meet to hear the royal command and to give notice to Karlomann: he states where and on what day and hour they should meet, and that Karlomann should send Goslin and Conrad to them, or, if it pleased him, should himself come to them, so that he might hear the king’s missaticum with them and there consider together how henceforth he should act for his salvation and honor [Col. 0245B].

To Count Harduin, concerning the aforementioned business of Karlomann, and how matters then stood: hostages had been exchanged; they had spoken with Karlomann and advised him to live peacefully in this kingdom and, when his father arrived, to go with them to meet him. But since Hincmar had heard that the king would arrive sooner than expected, he confesses that he does not know what Karlomann will then do. Yet he warns the count to be prepared to execute whatever commands the king may give.

Likewise, concerning certain evil men belonging to a certain Wipert, who committed robberies, arsons, murders, and other evils: he admonishes Harduin to strive with his brother Hadebald to have these evils corrected and stopped by the laws, lest they, who were the king’s envoys in this kingdom, incur the king’s displeasure because of such matters. He too would strive to do this, were he not detained by bodily illness [Col. 0245C]. Moreover, Harduin should speak with Gaulf [read: Grimulph], a faithful man of the king, who was said to receive these evildoers, and show him how much danger he incurred by receiving them, warning him henceforth to guard himself from such people. Likewise, concerning the matters in which Harduin had informed him that he had been accused before the king, and because he had not explicitly stated that accusation in his letters [read: omit *non*], Hincmar directs him to send a faithful and sensible messenger to him, through whom he may learn the truth of the matter more carefully, give him true counsel, and assist him in the matter according to his ability.

To his friend Maingand [read: Manigaud], concerning possessions of Saint Remigius in the Vosges, from which certain people were trying to take a small dwelling. The envoys of King Louis had already investigated and found that the church of Rheims held it justly, and that it was clear that, within the boundaries of the possessions which Saint Remigius had bought there, no authority had any right except the church of Rheims. He asks him, if he can quietly vindicate the property for this church, to do so; otherwise, to hold it so that it may neither be restored nor adjudged to another authority until he and Archbishop Luitbert come together and the matter is duly determined according to law through the church’s advocate [Col. 0246A], and so forth. Likewise, concerning the same matter, exhorting and asking him to apply greater care to those possessions, and so forth.

Likewise, to his friend Erluin, concerning the aforesaid possessions and the small dwelling mentioned above. Giving thanks for the assistance he was providing to the aforesaid property and dependants, he asks him to complete what he has begun well, to assist so that the monasteries of God’s servants may have peace from the aforesaid property, and to lend aid so that certain holdings unjustly taken away by that authority may be justly recovered. He sends him gifts in gold and silver and promises service worthy of him, both special and temporal. Likewise, reporting what he had heard, he asks him to suggest to King Louis that, for the redemption of his soul, he have the possessions that had been taken restored to the church of Rheims, entrust them to Erluin, and appoint Erluin as his envoy to investigate and carry out justice concerning them; he also sends Erluin gifts of silver vessels [Col. 0246B]. Likewise, he reports that he had heard a certain Lantfrid boast that he had obtained the aforesaid possessions from Emperor Charles to hold as a benefice with the consent of Lord Hincmar. He says this is wholly false, and that all the kings under heaven could not obtain from him consent that those possessions should ever be held by anyone, because of the prohibitions which Saint Remigius had laid down in his testament.

To Odalricus, the illustrious count and his friend, concerning [Col. 0246C] the case of his men whose property King Louis of the Trans-Rhine, the lord of this Odalricus, was treating badly and unjustly: he warns him to fear therein the judgment of God, the King of kings, and to take care to amend what he had done unjustly. He also says that he had heard that Lord Hincmarus had advised his own king to confiscate the estates which Louis’s faithful men possessed in his kingdom, and that for this reason he had taken those estates from these men. He says that it was unbecoming for a king to believe such things about his Catholic and faithful bishop before learning the truth concerning them, and also because he had contradicted the king’s counsellors, who had urged their lord to undertake this action. He also shows how King Karlomannus, the brother of the great Charles, had handed over the estate of Noviliacum to Saint Remigius, and how thereafter, [Col. 0246D] down to that time, the same estate had been administered; and because the matter concerned his danger both to his honor and to his soul, if he consented to defraud the property of the Church entrusted to him and concealed from his own lord, the king, the danger threatening him. He would not wish to lose his office and his soul even for the whole world, and so forth.

Likewise, giving thanks for what he had conscientiously carried out at his request on behalf of the latter’s faithful men, and because he remained in his affection, he asks him not to cease doing the same in the future.

To Bertrannus, the illustrious count of the Tardunensis district and his kinsman, concerning the oath to be rendered to the king, namely, how those who resided in his county ought to swear fidelity to the king. Likewise, concerning a vacant place without a priest, where Saint Patricia [Col. 0247A] rests, he warns him to present as soon as possible to the ecclesiastical ministers a cleric suited to the sacred ministry who could be ordained there. He should know for certain that after the ordination, which was to take place shortly, he would not leave that place without a priest, because he did not consent to leave those people either with a hireling or without their own shepherd. If he himself did not present someone who could be found worthy, he would ordain the best man he could find. Likewise, concerning Haimo, his faithful man, whom the same count had ordered to be summoned to his assembly by public ban, although he had departed for the king’s service at the king’s command.

To Boso, the illustrious count, concerning the election of the bishop of Silanectum, showing that it was not part of his ministry to designate any particular person, and so forth. Likewise, to Boso, the renowned man, giving thanks for the property of the Church of Reims situated in the province, which he was protecting as he had promised him, and warning him to prepare himself in such a way that the prayers of Hincmarus and of the Church entrusted to him might benefit him. He did not conceal what he had heard about him that was dangerous: namely, that he had given property belonging to various churches to his own men. He therefore declares that it was greatly to be feared that the prayers of God’s faithful might be obstructed on his behalf by the outcries of the saints reigning with God in heaven, and so forth.

To Coirannus [i.e., Coirandus], the count, concerning one of his men who was reported to have committed certain serious crimes; and because the bishop did not dare leave these matters unexamined, he begs him, for the sake of affection, to order the man to come to him to be examined by him, [Col. 0247C] because if he did not do so, he would be subjected to more severe pressure by him, both on account of his episcopal ministry and on account of the king’s commission.

To Isembertus, the illustrious man and his friend, begging on behalf of his nephew Hincmarus, whom he calls wretched, since he was enduring such severe things because of his offenses, and asking him to assist him in his needs.

To Rainoldus, the count, concerning the property of the Church of Reims, which he had indicated that he possessed after recovering it and wresting it from the hands of those who had seized it.

To Theudericus, the illustrious count, sending him the names of his men who were hastening to the expedition and the king’s service. Likewise, concerning gifts of silver which he was sending to the king, who was tarrying in a land laid waste by the pagans for the service of God. Likewise, concerning the concern which the same Theudericus had undertaken during the reign of the recently deceased King Louis for the king’s sons, he asks him not to take it badly if he admonishes him, out of affection, that he ought to remain vigilant with regard to those same king’s sons. He shows that it is not only a great presumption but also a great danger for one person alone to manage the general government of the kingdom without the counsel and consent of many. He also informs him about what the king had commissioned him to do, explaining how matters had once been handled between the kings Louis, Lothar, and Karlomannus, and how they ought to be handled now. He adds certain chapters which had been established and confirmed by the three kings—Louis, Charles, and Lothar—when they met together.

Likewise, concerning a certain religious bishop, he asks him to give that bishop an opportunity to speak with him, so that through his intervention he might gain access to the king’s presence, [Col. 0248A] and obtain what he reasonably requested. He also writes certain other things to Hugh, the son of King Lothar, indicating that he had had his father and grandfather, the emperor Lothar, as friends and intimates. Since he desired Hugh’s safety, he made known to him, out of affection, what he had heard about his danger: namely, that many plunderers had conspired and were conspiring with him, and that innumerable and horrible depredations were being committed with that prince as their leader and instigator, together with many other crimes, all of which would rebound upon his own head. He shows how dreadful it was to deserve everlasting punishments for such crimes, and demonstrates that these very matters had reached the synod of bishops held in Neustria (Synod in Neustria, A.D. 877).

Moreover, since he was plotting an invasion of the kingdom, and since he had been instructed by the aforesaid assembly to send to him and admonish him—just as the laws command—to recover from such great evils, separate the evildoers from himself, and restrain himself from sedition and invasion of the kingdom, he says that if Hugh did not wish to obey his admonition and the synod’s commands, he would summon a synod of the bishops both of his own diocese and of the neighboring provinces, and by the synodal judgment of the bishops would excommunicate him, his accomplices, and his supporters [ms., perpetrators]. Afterwards all those bishops would make that excommunication known to the Roman pontiff and to all bishops and princes throughout the surrounding kingdoms.

Therefore he warns him as a son to consider the great danger in which he stood, placing before him the statements of divine authorities so that he might recognize his danger. He exhorts and warns him not to believe any flatterer who urged him to undertake an invasion of the kingdom. He adds that he should consider what benefit it had brought his uncles that they had begun an invasion of the kingdom against the law of God, and that his father, for the labor by which he had labored against the will of God, had lost both his life and his kingdom. He adds what the laws prescribe concerning invaders of kingdoms.

He further says that the king had promised him, and had partly shown him, that he wished to increase his honors and hold him in honor if the fault were not his. He also warns him not to listen to the exhortations of wicked men or imitate evildoers, who flourish for a time and soon wither like hay, but to obey Holy Scripture, which says clearly: “Wait for the Lord and keep his way” [Col. 0248D] (Psalm XXXVI), and so forth. He also adds that he should send him a definite and truthful reply concerning these matters.

He sent a letter of the following kind to a certain illustrious man, Engilgarius:

> “Hincmarus, bishop, sends greetings to Engilgarius.
>
> “It has come to our attention that you made your man Rathrannus swear an unreasonable and inappropriate oath that endangered him. Although he owes you service, nevertheless both you and he are under our care and ought to be concerned for your salvation. Therefore I command you, because I am greatly astonished that you have not understood that the danger is more serious when, whether by persuasion or by fear, you lead a man into perjury—whereas if you alone committed perjury, you would incur a single perjury—indeed, commit homicide through perjury [Col. 0249A]. But when you cause another to commit perjury, you destroy both yourself and him.
>
> “Therefore we command that, if the matter is as it has reached us, you abstain from the church and altar until you come to us and either offer a fitting excuse for such carelessness or receive a fitting penance.”

To Leudowinus, his friend, he often sent letters concerning the property and dependents of the Church of Reims located in Provence. Likewise, he sent written messages to Letuardus, Hilduardus, and others living in the same district, both concerning that property and concerning the salvation of their souls.

To Achadeus, the count, concerning the robberies which he heard were being committed by his men in his county, and concerning the estate of Spantia, from which Achadeus intended to take the grain belonging to the Church of Reims. He informs him that if he carried off anything from it, he would excommunicate both him [Col. 0249B] and his men, make them alien from all Christian fellowship, and see to it through his royal commission—by which action against a count who committed injustice in his county ought to be undertaken—that the matter was enforced.

To Amalbertus, the illustrious count, concerning the injustice which he had heard that Amalbertus had committed in his court by exacting the property of a certain man slain by him from the person who, according to that man’s instruction, had distributed it as alms for him. He expresses horror that a Christian and a dying man had not feared to admit such things, and he fears the future judgment of God. He demonstrates by divine authority how grave a crime he had committed, bringing before his mind’s eye the possibility that he might be regarded as a hireling rather than a shepherd, since he saw injustice and kept silent. He also points out that he was an imperial envoy and possessed the emperor’s chapters [Col. 0249C] for the protection of newcomers and persons involved in incest.

Accordingly, both to that count and to all the exactors and judges who had sat in that judgment, he commands by the word of almighty God and by the emperor’s ban, with episcopal authority, that no one condemn, trouble, or oppose that man on this account until the bishop himself, either personally or through his envoys, had carefully investigated the case and defined it justly and reasonably according to ecclesiastical and human laws. He declares that whoever presumed to act against God’s command in this matter should first be compelled to amend it according to the legal chapters; then, according to ecclesiastical laws, he would exclude him from the communion of Christians until satisfaction had been made.

He also declares that whomever he ordered to come to his assembly so that he might carefully investigate and define this case legally and canonically, if they neglected to come, he would exclude from all fellowship with Christians until satisfaction had been made after a third admonition, unless they produced a reasonable excuse.

He adds something about the scourges which many were suffering [i.e., “which were suffering many”], and shows that he proclaimed these matters so sternly from the word of God in order that they might understand how great the offense was in this case: presuming against God’s command and against the sacred Scriptures. He warns them not to pile their own sins upon the sins of others.

To Sigebertus, concerning the presumption and prejudice which he had exercised against a certain priest on behalf of a church, he commands him to amend this personally and to beware of such frivolities and presumptions, because if he did not do so, he would take action against him by virtue of his own ministry and would notify the other bishops to do the same.

## CHAPTER XXVII. What he wrote to certain queens

Writing to Irmingard Augusta, he congratulates her after hearing of the fervor of her religion, asserting that he continually discharged duties of prayer for her. He also replies to the letter which she had sent him, indicating that certain men had told her that, by that bishop’s command, many evils were being done to the property of the monastery of Avenay (Avennacum), belonging to Bertha, daughter of the empress. He affirms that the devil, the father of lies, had spoken falsehood through their mouths. [Col. 0250B] If her men had done anything unjustly against the property of that monastery, he does not deny it; nevertheless, he indicates that she had been ignorant of it, had not consented to it, and had not wished it.

Concerning a certain estate which she had reported as unjustly taken from the aforesaid monastery, he asserts that, as far as his conscience testified to him, he had never unjustly taken an estate from anyone. Instead, he had petitioned the king concerning it and obtained permission for him to send his envoys, who, investigating most carefully with an even balance the possessions of the Church of Reims and of the monastery of Avenay, would decide the matter. For he who had abandoned his own possessions for Christ neither wished nor needed them, but he did not dare negligently abandon without reason or law the things entrusted to him.

He adds that there were many matters concerning that monastery in which he needed her help and that of her daughter. He asks her to send her vigorous and faithful envoy together with her daughter’s envoy, so that he might correct there with them whatever required correction and see what intention and purpose she herself had in such matters, lest danger, God forbid, remain as a result for them and for her. He asks that her mind always remain watchful and that she not readily believe the tongues of others, especially concerning Christ’s priests, since, if the devil could not do so in another way, he would wish to darken her intention in this matter, so as to make her err in an unwarranted opinion about priests.

Finally, concerning what she had added—that she had spoken on his behalf to the mind of the emperor Lothar—he testifies that she had acted against him in doing so, not as a great and God-devoted wife ought to act.

> “I know,” he says, [Col. 0250D] “that many contrary things have been said about me to him; but if he wishes, he can learn that they are not true. Nevertheless, I do not dare rebuke him, because he is my lord, nor do I say of his person what is written in Scripture: ‘He who willingly listens to words of falsehood will also have wicked ministers’ (Proverbs XXIX)—that is, men who willingly speak wickedly to him about the devout.
>
> “The person who told him, on my behalf, what you had instructed me to say, stated it differently from the truth and wrongly interpreted words that had been well spoken. If he had wished to learn the truth, and some envoy had come down to me from him so as to learn the truth from me—as one did come and disparage me, however unworthy a priest of Christ the Lord—I would most gladly have satisfied his mind.
>
> “As for my envoy, concerning your most gracious Ladyship’s instruction that I should send him to affirm to the emperor that I wished to undertake nothing concerning his infidelity: you know how many lies are now circulating throughout this age, how much sincerity ought to exist in a priest, and how faithfully I wish, as is right, to remain loyal to my lord. Therefore, lest evil interpreters interpret good evilly, I cannot yet do this.
>
> “Nevertheless, if my lord Lothar wishes to believe, he can truly learn that I am unfaithful not only to him but to no person in the world; and if he wishes to believe, let him believe. Otherwise, when he among the princes and I among the bishops come before the King of kings and the Bishop of bishops, then he will learn fully, without anyone’s report, what is true in this matter,” and so forth.

To Bertha, abbess of the monastery of Avenay, concerning the impediments which the brothers and servants of the monastery of Altvillar and of other estates of the Church of Reims suffered at the hands of her men after she had come into this kingdom. He therefore asks her to order that diligence and care be applied, so that this Church might not suffer such great and unprecedented prejudices from her neighborhood, from which it ought to have received comfort and joy because of her good life and sober conduct. If she did this, she would thereby make God propitious toward her and reconcile Saint Mary and Saint Remigius to her; she would also receive episcopal service from him.

But if she thought little of correcting her people, he, although unwilling, would knock at the king’s ears concerning the matter, so that, if necessary, the case might grow to such an extent that he would exercise ecclesiastical authority over her and her people according to the canonical rules.

To Irmintrud, the queen, concerning the administration of the Church of Beauvais in the election of its shepherd. He asks her to suggest to the king that no one should improperly turn his mind in any direction concerning the administration of that Church until he himself, coming into the king’s service, had informed him of what was necessary and laid its rights before him. In this way, with the Lord’s assent, he might endeavor to arrange what was pleasing to God and useful to them.

To Rotrud, consecrated to God, and to the other sisters of the monastery of the Holy Cross and Saint Radegund, concerning the election of the abbess of that monastery. The king had ordered Archbishop Frotarius, Erardus, and Angenoldus to go to the aforesaid monastery and conduct a canonical election there. If the entire congregation in agreement, or even a smaller but better portion of it, elected Rotrud, she would be appointed to the office of abbess. But if the whole congregation unanimously rejected her and elected another, the woman whom it had elected unanimously would remain in the office of abbess until the matter was reported to the king, and whichever woman had been elected there would assume the burden of the abbacy, while Odila would return to her own monastery. The leading clergy and vassals, however, were to come to the queen, under whose protection, after God and his saints, they ought to remain.

> “Therefore,” he says, “love the sisters above all else. In private conversations and in your public assembly, forgive and cast away completely from your hearts all injuries and sources of scandal which have arisen among you up to now, so that none of you may seek vengeance upon her sister, whether for a word, an action, or any slight, either from God or in this world. For, as the Lord declares, whatever you offer him without concord will not please him. Whether you pray, offer sacrifice, or afflict yourselves, nothing will be pleasing to God without this concord of charity.
>
> “For as the Apostle says: ‘Even if I hand over my body to be burned, but do not have charity, I am nothing’ (1 Corinthians XIII). And you know that the rule which you have professed (Saint Benedict, chapter 13), because of the thorns of scandal that commonly arise in a monastery, commands that the Lord’s Prayer be recited at the morning and evening offices by the superior, so that everyone may hear it, in order that, fearing the agreement expressed in the words ‘Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors,’ we may drive all resentment from our hearts.
>
> “After you have done this first, lest, God forbid, the canonical election from your monastery perish because of your discord, gather yourselves according to God’s will, the unanimity required by royal devotion, and your own salvation—present and eternal—with the concord of charity, which is the mother of all virtues; with humility, which is the guardian of those virtues; and with true obedience, which is the ladder by which one reaches heaven. Having been brought into agreement among yourselves through a salutary election, restore, bind, and preserve yourselves according to the canonical rule; for otherwise, as you yourselves know best, you cannot possibly be saved.
>
> “And just as you guard your minds from restless impulses, so guard your tongues from words that provoke anger and harm you. The Apostle testifies: ‘Let every outcry and indignation be taken away from you, together with all malice, and let no evil speech proceed from your mouth’ (Ephesians IV). Do not let any of you, like people who are first moved by grief and then made cheerful by some joy, as though victorious because they have obtained what they desire, say something improper about anyone. Otherwise you will lose before God the merit of your patience through useless words.
>
> “And if someone should try, by any provocation, to incite one of you to utter something improper about anyone, so that he might find a way to seize upon her words and condemn her reasonably, give neither the devil nor a cunning person any opportunity whatsoever for this. Rather, conduct yourselves in such a way that, inwardly and outwardly decently adorned, you may send worthy and acceptable prayers to God’s ears both for yourselves and for your lord and lady [ms., our lord and lady], and not only for your friends but also for your enemies.”

To Teutberga, abbess, concerning the organization of the monastery of Avenay, which he had once arranged with Queen Irmintrud, including the number of clerics and nuns and the property of the monastery’s estates, namely, 1,150 mansi (landholdings). He indicates that he had arranged for twenty clerics and forty nuns to be able to reside there, had provided them with sustenance, and had established the necessary supplies and services, apart from lighting and the other necessities of the monastery.

He shows [Col. 0253A] that Nivardus, archbishop of Reims, had built the monastery of Altvillar from the property of the Church of Reims, and that his brother had built the monastery of Avenay from his own property and from what other good men had given to the same place, and that he had handed it over to the Church of Reims. Documents were therefore held which clearly disclosed this. Yet through a royal grant, like the other property of this Church, it had long been held by outsiders, and so forth.

To Queen Richild, indicating that when [ms., “at one time”] the diocese of Laon was vacant of a bishop, it was especially under his own care, and that the alms of Queen Irmintrud had been wrongly treated by a certain provost of the monastery of Origny. Later, however, this Richild had been wrongly obeyed, contrary to the sacred laws, by the priest Uvinifridus, so that the regular abbess was expelled from that monastery.

He shows from sacred authority how great a danger the queen thereby faced, and that he had sent someone to her to warn her to escape this evil. She, however, had not only failed to correct it but had added a worse evil to the bad one, contrary to divine authority: namely, promoting a novice, a newcomer to religious life, to its governance because of the worldly property she had received from her.

He further explains how, when Hedenulfus had been ordained bishop of the Church of Laon, he had warned him to urge King Charles to dissolve so pernicious an action and free both himself and the queen from such great danger. But because he had not seen what he had advised brought to completion, he himself had admonished the aforesaid king about it. The king, however, so as not to distress the queen, had not corrected what he knew had been wrongly done.

He also recalls how the aforesaid king, at the request of Queen Irmintrud, had asked that, through a council of Pardulus, bishop of Laon, a privilege concerning the monastery of Origny be dictated by him, confirmed by the other bishops, and then confirmed by the king himself. This bishop, obeying the king’s command, did not compose that privilege in his own words; rather, just as Blessed Pope Gregory had dictated, at the request of a certain queen, a privilege concerning a monastery built by that queen, so he too had dictated or translated it. He repeats the curse which that same lord Gregory had hurled against the usurper of that monastery (Book II, Letter 10).

He adds that, as long as she remained in this presumption and evil deed, whenever she presumed to receive the body and blood of the Lord, she would receive judgment—that is, condemnation—for herself. He earnestly begs and warns her not to let her own judgment or anyone’s suggestion deceive her, but to think about the remedy for the king’s soul and her own redemption, and to hasten to correct what had been wrongly done.

He also explains how great an evil she had committed, as he had heard, by taking away the aforesaid privilege and royal order concerning that monastery, and he says this so that she might correct herself and not incur condemnation. Moreover, if she had received property and dependents, as he had heard, from the aforesaid female novice in exchange for entrusting her with the governance of the monastery, she had incurred the heresy of simony. Whoever favored that heresy, so long as he did so, could not stand in the body of the unity of the Catholic Church before the eyes of the Lord.

He warns her to read the chapters of Saint Benedict’s Rule (chapter 665) concerning the appointment of an abbot or abbess, and she would find how gravely she had sinned in this appointment against the Holy Spirit, through whom that Rule had been promulgated. From divine institutions he makes clear what a dangerous evil both the queen herself and that purchaser had undertaken.

He asks her to receive kindly what he writes with groaning as part of his duty, for her salvation and for the remedy of the king’s soul, and to recognize that he had taken care to write this out of great fidelity.

To Leutgard, the wife of Louis of the Trans-Rhine, concerning his envoys, whom he was sending to that same King Louis, so that through her intervention they might reach his presence, and so that through her intercession and arrangement the same king might send capable envoys to the city of Reims who could save her and the monasteries subject to her from the attack of the approaching Trans-Rhenish army.

To Irmingard, the wife of Boso, the renowned man, concerning the property of the Churches of God. He had heard that she was sufficiently instructed in the sacred writings by a certain teacher named Anastasius. Therefore he asks that the one who had given her the ability to know might also give her the will, the power, and the completion of good action. He warns her to exhort her husband to fear God and keep his commandments.

He also writes concerning ecclesiastical property which, as he had heard, Boso had taken from the churches and distributed among his own men, asking her to show him from the Holy Scriptures how grave a judgment God had pronounced on account of this, and so forth.

Likewise, to Bertha, the wife of Count Gerardus, concerning the property of the Church entrusted to him and situated in Provence, which he had entrusted to that Gerardus to protect and administer. He asks her to act energetically as an intermediary with her husband on behalf of that property.

To a certain matron, Irminsinda, concerning a certain deacon whom she had ordered to be seized and reduced to her service. He explains that the same deacon had legitimately become a free man and that, after receiving his freedom, he had lawfully ordained him as a deacon.

He shows that, if he had been her slave, had not possessed freedom, and had remained for so long after his ordination without her claiming him, he could no longer, according to the sacred laws, be reclaimed into servitude—how much less one who had been a Church tenant and belonged to no individual, had been legally made free, canonically ordained, and made the property of the Church and of his ordinator. He warns her not to presume to undertake such an action again, because if she presumed to do so, he would strive to prosecute the matter legally and canonically. He adds that he warned her in this way because he held her in dear familiarity.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. What admonitions for salvation he issued to those subject to him.

Scrib[ing] also to some of those subject to him, like a father to his sons, he diligently instructed them about many necessary matters, both spiritual and temporal.

To Richald, chorepiscopus, and Rodoald, archpresbyter, concerning the provincial synod to be held at the royal palace at Carisiacum (above, chap. 24): he ordered them to make known throughout the entire parish of Reims that those who considered themselves injured should arrange to assemble at that synod, and that they should invite certain persons with authority and admonish them to come. They were also to order Milon, together with his daughter, whom Fulcricus had abused, and all who had consented to that presbyter’s unlawful union, as well as those in whose parishes they resided, to assemble at the same synod by the word of God, by his own authority, and under the king’s ban.

To Ansold, Gerold, and Hadrich, concerning an inquiry into a certain brother of his, Ragamfred, his ministerialis, and so that, if necessary, he might be detained in free and safe custody lest he flee, and brought to him. He also commanded that same Ragamfred, by the authority of God and by his own order, to remain with them throughout the same inquiry. After Ragamfred had departed and was staying in other parishes, he sent him a letter recalling him by canonical authority, so that he should return to his metropolitan church and present himself before his humility; or, if he were concerned about his judgment, that he should hasten to attend a regular synod.

To Gislold, provost of the canons, concerning the resources entrusted to him and unlawfully usurped—he had irregularly withdrawn from him on this account—he gave a canonical admonition to return and strive to make satisfaction concerning the matters laid against him.

To Theodacrus, likewise a provost, concerning the same Gissold, for whom Queen Irmintrudis was interceding, he ordered that the portion of his service which reasonably belonged to him should be given to him; and if anything was owed to him in that bishopric, that it should be restored to him. The bishop also ordered this to be done. Since Gissold had said that he possessed a message from the queen for the canons, he commanded that, if he came to them, he should be received as the queen’s envoy with due honor.

To Gerard, dean, concerning a certain excommunicated Radulf who had come to him seeking penance. He ordered Radulf to come to Reims to receive it, together with the consecrated woman whom he had taken as his partner. He instructed this presbyter to commend them to the other presbyters, so that they might take great care of them—namely, so that if either of them were overtaken by an illness from which he or she thought there was no escape, and promised that he or she repented from the heart of the sin and would amend it before witnesses through worthy fruits of penance, while professing obedience to the bishop’s command, that person might be considered absolved.

To Sigloard, archpresbyter, and also to Ansold and certain others whom he had ordered to investigate a certain presbyter, he prescribed the following procedure for the inquiry. Since he had heard that this presbyter had been stripped contrary to the laws of some of his possessions, he was first to be restored to all his property before being compelled to answer his accusers. Otherwise the law would be violated, and the bishop himself, by taking the law away from the presbyter, would also deprive himself of it. He further ordered that, if the count himself had ordered the presbyter to be stripped of his property, the count should make amends to him by means of a pledge, with arrangements made for how this was to be done. But if the count denied having caused this to happen [i.e. had not ordered it], those who had taken the presbyter’s property from him were to make legal restitution to that presbyter; the bishop himself would determine their penance according to their acknowledgment of guilt.

If the count refused to do this, they were to report to him that he himself should bring the matter before the king. After these things had been done, they were to undertake the proceedings of this judgment in such a way as to ensure that, through ignorance, the presbyter’s accusers did not presume, at someone’s instigation, to bring forward a charge by which they themselves could be condemned—just as care had to be taken that the presbyter not be unjustly condemned.

After this they were to adjure the accusers, or their witnesses, by their baptism and by other various adjurations, not to speak falsely about the presbyter out of hatred, envy, fear of anyone, or encouragement from anyone; nor, out of favor, affection, or reward, to conceal the truth. The accusers and witnesses were also to be informed which persons the sacred canons did not permit to be admitted either for accusing a presbyter or for testifying against him, and how both accusers and witnesses ought to be examined.

Everything that the accusers or witnesses testified concerning each individual charge was to be written down and read aloud before everyone, so that it could be established that those things had indeed been said. All who were present at this placitum, both presbyters and laymen, were likewise to be recorded, insofar as necessity appeared to require.

The accusers were to promise under oath that they would give their presence, and the witnesses that they would give their oath, at the next placitum, which the canons granted the presbyter for the opportunity to defend or answer himself. That placitum was to be announced to the presbyter thirty days in advance, so that he might come prepared either to clear himself canonically or to submit himself. If he did not do so, he was to know that he would receive a canonical sentence.

They were also to issue a ban, by the authority of God and the sacred canons and under the prohibition of the king and the bishop, so that no one should lay any ambush for the presbyter or inflict any violence upon him; nor upon his accusers or witnesses, until this case had received a legal determination. He also prescribed what should be done regarding those men who, on the previous occasion when the presbyter had been accused, had sworn and had their oath approved by judgment, but had then declared that they had committed perjury.

Regarding the land belonging to the Church over which the count and the presbyter were disputing, he also prescribed what should be done, and ordered the presbyter to obey the count’s commands; or, if he did not wish to do so, to come for that reason to a placitum before the king and his faithful men, both bishops and laymen. If the presbyter refused to obey those whom the others obeyed, he was to be canonically summoned before the provincial synod.

Likewise, concerning the same inquiry, he expressed anger at Sigloard and Ansold because they had carried it out negligently, and so forth.

Likewise, concerning a certain presbyter who, after his ordination, had carelessly forgotten what he had once learned about his ministry, he had ordered that he be kept confined under guard for some time, so that at least by this means some bitterness might touch his mind and cleanse him from sin, and so forth.

Likewise, concerning the three-day fast which the king had arranged with his bishops and other faithful men for the peace of the holy Church of God, he instructed how it was to be observed.

Likewise, concerning a certain presbyter of the monastery of Avennacum who was accused in connection with the treasure of that church, lost long ago.

Likewise, to Si[g]loard and Rodold, concerning a certain presbyter whom he had agreed, at Sigloard’s persuasion, to permit to declare himself disqualified from governing the parish entrusted to him by a written statement of his profession and to request that another be ordained in his place. But the presbyter had concealed from him the collusion that had been arranged—namely, that his protégé should be ordained in his place without the consent of his superior—and he had deceitfully arranged to recover the gift [xenium] that had been given. He had done this so as to install that same protégé contrary to the bishop’s prohibition, and so forth concerning what was subsequently to be done about it.

Likewise, to Sigloard, concerning the presbyter of the church of Saint Julian who had stolen the lamp of Saint Remigius. He severely rebuked Sigloard because, having discovered that this had happened, he had kept silent about it, although the bishop, with the Lord as witness, had entrusted his own authority to Sigloard. He ought to have confined that presbyter in the strictest custody, not released him through sureties. Since he had not done this previously, he was now to do so. The prison was also to be securely restored by the vicedominus, and guards were to be assigned if necessary.

Likewise, to Rodold, rebuking him because he had incautiously released what the bishop had canonically bound, and had permitted other presbyters to celebrate Mass in a certain chapel subject to the basilica of the church’s court; he prescribed what was to be done about it.

To a certain monk named Anselm [i.e. Anselin], he ordered that he record everything which, as it appeared, had been done or granted in the monastery of Altvillar before the bishop’s ordination, and everything afterward; also the number of brothers and servants serving them, and whether anything from those resources had been distributed during his own time, for what purposes, or through which persons. Everything was to be recorded so truthfully that the royal envoys could find nothing false there. He gave a similar order to Ratramn, provost of the monastery of Orbais.

Likewise, to Ratramn, concerning a certain benefice [praestaria] held by Amalraus the canon, whose service the same provost had ordered to be seized after Amalraus’s death. For this reason he excommunicated him, placing both him and his accomplices in this act on bread and water until the things they had unjustly taken were restored.

To a certain priest or dean named Altharius [ms., Alchanus], concerning a presbyter from the church of Vindonissa whom Leutard, the senior of that village, had expelled from that church, stripping him of his legal standing and all authority there, and had entrusted the same church to another presbyter from a different bishopric. He excommunicated the intruding presbyter, forbidding him to presume to celebrate Mass anywhere in the entire parish of Reims or to receive ecclesiastical communion, except perhaps the viaticum on account of serious illness—and even then, if he recovered, he was immediately to depart from that parish.

He ordered the parishioners of the aforesaid church, by the authority of God, not to hear the Mass of any presbyter in that church except that of the presbyter who had been unjustly expelled, until his case had been determined; unless, perhaps, that presbyter were unable to celebrate Mass for them because of illness, and so forth.

To the monk and presbyter Altmann, whom he had sent far away for the sake of obedience, concerning what he had found in certain letters delivered to him by a man of Archbishop Harduic: namely, that Altmann was suspected of aspiring to benefices and secular affairs, which were not fitting for his profession and salvation. He therefore ordered him to return as quickly as possible to his monastery, where he should devote himself to reading and prayer while lamenting the sins of his youth, and so forth.

To a certain priest named Lantard, who had left the parish of Reims because of the case of Bishop Ebo, he sent a request that, if he possessed—as he had heard—any written accounts concerning the life and deeds of blessed Remigius beyond those that had long been read in the church of Reims, he should either bring them to him as soon as possible or send them under seal. He offered afterward to be ready and prepared to assist him in whatever he might need.

If Lantard wished to return to his own place, he promised to receive him willingly and kindly and, as soon as he came, to grant him a canonical prebend and his former rank among the brothers; he would also provide him with support, according to what was convenient for himself and suitable for Lantard, so that Lantard might be pleased to remain with him. He explained the reason for Lantard’s apprehension—namely, why he had removed from their orders those ordained by Ebo after Ebo’s deposition, and how he had afterward moderated his judgment.

To Rodoard, provost, and the other canonical brothers of the church of Reims, concerning the reception of Odalhard and Waltarius, nephews of Isaac, bishop of Langres, who had irregularly departed from that community. He prescribed how they were to be received and how they were to be treated and maintained. He had also sent them letters of admonition concerning their return.

He likewise wrote to the canons and monks concerning the reception of Adalgaud [ms., Addagaud], the deacon, explaining that he had received into the embrace of his affection and fatherhood the man who had acknowledged that, through his own negligence, he had offended the bishop’s mind. He ordered that Adalgaud be received kindly and familiarly as a brother and son, and that the benefits of kindness be bestowed upon him. King Louis had also sent the bishop a letter of intercession on Adalgaud’s behalf.

To Rotfrid, provost, concerning the correction [i.e. reprimand] of the monk Odelcalc, whom he had heard to be disobedient, harsh in character, and stubbornly attached to his own will. He supplied examples from sacred authority for them to read to him, so that he might correct himself.

For Gontramn and Odelhard, archpresbyters, he composed an admonitory instruction suited to their ministry in thirteen chapters.

To Gontramn [i.e. Guntramn], provost, concerning the servants of the monastery entrusted to him, who complained that their small plots of land and the stipends owed to them were being taken away by him: he ordered that this be corrected according to what was just.

To the monk Gottschalk, who had fallen into heresy concerning certain statements of authors which he did not properly understand or explain, especially those of Prosper. He expounded their meaning chiefly through the statements of blessed Augustine and proposed other suitable witnesses, the teachers of the apostolic faith. He admonished Gottschalk to follow their teaching in all things and demonstrated by clear testimonies that God foreknows both good and evil, but foreknows evil alone, whereas he both foreknows and predestines good.

Thus foreknowledge can exist without predestination; predestination, however, cannot exist without foreknowledge. God foreknew and predestined the good for the kingdom, but merely foreknew the wicked and did not predestine them, nor did he compel them by his foreknowledge to perish. Gottschalk obstinately refused to subscribe to this definition.

The same lord Hincmar also wrote to the monks of the monastery of Altvillar concerning that same Gottschalk, instructing them that, if he came to acknowledge himself before his soul departed from his body, they should show him both spiritual and bodily humanity. He demonstrated from the words of orthodox authorities the authority of the Church regarding excommunicated persons of this sort.

To his faithful men Amalgis and Ragbert, concerning the property of his Church situated in Aquitaine, about which he had sent letters to Regimundus, asking that he provide his envoys with assistance in vindicating that property. He ordered these men to receive the same property in its entirety and to keep it under their care.

To his faithful man Peter, concerning the property situated in the province, he sent certain brothers to him, who, with his counsel, were to discuss his loyalty and the welfare of the property and arrange the property itself, its revenues, and its resources. Since he had heard that certain things had been done there without Peter’s counsel, as though by Peter’s authority, he excused himself by saying that he had neither ordered nor wished this. In separate chapters he instructed Peter how they wished the property to be administered and which persons, from which estates, were to come to him from those possessions.

To Evrard, son or son-in-law of his sister Hildegund, he explained in writing how he ought to conduct himself toward King Louis across the Rhine, lest Louis take away the allod which Evrard possessed in Alemannia because Evrard had abandoned Louis’s lordship. On this matter he also wrote to his aforesaid sister, asking her prudently to organize and arrange her lord’s affairs.

He also sometimes wrote to certain persons of the lower orders, namely the administrators of estates, concerning the property of their offices, prudently and reasonably setting out how they should manage the resources entrusted to them.

In general, he instructed all those entrusted to him, both by word and by letter, how they should live justly, piously, and chastely, and how reverently and devoutly they should observe the appointed fasts. Concerning those who had died, both bishops and any other persons, he taught them how to beseech the Lord’s mercy. He also instructed them to ask the Lord, through fasts and prayers, that persons pleasing to God might be chosen as bishops for vacant sees.

At various synods he also issued several very useful chapters and entrusted them to his people for observance. To various churches of his diocese, especially when it happened that they were deprived of their pastors, he sent letters of consolation, instructing them first to seek such consolation from God. He also taught them to seek from earthly rulers that a free election be granted to them, and he diligently worked to secure this both in person and through his letters and envoys.

Once it had been obtained, he took care to teach them how to exercise it and how to guard themselves, in carrying it out, from every deceit of perversity, giving them a prescribed form for the election. He directed his attention to no particular person, but considered whom all might choose unanimously, or whom the greater number and the better people might choose advantageously.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Concerning the book he published on how images of the Lord and of the saints are to be venerated, and so forth

At the request of his fellow bishops and brothers, he also wrote a book explaining how images of our Savior and of his saints are to be venerated, together with a certain epilogue arranged in verse.

He also answered the questions of a certain person: why baptized apostates, who had been marked by the laying on of a bishop’s hand, receive the laying on of hands outside the order of the diaconate or priesthood in order to perform penance.

He also wrote to a certain archbishop, treating of the principal sacraments of human salvation.

Likewise, to a certain bishop, answering his questions concerning the ordinations of bishops and translations from one city to another; and concerning Actard, bishop of Nantes, who, after being expelled by a certain Breton leader, had stayed for some time in the vacant church of Thérouanne and, at the request of the clergy and people of the province of Tours, with the bishops assembled, had been incardinated in that metropolitan church.

Likewise, to a certain brother, concerning a man who had had intercourse with a certain woman and afterward married her sister.

He also wrote an apology for himself (above, chap. 21), for all who wished to read it, against those who had slandered him before Pope John, who held a synod at Troyes [i.e. at Troyes]. The same bishop received him kindly, and at that time he answered them at the synod as circumstances required. Later he did not neglect to excuse himself in writing, asserting that he reverently received and upheld the decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs, although his enemies accused him of refusing to accept them as authoritative.

Likewise, he wrote concerning the Council of Nicaea and the deposition and restoration of Hincmar, bishop of Laon.

He also addressed the accusation that he had said that the Roman pope was not of greater dignity than he himself. He wrote as well concerning Carloman and the other insults brought against him through slander, from which the truth rendered him excusable.

He wrote many further works, which we do not think it necessary to enumerate here.

## CHAPTER XXX. Concerning the transfer of the body of Saint Remigius from his monastery and the death of Bishop Hincmar

[Col. 0260D]

At last, as crimes multiplied, against which he had always stood like an impenetrable wall, the people of the Northmen spread throughout the entire kingdom of the Franks (AIMONIUS, book V, chap. 41). Since this city was then inhabited without walls, he took what he held most dear among its treasures—namely, the body of blessed Remigius—sought the wooded regions beyond the river Marne, and kept that sacred body for some time at the estate of Épernay.

While he was staying there, he finally ended his earthly life at the same estate. His body was brought back to the monastery of Saint Remigius and, behind the tomb of that saint, was buried in the grave which he himself had prepared for himself. His epitaph, dictated by him, is preserved as follows:

> In name, not merit, Hincmar the bishop, from the tomb,
>
> I ask you, reader, to remember me by this inscription.
>
> Dionysius once gave me as shepherd
>
> To the peoples of Reims, as they requested.
>
> I ruled, according to my ability, the government
>
> Of the humble great people of Reims; now here I am devoured by worms.
>
> Therefore ask now for rest for my soul,
>
> And, when it has taken up the flesh again, ask these full joys for me as well.
>
> O Christ, mercifully have pity on your faithful servant;
>
> Holy Mary, be gracious to your worshiper.
>
> May devotion to sweet Remigius benefit him,
>
> By which he loved you with heart, mouth, and hand.
>
> Therefore here he humbly requested that his limbs be placed,
>
> Since this pleased him well; finally, thus he died.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 882; in the thirty-second year of his episcopate, in the seventh month and on the fourth day.

# BOOK FOUR

## CHAPTER ONE. Concerning the episcopate of Fulco and the writings he sent to certain Roman pontiffs

[Col. 0261B]

After the man of God had been gathered to his fathers, Fulco, a very noble man accustomed to courtly offices, succeeded him in the bishopric of Reims. Entrusting the tenor of his faith to Pope Marinus, he received the pallium from him, according to the custom of his predecessors.

He also sent him letters requesting that the privilege owed to the church of Reims be granted, and commending King Carloman. In them he indicated that the same pope had known him previously, in the time of Pope John, when Fulco had been at Rome with Emperor Charles.

Likewise, he wrote concerning a certain monastery which his brother, named Rampo, had commissioned to be built by him in his will from property belonging to his own estate. Later a certain Erminfrid had seized these possessions and had taken Rampo’s widowed wife as his own.

For this reason the same pope (John VIII) sent letters to Evrard, archbishop of Sens, in whose parish the monastery had been built. He also wrote to John, archbishop of Rouen, in whose diocese the same Erminfrid lived, ordering him to admonish Erminfrid to cease this seizure of sacred property; if he refused, he was to undergo canonical punishment.

He also sought to visit Pope Hadrian (Hadrian III, in the year 884), the successor of Marinus, by letter at the beginning of his pontificate, rejoicing in his honor and indicating that he wished to travel to Rome if, with God granting peace, he were able to do so.

He asked him to have copies of the privileges granted to the see of Reims by the Roman pontiffs Leo (Leo IV), Benedict (Benedict III), and Nicholas (Nicholas I) read before him and preserved, confirmed, and enlarged by him.

Concerning the aforesaid monastery, whose property the aforementioned Erminfrid had seized, he also requested that the pope send his authoritative order to the previously mentioned archbishops, Evrard and John, prescribing what should be done against Erminfrid, and so forth.

Likewise, he wrote to commend the aforementioned King Carloman and to defend Frothar, archbishop of Bourges, who was said to have been accused before the same pope by a monk of his diocese. The accusation was that, after his city had been overthrown by the pagans, Frothar had rashly invaded the see of another.

Fulco showed that Frothar had been sought out and elected by the bishops of his diocese and by the entire clergy and people of that city, and that Pope Marinus, the predecessor of the pope addressed, had graciously consented to this at their request. He had moreover bestowed the pallium on him and confirmed his promotion to the church of Bourges in writing, and so forth.

He also sent letters to Stephen (Stephen VI), the successor of Hadrian, taking care to give thanks because Stephen had deigned to visit him and his church through letters of his apostolate and to console him amid the world’s many pressures, and because he had wished to honor him by calling him brother and friend. Fulco stated that he himself did not wish to seek this title, but rather to remain a servant and subject.

He indicated that he would have hastened to see the pope himself if he had not been surrounded by a pagan siege: the pagans were only ten miles from his city, and they were then besieging the city of Paris. This invasion had afflicted the kingdom for eight years already, so that no one seemed to have free access far beyond the fortified places.

Finally, he added that he had heard of plots being devised against the pope by certain wicked men, and that he had taken this very badly. He wished to offer assistance if permitted, but the one thing he could do was persist in prayers for him.

He also mentioned his kinsman Wido [Note: Wido, formerly duke of Spoleto, became emperor in the year 892], whom the same pope had adopted as a son. He said that both he himself and his other relatives, to whom he had reported this, would show the pope the reverence owed to him.

He also referred to what the pope had written to him, saying that he was ready to confirm whatever necessities for the Church of God might be indicated; that in every way he had fulfilled the pope’s request, being bound to his fidelity; and that, together with his fellow bishops and suffragans, he would persevere in the proper veneration of the holy Roman See. If anything contrary to sound faith should arise against it, he declared himself ready, with God’s help, to refute it in every way.

He further asked the pope to know that the see of Reims had always been honored by his predecessors above all the Gallican churches, since blessed Peter, the first of the apostles, had first sent Saint Sixtus as bishop to this city and had granted him primacy over the whole Gallican region. Pope Hormisdas, too, had entrusted Saint Remigius with his own authority in the regions of Gaul.

He recalled this so that the see of Reims might not be permitted to be dishonored in his days. He also appended a discussion of the privileges granted to him in everything he had requested from the predecessors of this pope, Marinus and Hadrian.

Likewise, he wrote concerning the possessions of Rampo already mentioned and their usurper, whom the aforementioned pontiffs had ordered the archbishops of Sens and Rouen to excommunicate. Since those archbishops had delayed imposing the excommunication, the same usurper still possessed what he had seized.

He therefore requested that the pope himself pronounce an apostolic sentence and order the aforesaid archbishops not to delay any longer in excommunicating him.

He also asked the pope to make representations to Emperor Charles (surnamed the Fat) concerning certain possessions of the church of Reims which certain invaders had taken away. The emperor had already restored a large part of them; Fulco asked that, through the pope’s intercession, he complete the good work he had begun. He also asked the pope to thank the emperor for what he had done, and so forth.

In reply, the pope declared that he had been greatly pleased to learn that Fulco was eager to honor the apostolic see. He urged him to burn ever more ardently with this devotion.

He also said that he had received the memory of Duke Wido with the greatest gratitude, confessing that he held Wido in the place of an only son.

Concerning the Northmen’s invasion, which our kingdom was suffering, he said that he grieved as over a personal affliction. He promised to pray to God, through the intercession of the princes of the apostles, for the defense of this people, and that this bishop might be brought safely to the threshold of the apostles, so that he might embrace him in his bodily arms and confer with him concerning the privileges about which Fulco had written.

He also said that he had sent letters to the archbishops for whom Fulco had asked, as well as a supplicatory letter to the emperor concerning the rights of the church of Reims, thanking him for the kindness he had shown [Note: These letters of Stephen are not extant].

The same bishop afterward sent another letter to the same pope, saying that he rejoiced in the pope’s prosperity amid the many tribulations and hardships inflicted upon them by the pagans. He also took care to commend the favor of the aforementioned Wido.

He renewed his complaint concerning the woman previously named and concerning Erminfrid, who, after being admonished by the aforesaid archbishops, had proved disobedient. He requested that the archbishops again be admonished by papal authority to rebuke Erminfrid more severely and, if he did not restore what he had seized, to strike him with ecclesiastical judgment.

He further asked that the pope write back to him whether it was lawful for the ordination of bishops to take place on any feast of the saints, rather than only on Sunday, and so forth.

In reply, the same pope gave thanks for Fulco’s love and concern for the apostolic see. He expressed compassion for Fulco’s affliction and promised to pour out prayers to the Lord for his relief, strengthening him and urging him to trust in the Lord’s consolation.

He also wrote to the same bishop concerning a certain Dominicus who had been oppressed or expelled by his own sons and relatives, urging Fulco to investigate the matter carefully and to become his helper in it.

Likewise, concerning the reception of certain Englishmen.

Likewise, to him and to Aurelian of Lyon, Adelgar, Geilo [i.e. Gerlo], Emmenno, and the others residing throughout Gaul, concerning the complaint of the church of Bourges against the usurper of Forthar, bishop of Bordeaux, who had also held the see of Poitiers for some time. Forthar had afterward been granted the see of Bourges for a time by Pope John because of the barbarian invasion, under the condition that, once that necessity had been removed, what necessity had required would also be removed.

For this reason Pope Stephen ordered the aforesaid archbishops to compel Forthar to return to his own see. If he disdained to obey the apostolic admonitions, they were to know that he had been bound by the judgment of the Holy Spirit with the chains of perpetual anathema.

Likewise, concerning Theutbold, bishop of Langres, the pope stated that a complaint from the church of Langres had reached him: after Bishop Isaac’s death, without consulting the clergy and people, Aurelian of Lyon had ordained a certain monk, Egilo, who had recently come from the secular world, as bishop and had imposed him upon them by force, although they did not wish it.

When Egilo died by divine calling, the clergy and people, so that they might not fall into the same situation again, unanimously chose Theutbold, a deacon of that church, and requested that the pope consecrate him as their bishop.

But the pope, wishing to preserve inviolate the privilege of each church, delayed doing this. He sent Theutbold to the aforesaid Aurelian, writing to him that, if the votes of the clergy and people agreed unanimously upon him and the sacred canons did not oppose it, Aurelian should not delay laying hands upon him.

If canonical reason prohibited this, Aurelian was to write the same back to him. In the meantime, however, he was on no account to presume to ordain another there without consulting the pope. At the same time he sent with him Olrannus, bishop of Senigallia, as an executor.

Aurelian deceived Olrannus by sending him ahead to the city of Langres, promising that he himself would follow immediately. Olrannus waited there for a long time, but Aurelian neither arrived nor took care to make known or report to the pope the reason for his delay [for *providerit*, “he had provided”].

Therefore the clergy and people, with a decree confirmed by the signatures of all, sent the aforesaid elected man to Rome again, earnestly requesting that he be consecrated for them.

But even then the pope did not agree to do this, wishing the privilege granted to the church of Lyon to remain unaltered. Accordingly, he wrote once more to the aforementioned Aurelian and ordered him, since the clergy and people unanimously desired the aforesaid deacon, either to consecrate him or to hasten to write back what he judged objectionable in him.

Aurelian, however, adding the obstinacy of a second disobedience to his first, not only scorned to consecrate the man presented to him or to write back what he judged objectionable in him, but also, contrary to the prohibitions and statutes of the sacred canons, presumed to force upon them an outsider, unknown to that church, ordained in some obscure corner.

But they preferred to undertake the labor rather than submit to an unknown man, and they returned to their own people, imploring that the ecclesiastical laws not be allowed to be violated.

> “But we,” he said, “who have undertaken the care of all the churches in blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, knowing that a man is not to be counted among the bishops who has been chosen neither by the clergy nor sought by the people, have been moved by the lamentable prayers of those people and have consecrated the often-mentioned venerable deacon Theutbold as bishop of the church of Langres, a fitting sentence having been imposed upon the transgressors, although they had also been hindered by other transgressions.
>
> “Therefore we enjoin upon your holiness that, when you have received these apostolic letters of ours, you should put aside all delay, go to the church of Langres, and restore to office that same Theutbold, solemnly consecrated by us as bishop. You are also to make known to all archbishops and bishops that, in punishment for such great contumacy, you have undertaken a special care for that church, for the alleviation of the suffering caused by so great a labor and for the relief of the oppression inflicted upon it.
>
> “Whatever that venerable bishop Theutbold reports to you on our behalf, believe it, and do not hesitate in any way to put it into effect, since we trust that your reverence remains devoted toward us.”

In reply to this, the same bishop Fulco gives thanks for the consolation afforded by his letter, declaring that he had been—and was—prepared to fulfill whatever had been enjoined upon him by the authority of that pope’s eminence [Col. 0265B]. He had indeed wished to carry out without delay the aforesaid command concerning Bishop Theuthbold, but, on the advice of his own king Odo, had meanwhile postponed it, while that king sent his envoys to the same pope and learned his command with complete certainty.

Regarding the matters pursued in the pope’s letter—namely, that he wished to preserve the institutions and privileges of all the churches inviolate, though in a confused order—Fulco reports that all the bishops were greatly pleased, in whose presence he had caused these things to be read. He asks the pope’s authority and requests that he send him a written reply stating whether his suffragan fellow bishops who belong to his diocese may, without his license, agreement [Col. 0265C] [ms. c., “restraint”], or permission, undertake the ordination of a king or of any other person, or presume to do anything else without consulting their metropolitan or contrary to the prohibitions of their primate.

Finally, that pope granted the privilege requested from the Roman See and sent it in writing to the bishop concerning the ecclesiastical properties bestowed, or to be bestowed, upon this Church of Reims, so that no one might presume to invade or retain them, and so that after his death no one might in any way dare unlawfully to seize this bishopric or its possessions. He forbade these things under threat of the censure of the Apostolic See.

He also writes to him concerning the dispute that had arisen between Herimannus, archbishop of Cologne, and Adelgarius, bishop of Hamburg and Bremen [j, “Bremen”]. Because of this dispute [Col. 0265D] Herimannus had sent his complaint to the same pope and had afterward gone to him in person, protesting that Herimannus was violating the privileges of his church. The pope had therefore summoned both of them to appear before him. But when Adelgarius came and Herimannus failed to appear, the pope postponed bringing so great a lawsuit to an end, lest he seem to judge anything hastily and thereby give rise to a renewed dispute in future times.

Accordingly, he instructs this bishop of ours, acting in the pope’s own place, to convene a synod at the city of Wangion, together with the neighboring suffragan and border bishops. He had ordered Herimannus of the Agrippine colony, Son deroldus of Mainz with his suffragans, [Col. 0266A] and also Adelgarius to attend, so that careful examination might declare what was owed to each party.

He also admonishes the fraternity of Lord Fulco not to delay, if it could in any way be done, presenting his own special presence to him with them; for he had arranged that these matters, and other ecclesiastical affairs that were imminent, should be discussed with Fulco and settled by his counsel. He would therefore rejoice greatly at Fulco’s arrival, wishing to have his presence for deliberating about ecclesiastical affairs. Otherwise, he advises him to send, together with them, a man of the episcopal order who was vigorous and could report truthfully how the matter actually stood.

If they lacked the ability to come, they were to send envoys with him who, serving as their representatives [Col. 0266B], would possess the freedom to debate and deliberate, so that once a final judgment had been received, it would no longer be necessary at any future time to reopen the question.

Concerning these matters Lord Fulco also sent letters to Formosus, the successor of this Stephen, informing him how these things had been enjoined upon him by the aforesaid Pope Stephen and asking him to send written authority of his own for carrying them out. In a subsequent letter he says that he is exceedingly surprised that, if his letter had reached Formosus’s presence, he had not deserved to receive a reply from that pope.

Meanwhile he gives thanks that Formosus had deigned to remember him and, through Abbess Bertha, to send him words of holy consolation [Col. 0266C], saying that he wished to see Fulco and converse with him in mutual speech. Fulco confesses that this had brought him immense joy, so that he desired even more strongly to see Formosus’s presence. He adds that Formosus should write back to him indicating the time and place at which he should come, and that he would diligently obey his commands.

Moreover, he asks that Formosus order a privilege for the Church of Reims to be issued under his authority, just as his predecessors are known to have done, and that he protect with perpetual firmness, against all adversaries, the properties acquired for this church through Fulco’s humility.

He also records how Margrave Evrard obtained from the Roman See the venerable body of Saint Calixtus, pope and martyr, and established in his own estate a monastery in his honor [Note: [Col. 0265] Cisonium monastery in Belgium, between Tournai and the islands]. After Evrard’s death, that estate passed by hereditary right to his son, the abbot Rodulf. Rodulf retained these properties, together with the remains of the aforesaid martyr, throughout his life without any opposition; and, as he was about to depart from this world, he assigned the same properties, together with the monastery and the sacred body, to the Reims church of Holy Mary, Mother of God, and appointed that church heir to all his possessions.

At that time a certain Hucboldus, the husband of Rodulf’s sister, claimed the gift made by that abbot and attempted to take it away from the right of the church of the Mother of God. Fulco therefore asks Formosus to instruct him by his sacred letters concerning what should be done in such matters, to strengthen the transfer of these properties with eternal stability, and to strike those who opposed it with the fitting punishment of excommunication [Col. 0267A].

Finally, he says that he had been stirred to anxiety and sobbing because he had heard from certain people that the holy Roman Church was being disturbed. He declares himself ready to fight in every way with all his strength for its honor and to obey that pope, as his lord and teacher, in everything.

He also adds a report concerning certain bishops of Gaul who were improperly seeking the pallium from the Roman See while scorning their metropolitans in this matter. He asserts that, unless this affair were guarded by prudent care, it would produce no small confusion in the Church and would cause great harm to charity. He therefore says that he prays, both for himself and for the whole Church, that the pope not consent to the unreasonable petition of anyone without general agreement and letters, lest ecclesiastical dignity begin to lose its honor if an improper request, rashly pursued, were imprudently granted [Col. 0267B].

## CHAPTER II. What Pope Formosus wrote to Fulco, and to King Charles and Odo

In reply, the same Pope Formosus warns Fulco that he ought to sympathize with the Roman Church and come to the aid of its impending ruin, nor deny it his presence. He adds that heresies and schisms were springing up everywhere and that there was no one who came forward to resist them.

He says that for a long time pernicious heresies had been troubling the East and that the Church of Constantinople was being disturbed by harmful schisms. At the same time, envoys from the African region were pressing for answers concerning the schism that had arisen some time earlier among the bishops of those provinces [Col. 0267C]. Legations from various regions were likewise persisting, seeking different answers.

For this reason he had determined to begin a general synod (the Roman council of 893) on the Kalends of March, in the eleventh indiction. He expressly urges Fulco to hasten to it without any delay, so that by speaking together they might discuss these matters more fully and respond more abundantly to each question.

He says that he greatly grieves over the storms of the Nortmannic people, by which Fulco had declared himself disturbed, and implores that the right hand of the Most High restrain them through the intercession of the chief apostles. The letters which Fulco had indicated he first sent to the pope through certain persons had not reached him at all.

He had also previously sent another letter to this bishop of ours concerning the celebration of the same synod, which he asserts he had decided to begin in the middle of May, in the tenth indiction [Col. 0267D]. In that letter he admits that Italy had then suffered terrible wars once and twice and had almost been destroyed. He says that he mourns the insane heresy of the eastern regions, which contained blasphemy against Christ Jesus [j, “conjecturing blasphemy against Christ Jesus”].

He further sends him the requested privilege concerning certain prebends, recalling that blessed Remigius had been constituted apostle to the Frankish people by the authority of the Roman See, with the grace of God. He also confirms that the village of Berna, which had long before been unjustly taken away, had been restored to the Church of Reims.

He likewise confirms by apostolic authority the restoration of Duodeciacum [Col. 0268A], as well as the properties which the same Lord Fulco had obtained by precarious tenure—namely Rodemiam and Margolium, Lastemnam and Guigleium, Virtus, the abbey called Campellis, Atteias, Maniacum, and other properties that had formerly been taken away and had then been returned to the Church of Reims—so that no one might presume to remove or invade them, or any other possessions of that church.

Moreover, by the authority of blessed Peter he decrees that no king, no bishop, and no Christian whatsoever, when the bishop of Reims dies, may appropriate that bishopric or the properties of its church for his own advantage or hold them under his own dominion, except the bishop of that city [Col. 0268B]. Nor may anyone compel that metropolitan church to remain without a suitable pastor beyond the period established by canon law and without the ecclesiastical regulations being observed; nor may anyone appoint a bishop there except as the sacred canons command.

He also promulgates and decrees that the properties of the villages of this church and their resources, which the same venerable Bishop Fulco had assigned to the uses of ecclesiastical furnishings and lamps, or to the stipends of canons, monks, nuns, matricularii, guests, and the poor, should remain perpetually undisturbed. He strengthens this authority of his decree by binding violators under the penalty of anathema.

He also reports that Emperor Wido had been crowned in that same year, in the tenth indiction.
