At the request of Lord Fulco he sent him another privilege concerning the monastery of Avennac and concerning the monastery which Abbot Rodulf, by hereditary right of his own property, had built in honor of Saint Calixtus, martyr and pope, and had granted to this Church of Reims. He confirms and establishes by apostolic power both these monasteries and all the possessions granted to the Church of Reims by royal generosity or by the munificence of other Christians, as well as those which the same bishop had acquired or would thereafter acquire [Col. 0268C].

Here too he states that Lantbertus [Emperor Lambert], son of Wido, had been made the new emperor in the second year of his father’s reign.

Likewise, concerning the bishops of the province of Reims, he writes to Fulco that he had heard that some of them were disregarding the hearing of their own archbishop. He instructs him to summon his fellow bishops and to announce that he should convene whatever other bishops he deemed appropriate, so that together they might investigate this great neglect by synodal action and, strengthened by canonical and apostolic authority, decree whatever was necessary [Col. 0268D]. He adds that no one who wished to remain a participant in the pope’s apostolic communion should withdraw from so God-worthy a work.

He also writes concerning the advancement to the rule of the kingdom of Charles, whom Lord Fulco had raised to the royal dignity while still a boy, and concerning the crimes of King Odo and how he should be corrected. On these matters the same archbishop had sent his letters to the pope, seeking counsel and help.

For this reason the same pope sent his letters to King Odo [Col. 0269A], instructing him to withdraw from unlawful actions and not to trouble King Charles or anything belonging to him. He was to grant a suspension of the war until the same Bishop Fulco might endeavor to visit the Apostolic See.

## CHAPTER III. What he sent in writing to certain bishops of France

He also writes to the archbishops and other bishops of Gaul, warning them to meet and admonish King Odo, so that unlawful acts would not be committed and the property of others would not be usurped, but the war would be brought to an end and every hostile disturbance quieted. Alternatively, they were to proclaim a truce until Fulco, as stated, went to Rome. Meanwhile they themselves were to strive to postpone everything and restore peace and the harmony of unanimity [Col. 0269B].

He also sends an appropriate admonition to King Charles, congratulating him on his eminence and devotion, which the king had indicated that he held toward the Apostolic See. He briefly and clearly demonstrates how Charles ought to act in the kingdom. He sends him blessed bread as a pledge, which he had requested, and warns him concerning the journey of the aforesaid bishop to the Apostolic See.

Writing also to Lord Fulco, he states that he had sent the foregoing letters to the persons mentioned above at Fulco’s suggestion, concerning peace or the postponement of the war between Odo and Charles. He also writes to him about ending the dispute that he had heard had arisen because of the killing of Maniguldus by Albericus [Col. 0269C].

He further asks Fulco to promote to the episcopate, wherever an opportunity arose, a certain Grimlaicus, a priest dear to him.

The same Bishop Fulco is also found to have sent several letters to the aforesaid pope beyond those already mentioned: concerning his own summons, by which the pope called him to the Apostolic See; concerning the dispute between Kings Odo and Charles; and concerning the oppression suffered by the Church of Reims. He asked that the pope, by writing to the kings, command peace.

He also asked that the pope command Arnulfus of the region beyond the Rhine by apostolic authority not to trouble Charles’s kingdom, but rather to assist him, as befitted a kinsman aiding a kinsman. He was to order Odo not to presume to invade or plunder that kingdom; and, if he dared to do so, to fear the judgment of the Apostolic See [Col. 0269D].

He adds that after the pope’s admonition neither Arnulfus had wished to aid Charles in his distress, nor had Odo ceased his invasion of the kingdom, his robberies, and his devastation. Arnulfus had even taken away the property of the Church of Reims—both property that he had restored to it after it had for some time been unjustly removed, and property that had never previously been taken away—solely because this bishop had refused to accept his rash invasion [Papir., “command”].

Odo had also besieged the city of Reims, carried out countless killings and acts of plunder, and given the property of the Church of Reims to his retainers, persisting in the robbery of that church until Charles arrived with a strong army and drove him from the besieged city [Col. 0270A].

Fulco also reports that Robert, a man of Arnulfus from the parish of Herimannus, bishop of Cologne, had invaded and plundered the property of this church, until Fulco had driven him away by force, as one would drive away a mad dog, from laying waste to those possessions. He asks that, unless Robert should come to his senses after being admonished, he be struck by the judgment of apostolic authority.

Fulco says that he was hemmed in by these disturbances of the kingdom and that it was impossible for him to hasten to the pope’s apostolic presence while war was constantly expected and the affairs of the kingdom were believed incapable of being settled in any other way. He had therefore always postponed the war—not because the opposing parties were inferior or unequal, or because they doubted the justice of their cause, but lest the strength of the kingdom, worn down by wars, be exposed to pagan invasions [Col. 0270B]. Accordingly, after an agreement had been made between them, they had given each other pledges of security by clasping right hands until the appointed time, and so forth.

He also writes concerning King Charles and Emperor Lambert [Note: [Col. 0269D] Fulco was Lambert’s kinsman in the paternal line], giving thanks that the pope had informed him about Lambert: that he was taking care of him as a father and loving him in the place of a most beloved son, and that he wished to preserve unbroken harmony with him.

Fulco asserts that the pope loved Lambert not only because of the relationship of blood by which he was bound to him, but much more because Lambert was a worshiper and lover of the pope. He asks that King Charles join the aforesaid Lambert in friendship and that the pope write to Odo and the nobles of the kingdom for the sake of peace, so that Charles might advance to the kingdom owed to him by hereditary right [Col. 0270C].

Even if Charles could not now receive the entire kingdom, Fulco asks that they at least preserve for him, by dividing the kingdom peacefully and justly, some portion worthy of his dignity. He adds that he would carry out what the same apostolic pontiff had ordered him concerning the transgressors and violators of sacred things—Richard, Manasses, and Rampo—as soon as he was able to gather his fellow bishops together.

The pope was to write back only on this point: since he had bound those men with the everlasting chain of anathema, whether any mercy might be shown to them if they turned to penance, or whether they might be received into penance, and what the nature of their penance ought to be.

Concerning Rampo, Fulco affirms that he was guilty only against Bishop Teuthbold; he had committed no fault against Walter, bishop of Sens [Col. 0270D], since he had neither been present for Walter’s arrest nor provided assistance or consent for it.

He also writes concerning Herilandus, bishop of Thérouanne. When that bishopric had been devastated by the Nortmanns and Herilandus, compelled by necessity, had come to Fulco, Fulco had received him as was proper and had appointed him visitor of a widowed church, so that, while visiting it until a bishop could be ordained there, he might receive his support from it.

But because the people of the aforesaid parish of Thérouanne seemed barbarous in character and language, Fulco asks to be informed by the pope’s reply whether he ought to place Herilandus over that widowed people, or whether he might appoint another in the previously mentioned church—one who, because of kinship and language, would be more acceptable and could remain in that place [Col. 0271A].

The same pope, replying to him, praises him and congratulates him on the affection and solicitude that he showed toward Emperor Lambert. He warns him always to be concerned for Lambert’s loyalty and stability, as one close to him by kinship. He asserts that he himself had such harmony of peace and affection with Lambert that they could no longer be separated from one another by any wickedness.

He also informs him that Richard, Manasses, and Rampo had been excommunicated by him and bound perpetually by anathema because they had committed such unspeakable deeds: they had put out the eyes of Teuthbold [ms., “Theobald”], bishop of Langres, and had imprisoned Walter of Sens after driving him from his own see [Col. 0271B]. He orders Fulco to share the pope’s judgment concerning these matters and, after summoning all his suffragan bishops, to determine in like manner the canonical judgment that he had exercised against them.

He also writes to the same archbishop concerning a certain priest named Bertharius. The clergy and people of the Church of Châlons were said to have chosen him for the episcopate with the consent of King Odo. The pope rebukes Fulco because he had refused to consecrate Bertharius, who had been canonically called, and had instead reportedly conferred that church, upon the death of its bishop, upon Herilandus, bishop of Thérouanne, in the manner of a benefice.

Afterward Fulco had ordained in that same church a certain Mancion, entangled in various crimes, as though he were bishop. When the aforesaid Bertharius wished to visit the Apostolic See, he was seized by a certain Conrad, a vassal of Lord Fulco, dragged from the church, and sent into exile for one month [Col. 0271C].

Therefore the pope summons Fulco and expressly, though fraternally, commands him not to delay presenting himself at the appointed time. He is to bring with him the aforesaid Mancion and the aforementioned Conrad, together with certain named fellow bishops, and so forth.

## CHAPTER IV. What Pope Stephen wrote to Fulco, and what Fulco wrote back to the same pope

Writing also to Stephen, the successor of Formosus (Stephen VII), the same Lord Fulco endeavored to show the devotion that he held toward the Roman See and that he had very frequently desired to visit the thresholds of the apostles. But various dangerous circumstances had prevented him from fulfilling these wishes [Col. 0271D]. He also reports that, through his efforts, Kings Odo and Charles had finally been joined in peaceful harmony.

In reply, this pope admits that he had received Fulco’s letters but does not accept—indeed, he reproves—his excuse: other men visited the same See, while Fulco admitted that permission had not been granted to him to do so.

He therefore announces that he had most certainly decided to celebrate a synod in the coming September, in the fifteenth indiction. Calling this archbishop to it under judgment, he expressly warns him that, putting aside every delay and removing every excuse, he must hasten to present his special presence to the pope and to the synod at that time. If he neglected to do so, the pope would not hesitate to pronounce a canonical sentence against him [Col. 0272A].

In reply, the venerable bishop endeavors to disclose how great his devotion had always been toward the glorious See of the chief of the apostles and toward its holy bishops. He asserts that he had then been weighed down by various oppressions and constrained by different disturbances, so that he had been unable to visit that See in person. He had nevertheless sent beloved sons of this church there to recount orally the hardships of his journey.

He had also sent one of his fellow priests to carry out this task. He had not dared to write more because he had felt himself punished with sufficiently harsh reproach in the letter sent to him by the pope. This had caused him no small astonishment: that the pope’s first letter had struck him so severely, whereas until then, when his predecessors had written to him, nothing but honeyed and sweet words had usually come from that See [Col. 0272B].

Yet, attributing this to his own sins, he says that just as he was rightly saddened by his misfortune, so he rejoiced at the pope’s correction. He suggests that what had happened might have occurred because, as a rumor brought to him indicated, Fulco had been reported differently by certain people less filled with charity than the truth warranted.

He therefore asks the pope not readily to lend an ear to such persons until, as it is written, he investigates most carefully a matter he does not know (Job XXIX).

He adds plainly that from almost his earliest cradle he had been brought up in canonical disciplines, until the glorious King Charles, son of the Emperor Louis, took him into his palace and household service [Col. 0272C]. Remaining in the palace court thereafter until the time of King Carloman, son of Louis the Younger and grandson of that same Charles, he was then elected by the holy bishops of the province of Reims, as well as by the clergy and people of that city, and ordained bishop.

He asks that the pope investigate through the account of his envoys or of others who knew these things how he had found this church suffering from pagan attacks and how he had labored to the utmost of his ability for its peace.

He asserts that he was explaining these matters not out of arrogance, but so that the pope might know—he reasons—that a man brought up in this way and having lived thus before becoming a bishop would regard the episcopal office as a burden rather than an honor, as a service of humility rather than an instrument of exaltation.

He adds that, if some quiet were granted to the kingdom and he were able to obtain permission from King Odo, he would at last endeavor to hasten to the pope’s blessed feet, as soon as the roads became open. At that time they were blocked by Zendeboldus, son of King Arnulfus, who was also inflicting many injuries upon the Church of Reims and distributing its possessions among his subjects [Col. 0272D].

Fulco asks that Zendeboldus’s tyranny be restrained by apostolic authority, saying that in so dangerous a time, filled with necessities, it would be harmful for him to abandon his church.

## CHAPTER V. What letters Fulco sent to certain kings

Thus, exercising care for the whole kingdom, the same Lord Archbishop Fulco sends a letter to Emperor Charles [Col. 0273A] [Note: [Col. 0273D] Charles the Fat, mentioned above], son of King Louis of the region beyond the Rhine, concerning the protection and defense of the kingdom of the Franks, which was being oppressed in many ways by the Nortmanns in those regions.

He asserts that, with God’s help, the kingdom had hitherto been protected so long as it was governed by the rule of Charles’s uncle and namesake, and by that man’s sons. But after those men had happily departed from human life, and after the nobles of the kingdom had entrusted themselves to Charles’s imperial protection, many misfortunes had overwhelmed them on every side.

He mentions the city of Paris, which he calls the head and gateway of the kingdoms of Neustria and Burgundy. It was surrounded by a barbarian siege and would soon be captured unless God’s mercy came to its aid. If it were captured, they would suffer the ruin of the entire kingdom. These evils were already spreading so dangerously that nothing remained secure from that city as far as Reims [Col. 0273B]. The only safe habitation belonged to wicked Christians who had joined the barbarians and agreed with them; many of these, abandoning the Christian religion, had joined the society of the pagans and submitted themselves to their protection.

He also wrote to the same emperor concerning receiving the pallium from the Roman See and confirming the privileges once granted to the Church of Reims by the Roman pontiffs.

Sending a letter to King Arnulfus of the region beyond the Rhine on behalf of King Charles, whom Fulco had anointed king while he was still a child, he explains the reasons for Charles’s advancement, since he had heard that Arnulfus’s mind had been stirred against him because of this act.

He recalls that, after Emperor Charles, Arnulfus’s uncle, had died, Fulco had entered Arnulfus’s service, wishing to accept his lordship and governance. But Arnulfus had dismissed him without any counsel or consolation. Since no hope remained for him in Arnulfus, Fulco had been compelled to accept the dominion of Odo, a man unrelated to the royal stock who had tyrannically abused royal power; against his will Fulco had until then endured Odo’s rule.

Because he had desired Arnulfus’s dominion, he had therefore entered his service. But after he could find no counsel in Arnulfus, he had done the only thing that remained: he chose to have as king the man who alone, after Arnulfus, remained from Arnulfus’s royal lineage and whose predecessors and brothers had been kings.

Regarding the matter for which that king also blamed him—why they had not done this earlier—Fulco gives the explanation. When Emperor Charles died and Arnulfus himself refused to assume the government of the kingdom, this Charles was still very young in both body and understanding and was unfit to direct the kingdom. Since the most savage persecution of the Nortmanns was pressing upon them, it had then been dangerous to choose him [Col. 0273D].

But when they saw that he had reached an age at which he knew how to assent to sound counsel, they received him, in accordance with God’s honor, so that he might provide for the kingdom. They wished to educate him in such a way that he would be useful both to this kingdom and to Arnulfus himself.

As for their having presumed to do this without Arnulfus’s counsel, Fulco asserts that they had followed the custom of the Frankish people. Their custom had always been that, when a king died, they chose another from the royal stock or succession without regard for, or inquiry of, any greater or more powerful king [Col. 0274A].

Following this custom, they wished to entrust this king to Arnulfus’s loyalty and counsel, so that he might use Arnulfus’s assistance and counsel in everything, and so that both the king and the entire kingdom might be subject to Arnulfus’s commands and arrangements.

Moreover, concerning the allegation that had been brought to Arnulfus—that Fulco had done this against Arnulfus’s loyalty and for his own private advantage—he replies that Aschericus, who appeared to have made these claims, had come to Fulco before the archbishop had attempted to do anything of this kind, in the presence of Counts Heribertus and Ecfridus [ms., Exfridus, Erfridus]. Aschericus had sought both advice and assistance about what he should do concerning Odo’s commands, since Odo was ordering him to undertake intolerable things.

On behalf of the sons of Godfridus he had also sought counsel concerning the evil that Odo was attempting to do to them. They had asked Fulco that, by common counsel, such a leader be established under whom their subjects could remain secure. They were considering either Wido or this Charles of royal stock. After examining together whom they ought to support, it seemed to them that, for the benefit of the kingdom, to avoid Arnulfus’s opposition, and because of the proper and fitting rule of royal lineage, they should turn to this Charles.

They believed that Arnulfus would welcome this action concerning his kinsman and would bring aid to him and to the kingdom.

As for the claim that Fulco had done this on Wido’s account, so that by this device he might introduce Wido into the kingdom and, once the boy Charles had been set aside, turn to Wido, Fulco asserts that these things had been falsely alleged against him knowingly, out of the malice of envy. Alternatively, he says that he recognized that the man who spread such reports could himself become the kind of person he accused Fulco of being; but Fulco neither expected to become such a man nor recognized himself as descended from such an origin.

The predecessors of that king had never encountered such schemes in Fulco’s forebears. They had found those forebears proven in complete loyalty and in the interests of the kingdom and had therefore raised them honorably. For this reason it would have been shameful for that king to believe such a thing about Fulco or to mark him with such infamy.

Finally, concerning what Fulco had heard being said to Arnulfus—that this Charles was not the son of Louis—he asserts that no one who saw Charles and recognized the appearance of his parents could fail to recognize that he had sprung from royal stock. He also bore certain features of his father Louis by which he could be recognized as his son [Col. 0274D].

Fulco therefore asks Arnulfus’s royal majesty to receive these statements [j, “words”] graciously, and not to allow anyone to turn his mind against this innocent king, his kinsman. But whether the matters Fulco asserted were in fact so, Arnulfus should have them examined in his presence and before his faithful men and bring them to a proper conclusion, considering how his predecessors had governed the condition of the kingdom and how the succession of royal dignity had continued to flourish up to that time [Col. 0275A].

At that time only that one prince and this little kinsman of his, Charles, remained from the entire royal stock. Arnulfus should consider what might happen if the fate owed to all men should one day claim him, when there were already so many kings from foreign stock and still more who desired the royal name. After Arnulfus’s death, who would aid his son in ascending to the inheritance of the kingdom owed to him, if this kinsman Charles should happen to fall?

Fulco adds that it had been known among almost all peoples that the Frankish people were accustomed to have kings by succession. He offers as testimony the words of blessed Pope Gregory (Homily 10).

He also cites from the Teutonic books the story of a certain king named Hermenricus, who consigned all his offspring to death through the wicked counsels of one of his advisers. Fulco begs Arnulfus not to heed criminal counsels like that king [Gregory, On the Gospels], but to pity this people and aid the declining royal line, taking care that during his days the dignity of its succession be strengthened, and that those who were kings, or wished to be kings, from a foreign lineage should not prevail against those to whom royal honor was owed by descent [Col. 0275B].

He asserts that he had sent Aledrannus [ms. Papir., Alerannus] to Arnulfus, suggesting that Arnulfus should order any of those who had established King Charles to go into his service whomsoever he pleased. These men could demonstrate reasonably before his majesty that matters stood as Fulco had stated.

He earnestly begs the king to consider these matters with a benevolent mind and to know that Fulco’s devotion and intention toward Arnulfus’s loyalty were such that Charles would look to Arnulfus’s counsel in everything he was going to do, remain secure under Arnulfus’s kindness, and that no one would be able to turn the king’s mind away from aiding this kingdom or Charles himself [Col. 0275C].

He also writes to the same king, informing him of the loyalty and devotion that he held toward him and of his desire to hasten into Arnulfus’s service at his command. The promise that his own king Charles had made to Arnulfus, who had entrusted the kingdom to him, was to remain unshaken, both in Charles himself and in his subjects.

Charles also proposed to attack with arms Odo, the king who was his enemy and was preparing ambushes against him.

Visiting Emperor Wido by a mission of his letters, Fulco admits that he greatly rejoiced at the glory and exaltation of Wido’s See. But he marvels and is troubled that, after so long a time, Wido had sent him no messenger to inform him of his condition and prosperity [Col. 0275D].

Fulco begs him to give assistance to his king Charles and to show himself toward Charles as was fitting for him to act toward a kinsman. He asks Wido to let Charles know more quickly what his intentions toward him were.

Concerning King Arnulfus, Fulco reports that Arnulfus did not wish to preserve peace with Wido.

Finally, he says that Charles was sending his letter to the Apostolic See, commending himself to the pope’s prayers and asking to be strengthened by the pope’s blessing. He also asks that the pope unite Charles with Wido in friendship [Col. 0276A].

Fulco requests that Wido write back to the same king concerning his friendship, either through his messenger or by letter. He also asks Wido to show compassion for the injuries suffered by Fulco and by the Church entrusted to him, which Fulco endured because of his loyalty.

He further reports that the king had granted him the abbey of Saint Martin [ms., “entrusted”]. He asks Wido to receive under his protection the abbey’s properties that lay within Wido’s kingdom.

Writing to King Odo, he asks that, after the death of Bishop Dido, a free election be granted to the Church of Laon, demonstrating that people ought not to be compelled by force to accept someone whom they do not want. He also begs him to order that the same Church live without disturbance and not allow its property to be plundered by usurpers, lest he become a participant with the plunderers if he permits such things to occur. [Col. 0276B]

Writing to his king Charles, he expresses great indignation that it had been reported to him that the king wished to ally himself, at the evil advice of certain men, with the Northmen, so that he might obtain their assistance in securing the dignity of the kingdom.

“For who,” he says, “if he is faithful to you as he ought to be, would not be terrified that you wish to seek the friendship of God’s enemies and, for the destruction and ruin of the Christian name, to accept pagan arms and detestable treaties? For it makes no difference whether someone allies himself with pagans or, having denied God, worships idols. For if—as the Apostle says—‘evil conversations corrupt good morals’ (1 Cor. 15), how much more is the chastity of a Christian soul corrupted by the counsels and companionship of heathens? Indeed, one cannot fail to imitate what one continually sees; rather, one will gradually become accustomed to it and, as though dragged by the bond of evil habit, will be drawn into wrongdoing. Certainly, your royal ancestors, having laid aside the error of paganism, submitted themselves nobly to divine worship and always sought help from God; because of this they both ruled successfully and handed down the inheritance of the kingdom to their descendants.

“You, on the contrary, are now abandoning God. I shall say it plainly, although unwillingly: you are abandoning God when you ally yourself with his enemies. Therefore that prophetic saying is rightly directed at you which was once addressed to the king of Israel [Note: These are the words of Jehu to King Jehoshaphat of Judah] when he acted similarly: ‘You give assistance to the wicked and join in friendship with those who hate God’ (2 Chron. 19).

“And certainly, when you ought to put an end to past offenses, renounce the plundering and despoiling of the poor, and do penance for all these things, you now provoke God to still greater anger by joining yourselves to those who do not know God and place their confidence in their own savagery. Believe me: by acting thus you will never attain the kingdom; rather, God, whom you provoke, will swiftly destroy you. Until now I had hoped better things from you. Now I see that you will perish, together with all your kinsmen [ms. j, *Papir.*: *consentaneis*, “associates”], if you truly wish to act in this way and heed such counsels.

“Indeed, those who give you such advice are shown to be not faithful but altogether faithless. If you are willing to listen to them, you will lose both the earthly and the heavenly kingdom. I therefore beseech you by God to abandon such counsel, lest you wish to plunge yourselves into eternal destruction and bring the loss of everlasting sorrow upon me and the others who are faithful to you according to God. It would have been better for you not to be born than to wish to reign under the devil’s patronage and to help those whom you ought in every way to oppose.

“For know that, if you do this and heed such counsels, you will never have me as a faithful man. Rather, I shall recall from your allegiance as many as I can, and, together with all my fellow bishops, I shall excommunicate you and all your people and condemn you with an eternal anathema. Because of the fidelity that I preserve toward you, I write these things groaning, since I desire you always to be honored according to God and according to the world, and to ascend to the royal height owed to you with the help not of Satan but of Christ. For the kingdom that God gives has a firm foundation; but what is acquired through injustice and plunder is unstable and soon falls, and you will not be able to endure for long.” [Col. 0277B]

Addressing Emperor Lambert with a letter of congratulation, he reports what Pope Formosus had communicated to him in his letters: namely, that he loved the same emperor greatly, wished to advise him in all things as a most beloved son, and desired to maintain unbreakable concord with him. He therefore exhorts this ruler and earnestly urges him to show himself grateful for so great a kindness from the same pope, to love him as a most devoted father, to preserve toward him every form of fidelity and obedience, to obey his admonitions as a true son, and to honor the Roman see with fitting reverence. [Col. 0277C]

“For in this way,” he says, “your empire will be established with everlasting solidity, and divine assistance will support you against all your enemies and adversaries. With God’s help you will always become superior and stronger than all those who oppose you. Recall, I beg you, your uncle and namesake, the most illustrious Lambert: consider what his attitude was toward the holy Roman see and what end he attained, and take care not to arrive at the same example if you wish to do anything similar.

“Also beg the apostolic lord to deign to absolve him and to intercede for him with God. On my behalf, too, I ask you most earnestly to obtain his goodwill toward me, so that he may deign to receive a reward both for me and for the see of Reims, and preserve its privileges inviolably, as all his holy predecessors are known always to have done. And if anyone should ever [j.: “never”] presume to trouble the ears of his clemency and say anything sinister about us, do not believe the slanderers before he can learn through me, or certainly through his own or my messenger, what the truth is.

“Moreover, let your imperial dignity know that Rampon, your kinsman and mine, has been excommunicated by the same apostolic lord, as we have learned from his letters. On his behalf I beg your gentleness [ms.: *magnitudinem*, ‘greatness’] to plead with him, so that he may not deny him a place for doing penance and correcting what he has committed, nor allow him to perish irrecoverably, bound by perpetual anathema; but may impose upon him whatever penance and measure of satisfaction pleases him. Let him also order us and all the bishops of Italy and Gaul to whom he wrote concerning Rampon’s condemnation to write back in turn about what he should do in his mercy and how the matter ought to stand.” [Col. 0278A]

Sending a friendly letter to King Albrado overseas, he gives thanks because the king had sent so good and devoted a man, one in accord with ecclesiastical regulations, as bishop in the city called Canterbury. He had heard that this bishop was striving to cut off with the sword of the word a most perverse sect [ms.: *pervertissimam*, “most subversive”], which had arisen from pagan errors and still remained among that people.

This sect appeared to teach that bishops and priests might keep women introduced into their households; that each man might approach whichever female relative he wished; that they might commit incest with women consecrated to God; and that a man might have both a wife and a concubine. How contrary all these things are to sound faith he demonstrates by the clearest proofs, drawing upon the approved authorities [ms. j: *prolatis*, “adduced”] of the holy Fathers. [Col. 0278B]

Admonishing and rebuking Queen or Empress Richildis, he confesses that he has been seized with great sorrow because of the bad reputation that had reached him concerning the life and conduct of that queen. It was said, namely, that the devil rather than God was present where she was, since there surrounded her things that war against the salvation of the soul: anger, quarrels, dissensions, arson, murders, lust, and also the plundering of the poor and the seizure of churches. Concerning all these matters he admonishes her with due concern and pastoral diligence, urging her to transfer herself from such great evils to the fruit of eternal salvation.

He sets before her the four-way road, or quadriga, of the virtues; if she takes it up and strives to ascend, she will grasp the things that belong to wisdom, holiness, and eternal happiness. He urges her to preserve uncorrupted the veil of Christ that she had assumed in widowhood, so that she may present it inviolate to God, and not hasten toward hell, where she would discover the immeasurable evil of the many miseries that he endeavors to disclose to her.

Let her consider whether she is a friend of God or his sister. If she is not, let her labor without interruption (Tit. 2) so that she may become one—not with the brightness of virginity, but through the practice of salutary continence: by believing rightly, loving God and her neighbor, performing works of mercy, and living soberly, justly, and devoutly (Heb. 3). Let her take care to correct her life while it is called “today,” lest she fall into the snare of eternal confusion while failing to reflect how swiftly the present day passes.

Let her spare her own soul and take care to draw near to God; let her be regarded as a dove through simplicity and innocence [ms.: “let her possess the simplicity of a dove”], so that when she departs from the body she may deserve to hear Christ say:

“Winter has passed and gone away; my dove, come and rest with me” (Song 2),

sitting at the right hand of my Father.

He asserts that he speaks at length for this reason: he is deeply concerned for her salvation and wishes that she may truly become a queen by adorning her widowhood with virtues, keeping before her eyes the day of her death or resurrection, and hearing the Apostle say: “Awake, you righteous, and do not sin” (1 Cor. 15). Let her finally give glory to her God and work out her own salvation; let her turn away from evil and do good (Ps. 36).

He prays and earnestly desires that his correction, necessary amendment, and salutary compunction may touch her heart, so that at last she may recover from the snares of the devil; and that God’s grace may raise her from the tombs of her vices (2 Tim. 2), and so forth. May God make her, who is feverish with evils, firm and stable, fixed in what is good, so that here and in eternal life she may rejoice with the saints.

“But if,” he says, “you listen to our counsel, we shall be toward you as we ought to be, in all fidelity, reverence, and due service. And, greater than all these things, God will be gracious to you, as we desire and pray. Otherwise, we wish you truly to know that we do not wish to incur God’s displeasure on your behalf; but, according to our ministry, we shall do with you what canonical authority commands us.

“God is witness how unwillingly we shall do this. For we cannot depart from the Apostle, who says: ‘As long as I am the Apostle of the Gentiles, I shall honor my ministry’ (Rom. 11); and: ‘We are God’s fellow workers’ (1 Cor. 3); and: ‘It is God who works in us’ (Phil. 2); and: ‘Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?’ (2 Cor. 13). Therefore I beseech God in my conscience that my words may cling to your heart, and that he himself who speaks through me may speak these things in your ears and, through himself, in your heart. May almighty God stretch forth his hand from on high in answer to our prayers and deliver you from the filthy depths of this world.” [Col. 0279C]

## CHAPTER VI. What he wrote to various bishops

He is also found to have sent various writings to various prelates, sprinkled with pious salt and filled with divine authorities.

To Archbishop Flother, concerning the possessions of the Church of Reims situated in his diocese, which were suffering considerable loss at the hands of usurpers, he sends a warning and a request that, remembering the ministry conferred upon him by God and the commands of the Apostles—of which he adds several examples—he forbid these men by canonical authority to presume any longer upon the property of this Church, if [the text has *sicut*; more correctly, *si*, “if”] they do not wish to incur the displeasure of the Lord and his saints. [Col. 0279D]

To Rostagnus, prelate of the people of Arles, he gives thanks because he had learned that Rostagnus was concerned for the property of the Church of Reims, which he had placed under his supervision and protection. But he had heard that certain wicked usurpers were harassing or appropriating it. He therefore exhorts him to strike those same usurpers with strict excommunication unless they repent, if he does not judge that the matter ought to be referred to the apostolic see.

To Herimann, Archbishop of Cologne, he reports that he desires to speak with him and with the other bishops of his diocese and to discuss, as Herimann had suggested to him, matters necessary to the Churches. [Col. 0280A] This, however, was prevented by the storms of persecution raised by the Northmen. As soon as an opportunity in time presented itself, he would strive to fulfill the matter with all speed.

He further informs him that certain possessions belonging to the Church of Reims were being held under an unlawful title in his parish by certain usurpers. For this reason he had asked King Arnulf at Worms to command Willebert, Herimann’s predecessor in the episcopate, to act in this matter according to the decrees of the canons. The same King Arnulf had also sent Herimann as his envoy to the aforesaid bishop concerning this very matter.

But since Willebert had been unable to carry out the king’s command in this matter, he warns and asks Herimann to strike those usurpers, or those who were attempting to disturb the possessions, with canonical punishment unless they repent of the presumption they had begun. He also sends Herimann Pope Symmachus’s decree, in which he could learn with the clearest statement what ought to be done in such matters.

Likewise, concerning certain possessions of this Church situated across the Rhine, in a place called Bothert [j.: Bobert], which he had entrusted to Maingaud [j.: Magnigaud], he asks that, after Maingaud’s death, the same prelate Herimann undertake their protection. He should also admonish a certain Wibert, who appeared to hold other possessions of the Church of Reims, to restore them amicably.

Concerning the property of a certain abbey granted to him by the king, which lay in the regions of Herimann, he asks that Herimann defend it against seizure by outsiders, and so forth.

To Walter, Archbishop of the Church of Sens, he writes concerning the case of Abbess Hildegard, for which he had arranged certain proceedings, but Walter—partly because of his occupations and partly because he was weighed down by illness—had attended to none of them. He therefore sets out for him how the matter itself is to reach a lawful conclusion and urges him not to fail in coming to that proceeding.

If he does not come, Fulco himself will nevertheless, preserving charity, strive by God’s authority to complete what must be done there. The fact that he had delayed it until then was not because he lacked the authority or privilege to act; rather, he had acted out of affection for Walter, which he wished to preserve inviolately in every respect.

He also asks that Walter warn the aforesaid abbess, as his diocesan, not to withdraw from Walter’s assembly as though she were ignorant of it, but rather to take care to present herself on the appointed day. [Col. 0280D]

Likewise, he sends Walter a consolatory letter concerning his illness, and concerning the absolution that Walter had asked to receive from Fulco and from Fulco’s brothers, as well as concerning the provision for their meeting with the same lord Fulco when this could be arranged.

To Pleonicus, Archbishop overseas, he offers congratulations on his good efforts, by which he had learned that Pleonicus was laboring to cut off and eradicate the incestuous encouragements of lust mentioned above in the letter he had written to King Albrado (chap. 5), which appeared to have taken root among that people. He instructs and arms him with sacred authorities of canonical censure [perhaps: “Scripture”], wishing to share in his pious labors. [Col. 0281A]

To a certain Roman prelate, John, he recalls the affection of love that he had toward him, saying that he could not remember having found anyone with whom he was so harmoniously joined by a mutual affection of charity. He recalls that John had once received him with great goodwill, treated him with the most generous kindness, and heaped upon him great expenditures of benefactions.

He asserts that, as soon as peace had been restored, he would demonstrate by worthy services his grateful devotion both toward John and toward Pope Stephen. He asks John to protect him by his favor before the pope’s excellence and, whenever he sees it necessary, to assist him—as he trusts most fully in John’s goodness.

To Dodilo, Bishop of Cambrai, he writes concerning the proceedings that Dodilo had assigned to him, which he had not attended. He warns and asks Dodilo to strive to come to the next proceeding, wherever King Odo might be with the bishops, since they ought to settle the matter then at issue concerning Hildegard and Hirmingard.

He should also have the accusers of Hirmingard, together with those who ordered that the priest be blinded and suspended, and all who obeyed that wicked command or became accomplices in the crime, admonished and canonically summoned, so that they might take care to present themselves at this assembly. [Col. 0281B]

Likewise, in the same case, he gives thanks because Dodilo had devoutly received his admonition and had arrived fully prepared on the appointed day. He nevertheless appears to express anger that, when ecclesiastical matters were being dealt with, Dodilo had wished to entrust the case to him not through a cleric but through a man of the lay order.

The lord Fulco himself had been unable to come as agreed, partly detained by service to his elder and partly hindered by the trouble of bodily illness. He also admonishes Dodilo that he ought to remember what Fulco had once been toward him and how, without the king and without anyone advising his side, he had used every means to ensure that Dodilo attained this episcopal honor, when Dodilo was not yet perfectly known to him.

Nevertheless, he had acted for him as for a most beloved brother because he had believed—and still believed—that Dodilo possessed simple prudence, unfeigned faith, and firm and unchanging constancy. He had also hoped that Dodilo would be his collaborator and helper in all things.

Therefore, because of that sincere affection which he believed to exist in Dodilo, he says that he admonishes him, ordering him to put aside every delay and occupation and take care to be present at the agreed assembly of the bishops, without exception of any cause except bodily illness. He should also have the persons mentioned above, whom Fulco had identified in another letter, canonically admonished so that, prepared for the solemn gathering of the bishops, they might take care to present themselves on the appointed day. [Col. 0281D]

Likewise, writing with the other fellow bishops—namely Dido of Laon, Hetilo of Noyon, Riculfus of Soissons, and Herinand [above, chap. 3: Herilandus] of Meaux—he informs this prelate Dodilo that these aforesaid bishops had assembled in the city of Reims to discuss Baldwin’s seizure [Baldwin the Bald, Count of Flanders], about whom he had written to Dodilo [j.: *Doddoni*], urging Dodilo to admonish Baldwin to repent of the wicked arrogance of his presumption. [Col. 0282A]

But since the same prelate had written back that he had been unable to come to the bishops because the sword of the Northmen had intercepted his journey, Fulco expresses common sympathy for him over their shared disaster.

As for what Dodilo had requested concerning Baldwin, Fulco agrees that Dodilo should diligently correct him by admonishing, exhorting, and reproving him, setting before him the divine judgments of the holy Fathers. He also reports that a letter had been sent to Baldwin on behalf of the bishops.

He urges Dodilo, if Baldwin is present, to read the letter to him; if he is absent, to send it to him through his archdeacon, who should also make Baldwin understand it. If the archdeacon too is unable to reach him, Dodilo should have the letter read publicly in his presence at the place where Baldwin had seized the religious foundation. Thereafter, unless Baldwin repents, neither a monk nor any properly Christian person should associate with him, if he does not wish to become entangled in the bond of anathema. [Col. 0282B]

If Hetilo should also come to the city of Arras, Dodilo should meet him, so that they might canonically carry out what ought to be done concerning this matter; and whatever they did there, Dodilo should report to Fulco by letter.

To the prelate Hetilo he commands by letter that Hetilo travel with the king’s faithful men to Arras, doing as far as possible what he had found indicated to him in another writing as needing to be done.

Likewise, concerning what he was suffering from Dodilo, Bishop of Cambrai, he asserts that for his good deeds he was receiving insulting treatment from Dodilo. He calls Hetilo as his witness to how he had advanced Dodilo to better things with a paternal and simple affection of kindness. [Col. 0282C]

He also explains how the devout man Rodulf had assigned to the Church of Reims an abbey situated in Hetilo’s parish, entrusting to it at the same time the body of the blessed Pope and martyr Calixtus, which Rodulf had obtained and brought from the city of Rome.

Fulco therefore reports that he had amicably asked the aforesaid Dodilo to come to the fortress of Arras, honorably lift up the relics of the aforesaid martyr, and escort them as far as the monastery of Saint-Quentin. He had also requested Hetilo to come to that monastery and accompany the sacred body until the lord Fulco himself arrived and could fittingly receive it and escort it as far as this city of Reims.

There it was to be kept until, once peace had been restored, it could be returned to its proper place in Hetilo’s parish. [Col. 0282D]

But when Dodilo ought to have done what had been requested, he instead, setting aside the respect due to their filial and fraternal relationship, met the procession in the middle of the road, snatched the holy relic from the hands of those carrying it, and kept it with himself. He said that he would return it to no one except Hetilo, in whose parish it was recognized to have been deposited. He had done this, Fulco says, as a pretext for a new fraud, in order to be able to hand the sacred body over to a certain Count Huchold [ms.: Buchold].

Therefore Fulco asks Hetilo to send his messenger to Dodilo and, rebuking and correcting him with paternal and fraternal love, to recall to him how Fulco, moved solely by religious devotion and by the faith that he perhaps believed Dodilo possessed, had placed him in the episcopal see without waiting for any king or prince. He should warn Dodilo to withdraw from the presumption he had begun, lest he compel this same archbishop to do something against him that Dodilo himself would not wish. [Col. 0283A]

He also earnestly begs Hetilo not to give Dodilo his assent in such a matter, but to favor the just side in everything. The heavenly treasure entrusted to the Church of Reims by the man mentioned above should be restored to its city and basilica; Hetilo should not merely consent to this but should also assist it with all his strength.

To Dido, Bishop of Laon, he writes concerning the reconciliation of the soul of a certain Valcher, who, having been found guilty of treason, had suffered the death penalty. He had heard that, at the point of death, Valcher had sought penance through confession and the viaticum of holy communion from Dido, but had been unable to obtain it.

Moreover, the benefit of burial had been denied him, and prayer for him had been prohibited. Fulco therefore expresses anger against the same prelate, horrified that he had wished to act in this way, since Dido knew very well that sacred authority had decreed that penance must not be denied at the end of life.

He adduces several testimonies of the holy Fathers on this matter and warns Dido, having considered the common danger, to imitate the common Lord’s mercy. He should grant this sinner the remedy of penance at the end of life when he begs for mercy; he should have prayer made for him and personally perform for him, according to Christian custom, reconciliation and commendation of his soul. He should also transfer him from the exposed place where he had not been buried but cast aside, and bring him to the cemetery of the faithful. [Col. 0283B]

Likewise, concerning this same case, he requests and adduces the example of blessed Gregory (*Dialogues* IV.55), concerning a certain monk whom Gregory had ordered not to be given common burial or assisted by prayers, but after a proper period [ms. c.: “a long period”] ordered that reconciliation be granted to him. He also adduces the Gospel saying: “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save what had perished” (Luke 19). He further cites the testimony of the Council of Nicaea (canon 13, or 12), by which it is generally prescribed that communion be granted to anyone lying at the point of death who asks for the grace of communion. [Col. 0283C]

He writes to a certain Roman bishop, Peter, concerning matters about which he had consulted Pope Formosus regarding Herinand, Bishop of the Morini, whom Fulco had decided to place over the widowed Church of Châlons. He asks Peter to make a suggestion to the pope on behalf of this consultation, so that Fulco might more quickly obtain the desired answer concerning it.

He recalls what had been done in the case of Actard, Bishop of Nantes: Pope Nicholas had afterward decreed that Actard should be placed over the Church of the Morini and had finally decided that he should be incorporated into the archbishopric of the see of Tours. Fulco also asks Peter to seek suitable authority concerning this matter and, once he has found it, send it to him for execution. [Col. 0283D]

He writes to Honoratus, prelate of Beauvais, and declares that he is exceedingly astonished at how it could have happened that Honoratus’s mind had become so opposed and hostile to him, since Honoratus knew what Fulco’s attitude toward him had been and how he had always regarded him in the place of a brother and son, and with what affection he had striven so that Honoratus might attain the same honor.

Nevertheless, Honoratus ought not despair but should return as soon as possible to maintain peace and concord with Fulco. Fulco therefore admonishes him as a most beloved son to return to himself, consider what order and profession he belongs to, and reflect that he had not been injured by Fulco in anything. If possible, he should come to Fulco, so that they might discuss these matters more fully in conversation. If this could not be done, he should send one of his familiar associates through whom he could report what his mind was bearing. [Col. 0284A]

Fulco also reports that he had heard certain things about Honoratus which he could not easily believe: namely, that Honoratus was persisting in plunder, invading the possessions of others, and seizing money. In particular, he says that a certain Rotbert had complained to him that Honoratus had taken away all his movable property.

“But I,” he says, “cannot believe this of you. Rather, I think that there is someone who, relying on your favor and authority, has presumed to do these things, and for that reason what was done by another is attributed to you. If therefore it was done by any of your people, I beg you to restrain the author of this evil suitably and order that the entire loss be repaired. But if it is true that you yourselves did this, I beg you to desist from such an intention and have what was lost restored in full to the one who suffered the damage.” [Col. 0284B]

Likewise, he rebukes Honoratus for certain matters that he appeared to have written to Fulco without a straightforward profession, as though the lord Fulco had disturbed peace and concord. Honoratus had also indicated that his Church was being harassed by certain wicked men and that, concerning this matter, he had received no answer from the archbishop despite requesting one.

Fulco therefore recalls that he had preferred to obtain from Honoratus, by entreaty rather than command, a temporary truce for those men until the bishops themselves could speak together. Concerning a certain Aledramn, whom Honoratus was then threatening to excommunicate and appeared to be ordering the archbishop to punish with his censure, Fulco asserts that he had never intended not to obey the common and jointly issued commands and requests of his fellow bishops.

Yet the Church of Reims could not have known how to obey the Church of Beauvais in an exceptional manner. And because in this excommunication he saw not ecclesiastical censure prevailing but rash hostility, he explains that the beginning of the matter was the abandonment of King Odo and the installation of Charles. [Col. 0284C]

After several further points, he adds a discussion of the vacancy of the Churches of Senlis and Châlons. The Church of Senlis had then elected Otfred, whom they had brought to the prelate of Reims and asked to have ordained as bishop. Fulco asks Honoratus to come to this ordination, with every excuse removed, as canonical authority commands.

He also adds a warning that Honoratus should not understand these words as meaning that, henceforth, he may not hope to enjoy Fulco’s friendship—the friendship by which they had been mutually joined and which the archbishop wished to preserve unshaken forever. Fulco also desired to honor and exalt Honoratus’s see for the honor of his own see.

But since Fulco had seen himself secretly gnawed by Honoratus’s mordant criticism in his letters, he wished to make himself excusable for so great a stealthy attack, lest by keeping silent he appear to assent to it. [Col. 0284D]

Likewise, concerning the ordination of Mancion, Bishop of Châlons, Fulco had commanded Honoratus to come to it. Honoratus did not come and had even marked the ordination with a statement of criticism. The archbishop nevertheless bore this criticism patiently out of a spirit of charity, commanding and asking Honoratus to take care to attend the ordination of the aforesaid Otfred, and so forth. [Col. 0285A]

Likewise, concerning letters that Honoratus had sent to him, in which he had exhorted Fulco to come to the aid of the condition and holy religion of the tottering Church, the archbishop declares that he offers vows of thanks to God, who had stirred Honoratus’s mind to give such advice. His earlier letters had appeared to display swollen resentment, whereas this one gave full evidence of brotherly love.

If Honoratus held in his heart what his words expressed, Fulco says that he was ready to respond to his charity and preserve it inviolably. But since the suitable time when they could meet together did not then appear to have arrived, Fulco would take care, when the time came with the Lord’s help, to announce it appropriately both to Honoratus and to the other suffragans. [Col. 0285B]

Likewise, concerning Pope Stephen’s command, the pope had instructed the lord Fulco—granting him permission in the meantime, as he had requested—to send this Bishop Honoratus and Rodulf of Laon to Ravenna for the synod to be held there. Fulco therefore warns Honoratus to obey the pope’s command, just as the pope ordered.

He sends Teuthbald, Bishop of Langres, friendly letters binding them to one another in charity [ms.: *continctrices*, “binding”], reporting private matters between them that Teuthbald had communicated through his messenger, their mutual conversation, and the royal kinship and friendship of Teuthbald himself—friendship pleasing to King Charles. He also asks Teuthbald to send him word about Richard, prince of Burgundy, and about the Aquitanians, whatever he may have learned, and so forth. [Col. 0285C]

To Rodulf, successor to the aforementioned Bishop Dido, he writes with congratulations on Rodulf’s honor and progress in the Lord.

He also writes concerning one of Rodulf’s subjects, whom Rodulf had rejected, warning him to take care that the episcopal reputation not be harmed in this matter, when what was being done out of zeal for righteousness might be reported as being done out of zeal for exercising vengeance.

He states that the Church of Reims had possessed this privilege from ancient times: that whenever any of its diocesan clergy felt that they had offended their own bishops in any way, they might flee to it, the mother of the other Churches, and beg from it assistance in obtaining pardon. [Col. 0285D]

“But I,” he says, “did not wish to use any authority in this matter. Rather, I wished to ask as a friend of a friend—or rather, as one asks a specially beloved son—because I trusted that I had some influence with you—indeed, more than I shall say [the transmitted wording is uncertain].”

After several further points he adds that mercy is not transgression: God, after threatening strict vengeance, daily customarily extends the inward compassion of a father to those who turn back to him; and no one ever falls so completely that the opportunity to rise again ought to be denied him, and so forth.

## CHAPTER VII. What he wrote to abbots and certain illustrious men
To a certain Stephen, an abbot and most noble man, who also appeared to have been elected to the episcopate but had perhaps then [Col. 0286A] been rejected or disapproved, he sent a consolatory letter, asserting that he would preserve forever the friendship he had promised him. He grieved and lamented that the man whose pre-election to the governance of the Church had rejoiced him, he now saw frustrated in its accomplishment. Nevertheless, he urged him, although struck down, to rise again all the more strongly and vigorously. He wished him to recall all his relatives and friends, or anyone else he could, to peace and concord, etc.

To Baldwin, count of Flanders, concerning his offenses, about which he had considered with his fellow bishops of the diocese what ought to be done. Among various other wicked acts, Baldwin had even flogged a priest. From divine authorities he demonstrated how great a crime this deed was. Baldwin had also taken certain basilicas away from the priests appointed there and had given them to others without consulting [Col. 0286B] their bishop. Moreover, when Baldwin invaded a certain possession that the king had granted to the Church of Noyon, he retained it by force. He therefore appended canonical and legal chapters concerning such crimes. He also rebuked Baldwin because he had usurped a monastery of monks for himself and had risen against the king with disloyalty and perjury. Although time had long since been granted him regarding these matters and episcopal admonition had been applied, he appeared to evade it by moving from place to place. Therefore, calling him in this letter with paternal admonition, he urged him to profess his amendment. If he did not do so, he should know himself to be excluded from Christian communion, etc.

Likewise, writing to the same man together with his fellow bishops from the synod held at Reims [Col. 0286C] in the year 892 of the Lord’s Incarnation, he accused him of despising both ecclesiastical and secular laws, invading ecclesiastical property and honors not granted to him, casting the fear of God away from himself, and renouncing by his deeds the faith he had promised God in baptism. He had invaded a place belonging to the sacred monastic order and usurped for himself the name of abbot. Therefore, by common decree of the bishops, it had been judged that he should be struck with the anathema of canonical authority. But because he appeared useful both to the Church and to the public interests of the kingdom, the censure of ecclesiastical punishment was for the time suspended, and an interval was reserved for him to reconsider and amend himself. He was entreated, by the mercy of God, to withdraw his mind from this presumption, no longer to provoke God’s anger against himself, and not in some manner to give him [Col. 0286D] occasion, etc. Testimonies from divine authorities followed, also brought forward for his correction. If he refused to heed them, he was to know that he would be separated from all fellowship with the Church and struck with perpetual anathema. He also made public the sentence of excommunication that, if he refused to correct himself, he intended to hurl against him as soon as possible.

To the clergy and people of the Church of Senlis, concerning the election of the pastor they were to set over themselves, he wrote in anger, asking why they had delayed coming to him, or why they had preferred to address him in writing rather than by living voice. He ordered them to hasten to send him persons chosen from their college, mature and suitable both in age and wisdom, who would appear not to deviate in any way from the straight path [Col. 0287A] through favor, hatred, or any pretext of greed [variant: “desire”]. He also wrote to the ministers of the Church of Laon because he had heard that there were contentions among them and that they were holding separate gatherings. Therefore he admonished them, as sons, that if these things were so, they should be entirely cut off; their assembly, however, should be temperate and cheerful, in which each should speak according to his age or the integrity given him by God, with all haughtiness laid aside, etc.

Concerning the establishment and preservation of true concord and charity, he sent them a copy of the letter he had sent to King Odo to obtain for them a canonical election. He exhorted them, gathered together unanimously with the assistance of the Holy Spirit, to strive with the greatest diligence and to implore God’s mercy most earnestly, so that he might deign to be present at their pastoral election.

Visiting the brothers of the monastery of Corbie by letter of admonition [Col. 0287B], he rebuked and severely reproached them for the expulsion of their abbot. They had cast him out with cruel rashness after he had been afflicted by a serious illness, and, when he came to them, had not received him even as a pilgrim or shown him any human kindness. Instead, driving him from their common dwelling, they had shut him away in a most wretched place outside the monastery’s enclosure and had confirmed by common statute that no one might come to visit or console him; nor, when he died, was he to be considered worthy of common burial.

He therefore marveled that such wickedness could have stolen into their minds. Setting before them the apostolic and monastic precepts concerning the obedience owed to superiors, he showed that they had no right to dishonor in such a manner, contrary to every law, an abbot regularly [Col. 0287C] elected and reasonably instituted by the archbishop’s ordination, nor to tear apart and confuse in him the rights and institutions both divine and human. For it was not within their decision or power, whenever they wished, to depose an abbot and appoint another according to the desire of their will.

He also proposed the curse of Ham, who mocked his father’s nakedness, and showed that they were his accomplices in that curse (Genesis 9). Accordingly, placing before them the danger to their order, he admonished them and commanded them by the authority and ministry entrusted to him by God to recover from this obstinacy. They were to honor and love him, the father of their place, as abbot, until, if he recovered and could no longer bear such a burden, he himself might go to the king to make his excuse, so that by the king’s command [Col. 0287D] and the archbishop’s authority another abbot might be substituted in his place.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the matters by which he enlarged the episcopal estate, and on the other good works he performed in the episcopate

Finally, this bishop accomplished many good works in this see of Reims. He enlarged the episcopal estate by obtaining many possessions from kings and various persons, both for the monastery of Avenay and for several others, and he adorned this Church of Reims with various gifts and ornaments.

He also surrounded the city with a new wall—the wall whose construction Ebo had destroyed for the building of the basilica of the Mother of God. He newly established certain fortresses [Col. 0288A], namely Altimont and another near the town of Épernay, which King Odo overthrew because it had revolted from him on account of the elevation of Charles.

He also brought back to the city of Reims the venerable body of the most blessed Remigius from the monastery of Orbais (Omont). In the account of this, many great miracles were displayed (Book I, chapter 21), some of which we have previously related.

At that time, while the Northmen were ravaging the lands of the Franks and laying waste to various places, this bishop kindly received and fatherly cared for many priests, as well as other clerics and monks, who flocked to him from every direction. Among them he received and supported the monks of Saint-Denis, together with the precious body of that martyr and the relics of other saints.

He also arranged for the body of Saint Calixtus to be brought to Reims, after the abbey of that saint had been granted to him or to the Church of Reims [Col. 0288B], and reverently placed it behind the altar of Saint Mary. Beside it he installed the relics of Saint Nicasius and of his holy sister Eutropia, honorably brought from the Church of the titular saint Agricola.

## CHAPTER IX. On Saint Gibrianus and his brothers

At that time the remains of Saint Gibrianus were also brought to the Church of blessed Remigius from the district of Châlons, where he is known to have lived as a pilgrim and to have been buried.

Seven brothers had come into this province from Ireland for the sake of pilgrimage undertaken for the love of Christ: Gibrianus, Helanus, Tresanus, Germanus, Veranus, Abranus, and Petranus, together with their three sisters [Col. 0288C], Francla, Promptia, and Possenna. They chose suitable places for living beside a river called the Marne.

Among them, Gibrianus, a holy priest, chose a certain village called Cossa in which to dwell. There, living soberly, justly, and devoutly for many years, he strove to wage the good battle until the end of his life.

His body is said to have first been buried beside the public road. Later, a small oratory was built over his tomb because certain distinguished miracles had been manifested there. People were accustomed to flock there in great numbers, especially when the feast of his deposition was celebrated. Many cures were attributed to that place; some of them have been written down, while the greater number remain unknown.

Three women, however, are recorded there by name as having received sight [Col. 0288D]. In addition, the hand of a certain Grimoara [variant: “named Grimoart”] was restored with complete health.

Finally, during the reign of King Odo, when the cruelty of the Northmen was raging and devastating the lands of the Franks, the little church of this saint was burned by fire, along with many others in the same district. After its burning, voices of persons singing, though no persons were visible, were frequently heard there; nevertheless, certain lights appeared to burn there at night.

When the fame of such miracles had spread far and wide, the devout count Hadericus [manuscript: Haidericus], led by heavenly love and by veneration for the saint, went to Bishop Rodoardus, bishop of the Church of [Col. 0289A] [the supplied text breaks off here and resumes mid-sentence:] “... are called Condominicati, restored to the bishops’ jurisdiction; he acquired many male and female servants,” and strongly fortified the damaged defenses of the town by renewing its walls with solid masonry and constructing new engines and ditches all around.

He also reduced by forty solidi the customary payment of three hundred solidi that was given each year to the count of Joigny for the fortification of the castle of Apogny. At the same place he planted vines, and at Gy he built a stone house and chapel for the bishops.

At Varzy he acquired very many benefits. He withdrew the Church of Saint Peter from lay control, and likewise freed the Pentecostal offerings, as well as those for the Nativity of the Lord and for the feast of the Virgin’s Assumption, from lay possession; he established them permanently as belonging to the right of the bishops [Col. 0289B]. He planted vines, built an enclosure, and provided male and female servants, houses, cultivated and uncultivated lands.

At Conada, moreover, the bishop of Auxerre lacked an episcopal residence. There he built an excellent house in an excellent manner and decently adorned the chapel of Saint Mary beside it. By his own initiative, though with great labor, he also removed the Church of Saint Laurence from lay hands and assigned it to himself and his successors to possess forever, acquiring many other benefits as well.

At Toucy he built an episcopal residence for the bishops and, through his prudence, acquired many goods there with much labor for the use and benefit of the bishops.

Nor should we have kept silent about the fact that he deserved to obtain from the aforesaid Pope Urban II, at the Council of Nîmes, the monastery of Saint Germanus, which had been taken from our church by the ancient kings of France [Col. 0289C]. It was provided that, by God’s disposition, the bishop of Auxerre should appoint an abbot in that monastery forever. While he lived, he diligently strove, as far as he could and ought, to support and order that church according to the regular discipline.

In the allod of Hildebert, a canon of our church, called Pontigny, at the request and initiative of that same Hildebert he established a monastery of monks living under the Rule of Saint Benedict, and placed there the devout Hugh as its first abbot.

He also raised by his benefactions, as far as he could, the monastery called Fons-Humidus, situated within the territory of the bishopric of Auxerre and built by Girard, a devout man who would later become its abbot.

He established the Church of Saint Peter, situated in the suburb of the city of Auxerre, as belonging to regular canons [Col. 0289D], and deserved to obtain from the lord pope the privilege of this ecclesiastical constitution.

> **Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, forever to the venerable brother Humbald, bishop of Auxerre, and to his canonically appointed successors.**
>
> It is fitting for us, who, although unworthy guardians and heralds of justice, are seen by the Lord’s disposition to have been placed upon the lofty watchtower of the chief apostles Peter and Paul, to give assent to just vows and to lend our ears to just petitions.
>
> Therefore, dearest brother in Christ, Humbald, assenting to your just petitions, we fortify by the authority of the apostolic see the holy Church of Auxerre over which, by God’s authorship, you preside. We decree that everything which your Church of Auxerre is known at present, in the fifteenth indiction, to possess from the ancient times of our predecessors [Col. 0290A], shall always be preserved for you and your successors free and inviolate.
>
> Let no one whatsoever, of whatever dignity or order, dare, against your will or that of your church, to invade, take away, or in any manner withdraw its subjection or your possessions. Rather, let everything remain under the obedience and administration of you and your canonical successors, who live honorably. For it is believed that this was established by the pontiffs of the holy Roman Church, our predecessors, at the petition of blessed [Col. 0290B] Germanus, whose patrimony the parish of Auxerre had been.
>
> If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly attempting rashly to act against this page of our constitution, should be admonished once, twice, or three times and fail to correct the matter by suitable satisfaction, let that person lose the dignity of his power and honor, recognize himself to be guilty before the divine judgment because of the iniquity committed, be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and at the final judgment be subject to strict punishment.
>
> But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who preserve what is just for that place, so that they may receive the fruit of good action and find the rewards of eternal peace before the strict Judge. Amen, amen.

Likewise [Col. 0290C], of the same man to the clergy:

> **Paschal, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the canons of the Church of Auxerre, greeting and apostolic blessing.**
>
> Because our fellow brother Humbald, bishop of your church, acted kindly toward our son Husgerius, your canon, and, with your consent, gave him the dignity of the provostship, we give thanks both to him and to you.
>
> We wish you to know that we desire both him and everything belonging to him to remain under the protection and guardianship of the apostolic see. Therefore, by the authority of this letter, we forbid any ecclesiastical or secular person to presume to disturb this son of ours concerning the benefit of the aforesaid provostship.

Among the other distinctions of his kindly deeds [Col. 0290D], this man of honorable life and praiseworthy in every respect established the Church of Saint Eusebius, where the burial place of our canons and servants is known to be, as belonging to regular canons. He placed there many brothers of approved life under a prior from the abbey, and took care, with the consent of the entire clergy and people, Herveus, bishop of Nevers and a canon of our church, assisting and commending the arrangement, that the prebend of each of our deceased canons should be given to them for one year. Thus the regular canons of Saint Eusebius would celebrate Masses for our dead and perform daily the other offices owed for the dead.

The same prebend—[the supplied source’s transition concerning his predecessor, Bishop Robert, is incomplete]—[Col. 0291A] he, because no one could approach him owing to the enormity of the stench, ended a most wretched life by a pitiable death.

## CHAPTER XI. On the episcopate of Lord Heriveus

Lord Heriveus succeeded in the pontificate of Reims. He too was taken from the king’s court and raised to the episcopate. He was noble by birth, specifically the nephew on his mother’s side of Count Hucbald. Although still young, he was advanced to this honor, with Riculf, bishop of Soissons; Dodilo, bishop of Cambrai; Otgarius, bishop of Amiens; Mancion, bishop of Châlons; Rodulf, bishop of Laon; Otfrid, bishop of Senlis; and the other diocesan bishops giving their consent and confirming the decree of his ordination.

He immediately strove to show himself capable of this high office [Col. 0291B], making himself beloved by all good people and even exemplary to the elderly. He was a kindly lover of the poor, a generous comforter of the religious, and greatly merciful in refreshing the grieving and afflicted. He was especially learned in ecclesiastical chants, outstanding in psalmody, and disciplined by its practice. Cheerful in mind and face, gracious and most gentle, distinguished by every virtue, he was the father of the clergy and the devout protector of the entire people. Slow to anger and swift to mercy, he was a lover of the Churches of God and, with God’s strength, a most valiant defender of the flock entrusted to him.

Finally, he recovered various possessions and estates of the Church that his predecessor had granted to different persons by leases or grants. As he diligently pursued spiritual things, temporal goods flowed abundantly to him [Col. 0291C]; he distributed them with honorable prudence, assigning suitable resources to the servants of the episcopal estate while he himself remained constantly devoted to prayer. Thus the Church’s various granaries and storehouses were filled with abundant goods; all the estates were administered both reasonably and mercifully; and he also repaired or established certain towns.

## CHAPTER XII. On the return of blessed Remigius to his monastery

This bishop decided to transfer the body of blessed Remigius, which had until then been kept in the city behind the altar of the Mother of God in the principal church, to the basilica of that saint’s burial (in the year 901, on the fourth day before the Kalends of January).

It was winter, and King Charles and several of his nobles [Col. 0291D] had gathered in this city to celebrate the solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity. Since during those days there was an excessive amount of mud everywhere and all around because of the heavy rains, many began to complain about how they would be able to carry that holy body to its appointed place.

It happened that, during the night after the feast of the Holy Innocents, on the following day being the day appointed for completing this work, the north wind suddenly arose at midnight and the entire mass of mud immediately froze. Thus, when the moisture of the earth and mud had dried, the sacred limbs of the bishop could be carried over the suddenly formed surface of ice with dry and unobstructed footsteps.

When they had gone outside the city to the place from which the monastery was then to be approached directly [Col. 0292A], a certain lame man, about whom we have already spoken above, was raised by divine power and restored to health.

While a great crowd was present there, with throngs converging from every direction, the scabbards of Richard, prince of Burgundy, decorated with gold and beautifully adorned with gems, were cut from his belt because of the crush of the procession. A certain merchant bought them and carried them through various markets, but could not sell them anywhere.
