After a year he brought them back to the same prince in Burgundy [manuscript: “in Burgundy”], and the prince received them with thanksgiving and the blessing of Saint Remigius.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the repair of the castle of Mouson and certain other fortifications and churches

[Col. 0292B] This bishop fortified the castle of Mouson (Mouson) by repairing its walls. He also rebuilt from the foundations the church there that had been destroyed and dedicated it, as it had formerly been, in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God. There he placed the bones of Saint Victor, which had been found not far from that castle.

He also established and strengthened a fortification at Coucy (Coucy), in a secure location. Likewise, he built another fortification at Épernay, on the river Marne.

He caused several churches that had been destroyed during the persecution of the Northmen to be restored and consecrated. In the Vosges, within the estate of blessed Remigius, he also built a church [Col. 0292C] and, with the consent of the bishop of Mainz, dedicated it after placing there the relics of that same saint.

At Reims he consecrated a church built by the city’s canons outside the city wall in honor of Saint Denis. There he deposited for safekeeping the remains of the holy bishop Rigobert and of Saint Theodulf the abbot.

He also cleansed and adorned the crypt beneath the seat of the principal church, which had long remained filled with earth, and consecrated it in honor of that holy bishop, who is said to have been accustomed to pour out his prayers to God there in secret.

He richly adorned the Church of Reims with many gifts, illuminating it with silver crowns and lamps, both gold and silver. He also enriched it with other vessels of these two precious metals and with jeweled objects [variant: “gems”]. Moreover, he constructed and dedicated an altar in the middle of the choir in honor of the Holy Trinity [Col. 0292D] and surrounded it with panels covered in silver.

He covered the greater cross with gold and adorned it suitably with gems and the most holy relics. He also decorated the venerable church with very many silk ornaments.

To me and to the others—clerics who were canons, monks, nuns, and all who sought him for various necessities—he gave many generous benefits.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the synodal councils held, the conversion of the Northmen, and the expedition against the Hungarians

Finally, he often held synodal assemblies with the fellow bishops of his diocese. In them he dealt prudently and suitably with the peace and religion of God’s holy Church and with the condition of the Frankish kingdom [Col. 0293A].

He also labored greatly for the pacification and conversion of the Northmen. At length, after the war that Count Robert of Chartres waged against them, they accepted the faith of Christ, receiving certain coastal districts together with Rouen, which they had almost entirely destroyed, and the other territories subject to it.

At the request of Witton, then bishop of Rouen, he compiled from various authorities of the holy Fathers thirty-three chapters concerning how those Northmen ought to be treated and entrusted them to that archbishop. Moreover, he took care to consult the Roman pontiff concerning this matter. In response to the pontiff’s directives, he did not cease to set forth what ought to be done regarding the conversion of that people.

When the Hungarians were ravaging the kingdom of Lotharingia [Col. 0293B], while Charles was summoning the nobles of the Franks to assist him against that people, this bishop alone of all the kingdom’s leading men came to the king with only his own forces for the defense of God’s Church, bringing with him, as is reported, fifteen hundred armed men.

## CHAPTER XV. On the support given to King Charles when abandoned by his own men

In the following year (920), when nearly all the nobles of the Franks had defected from their king Charles at the city of Soissons because of his counselor Haganon—whom Charles had chosen from among men of modest rank, heard, and honored above all the princes—and had completely abandoned him, this bishop, always faithful, devout, and steadfast in dangers, fearlessly received the king from that place and led him to his camp.

From there he brought him with him to the city of Reims and followed and accompanied him for almost seven months, until he restored to him his counts and the kingdom itself.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the excommunication and absolution of Count Erlebald

This bishop excommunicated Erlebald, count of the district of Castrum, because he had invaded land belonging to the episcopal estate of Reims and had built a fortification there over the Meuse, from which he repeatedly inflicted harm on the Church’s household. Moreover, he had secretly attacked the castle of Altimont.

Since he nevertheless did not cease from the evils he had begun, the archbishop proceeded with his men to capture the fortification he had built, which he called Masières (Masières-sur-la-Meuse). After besieging it for almost four weeks, he captured it when Erlebald finally abandoned it, placed guards there, and returned to Reims.

Erlebald, however, went to the king, who was then staying in the district of Worms against Henry, the prince beyond the Rhine. There he was killed by the king’s enemies, who unexpectedly attacked him.

Nevertheless, afterward, at a synod that the same lord archbishop held with his diocesans at Trosly, he absolved him from the bond of excommunication, at the king’s intervention and earnest request.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the death of Bishop Heriveus

Finally, as discord increased between King Charles and Robert, when nearly all the nobles of the kingdom had gathered at Saint Remigius to establish Robert as king, the same archbishop, overcome by illness, died. This occurred on the third day after Robert had become king and on the fourth day before he completed the twenty-second year of his episcopate.

It happened that on the very day of his death several bishops who had come to the city entered Reims. They celebrated his funeral with fitting rites and, amid the greatest mourning of his own people and of outsiders alike, committed him to a worthy burial.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the succession of Bishop Seulfus

Seulfus succeeded this bishop. At that time he was serving this city in the office of archdeacon. He was sufficiently instructed in both ecclesiastical and secular disciplines, and had studied the liberal arts under Remigius, his teacher at Auxerre.

After he had been ordained bishop with the consent and command of King Robert by Abbo of Soissons and the other bishops of the province of Reims, Odo, once the brother of Archbishop Heriveus, and Heriveus, his nephew, were brought before the same bishop. They were accused of failing to keep the fidelity they had promised him.

Because they refused either to come before that bishop to render an account or to decide the matter by single combat with their accusers, the Church’s possessions, which they had held from that episcopal estate, were taken from them. The two men were led by Count Heribert to King Robert. They were held under guard until King Robert’s death: Odo with Heribert himself, and Heriveus at Paris [Col. 0294C].

It is reported that the archbishop and his counselors had made an agreement with Count Heribert concerning the election of his son to this see in exchange for the expulsion of the aforesaid men.

Finally, this bishop sent legates of the Church to Rome to obtain Pope John’s consent (John X) to his ordination. From the pope he received the pallium and letters of privilege for this see.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the synod he held, his other acts, and his end

This bishop also held a synod (924) at the village of Trosly with the bishops of the diocese of Reims, at which several counts were also present. At it, Count Isaac came to make satisfaction for the evil acts he had committed against the Church of Cambrai: he had seized by deceitful invasion and burned a certain castle belonging to Bishop Stephen of that city.

For this crime he was placed under bond at the synod and made peace with the aforesaid Bishop Stephen for one hundred pounds of silver, through the efforts of Count Heribert and the other counts of France who were present.

This bishop surrounded the monastery of Saint Remigius with a wall, together with the ruined churches and houses lying around it, and established a fortress there. He repaired the episcopal residence with chambers and adorned it with paintings.

He also made a large golden chalice set with gems, weighing ten pounds, in honor of the Mother of God, and prepared certain other ornaments for the church.

He began to cover the ciborium over the altar of Saint Mary with silver [Col. 0295A], but, overtaken by death, could not complete the work.

It is reported that he ended his life after being given poison by the household servants or retainers of Count Heribert.

## CHAPTER XX. On the election of Hugh, Heribert’s son

Soon after his death (925), Count Heribert came to Reims and summoned Abbo, bishop of Soissons, and Bovo, bishop of Châlons. Joining them to himself and deliberating about the election of a ruler for this Church of Reims, he compelled both clerics and laymen to follow his will.

Therefore, following his counsel, lest the bishopric be divided among outsiders, they elected his son, named Hugh, who was extremely young and had not yet completed five years.

After this had been done, they hurried to the king [Col. 0295B] to obtain his authority. When King Rodulf learned of the election, he entrusted the bishopric of Reims to Heribert, to be administered and governed by him according to the standard of equity.

He also hastened to send the Church’s legates to Rome with Bishop Abbo. They carried with them the decree of this election and sought the pope’s consent to it.

Accordingly, Pope John, with Bishop Abbo intervening, gave his consent to their petition and entrusted the episcopal estate of Reims to Bishop Abbo, decreeing that he should conduct and settle there the matters belonging to episcopal administration.

Having obtained power over the episcopal estate of Reims, Count Heribert unjustly deprived both me—for I had not been present at the election described above—and several others, clerics and laymen, of the benefits of ecclesiastical possessions with which we appeared to have been rewarded by earlier bishops in return for our service. He distributed these possessions according to the pleasure of his will to whomever he wished.

Not long afterward, when a disturbance arose among the clerics within the canons’ enclosure, certain armed soldiers arrived, and two clerics were killed there, one of whom was a deacon and the other was regarded as a subdeacon.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the invasion of the Hungarians and the discord between King Rodulf and Count Heribert

In 926, when the Hungarians had crossed the Rhine and were raging through the district of Voncq with devastation and fires, the body of Saint Remigius and the relics of certain other saints were carried away from their places in Reims by those responsible for them, because of this fear.

In the following year discord arose between King Rodulf and Count Heribert over the county of Laon, which Heribert requested for his son Odo, while the king had granted it to Rotger, son of Count Rotger.

On a certain Sunday in March, fiery battle-lines were seen in the sky over Reims. A plague immediately followed this sign, resembling fever and cough; as the mortality continued, it raged among all the peoples of Germany and Gaul.

Count Heribert sent his legates across the Rhine to Henry. Summoned by Henry through them to meet him, he hastened there with Hugh, son of Robert. After making a pact with each other, they honored Henry with gifts, and were themselves honored by him.

A synod of six bishops of the diocese of Reims was held at Trosly (the Trosly synod of 927), convened at the command of Count Heribert, though King Rodulf opposed it.

After the synod, Heribert released Charles from the custody in which he had held him and led him to Saint-Quentin. From there he sought a meeting with the Northmen together with Charles. There William, son of Rollo, prince of the Northmen, commended himself to Charles and confirmed his friendship with Heribert.

Then Count Heribert came to Reims with Charles and sent a letter to Pope John in Rome, informing him of Charles’s restoration and honor, and stating that, as John had commanded him—even under threat of excommunication—he would strive with all his strength on Charles’s behalf.

When the messenger who had carried the letter returned, he announced that Pope John was being held confined in custody by Wido, King Hugh’s brother.

Count Heribert, having gained possession of Laon, then went to meet the Northmen at their assembly and made peace with them. His son Odo, whom Rollo held as a hostage, was not returned to him until his father, Heribert, committed himself to Charles, together with several other counts and bishops of France.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the introduction of Bishop Odalric of Aix at Reims and the placing of King Charles under guard

At approximately the same time, Bishop Odalric of Aix, who had withdrawn from his see because of the persecution of the Saracens, was received into the Church of Reims by Count Heribert, solely to celebrate episcopal functions in place of Hugh, the count’s son, who was still a child. The bishop was granted the abbey of Saint Timothy, together with only one cleric’s prebend.

Counts Hugh and Heribert went to meet Henry. After returning from there, they went to meet King Rodulf, and Heribert again committed himself to him, while Charles was once more placed under guard.

King Rodulf came to Reims, where Charles was being held. He made peace with him, humbling himself in his presence and restoring to him the fiscal estate of Attigny. He also honored the king with certain royal gifts.

Count Heribert captured the castle of Vitry (929), belonging to Boso, the brother of King Rodulf. Then, together with Hugh, he besieged Montreuil, the fortification of Count Erluin situated beside the sea. After finally receiving hostages, he withdrew from the siege.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the discord that arose between Counts Hugh and Heribert and King Rodulf
Not long afterward, discord arose between those same counts, namely Hugh and Heribert, when Hugh received Erluin together with his lands, while Heribert received Hilduin and Arnald, who had belonged to Hugh. From this, various movements of war were stirred up throughout Francia between Hugh and Heribert. For this reason King Rudolph, coming from Burgundy, brought about peace between them and Boson, though only after much labor at various assemblies; and Heribert restored Vitry to Boson. [Col. 0297A] After peace had been maintained for a few days, Heribert received Ansellus, Boson’s dependent who was guarding the aforementioned castle, together with the castle itself, and granted him Codiciacum, the township of Saint Remigius, along with other land. Not long afterward, Boson’s loyal men, through the treachery of the townsmen, recovered Vitry and seized Mouzon by a ruse. But when Heribert, summoned by some people of Mouzon, arrived unexpectedly, crossed the Meuse at unanticipated fords, and entered the town through a gate secretly opened by the citizens, he captured on the spot all of Boson’s soldiers who were stationed there to guard the place. At the same time, shortly before the Nativity of the Lord, a great light was seen at Rheims, below and around the church of Saint Mary, appearing from the northern and eastern sides shortly before daybreak and seeming to pass across toward the southern side. In the year after [Col. 0297B] this, Count Heribert deserted King Rudolph, and his soldiers, setting out from the city of Rheims, captured and destroyed a certain castle of Hugh’s situated on the Vesle, called Braine (Braine-sur-Vesle), which Hugh had taken from the bishop of Rouen.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the ordination of Lord Artold, bishop.

King Rudolph sent a letter to Rheims to the clergy and people, for the purpose of holding an election of a bishop. They replied that they could not do this without preserving their own elected candidate and maintaining the election they had made. Meanwhile Count Heribert went to Henry and submitted himself to him, while the armies of the king and of Hugh ravaged the countryside of Rheims and Laon. After the city of Rheims had been besieged, the king finally gained possession of it in the third [Col. 0297C] week of the siege, when the soldiers of the church opened the gates to him. Having therefore joined to himself several bishops from Francia and Burgundy, he had a certain Artold, a monk from the monastery of Saint Remigius, ordained bishop in this see. The king then proceeded to Laon and besieged Heribert there. After resisting for some time, Heribert at last requested a place through which he might leave. Having obtained it, he withdrew from Laon, leaving his wife in the fortress that he himself had built inside the same stronghold; later, the king required greater effort and delay to capture it (933).

A year after his ordination, Bishop Artold received the pallium sent to him through legates of the Church of Rheims by Pope John (John XI), son of Maria, who was also called Marozia, or by Alberic, the patrician and brother of that pope. Alberic held his brother John [Col. 0297D] in his power and kept their aforementioned mother confined in custody; he had also driven King Hugh out of Rome. While King Rudolph was besieging Heribert’s stronghold, called the Castle of Theodoric, and several prelates of Francia and Burgundy had gathered for this siege, a synod was apparently held there (Theodoric’s, at the Castle), presided over by Teutilo, bishop of Tours, together with Artold of Rheims. At that time he ordained Hildegarius bishop of Beauvais. In the same year he consecrated Fulbert bishop of the city of Cambrai.

## CHAPTER XXV. On signs seen at Rheims and the illnesses that followed.

In the following year (934), fiery battle-lines and certain darts were seen moving through the sky at Rheims. A fiery serpent was also seen being carried rapidly through the sky; soon afterward, a pestilence afflicted human bodies with various illnesses. In the year following that one (935), a synod of seven bishops convened at Saint Macra at the summons of Bishop Artold. At it, plunderers and those who had seized ecclesiastical property were summoned to make satisfaction.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the reception of Louis after the death of King Rudolph.

Finally, in the following year (936), after King Rudolph had died, Count Hugh sent across the sea to summon Louis, son of Charles (Louis, son of Charles the Simple), whom his maternal uncle, King Æthelstan, was raising. After receiving an oath from the envoys of the Franks, Æthelstan sent him to Francia. Hugh and the other nobles of the Franks went out to receive him and, as soon as he had come ashore, submitted themselves to him on the very sands of the coast near Boulogne, as had been agreed on both sides. From there he was led to Laon and was endowed with royal blessing, anointed, and crowned by Archbishop Artold in the presence of the leading men of the kingdom and more than twenty bishops.

The bishopric of Laon was also given to Rudolph, a priest of that place unanimously elected by its citizens; the aforementioned archbishop likewise ordained him. In the other sees of the diocese of Rheims also, excepting those of Châlons and Amiens, he ordained various bishops. After Heribert had again made peace with Hugh (936), men of that same Count Heribert, through the treachery of a certain Wicpert, captured a castle of the Church of Rheims, called Causostis, situated on the River Marne and built by Bishop Artold, [Col. 0298C] and seized Ragembert, Artold’s cousin, who was in charge of the fortress. They repeatedly ravaged the surrounding estates belonging to the church.

Meanwhile King Louis, summoned by Bishop Artold, came to Laon and besieged the new fortress recently erected there by Heribert. After many siege engines had been tried against the wall, and after it had finally been undermined and brought down, he captured it by a great assault. He also recovered by warfare the castle of Corbeny, which his father had given to Saint Remigius and which the monks of that monastery had entrusted to him, from Heribert’s subjects. The men of Heribert who were captured inside it he permitted, at the request of Bishop Artold, to depart safely to their own people. [Col. 0298D]

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the excommunication of Count Heribert.

(939.) Finally, Bishop Artold, after consulting with certain other bishops, excommunicated Heribert, who had seized and occupied certain towns and estates belonging to the Church of Rheims, and did so even in the presence of the king (940). After this, King Louis granted Bishop Artold—and through him the Church of Rheims—by a royal charter, the mint of the city of Rheims, to possess in perpetual right. He also granted the whole county of Rheims to the same church.

Bishop Artold besieged the stronghold of Causostis. On the fifth day, when King Louis arrived there, those who were inside surrendered and abandoned it. [Col. 0299A] Not long afterward, it was utterly overturned and dismantled by those who had taken possession of it. Hugh’s envoys came to the king, and the king worked to establish peace between Bishop Artold and Heribert through them. Then he proceeded with Bishop Artold to a certain castle held on the River Marne by Heriveus, nephew of Heriveus, formerly archbishop; from there he was also ravaging the villages situated all around the bishopric of Rheims. Without delay, after receiving hostages from Heriveus himself, the king returned to Rheims. On the following day he went to Saint Remigius and entrusted himself to the intercession of that saint, promising to give as a pledge a pound of silver every year. He also gave the monks of that place a charter of immunity concerning the same castle.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the expulsion of Lord Artold from the city of Rheims.

[Col. 0299B]

Hugh, called the Great, prince and son of Rothert, having joined to himself certain bishops from both Francia and Burgundy, together with Count Heribert and William, prince of the Normans, besieged the city of Rheims. On the sixth day of the siege, almost the entire military force abandoned Bishop Artold and went over to Heribert. Count Heribert then entered the city. Bishop Artold, having gone to Saint Remigius at the summons of the leading bishops, was persuaded—or terrified by the princes of the bishopric—into renouncing the administration and authority of the see. The abbey of Saint Basolus and the monastery of Avenay were granted to him, and he withdrew to Saint Basolus to reside there, after spending eight years [Col. 0299C] and seven months [manuscript: six] in the episcopate.

Hugh and Heribert, after conferring with certain Lotharingians, set out with William to besiege Laon. They left at Rheims Hugh the deacon, Heribert’s son, who had long before been summoned to the episcopate of that city. In the third month after his return, he was ordained priest by Wido, bishop of Soissons. After his election he had completed fifteen years, which he had spent at Auxerre occupied with the study of letters, in the household of Wido, bishop of that city, by whom he had also been ordained deacon. He had received the other lower orders at Rheims from Abbo, bishop of Soissons.

After King Louis returned from Burgundy, Bishop Artold left the monastery of Saint Basolus and went to the same king [Col. 0299D] with certain relatives of his, from whom Count Heribert had taken the ecclesiastical benefices they held. He also took from me the church of the village of Cormicy, together with the land belonging to the benefice that I held at that time.

Finally, as I was intending to visit the tomb of Saint Martin for the sake of prayer, he detained me. Certain people secretly accused me before him of intending to go away for the harm of himself or his son, and because I refused to entrust myself to our elected candidate, not knowing whether it pleased God that he should become our bishop. Thus, for a full five months, by order of the count, I was held among our brothers, partly under free custody.

[Col. 0300A] It happened, however, through the intercession of my lady, the blessed Mother of God, that on the very day of the Conception (25 March) and Passion (27 March) of our Lord Jesus Christ I was released from custody. On the third day, namely the sixth day before the Kalends of April, on which the Lord rose from the dead, I left and proceeded with our aforementioned elected candidate to the city of Soissons.

There the bishops of this diocese, together with the princes Hugh and Heribert (Synod of Soissons, 941), assembled and discussed what ought to be done concerning the episcopal ordination of this Hugh. They decided that he should be ordained, after certain sons of the Church of Rheims—both clerics and laymen—had done penance. His supporters asserted that Artold had not been elected at all, but had been introduced by force, and that he had renounced [Col. 0300B] episcopal authority.

There Prince Hugh then took me by the hand [manuscript: hands] and entrusted me to this Hugh, his nephew, for the purpose of doing me good. Indeed, he gave me the church of Saint Mary situated at Colrido, restored to me the land that his father had taken from me, and added another tract in the aforementioned village.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the evils that followed afterward.

Without delay, the bishops came from the aforementioned assembly to the city of Rheims and elevated our aforesaid elected candidate to the archiepiscopal dignity in the church of Saint Remigius.

At about the same time, the monastery of Saint Theodoric was made illustrious by several miracles, some of which we have already related above (Book I, [Col. 0300C] final chapter), where we made mention of that blessed man. From the church of Saint Mary at Rheims, a large cross that Lord Heriveus, the archbishop, had covered with gold and adorned with gems was stolen by thieves at night—lovers, that is, of darkness. After it had been sought for a long time, part of its gold and gems was finally recovered a year later from the thieves, who had been fined. From this gold the bishop afterward had a chalice made in honor of the Mother of God, adding a certain quantity from his own resources as well.

While Hugh and Heribert were jointly besieging Laon, King Louis came into the district of Port after gathering with him as many men as he could from every quarter. When Hugh and Heribert heard that the king was approaching them, they abandoned the siege and hurried against him. Attacking the king’s army unexpectedly, they struck down some and put the rest to flight. The king himself, led away by his men with only a few companions and forced to extricate himself from the battle, barely escaped, accompanied by Bishop Artold and Count Rotger.

Bishop Artold, having lost the property he had possessed there, went to Hugh and Heribert, brought by his friends. After the abbeys of Saint Basolus and Avenay, together with the estate of Vendeuvre [Vendeure], had been restored to him, and peace had been made with Bishop Hugh, he went to Saint Basolus to live there.

In the following year (942), certain traitors were discovered at Rheims and put to death; others, deprived of their property belonging to the church, were driven from the city. The envoys of the Church of Rheims returned from Rome bearing the pallium for Archbishop Hugh, sent by Pope Stephen [Col. 0301A] (Stephen VIII). Along with them came an embassy to the leading men of the kingdom, instructing them to receive King Louis and then to send their own envoys to Rome.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the seizure of the castle of Altimont and of Mouzon, and the death of Heribert.

In the year after that (943), Bishop Artold left the monastery of Saint Basolus and went to the king. The king promised him that he would restore to him the bishopric of Rheims. Artold then took with him his brothers and certain others who had been expelled from the bishopric of Rheims, and seized the castle of Altimont.

King Louis also attacked Mouzon with them, but was repulsed by the loyal men of Bishop Hugh, several of his own men being killed. Nevertheless, he advanced upon certain suburban houses [Col. 0301B] of that castle.

Meanwhile, after Count Heribert died, frequent negotiations took place between the king and Prince Hugh concerning the reception of Heribert’s sons. The king first received Archbishop Hugh, through the mediation of Duke Otto of Lotharingia and Bishop Adalbero, with Duke Hugh especially insisting on the matter, on the condition that the abbeys which Artold had left when he went to the king should be restored to Bishop Artold, that another bishopric should also be provided for him, and that the honors which his brothers and relatives had held from the bishopric of Rheims should be restored to them. Later the other sons of Count Heribert were also received by the king.

Finally, Bishop Hugh captured and burned the castle of Ambly, which Robert and Rudolph [Col. 0301C]—brothers who had been expelled from Rheims—held and from which they carried out plundering throughout the bishopric of Rheims. The aforementioned archbishop also besieged the stronghold of Altimont, which Dodo, Bishop Artold’s brother, held. At last, after taking Dodo’s young son as a hostage, he withdrew, also at the king’s command.

In the following year (944), the king’s soldiers ravaged the bishopric of Rheims. Heribert’s sons ravaged the abbey of Saint Crispin, while Bagenold ravaged the abbey of Saint Medard. Thus each side raged through the other’s possessions with robbery and plunder.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the siege of the city of Rheims by King Louis’s army.

[Col. 0301D] In the year after this (945), which was the fifth year of this bishop’s episcopate, King Louis, having gathered a Norman army with him, ravaged the district of Vermandois. Taking with them Erluin and part of Arnulf’s soldiers, as well as Bishop Artold with those who had long before been expelled from Rheims, and also Count Bernard and his nephew Theodoric, they surrounded the city of Rheims.

The crops all around were devastated, the villages plundered and partly burned, and many churches broken into. Whenever fighting took place at the gates or around the wall, many on both sides were wounded, and some were also killed. Finally, the aforementioned Duke Hugh routed the Normans, who had entered his territory, in a considerable slaughter and drove them from his borders.

After this he sent certain hostages to the king at Rheims, so that Ragenold might meet him on the king’s behalf for a conference. When Ragenold had departed, Hugh negotiated with him that the king should receive hostages from Archbishop Hugh and withdraw from the siege of Rheims, provided that the same prelate, at a designated assembly, would come to give an account of everything that the king might demand from him. When these terms had been granted to him, the king withdrew from the siege on the fifteenth day after the city had been besieged. Not long afterward, that same king was captured by the Normans and detained at Rouen.

Bishop Hugh, while besieging the castle of Altimont, received it after nearly seven weeks of siege, when Dodo, Lord Artold’s brother, surrendered it to him. The condition was that, after receiving Dodo’s son and his brother’s son, the bishop would grant them the land of their fathers.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the restoration of the rule in the monastery of Saint Remigius and the appointment of Abbot Hincmar.

[Col. 0302B]

Finally, this bishop summoned Ercambold, abbot of the monastery of Saint Benedict, and labored to restore the monastic rule in the monastery of Saint Remigius, appointing Hincmar, a monk of that place, as abbot.

Queen Gerberga had recently sent an embassy to her brother, King Otto, requesting his assistance against Prince Hugh, to whom she had restored Laon, that he might recover King Louis, whom Hugh had detained in custody after receiving him from the Normans (946). Otto gathered the greatest army from all his kingdoms and came to Francia, bringing with him Conrad, king of Cisalpine [Col. 0302C] Gaul. King Louis went out to meet them and was received by them with considerable friendliness and honor.

Thus they came together to Laon and, after considering the strength of the castle, turned away from it and attacked the city of Rheims. Surrounding it with a siege, they enclosed it with a vast army.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the repulse of Bishop Hugh.

Bishop Hugh, seeing that he could not endure the siege or resist so great a multitude, consulted certain princes who appeared to be his friends: namely Arnulf, who had his sister as wife, and Wido [manuscript: Uddo; below, Uddo’s], because he had his aunt as wife, and also [Col. 0302D] Herimann [manuscript: Hermann], Wido’s brother. He asked them what he ought to do.

They gave him this advice: that he should leave with his men and abandon the city, because the kings had determined to expel them by every means, and they could not intervene on his behalf with the kings to prevent his eyes from being torn out if the city happened to be captured by force.

After receiving this advice and communicating it to his men, he left on the third day of the siege with nearly all the soldiers who were then with him. Thus the kings entered with the bishops and princes, and caused Lord Artold, the prelate who had previously been expelled, to be enthroned again. Robert, archbishop of Trier, and Frederick of Mainz took him by both hands and restored him to that see.

Then, leaving Queen Gerberga [Col. 0303A] at Rheims, the kings themselves entered Hugh’s territory with their armies and crushed it with severe ravaging. They also traversed the territory of the Normans, devastating every place, and thereafter returned to their own lands, each to his own destination.

In the following year (947), King Louis besieged the castle of Mouzon, which Hugh, expelled from Rheims, held. But, accomplishing nothing according to his wishes, and after the Lotharingians who were with him finally withdrew after a month, he himself returned to Rheims.

When King Louis had set out to King Otto to celebrate Easter, Prince Hugh, rashly influenced by certain people, attacked the city of Rheims with Bishop Hugh, as though he would soon capture it. But the attempt failed: the soldiers of the king and of Bishop Artold resisted, and on the eighth day after their arrival they withdrew in confusion.

After the death of Derald, bishop of Amiens, a certain Tetbald, archdeacon of the Church of Soissons, was ordained bishop of Amiens by Hugh. At the assembly of the legal hearing of Kings Louis and Otto, gathered on the River Cher, the bishops heard the matter of the dispute between Aldo and Hugh, the prelates of the Church of Rheims. Since no synod had then been assembled, however, the dispute could not be settled. It was announced that a synod would be held around the middle of November.

Meanwhile the see of Rheims was granted to Artold, while Hugh was permitted to remain at Mouzon. Heriveus, nephew of Archbishop Heriveus, possessed a fortress that he had built on this side of the River Marne, and he ravaged the villages situated all around in the bishopric of Rheims. He was excommunicated by Bishop Artold because of the property of the church that he had seized.

One day Count Ragenold and the brothers of Bishop Artold, with certain soldiers of the church, went out against his plunderers and put the raiders to flight. When Heriveus heard this, he left his fortress with the soldiers he had with him, armed for battle, and came against our men. He engaged them and was killed, along with some of his men; all the rest were put to flight, while several on both sides were wounded. The victors carried his body to Rheims.

Bishop Hugh took with him Theobald of Montaigu, his sister’s husband, and certain others from among the raiders, and came to the villages adjoining Rheims at the time of the vintage. They gathered nearly all the wine from there and carried it away into various districts.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the synod held at Verdun.

A synod was afterward held at Verdun (947), presided over by Robert, bishop of Trier, together with Artold of Rheims, Odalric of Aix, Adalbero of Metz, Gozlin of Toul, Hildebold [manuscript: Hildebaldo] the Transrhenish, and Israel the Breton. Also present were Bruno, abbot and brother of King Otto, as well as the abbots Agenold and Odilo, with several others.

Hugh was summoned to it, but, although two bishops were sent to escort him, he refused to come. The entire synod, however, decreed that the bishopric should be governed by Artold of Rheims. [Col. 0304A] A synod was therefore announced, and it met in the church of Saint Peter in sight of Mouzon, from the dioceses of Trier and Rheims.

When Bishop Hugh came there and spoke with Archbishop Robert, he refused to enter the synod. He sent certain letters in the name of Pope Agapitus (Agapitus II) to the bishops through his cleric, who had brought them from Rome. They contained no canonical authority, but merely commanded that the bishopric of Rheims be restored to Hugh.

After these letters had been read, the bishops replied that it was neither worthy nor fitting for them to disregard the mandate of the apostolic legation, which Archbishop Robert had previously received in the presence of kings and bishops, when it was delivered by Frederick, bishop of Mainz, because of these letters presented by the schemer against and rival of Bishop Artold. Rather, what they had begun in accordance with the canons should be dealt with canonically.

They therefore ordered the reading of chapter 19 of the Council of Carthage, concerning the accused and the accuser. After it had been read, it was judged, according to the determination of this chapter, that while Artold retained communion and the diocese of Rheims, Hugh—who had already twice refused to come when summoned to synods—should abstain from communion and from governing the bishopric of Rheims until he should appear at a universal synod to clear himself.

The bishops immediately had this chapter written out on parchment in their presence, adding this decision of theirs, and sent it to Hugh. Two days later he sent the same document back to Bishop Robert, replying [Col. 0304C] in these words that he would in no way obey their judgment.

Meanwhile letters of appeal from Bishop Artold were sent to the Roman see. Lord Pope Agapitus therefore sent his legate, Bishop Marinus, to King Otto in order to summon and assemble a general synod. The pope’s own letters were also sent from the city to certain bishops individually, calling them to the same synod.

Finally, when the synod had assembled in the palace at Ingelheim (948, 7 June), the following matters were read out before the kings and bishops:

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the synod assembled at Ingelheim and the excommunication of Bishop Hugh. The course of the dispute conducted between Bishops Artold and Hugh.

[Col. 0304D]

To Lord Marinus, vicar of the holy Roman and apostolic see, and to the entire holy synod assembled at Ingelheim: Artold, by the favor of the divine mercy, bishop of Rheims.

Lord Pope Agapitus sent letters to us and to the other bishops of our diocese, in which he commanded us to make every effort to assemble at this council of your holiness, instructed concerning everything, so that the truth of the misery of our see, which we suffer, might be made manifest before your holiness.

For this reason we consider it useful to disclose to your prudence how the matter that began this dispute, which is still being most miserably contested between Hugh and me, first arose.

After Archbishop Heriveus had died, we elected Seulf, who at that time held the office of archdeacon of our city, to the episcopate of the same see. After he had been ordained bishop (see above, chapter 18), he took zeal against the relatives of his predecessor. Since he was unable to drive them from their position by himself, he formed a plan with certain laymen, his advisers, and sought the friendship of Count Heribert. He obtained it through an oath administered by those same advisers, on the following condition: after Seulf’s death, the soldiers of the church were not to seek the election of a bishop in any way without Heribert’s counsel; and the count, for his part, was to separate the brother of Bishop Heriveus and his nephews from participation in the property of the bishopric of Rheims.

After these arrangements had been made, the same relatives of Bishop Heriveus were accused by Seulf’s advisers [Col. 0305B] of disloyalty to their lord. Count Heribert was summoned with many of his men, and they were ordered to come before them to give an account. Because they refused to engage in single combat against those by whom they had been accused, their property, which they held from the bishop, was taken from them, and they were arrested and led by Count Heribert to King Robert. The king kept them in custody until his own death.

Finally, in the third year of his episcopate, Seulf died—many assert that he was poisoned by Heribert’s household. Count Heribert immediately went to the city of Rheims and had the soldiers of the church, together with certain clerics, attend his council concerning the election of a rector, as had been sworn. With them he went to King Rudolph in Burgundy and obtained from him that the same bishopric should be entrusted to him, on the condition that he grant and preserve the honor due to both clerics and laymen, do no one an injustice, and govern the bishopric according to equal right until he could present to the same king a cleric capable of being duly ordained to carry out the episcopal ministry.

When the count returned to the same city, he divided the property of the bishopric among his supporters as he pleased, took it away from the others, and, without any judgment or law, stripped those whom he wished of their possessions or drove them from the city. Finally, receiving Odalric, bishop of Aix, in the same city, he ordered him to celebrate the episcopal ministry there.

Thus for six years and more he claimed the same bishopric as his own dominion, treating it according to his personal will and sitting in the bishop’s seat—both he himself and his wife—until, in the seventh year, certain disputes arose between him and King Rudolph and Count Hugh. King Rudolph, together with Hugh and his brother Boson, and many others, both bishops and counts, besieged the city of Rheims. The bishops were incensed against him and complained that, contrary to the authorities of divine law, he had allowed this city to remain without a shepherd for so long.

Moved by their complaints, the king admonished the clergy and people concerning the election of a shepherd, giving them permission to act for the honor of God and their loyalty to him. [Col. 0306A] Thus, when all the clerics and laymen who were outside the siege agreed, and many of those who were shut inside also supported the same decision, my person was elected, undertaking this office more as a burden than as an honor.

At last, when both the soldiers and the citizens opened the gates of the city to King Rudolph, and the eighteen bishops who were present gave me the episcopal blessing, and the whole clergy and the remaining citizens received my humility, I was enthroned there by the bishops of our diocese. As God granted, I administered the ministry entrusted to me for nearly nine years, ordaining eight bishops throughout the diocese and many clerics in the bishopric, as seemed appropriate.

Then, in the ninth year afterward, after I had blessed King Louis—with Hugh and all the leading men of the kingdom supporting him—and Queen Gerberga, and had anointed them with the sacred chrism, Count Hugh, provoked by anger because I was unwilling to agree or join myself to him in the king’s disloyalty, besieged the city of Rheims, bringing with him Count Heribert and William, prince of the Normans.

Not long afterward—on the sixth day of the siege—I was abandoned by nearly the entire body of the lay military force. Thus, abandoned by them, I was compelled to go out to Hugh and Heribert. They constrained and terrified me, forcing me to renounce the administration of the bishopric (above, chapter 27), and, driving me out in this way, established me to live in the monastery of Saint Basolus. They brought into the city Hugh, Heribert’s son, who had been ordained deacon at Auxerre, [Col. 0306C] and took possession of the city.

But when King Louis returned from Burgundy, he found me at Saint Basolus. Taking me with him, together with my relatives whose property Count Heribert had taken, he led us to Laon, which Heribert and Hugh were then besieging. After the siege was lifted, they entered the town, and arrangements were made for us to live there.

Meanwhile, the clerics of our place and certain laymen were treated most harshly by Heribert. Some of the clerics were thrust into custody, their property was taken and plundered, and robberies were openly committed throughout the entire city.

Meanwhile the bishops of our diocese were summoned by Hugh and Heribert, who were striving and asking them about the ordination of Hugh, Heribert’s son. They assembled at Soissons and sent Hildegarius, bishop of Beauvais, with certain other envoys to me at Laon, ordering me to come to them—in other words, to consent to the perversity of this ordination.

I sent back word that it was not appropriate for me to go to them where my adversaries and enemies were gathered with them. If they wished to speak with me, they should come to a place where I could approach them without danger.

When they came to a place chosen by them, I went to them. On arriving, I prostrated myself before them, begging them, for the love and honor of God, to strive to give both me and themselves sound counsel.

They began to question me about the ordination of the aforementioned Hugh and to urge me by every means to give my consent to this ordination, promising that they would obtain for me certain properties belonging to the bishopric.

But after I had delayed my answer for a long time, seeing that they all persisted in the purpose they had undertaken, I rose and publicly forbade it in the hearing of everyone. By the authority of God the almighty Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, I excommunicated them, so that none of them should participate in the same ordination, nor should any of them, while I lived, lay hands upon anyone for episcopal office. Nor should anyone presume to receive that same blessing. If it should happen, I would summon them before the apostolic see.

When they then raged, I moderated my reply so that I might leave their midst and return to Laon, saying that they should send someone with me who could report to them what counsel I might be able to find concerning this matter from my lady the queen and her faithful men, since the king was absent.

For this purpose they sent Bishop Derold, thinking that I would change my mind. When he came and questioned me about the matter before the lady queen and her faithful men, I rose again and hurled the aforementioned form of excommunication against those same bishops. I also took care to repeat the summons before the apostolic see, excommunicating Derold himself, so that he would not keep this entirely silent from them but would openly proclaim it to all.

These things having been done, they, making light of our excommunication, went to Rheims; some of them laid hands upon this ordination, while others are known to have withdrawn. But I, remaining with the king, endured with him the anxieties that he is known to have suffered. And when Hugh and Heribert attacked him in war, I was with him and scarcely escaped the danger of death. Having thus escaped from the midst of his enemies through God’s help and protection, I fled and wandered through every inaccessible place and forest, not daring to settle in any fixed location.

The counts Hugh and Heribert, addressing certain of our friends who were subject to them, urged them to search for me and bring me to them, promising that they would do me good and enrich me with whatever possessions they themselves requested. Accordingly, while my friends were searching for me, they found me wandering in various places, and so I was brought by my brothers and friends to the aforesaid counts. After they saw me in their power, they began to demand that I hand over the pallium conferred upon me by the Roman See and utterly renounce my priestly ministry [Col. 0307D]. I testify that I would do this under no circumstances, not even for love of the present life.

Thus constrained and pressed by them, I was finally compelled to renounce the possessions of the bishopric. And so I was again led to Saint Basolus, as though I were free of office, to dwell there. I remained in that monastery for a few days, until I learned through reliable messengers from the household of Count Heribert that he was plotting my destruction. Again and again frightened and driven on by such messages, I abandoned the place, returned as a wanderer to the hidden recesses of the forests, and, while the hours were silent, came back to Laon by a byway. There I was received by the king and appointed to remain with him.

I stayed there with him and his faithful followers, awaiting and praying for the mercy of God [Col. 0308A], until He deigned to put it into the heart of Lord King Otto that he should hasten into Francia to aid my lord king and us (see above, ch. 32).

Finally, after our lady the queen had left Laon for the absolution of Lord King, I departed from there with my elder king and came to Lord King Otto; together we also approached Rheims (above, ch. 33). The city was accordingly surrounded by armies, and the bishops who were present judged that I should be restored to my see. Lord King Otto therefore ordered Hugh to leave and surrender the city he had seized. But after hesitating for some time and resisting as far as he could, when he saw that he was wholly unable to withstand the attack and that the support of his friends could not help him, he decided that he must depart [Col. 0308B], requesting that he be allowed to leave freely with his men.

He was therefore permitted to depart unharmed, with all who wished to accompany him, and he carried away whatever he wished to take with him, no one objecting. Thus, having entered the city with the kings, I was placed in our position and restored to my dignity. I was received by Lords Archbishop Robert of Trier and Frederick of Mainz, accompanied and congratulated by the other clergy of our church and by the remaining citizens, and by them I was restored to the episcopal chair.

Hugh, however, after leaving Rheims, occupied with his men the fortress of Mouzon and, fortifying it against the faithful of our senior king, retained it. Finally, when a conference was arranged between the kings—namely, my senior king and Lord Otto—we met beside the Chiers [m., Karam] River, both I and Hugh himself with those who had ordained him [Col. 0308C]. There the bishops heard the matter at issue. He produced letters supposedly issued by me and addressed to the Roman See, presenting my defense as though I had requested that the administration of my bishopric be suspended. I protested, and still protest, that I had never dictated these letters nor in any way confirmed them by signing them.

Because a synod had not then been convened—this being urged by Hugh’s supporters—our dispute could not be decided. A synod to be held at Verdun around the middle of November was therefore announced, with the bishops of both parties agreeing. Meanwhile, it was decreed that I should govern the see of Rheims, while Hugh was permitted to remain at Mouzon.

Before long, however, when the time of the grape harvest was approaching, our rival Hugh, taking with him Theobald, an enemy of the king and of our realm, together with many other evildoers, came to the villages of the bishopric of Rheims adjoining the city. Gathering nearly all the wine from them, he had it carried off to various districts. Much evil was then perpetrated there; men of our church were carried away captive and subjected to various tortures to force them to pay ransom (above, ch. 34).

The synod announced for the middle of the month was held at Verdun, with Robert, bishop of Trier, presiding by command of the lord Roman pope; Lord Bruno was also present, together with several bishops and abbots.

The aforesaid Hugh was summoned to it, and two bishops, Adalbero [Col. 0309A] and Gozlin, were even sent to bring him. He nevertheless refused to come. The entire synod decreed that I should govern the bishopric of Rheims. A further synod was announced for the Ides of January, and it was duly convened, as had been proclaimed, in the church of Saint Peter before the fortress of Mouzon, by Lord Robert, with the other bishops of the diocese of Trier and some from Rheims attending.

Our rival Hugh came there, but after speaking with Lord Robert he refused to enter the synod. Instead, through his cleric, who was said to have brought them from Rome, he sent the bishops letters supposedly issued in the name of the lord pope. These contained no canonical authority, but merely ordered that the bishopric of Rheims be restored to Hugh.

After they had been read, the bishops took counsel with the abbots and the other wise men who were present [Col. 0309B]. They replied that it was neither proper nor fitting for the mandate of the apostolic legation—which Archbishop Robert had previously received, through Bishop Frederick of Mainz, before the kings and bishops of both Gaul and Germany, and of which he had already carried out part—to be suspended because of those letters produced by our conspirator. Rather, they unanimously judged that what had been begun according to rule should be pursued canonically. The nineteenth chapter of the Council of Carthage, concerning the accused and the accuser, was ordered to be read.

After it had been read, judgment was given according to the determination of that chapter: while I retained communion and the parish of Rheims, Hugh, who had already refused to attend two synods to which he had been summoned, was to abstain from communion [Col. 0309C] and from the governance of the bishopric of Rheims until he presented himself at the universal synod that had been announced, either to purge himself or to render an account.

They immediately had this chapter copied onto a sheet in the presence of the bishops, adding this decision of theirs as well, and sent it to Hugh. On the following day he returned the same document to Bishop Robert, sending back this reply: that he would in no way obey their judgment.

Thus, when the council had concluded, he retained Mouzon contrary to the commands of the kings and bishops. I, having returned to Rheims, sent the complaints of my protest through envoys of Lord King Otto to the Roman See, awaiting the commands of that holy see and ready to obey its decrees and the judgments of your universal holy council [Col. 0309D].

After these letters had been read, and after they had been interpreted for the kings in the Teutonic language [ms., Teutonicam; j, Theotiscam], a certain Sigebald entered. He was a cleric of the aforementioned Hugh and brought letters that he had brought from Rome, letters that he had already made public at another synod at Mouzon.

He asserted that these letters had been given to him at Rome by the very Marinus who was present as vicar. Lord Marinus, producing the letters that the same Sigebald had carried to Rome, ordered them to be read before the synod. During their reading it was found, as the letters themselves acknowledged, that Wido, bishop of Soissons, Hildegarius of Beauvais, Rodulfus of Laon, and all the other bishops of the diocese of Rheims [Col. 0310A] had sent these same letters to the apostolic see for Hugh’s restoration to the see of Rheims and for Artoldus’s expulsion.

After the reading, Bishop Artoldus, the aforesaid Rodulfus, who was named in those letters, and Bishop Fulbertus of Cambrai rose and repudiated the letters. They asserted that they had never before seen or heard of them and had given no consent to their dispatch. When that cleric could not contradict them, although he loudly opposed them with accusations, Lord Marinus urged the entire synod to offer counsel and a just judgment concerning such an accuser and informer against bishops.

After the informer had been publicly refuted as having brought false charges [Col. 0310B], they read the chapters concerning such accusers and judged, unanimously decreeing, that he should be deprived of the honor he enjoyed and, according to the tenor of those chapters, sent into exile. Thus deprived of the diaconate, the ministry he held, and rejected from the presence of the synod, he departed.

But concerning Bishop Artoldus, who had presented himself at all the synods and had not evaded synodal judgment, they decreed, approved, and confirmed that the bishopric of Rheims was to be retained and governed by him in accordance with the ordinances of the canons and the decrees of the holy Fathers.

On the second day of the session, after readings from divine authority and an address by the vicar Marinus, Lord Robert, archbishop of Trier, proposed that, since the bishopric of Rheims had been restored and reinstated to Bishop Artoldus [Col. 0310C] according to the ordinances of sacred law, synodal judgment should be carried out against the invader of that see.

The vicar Marinus therefore ordered the synod to pronounce a canonical sentence concerning this presumption. The chapters of the Catholic sacred law were accordingly ordered to be read. After they had been read, in accordance with the ordinances of the sacred canons and the decrees of the holy Fathers—Sixtus, Alexander, Innocent, Zosimus, Boniface, Celestine, Leo, Symmachus, and the other holy teachers of the Church of God—they excommunicated the aforesaid Hugh, invader of the Church of Rheims, and expelled him from the bosom of the Church of God, until he should undertake to come to repentance and make worthy satisfaction.

On the remaining days of the synod, certain necessary matters were also discussed concerning incestuous marriages and the churches that were improperly given—or rather sold—and unlawfully taken away from priests in the regions of Germany [Col. 0310D]. It was prohibited and decreed that no one should presume to do this at all. Other matters useful to the Church of God were also discussed, and several decisions were established.

Meanwhile King Louis asked King Otto to bring him aid against Hugh and his other enemies. Otto granted the request and ordered Duke Conrad to go to his assistance with an army of Lotharingians. While the army was being assembled, King Louis was to remain with the duke, while the bishops—namely Artoldus and Rodulfus, who were with the king—were to stay with the Lotharingian bishops so that they would suffer no misfortune on the road.

We therefore remained with Robert of Trier [Col. 0311A] for nearly four weeks, while Rodulfus of Laon stayed with Adalbero of Metz. When the army had finally been gathered, the Lotharingian bishops went to Mouzon. They besieged and attacked the fortress and compelled the soldiers who were there with Hugh to surrender. Having received hostages from them, they went to meet King Louis and Duke Conrad in the region of Laon.

There the duke and the army besieged a fortification that Theobald had built and held at a place called Mons Acutus, and who was also holding Laon against the king. After attacking this stronghold, they eventually captured it, though not without delay. From there they went to Laon and, assembling in the church of Saint Vincent, the bishops excommunicated the aforesaid Theobald. Through letters issued in the name of Marinus, legate of the apostolic see, and in their own, they summoned Hugh, the actual prince, to come and make amends for the evils he had committed against the king and the bishops [Col. 0311B].

Finally, Wido, bishop of the city of Soissons, came to King Louis, committed himself to him, and made peace with Archbishop Artoldus, satisfying him concerning Hugh’s ordination. Duke Conrad also lifted King Louis’s daughter from the sacred font. Thus, after the fortress of Mouzon had been recovered and demolished, the Lotharingians returned to their own lands.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Concerning the siege and burning of the city of Soissons by Count Hugh

Hugh, therefore, making no delay, gathered a large force of his own men and of the Northmen, attacked the city of Soissons, besieged and assaulted it, and struck down several people [Col. 0311C]. He also set fire to the mother church by hurling flames into it, and at the same time burned the canons’ cloister and part of the city. Nevertheless, unable to capture the city, he abandoned it and went to a certain fortification that Count Ragenold of Louis was building above the Aisne River at a place called Rauciacus (Roucy), and, though it was still unfinished, surrounded it with his camp.

He did not capture that place either. He did, however, devastate the villages of the Church of Rheims adjoining his camp. His marauders also killed many peasants, violating churches and raging so savagely that in the village of Culmiciacum, both inside and around the church, they killed nearly four hundred people and completely stripped the church itself of its goods. After many such crimes had been committed, Hugh at last withdrew with his plundering men [Col. 0311D].

The soldiers who had until then been with the excommunicated Hugh returned to Bishop Artoldus. He received some of them, restoring to them the possessions they had held, but rejected others.

After this he went to Trier for a synod with Wido, bishop of Soissons, Rodulfus of Laon, and Winefredus of Thérouanne. When they arrived, they found Marinus awaiting them with Archbishop Robert; they found none of the other Lotharingian or German prelates there.

When they had taken their seats, the vicar Marinus began to inquire what Prince Hugh had done against them and against King Louis after the preceding synod. They reported the evils mentioned above that he had inflicted upon them and upon their churches [Col. 0312A] [ms., j, the Church of Soissons].

Marinus therefore asked about summoning the prince, whether the summons letters that he had commissioned for delivery to Hugh had reached him. Archbishop Artoldus replied that some of them had been delivered, while others could not be delivered because their bearer had been intercepted by Hugh’s marauders; Hugh had nevertheless been summoned both by letters and by certain intermediaries.

It was then asked whether any envoy on Hugh’s behalf was present. When none could be found, it was decided to wait in case he might arrive the next day. When this did not happen, and all who were present—both clergy and distinguished laymen—called out that he should be excommunicated, the bishops decided that this excommunication should nevertheless be postponed until the third day of the synod [Col. 0312B].

They discussed the bishops who had been summoned but delayed coming, and those who had participated in Hugh’s ordination. Wido, bishop of Soissons, confessed himself guilty, prostrating himself before the vicar Marinus and Archbishop Artoldus. At the intercession of Robert and Artoldus, archbishops, before Marinus, he deserved to be absolved from this offense.

Wicfredus of Thérouanne was found to be free of participation in that ordination. A certain priest, an envoy of Transmarus, bishop of Noyon (Transmarus Noviom. 42 episc. in tab. Democh.), was present and asserted that the bishop had been held by such a grave illness that he had been unable to come to the same synod. The bishops of our region who were present also testified to this.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Concerning the excommunication of Count Hugh

On the third day, chiefly at the insistence of Luitdulf, envoy and chaplain of King Otto—for the same king had ordered that this be done without fail—Count Hugh, enemy of King Louis, was excommunicated for the evils mentioned above that he had committed. This was done, however, on the condition that the sentence would last until he came to his senses and appeared before the vicar Marinus or the bishops whom he had injured to make satisfaction. If he refused to do this, he was to go to Rome to seek his absolution.

Two false bishops ordained by the condemned Hugh were also excommunicated: Theobald [ms., Theobaldus] and Ivo. The former had been installed in the city of Amiens after Hugh’s expulsion; the latter had been installed by Hugh in the city of Senlis after Hugh’s condemnation [Col. 0312D].

A certain cleric of Laon named Adelonus was also excommunicated. His bishop Rodulfus accused him of having introduced the excommunicated Theobald into the church.

Bishop Hildegarius of Beauvais was summoned by letters from the aforesaid Marinus to come before him, or to go to Rome to render an account before the lord pope, because he had taken part in the unlawful ordination of the aforesaid false bishops. Heribert, son of Count Heribert, was also summoned to come and make satisfaction for the evils he had committed against the bishops.

These things having been done, the bishops returned to their own regions. Luitdulf, Otto’s chaplain, led the vicar Marinus to his king in Saxony, where Marinus was to consecrate the church of the monastery of Fulda. After that consecration [Col. 0313A], Marinus returned to Rome when winter had ended.

A son was born to King Louis, and Bishop Artoldus lifted him from the sacred font, giving him his father’s name.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Concerning certain churches and monasteries of the city of Rheims

There were once many basilicas of saints among us, as well as monasteries within and around this city of Rheims, which are now demonstrably no longer in existence. Two monasteries of women, however, still remain within the city. One of them—called by a name derived from the location, as stated above—is traditionally said to have been built in honor of Saint Mary or Saint Peter by Saint Balderic the priest together with his sister Bova, who later became abbess of the same monastery.

They are said to have been descended from royal stock, their father being King Sigebert. They had a niece named Doda, a most chaste girl, who is said to have been betrothed to a certain magnate of that same King Sigebert. Her aforementioned aunt Bova instructed her to serve God and preserve perpetual virginity, and turned her away from love of her earthly bridegroom.

When he opposed this and attempted to seize the bride, he mounted a horse and tried by every means to carry out his purpose. But, thrown from the horse in its fury, he is said to have died with his neck broken.

Blessed Doda, remaining firm in her resolve of chastity, succeeded her aunt in the governance of the same monastery. She later obtained from Prince Pippin a charter of immunity, which is still preserved among us, for that monastery [Col. 0313B].

Their bodies long rested buried in the church outside the walls of the city, where the first monastery of women had been. Later, after being raised through certain revelations, they were carried to this new church and reverently placed there. They continue to be honored there by the constant reverence of the women serving God.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. Concerning Saint Balderic the abbot

After building this monastery, Saint Balderic (Saint Bauldry), seeking a place where he could also establish a dwelling in which he might live religiously with men gathered around him and serve God devoutly and peacefully, finally found a place he liked called Montem Falconis, “Falcon’s Mountain” (Montfaucon).

At that time the place was uninhabitable and covered with dense forests [Col. 0313D]. Cutting them down, he built himself a dwelling by his own labor.

It is said that, while he was seeking that place, he had as a guide and, as it were, a leader on his journey a bird that we call a falcon. The bird settled at that place and, returning there for three days, remained without moving at the spot where the altar is now kept in honor of Saint Peter the Apostle. Hence, many assert, the monastery received its name from this event.

When he had begun to serve God there more devoutly, some God-fearing people bestowed their possessions upon him. Gathering monks around him, he established the monastery under a regular rule and built the same monastery in honor of blessed Germanus.

After accomplishing these things, he returned to his sister at Rheims [Col. 0314A] and there ended the final day of his earthly course. There, too, he was buried and rested for a considerable time.

## CHAPTER XL. Concerning miracles displayed after his death

In the course of time, through the diligence of the clerics inhabiting the monastery of that blessed man mentioned above, his body was secretly carried there after being taken from Rheims, the guards having been deceived by a trick.

Certain citizens of Rheims pursued them and continued after them until some of them caught sight of the fugitives. When the bearers of the sacred relic became alarmed at their arrival, a dense mist, believed to have been sent by God, arose between the two groups. The pursuers, obscured by it and led astray onto byways, could no longer follow the tracks of those ahead.

But, during the night, a radiance sent from above shone upon the bearers of the sacred body until, tireless, they reached the nearest estate belonging to the monastery, called the village of Spanulfus [al., Spamulfi] [Col. 0314B]. Because they laid the sacred remains there, a church was later built in his honor.

When they proceeded from there with the sacred relic, and began to draw near the monastery, the bells of the monastery church are said to have rung of their own accord, without human impulse. Hearing this, the brothers came out to meet them. Receiving the long-desired gift, they attempted to carry it into the church of Saint Germanus, but before the entrance to the basilica they felt it fixed with such weight that they were utterly unable to move it farther, although for three days they tried to do so with every effort.

At last they built a roof over the remains, which were fixed in place, and the body of the confessor is said to have remained there for three years [Col. 0314C]. After that period had elapsed, his venerable body was carried, following a three-day fast, to the church of Saint Lawrence, where he had prepared his own tomb while alive, and was reverently placed in his sarcophagus.

It is known to have been preserved there with venerable honor until the time of King Charles and Archbishop Hincmar, when the Northmen began to ravage this kingdom. Compelled by fear of them, the canons of that place lifted the body of their patron from the tomb and placed it upon the altar of Saint Lawrence.

As this was being done, three drops of blood flowed from his head, so fresh and warm that they seemed to flow from a living body. The body was then carried to Verdun. From there it was brought back and placed in the church of Saint Germanus [Col. 0314D].

While it was absent from its monastery, the Northmen reached the place. But because the Lord protected it, they neither burned the churches nor killed anyone except one woman. When they withdrew, they left the altars heaped with their own gifts.

On another occasion, when the Northmen again approached the same place, a certain canon named Ottradus took up the saint’s body. After the others had fled, he himself climbed a certain tree with the sacred body. The pagans pursued him and reached the very tree. Looking upward, they could not discover that anyone had climbed it.

That brother remained there for nine days and, taking no food except a single acorn, is said to have suffered neither hunger nor thirst [Col. 0315A]. Once again, through the merits of this blessed man, that place was freed from the pagans’ slaughter and burning.

Afterward it happened that certain robbers, faithless to royal majesty, came to the same place. Finding no hand resisting them, they began to plunder the deserted site. While they were doing this, the bells of the church of Saint Lawrence began to ring, though no one struck them, and two candles were miraculously kindled by heavenly fire.

The robbers were struck with fear and fled. One of them fell at the very gate of the monastery and collapsed. He and his proud horse were so crushed by the fall that the skins in which he was carrying wine were also broken [Col. 0315B]. Seeing this, the others enriched the church with gifts and withdrew in fear.

## CHAPTER XLI. Concerning the village of Waslicia

The canons of this venerable place, once compelled by hunger, took relics from the body of their venerable patron and traveled to one of their estates situated on the bank of the Rhine, called Waslicia. One of their abbots, Adelardus by name, had bestowed it upon that monastery.

When the country people there began to bring their gifts while venerating the life-giving relics, an abbot of a monastery called Bonn, going to Willebert, bishop of Cologne, began to denounce this devotion. He asserted that no relics of any saint had truly been brought there [Col. 0315C].

The visiting canons, fearing that they might be detained and examined by the bishop, since they were carrying the entire body of the saint with them, immediately upon hearing this returned to their monastery in two days, covering nearly one hundred leagues. Taking with them the blessed man’s body intact, they returned to the aforesaid village in the same number of days.

When they began to approach it, while they were still about a league from the village, the church bells began to ring without anyone setting them in motion. The clerics who had remained at the place heard this, understood that their patron was arriving, and went out to meet him with crosses. They received their protector with due honor.

While they were celebrating the solemnities of Mass, three remarkable things suddenly occurred there. One crippled man was straightened, a blind man received sight, and a mute man acquired speech [Col. 0315D].

The aforesaid abbot nevertheless did not cease blaspheming the miracles of God, turning away from the saint’s visitation as many people as he could.

While he was doing this, he was seized by a fever and afflicted so severely that he could neither eat, drink, nor walk. Forced by the burning of this illness [al., “consumed by it”], he finally recognized his sin. He had himself carried in a sedan chair as far as the Rhine and from there by boat to the aforesaid village. Thus he was brought before the presence of the holy body.

There he confessed his fault and asked to be absolved. He gave an amount of wax equal to the weight of his own body and made vows to be paid annually. After remaining there for six days [Col. 0316A], he deserved to recover complete health and, departing sound, returned on his own feet to his home.

The clerics mentioned above remained there with their patron for a full year. They say that no day passed without miracles of God being performed there. At the very vigil of Saint John the Baptist, when many people came from Saxony and even from distant regions, eighteen notable miracles are attested to have been displayed; scarcely any sick person came who did not depart restored and joyful.

Such an abundance of goods was brought there that the clerics themselves lived from it, supported the others who had remained in the monastery, and enlarged or adorned the church of that village.

Afterward it happened that, because of a lack of water, the same sacred body was carried outside the monastery and brought to meet the relics of Saint Jovinus [Col. 0316B]. When it had been carried to meet them, as soon as the two groups came together, although the sky had been clouded and there was a severe drought, a plentiful downpour of rain fell. While everyone’s clothing and cloaks were soaked by the rain, the pallia carried above the bodies of the aforesaid saints alone remained completely untouched by it.

There a one-eyed man recovered the sight of the eye he had lost. Immediately fleeing without glorifying God, he departed ungratefully, as was his playful custom. But when he reached home, he again lost the sight he had recovered.

When they arrived at the monastery with the bodies of both saints, the relic of Saint Balderic became so heavy that it could not be moved at all, until they caused the remains of Saint Jovinus to go ahead as far as the monastery.

When Lord Dado, bishop of Verdun, had obtained this abbey from the king—Arnulf from across the Rhine—and had begun to hear of these miracles, he arranged that each year the sacred relics of the three monasteries should be brought together to a certain central place called Gaudiacum.

From the see of the city of Verdun came Saint Vitonus and Saint Agericus; Saint Balderic came from his monastery, and Saint Rodvicus from Wasloi. At this gathering countless miracles were later performed, so that scarcely any such assembly passed without one of the sick being restored to health—especially those who appeared to seek the patronage of blessed Balderic.

At one such gathering, a mute man spoke. The people of Verdun seized him and began to take him away with them, asserting that the virtue of the saints they had brought had performed this miracle [Col. 0316D]. As the various groups were then being carried back to their own places, the bones of Saint Balderic became so heavy that they seemed entirely immovable.

Many people returned in wonder at this miracle. When they asked the saint’s people why he wished to remain there and what he intended to accomplish, it happened that they inquired about the man who had been mute and had spoken. At last he was summoned back. When he had been brought to the place where the relic had been fixed, it was immediately lifted without difficulty, and the monastery gladly carried it back to its sacred body.

After the aforesaid Bishop Dado had obtained this abbey of Saint Balderic, he exchanged with Abbot Adelardus certain lands across the Rhine [Col. 0317A], which had formerly been given to the same monastery, for the village of Gerlani Monte, situated above the Moselle.

When he ordered the brothers of this congregation to travel to that village in order to ratify it for himself, they took with them the remains of their patron, Lord Balderic, and went to carry out his orders.

When they reached a village called Deva [j, Dena], the sacred relic became so heavy that those carrying it could not proceed any farther. After taking counsel, they received the ability to carry it onward to the church of that village, dedicated to Saint Martin. Once the relic had been brought there, after prayer it was carried out of the church, but again Saint Balderic’s body became heavy.

While everyone wondered, and some of the bearers thought that God wished to display signs there for the glorification of His saint, they asked whether any sick people might happen to be present [Col. 0317B].
