Some injured people arrived and others were carried there. A lame man was straightened; a woman whose arms had been contracted for eight years was released; two blind women received sight; and a seven-year-old mute child began to speak.

The people of the village later set up a cross at that place. There afterward two women received the light of their eyes, candles were kindled by divine power, and many people were freed from various illnesses.

## CHAPTER XLII. Concerning the church of Saint Romanus and the miracles at Gallani Monte [j, Gerlani]

Milo, provost of the canons of this place, had formerly taken away from them the church of Saint Romanus, built in the aforesaid village of Gerlani Monte [Col. 0317C]. When they received it back after Count Boso had returned it to them, and had brought the remains of Saint Balderic there, many people began to flock to his patronage.

Among them two noble blind women were brought, as well as a poor woman who had been contracted in nearly all her limbs.

On the night of the vigil of Saint Romanus, while the customary all-night watch was being held in the church, such a great light was suddenly poured down from heaven that it seemed to surpass all the lamps that had been lit. Only the altar, above which the saint’s bones had been deposited, appeared to be covered by a dense mist, and the container of the sacred relic itself seemed to move [Col. 0317D].

Suddenly one of the blind women first, and then the other, proclaimed that they could see. Then the contracted woman lying in the middle, when she began to cry out and pray for the help of God and of Saint Balderic, gradually became free: first in her arms, and then in her knees, until she stood upright on her feet.

Afterward restored to health, she has continued to be supported by the clerics’ charity.

While the clerics were staying in the aforesaid place with the sacred relic, it happened one evening, as they were sitting together, that a man who was a friend of a certain Milo, inflamed by drunkenness and fury, began to ask them what they were doing there and why they had entered Milo’s village.

They replied that the property belonged to Saint Balderic, not to Milo. When he contradicted them, saying that it belonged to Milo, not Balderic, the clerics threatened him, and he withdrew. Climbing a high cliff adjoining the village, he threw himself headlong from it and lay crushed, appearing dead or near death.

He was taken up and carried before the presence of the holy body. There at last he acknowledged his guilt, was unexpectedly healed, and within a short time was restored to complete health [Col. 0318A].

Again, when the relics of this saint had recently been brought back to the aforesaid village of Waslicia, since Godefrid, Count Palatine of Prince Henry, had overrun that village, some of Saint Balderic’s clerics went to the same Godefrid for this reason. When they could obtain no worthy answer from him, and he declared that he would do no more for them there than for his own dog, [Col. 0318B] one of the clerics added pointedly that he would therefore sweat hot sweat, and that his dog would not help him. At this he, enraged, ordered them to be driven from his sight. As they withdrew, he was immediately struck by divine vengeance: seized by a violent fever, he began to suffer most grievously, to burn with excessive heat, and to pour forth the hottest sweat.

He therefore sent to Wicfrid, bishop of Cologne, asking him to come to him. He reported the matter to him and received this counsel: he should send to the aforesaid clerics, summon them to him, correct his errors, and seek from them both advice and help concerning his illness. Obeying, he sent to them and ordered them to come to him. But his messenger, puffed up, as it seemed, with the pride of arrogance, began imperiously to command [Col. 0318C] that the clerics should immediately go to his master. They refused, asking him instead to share fellowship with them [*charitatem secum facere*]. He despised them; and as he departed, at the very moment of his leaving, his horse, spurred on by him, sprang forward, fell, and died with its neck broken.

Thus humbled, he returned to the brothers, shared the fellowship he had refused, and departed corrected. Called and requested again, and then a third time, they finally learned of this man’s misfortunes and came to him. They sympathized with his sufferings and strove by their prayers to absolve him when he confessed his sin and promised amendment. He immediately declared that he was feeling better; and when the brothers had departed, he recovered, restored the things he had seized, and thereafter refrained from harming them. [Col. 0318D] Yet his household is said to have been afflicted by so great a calamity that scarcely any survived who had used those possessions; even the horses and dogs perished, while the invader himself, having lost his hair together with his skin and his nails, barely escaped.

## CHAPTER XLIII. On a miracle performed in the river Rhine

At that time, because of the invasion of the Hungarians, which had first arisen in that period against this kingdom, the canons of Saint Balderic crossed the Rhine with their lord after taking counsel together. Returning from there one evening, they cast anchors in the middle of the river and brought the ship to a halt. Leaving a few men in the ship as guardians of the sacred relic, they themselves hastened to the aforesaid farmstead of their possession [that is, Wastitia].

[Col. 0319A] Three robbers, having learned that only a few guardians remained in the ship and supposing that treasures or the saint’s ornaments had been left there, boarded a small boat and set out for it. But before they reached the ship they sought, they were divinely blinded, and, having lost their senses and being unable to row, began to be carried along by the force of the river. Their little boat struck the ship that guarded the saint’s body and was smashed, leaving them amid the waves. Two of them were immediately swallowed by the river. The third, who was also a servant of Saint Balderic, reached out his hand and seized the saint’s ship. Thus escaping death, and being brought into the presence of the clerics, he could say nothing about what he had suffered until the following day, when he had recovered his strength and regained his senses; then at last he related what had happened.

[Col. 0319B] After the bones of this blessed man had been brought from the aforesaid place to his monastery, many miracles are said to have been displayed there, but because of their number they have not been written down. Recently a poor man brought there a candle rolled into a ring and, shortly before evening, placed it above the reliquary of the sacred bones. When he withdrew after saying his prayer, the candle, suddenly kindled by fire from above, began to burn. It burned completely away before the church custodian came to ring the bells for vespers; the cloak on which it lay was unharmed, and the candle caused no damage to the cloak to which it adhered.

Moreover, the Lord very frequently deigns to display there many miracles of healing and enlightenment, in order to manifest the merits of his saint—to the honor and praise, of course, of his name, which is blessed forever.

## CHAPTER XLIV. On miracles performed in the monastery of Saints Bova and Doda

[Col. 0319C] Finally, in the aforesaid women’s monastery (above, chapter 28), where, as we have said, the bodies of the aforesaid holy women Bova and Doda were transferred, certain miracles are subsequently attested to have been performed. Those who come there suffering from fevers or afflicted by various illnesses deserve to be granted the health they desire, especially on the day of their solemnity, that is, 24 April.

Recently, a certain girl who had been deprived of hearing—because the passages of this sense had been obstructed by the force of her illness—through the intervention of these holy brides of Christ deserved to receive again the long-lost function of her ears.

## CHAPTER XLV. On the vision of a certain girl

[Col. 0319D] There is in this monastery a certain religious virgin, the niece of the late devout priest Guntmar, named Ricuidis. The blessed apostle Peter and the blessed Remigius formerly appeared to her in a vision, signifying that they would impose upon her a journey to Rome when they returned to her. They also declared that they would return in the middle of September, namely on the day of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross.

Suspended in expectation of this, and forbidden by them, she dared to disclose it to no one. On the day they had foretold for their return, they appeared to her again, ordering her to summon her brother, the priest Frederic, and exhorting him, as far as he could, to follow the footsteps of the aforementioned [Col. 0320A] priest Guntmar. At their command she was to impose upon him the duty of undertaking that journey with her, in the following manner: from that day neither he nor she was to eat meat or drink wine until they undertook the journey, except that she alone might drink as much wine as could be purchased with the money she would find upon a certain altar designated to her by them.

So that this might be believed more readily, she was to take three sisters of this monastery, namely three religious women, as witnesses to investigate the matter, specifically those persons whom she was to summon. Saint Remigius added this further instruction: she was to tell her brother to remember that he had once appeared to him and spoken with him. As a sign by which he might recognize him, he added that he had seemed to strike him in the palm with a knife.

[Col. 0320B] She immediately sent to her brother and ordered him to come to her quickly. When he arrived, he found his sister still fasting at the hour of evening and greatly astonished by the vision. She summoned the religious women she had named, and together they sang the seven penitential psalms before the indicated altar, adding the prayers of the litanies. They then approached the altar and, removing its coverings, found in one corner of it a small coin. Taking it with thanksgiving, they gave it in exchange for wine. This was the only wine the religious woman drank; thereafter she was to take no more until both she and her brother had begun the journey imposed upon them.

They undertook it faithfully and confidently and, with God’s help and with Saints Peter and [Col. 0320C] Remigius assisting them, completed it successfully, just as the saints had promised. Thereafter she abstains from meat except on Sunday; and on three days each week she does no work until the signal sounds for the second hour, devoting herself to prayers and psalmody. She recalls that she was commanded to observe this for seven years.

Her aforesaid brother was likewise instructed through her by the saints to abstain from meat four days each week and from wine every Friday throughout his life. They have been seen to observe these practices.

## CHAPTER XLVI. On another women’s monastery at Reims

There is also another women’s monastery situated at Reims by the gate once called Collaticia, [Col. 0320D] from the delivery of merchandise, and now called Basilicaris [perhaps Baseillo], because it is said formerly to have abounded in basilicas more than the other gates, or because it provided passage for those going to the basilica in the district of Saint Remigius [printed *consistentes*, with defective agreement]. We have mentioned that Lord Rigobert had a residence above it [Book II, chapter 12].

This monastery is traditionally said to have been built in honor of Saint Peter by Lord Guntbert, an illustrious man. It is called royal or fiscal because it remained under royal authority until recent times. The Emperor Louis gave the monastery to his daughter Alpheid [elsewhere Alpaid and below Alpaid], the wife of Count Bego, and granted that sacred place a charter of immunity, just as his father, the Emperor Charles, [Col. 0321A] had once done.

Later, through a conditional grant (*precaria*) by Alpheid herself or by her sons Letard and Ebrard, this convent passed into the share and possession of the church of Reims. It is said to possess a tooth of the apostle Saint Andrew, whose benefits many sick people frequently experience when they are deemed worthy to kiss it.

Here, in the church of this convent, we saw a candle kindled three times by heavenly fire. Certain citizens of Reims had made this candle from wax collected together when they had recently set out to visit the thresholds of the Apostles. In this monastery too we saw a girl sweat blood. She then lay motionless for a full week, as though dead, and several visions were shown to her.

## CHAPTER XLVII. On Lord Guntbert and his wife Berta

[Col. 0321B] The aforementioned Lord Guntbert, founder of this convent, is said, after leaving his wife and seeking the coastal regions, to have founded another monastery. There he is also said to have been beheaded by barbarians.

His wife, Lady Berta, left behind, built a monastery for women at Avennac, after the Lord had shown her the place through an angel. Since there was no water there, she obtained from the owners of the neighboring forest, upon payment of a pound of silver, a spring situated nearly two miles from her monastery. A stream immediately flowed from this spring and followed her as she returned to the convent. Still flowing abundantly, it is called Libra because it was purchased for that amount.

Finally, the stepsons of Lady Berta rose up against her and killed her. [Col. 0321C] Immediately handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, they are said to have died (*decessisse*; MS r. *defecisse*, “to have failed/perished”), transformed from human understanding into bestial savagery.

Lady Berta is said to have appeared by night to Montia, the niece of Lord Guntbert, while Montia was awake; she had been an accomplice in this crime. She ordered her to strive to bring Lord Guntbert’s body back to this place and place it beside her own remains; thus, she said, the Lord would forgive her sin in consenting to the murder.

When Montia asked for a sign by which she might know that this had been forgiven her, she heard that, as soon as she had fulfilled the command, blood would burst from her mouth or nostrils. This was fulfilled when Lord Guntbert’s body was buried beside Berta’s relic.

After approximately one hundred years, the body of Lady Berta was found intact, and [Col. 0321D] blood flowed from her wounds as freshly as if they had been inflicted upon a living woman at that very hour. To display the honor and merit of these saints, the Lord later deigned to perform many miracles, which, through negligence, have not been recorded.

In all their tribulations, the community sought the Lord’s mercy through their intercession and deserved to receive the consolation mercifully provided to them. Recently, moreover, a certain woman stole a linen cloth from another woman of this monastery and wished to carry it away with her, but she could not leave the church in any way until she confessed her guilt and restored the veil she had taken to the altar.

Lord Fulco, the bishop, obtained from King Odo, [Col. 0322A] by a charter of that king, the grant of this monastery or abbey to the church of Reims; and, to confirm it to this church, he obtained from Pope Formosus a privilege of the Apostolic See.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. On two churches of Saint Hilary at Reims

There are two churches at Reims in honor of Saint Hilary. One is within the city, where recently a certain girl who was crippled and paralyzed was raised up by divine power. The other, the older church, is situated before the Gate of Mars; Bishop Saint Rigobert gave it to the clerics who were our predecessors for their burial. Long ago, namely before the departure or expulsion of Bishop Artold, it was distinguished by frequent miracles. At that time, therefore, with the citizens also contributing their assistance, he had it [Col. 0322B] repaired with roofs and new ceilings.

A certain blind man named Paul, having been warned in a dream to go to that church, where he would receive sight, came there and, having recovered his sight, departed seeing without delay.

One of the bishop’s servants, when he was going to that church, encountered a fisherman with fish before the church doors. He seized the fish as though he intended to buy them. But the poor fisherman, sorrowfully calling upon Saint Hilary to settle the matter with him, hurled imprecations at him. He, however, disregarding such words, entered the church as though he were going to hear Mass. While he was standing there, he suddenly fell, was afflicted with severe torment, and was thrown out. He suffered from this affliction for a considerable time.

In the cemetery of this church a certain Scot, a servant of God, had formerly been buried. But when [Col. 0322C] both his name and the memory of his burial seemed already to have been erased by our people, he began to make himself known through appearances.

A certain citizen, not from the lower classes but poor in possessions, had once died in our own day. His friends approached Hildegarius, the priest of this church, and asked him to grant them a burial place where they might find a sarcophagus in which they could lay the man’s body, since they had no resources with which to purchase one. When he granted their request, they opened the burial place of the servant of God, but they could not open his sarcophagus.

When the priest heard this, he approached and, attempting to lift the sarcophagus cover, opened the tomb slightly. Immediately such a fragrance of extraordinary sweetness poured forth that he declared he had never breathed [Col. 0322D] a more delightful scent. Looking inside, he saw an intact body clothed in priestly vestments. Replacing the tomb’s covering, he did not dare violate the burial further; nevertheless, he allowed the other body to be placed above it on boards.

That same night his uncle, a priest who had died long before, appeared to him in a dream and declared that he had greatly offended God on the previous day, especially if he had presumed to violate the saint’s tomb. The blessed man himself also appeared during those same days and declared that he was greatly burdened by the weight and indignity of the corpse placed above him. He ordered the priest to be told that, unless he quickly removed that fetid body from his burial place [printed *id fetidum*, “that fetid”; MS *jam fetidum*, “already fetid”], he would soon be punished by divine vengeance.

[Col. 0323A] Terrified by these warnings, the priest had the corpse that had been placed above the saint’s burial removed at once and buried it in a tomb opened elsewhere.

The same saint of the Lord later appeared to a certain peasant and ordered him to go to Bishop Artold and tell him, in his name, to transfer his body, which lay outside, into the church. The peasant was afraid to report this and neglected the command. Not long afterward, the saint appeared to him again while he was awake, harshly rebuked him for neglecting the order, and struck him on the cheek with a slap.

Immediately he lost the hearing of the ear on the side where he had been struck and suffered from a headache for nearly half a year.

Then, on a certain Sunday night, the saint appeared in a vision to a priest serving in that same church under the aforementioned priest. [Col. 0323B] He warned him to tell the bishop to transfer his body into the aforesaid church. He did not fail to show him the place where it was to be laid, and he revealed his death, the cause of his death, and the reason for his coming. He said that he had been a Scot, traveling with companions to Rome for the sake of prayer, and that he had been killed by robbers on the river Aisne. His companions had brought his body here and buried it there. He also disclosed his name, saying that he was called Merolilanus [that is, Merolianus], and ordered the priest to have the name written down lest it slip from memory.

Bending down and taking a piece of chalk that happened to be lying there, he gave it to him and ordered him immediately to write the name on a chest attached to his bed. [Col. 0323C] The priest seemed to receive the chalk and write down the name. When he wrote an R in place of the letter L, the saint told him to correct it. The name was found written down in this way the next day, as the same priest testified, although he could not have written it so well during the day while awake.

Warned by these revelations, the bishop did have the church restored, but he did not transfer the holy body. Not long afterward, however, it happened that in that same church he resigned the administration of the bishopric before Prince Hugh.

## CHAPTER XLIX. On churches built in honor of Saint Martin throughout nearly the whole diocese

There are also many churches throughout nearly the entire diocese in honor of blessed Martin, [Col. 0323D] illumined by divine miracles—miracles which, we believe, no one could adequately recount.

In the district of Saint Remigius there stands a church of this blessed confessor, which is said formerly to have housed a community of clerics. A miracle of the following kind is related among us concerning it.

A certain illustrious man had taken a wife. Not long afterward, he departed on campaign at the king’s command and remained away for a long time. When he had returned home, he was told that his wife had been corrupted by adultery. Since the man loved his wife, he wished to test what he had heard by this examination: he required his wife to swear before the sacred altars of the churches in this district that she was innocent of the crime, so that afterward she might be free from the accusation.

She did not refuse, but readily accepted. [Col. 0324A] Having pledged faith to her words, she came with her husband to the district and swore an oath upon the altars of certain churches. At last she reached this church. As she approached the altar and wickedly swore falsely, her womb suddenly burst open; her entrails fell upon the ground, and she collapsed dead, showing how true had been the report that had been brought to her husband about her.

Moved by God’s sign through the miracle, he is said to have vowed never again to take a wife. He assigned to the same church the household that had belonged to his wife and gave them this law: they were to pay a head-tax there and were to be liable to no other service. Preserved for itself under this law, that household is found to have grown to two thousand persons or more, so that formerly, before it was devastated by the barbarians, it paid twelve pounds [Col. 0324B] of silver to the church.

## CHAPTER L. On miracles of Saint Martin displayed at Reims

Our city is also said to be distinguished by several other miracles of this blessed Father. Among these, we have decided to insert here those which Saint Gregory of Tours recounts in his books of miracles (Gregory, Book IV of the *Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 26), so that if any readers have not happened to read them, they may find them here.

He relates that, when he was once traveling through the district of Reims, a man of Reims told him that the prison in which that man’s servant was being held among other prisoners had been opened by the power of blessed Martin, and that the prisoners, released from the dungeon, had departed free.

The prison was constructed in such a way that strong planks were laid over a framework of beams [Col. 0324C] to form a platform; above it, great stones had been placed to weigh it down [printed *eumdem*, “it”; original *eosdem*, “them”]. Nevertheless, the prison door was secured with an iron bar, shut with a key, and locked with a bolt. But, as the informant himself asserted, the power of the bishop scattered the stones and planks, broke the chains, and opened the beam that confined the prisoners’ feet. Without unlocking the door, he lifted the men through the air and brought them out through the opened roof, saying:

> “I am Martin, the soldier of Christ, your liberator. Depart in peace and go away without fear.”

“But when we,” Gregory says, “approached the king and spread abroad the miracle of this power, the king declared that some of those who had been released had come to him, and that he had remitted to the accused the composition owed to the treasury, which they call the *fredum*.”

[Col. 0324D] The same Gregory also reports (in the place cited above, Book II, chapter 17) that he once visited this city, and that in the sacristy of this church at Reims the deaf ear of Sigo, referendary of King Sigebert, was suddenly opened and healed by the power of blessed Martin, whose relics Gregory had with him, while Sigo was conversing with Gregory.

## CHAPTER LI. On Saint Macra the virgin

In this district of Reims the blessed virgin Macra suffered under the prefect Rictiovarus. After enduring the most grievous tortures for her unconquerable confession of Christ, and after the cutting off of her breasts and their sudden healing through an angel’s visitation in prison, she was rolled naked over burning coals and potsherds [Col. 0325A] while offering prayers and thanksgivings. Giving her undefiled spirit back to God and triumphing over the adversary, she joyfully sought heaven there.

Her body was then buried not far from the place where she suffered. Many years later, the place where the most blessed virgin had been buried was revealed in a vision to a certain herdsman, beside a church built in honor of blessed Martin. In the vision he was warned that the body of the most sacred virgin should be reburied more honorably within the aforesaid church, so that her presence might become more clearly known to the inhabitants of that place, as was fitting.

This was soon accomplished with great ceremony by men beloved of God. As long as her venerable body rested there, notable miracles were performed through her intercession. There the blind obtained sight, the lame [Col. 0325B] received the power to walk, and the deaf received hearing, as the Lord granted these gifts through her.

Later, a certain energetic founder and cultivator of holy churches named Daugulfus [j, Dangulfus] founded the church where she is now venerated. In it he transferred her most sacred remains during the reign of the great Emperor Charles. There too, through the Lord’s favor, many miracles frequently occur.

[Note: [Col. 0325D] The name of the place is Fismes.]

Recently, during the time of the Hungarian persecution, those same barbarians wished to set the church on fire. They ignited great heaps of grain that had been piled against its wall. Although the crops were consumed and the flame licked the roof of the church, they were nevertheless unable to set the church itself alight.

## CHAPTER LII. On Saints Rufinus and Valerius, martyrs

[Col. 0325C] At the same time that this holy virgin suffered, her torturer Rictiovarus passed through the city of Reims and compelled certain Christians to worship the gods. When he could not overcome them, he ordered them to be slaughtered.

After leaving there, he found two men, Rufinus and Valerius, strong in the faith of Christ but guardians of the royal granaries. He seized them, and when he discovered that they were utterly steadfast in their love and confession of Christ, he afflicted them with blows and tormented them by a prolonged confinement in prison. There they were relieved and strengthened by an angelic visitation and consolation.

At last, since they were found unconquered, they were condemned to death.

After not many intervals of time, their most sacred remains were being carried in biers to the city of Reims. [Col. 0325D] At the place where their bones now lie buried, the biers became so heavy that they could not be moved from the spot [printed *sunt*, “were”; c. i. *feruntur*, “are reported to have been”]. Thus it is shown to have happened by God’s command: where they had distributed generous alms to the poor, there they were to receive the pleasant repose of their bodies.

But when, not long ago, the barbarian people of the Northmen poured into Gaul in a frenzy of devastation, their relics were carried to the city of Reims to avoid the storm of that persecution. They were placed in the church of Saint Peter and kept there under honor for many days.

When at last the barbarians withdrew and the storm that had raged so long against us subsided [*desedisset*, “had subsided”; i. *desaevisset*, “had ceased raging”], [Col. 0326A] tranquility returned at God’s command. The priest who served the saints, and who had long wished to return to his own place, hastened to take up the remains of the holy martyrs and carry them back to the place dedicated to them.

After the celebration of Mass, the bodies consecrated to Christ were lifted by the priests, who carried them back amid a great accompanying crowd. It happened that the day, which was a Sunday, was stormy with wind, so that all the candles carried in service of the saints were extinguished by the force of the whirlwind.

When they had entered part of the river on their journey, the candle carried before the relics of the saints, having been extinguished, was suddenly kindled from heaven and presented a wondrous spectacle to all. Amid mingled hailstorms [Col. 0326B] and blasts of wind, the miraculous flame lasted for nearly four miles.

Later the priest decided to remake the candle itself into a better form from the same wax. While this was being done by the priests subject to him, the soft wax, wondrous to relate, began to grow in their hands and to increase to a great quantity.

## CHAPTER LIII. On miracles of the same saints

While they stood astonished and marveling, the priest entered. Seeing that the wax had increased in this way, he believed that they had added other wax to it, although he had not ordered them to do so. But when he learned from the priests what miracle had occurred, he gave thanks to God and stored the wax in the church as a memorial of so great an event.

[Col. 0326C] Riculfus, the venerable bishop of Soissons, ordered relics of this wax to be brought to him. Religious priests of neighboring churches likewise requested portions out of devotion and reverently deposited them in their churches.

On another occasion, when the saints’ bodies were being carried back from the city of Soissons, to which they had been brought because of a similar persecution, to their proper place, a certain lame man accompanied the others who were escorting the saints’ bodies with devout service. He crawled forward, moving as best he could. Nature had not made him lame; rather, a painful weakness had later come upon his gait.

When they reached the village called Vasneia, he was immediately restored to his natural uprightness. Throwing away his supports, he began to walk on his feet and, with grateful voice, to praise God, wondrous in his saints.

[Col. 0326D] Furthermore, one example will suffice to show how quickly divine vengeance is exercised against those who try to violate the sacred place and seize the possessions entrusted to the holy martyrs.

At a time when serious disputes were taking place in the kingdom of the Franks between Kings Odo and Charles, the occasion permitted robbery and plundering; right and wrong were confused, and nowhere was there fear of God or of human laws. Everything was determined by force and power.

On one occasion, raiders came to a village called Basilica and began to carry off all the little possessions of the poor. A certain poor woman then fled with her household goods toward the church of the holy martyrs, making her way at great speed.

[Col. 0327A] One of those who had come to plunder began to pursue her at full speed while seated on his horse, wishing to seize her and take away her belongings. One of the bystanders said:

> “Do not, poor man, do not pursue her into the courtyard of the holy martyrs, lest something bad happen to you.”

He feared nothing, however, but drove his horse rapidly after the fleeing woman. As soon as the horse set its front feet in the courtyard, it suddenly stumbled headlong and fell.

Its rider was so gravely injured by the impact that, from the top of his knee to his foot, his shinbone having been broken, the flesh gaped as though cut by iron, and the bone itself lay exposed, stripped of its covering of flesh [*tegimine*; MS i. *tegmine*, another form meaning “covering”]. The proud horseman who had arrived was now humbled: unable to walk on his own feet, he was carried out of the church courtyard by other men’s hands.

[Col. 0327B] After his horse and whatever he could possess had been given to the holy martyrs on his behalf, he was indeed rescued from death. But for the remainder of his life he was useless and fit for no work, carrying in his bodily weakness a testimony to divine power and instilling in others a salutary fear through the example of the vengeance inflicted upon him, lest those who commit such acts suffer similar things.

It is also very well known and widely reported by all that oil once increased at the tombs of the holy martyrs. A priest had placed a certain earthen vessel beside the altar to preserve oil that was to burn there for the light. Only a little oil remained in the vessel, most of it having been consumed in the lamps, when suddenly it began to increase and, with no one watching, to grow greater, until the oil rising in the vessel reached its mouth.

[Col. 0328A] When this continued for several days, and the divinely increased liquid could no longer be contained within the narrow vessel but flowed drop by drop onto the ground, the cleric who was custodian of that church alone noticed it. He placed another vessel beneath it and, within a few days, collected a sextary. Unfortunate man that he was, he secretly hid it, thinking that the divine miracle would serve as a resource for his greed and believing that what had been provided as protection for all could secretly be turned into theft for himself.

But Christ, who had determined to make his saints wondrous before all, did not long permit either his shameful deed or the gift he had granted for the glory of his martyrs to remain hidden.

One day the priest entered, for some reason I do not know, a house adjoining the basilica, where the bishop of Soissons customarily stayed whenever he came there. [Col. 0328B] He saw the vessel overflowing with oil and marveled at the source of such abundance, since oil of this kind could rarely be found there. He began to question the cleric who knew of so great a crime: whose oil was it, or who had placed it there?

The cleric replied that he did not know where it had come from. But the boys who were staying there to learn the psalms and who knew the whole matter told the priest both of the miracle and of the custodian’s theft.

When he heard this, the priest quickly ran to the vessel standing beside the altar and found the pavement still wet from the overflowing oil. While he glorified God, wondrous in his saints, another of the custodians arrived and confessed that he had taken a large part of that oil, with no witness present, and had spent it wherever and however he wished.

[Col. 0327]

# FLODOARD’S ADDENDUM

From the Igniacensis codex, which contains Flodoard’s *Breviary* in two books together with an appendix.

(From Labbe, *Bibliotheca manuscriptorum*, vol. II, p. 363.)

[Col. 0327C] (After the epitaph of Bishop Fulco, Book IV, chapter 8): “Finally, Winemar, his murderer, etc., up to ‘he finished.’”

The aforementioned Fulco, however, being a wise and God-fearing man, had long before arranged his will and distributed certain parts of his patrimony among churches. Among these he granted to the church of Reims, for the remedy of his soul, the village of Nemincum, which is situated in the diocese of Noyon. Its revenues are distributed among the canons of Reims in order that his memory may be commemorated annually.

From the revenue of this same village, the canons of Noyon receive sixty solidi each year in that currency. We think it not inappropriate to set down here the reason for which these coins are paid by the church of Reims to the church of Noyon. To make this clearer, we shall append to this work [Col. 0327D] the written record of that agreement.

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, [Col. 0328C] let the agreement made between the canons of Saint Mary of Reims and Saint Mary of Noyon concerning the third part of the village called Bidricus be known to the sons of the holy mother Church, present and future.
>
> “Harduinus, archdeacon of the church of Noyon and later made bishop of Langres, had granted that third part of the aforesaid village—which had come to him from his parents by hereditary right—to the brethren of the church of Noyon for the remedy of his soul. While they held it at a distance, however, the robbers of the region were violently devastating it through frequent invasions and plundering.
>
> “Compelled by this necessity, and also warned by the brethren of the church of Reims, they granted it on what appears to be a rent-paying tenure [printed *ad Trecensum*, uncertain wording] for three pounds of Vermandian coins, which they were to receive each year from the revenue at Nemineum on the feast of Saint Dionysius.
>
> “If injustice is committed [Col. 0328D] in the payment of the revenue, let it be corrected according to the law of the court. But if the village itself is devastated, let the brethren of Reims not withdraw from this agreement on that account; and if it is restored, [Col. 0329A] let the brethren of Noyon nevertheless remain in their agreement without alteration.
>
> “This agreement was made with the counsel and consent of Archbishop Wido, Provost Odalric, Dean Richard, Cantor Odo, and the entire community. On the other side, this agreement was likewise granted with the consent of Baldwin, bishop of Noyon, and with the counsel of Provost Haganus, Dean Rotbert, and the common assent of the entire community.
>
> “Moreover, since both parties wished this pact to be perpetual, they commissioned it to be written, so that it might remain forever a testimony to the aforesaid agreement.
>
> “Done in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1051, indiction 3, during the reign of King Henry, in the twenty-third year; in the nineteenth year of the archiepiscopate of Lord Wido; and [Col. 0329B] in the eighth year of Baldwin’s episcopate at Noyon.”

(Item, Book IV, chapter 19, after the end of the chapter): Concerning this Seulf our predecessors used to say that he enlarged this church by as much as the length of three arches encompasses. They also said that he had built the old tower, which the lord archbishop Samson had demolished, when he likewise enlarged the church by the length of two arches and began to construct one tower on each side, in the year of the Incarnation of the Word 1152. But since no mention of the aforesaid opinion is found in Flodoard’s book, it seems uncertain, since it is confirmed neither by writing nor by any witness. Moreover, this Flodoard, who is the author of this work, was a contemporary of Archbishop Herivaeus, as well as of Seulf and Artold, as can be judged from his own words; and he who recounted their lesser works would perhaps not have omitted this important matter, had he known it to be true. Certainly, as we have it written, the aforementioned Seulf granted us exemption for the cloister—namely, the right to sell, purchase, or exchange houses among ourselves. In return for this grant, we annually commemorate the day of his death; and to this observance we rightly add the memory of Tilpin and Wido, who died on the day before him and bestowed many benefits upon the Church. Now, having digressed a little, let us return to the thread of the narrative.

[Col. 0329]

## Scholia or Notes on the Books of the History of the Church of Rheims

By which obscure matters are clarified, doubtful and confused matters explained, and mutilated or corrupt passages supplied and corrected.

By George Colvenerius, Doctor of Sacred Theology, royal and ordinary professor at the Academy of Douai, provost of the collegiate church of Saint Peter, and chancellor of the Academy.

(From the Library of the Fathers, volume XVII.)

## Notes on Book One

### Prologue

[Col. 0329C]

“Flodoard to the distinguished bishop R.” Thus, with the Reverend Father Jacques Sirmond, we expand the passage, since the manuscript has R F L. As Sirmond himself says, some think that the letter R. is to be understood as referring to Rodulf, bishop of Laon, whom our author writes in his Chronicle to have died in the year 948; nor does this history proceed any farther.

### Chapter One

“Slain by the brother’s soldiers . . .” Thus all the copies read, and he frequently speaks in this way, with the preposition understood, instead of “by the brother’s soldiers,” which J. supplied. Thus below, chapter 6: “removed from the popular crowds.”

[Col. 0330C]

“Whose arch is on the right for those going out.” That is, the one which is on the right for those entering the city.

“For sailors say that the swan gives a favorable omen, as Aemilius says.” These words, together with the following distich, are taken from Isidore, Book XII of the *Origins*, or *Etymologies*, chapter 7; I therefore added the little word “says.” Isidore took them from Servius on Book I of the *Aeneid*, at the verse:

“Behold the happy swans, twice six in procession.”

Aemilius Macer also has this distich in his *Ornithogony*, a work cited by Servius; likewise Nonius Marcellus, under the word *prosecta*. There, however, “Licinius” is wrongly read for “Aemilius,” as learned scholars have noted. Servius, in the passage cited above, at the verse “The sluggish drones,” names Marcus Aemilius. What is added here concerning geese is taken from the same passage of Isidore, where, concerning the Capitol saved by geese, he cites Livy, Plutarch, and Florus. To these may be added Pliny, Book X of the *Natural History*, chapter 22, and Book XXIX, chapter 3, as well as Virgil himself, near the end of Book VIII of the *Aeneid*.

“Now the name of our city was once called Durocortorum.” Thus the copies C, M, and J always read here and below, whereas S. everywhere substituted *Durocortum*. This form is indeed read commonly in the text of Julius Caesar at the passage cited here. But Fulvius Ursinus, in his emendations, testifies that in a book written nearly six hundred years ago, and in another Vatican codex, *Durocortorum* is read, as Ptolemy also reads it: Δουροκόρτορον (*Douro-kortoron*). The same reading is supported by Aethicus, by the commentary of Hieronymus Surita on the *Itinerary of Antoninus*, and by Hincmarus, Letter 6, among those published by the Reverend Father Busaeus, chapter 18. Peter Divaeus and Abraham Ortelius write *Durocottorum* in their *Geographical Treasury*, changing the letter r into t.

“Having laid waste the regions, Caesar [assembled] an army.” Thus the Original and C read, whereas manuscript J wrongly reads “having formed legions,” as is made clear by what precedes in Caesar.

“Aethicus also records it in his *Cosmography* as follows.” The words he cites are found in the *Itinerary of the Provinces*, which is attributed to Antoninus Augustus, also called the Emperor Antoninus, and which is appended to the Basel edition of Aethicus’s *Cosmography* of 1575. It is likely that Aethicus was the author of both works. See the preface to that edition. Saint Everard of Cisonium mentions the *Cosmography of the philosopher Aethicus* in his testament.

“M. P. M.” Thus our copy everywhere has M. Read this as “more or less thousands,” or rather “thousands of paces,” as Hieronymus Surita wishes at the beginning of his commentary on the aforementioned *Itinerary*, rejecting another interpretation. “For,” he says, “we can clearly establish that those roads were measured by definite and consistent dimensions of stones.” This is also supported by the fact that in the *Itinerary* itself only the two letters M. P. are read. J., with separate points, wrote M. P. M., omitting the comma placed above.

“Likewise, from Durocortorum to Divodorum, and shortly afterward, Divodorum.” In the aforementioned *Itinerary* *Divodorum* is written more frequently, and it is therefore likely that it should be read in the second place as well, as J. reads it. This is now the city of Metz, or is thought to be Theon’s town.

“Likewise, from Bagacum of the Nervii.” I restored this in place of “from Agraccum,” on the basis of the aforementioned *Itinerary*, though some copies there read *Bajacum*. The town of Hainaut seems to be intended, which was then called Bavacum.

### Chapter Two

“He orders the camp to be fortified to a height of twelve feet and with a ditch eighteen feet deep.” The Original is clearer: “He orders the camp to be fortified with a rampart twelve feet high and a ditch eighteen feet deep.”

“When night had put an end to the siege.” I restored this from the Original in place of “when they had not brought it to an end.” Shortly afterward likewise: “At midnight,” in place of “on that day at midnight.”

“And the docile ruler of the beaked Belgian covinus.” Thus it was corrected in S. from the Original, and J. reads it in the same way, whereas M. reads “of the displayed Belgian, to conquer.” In the *Corpus of Poets*, published at Lyon in 1603, *monstrati* is also read, and in the first verse *Aturi* is read for *Satyri*, although the correct reading, as Ortelius teaches in his *Treasury*, is *Atyri*. Atyrus is a river of the Tarbelli in Aquitanian Gaul that flows into the Ocean. A *covinus* is a type of chariot or sickle-bearing vehicle used by the Britons and Gauls in battle.

### Chapter Three

“Saint Sinicius, first bishop of the see of Soissons, and afterward our bishop.” Below as well: “of Soissons” and “to Soissons.” This is the nearly uniform reading of the older manuscript M, which S. changed everywhere by adding the letter i, writing *Suessionicae* and *Suessioni*, and so forth. I preferred to retain the ancient form, since it has support from Ptolemy, Aethicus, and others, as well as from the French form *Soissons*, even though the later form is more usual and is sometimes found in Julius Caesar. It makes no difference whether it is pronounced in one way or the other.

The historical truth of the account given here is confirmed by the fact that Saints Sixtus and Sinicius—concerning whom the Martyrologies speak on the first of September—are placed first in the catalogue of the bishops of Soissons, just as they are in that of the bishops of Rheims, as may be seen in the tables of Antonius Demochares. There they are said to have suffered martyrdom under Nero, together with Amantius, their successor. For this reason, according to the same Demochares, the bishop of Soissons holds the first place among the suffragan bishops of the province of Rheims and is called their dean; he also has the first voice in deliberations, and so forth, because these same men were the first bishops of Soissons and Rheims.

The names of the bishops who formerly were accustomed to be subject to the archbishop of Rheims are these: the bishop of Soissons, Châlons, Laon, Beauvais, Amiens, Noyon, Senlis, Cambrai, Arras, Tournai, and Thérouanne. After the Morini were abolished by Emperor Charles V in 1533, the episcopal see was partly transferred to Boulogne, and the bishop of Boulogne remains subject to the same metropolitan of Rheims. But in 1559, when new bishoprics were erected in the Low Countries by the bull of Paul IV, Cambrai, Arras, and Tournai were withdrawn from the metropolitan see of Rheims. The see of Cambrai was made metropolitan, with Arras and Tournai subject to it, together with two others newly erected, namely Saint-Omer and Namur.

“And Saint Memmius, ruler of the city of Châlons.” He is placed first in the catalogue of the bishops of Châlons. The Roman Martyrology, Usuard, and others speak of him on 5 August.

“His nephew, as they say, Saint Divitianus, whom he ordained bishop of Soissons.” C lacks “saint,” and the title of sanctity is not added in the tables of Demochares, in which he occupies third place. Although all our copies read *Suessoni* in the dative, the form *Suessonis* is found.

“He cherished his pledges.” Almost all the copies read this way, although manuscript J has *pignora* here and nearly everywhere else. The former agrees with antiquity. Hence Aldus Manutius says in his *Epitome of Orthography*: “The ancients said *pignus, pigneris*; later writers, *pignoris*.”

“Likewise adorned, he shone through the ministries of the clergy.” Those who are now called canons were formerly called simply clergy, as is clear from the writings of the ancients and from John Molanus, Book I, *On Canons*, chapter 2.

### Chapter Four

What is related in this chapter concerning the first martyrs of the city of Rheims—Timothy, Apollinaris, and the others—is taken from the acts which Baronius testifies that he possesses in manuscript, in his notes on the Roman Martyrology, 23 August. Their beginning is as follows: “Under the emperor Nero, with Lampadius as governor,” and so forth. For on that day, in agreement with Flodoard, their feast day is assigned, and on the preceding day that of Saint Maurus and his fellow martyrs. Peter de Natalibus also gives the date, Book VII, chapter 95, namely around the year of the Lord 57.

John Molanus discusses these men, especially the blessed Maurus, at length in the *Feasts of the Saints of Belgium*, 22 August. For the body of that same blessed Maurus, which Flodoard writes in this chapter to have been preserved in the church of Saint Celsinus, was transferred to Belgium after Flodoard’s time, under Arnulf, archbishop of Rheims, while the head remained behind, around the year of the Lord 1012. It was transferred to a place called Florennes, in the diocese of Liège, as is clear from Arnulf’s own letter to Balderic, bishop of Liège, which may be seen in Molanus.

“Where the illustrious man Lord Gondebertus was, with his wife Bertha.” These persons are discussed at length below, Book IV, chapters 46 and 47.

### Chapter Five

“Under whom Betausius is found, who, together with his deacon Primogenitus, is recorded as the first from this Belgian province to have attended the First Synod of Arles, reported by Bishop Marinus to the most blessed Pope Sylvester, during the consulship of Volusianus and Anianus.”

M and J read *Berausius* in the list of the archbishops of Rheims; the same form is also found in the margin of Volume I of the Councils, in the subscription. In the letter written by the synod to Sylvester, the name is *Ambitausus*, and in the margin *Bethausus*, as Baronius corrects it under the year 314. C, S, and J read *Betansius* here, apparently following the tables of Demochares, who testifies that at the Second Council of Arles he is called *Bethanius*. Demochares notes that this council took place in 316. But Baronius and the named consuls show that it was held in 314, which was the first year of Sylvester’s pontificate and the ninth of the Emperor Constantine.

The present passage of Flodoard therefore confirms the opinion of Caesar Baronius, who says that those bishops whose names are subscribed in the volumes of the Councils to the Second Council of Arles ought to be subscribed to the First. This was followed by the very learned Severinus Binius in the newest edition of the Councils, published at Cologne in 1606. The text of the subscription can also be corrected from this passage. Since it reads there: “From the province of Gaul, from the city of Rheims: Ibethanius the bishop, Prigenius the deacon,” while the margin has *Betausius, Prigemus*, the text should rightly read *Betausius and Primogenitus*. The text continues.

“After him Aper, then Maternianus.” Concerning the latter, Molanus adds to Usuard’s Martyrology on 30 April: “On the same day, the feast of Saint Maternianus, archbishop of Rheims, who governed that same Church as its sixth bishop.”

Between Aper and Maternianus, Demochares inserts Discolius, whom he makes the sixth bishop of this see. He is recorded as having subscribed to the Council of Cologne, held under Pope Julius I against Euphrates, around the year of the Lord 346. But perhaps he was only a chorepiscopus, or a bishop of Rheims in title only, as some have answered concerning Abel.

That Discolius should not be added is proved first by the testament of Saint Remigius below, chapter 18: “The church of Saint Sixtus, where he rests with three of his successors.” And above: “The church of Joviniana, and so forth, where also five confessors, the immediate predecessors of Lord Nicasius, have been buried.” There are therefore no more than nine who preceded Saint Nicasius.

Second, it is proved by the letter of Ebo to Baldwin Ferreus, margrave of Flanders, which is found in Molanus’s *Feasts of the Saints of Belgium*, 14 October. In it he expressly writes that Saint Donatianus was the seventh bishop of the see of Rheims.

Third, it is proved by Hincmar’s letter, found below in Book III, chapter 22, where he calls Saint Remigius the fifteenth archbishop of Rheims.

Ebo gives the reason why little is written about these bishops and the other saints of this province in the letter cited above: “Know that the written lives of him”—that is, Donatianus—“and of Saint Remigius and innumerable other saints were destroyed by the devastation of the Vandals.”

“From this point Donatianus became bishop, whose relics were also carried to the maritime regions by the bishop of Noyon or Tournai.” The author speaks in the same way below, specifically in Book III, chapter 23, because the churches of Noyon and Tournai were united for six hundred years, namely from the time of Saint Medard, who died in the year of the Lord 556, until the time of Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux.

Noyon is also called *Noviomensis* and *Noviodunensis*; in French, Noyon. This blessed bishop was transferred to the distinguished Flemish maritime city called Bruges, which had previously been subject to the Church of Tournai. More recently, namely in 1559, the church of Saint Donatianus itself was erected as a cathedral. He was transferred there during the time of the aforementioned Ebo, archbishop of Rheims, and of Charles the Bald, in the year 863, as Jacobus Meyerus writes in his *Annals of Flanders*.

Yet the claim cannot be true which Meyerus does not assert but says that he found recorded: namely, that Donatianus was baptized by Dionysius, bishop of the city of Rome, and was appointed by him bishop of Rheims around the year of salvation 270. For, as is clear from what has been said, Betausius was bishop of Rheims in 314. Aper and Maternianus succeeded him, and then Donatianus.

To omit nothing, in the tables of Demochares he is called “L. Donatianus the Roman, son of Cornelius and Lucina.” Molanus notes what accounts of his life exist in his additions to Usuard, 14 October; Laurentius Surius discusses his translation on the same day.

“Whom the blessed Viventius [succeeded].” Molanus mentions him in his addition to Usuard, 7 September.

### Chapter Six

“It is said to have existed in ancient times in the church called ‘at the Apostles.’” Thus M. and the others read. But in M, in a later hand, “of Saint Symphorianus” was written above the line. S. incorporated this into the text, as well as certain other explanatory additions, in the following form: “Which was formerly called ‘at the Apostles’ but is now called Saint Symphorianus,” as J. also reads it. Nicholas Chesneau, dean and canon of that same church of Saint Symphorianus, has the same annotation in his French copy. But I do not approve of transferring marginal annotations into the text. Nevertheless, all copies have the same wording in the text in Book II, chapter 6.

What the author relates in this chapter concerning the martyrdom of Saint Nicasius, Eutropia, and their companions he took for the most part from the acts of those martyrs. These acts, taken from a manuscript codex, are found in Surius, Volume VII; in Vincent of Beauvais, *Historical Mirror*, Book XXI, chapters 37 and 38; in Peter de Natalibus, Book I, chapter 69; and in Saint Antoninus, Part II of the *History*, title 11, chapter 8. They are fuller and more complete, however, among the *Lives of the Saints* printed at Cologne in folio, almost at the infancy of printing, in 1483. They are also found in the proper breviaries of the cathedral churches of Rheims, Amiens, Arras, and Bruges.

First, the time at which these events occurred must be established. In this matter the passage cited at the end of this chapter from Saint Jerome’s letter to Ageruchia, or Gerontia, gives us considerable light. Baronius teaches that this letter was written in the year 407. It is therefore likely that the events occurred in that same year.

For the Vandals and Alans entered Gaul after crossing the Rhine on the day before the Kalends of January in the year 406, as Blessed Prosper records in his *Chronicle*, during the sixth consulship of Arcadius and the consulship of Anicius Probus. Christian Massaeus and Baronius assign these consuls to this year, although Prosper assigns them to the year 408. Other chronicles exceed Baronius’s chronology by two years. Cassiodorus in his *Chronicle* and Zosimus, Book VI, report the same event under the same consuls.

Arnaldus Pontacus, in his notes on Prosper’s *Chronicle*, says that the passage about this disastrous invasion in the aforementioned letter of Jerome belongs to the same period, around the same year. This opinion is especially approved by Baronius, who, under the year 407, after quoting the same words of Jerome, adds:

“But since he reports that Rheims was devastated by the Vandals among the calamities of the other cities of Gaul, this opinion draws me more strongly to suppose that Saint Nicasius, bishop of that city, together with his sister Eutropia and his companions, received the crown of martyrdom, although some assign this to the time of the Huns. Their acts of passion likewise state that they suffered under the Vandals, but they must plainly be corrected in saying that the Vandals were pagans, since it is clear that they were Christians.”

Thus he. As for the latter point, however, it is likely that not all the Vandals were Christians, but that many pagans were mixed among the Arian Vandals.

That this martyrdom occurred at the time just mentioned—not, as Sigebert records in his *Chronicle*, following popular, and presumably Frankish, annals, under the Huns in 453, nor, as Demochares says, in 454—is proved by our Flodoard. Four other bishops, who are listed below in chapter 9, intervened between Saint Nicasius and Saint Remigius.

Saint Remigius died in the year of the Lord 544, in the seventy-fourth year of his episcopate and the ninety-fifth year of his life, as is clear from his epitaph below in this same book, chapter 21. It follows that he became bishop in the year 470. Thus, for the four intervening bishops, only sixteen or seventeen years would remain.

Moreover, Saint Jerome died in the year 421 or 422. The martyrdom must therefore have occurred before that time, at the latest.

Finally, this opinion is supported by the fact that Blessed Servatius is named among the contemporaries of Blessed Nicasius. He could by no means have lived until the year 453, for he would then have been bishop for more than a hundred years. He attended the Councils of Sardica and Cologne, held respectively in 343 and 346. Nor is it at all probable that he lived for three hundred years, as is read in some accounts.

As for the aforementioned letter of Saint Jerome, without detracting from the authority of Baronius, I am more inclined to believe that it was written in 408. Since the destruction of the city of Rheims occurred at the end of 407, namely on 14 December, news of that event could not have reached Saint Jerome, who was residing in Bethlehem, in the same year.

There is another difficulty here: whether they suffered at the hands of the Vandals or of the Huns. But this is already made clear by the resolution of the preceding question. The persecution of the Huns and their devastation of Gaul under King Attila occurred later, around the year 450. At that time Blessed Anianus, bishop of Orléans, and Blessed Lupus of Troyes were living. The author prematurely names them here, and says that by their prayers and merits they delivered their cities from the devastation of Attila, king of the Huns.

A reconciliation concerning Saint Lupus might easily be proposed, since he was bishop for fifty-two years. But it is contradicted by the fact that he was not raised to the episcopal throne until 427, according to Baronius’s calculation, who records his death in 479.

Flodoard must nevertheless be excused, since in this matter he follows Hincmar, Letter 5, chapter 17, among those published by the Reverend Father John Busaeus.

I do not find in the histories how many years Saint Anianus occupied the see, but he is said to have died in 453. It may nevertheless be inferred that he lived long in the episcopate and could have witnessed both persecutions, because Vincent of Beauvais discusses him in connection with the death of Blessed Jerome and the persecution of the Vandals, as though Anianus had already been bishop at that time—namely in Book XX, chapters 11–13—following, as he himself says, Hugh of Fleury.

Certainly, all their acts, both those in the breviaries and those published separately, mention the persecution of the Vandals, not that of the Huns. Francis Haraeus, in his abridgment of the *Lives of the Saints*, joins the Huns to the Vandals on his own authority, perhaps moved by that of Sigebert, since he does not possess the complete acts.

Finally, Jerome and Ebo, in the passages cited above, mention the Vandals, not the Huns. The Martyrology of Usuard, enlarged by John Molanus, and the proper Martyrology of the Church of Cambrai do the same.

Otto of Freising, in his *Chronicle*, Book IV, chapter 28, followed Sigebert, as did John Tilius in his *Chronicle of the Franks* and the French *Lives of the Saints* published by the doctors of Paris.

After arranging all this material, I find that Massaeus, a diligent historian, held the same opinion as I do in Book XI of his *Chronicle of the World*, under the year 406. He says:

“In that consulship”—namely, the sixth of Arcadius and that of Anicius Probus—“as Prosper testifies, on the day before the Kalends of January, after crossing the Rhine, the Vandals, Alans, and other barbarian nations invaded Gaul and carried out countless massacres. Among these, Saint Nicasius fell at Rheims. His own history testifies to this, making no mention of the Huns but only of the Vandals. Saint Jerome also clearly bears witness to the same in his letter to Gerontia; he died long before the arrival of the Huns in Gaul. We therefore rightly condemn the negligence of those who place the martyrdom of Saint Nicasius more than forty years later, leaving scarcely any time at all between him and Remigius.”

Thus he.

Nicolaus Camuzar makes the same observation at the end of his *Promptuary of Sacred Antiquities of the Diocese of Troyes*. He shows that Sigebert wrongly attributes the killing of Saint Nicasius to Attila:

“Flodoard,” he says, “perhaps following a somewhat earlier author, makes the most holy bishops Servatius of Tongeren, Nicasius, and Lupus contemporaries and of the same age, although it is plainly evident that Lord Lupus was not raised to the episcopal dignity until twenty years after the death of those bishops.”

Thus he.

As for the reasoning of some who say that, because Eutropia is reported here to have feared for her chastity on account of her beauty, the event must have been caused by the Huns rather than the Vandals, since the race of the Huns was more inclined than others to lust and immorality, as Salvian testifies in Book IV, *On Right Judgment and Providence*: this is a very weak argument. Such things ought rightly to be feared in any hostile invasion.

“And several others distinguished by their virtues.” For example, Saint Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse, a contemporary of Nicasius, whom Jerome mentions in the passage cited above; and Saint Germanus of Auxerre, a contemporary of Lupus of Troyes but later than Saint Nicasius.

“Whence also, according to the opinion of Blessed Augustine, he found the greater fruit of charity,” and so forth. The passage is from Letter 180. From almost its very words the author wove the thread of his account, beginning at: “Blessed Nicasius therefore laid down his life for the brethren,” and continuing to: “not like a hired servant, seeing the wolf coming.”

Augustine’s complete statement reads as follows:

“For one who does not flee hostile calamities, although he could escape, lest he abandon the ministry of Christ, where people cannot become Christians or live as Christians, finds a greater fruit of charity than one who flees not for the sake of the brethren but for his own sake, and, when captured, does not deny Christ but accepts martyrdom.”

“Aggeruchia the widow.” Thus M. J. has *Ageruchiam*, C. *Geruntiam*, and S. likewise *Gerontiam*. Erasmus preferred this reading in Jerome’s works; Marianus reads *Ageruchia*. See our notes on the *Chronicle of Cambrai*, Book I, chapter 5.

“Nemetes and Argentoracus transferred into Germany.” Jerome now reads: “The Nemetae and Argentoratus, transferred into Germany,” which S. altered. But *transferred* is correctly feminine, so that it refers to the cities.

“For he was living there, intent upon these duties.” M. has *isto*, “there.” The correct reading is *isthuc* or *isthic*, as it is read in the *Life of Blessed Remigius* by Hincmar, where what is said here concerning the burning of the city of Rheims and the impressions of his feet in the stones is explained at greater length, as also below by the author in chapter 12.

### Chapter Seven

Everything related in this chapter—apart from the translation carried out by Fulco—is found in nearly the same words in the acts of these martyrs printed at Cologne in 1483, mentioned above.

“Which, as is said, are still preserved at the fortress of Tournai.” In former times notable relics of Saint Nicasius were kept at Tournai, in the church of Saint Mary. But one hundred years after Flodoard’s time they were brought back to Rheims, during the time of Gervasius, archbishop, who had previously been bishop of Le Mans. For this reason the Church of Rheims celebrates the feast of the translation of Saint Nicasius on 23 July.

On that day the breviary of the same Church reads:

“When one of the clerics of Tournai heard that the aforementioned Gervasius had begun to restore the shrine of Saint Nicasius at Rheims, he made every effort to restore to the church at Rheims that part of the body of Blessed Nicasius which was preserved in the church at Tournai. He sought a time and place for fulfilling his desire. Since he could not accomplish this by himself, one night the church of Tournai caught fire; the blaze threatened ruin to the entire city. The aforementioned cleric, finding an opportunity, entered the burning church without fear, carried away the glorious treasure, and reached Rheims. He explained the whole matter to Gervasius in due order. Gervasius joined the part of the blessed body he had received to the other part, which had been kept in a chest, and found everything equal. Later, the entire body was transferred to the church dedicated to the Blessed Virgin, where it is now devoutly venerated.”

Thus far the breviary.

### Chapter Eight

Molanus discusses Saint Oriculus and his companions in his addition to Usuard’s Martyrology, 18 November, in these words:

“On this same day, [the feast] of the blessed martyr Oriculus and his companions, who suffered during the persecution of the Vandals.”

The Roman Martyrology likewise reads:

“On this same day, Saints Oriculus and his companions, who suffered for the Catholic faith during the persecution of the Vandals.”

In his notes there Baronius added only this:

“Concerning him, namely Oriculus, the other manuscripts read the same, from which Molanus [compiled his text] in Usuard. I read the same in the Cologne addition made to Usuard in the year 1521.”

“Which is still said clearly to appear.” Thus M. In C, a later hand added the syllable *ap*. Hence C and J read *apparere*, “to appear,” whereas *parere*, “to be evident,” is extremely common in place of *apparere*, as in Matthew 24: “Then the sign of the Son of Man will be evident.”

“The priest of that same place, named Betto.” The manuscript has *Becco*; C has *Beto*. By “priest of this or that place,” both in this history and frequently in the writings of the ancients, the person now called a pastor, parish priest, or, in French, a *curé*, is understood. Thus in the *Life of Saint Bavo*, the priest Domlinus is said to have come from Thurolt; he was the pastor of that place.

### Chapter Nine

“Then Bennadius, whose name in his testament is nevertheless Bennagius.” In the tables of Demochares and in Baronius’s *Annals*, *Gennadius* is wrongly read, and it is also said that he died in the year 471, although he died rather one year earlier. For, as is clear from the notes on chapter 6 and below on chapter 13, Remigius assumed the episcopate in the year 470.

### Chapter Ten

What this chapter and the following chapters discuss concerning the birth and life of Saint Remigius is drawn for the most part from the *Life* written by Fortunatus and Hincmar. The former is found in Surius on 1 October, the latter on 13 January. I have carefully compared both with what Flodoard relates here. In Hincmar, everything is reported more fully and sometimes more clearly. Flodoard nevertheless added certain matters taken from elsewhere.

According to Sigebert, Christian Massaeus, and others, Saint Remigius was born in the year 449. See the notes below on chapter 13.

“Principius, afterward the holy bishop of the city of Soissons, and the father of Blessed Lupus, the successor of that same Principius.” Saint Principius is the twelfth blessed bishop in Demochares’ catalogue of the bishops of Soissons, while Lupus is the thirteenth. The Roman Martyrology mentions Principius on 25 September, as does Molanus’s addition to Usuard on the same day. The elevation of both Principius and Lupus is commemorated on the Kalends of June.

These words might be understood to mean that Blessed Clinia, the mother of Saint Remigius, had not two sons in her youth, but that Principius himself was the father of Blessed Lupus, as is expressly stated in the French translation. Yet in Hincmar’s *Life of Saint Remigius* it is clearly indicated that she had two sons. It reads as follows:

“She had borne in the flower of her youth, by her one husband Aemilius, Principius, afterward the holy bishop of the city of Soissons, and his brother, the father of Blessed Lupus, the successor of that same Principius.”

There is no doubt that Flodoard intended to say the same thing, abbreviating Hincmar. Baronius is therefore mistaken when, in his *Annals* under the years 463 and 507, he says that Saint Lupus of Soissons was the son of Saint Principius, bishop of Soissons. It is true, however, that he was Principius’s successor and Saint Remigius’s nephew, as is clear from the acts and from the testament of the same saint.

John Savaro, in his notes on Letter 14 of Sidonius, Book VIII, and Letter 8 of Book IX, says that Principius was the paternal uncle of Lupus, bishop of Soissons and his own successor, not his father.

When I consulted Lord Guillaume le Begue, Doctor of Sacred Theology and head master of the College of Rheims, about this difficulty, he replied in agreement with Hincmar and Savaro. He added the testimony of an anonymous writer from the monastery of Saint Remigius, whom he says lived around the year 1400. It reads as follows:

“Cilinia, in the flower of her youth, bore by her one husband Aemilius two sons, namely Principius and another whose name is unknown to us. This other son took a wife, by whom he fathered a son named Lupus. After Saint Principius, his uncle—he means his paternal uncle—the bishop of Soissons, Lupus succeeded to the see.”

“During whose nursing.” Thus all the copies read, but from Hincmar it seems that *ablactatione*, “during whose weaning,” should be read.

“Already, however, an old man.” Thus C and J. In M, “although still” is read; S joins it into a single expression and explains it as meaning “nevertheless.”

“And he is still held especially distinguished in the prayers of the righteous.” “Of the righteous” means of good and pious men, in opposition to the wicked.

“In whose church his own blessed mother also rests.” He is speaking of Blessed Balsamia, or, as C has it, Balsemia, Saint Remigius’s nurse. She rests in the church of Saint Celsinus, her son, which is now called the church of the Holy Nurse. Molanus mentions Celsinus in his addition to Usuard, 25 October, in these words:

“At Rheims, Saint Celsinus, confessor and priest, disciple of Blessed Remigius.”

### Chapter Eleven

“Whom ecclesiastical regulation would not admit to such a dignity at that age.” According to the ancient canons, as is clear from the decrees of Pope Fabian and from canon 11 of the Council of Neocaesarea, no one was permitted to be ordained priest before the age of thirty, even if he was exceptionally worthy. These canons are also found in Gratian, Distinction 78. Much less, therefore, could he be ordained bishop.

“Paul appeared to be in the spirit.” All the copies read this except C, which has *inspectu*, “in sight.” But *in spiritu* is clearly the correct reading, both from Hincmar and from the beginning of the *Life of Saint Rigobert* in Surius, 4 January, where the same statement occurs.

### Chapter Twelve

“He came to a village called Calmiciacum out of devoted zeal for this undertaking.” Thus manuscript J, and below in chapter 21 and in Book II, chapters 7 and 11, all the copies read the same. Likewise in Fortunatus, from whom this miracle is taken:

“He came to a village whose name was Calmaciacus, out of zealous devotion.”

Here C reads *Culmiciacum*. Below there is sometimes *Calmisciacum*, as in chapter 18 in Saint Remigius’s testament; elsewhere *Colmisciacum*, *Culmisciacum*, and *Culmissiacum*, as at the end of chapter 20.

Flodoard himself was pastor of that place, as is clear from Book IV, chapter 28. In French it is translated as *Cormicy*, and in the margin *Chaumusy* is given as an alternative; this is how it is translated in chapter 20 of this book, and in Book II, chapter 7, as *Chaumuci*. In chapter 12 it is again *Cormicy*, and so thereafter.

“For the purpose of saving the same.” The vessel is understood: that is, lest the vessel be spoiled if it were completely empty.

“Through the Open Gate.” Hincmar gives the reason for the name, adding this parenthesis:

“But at that time it was called this because, while the other gates were closed for the protection of the city, this one stood open during the day for the convenience of those going out and coming in.”

The place is at Rheims, where the church of the Temple now stands; I believe it received its name from the Templars.

Relying, as is reported, on the letters which they had given to blessed Remigius. The letters of Saint Benedict to blessed Remigius still exist today at the end of the Cassinian Chronicle, in the Benedictine Breviary on the Kalends of October, and several times elsewhere, according to Arnold Wion, *Lignum vitae*, book I, chapter 1. They are also found in volume VI of Baronius’s *Annals*, under the year 507, where he suspects them of being forged—both because of the superscription, which seems to him unusually worded, and because in Saint Remigius’s testament the man whose daughter he cared for, freeing her from a demon and raising her from the dead, is called Benedictus. Baronius thinks Hincmarus made an error, and that Flodoardus, taking the account from him, substituted Saint Benedict—who at this time was practicing monastic life in Italy—for that Benedict, the girl’s father, a very wealthy man in Provence.

Yet this letter and Hincmarus’s account of Saint Benedict are in no way inconsistent with Saint Remigius’s testament. For, according to the history of Saint Remigius’s Life, this Benedict first brought his daughter to the thresholds of the Apostles and to Saint Benedict; afterward Saint Benedict sent the parents back to Gaul with this letter. That this letter does not belong to the Benedict whom Baronius supposes is shown by the fact that Benedict himself came in person, not by letter, to Saint Remigius. Moreover, neither the title nor the wording of the letter can in any way fit Benedict, the girl’s father. Nor should anyone be troubled by Flodoardus’s statement “as is reported,” the way we customarily speak when a matter is not entirely certain, since those words are not in Hincmarus but were added by Flodoardus—both here and often elsewhere, even where there is no doubt, specifically below in chapter 17. Hincmarus, however, reports the matter positively, speaking both of letters from the man of God Benedict—for that is what he calls him—and of letters from Alaric, king of the Goths. Fortunatus the priest, in his *Life of Saint Remigius*, mentions both letters long before Hincmarus; and one should not lightly depart from ancient testimony.

Nor should this seem wholly unusual. Considering especially the truly candid and Christian simplicity of the ancient monks, it is understandable that a writer inferior in age and rank should address a superior as “brother and fellow servant in Christ Jesus,” and should not authoritatively bestow upon him the name of eternal blessing, but humbly wish it for him—just as we commonly write to anyone wishing him health, eternal life, or some other blessing. So that everyone may form his own judgment on this matter, I have thought it appropriate to insert here the short letter from the aforementioned Chronicle, and in a somewhat more accurate form than that in which Nicolaus Chesneau inserted it into his French version, from manuscript papers belonging to the venerable religious of the monastery of Saint Remigius at Reims. It runs as follows:

> To Remigius, lord priest: Benedict, a humble cultivator of the monastic life, your brother and fellow servant in Christ Jesus, offers the gift of eternal blessing. Rejoicing in your most holy progress, priest of the supreme King—for we are members of the supreme Head—I believe that I possess wholly in you, praise be to God, what I feel to be lacking in myself. Behold: what my sins prevented from taking place is now supplied by the priestly merits of your authority; and from now on let human rumors concerning me cease, since in your presence the perfection of all virtues is established. I entrust this captive woman, besieged by the ancient enemy, to your eminence, so that you may offer a sacred sacrifice to God for her liberation and make my littleness rejoice greatly in that victory. Farewell, clearest jewel of Christ’s priests.

With their child bound, they arrived. “Bound” means tied, constrained by bonds. For in Hincmarus we read: “Bringing her with them, bound.”

“Sidonius sends greetings to Lord Pope Remigius.” That the title *pope* was customarily applied to all bishops is clear from countless examples in the writings of Cyprian, Jerome, Augustine, Sidonius, Fortunatus, Eulogius of Córdoba, and other Fathers.
