This Eulogius flourished in the year 850; until that time the title was common to all bishops, although it had gradually begun to be applied more frequently and more particularly to the Roman pontiff, as can easily be observed in the writings of Cassiodorus. When, therefore, in later times common usage established that the title *pope* should be given only to the Roman pontiff, and when certain schismatic bishops, out of hatred for that Roman prelate, arrogated it to themselves with proud presumption and assumed other privileges not granted to them, a synod was finally held at Rome under Gregory VII, in the year of the Lord 1073. Among other things, it decreed against those schismatics that there should be only one pope throughout the Christian world, and that no one might call himself or another by that name. The synod is preserved in the register of Gregory VII’s letters in the Vatican Library. This is taken from Baronius’s notes on the Roman Martyrology, 10 January.

Would that the writings of blessed Remigius mentioned by Sidonius in this letter might one day be brought to light, if they have not perished. The Roman Breviary on the Kalends of October likewise testifies that blessed Remigius wrote much, saying that he interpreted many books of Holy Scripture. Hincmarus calls him “learned in every respect” and “most learned in the Holy Scriptures.” Gregory of Tours, book II of the *Histories of the Franks*, chapter 31, quotes the beginning of a consolatory letter from blessed Remigius to King Clovis on the death of his sister Albofledis. Aimo, book I of *The Deeds of the Franks*, at the end, quotes the epitaph of that same King Clovis, believed to have been composed by Saint Remigius. Guilelmus Eysengrein, in his *Catalogue of Witnesses to the Truth*, says that Remigius, in books he published, exposed the Arians’ adulterous opinions concerning the faith of Christ, and left many other literary monuments.

Recently, in Mainz, his explanations of Paul’s Epistles were printed in folio in the year 1614, through the work of the Reverend Father Johannes Baptista Villalpandus, theologian of the Society of Jesus. In his preface to the reader, Villalpandus plausibly demonstrates that these works belong to this Remigius, not to Remigius of Auxerre, and answers the objections raised against that attribution. Certainly not only Bellarmine, but before him Cuthbert Tunstall, bishop of Durham, in book I of *On the Truth of the Body and Blood of the Lord in the Eucharist*, and after him Johannes Garetius, in the sixth centenary of the same subject, cite from Remigius, archbishop of Reims, a notable passage preserved in these explanations. Cuthbert adds:

> We once saw one or two books of this Remigius, written in an ancient hand and bearing his name.

Villalpandus, in the preface just mentioned, also testifies that various homilies are preserved in different books of the monastery of Cassino which retain the name and attribution of Bishop Remigius. The matter, however, is not yet certain to me.

There is a folio work printed at Hanau in the year 1613, entitled *Corpus of the Ancient and Genuine History of France*. It contains a treatise with many letters of kings and bishops. Among them are four letters of Remigius: two to Clovis, the first being the consolatory letter mentioned above; the third to the bishops Heraclius, Leo, and Theodosius; and the fourth addressed to Bishop Fulco.

Whatever he had brought, although you were ready to purchase it, he brought in as a gift, as a citizen—which was not unjust. From the works of Sidonius corrected through the labor of Johannes Savaron, I restored the word *paratis* in place of *paratus*, and *civis* in place of *cujus*, as well as three other words below. Conversely, nine or ten passages in the same letter of Sidonius may be restored from our author. The sentence is there read as follows:

> Whatever he had brought, although you were ready to purchase it, he nevertheless brought it in as a gift, as a citizen—which was not unjust.

The edition with the notes of Johannes de Wouweren and Petrus Colvius reads the same way, except that in the middle it reads and punctuates the words as a parenthesis:

> *(quod tamen cujus nec erat, injustum)*—that is, “which, however, as a citizen, was not unjust,” with *cujus* in place of *civis*.

Like other editions of the same letter, it contains errors. Thus Savaron’s edition deserves preference, if one may judge the lion from its claw.

## CHAPTER XIII

Syagrius, a certain Roman prince. He was the son of Aegidius, commander of the Romans, and resided at Soissons. See Gregory of Tours, book II of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 27; and Sigebert in the *Chronicle* under the year 489, where he writes that Syagrius was killed.

When once he was passing near the city of Reims. Specifically, along the road which, as Hincmarus says, is still called “Barbarian” because barbarians traveled along it; in French, *rue de Barbâtre*. There was also a village called Barbastre, as Nicolaus Chesneau noted in his manuscript copy. Gregory of Tours discusses the events described in this chapter above, chapters 27–31.

When he entered the everlasting fountain of life. It should be noted that in ancient times those being baptized customarily entered the baptismal font at least up to the waist, rather than merely having water poured over the head, as is now done. Ancient paintings and histories prove this. Thus, in the *Life of Saint Vulfran*, bishop, written by Jonas, a monk of Fontenelle, and printed by Surius, volume II, on 20 March, we read that after Rabbodus, duke of the Frisians, had advanced to the font, he withdrew his foot from it, saying:

> He could not be deprived of the company of his predecessors, the princes of the Frisians, and sit with the small number of the poor in the heavenly kingdom.

For he had asked the bishop whether the greater number of the princes or nobles of the Frisian people were in that heavenly region or in the region he called Tartarus, which the bishop described. Sigebert reports the same in his *Chronicle* under the year 718, in these words:

> Rabbodus, duke of the Frisians, moved by the preaching of Bishop Vulfran to the point that he ought to be baptized, had dipped one foot into the bath. Withdrawing the other foot, he asked where the greater number of his ancestors were: in hell or in paradise? And so forth.

“Gently lower your neck, Sicamber.” From this it may be inferred that Clovis was Geldrian by birth or origin. For many consistently assert that the peoples of our Belgium, once called Geldrians, were formerly called Sicambri; among them are Hermannus a Nuenare, in his account *On the Origin and Settlements of the Ancient Franks*, and in his brief work on Belgic Gaul. On this matter see Molanus, *The Saints of Belgium*, 13 January.

Not everyone agrees, moreover, in which year of the Lord Clovis’s baptism took place. After the end of manuscript M, in the same hand in which that manuscript was written, the following has been added in full words rather than numerical symbols, in which mistakes are easily made:

> From the Incarnation of the Lord to the passing of Saint Martin are 443 years. From the Incarnation of the Lord to the baptism of the Franks are 542 years. From the Incarnation of the Lord to the passing of Clovis are reckoned 556 years. From the Incarnation of the Lord to the passing of Saint Remigius are reckoned 575 years.

So it stands there. But these figures are wrong in many respects. Nicolaus Chesneau added in the margin of his French translation at this place that Clovis was baptized on Easter Eve in the year 497, the twenty-fifth year of his reign, although in his preface to the clergy and people of Reims he likewise said that Clovis was baptized in the year 542, as appears at the end of the aforementioned manuscript.

Margatinus de la Bigne, in the chronological index of the second and third editions of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, under the fifth century and Claudianus Mamertus, says that Clovis was baptized in the year 452—that is, almost one hundred years earlier. According to the chronological accounts of Sigebert, Sebastian Münster, Johannes Tielius, and Baronius, however, he was baptized in the year 499. Aimo is not far from them at the end of book I of *The Deeds of the Franks*, where he writes that Clovis reigned for thirty years and died in the year 514 of the Lord’s Incarnation. Most agree that he was baptized in the fifteenth year of his reign, including Johannes Trithemius, Franciscus Belforestus in the *Annals of France*, and others. Those who teach that he was washed in the baptismal font in the year 500 differ little or not at all from these authorities, including Massaeus, Belforestus, Genebrardus, and other more recent writers.

Since it is certain that he was baptized on Easter Eve, and since according to the Gallican reckoning—still used in our own time in Belgium—the year of the Lord is ordinarily begun at the feast of Easter, according to the former authorities he was baptized on the last day of the year 499, whereas according to the latter he was baptized on the first day of the year 500.

From antiquity Hincmarus also supports this view in the epitaph of blessed Remigius, cited below in chapter 21, where the exact time of his age, ordination, episcopal tenure, and the baptism of the Franks is given. That epitaph establishes that blessed Remigius was made bishop of Reims in the twenty-second year of his age, presided for seventy-four years, died in the year 544 at the age of ninety-six, and that the Frankish people were baptized in the year 500. It follows that he must have been made bishop in the year 470.

Sigebert does not disagree with this as to the year of his death. He says that Remigius was born in 449, made bishop in 471, and died in 545; Jacobus Meyerus says the same in the *Annals of Flanders*. Since Remigius died on 13 January, the same year is 545 when reckoned from January, but 544 when reckoned from Easter, as the Gauls continued to do until the time of Charles IX.

These authorities are nevertheless contradicted by the fact that Flavius, who succeeded blessed Remigius after Romanus, is said to have signed the Council of Arvernum, held in the year 541 according to Baronius. The aforementioned Guilelmus le Bègue agrees with me in placing the council in that year, although it was in fact held fifteen or sixteen years later.

With a certain prince named Raganarius beyond the River Somme. That is, at Cambrai, as Baldericus explains these words, author of the *Chronicle of Cambrai*, book I, chapter 4, where he says more about this Raganarius—or, as he himself writes, Ragnacharius. Manuscript M and the codex of the monastery of Saint Remigius, as Nicolaus Chesneau notes, read *Somnam*; yet the text of that codex has *Somenam* and translates it into French as *Somne*. J likewise has *Somenam*, as does Sigebert under the year 445.

The aforementioned King Louis. Thus M and C, although M almost always below writes *Ludowico* and the same Saint Remigius codex, as Nicolaus Chesneau noted, also reads it here as *Ludowico*. The name is found written in many other forms as well, as I noted in the *Chronicle of Cambrai*, book I, chapter 37. Some observe that after his baptism Clovis was called Louis, because he was given that name in baptism, as Laurentius Surius noted on 13 January. Therefore, despite the testimony of all the manuscripts, the name Louis should not here be changed to Clovis, as was done in S and J, even though it must be acknowledged that the names are identical.

## CHAPTER XIV

He gave to the church of Saint Mary at Laon-Chevet, a castle of the diocese of Reims where he had been raised, a considerable portion of the same possessions, and likewise a portion of the other goods. The subject is Saint Remigius. Since the castle of Laon-Chevet and the county of Laon belonged to the parish or diocese of Reims, blessed Remigius established a new bishopric at Laon, as is clear both from this chapter and from Sigebert’s *Chronicle*. He writes under the year 500:

> King Clovis bestowed many estates upon the church of Reims. Remigius, giving a large part of them to the church of Laon, established the episcopal see there. He restored to his see a man who had fallen into fornication with his former wife, had been purified by seven years of penance, and had been brought out of confinement by divine command.

Flodoardus follows Sigebert in this account.

There he found Genebaud, a man noble by birth. Nicolaus Chesneau calls him a count in the margin of his French translation. Our manuscripts consistently read *Genebaudum*. In Hincmarus, as printed by Surius, he is called *Genebaldus*, as also in the tables of Democharis, who adds that some call him Geraldus and others Genebaudus. Hincmarus’s manuscript at Mont-Saint-Éloi likewise reads *Genebaudus*. The variation seems to have arisen because, from the French form *Genebauld*, some omit the *u* and others the *l*.

And the silent passion of both the man and the woman burned in the heart of lust. The manuscript incorrectly reads *totiusque* instead of *tacitusque*. In Hincmarus the complete sentence reads:

> Thus it happened that, while the fault was concealed from men and the passion of lust was concealed in the hearts of both the bishop and the woman—for, as is known, the more fire is covered, the more fiercely the covered fire burns—the bishop, pierced with remorse over his fault, …

Here, therefore, he called it “silent,” meaning covered and secret. This history of Saint Genebaud clearly shows how far from the truth is the teaching of the sectarians of our time, who want the Apostle’s words “the husband of one wife” to mean a man who had a wife, although intercourse with a wife whom he had separated from his bed had to be expiated by such profound penance. It is entirely true what Jerome says in book I *Against Jovinianus*:

> Certainly you admit that a man who fathers children while he is bishop cannot be a bishop. Otherwise, if he is discovered, he will not be treated merely as a husband but will be condemned as an adulterer.

He asks Saint Remigius to go to Laon. That is, to go or come there. Hincmarus states it more clearly:

> He sent to Saint Remigius, asking him to come to Laon.

Genebaud therefore died in peace, numbered among the saints of God. He is mentioned in the Cologne addition to Usuard and by Molanus on 5 September. The Cologne addition says that his deeds are recorded in the *Acts of Saint Remigius*. Everything mentioned here about him is explained more fully by Hincmarus in the *Life of Saint Remigius*. Petrus Equilinus discusses him and his son Saint Latro in book I, chapter 41.

Juliacus and Codiciacus are the estates of these possessions. All our manuscripts consistently read this both here and in many places below, as does Hincmarus’s manuscript. Therefore the reading found in Surius’s printed Hincmarus, *Judaicus and Ociliacus*, should be corrected from our present author.

## CHAPTER XV

Gondebaudus and Godegiselus. Thus the Remigius codex reads, in agreement with Gregory of Tours, book II of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 32 and following chapters, and with Aimo, book I of *The Deeds of the Franks*, chapter 19. The same history is described in those places, and the name is written *Godegisilus*, as J reads here. Hincmarus, as printed by Surius, has *Godeglissus*. Our other manuscripts read *Godigeselus*. This Gondebaudus—or, as Hincmarus and Aimo write, Gundebaldus, and Gregory, Gundobaldus—was king of the Burgundians, who, according to that same Gregory, were infected with the Arian heresy. Massaeus, at the beginning of book XII of his *Chronicle*, writes *Gundebaldus* and *Gundegisilus*.

They came upon the River Ouche, near the castle of Dijon, and Gondebaudus, shutting himself inside the castle of Avignon, and so forth. Hincmarus has *Oscharam*, as S reads. All the manuscripts except J had *Avionem*, but we have written *Avinionem* on the authority of Hincmarus and Gregory, who says that Gondebaudus entered the city of Avignon. Massaeus likewise calls it Avignon. Nicolaus Chesneau translates it as *Avignon*.

And a synod was held in the city of Orléans at the advice of his holy patron Remigius. This was the First Council of Orléans, preserved in volume II of the councils. Baronius places it in the year 507; Sigebert, Massaeus, Onuphrius, and others place it in 512. Among those whose signatures are recorded are Saint Gildaldus, bishop of Rouen, and Saint Lupus, bishop of Soissons.

And a purple tunic. Thus M, J, and Hincmarus’s manuscript, as printed by Surius, who also noted in the margin:

> Sidonius uses *blatta* for purple.

Sigebert likewise has this reading, in an edition prepared from manuscript codices by the very learned Aubert Miraeus, although the French manuscripts read *blacteam*, the German ones *bracteam*, C *baltea*, and S *blattrea*. We should not depart from the first reading. For Eutropius, Cassiodorus, and others also use *blatteum* for “purple.” Moreover, Gregory of Tours reads *tunica blatteam* in book II of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 38.

Sigebert gives the same account in almost the same words under the year 510:

> King Clovis received from the Emperor Anastasius consular documents, a golden crown adorned with jewels, and a purple tunic; from that day he was called consul and Augustus. The king himself sent to Rome, to Saint Peter, a golden crown adorned with jewels, which is commonly called a kingdom.

For a clearer understanding of the matter, consider what Papirius Massonus says in book I of the *Annals of the Franks*:

> Caesar Anastasius, admiring Clovis’s name and achievements, sent envoys to him in Celtic Gaul from Greece, to honor the king of the Franks with the dignity of a patrician, which differs greatly from the consulship: the former is perpetual, the latter annual.

So he writes.

The letters he sent to him. The letters of Pope Hormisdas, by which he entrusted blessed Remigius with his own authority in the kingdom of Louis, are preserved in volume II of the councils and in volume I of Surius’s *Life of blessed Remigius*, written by Hincmarus.

## CHAPTER XVI

I nowhere find the name of the synod at which Saint Remigius converted the heretic. Baronius, volume VI, under the year 514, says that it was a synod convened at Reims by Saint Remigius himself after he had received letters from Pope Hormisdas, by which Hormisdas entrusted him with his own authority. Severinus Binius follows Baronius in all respects, volume II of the councils, placing the synod in that year, under Hormisdas, in the matter of reforming ecclesiastical discipline in Gaul.

The beginning of the chapter, however, contradicts this: it says that the bishops of Gaul asked blessed Remigius to come to that council. Hincmarus says the same, and both writers state that the council was held on a matter of faith, not only by the bishops of Gaul but also by those of the provinces of Belgic Gaul, as Hincmarus explicitly asserts. Nor do the people of Reims recognize this synod, as the aforementioned Guilelmus le Bègue wrote to me. He therefore thinks that the event took place at the aforementioned Council of Orléans. But this clearly conflicts with Hincmarus and Flodoardus, who record two synods, identifying this one as distinct from the earlier council.

## CHAPTER XVII

“‘There is always a good fire, if it cannot be increased,’ he said.” Thus all the manuscripts and Hincmarus. The meaning seems to be: “if nothing more can be obtained.” This agrees with what precedes in Hincmarus, namely, that blessed Remigius spoke these words with a peaceful heart and mouth. In French it is translated: “If it does not exceed the limit and is not too powerful.”

Let men become ponderous, and let women be punished with an affliction of the throat. Here “ponderousness” is a defect of the sexual organs, the nature of which Saint Gregory explains in part I of *Pastoral Care*, at the end.

Because they killed the vice-lord of the Church of Reims in that same village. What this office formerly was may be seen in the canons collected by Gratian, distinction 89, chapter *Volumus*, and those following. From that passage, and below from Flodoardus, book II, chapter 13, it is clear that the vice-lord and the steward of the church were the same office. Onuphrius explains it in the same way in his interpretation of ecclesiastical terms. In French it is translated *vidame de Reims*. In former times, *dame* was used in French in the masculine gender for “lord,” as Sebastian Roulliard proves in his *Parthenia Carnotensis*, chapter 17, where he discusses at length the vice-lords of the Church of Chartres and explains what their office was and what kind of office it was.

“When he gives sleep to his beloved, this is the inheritance of the Lord.” Thus the Roman Psalter reads. Our Vulgate edition, which agrees with the Gallican Psalter, reads somewhat differently.

And no body of any celebrated saint was preserved in it, although it, together with the surrounding courts, had from ancient times been regarded as the cemetery of the church of Reims. S and J have *Remense*, and the entire sentence is clearer in Hincmarus, as follows:

> But no body of the named saint lay there; and it, together with the courts surrounding it, had from ancient times been the cemetery of the church of Reims.

As Nicolaus Chesneau noted in the margin of his French translation, the ancient cemetery of Reims was outside the city.

Have mercy also on your servant Adeloldus. This seems to refer either to the author of the monument placed there, or rather to the author of these rhythmic compositions, which we had printed in verse form because they were made like prose sequences, which were once frequently recited during the sacred office of the Mass.

## CHAPTER XVIII

Barnabas Brissonius transcribed the testament of blessed Remigius in full in book VII of *On the Forms and Solemn Words of the Roman People*, from our present author and from other sources. He introduces it as follows:

> There exists an elegant testament of Lord Remigius, archbishop of Reims, who has as the outstanding herald of his praises Sidonius Apollinaris, his contemporary, in letter 7 of book IX. I copied it long ago from the archives of Hincmarus and Flodoardus and from those of the Church of Reims; it was recently published, with a translation, by Nicolaus Querculus in his French version of Flodoardus, and so forth.

In the same place Brissonius gives the testament of Hadoindus, bishop of Le Mans. Flodoardus mentions it in book II, chapter 5. It belongs to nearly the same century and has a similar style. It begins as follows:

> In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and of the Holy Spirit, on the eighth day before the Ides of February, in the fifth year of the reign of the most glorious King Clovis. I, Hadoindus, although unworthy and a sinner, bishop of the holy Church of God in the city of Le Mans, being sound, by God’s favor, in mind and body and of sound judgment, fearing the fate of human frailty, have drawn up a testament, and have dictated it to the deacon Cadultus to be written. If, for any reason, my testament should not be legally valid under the civil law, the praetorian law, or through the intervention of any new law, I wish it to be valid as a codicil, as though I had died intestate, and let it be valid. Therefore, whenever I, Hadoindus, the bishop named above, shall have departed this life and fulfilled the debt of the time to come, then you, holy and venerable Church, shall be my heir, and I appoint you as my heir, so that wherever in this testament I have given, bequeathed, or ordered anything to be given, I entrust to your faith, as my heir, that it be given, done, and provided, and so forth.

I have inserted this here because it contributes to a fuller understanding of blessed Remigius’s testament. Although Brissonius edited it with complete fidelity, there are nevertheless places where greater care and correction may be admitted.

If anything in the law should appear to be lacking for it. I restored *si ei* in place of *fieri*. The manuscript incorrectly has *affuisse* for *defuisse*, unless perhaps *abfuisse* was written.

I shall have given, bequeathed, or ordered to be given. Thus manuscripts M and J and Brissonius. C has “having bequeathed by making a gift.” A little later Brissonius incorrectly has *Pontensi* for *Portensi*, perhaps a typographical error; likewise, much later, *colonos* for *colonas*. Three words afterward he omits the words “with all those whom I shall leave intestate.” These are also absent from C, along with several other passages that I supplied from other manuscripts.

You shall claim it for your ownership. Thus all the manuscripts have it both here and twice in the middle of the testament, as does Brissonius, although it seemed that *vendicabis* should be read. Learned men even today judge that it should be written this way, and Aldus Manutius teaches in his *Orthography* that it was written so in ancient times. Hence *vindex*, not *vendex*, and *vindiciae*. Certainly *vindicare*, among other meanings, signifies “to assert a claim.” See Ludovicus Rhodiginus, book XVII of the *Ancient Readings*, chapter 29.

In poorhouses, monasteries, martyries, and deaconries. A *ptochium*—Greek *πτωχεῖον*—means a house for the poor. *Martyria* were churches or oratories in which martyrs were venerated. *Diaconiae* were so called from deacons. These were public hospices for the poor, with oratories and chapels attached, in which the head of the deaconry, or the deacon, supplied the needy with what they required. See Onuphrius above. Pope Zacharias mentions these institutions in letter 7.

A village from the estate at Portensis, and [lacuna] also at Villani, and so forth. Here manuscript M, and shortly afterward below, read *Porcensi*; they likewise read *villaris*, and in M a space is left blank to indicate that a word is missing, as also below. Brissonius and the others did not notice this and therefore write everything continuously. A similar variation occurs in book II, chapter 11. At the beginning of that chapter M and J again read *Porcensi*, but C translates it as *Postez*, with a *t* written above the *s*. At the end, M and C have *Portensi*. In book III, chapter 7, all the manuscripts read *Porcensi*, and the French translation gives *Potez*, adding in the margin, “or Portiam.” Likewise, in book IV, chapter 29, the manuscripts have *pagum Portensem* or, in C and J, *Porcensem*, translated into French as “the territory of Portiam.”

Duodeciacus, however, just as from Clodowallus, and so forth. M has *Ludowallus*, and likewise below *Ludowaldus*. Brissonius has *Hlodowaldus*, and likewise below in book III, chapter 20. In all the manuscripts Saint Clodoaldus is mentioned twice. Blessed Remigius shortly afterward calls him “a most holy boy” and “of one mind with him.” Usuard, the Roman Martyrology, Arnold Wion’s monastic Martyrology, and others discuss him on 7 September. He rests near Paris, in French *Saint-Cloud*. Gregory of Tours discusses him in book III of the *History of the Franks*, chapters 6 and 8, where the name is written *Chlodovaldus*, and Sigebert mentions him under the year 531. He was the son of King Clodomer and grandson of the first Clovis.

In Austrasia, or Thuringia. Thus all the manuscripts; S has *Thoringa*; Brissonius and J, *Toringia*.

For my future episcopal successor I leave a white paschal *amphibalus*. Thus all the other manuscripts except the third copy used by Nicolaus Chesneau, which reads *pastoralem* instead of *paschalem*. An *amphibalus* designates a garment, from the Greek *ἀμφιβάλλω*, “to place around,” “to cover,” or “to clothe.”

Between you, my heir, and your diocese, the Church of Laon, and below, at Laon. S correctly restored this reading both here and below. Brissonius and J likewise consistently read it, whereas M and R everywhere have *Lugdunensem* and *Lugdunum*, incorrectly. For what connection could the Church of Reims have with the Church of Lyon? The Church of Laon, however, since it was a part of the diocese of Reims, was established by Remigius himself as a cathedral subject to the Church of Reims, as we noted above in connection with chapter 14. Therefore he calls the Church of Laon here a diocese of Reims.

That this is the correct reading is also clear from chapter 20 below, where Anisiacus is expressly assigned to the Church of Laon, and from chapter 14 above, where Saint Remigius is said to have transferred a considerable part of the possessions given to him by Clovis and others to the church of Saint Mary at Laon-Chevet. This is likewise how the passage should be read in Gregory of Tours, book VI, chapter 4, where the printed reading is *Lugduni Clavati*.

That other golden vessel of ten pounds. Thus manuscript J and C in the margin. In the text, however, it reads:

> Another silver vessel of ten pounds.

Brissonius followed that reading. But *golden* is clearly correct from the contrast with what follows, where he says:

> which at Laon I myself dictated upon a silver vessel.

I order a little tower and a figured chalice to be made. Thus M and J. From this another made a censer, as C reads in the text, and as Brissonius also has; but in the margin C notes that it elsewhere reads *turriculum*:

> In its place, he says, I think *turricula* should be restored. A *turricula* is what is commonly called a ciborium.

S likewise wrote *turriculam* for this reason. The reading *thuribulum* should first be rejected because it is much more likely that, from a golden vessel—as we have shown the text should be read—he ordered a vessel to be made for the use of the venerable sacrament of the Eucharist rather than a censer. Secondly, he adds:

> And I wish the epigrams that I myself dictated at Laon upon a silver vessel to be inscribed upon this one as well.

These seem plainly to be the verses found above in chapter 10. He calls it a “figured chalice” because it was carved with images and figures.

Below, in book II, chapter 6, there is also mention of a golden tower placed upon the altar of blessed Mary. Nicolaus Chesneau likewise interprets it there as a *ciborium*, that is, a repository for the venerable sacrament of the Eucharist, named from its shape. Below, in book IV, chapter 19, Flodoardus mentions a ciborium over the altar of Saint Mary. Venantius Fortunatus likewise mentions a golden tower used for the same purpose in book III, chapter 23, in an epigram to Felix of Bourges, who signed the Second Council of Tours, held in the year 570.

Gregory of Tours simply calls it a “tower” in book I of *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 86, saying:

> The deacon took the tower in which the mystery of the Lord’s body was contained and began to carry it toward the door. Once he had entered the church, intending to place it upon the altar, it slipped from his hand and was carried through the air, and so forth.

Nevertheless, so that we do not depart from the ancient manuscripts, which consistently read *turriculum*—and generally the less likely reading is the more accurate one—it may be accepted as an adjective meaning “towered” or “provided with little towers.” For *turricus, -a, -um* is found with this meaning in the *Summa* of Johannes Januensis, called the *Catholicon*.

Moreover, from the fact that he wanted the verses found above in chapter 10 to be inscribed upon this chalice, we understand that it was a ministerial chalice, as Onuphrius explains above. Ministerial chalices were so called because they served for administering the blood of Christ to the people.

Balatoforum. Thus all the manuscripts, except that manuscript C has *Badatoforum*. It appears to be a proper name.

For those awaiting alms. Thus manuscript J and Brissonius; C and R have “for those requesting.”

Calmisciaco, Tessiaco. Thus S, J, and Brissonius. Elsewhere, as in M, *Colmisiacum*; elsewhere it is read as *Tamacum* and *Trissiacum*.

At the Soissons gate, two solidi. Thus C, S, J, and Brissonius, and likewise in the fifteen articles that follow, up to “the church of the holy martyrs Cosmas and Damian.” M, however, everywhere has the nominative *solidi duo*, as does the Remigius codex. This difference seems to have arisen because the words were not written out in full but represented by the numerical notation *sol. 2*, as is still found in many places in M, which another copyist expanded into letters.

I built above the crypt of Reims. Thus all the manuscripts. Brissonius is therefore wrong to read *supra scriptam*, unless this is a typographical error.

I added to the earlier possessions. Thus manuscript J. Brissonius and C, however, have “I added to the upper possessions,” and Brissonius does not connect the phrase properly with what follows, contrary to all the manuscripts.

Plebeias I added above the Matrona. Brissonius and all the exemplars read this way, as it is also read twice below in this testament, except that C in the printed edition has *Maternam* here, which is the more recent name of the same river, in French *Marne*. Thus in Flodoard one or the other is read indiscriminately. For in Book Three, at the final chapter, all the exemplars and Aimoinus read *Matronam* at the place I have marked in the margin. Below, however, in Book One, Chapter Twenty-Four, MS and all the exemplars read *Maternam*; likewise in Book Two, Chapters Seven and Eight. Again, in Book Four, Chapters Nine, Thirteen, Twenty-Six, and Twenty-Seven, all our exemplars except J read *Maternam*, as does MS in Chapter 33. *Materna* is similarly read in the foundation charter of the monastery or priory of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, founded at Paris in the year 1060 by Henry I, king of the Franks. Gregory of Tours has *Matronam* in Book Six of his Histories, Chapter Twenty-Five, and in Book Eight, Chapter Ten.

And Paschasidem, his wife. C S and Brissonius read this way, but M has *Pascasidam*, J *Pascasidem*, while C notes that elsewhere *Pascasiolam* is read.

Theodonima. Brissonius and C in the printed edition have *Theudonima*; J, *Theodonivia*.

Edoneifan, who belongs to your man. Brissonius likewise reads *Edoneifan*, but MS reads *Edoversam*. In codex R one can read *Edoveifan* [as it has it] and *Edoveresam*.

Ad imitatem montium posito. J and Brissonius read this way, but MS C has *ad unitatem*.

And the little meadows that belong to Jovia. All the exemplars read this way. Nicolaus Chesneau notes that it should perhaps read *quae juxta sunt*, “which are nearby.”

And his wife Moria. MS J and C in the margin read this way, but in the text they have “his wife Mora,” as does Brissonius.

Medaridus, their son. C J and Brissonius read this way; MS has *Medarius*.

And I bequeath Moderatus to my grandson Praetextatus. This is the authentic reading, restored from the various witnesses; it is found in C and J, so that Praetextatus is a proper name. Thus below he mentions his great-granddaughter Praetextata. But C in the printed text, S, and Brissonius read *Moderato*, so as to make it agree with *Praetextato*, as though it were a cognomen; M has *praetaxato Moderatum*, making it a common noun meaning “the aforesaid,” a reading which the codex records in the margin.

Totticionem. So MS. The others have *Tottionem*.

A lacerna. C R and Brissonius read this way; elsewhere *laternam*, and MS J *lucernam*. A *lacerna* is the same as a *paenula*, namely, a kind of garment worn over the tunic to ward off rain. It is mentioned in the Acts of Saint Cyprian and in Sulpicius, Book One of the Dialogues, Chapter Fourteen. Martial and other secular authors use the word. See the passages in Baronius, volume Two of the *Annals*, under the year 261.

And a figured silver *cabuta*. All the exemplars read this way. Brissonius has *cambutam*, but he incorrectly joins the following words, “to his little son Parovius,” with what precedes, whereas a new sentence begins there, as four of our exemplars make clear. The person to whom something is bequeathed is normally named at the beginning. MJ reads *parvulo*; C, *Parovio*; S joins both, *parvulo Parovio*. *Parovio* seems to be the correct reading. Let others explain what *cabuta* may be. This alone occurs to me: since Brissonius reads *cambutam*, if *cambuca* were read, it would signify an episcopal crozier, or rather the staff of a bishop’s crozier. Peter Comestor uses the word in his *History of Exodus*, Chapter 52: “As is customarily done with the ivory staff of a bishop’s *cambuca*.” Hence, in the *Pontifical* of William Durandus, which I possess in manuscript, Part Two, where the consecration of a church is treated, when the bishop approaches the church door, it reads: “Let him make a cross with the *gambuca* on the upper and lower threshold.” In its place the Roman *Pontifical*, printed in 1503 and at Venice in 1561, as well as other editions, say “with the pastoral staff.” Earlier the same Durandus *Pontifical* expressly says, “with the lower part of the *gambuca*, or pastoral staff.” By these words it plainly indicates that the two are the same.

I also give him a *hichinaculum*. So CR and Brissonius; MS J has *hiclinaculum*.

A vine’s *pedatura*. Below CMS has *peditura*, but incorrectly. I take it to mean what Columella calls the vine’s *pedamentum* and *statumen*, that is, the poles and stakes that support the vine.

To my grandson Actio. C in the margin and below in the text, together with Brissonius and J, read this way. MS has *Actio* here, but a little farther below and in Chapter 23 M also has *Etio*, while S J have *Aetio*. The name Aetius is found in Letter 56 of Pope Leo I.

So that from his own shares. J reads this way. The others have *patribus*.

Whom I command to be freed, Catusio and Auliatena. MS C J read this way. Brissonius has *percupio*, “I especially desire,” and *Cattusionem et Aulietenam*, as does C in the printed edition.

Leutiberedum. MS reads this way. C J and Brissonius have *Leuberedum*.

Vasantem, the cook. MS C and Brissonius read this way; but C notes in the margin that elsewhere *Adcum* is read. J has *Vasantem cocum*, so that it is a common noun rather than two proper names.

Dagarasena and Baudorosena. And below, *Flavarasena*. C J and Brissonius read this way. S likewise, except that with M it reads *Dagaraseam*. The other two exemplars, M, read the final syllable with *u*: *Baudoroseuam*, *Flavaraseuam*.

Modorosena. C and Brissonius read this way; M has *Odoresevam*. SI, *Odorosenam*.

Leudonera. C S and Brissonius read this way. MJ have *Leudoueram*, with *u*.

Salvonarias above the Mora. All the exemplars and Brissonius read this way, except that M has *Salvanarias*. C added this note in the margin: “Perhaps *Salinarias above the Mosa* should be restored, or *Sablonarias*, as below.”

Domitextilis, a fine little cloak. In all our exemplars these are two separate words, but I have joined them as Brissonius does.

Let all the others be, and remain, disinherited. All the exemplars read this way, except that M omits the second expression, but incorrectly. Such wording is customarily used in testamentary formulas for greater force and emphasis.

“If any erasure or scraping is found in it, it was made in my presence, while it was being reread and corrected by me.” A similar clause occurs at the end of the testament of Saint Berthicrannus in Brissonius, in these words:

“If any erasures, if any scrapings, if any letters have been added or removed, I made them or ordered them to be made while I repeatedly reread my own will to myself and reviewed or corrected everything item by item, as the law instructs. I entrusted it to be secured by the subscriptions and seals of seven honorable men, and for the full security and legal force of the whole matter I ordered this to be appended. Done at the city of Le Mans, on the day and in the year stated above.”

There *caraxatura*, or rather *charaxatura*, signifies an erasure or deletion. Gregory of Tours uses *caraxare* and *caraxari* for “to engrave” and “to be engraved” in Book Seven, Chapter Thirty-Six, and Book Eight, Chapter Twenty-Nine. Our author uses *charaxatorum indigentia* in the prologue, meaning “the lack of writers or scribes,” and *caraxatum* in Book One, Chapter Nine, meaning “written.” Below, in Book Three, Chapter Sixteen, it seems to have the same meaning as “to mark” or “to censure.” See our index of obscure words in the *Chronicle of Cambrai*, where we have also cited the passage from Prudentius.

Completed at Reims, on the day and in the consulship stated above. From this it is clear that, despite all the care we have taken to publish this testament faithfully and completely, something is still missing at the beginning, since no mention is made there either of the day or of the consul. This is regrettable, because the date when this testament was made is thereby unknown.

With the intervening and intermediate signatories. C J read this way. Brissonius agrees with M, which reads *meridicis*. From this S produced *veridicis*. That reading might seem correct, were it not obstructed by the following words, “and …”

The bishops who subscribed to the testament, listed in this order, are these: Saint Vedastus of Arras; Saint Genebaudus of Laon; Saint Medardus of Noyon and Tournai, united; Saint Lupus of Soissons; Benedictus; and Eulogius.

In exemplar M, two names seem to need adding after Medardus. For the words “to whom my father Remigius,” and so forth, are inserted twice again, with a cross added but the names omitted, and therefore the passage has been passed over by the others. It would therefore be worthwhile to investigate whether a more correct exemplar of this testament might be found in the archives of the Church of Reims or among the writings of Hincmarus. For it is certainly plausible that all the bishops of that province, who at that time numbered nine, subscribed.

In manuscript C, after Agricola the presbyter, Eulogius the bishop follows again, with “to whom my father,” and so forth; then again: “Agricola the presbyter.” This, however, is a scribal error. For although it is possible that two bishops of the same name might subscribe, a bishop would never subscribe after a presbyter. I have therefore omitted these words, together with all the other exemplars and Brissonius.

The presbyter Theodonius. Brissonius and C read this way, noting that elsewhere *Theodonus* is read; MS J has *Theodericus*. Perhaps *Theodorus* should be read.

I, Pappolus, an illustrious man, was present and subscribed. In exemplar M, the following six or seven laymen have these two letters prefixed to their names; I have supplied them from that exemplar, and J likewise reproduces them. Since they were perhaps not understood or noticed by the others, they were omitted by C S and Brissonius. They should be read *vir clarus* or *vir clarissimus*, “an illustrious or most illustrious man,” or *vir consularis*, “a man of consular rank.” Between the subscriptions of Eusebius and Rusticola, M inserts: “I, an illustrious man, was present,” and therefore one person seems to have been omitted here, perhaps Attolus, about whom below in Chapter Twenty-Three; alternatively, those words may be superfluous. Certainly below, in Chapter 23, only six laymen are named as having subscribed, and their names are explicitly given.

CHAPTER XIX

In manuscript MS this chapter precedes the chapter on the testament; in the others it follows it, and this order is more consistent with the sequence of events.

When he devastated the people of First Germany. That is, Upper Germany. He means Trier and the surrounding region. “First Germany,” says Papirius Massonus in Book One of his *Frankish Annals*, under Meroveus, Salvianus, Sidonius, and the ancient writers, is the region along the Rhine, to which Ammianus says that, among other places, Mainz, the Vangiones, the Nemetes, and Strasbourg belonged. The same Massonus, under Clovis, says that Cologne Agrippina held first place among the cities of Second Germany. The city of the Tungri was likewise in that region. See below at Chapter 23. This pestilence occurred in the year 565, according to Baronius.

CHAPTER XX

On the mountain of the Bardoni. This is the mountain otherwise called the Apennines, which divide Italy lengthwise. See Ortelius’s *Geographical Thesaurus*.

Which is called Bercetum. Elsewhere *Berterum*, *Bertecum*, and *Berletum*. But that *Bercetum* is the correct reading, as found in the better exemplars, is also confirmed by Paul the Deacon, who mentions this monastery in the Alps of the Bardoni, built by Liutprand.

When the three brothers, Lothar, Louis, and Charles, divided the kingdom of the Franks among themselves after their father’s death. MS omits the word “of the Franks,” and Hincmarus does not have it either; this may perhaps be the better reading. These three were the sons of Emperor Louis the Pious. The empire fell to Lothar, Germany to Louis, and Francia to Charles the Bald.

The estates of the bishop of Reims, which the presbyter Fulco held. All the old exemplars and Hincmarus read this way, so that *quod tenebat* refers to the bishop, who held them after Ebo had been deposed, as is also clear from the final chapter of Book Two and Chapter One of Book Three, when the see remained vacant for ten years. J therefore reads incorrectly, having changed it to *quas*, so that it refers to the estates, as C likewise rendered it in French.

He gave the estate of Juliacum to a certain Ricuinus. How the same Charles the Bald later revoked this donation and restored this estate, together with all the other goods that had been alienated, to the Church of Reims by a public edict, may be seen in Book Three, Chapter 4.

In modern times, a certain tenant farmer. This occurred in Hincmarus’s time, for he himself says *nostra aetate*, “in our time.”

For which matter, last year, when we spoke with King Otto and the aforementioned duke, at the time when we had been sent to him at Aachen. The reference is to Otto I, discussed below in Book Four, Chapters 33 and following. The correct reading is *Aquis*, in French Aix, as all the exemplars read; S substitutes *Aquisgranum*, the name of the same city. But the former is found very frequently in earlier authors.

CHAPTER XXI

And he placed the whole thing, together with the *brandeum* in which it had previously been found wrapped. Hincmarus, in the *Life of Saint Remigius*, has “wrapped in a red *brandeum*.” Nicolaus Chesneau translates this into French as *drap de samy vermeil*, “a cloth of crimson silk,” as in the preceding chapter. A *brandeum* signifies a silk or linen cloth in which the bodies or relics of saints were wrapped. It was customary, as was decreed in some places by councils, for the bodies of saints to be wrapped in such precious cloths. Saint Gregory the Great uses the same word in Book Three, Letter 30, for silk or a veil sent for this purpose and placed in contact with the bodies of saints. Thus he writes to the Empress Constantia:

“Let the most tranquil lady know that it is not the Roman custom, when they give relics of saints, to presume to touch anything from the body, but only to place a *brandeum* in a small box and set it beside the most sacred bodies of the saints. Once it has been lifted up in the church that is to be dedicated, it is deposited with due reverence; and through it such great miracles occur there that it is as though their bodies themselves had been specially brought to that place. It happened, therefore, in the time of Pope Leo of blessed memory, as handed down by our elders, that when certain Greeks doubted such relics, the aforesaid pontiff cut this very *brandeum* with scissors brought for the purpose, and blood flowed from the incision itself.”

So much for Gregory. Gregory of Tours, in Book One of his *Miracles*, Chapter Twenty-Eight, also mentions the very ancient custom of placing veils or other objects of the same kind over the tomb of the Apostle Peter, so that they might be received enriched by his blessing.

And Charles the Third arranged the affairs of the kingdom. This is Charles the Bald. The first Charles was Charles Martel, the second Charles the Great.

Octimber the first, and so forth. The exemplars read this way, but J has *Octember*. S changed it to *October*, although the former has the flavor of antiquity and expresses the origin of the word; it is likewise read in the metrical *Martyrology* of Wandelbert of Prüm.

There had been three hundred, four times thirteen years, and so forth. That is, three hundred and four times thirteen, which is fifty-two: fifty-two years had elapsed since the baptism of Clovis and of the Franks when this translation of the body of Saint Remigius took place, namely, in the year 952. It follows that Clovis’s baptism occurred in the year 500. The meaning is not, as it might appear, three hundred forty-three years. In that case he would have had to be baptized in the year 509, contrary to the common opinion, as we noted above at Chapter 13.

Accompanied on every side, surrounded by throngs of peoples. *Secus* means “near,” and all the exemplars read it this way, lest anyone think that *secum*, “with him,” should be read.

CHAPTER XXII

A certain woman from the district of Troyes, afflicted with convulsive movements of all her limbs. Augustine recounts a similar punishment, arising from a mother’s curse, and its healing at the memorial of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, in Book Twenty-Two of *The City of God*, Chapter 8.

From the estate called Caucella. R and MS J read this way, but C has *Caurella*. Concerning the translation of Saint Remigius to the place of his burial, or to his monastery, carried out by Archbishop Herivaeus in the year 901, the author treats somewhat more fully at the end of this chapter and in Book Four, Chapter 12.

But in that place where this gift of healing occurred, a column was afterward erected, with a cross fixed to it, containing a memorial of this glorification. Around the foot of the column bearing the cross, situated in the suburb of Saint-Denis at Reims, this inscription bears witness to the event:

“In the nine-hundred-and-first year of the Lord’s incarnation, on the fourth day before the Kalends of January, and on the second Sabbath, when the glorious body of our Lord and patron, the blessed Remigius, had been brought from this city, the people of both orders of rank gathered devoutly around Herivaeus the bishop, with King Charles following, together with Prince Richard, and, with one mind, loudly singing praises to Christ. When the most sacred relic had been brought here, a heavenly power immediately descended and caused a certain lame man—wondrous to relate!—to leap forth with his knees straightened. From that moment he pursued his own healing with a new step, by whose aid may we be helped here and forever.

“Saint Sigloardus, have mercy on your monk,

Who, led by love of this miracle,

Erected this inscription in memory of it.”

CHAPTER XXIII

A certain man of the province of Second Belgica. Second Belgica contains Reims, Châlons, Amiens, and so forth. As Jacobus Meyerus learnedly writes in his *Annals of Flanders*, under the year 453, the Romans divided Belgic Gaul into First Germany, or Upper Germany, which contained Strasbourg, Mainz, the Nemetes, the Vangiones, and other peoples near the Rhine; and Second Germany, or Lower Germany, whose chief city was Cologne Agrippina, together with the Tungri and the coastal peoples of the Nervii and Morini, who are now called Brabanters and Flemings. Again, they divided the same Gaul into First Belgica, whose chief city was Trier, together with the Mediomatrici, Leuci, and Virodunenses; and Second Belgica, in which the Remi held primacy, with the Suessiones, Châlons, Laon, Cambrai, Nervii, Morini, Atrebates, Amiens, Beauvais, and Nijmegen subject to them. Flanders is included within this Second Belgica.

CHAPTER XXIV

There is a little wood situated on a mountain three miles from the city. The mountain is called Hor, as it is in the *Life of Theodoric*, the saint under discussion here, in Surius.

Unless he is called Theodoricus. C and R read this way, but S J have *Theoderius*, and others *Theodericus*. Whatever the reading, the author intended to express a diminutive name, such as among the French end in *-o*, for example *Pierrot* from *Petrus*.

On the Kalends of July. The Roman *Martyrology* of Usuardus, with Baronius’s notes, assigns the feast of Saint Theodoric or Theoderic to this day; so do Peter Galesinius, Francis Maurolycus, who calls him Theodorus, and Arnoldus Wion in Book Three of *The Tree of Life*. His life is also found on this day in Surius, agreeing with what is related in this chapter, although here it is somewhat fuller.

Finally, on a certain Sabbath day, when evening was already approaching the Lord’s Day, a certain poor woman, and so forth. This woman was severely punished because she was working on the evening of the Lord’s Day, since at that time the celebration of Sunday began at the hour of Vespers, a practice that continued almost to our own times. See what I wrote in the notes to Thomas of Cantimpré, Book Two, Chapter 53, Part Nine. The same is clear from this author above, Chapter 20, where a certain Ragenbaldus was punished for the same reason.

CHAPTER XXV

Molanus discusses Saint Theodulf, the subject of this chapter, in his addition to Usuardus under the Kalends of May. Peter Galesinius and Arnoldus Wion do so on the same day. Sigebertus mentions both, Saint Theodoric and Theodulf, in his *Chronicle* under the year 534, in these words:

“Theodoricus the abbot, disciple of Saint Remigius, and Theodulfus the abbot, disciple of that Theodoricus, shine forth in Francia.”

The discovery of the body of Saint Theodulf at Trier is noted, from Trithemius, by the said Arnoldus Wion on the last day of February; Thomas of Cantimpré describes it at length in the work cited above, Part Two. But I have considerable doubt whether that Theodulfus is the same as this one. Trithemius identifies them in Book Three of *Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, Chapter 260, where he writes:

“Theodulfus, abbot on Mount Hor, a man of holy conduct and innocent life, shone forth, distinguished by many virtues. His body, discovered whole and incorrupt not many years ago, was deposited with great honor at Trier among the Preachers, on the high altar. This discovery is celebrated on the day before the Kalends of March.”

So he writes. Nevertheless, I think it more likely that they were different men.

SCHOLIA ON BOOK TWO

CHAPTER ONE

Romanus is said to have succeeded blessed Remigius. This was evidently around the year 545. Blessed Romanus founded a monastery in a village called Mentuniacum, two leagues from the city of Troyes, and was its first abbot. It has been completely destroyed for six hundred years, and nothing remains of it except a cross placed there in memory of the event. Concerning him, the *Life of Saint Leo the Abbot* in the Breviary of Troyes reads as follows:

“When blessed Romanus, abbot of the monastery of Mentuniacum, was elected bishop of Reims, blessed Leo became abbot of his monastery.”

Another, though mutilated, life of Saint Leo testifies that this same Saint Romanus obtained from King Clovis the Elder confirmation of the donation of certain estates that the patrician Merobaudes had most generously granted to the same monastery. The text continues.

Flavius succeeded Romanus. This Flavius is recorded as having subscribed to the Council of Clermont. See the scholia on Chapter 13 of the preceding book.

CHAPTER II

Some of the passages cited in this chapter from Fortunatus could be restored in the text itself, especially *Egidi* for *Igidi*, in verse 4 *favens* for *fovens*, in verse 24 *sonet* for *sonat*, and several others.

Who, as envoy from King Childebert, the son of King Sigebert, to King Chilperic, the uncle of that Childebert, and so forth. This Sigebert was the king of Austrasia who married the wicked Brunhilda. His brothers were Guntram, king of Burgundy, Charibert, and Chilperic; all were sons of Clotaire I. Sigebert died in the year 578, and his son Childebert succeeded him.

So that, once the kingdom of King Guntram, the brother of Chilperic, had been taken away. The name Guntram or Gontram is written in various ways. M consistently reads *Gunthramnus*, with *m* in the second syllable; J always has *Guntrannus*, as C sometimes does. The former reading is supported by Gregory of Tours, who, in the passages cited in the text, writes the name in full as *Gunthchramnus*; in the volumes of the Councils and elsewhere it appears as *Guntheramnus*.

He had been sent by Queen Fredegund. She was the wife of Chilperic, whose murder was eventually brought about by her treachery. Aimoinus discusses her in Book Three of *On the Deeds of the Franks*, Chapter 56: “Fredegund,” he says, “was outstanding in beauty, clever in counsel, and, apart from Brunhilda, acknowledged no equal in deceit,” and so forth. What follows in this chapter is taken almost word for word from Gregory of Tours, Book Ten of the *Histories*, Chapter 19. This synod of Metz, and the deposition of Aegidius, took place in the year 594, as Severinus Binius noted in Volume Two of the Councils.

For many weights of gold and silver were found in this bishop’s *regestum*. Gregory has exactly the same words; MS corruptly reads *regesta* instead of *regesto*. The word *regestum* occurs above in the same chapter in Gregory, when he says: “For these writings were found together in a *regestum* of King Chilperic, in one of the chests.” Nicolaus Chesneau translates it into French as *épargne*, “treasury.” “In Latin,” says Budaeus, “*regestum* may mean what we commonly call a register. Here it seems to signify a treasury, or a place where treasure is kept.” Gregory uses it in this sense in Book Nine of the *Histories*, Chapters 10 and 34.

CHAPTER III

Molanus discusses Saint Basolus, in French Saint Basle, in his addition to Usuardus under 26 November, the day on which this chapter says he died. The Roman *Martyrology* likewise mentions him from ancient manuscripts, as Baronius notes there; so do Peter in Book Nine of his *Catalogue*, Chapter 69, and Arnoldus Wion in his monastic *Martyrology*, or Book Three of *The Tree of Life*, under the same day, citing Galesinius and others, specifically Vincentius in the *Speculum*, Book 21, Chapter 116. Trithemius also discusses him in *Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, Book Three, Chapter 45, and Sigebertus in his *Chronicle* under the year 567. Molanus discusses the translation of his relics by Hincmarus under 15 October.

Which the grove beginning there overshadows, Rigetium. C and J read this way, but MS has *Rigentium*. In the breviary of the Church of Reims it is *Rietum*, rendered in French as *Forêt de la Route*.

He sent to his nephew named Balsemius, so that he might bring him to himself from the region of Limoges. J corruptly has *Balsennum*. In French, Saint Bassange. A fragment of the life of this martyr Balsemius is found in the *Promptuary of Sacred Antiquities of the Diocese of Troyes*; Molanus added him to Usuardus under 16 August, the day on which his feast is celebrated in the diocese of Troyes.

And establishing their encampment there, they began to return hither from raiding wherever they had been. All the exemplars read this way, that is, “from raiding” or “from plunder.” S therefore changed it incorrectly to *praedati*. The preceding words indicate that they had established a fixed camp or tent there, in French *retraite*, from which we derive the Latin expression *castrametari*, “to encamp.” See below at Book Four, Chapter 10.

CHAPTER IV

After Aegidius, Romulfus. M reads *Remulfus* here and in the following chapter; but in the summary of this chapter, above in Chapter 2, and in the text, it has *Romulfus*, as do the other exemplars and Gregory of Tours, Book Nine of the *Frankish Histories*, Chapter 30, where he is named count of the palace of King Childebert, and Book Ten, Chapter 19.

CHAPTER V

Concerning Bishop Sonnatius. This is the common spelling in the exemplars, both in this chapter and in the preceding one. M generally writes *Sompnacius*, and sometimes *Sompniacius*; C, *Sonnacius*. The synod of Reims held under him, which was extremely celebrated and more than provincial, since many archbishops from other provinces also attended, would that it still existed in the volumes of the Councils.

Palladius of Auxerre. MS has *Altissiodorensi*. J consistently writes *Autisiodorensi*, supported by the French form *Auxerre*.

Ansaricus of Soissons. C J have *Ansericus*.

Claudius of Riez. All the exemplars read this way. He seems to be the bishop of Riez in the archbishopric of Toulouse, who is otherwise called *Rivensis* and *Rivenensis*. Unless someone thinks that *Regiensis* or *Regensis* should be read. For Claudius, bishop of Riez, is recorded as having subscribed to the Second Council of Chalon, held around this period, namely in the year 658, or, according to others, 664. Two others who attended this Council of Reims also subscribed there: Donatus of Besançon and Palladius of Auxerre. Yet in the volume of the Councils *Reiensis* may perhaps be the correct reading, a less familiar form, instead of *Regiensis*.

Vero of Rodez. J reads this way, and MS has *Rutemensi*; C, *Tervensi*. There is a bishopric of Rodez, in French *Rodez*—for *Ruthenum* is elsewhere called *Rhodium—in the archbishopric of Bourges.

Agricola of Gévaudan. This is what in later centuries was called the bishopric of Mende, in the same archbishopric of Bourges, in which are Clermont and Rodez, just mentioned. For Gabal, also called Gabali by the Prologue and Fortunatus, and Gabales by Caesar, Pliny, and Strabo, is Mende in French, that is, Mimat in Aquitaine, in the region of the Gabalitani, now called Gévaudan. It is the principal city and chief town, as Philip Ferrarius teaches in the new *Topography of the Roman Martyrology*. I note this lest anyone think that it is the town of Chalon, which is under the archbishopric of Lyon, especially since Robertus Caenalis believes the Gabales to be the people of Chalon. Indeed, Agricola, bishop of Chalon, is recorded as having subscribed to the Fourth and Fifth Councils of Orléans, the latter held in the year 552, and also to the Second Council of Paris and the First Council of Lyon, held in the year 570. He governed his church for forty-eight years and lived to the age of eighty-three, as Gregory of Tours reports in Book Five of the *Histories*, Chapter 45, and Baronius, following him, in his notes to the Roman *Martyrology* under 17 March. But that he should be the same man as the one who attended this Council of Reims also seems to be ruled out by the difference in dates—

Audericus of Auch. Auch, otherwise called Auxitanum, gives its name to the archbishopric of Auch. In French, Auch in Gascony.

So that the chapter of canons enacted at Paris in a general synod, assembled in the Basilica of Saint Peter through the efforts of King Lothar, may be preserved with full force. The reference seems to be to the Third Council of Paris, whose nine chapters are preserved in Volume Two of the Councils edited by Binius. It is no objection that it is said there to have been celebrated under Childebert, since this means Childebert I, the son of Clovis the Great, who died in the year 559. At the same time his brother Clotaire I reigned, here called Lothar, and he died in the year 565. Childebert held the royal throne at Paris, while Clotaire held it at Soissons, although eventually he ruled all Gaul as well. It is therefore likely that this Parisian synod was celebrated after the year 559, as Binius explicitly teaches.

Moreover, to the register of the holy Church of Reims. Before these words MS and J add: “to the Basilica of Saint Medard, fifteen solidi.” We omitted this, following the other exemplars, because the church of Saint Medard had already been mentioned above.

CHAPTER VI

After this blessed man, Leudegiselus, the brother of Bishop Attila, succeeded him. As is clear from the following chapter, this Attila was bishop of Laon. In the tables of Democharis he occupies sixth place, where he is called Attola, as he is also by Hincmarus in *Opusculum* 55, Chapter 1. He consecrated Saint Autbert of Cambrai as bishop in the year 642, as I noted in the *Chronicle of Cambrai*, Book One, Chapter 19. The text continues:

He governed the bishopric during the time of King Dagobert. This was Dagobert I, who, after his father Clotaire II, reigned for another fourteen years and died in 645. His eldest son Sigebert succeeded him; he is mentioned at the end of the chapter and died in 656.

Anglebertus succeeded him. All the exemplars read this way except J, which throughout this chapter has *Angelbertus*.

CHAPTER VII

At the request of Berccarius the abbot. All the exemplars read this way; S changed it everywhere to *Bercharius*, as did J. The contracted form is found in Sigebertus’s *Chronicle* and in Nicolaus Camuzaeus’s *Promptuary of Sacred Antiquities of the Diocese of Troyes*, which contains his complete life and passion written by Asson, abbot of Derventum, and in Surius, Volume Five, where a brief version of his life is given from Vincentius’s *Historical Speculum*, Book 24, under 16 October.

The church at Viriziacum. That this is the correct reading is clear from Chapters 1 and 3 of this book, where it is consistently read this way. In French, Verzy. Elsewhere, both here and below in Chapter 10, the exemplars vary: M has *Viriacum*; C, *Viriciacum*, as M reads in Chapter 10, where C has *Virigiacum*.

To whom King Louis also. This refers to Clovis II, who died in 662.

Also in his time the illustrious man Grimoaldus gave to Saint Remigius, and so forth. He seems to have been the mayor or master of the palace of the Franks, the son of blessed Pippin of Landen and brother of Saints Gertrude and Begga; he died in the year 658. The council of the bishops of Gaul held at Nantes by order of the Roman pontiff, which the author mentions here, seems to be missing from the volumes of the Councils. Unless it is perhaps the council containing twenty chapters, placed in Volume Three after the Council of Tribur, held in the year 895. Concerning it Binius notes there: “We are uncertain at what time this council was held, and so we have placed it here.”

After this he is said to have died in the little church of Saint Mary, which he had built in the same monastery. How solemn the funeral rites offered for Nivardus were is reported above, in the *Life and Passion of Saint Bercharius the Abbot*. He died on the Kalends of September; under that day Molanus added to Usuardus: “At Hautvillers, the deposition of Saint Nivardus, bishop of Reims.” Peter Galesinius places him in his *Martyrology* on the same day. Sigebertus mentions him in his *Chronicle* under the year 661, in these words:

“Saint Nivardus, archbishop of Reims, and his successor Reolus; Bercharius also, the martyr, who was the first abbot of Hautvillers; and Saint Bertha, martyr and abbess, shine forth in holiness in Gaul.”

Some people corruptly call him Viviardus.

CHAPTER VIII

It is established that the body of the blessed Queen Helena was brought from the city of Rome to the aforementioned monastery of this holy man Nivardus, that is, to Hautvillers. The day of the translation and of its arrival at this monastery is noted under 7 February in Molanus’s additions to Usuardus. Almannus, a monk of Hautvillers, wrote the history of this translation, according to Sigebertus in *On Illustrious Men*, Chapter 99; as he reports in the same place, Almannus also wrote the lives of Saint Nivardus and Saint Sindulfus, who is discussed in the following chapter. According to the same Sigebertus in his *Chronicle*, this translation from Rome to Gaul took place in the year 849, as Baronius also reports after him in Volume Ten, at the end of that year, adding:

“But concerning her body there is an ancient controversy between the Latins and the Greeks as to where it was buried. The Venetians also boast that they possess it, having brought it from the East, and they honor it with fitting devotion.”

So Baronius.

They rejoice, enlarged by a double *esox*. MJ read this way. S left the place blank. It is thought to signify a fish otherwise called a salmon. Sulpicius Severus, in Book Three of the *Dialogues on the Virtues of Blessed Martin*, Chapter 13, writes: “At the first cast of a very small net, the deacon drew out a huge *esox*.” In the margin at this passage Surius, Volume Six, noted: “*Ezox*, that is, salmon.” He himself writes it with *z*. Adrian Junius, listing the names of fish in his *Nomenclator*, writes *Exos*, because it lacks bones, or, as others read, *esox* in Pliny. In English, “a lax,” and he distinguishes it from the salmon. Pliny, *Natural History*, Book Nine, Chapter 15, writes: “There are also fish in certain rivers no smaller than these: the silurus in the Nile, the *esox* in the Rhine, and the *attilus* in the Po.” In the same place, Chapter 18, he discusses the salmon.

CHAPTER IX

Molanus discusses Saint Sindulfus in his addition to Usuardus under 20 October; so do the Roman *Martyrology* with Baronius and Peter Galesinius under the same day, as does Wion. Trithemius likewise discusses him in *Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, Book Three, Chapter 46; he writes that Sindulfus flourished in the year 600 and was the companion of blessed Basolus the abbot, discussed above in Chapter 3. Hence Sigebertus speaks of them together in his *Chronicle* under the year 567:

“Basolus the abbot, and Sindulfus the presbyter and recluse, shine forth in Francia.”

CHAPTER X
## On Saint Reolus, Bishop

I find nothing about him in the Martyrologies. Before becoming bishop, he had as his wife a niece of Saint Nivard, the daughter of King Childeric, as is established by the author above, chapter 7. After her death, he presided over this archbishopric for twenty-six years, as is stated in the *Life of Saint Gumbert*, the brother of Saint Nivard, which appears in the *Lives of the Saints* published in French by the Parisian editors, under 29 April. Others call him Regulus, such as Papirius Masson in his *Annals* and Jacobus Sirmondus in his *Catalogue of the Archbishops of Reims*.

Cruciniacum mountain, Curbam estate, together with Aciniacum in the district of Tardenois. Nicolaus Chesneau translated these names into French as “the mountain of Cruny, Courville, and Acini in Tardenois.” Almost all copies read them in this way, both here and in chapter 17 of this book, except that the manuscript reads Torbam here and in chapter 11, and Tardonisse here.

## CHAPTER XI

Gerniacum court. Thus all the copies read here and frequently below; in French, Gernicourt. In several places S substitutes Germanicam, which above, in chapter 5, is rendered Germyni. From this passage Surius, Haraeus, and Lippelus should be corrected, since in the *Life of Saint Rigobert* under 4 January they read Gremaca. The place is not far from Reims, as is clear from the following chapter. The same authors must also be corrected for placing the battle of Charles against Chilperic and Ragemfrid on 21 July, whereas April should be read. For it occurred during Lent, on the Sunday before Easter, as stated by the *Annals of the Franks* published by Pithoeus and by the appendix to Gregory of Tours, whose author is Fredegarius Scholasticus, who describes the events of his own time.

An estate named Cartobram. Thus CR and J. Another copy has Carobram. In French, Chartreune.

And in an estate whose name was Turba. Thus all the copies read here. In French, Tourbe.

From the estate of Bracaneium on the river Rotumna. RM has Bracaneco; J, Bracaneto.

Finally, from King Dagobert. The second of that name is meant, the son of Childebert, who died in the year 715 and was succeeded by his son Theuderic II.

Also in Rodonicum. Thus J; but the manuscript has Rodinicum, C has Rodolitum, and another copy Rodocinum.

[Col. 0364D]

This venerable prelate is said to have held Pippin, mayor of the palace of the royal household, in the highest friendship; he frequently used to send him *eulogiae* as a blessing. This was Pippin of Herstal, the son of Saint Begga and the father of Charles Martel by a concubine. *Eulogiae* were blessed loaves, symbols of mutual communion and friendship; Baron gives a lengthy account of them in volume III of his *Annals*, under the year 313. The Council of Nantes, chapter 6, mentioned above, sets out the form of the blessing.

On Mount Betelinus. Thus R and J, with which the manuscript agrees; C has Berelinus, and another copy Belinus.

In the district of Castricus. Thus also below, chapter 18; elsewhere, “in the village of Castricus.” Here the manuscript combines both readings: “in the village, in the district of Castricus.”

## CHAPTER XII

[Col. 0365A]

Finally, when hostility had arisen between King Chilperic and Charles, the aforesaid Pippin’s son, and Ragemfrid, the mayor of the palace. This was Chilperic II, the brother of Dagobert II; he died in the year 719 or, according to others, 726. These events, however, took place in the year 717, as reported by the *Annals of the Franks* published by Pithoeus. Sigebertus and Meyerus assign them to the year 718. The issue concerned the acquisition of the principate, or the office of master of the horse, as stated in the *Life of Saint Rigobert*. For Chilperic had appointed this Ragemfrid master of the horse, or mayor of the palace.

That he did not open it to him beforehand. Thus CR and J. M also once read *nonnulli* (“some”), but the word was not struck through and was left as *nulli*, as S reads it.

[Col. 0365B]

He expelled Rigobert, his patron, from the episcopate; Rigobert was said to have received him from the sacred font. S wishes *patrinum* to be corrected to *patronum*, but all the copies oppose this. In his *Life*, Saint Rigobert is said both to have baptized Charles and to have received him from the sacred font. Moreover, those who receive a person from baptism are properly called patrons. Sigebertus and Massaeus record his deposition from the episcopate, as well as that of Eucherius of Orléans, under the year 723.

Of which it is handed down in the fathers’ written account, and so forth. The story of the vision of Saint Eucherius, bishop of Orléans, concerning the eternal damnation of Charles Martel on account of his seizure of ecclesiastical property appears in nearly the same words in the manuscript capitularies sent by the bishops of the provinces of Reims and Rouen to King Louis. It is also appended in the notes to the new *Corpus Canonum*, revised under Gregory XIII, 16, q. 1, chapter *Quia*. It likewise appears in the *Life of the same Saint Eucherius* in Surius under February, written by a contemporary, and in the *Life of Saint Rigobert* under 4 January. In all these works it is asserted that the said Martel was from that moment consigned, in body and soul, to eternal punishments. Hincmar mentions the same matter in the preface to the *Life of Saint Remigius*; among more recent authors, Paulus Aemilius does so in book II of *The Deeds of the Franks*, and Petrus Despinac, archbishop of Lyon, in an address delivered before King Henry III of France at Blois in 1575, as Arnold Wion testifies in book III of the *Tree of Life*, under 20 February.

[Col. 0365D]

Peter Pithoeus, however, contradicts these claims in his *Glossary of the Capitularies*, under the letter R, as does Baronius in volume IX of the *Annals*, under the year 741. Their reason is that Eucherius died at least ten years before Martel. Baronius further adds that one may have good hope for Martel’s salvation because he performed penance. Let others examine what should be thought about this matter. Flodoard faithfully relates what he received from the writings of the Fathers; these should not be rashly overthrown, especially the acts of councils.

Whose body was buried in the monastery of Saint Trudo. This place is in Hasbania, a part of Brabant, within the town of Saint Trond, where Saint Eucherius was buried. Nicolaus Chesneau translated the passage into French in the opposite way, saying: “The body of Saint Trudo was buried in the monastery of Saint Eucherius.”

Who, after returning, is requested by Milo, and so forth. That is, he is asked for or required. For it is passive, in the same way as above in chapter 3 of this book. “And he was requested to grant a dwelling for a more secluded way of life.” Here S incorrectly corrected the text against all the copies to *petentisque*. The meaning, therefore, is that Saint Rigobert was requested by Milo.

He lived for a considerable time in the court of Gerniacum. For fifteen or seventeen years, as the same William Le Bègue, mentioned above in book I, noted in the margin; he likewise notes that Rigobert lived in exile in Gascony for five or seven years.

## CHAPTER XIII

[Col. 0366B]

Adrian, pontiff of the apostolic see, mentions this blessed prelate in his letter addressed to Tilpin, later bishop of Reims. This fragment appears in volume III of the Councils among the writings of Gregory II, and this attribution was made on Baronius’s authority, volume IX, under the year 717. He would certainly have judged otherwise if he had read through the remaining part of the same letter, which is quoted below in chapter 16. For it is plainly proved from that passage that the letter truly belongs to Adrian, not Gregory, since it mentions Zachary and Stephen, his predecessors, who came after Gregory II. The letter can be completed by adding the two sections quoted below in chapters 16 and 17. The note of Severinus Binius should also be corrected: he observes that Adrian’s name was mistakenly introduced for Gregory II in Surius under 4 January. Nicolaus Serrarius makes the same observation in his notes on letter 142 of Saint Boniface.

Together with another episcopate. Namely, that of Trier, as is proved by Hincmar’s letter 16, chapter 19, among those printed, and by Hincmar’s preface to the *Life of Saint Remigius*, where he says that Milo—the person under discussion—usurped the episcopates of Reims and Trier simultaneously and ruined them for approximately forty years.

## CHAPTER XIV

He died on the day before the Nones of January—that is, 4 January—Saint Rigobert. One copy adds in the margin: “Around the year 773 of the Lord’s incarnation.” The manuscript and CJ do not have these words, although they appear in the *Life* preserved by Surius, from which most of what has so far been reported about him in this *History* was taken. The *Life* also adds, for greater chronological precision, that he died in the eighth indiction. It appears in Surius under 4 January. His memory is commemorated on that day in the Roman Martyrology, both in that of Peter Galesinius and in that of Baronius. Molanus likewise added him to Usuardus on the same day.

Baronius writes in his notes there that Rigobert lived down to the time of Pope Adrian, who, he says, after Rigobert’s death, rejected Milo and substituted Turpin in his place, as his acts testify. This agrees with what has been said about the year of his death, since Adrian began to sit as pope in the year 772. Sigebertus likewise mentions him in his *Chronicle* under the year 723, when he says that Rigobert was removed or expelled from the episcopate.

[Col. 0367A]
