If these things are true, he must have spent fifty years in exile. Franciscus Haraeus, however, in the *Lives of the Saints* published by him, places Rigobert’s death around the year 733, adding the following note after his *Life*:

“He was said to have died in the year of Christ 773, but there seems certainly to be an error in the numbers. For Martel, the prince whom that bishop washed in baptism when he was a child, died at the age of fifty in the year of salvation 741; thus Saint Rigobert ought to have held the episcopate for a full eighty years. The historian Sigebertus likewise reports that in the twenty-third year of that century he was driven from the episcopate by Martel. Add that he is said to have lived only under these three kings—Childebert, Dagobert, and Chilperic—the last of whom certainly ceased to live in the year 727. Therefore I suspect that *XXXIII* was formerly replaced by *LXXIII*, so that Saint Rigobert died in the thirty-third year of that century, not the seventy-third.”

Haraeus’s conclusion is sufficiently probable.

## CHAPTER XV

Into the district of the Veromandui, to the estate of Nemincum. J has Memnicum. In this part of the Veromanduan territory stands the distinguished city of Saint-Quentin, not far from Cambrai.

These precious relics carried there. The manuscript and J have *munera* (“gifts”), as does C, which translated the word into French. But the other reading is better, and all the copies have it shortly afterward.

Not long after this, and so forth. This was the fourth translation of Saint Rigobert’s relics, carried out by Archbishop Herivaeus, about which see below, book IV, chapter 13.

## CHAPTER XVI

Although some report that he was only a chorepiscopus. Elsewhere, *coepiscopus*. But the correct reading is *chorepiscopus*. Chorepiscopi received their name from Greek χώρα, a word meaning “region” or “district,” as though they were overseers of particular small regions within each diocese. This office seems to correspond especially to those now called archdeacons, archpriests, rural deans, and deans of Christianity. Hincmar, below in book III, chapter 22, interprets the same title as “vicar bishop,” from *vicus*, “village.” For this reason Nicolaus Chesneau translates it here and below into French as *doyen rural*, “rural dean.”

In M the word was written *corepiscopus*, but the letter *r* was erased by a later hand belonging to some ignorant person, in order to produce *coepiscopus*. That Abel truly was archbishop of Reims is sufficiently proved by this chapter of Flodoard. The same conclusion follows from the *Life of Saint Rigobert* in Surius, where Hincmar is said to have been the fifth archbishop of Reims after Saint Rigobert. If Abel is not counted, Hincmar will be only the fourth.

[Col. 0367D]

We also have the reason why some omit Abel from the catalogue of the archbishops of Reims in the passages cited in this chapter from Adrian’s letter. Although Abel was appointed bishop there, he was not permitted to remain there; he therefore returned to Lobbes, a celebrated monastery in Belgium, where he is believed to have labored for the conversion of unbelievers, so that by holy living and preaching he reached the prize of eternal life. Molanus added his name to the sacred Martyrology of Usuardus under 5 August. On that day Molanus also discusses him in the *Birthdays of the Saints of Belgium*, assigning him the title of archbishop of Reims; Peter Galesinius and Arnold Wion do the same in their Martyrologies. So too does Trithemius in book III, chapter 298, and book IV, chapter 118, of *On the Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*. In the latter passage he writes that Abel’s feast is celebrated on 23 September. He was Scottish by nationality.

Grimo in the city called Rodomus. M and another copy have *Rodomis*, for which S and J substituted *Rothomagus*, the name of the same city, which is also called Rodoma. See the note of Nicolaus Serrarius on letter 143 of Saint Boniface. I do not approve of replacing old names with newer ones, even when the newer ones are more familiar, because by this method knowledge of antiquity is lost. Thus also below, in book IV, chapter 31, all the copies read *Rodomi*, except that C corruptly reads *Rodonii*; in both places the French translation has Rouen.

Sigebertus uses that designation under the year 751: “Remigius,” he says, “the brother of King Pippin, archbishop of Rodomus in Gaul, flourishes.” This Grimo is the twenty-seventh archbishop of Rouen in the catalogue of Democharus, having been appointed in place of Robert in the year 733.

Finally, the third, Hartbert, in the city called Senones. Thus C and J. But the manuscript has *Hartbertum*. In the volumes of the Councils the name is *Artbertus*; in the catalogue of Democharus, *Otbertus* or *Ochibertus*, cardinal in the year 762; he is the thirty-sixth in order. Moreover, from the passages cited here from two letters of Zachary, not a few things may be restored in the volumes of the decretal letters and in volume III of the Councils.

## CHAPTER XVII

Concerning Bishop Tilpin. Thus all the copies consistently read. Other authors call him simply Turpin or John Turpin. A history of the life of Charlemagne and Roland exists under his name, although Papirius Masson, in book II of the *Frankish Annals*, believes that it is not his work but that of an idle man who wrote those stories after the empire of Charles the Bald for the entertainment of the young. Antonius Possevinus teaches the same, correctly, in the *Sacred Apparatus*, under “Tilpin.”

Concerning the ordination of a bishop named Lul of the holy Church of Mainz. Thus all the old copies, whereas S and J substituted *Lulli*. But in the volumes of the Councils he is often called Lul, specifically in letter 12 of Pope Zachary, and likewise in the letters of Saint Boniface. This blessed Lull was the successor of Saint Boniface the martyr and the second archbishop of Mainz.

Noviliacum in the district of Urtinse. C has *Ursince*; J, *Urcinse*.

## CHAPTER XVIII

He had been appointed, before his episcopate, as the royal envoy for administering justice properly. *Missus* means “legate.” Envoys are frequently mentioned in the Capitularies of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious; their office is described in this chapter. A count was generally added to the royal envoy, as is clear from book II of the *Capitularies*, chapter 25. The name referred to an office, not—as it does today—to rank or eminence. On royal envoys, see book I, chapter 122; book II, chapters 11, 16, 17, 19, 25, 26, 27, and 28; and book III, chapters 17, 18, and 33, among others. On counts, see book II, chapters 6, 9, 10, 12, 18, 23, 24, 25, 26, 28, and 32, among others. On these matters see also Petrus Pithoeus in his *Glossary of the Capitularies*, under “Royal Envoys”; Florentinus Van der Haer in *The Castellanies of Lille*; and Petrus Louvet in book III, chapter 9, of his *History of Beauvais*.

In these districts also, namely Dolomense, Vongense, and so forth. The manuscript reads all these names with *e*, as was frequently customary in earlier usage; we have chosen to preserve this. CJ has *Dolomensi*, *Vongensi*, and so forth, with *i*.

So that they might have good and suitable vice-lords (*vicedomni*) and advocates. Thus M. The other copies have *vicedomini*. A chapter on these viscounts and advocates appears in book III of the *Capitularies*, chapter 11, where *vicedomnis* is likewise read. For if *dominus* was then pronounced *domnus*, correspondingly they pronounced and wrote *vicedomnus*.

[Col. 0369B]

He is found to have held a synod in the year 814 from the incarnation of Our Lord Jesus Christ, in the church of Noyon. This synod is absent from the volumes of the Councils. Yet volume III contains the first Council of Reims, held under the same Vulfarius and Charlemagne in the preceding year, 813, in the month of May; it has forty-four chapters or canons. Our author mentions it shortly below, saying that forty-three chapters were established there. It could easily have happened, however, that one was divided into two.

Having gathered with him his fellow bishops Hildoard, Ermeno, Jesse, Ragumbert, Grimbold, Rothard, Wendilmar, and Ostroald. J writes *Hildoald*. He was bishop of Cambrai; Ermeno was bishop of Senlis, and is called Herminius in the catalogue of Democharus. Jesse was bishop of Amiens; Ragumbert—or, as CJ has it, Ragimbert—was bishop of Beauvais, succeeded by Saint Hildemannus, discussed below in chapter 20, who died on 8 December 848. Grimbold was bishop of Thérouanne; elsewhere he is called Grimbald and Erembald. Rothard was bishop of Soissons; below in chapter 20 and throughout book III, almost all the copies call him Rothadus, though they vary here. In the volumes of the Councils and in volume III of the second edition of the *Library of the Fathers*, the name is Rothaldus. Wendilmar was bishop of Noyon, and Ostroald bishop of Laon.

Adalbard. CJ has *Adalard*.

Fulrad, Ericho. Thus C and J. Another copy has *Folrad*, *Eriono*. Shortly afterward, in place of *Otnerus*, CJ reads *Otherus*.

That is, Varina, Urbs-campus, Trapiacus, Jerusalem, Harbaudianisva, or the church of Saint Leodegarius. Thus the copies read, except that the manuscript has *Varinne* and divides the final name into two, reading *Haer Haudiavisna*. Nicolaus Chesneau translates these names into French as Varesnes, Urcamp, Trapi, Jerusalem, Herbaudia Vispa.

Of grain, 1,975 *modii*. Thus J, but the manuscript omits the word *modii*, so that it is uncertain whether the *MD* is not itself the measure *modii*, as shortly afterward the manuscript writes: “*md. j. lijo. vini*,” that is, 1,052 *modii* of wine.

## CHAPTER XIX

At the urging of this prelate, Alitgarius, bishop of Cambrai, wrote six little books on remedies for sins and on the order or judgments of penance. These little books appear in volume V of the *Ancient Reading*, published by Henricus Canisius, together with the two letters cited here placed before them. From this passage of our author it is proved that the sixth book, which Canisius places separately, also belongs to Halitgarius—or, as the *Chronicle of Cambrai*, book I, chapter 38, reads, Halitcharius. These books deserve to be counted among the earliest works of casuistry.

There were nevertheless others who wrote on the same subject before Halitgarius’s time, as is clear from this very letter of Ebo: for example, the Roman *Penitential* and that of Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury, whom Bede mentions in his *Chronicles* under Dagobert. There is also Bede’s own book *On Remedies for Sins*. In addition, there were the works of Otlibert and Hatto, bishop of Basel, and later those of Theodulf of Orléans, Rabanus, and others, whom Rhenanus mentions in the argument to Tertullian’s book *On Repentance*, as does Jacobus Pamelius in note 1 on the same book. It is evident from this work of Halitgarius that even at that time penances were customarily imposed according to the requirements of the canons.

When they had prayed for a long time. The manuscript reads, “when they had prayed to God.” But the other reading, found in the remaining copies, is rightly preferred; it agrees with Theganus in *On the Deeds of Louis the Pious*, chapter 16, from which Flodoardus probably took the passage, since he uses the same words. Both the war against the Slavs and Louis’s coronation as emperor took place in the year 816, as is clear from the same Theganus and from Baronius.

They are found to have conferred apostolic offices. Thus all the copies read. Someone may think that *imperialia* (“imperial”) should be read in place of *apostolica*, as in the diploma of this chapter: “We assumed the imperial insignia.” But the true reading is *apostolica munia*, that is, “offices that are customarily conferred by the apostolic see.” For it belongs to the apostolic see to crown the emperor. This reading is confirmed by book III, chapter 10, where what is quoted here from a letter of Emperor Lothair is reported.

And Lothair brought his father with him to the palace of Compiègne, where he afflicted him together with the bishops. Volume III of the Councils contains a council held at Compiègne, at which Emperor Louis was deposed in the year 833.

Of Moderamnus, bishop of Rennes. Thus S and J correctly read, as do all the copies in chapter 20 of book I. The name is translated into French as Rennes. The see is under the archbishopric of Tours. The other copies read here “archbishop of Rouen.” This presumably arose because someone wrote *Rodomensis* for *Redonensis*, after which another wrote *Rothomagensis*. For Rouen is also called Rodoma and Rodomus, as we established above in the note on chapter 16. Moreover, no Moderamnus is found in Democharus’s catalogue of the archbishops of Rouen.

## CHAPTER XX

Later, when Pope Nicholas asked the bishops of Gaul, and especially those of the Belgian province, he received among other things the following in their replies. The letter of the bishops of Gaul to Nicholas I, from which the author drew all these materials, does not survive, at least not in full. For it is clear that he is quoting these matters from other sources when, after recounting many things, he adds: “Likewise, shortly afterward”; and again: “Likewise, a little later.”

Namely Aiulf, archbishop, and Badarad, bishop. R, M, and J read *Aiulf*, from which S produced *Anulf*, while C has *Arnulf*. C and J read *Badarad*, as is also found below in this same chapter, consistently in almost all copies, except that the manuscript has *Baradus*. The synod of Soissons, likewise, which is mentioned near the end of this chapter, reads *Badarad* and *Aiulf*. The manuscript and R read *Hadarad* here.

Whom he had chosen as his judges according to the canons of the African province. The African Council, which is cited several times in this chapter, seems to be the council found in volume I of the Councils, held under Popes Boniface and Celestine. There are 105 canons belonging to various councils of the African province. The canon cited here is chapter 63, which Hincmar specifically cites in the Council of Soissons, discussed in book III, chapter 11. But the passages cited below from chapters 59 and 74 are not found in that council as it now survives.

Namely Bishop Theodoric. He was bishop of Cambrai, as is clear from the *Chronicle of Cambrai*, book I, chapter 41.

In the year 835 from the incarnation of Our Lord Jesus Christ, and also in the twenty-first year of the reign of the glorious Caesar Louis. Thus C. But R, the manuscript, and J have XXIII, incorrectly. Since he began to reign at the beginning of the year 815, the year 835 was the twenty-first year of his reign, as Sigebertus agrees in his *Chronicle*.

Bishop Hartgarius. Thus RC and J. But the manuscript and another copy have *Harogarius*.

Bishop Rambert. M has *Hranbertus*, S *Hrambertus*.

Bishop Haiminus. Thus RJ and C in the French version. The manuscript has *Hamus*, and C in the Latin text has *Hamius*.

To whose restoration the aforesaid synod held at Soissons offered opposition. R and the manuscript have *contradicit*, “offers opposition.” This synod was mentioned implicitly at the beginning of this chapter.

From whom he obtained an episcopate in the region of Saxony, and so forth. For he became bishop of Hildesheim, fourth in succession, and remained there for twelve years, as Albert Krantzius writes in book I of the *Metropolis*, chapter 30. This agrees sufficiently with Flodoardus’s statement in book III, chapter 2, that he lived until the year 851.

# SCHOLIA ON BOOK THREE

[Col. 0371]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0371C]

Finally, in the year 845 of the Lord’s incarnation, Charles held a synod of the bishops of his kingdom at Beauvais. Thus all the old copies read, as it is also read three or four times in the Breviary of Arras under 15 July. S and J changed it to the name more commonly used in this century, Beauvais. Baronius, in volume X of his *Annals*, under that year, inserted this entire first chapter into his *Annals*, translated into Latin from our Flodoard as published in French; Binius then did the same in volume III of the Councils.

To Wenilo, archbishop of the Church of Sennensis. Thus all the old copies read; S and J again changed the form everywhere to *Senonensis*. Someone likewise corrected it in M, although the original reading was *Sennensis*, as it is consistently read below in chapters 20 and 21. The same change was made below in chapter 2. For there too M originally read “with Wenilo of Sennis.” The *Chronicle of Cambrai*, book I, chapter 43, likewise reads “with Venelo of Sennis.” Below, in chapter 20, all the copies call him Egilo; in chapter 22, Wanilo. In the *History attributed to Tilpin* he is called Ganelo.

The manuscript copy of Peter of Troyes’s *Scholastic History*, preserved in the library of the cathedral church of Saint-Omer, likewise reads “with William of Sennis,” where the printed editions have *Senonensis*. The French word Sens also supports this reading. In a manuscript catalogue of the bishops of the whole world, which I possess, I read *the archbishopric of Siennis*. Finally, Pope Zachary, speaking of this church in his letter to Saint Boniface—letter 143 among the letters of Boniface—says: “Finally, Hartbert in the city which is called Sennis.” Serrarius rightly suspects that the city of Sens is meant here, and this is clear from our Flodoard above, book II, chapter 16.

Finally, *Sennensis* is read consistently in the letters of Nicholas I to King Charles and to Egilo, which Joan Cordesius published together with Hincmar’s letters.

## CHAPTER II

The material contained throughout this chapter concerning the Council of Paris held in the case of Ebo is likewise included by Baronius, translated from French into Latin, under the year 847; Binius then included it in volume III of the Councils.

## CHAPTER III

And let them obtain that sacred offerings be presented for us. Thus C and J. Other copies have *imperent* (“let them command”). M has *intrent pro nobis offerre* (“let them enter to offer for us”), for which S reads *instent pro nobis offerre* (“let them persist in offering for us”). But the first reading seems better. From this we learn that the suffrages of the living benefit the dead.

## CHAPTER IV

And to the little ones, the dwarf. It is uncertain whether these are proper names or common nouns, though the latter seems more likely. Hence the French translation is *le petit nain*, that is, “the little dwarf.”

He should know that he will correct matters according to the capitularies of his grandfather, worthy of honorable memory, and of our father, worthy of pious remembrance. We have noted the relevant passages from the Capitularies of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious in the text. On the same subject, Pithoeus, in his *Glossary*, under “Nones and Tithes,” cites canon 42 of the Synod of Mainz, canon 46 of the Synod of Tours, and canon 62 of the Synod of Meaux.

They can provide counsel. Thus C and J read. All the copies read the same above in book II, chapter 19, in the letters of Emperor Louis. Elsewhere the reading is *consilium* (“counsel”), as in the manuscript here. Pope Nicholas I uses the same word in letter 32: “We have heard,” he says, “that Lothair did not await the counsel requested from the apostolic see.” The same word occurs in Rothad’s appeal to the apostolic see: “Without my consent or counsel.” It also appears in the *Chronicle of Cambrai*, book III, chapter 26: “So that he might keep him far from the counsel of the pontiff.” In these passages *consultus* means consultation or counsel. Bishop Fulbert of Chartres uses the same word in letter 39.

## CHAPTER V

Endowed with authorities of this kind of royal benevolence. Thus all the copies read, whereas S substituted *fretus* (“relying on”). The meaning is: “Since he possessed authorities of this kind,” that is, edicts or diplomas.

He also adorned the Book of Sacraments and the Lectionary, which he had caused to be written, with ivory and silver. Among the ancients, and specifically for Saint Gregory, the Book of Sacraments was what we call the Missal, or, in the neuter gender, the *Missale*. The Lectionary was the book containing the readings for each day. Similar statements appear below in chapter 9, given by the same Hincmar to the church of Saint Remigius.

## CHAPTER VI

And preparing little gifts of candles. This is the correct reading. But M has *candelabrum munuscula*, from which S and J produced *candelabrum et munuscula*, “a candlestick and little gifts.” From this we learn that even at that time the devotion of the faithful was customary: they lit lamps for the saints, as we still see today.

## CHAPTER VII

A certain veil spread over the place was seen there. Thus M and R. But CJ has *appensum*, “hung up,” and S *oppensum*.

## CHAPTER VIII

He returns the carpets to the benches. That is, he puts them back. Thus all the copies except the manuscript, which has: “He returned the holy carpets.” From the matters related here we learn that church ornaments were not to be applied to profane uses.

## CHAPTER IX

He placed above it verses distinguished by gold. Thus the manuscript. J has *inlitis*, “smeared with,” and C *inditis*, “inserted.”

## CHAPTER X

He had never granted to any archbishop the daily use of the pallium. The authority and use of the pallium are treated in title 8 of book I of the *Decretals*. Baronius, in volume X, under two years—namely 849 and 852—writes that Pope Nicholas denied that the daily use of the pallium had been granted to Hincmar by Pope Leo, “as,” he says, “will be stated in its proper place.” Yet in the deeds of Pope Nicholas he nowhere demonstrates that this was false, although he does rebuke Hincmar on other matters.

He is found to have commended them to bishops and legates. Thus the manuscript. CJ has *epistolis*, “in letters.” The first reading is preferable, because letters are mentioned shortly afterward.

## CHAPTER XI

Concerning the provincial synod held at the city of Soissons. It appears in volume III of the Councils, part one, as having been celebrated in the year 853, under Leo IV. But, as is noted there and as our author admits below in this same chapter, it was rejected by Pope Nicholas I.

The author drew from the acts of this synod the material he writes here, in many places borrowing its very words. Pope Nicholas later retracted and condemned it with respect to the deposition of those clerics who had been ordained by Ebo. Hincmar had obtained approval of that synod from Pope Benedict and from Nicholas himself earlier, but by concealed means, as Nicholas’s letters 52 and 5 demonstrate among those in the appendix to his letters; Baronius himself admits this in volume X under the year 863, where he inserts the same letter.

[Col. 0374A]

That the synod was rejected by Pope Nicholas is clear from his letters 46 and 47, and from letters 13 and 15 in the appendix. In them he ordered another synod to be convened in the same city of Soissons concerning the same difficulty; that synod decreed that the said clerics were to be restored. It was held in the year 866.

To Amalric of Tours. Thus CJ, the volume of the Councils, and the *Chronicle of Cambrai*. The manuscript has *Almarico*, and below *Almaricum*, and likewise twice in chapter 21. The full form is *Amalaricus*, the name of a king of the Visigoths. M also has *Turonense*, *Catalaunense*, *Noviomagense*, and so forth, all with *e*, except that it reads *Sennensi*, which was changed to *Senonensi* and *Cameracensi*. Here, however, we have retained the more usual declension, following the other copies and the form found in the volumes of the Councils, so that the ablative is pronounced with *i*.

To Hubert of Meaux. Thus CJ, as do the tables of Democharus. The remaining copies have *Hucbertus*, as in the volumes of the Councils; the same form is also consistently found in the manuscript copies of Sigebertus for the name of the bishop of Liège.

To Jonah of Autun. M has *Augustidunense*, for which S and J have *Augustodunense*, now the more usual form.

To Godelsad of Chalon. Thus all the old copies; S and J substituted the more recent name *Cabillonense*.

To Hildebrand of Sées. M has *Sagense*, J *Sagensi*, as this passage is also read in the volumes of the Councils. But in the subscriptions of the Council of Toul and the Second Council of Soissons the form is *Hildebrandus Sagiensis*. Likewise, in the tables of Democharus, Saint Hildebrand is listed ninth among the bishops of Sées. The town is called Sagium and Saium, in French Séez in Normandy.

To Rigbold, chorepiscopus of Reims. Thus C and the volumes of the Councils, where he is called Rigbaldus; the manuscript and J incorrectly read *coepiscopus* in his place.

To Lupus, abbot of the monastery called Ferrarium. Thus all the copies. In the volumes of the Councils: “Lupus, abbot of the monastery of Bethlehem, which is called Ferraria.” It was called by both names. A book of letters by this Abbot Lupus survives.

Heriacum. M and another copy have *Heiricum*; S and J, *Hericum*; the volumes of the Councils, *Ericum*.

Hairohald. Thus the manuscript. Another copy has *Hairoldus*, as CJ; the volumes of the Councils have *Harowaldus*.

Named Halduin. Thus RC and the volumes of the Councils. But the manuscript has *Balduin*, although M reads *Halduinum* below, which was incorrectly corrected to *Balduinum*. J has *Harduinum* in both places.

[Col. 0375A]

Finally, the aforesaid prelates of the council, obedient to the commands of the apostolic see, and so forth, presenting a letter of the following kind. This letter, whose principal points alone are inserted here, is the synodal letter of the Council of Troyes, discussed below in chapter 17. It was held by the same bishops in the following year, namely 867, by whom the Council of Soissons had been held in 866, as the title itself indicates. It was addressed to Nicholas but delivered to his successor Adrian II.

It appears in volume III of the Councils at the end of the first part. Before it stands another letter of the same bishops, written from the Council of Soissons in the preceding year, which our author mentioned shortly above. In this second letter they fully satisfy what Pope Nicholas had enjoined upon them in letter 46. The inscription is somewhat fuller in the volumes of the Councils and in Hincmar’s little works recently published by John, canon of the Church of Limoges:

“To the most reverend and most holy lord Father and universal pope Nicholas, the bishops who in the previous year, by the grace of God and by your decree, assembled at the city of Soissons with the others who were then unable to attend, on the eighth day before the Kalends of November, in the first indiction, having gathered at Troyes.”

In addition to the synodal letters from the Second Council of Soissons, Hincmar also sent Pope Nicholas a private letter in which he excused himself for not immediately restoring those clerics. It appears in Baronius under the year 866, after the synodal letter. Both letters were sent through Egilo, archbishop of Sens.

Since the synodal letter of Troyes is not inserted in full in this chapter, some passages missing from the volumes of the Councils and from Cordesius could have been supplied from what Flodoardus preserves.

To have hastened to restore them to their orders. Thus S and J, but this is incorrectly placed here; the correct reading, found in M and C, is *maturaremus*, “we would have hastened.” This is how it appears in the volumes of the Councils, in the same letter published by Cordesius, in Hincmar’s letter to Pope Nicholas—which is the second among those published by Cordesius—and in the letter of the Second Council of Soissons to the same Nicholas.

The writings also which were sent from here by your authority. Thus CJ. The reading in the volumes of the Councils agrees, except that it has *huc* in place of *hinc*. But *hinc* can be understood not as an adverb of place, but as “from here,” that is, “concerning this matter.” The manuscript has: “the writings which were sent from here by our authority.” The preceding and following material, however, requires the first reading.

## CHAPTER XII
He caused the sentence of excommunication against the aforementioned Baldwin and Judith to be pronounced by the bishops, in accordance with the decrees of blessed Gregory. That is, he arranged for them to be excommunicated. The reference is evidently to Decrees 10 and 11 of Gregory II at the Roman synod, chapter “If anyone abducts a virgin,” *Causa* 36, question 2, where the excommunication of abductors of virgins and widows is ordered.

And he bestowed honors upon Baldwin solely at your request. This Baldwin, surnamed “the Iron,” is said to have been the first created count of Flanders, or count of the realm, by Charles the Bald, Judith’s father. See Jacobus Meyerus, *Annals of Flanders*, under the year 863. Among Nicholas’s letters, those concerning Baldwin are numbers 20, 21, 30, 32, and 52; almost all of them are addressed to King Charles, asking him to spare Baldwin. One is addressed to Queen Hermentrude. Those addressed to Hincmar, which this chapter mentions, are not extant.

## CHAPTER XIII

### On the case of Rothad, deposed bishop of Soissons

This Rothadus, or, as he is more commonly called in the volumes of the Councils and in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Rothaldus, was deposed at Hincmar’s initiative by several bishops assembled in the synod of Senlis in June 863. After confining him to a monastery, they appointed another in his place, notwithstanding his appeal to the Apostolic See. He was later restored to his own see, since no accusers appeared against him at Rome, nor did Odo, bishop of Beauvais, who had been sent to Rome by this synod, accuse him. On all these matters see at length Letter 28 of Pope Nicholas I and those that follow, through Letter 44. These sixteen letters also appear in volume III of the second edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. Certainly Hincmarus, in his apologetic letter, which occupies this entire chapter, writes that he is sending his representatives “not as accusers to engage in conflict, but, having been accused by Rothad and by those nearby, to make known that we judged regularly—not, in contempt of the Apostolic See, Rothad, who appealed to the Apostolic See according to the canons of Sardica, but the man who appealed to the judgment of the chosen concerning specific charges, in accordance with the Carthaginian and African canons and the decrees of blessed Gregory.” So he writes. Rothadus, however, denies this in his appeal, which is preserved after Letter 37 of Pope Nicholas; and the chief controversy in this case appears to lie precisely here. This entire chapter appears in Baronius, volume X, under the year 861, but from a single copy and, as Baronius admits, not without errors.

Certain bishops of King Lothair’s realm, led against us by bitter zeal because we did not yield to their counsels concerning Waldrada. King Lothair, son of Emperor Lothair, had repudiated his lawful wife Theutberga and taken this Waldrada, his concubine, in marriage. Numerous letters of Pope Nicholas and Hincmar’s lengthy work *On the Divorce of King Lothair and Queen Theutberga* also survive concerning this matter.

And therefore, in order that he might support himself, to promise him a *locarium*. Thus read C and J. The word *locarium* is derived from *locus*, “place,” where one may *locare*, that is, “to place” or “settle” oneself. According to Varro, it means the payment made in a stable or tavern. Hence it is translated into French as *moyens de vivre* (“means of living”). The manuscript and another copy read *jocarium*, which could mean the same as *jocale*, French *joyaux* (“jewels”); but that does not suit this passage. The earlier reading and meaning are confirmed by what precedes not long before.

And constrained by the length and insecurity of the journey. He calls an insecure journey *iter insolidum*, that is, one that is unsafe, in French *mal sûr*. Some copies make the two words *in soliditate*, but incorrectly.

[Col. 0377A] Unless for as long as his own bishop had been expelled by her without any crime. Evidently Rigobertus, mentioned above in Book II, chapter 12. This phrase was written by another hand above the line in M, and S and J transferred it into the text.

That he had stolen the property and treasure of the church. Thus reads C, and this appears to be the true reading. The others have *fraudatus* (“defrauded”).

## CHAPTER XIV

To the recently held conventicle at Metz, which you forbade to be called a synod. It appears in volume III of the Councils, at the end of the first part. It was held in June 863 concerning King Lothair’s repudiation of Queen Theutberga. Nicholas I condemned it at the Third Roman Council, held under him in the same year.

Finally, at the synod held in the city of Mainz, presenting to Archbishop Rabanus a written statement of his error, [Col. 0377B] condemned by all the bishops of Germany, and so forth. This is the Second Synod of Mainz under Rabanus, in the year of the Lord 848, during the pontificate of Pope Leo IV. Baronius discusses it under that same year, but only from Flodoard’s writings as translated from the French.

Afterward, having been heard by the bishops of the provinces of Belgica, Rheims, and Gaul. Namely, at the Synod of Valence in 855, by bishops of three provinces, which is found in volume III of the Councils, part I; and at the Synod of Toul, in the suburb of that city, at a place called Saponaria, by bishops of twelve provinces in the year of the Lord 859. That synod is not preserved there in full. See Baronius in his *Annals* under this year. The author mentions both below, in chapter 16.

Which appears to speak against the Catholic faith from the old Predestinarian heresy, and so forth. He correctly says “appears,” because some of these statements, properly understood, are not contrary to the faith—for example, the second point, if one distinguishes between God’s will of good pleasure and his signified will. Likewise the third point, namely, that Christ died and was crucified sufficiently for all, because the price he paid was sufficient, though not efficaciously for all, because it is not applied to all. In this sense Saint Prosper formerly replied to the *Chapters of the Gauls* and the Vincentian objections.

What Hincmarus adduces first is expressed in these words: “He”—namely, Gothescalcus—“says what the ancient Predestinarians also said: just as God predestined some to eternal life, so he predestined some to eternal death.” This was impiously said by them and by Gothescalcus, because they claimed that by a fatal necessity arising from God’s predestination people were compelled first to sin and then to death. This is clear from the first objection in the *Chapters of the Gauls*, from the final canon of the Second Council of Orange, and from chapter 3 of the Council of Valence, where, with that same Council of Orange cited, it is said:

“We truly do not merely refuse to believe that some have been predestined to evil by divine power, so that, as it were, they could not be anything else; if there are people who wish to believe such a great evil, we anathematize them with complete abhorrence, as did the Synod of Orange.”

Let them read, and consider carefully for themselves, chapter six of that same Council of Valence—those who have revived such questions in this age.

Moreover, among the ancients there is little mention of the Predestinarian heresy under that name. [Col. 0378A] Later writers on heresies merely report what Sigebertus says in his *Chronicle* under the year 415:

“The heresy of the Predestinarians began to spread at this time. They are called Predestinarians because, disputing about predestination and divine grace, they asserted that the labor of good works benefits neither those who live piously, if they have been predestined by God to death, nor does wicked living harm the impious, if they have been predestined by God to life. This assertion both drew the good away from good things and incited the wicked to evil.”

So he writes.

What the ancient Predestinarians did not say, this man says both more boldly and more perniciously: that the deity of the Holy Trinity is threefold. This is said less correctly and improperly, since in the Holy Trinity there is only one deity numerically, belonging to three persons. Yet one may speak of a threefold deity in the sense that it exists in three persons. Thus, for approximately three hundred and fifty years, that hymn of Saint Thomas on the Blessed Sacrament has been sung in the Roman Church, in which it says:

> We ask you, threefold and yet one Deity.

And when the question of changing it arose during the final revision of the Roman Breviary under Clement VIII, as I learned from the men concerned, nothing was changed because of the authority of so great a doctor. Likewise, in Chrysostom, volume III, in the homily *On Saint John the Baptist*—which is not actually his, but by an unknown author—we read: “In the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit there is a threefold and one divinity.” There *triplex* (“threefold”) is used for *trina* (“threefold,” in the sense of three persons), just as in Prudentius’s hymn on the Paschal candle, when he says of God:

> He extends his kingdom by a threefold divine power.

For God is not properly called *triplex* (“threefold”), but *trinus* (“triune”), as the scholastic doctors teach in Book I of the *Sentences*, distinction 19.

And he seeks not only to appear the teacher of his own teachers, and so forth. Thus read all the copies, and this is the true reading. Accordingly, *dictorum* (“of the things said”) was wrongly corrected in M, a reading followed by S. The meaning is that he seeks to appear the teacher of his teachers—that is, of those who teach and instruct him—and tries to convict them of teaching something contrary to themselves and to their own doctrine.

## CHAPTER XV

Moreover, the synodal chapters of our venerable fellow priests, namely, of the three provinces, as is contained there, and so forth. He is speaking of the Council of Valence, as is clear from what follows. Thirteen or fourteen bishops in all attended it, including three metropolitans: Remigius of Lyons, Egilmatus of Vienne, and Rodlandus of Arles. At the beginning, only their names are given, together with that of Elbo, bishop of Grenoble. In chapter 4 of this council are found the statements that Hincmarus acknowledges in this letter to have been made against him, both concerning the four and concerning the nineteen chapters he had collected.

In the African and Arausican synod. This is the Second Synod of Orange, which still survives today. Three councils concerning this matter were held in Africa: two at Carthage and one at Milevis in Numidia. This is clear from Letter 47 of Saint Augustine, where he calls one of them the plenary council of all Africa. It is regrettable that this council is no longer extant, though Prosper quotes some fragments from it in his *Reply to the Chapters of the Gauls*, chapter 8, and in Book Against the Collator, chapter 10.

As if there had existed a letter of the Chapters, which the venerable bishop Ibas denied at the synod was his own. This is Ibas, bishop of the Church of Edessa, concerning whom the ecclesiastical councils—or rather judgments—at Tyre and Berytus and the Council of Chalcedon, action 10, speak. See also Baronius under the year 448. He says that the letter was indeed Ibas’s, but denies that Ibas said these or similar words: “I do not begrudge Christ his having been made God; if I wish, I too can become one.” After the testimony of the clergy of the Church of Edessa had been heard, he was acquitted of that charge.

In the time of the emperor Charles of blessed memory, when a synod was held concerning Felix’s known infidelity. S reads *infelicitate* (“misfortune”) instead. He is speaking of Charlemagne and Felix, bishop of Urgel. The Frankish Annals published by Pithoeus discuss this Felix and his error under the year 792; Sigebertus in his *Chronicle* under 793; Aimoïnus, Book IV, chapters 83 and 85; Jonas of Orléans, Book I *On the Worship of Images*; and Paul of Aquileia, who wrote a book against his error, preserved in volume IV of the second edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. His heresy was condemned at the Council of Frankfurt, which appears in volume III of the Councils under the year 794.

And thus at last we shall submit those nineteen chapters. Thus read all our copies and the Council of Valence. [Col. 0379C] Therefore J incorrectly reads “sixteen.”

## CHAPTER XVI

Is it because you are separated from the ancient faith of the fathers? Thus reads C: *cana*, that is, “ancient,” as Chesneau translates it into French. The manuscript agrees, reading *arcana* instead of *a cana*. J substituted *sana* (“sound”). Thus Sidonius Apollinaris, poem 2: “the hoary age of the fathers,” that is, the ancient age; and Isidore, in manuscript glosses: “hoary faith, ancient old age.” And before them Virgil, *Aeneid* I:

> Hoary Faith, Vesta, and Quirinus with his brother Remus  
> shall give the laws.

At the assembly of bishops held in the territory of Toul, in a village called Saponaria. I noted this council above, under chapter 14.

And in the suburb of the city of Langres. This synod is not extant. [Col. 0379D]

Because the chapters themselves were not brought forth by them, to say nothing of being brought forth through them by the synod. The meaning is that they were not put forward as though they had originated with them.

I fear that “to connive” means “to keep silent about this.” I restored this from the original of Celestine’s first letter; in place of *cohibere* (“to restrain”), J substituted *committere* (“to entrust” or “commit”).

In a village belonging to the bishopric of Rouen called Melpsa. Elsewhere it is called Melpha or Anelpha, or Avelpha, as in the manuscript. J has Nelpha.

## CHAPTER XVII

### On the synod of six provinces of Gaul held at Troyes

This synod appears in volume III of the Councils, part II. In the same part there is also Adrian II’s answering letter to this synod, which is number 9 among his letters. Above, in chapter 11 of this book, a substantial portion of the synodal letter of this same Council of Troyes has been included.

Through Actardus, the venerable bishop of Nantes. Thus also in the volumes of the Councils. The manuscript has *Acardus* here and below several times, and sometimes *Accardus*, *Arctardus*, and *Artardus*. But the first reading is the more common.

Pope Nicholas, however, gratefully receiving what Hincmarus had written to him, replied that he had been satisfied concerning everything. This apologetic letter of Hincmarus, quite lengthy, appears in Baronius under the year 867, but Nicholas’s reply is not extant.

The Greeks themselves saying that we Latins make chrism from river water. I understand this to mean that “we Latins make chrism from river water.” Hence the Roman edition of the decretal letters reads: “They deceitfully suppose that we make chrism from river water.” I am surprised that Nicolas Chesneau translated it as though *Latini* were a genitive depending on *fluminis*, with the marginal note: “The Latin River, the Tiber.” For in the refutation of the ten calumnies brought forward by the Greeks, which Baronius places after the letter of Nicholas cited here, the only statement is: “That the Western Church uses water in place of chrism is, by everyone’s testimony, a manifest calumny.” Certainly the Greeks do not seem to have intended to say that the entire Western Church used Tiber water for chrism, but rather water from some river or other.

## CHAPTER XVIII

In the vision of the revived Bernoldus. Similar things concerning Bernoldus’s vision of a dark place and another luminous place are written by the Venerable Bede, Book V of the *History of the English People*, chapter 13, and by Lupoldus of Babenberg, *On the Zeal of the Ancient Princes of Germany*, chapter 14. There, drawing on Vincent’s *Speculum* and the *History of the Franks*, he discusses Emperor Louis the Pious detained in punishments and asking help from his son Louis the German. Sigebertus also discusses him in his *Chronicle* under the year 875.

For if they have contended over this, I shall soon be freed from this punishment. That is, if they do this zealously, as is said above, so that they may act and contend with one another to establish the peace that the king commands.

Likewise, concerning the passion of Saint Dionysius by Methodius, and so forth. This letter appears in Surius, *Lives of the Saints*, under October 9.

## CHAPTER XIX

[Col. 0380D]

### On the payment of the *conjectum* to the Normans

The *conjectum* was a type of tribute, its name deriving from *conjacere*, as is clear from Book IV of the Capitularies, chapter 69, and from Charles’s edict at Quierzy in 861. See Pithoeus’s *Glossary*, under *Conjectum*. Papirius Massonus, Book II of the *Frankish Annals*, while quoting these words of Flodoardus under Louis the Stammerer, notes in the margin: “*Conjectus* means grain-supply.”

To the sons also of that deceased king, Louis and Carloman. These were the sons of Louis the Stammerer by his first wife, Ansgarde. By his second wife, named Adelaide, he fathered Charles the Posthumous, surnamed the Simple. He mentions them again below, in chapter 24, when listing the letter to Abbot Hugh concerning the same affair. Sigebertus, in his *Chronicle* under the year 880, calls them sons by a concubine. Papirius, however, in the passage already cited, proves that they were born from a lawful marriage.

After the death of Bishop Ragenelinus. Thus the manuscript consistently reads *Ragelini* here and below, in chapters 23 and 24; J almost everywhere has *Ragenelmi*, as Papirius Massonus also twice reads it in Book II of the *Frankish Annals*. But in chapter 23 all our copies have *Rainelini* in the section concerning Berno, while J has *Rainelmi*. This is the man who is called the thirty-seventh in the catalogues of the bishops of Tournai and Noyon, *Rancelinus* or *Raymelinus*, and in the subscription to the Council of Soissons, held in 866, *Remelinus*. He was succeeded by Hedilo.

## CHAPTER XX

To Arduicus of Besançon. Thus read C and J, and in the following chapters all the copies, sometimes with aspiration, *Harduicus*. The manuscript has *Radvicus* here; C has corrected it above the line, and also reads it so in French.

For the estate of Deduciacus. Thus the manuscript also reads below, but there it makes two words; J has *Dudiciacus* here and *Dudeciacus* below. In the testament of Saint Remigius, all copies consistently give the complete name *Duodeciacus*, as also below in this Book III, the following chapter, *the estate Duodeciaca*, although the manuscript, omitting one letter, reads only *Dudeciaca*. Likewise, in chapter 26 the manuscript twice reads *Dudeciacus*, where J has the complete *Dudeciacus* at the first occurrence; all the copies likewise read it in Book IV, chapter 2.

But also concerning the estate of Noviliacum, and so forth. On this estate see above, Book II, chapter 17, and at greater length in the fragment of Hincmarus that Jacobus Sirmondus appended after the end of this work. It appears to contain part of this letter.

Also to Charles, son of Louis the German. This is Charles the Fat, son of the king of Germany, brother of Charles the Bald.

## CHAPTER XXI

To Lothair, king of Italy, who, having abandoned his own wife, had joined himself to a certain woman. This is the Lothair mentioned above under chapter 13 and again in chapter 20, namely, the son of Emperor Lothair. Baronius, however, under the year 855, when Emperor Lothair died, says that after dividing the kingdom he gave Italy to Louis, who also succeeded him in the empire, while he gave Lothair the kingdom he possessed in Francia, except Provence, which he gave to Charles. Baronius repeatedly, under the year 868, calls this Lothair the adulterous king of Gaul and the Franks; Sigebertus likewise says in his *Chronicle* under the year 855 that he held Lotharingia, and under the year 862, when he took Waldrada as his concubine, calls him king of Lotharingia. Papirius Massonus similarly writes in Book II of the *Frankish Annals*, under Charles the Bald:

> He died, leaving his sons Louis, Lothair, and Charles. The latter held Provence; the second held the lands of the Leuci and Mediomatrici, which changed their ancient name into Lotharingia. Louis was king of Italy.

Therefore *king of Lotharingia* seems to need to be substituted for *king of Italy*.

I also wrote certain things to Pope Adrian. Among Hincmar’s letters edited by Cordesius, only one is addressed to Adrian II. Adrian’s letters to Hincmar that are extant are in volume III of the Councils, numbers 13 and 28.

To Formosus, the religious bishop of that same see—that is, of the Roman see. Understand this as “suffragan,” as Baronius explains when citing the same words under the year 891. Formosus, long after Hincmar’s death, was then made supreme pontiff, having previously been bishop of Porto. Likewise, below in Book IV, chapter 6, during the pontificate of Stephen VII, Fulco writes to a certain Roman prelate named John, whom Baronius under the year 897 says was one of the suffragans of the Holy Roman Church. Understand Gaudericus and John in the same way, for they are mentioned shortly afterward.

Also asking that the Gospel of the Nazarenes be sent to him for copying. Saint Jerome mentions this several times, writing in *On Illustrious Men*, under James, that he translated it from Hebrew into Greek and Latin. On this see Sixtus of Siena, Book II of the *Bibliotheca Sancta*, under “The Gospel of the Hebrews.” For it is also called by that name.

To Vulfadus, archbishop of Bourges. He is the man who had been ordained priest by Ebo, concerning whom there has been frequent mention above, as is clear from the letter of King Charles to Pope Nicholas, which appears among Hincmar’s letters edited by Cordesius.

To Immo, bishop of Noyon. Elsewhere he is called Himmo, and he is recorded as a signatory at the Council of Toul in 859. He is also called Emmo and Emino. Meyerus writes that he was killed by the Northmen during the sack of his city in that same year.

To Prudentius of Troyes. In the catalogue of the bishops of Troyes he is the thirty-seventh. He died around the year 864, according to the *Storehouse of Sacred Antiquities of the Diocese of Troyes*, by Nicholas Camuzat, its author or compiler. His feast is celebrated with nine lessons on April 6. The same *Storehouse* preserves a sermon of his entitled: “Sermon of Blessed Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes, on the Life and Death of the Glorious Virgin Maura.” He also wrote a book learnedly refuting a short work filled with Origenist and Pelagian errors, which John Scotus had composed from the writings of Gothescalcus of Orbais, the monk. He was succeeded by Fulchricus, then by Atulfus, or Octulfus, concerning whom see below, chapter 23.

To Aeneas of Paris, on behalf of Rothadus of Soissons. He also sent other letters to this Aeneas on behalf of the cleric Berno, which appear in Baronius under the year 912, together with Aeneas’s reply to Hincmar.

## CHAPTER XXII

In the synod of bishops of ten provinces. This is the Synod of Douzy in the province of Rheims. Joannes Cordesius published a fragment of this synod’s letter to Adrian II among Hincmar’s letters. Aimoïnus mentions the same synod in Book V, chapter 24, at the end: “It was held in the year 817.” It appears in volume III of the Councils, part II. There also precedes it the council held at the palace of Verberie by twenty bishops, and the council held at the estate and palace of Attigny in 870. Baronius says that the latter was illegitimate and a robber council, and that Hincmarus of Laon was unjustly deposed there. [Col. 0383A]

Perhaps Hincmarus of Rheims—who was evidently forceful in all his actions and a great defender of the ancient discipline—was somewhat too severe toward his nephew Hincmarus of Laon, whom Baronius calls a defender of the rights of the Roman Church. Yet Baronius also shows in his *Annals*, under the years 870 and 871, that he acted unjustly toward him. Accordingly, Adrian II’s Letter 27 and the three that follow support Hincmarus of Laon. His complaint, or appeal, to the Apostolic See is preserved in the same volume of the Councils after Letter 3 of John VIII. Finally, at the Council of Troyes, under the same John VIII, in 878, Baronius says that he was restored to his former rank, and proves it from Ado at the end of his *Chronicle*. Aimoïnus, however, in the cited book, chapter 37, seems rather to indicate the opposite when he says:

> Pope John said that Hedenulfus, a bishop ordained by his own authority, should retain his see and exercise the episcopal ministry; and that Hincmarus, if he wished, should celebrate Mass and receive a share of the property of the bishopric of Laon.

Certainly Pope Nicholas I, although in a letter sent to Hincmarus of Rheims, preserved in volume III of the Councils, he reproves him in certain matters, nevertheless gives him splendid testimony in the letter whose fragment Ivo quotes in his *Decretum*, part XIV, chapter 46, and Gratian, *Causa* II, question 3, chapter 102, under the heading “Most Excellent,” saying:

> Therefore we now charge your Blessedness, having been strengthened in this matter by our authority, to strive to take responsibility for it; for your holiness, taught by God, knows very well that one thing is done from necessity, another from ignorance, and another through deliberate choice.

And so forth.

Meyerus, in his *Annals of Flanders*, under the year 885, testifies that he was a pious and highly learned man. The letter of that same John VIII also supports Hincmarus of Rheims. Since it is absent from the volumes of the Councils, it seemed worthwhile to copy it here, having first been transcribed by the Reverend Father Jacobus Sirmondus from the Library of Saint Remigius:

> John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hincmarus, archbishop of Rheims.
>
> Although we had never doubted the judgment of your holiness, nevertheless, because our dearest son Charles, the most invincible emperor, whom we had diligently questioned, reported to our apostolate the circumstances of the judgment pronounced by your Blessedness and your fellow bishops against Hincmarus, formerly bishop of Laon, we have recognized that the judgment was entirely just. [Col. 0383D] For so great a prince could affirm nothing unless supported by the truth. Therefore we have judged it wrong not to give his report an immediate hearing in good faith.
>
> Do not now leave the Church of Laon widowed and without pastoral governance. Instead, appoint as its bishop an appropriate man, chosen without partiality from the clergy of the Church of Laon, one in whom the votes of all may agree. We also wish the envoy of the aforementioned most devout emperor to be present at this election, so that, without secular tumult, a man may be chosen from every side who is proved in every respect suitable for the sacred canons.
>
> We wish your holiness good health in Christ.
>
> Given at Rome by Theodoricus, at the command of Pope John and of Charles, our lord, the new emperor, through the hands of Anastasius the Librarian, in the sacristy of the Church of Saint Peter. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 877, on the Nones of January, in the ninth indiction. It was carried by the same Theodoricus to Hincmarus, archbishop of Rheims, in the city of Rheims, in the same year and indiction, on the fifth day before the Ides of March.

And accused by a Northman at the synod. On this see Letters 28 and 29 of Adrian.

The municipality of Laon, and so forth, from its foundation, after it had been established by the praetor Marcobrius, as the histories relate. Hincmarus himself says the following about the same matter in his *Work of Fifty-Five Chapters*, chapter 16:

> This fortress of Laon, as the ancient historian Eutropius says, was founded by the praetor Marcobrius. From its beginning, while paganism still prevailed, it had neither the name nor the status of a city or provincial see.

Formerly possessed by *horno*. Thus read the manuscript and the original. J has *orno*, as M reads in Book I, chapter 20. *Horno* means the same as “this year.” It is also written *hornus, -a, -um*, as in “the fruits of this year” and “the apples of this year.”

Although he inclines his head toward a volume, the man who does not obey them, but rather, extending his hands forward to meet them. Thus read the original and J. The phrase is quite obscure. The manuscript has *thomum*. The copy used by Baronius reads *Thomam*, and he thinks *Romam* should be restored. In place of *porro* (“forward”), it reads *Petro* (“Peter”). The manuscript has *obvians*. A *tomus* properly means a fragment cut off from a book, and is used for an incomplete book or volume.

## CHAPTER XXIII

[Col. 0384C]

To hold a synod at Pistas. This means the Council of Pistes, at a place called Pistes on the River Seine, held in 863 under Pope Nicholas I. It appears in volume III of the Councils, at the end of the first part. Hence above, in chapter 21, all the copies read *at Pistas on the Seine*. Here the manuscript reads *Pestas*, but incorrectly. It is also called Pisciacum and Pistae, as though from *Pisciatae*, because, as Sebastian Roulliard writes in his *Parthenia*, or *History of the Church of Chartres*, chapter 12, number 9, it is customarily the swimming pool of all France. In French, Poissy.

To Walo, prelate of Metz. Thus reads the manuscript, but J has *Wala*, as Aimoïnus calls him in Book V, chapter 41.

## CHAPTER XXIV

[Col. 0384D]

Into the parish of Paris. Thus C reads in the French translation, which is supported by the fact that he writes to the abbot of Saint-Denis near Paris. C in Latin and J have *Pariacensem*; the manuscript has *Parnacensem*.

## CHAPTER XXV

To Magenardus, the provost. The manuscript has *Agenardus*.

## CHAPTER XXVI

To the most illustrious man Eberardus. M has *Ebarardus*; J has *Ebrardus* by contraction.

To Roricus, a Northman converted to the faith of Christ. This Roricus is different from Rollo, leader of the Northmen, concerning whom the *Chronicle of Cambrai*, Book II, chapter 29, says that he was converted to the faith and baptized in the year 912, as I noted there.

## CHAPTER XXVII

[Col. 0385A]

To Queen Irmintrude. This is the first wife of Charles the Bald, whom other writers call Hermentrude. After her death he married Richildis.

So that, fearing the agreement of which we say, “Forgive us our debts, as …,” and so forth. By “agreement” he means a pact, concord, or legal covenant. He is referring to the covenant of the Lord’s Prayer and to chapter 13 of the Rule of Saint Benedict, where it says: “Those who have been bound by the pledge of that prayer, in which they say, ‘Forgive us …,’” and so forth.

How dangerous an evil both the queen herself and that empress underwent. M has *periculum* (“danger”); J reads: “How dangerous an evil both she herself and that empress underwent.”

## CHAPTER XXVIII

[Col. 0385B]

Of a certain brother of Ragamfredus. Thus M reads here and shortly below. S has *Ragemfredus*; J, *Raganfredus*.

But if the count himself denied that this had been done. Thus reads the manuscript. J, however, has: “But if the count himself did not ask that this be done.” The apparent meaning is: “If the count denies that he did it.”

Or through fear of someone, or at the instigation of the priest himself. Thus J reads. The manuscript, however, has: “Or through fear of someone, they presume to be condemned because of that impulse, or by an oath concerning him,” and so forth.

He merely foreknew the evil, but did not predestine them, nor by his foreknowledge compel them to perish. Thus J reads. The manuscript adds two words, *ad regnum* (“to the kingdom”), as follows: “He did not predestine them to the kingdom, nor [predestine them] to perish,” and so forth. [Col. 0386A] This reading is certainly faulty; instead, it should have said “to destruction.”

## CHAPTER XXIX

On the book published by him: *How the Images of the Lord and of the Saints Are to Be Venerated*. If this book existed, it would then be clear what Hincmarus thought about this matter. Certainly it is evident that he held the Catholic position from his own *Work of Fifty-Five Chapters Against Hincmarus of Laon*, chapter 25. As for the passage Matthias Flacius Illyricus cites from chapter 20 of the same work, by which Hincmarus appears to condemn the Seventh Synod concerning images, namely the Second Council of Nicaea, one should know that he cites Hincmarus’s text corruptly, substituting *Nicaea* for *Constantinople*. The words he cites are found in Alanus’s fourth dialogue, chapter 18. They also appear in Baronius, volume IX, under the year 794. But the complete work of Hincmarus should be consulted; it was finally published in Paris in the preceding year, 1615, where *Constantinople* is read without any textual variation. See also Alanus at the passage already cited and in the following chapter, and Severinus Binius, who discusses these matters at great length in his notes on the Council of Frankfurt, volume III.

## CHAPTER XXX

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 882. Thus read all the copies. On this matter the author should be trusted more than Sigebertus and Meyerus, who write that Hincmarus died in the year 885.

# SCHOLIA ON BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0385]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0385C]

Fulco, a man of very noble rank. Elsewhere *Folco*, as M writes almost everywhere.

Delegating to Pope Marinus. This is the true reading, as it is consistently read below, although in M a recent hand has added the letter *t*, making it read *Martinus*, and identifies him as Martin II. But Baronius and Binius attest that the reading should be *Marinus*, asserting that he is wrongly called Martin II.

For the defense of Frotharius, archbishop of Bourges. He had previously been archbishop of Bordeaux, as is clear above, Book III, chapter 21, and below in this same chapter.

To which those letters responded. This chapter lists ten or more letters of Pope Stephen VI, none of which appears among the decretal letters or in the volumes of the Councils. Likewise, none of Fulco’s letters listed in this chapter—eight or nine in number—or several in the following chapters is extant.

By which, through divine calling, he passed beyond humanity. That is, he died. Thus below, chapter 5: “When they had happily passed beyond human life.” Likewise the *Chronicle of Cambrai*, Book III, chapter 19: “Baldricus the bishop left humanity,” that is, died. See my notes there.

[Col. 0386C] But after consultation with his king Odo. This Odo, son of Duke Robert, was tutor of King Charles the Simple, the posthumous son of Louis the Stammerer. See the scholia below, chapter 5.

To summon a synod at the city of the Vangiones. The manuscript has *Vangionem*. Sigebertus and others call this city Worms by another name. Hence Luitprandus, in his little work *On the Lives of the Pontiffs*, in his Life of Stephen VI, says that he ordered a synod to be summoned at Worms. The Council of Worms is listed in volume III of the Councils, part II, under the year 890. His words are as follows:

> He ordered Herimannus, archbishop of Cologne, and Adalgar, archbishop of Hamburg, who were disputing concerning the Church of Bremen, to come to Worms for a synod. There, entrusting their case to Fulco, bishop of Rheims, as his representative, he ordered it to be examined.

Who, having discharged their representative duties, might possess the freedom to debate and deliberate. Thus reads C. M has *viricatione*, which S changed to *juriscautione*; J has *vicariatione*; Baronius has *vicatione*, with “in place of” written in the margin. In the same sense, in the letter of Saint Radegund, one reads in Gregory of Tours, Book IX of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 42, *epistolae vicarietate* (“by the authority of the letter of representation”). The meaning is: “Those who undertake their representative duties,” or, as we would say today, “who are their agents with full power to settle the matter completely.” The following then appears:

So that, once a definitive sentence has been delivered, it may no longer be necessary at any future time to reopen the question concerning this matter. Thus C and I read; J has *infinitima*. In the manuscript, *perfecta* appears in place of *percepta*, and M has *nectere* in place of *vertere*, as Baronius also reads both.

## CHAPTER II

Rodemia, namely. Thus J reads; S has *Rodenna*; M, *Todenna*.

Also indicating that the emperor Wido had been crowned in the same year, in the tenth indiction. Namely, in the year 892, although immediately after the death of Charles the Fat—that is, from the year 888, according to Regino and Baronius—he had occupied the empire, having been duke of Spoleto. Throughout his life he had contended over it with Arnulf and Berengar, duke of Friuli. Baronius writes that both Wido and Arnulf died in 899; Sigebertus places Wido’s death in 901 and Arnulf’s in 902, and Wido’s son Lambert’s in 903. Baronius, however, is more reliable on all these matters and assigns the death of Emperor Lambert to the year 910.

## CHAPTER III

For if he dared, he would fear the judgment of the Apostolic See. Thus C and J read. The manuscript, however, has: “For if he did not listen, he would fear the judgment of the Apostolic See,” and so forth. In M a recent hand has added the negation *non*. There is therefore no doubt that the earlier reading is the true one.

He also writes to the same archbishop—that is, Pope Formosus writes to Fulco—on behalf of a certain priest Bertharius. Thus read the manuscript, C, and J; elsewhere *Vertarius*; C in the French version, here and below, *Bercharius*.

## CHAPTER IV
Those [things], then, [were done] by Zendebold, son of King Arnulf. J reads *Zeudeboldo*, as does C. Sigebert calls him *Zuendebaldus*. He was Arnulf’s son by a concubine, as the same Sigebert records in his *Chronicle* under the year 896, where he writes that his father made him king of Lotharingia and that he was killed by them in 903, or, according to Regino, in 900.

## CHAPTER V

Sending a letter to King Arnulf of the Trans-Rhenish realm concerning the cause of King Charles, whom he had anointed king while still a little child. This Arnulf was the son of Carloman, and Carloman was the son of Louis the German. For this Louis, son of the Emperor Louis the Pious—called the German and the Trans-Rhenish, and brother of Charles the Bald—had three sons: Carloman, Louis, and Charles the Fat, who became emperor. Arnulf succeeded this paternal uncle in the kingship rather than in the empire. Hence both Flodoard and other writers more often call him king than emperor. See Baronius, volume X, under the year 888.

The material that follows, up to the words “Also, to the same king, informing him of his fidelity,” Severinus Binius presents as part of the acts of the Council of Rheims, held in 892. At that council Charles the Simple, the posthumous son of Louis the Stammerer by Adelaide and the legitimate successor to the Frankish kingdom, was anointed by Fulk, archbishop of Rheims, while Odo, count of Paris and guardian of that same Charles, was rejected. Odo had tyrannically usurped the title of king of the Franks after the death of the Emperor Charles the Fat, who, according to Regino—whom Baronius follows under the year 888—had departed this life.

In his *Chronicle* under the year 890, Sigebert writes that Charles the Fat was rejected by the nobles and that the aforementioned Arnulf was raised in his place, while Charles died in the following year. He adds that, in that same year 890, the Franks, disregarding Charles, the barely ten-year-old child of Louis the Stammerer, appointed as their king Odo, son of Duke Robert.

At the same synod, the case of Baldwin, count of Flanders, was also discussed, as is clear from the following chapters 6 and 7. Sigebert assigns the events just mentioned to the year 894, in which year he writes:

> “While King Odo was staying in Aquitaine at the counsel of the Franks, the Franks recall the twelve-year-old boy Charles, son of Louis the Stammerer, to his paternal kingdom and have him blessed as king at Rheims by Archbishop Fulk.”

And under the year 899:

> “Odo, king of the Franks, dies, urging the leading men to receive Charles into the kingdom.”

Meyer gives a fuller account of this under the same year, 899.

### Aschericus himself

So CR and J; but M has *Addericus*, for which S has *clericus*, as it is read in Baronius, volume X, under the year 892, and in Papirius Masson.

### The sons of Godfrey

The manuscript of Papirius has *Goffridi*; J, *Gosfridi*.

### So that he may deign to receive a reward both from me and from the see of Rheims

Thus R, the manuscript, Baronius’s exemplar, and J, which reads *de sede*. The others omit *de*, so that the phrase is understood in the French sense of *merci*, that is, “to grant pardon and indulgence.” Elsewhere *memoriam* is read, as it is translated in French.

## CHAPTER VI

### To Archbishop Frother

So R and J; but the manuscript has *Flothero*. We prefer the former reading, because it seems to refer to Frotharius, archbishop of Bourges, mentioned above in chapter 1 and in Book III, chapter 21. In Democharis’s tables he is also called *Froterius*. He subscribed to the Council of Soissons held in 866 and to that of Troyes in 867, where he is called sometimes *Frotarius* and sometimes *Frotharius*, with the aspirate added.

### To Rostagnus, prelate of the people of Arles

This is undoubtedly the man who above, in Book III, chapter 21, is called Rothstanus.

### To Archbishop Pleonicus of the Transmarine realm

This is the man who is called Pleimundus, nineteenth in the catalogue of the archbishops of Canterbury.

### To deal with Baldwin’s seizure

This Baldwin, count of Flanders, had invaded the monastery of Saint Bertin under a grant from Charles the Simple. On this matter, Molanus writes from Folchard and John of Ypres in *The Feasts of the Saints of Belgium*, under 9 September and 17 June.

### A certain abbey situated in the parish of this Hetilo

He means Cisonium in the diocese of Tournai, mentioned above in chapter 1. It is said to have been situated in the parish of Hetilo, bishop of Noyon, because, as we noted in the commentary on Book I, chapter 5, the churches of Tournai and Noyon were united for six hundred years.

### Which he had brought back after obtaining it from the city of Rome

Saint Everard, the margrave, as stated above in chapter 1 of this book, obtained from the Roman see the body of Saint Calixtus, pope and martyr. It is possible, however, that his son Rudolf, who is being discussed here, finally brought it from there.

Nevertheless, Jacob Meyer in his *Annals of Flanders* and John Molanus in *The Feasts of the Saints of Belgium*, under 14 October, write that the relics of Saint Calixtus were brought to Cisonium by Everard, founder of the place, in 854. Molanus adds that they were at Rheims, where they are said to have been brought below, in chapter 8. Yet the inscription on the reliquary states that they were brought to Cisonium in 855.

Therefore Sigebert—or whoever added this statement to Sigebert—seems to be mistaken in assigning it to 884:

> “At this time a certain Rudolf transferred the body of Saint Calixtus, pope and martyr, from the city of Rome to Francia.”

### The aforementioned Otfrid

He is named this way below in chapter 11 in all the exemplars, in Democharis’s tables, and in the *Chronicle of Cambrai*, Book I, chapter 64. Above, however, in this chapter, the manuscript reads *Etfredus*; J, *Otfredus*.

### Seeking assistance for themselves from her in obtaining pardon

J omits *veniae*; perhaps *venire* should be read.

## CHAPTER VII

### He reproves him on the basis of the synod held at Rheims in the year 892 of the Lord’s Incarnation

This is the Council of Rheims at which Charles the Simple, son of Louis the Stammerer, was anointed king of the Franks. I have commented on him above, under chapter 4.

## CHAPTER VIII

### From the church of the title of Saint Agricola

This is now Saint Nicasius.

## CHAPTER IX

### Namely, Gibrianus, Helanus, and so forth

So the manuscript reads. In M, however, *Helanus* was added by another hand, since it had been omitted. C, both in Latin and French, and J read *Tesanus* instead. John Molanus mentions both in his additions to Usuard.

For the former, under 8 May, he writes:

> “At Rheims, the deposition of Saint Gibrianus, confessor, who rests in the church of Saint Remigius.”

For the latter, under 7 October:

> “In the district of Rheims, in a village called Buxiolus, the deposition of Saint Helanus, priest and confessor.”

Peter Galesinius also includes this same Saint Helanus on that day in his *Martyrology*, from the tables of the saints of the Church of Rheims. In both places he is called *Helanus* without any variation, as also in Molanus’s *The Feasts of the Saints of Belgium*, under 3 December, where he distinctly lists Helanus, Tresanus the German, and Veranus.

Concerning the age of these saints, Sigebert writes in his *Chronicle* under the year 509:

> “Gibrianus the Scot, having travelled through Gaul as a pilgrim with his brothers and sisters, glorified the city of Rheims by his life and death.”

### Francla

So CR; but the manuscript has *Franda*, and J, *Frauda*.

## CHAPTER X

For the account of the killing, or martyrdom, of Fulk, see Molanus in *The Feasts of the Saints of Belgium*, under 17 June, drawing on the chronicles of Saint Bertin. He was killed in 900, as stated there, and Sigebert, James of Guise, Meyer, Baronius in his *Annals*, and others agree. This is also demonstrated by the fact that, as was shown above at the end of Book III, Hincmar died in 882, while Fulk occupied the see for seventeen years, three months, and ten days, according to the epitaph given here.

Nicholas Chesneau is therefore mistaken when, in his French edition, he notes in the margin that Fulk died in 903. The same is proved by chapter 17 below. For when his successor Herivaeus, as stated in the author’s *Chronicle*, died in 922, on 2 July, and had held the see, as is said there, for twenty-two years less four days, he must have been ordained on 6 July 900.

### Investigating how he used to proceed from his lodging to an audience with the king, and so forth

All the exemplars read this way. The meaning is: how he used to set out from the place where he normally lodged, or from his lodging. Hence the following statement:

> “The others who survived those who had remained at the lodgings,” and so forth.

He uses the same word, *metatus*, below in chapter 15. That it signifies a lodging is clear from the fact that what he says there, “He led him to his lodging,” is expressed in his *Chronicle* as “He led him to his lodgings.”

He also uses the same word above in Book I, chapter 20, and Book II, chapter 3, where see the commentary. Therefore S is wrong to propose, against all the exemplars, that it should be corrected to “those in his entourage.”

Gregory of Tours frequently uses *metatus* in his *History of the Franks*: for example, in Book III, chapter 8, “having returned to his lodging”; chapter 15, “in his lodging”; Book V, chapter 15, “when the king had withdrawn to his lodging”; also in the same book, chapter 39; and Book VII, chapter 29, twice, “he arrived at our lodging.” The phrase that follows, “in my dwelling,” means “in my residence,” and so forth.

## CHAPTER XII

### And received it through the blessing of Saint Remigius

This was attributed to the merits of Saint Remigius: the man who had honored the translation of his body was not to lose what had been stolen from him.

## CHAPTER XIV

### Finally, he frequently held synodal assemblies with the co-bishops of his diocese

Two are mentioned by name. The first was held in 909, under Pope Sergius III, in the district of Soissons at Trosleium; it is mentioned below in chapter 16, where the manuscript reads *Trosleium*, as do all the exemplars in chapters 19 and 21. The place is found under both names: one form is complete, the other abbreviated, as with *Herivaeus*.

A summary of its acts, drawn from Baronius, is found in volume III, part II, of the Councils. The second was held in 921. Our author mentions it in his *Chronicle*, as does Severinus Binius after the synod held there under Seulfus; this is discussed below in chapter 19.

### After the war that Count Robert of Chartres waged against them

So all the exemplars read. The French translation correctly renders this as *vers Chartres*, that is, “toward Chartres.” Hence S changed *Carnotenus* to *Carnototenus*.

How Rollo, duke of the Normans, while besieging Chartres, was miraculously driven back from the city, around the year 908, through the shirt or undergarment of the Blessed Virgin Mary, is described at length in French by Sebastian Roulliard in his *History of the Church of Chartres*, chapter 7, no. 5.

### They received the faith of Christ

Thus C and J. But the manuscript, Baronius, Papirius, and the author himself in his *Chronicle* read *ceperunt*.

### Moreover, he also endeavored to consult the Roman pontiff concerning such a matter

“Upon whose replies,” and so forth. Pope John IX’s reply to Archbishop Herivaeus concerning what ought to be done regarding the conversion of the Normans is preserved in Baronius, volume X, under the year 905, and in volume III, part II, of the Councils.

## CHAPTER XV

### In the following year, and so forth

From this point onward, the year numbers that I have added are taken from the *Chronicle* of our Flodoard, which Pithoeus published among twelve contemporary authors.

### On account of Haganon, his counsellor

Thus J and C, both in Latin and French. M, however, has *Hagonem*, from which S made *Hugonem*. The reading we have retained is clearly correct from the author’s *Chronicle*, where he consistently reads it this way in many places.

Sigebert gives another reason for King Charles’s abandonment in his *Chronicle* under the year 920, in these words:

> “Robert, duke and brother of King Odo, desiring the kingdom of the Franks against Charles, disturbed Francia; at his instigation nearly all the leading men of Francia opposed Charles.”

## CHAPTER XVI

### Concerning the excommunication of Count Erlebald

J reads this consistently. Otherwise the reading varies even within the same exemplar. The manuscript has *Heriboldi* in the title, then M has *Herlebaldum* in the text, and later *Erbebaldus*; S has *Heribaldus*. The forms *Erebaldus*, *Ereboldus*, and *Erleboldus* are also found.

From the end of the chapter, however, it is clear that he was absolved from excommunication after his death.

## CHAPTER XVII

### Namely, on the third day after Robert had become king

He had become king on the last day of June 922. This Robert, brother of King Odo, was killed in the same year, according to Odorannus and Sigebert, with the assistance of the Lotharingians, near Soissons. Greater credence should be given, however, to our author, who was writing about events of his own time and states in his *Chronicle* that Robert was killed in the following year, 923.

## CHAPTER XIX

### To have ended his life
