Seulfus died in 925, after completing three years and five days in the episcopate. Thus the author states in his *Chronicle*. This agrees with what is said about him below, in chapter 35.

## CHAPTER XX

### King Rudolf, therefore

Meyer writes about this Rudolf under the year 890:

> “In that same year the Burgundians placed the diadem on Rudolf, son of their duke Richard, and hailed him as their king.”

This Rudolf, son of Richard, margrave and governor of Burgundy, was king of Burgundy. After King Robert, his father-in-law, was killed in battle in 923, the Franks, unwilling to return to Charles the Simple, chose Rudolf as their king. He ruled the kingdom of Francia for two years, according to Sigebert, while Charles was held in custody at Péronne.

From the following chapters, however, it is clear that Rudolf ruled in Francia until 936, when he died, as stated below in chapter 26. He died on 15 May and thus reigned for twelve years. This agrees with Robert Gaguin, Paul Aemilius, and many others.

Papirius writes of him in Book II of his *Annals*, under Charles the Simple:

> “Rudolf, son of Richard, had Emma, Robert’s daughter, as his wife; Heribert had married another of Robert’s daughters; the father-in-law, the sons-in-law, and Hugh the son possessed great influence, favor, and resources.”

## CHAPTER XXI

### Heribert expelled Charles from the custody in which he was holding him

Heribert had captured him by treachery in 923, after Robert’s death, and Charles was released from prison in 927. In the following year, however, he was again placed in custody, where he died in 929. This is taken from the author’s *Chronicle*.

Sigebert gives similar information but is mistaken about the date when he writes that, in 924, Count Heribert thrust Charles into custody at Péronne because of the killing of Duke Robert, whom Charles had killed. Under the year 926 he writes:

> “Charles, king of the Franks, an exile and martyr under Heribert’s custody, dies.”

He is likewise mistaken about the date when he writes that, in 928, Louis, Charles’s son, returned to Francia, although this did not happen until 936, after the death of Rudolf, king of Burgundy.

## CHAPTER XXIII

### And also Arnaldus

So J; another exemplar has *Arnoldus*. Likewise, in what follows, some read *Artoldus*, as C and J often do, while the manuscript more frequently reads *Artaldus*. Similarly, *Sigeboldus* and *Sigebaldus*, and below, in chapter 33, *Deroldus* and *Deraldus*.

## CHAPTER XXIV

### Concerning the ordination of Lord Artoldus, bishop

This took place in 931, and he died in 961, on the day before the Kalends of October, according to the author in his *Chronicle*. It is therefore established that he governed the Church for thirty-one years.

## CHAPTER XXV

### The synod of seven bishops at Saint Macra

M has *Magram*; S, *Machram*. In volume III of the Councils it is assigned to the year 935 under the name of the Council of Rheims, although it was a certain district of that diocese, otherwise called Fismes, as Nicholas Chesneau noted.

For the passion of Saint Macra, virgin, see below, chapter 51.

## CHAPTER XXVI

### To Louis, son of Charles, whom King Alstannus, his uncle, was raising

R has *Alstanus*; J, *Astranus*. In the catalogue of the kings of England in John Carion, he is called *Adelstanus*; Meyer calls him *Athelstanus*.

This Louis was the son of Charles the Simple and was called Transmarine because he had been raised across the sea by the king of England, since his mother was the daughter of the king of the English.

### Which his father, namely Charles the Simple, had handed over to Saint Remigius

That is, to the monastery of Saint Remigius, as is clear from the words that follow. The expression is understood in the same way below, in the next chapter, and elsewhere.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

### Hugh the prince, son of Robert

Below, in chapter 35 and elsewhere, this man is called Count Hugh. He was called Hugh the Great, count of Paris and duke of Aquitaine, son of Robert, count of Anjou and Paris, who had been elected king and was discussed above in chapter 17.

The same Hugh is called duke of the Franks. He rebelled against Louis, king of the Franks and son of Charles the Simple, and died in 956. By his wife Aurea, who was the daughter of Henry the Fowler and sister of the Emperor Otto I, though others call her Havidis, he fathered Hugh Capet, later king of Francia. After the extinction of the line of Charlemagne, Hugh Capet obtained the kingdom of the Franks.

The history is described in Aimoinus, *On the Deeds of the Franks*, Book V, chapters 44 and 45. The Robert in question was the brother of King Odo and was married to the sister of the very powerful Heribert, count of Aquitaine and Vermandois, who is frequently mentioned here. Hence Sigebert, in his *Chronicle* under the year 949, calls Hugh, son of Heribert, the nephew of Hugh the Great, as does our author in his *Chronicle* under 943.

### He also took from me the church of the village of Colmisiacum

In his *Chronicle*, under the year 940, he says:

> “The church that I governed at Culmisiacum.”

It is therefore clear that he had once been the rector or pastor of that place, which he frequently mentions in this *History*. The name is written in various ways, as we noted in Book I, chapter 12.

## CHAPTER XXX

### They occupy the fortress of Altimont

This is the complete spelling. R and J, however, usually read *Almontem*, both above and below.

### The other sons of Count Heribert are subsequently received by the king

Papirius Masson writes of this Count Heribert in Book II of his *Annals of the Franks*:

> “He left behind Heribert, an illegitimate son and bishop of Rheims; Hugh; Odo; Adelbert; and one daughter, the wife of Arnulf of Flanders.”

### He captured the fortress of Amblicum

Thus J; C, *Amblecum*; the manuscript, *Amblidum*; in French, *Ambli*.

## CHAPTER XXXI

### So that the same prelate, receiving the son himself and the son of his brother

Thus C, in both the French and Latin versions, and J. But another exemplar, the manuscript, and the author in his *Chronicle* read: “receiving the son of that man,” and so forth.

## CHAPTER XXXII

### The abbot of the monastery of Saint Benedict

All the exemplars read this way. S therefore wrongly wrote “Saint Remigius” in place of “Benedict.” As Nicholas Chesneau noted, the reference is to the abbot of Saint Benedict on the Loire, in the diocese of Orléans.

### Queen Gerberga had recently sent an embassy to her brother, King Otto

This Gerberga, sister of Otto I, emperor or king—for historians often call him king because he had not received the imperial blessing, just as his father, Henry the Fowler, had not—had first been the wife of Giselbert, duke of Lotharingia. After Giselbert was killed, King Louis of the Franks married her, as Sigebert writes in his *Chronicle* under the year 943.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

### He attacks the city of Rheims with Bishop Hugh, as though he were about to capture it

After the word *praesule*, the manuscript adds “and a certain Theobald,” which is absent from the other exemplars and from the *Chronicle*. The construction of the sentence does not seem to permit its inclusion.

### After Deraldus, prelate of Amiens, had died, a certain Tetbaldus

Thus C and R; but the manuscript has the corrupt form *Derordus*. J and C in the French version have *Deroldus*, as do all the exemplars below, twice in chapter 35. For *Tetbaldus*, M has *Theobalus*, from which S produced *Theobaldus*, as the manuscript reads in chapter 37.

In Democharis’s tables we find *Deraldus*, followed by Raimboldus and then Theobudus. The author reads *Deroldus* and *Tetbaldus* in his *Chronicle*.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

### With Bruno, abbot and brother of King Otto, also present

The author likewise reads this way in his *Chronicle*. C has *Brimo*, and the French version renders it *Brimon*, as it can also be read in M. But below, in chapter 35, *Brunone* is written very clearly, although there too the French version renders it *Brimon*.

The other reading is preferable, because the passage seems entirely to concern the man who shortly afterward became archbishop of Cologne, succeeding Wicfredus in 953, according to the author’s *Chronicle* and Sigebert. Everyone calls him Bruno. He was the brother of Otto I, emperor, and the son of Henry the Fowler.

### He also sent two bishops to escort him

Namely, Adalbero and Gossinus, as is stated in the following chapter in the booklet of Artoldus and as the author specifies in his *Chronicle*.

### From the diocese of Trier and that of Rheims

The meaning is that, at that synod of Mouzon, there were bishops from both dioceses. C did not understand this in the French version. For the author himself writes in his *Chronicle*:

> “In the year 948, the aforementioned synod was held in the church of Saint Peter, before the view of the fortress of Mouzon, by Lord Robert and the other bishops of the diocese of Trier, together with some from Rheims.”

### Chapter 19 of the Council of Carthage concerning the accuser

This seems to refer to chapters 9 and 10 of the Third Council of Carthage. This is supported by the fact that below, in chapter 35, “the nineteenth” is read, where the conjunction *and* could easily have been omitted.

## CHAPTER XXXV

### Concerning the synod convened at Engelenheim

It was held on 7 June 948 in the church dedicated in honor of the Blessed Remigius, as stated in the author’s *Chronicle*, where he also lists the names of those who attended, at no. 31. Regino, in Book II of his *Chronicles*, writes that thirty-four bishops attended. In volume III, part II, of the Councils, thirty-one signatories are recorded.

### Finally, after our lady the queen had left Laon for the absolution of the lord king

The meaning is clear from what the author said above in chapter 32. Hugh the prince, called the Great, was holding King Louis himself in custody, and Queen Gerberga had returned Laon to Hugh so that she might recover King Louis. His absolution, that is, his liberation, could not have been obtained in any other way, as the author states in his *Chronicle* under 948.

### After the reading of these letters, and so forth

Everything that follows to the end of the chapter, as well as the next two chapters, is identical, even word for word, in the *Chronicle* under the year just mentioned.

### After the chapters concerning such accusers had been read

He seems to mean chapters of the Council of Carthage, or the capitularies of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious. I do not find this particular matter in them, however.

### But to Bishop Artoldus, who had made himself present at every synod

Many synods were convened concerning this matter, as is clear partly from the preceding material, partly from the author’s *Chronicle*, and partly from volume III, part II, of the Councils. These were the synod of Verdun in 947; that of Mouzon in 948, on the Ides of January; that of Engelenheim in 948, on 7 June, discussed in this chapter and more famous than the others; and finally the Roman synod of 949, at which Pope Agapitus II confirmed the condemnation of Bishop Hugh made at Engelenheim.

### On the remaining days of the synod, certain necessary matters concerning incestuous marriages were also discussed, and so forth

This may be seen in the acts and ten canons of this council, edited by Henri Canisius and appended by Severinus Binius to the end of volume III, part II, of the Councils. The canon concerning incestuous marriages is nevertheless absent there.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

### They killed nearly four hundred men

Thus C, in both the French and Latin versions, and J. The manuscript, however, reads “forty,” as does the author in his *Chronicle* under the year 948, when these events took place.

### To Winefredus of the Morini

The manuscript reads this way here, but below has *Huicfredus*. C has *Winefrede* in the French version in both places, but *Wifredus* in the Latin version, as does J.

The author’s *Chronicle* likewise has two readings, *Vincfredus* and *Wicfredus*. In the manuscript of the Chronicle of Meaux he is called *Wycfridus*. The complete form seems to be *Winefredus*, from which *Vincfredus* and *Wicfredus* arose through contraction.

The latter name belonged at the same time to the archbishop of Cologne, who is also called Wicfredus below, in chapter 42. There M reads *Hincfridus*, which S changed to *Huicfridus*.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

### With Luitdulfus, chaplain of King Otto, taking the leading role

This is the true and complete reading in all the exemplars, but it varies below. C has *Lindulfus*; M, *Ludulfus*. In the *Chronicle* we find *Luidulfus* and *Laudulfus*.

The subject is Otto I, emperor of that name, also called Otto the Great because of his celebrated victories in war, as Lupoldus Bebenbergius states in *On the Zeal of the Ancient Princes of Germany*, chapter 2. C reads *Odonis* below. For the same person, the forms *Ottho*, *Otho*, *Odo*, *Ado*, and *Udo* are sometimes used interchangeably.

### By the name Adelonus

Thus C and J; but the manuscript has *Adelonius*. In the *Chronicle*, *Adelomus*; in French it is rendered *Adeloin*.

Pope Agapitus II approved the acts of the synod of Ingelenheim, mentioned above in chapter 35, and of the synod of Trier, discussed in this and the preceding chapter. He did so at a council held at Saint Peter’s in Rome, confirming the condemnation of Bishop Hugh and the excommunication of Hugh the prince until he should make satisfaction to King Louis, as the author testifies in his *Chronicle* under the year 949.

That *Chronicle* extends farther than this *History*. It reaches as far as the year 966. Artoldus died in 961, on the day before the Kalends of October, according to the same *Chronicle*, and in the following year Odalricus succeeded him.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

### Is said to have built it in honor of Mary or Saint Peter

S correctly notes in the margin that *vel* should be read for *et*. The same occurs in certain other places, especially in chapter summaries.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

### Concerning Saint Balderic, abbot

John Molanus writes of him in his additions to Usuard, under 16 October:

> “At Falcon Mountain, of the most blessed Baldricus, confessor, whose life is made illustrious by frequent miracles.”

Arnold Wion likewise writes of him in Book III of his *Lignum Vitae*, in his monastic *Martyrology*, under the same day, as does John Trithemius in *On Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, Book III, chapter 152.

## CHAPTER XLI

### Concerning the estate of Waslicia

Thus R, M, and J, and this seems to be the correct reading; S has *Vassicia*, while C has *Wasticia*. In the French version, both forms occur here, *Walstice ou Valliche*, but below it is always *Walstice*.

### Namely, from the see of the city of Verdun: Saints Vitonus and Agericus

Both were bishops of that see: Vitonus was the eighth, and Agericus the tenth, in Democharis’s tables. Concerning them he writes:

> “8. Saint Videnus, or Vitonus, was elected in 502 at the First Council of Orléans, in the time of Clovis. 10. Saint Agericus was elected in 554.”

For information about them, see Richard de Wassebourg, archdeacon of Verdun, Book II of *The Antiquities of Belgic Gaul*. He wrote this work in French, in which language their names are Saint-Vanne and Saint-Agry.

### And Saint Roduicus of Wassoio

C has *Rodincus de Vassoio*.

### In place of the estate of Gerlanimons, situated on the Moselle

Thus R, C, and J. But the manuscript has *Gelani*, as does the following chapter, both in the title and in the text. This is also found in C; M has *Gelani* there, while C and S have *Gellani*.

### When he came to that estate in order to take possession of it

Thus C and J, but the manuscript has *faciendi*. The French version renders it “for the purpose of taking possession,” which in French is *saisir* and *saisine*, that is, possession.

The proper Latin word would be *sancire*, “to confirm,” because possession confirms the thing acquired.

## CHAPTER XLIV

### Saints Bova and Doda

John Molanus discusses them in his additions to Usuard, under 24 April, in these words:

> “At Rheims, the city, of Saints Bova and Doda.”

From this Baronius evidently copied the entry into the Roman *Martyrology* under the same day. Peter Galesinius, Felix, and Arnold Wion likewise mention them in their *Martyrologies*. All of them must be corrected because they read *Bona* instead of *Bova*.

All our exemplars prove that the latter is the true reading, both above in chapter 38 and in this chapter. Likewise, above in chapter 20, we read *Bovo*, bishop of Châlons, which S incorrectly changed to *Bavo* and C to *Bono*.

Moreover, this same female saint is called *Boba* in Book II, chapter 10, in all the exemplars. The letter *b* is often changed into *v*, or the reverse, as in *Bibiana* and *Viviana*, *Jobita* and *Jovita*.

## CHAPTERS XLVI AND XLVII

### Concerning Lord Gunther and his wife Berta

This name is written variously in the exemplars, but this is the most frequent form; it also occurs with *o* as *Gontbertus*. The complete pronunciation is *Gondebertus*, as it is read above in Book I, chapter 4, at the end, or *Gundebertus*, as in Book II, chapter 10.

Here it is usually *Guntbertus* or *Gontbertus*, but the manuscript has *Gombertus* in the title of chapter 47. Under this name his life is included in the *Lives of the Saints* published in French by the Parisian scholars, under 29 April. There he is said to have been the brother of Nivardus, bishop of Rheims, as Flodoard also testifies in the chapter already mentioned, chapter 10.

He also seems to be the man whom Molanus mentions in his additions to Usuard, under 23 November:

> “In the territory of Rheims, of Saint Gobertus, confessor.”

It is an objection, however, that Saint Gontbertus died a martyr, as did Saint Berta. Concerning her, Sigebert writes in his *Chronicle* under the year 661:

> “Berta, martyr and abbess, shines in holiness in Gaul.”

Her *Life* is included in the *Lives of the Saints* published in French by the doctors of Paris, under 1 May.

## CHAPTER XLVIII

### Concerning the two churches of Saint Hilary at Rheims

This is the common and more frequent reading. M, however, has *Hillari* here and *Hilari* in the chapter index. In the same way Baronius calls the Roman pontiff who succeeded Saint Leo the Great *Hilarus*, although he is more frequently called *Hilarius*.

### Which was called Merolilanus

Saint Merolilanus the Scot now rests at Rheims in the church of Saint Symphorianus.

## CHAPTER XLIX

### His entrails slide onto the ground

That is, his intestines. The manuscript renders this in French as *entrailles*; C has *humi*. The other reading is more correct, so that it means “onto the ground,” rather than “from the ground.”

This punishment was prescribed by God for an adulteress in Numbers 5.

## CHAPTER L

### The composition owed to the treasury, which they call *fredum*, had been remitted by him to the guilty parties

I have restored *fredum* in place of *fretum*, although the latter is also found in the printed edition of Gregory of Tours, whose passage is cited here. That text too must be corrected in many places, as will be clear if one compares what Flodoard reports here with the corresponding passage of Gregory.

Certainly Pithoeus reads *fredum* in his *Glossary of the Capitularies*, under *Freda*, and James du Breul reads it in his note on Book V, chapter 17, of Aimoinus, citing the same passage of Gregory.

Likewise, the plural *freda* is consistently found in various charters preserved in the *Chronicle of Cambrai*, Book I, chapters 37, 62, 76, and 107, and in the foundation charter of the priory of Saint Martin in the Fields near Paris, issued in 1060 by Henry I, king of the Franks, where the phrase is *in fredis*. These records are preserved in the Martinian collection.

In the epitome of Charlemagne’s constitutions, however, *freta* is read for *freda*, in the chapter that is numbered 30 of Book III in the books of the Capitularies edited by Pithoeus. There it says:

> “Except the *freta* that is written in the Salic law.”

On this passage Vitus Amerpachius writes:

> “*Freta* is what those ages otherwise call *freda* and *fredum,” and so forth.

But since the exemplar from which these constitutions were printed was extremely defective, there is scarcely any doubt that this is a copyist’s error.

What *fredum* means is indicated here: it is a word of Teutonic origin signifying peace. The Germans call it *fred* and *frid*, and we Teutons call it *vrede*. *Fredas* is also read elsewhere, including in the privilege of Charles the Bald preserved in the *Tricassine Promptuary*, folio 84.

## CHAPTER LI

### Blessed Macra, virgin, under the prefect Rictiovar

This is read as one word in C and J here and in the manuscript in the following chapter. In the manuscript here, however, *Rictio Varo* is written as two separate words, a form Baronius prefers in his notes on the Roman *Martyrology* under 6 January. Usuard also commemorates this virgin on that day.

Rictiovar was an exceedingly cruel prefect or governor of Gaul under Diocletian and Maximian, around the year 300. Baronius lists many martyrs who suffered under him in volume II of his *Annals*, under the year 303, where he also recounts his pitiable death.

## CHAPTER LII

### Concerning Saints Rufinus and Valerius, martyrs

Baronius, Usuard, and others mention them in their *Martyrologies* under 14 June.

## CHAPTER LIII

### He suddenly fell forward, headlong

This is the true reading, found in C and J. Since it was not understood, it was altered in the other exemplars. One reads *cernatiis*. In M the reading was *conternatiis*, but a later hand corrected it to *consternatus*, as S wrote it.

*Cernuus* means “inclining toward the front” or “falling headfirst.” Hence Virgil’s line in *Aeneid* X:

> “And, leaning forward, he falls headlong upon the field.”

Servius says:

> “A horse is called *cernuus* when it falls upon its face, as though toward the part that we see.”

Hence also the following line in a hymn of the Church:

> “Therefore, before so great a sacrament,  
> We bow down in worship.”

## EXPLANATION OF OBSCURE OR BARBAROUS WORDS IN ALPHABETICAL ORDER

These words occur in the four books of Flodoard, whether they belong to Flodoard himself or to others whose testimonies or letters are inserted. An asterisk is placed before those that do not belong to the author.

### A

**Abinde**, in place of *inde*, that is, “from that time” or “from that place.” He uses it in both senses.

* **Acetabulum**, Book I, chapter 18, in the testament of Saint Remigius. It seems to be understood as in Numbers 7, where the Hebrew has *scutella*, “bowl” or “dish.” The *Nomenclator* of Hadrian Junius lists it among measures of liquids and says that it holds one and a half *cyathi*.

**Aequivocus**, “of the same name.” See our index of obscure words in the *Chronicle of Cambrai*.

**Alodis**, the same as *alodium*. See the index just mentioned and the glossary of Peter Pithoeus on the capitularies, under *Alode*.

* **Amphibalum**. See the commentary on Book I, chapter 18.

**Atrium**, “cemetery.” French *l’âtre*.

### B

* **Beneficiare**, “to grant as a benefice.”

**Blattea**, “purple.” See the commentary on Book I, chapter 15.

**Brandeum**, Book I, chapters 20 and 21: a silk cloth or linen in which the bodies or relics of saints are wrapped; or also a cloth brought from elsewhere that has touched their relics, as is done today. See the commentary on Book I, chapter 21.

**Breviculus**, Book III, chapter 22: a sheet or small document, derived from *breve* as a diminutive. Thus in the works of Saint Augustine, volume VII, there is *Breviculus Collationum cum Donatistis*, “A Brief Summary of the Conferences with the Donatists,” that is, as Augustine elsewhere calls it there and in Letter 158, a *breviarium* and *breviatio*, or abridgment.

Similarly, according to Alciatus and others, Book VII of the *Code*, title 44, is *On Sentences to Be Recited from a Breviculus*—for which the common reading is *periculo*. On this passage Christophorus Hegendorphinus writes in his exposition of the titles of the *Code*:

> “This title is read corruptly. For *breviculo* should be read in place of *periculo*, since the subject here is how sentences are to be recited from a written document. *Breviculus* is a diminutive word from *breve*, that is, from a small document, a written or dictated record.””

### C

* **Cabuta**, or **Cambuta**. See the commentary on Book I, chapter 18. To this I add that the pastoral staff of Saint Burchard, first bishop of Würzburg, was a staff of elder wood, as stated in his *Life*, Book II, chapter 1, volume V of Surius.

**Caraxatum**, Book I, chapter 9, “written.” Likewise *caraxare*, *caraxatura*, and *caraxatores*, or rather, with aspiration, *charaxatum*, and so forth. See the commentary there on chapter 18.

Cellerarius, Book I, chapter 12; or, as J and C have it, *cellarius*, the same as *cellerarius*, as S altered it; likewise, as is still read in Hincmar: the servant of the cellar, or steward, or keeper of provisions. See the index of obscure words to Thomas of Cantimpré.

Cernuatus, *cernuus* (“bowed,” “stooping”). See the scholia on Book IV, chapter [number not supplied].

Comes, the name of an office, Book II, chapter 18, and elsewhere. For these counts, together with the royal envoys, exercised judicial authority in each province, as is clear from the same chapter and from the capitularies of Charlemagne. See the scholia on that chapter.

[Col. 0400A] Conjectus, or *conjectum*, a kind of tax. See the scholia on Book III, chapter 19.

Consuerant, for *consueverant* (“they had been accustomed”), Book I, chapter 12.

*Consultus*, *consultus* (“consultation”), *consultatio* (“consultation”), *consilium* (“counsel”). See the scholia on Book III, chapter 4.

Cors, *cortis*, used for the royal court, French *cour*, Book III, chapter 13, twice in Hincmar’s letters; sometimes used for *curtis*, as in Book I, chapter 17, and Book II, chapter 6.

Curs, *curtis*, that is, an estate or villa. Charlemagne’s Capitularies, Book III, chapter 19: “Our estates remain deserted.” See the index of obscure words to the Chronicle of Cambrai.

D

Decania, *decanatus* (“deanery”), Book III, chapter 25, just as *canonia* is used for *canonicatus* (“canonry”).

Decubavit, for *decubuit* (“he lay down”), Book I, chapter 8.

Depactum, for *pactum* or *conventum* (“agreement,” “compact”).

*Diaconiae.* See the scholia on Book I, chapter 18.

Domnus, for *dominus* (“lord”). See the notes to the Chronicle of Cambrai, Book I, chapter 27.

[Col. 0400B] E

Emovere, for *movere* or *dimovere* (“to move,” “to remove”), Book IV, chapter 40; French *émouvoir*.

Episcopium, an episcopal see or bishopric. See the index of obscure words to the Chronicle of Cambrai.

Esox, *esocis*, a kind of fish, Book II, chapter 8, where see the scholia.

Eulogiae. See the scholia on Book II, chapter 11.

Exinde, for *inde* (“from there,” “thereafter”), that is, from that place or time. Fortunatus uses it in the Life of Saint Medard.

F

Fiscalini, so called from *fiscus* (“the royal treasury”), Book I, chapter 20: those who held estates belonging to the royal treasury. “Fiscalini servants” are found in Aimoinus, Book III, *On the Deeds of the Franks*, chapters 42 and 55; in Book III of the Capitularies, chapter 16, “royal fiscalini” are mentioned; and in the epitome of the Constitutions of Charlemagne, Ripuarian law 2: “A royal man, that is, a fiscalinus.” See Pithoeus’s Glossary.

[Col. 0400C] Flasco, Book I, chapter 15, a type of vessel, French *un flacon* (“a flask”). Blessed Gregory uses the word *flasconis* in Book II of the Dialogues, chapter 18.

Francisca, Book I, chapter 13, a double-edged axe, as Hincmar has it in the Life of Saint Remigius, and Flodoard himself also in the chapter just mentioned. Gregory of Tours likewise, in Book II of his History of the Franks, chapter 27, describing the same story, names both a double axe and an axe. Aimoinus, Book I, *On the Deeds of the Franks*, chapter 12: “And, extending his hand, he cast his *francisca* upon the ground, which is called a sword.”

*Fredum.* See the scholia on Book IV, chapter 50, and the notes to Book I, chapter 37 of the Chronicle of Cambrai.

Frigoritici, Book II, chapter 14, and Book IV, chapter 44: people suffering from fever, afflicted by a cold disease. Fortunatus uses the same word in Book I of the Life of Saint Radegund, chapter 10, which is found in Surius, volume IV, under 13 August; there one reads *frigoreticus*, and Surius noted in the margin: “*Frigoreticus*, for one suffering from fever.” Gregory of Tours, Book V of the History of the Franks, chapter 10: “those suffering from *frigoritic* pustules.” The same author, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 64: “The *frigoritici* and other sick people are healed.” See more in the index of obscure words in the Chronicle of Cambrai.

[Col. 0401A] G

Glaucoma, *glaucomae*, Book [number omitted], chapter 24. Plautus uses the word in *The Soldier*. More commonly it is called *glaucoma*, genitive *glaucomatis*, and also *glaucomatum*, genitive *glaucomati*; it means an affliction of the eye.

H

Hichinaculum, or *hiclinaculum*, Book I, chapter 18, in the testament of Saint Remigius.

Homo hujus aut illius, “the man of this or that person,” as in *homo Arnulfi*, “the vassal of Arnulf.”

Horno, that is, “this year,” Book I, chapter 20, and Book III, chapter 22, where see the scholion.

I

Imaginatum, carved and decorated with images and figures. See the scholia on Book I, chapter 18. The same word is mentioned in Book III, chapter 5.

*In ante*, Book II, chapter 17, that is, “thereafter,” which others more often say as *in antea*. See the index of obscure words in the Chronicle of Cambrai. Besides the passages noted there, Gregory of Tours uses it in Book VIII of the History of the Franks, chapter 28, and Pope Eutychianus in question 6, chapter *Episcopus*. Likewise Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, Letter 89: “From that time onward let him be excommunicated.”

Incardinari, to be instituted or appointed to a bishopric or another dignity, Book III, chapter 21. Pope Adrian II uses the word in Letter 11. John the Deacon likewise frequently uses the verb *incardinare* and *incardinari* in Book III of the Life of Pope Gregory, chapters 15 and following, in the sense of “to appoint”; Pope Gregory himself also uses it in a letter. See Onuphrius Panvinius’s booklet *On the Interpretation of Ecclesiastical Words*, under the entry *Cardinalis*.

Incardinatus, instituted or appointed, Book III, chapter 29. Ivo of Chartres, Letter 131; see there the observations of François Juret, who cites many passages from Pope Gregory concerning the same word.

Insigne, for *insigniter* (“conspicuously,” “notably”), Book I, chapter 10.

Intentio, for a lawsuit or dispute, Book II, chapter 10.

[Col. 0401C] Intranea, intestines, Book IV, chapter 49. See the scholia.

Isdem, for *idem* (“the same”), Book I, chapter 25, and Book III, chapters 13, 17, and 19; in the last passage manuscript C has *idem*.

L

*Lacerna.* See the scholia on Book I, chapter 18.

Legatarius, an envoy or legate, Book I, chapter 25.

Libitudo, *libitus*, *libido* (“desire,” “lust”), Book IV, chapter 7. See the scholia.

Licito, for *licite* (“lawfully”), Book IV, final chapter.

*Locarium.* See the scholia on Book III, chapter 13.

M

Majordomus, Book II, chapter 12, the prefect of the palace.

Mallus, Book II, chapter 18; Book III, chapter 26. See our notes to Book I, chapter 72 of the Chronicle of Cambrai, and the notes of John Busaeus to Hincmar’s Letter 4.

Mandare, to signify; *remandare*, to announce or report back—both according to French usage.

Maniaticus, insane, from the Greek word *mania* (μανία), meaning madness. Gerson and John Nider also use the word *maniacus* in the same sense in the *Formicarius*.

Mansionile, Book III, chapter 26. It seems to be the same as *mansio*, a dwelling or habitation, belonging to farm managers.

Mansus and *mansum*. See the index of obscure words to the Chronicle of Cambrai. Nicolas Chesneau translates *mansos* or *mansa* into French as *arpents* or *arpents de terre* (“acres” or “acres of land”).

Matricula and *matricularii*. See the aforementioned index. The word is read in Book I, chapter 18, in the testament of Saint Remigius, and frequently elsewhere. It also occurs in Hincmar’s Letter 7, chapter 35, among those edited by Busaeus.

Matutinorum solemnia, Book I, chapter 25. Thus people formerly spoke, understanding “of hymns”; now we say *matutina* (“Matins”), namely, “of prayers.” See the same index.

Metatus, *metatus*, a place where someone customarily pitches a tent or lodges. See the scholia on Book II, chapter 3, and on Book IV, chapter 10.

[Col. 0402A] Mirum, a miracle.

Missaticum, an embassy or commission from a *missus*, that is, an envoy; or a message. French *message*. It is found in Hincmar’s *Opusculum of the Fifty-Five Chapters*, after chapter 55.

Missaticus, the same as *missus*, an envoy or messenger, as is clear from Book III, chapter 28.

Missorium argenteum, “a silver serving dish,” in the testament of Saint Remigius and in Book II, chapter 5: “a gilded silver serving dish.” In both places it is translated into French as *vase d’argent* (“silver vessel”). Gregory of Tours, Book VI of the History of the Franks, chapter 2: “The king showed us a large serving dish, which he had made of gold and jewels, weighing fifty pounds.” In Book VII, chapter 4, a golden serving dish is mentioned.

Missus, a messenger, envoy, or commissioner. See the scholia on chapter 18, section 2, and the index of obscure words in the Chronicle of Cambrai.

Molendimus, for *molendinum* (“mill”), from *mola* (“millstone”), Book I, chapter 14. Likewise, in Appendix 2 to Gregory of Tours’s History, in the description of the dedication of the church of Marmoutier, one reads *molendinos nostros* (“our mills”). See the notes to Book I, chapter 52 of the Chronicle of Cambrai.

N

Nec estuosi, Book III, chapter 26: poor people lacking the necessities of life, *nécessiteux* (“the needy”). Hincmar uses the expression in Letter 7, final chapter.

Nomenclator, Book III, chapter 21. See Onuphrius above.

Nonna, a nun, Book III, chapter 27. Jerome, in his letter to Eustochium, *On the Preservation of Virginity*: “And because, having experienced the domination of husbands, they prefer the freedom of widowhood, chaste women are called *castae* and *nonnae*.” Erasmus conjectures in his note on this passage that the word may belong to the Egyptian language. Saint Benedict, in the Rule, chapter 63: “The younger monks call their elders *nonnos*, which signifies the reverence due to a father.” Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, Letter 19, and Book V of the Capitularies, chapters 2 and 3, use the same word. On this word see further the Reverend Father Heribert Rosweyde in his *Onomasticon of More Difficult Things and Words* for the Lives of the Fathers.

O

*Octimber*, for *October*. See the scholion on Book I, chapter 21. To this may be added Bede’s *On the Reckoning of Time*, where, reviewing the names of October among various peoples, he says: “*Theseri* among the Hebrews, *Paophi* among the Egyptians, *Hyperberetaeus* among the Macedonians, *Octimbrios* in Greek—which was undoubtedly formed from the Latin *Octimber*—and *October* in Latin.”

*Omnimodis*, entirely, in every way. See the index of obscure words to the Chronicle of Cambrai.

P

Pagus, a region, district, or territory; French *pays*, as in *pagus Laudunensis* (“the district of Laon”). Thus, according to Petrus Divaeus in *The Antiquities of Belgian Gaul*, chapter 14, Julius Caesar frequently uses the word. “They had many *pagi*,” he says, speaking of the Morini, “not indeed villages, as the word *pagi* is understood at that time, but regions; in this sense the word is familiar to Caesar.” Thus Divaeus.

Pallium, the insignia of an archbishopric, is a band woven of white wool, having above it a circle fastening the shoulders and two strips hanging down from either side, with four purple crosses—front and back, and on the right and left. See Onuphrius above and Pithoeus’s Glossary to the *Capitularies*.

Parisius, indeclinable, Book I, chapter 15; Book II, chapter 2; and elsewhere, used for *Parisii*, *Parisiorum*. Ivo also uses it indeclinably in Letter 16; see the observations of François Juret on that letter.

Parochia, or *parrochia*, as M generally writes it. It is frequently used by medieval writers and in the canons for a diocese. Sometimes, however, the terms are distinguished so that *dioecesis* denotes the whole province of an archbishopric, while *parochia* denotes only a bishopric. Hence Hincmar, in the *Opusculum of the Fifty-Five Capitularies*, chapter 16: “Saint Remigius caused the see of Laon to sit in the bench of the metropolitan church of Reims; he separated it from his own parish, but not from the province of the diocese.” The same Hincmar, in Letter 2 to Pope Nicholas, among those published by John Cordesius: “But since not only my diocese, but also my parish, is divided between two kingdoms, under two kings.” Likewise, in his letter to Pope Adrian: “In whose—that is, Lothair’s—part of the kingdom there lay not only part of the diocese, but also part of my parish.” And below: “In whose kingdom my parish and my province are situated.” The same author, finally, in his letter to the clergy and people of the church of Beauvais: “Likewise concerning the diocese of another archbishop, or the parish of a bishop,” and so forth.

Pedatura viti, that is, a support or prop for a vine. Hence *vitis pedata et statuminata* in Pliny, meaning a vine supported and strengthened by stakes and poles. See the scholion on Book I, chapter 1. It is derived from the verb *pedare*, which means to provide a vine or another small tree with a support.

*Praedonare*, for *condonare* (“to pardon”), French *pardonner*. It is found in the Capitularies, for example in Book IV, chapter 37, and elsewhere, and in Goffrid, abbot of Vendôme, Book V, Letter 19.

Pitatium and *pitatiolum*, or, as J generally has it with *c*, *pitaculum*, Book III, chapter 22. This was the title of a short work by Hincmar, bishop of Laon and nephew of Hincmar of Reims, prefaced by a poem beginning:

> This little *pitatiolus* clearly and aptly sets forth  
> the See that is freely to be called Apostolic.

Hincmar of Reims refutes this work at length in his extensive *Work of the Fifty-Five Capitularies*, also prefaced by a poem in these words:

> Concerning this title, young priest Hincmar,  
> it is fitting that I answer you with equal art, and so forth.  
> For earlier writers used *pitatiolum* as a neuter,  
> and this languid heading shows that the rest is lax, and so forth.

Otherwise, *pitacium* means a small sheet or brief letter. Adrian Junius, in his *Nomenclator*: “*Pyctatium*, or rather *pyctacium* according to Cassiodorus and Lampridius, is a small tablet; in Greek, πιττακίον, according to Moschopulus. In Belgian, *een cleine cedulle* (‘a small note’). In Celsus, *pitacium* means the same as a plaster. Isidore’s Glossary B: *Pictacium*, a short and modest letter; a little written note, a membrane.” Heribert Rosweyde discusses *pittacium* further in the work cited above.

Placitum, a public assembly, or an assembly of the kingdom’s nobles; a diet or parliament, French *plaids*. See the index of obscure words to the Chronicle of Cambrai, the notes of Busaeus to Hincmar’s Letters 3 and 4, and the notes of Jacques Sirmond to Letter 36 of Book III of Goffrid, abbot of Vendôme.

Praeceptum, a princely rescript or royal decree; a privilege or charter of immunity. See our notes to Book I, chapter 85 of the Chronicle of Cambrai.

Praestaria and *precaria* are the same, as is clear from Book IV, chapter 11, where Nicolas Chesneau translates it into French as *usufruit* (“usufruct”). For the meaning of *precaria*, see the aforementioned index. In addition to the passages noted there, Ivo mentions *precariae* in Letter 271.

[Col. 0403D] Praesentaliter, for *praesentialiter* (“presently,” “in person”).

Praevidere, for *providere* (“to provide for”), Book IV, chapter 1. Balderic also uses it several times in the Chronicle of Cambrai. See our index of obscure words.

Precatoria, Book II, chapter 5, the same as *precaria*.

Presbyter, a pastor or parish priest. See the scholion on Book I, chapter 8.

*Ptochium*, Book I, chapter 18. In Greek πτωχεῖον, a house for the poor, or a place for receiving beggars. Bishop Bassianus, in a letter to the emperors Valentinian and Marcian preserved in the Council of Chalcedon, session 11: “But from my youth I have lived with the poor, and I established a *ptochium*, and placed seventy beds in it; and I received all the sick and ulcerated as guests.” Likewise in the same council, canon 8: “Clergy who are placed over *ptochodochia*, and who are appointed in monasteries and basilicas of the martyrs, shall remain under the authority of the bishops,” and so forth. The second edition, or translation, in the volumes of the Councils has *in ptochiis* (“in poorhouses”). The third, that of Gentianus Hervetus, has “the clergy of the poorhouses (*ptochotrophia*).” In Gratian, question 18, section 2, chapter 10, *In ptochiis* is read in the corrected edition of Gregory XIII, as in the second edition: “Certain monks”; the corrupt standard copies had *in parochiis* (“in parishes”), and it is noted there that *ptochiis* is the word of the Greek canon. Rosweyde discusses the same word in the work cited above.

Q

Quaeque, for *quocunque* (“whatever,” “whichever”).

Quique or *quisque*, for *quicunque* (“whoever”), frequently in Book III.

Quibusque, for *quibuscunque* (“to whomsoever,” “whatever persons”).

Quisque, for *quisquis* (“whoever”). François Juret, in his observations on Ivo’s Letter 8: “Earlier writers said *quisque* for *quisquis*; because most people did not observe this, they often altered and corrupted the authors contrary to the testimony of the ancient manuscripts.” Thus he writes. He proves the point there with examples cited from Tertullian, Hilary, and others.

R

Refutare, to refuse, reject, or decline, French *refuser*, Book II, chapter 19. Ivo uses it in the same sense in Letters 131, 173, 178, and 186, and frequently elsewhere.

Regestum, Book II, chapter 2, where see the scholia.

Remandare, to announce or report back.

Repedare, to return. Lucillus: “To return and turn back, so as to avoid Rome.”

Revadiare, Book III, chapter 4, is derived from *vas, vadis* (“surety”), and is translated into French there as “to acknowledge oneself a debtor.” It is found in the same book, chapter 28. See the index of obscure words to the Chronicle of Cambrai.

Revestitus, Book III, chapter 18, “clothed in ecclesiastical vestments,” French *revêtu*. Sometimes *revestire* means to restore someone to possession after deprivation, as in the same book, chapter 26, and Book IV, chapter 1. Hence *vestitura* (“investiture”); Pithoeus discusses the word in his Glossary.

Rotula and *rotulus*, Book III, chapter 11, and elsewhere, a sheet, volume, or rolled-up writing. In the same book, chapter 22, Hincmar says *rotulam prolixissimam* (“a very lengthy roll”). He also uses the word in the *Opusculum of the Fifty-Five Capitularies*, chapter 43. Stephen, bishop of Paris, uses *rotulus* several times in the sense of a sheet in the letter prefixed to the condemnation of several articles at the end of Peter Lombard’s *Sentences*. *Rotula* is a diminutive of *rota* (“wheel”).

S

Satarium argenteum, a silver saltcellar, Book III, chapter 5, where the manuscript incorrectly reads *solarium*. In Book II, chapter 23, we read: “two salt vessels sent by King Saint Stephen.” There, perhaps, he means something else.

Sancire, to take possession, French *saisir*. See the scholion on Book IV, chapter 41. Ivo of Chartres uses the verbs *saisivit* and *resaisivit* in Letter 101.

Senior, lord, French *seigneur*. Hincmar uses it in Letter 1 among those edited by Busaeus, and medieval writers use it frequently. See the index of obscure words to the Chronicle of Cambrai and Peter Gregory, Book VI of the *Syntagma of Universal Law*, chapter 11.

Signa ecclesiae, bells. Hence in the *Pontifical*, Part II, the title is: “On the blessing of the church sign, or bell.” See Pithoeus’s Glossary under *Signa*.

Succensere eum, or *eos*, with the accusative: to become angry with him or them.

*Suetum*, customary or accustomed.

Sumptorium, Book III, chapter 5, a spoon, as it is translated into French; namely, the spoon used in the sacred chalice.

T

Tantitas, smallness or littleness, in the author’s prologue.

Thudestica lingua, Book IV, chapter 35, where the manuscript has *Teutonica*; J has *Theotisca*, that is, German.

Thuytsche. Among the letters of Hincmar edited by Cordesius there is a letter from Otfried, a monk, to Liutbert, archbishop of Mainz, together with a preface to an old book written in the Saxon language. There it is called *Teudisca*, and the adverb *Theotisce* is used. An example of the Theodisc language is also found in Book III of Nithard’s History.

Titulare, to entitle, inscribe, or distinguish with a title.

*Turriculum.* See the scholion on Book I, chapter 18.

U

Unguen, ointment, Book I, chapter 11, from Hincmar’s Life of Saint Remigius. Persius uses the word.

Utillimus, for *utilissimus* (“most useful”).

V

Vadatus, Book IV, chapter 19, from the common verb *vador, vadari*, that is, to become surety for another. See the index of obscure words to the Chronicle of Cambrai.

Vadius, Book III, chapter 28: “Let him cause this to be corrected for him through a *vadium*.” It seems to mean the same as *vas, vadis*, that is, a surety. According to Jacques Spiegelius in his *Legal Lexicon*, it was first called *vadis*, and later, through syncope, *vas*. *Vadimonium* is a pledge to appear in court. [Col. 0405B] Others write it with a double *w*, *wadius*, as in Book II of the Capitularies, chapter 38: “Let them take *wadia* from those who do not pay tithes.” In Book III, chapter 29, the title is: “Concerning a free man who has surrendered himself in place of a *wadius*.” In the epitome of the Constitutions of Charlemagne concerning Ripuarian law, chapter 3: “A free man who is unable to pay any fine and has no sureties may send himself as a pledge to the person to whom he is indebted, until he has paid the fine that he owed.” On this passage Vitus Amerpachius notes: “To give in pledge means to pledge or assign.” See Rubricus, Book II of the Lombard Laws. Pithoeus cites many passages in his Glossary under *Wadii*, and the verb *wadiare* is frequent in the laws of the Lombards.

Vasalli, or *vassalli*, dependants or clients. See the same Glossary under *Vassi*.

Vel is often used for *et* (“and”), especially in chapter summaries. The French translator likewise renders it in this way, for example in Book IV, chapters 19, 36, and 38.

Vicaricatio, substitutions or deputies. See the scholia on Book IV, chapter 1.

Vicedominus, Book I, chapter 17. See the scholia. The word is also used elsewhere.

Villa is often used for a district or city, according to French usage, as in Book I, chapter 14: “Sparnacum, his villa,” that is, “his city.” Elsewhere he calls the same place an *oppidum* (“town”).

Villaris, masculine, Book II, chapters 2 and 5, a villa or estate.

[Col. 0405]

# APPENDIX TO THE HISTORY OF THE CHURCH OF REIMS

## SYNODAL STATUTES OF THE CHURCH OF REIMS

These statutes, received from Marmoutier (in French, *Marmoustier*), founded by Saint Martin in the suburbs of the city of Tours, reached our hands only later; it seemed appropriate, therefore, to append them here. Although there are certain features in them that do not seem to bear the stamp of antiquity—for example, that they give parish priests the title of pastor, whereas in Sonnacius’s time and long afterward they were usually called merely presbyters or priests; and likewise that they place the feast of the Nativity of Blessed Mary among the feasts to be celebrated, which does not seem to have been so ancient in these regions, since Fulbert of Chartres, who lived in the year 1017, is said to have first celebrated it in Gaul, if we believe Demochare—nevertheless, it could easily have happened that the name “pastor” was substituted for “presbyter” by someone of a later period, and that the feast was added by someone else. Saint Hildefonsus, however, who lived at the same time as Sonnacius, writes in his book *On the Virginity and Childbirth of Blessed Mary* that her nativity was celebrated and venerated by the authority of the whole Church. Similar provisions are written by Jesse, bishop of Amiens, in his letter to the priests of his diocese, and by the constitution of Riculfus, bishop of Soissons, which John Cordesius published together with Hincmar’s works.

The Reverend Father Jacques Sirmond added what follows to his edition; we also wished not to omit it from ours, but have arranged it in chronological order.

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0405C]

Without faith, as the Apostle testifies (Hebrews 11), it is impossible to please God; therefore we command everyone to hold and follow exactly the doctrine of faith according to the word of God and the tradition of the holy Roman Church. And whoever are pastors must learn and know the things that pertain to instructing the people and the flock, and must rouse their people to the practice of virtue.

## CHAPTER II

Let them administer the sacraments piously to the faithful, and always provide whatever pertains to explaining the benefit of the sacrament and to instruction.

## CHAPTER III

Let them accept no payment, but trust in God, who gives food to the young ravens that call upon him (Psalm 146).

## CHAPTER IV

The person who is to baptize must be sober and must perform the act properly; he must pronounce the words attentively and duly inquire about the parents.

## CHAPTER V

The sacrament of Confirmation contains the gift of the strengthening Holy Spirit and conveys more abundant grace; therefore it must not be neglected.

## CHAPTER VI

The forgiveness of sins and expiation rest chiefly upon, and depend upon, the Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ.

## CHAPTER VII

Let the pastor care for his sheep and not neglect it; let him enjoin it to attend the sacrifice of the Mass on solemn and Sunday days; let him know its face (Proverbs 27). If it is absent twice in a year, let it be forbidden to enter that church and let it be deprived of pastoral burial and consolation.

## CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 0407A]

During Lent no one except the pastor may hear the confessions of penitents. For it is his responsibility to recognize the sheep for which he pledges his own soul to the Lord.

## CHAPTER IX

The priest who is to celebrate the most holy Eucharist must prepare and examine himself, and must do so at least twice a month.

## CHAPTER X

Let it be carried to the sick in a proper vessel, with a light preceding and leading the way; and let all who wish to travel receive it as viaticum.

## CHAPTER XI

And why is it refused to those condemned to death, when it is especially beneficial to them for the hope and reassurance of a certain death and of their present struggle?

## CHAPTER XII

Those who wish to be promoted to orders must possess a benefice sufficient for their support, subject to the examination of trustworthy and sworn men.

## CHAPTER XIII

Let tonsure be given to no one except a suitable person who may afterward reasonably advance to sacred orders. For what need is there to send the children’s bread to dogs (Matthew 25), and spiritual things to lovers of the world?

## CHAPTER XIV

In marriage there exists an image of the most holy union born between Christ and the Church (Ephesians 5); therefore it is a bond established by God, which greatly contributes to the prosperity of the household, to peace between the parties, and to the raising of children.

## CHAPTER XV

Let extreme unction be brought to the person who is suffering and requests it; and let the pastor visit him frequently in his own home and attend to him piously, both encouraging him toward future glory and duly preparing him.

## CHAPTER XVI

Concerning clerics. Let them shine like stars and perpetual lights in the firmament of the Church (Daniel 1). Let them not be drunkards, triflers, or involved in secular affairs.

## CHAPTER XVII

Nor let them converse with women or keep them in their homes; let them live in community and inhabit houses open to the poor.

## CHAPTER XVIII

We command that the suffrages for the dead be observed in every respect, and that the solemn rites of Mass not be diverted in any other manner contrary to the intention of the founders.

## CHAPTER XIX

Let bishops be faithful and diligent dispensers of the word of God. Their charity is also recognized in this: that they feed the flock by example and by word.

## CHAPTER XX

[Col. 0408B]

The following feasts are to be honored without any legal or secular work and celebrated with due veneration: the Nativity of the Lord, the Circumcision, the Epiphany, the Annunciation of Blessed Mary, the Resurrection of the Lord together with the following day, the Ascension of the Lord, Pentecost, the Nativity of Blessed John the Baptist, the feasts of the apostles Peter and Paul, the Assumption of Blessed Mary, her Nativity, the feast of Andrew the apostle, and all Sundays.

## CHAPTER XXI

Let churches be adequately endowed for the support of the pastor and clergy, so that they may more securely watch over the flock and be anxious and solicitous for its salvation.

## CONCERNING THE MINISTERS OF THE CHURCH OF REIMS

Bishop Ebo, having found them in disordered condition, dictated the following at their request, under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0407]

[Col. 0407C] It is fitting that the provost have responsibility for both internal and external affairs. His external responsibility lies in preserving and governing, according to God, the goods and household, with the utmost attention, piety, and benevolence. It also consists in every form of diligence required for their maintenance: carefully arranging all profitable kinds of labor in the fields, vineyards, woods, and gardens, and the various kinds of purchases; and, in addition, attending to the necessary quality and quantity of the buildings.

It is clear that his internal concern must be the public provision for the brothers, honorably arranged in food and drink and in every bodily support that divine piety supplies, whether through the effort of his labor, through the alms of the faithful, or through the gift of his own public administration. Another necessary provision is also plainly required of him for the sick and the elderly, according to the differing needs of each person.

From this follows the care that embraces every bodily and spiritual form of the brothers’ adornment: bodily care first in the cloister, then in the refectory, dormitory, cellar, kitchen, and all other necessary dwelling places, as well as in all the vessels. Spiritually, such a minister of true religion must possess zeal for holy conduct, day and night, according to the canonical hours as they are distributed.

He must correct morals, detecting by gravity the movement of levity; he must entirely drive away idle talk with appropriate severity in private places and at suitable times; and he must punish, by the judgment of all the brothers in chapter, all negligences publicly discovered, in these ways: either by imprisonment, separation from the table, or various forms of beating. His most prudent vigilance must also watch over the deans subordinate to him, so that not one person, from the greatest to the least, may be absent from the place of his office for even a single day without his knowledge and permission.

The office of the archdeacon is to arrange the ecclesiastical grades with the greatest foresight, taking account of age and merit; at stated times to assign, by definite names, each person’s office throughout the entire region, carefully to test his merit, and, by investigating, to minister the grace of the Holy Spirit to each one; to train and form faithful ministers for all the divine offices of the holy Church of God; and, for all feasts and weekdays and for the offices of the whole year, to correct not only the learning contained in the chants and readings but also to hand on spiritual understanding to the entire clergy in chapter.

He must establish with witnesses the freedom of free persons, require freedom for slaves of others who wish to enter the orders, and also have authority to make free members of the church’s own household and to require freedom from outsiders. [Col. 0409A] For neglected reading or neglect of the office belonging to his grade, he must excommunicate anyone from the deacon down to the lowest rank; he must also restrain young men from such excesses by beatings; and he must provide for and deliver a discourse to the people on feast days. Thus, with the most devoted attention to true religion, he must lead everything worthily and in order all the way to the consecration of a priest.

He must also take charge, on the solemn feasts of the Lord, of the prisoners held in the public prison of the city—that is, on the Nativity of the Lord, the Epiphany, the beginning of Lent, mid-Lent, Palm Sunday, Holy Saturday, and holy Easter day, and likewise on the Ascension of the Lord and Pentecost—receiving them with the greatest diligence and preparing for them, from divine and human benefactions, the refreshment of blessing through bodily and spiritual services.

The ministry of the chorepiscopi is to correct and direct the entire priestly conduct of the region entrusted to them: that is, by opening and awakening everyone’s understanding in the celebration of the divine sacraments and in baptism; to preach to the people of the region; to require confessions; to impose penance cautiously and with discretion; to practice hospitality; to visit the sick, bringing services of kindness, blessing, and holy [Col. 0410A] unction; to exercise the peoples so that they may become worthy of holy communion through constant admonition; to consign the dead reverently to burial, with commendations of the soul, prayers, and worthy services; and to intercede with reasonable assiduity for the living and the dead, the children of the whole Church.

Moreover, in everything whatsoever, within the church and outside the church, in the cloister and in all the dwellings, from the greatest to the least, whoever he sees neglecting anything, he must always correct according to the ecclesiastical manner of correction; and, by practicing every true religion himself first, he must teach everyone to practice it. He must in no way exceed this procedure, except at the command of the bishop, in the matters that follow concerning every right of consecration.

[Col. 0410B] It is proper for the bishop of the city himself to make arrangements concerning consecration, Confirmation, reconciliation, and the proclamation of a public fast, or anything else belonging to public jurisdiction that is appropriate to the time and owed to God. The chief purpose of this office is that, by the most careful foresight, he should diligently ensure how he may govern all offices with the greatest zeal and direct them toward the harbor of perfection. In these matters the chorepiscopus must in no way exceed his authority unless ordered to do so.

[Note: We copied the preceding work of Ebo from the library of Saint Remigius at Reims, together with the letter of John VIII and the decree of the election of Laon, which follow below. The next Notice concerning the estate of Novilliacum, whose author appears to be Hincmar himself, was kindly communicated to us by Nicolas Faber from the library, as he said, of the most distinguished Claudius Puteanus, senator of Paris.]

# THE DEEDS FOLLOW

## How Lord Hincmar obtained the estate of Novilliacum from Lord Charles the Emperor, son of the Emperor Louis

[Col. 0409]

[Col. 0409C] King Pippin died on 24 September (765) in the monastery of Saint Denis. His sons Carlomannus and Charles, according to their father’s arrangement and the counsel of the kingdom’s leading men, divided their paternal kingdom between themselves, and were raised to the kingship on 9 October: Carlomannus at Soissons and Charles at Noyon, as we have it written in the *Annals of the Kings*.

In the fourth year of his reign Carlomannus fell ill with the illness from which he died at Salmuntiacum. Before his death, by a royal charter of his authority, which we possess, and during the time of Archbishop Tilpin, he granted the estate of Novilliacum, with everything belonging to it, for the remedy of his soul and as the place of his burial, to the church of Saint Mary of Reims and the basilica of Saint Remigius, in which he was also buried. After his death, his brother Charles, by a charter of his authority that we possess, confirmed the same grant.

After Archbishop Tilpin died, in the twenty-third year after Carloman had given the estate of Novilliacum to the church of Reims, Lord King Charles held the bishopric of Reims under his own authority and granted the estate of Novilliacum [Col. 0410C] as a benefice to Anscher the Saxon. Anscher paid the ninths and tithes from that estate to the Reims Church until his death. After Lord Charles and Anscher himself had died, the Reims Church continued to hold its investiture in the estate, as stated above, for thirty-seven years, since Carloman had transferred the aforesaid estate with all its appurtenances and in its entirety to the Reims Church.

After the death of Lord Charles and of Anscher himself, Emperor Lord Louis granted the estate of Novilliacum as a benefice to Donatus. Donatus, through the intervention of Bigo, fraudulently obtained by an imperial charter from Lord Emperor Louis certain estates belonging to that villa as his property, as though they were part of the royal fisc. When Lothair, the son of Lord Emperor Louis, came to Chalon and attacked it, Donatus defected from the emperor at the estate above the Marne called Pomarius, lied to him, and fled to Lothair. When Emperor Louis came in hostility to the estate called Caleiacus, Lothair came to him with his men under constraint, and he and his followers swore the oath that the emperor demanded of them. Among them, Donatus, whose infidelity was proved, swore the oath demanded by the emperor. The emperor took from him the county of Meaux and the estate of Novilliacum with its appurtenances, and granted them as a benefice to Atho, who had been Emperor Charles’s doorkeeper.

During the lifetime of Emperor Louis, Donatus recovered neither the county nor any legal security for his property. After Lord Emperor Louis died, the kingdom was divided among the brothers, peace was made between them, and Atho died; then Charles the Bald granted Novilliacum as a benefice to Donatus. In due course Donatus commended his son Gozelin to King Charles, and Charles granted him the estate of Novilliacum with its appurtenances as a benefice.

Then, when King Charles was proceeding to besiege the Normans who were settled on the island called Oscelsus, Donatus’s wife Landrada and their sons, together with others, defected. It was judged that their honors and properties should be taken from them by the Franks and reduced to the fisc. Consequently, Landrada and her sons did not thereafter obtain the authority of King Charles. For these reasons, in the twentieth year of his reign, Charles granted the royal estate to the monastery of Orbais by a charter of his authority, which we possess.

In the thirty-second year of his reign, the glorious Lord King Charles came to the basilica of Saint Remigius. There I showed him the burial place of King Carloman, the charters of Carloman himself and of his grandfather Charles concerning Novilliacum, and the authorities of the sacred canons, which condemn by the judgment of the Holy Spirit those who retain the alms of the dead and delay handing them over to churches. Such people are judged to be rejected from the Church as faithless, regarded as murderers of the needy, and considered unbelievers in God’s judgment. By a charter of his authority, which we possess, he therefore restored to the Reims Church the estate itself with everything belonging to it. At that time Bernaus held it as a benefice after his brother Rothan.

Later it came to his attention that certain men from the estate of Novilliacum were fraudulently retaining as their property goods and serfs obtained both from his father and from him—namely, Landrada, the former wife of Donatus, Cuntharinus, Hugo and Waltrudis, her son Elampodus, Rotbertus, and Boso. He sent his agents to investigate this matter. When an inquiry had been held and the truth discovered, as it had been reported to him, and when the aforesaid persons failed to appear for judgment and were therefore outlawed, he ordered the charters of Carloman and Charles, as well as his own charter, to be read before his faithful men at his general assembly at Douzy, in the palatine court.

Accordingly, his faithful men—both counts and royal vassals, whose names we have in writing, as well as all the others who were present—leaving aside the same charters, judged that whoever had obtained any of the goods or serfs of the estate of Novilliacum by anyone’s charter or in any other way after Carloman’s gift, by which he transferred the estate of Novilliacum with all its appurtenances or in its entirety, just as it then belonged to the fisc, to the Reims Church, and after the confirmation of his brother Charles had acquired it as property, should restore those goods and serfs to that house of God unless he could produce evidence of an exchange proving that they had been exchanged justly and reasonably. For he had obtained them not from the royal fisc but, through the gift, from ecclesiastical goods and serfs. This is set out more fully in the charter of restitution issued by Lord Charles, which we possess.

But when Lord Charles went to Rome and his brother Lord Louis came to Attigny, certain men of our group obtained from Lady Queen Richildis and from Lord Louis, son of Lord King Charles, that the estate of Novilliacum with its appurtenances should be handed over to the sons of Donatus and Landrada. They paid no attention to what is written in the capitularies of the emperors: such men are to be judged faithless with respect to royal property, and under ecclesiastical law they are judged guilty of sacrilege regarding ecclesiastical goods.

When Lord Charles, the emperor, returned and came to Reims, he took the news of this action very seriously and sent his agents. They restored the said estate to the Reims Church and to our advocate, as we have set out more fully in writing.

Here there followed a letter with the title: “Pope John VIII’s Order Concerning the Ordination of a Bishop for the Vacant Church of Laon.” Since we have inserted it in our scholia on chapter twenty-two of book three, we omit it here.

## Decree of the Laon Clergy Concerning Hedenulf, the Elected Bishop

[Col. 0411]

[Col. 0411D] To the most reverend and holy Lord Hincmar, archbishop, and to the other holy Fathers and bishops of our diocese: the clergy of Laon, together with the people of the entire parish and the bishops associated with it, send eternal salvation and peace in the Lord Jesus Christ.

We recall that the canonical rules and apostolic institutions have established that whenever any city lacks the ministry of pontifical dignity and is without its own shepherd, its clergy must approach the metropolitan pontiff with a decree of election confirmed by the hands of each petitioner, and must humbly petition him concerning the appointment of a shepherd in place of the one who has died. Thus the city, deprived of pastoral care, may recover its own bishop, and the man who is to be ordained may approach with greater favor. For the one whom all must obey should certainly also be chosen by all, lest the city either despise or hate a bishop whom it did not desire, and become less religious than it should because it was not permitted to have the man it wanted. Those who are to ordain him will then be able to lay their hands upon the one in whom they see the votes of all most strongly united, freely and without delay.

Therefore, approaching your paternity with the decree of our election, confirmed by the hands of each of us, we implore, beseech, and petition you that Hedenulf, a son of our Church, advanced in our Church through the merits of his service even to the burden of the priesthood, approved as suitable in life, conduct, and holy behavior, and whom with your permission, with the favor of the most Christian Emperor Charles, we have chosen with equal consent, harmonious devotion, and unanimous will, may be consecrated through your hands and those of the other holy bishops of your diocese, and may be appointed our teacher and bishop, as well as the bishop of our church. We confidently believe, with the grace of Christ cooperating, that we are choosing as our shepherd one who corresponds to the apostolic model by which Blessed Paul demonstrates that a bishop should be adorned, and who does not violate the sacred canons. We pray that your holy paternity may now and always prosper in Christ.

Done on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, in the basilica of Saint Mary, Mother of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 877, in the thirty-seventh year of the reign of Lord Charles the emperor and the first year of his empire, in the ninth indiction.

## By an Unknown but Ancient Writer

A canon of the Same Reims Church, who had abridged Flodoard

## Supplement to Flodoard’s History

[Col. 0413]

[Col. 0413B] Thus far we have arranged our account of the archbishops of Reims according to Flodoard’s tradition, describing how one succeeded another. Now, however, with God’s help, we shall append to the work already begun an account of those who arose after Flodoard’s death, according to what we have heard from our elders or found in ancient charters.

The aforesaid Artold, whose death is not mentioned in Flodoard’s book, transferred to Saint Remigius the abbey of Saint Timothy, which until that time had belonged to the bishops of Reims, because he had himself been taken from that monastery. After governing the diocese of Reims for thirty years amid great adversity and, at times, tranquility, he entered the way of all flesh with a good end.

After his death, Lord Odalric, a noble and honorable man, assumed the episcopal burden. We possess few records of his works. It is nevertheless clear that he gave the estate of Vindenissa to the Reims Church. In memory of this benefaction, he is commemorated every year at the Reims assembly. On that same day, for the remedy of his soul, individual loaves are distributed to twenty-four poor people, together with an equal number of measures of wine and one denarius each.

The aforesaid estate lies in the territory of the count of Registestum, and is now held by a count named Guiter under a rent of thirty solidi. In the time of his predecessors, moreover, many goods were granted to the Reims Church in exchange for this same estate; we shall explain this more fully below.

The aforesaid Bishop Odalric worked faithfully for the benefit of the Church entrusted to him, especially for the restoration of the valley of Rodigion, which Hugo, son of Count Roger, had given to the Reims Church, but which certain wrongdoers from his lineage had seized and wished to claim for themselves by hereditary right. The venerable archbishop Odalric, as a noble and powerful man, resisted their attempt manfully and restored the aforesaid valley free to the jurisdiction of the Reims Church. To make this known more clearly to later generations, we shall set down on this page the charter of the valley’s donation and a written memorial of what took place.

> “It is known to nearly all the leading men of the whole of France that Hugo, born of noble lineage, in the first flower of youth, when he knew that the day of his departure from this age had come upon him, although he could have found many heirs eager for his inheritance, made God and his saints heirs of his patrimony with all the effort of his mind. At the beginning of his disposition, therefore, invoking the protection of the blessed Mother of God, the ever-virgin Mary, our Lady and Mistress, he gave to the table of the brothers who devoutly serve God and his immaculate Mother in the Reims Church a certain jurisdiction of the valley of Rodigion, commonly named from the stream running through its middle, so that the memory of this man of good character might be kept in that Church.
>
> “After his departure, a great dispute consequently arose between that Church and certain relatives of the aforesaid illustrious man. Since Lord Odalric, the lord and venerable bishop, vigorously opposed them, their controversy was reduced to nothing and could achieve no result. Therefore it should rightly be considered not undeserved if an ear is lent to the petitions of any member of that lineage.
>
> “Let it therefore be known to all present and future canons, monks, laymen, and nobles of the holy Reims Church that Emma, the niece of that venerable bishop, came before the aforesaid brothers and asked that they grant her the same jurisdiction under a rent of ten silver solidi, payable on the Assumption of Saint Mary, for her two sons Arnulf and Odalric. Whichever of them, through affection and love, should obey her more amicably during her lifetime was to succeed to the inheritance, while the following were retained under the direct control of the aforesaid brothers: the small estate called Sevivald’s court, with its wood and half its meadow belonging to it.
>
> “This was provided, however, that the pigs dwelling in that small estate, and those brought there with the pigs of the Reims canons—for they are nevertheless members of their household—might feed upon the produce of the wood; the people dwelling outside the jurisdiction also being excepted; but as to the rest she might freely act, subject to preserving the jurisdiction, as over her own property. Since her wish could not reasonably be opposed in any respect, she obtained what she requested and committed the transaction to writing as a memorial.
>
> “Done at Reims in the fourteenth year of King Lothair, in the sixth year of the episcopate of Lord Odalric the archbishop. Saint Odalric the archbishop, with whose permission and consent this document was made, confirmed it with his own hand and caused it to be strengthened by the hands of noble men.”

After the aforesaid Odalric had been gathered to his fathers seven years after assuming the government, Lord Adelbero, brother of Count Henry and from the land of Lotharingia, was raised to the episcopal throne through the favor and foresight of King Lothair. This noble man, distinguished by honorable conduct and instructed in ecclesiastical disciplines, restored the religion of the Reims Church, which had grown excessively lukewarm, to a good condition, and devoted earnest labor and expenditure to the interests of those serving God there.

He also reformed the monastery of Mouzon, which had fallen from its former dignity, into the monastic order, and confirmed the substance of that reform, so that it would not be altered in succeeding times, by the following privilege of his authority:

> “Adalbero, by the gracious mercy of God archbishop of the holy Reims Church. Let it be known, etc. For the remainder, see under Adalbero. EDITOR OF THE PATROLOGY.”

[Col. 0415C] In the time of this same Adalbero, the following agreement was made concerning the estate of Vindenissa between Count Manasses and the Reims canons.

> “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Let it be known to all the faithful, present and future, that Manasses the knight, with the favor also of Lord Adalbero the archbishop, effectively obtained from the canons of the Reims Church the entire jurisdiction called Vindenissa for himself and his wife Oidela, except for the churches reserved by right of lordship for the use of the canons, subject to an exchange of property.
>
> “In return, Manasses gave to the canons’ portion, in a suitable manner, everything he possessed in the estate of Tencauda: namely, nine manses and a mill; in Verniacum, eight and a half manses; and in the estate of Colummis, two holdings in the county of Reims. He also gave another estate called Loeium, containing seven and a half manses and one quarter, except for one demesne mansus and one quarter of the church, a meadow, a mill, and a wood with seventy-one male and female serfs, in the county of Châlons on the river Bair.
>
> “Also, in the estate called Eccleis, he gave two parts of the church and whatever rights were held there—namely, five manses and one meadow, with lands and male and female serfs—in the county of Porcien. The precarial arrangement was established between both parties on this condition: that the same canons should retain Tencauda and Verniacum in their own hands as compensation and for possession, while he and his aforesaid wife should retain and possess all the rest, together with the jurisdiction of Vindenissa, with unrestricted authority, only during their lifetimes.
>
> “When they have departed from human affairs, the entire estate, with all its contents, namely the properties granted by precaria, which remain perpetually attached by inviolable right to the canons’ share, shall return into their hands by legal obligation for them to possess. If anyone in the future attempts in any way to oppose this precaria—which we do not believe will happen—let his foolish rashness be utterly empty and void, and let this same precaria, legally established by the authority of our predecessors, remain stable and firm, on the express condition that Manasses securely confirm to the canons by peaceful right all the properties returned in exchange. Otherwise, let him return equivalent properties, or let the Reims Church justly recover what is hers.
>
> “Done at Reims, at the see, on the eighth day before the Ides of November, in the twentieth year of the reign of Lord Lothair, king of the Franks, and in the fourth year of the episcopate of Lord Adalbero. Lord Adalbero the archbishop subscribed and confirmed it.”

Another agreement concerning the estate of Virtus was also established in the time of the aforesaid Adalbero between Count Heribert and the Reims canons. To prevent the memory of this matter from being erased by the passage of time, it was confirmed by the following written document:

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Leudo, provost of the Reims Church, and the entire congregation of the canons of that place, do not wish the knowledge of all present and future to be unaware that Count Heribert, coming before our humility, asked us to grant him, from our jurisdiction, the estate called Virtus, which he had claimed for himself by seizure.
>
