> “This was on the condition that, as compensation for possession, we should retain from it for the present two free, inhabited manses, and that he should pay us annually, as compensation, one pound of denarii of Reims coin on the feast of Saint Remigius, the Kalends of October, during the days of his life only, excluding his wife, his children, and all his heirs.
>
> “Favoring his petition, and with the advice and consent of all, we granted him the aforesaid estate according to the arrangement prescribed and determined by him. If he should be negligent concerning the rent and refuse to make amends, let him lose the usufruct.
>
> “To enable him to possess the aforesaid properties more securely during his lifetime, and to enable us after his departure to recover the aforementioned estate in its entirety for our use, it has been decreed not only by us but also by him that we should draw up a charter concerning this matter. We further add that if, after the end of his life, anyone should attempt to inflict any disturbance or injustice upon us, let that person be condemned and bound irrevocably under the excommunication of a curse and anathema. Let it be done, let it be done, let it be done.
>
> “The sign of Lord Adalbero the archbishop, confirming and consenting.”

After the aforementioned Adalbero had governed the Reims diocese courageously for nineteen years [Col. 0416D] and the good reputation of his honorable conduct had spread everywhere, he was finally worn out by old age and closed his last day with a good end. His body was buried in the greater church beneath the altar consecrated in honor of the holy cross. His epitaph, written in gold letters on a bronze tablet, still reads:

> Nature, the mother, had bestowed what she deemed supreme  
> To increase your merit, Bishop Adalbero, when she  
> Took you, outstanding above all mortals, from the world.  
> On the fifth day, when the waters pour forth beneath the weight of things.

Nor should I omit the fact that every year the day of his death is reverently commemorated, and a plentiful alms of bread and wine is distributed to the poor. This alms is called the Mandate of Adalbero. It should also be known how the expense of this alms is prepared: from the house called the Hospital of the Poor, four sextarii of grain; from the treasury, four of wheat; from the demesne granary, one modius of grain; and sufficient wine.

There was nothing more in the Igny codex from which these excerpts were taken.

[Col. 0417]

# Flodoard’s Annals

(Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*)

## Notice to the Reader Concerning the Following Book

[Col. 0417B] Just as in the ninth century the Reims Church produced Hincmar, archbishop, so in the tenth it produced Flodoard [Note: [Col. 0417D] He should be written Flodoardus, not Frodoardus, both from the epitaph and from certain manuscripts of the *History of Reims* that abbreviate the name as Floardus, as well as from the excellent manuscript of the *Annals* at the year 963, from Richer, and from the old calendar of Saint Mary of Reims; he himself writes the name of his mother’s uncle as Flavardus in book II, chapter 3. In any case, Frodoardus is plainly the same name, and both forms are corruptions of Chlodouvaldus.] the priest and Richer the monk, distinguished writers of history.

The former was born in 893 or 894 [Note: [Col. 0417D] From the *Annals*, year 962.] at Épernay [Note: [Col. 0417D] Gallic epitaph.], an estate of the Reims diocese. He was educated in letters at the Reims school restored by Fulk, was enrolled in the clergy of the Reims Church by Archbishop Herivaeus, and was endowed with benefices [Note: [Col. 0417D] *History of Reims* IV, 13.]. Around the twenty-fifth year of his age he began to turn his attention to public affairs [Note: [Col. 0417D] I infer this from the fact that, if not in writing the *Annals*, at least in recording events, he seems to have begun work around the year 919.], as may be inferred from the beginning of the *Annals*, which he continued from the year 919 to 966. Certainly from that time onward he was highly esteemed by the Reims archbishops Herivaeus, Seulf, and Artold, and was employed in conducting their affairs.

In 924 he accompanied Seulf and attended the meeting held in the territory of Autun between King Rudolph and Hugh, count of Provence, and William, prince of Aquitaine [Note: *Annals*, year 924.]. In the following year, after Seulf died, Heribert, count of Vermandois, imposed his young son Hugh upon the see as successor, and deprived of the benefices of ecclesiastical possessions all who did not almost entirely support his efforts [Note: *Annals*, year 925.]. Among these was Flodoard, who was treated unjustly. He thereafter followed the opposing party and attached himself to Archbishop Artold, whom King Rudolph had substituted in Seulf’s place.

In the following years he celebrated in heroic verse the triumphs of Jesus Christ, of the saints, and of the martyrs of Italy [Note: He gave one manuscript of the work to Robert, archbishop of Trier; another he may perhaps have brought to the church of Saint Julian of Tours. It is said to exist at Clermont, in the *Acts of the Saints*, May VII, p. 69.], adding accounts of the deeds of the Roman pontiffs down to his own time. He thereby gained a reputation even among outsiders, so that Bishop Rather of Verona sent him for judgment a book he had written about his exile [Note: Folcuin, *Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*, chapter 20.].

In 936, or shortly thereafter [Note: Leo occupied the papal see from January 936 through July 939.], it is uncertain whether on his own affairs or those of the Reims Church, he went to Rome. There Pope Leo VII received him kindly, granted his request, and promoted him to the priesthood [Note: See below.]. Returning to his homeland, he completed his heroic work [Note: In Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, series III, part II, p. 596.].

In October 940 he intended to visit the tomb of Saint Martin as an act of devotion, but he was secretly accused before Count Heribert of planning to act against him or his son because he refused to join Hugh’s party [Note: *History of Reims* IV, 28. Compare the *Annals*, year 940.]. After the goods he held from the Reims bishopric and his church at Cormicy had been taken from him, he was handed over to custody. He did not recover his freedom until five months later, on 25 March 941 [Col. 0418C]. Then, at the synod of Soissons, he was entrusted by Prince Hugh to Archbishop Hugh, and recovered another church, namely that of Saint Mary at Colrido, together with land unjustly taken from him [Note: *History of Reims* IV, 28.].

Later, after Artold had also been restored to his see, Flodoard remained faithful to him and assisted him in conducting ecclesiastical affairs both at home and at assemblies of princes and synods. He seemed all the more suitable for this because he was in charge of the Church archive [Note: *History of Reims* II, 19.].

In 948 he attended the synod of Ingelheim, where he became known to several distinguished men. After the synod, by royal decree, he stayed for four weeks with Artold at the residence of Robert, archbishop of Trier. The previous year, Artold had sent him [Note: *History of Reims* I, 20: “Lord Artold the bishop had formerly entrusted these properties to Duke Conrad; he had delegated them to a certain Ragenbald, one of his men. Ragenbald greatly afflicted the tenants of those properties. Because of their affliction they often cried out to Saint Remigius, coming to Reims and seeking the protection of their patron. For this reason, the previous year, when we were sent to King Otto at Aachen, we spoke with the king and the aforesaid duke. But we were unable to obtain a promise that Ragenbald would desist from plundering those properties. It happened this year [the Colvenerus manuscript reads ‘this year’], that when one Saturday he had gathered the same tenants to perform some work and ordered the priest not to ring the evening bells until nearly nightfall but to persist in completing the work, he was struck by an unseen striker. When he asked who had struck him, and everyone denied having seen it, he was driven mad by the Furies, lost his reason, suffered severely, and died. When Duke Conrad learned this, he was exceedingly frightened, came to Saint Remigius, and restored the properties to him. The bishop Artold, as previously stated, assigned them to Abbot Hincmar and the other monks for the support of their livelihood.”] after he had spoken with King Otto and Duke Conrad at Aachen about the properties of the Reims Church in the Vosges, which had been seized by a certain Ragenbald.

Amid these affairs, he undertook to write the history of the Reims Church. Gathering materials from every source, especially charters preserved in the archive and books kept in the Church library, he carried the work through four books, from the origin of the Reims people to the end of the year 948. At the request of Robert, archbishop of Trier, he revised it and dedicated it to him with this letter:

> “To the venerable Lord,” etc.  
> (This letter is prefixed above to the *History of the Reims Church*.)

In the first book he recounts the history of the Church down to the death and translation of Saint Remigius; in the second, the successors of Saint Remigius down to Hincmar; in the third, the deeds and writings of Archbishop Hincmar; and in the fourth, Fulk, Herivaeus, Seulf, and Artold down to the completion of the synod of Ingelheim.

The work, published to the great benefit of the history of Gaul—not only ecclesiastical but also civil and literary history—is especially valuable because, since the sources used by the author have been lost, one finds there many important details nowhere else. Yet he deserves particular praise for his history of Hincmar and Fulk [Note: In his letters to Emperor Arnulf on behalf of Charles the Simple, Fulk also reports the following, IV, chapter 5: “He adds that it was known among nearly all peoples that the Frankish nation was accustomed to have kings by succession, producing in support the testimony of Blessed Pope Gregory. He also adds from German books an account of a certain king named Hermenricus, who had condemned his entire lineage to death through the wicked counsels of one of his advisers. He begs that this king not heed criminal counsels but take pity on this people and assist the declining royal line, striving that in his days the dignity of his succession may be strengthened and that those who were kings, or wished to be kings, from another lineage might not prevail against those to whom royal honor was owed by descent.”], to whose deeds and writings he devoted particular attention in his account. We read most of the remainder repeated in his *Annals*.

From that time onward he devoted unbroken attention and care to them [Note: Especially down to the year 954.]. Amid affairs and during the great upheaval of events throughout Gaul, he carefully recorded, as an eyewitness, the kingdom and the leading men of Gaul and Germany, distinguished either by learning or by power [Note: For example, Rudolph of Trier; Adaldag, archbishop of Hamburg; and Anno, abbot of Magdeburg, later bishop of Worms. Concerning him the *History of Reims* I, 4, reports: “Finally, King Otto, with the permission of Archbishop Artold, had the bones of Blessed Timothy transferred to Saxony and established a monastery of monks in his honor. Many marvels are said to have been displayed during this translation. For, as Anno—then abbot, now bishop—reported to me, and from him those sacred relics were transferred, besides many other cures, twelve persons among the lame and blind were healed. Saint Apollinaris also, after his bones had been transferred to the monastery of Orbais, is seen there to flourish through notable signs of grace.”]. He did so with the fidelity proper to a pious and candid man, free from violent partisan zeal, as is also demonstrated by his pure, simple, serious style, adorned without affectation.

He completed the *Annals* in the monastery to which he had gone after resigning his benefice, becoming a monk [Note: Letter of Adaldag, in Colvenerus’s *History of Reims*.] and soon afterward, apparently, an abbot [Note: He seems to have been an abbot, writing in 962 about having resigned the prelacy.]. While he was devoted to such occupations and studies, in 952 or 953 [Note: See the second edition of *Gallia Christiana*, under the bishops of Noyon.] the clergy and people of Noyon and Tournai elected him as their bishop. Since royal favor did not follow, however, another man was imposed upon the see for money, despite Flodoard’s opposition [Note: From the letters of Adaldag.]. On this matter he was visited by letters sent to him by Adaldag, archbishop of Hamburg.

Thus Flodoard spent his life as a priest and prelate of the Reims Church under Artold. After Artold died and Hugh, who survived him, was excommunicated, Flodoard himself, in 962, together with the other canons of the Church, and with the support of King Lothair, his mother the queen, and Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, elected Odelric, son of a certain Count Hugh, as archbishop [Note: *Annals*, year 962.]. The following year, feeling himself weighed down by old age [Note: Ibid., year 963.], at the age of seventy he resigned the ministry of the prelacy before the same prelate and accepted his nephew Flodoard as his successor.

During the four years he survived, broken by age and worn down by illness, he added only a few lines to his *Annals*. Finally, in 966, “a man venerable for the life he led, worthy of reverence for the honor of his holiness, angelic in the splendor of his chastity, heavenly in the radiance of his wisdom, abundantly filled with the marks of every virtue, an excellent writer, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, leaving the exile of his earthly pilgrimage, attained, as we believe, the rights of a citizen.” [Col. 0420C]

His epitaph, at the end of the manuscript of his poems, perhaps composed by him himself, reads:

> Here lies Flodoard, an unworthy priest in honor,  
> Awaiting the heavenly Judge’s return.  
> Trusting that pardon will be granted him by mercy,  
> Though burdened with countless offenses.  
> Whoever reads this inscription, mindful of your future lot,  
> Thus seek the Lord because he lies beneath the earth.  
> Christ, kindly spare your servant Flodoard,  
> And grant your servant pardon at the judgment. Amen.

Another epitaph of his, written in the Gallic language [Note: Found by Colvenerus in a manuscript of the *History of Reims*:

> If you wish to know the bishops of Reims,  
> Read the tale of wise Flodoard.  
> He died in the time of Bishop Odalric,  
> And was born of Épernay lineage.  
> He lived as a chaste cleric, a good monk, and a worthy abbot.  
> And at Rome he was made white by Agapitus.  
> Through his history you will learn many new things,  
> And from it drink all antiquity.]

draws from the *Annals* at the year 962 and from the appendix at the year 966. It also calls Flodoard a monk and abbot and says that he was “made white” by Pope Agapitus—that is, clothed in a white tunic—or consecrated as a priest. Since it is certain that this occurred before the year 940, Leo VII must be understood in place of Agapitus.

Among his writings, the *Annals* claim the foremost place for themselves among the *Monumenta Germaniae*. For purposes of illustration, we have thought it appropriate to place beneath them passages from the *History of Reims* in which the same events are expressed in different words. For this purpose we have used Colvenerus’s edition, collated by the learned Waitz with manuscript no. 186 of the Montpellier library, a thirteenth-century parchment manuscript; for the Paris manuscript no. 5209 ends at chapter 4 of book III.

The *Annals* were first published by Pierre Pithou among the *Scriptores* XII, Paris, 1588, pp. 147 ff. (reprinted at Frankfurt in 1594, pp. 109 ff.), from three manuscripts. He calls one of them the Dijon manuscript and the other the older one. One or the other of these was present in the manuscript from which the *Fulda Annals* were published, formerly preserved in the Vatican in the library of Queen Christina under no. 994, but now, according to the learned Papencordt, excised.

Chesne used Pithou’s edition in the *Scriptores of the Franks* II, pp. 590 ff., together with the Thuaneus manuscript. Without consulting Pithou’s edition, Bouquet corrected Chesne’s edition in volume VIII, pp. 176 ff., from the same manuscript, which had by then been placed in the Paris Royal Library under no. 5354, and from the Paris manuscript of Saint-Victor.

Our edition is based on these resources [Note: The now-burned Cotton manuscript Otho B. III, containing *Frodoard’s Chronicle of Saint Alban*, from the year of Christ 966, and Ragenald of Angers to 1277 (Smith, *Catalogue of the Cotton Library*, p. 69), seems to have contained a later work derived from Flodoard.].

1) Manuscript of the former library of the college of Troyes, now preserved in the library of the University of Montpellier under no. 151; a parchment volume in small folio, from the eleventh century. That it is the same manuscript as Pithoeus’s Divionensis is demonstrated by its readings, appendix, and the visions of Flothild prefixed to the work. In 1837 the distinguished scholar Georg Waitz collated it most diligently for our use with the printed editions. I judged that it should be assigned first place among our aids. For it contains the text as Flodoard had given it up to his death, without the appendix; and therefore it appears to have been derived from an authentic copy, a conclusion further confirmed in general by its readings and continuous text, since all the other manuscripts gape here and there with the same lacunae and present an appendix of the years 966, 976, 977, and 978. The book consists of seven quires, marked VI, VII, VIII, IX, X, XI, and XII, together with an eighth unmarked quire. It has already been bound into a larger codex, whose pages are numbered from page 27 onward. On page 27 it first presents the visions of Flothild, edited by Pithoeus on page 278; on page 31, without a rubric, it presents our Annals. Each year is marked by a Greek letter indicating the number by which it is distant from the year 893, the beginning of the reign of Charles the Simple—for example, at the end of the year 925, ΛΓ; 926, ΛΔ; and so forth.

2) The royal Paris manuscript no. 5354, a parchment volume in folio from the eleventh century, entitled “Here begins the chronicle of Flodoard the priest concerning the deeds of the Normans.” [Note: According to an old catalogue, the following works are contained in this manuscript: *The Passion of Saint Emanus and his companions; The Life and Passing of Saint Martial, bishop and confessor; The Chronicle of Frodoard the priest concerning the deeds of the Normans; The Passion of the holy bishops Savinianus and Potentianus and their companions, Altinus, Eodaldus, Victorinus, and Erotianus; The Life and Conduct of King Charles the Great; The Life of the Emperor Louis; The Life of Saint Mary of Egypt; Helmo’s Exposition of the Apocalypse.*—Flodoard occupies folios 21–41.]

The manuscript was copied for our use with exceptional diligence by the highly learned Otto Jahn, Ph.D., of Kiel. You would judge it to be the same as Chesne’s Thuaneus, except that the name of Thuaneus is absent from it. It prefixed to the Annals a notice concerning the death of Charles the Bald, copied from a certain book of the abbey of Saint-Fare at Meaux. This, however, was the reason why several learned men concluded that Flodoard had begun writing from that point and that the years 878–918 of his work were missing. How contrary this is to the truth is clear both from the manuscripts themselves and from Richer, who copied Flodoard beginning with the year 919. [Note: The *Chronicle of Angers*, in Labbe I, p. 285, incorrectly gives the year 917.]

We insert that notice here:

> In the year 877 and the tenth indiction, on the second day before the Nones of October [Pithoeus: the twelfth indiction, on the Nones], the most excellent Emperor Charles, of holy remembrance and distinguished memory, bringing his earthly course to an end, happily, as we believe, departed to eternal joys. He was indeed the son of the most serene Emperor Louis and the grandson of the glorious Caesar Charles of the same name. His most noble kinswoman Bertrada, abbess, together with the entire community entrusted to her, constantly remembering him in most devout supplications, had this memorial, set down in a concise written form, copied out so that it might be read annually on his anniversary and that his memory might always be preserved.

From this manuscript derives:

2a) A manuscript of the library of Albi, on paper and in folio, from the seventeenth century. It is entitled *The Annals of Fredoard the Priest* and occupies 58 pages. At Waitz’s request, the city librarian transmitted notes of readings possessing some significance. It presents the annals for the years 919–966, together with an appendix for the year 966 such as we read in manuscript 2.

3) In third place must be cited Pithoeus’s edition, together with

3a) the readings of a certain manuscript, marked with the siglum M in the margin of Pithoeus’s edition, and

3b) the manuscript of Saint-Victor in Paris, whose readings, cited by Bouquet, assign it this place.

We have also used authors who excerpted Flodoard in the same century and in the immediately following centuries: Richer and Hugh of Flavigny [Note: We designate his readings as “Hugh V”; Hugh of Floriacum as “Hugh II.”]. They agree in some places with our manuscript 1. We have also drawn here and there on their readings or additions, as well as on those of Baldric and Hugh of Floriacum.

## ANNALS

In the year of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ

### 919

Remarkable hail fell at Rheims, exceeding a hen’s egg in size. As for the breadth to which it spread, it covered half a palm. Yet in certain other places it was seen to have fallen even larger. In this year there was scarcely any wine in the district of Rheims. [Note: *remensi* in manuscripts 2 and 3.]

The Normans ravaged, crushed, and destroyed all Brittany situated in Cornouaille, in Lesser Brittany—that is, along the coast—carrying away, selling, and expelling all the Britons. [Note: Manuscript 1 usually writes *Nortmanni*, but also *Nordmanni*; manuscripts 2 and 3 use both; Richer usually has *Nortmanni*. Manuscript 2 frequently has *Britanniam*.]

The Hungarians ravaged Italy and part of Gaul, namely the kingdom of Lothair. [Note: Manuscript 3 has *Hungarii*; manuscript 3 has *partem*; manuscript 3 has *Lodharii*. Compare Mabillon, *Annals of the Benedictines*, book XLII, no. 30.]

In the year of the incarnation of the Lord

### 920

Almost all the counts of Gaul abandoned their king Charles at the city of Soissons because he refused to dismiss his counsellor Haganon, whom he had raised from among men of modest rank and made powerful. [Note: *Suessionicam* is frequent in manuscript 1; manuscript 3 has *Suessionem*. Manuscript 2 has *relinquerunt*.]

But Heriveus, archbishop of Rheims, received the king when everyone else had deserted him and led him to his lodging in a settlement called Carcarisia. [Note: Manuscripts 2 and 3 have *villa*. Manuscript 2 has *Carcasiria*; Hugh of Flavigny has *Carisia*.] On the following day they came to Crusniacum, a settlement of the church of Rheims, [Note: Manuscript 3 has *Crusin acum*.] and remained there until they came to Rheims. Thus he escorted him for nearly seven months, until he restored his princes to him and restored him to his kingdom. [Manuscript c reads *contutatus* for “accompanied.”]

[Note: *History of Rheims* IV, 15: “Since nearly all the leading men of the Franks had defected from their king Charles at the city of Soissons because of Haganon, his counsellor, whom he had chosen from among men of ordinary rank and honored above all the nobles, they had completely abandoned him. This faithful, pious, and steadfast bishop, always present in dangers, fearlessly received the king from that place, led him to his lodging, and from there brought him with him to the city of Rheims. For nearly seven months he followed and accompanied him, until he restored his counts to him and restored him to his kingdom.”]

[Note: *History of Rheims* IV, 16: “This prelate excommunicated Erlebald, count of the Castrician district, because of the land of the bishopric of Rheims which he had seized and on which he had built a fortification over the Meuse, from which he repeatedly inflicted harm upon the ecclesiastical household. In addition, he had secretly stormed the castle of Altimont. But when he did not cease from the evils he had begun, the archbishop went with his men to capture the fortification that he had built and called Macerias. After besieging it for nearly four weeks, when Erlebald finally abandoned it, he captured it and, having placed guards there, returned to Rheims. Erlebald then went to the king, who at that time was staying in the district of Worms against Henry, the ruler beyond the Rhine; there he was killed by the king’s enemies who came upon him. Nevertheless, afterward, at a synod which the same lord archbishop held at Trosly with his diocesan clergy, he absolved Erlebald from the bond of excommunication at the king’s intervention and earnest request.”]

Afterward Archbishop Heriveus went to the Meuse to recover a certain castle situated in the territory of his bishopric, which they call Macerias, held against him by Erlebald, count of the Castrician district. [Notes: Manuscripts 2 and 3 have *Macherias*, as also below. “Maisières.” The Castrician district contains Mézières and Donchery.] Erlebald was then also excommunicated because he continually inflicted evils upon the household of the bishopric, and because he had secretly stormed the castle of Altmont, belonging to the church of Rheims. [Note: “Omont.”]

After the archbishop had besieged the aforesaid castle, that is, Macerias, with his faithful men for nearly four weeks, Erlebald finally abandoning it, he recovered it and, having stationed guards there, returned to Rheims. Erlebald went to the king, who at that time was staying in the district of Worms, seated opposite Henry, the ruler beyond the Rhine. There he was killed by the king’s enemies who had come upon him. [Notes: Manuscript 3 has *Henricum*. Manuscripts 2 and 3 have *Transrhenensem*. Manuscript 3 has *sibi regis*.]

In this year and the following, a dispute was carried on between Bishop Hilduin and Abbot Richard concerning the bishopric of Tongeren. For the king had given that bishopric to Richard because Hilduin had defected from him, although he had previously granted it to Hilduin. Archbishop Herimann, however, ordained Hilduin bishop there, with the clergy electing him and the people supporting him, as did Gislebert, whom many of the Lotharingian nobles had chosen as their ruler after abandoning King Charles. But when the Lotharingians and Gislebert himself returned to him, Charles supported Richard the abbot, not Hilduin the bishop, in that bishopric. [Notes: manuscript 2 has *episcopum* for *episcopium*; manuscript 2 corrects *delegerent* to *delegerant*.]

At Rheims, in the monastery of Saint Peter near the basilica gate, a candle which the citizens who had gone to Rome to visit the thresholds of the apostles had placed there was lit three times, also by heavenly fire. [Notes: Manuscript 1 lacks *accensus est*; manuscripts 2 and 3 have *igni*.]

A certain girl named Osanna had also come to that monastery from the district of Vonzinse. [Notes: Manuscript 1 corrects *pago* from *paco*. Manuscript 2 has *Voxinse*. “Near Vouzy in Champagne.”] She ate no meat and had been unable to eat bread for two years. Many visions were shown to her. During those very days she lay motionless for a full week and, to everyone’s astonishment [manuscripts 2 and 3: *omni admiratione*, “to the astonishment of all”], sweated blood, so that her entire forehead and face down to the neck were covered with blood; yet life, or at least some warmth, remained in her, as she breathed even then with extreme faintness. She also declared that she had seen many things. Of some she spoke, but of most of what she had seen [omitted in manuscripts 2 and 3] she professed that she did not dare to speak. At that time honey was found in ears of grain around the city of Rheims, and flowers appeared on certain trees after their fruits had already ripened or been gathered. [Note: Manuscripts 2 and 3 have *inventum est*.]

### 921

Rodulfus, bishop of the Mount of Laon, died; Adelelmus, the treasurer of that place, succeeded him and was ordained bishop at Rheims by Lord Heriveus. [Note: Manuscript 2 has *thesaurarius*.]

Many Englishmen traveling to Rome were crushed beneath stones by the Saracens amid the Alpine passes. [Note: Manuscript 3 has *obruti sunt*.]

A synod was held at Trosly, [Note: Trosly near the Aisne, in the district of Soissons. Bouquet.] presided over by Archbishop Heriveus, with King Charles also present. Through the king’s influence, Erlebald, the Castrician, was absolved there. [Note: Manuscripts 2 and 3 have *Herlebaldus*.]

Richard, marquis of Burgundy, died. King Charles went into the kingdom of Lothair; after forcibly recovering certain strongholds of his disloyal Ricuinus and making a truce with Henry, the ruler beyond the Rhine, lasting until the feast of Saint Martin, he returned to the Mount of Laon. [Notes: Manuscript 2 has *habiit*. Manuscript 2 lacks *reversus est*. Manuscript 3 frequently has *Transrhenensem*.]

There were many storms in various places this year; people were also struck dead by lightning and houses were burned. There was great heat in summer and an abundance of hay. A severe drought lasted almost three continuous months—July, August, and September.

Count Robert besieged the Normans who had occupied the Loire for five months. After receiving hostages from them, he granted them Brittany, which they had ravaged, together with the district of Nantes; and they began to accept the faith of Christ. [Notes: Manuscript 2 has *acceptumque* for *acceptisque*; manuscript 3 has *Nannetico*.] Erluin, bishop of Beauvais, died. Charles again established peace with Henry.

### 922

Charles ravaged the kingdom of Lothair because of the persecution of Gislebert and Otto, with plunder, sacrilege, and arson, even during Lent, as throughout the entire winter.

Richard, who had gone to Rome because of the bishopric of Tongeren, returned, having been ordained bishop by Pope John; Hilduin, who had also gone there as bishop, had been excommunicated by that same pope. Bishop Drogo of Toul died; Gauzlin succeeded him. [Notes: Manuscript 3 has *Rogo*. Manuscript 3 has *successit*; manuscript 2 has *Goslinus*, manuscript 3 *Gauclinus*. Gauzlin was also ordained on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April. Hugh V.]

After Berengar, king of the Lombards, had been driven from his kingdom by his nobles because of his arrogance, Rodulf, king of Cisalpine Gaul, was admitted to the kingdom by those same nobles. The Hungarians, acting at the instigation of the aforementioned Berengar, ravaged Italy after capturing many towns. [Notes: Manuscript 2 has *Langobardorum*. Manuscripts 2 and 3 have *imperatore*. Manuscripts 2 and 3 lack the words concerning his arrogance.]

When Charles had returned to Laon, Hugh, son of Robert, came after Easter above the Vidula. [Notes: Manuscripts 2 and 3 have *super*. Manuscript 2 has *Vidolam*. “La Vêle, which flows into the Aisne.”] There, near the settlement of Fimes, [Note: Manuscript 3 has *Fimmas*. “Fismes.”] he encountered the faithful men of Archbishop Heriveus together with certain counts of Gaul.

When Hugh had proceeded with them across the Aisne into the district of Laon, Charles, because of the aforementioned Haganon, to whom the king had given the abbey of Rothildis, his paternal aunt and Hugh’s mother-in-law, called Gola, [Notes: Manuscripts 2 and 3 have *Cola*. “Apparently Chelles, not far from Paris.”] secretly left Laon with Heribert and Haganon and, because of his affection for Haganon, went across the Meuse out of fear of this man.

Hugh pursued him with the rest of his force, numbering two thousand warriors, as far as the Meuse. There he met Gislebert of Lotharingia. Recalled to a conference with him by his father, who had pursued him and was stationed above the Aisne in the district of Laon, Hugh returned. When Charles learned of this, he crossed the Meuse again with some of the Lotharingians who had come to him and began to plunder and burn the villages of the church of Rheims. He also captured and plundered the castle of Altmont by force, not without the loss of some of his men. [Note: Manuscript 3 has *clade suorum*.]

Robert therefore advanced toward the river Marne to meet his son-in-law Rodulf, son of Richard. Charles followed him with the Lotharingians, crossed the Marne, and the castle of Epernay was plundered by Haganon’s accomplices. [Notes: Manuscript 1 has *Sparnau*. “Epernay.”] When the aforesaid Rodulf came with the Burgundians, Robert also crossed the river below Epernay and pitched camp no more than three leagues from Charles’s army. The two sides remained there for more than a week, while everyone except Haganon and Charles came to a conference. [Notes: Manuscript 1 has *utrimque* in an erased place; manuscripts 2 and 3 have *utrimque*. Manuscript 1 lacks *ceteri*. Manuscript 1 has *Aganonem*.]

Meanwhile Hugh, son of Richard, came to Robert and encountered about two hundred men who had been with Haganon and were going to plunder the villages of the bishopric of Rheims. After capturing them and killing only three, he took their horses and weapons and sent the rest back to their own men loaded with disgrace. [Notes: Manuscript 2 has *aequos*; manuscript 2 has *oneratos*.]

Robert then pitched camp at Calmiciacum, [Note: Chermizy or Chaumuzy, near Rheims.] and Charles near Rheims. After remaining there for three continuous days, about one league from the city, and after some of their horses had been captured by the citizens of Rheims, they fought against the city on only one day, namely Pentecost Sunday. [Notes: Manuscript 2 has *Rhemin*; manuscript 3 has *pugnaverunt*.] Some of the Lotharingians were killed and many wounded, and night brought the battle to an end.

When it was finally heard that those who were with Robert had captured Laon, distributed Haganon’s treasures that had been there, and seized one of his brothers, Charles went with Haganon toward Laon. Some of the Lotharingians returned to their own homes; others went on with Charles. Robert pitched his tents above the Aisne.

When Charles was denied entry into Laon, he took his position on the river Sère, [Notes: Manuscript 2 has *Isaram*. “The Sère and the Ailette in the district of Laon; they flow into the Aisne at La Fère.”] and Robert pitched camp on the Ailette. As Robert’s forces grew daily while Charles’s diminished, Charles finally withdrew secretly with Haganon and went across the Meuse.

The Franks chose Robert the Elder and submitted to him. Accordingly, Robert was established as king at Rheims, at Saint-Remigius, by the bishops and leading men of the kingdom.

Archbishop Heriveus of Rheims [manuscript 2: *Heinricus*] died on the third day after the consecration of King Robert, namely on the sixth day before the Nones of July, four days before completing the twenty-second year of his episcopate. [Note: Manuscript 1 has *consecratione*.] Seulfus succeeded him in the episcopate; he had then been serving as archdeacon in that same city. [Note: Manuscript 3 has “the ministry of that city’s archdeaconry.”]

[Note: *History of Rheims* IV, 17: “As the disagreement between King Charles and Robert increased, and nearly all the nobles of the kingdom had gathered at Saint-Remigius to establish Robert as king, that same archbishop, overcome by illness, died—on the third day, namely, after Robert had become king, and on the fourth day before he completed the twenty-second year of his episcopate. It happened [lacuna in manuscript c] that on the very day of his death several bishops who had come there entered the city of Rheims. They celebrated his funeral with fitting rites and, amid the greatest grief both of his own people and [lacuna in manuscript c] of outsiders, committed him to a worthy burial.”]

At Cambrai three suns seemed to appear, or the sun seemed to have three circles separated from one another. Likewise, two darts in the sky approached one another from opposite sides until they were covered by a cloud. Likewise, two trunks approached each other in the sky until they too were covered by a cloud. [Notes: Manuscript 3 omits *visi sunt*. Manuscript 1 omits *nube*.]

Robert sent his son Hugh into the kingdom of Lothair with a certain force of Franks to relieve Gislebert’s castle of Capraemont, which Charles was pressing under siege. [Note: Manuscript 1 has *Caprae Mortem*.] When Charles learned this, he abandoned the siege, and Hugh, after receiving hostages from certain Lotharingians, returned to his father.

An earthquake occurred in the district of Cambrai, as a result of which several houses there were overturned. In the district of Paris, too, in a settlement called Jesedis, many miracles are reported to have occurred in the church of Saint Peter beginning in the preceding year, when relics from the apostle’s beard were brought there. More than one hundred and seventy persons among the blind, lame, and crippled are said to have been restored to health. All the demoniacs who went there returned with sound minds after the demons had been expelled, in addition to countless other things that occurred there.

### 923

Robert went into the kingdom of Lothair to confer with Henry, who came to meet him in the district of the Ripuarians, above the river Roer. There they entertained one another; after making a pact of friendship and exchanging gifts, they departed. There, too, certain Lotharingians gave hostages and received from Robert a truce lasting until the Kalends of October. [Notes: Manuscripts 3 have *Ribuariarium*; manuscript 2 lacks the date.]

The Normans plundered Aquitaine and Auvergne. Against them William, duke of the Aquitanians, and Raimund fought, and twelve thousand of the Normans were killed. [Notes: Manuscript 1 frequently has *Willelmus*. Manuscript 2 has *Aquitanorum*.]

Boso, son of Richard, killed Ricuinus while he lay sick in bed.

Charles, with his Lotharingians, broke the truce that they had recently received from Robert, crossed the Meuse, and came to Attigny. Before Robert could gather his faithful men, Charles unexpectedly approached the Aisne, where he had learned that Robert was stationed below the city of Soissons. On the following day, a Sunday, after the sixth hour had already passed, when the Franks were not expecting battle that day and many were dining, Charles crossed the Aisne and came against Robert with his armed Lotharingians.

Robert, for his part, advanced against him with the armed men who were with him. When battle had been joined and many had fallen on both sides, King Robert also fell, pierced by lances. Those who were on Robert’s side—namely his son Hugh, Heribert, count of Vermandois, [Note: Hugh V and Hugh of Flavigny identify him as Count Heribert of Vermandois.] and the others—nevertheless won the victory and put Charles and the Lotharingians to flight. But because their own king had died, they ceased pursuing them. They held the field, however, and the spoils were plundered from them, especially by peasants and by those who had streamed out from the suburb of Soissons. [Notes: Manuscript 2 has *optinuere*; manuscripts 2 and 3 omit the preposition *a* before *rusticanis*.]

The Lotharingians, having lost many baggage animals, which Count Rothgarius seized and carried away into the castle of Laon, and leaving Charles within the kingdom of the Franks, returned to their own lands. [Notes: Manuscripts 2 and 3 have *Rotgarius*. Manuscript 2 has *in* for *infra*.]

Charles then begged Count Heribert, Archbishop Seulfus, and the other leading men of the kingdom, through many embassies, to return to him. When they refused, they sent Rodulfus to Burgundy. [Note: Rodulfus, son of Richard the Justiciar; Hugh V: Rodulfus, son of Richard, the great prince.] He promptly came to meet them with a large force of his men.

When the Franks heard that Charles had summoned the Normans to come to him, they took up a position between Charles and the Normans above the river Oise with Rodulf, so that the Normans might not join him. When Charles fled across the Meuse, they all chose Rodulf as king.

Rodulfus, son of Richard, was established as king at the city of Soissons. [Note: In the monastery of Saint-Medard, as marked by Pithoeus with asterisks. This is found neither in Richer nor in Hugh V.]

[Hugh of Flavigny continues as follows: “And his brother Boso was established as king of Upper Gaul, which is called the long-haired land—that is, Upper Burgundy—and Hugh Capet as duke of Lower Burgundy.”]

Count Heribert sent his cousin Bernard, together with other envoys, to Charles, although, as is said, those envoys were unaware of the plan being conducted through them. Persuaded by their oaths, Charles went with a few men to Heribert. Heribert received him in his castle above the Somme near Saint-Quentin. [Note: “Saint-Quentin.”] After sending back those who had come with him, Heribert had Charles led to one of his fortifications called Château-Thierry, above the river Marne. [Note: “Château-Thierry.”] There he detained him under guard, supplying him with the necessities of life. He himself then followed King Rodulf into Burgundy.

Meanwhile Ragenold, prince of the Normans who were operating on the Loire, having long before been summoned by Charles through repeated messages, ravaged Gaul beyond the Oise, joining to himself many men from Rouen. [Note: Manuscripts 2 and 3 have *praedatur*.] Heribert’s faithful men who had remained in the castles came upon his camp, joined by Rodulf, stepson of Count Rotger, and by Counts Ingobrandus. They seized an enormous amount of booty, and one thousand captives were freed there. [Notes: Manuscript 1 has *eripierunt*; manuscript 2 has *Ingobrandus*.]

When Ragenold learned this, driven by fury he advanced to plunder the district of Arras. Count Adelelmus met him and struck down six hundred of them, while the rest fled. Ragenold hurried with the survivors to the refuge of his fortifications and did not cease from carrying out as much plunder and brigandage as he could.

Pressed by these circumstances, King Rodulf, summoned by Hugh, son of Robert, came from Burgundy to Compiègne on the Oise. When he heard that the Normans were ravaging the district of Beauvais, he crossed over there with Archbishop Seulfus, Count Heribert, and certain other chosen and brave men.

After crossing the river Itta, [Note: The Epte, which flows into the Seine midway between Paris and Rouen.] he entered the land that had formerly been given to the Normans when they came to the faith of Christ, so that they might observe that faith and have peace. The king and the Franks also devastated part of that land with slaughter and fire because the Normans had broken the peace they had made on account of the promises of Charles, who had promised them an extensive territory. [Notes: Manuscript 1 has *ipsius* for *ipsi*; manuscript 2 has *infringere* for *infregere*.]

While he was occupied with these matters, envoys of the Lotharingians approached him, promising to submit themselves and their possessions to him. Recalled from this devastation by their embassy, he went, on the advice of the leading men who were with him, to meet the Lotharingians, leaving Counts Hugh and Heribert behind to defend the homeland beyond the Oise.

The Lotharingians came to meet him near Mouzon. Meanwhile his wife Emma, daughter of King Robert, was consecrated queen at Rheims by Seulfus, the archbishop.

Rodulf, received as king by many of the Lotharingians, was asked by Wigericus, bishop of Metz, to go and recover a certain castle in the district of Alsace called Zabern. [Note: “Zabern.”] He spent almost the whole autumn there, while the castellans, because they were beyond the Rhine, waited in vain for assistance from Henry. At last, after receiving hostages from them, he returned to Laon to his wife. [Notes: Manuscript 1 has *autumnus* corrected from *auttumnus*; manuscript 3 has *autunno*. Manuscript 3 has *castellani*.]

Meanwhile, while the Normans were plundering certain of our districts beyond the Oise and our people were plundering their land, they promised peace through frequent embassies sent alternately to Count Heribert and Archbishop Seulfus, as well as to the other Franks who were encamped with them against the Normans—provided that they were given the extensive territory they requested beyond the Seine. When King Rodulf had returned, as stated, to Laon, they sent him hostages and received from him a truce until the middle of May.

While these things were taking place, it was reported that Henry, invited by Count Gislebert and by Rotger, archbishop of Trier—who had not yet submitted themselves to Rodulf—had crossed the Rhine and was ravaging the kingdom of Lothair. [Notes: Manuscript 3 always has *Rhenum*. Manuscript 2 has *nuntiatur* corrected from *nuntiantur*; manuscript 3 has *nunciantur*.]

He ravaged the land lying between the Rhine and the Moselle, carrying away flocks and herds and exhausting the rest of its resources, while also taking many young people captive. When he heard that Rodulf was gathering an army not only from Gaul but from all Burgundy, he withdrew into his own kingdom and granted the Lotharingians a truce until the Kalends of October of the following year. [Notes: Manuscripts 2 and 3 have *sequentis anni*, “of the following year.”]

Only Otto defected to Henry from among those who had submitted to Rodulf.

When Bishop Wigericus recovered Zabern, he demolished it. Cambrai was disastrously consumed by a fire that had been poorly guarded against.

The other Rodulfus, king of Cisalpine Gaul, whom the Italians had admitted to the kingdom after rejecting their king Berengar, fought Berengar himself and defeated him; one thousand five hundred men are said to have fallen there. [Notes: Manuscript 3a has *accepto* for *abiecto*; manuscript 2 omits the indicated phrase, “having received into the kingdom their king Berengar.”]

Pope John sent Archbishop Seulfus the archiepiscopal insignia called the pallium. A multitude of Englishmen traveling to the threshold of Saint Peter for the sake of prayer were massacred by the Saracens among the Alps. [Notes: Manuscripts 1 and 3 have *Saracenis*; manuscript 2 has *trucidantur*.]

Dado, bishop of Verdun, died, and his bishopric was granted by King Rodulf to Hugh, who, being a priest, was consecrated at Rheims by Archbishop Seulfus. [Notes: Manuscript 1 has *ab* and *episcopo*. Hugh of Flavigny continues: “After completing thirty-seven years in the episcopate, he earned a fitting burial among the tombs of his predecessor bishops in the church of Saint Vito.”]

Textual readings not otherwise noted above: In 921, manuscripts 2 and 3 have *sinodus* for *synodus*; manuscript 3 has *Ricardus* and *Lodharii*. In 922, manuscript 3 has *Lodhariense*; manuscript 2 corrects *obviam* to *obvium*; manuscript 1 reads *sequi* on one line and *quens* on another, while manuscript 3 has *subsequens*; manuscript 2 has *Haganonem*; and manuscript 2 has *conp.* for *comprehendissent*. In the Cambrai account, manuscript 3 has *Camaracum*; manuscript 1 has *frangorum* for *Francorum*, *Caprae mortem* for *Capraemontem*, and omits *nube*; manuscript 2 has *relinquid*, manuscript 3 *relinquit*, for *reliquid*; manuscripts 2 and 3 have *gesedis* for *Jesedis*; manuscript 1 corrects *claudus* to *claudos*; and manuscript 2 has *sanitatem*.

In 923, manuscript 1 has *Normanni*; manuscript 2 has *depraedantur*, *acceperat*, *cum eo*, *Axonem*, *ocius*, *compendia*, *normandni*, *exercitus*, and *cogeret*; manuscript 1 has *insperante*, *medii medii*, *dehin*, and *a* for *ab*; manuscript 3 omits the passage from *Rotbertus* through *processit*, has *suis Lodhariensibus*, *Otho*, and *cogeret*, and reads *Ita* (as does manuscript 3a) for *Itta*. At the notice that Charles summoned the Normans, the source records the abbreviated readings *ad se v.* and, in manuscript 2, *Normannos* (manuscript 3: *ad s. v. n.*). Manuscripts 2 and 3 omit *regem* after *cuncti*; manuscript 1 has *Rhenum*’s spelling *renum* throughout. Wigericus is *uuigerius* in manuscript 1, *uuitgericus* in manuscript 2, and *wilgericus* in manuscript 3. Manuscript 1 has *Iohhanne* for *Johanne*.

### 924
With [the year] beginning, a levy of the contributory money-tax was imposed throughout Francia [Note: [Col. 0431] *franciam* in witnesses 2 and 3, frequently], to be given to the Northmen according to the peace agreement. King Rodulf was preparing an expedition into Aquitaine, because William [Note: [Col. 0431] *uuillemus* in witness 1, frequently], ruler of that region, was delaying in submitting to him. When William learned that Rodulf was hastening into Aquitaine with a hostile force, he came to meet him above the Loire. After messengers had gone back and forth, they finally came to a conference on the Loire itself, within the district of Augustodunum [Note: [Col. 0431] *augustidinensem* in witness 1]. They remained there all day, Rodulf on one bank and William on the other, with messengers advancing from both sides. When the day had thus been spent, William at last crossed the river and reached Rodulf at night. Jumping down from his horse, he approached the king, who was seated on his horse [Note: [Col. 0431] *aequo* in witness 2], on foot. After the king had kissed him, they withdrew on both sides.

On the following day William returned to the king. Having received an eight-day truce, he submitted himself to the king after the week had ended. The king restored to him the district of Bourges [Note: [Col. 0431] *bituricensem* in witness 2], which he had recently taken from him by force, relying on the assistance of Robert, who was not yet king, together with the city of Bourges. Finally, he gave Péronne [Note: [Col. 0431] *perronam* in witness 2; *parronam* in witness 3; *paronam*, Hugo of Flodoard] to Heribert, and Le Mans to Hugh, Robert’s son.

Archbishop Seulfus also recovered from Hugh of Vienne—who had taken part in that same conference [Note: [Col. 0431] *eodem* in witness 2]—the land of Saint Remigius lying in the province of Lyon [Note: [Col. 0431] *ludunensi* in witness 2], from which Bishop Heriveus had received nothing [Note: [Col. 0432] Later, king of Italy]. From there, returning, we came near a certain castle called Mount Saint John. Raginard [Note: [Col. 0431] *raienardus* in witness 2, consistently; *ragenardus* in witness 3] had invaded and held it. At the urging of his nephews Walon and Gislebert, and of the others whom the king had sent to capture it, he sent his son as a hostage to the king. The king, having been entreated by Raginard’s relatives [Note: [Col. 0431] *raginardi* in witness 3] and by his brother Hugh, ordered the son to be received and granted Raginard a truce; all the others who were with Raginard he left bound by oath [Note: [Col. 0431] *obstricto* in witness 2].

Meanwhile Berengarius, who had Gislebert’s sister as his wife [Note: [Col. 0431] absent in witness 3], captured Gislebert [Note: [Col. 0431] *conp.* in witness 2]. He released him after the sons of Ragenarius, his brother [Note: [Col. 0431] *fratri sui* in witness 2], had been offered to him as hostages in Gislebert’s place [Note: [Col. 0431] the witnesses transpose the references to the hostages]. Once released, Gislebert devastated by numerous raids the land of Berengarius, of his brother Ragenarius, and of Count Isaac. After this he sent envoys to King Rodulf, asking to be received by him. But the king, on the advice of his faithful men, despising Gislebert’s perjuries and fickleness [Note: [Col. 0431] *abhom* in witness 2], refused to do so.

The Hungarians, led by King Berengarius, whom the Lombards had driven back [Note: [Col. 0431] *lamgobardi* in witness 2; *pepulerant* in witnesses 2 and 3], ravaged Italy. They also set fire to Pavia, a very populous [Note: [Col. 0431] in witness 2, *de* is written above *populosissimam] and exceedingly wealthy city. Countless riches perished there. Forty-four churches [Note: [Col. 0431] forty-three in witness 3] were burned; the city’s own bishop and the bishop of Vercelli, who was with him, were killed by fire and smoke. Of that almost innumerable multitude, only two hundred are said to have survived. From the remnants of the burned city, which they had gathered among the ashes, they gave the Hungarians eight modii of silver [Note: [Col. 0431] *md.* in witness 1], thereby purchasing their lives and the walls of the empty city.

When this was finished, the Hungarians crossed the rugged passes of the Alpine ridges and came into Gaul. Rodulf, king of Cisalpine Gaul [Note: [Col. 0431] witnesses 2 and 3 read “Rodulf, king of Gaul”; witness 2 also has “king of Cisalpine Gaul”], and Hugh of Vienne shut the Hungarians in among the narrow Alpine valleys [Note: [Col. 0431] *alpinarum* in witnesses 1 and 3]. Escaping from there through an unexpected place along the mountain’s trackless ways, they attacked Gothia [Note: [Col. 0431] “They were compelled to make for the province of Toulouse. But there, hindered by the power of almighty God, they later perished from dysentery and various disasters.” Hugo of Flodoard; compare the end of this year]. The aforesaid commanders pursued them and struck down as many as they could find. Meanwhile Berengarius, king of Italy, was killed by his own men [Note: [Col. 0431] *interemitur* corrected to *interimitur* in witness 1. At this point witness 2 inserts the sentences written below, beginning “The Northmen made peace with the Franks” and ending “the Hungarians who were ravaging Gothia are reported to have been destroyed”; witness 3 preserves them here in parentheses].

King Rodulf held a royal assembly at Attigny [Note: [Col. 0431] absent in witness 2; *habuit* in witness 3]. Then, while preparing to depart for the kingdom of Lothar, he was seized by a very serious illness [Note: [Col. 0431] *langore* in witness 2]. When its force returned, although he was already thought to be recovering, he was overcome and, regarded by many as almost beyond hope, asked to be carried at Reims to Saint Remigius [Note: [Col. 0433] *fecit* in witnesses 2 and 3]. There he bestowed some gifts and sent whatever treasures remained to him—apart from his wife’s share—to monasteries throughout Francia and Burgundy. After spending four weeks at Saint Remigius, he finally regained his health and went to the city of Soissons [Note: [Col. 0433] *civitatem* in witness 2], and from there returned to Burgundy.

Heinricus likewise spent the whole summer ill in the very territory of the Sarmatians [Note: [Col. 0433] *parmatarum* in witness 2]. Meanwhile conflict, with killings, burnings, and plundering on both sides, arose between Gislebert and his brother Ragener [Note: [Col. 0433] *ragenarium* in witnesses 2 and 3], and no less between Boso and Otto [Note: [Col. 0433] *ottonem* in witness 3]. The Northmen made peace with the Franks by oaths, through Counts Hugh and Heribert and also Archbishop Seulfus [Note: [Col. 0433] *hugone* in witness 1]. King Rodulf was absent, but with his consent their territory was enlarged: Le Mans and Bayeux were granted to them under the peace agreement.

Count Isaac deceitfully seized and burned a certain castle belonging to Stephen, bishop of Cambrai. Heribert’s fortified tower above the River Marne, where Charles was being held, also burned in a sudden conflagration. Raginold [Note: [Col. 0433] *rainoldus* in witness 1; *raienoldus* in witness 2; *ragenoldus* in witness 3], with his Northmen, because he had not yet received a possession within Gaul, ravaged Hugh’s land between the Loire and the Seine.

A synod of the bishops of the diocese of Reims was held at Trosly in October, with Archbishop Seulfus presiding. There Count Isaac came to make amendment and satisfaction for the wrongs he had perpetrated against the church of Cambrai; having been bound by a pledge of one hundred pounds of silver [Note: [Col. 0433] *libras* in witness 3], he was reconciled with Stephen, bishop of that city, in the presence [Note: [Col. 0433] *satagente*, History of Reims] of Heribert and several counts of Francia.

King Rodulf recovered the castle of Mount Saint John, although Raginard abandoned it unwillingly, and then returned to Francia [Note: [Col. 0433] *repetiit* in witness 3]. William and Hugh, Robert’s son [Note: [Col. 0433] “son of Robert” in witnesses 2 and 3], made a security agreement concerning their land with Ragenold [Note: [Col. 0433] absent in witnesses 2 and 3], and Ragenold with his Northmen departed for Burgundy.

Many candle-lights appeared this year in various parts of Francia, suddenly arising as a light. Visions of saints were also shown to a certain priest named Ebrulf, living in a village near Mouzon [Note: [Col. 0433] *conmanti* in witness 1]. At Reims, in the church of Saint Mary, on the feast of All Saints, a certain man who had long been crippled—his thighs had adhered to his legs, with the tendons of his knees so contracted—was released and made upright by divine power [Note: [Col. 0433] *ereptus* in witness 3]. The Hungarians who had been ravaging Gothia are reported to have been almost entirely destroyed after suffering a certain plague, with swelling of the head and dysentery; only a few escaped.

The year

## 925

As the year began, Raginold [Note: [Col. 0433] *ragenoldus* in witness 3], with his Northmen, was ravaging Burgundy [Note: [Col. 0433] *depopulatur* in witness 2]. Count Warnerius and Count Manasses, together with the bishops Ansegisus and Gotselinus [Note: [Col. 0433] *getselinus* in witness 1; *gotselinus* in witness 2; *gozcelinus* in witness 3], engaged them at Mount Calaus [Note: [Col. 0433] *calaun* in witness 3] and struck down more than eight hundred Northmen. Count Warnerius was captured and killed there after the horse on which he was sitting had been killed, and Ansegisus, bishop of Troyes [Note: [Col. 0433] *trecassinae* in witness 3], was wounded.

When King Rodulf learned this, he set out for Burgundy with some men from Francia—namely, soldiers of the church of Reims—and with Abbo, bishop of Soissons [Note: [Col. 0433] *ebbone* corrected to *abbone* in witness 1], accompanied by a few others. Count Heribert also followed him. After gathering a considerable force of soldiers from Burgundy, he came as far as the Northmen’s camp above the Seine. There the men who had come from Francia fought on foot against those at the camp.

When they saw that the men with the king—by far the greater part of the army—were attempting neither to storm the camp nor to dismount from their horses, they drove back into the camp the Northmen who had gone out to fight [Note: [Col. 0433] *fugerant* in witness 3; *pugnandum* in witnesses 2 and 3], striking some of them down. They then abandoned the assault on the camp and pitched their own camp in a circle two or three miles from the Northmen’s, while Hugh, Robert’s son, pitched his camp on the opposite bank of the Seine.

Because the Franks postponed closing in on the camp and delayed from day to day [Note: [Col. 0433] *proferentibus* in witness 2] while waiting for ships to come from Paris, the Northmen made a secret sortie—so it is said, with the assent of some of our men—left their camp, and escaped by making for a certain forest in order to protect their route. All our men then returned to their own positions.

When the Lenten fasts had begun, Heribert spoke with Gislebert and then with Hugh, and summoned the king from Burgundy. He came quickly and went to meet the Lotharingians and Gislebert at Cambrai. They abandoned this planned meeting and came to him above the Meuse; Gislebert and Otto [Note: [Col. 0433] *otho*, written above the line in witness 1; *otho* in witness 2] then became his men.

The Northmen of Rouen broke the treaty that they had once made and ravaged the districts of Beauvais and Amiens. The city of Amiens was burned by a fire of refugees that had been badly attended; Arras likewise burned in a sudden conflagration. The Northmen came to Noyon to plunder and set fire to its suburbs. The castellans went out with the townspeople, drove back the Northmen, struck down as many as they could, and freed part of the suburb.

Meanwhile the men of Bayeux plundered the Northmen’s territory beyond the Seine. When the Parisians learned this [Note: [Col. 0433] so in witness 1, which supplies punctuation], they too, together with certain retainers of Hugh, Robert’s son, and with the townsmen of certain castles, ravaged part of the district of Rouen [Note: [Col. 0435] *quendam* in witness 2; *rothomag.* in witness 3], which the Northmen possessed on this side of the Seine. They burned villages, drove away livestock, and killed some of the Northmen.

Meanwhile Count Heribert, with a few Franks, remained above the Oise to prevent the Northmen from crossing, since scarcely any grass was yet available for the horses [Note: [Col. 0435] *aequis* in witness 2]. When the Northmen learned that their land had been ravaged, they hurried to return to it [Note: [Col. 0435] *festinanter* in witness 2; *festinanter rediere* in witness 3].

Heinricus, finally crossing the Rhine, captured by force a town called Tolbiac [Note: [Col. 0435] Zülpich], which Gislebert’s supporters were defending. He did not remain long within the kingdom of Lothar but returned across the Rhine to his own lands, having received hostages from Gislebert. Count Hilgaud and the other maritime Franks invaded and devastated neighboring places recently possessed by the Northmen.

Meanwhile Rodulf returned from Burgundy to Francia and announced by royal ban that the Franks should prepare for war against the Northmen [Note: [Col. 0435] *praeparent* corrected from *praeparant* in witness 2; *praepararent* in witness 3]. Heribert therefore began an expedition against the Northmen with the soldiers of the church of Reims. Count Arnulf [Note: [Col. 0435] absent in witness 1] and the other maritime Franks also attacked a certain Northman stronghold, to which their ruler Rollo had sent a thousand Northmen from Rouen, besides the town’s own inhabitants.

That castle, situated beside the sea, was called Eu [Note: [Col. 0435] Eu, between Dieppe and Abbeville]. The Franks surrounded it, broke through the rampart that enclosed it as an outer defense, breached the wall, and climbed up. After gaining possession of the town by fighting, they killed all the males and burned the fortification.

Some, however, escaped and occupied a nearby island. The Franks attacked and captured it, though only after a longer delay than that in which they had taken the town. When the Northmen who were defending their lives as best they could with weapons saw this, and had lost hope of survival, some were killed as they swam out. Some of the Northmen were killed by Frankish swords, while others met death by their own weapons [Note: [Col. 0435] *oppetebat* in witness 2]. Thus, after all had been struck down and a considerable amount of booty seized, the Franks returned to their own lands. King Rodulf, meanwhile, was staying in the district of Beauvais with Hugh and the Burgundians.

At about this time Seulfus, archbishop of Reims [Note: [Col. 0435] History of Reims IV.19–20 reports: “He is said to have ended his life after being given poison by Heribert’s household or retainers. Immediately after his death, Count Heribert came to Reims, summoned Abbo, bishop of Soissons, and Bovo of Châlons. Joining them to himself, he deliberated about the election of a ruler for this church of Reims and compelled both clergy and laity to follow his will. Following his advice, lest the bishopric perhaps be divided among outsiders, they elected his son, named Hugh, a very small child who had not yet completed five years. After this was done, they hurried to the king to obtain his authorization. When King Rodulf learned of the election, he entrusted the bishopric of Reims to Heribert, to be administered and governed by him according to the standard of equity. He also hastened to send the church’s envoys to Rome with Bishop Abbo, carrying with them the decree of this election and seeking the pope’s approval of it. Pope John, with Bishop Abbo intervening, granted their request and assigned the bishopric of Reims to Bishop Abbo, decreeing that the matters belonging to episcopal ministry should be handled and concluded by him in that bishopric. Thus Count Heribert, having obtained control of the bishopric of Reims, unjustly deprived both me, who had not taken part in his aforesaid election, and several others, clergy and laity alike, of the benefits of ecclesiastical possessions, with which we seemed to have been rewarded by earlier bishops in return for our service. Whatever he wished, he distributed to those whom he favored. Not long afterward, when an uproar arose among the clergy within the canons’ enclosure, some soldiers arrived with weapons, and two clerics were killed there, one of whom was considered a deacon and the other a subdeacon.”] died after completing three years and five days in the episcopate [Note: [Col. 0435] the five days are absent in witness 1].

Count Heribert came to Reims and compelled the vassals of that church, as well as the clergy, to follow his counsel concerning the election of a ruler. Hugh, Robert’s son, received a security agreement from the Northmen [Note: [Col. 0435] *accepit* in witness 2], while the land of Baldwin’s sons, and also that of Rodulf of Gaugé and Hilgaud [Note: [Col. 0435] *hilgaldi* in witness 3], was left outside the security.

The bishopric of Reims was entrusted to Count Heribert [Note: [Col. 0435] *herberto* in witness 1] under the pretext of his son Hugh, a very small child, not yet, as was generally reported, five years old. Bishop Abbo went to Rome [Col. 0436C] with envoys of Count Heribert.

All the Lotharingians submitted themselves to Heinricus. He granted the bishopric of Verdun to Bernuinus, nephew of Bishop Dado [Note: [Col. 0435] *dadanis* in witness 2], who was ordained bishop there after expelling the priest Hugh, to whom Rodulf had given it [Note: [Col. 0435] Hugh adds: “From this point Verdun and the other cities defected from the kingdom of the Franks.”].

## 926

The year was beginning, and King Rodulf, with Count Heribert and certain maritime Franks, was besieging the Northmen, who had been confined in a certain forest in the district of Arras. Suddenly, after several days, the Northmen began a nighttime sortie and attacked the king’s camp. Heribert came to the king’s aid so that he would not be captured by the Northmen. Some huts were burned, and fighting took place at the camp [Note: [Col. 0435] absent in witness 2]. At last the Northmen were driven back from the assault on the camp and withdrew. The king was wounded there, Count Hilgaud was killed, and eleven hundred Northmen are said to have been killed there.

Rodulf thus returned to Laon, while the Northmen ravaged the wooded places as far as the district of Porcien [Note: [Col. 0436] In Champagne; for example, Château-Porcien in the department of Ardennes]. The Hungarians, after crossing the Rhine [Note: [Col. 0435] absent in witness 2], raged with plundering and burnings as far as the district of Vimeu [Note: [Col. 0437] *uotinsem* in witness 2; *vozinsem* in witness 3].

On the fourteenth day of the moon, on Holy Saturday of Easter [Note: [Col. 0437] absent in witnesses 1 and 3], on the day of the Kalends of April, the moon suffered an eclipse and was turned pale, with only a small portion of its light remaining, as though it were a second [moon] [Note: [Col. 0437] *veluti* in witness 3]. As dawn was already beginning, it was wholly changed to the color of blood [Note: [Col. 0437] *inmutata* in witness 2; *colorem* absent in witness 2].

The body of Saint Remigius and the relics of certain other saints were carried from their monasteries at Reims because of fear of the Hungarians. Among them were also the relics of Saint Walburga [Note: [Col. 0437] *walleburgis* in witnesses 2 and 3; *galburgis*, Hugo of Flodoard], through which several miracles were being performed [Note: [Col. 0437] “often occur,” Hugo of Flodoard].

The levy of the contributory money-tax to be given to the Northmen under the peace agreement was publicly imposed throughout Francia and Burgundy. After the money had been paid, peace was confirmed on both sides by oath [Note: [Col. 0437] “with an oath” is absent in witness 2]. From there an army from Francia and Burgundy, with King Rodulf and Count Heribert, set out along the Loire. They received hostages from the city of Nevers, which William’s brother was defending against the king, and crossed into Aquitaine to pursue William, who had perhaps defected from the king. They pursued him as he fled [Note: [Col. 0437] *fugientem* in witnesses 2 and 3], until the report of the Hungarian invasion—that they had again crossed the Rhine—compelled the army to return to Francia.

Hugh, Berta’s son, was established as king at Rome over Italy, after Rodulf, king of Cisalpine Gaul, who had seized that kingdom and had joined himself to another woman while his wife was still alive, was expelled. Berta’s sons also killed Burcard, ruler of the Alamanni [Note: [Col. 0437] *buchardo* in witness 3], Rodulf’s father-in-law, who had crossed the Alps with him in order to recover the kingdom of Italy for his son-in-law [Note: [Col. 0437] *italia* in witness 2; *italiam* in witness 3].

The priest Hugh, expelled from Verdun, died. A certain Ebrardus [Note: [Col. 0437] *quoque* in witnesses 2 and 3], from across the Rhine, was sent by Heinricus into the kingdom of Lothar to administer justice, and he reconciled the Lotharingians among themselves in peace. Count Rodulf, son of Heilwidis [Note: [Col. 0437] *heiloidis* in witness 2; *heloidis* in witnesses 3 and 3b], died. Not long afterward, his stepfather Rotgarius [Note: [Col. 0437] *rotgardus* in witness 1], count of the district of Laon [Note: [Col. 0437] *victricus* in witness 2], also died.

Hugh, Robert’s son, married the daughter of Edward [Note: [Col. 0437] *eaduardi* in witness 2], king of the English and sister of Charles’s wife.

## 927

A quarrel arose between King Rodulf and Count Heribert over the county of Laon. Heribert wanted it given to his son Odo, but the king granted it to one of Rotgarius’s sons, named Rotgarius [Note: [Col. 0437] *rotgerio* in witness 1; *rotgarii* in witness 2] [Note: [Col. 0437] *exoritur* in witnesses 2 and 3].

Fiery ranks were seen in the sky at Reims on a Sunday morning in March. A pestilence followed immediately after this sign, resembling fever and cough; combined with mortality, it spread among all the peoples of Germany and Gaul.

Widricus, bishop of Metz [Note: [Col. 0437] *metensis* in witness 3, and below], died. Count Heribert sent his envoys across the Rhine to Heinricus. When they returned, Heinricus summoned Heribert to a conference through those same envoys [Note: [Col. 0437] *pro eodem* in witness 3]. As Heribert hurried there, peace was established with Hugh, Robert’s son; he honored Heinricus with gifts and was honored by him in return. There Heinricus, disregarding the election of the people of Metz, gave their bishopric to a certain man, reportedly a servant of God, surnamed Benno [Note: [Col. 0437] *episcop: um* in witness 2].

Hugh, Robert’s son, and Count Heribert marched against the Northmen, who were staying on the Loire. A very great storm shook the districts of Laon and Soissons. Houses were overturned, many trees were uprooted, and many people were killed in various places [Note: [Col. 0437] *plures* in witness 1].

William, ruler of the Aquitanians, died. After the Northmen on the Loire had been besieged for five weeks by Heribert and Hugh [Note: [Col. 0437] absent in witness 2], they gave and received hostages and were granted the district of Nantes; then they made peace with the Franks.

A synod of six bishops was held at Trosly. King Rodulf opposed it through messengers of Count Heribert, ordering Heribert to postpone the synod and come to meet him at Compiègne [Note: [Col. 0437] *conpendium* in witness 2]. Heribert refused to do this [Note: [Col. 0437] *rennuit* in witness 2], but attended the synod. There Count Herluin came to perform penance for the wife whom he had married while another wife was alive.

After the synod had concluded, Count Heribert wished to enter Laon. King Rodulf, however, forestalled him by sending soldiers there to guard the place; then he himself followed and entered the same castle. Heribert expelled Charles from custody and took him with him into the district of Vermandois [Note: [Col. 0437] *ueromandissem* in witness 2], namely to Saint-Quentin [Note: [Col. 0437] *deducit* in witnesses 2 and 3].

Rodulf returned to Burgundy, leaving Rotgarius’s sons with his wife to guard Laon. They went out and devastated all the places around Coucy [Note: [Col. 0437] Coucy], a castle belonging to the bishopric of Reims.

Charles therefore sought a conference with the Northmen at the castle called Eu [Note: [Col. 0437] *Alga*, Hugo of Flodoard]. There Rollo’s son submitted himself to Charles [Note: [Col. 0437] *conmittit* in witness 2] and established friendship with Heribert. Meanwhile fear prompted by a false report about the Hungarians, and panic, spread through the kingdom of Lothar and Francia.

## 928

At the beginning of the year, during the very solemn celebration of Christ’s birth, Rodulf came from Burgundy into Francia with a hostile force of Burgundians, plundering and also burning certain places. Hugh, Robert’s son, hurried to meet him. When they came to the Oise, Hugh acted as mediator and intermediary between Rodulf and Count Heribert, and received hostages from Heribert until they should meet again at the appointed assembly.

After this had been done, Rodulf returned to Burgundy, unable to persuade his wife to leave Laon. Count Heribert came to Reims with Charles and from there sent a letter to Pope John at Rome, informing him of Charles’s restoration and honor, just as the pope had instructed him, even under threat of excommunication, to strive with all his strength for this [Note: [Col. 0439] absent in witness 1].

King Rodulf and Count Heribert again came to an assembly, now during Lent. Queen, Rodulf’s wife, left Laon [Note: [Col. 0439] *reliquit* in witness 3; *relinquit* corrected in witness 2] and returned to Burgundy. Count Heribert took possession of Laon and afterward held an assembly with the Northmen; he and Hugh [Note: [Col. 0439] Hugh, Robert’s son, in witness 3] made a pact of friendship with them [Note: [Col. 0439] *amicitiamque* in witness 2].

Heribert’s son Odo, however, whom Rollo held as a hostage, was not returned to him until Heribert the father submitted himself to Charles together with certain other counts and bishops of Francia. Various storms broke out in different places [Note: [Col. 0439] *effulsere* in witness 2].

Otgarius, bishop of Amiens, a holy man of advanced age, died. His life is said to have extended to one hundred years and more [Note: [Col. 0439] *prolata* in witnesses 2 and 3]. Count Heribert captured by force and destroyed a certain stronghold of Rotgarius’s sons, called Mortaigne [Note: [Col. 0439] *moritamam* in witness 1; [Col. 0439] Mortaigne], above the River Scheldt [Note: [Col. 0439] absent in witness 2].

Meanwhile Heribert’s envoy returned from Rome, reporting that Pope John had been imprisoned by Wido, the brother of King Hugh [Note: [Col. 0439] *lihugonis* in witness 2], because of a certain quarrel that had arisen between them [Note: [Col. 0439] *reclusum* in witness 3].

A certain bishop Odalricus of Aix [Note: [Col. 0439] In Wasconia. Bouquet] [Note: [Col. 0439] History of Reims IV.22: “A bishop who had withdrawn from his see because of persecution by the Saracens”] was received by Count Heribert in the church of Reims to perform episcopal ministry only in place of Hugh, the count’s son, who was still a child. Odalricus was granted only the abbey of Saint Timothy, together with a canonical prebend.

Heinricus, ruler of Germany [Note: [Col. 0439] *germanicus* in witness 3], crossed the Rhine with a multitude of Germans. Coming above the Meuse, he besieged a certain castle belonging to Count Boso, called Durofostum [Note: [Col. 0439] Regino has *Durfos*; perhaps Delft?], because Boso refused to submit to legal judgment concerning certain abbeys and lands of bishoprics [Note: [Col. 0439] *episcopii* in witness 3] that he had seized by the authority of his power and stubbornly retained, scorning Heinricus’s commands.

He sent to Boso and promised peace if Boso would come to him. After receiving hostages under a security agreement from Heinricus, Boso came to him and promised him loyalty and peace for the kingdom by oath. He returned the land he had seized by force and received other land in compensation [Note: [Col. 0439] *reconp.* in witness 2]. Thus both he himself and Ragenarius made peace with Gislebert and the other Lotharingians.

Hugh and Heribert went to Heinricus for a conference. Returning from there, they went to meet King Rodulf. Heribert again submitted himself to Rodulf, while Charles was once more placed under guard. Then Heribert went with Rodulf into Burgundy to meet Hugh, king of Italy.

The grape harvests were almost completed during the month of August. King Hugh held a conference with Rodulf and gave Count Heribert the province of Vienne [Note: [Col. 0439] *viens* in witness 2; *viensem* in witness 3a] in place of his son Odo.

Benno, bishop of Metz [Note: [Col. 0439] *metensis* in witness 3, frequently], was attacked by ambush, castrated, and deprived of his eyesight. King Rodulf came to Reims and made peace with Charles [Note: [Col. 0440] “There, Charles humbled himself before his presence and handed himself over,” and so forth], restoring Attigny to him [Note: [Col. 0439] *ei* in witness 3] and honoring him with gifts.

## 929

Heribert and Hugh set out against Boso, King Rodulf’s brother, because of certain allodial lands of the recently deceased Rothildis, which Hugh, her son-in-law, sought to recover from Boso after Boso had seized them. Count Heribert captured Victoriacum [Note: [Col. 0440] Vitry-en-Perthois], Boso’s castle, and afterward granted Boso a truce until the end of May.

Boso went to Heinricus and was compelled to swear publicly to the peace. Deroldus, a physician, obtained the bishopric of Amiens [Note: [Col. 0439] *ambianensis* in witness 1], and Albero obtained that of Metz. A certain abbey was granted to Benno as a means of support [Note: [Col. 0439] “with a provision for support” in witness 3].

Heribert and Hugh besieged Monasteriolum [Note: [Col. 0440] Montreuil, south of Boulogne toward Marchiennes], the castle of Herluin [Note: [Col. 0439] *herluini* in witnesses 2 and 3], son of Count Hilgaud. At last, after receiving hostages, they returned.
