Pope John, while being held under guard after being deprived of power by a certain powerful woman named Marozia, died—some say by force, but most maintain that he was driven to it by anguish. King Charles also died at Péronne [Note: [Col. 0439] *parronam* in witness 1; *parronam*, Hugo V].

A quarrel arose between Counts Hugh and Heribert. Hugh received Herluin with his land, while Heribert received Hilduin [Note: [Col. 0440] History of Reims IV.23: “And also Arnaldus”], who had belonged to Hugh. The Alpine roads were blocked by Saracens, and many who wished to travel to Rome were prevented and turned back.

## 930

King Rodulf almost annihilated in a single battle, in the district of Limoges [Note: [Col. 0440] *lemocino* in witness 2; the letters *ui* are written above the word in witness 1] [Note: [Col. 0440] History of Reims IV.23: “The town of Saint Remigius”], the Northmen from the Loire who were harassing Aquitaine with their plundering [Note: [Col. 0439] *depraedationis* in witness 2], and he subjected the Aquitanians to himself.

Heribert received Arnulf [Note: [Col. 0439] *harnoldum* in witness 2; *arnulfum* in witness 3b], who had belonged to Hugh. Various movements of war were stirred up throughout Francia between Hugh and Heribert. King Rodulf came into Francia and, with great effort through several assemblies, established peace among them and with Boso [Note: [Col. 0441] *a. inter b.* in witness 2]. Heribert returned Victoriacum [Note: [Col. 0441] *uicturiacum* in witness 2] to Boso.

After Adelelmus, bishop of Laon, had died, his nephew Gozpertus [Note: [Col. 0441] *gozbertus* in witnesses 2 and 3] obtained the bishopric [Note: [Col. 0441] “his nephew obtained the bishopric” in witness 2]. Heribert received Ansellus, Boso’s vassal, who held Victoriacum [Note: [Col. 0441] *nicturiacum* in witness 2, consistently], together with the castle, and granted him Coucy and other land.

When King Rodulf had returned to Burgundy, the Lotharingians came into Francia with Gislebert to meet Hugh [Note: [Col. 0441] *v. h.* in witnesses 2 and 3]. They captured by siege a certain town called Douai [Note: [Col. 0441] Douai], which Arnulf held.

Meanwhile Boso’s men recovered Victoriacum by treachery and seized Mouzon by fraud. Boso, leaving some of his own loyal men to guard Mouzon, went to besiege the castle mentioned above. Heribert, summoned by certain men of Mouzon [Note: [Col. 0441] *mosomansibus* in witness 2], arrived unexpectedly. Crossing the Meuse at an unexpected ford and entering the town through a gate secretly opened by the castellans [Note: [Col. 0441] “citizens,” History of Reims], he captured all Boso’s vassals who had been left there to defend the place [Note: [Col. 0441] *q. i* is absent in witness 2].

At Reims, within and around the church of Saint Mary, a great light appeared shortly before daybreak from the northern and eastern side [Note: [Col. 0441] “At the same time, before the Nativity of the Lord, at Reims, and so forth—it appeared to have passed across toward the southern side.”].

## 931
[Col. 0441C] King Rodulfus, having gone to Vienne, returned after Karlo Constantino, son of Lucdowicius Orbi, who held it, had promised submission to him. He then went to Tours, to Saint Martin, for the sake of prayer. Meanwhile the Lotharingians captured Duvagium, and Hugo granted it to Rotgarius, the son of Rotgarius. Heribertus, for his part, returned the castle of Saint-Quentin to Arnolfus in exchange for it.  
[Note: One witness omits “Vienne” here; another reads *Viennem* (“Vienne”). One witness has *Karolo* for *Karlo*. The name *Lucdowici* is transmitted as *Lugdovici* in witness 3. One witness reads *orbis* (“of the world”) for *Orbi*. *Duaglum* is another reading for *Duvagium*. *Reddidit* (“returned”) is found in two witnesses instead of *reddit* (“returns”).]

The Greeks, pursuing the Saracens by sea as far as the Forest of Fraxinidus, where their refuge was and from which they went out to plunder Italy in continual raids, and after they had also occupied the Alps, struck them down in a swift destruction, with God’s favor, and restored peace to Italy and the Alps.  
[Note: One witness omits “as far as.” The readings are *internitione* (“destruction”) and *internicione* (“slaughter”). For *quietam* (“peaceful”), two witnesses read *qui eam* (“which it”), while another has *quidam*, together with the letters A.R.I.; the precise force of this variant is uncertain.]

On the day of the Purification of the blessed Mother of God, Mary, in her church at Reims, a servant of one of the canons, keeper of the church of Saint Dionysius and Saint Tedulfus, was suddenly struck and became rigid in the nerves of both his hands and his feet. When he fell, his mouth seemed to him to have adhered to a stone in the pavement. A little later, after the stiffness had tightened both his hands and his legs, he was carried away motionless. On the fifth day his hands were released during Mass, and likewise his legs during Mass on the fifteenth day. A similar event had happened to him in the same church on the day of the Lord’s Circumcision five years earlier; he had then been released there after thirty days, on the very solemnity of the Purification.  
[Note: One witness omits “on the day of the Purification of the blessed Mother of God.” Another has *perculsus, contractis obriguit nervis* (“struck, he became rigid with contracted nerves”) instead of the longer wording. One witness reads *immobili* (“motionless”) rather than *immobilis*. Another transmits a difficult abbreviation, *m. ei d. r.*, in place of “on the fifth day his hands were released.” One witness omits “after thirty days.”]

Rotbertus, archbishop of the church of Tours, returning from Rome, was killed at night beneath the Alps, inside his tents, together with those accompanying him, by robbers.  
[Note: One witness calls him a bishop rather than an archbishop.]

Gislebertus, son of Manasses, defected from King Rodulfus because of the castle of Avalon [Avallon], which Queen Emma had taken from him. At the same time Ricardus, son of Warnarius, also withdrew for the same reason.  
[Note: Two witnesses read *descinit* rather than *desciscit* (“defected”). One reads *Avalonem* instead of *Avalonum*.]

A quarrel likewise arose between Gislebertus of Lotharingia and Boso; Boso was reconciled with Heribertus. Gislebertus captured Boso’s castle of Durofostum, and during those same days Moritania, a stronghold of the sons of Rotgarius, was captured by Arnulfus, son of Balduinus. Heribertus also received the friendship of Gislebertus of Lotharingia.  
[Note: One witness reads *Moritama* for *Moritania*.]

Boso, leaving Heinricus, went to King Rodulfus. On his return he captured the castle of Catalonicum by force, burned it, and overturned it, because of his enmity toward Bishop Bovo, whose men had mutilated some of Boso’s men.  
[Note: One witness reads *catalaucum* for *Catalonicum*. Another has *membra* (“limbs” or “members”) instead of *membris* (“with the limbs”).]

King Rodulfus returned to Francia. After Count Heribertus had defected from him, the king, joining Hugo to himself, captured and destroyed one of Heribertus’s castles, called Domincum [Doulens]; afterward he besieged Arras.  
[Note: Two witnesses and Hugo of Fleury read *castellum* (“castle”) for *castrum*. The name is also transmitted as *Donincum* and *Donineum*.]

Count Heribertus, having had the Lotharingians joined to him through Gislebertus, duke of Lotharingia, went against the king. A truce was arranged until the Kalends of October, and both sides withdrew. Meanwhile some of Heribertus’s retainers, setting out from the city of Reims, captured and destroyed a certain castle of Hugo situated on the Vidula, called Braina [Braine-sur-Vesle], which Hugo himself had taken from the bishop of Rouen.  
[Note: One witness omits “through Gislebertus, duke of Lotharingia,” because a new page begins there. One witness omits the words “setting out from the city of Reims.” Another omits “situated on the Vidula.” Two witnesses omit “which Hugo himself had taken from the bishop of Rouen.”]

King Rodulfus sent letters from Reims to the clergy and people requesting that a prelate be elected. They replied that they could not do so without preserving their own elected candidate and the election they had made.  
[Note: The source has *praesulis*, “of a prelate,” rather than specifically “of an archbishop.”]

Count Heribertus went to Heinricus and entrusted himself to him. The king’s army and Hugo’s army then ravaged the Laonnois and the Rémois. King Rodulfus, proceeding to Attigny, sent Hugo to Heinricus. After Heinricus had received hostages and security had been agreed, he withdrew across the Rhine.  
[Note: One witness reads *opsidibus* for *obsidibus* (“hostages”).]

Meanwhile the Bretons who had remained under the authority of the Northmen in Cornouaille, being subject to Gaul, rose against those who had occupied their land. During the very festival of Saint Michael they are said to have killed all the Northmen living among them, after first killing their leader, whose name was Felecan.  
[Note: One witness has *corna* for *Cornu*. Another transmits the phrase concerning the leader merely as *f.*, an abbreviated or incomplete reading.]

King Rodulfus, together with Hugo, Boso, and his other men, besieged the city of Reims. At last, in the third week after the beginning of the siege, he entered it when those who were in the city opened it to him.  
[Note: One witness reads *obsidet* (“besieges”) rather than *obsident* (“they besiege”). Two witnesses preserve a fuller order of the sentence: “After the siege had lasted three weeks, and after they had opened the city to him, he entered.” A historical witness adds: “Some soldiers of the church joined him.”]

He had Artoldus, a monk from the monastery of Saint Remigius, ordained there as prelate. Artoldus had already, in that same year, left Heribertus and passed over to Hugo.  
[Note: One witness has *Artaldum* for *Artoldum*.]

The king also captured Bovo, bishop of Châlons, who had defected from him together with Heribertus, and handed him over to Hugo to be kept in custody. He granted Bovo’s bishopric to the cleric Milo.  
[Note: The phrase *episcopatum ipsius* means “his bishopric,” that is, Bovo’s. Two witnesses read *tradidit* (“handed over”) rather than *tribuit* (“granted”).]

He then proceeded to Laon and besieged Heribertus, who had shut himself up there with his men. He did not continue the siege long but requested permission to leave. After time had been granted him, he withdrew, leaving his wife in the fortress that he himself had built below Laon. The king later required greater labor and delay to capture it. Having scarcely at last gained possession of it, he returned to Burgundy, setting out to meet the Aquitanians, who were in disagreement.

Meanwhile Incon, a Northman who was staying on the Loire, invaded Brittany with his men. After defeating—and, according to another reading, expelling—and killing the Bretons, he took possession of the region.  
[Note: One witness omits “and expelling.” Another witness supplies the variant *vel ejectis* (“or expelled”) in this place.]

## Year 932

King Rodulfus, having returned to Burgundy, recovered certain castles of Gislebertus and Ricardus, who had defected from him.  
[Note: One witness has the singular *desciuerat* (“had defected”) rather than the plural *desciverant*.]

Airardus, bishop of Noyon, died. A certain cleric of that city, who wished to become bishop, secretly admitted Count Adelelmus into the city at night by climbing over the wall. In the morning the local soldiers expelled from the city gathered a number of men from the suburbs and attacked the city. While the citizens who had remained inside the walls gave their support, some entered after burning the gate and others through a window of the church.

Adelelmus fled into the church and was killed beside the altar together with some who had entered with him. The citizens recovered the city.  
[Note: One witness reads *civitatem* (“the city”) where the text has *civitate* (“in the city”).]

Count Heribertus, having recovered the castle of Hamme [Ham in Picardy], captured Ebrardus, the brother of Erluinus, who held it.  
[Note: The name appears as *Hebrardus* and *Herluinus* in different witnesses.]

King Rodulfus, having spoken with Hugo, received Bishop Bovo back into his favor and restored to him his bishopric, namely Châlons.

Waltbertus, abbot of Corbie, was ordained bishop for the people of Noyon.

King Rodulfus, having recovered Gislebertus, returned from Burgundy to Francia. There he took possession of the abbey of Saint Medard, which Heribertus held, and returned to Burgundy.  
[Note: One witness reads *abacia* for *abbatia*, “abbey.”]

Hugo, besieging Amiens with certain bishops of Francia—a city held by Heribertus’s loyalists—and repeatedly attacking it in battle, finally withdrew after taking hostages, and surrounded the fortress of Saint-Quentin with a siege.

Milo, who was plundering the bishopric of Châlons, was excommunicated by Artoldus the archbishop and the other bishops of the diocese of Reims.  
[Note: One witness reads *Artaldo* for *Artoldo*; another uses that form almost consistently.]

After Hugo had besieged the castle of Saint-Quentin for two months, he finally captured it when the townsmen surrendered. On the day after he entered it, a certain cripple in the church itself was raised upright.

Ragemundus and Ermingaudus, princes of Gothia, entrusted themselves to King Rodulfus. Lupus also, called Acinarius, a Basque, who was said to have a horse more than a hundred years old but still exceptionally strong, did so.  
[Note: Hugo of Fleury gives the names as Raimundus and Herminigaldus. One witness reads *Lacinarius* for *Acinarius*.]

At Hugo’s invitation, Gislebertus with the Lotharingians besieged Perrona. There, in frequent engagements, many Lotharingians were killed. The survivors, unable to capture the fortification, withdrew, after Duke Gislebertus had first spoken with King Rodulfus through the mediation of Hugo.  
[Note: The place-name appears as *Parrona* and *Perona* in different witnesses.]

King Rodulfus and Hugo besieged Hammum, Heribertus’s castle, and then left it after taking hostages.

After Gozpertus, bishop of Laon, had died, Ingramnus, dean of the monastery of Saint Medard, was ordained bishop of Laon.  
[Note: The names appear as *Gozbertus* and *Ingrannus* in other witnesses.]

Boso, the king’s brother, and Bernuinus, bishop of Verdun, raged against one another with fires and plundering.  
[Note: Two witnesses read *bacchantur* (“rage” or “run riot”) rather than *bachantur*. A historical note adds: “For this reason the city itself suffered greatly.” Another historical witness identifies Boso as “the king of Gaul, which is called long-haired Gaul.”]

Heribertus went across the Rhine to Heinricus.

## Year 933

The envoys of the church of Reims, Giso and Amalricus, returning from Rome, brought the pallium to Archbishop Artoldus. They reported that Pope John, son of Maria, also called Marocia, was being held in custody by his brother, named Albericus, who was also keeping their mother Marocia confined and held Rome against King Hugo.  
[Note: The name Marocia appears as *Matrocia* in one witness.]

The Hungarians divided into three groups. One group went toward Italy; another invaded Heinricus’s territory across the Rhine. Against them Heinricus marched with the Bavarians, Saxons, and certain other peoples subject to him, and slaughtered them all. Thirty-six thousand of them are reported to have been killed, apart from those whom the river swallowed and those who were captured alive.  
[Note: One witness reads *terra* (“land”) rather than *terram*. Two witnesses read *omnibus* (“all”) rather than “certain others.” Two witnesses omit the number, but there can be no doubt that XXXVI—thirty-six—should be read. The text has *internetionem* in one witness and *internicionem* in two.]

Richarius, bishop of Tongeren, destroyed a certain castle of Count Bernardus, which Bernardus himself had built at Arches in the pagus of Porcien. He did so because it was situated on the land of his church.  
[Note: The place-name appears as *Archeias* in two witnesses.]

Vienne was surrendered to King Rodulfus by those who held it. Willelmus, prince of the Northmen, entrusted himself to the same king. The king also granted him land situated along the coast of Brittany.

King Rodulfus besieged for six weeks Heribertus’s stronghold called Castellum-Theoderici. Afterward Walo, who guarded it, entrusted himself to Queen Emma, and the castle was left under her protection and care.  
[Note: The name appears as *Teoderici* in two witnesses.]

Waldricus, bishop of Auxerre, died, and Wido, archdeacon of that place, obtained the bishopric.  
[Note: One witness omits “of that place”; another supplies the form *Widolus*.]

While the aforementioned fortress was being besieged, a synod was held. Several prelates of Francia and Burgundy assembled, presided over by Lord Artoldus, bishop of Reims, and Lord Teutolus, bishop of Tours. At that time Lord Artoldus also ordained Hildegarius bishop of the city of Beauvais.  
[Note: The name of the bishop of Tours appears as *Teutolo*, *Teudolus*, and *Teutilo* in different witnesses and in the History of Reims. One witness has *ordinavit* (“ordained”) instead of *ordinat*.]

Odo, the son of Heribertus, holding the fortress of Hamme, ravaged the Soissonnais and Noyonnais with plundering and fires.

Heribertus, his father, came secretly to Saint-Quentin. On the third day after his arrival he captured the castle by fighting, since the townsmen did not resist and only Hugo’s guards opposed him. Heribertus captured them, but after receiving their oath, he released them there, leaving some of his own associates to protect the town.

When Hugo heard this, he immediately arrived and recovered the castle. He seized a certain noble cleric named Treduinus, who had been left there by Heribertus, and hanged him together with certain others. He inflicted various mutilations on several others.  
[Note: One witness reads *Tedu[inus]* for *Treduinus*. Another says explicitly that he “killed him by hanging.”]

Then, setting out with Lord Artoldus the bishop, he captured without difficulty a stronghold called Rauga [Roge], as Heribertus’s guards surrendered it. King Hugo of Italy besieged Rome.

The Saracens occupied the Alpine passes and plundered all the neighboring places.  
[Note: Two witnesses read *atque* (“and also”) rather than *et* (“and”).]

Archbishop Artoldus ordained Fulbertus bishop of the city of Cambrai.

Heribertus recovered Castellum-Theoderici, situated on the River Materna, after certain men whom Walo had left there as its guards surrendered it to him. Having arranged the guards, he withdrew.

When Hugo heard this, he immediately arranged to besiege the same castle.  
[Note: Two witnesses read *quantociens* (“as soon as possible” or “as often”) rather than *quantotius* (“as quickly as possible”).]

## Year 934

King Rodulfus and Count Hugo besieged the aforementioned fortress. At last, in the fourth month, Walo and his men climbed the walls at night while the guards were sleeping, and part of the town was captured. The citadel, however, safer than the town, was retained by Heribertus’s loyalists. When the king’s soldiers pressed them, they soon afterward surrendered hostages, and the siege was abandoned.  
[Note: One witness reads *obsidentibus* for the corrupt form transmitted in the text. Another reads *regis* (“of the king”) rather than *regiis* (“royal”).]

At Reims, in the church of the blessed Mother of God, during the solemnity of the Lord’s Annunciation, while the sacred Masses were being celebrated there by Bishop Artoldus, a certain young man who habitually crawled because the tendons behind his knees were contracted was suddenly released. The joints of his knees and legs extended, and he stood up; testing his step, he recovered the footsteps long forgotten.  
[Note: One witness omits “the blessed Mother of God.” Another has *sacrarum* (“of sacred things”) rather than *sacrae* (“sacred”). One reads *recipit* or *recepit* (“recovers”) rather than *repetit* (“retrieves” or “repeats”) the forgotten footsteps.]

Likewise, in the church of Saint Hilary before the Gate of Mars, a certain blind man named Paulus received his sight. He had first been warned in a dream to come to that place, where he was to receive light.  
[Note: One witness omits “to come to that place.”]

The king, again together with Hugo, resumed the abandoned siege, since Heribertus had disregarded the hostages his own men had given.  
[Note: One witness reads “the hostages whom his men had seen” rather than “the hostages whom his men had given.”]

Heinricus sent Gislebertus and Ebrardus, together with the bishops of the kingdom of Lotharingia, to King Rodulfus on behalf of Heribertus. After Castellum-Theoderici had been returned to the king, Hamme and Perrona were granted to Heribertus until the Kalends of October.  
[Note: The name Ebrardus appears as *Eubrardus* in one witness. The place-name Perrona is also transmitted as *Parrona*.]

Arnulfus of Flanders took as his wife Heribertus’s daughter, who had formerly been pledged to him by mutual oaths. The phrase indicates that each had given an oath to the other.

Heribertus, gathering the crops in the Vermandois from those who had abandoned him or to whom Hugo had given that land, had them brought to Perrona.

At Reims, fiery armies were seen moving across the sky, together with what appeared to be a fiery serpent and certain darts flying on the morning before the light arose, on the day before the Ides of October. A plague immediately followed, afflicting human bodies with various diseases.  
[Note: One witness omits “were seen.”]

A certain deacon of Verdun named Adelmarus, overcome by illness, seemed to have lost his breath. Before he was placed on a bier, however, he returned to life and rose so strong that he seemed to himself to have suffered no illness at all.  
[Note: One witness has *perpessum* rather than *perpessus*; Hugo of Verdun preserves the same phrase.]

He testified that he had seen various places of punishment and refreshment, and that he himself had been assigned to a place of punishment. Through the prayers of the Mother of God and with blessed Martin interceding, he was restored to the present life in order to perform penance.

[Col. 0446D–0448C] Hugo of Verdun continues:

“For this reason, encouraged by his example, certain canons of blessed Mary of Verdun abandoned the world. Since there was no community of monks in that same city—for clerics served in the churches of Saint Peter and Saint Vitonus—they went to Toul and, after changing their habit in the monastery of Saint Aper, strove to abandon the world and be incorporated into Christ the Lord as faithful members into their head.

This caused the bishop great sorrow, as it did the remaining canons and the leading men of the people, because they would have preferred them to serve in that same bishopric rather than depart for another. Nevertheless, through their good and praiseworthy efforts and examples, the devotion to the monastic rule and the fervor of the order were restored in that monastery and in certain others throughout the kingdom of Lotharingia.”

Gislebertus came into Francia with the Lotharingians to aid Heribertus, as though he intended to besiege the town of Saint-Quentin. Before he reached it, however, Hugo’s envoys came to meet him and arranged peace between Hugo and Heribertus, each side giving an oath, until the month of May. The Lotharingians then returned to their own lands.

The devotion to the monastic rule was restored in certain monasteries throughout the kingdom of Lotharingia. Queen Emma also died.

## Year 935

King Rodulfus besieged and captured a certain castle called Viriliacum, belonging to Gosfridus, which certain Aquitanians held against him; he restored it to Gosfridus. He then returned to Francia and sent Gosfridus across the Rhine to Heinricus.  
[Note: One witness has *Gosfredus* rather than *Gosfridus*.]

While this king was staying at Laon, a riot arose on Easter Day itself between the king’s men and the bishop’s soldiers. Several people were wounded or killed there, not only laymen but also certain clerics.

For this reason the king held a council at Soissons with the leading men of the kingdom. He then spoke with Heinricus’s envoys and hastened to meet him. King Rodulfus of the Jura was also present. After friendship had been agreed between them, they also reconciled Heribertus and Hugo, restoring to Heribertus certain of his possessions.

Heinricus likewise, having received Boso, restored to him a large part of the land he had previously held.

The Hungarians spread through Burgundy, ravaging with plunder, fires, and killings. They did not continue for long, however, and, learning of King Rodulfus’s arrival, crossed over into Italy.

Hugo of Verdun continues:

“When Bishop Herveus died, Romundus was appointed in his place under King Rodulfus. He destroyed the abbey of Colticum, built the castle of Coltica, and likewise constructed Curense and Petraepertusum; he gave his sons and daughters the goods of the churches and the castles he had built. After perpetrating many evils, he was scourged by Saint George and died.”

Archbishop Artoldus ordained a certain monk named Wifredus bishop of the church of Thérouanne.  
[Note: One witness reads *Umfredus* for *Wifredus*; another has *Tarvianensis* for the church’s name.]

King Rodulfus besieged the castle of Dijon, which Count Boso had captured and his associates held.

The Lotharingians, together with certain counts from Saxony—namely, Heribertus’s friends—came with a large army as though to meet Hugo. Because Hugo refused to return the castle of Saint-Quentin to Heribertus, they besieged that stronghold. Having pressed it in battle, they finally received it through the surrender of its defenders and destroyed it.

As they were preparing to besiege Laon, they returned to their own lands at the command of King Rodulfus.

Meanwhile Boso, King Rodulfus’s brother, died during the expedition for the siege of the castle of Saint-Quentin. He was carried to Saint Remigius and buried there.

King Rodulfus lay seriously ill throughout the autumn.

The Northmen who were plundering the Berry region were attacked in battle by the people of Berry and Tours and were killed.

A synod of seven bishops was held at Saint Macra [Fismes], with Lord Artoldus the archbishop presiding. In it, plunderers and those who had seized ecclesiastical property were summoned to correction.  
[Note: Two witnesses read *correptionem* (“reproof” or “discipline”) rather than *correctionem* (“correction”).]

## Year 936

Ingramnus, bishop of the church of Laon, died. At nearly the same time King Rodulfus died and was buried at Sens, at Saint Columba, whose church had shortly before been burned through the faction of certain men.

The Bretons, returning from overseas regions under the protection of King Alstanus, reclaimed their land.  
[Note: One witness reads *revertuntur* (“they return”), while another has *revertentes* (“returning”), as on the following page.]

Count Hugo sent across the sea to summon Ludowicus, son of Karolus, to assume the kingship. King Alstanus, Ludowicus’s maternal uncle, after first receiving an oath from the envoys of the Franks, sent him to Francia with certain bishops and other loyal men.

Hugo and the other leading men of Francia went out to meet him. As soon as he had left the ship, they entrusted themselves to him on the shore sands at Boulogne, as had been agreed on both sides. From there they led him to Laon. Enriched with the royal blessing, he was anointed and crowned by Lord Artoldus the archbishop, in the presence of the leading men of the kingdom and more than twenty bishops.

The bishopric of Laon was given to Rodulfus, a priest of that place, unanimously elected by the citizens. Lord Artoldus consecrated him bishop.

[Col. 0448C] A historical continuation states: “In the other sees of the diocese of Reims also, except Châlons and Amiens, he ordained various bishops.”

The king and Hugo went to Burgundy and besieged the city of the Lingones, which Hugo, the king’s brother, had captured for Rodulfus. When those who seemed to be guarding it fled, they recovered it without battle. After receiving hostages from the bishops and leading men of Burgundy, they came to Paris.

During those same days King Heinricus died, and a dispute over the kingdom arose among his sons. In the end, supreme authority fell to the eldest, named Otto.  
[Note: One witness regularly has *Ottonus* or *Ottoni* for Otto.]

On the fourteenth night of the moon, on the second day before the Nones of September, the moon, covered in a bloody color, seemed scarcely to illuminate the night.  
[Note: One witness reads *nocte* (“by night”) rather than *noctem* (“the night”).]

After Pope John, the brother of the patrician Albericus, died, a certain servant of God named Leo was established as pope at Rome.  
[Note: One witness omits the word “patrician.”]

King Hugo of Italy attempted to capture Rome. After his army had been afflicted by hunger and the death of its horses, he finally made peace with Albericus, giving him his daughter as a wife, and abandoned the siege. Later, having discovered certain men—reportedly his brother Boso’s—plotting against him, he deceitfully captured that same brother and sent him into custody.  
[Note: One witness transmits the phrase “certain men of his brother” only incompletely, with the words *fratris sui* omitted.]

The Saracens went into Alamannia to plunder. On their return they killed many who were making for Rome.

Hugo, son of Rotbertus, made peace with Hugo, son of Richardus, after dividing Burgundy between them.

Adelelmus, bishop of Senlis, died.

## Year 937

Bernuinus, from the monastery of Saint Crispinus, was ordained bishop of Senlis.

After Waltbertus, bishop of Noyon, had died, Transmarus, provost of the monastery of Saint Vedastus, succeeded him.  
[Note: An appended source note records that Waltbertus died on the seventh day before the Kalends of January. The list of the abbots of Corbie indicates that Waltbertus had been transferred from that monastery to the see of Noyon. One witness calls the successor *Fransmarus*.]

King Ludovicus, separating himself from the administration of Prince Hugo, received his mother at Laon.

Hugo made peace with Heribertus. Heribertus, recovering the castle called Theoderici after Walo opened it to him, cast Walo into chains once Walo had become his man.  
[Note: Two witnesses read *pacatur* (“is reconciled” or “makes peace”) for *paccatur*.]

A part of the sky seemed to burn, and a pursuit by the Hungarians followed from that same direction across Francia. Villages and fields were devastated, houses and basilicas were burned, and a multitude of captives was carried away.

Nevertheless, they were unable to burn certain churches even after applying fire to them. They could not set fire to the church of Saint Macra, although two stacks of grain, which almost touched its walls, had been burned.

[Col. 0449C–0450B] Flodoardus relates the matter as follows in *History of Reims*, Book II, chapter 3:

“When recently these lands of Gaul, driven by our sins, were handed over to be torn apart by the swords of the Hungarians, certain barbarians entered the monastery of Saint Basolus. Since the clerics had already fled to the city with the relics of their patron, they found the dwellings of the monastery almost empty of people. There they established their camp and began to return there from every direction after plundering.

One of them, seeing gilded metal glittering in the little tower of the church bells, greedy for gold and money, climbed onto the roof of the basilica. As he tried to tear apart the little tower, he suddenly slipped and fell to the ground, dying with his limbs broken.

Another tried to climb upon the altar of that church, consecrated in honor of blessed Martin. When he placed his hand upon the horn of the altar, his hand adhered so firmly to the marble that afterward it could not be pulled away by any means. Since his companions refused to leave him there, they cut away with axes a portion of the stone around his hand and led him away with them, unwillingly carrying the piece of marble that remained attached to his hand.

According to the report of the captives who returned, he carried that stone all the way to his own land, his arm already withered, proclaiming that this had happened through the power of Basolus.”

In the church of Saint Basolus, when one of the Hungarians tried to climb upon the altar and placed his hand on it, his hand adhered to the stone of the altar. It could not be pulled away at all until the other Hungarians cut away the stone of the altar around his hand. Thus, to everyone’s amazement, the pagan was forced to carry away the part of the stone that had adhered to his hand.  
[Note: One witness reads *lapidibus* (“stones”) in the plural rather than *lapidi* (“stone”). Another reads *perferre* (“carry away”) rather than *proferre* (“bring forth”). Hugo of Verdun also preserves the account.]

A certain priest from Bovo’s estate—for that is what the village of his church is called—named Adalgarius, was captured by them and carried away as far as the pagus of Berry. While he was in chains and iron fetters, a vision appeared at night to one of his fellow captives. She was commanded to tell the priest to flee, so that he might see himself released; and at the same time, in accordance with the vision, his chain was unlocked.

But the priest feared death, which the barbarian often threatened him with if he caught him attempting to flee. He therefore fastened the chain around his feet again, searched for the lock that had sprung from the fetter, and tried to secure his bonds again with the lock, not daring to escape.

The next night the aforementioned captive again had a vision, strengthening her to urge the priest to undertake his flight. His bonds were again released. At last the priest, encouraged to do so, fled. He hid for several days in a marsh, and, when he learned that the barbarians had passed by, finally returned to his homeland.

He told us that during this captivity he had seen a certain monk of the monastery of Orbais named Hucbaldus, whom the pagans often tried to kill but could not cut into his flesh. Therefore they said that he was a god.  
[Note: Flodoardus also narrates this in *History of Reims*, Book II, chapter 10. In witnesses 2, 2a, 3a, and 3b, intervening text is absent after the variant “the Bretons began to say”; that text is preserved in Hugo of Verdun.]

As this priest reports, one man saw Hucbaldus placed naked in the middle and attacked from every side with arrows; yet not even the surface of his skin was wounded. The arrows rebounded from his body, as from diamond, and no mark of a blow appeared on his skin. The priest also says that he saw him struck naked with a sword with all the attacker’s strength, yet his flesh nevertheless remained unharmed.  
[Note: One witness corrects *ullus* (“no one”) to *ullum* (“no mark” in the phrase as construed).]

The Bretons, after returning to their own places following a long period of exile, fought frequent battles with the Northmen who had occupied the land adjoining theirs. They prevailed in many encounters and recovered the places that had been occupied.

Rodulfus, king of the Jura and of Cisalpine Gaul, died. His young son Chonradus succeeded him in the kingdom.  
[Note: One witness reads *Conradus* for *Chonradus*.]

Abbo, bishop of Soissons, died. Wido, son of Fulco of Anjou and a canon of Saint Martin of Tours, obtained his bishopric.  
[Note: One witness has *Folconis* for *Fulconis*.]

## Year 938

King Ludowicus captured by force a certain castle called Montiniacum [Montigny in the pagus of Soissons], which a certain robber named Serlus held while practicing brigandage. At the request of Lord Artoldus the archbishop, he spared Serlus’s life, but destroyed the town.  
[Note: One witness reads *quoque* (“also”) rather than *vero* (“indeed” or “however”).]

At Hugo’s request, he received Heribertus back into peace.

He recovered Tusciacum [Tully] on the Meuse, together with the other villages belonging to it, which his father had given to his mother by right of dowry and which Count Rotgarius held. Rotgarius returned them when the king sought to recover them by force.  
[Note: One witness reads *Rotgerius* for *Rotgarius*.]

On his return from there, the king forcibly recovered the castle of Corbenacum [Corbeny], which his father had given to Saint Remigius and which Heribertus had occupied. The monks had entrusted it to the king. He allowed Heribertus’s men who were in it to depart after Lord Artoldus the archbishop requested it.  
[Note: One witness has *commissam* (“entrusted,” feminine) instead of *commissum* (“entrusted,” neuter), agreeing it differently with the implied noun.]

Prince Hugo, son of Rotbertus, married the sister of Otto, the king beyond the Rhine, the daughter of Heinricus.

King Ludowicus, traveling toward the coastal regions, attempted to restore a certain castle and harbor on the sea called Guisum [Wissant, west of Calais].  
[Note: One witness reads *castrumque* (“and a castle”) rather than *castrum portumque* (“a castle and harbor”). Two witnesses read *quod* (“which,” neuter) rather than *quem* (“which,” masculine).]

While he was staying with Arnulfus, Heribertus’s men captured, through the treachery of a certain Wipertus, a castle of the church of Reims called Causostem [perhaps La Chaussée], situated on the River Materna and built by Bishop Artoldus. They carried away Raegibertus, who commanded that castle.  
[Note: One witness reads *Wilbertus* for *Wipertus*. A historical note identifies Raegibertus as Ragenbertus, a cousin of Bishop Artoldus.]

They also repeatedly ravaged the surrounding villages.

II, cap. 3, haec ita narrat: Quando nuper hae Galliarum patriae, [Col. 0449D] peccatis nostris impellentibus, Hungarorum gladiis dilacerandae sunt traditae, quidam barbarorum sancti Basoli monasterium ingressi, dum clerici jam cum patroni sui pigneribus ad civitatem [Col. 0450A] confugissent, habitacula coenobii hominibus pene vacua repererunt, ibique metatum suum constituentes, huc undecunque praedatu reverti coeperunt. Quorum quidam in ecclesiae signorum terricula, deaurata conspiciens relucere metalla, cupidus auri pecuniae, tectum conscendit basilicae, nisusque dissipare turriculam, subito delapsus ad terram corruit, membrisque confractis interiit. Alius horum super aram ipsius ecclesiae, in honore beati Martini consecratam, conatus ascendere, dum manum supra cornu altaris apposuisset, ipsa manus ejus ita inhaesit marmori, ut nullo modo ab eo postea potuisset avelli. Et quia hic eum sui noluerunt relinquere, partem lapinis circa manum ipsius bipennibus abscindentes, eum secum particulam marmoris, quae manui ejus adhaeserat, invite ferentem deduxerunt. Qui etiam, ut captivi qui reversi sunt referunt, usque ad terram suam, arente jam brachio, hunc lapidem ferens, et Basoli [Col. 0450B] virtute factum proclamans, reversus est. — Flodoard, *History of Reims* II.3 supplies the retained miracle narrative; its full English translation appears in the main text at Cols. 0449C–0450B.

Meanwhile King Louis, summoned by Archbishop Artold [Note: [Col. 0451] “King Louis,” lines 2–3], returned and, entering Laon, besieged the new fortress recently built there by Heribert [Note: [Col. 0451] “which he had recently,” line 1; “by Heribert,” lines 1–3]. After undermining and overthrowing the wall with many siege engines [Note: [Col. 0451] “excavated” for “undermined,” line 1; “undermined,” line 2], he finally captured it with great difficulty. From there he went to meet Hugh, formerly the brother of King Rudolf, leaving Odo, Heribert’s son, who had most recently entrusted himself to him [Note: [Col. 0451] “recently,” line 3], behind to guard Laon.

Hugh, however, was sent ahead and came to the king [Note: [Col. 0451] “had come,” line 3], promising him friendship under oath. Gislebert, with the Lotharingians, came to Hugh and Heribert’s assistance against King Louis, and they captured the fortress of Pierrepont by force [Note: [Col. 0452] Pierrepont in the district of Laon]. Count Arnulf and Heribert obtained a delay between King Louis and Hugh, arranging peace by oath until the end of January [Note: [Col. 0451] absent in witness 2]. Thereupon King Louis [Note: [Col. 0451] “Louis,” line 3], on the advice [Note: [Col. 0451] absent in witness 2] of Odo [Note: [Col. 0451] “Hodowin,” witnesses 2–3] and Gerard, who had abandoned Rudolf, bishop of Laon, and gone over to Hugh, seized and distributed the goods or treasures found at Laon.

## 939

King Louis [Note: [Col. 0451] “Ludovicus,” line 3, frequently elsewhere] went to meet Hugh, son of Richard. Returning with him from Burgundy, he proceeded against Hugh, son of Robert, and William [Note: [Col. 0451] “of William,” witness 2], prince of the Normans. Because William had recently devastated certain estates of Count Arnulf with plunder and fires [Note: [Col. 0451] “plunder and with certain fires,” witness 2], he was excommunicated by the bishops who were with the king, together with Heribert [Note: [Col. 0451] “Heribert,” line 3], who stubbornly retained certain towns and estates of Saint Remigius after invading them. Hugh, giving hostages, made peace until the Kalends of June.

The Lotharingians abandoned their king, Otto [Note: [Col. 0451] “their king,” lines 2–3], and came to King Louis, who delayed receiving them because of the friendship that had been arranged between them through the envoys of Otto himself and Count Arnulf.

Count Arnulf captured Erluin’s coastal fortress called Monasteriolum, after a certain traitor surrendered it to him, and sent Erluin’s wife across the sea with her sons to King Athelstan [Note: [Col. 0451] “Athelstan,” line 3]. Before long Erluin gathered a considerable force of Normans, recovered the fortress by fighting, killed some of Arnulf’s soldiers whom he found inside, and kept others alive in order to recover his wife.

The Lotharingians again came to King Louis. The leading men of that kingdom—namely Duke Gislebert and Counts Otto, Isaac, and Theoderic [Note: [Col. 0451] “Theoderic,” line 1, and frequently elsewhere]—entrusted themselves to the king [Note: [Col. 0451] absent in witness 2]. The bishops, however [Note: [Col. 0451] absent in witness 2], because King Otto [Note: [Col. 0451] absent in witness 2] was holding their hostages with him, delayed entrusting themselves to King Louis. King Otto, having crossed the Rhine, toured the kingdom of Lotharingia and devastated many places with fires and plunder.

A fleet of Englishmen, sent by their king Athelstan to assist King Louis, crossed the sea [Note: [Col. 0451] “by sea,” witnesses 2–3] and plundered all the places bordering on the sea in the land of the Morini. Having accomplished none of the business for which they had come, they crossed the sea again [Note: [Col. 0451] “having rowed back,” witness 2] and returned to their own lands.

King Otto held a conference with Hugh, Heribert, Arnulf, and William, prince of the Normans. After receiving from them the oaths of their agreement, he returned across the Rhine.

Meanwhile King Louis went to the district of Verdun [Note: [Col. 0453] “Verdun,” witnesses 2–3], where certain bishops of the kingdom of Lotharingia became his men. From there he proceeded to Alsace, spoke with Hugh of Italy, received certain Lotharingians who came to him, and drove some of King Otto’s loyal men across the Rhine. Then he returned to Laon and expelled Rudolf, bishop of Laon [Note: [Col. 0453] thus witnesses 2 and Richer; witness 1 reads “bishop of Verdun”], accused of treachery, from the fortress. He also deprived Rudolf’s men of the episcopal property and gave it to his own men.

Duke Gislebert of the Lotharingians went across the Rhine to plunder. While returning, with the Saxons pursuing him, he is said to have leapt into the Rhine with his horse [Note: [Col. 0453] “to have leapt apart,” witness 2]. There he was violently killed by the waves, and afterward, so it is reported, could not be found. Some, however, say that fishermen found and buried him, and concealed him because of the ornaments among his spoils.

King Louis, having returned to the kingdom of Lotharingia, married Gerberga, Gislebert’s widow, namely the sister of King Otto [Note: [Col. 0453] Hugo of Verdun adds: “Otto—that is, Gislebert’s son—received the duchy”]. A gathering of various people traveling to Rome was attacked and destroyed by the Saracens [Note: [Col. 0453] “Saracens,” line 3, and frequently elsewhere]. The Bretons, fighting with the Normans, won a victory and are said to have captured a certain Norman fortress. Some of Arnulf’s men, plundering Erluin’s land, were killed by Erluin. King Otto, returning to the kingdom of Lotharingia, compelled nearly all the Lotharingians to return to him [Note: [Col. 0453] “compelled,” witness 3].

Hugh the White went with Heribert to confer with him. On their return they plundered certain lands belonging to the faithful of the church of Reims and burned some of them [Note: [Col. 0453] In the margin, in another hand, witness 1 has *autanda*, followed by the Greek numerals ΜΖ (47), incorrectly].

## 940

[Note: [Col. 0453] This is found only in the margin of witness 1: “Berengar, bishop of Verdun, is consecrated by Artold, archbishop of Reims.” In Hugo of Verdun these matters are related more fully.]

King Louis [Note: [Col. 0453] “Louis,” line 3] went to meet William, prince of the Normans. William came to him in the district of Amiens and entrusted himself to him. The king gave him the land that his father Charles had granted to the Normans, and from there proceeded against Hugh [Note: [Col. 0453] “against Hugh,” witnesses 2–3]. When Hugh refused to come to him, Louis returned to Laon.

The king gave Archbishop Artold [Note: [Col. 0453] “bishop,” witness 2], and through him the church of Reims [Note: [Col. 0453] absent in witness 2], by a royal charter, the mint of the city of Reims, to be possessed in perpetuity by right. He also granted the entire county of Reims to that church.

Archbishop Artold besieged the fortress of Causost [Col. 0454A]. On the fifth day, when King Louis arrived there, those inside surrendered and abandoned it. Soon afterward it was utterly overthrown and dismantled by those who had captured it.

Hugh’s envoys came to the king, and the king tried through them to work out peace between Archbishop Artold and Heribert. He then proceeded with Archbishop Artold to a certain castle held by Heriveus, nephew of the former Bishop Heriveus [Note: [Col. 0453] “archbishop,” witnesses 2–3], above the River Marne. From there Heriveus had been plundering the surrounding estates of the church of Reims. No sooner had the king accepted hostages from Heriveus [Note: [Col. 0453] “having accepted hostages from him,” witnesses 2–3] than he returned to Reims. On the following day he went to Saint Remigius, commended himself to the intercession of that saint, and promised to give a pound of silver annually as a pledge [Note: [Col. 0453] “each year,” witnesses 2–3]. He also gave the monks of that place a charter of immunity concerning the same castle.

Hugh, prince and son of Robert [Note: [Col. 0453] “the source of iniquity, Hugh the Great,” Hugh of Verdun; “Hugh V,” another reference], joined certain bishops of both France and Burgundy and, together with Count Heribert and William, prince of the Normans, besieged the city of Reims. On the sixth day of the siege [Note: [Col. 0453] “on the sixth,” witnesses 2–3], when almost the entire military force abandoned Archbishop Artold and went over to Heribert, Count Heribert entered the city [Note: [Col. 0453] absent in witness 3].

Archbishop Artold went to Saint Remigius at the summons of the nobles and bishops. There he was persuaded, or terrified, by the princes into renouncing the administration and authority of the episcopate. After being granted the abbey of Saint-Basle and the monastery of Avenay [Note: [Col. 0453] “Alvenay,” witness 3; [Col. 0454] Saint-Basle and Apenay], he withdrew to live at Saint-Basle [Note: [Col. 0453] “having lived,” witness 3].

[Note: [Col. 0454] [H. R. IV, 28] After spending eight years and seven months in the episcopate, and so forth.]

Hugh and Heribert, having spoken with certain Lotharingians, went with William to besiege Laon [Note: [Col. 0453] “and went with William,” witnesses 2–3]. They left at Reims Hugh the deacon, Heribert’s son, who had long before been summoned to the episcopate [Note: [Col. 0453] “from the episcopate,” witness 2] of that city [Note: [Col. 0453] “elected,” witness 1].

[Note: [Col. 0454] [H. R. IV, 28] In the third month after his return, he was ordained priest by Guido, bishop of Soissons, after completing fifteen years from the time he had been elected. During those years he had lived at Auxerre, occupied with literary studies under Guido, bishop of that city, by whom he had also been ordained deacon. For he had received the other lower orders at Reims from Abbo, bishop of Soissons.]

After six or seven weeks, King Louis returned from Burgundy. Taking Archbishop Artold with him, together with his relatives, whose benefices Count Heribert had taken away, he entered the Reims region. After crossing the River Aisne, he hurried to Laon.

When Hugh and Heribert learned this, they abandoned the siege of Laon and hastened by night to the fortress of Pierrepont. From there they went to meet King Otto. Joining him, they led him to Attigny, where, together with Count Rotger, they entrusted themselves to Otto [Note: [Col. 0455] “Otto,” witness 3].

King Louis entered Laon and provided his men with the necessities [Note: [Col. 0455] “his own men,” witness 2; “with necessities and provisions,” witness 3]. Then, with Hugh the Black and William of Poitiers, he returned to Burgundy.

King Otto [Note: [Col. 0455] Hugo of Fleury prefaces this: “Otto of the Trans-Rhine received the kingdom of Lotharingia from Louis,” and so forth] entrusted the kingdom of Lotharingia to his brother Henry. Then, with the multitude of various peoples whom he had brought with him [Note: [Col. 0455] “led away,” witnesses 2–3], he proceeded after Louis into Burgundy. He had with him Conrad, son of King Rudolf of Jura, whom he had captured by deceit, brought to himself, and continued to detain for a long time.

After pitching camp above the Seine [Note: [Col. 0455] “over,” witnesses 2–3], Otto received hostages from Hugh, under oath that he would not harm Hugh or Heribert, who had submitted themselves to that Otto [Note: [Col. 0455] “to Otto,” witnesses 2–3]. Having done this, he returned to his own lands.

Hugh, Heribert’s son, was ordained priest at Reims by Guido, bishop of Soissons.

King Louis returned to Laon.

Finally, as I was preparing to visit the tomb of Saint Martin for the sake of prayer, I was detained by Count Heribert. Certain people secretly accused me before him of intending to leave for the harm of himself or his son [Note: [Col. 0455] “or for the harm of his son,” witnesses 2–3].

[Note: [Col. 0455] [H. R. IV, 28] And because I refused to entrust myself to this man elected by us, not knowing whether it pleased God that he should be our bishop. And so forth.]

He had me kept under guard, after taking from me the possessions that I held from the episcopate, together with the church that I governed at Cormicy [Note: [Col. 0456] Cormicy]. Thus I was detained for five full months.

[Note: [Col. 0455–0456] [H. R. IV, 28] By order of the count I was detained partly under free custody among our brothers. It happened, through the intercession of my lady, the blessed Mother of God, that on the very day of the conception and Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ I was released from custody. On the third day, namely the sixth day before the Kalends of April, when the Lord rose from the dead, I left and went with our aforementioned elect to the city of Soissons. There the bishops of this diocese, meeting with the princes Hugh and Heribert, discussed what ought to be done concerning Hugh’s episcopal ordination. They decided, at the request of certain sons of the church of Reims, both clerics and laymen, that he should be ordained, his supporters asserting that Artold had not been elected at all, but had been introduced by violence, and had renounced episcopal authority. Thereupon Prince Hugh took me by the hand and entrusted me to this Hugh, his nephew, for good treatment. He gave me the church of Saint Mary situated at Colridus, and also restored the land that his father had taken from me, adding another portion in the aforementioned village.]

King Louis attacked the fortress of Pierrepont by force and, after taking hostages, withdrew from it. Then he went into the kingdom of Lotharingia with Archbishop Artold and his other loyal men. King Otto also crossed the Rhine and came against him, but their loyal men arranged a truce between them.

A certain poor little virgin girl from a village called Lavenna, named Flothildis, had clearly become accustomed, while awake and in the spirit, to seeing visions of the saints, and she foretold certain future events [Note: [Col. 0455] “had come to see,” witness 2; “affirmed,” witness 3].

[Note: [Col. 0456] These visions are recorded in manuscript 1.]

She died the following year on the very night of the Nativity of the Lord. This year, formations of various colors were seen in the sky on a Sunday night in December [Note: [Col. 0455] “December,” witnesses 2–3].

A gathering of people from overseas and of Gauls, traveling to Rome, returned, with some of them having been killed by the Saracens. They could not cross the Alps because of the Saracens who had occupied the village of the monastery of Saint Maurice.

## 941

Gerland, archbishop of Sens, was driven from his city by Frotmund, whom Hugh the White [Note: [Col. 0455] “the abbot,” witness 3] had placed in charge of that city. Gerland was blamed because he had favored Walo, in the name of Count Heribert, who had expelled Frotmund or his men from the aforesaid city.

Count Heribert summoned a synod to settle the dispute between his son Hugh [Note: [Col. 0455] absent in witness 1 and “and Hugh,” witness 3] and Archbishop Artold. Hugh, however, obstructed it and worked to prevent the assembly from becoming an occasion for gathering support and aid for King Louis; therefore they abandoned the meeting.

As King Louis was going to Burgundy, he discovered that Count Rotger had by chance pitched camp near him. Attacking him, Louis captured him together with those who were with him on the River Marne and took him with him into Burgundy [Note: [Col. 0455] “Rotger,” witness 1].

Counts Hugh and Heribert summoned the bishops of the diocese of Reims. Meeting at Soissons in the church of Saints Crispin and Crispinian, they discussed the condition of the episcopate of Reims, deciding [Note: [Col. 0455] “and they decided,” witnesses 2–3]—after clerics and noble laymen complained that the see had long been vacant—that, since Bishop Artold had sworn that he would never again involve himself in that episcopate [Note: [Col. 0455] “intervene,” witness 1; Hugo V], he should not return to govern it, but that Hugh, son of Count Heribert, who had previously been summoned to that episcopate [Note: [Col. 0455] corrected from “elected” to “summoned,” witness 1], should be ordained bishop at the request of the clergy and people.

There Hugh first summoned me from exile by his command [Note: [Col. 0455] The words from “and there” through “summoned” are absent in witnesses 2, 2a, and 3b]. Then the bishops went to Reims and consecrated our aforementioned elect as bishop at Saint Remigius [Note: [Col. 0455] absent in witness 2 and in part in witness 3].

Count Rotger was released by King Louis after giving hostages and surrendering the castle of Douai to Arnold.

The monastery of Saint Theoderic was illuminated by divine miracles.

The great cross of the church of Reims, covered with gold and adorned with precious gems, was secretly taken away from that same church.

The canons of Montfaucon [Note: [Col. 0457] Montfaucon], oppressed by the heavy-handedness of the bishop of Verdun [Note: [Col. 0457] “as they asserted,” according to Hugo V], abandoned their monastery and carried the body of their patron Saint Balderic to Reims.

King Louis, going to Burgundy, reconciled Count Rotger with Hugh the Black and Gislebert. Returning from there to Laon, he expelled Arnold and his brother Landric from the same castle, accusing them of treachery, and gave the county of Laon to Rotger [Note: [Col. 0457] “Rotger,” witness 1]. When he learned that Hugh the White was hurrying to besiege Laon, he returned to Burgundy with Bishop Artold and Count Rotger.

While he was staying near the castle of Vitry [Note: [Col. 0457] “Vitry,” witness 2; “Victoriacum,” witness 3], Hugh and Heribert besieged Laon. The king gathered as many men as he could from every quarter and came into the district of Porcien. When Hugh and Heribert heard that the king was approaching them, they abandoned the siege and hurried against him. Attacking the king’s unsuspecting army, they struck down some and put the rest to flight.

The king himself, led away by his men with only a few companions and forced to extricate himself from the battle, barely escaped, accompanied by Bishop Artold and Count Rotger.

Bishop Artold, having lost the possessions he had there, went to Hugh and Heribert [H. R. IV, 29 adds: “brought there by his friends”]. After giving the oaths they demanded of him, and after the abbeys of Saint-Basle and Avenay had been restored to him, together with the village of Vindenissa, and after peace had been arranged with Bishop Hugh, he went to Saint-Basle to live there.

Hugh and Heribert abandoned the siege of Laon.

A son was born to King Louis. The counts who had been sent ahead spoke with William, and soon returned to resume the siege of Laon, believing that the castle had been betrayed to them. Since nothing had been accomplished as they had supposed, they returned to their own lands.

King Louis was received at Vienne by Charles Constantine. The Aquitanians came to him and received him.

Hugh and Heribert, William and Arnulf, held a conference. From there Heribert went across the Rhine to King Otto [Note: [Col. 0457] “to the king,” witness 3].

## 942

Having secured the Aquitanians for himself, King Louis returned to Laon. He did not remain long [Note: [Col. 0457] “having remained,” witness 3], and, having obtained no peace, returned to Burgundy [Note: [Col. 0457] “returned,” witness 3].

A legate of Pope Stephen, named Damasus, who had been ordained bishop of Rome in order to carry out this legation, came to France. He brought letters from the Apostolic See to all the princes of the kingdom and to all the inhabitants of France and Burgundy, instructing them to receive their king Louis. If they neglected to do so and continued to pursue him with the hostile sword, he declared that the threat of excommunication would be proclaimed [Note: [Col. 0457] “proclaiming,” witnesses 2–3].

For this reason the bishops of the diocese of Reims conferred with Count Heribert and begged him [Note: [Col. 0457] “prayed,” witness 1] to intercede with Prince Hugh for the reception of the king.

Certain traitors were found and killed at Reims. Others, deprived of their church property, were driven from the city.

The envoys of the church of Reims returned from Rome, bringing a pallium sent by Pope Stephen to Bishop Hugh. An embassy also came with them to the princes of the kingdom, instructing them to receive King Louis [Note: [Col. 0457] “Louis,” witness 3] and then send their own envoys to Rome. If they failed to arrange this by the Nativity of the Lord, they were to understand that they would then be excommunicated.

Lord Odo, abbot, was laboring with King Hugh of Italy for peace between him and Alberic, the Roman patrician.

That same King Hugh was trying to drive the Saracens from their fortress at Fraxinetum.

Count Rotger, while serving as an envoy to William, prince of the Normans, on behalf of King Louis, died there.

William received King Louis royally at Rouen [Note: [Col. 0457] “Rouen,” witness 2]. William of Poitiers and the Bretons also came to the king with their princes.

With these men the king came to the River Oise [Note: [Col. 0457] absent in witness 2]. Hugh and Heribert, together with Duke Otto of the Lotharingians, destroyed the bridges and removed the boats. With the men they could gather, they settled on the opposite bank of the river.

After the dispute between them had been conducted through intermediaries, a truce was finally granted [Note: [Col. 0457] “then a truce was granted,” witnesses 2–3] from the middle of September until the middle of November, and hostages were taken on both sides. From the king’s side, Heribert’s younger son was given as hostage.

The king, William, and Hugh also sent hostages to King Otto through Duke Otto.

A great famine spread throughout France and Burgundy, and an exceedingly great mortality among cattle, so that very few such animals remained in those lands.

King Louis [Note: [Col. 0457] “Lodhuuicus,” witness 3] went to meet King Otto. They received each other amicably and confirmed their friendship by agreements [Note: [Col. 0457] “their mutual friendship,” witness 3].

Otto worked hard to establish peace between King Louis and Hugh and finally brought Hugh over to that king. Heribert likewise, together with his son of the same name, became a man of King Louis.

When the king returned, the bishops of the diocese of Reims came to him. He also received Rudolf [Note: [Col. 0457] “who had been seeking Rudolf,” witness 3] of Laon and restored his episcopate to him.

The venerable Lord Odo, abbot, restorer of many monasteries and renewer of the holy rule, died at Tours and was buried at Saint Julian [Note: [Col. 0457] thus witnesses 2–3; Hugo of Fleury reads “Saint Martin”; Hugo of Verdun; compare below under 945].

[Note: [Col. 0457] Hugo of Verdun adds: “And Heimard, a venerable man, succeeded him.”]

## 943

Count Arnulf, having summoned William, prince of the Normans, to a conference, had him treacherously killed [Note: [Col. 0459] Hugo V adds: “Richard I succeeded him and obtained Normandy as a gift from King Louis”].

King Louis gave the land of the Normans to William’s son, born [Note: [Col. 0459] “born,” witnesses 1 and 3] of a Breton concubine. Some of William’s princes entrusted themselves to the king, while others went over to Duke Hugh.

Count Heribert died, and his sons buried him at Saint-Quentin [Note: [Col. 0459] “his own,” witness 2]. When they heard that Rudolf, son of Rudolf of Gouy [Note: [Col. 0459] “Gaugiacum,” witnesses 2–3; [Col. 0459] Gouy in the Brabant district. BOUQ.], had come, as they supposed, to invade their father’s land, they attacked and killed him.

When King Louis heard this, he became very sorrowful.

Bishop Artold left the monastery of Saint-Basle and went to the king. The king promised him that he would restore the episcopate of Reims to him. Artold, taking with him his brothers and certain others who had been expelled from the episcopate of Reims, seized the castle of Altmont [Note: [Col. 0459] “he seized,” witnesses 2–3; H. R.].

King Louis also attacked Mouzon with them [Note: [Col. 0459] “Louis,” witness 3], but was repelled by the loyal men of Bishop Hugh, some of his own men being killed. He nevertheless burned certain suburban houses of that castle, in which a large quantity of stored grain perished.

Hugh, duke of the Franks [Note: [Col. 0459] “Hugh the Great,” Hugo V], repeatedly engaged the Normans who had come as pagans or were returning to paganism. They killed a large number of his Christian foot soldiers.

Hugh himself, after killing some of the Normans and putting the rest to flight, obtained the castle of Évreux [Note: [Col. 0459] “city,” witnesses 2–3; “Ebroicas,” witnesses 2–3; [Col. 0459] Évreux], with the support of its Christian Norman defenders [Note: [Col. 0459] absent in witness 2].

As Louis was returning to Rouen, he engaged Turmod [Note: [Col. 0459] “Trumond,” witness 3b], a Norman who had returned to idolatry and pagan rites, who was also compelling William’s son and others to do the same [Note: [Col. 0459] “still,” witness 3] and was plotting against the king. Fighting together with the pagan king Setric, Louis killed them [Note: [Col. 0459] “kills,” witnesses 2–3].

He entrusted Rouen to Erluin and returned to Compiègne, where Duke Hugh was awaiting him with his nephews, Heribert’s sons. Much discussion had been taking place concerning their reception.

The king first received Hugh, the bishop, through the mediation of Duke Otto of the Lotharingians and Bishop Adelbero, with Duke Hugh taking the leading role. The arrangement was that the abbeys which Hugh had abandoned [Note: [Col. 0459] “left,” witness 2; “relinquished,” witness 3] when he went to the king should be restored to Bishop Artold [Note: [Col. 0459] “Artold,” witness 1]; another episcopate should also be provided for him; and the honors that his brothers and relatives had held from the episcopate of Reims should be restored to them.

Afterward the remaining sons of Count Heribert were also received by the king.

King Louis [Note: [Col. 0459] “King Louis,” witnesses 2–3] then went to Rouen [Note: [Col. 0459] “Rouen,” witness 3], received Évreux from Duke Hugh, and, having been weakened by illness at Paris, lay sick for almost the whole summer [Note: [Col. 0459] “almost,” witness 2; “lay sick,” witness 2].

Bishop Hugh captured and burned the castle of Amblidum [Note: [Col. 0460] Ambli on the River Bar, which flows into the Meuse below Sedan], which had been held [Note: [Col. 0459] “detained,” witnesses 2–3; H. R.] by Robert and Rudolf, brothers expelled from Reims. From there they had been conducting raids throughout the episcopate of Reims.

Erluin engaged Arnulf and, after gaining the victory, killed the man who had slain William, prince of the Normans. He cut off that man’s hands [Note: [Col. 0459] “his hands cut off,” witnesses 2–3] and sent them to Rouen.

The aforementioned Bishop Hugh besieged the fortress of Altmont [Note: [Col. 0459] “Almont,” witness 3], held by Dodo, brother of Bishop Artold. At last he received Dodo’s little son as a hostage [Note: [Col. 0459] “his son as hostage,” witnesses 2–3] and withdrew, also at the king’s command.

Duke Hugh lifted the king’s daughter from the sacred font, and the king entrusted the duchy of France to him, subjecting all Burgundy to his authority.

Hugh also reconciled Arnulf with the king, who had been hostile to him because of William’s death.

King Otto [Note: [Col. 0459] “Odo,” witnesses 2–3 and 3b] arrested certain of Louis’s loyal men who were plotting against him [Note: [Col. 0459] “arrested and placed in custody,” witnesses 2–3] and placed them in custody. From this a quarrel arose between the two kings.

## 944

King Louis went into Aquitaine with Queen Gerberga [Note: [Col. 0459] “Queen Gerberga … with” is absent in 3b]. After speaking with Raymond [Note: [Col. 0459] “Ragimund,” witnesses 2–3 and 3b], prince of the Goths, and the other nobles of Aquitaine, he returned to France.

A certain castle called Montigny, situated in the district of Soissons and belonging to the abbey of Saint Crispin—which Louis had long before recovered [Note: [Col. 0459] “acquired,” witness 2; “ordered,” witness 3] and had given to Ragenold after Heribert’s sons surrendered it to him—was captured by the king’s loyal men through the treachery of certain townsmen. A man named Andrew, who held it in fidelity to Heribert’s sons, was killed, as was the traitor killed by Andrew.

The king’s household also took the city of Amiens, which Odo [Note: [Col. 0459] “Odo,” witness 2], Heribert’s son, held, with the support of Bishop Derold and through the surrender of the bishop’s loyal men.

From these events another quarrel arose between the king and Heribert’s sons.

Duke Otto of the Lotharingians died.

Hugh, duke of the Franks, made a treaty with the Normans [Note: [Col. 0459] “made a treaty with the Normans,” witnesses 2–3], with hostages given and received on both sides. He then prepared to depart with Heribert’s sons to meet King Otto in the kingdom of Lothar. But that king, delaying his own arrival, sent a certain Duke Herman with a huge army.

After peace had been made between Erluin and Arnulf, King Louis gave the castle of Amiens to Erluin.

Heribert’s sons treacherously captured a certain fortress belonging to Rudolf [Note: [Col. 0461] “Radulf,” witnesses 2–3], a loyal man of King Louis, called Clastris, situated in the district of Vermandois [Note: [Col. 0461] corrected from “Vermandois” to “Vermandense” in witness 1]. Rudolf secretly escaped [Note: [Col. 0461] “Radulf,” witness 2], and they seized and plundered his treasures, leaving the town empty.

Duke Hugh sought a conference with Herman, who had been sent to besiege the castles of the brothers Ragnarius [Note: [Col. 0461] “Ragenarius,” witness 3] and Rudolf, loyal men of King Louis. Since they had no force with which to resist Herman, they asked King Otto for pardon, giving many gifts [Note: [Col. 0461] “to Otto the king,” witnesses 2–3].

Otto, arriving at the palace of Aachen, held a conference with the Lotharingians. There envoys of King Louis and legates of Duke Hugh also came to him.

Otto received the king’s envoys honorably but opposed the duke’s envoys [Note: [Col. 0461] “adversus,” witnesses 2–3]. Then a certain Manasses, sent by Hugh, saw that Louis’s envoys were strongly hostile to his embassy. He brought forward certain instructions recently given to him by this king to deliver to Otto—instructions that he had previously been unwilling to disclose [Note: [Col. 0461] “which,” witness 2].

He revealed considerable reproaches that King Louis had ordered him to deliver to King Otto [Note: [Col. 0461] absent in witness 3]: namely, that Otto was perjured concerning the oaths he had sworn to Louis. He added several other disgraceful accusations.

Greatly angered by this, Otto dismissed Louis’s envoys, since they could not contradict Manasses’s words, but treated Hugh’s envoys honorably. He ordered all his own loyal men to withdraw from aiding or supporting Louis [Note: [Col. 0461] “participation,” corrected from “participation” in witness 1].

In the German regions across the Rhine there was a certain man whose hand had been cut off [Note: [Col. 0461] “cut off,” witnesses 2–3]. After fourteen years, as those who knew him assert, it was suddenly restored to him whole while he slept at night [Note: [Col. 0461] “by night,” witnesses 2–3].

In the same regions [Note: [Col. 0461] “those same,” witness 3], in certain districts, fiery balls were seen flying through the air [Note: [Col. 0461] “to fly,” witnesses 2–3]. Some of them, flying about there, set houses and estates on fire [Note: [Col. 0461] “and,” witnesses 2–3]. In certain places, however, they were driven back by placing crosses against them [Note: [Col. 0461] “legs” for “crosses,” witnesses 2–3], together with episcopal blessing and holy water. The king’s soldiers plundered the episcopate of Reims, and Heribert’s sons plundered the abbey of Saint Crispin, while Ragenold plundered the abbey of Saint Medard. Thus both sides raged against one another with thefts and plundering.

A great storm arose in the Paris region, together with a very violent whirlwind. The walls of a certain extremely ancient house, built with very strong cement on the mountain called Martyrs’ Mountain [Note: [Col. 0461] Montmartre], which had long stood unmoved [Note: [Col. 0461] “which,” witness 2; “construction,” witness 2], were utterly overthrown.

It is said that demons were then seen there in the form of horsemen. They destroyed a nearby church [Note: [Col. 0461] “a certain church,” witness 2], drove its beams against the aforementioned walls [Note: [Col. 0461] “against the aforesaid walls,” witnesses 2–3], and thereby overthrew them [Note: [Col. 0461] witness 3 reads “overthrew,” “tore out,” and “devastated” in place of the corresponding verbs]. They also tore up the vineyards of the mountain itself and devastated all the crops.

Soon afterward came the destruction of the Bretons. Divided among themselves by the dispute between their princes Berengar and Alan, they were invaded by the Normans, with whom they had made a treaty, and were crushed in a great slaughter [Note: [Col. 0461] “crushed,” witness 2].

Their city called Dol was captured, and its bishop, surrounded and overwhelmed by the multitude who had taken refuge in the church, was killed.

At last the Bretons restored their strength and entered into battle, in which they appeared to prevail over the Normans [Note: [Col. 0461] absent in witness 1].

Then, in a third engagement [Note: [Col. 0461] “after a third engagement,” witness 1], a great multitude fell on both sides [Note: [Col. 0461] absent in witness 2]. The Normans, however, won the victory, slaughtered the Bretons to extermination, and drove them from their land [Note: [Col. 0461] “and drove them,” witnesses 2–3].

Those Normans themselves, who had recently come from overseas regions [Note: [Col. 0461] “had come,” witness 3], invaded the Bretons’ lands [Note: [Col. 0461] singular “land,” witnesses 2–3].

King Ludowicus set out into the land of the Northmen with Arnulf and Erluin and certain bishops of Francia and Burgundy. Arnulf, going ahead of the king, routed some Northmen who were keeping watch at Arcas [Note: [Col. 0462D] Arques.] and prepared the king’s passage. Thus, when the king reached Rouen, he was received in the city by the Northmen; some who did not wish to receive him went to sea, while all the rest submitted to him. Duke Hugo, traveling with his men and certain nobles of Burgundy across the Seine, reached as far as Bayeux and besieged the city, which the king had granted him if he would help him subjugate this people of the Northmen. But after the king had been received by the Northmen, he ordered the duke to withdraw from the siege of the aforesaid city. When the duke withdrew, the king entered it. Hence a source of discord was stirred up between the king and the duke, especially because the king had received hostages from the people of Évreux, who were subject to Hugo, and refused to return them to that same duke.

## Year 945

While King Ludowicus was still staying at Rouen [Note: [Col. 0461] “King Ludowicus” 2, 3.], Queen Gerberga gave birth to a son at Laon, who was called Karolus for catechizing [Note: [Col. 0461] “catetiz.” corrected to “cateciz.” in witness 1.] [Note: [Col. 0461] “vocatus” in witnesses 2, 3.]. The king returned to Laon and spoke with Arnulf; after arranging certain matters, he returned to Rouen.

But Count Bernard of Senlis and Tetbald of Tours [Note: [Col. 0461] Omitted in witnesses 2, 3.], together with Heribert, attacked the king’s fortress of Montigny during the Easter season. They captured it, set it on fire [Note: [Col. 0461] “They set it on fire and destroyed it” in witnesses 2, 3.], and demolished it. That same Bernard, attacking the king’s huntsmen and dogs, carried off their horses and whatever else seemed useful to him. He also invaded Compiègne, a town belonging to the royal seat, together with certain villages subject to that seat.

King Ludowicus, gathering a Northmen army with him, plundered the district of Vermandois and, taking Erluin with them [Note: [Col. 0463] “with those men” in witnesses 2, 3.], together with part of Arnulf’s soldiers [Note: [Col. 0463] “with the father” in witness 2.], as well as Bishop Artoldus and those who had long before been expelled from Reims [Note: [Col. 0463] “who had previously been expelled” in witnesses 2, 3; also H. R.], and Counts Bernard and Theoderic, his nephew [Note: [Col. 0463] “Theoderic” in witness 2.], he besieged the city of Reims.

The crops were devastated all around, the villages were plundered and partly burned, and many churches were broken open. Whenever fighting took place at the gates or around the wall, many on both sides were wounded, and some were even killed. Finally, Duke Hugo fought against the Northmen who had entered his territory; he routed them with considerable slaughter [Note: [Col. 0463] “with considerable destruction” in witness 3.] and drove them from his borders. After this, he sent to the king at Reims, giving hostages so that Ragenold, on the king’s behalf, might meet him for a conference.

When Ragenold had gone, Hugo negotiated with him that the king should receive hostages from Bishop Hugo and withdraw from the siege of Reims, so that the same prelate might come at the appointed meeting to give an account of everything that the king had demanded from him [Note: [Col. 0463] “had demanded” in witness 2 and H. R.; the text reads “will have demanded.”]. After these terms had been given to him, the king withdrew from the siege on the fifteenth day after the city had been besieged.

Therefore, around the feast of Saint John, Duke Hugo held a meeting with the king through intermediaries [Note: [Col. 0463] “through intermediaries” in witness 2.]. Nothing definite was accomplished concerning the establishment of peace between them [Note: [Col. 0463] “definitely” in witness 1; “a definite settlement” in witnesses 2, 3.], except that they granted each other a truce until the middle of August [Note: [Col. 0463] Omitted in witness 2.].

After these events, King Ludowicus, taking Erluin and certain members of his household with him, set out for Rouen.

The venerable lord Theotilo, bishop of the city of Tours, died. While he had been striving to establish peace between the king and the leading men, and while returning from Laon occupied with these efforts, he was overcome by bodily illness on the journey. As he was already breathing out his final breath [Note: [Col. 0463] “breathing out” in witnesses 2, 3.], a certain sign of light appeared moving through the air. It seemed to be one cubit in length, and those escorting his funeral were sufficiently aided by its light to dispel the darkness of night [Note: [Col. 0463] Superscript in witness 1; omitted in witness 2.]. Having obtained such consolation, they carried his body, as is said, for nearly two hundred miles, all the way to the city of Tours.

He was reverently buried in the monastery of Saint Julian, which that holy man had established with the greatest devotion, beside the tomb of Lord Odo. From that time onward, it was declared that the church itself was illumined by divine miracles [Note: [Col. 0463] “to illumine” in witness 2.].

While King Ludowicus was staying at Rouen [Note: [Col. 0463] “Lodhuuicus” in witness 3.], Hagroldus [Note: [Col. 0463] “Haigroldus” in witnesses 2, 3, and below.] the Northman, who governed Bayeux, sent word to him that he would come to meet him at an agreed time and place if the king came to that location.

At last, when the king came with a few men to the appointed place, Hagroldus arrived armed with a multitude of Northmen [Note: [Col. 0463] “came”; corrected to “arrived” in witness 1; “had arrived” in witness 2.].
