Attacking the king’s companions, he killed nearly all of them [Note: [Col. 0463] “kills” in witness 3.]. The king alone fled, pursued by a certain Northman who was loyal to him [Note: [Col. 0463] “a Northman” in witness 3; “a certain Northman” in witnesses 2, 3.]. Coming with him to Rouen, he was captured [Note: [Col. 0463] Omitted in witness 3.] by other Northmen whom he had thought loyal to him, and was held under guard.

Hugo, king of Italy, was also expelled from the kingdom by his own people, and his son was received into the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0463] “received” in witnesses 2, 3; “Lotharius, his son, succeeded him,” in H. V.].

Bishop Hugo, besieging the fortress of Altmont, received it after nearly seven weeks of siege [Note: [Col. 0463] “of the siege”; corrected from “of the form” in witness 2.], when Dodo surrendered it [Note: [Col. 0463] “Odo” in witnesses 2, 3; H. R. IV, 31 identifies him as Dodo, brother of Lord Artoldus], on the following terms: the archbishop would receive Dodo’s son and his brother’s son and would grant them the land of their fathers [Note: [Col. 0463] “bishop” in witnesses 2, 3.].

While Duke Hugo was laboring for the king’s release, the Northmen demanded that the king’s sons be given to them as hostages and asserted that they would release the king on no other condition. A messenger was therefore sent to the queen for the boys. She sent the younger one and declared that she would not send the elder. The younger was therefore handed over, and, so that the king might be released, Wido [Note: [Col. 0463] “Vindo” in witness 3.], bishop of Soissons, surrendered himself as a hostage.

The king, thus released by the Northmen, was received by Prince Hugo. Entrusting him to Tetbald, one of his men [Note: [Col. 0463] “Tetbald, count of Chartres; Hugo V.”], Hugo set out to meet King Otho. Since that king did not wish to speak with him, he sent Duke Conrad of Lorraine to him. After speaking with Conrad, Hugo returned, angry with King Otho.

When Richarius, bishop of the people of Tongeren, died, King Otho gave that bishopric to Hugo, abbot of the monastery of Saint Maximinus, though Hugo was unwilling and refused it, and had him ordained bishop. Thus he returned across the Rhine.

In the district of Paris, and likewise throughout various surrounding districts [Note: [Col. 0463] “various” corrected to “divided” in witness 1; “divided” in witnesses 2, 3.], a fiery affliction attacked different limbs of human beings. Whatever parts were gradually burned were consumed, until death finally ended their suffering [Note: “Gradually” is omitted in witness 1.]. Some of them, seeking certain holy places, escaped the torments. More, however, were healed at Paris in the church of Holy Mary, Mother of God, so thoroughly that all who were able to reach that place are said to have been saved from this plague. Duke Hugo also supported them with daily provisions.

When some of them wished to return home, the fire, having been extinguished, flared up again; but when they returned to the church, they were freed [Note: [Col. 0463] “might be freed,” corrected to “were freed” in witness 2.].

## Year 946

Certain disturbances arose among the sons of Count Heribert [Note: [Col. 0463] Omitted in witnesses 2, 3.] concerning the division of their inheritances. Nevertheless, through the mediation of their uncle, Prince Hugo [Note: [Col. 0465] “auumculo” in witness 2.], they were reconciled, their possessions being divided among them as seemed appropriate to them.

Hugo, king of Italy, was received back into the kingdom by his own people. Edmund, king of the English, sent envoys to Prince Hugo for the restoration of King Ludowicus. For this purpose the prince held public assemblies with his nephews and with the other leading men of the kingdom.

Pope Marinus died, and Agapitus succeeded him. Peace was negotiated between the patrician Alberic and Hugo, king of Italy.

Hugo, duke of the Franks, taking with him Hugo [Note: [Col. 0465] “the Black,” son of Richard.] and the other leading men of the kingdom, restored King Ludowicus to the kingdom. He received the fortress of Laon, which Queen Gerberga held, and entrusted it to the same Tetbald.

The Duke, renewing for King Ludowicus his royal honor and title, committed himself to him together with the other leading men of the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0465] “and committed himself to him” in witness 1.]. King Edmund overseas died; the wife of King Otho, who was Edmund’s sister, also died.

Queen Gerberga had recently sent an embassy to Otho, her brother, asking him for aid. Gathering a very large army from all his kingdoms, he came to Francia, bringing with him Conrad, king of Cisalpine Gaul [Note: [Col. 0465] “Conrad” in witness 2.]. King Ludowicus went out to meet them and was received by them with sufficient friendliness and honor. Thus they came together to Laon. After examining the strength of the fortress, they turned away from it and attacked the city of Reims. Surrounding it with a siege, they fortified it with a huge army.

When Bishop Hugo saw that he could not endure the siege or resist so great a multitude, he spoke with certain leading men who seemed to be his friends: namely, with Arnulf, who had his sister as wife; with Uddo [Note: [Col. 0465] “Oddo” in witness 1; “Uuiddo” in witness 2.], who had his aunt as wife [Note: [Col. 0465] “his kinswoman” in witness 2.]; and with Hermann [Note: [Col. 0465] “Herimann” in witness 2, 3.], Uddo’s brother [Note: [Col. 0465] “Uuiddo” in witness 2.]. He asked them what he ought to do.

They gave him this advice: that he should leave with his men and abandon the city, because the kings had arranged that he should be expelled by every means, and they would be unable to intervene with the kings on his behalf; if the city happened to be captured by force, his eyes would be torn out.

After hearing this advice and making it known to his men, he left on the third day of the siege [Note: [Col. 0465] “the third sieges” in witness 2.] with nearly all the soldiers who were then with him.

Thus the kings, entering the city with the bishops and leading men, had Lord Artoldus, the prelate who had formerly been expelled, enthroned again [Note: [Col. 0465] Omitted in witness 1.]. Robert, archbishop of Trier, and Frederick of Mainz, receiving him [Note: [Col. 0465] “because the authority of the Roman See had so decreed,” in H. V.], restored him with both hands to that see.

Then, leaving Queen Gerberga at Reims, the kings themselves with their armies attacked Hugo’s territory. They besieged the city of Senlis, but when they saw that it was strongly fortified and were unable to take it, they killed some of their own men and abandoned the siege [Note: [Col. 0465] “and withdrew”; the remainder is omitted in witness 2.].

Thus, pressing across the Seine, they inflicted heavy plundering on every place except the cities [Note: [Col. 0465] “raids” in witness 3.]. They traveled through the land of the Northmen and devastated many places. Then, returning from there [Note: [Col. 0465] “turning back” in witness 2.], they went back to their own lands [Note: [Col. 0465] “those lands” in witness 1.].

Deroldus, bishop of Amiens, died [Note: [Col. 0465] “dies” in witness 3.].

## Year 947

Prince Hugo, having set his army in motion, went into Arnulf’s territory and besieged certain fortifications belonging to him. Since he accomplished none of the business he had hoped for, he returned to his own lands.

King Ludowicus likewise besieged Mosomum [Note: [Col. 0465] “Mouzon” in witness 3.], which Bishop Hugo, expelled from Reims [Note: [Col. 0465] “rejected” in witness 1 and R.; “expelled” in witnesses 2, 3 and H. R.], was holding [Note: [Col. 0465] “retaining” in witnesses 2, 3 and H. R.]. But since he too achieved nothing according to his wishes, when the Lotharingians finally withdrew after a month, he himself returned to Reims [Note: [Col. 0465] “to Mouzon,” corrected to “to Reims” in witness 1.].

Bovo, bishop of Châlons, died. The people of Châlons chose for themselves a certain noble young cleric named Gibuinus.

King Ludowicus celebrated Easter at Aachen with King Otho and was honored by him with royal gifts [Note: [Col. 0465] “and was honored by him with gifts” in witnesses 2, 3.].

Prince Hugo, rashly persuaded by certain people, attacked Reims with Bishop Hugo, as though he were about to capture it immediately. But his hope was frustrated by the resistance of the king’s loyal men and of Archbishop Artoldus. On the eighth day after they had arrived, they withdrew in confusion.

Bishop Hugo, with the support of his uncle Hugo, ordained as bishop of Amiens a certain Tetbald, a cleric of the church of Soissons.

At the request of Count Arnulf, King Ludowicus set out for Arras with Bishop Artoldus. From there he and Arnulf advanced to besiege Monasteriolum, the fortress of Rotger’s son Erluin [Note: [Col. 0465] “Rotgarius” in witness 1.]. After fruitless labor and the death of many of their men [Note: [Col. 0465] “of very many”; corrected to “of many” in witness 2.], deprived of hope, they returned to their homes.

A great storm poured down upon Reims for the entire span of one night, with continual flashes of lightning [Note: [Col. 0465] “chor.” in witness 2.] and an earthquake, so that wells were filled and some houses were overturned.

A meeting of Kings Ludowicus and Otho was held over the river Chara [Note: [Col. 0465D] Cher.] at the beginning of August. Prince Hugo had pitched his camp near Mosomum and Duodeciacum [Note: [Col. 0466D] Douzy.]. There the dispute between Artoldus and Hugo, the prelates of the church of Reims, was heard by the bishops. Since no synod had then been summoned, the dispute could not be settled.

A synod was therefore announced for the middle of November [Note: [Col. 0467] “announced” in witness 2.]. Meanwhile the see of Reims was granted to Artoldus, while the other Bishop Hugo was permitted to remain at Mosomum. Through the mediation of King Otho, a truce or cessation of war between King Ludowicus and Prince Hugo was arranged until the time of the synod.

Heriveus, nephew of the former Archbishop Heriveus, possessed a fortification which he had built on this side of the river Marne. From it he plundered the surrounding villages belonging to the bishopric of Reims [Note: [Col. 0467] “circumquique” in witness 3; below, “ad Artoldus” is a typographical error.]. For seizing these possessions of the church, he was excommunicated by Bishop Artoldus.

One day Count Ragenaldus [Note: [Col. 0467] “Ragenoldus” in witnesses 2, 3.] and Dodo, the brother of that prelate [Note: “and the brothers”; H. R.], went out with certain soldiers of the church against Heriveus’s raiders and put the marauders to flight. When Heriveus heard this, he left his fortification with the soldiers he had with him, armed for battle against our men [Note: [Col. 0467] “against us” in witness 2.]. He engaged them and was killed together with some of his men [Note: [Col. 0467] “with some of his men” in witnesses 2, 3.]. All the rest were put to flight, while several on both sides were wounded.

The victors carried his body to Reims.

Bishop Hugo, taking with him [Note: [Col. 0467] “with him” is omitted in witness 1.] Tetbald of Laon [Note: [Col. 0467B] H. R. IV, 33 identifies him as Tetbald of Montaigu, the husband of Hugo’s sister; this is absent from the Montpellier manuscript.] and several other evildoers, came during the vintage season to Culmisciacum [Note: [Col. 0467] “Colmisciacum” in witness 1.] [Note: [Col. 0467D] Cormicy.] and the neighboring villages. Gathering nearly all the wine from them, they carried it away into various districts.

The aforesaid synod was held at Verdun [Note: [Col. 0467] “The synod announced for the middle of November was held at Verdun”; Hugo V.], under the presidency of Robert, bishop of Trier, together with Artoldus of Reims [Note: [Col. 0467] “Robert of Trier, Berengarius of Verdun, and Hugo”; Hugo V.], Odalricus of Augsburg [Note: [Col. 0467] “Odo”; “Hugo of Fleury”], Adalbero of Metz [Note: [Col. 0467] “Adhelbero” in witnesses 2, 3; “Alberone,” Hugo of Fleury.], Goslenus of Toul [Note: [Col. 0467] “Goslinus” in witnesses 2, 3, and below.], Hildeboldus of the trans-Rhenish region [Note: [Col. 0467] “Mirnegardus of Werden” in witness 3; Hildeboldus was in fact bishop of Minden.], Israhel the Breton [Note: [Col. 0467] Witness 1 and Hugo V read: “with Israhel the Breton present; Bruno.”], and, in the presence of Bruno the abbot [Note: [Col. 0467D] Of Lorsch.], the brother of King Otho, as well as Agenoldus [Note: [Col. 0467D] Of Gorze.] and Odilo [Note: [Col. 0467] “Odilo, abbot of Cluny” in Hugo of Fleury; [Col. 0467D] “of Stavelot.”], together with certain other venerable abbots.

[Note: [Col. 0467D] Hugo V adds: “This synod was announced at Verdun for this reason: so that at least in this way the aforesaid Berengarius of Verdun might attend the assembly of bishops, since his authority was so great that it seemed improper for what was not confirmed by the authentic presence of a man of such steadfast nobility to be rejected.”]

Bishop Hugo was summoned to it, and two bishops, Adalbero and Goslenus, were even sent to escort him there; but he refused to come. The whole synod adjudged the bishopric of Reims to be held by Lord Artoldus [Note: [Col. 0467] Omitted in witness 1.]. A synod was again announced for the Ides of January [Note: [Col. 0467] Omitted in witness 1.].

## Year 948

The aforesaid synod was held in the church of Saint Peter, before the fortress of Mosomum, by Lord Robert and the other bishops of the diocese of Trier [Note: [Col. 0467] “of Trier” in witnesses 2, 3.] and by some from Reims.

When Bishop Hugo arrived there and spoke with Robert, he refused to enter the synod. Through his cleric, who had brought them from Rome, he sent certain letters in the name of Pope Agapitus to the bishops. They contained no canonical authority, but merely commanded that the bishopric of Reims be restored to Hugo.

After the letters had been read, the bishops took counsel with the abbots and the other wise men who were present. They replied that it was neither worthy nor appropriate for them, because of those letters presented by a plotter against Bishop Artoldus, to interrupt the apostolic legation which Archbishop Robert had previously undertaken before the kings and bishops of both Gaul and Germany, delivered by Bishop Frederick of Mainz, and of which he had already carried out part of the mandate. Rather, what had been regularly begun should be treated canonically.

It was therefore ordered that chapter 19 of the Council of Carthage, concerning the accused and the accuser, should be read. After it had been read, it was judged, according to the definition of that chapter, that, while Bishop Artoldus retained communion and the parish of Reims [Note: [Col. 0467] “parish” in witnesses 1, 3.], Hugo—who had already been summoned to two synods but had contemptuously refused to come [Note: [Col. 0467] “to two synods” in witnesses 1, 2.]—should abstain from communion and from the governance of the bishopric of Reims until he should appear at the universal synod announced for the Kalends of August to clear himself [Note: [Col. 0467] “annual synod” in witness 1.].

The bishops immediately had the chapter written out before them on a document, adding this judgment of their own, and sent it to Hugo. The next day he sent the same document back to Bishop Robert, replying in these words that he would in no way obey their judgment.

Count Arnulf, with the support of Prince Hugo, captured the fortress of Monasteriolum.

Meanwhile, Lord Artoldus sent a letter of complaint to the Roman See. Lord Pope Agapitus therefore sent his legate, Bishop Marinus, to King Otho to summon and assemble a general synod. The pope’s own letters were also sent from Rome to certain bishops of Gaul and Germany, calling them to the same synod [Note: [Col. 0467] Omitted in witness 3.].

This synod was assembled by order of the aforesaid pope at the royal palace of Engulenhein [Note: [Col. 0467] “Eungulenhein” in witness 1; “Eglehem” in witness 3.], in the church dedicated in honor of blessed Remigius, on 7 June [Note: [Col. 0467] The numeral is omitted in witness 1. Hugo V gives: “1 June 948, indiction 6, in the third year of Lord Agapitus’s papacy, and the thirteenth year of the reign of King Otho and likewise of Ludowicus.”], on account of the greatest disputes that were being stirred up between King Ludowicus and Prince Hugo, and likewise between Artoldus, archbishop of Reims [Note: [Col. 0469] “bishop of Reims” in witnesses 2, 3; “archbishop of Reims,” Hugo V.], and Hugo, who had been unlawfully substituted as prelate of that city. These disputes had thrown the whole kingdom of the Franks into disorder.

When the aforesaid Marinus, the legate of the Apostolic See, arrived to celebrate the synod, the bishops of Germany also assembled with certain bishops of Gaul [Note: [Col. 0469] Hugo V adds: “Thirty-two bishops of Gaul and Germany assembled, whom we have judged worthy to note below.”]: namely, Robert, archbishop of Trier [Note: [Col. 0469] “Trier” in witness 2, 3, and frequently below.]; Artoldus of Reims [Note: [Col. 0469] “Astardus” in witness 2]; Frederick of Mainz [Note: [Col. 0469] “Mainz” in witnesses 2, 3]; Wicfredus of Cologne [Note: [Col. 0469] “Wifredus” in witness 2]; Adaldachus of Hamburg [Note: [Col. 0469] “Adeldacus” in witnesses 2, 3; “Adalbertus” in witness 2]; Hildeboldus of Minden [Note: [Col. 0469] “Hildeboldus” in witnesses 2, 3; “Heldeboldus” in witness 2]; Goslenus of Toul [Note: [Col. 0469] “Gauslinus” in witness 2; “Goslinus” in witness 2]; Adalbero of Metz [Note: [Col. 0469] “Adelbero” in witnesses 2, 3 and 2]; Berengarius of Verdun [Note: [Col. 0469] “Berungarius” in witness 2]; Fulbertus of Cambrai; Rodulfus of Laon [Note: [Col. 0469] “Licudunensis” in witness 3]; Richoo of Worms; Reimboldus of Speyer [Note: [Col. 0469] “Reinboldus” in witness 2; “Rainbaldus” in witness 3; “Rambaldus” in witness 2]; Poppo of Würzburg [Note: [Col. 0469] “Popo” in witness 2; “Wilsib.” in witness 2; “Wizib.” in witness 3; “Witsib.” in Hugo V.]; Chounradus of Constance [Note: [Col. 0469] Thus in witness 2; witness 1 corrected from “Choonradus”; “Conradus” in witness 2]; Odelricus of Augsburg; Thethardus of Hildesheim [Note: [Col. 0469] “Tethardus” in witnesses 2, 3 and Hugo V.]; Bernardus of Halberstadt [Note: [Col. 0469] “Alfurcestensis” in witness 2]; Dudo of Paderborn [Note: [Col. 0469] “Dodo” in witness 2; “Poderbrumensis” in witness 2; “Poderburnensis” in witness 3]; Farabertus of Tongeren [Note: [Col. 0469] Witnesses offer variants assigning these names differently: “Liopt. R., Michael R., Farab. T.” in witness 2; “Michael R., Far. T., Liop. Rib.” in witness 3]; Lioptacus of Ribemont; Michahel of Regensburg; Doddo of Osnabrück [Note: [Col. 0469] “Dodo Osneburgensis” in witnesses 2, 3]; Everis of Minden; Baldricus of Utrecht; Heroldus of Salzburg [Note: [Col. 0469] “Saleb.” in witness 1; “Salb.” in witness 3]; Adalbertus of Passau; Starchandus of Eichstätt [Note: [Col. 0469] “Eistenensis” in witness 1; “Eistentiensis” in witness 2; “Eistanciensis” in witness 3]; Horath of Schleswig [Note: [Col. 0469] “Leowicensis” in witness 3; “Horachs l.” in witness 2]; Wichardus of Basel [Note: [Col. 0469] “Wikardus” in witness 3]; and Liesdac of Ribe [Note: [Col. 0469] “Liesdao” in witness 1 and Hugo V.; “Lidac Ripuensis” in witness 3.].

When these prelates were seated in the church of the aforementioned place, after the preliminary prayers according to the order for celebrating a council, and after the readings from sacred authority, the glorious kings Otho and Ludowicus entered and sat together. After the address of Marinus, the aforesaid legate of the Apostolic See, King Ludowicus rose from the side and seat [Note: [Col. 0469] “consent” in witness 2.] of Lord King Otho and disclosed the complaint of his accusation before the aforementioned vicar of the Roman See and the other bishops seated there [Note: [Col. 0469] “those sitting” in witnesses 2, 3.].

He related how he had been summoned from overseas by the envoys of Hugo and the other princes of Francia to receive the kingdom of his paternal inheritance; how, by the votes and acclamations of all the nobles and military men of the Franks, he had been elevated and consecrated to assume the height of royal rule; and how afterward he had been expelled by the aforesaid Hugo, attacked by treachery, captured, and held by him under guard for an entire year. His release could not otherwise be obtained unless he abandoned the fortress of Laon, which Queen Gerberga alone, with her loyal men, still held among all her royal seats, while Hugo occupied it.

If anyone should object that all these evils which he had suffered after receiving the kingdom had been inflicted upon him because of his own wrongdoing, he would clear himself of that charge according to synodal judgment and the order of King Otho, or defend himself by single combat [Note: [Col. 0469] Omitted in witness 2.].

Then Archbishop Artoldus rose and, in accordance with the command of the Roman pope that had been entrusted to him, presented the beginning and substance of the dispute between himself and Hugo, who had been substituted for him as bishop of the church of Reims.

After these letters had been read [Note: [Col. 0469D] Mon. Germ., Leg. II, 21; Patrologia, vol. CXXXVIII, among the ecclesiastical constitutions of Otho the Great, “Acts of the Synod of Ingelheim.”], and after they had been interpreted for the kings in the Teutonic language [Note: [Col. 0469] “Teustic” in witness 1; “Teutonic” in witnesses 2, 3. Note: [Col. 0470D] “Thus Ludowicus also knew the Teutonic language.”], a certain Sigiboldus [Note: [Col. 0469] “Sygibaldus” in witness 2; “Sigebaldus,” H. R.; “Bald.”] entered the synod, a cleric of the aforementioned Hugo. He brought letters which he had carried from Rome and which he had already produced at another synod at Mosomum [Note: [Col. 0469] “Mosoni” in witness 1.], asserting that the same letters had been given to him at Rome by Marinus himself, the vicar who was present.

Marinus produced the letters which that same Sigiboldus had brought to Rome [Note: [Col. 0469] “had carried” in witnesses 2, 3.] and ordered that they be read before the synod. During their reading it was discovered, as the letters themselves acknowledged, that Wido, bishop of Soissons, Hildegarius of Beauvais, Rodulfus of Laon, and all the other bishops of the diocese of Reims had delegated those same letters to the Apostolic See for the restoration of Hugo to the see of Reims and the expulsion of Artoldus.

After the reading, Bishop Artoldus and the aforementioned Rodulfus, who was named in the letters, rose, together with Fulbertus, bishop of Cambrai, and rejected the letters. They asserted that they had never before seen or heard them and had given no consent to their delegation.

When that cleric could not contradict them, although he loudly objected with accusations against them [Note: [Col. 0469] “although objecting with accusations” in witness 2.], Lord Marinus, advising the whole synod, ordered them to offer him counsel and a proper judgment concerning such an accuser [Note: [Col. 0469] “accuser” in witness 2; “firmly” in the same witness.] and informer of accusations against bishops.

After the informer had been publicly refuted for bringing false charges, they read the chapters concerning such accusers [Note: [Col. 0471] “such an accuser” in witness 2.]. They judged and unanimously decreed that he should be deprived of the honor he enjoyed and, according to the tenor of the chapters, be driven into exile.

Thus stripped of the diaconate, the ministry he had held, and rejected from the presence of the synod, he departed.

As for Bishop Artoldus, who had made himself available to every synod and had not evaded synodal judgment, they decreed, approved, and confirmed that the bishopric of Reims should be entirely retained and administered by him according to the institutions of the canons and the decrees of the holy Fathers.

On the second day of the session, after the readings of divine authority and the address of Marinus the vicar, Lord Robert, archbishop of Trier, proposed that, since the bishopric of Reims had been restored and returned to Bishop Artoldus according to the institutions of sacred law, synodal judgment should be carried out against the invader of that see.

Marinus the vicar therefore ordered the synod to pronounce a canonical sentence concerning this presumption. The Catholic chapters of sacred law were accordingly ordered to be read. After they had been read, and in accordance with the institutions of the sacred canons and the decrees of the holy Fathers—Sixtus, Alexander, Innocent, Zosimus, Boniface, Celestine, Leo, Symmachus [Note: [Col. 0471] “Simmachus” in witnesses 2, 3.] and the other holy doctors of the Church of God—they excommunicated the aforesaid Hugo, invader of the church of Reims, and expelled him from the bosom of the Church of God, until he should undertake to come to repentance and make worthy satisfaction [Note: [Col. 0471] “until he should come”; Hugo V: “until he should undertake to make satisfaction”; H. R.].

On the remaining days of the synod, certain necessary matters were also discussed concerning incestuous marriages and churches which in the regions of Germany were improperly given to priests, or rather sold, and unlawfully taken away by laymen [Note: [Col. 0471] “unlawfully” in witness 2.]. It was prohibited and decreed that no one should presume to do this at all [Note: [Col. 0471] “and” omitted in witness 2.]. Certain other matters useful to the Church of God were also discussed and defined [Note: [Col. 0471] “determined” in witness 3.].

Meanwhile King Ludowicus begged King Otho to bring him aid against Hugo and his other enemies. Otho granted the request and ordered Duke Conrad to go to his aid with an army of Lotharingians. In the meantime, while the army was being assembled, King Ludowicus was to remain with the duke, while Bishops Artoldus and Rodulfus, who were with the king, were to stay with the Lotharingian bishops so that they might suffer no adversity on the journey.

We therefore remained with Robert of Trier for nearly four weeks, while Rodulfus of Laon stayed with Adalbero of Metz [Note: [Col. 0471] “Adhelbero” in witnesses 2, 3.].

When the army had finally been assembled, the Lotharingian bishops went to Mosomum. Besieging and attacking the fortress itself, they compelled the soldiers who were there with Hugo to surrender. After receiving hostages from them [Note: [Col. 0471] This phrase is absent in witness 3.], they went to meet King Ludowicus and Duke Conrad [Note: [Col. 0471] “Conrad” in witnesses 2, 3, throughout.] in the district of Laon.

There the duke and the army besieged a certain fortification which Tetbald had built and held at a place called Mons Acutus [Note: [Col. 0471] “He captured the fortification called Mons Acutus before Laon”; Hugo V.] [Note: [Col. 0471D] Montaigu.], and by which he held Laon against the king. Attacking this stronghold, they finally captured it, though not without delay, and from there went to Laon.

The bishops assembled in the church of Saint Vincent and excommunicated the aforementioned Tetbald. They summoned Prince Hugo by letters in the name of Marinus, the legate of the Apostolic See, and in their own name, ordering him to come to make amends for the wrongs he had committed against the king and the bishops.

Finally, Wido, bishop of the city of Soissons, came to King Ludowicus, committed himself to him, and made peace with Archbishop Artoldus, giving him satisfaction for the ordination of Hugo.

Duke Conrad also took King Ludowicus’s daughter from the sacred font.

Thus, after the fortress of Mosomum had been recovered and destroyed, the Lotharingians returned to their own lands.

Therefore Hugh, making no delay, gathered a large force of his own men and of the Northmen, attacked the city of Soissons [Note: [Col. 0471] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “adgr...”], and besieging it assaulted it [Note: [Col. 0471] “assaulted”: manuscripts 2 and 3 read “was assaulting”], killing some people. Having also set fires, he burned the house of the father of the church, together with the canons’ cloister and part of the city. Yet, unable to capture the city itself, he abandoned it and came to a certain fortification [Col. 0472C] which Count Ragenold was building for Louis over the river Aisne [Note: [Col. 0471] “Aisne”: manuscript 2 has the accusative form “Axonem”], at a place called Roucy [Note: [Col. 0472D] Roucy], and surrounded it with a siege camp while it was still unfinished. But he did not capture that either; nevertheless, he devastated the villages of the church of Reims adjoining his camps. His brigands also killed many of the peasants, violating the churches [Note: [Col. 0471] manuscript 1 reads “vallantes”] and raging so violently that in the village of Culmisiac, both inside and around the church, they killed nearly forty men [Note: [Col. 0471] “forty”: H. R. IV. 36 reads “four hundred”; the Montpessulanus manuscript reads “four hundred”], and stripped the church itself of almost all its possessions [Note: [Col. 0471] “stripped ... of almost all its possessions”: manuscripts 2 and 3, and H. R., read “completely stripped”]. After many such outrages had been committed [Note: [Col. 0471] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “and with many”], Hugh at last returned with his marauders.

Thus the soldiers who had until then remained with the excommunicated Hugh returned to Archbishop Artoldus. He received some of them, after they had been restored the possessions they had held [Note: [Col. 0471] “received”: manuscript 1 reads “receives”; manuscripts 2 and 3b read “rejects”], but rejected others. After this he set out to Trier for a synod with the bishops Wido of Soissons [Note: [Col. 0471] absent from manuscripts 2 and 3], Rodulfus of Laon, and Wicfredus of Thérouanne [Note: [Col. 0471] manuscript 3 reads “Vincfredus”]. When they arrived there, they found Marinus, the papal legate, awaiting them [Col. 0473A] with Archbishop Rotbertus; but they found no bishop there from among the other Lotharingians or Germans.

As they considered these matters, Marinus the vicar began to inquire [Note: [Col. 0473] manuscripts 2 and 3, and H. R., read “Marinus the vicar began to inquire”] what the prince Hugh had done after the previously mentioned synod against them or against King Louis. They reported the evils already mentioned, which he had inflicted upon them and their churches. Marinus therefore asked about the summons issued to the prince: whether the letters of summons that he had commissioned to be delivered to him had reached him. Archbishop Artoldus replied that some of them had been delivered [Note: [Col. 0473] manuscript 3 reads “were delivered”], while others could not be delivered [Note: [Col. 0473] manuscript 3 reads “were not able to be delivered”], because their bearer had been intercepted by Hugh’s marauders; nevertheless, Hugh had been summoned both by letters and by certain messengers [Note: [Col. 0473] manuscript 1 corrects “fuerat” to “fuerit”].

They then asked whether anyone had arrived as his representative [Col. 0473B]. Since no one was found, it was decided to wait, in case he might perhaps arrive on the following day. When this did not happen at all, and all who were present [Note: [Col. 0473] manuscript 2 corrects “aderent” to “aderant”]—both clergy and [illustrious [Note: [Col. 0473] absent from manuscripts 1 and 3]] laymen—were loudly proclaiming that he ought to be excommunicated [Note: [Col. 0473] manuscript 2 reads “to proclaim”; manuscript 3, “they proclaimed”], the bishops determined that this excommunication should still be postponed until the third day of the synod [Note: [Col. 0473] manuscript 3 reads “until the day”].

They discussed the bishops who had been summoned but had delayed coming, and those who had taken part in Hugh’s ordination. Wido of Soissons confessed himself culpable, prostrating himself before Marinus the vicar and Archbishop Artoldus [Note: [Col. 0473] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “a certain man”]. But, when Archbishop Rotbertus and Archbishop Artoldus interceded for him before Marinus [Note: [Col. 0473] the text reads “Marimum”], he deserved to be absolved from this offense. Wicfredus of Thérouanne was found to be free from participation in that ordination.

There appeared a certain priest, a legate of Transmarus, bishop of Noyon [Note: [Col. 0473] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “of the bishop from overseas”], asserting that the same bishop had been so weakened by severe illness [Note: [Col. 0473] manuscript 2 reads “illness”] that he had been unable to come to that synod [Note: [Col. 0473] manuscript 2 corrects “eundem” to “eandem”]. The bishops of our region who were present also testified to this [Note: [Col. 0473] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “testified”].

At last, on the third day, with Liuddulfus [Note: [Col. 0473] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “Liutdulfus”], the legate and chaplain of King Otto, pressing the matter especially—for the same king had commanded that it be done without fail—Count Hugh, enemy of King Louis, was excommunicated for the evils mentioned above that he had perpetrated. This was done on the condition that the excommunication would remain until he repented and came to make satisfaction before Marinus the vicar or before the bishops whom he had injured; but if he refused to do so, he was to go to Rome for his absolution.

The two pseudo-bishops ordained by the condemned Hugh, Tetbaldus and Ivo [Col. 0473D] [Note: [Col. 0473] perhaps “Iuo” in manuscript 1], were also excommunicated. The first had been appointed in the city of Amiens after Hugh’s expulsion; the other, in the city of Senlis after Hugh’s condemnation, by Hugh himself [Note: [Col. 0473] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “by him”]. A certain cleric of Laon named Adelomus was also excommunicated. His own bishop, Rodulfus [Note: [Col. 0473] absent from manuscript 2], had accused him of having introduced the excommunicated Tetbaldus into the church [Col. 0474A].

Hildegarius, bishop of Beauvais, was summoned by letters from the aforesaid Marinus to come before him [Note: [Col. 0473] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “and” for “that”] or to go to Rome, where he was to give an account before the lord pope for the unlawful ordination of the aforesaid pseudo-bishops, in which he had taken part. Heribertus, son of Count Heribertus, was also summoned to come and make satisfaction for the evils he was committing against the bishops.

When these matters had been accomplished, the bishops returned to their own regions. Liuddulfus [Note: [Col. 0473] manuscript 1 reads “Laudulphus”; manuscript 2, “Liutdulfus”; manuscript 3, “Luidulfus”], Otto’s chaplain, escorted Marinus the vicar to his own king in Saxony, where Liuddulfus was to consecrate the church of the monastery of Fulda [Note: [Col. 0473] “was to consecrate”: manuscripts 2 and 3 read “had been to consecrate”]. After its consecration, the same Marinus [Note: [Col. 0473] absent from manuscript 1], when winter had ended, returned to Rome.

In this year Bishops Geruncus of Bourges [Note: [Col. 0473] manuscript 2 reads “Bituricensis”] and Rodulfus of Laon died. A son was born to King Louis, and Bishop Artoldus lifted him from the sacred font, giving him his father’s name [Note: [Col. 0473] up to this point: History of Reims IV. 37]. In the year—

## 949

[Note: [Col. 0473] manuscript 3 reads “948.”]

The people of Laon, who remained loyal to King Louis [Note: [Col. 0473] manuscript 1 corrects “fidelitate” to “fidelitati”], chose for themselves as bishop Rorico, a deacon and the king’s brother; Archbishop Artoldus consecrated him at Reims. Since he was not accepted at Laon, however, he settled at the fortification of Pierrepont.

The people of Amiens, hating Tetbaldus, whom Hugh had appointed bishop over them, betrayed the castle to Count Arnulfus. He summoned King Louis, captured the town itself, expelled Tetbaldus, and installed there a certain monk named Ragembaldus of Arras [Note: [Col. 0473] manuscript 3 abbreviates “Arras”], whom the same people of Amiens had previously chosen for themselves [Note: [Col. 0473] manuscript 2 reads “had appointed”]. He was then brought by the king to Reims and ordained bishop by Archbishop Artoldus.

The soldiers of the church of Reims, who had not been received by that bishop, secretly captured the fortification of Altmont, which Dodo, brother of Lord Bishop Artoldus, held through a treacherous seizure. They summoned the excommunicated Hugh and received him into the town [Note: [Col. 0473] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “the town”], and from there they raged through the surrounding villages belonging to the bishopric with plunder.

As the solemnity of Easter approached, Queen Gerberga set out for her brother King Otto and celebrated Easter with him at the palace of Aachen [Note: [Col. 0473] manuscript 1 reads “of the palace”]. At that time embassies from various peoples were present there—namely, from the Greeks, Italians, English, and certain other nations.

The queen returned to Reims with a promise of her brother’s assistance [Note: [Col. 0473] manuscript 1 reads “with her brother”]. King Louis unexpectedly attacked Laon. At night his men secretly climbed the wall, broke the locks of the gates, entered the town, and captured the guards, except those who had climbed the tower [Note: [Col. 0473] “tower”: the editor writes, “I saw it still standing in May 1827; but now it no longer exists, having, as they say, been demolished for the public benefit”] of the royal residence, which Louis himself had founded at the gate of the castle. Unable to capture this tower, he separated it from the city by constructing an inner wall.

When Hugh learned of this, he went there with his men, while the king sent an embassy to request the assistance of Chonradus [Note: [Col. 0475] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “against”], duke of the Lotharingians. Hugh, approaching the tower, pitched his camp before the gate; then, having introduced guards into the fortress with sufficient provisions, he withdrew from the hill.

The king therefore went to meet Chonradus. The duke spoke with the king and arranged a truce in the war between him and Hugh until the month of August, while the king was to go and speak with King Otto. After he had spoken with Otto, Louis returned to Reims. There Adalbertus, son of Heribertus, came to him and became his man.

Count Ragenaldus [Note: [Col. 0475] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “Ragenoldus”], having joined to himself certain of the faithful men of Bishop Artoldus, built a fortification on the river Marne, at a place called Mareuil [Note: [Col. 0475] manuscript 1 reads “Marcilum”; manuscript 3, “Maroillum”] [Note: [Col. 0475D] Mareuil].

The castle of Coucy was returned to Lord Bishop Artoldus by those who guarded it on behalf of Count Hugh or Tetbaldus; they also placed themselves under the archbishop’s authority. Dodo, brother of Lord Artoldus, together with his faithful men, and Count Theoderic besieged the fortress of Altmont, which Hugh, once a bishop, had entered and held with his men. They established and fortified their camps before the gate of the castle.

Count Hugh gathered a large force of his own men and of the Northmen, went to Laon, brought out his men who were holding the fortress [Note: [Col. 0475] manuscript 2 and 3 read “castle”], and introduced others as guards with sufficient provisions. From there he went into the district of Porcien and pitched camp above Chaudion [Note: [Col. 0475] manuscript 2 reads “Caldionem”]. He then sent to King Louis, who was staying at Reims, as though to request peace.

Meanwhile, unexpectedly attacking Laon [Note: [Col. 0475C] manuscript 2 reads “Laudun”], he tried to capture it; but when his plan failed [Note: [Col. 0475] manuscript 1 corrected “a failed plan” to “when the plan failed”], he returned to his own territories. The king, however, summoned Arnulfus and certain Lotharingians [Note: [Col. 0475] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “and”], and pursued him as far as the district of Senlis. Arnulfus then burned the suburb of that city, and they returned to their own lands.

Hugh therefore assembled a considerable army of both his own men and Northmen and came into the district of Soissons. He sent Bishops Wido of Auxerre [Note: [Col. 0475] manuscript 3 reads “Vindone”; manuscript 2, “Antisioderensi”; manuscript 3, “Autisiodorensi”] and Ansegisus of Troyes [Note: [Col. 0475] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “Trecasino”] to the king and summoned Count Ragenaldus [Note: [Col. 0475] manuscripts 2 and 3 consistently read “Ragenoldus” here and below] to himself. After each had given an oath to the other [Note: [Col. 0475] manuscript 3 reads “to one another”], a truce was accepted until the octave of Easter [Note: [Col. 0475] manuscript 2 reads “octaves”]. Not long afterward, the king spoke with Arnulfus.

Count Ragenaldus captured by night the castle of Heriveus, namely Châtillon, having climbed its wall [Note: [Col. 0475D] manuscript 2 reads “with consent”]. Then, on the third day [Note: [Col. 0475] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “thereafter”], Dodo, brother of Lord Artoldus, recovered Altmont in almost the same manner [Note: [Col. 0475] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “recovers”].

Pope Agapitus held a synod at Saint Peter’s, in which he confirmed the condemnation of Bishop Hugh made at Ingelheim. He also excommunicated Prince Hugh until he should make satisfaction to King Louis [Note: [Col. 0475] manuscript 3 reads “until they make satisfaction”].

A certain Bernardus, a partisan of Hugh, held a castle on the river Oise called Chauny [Note: [Col. 0475] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “Calnacum”] [Note: [Col. 0475D] Chauny]. He placed himself and the castle under Count Adalbertus [Note: [Col. 0475] “Count Adalbertus” is absent from manuscript 1]. A certain church dedicated in honor of Saint Mary, situated on the river Arne, was illuminated by notable miracles and by the protection of healings. Another church, likewise dedicated in her honor and situated on the little river Pidum [Note: [Col. 0475] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “Rinulum”], shone with an almost similar brilliance.

## 950

King Louis went across the Moselle to King Otto, seeking from him counsel and assistance concerning the making of peace between himself and Hugh. Otto promised that he would send Duke Chonradus with the Lotharingians to carry this out. When the duke arrived with certain bishops and counts, he spoke with Hugh about establishing peace and reported to King Louis what he had found with Hugh. Thus he returned to Otto, leaving with Louis certain counts who would communicate the king’s will to Hugh.

Accordingly, King Louis and Prince Hugh came with their men to the river Marne to make peace. The former sat on this side of the river, the latter on the other, and they sent messengers to one another [Note: [Col. 0475] manuscript 2 and 3 read “they sent one another”]. Through the mediation and arbitration of Duke Chonradus, Hugh the Black, and also Bishops Adalbero [Note: [Col. 0475] manuscripts 2 and 3 abbreviate the name] and Fulbertus, Hugh came to the king and became his man. He made peace with Count Arnulfus, with Ragenoldus, and with Archbishop Artoldus, returning the tower of Laon to the king [Note: [Col. 0475] manuscripts 1, 2, and 3 read “to the king”].

After this Hugh again held a conference with the king at Compiègne [Note: [Col. 0475] manuscripts 2 and 3 omit “after this Hugh”]. There the bishopric of Noyon was granted to Rodulfus, who served as archdeacon of that church and whom the people of Noyon had chosen to be given as their bishop [Note: [Col. 0475] manuscript 2 reads “Noyon”; manuscript 3 reads “they had chosen”].

Not long afterward Hugh went with an army to the city of Amiens. He was received into the tower held by Bishop Ragembaldus [Note: [Col. 0475] manuscript 3 reads “Ragenbaldus”]; but he besieged the other tower, which the men of Count Arnulfus were guarding, while the king lay sick at Laon.

King Otto, who had besieged a large city of the Wends called Prague [Note: [Col. 0475] manuscripts read “Winedorum” corrected to “Wenedorum”; “Prague”], received their king into submission; he also made the Hungarians subject to him. The men of Count Ragenoldus secretly captured a fortification belonging to the church of Rouen, situated on the river Vidula [Note: [Col. 0477] manuscript 2 reads “Vidulla”; manuscript 3, “Indella”], called Brain [Note: [Col. 0477] manuscript 1 reads “Bramam”].

Prince Hugh was angered by this and sent to the king. The king went there, expelled the invaders, and returned the castle itself to its former guards [Note: [Col. 0477] absent from manuscripts 2 and 3]. He then sought a conference with Hugh. While he was having it [Note: [Col. 0477] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “while it was being held”], the guards of the castle of Coucy, who had defected from Lord Artoldus, received Count Tetbaldus into the town.

The king, angered by this, asked Hugh to return that fortification to him. But since he could not obtain it [Note: [Col. 0477] manuscript 3 omits “this”], because Count Tetbaldus resisted in every way [Note: [Col. 0477] manuscript 3 reads “in every way”], he angrily left Laon without consulting Hugh [Note: [Col. 0477] one text reads: “Tetbaldus left Coucy, and ...”; manuscript 1 reads “and he left”]. Tetbaldus expelled from Coucy [Note: [Col. 0477] manuscript 1 reads “Codiacum”; manuscript 2 perhaps the same] many of those whom he had found inside.

Lord Artoldus ordained the aforesaid Rodulfus, the elected bishop of Noyon, bishop at Reims.

A certain Berengarius, a prince of Italy, became king of Italy after, as they say, killing King Lotharius, Hugh’s son, with poison.

## 951

King Louis set out for Aquitaine with an army [Note: [Col. 0477] manuscript 2 reads “set out”; manuscript 3, “goes”]. Before he entered that province, Karlus Constantinus, prince of Vienne, and Stephen, bishop of Auvergne, came to him and became his men; the same bishop honored him with rich gifts. William of Poitiers also came to meet him [Note: [Col. 0477] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “was present to meet him”].

While the king delayed entering Aquitaine, he was seized by a severe illness. Letaldus [Note: [Col. 0477] manuscript 2 reads “Letoldus”; manuscript 3, “Letodus”], a certain count of Burgundy who had then recently become his man, took proper care of him during that illness. When his strength had been restored, the king returned to Francia [Col. 0477C].

Meanwhile Fredericus [Note: [Col. 0477] “Federicus” in the source; manuscript 3 reads “Adalbero”], brother of Bishop Adalbero, who had betrothed to himself the daughter of Prince Hugh, came into this kingdom. Without consulting the king or queen, he began constructing a fortification at a place called Fains [Note: [Col. 0477] manuscript 3 reads “Banis”] [Note: [Col. 0477D] Fains, near Bar], and repeatedly plundered the surrounding places.

King Louis was greatly troubled by this and sent an embassy to Otto. Prince Hugh, going to the same King Otto at his invitation [Note: [Col. 0477] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “invited by him”], sent two lions ahead to him, and soon followed himself [Note: [Col. 0477] manuscripts 2 and 3 omit “himself”]. Otto received him honorably during the days of Easter. Hugh was suitably treated by him and remained joyfully with him at Aachen throughout the days of the Easter solemnity [Note: [Col. 0477] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “with him”]. He returned richly endowed with many gifts, while Duke Chonradus escorted him as far as the river Marne [Col. 0477D].

Duke Chonradus, angered at certain Lotharingians [Note: [Col. 0477] manuscript 2 reads “at those who were angered”], demolished the towers of some of them and deprived certain men of Verdun of their honors. He captured a castle of Count Ragenarius [Note: [Col. 0477] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “Ragenarius”], and had the rest of his possessions besieged [Note: [Col. 0477] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “had the rest besieged”].

The envoys of King Louis, returning from Otto, reported that King Otto did not wish—in fact, he forbade it—that Fredericus or any of his men should possess any fortification in this kingdom unless he could obtain King Louis’s consent in the matter [Note: [Col. 0477] manuscript 3 reads “any village”].

The Hungarians, having crossed the Alps from Italy [Note: [Col. 0477] manuscript 3 reads “having crossed”], entered Aquitaine. They spent almost the whole summer there and ravaged that region with many plunderings and killings [Note: [Col. 0477] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “threats”]; then they returned through Italy to their own land.

King Louis besieged a fortification called Brenne, which certain brigands—namely, Gotbertus and his brother Angilbertus—had fortified [Note: [Col. 0477] manuscript 2 reads “had enriched”]. He finally captured it, weakened by hunger [Note: [Col. 0477] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “captured it at last”], and demolished it. Returning from there, he went to a conference with Arnulfus and Hugh.

But Hugh, because he was angry with Arnulfus over the castle of Monastery and the land formerly belonging to Erluinus, which Arnulfus had occupied, did not wish to come to the conference. Instead, he entered that land with Rotgarius, son of Erluinus, and besieged a certain castle. At Arnulfus’s request [Note: [Col. 0477] manuscript 2 reads “at the request of the one who was able”], the king sent to Hugh, caused the siege to be lifted, and obtained a truce [or truce-period] between them until the Kalends of December [between them [Note: [Col. 0477] absent from manuscript 1]].

Queen Ottogeba [Note: [Col. 0477] thus in manuscript 1; Aethgiva in Richer; Gerberga in manuscripts 2, 2a, and 3], mother of King Louis, left Laon. Escorted by certain men of both Heribertus and her brother Adalbertus, she went to Heribertus, who received her and took her as his wife.

King Louis, angered by this, took back the abbey of Saint Mary, which she held at Laon, and gave it to his wife Gerberga. He also subjected the royal estate of Attigny to his own authority [Note: [Col. 0477] the words “the estate ... to his own authority” are absent from manuscripts 2 and 3b].

King Otto went to Italy. When King Berengarius of the Lombards fled from the city of Pavia at Otto’s arrival, Otto himself entered that city. He also took as his wife the widow of the deceased King Lotharius, Hugh’s son, the sister of King Chonradus of Burgundy [Note: [Col. 0477] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “takes”]. The Saracens, blockading the Alpine passes, collected tribute from travelers going to Rome and thus allowed them to pass.

## 952

King Otto sent an embassy to Rome to secure his reception. When he did not obtain it, he returned to his own lands with his wife [Col. 0478D], leaving some of his men to guard Pavia.

Louis returned to Laon with Queen Gerberga [Note: [Col. 0477] manuscript 3 reads “captured”]. King Berengarius came to Duke Chonradus, who had remained at Pavia. Chonradus received him under his protection and brought him to Otto. Otto received him kindly and, granting him such possessions in Italy as he thought appropriate [Note: [Col. 0479] manuscript 2 reads “granting certain possessions, to return peacefully into Italy”], allowed him to return peacefully. Otto himself, after celebrating Easter, returned to Pavia [Note: [Col. 0479] the editor observes: “Flodoardus seems to have been thinking of Berengarius; Otto certainly did not come to Italy in this year.”].

Count Hugh came with his men to the river Marne. Duke Chonradus met him there with certain Lotharingians. Together they besieged the fortification at Mareuil [Note: [Col. 0479] manuscript 3 reads “Maroillum”], which Count Ragenaldus [Note: [Col. 0479] manuscripts 2 and 3, frequently, read “Ragenoldus”], together with the men of Lord Bishop Artoldus, had recently built within the river. Having set up many siege engines on every side, they pressed it vigorously. At last, not without loss among their own men, they captured and burned it; those who were inside came out under Chonradus’s protection [Note: [Col. 0479] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “to them”].

Meanwhile Hugh’s nephews, Heribertus and Rotbertus [Note: [Col. 0479] manuscript 2 reads “Robertus”], built a fortification for themselves at a place called Mont-Félix [Col. 0479B]. Thus both Hugh and Chonradus returned to their own territories.

Without delay, King Louis and Archbishop Artoldus, together with Count Ragenaldus [Note: [Col. 0479] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “after proceeding with Count Ragenaldus”], went to the river Marne and rebuilt the fortification that the aforesaid princes had burned; they also stationed many guards there.

From there the king went with Ragenaldus into the region of the castle of Vitry, which a certain Walter held. Walter had recently defected from the king and submitted himself, together with the castle, to Heribertus. They devastated Walter’s villages with plundering and fires, as well as the royal estate of Pontigon, which Heribertus had seized.

The king built another fortification against Vitry and left there, to guard it, certain of Walter’s peers [Note: [Col. 0479] thus in manuscripts 1, 2, and 3; Du Chesne and Bouquet read “from Walter’s parties”]. He entrusted the fortification itself to a certain Abbot Odalricus from Burgundy [Col. 0479C], and thus returned to Laon. Not long afterward, he returned to Reims with the queen.

Archbishop Artoldus sent monks to the monastery of Saint Basolus, expelling the clerics who served there [Note: [Col. 0479] manuscript 1 reads “who served him”], and entrusted it to Abbots Hincmarus and Rotmarus.

## 953

At the beginning of the year, Prince Hugh sent envoys to King Louis to establish peace and concord between them. He asked that Queen Gerberga seek a meeting with him [Note: [Col. 0479] manuscript 1 reads “conversation”]. She did so, was honored by him with gifts [Note: [Col. 0479] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “by him”], and returned to Reims. Hugh obtained from the king that the fortification constructed against the castle of Vitry should be dismantled.

Thus, in the middle of Lent, the king and Hugh entered into an agreement of concord and peace at Soissons.

Meanwhile discord arose between King Otto and his son Liudulfus, as well as between Duke Chonradus and certain leading men of Otto’s kingdom. For when a son had been born to the king by his present wife, it was reported that the king promised that child his kingdom [Col. 0480A], which he had formerly assigned to Liudulfus before going to Italy, and had made his magnates swear an oath of loyalty to Liudulfus.

The king therefore removed Chonradus from the duchy of the Lotharingians [Note: [Col. 0479] manuscript 2 reads “from the duchy, so that ...”], and Chonradus sought to capture the king. When the king learned this, he began to act cautiously [Note: [Col. 0479] absent from manuscript 2] and to seek Chonradus’s death; Chonradus, meanwhile, fortified his towns.

Ragenarius [Note: [Col. 0479] manuscript 2 corrected “Regenarius” to “Ragenarius”], who had long been his enemy, besieged one of his most strongly fortified castles [Note: [Col. 0479] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “besieged a very strongly fortified castle”]. Chonradus therefore gathered as large a force of soldiers as he could and hastened to raise the siege. When they engaged one another and many on both sides were killed [Note: [Col. 0479] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “killed”], Chonradus was put to flight [Note: [Col. 0479] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “was turned in flight”] and entered the city of Mainz [Note: [Col. 0479] manuscript 3 reads “into the city”; manuscripts 2 and 3 consistently spell the city “Maguntia”].

Meanwhile Queen Gerberga gave birth at Laon to twins [Col. 0480B], one of whom was called Charles and the other Henry. But Henry died soon after baptism [Note: [Col. 0479] absent from manuscript 2].

A synod of five bishops was held at Saint-Thierry in the territory of Reims, with Archbishop Artoldus presiding. Count Ragenaldus had been summoned to it because of the ecclesiastical possessions he had seized from the bishop, but he refused to come. He begged the king not to have him excommunicated and to send him to the synod; at the king’s request, his excommunication was then suspended.

King Otto besieged the city of Mainz, where Chonradus had taken refuge. At last, after nearly two months, he spoke with Chonradus, who had come out to him, received hostages from him, and returned across the Rhine.

Without delay Chonradus, leaving a garrison of his soldiers at Mainz, went to the city of Metz, which he soon entered by a secret incursion [Note: [Col. 0479] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “secret invasion”]. King Otto, summoned by his brother Henry, went to Bavaria, which his son Liudulfus was devastating after capturing certain cities.

Chonradus also abandoned the city of Metz after extensively plundering it, at the urging, as is said, of Abbot Agenoldus [Note: [Col. 0479] manuscript 2 reads “at the urging”]. Wicfredus, bishop of Cologne, died, and Bruno, King Otto’s brother, was ordained bishop there. King Otto also entrusted the kingdom of Lotharingia to him.

## 954

The aforesaid Chonradus, having made a pact with the Hungarians, led them through the kingdom of Lotharingia as far as the land of Ragenarius [Note: [Col. 0479] manuscript 1 reads “Ragnarius”—namely, that of his rival and of Bishop Bruno]. After they had carried out enormous plundering [Note: [Col. 0479] “enormous” is a typographical error in manuscript 3], they entered the kingdom of Louis with great booty and a multitude of captives [Col. 0480D].

Thus passing through the districts of Vermandois, Laon, Reims, and also Châlons, they entered Burgundy. A considerable number of them perished both in battles and from disease [Col. 0481A]; the rest returned through Italy to their own country.

Louis, the king’s son, died at Laon. King Louis left Laon and returned to the city of Reims, intending to remain there [Note: [Col. 0481] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “returned”]. Before he reached the river Aisne [Note: [Col. 0481] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “Axonem”], a wolf seemed to appear before him. He pursued it at a gallop, fell, and was severely bruised. He was carried to Reims, where, lying ill for a prolonged period [Note: [Col. 0481] manuscript 2 reads “illness”], he was afflicted by the disease of elephantiasis [Note: [Col. 0481] manuscript 2 and Richer read “elephantiasis”; manuscript 1 reads “of elephantiasis”; manuscript 3 reads “elephantiasis”]. Overcome by this illness, he ended his days and was buried at Saint Remigius.

Queen Gerberga sent to Hugh, asking his counsel and assistance. He summoned her to a conference, received her honorably when she came, and consoled her. He also promised to advance her son to the kingdom.

Liudulfus, having expelled his uncle Henry [Note: [Col. 0481] manuscript 1 reads “his father”], obtained the rule of all Bavaria. The Lotharingians were torn apart both by the attacks of Duke Chonradus and by mutual plundering among themselves.

Fulcharius [Note: [Col. 0481] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “Fulcarius”; manuscript 3a, “Fulcanus”], dean of the monastery of Saint Medardus, was ordained bishop of Noyon at Reims [Note: [Col. 0481] manuscript 3 reads “was ordained”]. Fredericus, brother of Bishop Adalbero [Note: [Col. 0481] manuscripts 2 and 3 abbreviate the name], took the daughter of Prince Hugh as his wife.

Roucy, the fortification of Ragenaldus. Count Heribertus secretly entered it through a sudden incursion [Note: [Col. 0481] manuscript 3 reads “invaded”; manuscripts 2 and 3 read “incursion”].

Lotharius, the son of Louis, was consecrated king at Saint Remigius by Archbishop Artoldus, with the support of Prince Hugh, Archbishop Bruno, and the other bishops and nobles of Francia, Burgundy [Note: [Col. 0481] absent from manuscript 2; present, together with the reading “at,” in Richer], and Aquitaine. Burgundy and Aquitaine were also given to Hugh by Lotharius himself.

The castle of Roucy was returned to Ragenaldus, while certain villages were given to Heribertus from Ragenaldus’s possessions. Queen Gerberga returned to Laon with her son the king [Note: [Col. 0481] absent from manuscript 1].

Not long afterward, Ragenaldus’s soldiers captured by a clandestine incursion [Note: [Col. 0481] manuscript 2 reads “secret”] the fortification of Heribertus called Mont-Félix, across the river Marne [Note: [Col. 0481] manuscript 2 reads “clandestine”; manuscripts 2 and 3 read “incursion”]. Heribertus and his brother Robert therefore besieged that fortification, and Heribertus sent envoys from Reims to Ragenaldus to ask for the return of the town.

Ragenaldus refused unless the siege were abandoned and they came to a judicial accounting concerning the castles they had mutually seized [Note: [Col. 0481] manuscript 1 reads “seized”]. When this had been done, he received back from Heribertus the villages that he had given for the aforesaid castle [Note: [Col. 0481] manuscript 2 reads “for the wrongfully seized castle”], and returned the town of Mont-Félix to Heribertus.

When Alberic, prefect of the Romans, died, his son Octavianus, although he was a cleric, obtained the prefecture [Note: [Col. 0481] Hugh of Flavigny reads “prefecture”]. Later, after Agapitus died, the Romans urged him to become pope of the city.

## 955

[Col. 0482A]

When the Hungarians set out from their own lands to plunder, King Otto went to meet them, fought them, and defeated them; he did not allow them to enter his kingdoms.

Prince Hugh honorably received Queen Gerberga and her son, King Lotharius, at Paris for Easter and kept them with him suitably for several days. From there he went with the king into Aquitaine and approached the city of Poitiers. They did not find William there, but nevertheless besieged the city. They remained at the siege for a long time without accomplishing anything. Count Ragenaldus, however, secretly captured the castle of Saint Radegund, adjoining the city [Note: [Col. 0481] manuscript 2 reads “secretly designated”], and it was burned [Note: [Col. 0481] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “incursion”]. At last, after two months, with the army exhausted by want, the siege was abandoned.

William gathered his army and pursued the king’s army [Col. 0482B]. When the king heard this, he and Hugh turned back against him. Seeing their great numbers at close quarters, William fled. The royal forces pursued him, killed many Aquitanians, and captured some of the nobles alive. William barely escaped with a few companions [Note: [Col. 0481] manuscripts 2 and 3 read “escapes”].

The Hungarians entered Bavaria with immense forces and a huge multitude, intending to come into Francia [Note: [Col. 0481] absent from manuscript 2]. Against them King Otto fought together with Burislaus, prince of the Sarmatians [Col. 0481D] [Bohemians], and with Chonradus, who had already been reconciled to him [Note: [Col. 0481D] Hugh V also noted the fourth day before the Ides of August]. He slaughtered those same Hungarians and almost completely destroyed them.

Chonradus, who had fought extraordinarily bravely that day and had especially encouraged the king by the victory, was killed there. After this battle King Otto fought with two kings of the Sarmatians [Col. 0482C]. With King Burislaus supporting him—the same king whom he had previously subjected—he won the victory.

After Bishop Fulcharius died, at last, five months later, a certain Hadulfus, a cleric of Laon, was elected by the people of Noyon and ordained bishop at Reims by Artoldus, Rorico, and Gibuinus [Note: [Col. 0481] manuscript 3 reads “and”].

## 956
King Otto held a formal assembly at Engulenheim [Note: [Col. 0481] “Engulehem” in 2; “Enguheein” in 3] with the Lotharingians, from whom he also received hostages from nearly all their towns. Another assembly was likewise held by him after Easter at Cologne, where he received not a few treasures from the Lotharingians. Soon afterward pestilence spread throughout Germany and all Gaul; some died, and more were exhausted by severe illness. Rotbert, bishop of Trier [Note: [Col. 0481] “Ragnarius” in 2 and 3, but the word is absent in 1 and 2], and Balderic [Note: [Col. 0481] “Baldricus” in 2 and 3] [Note: [Col. 0482D] of Liège], together with two other bishops, died without delay from that pestilence. King Lothar recovered by fighting a certain stronghold on the river Chiers [Note: [Col. 0481] “Carum” in 2 and 3], which Count Ragenarius [Note: [Col. 0481] “Ragnarius” repeatedly in 1; “Ingenarius” in 3] had taken from a certain Ursio, a soldier of the church of Reims [Col. 0483A]; he carried away with him Ragenarius’s children and some soldiers found there, and, after plundering the castle, burned it. Prince Hugh died. Queen Gerberga held a conference with her brother Bruno, at which Ragenarius’s soldiers and children were restored to him; the queen’s possessions, which Duke Gislebert had once given her as a dower, were restored to the queen. The bishopric of Trier was given to a certain Haynricus [Note: [Col. 0483] “Hayricus” in 1; cf. Hugh V.; “Hainricus” in 2; “Heinricus” in 3], a kinsman of King Otto. Fulbert, bishop of Cambrai, died; and the bishopric itself was granted to a certain Berengarius, a cleric from across the Rhine, nephew of Bovo, formerly bishop of Châlons [Note: [Col. 0483] “Catalaunensis” in 2], and he was ordained at Reims by Archbishop Artoldus [Note: [Col. 0483] “bishop” in 2 and 3]. In the year

## 957

[Col. 0483B] One night in January the church of the holy Mother of God at Reims was suddenly illuminated shortly after midnight [Note: [Col. 0483] “at midnight” in 2] with a great brilliance, in the presence of Lord Archbishop Artoldus, while Withardus, the custodian, likewise gazed on in wonder. King Lothar went into Upper Burgundy. The turmoil of wars was stirred up between Bruno, formerly a bishop and now duke, and Count Ragenarius and the other Lotharingians; likewise in Francia between Baldwin, son of Arnulf, and Rotgarius, formerly associated with Erluin, over the castle of Amiens [Note: [Col. 0483] “Amiens” in 1]. Rotbert, son of Heribert, entrusted himself to King Lothar. King Lothar, with his mother [Note: [Col. 0483] “his mother” in 2 and 3] and his aunt [Note: [Col. 0483] “friend” in 3], the widow of Hugh [Note: [Col. 0483] “to Hugh” in 1 and 3], went to meet his uncle Bruno in the district of Cambrai. When Ragenarius saw that he could not resist the multitude coming against him [Col. 0483C], he came to Bruno [Note: [Col. 0483] “came to Bruno” in 2]. But because he refused to give the hostages who had been demanded, Bruno seized him and led him away under guard; not long afterward he sent him across the Rhine into exile. Liudolf, son of Otto, who had obtained nearly all Italy, died and was buried at Mainz at Saint Alban’s.

## 958

Certain faithful men of Bishop Artoldus captured the castle of Codiciacum in a clandestine attack [Note: [Col. 0483] “by stealth” in 2; “by surprise” in 3]. Harduinus, a subordinate of Tetbaldus, to whom Tetbaldus had entrusted the castle, seeing the town captured, fled with his men into the citadel [Note: [Col. 0483] “fled with his men” in 2 and 3]. That tower was exceedingly strong. King Lothar came to storm it with Lord Artoldus and several other bishops and counts, and besieged it for nearly two weeks; [Col. 0483D] at last, after receiving Harduinus’s nephews as hostages [Note: [Col. 0483] “Harduinus” in 2 and 3], they withdrew from the siege. Then Tetbaldus arrived, but was not admitted into the town; returning through the districts of Laon and Soissons, he raged through them with plunder and returned to his own territory. Tetbaldus’s men captured a stronghold called Fara [Note: [Col. 0483] “Materias” in 2], after certain traitors had handed it over to them. To besiege it, Rorico, bishop of Laon, came with the soldiers of the church of Reims and with other friends whom he was able to summon [Col. 0484A]. When King Lothar finally arrived, the castle was surrendered by Tetbaldus’s command, through the mediation of the brothers Heribert and Rotbert. King Otto waged war [Note: [Col. 0483] absent in 2 and 3] against the Sarmatians [Note: [Col. 0483] “waged war” in 2]. Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, set out with an army of Lotharingians through Francia into Burgundy to speak with his sisters and nephews.

## 959

Bruno came again [Note: [Col. 0483] “also” in 2 and 3] into Francia and held a conference at Compiègne with his sister the queen and his nephews, who were at odds over certain castles that King Lothar had recovered from Burgundy; after hostages had been given, he established peace between them until the forthcoming assembly [Note: [Col. 0483] “until the time of the assembly” in 2 and 3]. During the days of Easter, King Lothar went with his mother [Col. 0484B] the queen to Cologne [Note: [Col. 0483] partly illegible, apparently “on Easter day,” in 1], intending to spend the festival there with his uncle Bruno. After security had been given to him concerning the Lotharingian kingdom, and after he had received certain gifts from his uncle, he returned to Laon.

The Lotharingians defected from Duke Bruno [Note: [Col. 0483] “from Duke Bruno” in 2 and 3], at the urging of a certain Immo, who had formerly been his counsellor but had recently withdrawn from him, because of certain new fortifications belonging to them, which the same duke ordered to be destroyed, and because of other burdens unfamiliar to them [Note: [Col. 0483] “to them” in 2], which he was said to wish to impose upon them. Afterward, when they had been summoned [Note: [Col. 0483] “recalled” in 2 and 3], he appointed a certain Count Frederick over them in his place.

Count Arnulf came to Reims and presented the church of Saint Mary with a considerable weight of silver. With it, the chests containing the relics of Saint Calixtus [Note: [Col. 0483] “Calixtus” in 3], Saint Nicasius, Saint Eutropia [Col. 0484C], and certain other saints were ornamented or covered [Note: [Col. 0483] “adorned” in 1]. He also decorated one of the Gospel books of this church with gold and silver; he likewise bestowed gifts upon the monastery of Saint Remigius.

Count Rotbert seized the castle of Dijon [Note: [Col. 0483] “Divionum” in 2 and 3], expelling the king’s faithful men. Therefore Bruno, summoned at the request of the king and queen, came into Burgundy with the Lotharingians and other peoples subject to him; he surrounded by siege both that castle and the city of Troyes, which the aforesaid Rotbert possessed.

## 960

At Altmont, certain traitors were discovered by Manasses, nephew of Lord Bishop Artoldus, and condemned to hanging; among them was also a certain priest [Col. 0484D]. A fortification called Maceriae [Note: [Col. 0483] “Materias” in 2], situated above the Meuse and below the territory of the church of Reims, was restored by Lantbertus to Archbishop Artoldus, in the presence of Frederick, duke of the Lotharingians [Note: [Col. 0483] the words “in the presence of Frederick, duke of the Lotharingians” are absent in 1],, who had been forbidden to retain it.

Richard, son of William, prince of the Normans [Note: [Col. 0483] “the prince” in 2 and 3], married the daughter of Hugh, formerly prince beyond the Seine [Note: [Col. 0483] “beyond the Seine” in 2 and 3; “Transequanus” in 1; Note: [Col. 0483] “he married” in 3].

Rotbert, brother of Heribert, deceitfully entered and seized a certain fortification called Dijon, which the faithful men of King Lothar held, pretending to be the king’s faithful man and expelling the royal guards. The king went with his mother the queen to recover it and besieged the castle [Note: [Col. 0485] “castle” absent in 1]. Bishop Bruno [Note: [Col. 0485] “castle Bruno” in 1], arriving there with the Lotharingians and others subject to him, received hostages from Rotbert and handed them over to the king. One of them, the son of Count Odelricus [Note: [Col. 0485] “Odalricus” in 2 and 3], was proved and judged a traitor and was beheaded; the other was kept alive in custody.

Otto and Hugh, sons of Hugh, came to the king through the mediation of their uncle Bruno and became his men. The king made Hugh duke, adding to him the district of Poitiers together with the land that his father had held; Burgundy was granted to Otto. When Bruno heard that certain Lotharingians were rising against him [Col. 0485B], he returned there in haste, leaving the king with his cousins at the siege.

One of Bruno’s enemies, named Rotbert, was fortifying the castle of Namur [Note: [Col. 0485] so in 1; “Manuvium” in 2 and 3] [Note: [Col. 0485D] Namur]. Another, Immo, was fortifying the stronghold called Capraemont. Bruno hastened to besiege it [Note: [Col. 0485] “hastened” in 2 and 3] and found the surrounding places exhausted of supplies [Note: [Col. 0485] “depleted” in 2]. Thus he besieged the enemy, who had an abundant supply of provisions [Note: [Col. 0485] “with abundant food” in 2 and 3]. After truces had been granted, he entered Cologne. King Lothar, having recovered the fortification of Dijon [Note: [Col. 0485] “Divione” in 2], installed his own guards and returned to Laon.

## 961 [Note: [Col. 0485] “after the nine-hundred-and-sixty-first year” in 1, 2, and 3]

Wido, bishop of Auxerre [Note: [Col. 0485] “Autisiodorensis” in 2; “Antisiodorensis” in 3], died. Otto, son of Hugh, formerly prince, came to King Lothar at Laon during the very days of the Easter festival, as did several nobles from both Francia and Burgundy [Note: [Col. 0485] absent in 1].

A royal assembly and a gathering of various princes [Note: [Col. 0485] “of various” corrected to “of various princes” in 1] was held at Soissons. Richard, son of William the Norman, approached it in order, if possible, to prevent it; but he was attacked by certain of the king’s faithful men, and, after some of his men had been killed, was put to flight [Note: [Col. 0485] “turned in flight” in 2 and 3]. Hugh, son of the former Count Rotgarius, died as a young man [Note: [Col. 0485] absent in 3] and was buried at Saint Remigius. Artoldus, archbishop of Reims, died on the day before the Kalends of October [Note: [Col. 0485] “withdrew” in 2]. King Lothar, with his mother [Gerberga the queen is absent in 1; Note: [Col. 0485]], and certain nobles of Francia, went to Burgundy; some bishops and leading men from Aquitaine came to him there [Note: [Col. 0485] “Aquitaine” in 3].

## 962

[Col. 0485D] Queen Gerberga sought a conference with her brother Bruno [Col. 0486A] [Note: [Col. 0485] “sought” in 2 and below], and this brother of hers advised him not to restore the bishopric of Reims to Hugh, as his brothers were requesting [Note: [Col. 0485] “his brother was requesting” in 2 and 3; Note: [Col. 0486D] that is, Hugh, son of Heribert].

King Otto went peacefully to Rome, was received graciously, and was there raised to imperial dignity. King Berengarius of Italy, bearing this with indignation, began to burn and ravage the regions that he ought to govern.

King Lothar spoke with his cousin Hugh, who requested that he restore the bishopric of Reims to the aforesaid Hugh. They therefore made a truce until the middle of April.

A synod of thirteen bishops was held in the district of Meaux, on the river Marne, from the dioceses of Reims and Sens, presided over by the bishop of Sens. Certain bishops were striving to have the bishopric of Reims returned to the aforesaid Hugh [Col. 0486B] [Note: [Col. 0485] “restored” in the Reims manuscript, 2, and 3]. But because Rorico, bishop of Laon, and Gibuinus, bishop of Châlons, were especially opposed, and asserted that one who had been excommunicated by so many bishops could not be absolved by a smaller number [Note: [Col. 0485] “could not have been absolved” in 2], the matter was left in this state until the pope of Rome could be consulted.

On the day of the Nativity of Our Lady, the Mother of God, a certain demoniac, a servant of Queen Gerberga, ran naked through the middle of the church to the altar and lay there as if dead. At length he rose, cleansed of the evil spirit [Note: [Col. 0485] “At length, after the unclean spirit had been expelled, he was cleansed” in 2 and 3b]. On that same day a certain blind man named Harbertus [Note: [Col. 0485] “Herbertus” in 2; “Heribertus” in 3] was given sight there [Note: [Col. 0485] “was illuminated” in 2 and 3].

King [Note: [Col. 0485] absent in 2] Lothar spoke with Prince Arnulf and made peace between him and his nephew of the same name [Note: [Col. 0485] “Ononmum” in 1], against whom he was hostile [the words “this count” are absent in 1; Note: [Col. 0485]], because of the killing of his brother, whom that same count had ordered killed after discovering his treachery [Note: [Col. 0485] “infirmity” in 2 and 3; “his” absent in 2 and 3]. Then the prince placed all his land in the king’s hands, but on the condition that he himself would remain honored in it during his lifetime [Note: [Col. 0485] “so that he himself would remain honored there during his lifetime” in 2].

A certain Tetbaldus [Note: [Col. 0485] “indeed” in 2 and 3], fighting with the Normans, was defeated by them and escaped by fleeing. Since he was consequently hostile to his lord Hugh [Note: [Col. 0485] “offended” in 2 and 3], he came to the king. He was kindly received by the king and by Queen Gerberga [Note: [Col. 0485] “by Queen Gerberga” in 2 and 3] and departed, refreshed by gentle consolation.

Vulfaldus [Note: [Col. 0485] “Vulfoldus” in 2 and 3], abbot of the monastery of Saint Benedict, was made bishop of the city of Chartres [Note: [Col. 0485] absent in 2 and 3].

An embassy came from Pope John [Note: [Col. 0485] “from” in 2 and 3] and announced that the aforesaid Hugh, formerly a bishop, had been excommunicated both by the pope himself and by the entire Roman synod [Col. 0486D], as well as by another synod held at Pavia.

[Col. 0487A] Having been informed of this embassy through Archbishop Bruno, we chose for the bishopric [Note: [Col. 0487] “the bishop” in 2 and 3] of Reims Odelricus [Note: [Col. 0487] “Odelricus,” corrected from “Odelrico,” in 1; “Odalricus” in 2 and 3], an illustrious cleric, son of a certain Count Hugh, with the favor of King Lothar, his mother the queen, and the aforesaid Bruno. He was ordained at Reims by the bishops Wido of Soissons, Rorico of Laon, Gibuinus of Châlons, Hadulfus of Noyon, and Wicfredus of Verdun.

## 963

Odelricus [Note: [Col. 0487] “Odalricus” in 2 and 3], archbishop of Reims, summoned the nobles of Francia who had occupied certain possessions of the church of Reims. But I, broken by age and worn down by illness, resigned the ministry of the prelacy in the presence of that same bishop. He, releasing me from this yoke, imposed it by election of our brothers [Note: [Col. 0487] “my brothers” in 3] upon my nephew Flodoardus [Note: [Col. 0487] “Frodoardus” in 2 and 3], in the seventieth year of my life.

After Bishop Gibuinus had departed, the brothers Heribert and Rotbert besieged the city of Châlons. At length, when the market-fairs had ended [Note: [Col. 0487] absent in 2], they set it on fire; but the soldiers were freed after climbing into a certain tower of the place [Note: [Col. 0487] “in the tower of the place” in 2 and 3].

## 964

The winter was very long and severe [Note: [Col. 0487] “hyemps” in 2] until the Kalends of February [Note: [Col. 0487] “Februarii” in 2 and 3].
