Lord Bishop Odelricus excommunicated a certain nobleman, Tetbaldus [Note: [Col. 0487] “excommunicated” in the past tense in 2], on account of the castle of Codiciacum and certain estates of Saint Remigius, which he had unjustly obtained and stubbornly retained.

Count Heribert returned the village of Épernay to him and obtained the friendship of the aforesaid bishop; he also did not hesitate to return to the same bishop, when he demanded them, the remaining villages of the church of Reims [Col. 0487C] that he had occupied [Note: [Col. 0487] “when he demanded them back” in 3b].

## 965

Otto, son of Hugh, who governed Burgundy, died, and the rulers of that land [the word “land” is absent in 1; Note: [Col. 0487] “and” in 2] turned to Hugh and Odo [Note: [Col. 0487] “Odo” in 2 and 3], his brothers, who were clerics.

When Prince Arnulf also died, King Lothar entered his territory, and its nobles were subjected to the same king through the mediation of Rorico, bishop of Laon. When Lothar returned to Laon [Note: [Col. 0487] “while returning” corrected to “when he returned” in 2], his mother, Queen Gerberga, remained there with her young son Charles.

Archbishop Odelricus received Épernay from Heribert [Note: [Col. 0487] absent in 2], and Codiciacum from Tetbaldus; he absolved Tetbaldus from the bond of excommunication [Note: [Col. 0487] “from his uncle” corrected to “from the bond” in 1], and granted that same castle to Tetbaldus’s son, who had entrusted himself to him.

[Col. 0488A] Returning from the city of Rome, Emperor Otto came to Cologne. There he received Queen Gerberga, his sister, who had come to meet him with her sons King Lothar and the boy Charles; and with them and many other nobles he held a great assembly.

At Rome, when Pope Octavianus, by whom Otto had been received and blessed to govern the affairs of the empire, had departed from the city and the emperor had often recalled him, but Octavianus refused to return because he was being reproved for his irreligious conduct, Otto summoned a synod and caused a certain illustrious cleric of that same church, John [Note: [Col. 0487D] Leo VIII; Hugh V is more mistaken in asserting that John XII had then been installed], to be ordained pope by election of the Romans.

But when John returned to Pavia [Note: [Col. 0487] “entered” in 2 and 3], Octavianus was accepted by the Romans; not long afterward he died. While John remained at Pavia with the emperor [Col. 0488B], the Romans chose a certain Benedict, a notary of that church, and caused him to be ordained pope for themselves. He had consented to John’s election [Note: [Col. 0487] “consented” in 2] and had remained subject to him.

Emperor Otto returned to Rome, summoned a great synod, and restored John to his seat. Benedict, who had been deposed by the judgment of all the bishops of the synod [Note: [Col. 0487] “Benedict, because he had ascended his father’s bed” in Hugh V], he took away with him and sent into Saxony [Note: [Col. 0487] “brought him away” in 2; “took him away” in 3].

## 966

King Lothar took as his wife Emma, daughter of [Note: [Col. 0488D] “Lothar, son of Hugh”] a former king of Italy [Note: [Col. 0487] “of Italy” in 3b]. Archbishop Odelricus excommunicated Count Ragenaldus because of the villages of the church of Reims that he stubbornly retained [Note: [Col. 0487] “held” in 2 and 3]. The count himself, entering certain places belonging to the same bishopric [Col. 0488C] with his men, ravaged them with plunder and fire.

[Note: [Col. 0488C] In Migne, the section headed “Addit Codex 1” and the section headed “Addit Codex 2” are printed in parallel.]

## Addition from Codex 1

[Col. 0488C]

At that time a letter was sent by a certain count to the duke of the Aquitanians, containing the following:

“To G., duke of the Aquitanians, from Count Raynaldus of Porcien: whatever any good man considers first and foremost.

“Concerning our conversation and concerning the journey about which you warned me, I altogether decline. For age and other impediments hinder our journey. But concerning the genealogy—or rather the relationship—which you intended to recount in my presence, I have taken care to send you by letter what I know of it.

“Mathilde and Alberada were daughters of Gerberga. From Mathilde came King Rudolf and his sister Mathilde. From Alberada came Ermentrudis. From Mathilde, daughter of Mathilde, came Berta. From Ermentrudis came Agnes. From Berta came Geraldus of Geneva. From Agnes came Wido” [Note: [Col. 0489] Here half a page of space is left blank in 1].

## Addition from Codex 2

[Col. 0488C]

In that same year a man venerable in life, a priest of the church of Reims named Frodoardus, worthy of veneration for the honor of his holiness [Note: [Col. 0487] “the honor of holiness” in 3], angelic in the splendor of his chastity, heavenly in the radiance of his wisdom [Note: [Col. 0487] “from heaven” in 3], abundantly filled with the marks of the other virtues [Note: [Col. 0487] “filled” in 3], an outstanding author of the preceding book and of other books, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April [Note: [Col. 0487] feminine “fifth” in 3], abandoning the exile of his earthly pilgrimage, attained, as we believe, the rights of citizenship [Col. 0489A]. A marvelous and unprecedented downpour of rain, with crashing thunder and flashing lightning, occurred on the tenth day before the Kalends of August [Note: [Col. 0489] Here manuscript 2a ends]. 967. 968. 969. 970. 971. 972. 973. 974. 975.

In the year 976 Adelbero, archbishop in name but not in merit, destroyed the arched structure that stood beside the doors of the church of Saint Mary at Reims [Col. 0489B]. Upon it stood the altar of Saint Saviour, and fountains had been set there with marvelous workmanship.

At that same time, during Lent [Note: [Col. 0489] “in the fortieth year” in 3], on the Wednesday of Holy Week, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the fourth indiction [Note: [Col. 0489] “in the fourth indiction” in 3], around midday, a battle was fought between Charles, the king’s son and brother [Col. 0489C] [Note: [Col. 0489] “son of Louis, brother of Lothar, the kings”], and the Lotharingian counts Godefridus and Arnulfus.

In that battle, on Charles’s side there fell among the nobles Emmo of Longia, who was a soldier of Duke Hugh, and Hetdo [Note: [Col. 0489] “Ahetdo” in 3], a faithful man of Charles, and others; on Godefridus’s side many more fell. Godefridus himself was pierced by a lance and fell to the ground; at last, after sunset, his men somehow lifted him and carried him away. He lived afterward for some time, but was never fully restored to his former health.

Arnulfus, some report, maintained his flight for so long, returning [Col. 0489C], until he reached his own territory and was able to rest. In that same year, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January, Bishop Rorico of the holy church of Laon, who had been grievously afflicted by paralytic illness [Note: [Col. 0489] “illness” in 2; “paralysis” in 3], departed this life after giving many and fitting thanks to God for that illness [Col. 0490A]—namely, on the vigil of Saint Thomas the Apostle, after the morning praises of God. In that same year, around the month of August, a modius of wine was bought for seven denarii.

In the year 977 Adalbero [Note: [Col. 0489] “Adalbertus” in 2; “Adelbero” in 3], a young man born from the realm of Lothar, succeeded Bishop Rorico in the following manner. On the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February [Note: [Col. 0489] “seventeenth” in 3b], on the feast of Pope Saint Marcellus, he received the gift of the bishopric of the church of Laon in that very church, by the generosity of King Lothar.

Then, on the ninth day before the Kalends of April [Note: [Col. 0489] “ninth” in 3; “on the ninth” in 3b], namely on the vigil of the Annunciation of the Lord, he was ordained priest in the aforesaid church of Saint Mary by Archbishop Adelbero at Reims [Note: [Col. 0489] “at Reims, finally” in 3]. Finally, afterward, on the Kalends of April, he was ordained bishop on the holy day of Palm Sunday.

Returning from there to Laon [Col. 0490B], he consecrated the sacred chrism according to ecclesiastical custom; on Easter day he first [Note: [Col. 0489] feminine “first” in 2? and 3b] took his seat in his own see.

Hadulfus, bishop of Noyon, who for a long period had been terribly struck by paralysis, breathed out his spirit on the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, which at that time fell on a Sunday [Note: [Col. 0489] “breathed out” in 3]. In that same year, at the time of the vintage, there was a great abundance of wine, so much so that sellers accepted from buyers no more than five, four, or even three denarii for a single modius of wine [Note: [Col. 0489] “whether five, four, or three denarii” in 3].

In the year 978 the man of God Malcallanus [Note: [Col. 0489] “Malcallinus” in 3; “Malcalnus” in 3b], an Irishman by nationality, abandoned the transient life, which he hated [Note: [Col. 0489] “hated” in 2], on the vigil of Saint Vincent the Levite and Martyr, and happily began to live with the living God, whom he had served without ceasing while he still lived [Note: [Col. 0489] “with the Lord, whose servant he had been” in 3].

The aforesaid abbot was buried in the body and rests in the church of the blessed archangel Michael; while he remained bodily alive in this world [Note: [Col. 0489] “while he remained” in 3], he governed its abbey with pious direction.

[Col. 0489] End.

# The Metrical Works of Flodoard, Canon of Reims, Now Published for the First Time

[Note: [Col. 0491] 1. The Mazarin Codex, marked L no. 2004, a paper quarto from the beginning of the sixteenth century, formerly belonging to the monastery of the Discalced Carmelites of Paris. 2. The Codex of the Library of Saint Geneviève in Paris, on parchment, a quarto from the tenth century, marked 4 Y, written in a large and clear script. It is defective at the beginning and end; it begins: “With our first fruits,” verse 8 of chapter 1 of Book I, *On the Triumphs of Christ and the Saints of Palestine*; it ends at the following words, verse 184 of chapter 1 of Book V, *On the Triumphs of Christ in Italy*. At the beginning the following words have been sewn in later: “In the year 1746, this parchment codex, breathing the fragrance of the earliest Christian piety and most highly distinguished by the noble summit of its ancient script, inherited by hereditary right from ancestors distinguished both by nobility of birth and by virtue and learning, the Lord Franciscus de Martigny of Laon, a man venerable for his ancient manners—which is rare—and for the singular number of his eighty-six years—would that they were more!—freely presents to the regular canons of the royal basilica of Saint Geneviève in Paris, as an everlasting memorial of grateful devotion toward the patroness of the kingdom. He, a parishioner of Saint Leodegarus of Soissons under the governance of those same canons, personally saw to it, at his own expense, that the altar intended for parish ministry should be transformed from wood into marble and adorned with four elegant statues; that six altar candlesticks and a central image of the Crucified One should be made of bronze and silver, skillfully wrought; and that sacred vestments for the more solemn services of the sanctuary and choir should be made magnificent instead of ordinary.”]

## Invocation

[Col. 0491A]

God, boundless light, making the world serene with radiance,  
Illuminating the heavens with the lovely brightness of eternal light,  
You paint the star-bearing sky with sidereal light;  
You restrain the sea and lands by divine reason,  
You expose the air to winged creatures and the sea to sailors;  
You adorn the green fields with grasses and forests,  
And fill them with living creatures of varied kind and form.  

Above all creatures and the whole world you set humankind in honor,  
Humankind whom you ordained to bear the mark of your luminous face,  
Breathing into it a soul adorned with the image of heaven  
And pouring into it the insignia of the light above,  
Distinguishing it from the other animals by profound understanding.  

When humankind, departing from you, the highest light, into darkness,  
Was consigned to Tartarean shadows and rolled down to the depths,  
Through the true light, a witness [testem; the reading is uncertain] radiant with light [Note: [Col. 0491B] The letters of this word are extremely unclear in the manuscript. “Testem” is written above it, but without intelligible sense],  
And through pious companions shining with heaven’s brightness,  
You call it back to the true light and everlasting life,  
Ravished by the divine power of an unparalleled triumph.  

Therefore, with my senses drawn from the true light, light from light,  
Illuminating minds, I strive to sing in verse of your lofty trophies,  
By which you adorn your servants above the stars.  
Filling hearts with your breath, direct me with kindly understanding;  
[Col. 0492A] Grant that I may celebrate your followers in my vows and in measured song,  
Those by whom your pupils adorn both heaven and earth,  
Seeking the heights of the stars on the wings of virtues,  
And searching with heavenly light the darkness of the deep.  

They have given radiant flowers and blessed fruits,  
While you remove filthy creatures from clean flocks;  
Those whom devotion to vigorous faith raises above all the kingdoms  
Of the world and places fittingly in the high seats of heaven,  
Where they rejoice in divine nectar and the highest light,  
And illuminate the ages with words and flashing palms.  

I do not attempt to encompass in my song everything  
That surpasses the waves of the sea and the stars of heaven.  
But, entering joyfully to pluck certain flowers,  
I seek the green places from which I wish to fashion a woven garland;  
Thus, while I sing of the wars and unfold the celebrated crowns  
Whose worthy trophies I strive to describe in humble prayer,  
May I, with their aid, conquer the savage enemy  
And escape the deceits of the crafty serpent;  
Thus may I atone with livid tears for the sins committed,  
[Col. 0492B] So that by my weeping I may deserve to quench the Stygian flames;  
And, clothed in white after my filth has been removed,  
May I be admitted by the cleansing hands of the Lamb who purifies the world.

# Three Books on the Triumphs of Christ and the Saints of Palestine

## Book One Begins

### Chapter One. On the Places Honored by Christ’s Bodily Presence

[Note: [Col. 0492B] Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, Book II, chapter 1.]

[Col. 0491B]

Bethlehem, mother of the King, illustrious in David’s origin,  
Rejoicing in the King of kings, brighter in his radiant rising,  
You were worthy to behold Christ’s first cradle,  
The first to see God clothed in human flesh,  
Taught by the angels’ message to the shepherds. In you  
The heavenly bread was revealed, by which the lofty hosts of heaven rejoice to live,  
By which the world rejoices to live.  

[Note: [Col. 0493D] Here the manuscript of the Library of Saint Geneviève in Paris begins.]

In you our salvation was first seen, with the star as teacher,  
And bestowed with a worthy gift.  
So that faith might remain more devout throughout all ages,  
This same shining star is marked at the wellspring  
With water drunk from the consecrated Virgin Mary,  
Revealed not openly to all, but only to those pure in heart.  

Egypt, which for a long time bore darkness and faithless hearts,  
You preserve the light of heaven lying hidden on earth.  
Nazareth, happy, you shine with the illustrious foster-child  
Who, cherishing earthly things, makes heavenly things serene with light,  
Adorning human souls with heavenly splendor,  
And from his own power supplying every good.  

Galilee, which once wandered in darkness and lay hidden far and wide,  
Look up to the advance of the true light from light.  
You too, worthy Cana, rejoice in grateful beauty,  
Where water took on the mighty flavor of wine.  

The hem of his garment heals the sick  
Who were touched among the people of Gennesaret,  
And, the storm driven away, makes them joyful.  
Village of Capernaum, rich in the gift of miracles,  
Growing wealthy, you sprinkle their fragrance far and wide,  
So that peoples hasten from various regions to share it  
And to grasp the breath of life with faithful understanding—  
The men of Sidon and Tyre, the inhabitants of Syria,  
And the peoples of Judea and the crowds of Samaritans.  

Land of Bethany, you shine with a twofold virtue:  
Where sterility withers, the faithful rise from death.  

O name of Solyma, with what song shall I celebrate you?  
[Col. 0494A] O Jerusalem, called “vision of peace,”  
You reject the King of peace! Why do you lose the gifts of peace,  
Daring, contrary to your own name, to destroy  
The author of peace, who seeks to reconcile human affairs  
With those above? You, most wicked, gaze with a terrible face  
Upon him who seeks the lost as he dies—  
A sight which the terrified elements flee to see!  

The earth trembles, the sun hides its rays as the light is driven away,  
The rocks crack, the tombs open, and the cloths are torn;  
Yet, harder than rocks, savage one, you do not know how to rend your heart!  
We know by what guilt you betrayed him, utterly overthrown,  
And that you paid worthy penalties with atonement.  

But now, shining, restored to a better state,  
You preserve the wood of the precious cross and display its lofty trophies,  
While we now honor the Christ-bearing tomb,  
From which the Lamb, descending to the gates of hell, shattered the gates of Avernus,  
And, rising from the tomb, carried back rich spoils.  

Illustrious land, radiant with snowy beauty,  
Filled and strengthened by the touch of the supreme body,  
You fill the world, having drunk in a varied splendor of brightness,  
Lifting diseased limbs and driving away black poisons.  

Therefore now you are more venerable throughout the whole world  
Than when you alone cared for the solemn rites of one people.  
Mountain rich in abundance, mountain exultant, mountain rich in olives,  
Happily retaining the footprints in unfading grass  
That the feet of the Lord impressed,  
As he ascended the throne of the Father and sought the vaults of heaven.

### Chapter Two. On the Church of Blessed Mary

[Note: [Col. 0494D] Gregory of Tours, cited above, chapter 9.]

[Col. 0493C]

O blessed Valley of Jehoshaphat, found worthy  
To contain the resting place of the body of the blessed  
Virgin and Mother of God, yet not worthy to conceal from the world  
For long the star, the hall of divine light,  
Flashing with brightness, surrounded by splendid lilies,  
Which shone forth as the radiant gate of light  
For the human race and opened the lofty palaces of heaven.  

When Constantine was preparing to build this hall,  
He is said to have brought here enormous columns  
To be fitted to the work. Then, with their strength,  
Craftsmen labored for many days in ordered fashion,  
But no art assisted them.  

At last, when every effort of human ingenuity had failed,  
The gracious Virgin showed by what power they should be placed.  
She instructed the builder, after his fruitless efforts and sleep,  
What art he should join to the work, and that earthly things must yield to divine things:  
He should call three boys from their rods  
And use their innocent hands to accomplish the task;  
The work would be overcome.  

Rising early, the man hastened to carry out the instruction  
And summoned three little boys from school. To show  
That God rejoices in simplicity, in one hour  
They accomplished what the hands of many men could not achieve  
With art and delay.  

She who graciously gave her breasts to the child Christ,  
The sole Mother of God and the sole virgin who gave birth,  
Who nurtured the infant limbs of the King of heaven,  
The guide of little ones and lover of simplicity,  
Shines forth and proves by her examples that she understands the small.

### Chapter Three. On the Boy Freed from Fire

[Note: [Col. 0494D] Gregory of Tours, cited above, chapter 10.]

[Col. 0493D]

Thus the boy whom a more savage fire of Babylon had seized,  
Whom his father, whose anger was fiercer than asps and wild beasts,  
Had thrown into the flames, adding fuel to the fires,  
And whom he had shut up in the blazing furnace,  
Fed with the bread of heaven, so that he would not be burned  
In his father’s furnace—  
While, as his mother lamented, the whole city ran together,  
He was seen reclining on the rosy coals as though on soft feathers.  

Carried away while the crowd surrounded him,  
They asked how he had escaped unharmed from such vast fires.  
He replied: “That woman who sits on a chair in the hall,  
From whom I received the bread, carrying the boy in her lap,  
Covered me with her little cloak so that the fire could not touch me.”

### Chapter Four. On Certain Benefits Granted through Blessed Mary

[Note: [Col. 0495D] Gregory of Tours, cited above, chapter 11.]

[Col. 0495]

[Col. 0495A]

She gathers these little ones who shine with such simplicity,
Those whom she shelters everywhere, she consoles throughout the world.

Among these she protects many in Solyma; she cherishes the needy and provides sustenance for those entrusted to her care:

[Col. 0496A] She supplies the poor in means with the comforts of food;  
she fills granaries with the abundance of a sudden harvest,  
or loads the sacred altars with golden masses.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning one who carried a pledge of the Mother of God

[Note: [Col. 0495D] Gregory of Tours, cited above, chapter 17.]

[Col. 0495]

[Col. 0495A] A certain man, taking from her these holy pledges, had been cleansed of leprosy by the waters of Christ’s sacred baptism—by which many others are often freed from such a stain. While returning to his homeland, he suffered the scrutiny of bandits within the wilderness. The bearer was stripped of his clothing, and the chest concealing the gifts was seized. Thinking that they had discovered a hidden fraud, they were disappointed in their hope of gold.

Soon, having found a pyre blazing with flames, they thrust the casket into it; they seized him, beat him with scourges, and left him bound and beaten. Scarcely had he risen when he looked back and saw the precious talents, after the ashes had settled again, lying spread over the burning coals untouched by them, unaware of the heat; he saw also the coverings themselves shining despite the despised smoke, having felt no fire and rejected all its vapor.

Forgetting his punishment, he joyfully took up the gifts that had been given to him; glad, he continued his journey and proceeded along the path he had begun.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning the waters of the Jordan

[Note: [Col. 0496D] Gregory of Tours, cited above, chapter 88.]

[Col. 0495]

[Col. 0495B] Many wounds of body and soul are washed in the waters mentioned above. A woman of Jericho, once devoted to excessive offenses, came according to the customary solemn rite, mingling with the ranks of the devout. As she tried to enter the river’s current, the waters turned away and fled, refusing to be touched by the pollution of so dreadful and unspeakable a crime.

The shameless woman pursued the retreating waters across the clear marble-like stream, yet could not touch the consecrated waters. The river sought farther reaches and abandoned its course.

The people were astonished. They asked her, conscious of her offense, to explain what had happened. She confessed, recounting the deeds she had committed and revealing, in the guilt that consumed her, that she had murdered eight of her own children.

While the people prayed that her crimes might be expiated, she, overcome by their prayers, breathed her last, lest she compound her offense.

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning Saint John the Baptist

[Col. 0495]

[Col. 0496C] No prophet greater in the pledges born of women existed than he. He was the first to teach that sins are washed away in the waters; worthy also to baptize the world’s Redeemer in the stream, he rejoiced to devote himself to the truths he proclaimed.

While he scatters the relics of his blessed body throughout the world, the world is opened to be cleansed by these outstanding trophies.

The most renowned city, deriving its name from Alexander, and the head of Egypt, conspicuous beside the great sea, is made more illustrious by his remains, where it shines enriched by them. His bones, gathered at Sebaste in Palestine, rescued from the flames and carried to Solyma by Philip, were entrusted to the faith of Father Athanasius.

But the hero’s head, placed in Phoenician harvest-land, is celebrated with brilliant honor in festive worship.

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the apostles Peter and Paul

[Col. 0495]

[Col. 0495C] Rome, distinguished head of the world, renowned for triumphs, began to become even loftier and more glorious through the faith of Christ, supported by the patrons of blessed faith: Peter, the keeper of heaven’s keys and prince of shepherds, and Paul, the pattern of teaching and guide of teachers.

[Col. 0495D] One is given as teacher to the Hebrews; by his word he releases and binds minds under judgment, the arbiter of the Church, as though the Spirit dictates to him the punishments corresponding to distinct merits and returns rewards.

Through the exercise of his office a thief falls, and his wife who clings to him; Simon perishes through deceit, Thabitha rises from death, and Aeneas rises as well, together with a countless multitude.

The other plows and fills the hearts of the nations with the word. The divine power addresses him as he is turned toward heaven, snatches him up, and raises him to the heights, eager for heaven. It teaches him in heaven, so that from there he might teach earthly beings, feed minds, and sow throughout the world the seeds of the sacred word. He also heals many in body,

[Col. 0496C] and raises a young man from death, but even more numerous hearts.

These two, carrying you, O exalted heaven, above the stars, bear instruments concerning you through the regions of the world for the soldiers of peace, through which victory rises.

Peter, you endured the cross; Paul, devoted one, you endured Nero’s sword. Thus you earned lofty seats in the ether.

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning James, the brother of the Lord

[Col. 0497]

[Col. 0497A] Aelia, now Jerusalem, by which name you are called after being transformed and renewed, bearing the wondrous trophies of Christ’s cross, venerate the tombs of his servants. After the Lord, James first continued for you the rule of faith. He is read to have been the brother of Jesus, preserving the sacred [reading uncertain: *Sacratui*], and was called Justus as his surname.

[Col. 0498A] Born among his companions, he first adorned you as bishop. Watering the dry and parched hearts of the people, piercing their darkened hearts with rays of light, while teaching that the Master sits above the lofty stars, he was thrown down from the temple parapets and made a sacrifice. He was received into heaven, blessed even as the people looked on.

## CHAPTER X. Concerning Saint John the Apostle

[Col. 0497]

[Col. 0497A] Thus the people of Ephesus exalt the remains of John, beloved of Christ, whose eloquence surpasses the world. With chaste zeal he followed the Lamb of the splendid fleece, leaving his father Zebedee and following with his brother.

He alone, in a special affection, was joined to Christ before the others, receiving the doctrines of eternal life from the fountain and being worthy to recline upon the Master’s breast.

When Christ was fastened to the cross, the holy Virgin was entrusted to him, that he might stand as guardian of the sacred virgin. Strong in faith, he endured violent torments.

Driven into exile, he learned the mysteries of heaven; with his mouth thundering, he gives his soul to the kingdoms and his limbs to rest.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning James, the brother of Saint John

[Col. 0497]

[Col. 0497B] Gallaecia, where wealthy Spain reaches its farthest limit, shines through the body of James his brother. He was the faithful disciple of the chief Shepherd, for he saw the Lord as he would see him throughout the ages.

He was so outstanding in merits that he deserved to be the third witness when Christ wished to show his disciples the splendor of his own light, granting them to behold it and promising that they would not see death before he enabled them to see the light of the coming kingdom.

[Col. 0498B] Cruel Herod, you killed him with the sword at Solyma; but, with you condemned, he adorns the ends of the world.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning Saint Andrew

[Col. 0497]

[Col. 0497C] Andrew, manly in deed and speech, fervent in his desire to behold the splendor of divine light, shone among the disciples with the mind of John.

When he heard that Christ was taking away the sins of the world, he followed him at once—not merely with his feet, but with his heart. He found the true light, with its lamp aflame,

[Col. 0498C] and, moved by love, led his brother to worship it.

When he had delivered the sweet words of salvation to the peoples of Scythia, he also followed the Master’s example in death, embracing the cross and attaining the desire of his heart.

Achaia held the blessed bones of this Father, whose Constantinople now reverently honors.

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning Saint Matthew

[Col. 0497]

[Col. 0497C] Matthew, endowed with the justice of God, you shine. The Lord made you holy from a publican, generous from a rich man, and pious from a tax collector, making you a giver; from the jurisdiction of the marketplace he transferred you to the jurisdiction of the high heavens.

You were the first to write the Gospel of Christ in your fatherly speech,

[Col. 0497D] so that the Exalted One clothed himself in servile limbs.

Therefore the face of heavenly glory, displaying you as a man, carries you above the ether.

[Col. 0498C] After preparing to bring light to the darkness, you taught the Ethiopian people, black in sin and body, to receive the shining whiteness of Christ.

[Col. 0498D] You deserved the palm of martyrdom and the honor of heaven.

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning Saint Philip

[Col. 0497]

[Col. 0497D] Hierapolis, made greater by Philip’s tomb, is distinguished. Seeking the Father of the Word from the true light, he was deemed worthy to learn that the Begotten One possesses the radiance of the Begetter, shining with light from light in equal brightness; that the power of the Father shines in the power of the Son; that the Father remains in the Son and the Son in the Father; and that, when the Son is seen, the Father too is rightly seen.

[Col. 0498D] Spreading this faith among the peoples of Scythia, the pious man filled the barbarian lands with the abundant seed of teaching. Then, after establishing churches and arranging them in sacred order, he sowed generously by his speech the devout doctrines of life throughout the vast regions of Asia and was placed in the seat of heaven.

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning Saint Thomas

[Col. 0499]

[Col. 0499A] Thomas, who is Didymus, examined the open side of the Lamb fastened to the cross by the weapon of a soldier. Through his doubt our faith is strengthened: that Christ returned to life after the law of death had been undone.

As he touched the scars with the guidance of his finger, the greatest wounds of the doubting heart were healed,

[Col. 0500A] and every scar in our own mind was healed when it became clear that Christ had returned with true flesh.

After scattering the seeds of the word among the Parthians and Medes, India saw him suffer for its king. From there, through the devotion of the faithful people, his body is said to have been transferred from the earth to Edessa, while his soul was placed in the high heavens.

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning Saint Bartholomew

[Col. 0499]

[Col. 0499A] Bartholomew, holy one, whom grace made a child of the One who suspends the waters, you are held to be a fruitful branch of the true vine, inseparably clinging to it and bearing clusters at the proper season.

From it you poured the unmixed wine of faith far and wide, generously giving it to the sober. India too received it;

[Col. 0500A] there, completing your glorious course for Christ’s name by the sword, you sought the secrets of heaven.

The island which the waves of the Sicilian sea call Lipara received your Gangetic remains, bearing witness to distinguished triumphs won through a powerful death. They protect the people of Benevento beneath their covering.

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning Saints Simon and Jude

[Col. 0499]

[Col. 0499B] Simon Zelotes, also called the Cananaean—so named, clearly, from the village bearing this name—in which water was changed into the power of wine, showed that Christ is mighty as Lord of all things.

Egypt, stained by the sacred rites of ancient gods, receives the power of the everlasting Word [the phrase *tetra dente* is uncertain].

But Jude, the son of James, also called Thaddeus—far removed from him who betrayed the Lord of the world—was called Lebbaeus; the name is rendered in our tongue as “little heart” (*corculus*).

You sowed the seed of light between two rivers, in the midst of a homeland bearing the name of rivers.

[Col. 0500B] Both of you received the gifts of sacred teaching from the good Shepherd and truly powerful Master. Made the salt of the earth, you were prepared to season foolish minds; called light, you were taught to drive away darkness.

When you had banished these things by your speech in various regions, you entered and penetrated the kingdoms of threatening Persia, ready, like sheep among wolves, to advance.

With the serpent’s cleverness joined to the dove’s simplicity, you were wise. While preparing many gains for God, you led an innumerable Christian people beneath the devout yoke. At last, completing your course in the worthy contest of martyrdom, you gave your souls to heaven and your bones to tombs.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning Saint Matthias

[Col. 0499]

[Col. 0499C] Matthias, chosen to fill the number, you shine. You were preferred to Justus, whom the Lord’s grace had sanctified, and were deemed worthy by lot of the ministry through which you would bring the joys of peace to the world, having attained in heaven the summit of the twelfth seat, from which the savage betrayer of the Author had fallen, a lover also of his own destruction.

[Col. 0500C] The Holy Spirit illumines you, giving you as a pledge of an exalted gift and strengthening you with heavenly grace, so that, made a witness to the Lord’s triumph over death, you might everywhere bear witness to the miracles of Christ that you had seen; and, calling the pupils of the Jewish people to heaven, you rest, raised to the honor of the heavenly throne.

## CHAPTER XIX. Concerning the other witnesses of Christ

[Col. 0499]

[Col. 0499C] We have passed through the lofty summit of the apostolic order, while our modest Muse has sung the distinguished titles, marking each name in a twelve-line verse.

But now let us sing the armies of heaven and the trophies of faith, the many palms and countless crowns—things far greater than our art—and matters capable of surpassing Maeon’s bard

[Col. 0500C] and even our own Maro.

Yet it is not our purpose to disclose the wars fought by each one, since we could not count them, nor would it be enough even to remember the places in a brief account. It will suffice to recall certain celebrated athletes of the Lord by their tombs.

Among these, venerable Aelia excels the others through the marvelous monument of the King who governs all things.

## CHAPTER XX. Concerning David, Simeon, and Anna

[Col. 0499]

[Col. 0499D] Here lies the skillful harpist, gentle, pious, and faithful King David, from whose seed Christ wished, by the law of chastity, to take mortal human limbs, sanctifying the Virgin’s womb for himself.

He is read to have been placed in a wealthy mausoleum;

[Col. 0500D] but, when the Lord carried off the spoils of Phlegethon, he is believed to have been snatched away and given the heavenly court.

Here too lie many illustrious kings and holy prophets whom ancient ages produced.

Here is just Simeon, renowned through the exalted Spirit, who received the answer that he would never undergo death until he had deserved to see the Author of life.

When he had seen him, he asked that the bonds of the flesh be released for him, not fearing death because he was worthy to see life; he did not dread death’s shadow because he had come to know the light. Having seen peace, his limbs desired to rest.

Here also is Anna the prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, a model of salvation even for widows, born of the tribe of Asher.

[Col. 0502A] Living diligently in the temple and observing frequent fasts, she prayed to God and served him night and day. She received the heavenly gifts of prophecy.

She was worthy not only to behold the newborn Emmanuel, but also, prophesying, to proclaim words about him: she foretold that he had been appointed for the downfall of many and that his coming would also be the rising of many.

## CHAPTER XXI. Concerning Saint Stephen

[Col. 0501]

[Col. 0501A] Here too the supreme contests of the soldiers are brought to completion. In the first contest after Christ, Stephen triumphed over death’s livid weapons and thereby is known to have received the crown of his own name, at the time when the Lord had conquered the dreadful enemy by the cross.

When the apostolic assembly appointed seven men, whom the gracious Spirit adorned, to assist at the sacred tables, Stephen, chosen by divine will, rich in this light, was placed over them as archdeacon.

Soon, pouring forth a shower of speech, he shone with power and displayed new flashes of wonder to the people through unprecedented signs.

Against him the Synagogue, clamoring with Satanic babble, fought furiously: the freedmen, the remiss and illegitimate Cyrenians scorched by zeal,

[Col. 0501B] the crowd of Alexandrians, and the impudent Cilicians, together with the rest of Asia. But they could neither overcome the wisdom of the Spirit nor stop the streams of the Holy Spirit.

They took him before the council and made serious accusations, saying that he had declared that the traditions of Moses’ law must be changed by Jesus, as the temple’s ruin approached.

In their midst, his face shining like an angel’s, he thundered in his native voice, bright with light, and said:

“Fathers and brother-men, receive my words.

“God, shining in majesty, once appeared to our father Abraham, who was pleasing to him in the flesh, and commanded him: ‘Depart from your ancestral land and hasten to other kingdoms that I shall show you.’

“Leaving Chaldaea, he dwelt again at Charran. After his father’s death, this land led him into these fields,

[Col. 0501C] and did not give him even enough ground to set his foot upon; yet God promised to give it to his descendants when he was old and exhausted, lacking bodily offspring.

“‘Your descendants,’ he said, ‘will be settlers in foreign lands. They will be harshly treated for nearly four hundred years, cruelly oppressed in servitude. They will depart and afterward serve me in this place, and I will judge the nation to which they have been enslaved.’

“After the covenant of circumcision had been received, the old man begot Isaac; from Isaac was born Jacob, who begot twelve fathers of noble blood, whom envy drove to sell Joseph.

“Joseph entered Pharaoh’s court, with the Lord accompanying him from above; the Lord rescued him from every affliction, and through him Joseph soon became wise and esteemed by Pharaoh.

[Col. 0501D] The Lord set him over the kingdom and over the court.

“Then oppressive famine weighed upon Egypt and Canaan. This distress first stirred our fathers; there they learned that grain was available in Canopus.

“When they returned there, Joseph became known to them. After these things were reported to King Pharaoh, Joseph summoned his father and his whole family.

“To him Jacob descended with seventy-five souls of his own line.

“After Jacob himself died, the fathers—the twelve—were carried to Shechem and placed in the tomb that Abraham had bought from Hamor for a price.

“When the time of the promise approached, which the Lord himself had declared to Abraham, the people grew and became a great nation, until a king who knew nothing of these things rose over Egypt. He oppressed the settlers and compelled them to expose their own newborn children to cruel death.

[Col. 0502B] “At that time Moses was born, and for three months he was hidden in his ancestral house from the enemy.

“But, when he was pleasing to the Most High, he was placed among the reeds of the river; the royal daughter snatched him up, nourished him, and loved him as a son. He excelled in Egyptian arts and in deeds of courage. After completing forty years of life, he considered visiting his brothers.

“When he saw an Egyptian inflicting violence upon a Hebrew man, he struck him and thought that his own people understood that, through him, the Lord intended to bring them salvation.

“When he rebuked those foolish men who were raging with hatred and quarrels, he heard: ‘Who appointed you prince or judge over us? Are you intending to kill me as yesterday you killed the Egyptian?’

“Terrified by these words, Moses became an exile in a foreign land, fleeing to Midian, where he was blessed with two children.

“After he had completed forty years in that land, an angel appeared to him in the fire of the burning bush.

“When he wondered at the flame and prepared to investigate the phenomenon, a voice came: ‘I am myself the God of your fathers.’

“Astonished, Moses did not dare to look directly.

“To him the Lord said: ‘Remove the sandals from your feet, for the place on which you stand is certainly sacred ground. I have seen the harsh blows suffered by my people, whom the land of Pelusium holds, and I have heard their groaning with my ears. I have descended to protect them; you shall go as the one sent.’

[Col. 0502C] “This Moses, whom they had refused to accept as their leader, God sent to them as prince and Redeemer, while the heavenly being was shown to him and accompanied him through the fire.

“By these signs he led them out through the lands of Syene,

[Col. 0502D] and through the Red Sea and the dry, trackless wilderness; for forty years he also prophesied, saying: ‘God will raise up for you from among your brothers one like me as a prophet; you shall obey him.’

“He was indeed the leader of the Church dwelling in the wilderness, supported on lofty Sinai by angelic aid.

“He received the words of life to give us, but our fathers were unwilling to submit to his commands, turned away in their hard hearts, and ordered Aaron:

“‘Make gods for us to go before us, for as for this Moses who led us out, we do not know what has happened to him.’

“Then they cast a calf and offered sacrifices according to profane custom, rejoicing in the works of their hands.

“And God gave them over to serve the hosts of heaven, as the book of the prophets says to our fathers:

“‘While you were traversing deserted places, did you offer me any victim? Jacob’s house burned, and you took up Moloch’s tents and the star of Rempha,

[Col. 0503B] the figures which you had fashioned for worship.’

“Therefore I will cast you beyond the walls of Babylon.

“The tabernacle was with our fathers in the wilderness, which God, having shown the pattern, instructed Moses to make.

“When our fathers brought it with Joshua into the land, the nations that possessed it were expelled by the heavenly command. It remained until the time of David.

“David, who found favor with God, asked to discover a dwelling for the God of Jacob; Solomon built him a temple.

“But the Most High does not dwell in shrines made by hands, as the prophet himself testifies:

“‘Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool beneath my feet. What house will you build for me, or what place for my dwelling? Did not my hand make all these things?’

[Col. 0503C] “You are always striving to oppose the Holy Spirit, with uncircumcised ears and an obstinate neck. As your fathers did, so do you: they repeatedly slaughtered the prophets, hostile to all who spoke beforehand of the coming of the Just One, whom you betrayed and killed.

“You received the law through the message of angels, yet you are shown truly not to have kept it.”

When the martyr’s words had entered their ungrateful ears, their entrails burst, their hearts broke with fury, and the gnashing teeth of those pressing forward resounded.

But the holy martyr, filled with the exalted Spirit, looked up to heaven and saw the divine glory, and Jesus standing at the right hand of the eternal Father. Thus he said:

“Behold, I see the summit of heaven opened for me, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of Power.”

[Col. 0503D] With blocked ears they filled the air with their cries. With one mind and a savage attack they rushed upon Stephen, drove him from the city, and stoned the venerable man who was accused: a savage hand against the gentle, a cruel hand against the kindly, a violent hand against the benevolent.

Struck by the dreadful shower of stones, the venerable martyr called out: “Lord Jesus, receive this soul.”

Then, kneeling, he prayed in a loud voice: “God, do not count this crime against them.”

Having spoken these words, he sought the sleep of peace in death, holding his spirit firm and unconquered. By this he conquered the assembly; by this he overcame the stones, praying even for those who stoned him.

Nor could the prayers of the martyr have fallen in vain through his utterance. They are known to have ascended to the throne

[Col. 0504A] of the Almighty Lord, while we see Saul, raging in mind and unafraid to consent to so holy a killing, transformed in name and heart: Saul into Paul, made patient through the cross.

The faithful hastened to celebrate Stephen’s funeral rites, and the God-fearing offered abundant tears.

Gamaliel, the leader, placed the bones of the holy witness in his own field, where they were kept until fervent persecution pressed upon the worshipers of Christ.

Afterward, when Honorius had reigned for seven years, Lucianus was sleeping in the baptistery. In an ecstasy of mind he suddenly saw a tall, peaceful, and dignified old man, with a long beard and covered in a shining garment.

At its lower edge beautiful crosses were radiant, woven with gold as a border to the hem.

His feet were protected by splendid and decorous sandals, and he was marked by a golden, flexible herald’s staff. Gently touching Lucianus, he revealed himself as Gamaliel, of whom the distinguished Paul had been an excellent pupil; after some further words he added:

“Carefully excavate our tombs and uncover the decaying graves in the humble countryside.”

When Lucianus asked whose bodies lay buried there, he said:

“Lord Stephen is here first, he whom the Jews killed at Solyma by a slaughter of stones for Christ. By order of the priests he was abandoned to be devoured by dogs and savage beasts along the road to Cedar.

[Col. 0504C] “But I, knowing that he had preserved the faith even in death, gathered the company of the saints and the faithful crowd, persuaded them to carry him to our field, and buried him there according to the customary honor of the fathers.

“Beside him you will find a small chamber holding my nephew Nicodemus. Christ Jesus taught him through the Holy Spirit and water to be reborn, as happened first to Peter and then to John.

“Therefore the leaders of the priests, raging indignantly, removed him from his office and tried to hand him over to death; but he was protected with reverence for us.

“Nevertheless, after we had been driven from the city, our possessions were seized and overturned, and they left him half-dead after subjecting him to torments.

“I received him and ordered that he be treated. He was then healed and is said to have survived for a short time afterward.

[Col. 0504D] “When he died, I placed him at the feet of the first martyr.

“The third man who shares the common tomb with me is my son Abibas, reborn in the gracious font.

“He spent twenty years of life with me. While the servants of Christ mentioned above were giving him sacred instruction, he devoted himself constantly with Paul to sacred studies in the temple, meditating and abounding in the light of the law.

“Freed from the vice to which the human race is accustomed to subject itself, sheltered by heavenly virtue, rich in a celibate life, he rested in peace.

“My wife and my firstborn, who avoided believing in Christ, were buried in another field.

“Why, then, will you see their sarcophagi empty? Because they were judged worthy not to rest with us.”

When Lucianus asked the name of the place where he should seek them, the old man said:

“In our field, which in the language now customary among the Syrians is called the possession of the blessed.”

The vision appeared to the presbyter again and again. At last he went to the city of Solyma and reported all these things to Bishop John.

The bishop blessed the Lord joyfully with many tears and summoned the holy fathers from the neighboring cities. While the mound was being excavated in their presence, the earth cracked with a tremor and fragrant breath rose from it.

Those who happened to be present declared that they had never experienced anything like it; they rejoiced as though they were being fed with the nectar of paradise.

The healing power of that fragrance was received by those relieved from various illnesses: seventy-three in all.

These men were witnesses of the work: with the Father already mentioned, Bishop Eleutherius of Jericho and Eustominus of Sebaste,

[Col. 0506A] accompanied by a worthy company of the clergy.

Pressing the holy bones with precious gifts, they closed the tomb and returned to their own sees.

Not long afterward the blessed bones of Stephen shone again in Sion, where he had first served in sacred ministry.

At that time the dry earth lay withered, the fields thirsting, hardened by heat and deprived of tempering water. Suddenly the face of heaven disappeared; clouds thickened in the air, and rain was sent down from the sky.

By the exceptional merits and earned honor of the martyr, it watered the parched fields with abundant consolation.

His pledges shine throughout various lands, revealed and everywhere adorned by magnificent signs. Many of these, Saint Augustine, you yourself acknowledge; but most of the things that happen or have happened are left unspoken.

## CHAPTER XXII. Concerning Saint Simeon and the remaining bishops of Aelia

[Col. 0505]

[Col. 0505B] After James, Simeon was raised to sacred office at Solyma. He was also called the Lord’s disciple and was related by blood, being the son of Cleophas, who was the brother of Saint Joseph, the husband of the eternal Virgin and incomparable mother.

This Simeon, exhausted by old age, lived at the time when the emperor Trajan was harassing Christ’s flock with the sword. Worn down by many beatings in the name of Christ, after he had completed one hundred and twenty years, he shone in martyrdom at his death, made a sacrifice of the cross.

The judge marveled at the strength of his spirit: so powerful was it that the extremely aged man bore the torture of this punishment with a willing heart.

The ancient bishops of Solyma shine in this succession: first Justus, then Zacchaeus, then Tobias,

[Col. 0505C] Benjamin as the sixth, and John, said to be the seventh. After him came Matthias, followed by Philip.

Justus Seneca succeeded; then again Levi.

After him came Ephrem and Joseph, and finally Jude. These are remembered in Judaea, approved by the people and appointed to lead them, maintaining the faith of benevolent Christ.

Among them Matthias, fighting in steadfast conflict and enduring much for Christ’s devotion, came to rest. His numerous deeds are recounted as full of faith.

But, Jerusalem, after you shone renewed, when the Jews had been expelled and their homeland and city denied to them, so that they were no longer permitted to see your fields or even gaze upon their ancestral land from afar, you became, with the nations admitted and preserving peace within you, Aelia, named after the Roman tyrant, a dwelling for the peaceful servants of Christ.

After these earlier bishops, Marcus adorned you. He was the first from our nations to obtain your episcopate,

[Col. 0506C] worthy of the palm of martyrdom in a renowned contest.

Casianus succeeded Marcus, and Publius followed him.

Then came Maximus, Julianus, Gaius, and another Julianus, Capito, Valens, and Dolicianus.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Concerning Saints Narcissus and Alexander

[Col. 0505]

[Col. 0505C] After them Narcissus, a fragrant and beautiful flower, spread a joyful scent through the Church of Solyma, whose many marvelous deeds shine brightly.

He changed the nature of liquid into rich olive oil.

Once, when the supply of oil was failing and the fire was being left without the lamp’s light, the servants of the Church had no fuel at all, and the day of Paschal joy was already at hand, great sorrow and confusion seized the people and clergy.

But Narcissus, firm in his profound faith, ordered the ministers to bring him water from the wells. Taking it, he prayed, blessed it, and gave it to the lamps.

Suddenly, at this marvelous deed, you would have been astonished to see the fuel, so that the flames might not flee from their own nourishment, become dense with the joyful richness of the water; the pale liquid changed to a green color, took on a supernatural strength, and supplied the flames with the nourishment by which they are usually extinguished, so that the lamp rejoiced and burned.

The splendor of the light then blazed more brightly than usual, shining with a more abundant radiance through Christ’s goodness.

Because of their faith, the brothers decided to preserve pledges of this great gift, keeping some of the liquid as a confirmation.

F. [Note: [Col. 0505D] Thus the manuscripts.]

Finally, while Narcissus’ mind remained steadfast, holding firmly and safely to justice and what was right, certain little men of corrupted mind, liars who feared to suffer punishments deserved for their crimes under a just judge, presumed to invent a disgraceful charge and contrived to add a savage crime to the holy man’s name.

They approached hearers and suborned witnesses, accomplices in fraud, and did not fear to bind themselves by oaths.

One swore that fire should consume him; the next, that a wasting disease should destroy him; the third swore by his eyes that he should be deprived of sight.

By such oaths they bound themselves to bring testimony against him, although at that time no faithful person believed their assertions. For Narcissus’ life and chastity, which he had maintained from his earliest years, were known to all.

Unable to endure such shameful and profane accusations, he sought the deserted places, reading and cultivating solitude. He hid there for many years, living a withdrawn and contemplative life without disturbance.

But the eye that sees all did not delay the punishment of these men for long. Rather, through the very acts by which they had sanctioned their crime, he soon repaid them as they deserved—the men who had driven the holy man away with the burning poison of deceit.

Each received the punishment selected by his own judgment.

First, at the silent spark of night, a fire ignited his house, and he himself burned together with the flames.

A disease then invaded another from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head and climbed upward until it reached him entirely.

After these two had been consumed, the third man, seeing that the Lord had not overlooked their hidden deceit, threw himself openly into the midst of the people and revealed the crime in order.

Striving to expiate the monstrous deed with tears, he avenged by abundant weeping the fraud that had brought him grief, while, overcome by mourning, he sat blind in the darkness.

While Narcissus was cherishing his hidden retreat, a bishop named Dius was chosen for the sacred office. Germano followed him, and Gordius followed Germano.

Then, as though recovering after the harsh breath of a cold winter, when the lands had been released by the blowing of the west wind, a purple flower rises and flourishes in the green grass.

[Col. 0507C] No differently did Narcissus return, as though restored to life in divine honor, and was given back to the Church. He was again asked to preside over the people and administer the divine offices.

But, weary and weakened by old age, he could no longer bear all the burdens of the people. Guided by heavenly will,

[Col. 0508A] he shared the sacred heights of the see with Alexander, who governed the laws of the priesthood among the Cappadocians.

Alexander, eager to see the holy places, came to this city, and it was revealed that he was to be retained by the people and the old bishop.

Thus, on the day when the people learned that he had arrived, they hurried to the walls to meet the man. Suddenly a voice resounded, touched by heaven and heard by all:

“Receive the bishop whom the Almighty appoints for your altars.”

When the highest will had been plainly revealed, the fathers who were present, together with the holy elder, suddenly accepted the decision in the unanimous agreement of the people. They received, compelled, retained, venerated, and honored him.

At last Narcissus, completing the course of his contest after living two hundred and eight years,

[Col. 0508B] left the right of protecting the city to Alexander and went to the Lord, rejoicing in the reward of his merits.

His successor diligently watched over his duties and adorned what had been entrusted to him, while Decius raged in a storm, attempting to scatter the flock of God in a whirlwind.

Alexander, resplendent with his beautiful white hair, was led under the cruel imperial law of the tyrant and rejoiced to be thrust into prison in the name of the Lord.

Afflicted for a long time, he completed his sacred contest and, through Christ’s gift, received the crown of martyrdom.

Eusebius relates that he drew material for recording these distinguished deeds, recounted among the monuments of Christ’s Church, from Alexander’s library.

[Note: [Col. 0507] See Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, chapter 11.]

This Alexander himself sent the venerable presbyter Clement to the Church of Antioch.

[Col. 0508C] He also commended him with praises of virtue, declaring him a priest blessed in integrity and an elder proved by radiant piety.

Through Christ’s gift, Clement’s presence among the people of Solyma had strengthened the growing people of God entrusted to him.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Concerning the bishops Macarius, Maximus, and Cyriacus

[Col. 0507]

[Col. 0507C] After these, several bishops distinguished for their virtue and renowned in doctrine were appointed in succession at Solyma.

Among them, Macarius, while the people were wavering over the knowledge of the precious wood when the cross was found, hastened to seek the remains of the dead.

He placed beside them the crosses that had happened to be discovered. The others were rejected, but the body remained unmoved.

As soon as it was touched by the life-giving cross, an inner strength entered it; restored to sudden action, it rose again.

Maximus, their companion and the soldier of the Lord, suffered for the devotion and faith of God. His left knee was cut off and his right eye was removed, and he rejoiced to bear this as a mark of great faith.

The martyr Cyriacus, also called Jude, after triumphing over varied and numerous punishments—after the severing of his hands, fires, cups of molten lead, burning bronze, the rack, blows from rods, and the heat of fat and salt

[Col. 0508C] extinguished by his prayers; after snakes and the fumes of oil; after being pierced in the breast and struck in the inward parts by a spear—shone steadfastly, having finally won the victorious palm.

Another Macarius is said to have followed Hermon in sacred office, bearing a name worthy of his elevated virtues.

Cyril shines with the splendor of distinguished doctrine. He endured many contests for the scepters of the faith, was often driven out, but was advanced to a more illustrious see.

John, supported by wondrous integrity, followed him.

Moreover, many others triumph in this city; God knows their names and number, for he knows all things.

The holy one’s homeland. Who could recount all those whom Christ’s disciples baptized here,

[Col. 0508D] and who earned merit in the true faith and at the summit of life, when it is read that the holy Peter consecrated three thousand on one day, and on another five thousand, and then thousands whose total is not known to us?

## CHAPTER XXV. Hesychius and Philagrius

[Col. 0509]

[Col. 0509A] The presbyter Hesychius, who drew the mystical shadows of the ancient law and of the sacred rites toward the radiant light, changes water into wine wherever anything more worthy or especially remarkable had flourished in some remote place.

Here Philagrius shone among the peoples with the splendor of wisdom, seeking sustenance by the labor of his hands, and willingly poor and a friend of poverty. Once, when he had found a rich purse of solid coins, he stayed and waited until the man who had suffered the loss might return. He returned the gold to the weeping owner; when the man begged him to take a share, he resisted, and did not touch a single coin out of the thousand. Then, while the man proclaimed his praises, he fled and hastened heavenward on swift wings.

Justinus, radiant with the brilliant splendor of wisdom, was born here. Joseph also arose in this region, from a family who, laboring vigorously for the holy religion, handed over to the emperors books polished with the honor of piety. He was not ashamed of the cross when he presented it before the senate, bringing divine things and refuting human ones. He triumphed over Jews, nations, heresies, and falsehoods; publicly acclaimed, he rejoiced to have shed his famous blood for Christ, thereby honoring Jesus the teacher.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Mary Magdalene, Lazarus, and Joseph Justus

[Col. 0509]

[Col. 0509A] This land shines with many pupils of the ancient law on one side and of the new law on the other, whom the grace of Christ saves. In this region Mary Magdalene also shines, where Jesus showed that she was capable of loving him fervently after the demons had been driven out.

Her pure love so pleased Christ that she was the first to see him returning from the Stygian regions. When the bars of Erebus had been violently broken, here, near Bethany, your tomb, holy Lazarus, remained—whence, after the sun had held you for forty days, Death, trembling and obedient to the Lord, sent you back to the realms above.

[Col. 0510A] Here is your church-house and that of your holy sisters.

Joseph, who was called Justus, completed his contest in this homeland. The companions of Christ judged him worthy, because he shone by apostolic right, to be chosen by lot in place of Judas.

[Col. 0510B] Yet although the lot, by inward judgment, chose Matthias, Joseph nevertheless fulfilled the office of holy teaching, inflamed by heavenly love. Hence the frenzied and insane crowd of Jews assailed him with many insults. It is said that, having drunk poison on account of the faith, he suffered no harm from it; and at last he completed his triumph, with God as victor.

# THE SECOND BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0509]

## CHAPTER I. Christ’s vengeance under Vespasian

[Col. 0509B] Many other trophies celebrated at Jerusalem shone forth in different ways. At one time the peoples were driven away, at another the city was conquered; the Jews were repeatedly overwhelmed by the storm of war. When the merits of the righteous had been exalted to the height of royal power, they were afflicted, captured, and slain by the enemy because of their contempt for the sacred law of God, while the temple and the books were burned to the ground.

They were seized and sent into exile, then received back into their homeland; afterward, raised up from the various carnage of war and preserved until the divine offspring arose—Emmanuel, born of a virgin, against whom their ruins struck themselves headlong like against a stone.

Yet they did not hasten to rise, while they refused to accept pardon through Christ’s companions, to whom the remission of guilt had been entrusted. For almost forty years the sword of vengeance was delayed, so that an act of pardon might prevail; but when God’s mercy was rejected, deserved punishment suddenly arrived.

Portents nevertheless hastened to announce the future beginning. Given these prodigies, they were terrified by threatening light.

[Col. 0509D] A star, said to have shone for an entire year, resembling a sword and hanging over the wicked city, was seen; and comets burned with fierce, pestilential flames.

As they were preparing to celebrate the solemnities of their Passover,

[Col. 0510B] shortly after midnight a brilliant light surrounded the temple and flashed fearfully, moving now in one direction, now in the other.

Some interpreted this as an omen of coming prosperity. But others, whose judgment may have been sounder,

[Col. 0510C] said that an ill-omened light had disturbed their rest.

After many had been stirred, they brought forth deadly signs. Yet those who were warned by them refused to punish their deeds with tears and disdained to mourn the expiation of their crimes.

Even during these festivals, when the ministers had led out a young cow for sacrifice and the axe flashed, poised to be driven into its neck, it gave birth. The unaltered sacred law taught, through the mysteries of this event, that the lamb—whose mother refused to acknowledge her bleating offspring—represented the harsh yoke of the law, opposed to the gentle one, and that it was to be driven from its own sanctuary by savage swords.

The inner gate of the temple, facing east, was heavy with ornament and covered with solid metal. Of extraordinary weight, it could scarcely be moved by twenty men who pushed against the bronze. Yet, when they had exerted all their strength, it opened of its own accord, although it had been secured with bars and iron bolts driven deeply into it at midnight.

[Col. 0510D] After the festival day had passed in a short span of days, at night, while the shadows had not yet withdrawn,

[Col. 0511A] chariots and horsemen seemed to fly through the sky. Armed companies mingled with the clouds and suddenly surrounded the walls in the air.

During another festival, the one celebrated after fifty days, the priests, entering the temple according to their customary rite in the darkness of night, heard resounding noises. Soon they also heard sudden voices crying out with a terrible crash: “Let us depart from these dwellings.”

After another festival, while they were living in green booths, as was customary for this people, a certain rustic suddenly cried out, disturbing those who were resting in peace:

“From the rising of the sun, a voice; a voice from the boundary of the sun; a voice from the fourfold rising of the whirlwinds!

A voice over Jerusalem, a voice over the walls of the temple;

[Col. 0511B] a voice over bridegrooms and brides, and over the people.”

For a full year before the fourth year of the war, this man diligently traversed all the streets by night and day, uttering these words. The leading men, indignant and bearing these omens as evil, seized the young man and scourged him with many lashes.

He gave no answer on his own behalf but did not cease uttering these cries. The Romans, seeing that he was driven by the force of a divine power, brought him before the governor. The governor wore him down with cruel blows, and the scourges furrowed him to the bones. He shed no tears and made no calm plea. Rather, repeating the very words with every blow, he added: “Woe, woe to Jerusalem!” in pitiful lamentation.

Having dismissed him as mad by his own authority, the wicked people immediately pursued him in their frenzy.

For from their sacred books they drew the prophecy that a king would arise from their nation to rule the world. But since they despised the permission granted them to believe in Christ, and read themselves as destined to become the authors of so great a kingdom, they rushed from the one by whom they were called to understand true life and sought the paths of deserved death.

They were compelled to turn their swords against the earthly rulers whose protection seemed to keep them safe, and those who were proved to have attacked the heavenly Lord strove at the same time to overthrow the earthly rulers.

Therefore they were assailed in various ways, from heaven and from earth. Yet signs were first displayed by which their hearts, hardened like stone, might finally soften. But their minds, harder than rocks and soon to be delivered to the supreme judgment, remained stubborn and uncorrected.

The servants of Christ who had remained in Jerusalem until that very time, warned by the Lord and receiving his instructions,

[Col. 0511D] soon left the guilty city. Crossing the waters of the Jordan, they withdrew to a fortress called Pella.

After the holy people had been brought out of the savage danger of death, the wicked city was pressed from every side by many calamities: fire, famine, the sword, bandits, and siege. Everything now seemed destined to perish together, including the famous temple, which a loathsome profanation had polluted and which had once been foretold by the sacred prophets.

Fathers perished with their children, wives with their husbands; there was no distinction of evil, no pity for infants or old men, no compassion for children, no mercy for age. The underworld had exceeded all number.

[Col. 0512A] For while Roman troops shook the city from without, its inhabitants were no less slaughtered by the brigands within, to whom the city had been surrendered and under whom it was collapsing.

They suffered no less from their own people than from external violence. If any food was discovered anywhere, they hastened to seize it by ambush or force.

If the wealthy appeared to possess anything at all, they were killed after the charge of treasonous desertion had been fabricated. The evil increased as the reckless crowd searched houses and seized hidden grain, killing its keepers as though they denied that anything could be found.

Those whom they discovered, they tortured as though they had stored food. Because they saw them alive, they took this as evidence that food existed; they concluded that, unless the victims had concealed provisions, they would have perished.

When they saw people wasting away and growing thin from the exhaustion of hunger,

[Col. 0512B] they despised striking them down with a gleaming sword.

Many hid themselves in secret inner chambers, each with his own store of whatever food remained. Some even rejoiced to consume raw crops; others snatched them from the fire and devoured them badly roasted.

Yet they were not safe from the interior war. Children continually took away the small means of life from their parents, and parents from their children. Food was suddenly snatched from the father’s mouth; the morsels were worn away by the teeth of the children.

Nor did it escape these robbers, from the sign of closed doors, that their victims had eaten. They rushed headlong upon them, pulled food back from their throats, beat the old men, and seized the mothers, dragging them by their loosened hair while pieces of bread clung to them.

[Col. 0512C] They dashed children to pieces; no pity was shown to anyone.

But those whom they were able to recognize as having consumed food, they delighted in tormenting by an even harsher method. They closed the shameful bodily passages with a bar and pierced the outlets of the belly with sharp stakes, so that the wretched might produce a cupful of bread and flour.

Citizens perished, while food remained for the brigands. The starving wretch was killed by the well-fed torturer.

And deservedly, those whom they had chosen as their robber were enduring the greatest danger of death [Note: Namely, Barabbas.].

Some, having happened to escape the enemy’s chains, tore up shrubs and gathered herbs. They snatched away the provisions collected by hand and, when adjured, returned nothing in exchange for the great service. They regarded it as a way of allowing the wretched to continue on without punishment.

[Col. 0512D] In their flight, lest any place be a refuge of safety, the enemies found coins hidden beneath coverings. They seized some people who had swallowed gold and killed everyone who proceeded toward the walls. No one was spared, if he was believed to be carrying a purse of gold.

But when no hope of safety remained for the refugees, the famine that had grown within the walls seized everything. It ravaged the entire city and struck down all living things.

In the deepest inner chambers, hidden behind closed doors, lay the bodies of women and children, while the bodies of old men, consumed by hunger, lay in the middle of the streets.

Young men and everyone in the strength of manhood wandered pale through all the streets like shadows.

[Col. 0513A] Wherever the plague deprived them of the power to walk, they collapsed in ruin. Disease and their number prevented their corpses from being buried. Some breathed their last above burial caves while preparing to bury others.

Others died while carrying out funerals, and neither gave burial to others nor were buried by anyone.

No lamentation sounded over death, for destruction claimed every right for itself; it had even taken the moisture from their eyes.

Vast silence had now subdued the whole city, and the shadow of death covered the appearance of the place.

Only the brigands’ hand was more terrible than all these punishments. Even after everything else, they considered it permissible to plunder the tombs and hack corpses with swords. They killed those still breathing, but refused to strike only those who were already dead.

The half-dead, stretching out their hands, begged the utterly wicked for death,

[Col. 0513B] and longed to see the sword as their final payment.

When they could no longer endure the stench of the black ones [Note: That is, the dead; for *niger* is derived from νεκρός (*nekros*).],

they entrusted the bodies to the common earth at public expense.

[Note: [Col. 0514D] The Mazarinus manuscript omits this verse.]

Soon the number of the dead grew so great that it overcame the expense of burial. Bodies were thrown over the walls, and the caves of the ramparts were filled.

Titus went around, and, seeing that the ditch had been filled by a circuit of corpses and that the earth was drenched with human decay, he raised his hands to heaven with a groan and a cry, calling the ruler of the stars to witness that these deeds were not his work and that he bore no guilt for so many things.

The deadly frenzy urged everything toward food. Even those things that nature, removing them from the desire to eat, had forbidden many animals to consume, fortune compelled them to chew, overcoming human custom.

At last they did not abstain from leather straps, belts, or footwear. They stripped doors of their coverings; some subdued old hay with their teeth, while others ground it in their mouths, empty of any effort of the belly.

[Col. 0513C] Some even sold filthy refuse and sweepings.

Moreover—horrible to say, and reprehensible to all—a disgraceful act of slaughter was committed: a notorious woman devoured the limbs of her offspring, concealing her own flesh within her own entrails.

At last the guilty city, worn down by these evils, was captured and given over to avenging flames.

Those who had dared to violate the saving Lord with bloody hands, while the Passover festivals were being celebrated, perished throughout the whole kingdom, as though shut up in an avenging prison while those festivals were observed.

They say that their number was thirty times one hundred thousand; of these, eleven hundred thousand wretched people are said to have been consumed by raging famine and the sword.

From this point the brigands were killed in mutual slaughter.

Chosen young men were led to accompany the triumphal chariot of the father and the son, who, with heaven as avenger, had struck down those profane violators of the Father and the Son.

Nor, up to that time, had such noble glory of triumph been found: the father and son were received together in the city and borne in a single triumphal procession, so that this honor might adorn the glory of Christ’s vengeance.

[Col. 0514B] The Jews, driven then by various conditions, were subjected. Many of the survivors were condemned to labor in the mines; others were made to feed wild beasts; some were killed by the sword of gladiators.

Many were sold—boys, beardless youths, and all those whom their eighteenth year had not yet spared.

Exiled to different regions of the world, they showed all peoples how great were the burdens of guilt they had committed, and how the entire people, so great a nation, had deserved to be destroyed and perish: the survivors were sold and scattered throughout the regions of the world.

At last, deprived of angelic protection, the temple was polluted, shaken, devastated, and consumed by fire.

The word of God spoken about this was fulfilled in its entirety, and all that the Lord Jesus had uttered by his divine mouth was accomplished, when he lamented the city that was destined to perish for its crime.

As the Church of Christ shone brightly, the darkness was removed and the old shadow of the temple was driven away.

## CHAPTER II. The failed restoration of the temple

[Col. 0513]

[Col. 0513C] Julian the apostate, a deserter from Christ, ordered after a long interval that the ancient temple be restored to its native inhabitants, to be worshiped according to the Jews’ customary practice.

They hurried there, driven from every region, as though summoned by a divine herald. They assembled and began preparing the site for the temple.

Private resources strengthened them; public funding encouraged the undertaking, and the urgency of pressing forward began to be put into action.

They began to insult our people, as though they had recovered and reestablished the times of their kingdom. They frightened them with threatening faces, displayed their savagery and swollen fury, and arrogantly directed everything against our people.

When the foundations had already been exposed, the earth began to rise of its own accord, filling the trenches. Yet everything else was ready:

[Col. 0513D] stones, bases, gypsum, lime, cement, and columns.

Nothing was lacking for new foundations to be laid, even after the old ones had been thrown down, so that the work might bring back the light that had been born—although Cyril, then bishop of Jerusalem, opposed it.

[Col. 0514C] He, as a prudent man, examined Daniel’s prophecies and, remembering the Lord’s words, testified that it could not happen that this stone should be fitted by them to the stone.

To test the matter, they waited. The night alone delayed the opportunity to begin the work. Suddenly an earthquake arose, and the ground shook.
