Stones were hurled far away; the foundations were scattered over a wide area, and the walls that had been set in place collapsed in a rapid fall. The cement split apart, and the lime flew through the air.

A great crowd of profane craftsmen, preparing to build their shrine, lay beneath the open porticoes; falling walls crushed them in the ruin.

The rest, who thought they had escaped death, hurried at daybreak to search for those who had been killed.

[Col. 0514D] Within, a certain hidden little room had kept the tools required for the work.

From it a fiery mass emerged and ran through the street, consuming and burning the searchers,

[Col. 0515A] Jews whose final fate thus made their identity clear.

Repeating this again and again, and frequently thereafter, the fiery mass pressed more fiercely throughout the entire day, restraining the reckless undertaking of the audacious people.

At last, driven by immense fear, they are said, against their will, to have acknowledged Christ as the true Lord and God.

And lest they attribute these events to mere chance, the emblem of the cross shone radiant in the blazing sky.

[Col. 0516A] On the following night, the cross was also clearly impressed upon the garments of the unbelievers, marked with wondrous blackness, so that the faithless might prove by their efforts that it could not be driven away.

At last, thus terrified, their supporting hand gave way. They themselves looked more reverently upon these signs of the cross than upon their ancient rites, and upon Christ’s new triumph shining forth in the life-giving city, which offers light to the nations and, through its unceasing radiance, flashes throughout the kingdoms of the world.

## CHAPTER III. The removal and restoration of the holy cross

[Col. 0515]

[Col. 0515B] Although once, compelled by the guilt of crime, the Persian ruler brought a cruel army here while he trampled with the sword the surrounding regions and profaned holy places with slaughter,

he carried away the ornaments, including the standards of the blessed cross, and joined them to a throne shining with metallic light. Falsely claiming the laws of the Thunderer, he prepared unworthy scepters and appeared as a god beneath the modest expanse of heaven.

But the energetic leader of the Roman army, employing the force of war and supported by the protection of the true God, broke the half-man’s troops, burst into the inner chambers, and released the mortal god enclosed in bronze through slaughter.

He subdued the devoted battalions and brought back the divine standards,

[Col. 0516B] rejoicing in the trophy won by the power granted to him, and carried them back to Jerusalem. Divine things were accomplished in the heavens.

Ancient miracles, restored through new prayers, shone forth. A dead man returned to life through the wood of life.

Four lepers, freed from long illness, came forward; cleansed lepers, in their full number, displayed clean bodies; fifteen blind men saw great wonders.

Demons were expelled and left their numerous dwellings. Many illnesses fled, leaving many people restored.

The leader of the descendants of Romulus rejoiced and poured forth abundant wealth. Bowing down, he restored the sacred buildings with worthy structures, urged on the fathers, and decreed that the festivals of the cross should be celebrated annually; thereafter we reverence its solemn honors.

## CHAPTER IV. The panel bearing Christ’s image

[Col. 0515]

[Col. 0515C] Yet the hostile people, chattering in blind whispers, did not rest, though they had been defeated by the conqueror.

Their sin of speech and the pride of their hearts laid them low. Since they could not direct their arrows against Christ, they turned them against themselves, displaying their ancient hatred and eternal fury.

One who, by signs, was permitted to rage with the dark poison of envy, a new enemy always stirred by hatred of honor, burned with anger and sought by what art he might be allowed to rage.

He pined at the beauty of the Church and was jealous of its splendor. One of these men, seeing a panel bearing an image of the Redeemer’s face, worthy to shine on the walls of the hall, burned with dreadful fire, concocting black poisons.

Hastening in silent fury, he secretly approached at night, armed with a weapon, and attacked the painted image.

[Col. 0516C] He scraped the image from the wall, intending to carry it home hidden beneath his garment and burn it.

But when a light was brought near, he saw himself wet with blood, with a mark spreading over him. Terrified by this, he threw away the pierced panel, concealed it in hiding, and fled. Frightened by the portent, he dared not handle it.

In the morning, the people of God entered the inner shrine and saw that the ornament of the building was gone. Discovering the traces left by the blood, they followed them. Finding the thief’s hut, they carefully searched the innermost part of the dark little dwelling.

The cell gave back the jewel when it was carefully examined, despite the denials of the thief.

When the savage robber was assailed by a cloud of stones, the celebrated image was restored to the church.

## CHAPTER V. The infants slain by Herod

[Col. 0515]

[Col. 0515D] Ephrata, bearer of fruit, most fertile land, hail! Hail, Bethlehem, renowned for your fertility, whose God is your glory!

Deign to honor the unskilled singer, unequal to great heralds—not merely inferior to the great, but seen as inferior even to a child.

Before Sophronius had yet become renowned for the overthrow of Serapis, when the King of heaven was born in you, earthly kingdoms were terrified and the heavenly realms flashed with celebrated light. The inhabitants of heaven rejoiced, and hostile kingdoms trembled.

Peace sent from heaven to the pious made savage hearts quake, and those who were not friends of peace prepared to disturb peace.

Herod feared that he might be succeeded by the one who stands before all the peoples and kings of the world, arranging all heights by his perpetual command.

When he learned from you, great one, who the king was, and fearing to lose his scepter, he burned to destroy the King of heaven.

[Col. 0516D] He killed those of the same age, thinking that by this stratagem the child too would be killed, so that no infant would remain in your cradles.

Yet supreme wisdom anticipated the attempt. While another year was passing, it afflicted the enemy with a pestilential ulcer and a punishment worthy of his deeds, destroying him, and fulfilled the mysteries of the flesh he had assumed, which had once been ordained before the foundation of the world.

But who will be able to count the number of those infants whose blood then drenched the land of Bethlehem? They fulfilled the duties of a king’s birth-funeral, offering Christ the first beginnings of tender life.

They were witnesses to the event not by words, but by their own blood.

[Col. 0517A] The grieving hearts of their mothers lost them, but the rejoicing realms of heaven received them.

[Col. 0518A] Though they did not know to whom their souls were being dedicated by death, they now behold the Lamb of eternity and follow him.

## CHAPTER VI. The holy monk George

[Col. 0517]

[Col. 0517A] George is said to have been born in this city as a monk, restraining himself wonderfully through a narrow path of abstinence.

Corduba received him after he had departed from Jerusalem for doctrinal instruction.

[Col. 0518A] It saw him strengthened by noble companions, pressing down earthly things and seeking for a long time the desired triumph.

## CHAPTER VII. Saint Jerome

[Col. 0517]

[Col. 0517A] It is known that many holy men shone in this land, which the saint desired to visit.

[Col. 0517B] The blessed Jerome came here to remain.

His father was Eusebius, born within the walls of Stridon, at the boundary between Dalmatia and Pannonia. In the Roman city he assumed the garment of Christ.

Here he was learned in Greek and Latin letters. Then, following the discipline and rule of an approved monk, he became a presbyter and was praised as worthy of the episcopal office.

Soon plots were prepared against him because of the envy aroused by his habit of exposing the faults of many in writing and revealing the hidden crimes and vices of others.

To avoid inflaming their fury against himself, he withdrew. Leaving his home, relatives, and parents, he departed from Rome and made his way toward Jerusalem.

Yet he could not live without the light of the cultivated library. He was constantly turning over its books with rhetorical vigilance and extraordinary zeal.

[Col. 0517C] Cicero pleased him above all, and he repeatedly reviewed him with undivided attention.

While he was captivated by the attractions of that table, he was seized by a salutary fever and the heat of illness.

He was shaken by numbing cold and burned by raging fire. Suddenly he was carried away and brought before a judge. There a radiance shining with immense light took away his courage; prostrate, he could not raise his eyes toward the heavenly tribunal.

When asked about his condition, he declared that he was a Christian.

“You lie,” said the examiner. “You are a disciple of Cicero, not of Christ; your heart and your treasure are there.”

At these words he collapsed, and in the awareness of that memory he was consumed even more than he had been when ordered to suffer blows from a harsh scourge.

Amid the lashes, however, he kept saying: “Lord, have mercy.”

When this voice resounded with nothing but mournful lamentation,

[Col. 0517D] at last those standing by fell on their knees before the supreme judge, begging pardon for his youthful years. They said that if he were asked for anything pagan, he would afterward suffer what was deserved.

He swore that this had been granted and, prepared to swear solemnly, was sent back under that condition.

He awoke and opened his eyes, drenched in tears, while the crowd looked on in wonder—if it is permissible to call it a dream.

He testified that he had endured the harsh pains of the beating and that his shoulders bore livid marks burned into them.

From that time he read divine writings with as much love of piety as he had previously devoted to the study of worldly literature.

Renewed by these things, he entered the Byzantine dwelling of Gregory of Nazianzus, then renowned for its teaching, and humbly submitted to him as a teachable disciple.

Satisfied by him with the nourishment of sacred Scripture,

[Col. 0518A] he gladly sought Syria and its deserted countryside.

Carried on the soft wings of a simple dove, he sought places scorched by the sun,

[Col. 0518B] inhabited only by the loftiest monks and deserted by settlers.

After spending four years in this desolate region, he ran like a prudent animal to Christ’s manger and chose to remain at the Lord’s cradle.

Here he prayed, meditated, and devoted himself to prayers and studies. Fasting, he led the day onward until the rising of night.

Immediately many young men of outstanding character and holy companions were drawn to him by his reputation. The increasing number of arrivals and companions compelled him to provide a cell capable of receiving guests.

Chaste disciples, out of love for religion, approached this father, ready to serve his commands.

Wisdom had built for itself a beloved dwelling in his household, as the library reveals,

[Col. 0518C] which he cultivated with the greatest zeal and immense labor.

For who could explain with what effort he learned the Hebrew language and grasped the Chaldaean words? With what exertion and sweat did he acquire these things?

How much did he endure whenever he despaired and yet dared to renew the contest after he had given up?

He subdued the movements of his body and fled the fires of passion. He overcame the youthful heat of a light and fleeting age.

Armed with faith and trusting in Christ’s help, he attempted to render the canon of Hebrew Scripture into our language, so that, like new wine soon drawn from its press, it might preserve its own flavor without defect once poured into a perfectly pure vessel.

He examined the Roman books by prophetic light, and, commenting on them in his writings, explained almost everything.

[Col. 0518D] In addition, he produced many little works, exhorting and encouraging the pious and reproving the wicked; examining hidden matters and recounting the deeds of the saints.

He wrote a chronicle of history, disclosing the names of writers; arming Catholics and battling those who followed falsehoods.

For fifty-six years he was devoted to these studies and sowed the sacred seeds of the word in the soil of reason.

Now, as his bodily strength withered in his exhausted body, he spread the strength of his unconquered spirit.

So that he might be able to arrange the rules of the monastery, the weary old man accustomed himself to raising his limbs from his bed with the help of a rope suspended from a beam.

At last, having been received by God and leaving behind the bonds of the flesh, on the eighth day of September, after ninety years, he obtained the rest he desired, the end and fruit of his labor.

[Col. 0519A] From there he sought the heavens, where pure light had sought the earth;

and where the pious Lord, in humility, had descended to the depths,

[Col. 0520A] from there the good servant ascended exalted to the heights.

## CHAPTER VIII. Saint Paula

[Note: [Col. 0519] See Saint Jerome’s Letter 108, to Eustochium.]

[Col. 0519]

[Col. 0519A] The number of Jerome’s writings concerning Paula and Eustochium is by no means fixed, for there are very many of them. Here he recounts Paula’s life and deeds.

Noble by birth, she was nobler in goodness; renowned for her wealthy household, she was more illustrious still in voluntary poverty.

She preferred Bethlehem to Rome and exchanged ceilings glittering with gems for a roof of fallen turf.

Her father descended from the great Agamemnon,

[Col. 0519B] who overthrew Pergamum in a long war; her mother traced her lineage from the Scipios.

She was joined in marriage to Toxotius, whose blood came from Julius, and whom the marriage bond had adorned with five children.

She mourned his death so deeply that she almost followed him in fact: free, released from the agreement and bonds of marriage, she bound herself to Christ’s service, so that one might think she had desired the funeral of her earthly husband.

As she distributed her wealth and took away inheritances from her children—whom nevertheless she raised and enriched with a divine gift—she strove to help the poor throughout the entire city.

By serving, she was deemed worthy to receive the great bishops: Paulinus of the city called Antioch by name, and the holy Epiphanius of Salamis, worthy of such a host,

[Col. 0519C] whom an imperial command had then compelled to come to Rome.

Inflamed by their pious virtues, she burned with the desire to see the desert and considered leaving Rome.

Removing from her mind her children, servants, and possessions, she thought of freeing herself by every means from the bonds of the world.

At last, after the cold season, when the sea became suitable for ships and the bishops were returning to their proper seats, she followed them with a blessed vow.

With her dear brother and relatives, and with her children accompanying her to the harbor, she set out. They, striving in piety to surpass their pious mother, were surpassed by her piety. In proving herself Christ’s servant, she no longer knew the natural claims of the flesh.

The winds filled the sails, and the force of their wings carried the stern forward—the swift vessel’s course.

[Col. 0519D] Little Toxotius, stretching out his hands on the shore, and Rufina, wet with tears, tried to hold back the mother who despised earthly things and sought the heavenly

[Col. 0520A] heights, denying the laws and claims of nature.

Yet leaving these possessions behind, now free of their burden, she went on, content with her Eustochium. Conscious of so great an undertaking and companion in the vow, Eustochium, devoted to heaven, comforted her mother’s heart, stripped bare of earthly things.

Meanwhile, as the vessel swiftly cut through the sea, it reached the place where Flavia Domitilla had endured exile. Paula revered the cells of her martyrdom.

Happy, she saw everything that had hastened along the sea appear slow.

[Col. 0520B] Through the Adriatic waters, between Scylla and Charybdis, she entered the mild waters of Methone as though she were moving beneath calm seas.

Here, after leaving the sea, she refreshed her exhausted limbs. Soon she flew between Malea and Cythera and cut through the waters strewn with the Cyclades and their many islands.

After Rhodes and Lycia, she turned aside toward the shores of Cyprus.

When the holy Epiphanius saw her approaching, he received her as an exalted member of Christ, kneeling before him.

After visiting the monasteries and providing consolation, she was seen only a short distance from the city of Seleucia.

She climbed the walls of Antioch and visited it in this way.

Here also the holy affection of Paulinus detained her briefly. Though winter was warmed by the fervor of her faith, she did not abandon her journey midway but continued on a donkey,

[Col. 0520C] sitting painfully upon the animal that once had borne her gently in a litter.

She crossed Coele-Syria and the fields of Phoenicia. Passing through Berytus and leaving ancient Sidon behind, she entered the tower of Elijah, a small structure that remains on the shore of Sarepta, worshiping the Lord of hosts.

Through him, the only child of the widow who had once been raised from death by the prayers of the heavenly prophet was restored.

Proceeding across the sands of Tyre, with her knees fixed to the sacred ground, she was led on to Acho [Acco]; the city, whose name has now been changed, is called Ptolemais.

The fields of Mageddo, drenched with the blood of Josiah, passed beneath her joyful steps as she crossed the lands of Palestine.

She marveled at the ruins of the once-famous city of Dor, which shines afterward under the name of Straton’s Tower.

[Col. 0520D] Herod earlier enlarged it at the height of the favor of Augustus Caesar, and it was called Caesarea after the Roman prince.

## CHAPTER IX. The holy centurion Cornelius

[Col. 0519]

[Col. 0519D] As Paula carefully examined the sacred places there, she discovered the church of Christ, the building that Cornelius once inhabited and worshiped under his own right of residence.

He was worthy of God’s light although he had not yet been washed in baptism. A heavenly being bore witness that his prayers had reached the ears of God, that gracious mercy had approached the Lord’s throne, and that it had been granted to the chosen people.

Yet it is clear that the heavenly judge is not a respecter of persons and that, in his goodness, he does not reserve salvation for one people alone. The gates of heaven are opened to all nations, and by God’s gift they are approached with holy force.

No miracles had been given to this man, and no seeds of life had been sown by the sprinkling of earthly water. Yet Christ, who retains the right to bless hearts, inspired him. He prayed and was judged worthy of the stars.

He summoned a teacher when warned, sought instruction, and, although lacking the sacred font, was revealed as already purified.

[Col. 0521A] He received the gifts of the heavenly grace; for the Spirit filling him showed that he was worthy of the gift.

He considered it too little to go away having received only the gifts of life. He called his relatives, invited his dear friends, and sought to add many as participants in his gift.

Though not yet instructed, he offered clear signs of a future office and assumed the role of teacher.

Thus, when Peter granted him the holy washing, he was changed in rank after receiving the pledge of the life-giving Spirit.

[Col. 0522A] While exhorting and teaching the people with pious instruction and preparing them to multiply, he was made a priest from a centurion.

He shone as a bishop appointed in this city, where, wisely bringing about abundant growth in souls, he excelled. Blessed by these gains, he rested at the end of his life, returning substantial profits from the flock entrusted to him.

Thus, receiving worthy rewards for his labor, he obtained a heavenly honor among the leaders.

## CHAPTER X. The holy deacon Philip

[Col. 0521]

[Col. 0521A] There Paula visits the little shrine of Philip the Levite, one of the seven who began the distinguished ministry of sacred service with Stephen.

In accordance with the law by which he was appointed a minister, he never ceased scattering the seeds of the eternal word among the peoples and calling the sheep to the fold.

He performed many signs, shining with the light of his virtues: he expelled demons, healed paralyzed bodies, restored walking to the lame, and sight to the blind.

He strengthened the foundations of faith among the Samaritans, instructed and warned them, and drove away the poisons of Simon.

Guided by an angel, he hastened southward from there. Seeing an Ethiopian eunuch reading the sacred writings, he was joined to the chariot at the divine command, and by diligent care the meaning of the law was opened to him.

While the ancient waters were thirsted for, a spring appeared, revealed as new, by which the dry heart was refreshed when he drank.

This black eunuch, representing the hearts of the Gentiles, changed his dark skin when he was baptized.

Bethsoros is a village on the road from Jerusalem to Hebron.

[Col. 0522B] There, washed in the waters that the sacred rites sanctified, he deserved to share in the radiant life.

The Spirit, carrying Philip away, resolved to transfer him elsewhere—to Azotus and the other places—where he explained the words of salvation, mentioning this city as he passed through it, building up the minds in which he found rest, and his…

Three born beside one another, having received tombs with the honor of virginity; the fourth, Ephesian, smiles brightly. The Spirit himself, filling them with the gift of prophecy, preserved them from the enticements of the dreadful serpent and joined them, above the stars, to the heavenly choirs.

## CHAPTER XI. On Saint Procopius

[Col. 0521]

[Col. 0521B] Procopius is said to have adorned this city with a triumph—Scythopolis, previously adorned by his word and power. Standing day and night in God’s gracious worship, he consumed his inward parts with rare nourishment, yet fed hearts by filling them with heavenly banquets.

Moreover, brandishing his weapons against the inward and outward wars, he overcame and drove off the hostile forces.

[Col. 0522B] Sent here also as a faithful man for the first responses, strong, found wise, and proved steadfast, he beautifies the contest by receiving the sword after the angry judge Fabianus had spoken against the righteous.

## CHAPTER XII. On Priscus, Malchus, and Alexander

[Col. 0521]

[Col. 0521B] Furthermore, it is reported that here strong athletes completed celebrated triumphs through a precious death. Three young men, shining with vigorous virtue—Priscus, Malchus, and Alexander—were living together in a certain small rural estate beneath this city, devoted to their studies. During the reign of Valerian, when they learned that the struggles of the faith were multiplying, kindled alike by love of divine virtue, they began to reproach themselves for shameful sluggishness:

when heavenly crowns were being won in the City, they themselves were not winning them, nor going, seeking, and acquiring them, but were sluggishly maintaining a torpid rest upon the ground, although God commands that the heavenly kingdoms be seized with force.

Armed with these words, they went into the City. They hastened to the battles and, having approached the judge, sternly accused him of raging savagely with righteous blood.

Immediately, replying with words as worthy as his exhortations, he said: “Submit them to the beasts, since it does not please them that the blood of the devout should flow beneath our sword.”

They were soon handed over to terrible jaws to be eaten; snatched from the mouths of the beasts and caught up into Abraham’s bosom, they gained everlasting crowns through a ready death.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Saint Marinus

[Col. 0521]

[Col. 0521D] There was here a certain man powerful in wealth and honor, Marinus by name, resplendent with the insignia of military service and distinguished by his merits, one of the citizens of Jerusalem. While the proper order of advancement was once approaching him in the light of military service, behold, the goad of envy attacks a colleague, who cries out that Marinus could not attain this rank because he was oppressed by the hated religion of Christ.

When Marinus was questioned by the quaestor whether this was true, he immediately confessed with living voice that he was a Christian, declaring that he truly served according to Christ’s laws.

Three hours were granted to him in which to deliberate whether he wished to sacrifice to the gods or to die in the name of Christ.

[Col. 0523A] At once Bishop Theotignus went out to meet him and armed him, led him into the church, strengthened him with words of faith, and finally, raising him up, brought him into the inner sanctuary of the altar. There he set before him the sword with which he was girded, and then offered him the Gospel, asking which of the two he preferred.

When he had promptly extended his hand toward the divine laws, the bishop said: “Complete now what you have begun, son. Despising this fragile life, hope for the life that remains. Go forward in confidence; take the crown offered to you, with which the exalted Lord chooses to crown the devout head.”

[Col. 0524A] Returning, he went back to the savage tribunal of the herald, who summoned him and, once the time granted him had elapsed, ordered him to appear. He did not permit delay when the governor inquired of him; rather, expressing that he was firmly established in steadfastness, he said that the command of his fathers’ law had been confirmed, and that the commands of God were to be feared rather than those of man.

Thus ordered to be punished by such a slaughter of the throat, he soon ascended above the stars to a greater rank of honor.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Saint Asterius

[Col. 0523]

[Col. 0523A] A certain Asterius was present here, a native of the city of Rome, a patrician by birth, a senator in splendor, adorned with merits and enjoying his wealth prosperously,

[Col. 0523B] vigorous in nobility and powerful in royal descent, but above all exalted by love of the faith of Christ.

While he stood beside the contest of the aforesaid martyr, he received the body struck down by the sword and reverently lifted it upon his shoulders, laying a garment beneath it. As a witness, he handed it over for burial and soon gained honor.

He is also handed down in many other glorious deeds, among which they report this memorable event accomplished through him.

The Phoenicians, they say, formerly called Paneas a city; our people called it Caesarea Philippi. Near it stands Mount Panium, from whose roots the Jordan is said to emerge in two springs.

It was the custom there, on a fixed and solemn day, for a victim to be sacrificed by the foolish Gentiles to demonic powers. Once the deceitful coloring of the fraud had been removed, the deception used to vanish and appear nowhere to the eyes; yet rumor persuaded those present that the victim of the Most High was miraculously seeking the inner sanctuaries of heaven.

[Col. 0524A] It happened that Asterius was present when such a deception was being carried out. Seeing the profane spectacle and the foolish minds dazzled by the phantom, grieving over human errors and moved to pity, he groaned and prayed. Raising his eyes and extending his palms toward heaven, he invoked the mighty Lord with an inward cry. With complete faith and abundant tears, he begged that He expose the serpent’s ancient deceits, removing from miserable mortals the clouds of this trickery and revealing the hidden monsters.

While he was making this request in pious prayers and tears, behold, a serpent was suddenly brought forth and carried overhead—the victim thought to have been lifted away by divine robbery—then cast down into the depths of the river before everyone’s eyes.

Thus, dissolved by the prayer of the Christian’s faith, the mechanism of that false and age-old spectacle perished, so that the error could no longer be restored in those places, once the clear light of truth had been revealed.

## CHAPTER XV. On the Statue of the Savior

[Col. 0523]

[Col. 0523C] A woman, a citizen of Paneas, is discovered here, whom the fringe of the Lord’s garment, touched by blood, had raised up.

Before the doorway of a building stood a fixed bronze base, bearing the sculpted figure of a woman, as though stretching out her hands and kneeling. Beside it, another bronze base carried a statue of the Savior, adorned with a robe, with his right hand apparently extending assistance [the text has *pergeret*, “were proceeding,” for *porrigeret*, “were extending”].

Next to this, a plant sprang up and grew from the ground, accustomed to grow beside the worn strip of cloth. As soon as its leafy crown touched the remnant of the garment, it acquired the power to drive away every disease, possessing no sacred virtue except through contact with the cloth.

A faithless bull, rushing at its master after breaking its reins and attempting to resist, attacked it and, in its charge, overturned it. In its fury it also smashed the likenesses of its own image; but the statue’s trunk, struck by a flash of heavenly lightning, was crushed, and the blow of the divine avenger was marked upon its neck.

## CHAPTER XVI. On Saint Pamphilus

[Col. 0523]

[Col. 0523D] Here the celebrated martyr Pamphilus flourished through a venerable deed. Bishop Agapius, most generous toward the poor and bound to them by paternal love, consecrated him as a presbyter worthy of praise. The Church experienced and tested his vigilance in governance, proven through much labor.

He shone here after Theotignus in the episcopal office, fulfilling that responsibility with great distinction.

The sacred volumes that the martyr Pamphilus copied are said to be more valuable than the treasures of Croesus. He recalled the marks of the hand and reproduced the traces of the blood with his own fingers, the signs that the holy martyr had inscribed with his own limbs.

Full of faith and full of divine love, he triumphed over the savage kingdoms of Maximian through a martyr’s death.

Eusebius undertook in his books to publish the history of Pamphilus: who and how great he had been, and from where he originated; from childhood, his true teaching, battles, victories, how much he endured, and what struggles he underwent, until he likewise received the crown worthy of such honor.

## CHAPTER XVII. On Eusebius the Writer

[Col. 0525]

[Col. 0525A] This martyr, a helper of sacred studies in the light of books, shines here through Eusebius, whom Jerome himself calls the key of Scripture and the guardian of the everlasting Testament. Jerome records that Eusebius examined very many works

[Col. 0526A] from almost innumerable sources, among which are especially renowned the *Ecclesiastical History*, the *Canons of the Gospels*, and the *Chronicle* in every form. His doctrine and faith shine through the excellence of his works.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On Theophilus, Acacius, and Gelasius—The Remainder of Paula’s Journey

[Col. 0525]

[Col. 0525A] Here Bishop Theophilus shone with gracious light, purifying those who were in error concerning the observance of Easter by his teaching.

The bishop Acacius also resisted this error in the city; by explaining the doctrines of Solomon concerning the faith, he brought them to light. Moreover, he adorned the Church with much radiance.

Gelasius, who set Felix in the see in place of Liberius, is said here to have flourished after Euzonius, a holy man of worthy wit but sparing in composition.

After Paula had visited the sanctuaries of Caesarea, she passed through a half-ruined fortress called Antipatris and strove without delay to go to Lydda, which is called Diospolis in the Greek tongue. The shining salvation of Dorcas and Aeneas accompanies her there.

Not far from here she enters the village of Arimathea, where Joseph, worthy to bury the Lord of heaven, placed him in the tomb.

From there she proceeds to the city of the priests, Nob [or Nobe], named by an ill omen after the tomb of the slain [Note: 1 Kings 22].

From here she enters the port of Joppa, belonging to the fleeing Jonah; then, retracing her route, she quickly turns aside to Emmaus.

This place is now Nicopolis. There the Lord was recognized by the breaking of bread by those whose genuine love shone forth in their deeds; their eyes are proved to have been illumined while they honored the heavenly commands through their actions. They recognize through their works what they could not recognize by hearing, and at the same time reveal that not everyone is to be blessed merely by the mouth, unless good deeds follow.

Here, at the spring where the Redeemer was seen to have washed his feet when he appeared with the disciples, animals afflicted by various diseases are washed and leave their plagues behind.

Here too the renowned Cleophas, whose sacred house shines as worthy to receive the Lord as a guest, is slaughtered within it, having suffered the fury of the Jews on account of Christ’s praise. In the same place, where he was buried with celebrated devotion, the Lord whom his own house had received upon earth now dwells above the stars of heaven, giving himself to those whom he has subdued.

Leaving Nicopolis, Paula climbs both Beth-horons, cities established with the honor of King Solomon,

[Col. 0525D] but long ago overturned by the varied storm of wars. On her right she sees Gibeon, where Joshua, relying on his companion’s name, was able to make the sun stand still.

At Gibeah she stops and remembers the six hundred men slain through lust, and those spared in Paul’s ancestry.

From there she enters Jerusalem, a city called by a mingled threefold name, on its left side admiring the famous mausoleum of the empress Helena of Adiabene, who fed Jerusalem when famine persisted, with grain from the countryside of Canopus.

The lofty palace is said to have served as Paula’s lodging,

[Col. 0526A] but a small cell received her, avoiding high roofs.

Then, going around all the places marked by Christ’s holy triumphs, she venerates them with great love of faith. Prostrate before the cross, she worships and asks the Lord to protect her—the Lord hanging there and atoning by his death for the sins of the world.

She fastens kisses upon the stone and embraces the tomb, which the angel opened by removing the stone, where the joys of life are revealed.

[Col. 0526B] She touches the place, pouring forth a stream of tears, the place sanctified by the right of the tomb because of the Lord’s limbs.

At last, leaving from there, she ascends to the fortress of Zion, among the holy mountains, whose foundations are strong. Its gates and camps are dear to God above all else, the God of Jacob.

They are not gates such as are consumed by the flames of the enemy, but gates through which one enters the royal hall of heaven.

She does not look with dry eyes upon the column stained by the blood of Christ, the bound and scourged one. Certainly it bears abundant safeguards of continual salvation, giving strength to the faithful who cling to its bonds and driving away various plagues through healing consolation.

Through the portico of the church, which supports and raises it, the place is opened to Paula where the gracious Spirit had descended upon one hundred and twenty lambs.

[Col. 0526C] Here also, distributing pious gifts to Christ’s poor, she reaches beloved Bethlehem with a long breath of desire.

Entering the cave, she sees the divine womb of the Virgin, where she gave birth; the manger and the animals of Christ, by which the Lord’s own people recognized him. She testifies that she saw with the eyes of faith the child’s limbs lying in the swaddling clothes, the body of God placed beneath the narrow shelter.

She reverently offers fitting service to the untouched mother; the shepherds come at night, and the Magi bring pious gifts and the star appears; the infants are slaughtered, while Herod rages in his massacre, and Joseph, accompanied by Mary, seeks Egypt.

Thus she venerates the house of bread with abundant tears and greets the sacred cradle of the King at its pious spring.

Not far from there she seeks the tower of the flock, marked by a clear sign, where Jacob had fed his sheep. There the shepherds drank in the honor of the angelic voice: “Glory to God Most High,” sung to mortals, and “Peace” bequeathed to the benevolent, while the heavenly choir resounded with praises.

[Col. 0526D] Nearby, while the sheep are grazing, a lamb of pure fleece is revealed, filled with heavenly dew—one worthy to dissolve the sins of the world and to drive the destroyer from his own people.

From there Paula proceeds tirelessly along the ancient road to Gaza, whose name the Persian language explains as “treasure.”

In that city Bishop Silvanus, together with his companions, overcame the fury of Diocletian,

[Col. 0527A] when forty men were sent together to the joys of heaven by the sword at Fanesus [or Fennus].

Soon she crosses Bethzur on the right, and Eschol, from which the bearers carried the cluster of grapes, a sign of Christ, who, hung upon the wood, poured forth sweet wine for his own people and gave a land flowing with sweetness.

From there she seeks Sarah’s cell and the traces of Abraham’s oak, by which he deserved, through the eyes of his heart, to behold the day of Christ and rejoice in the Lord himself.

From there she climbs to Hebron, which is called Kiriath-arba, “the city of four,” after the tombs of four great men: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the first father. Caleb is joined to these and reckoned as the fourth among them.

[Col. 0527B] She leaves Kiriath-sepher, whose name was given by its writing, admiring the upper and lower waters that Othniel received, scorning the dry fields, so that he might enrich the irrigated little farms [Note: Judges 1].

From there she passes through Caphar-baruch, “the village of blessing,” where Abraham came as far as the starry Lord as his companion.

Paula marvels at the fields of Sodom and Gomorrah, burned by heavenly fire as their merits demanded.

She looks upon the vineyards of Engedi, whose shrubs sweat balsam, a gift denied to other lands.

Contemplating Segor, which the Syrians call Zoara, she remembers Lot’s cave and, turning to tears, warns how wine must be avoided: it ruled the man whom his fellow citizens could not overcome.

[Col. 0527C] Returning thence from the warm south, where the bride found her bridegroom lying down, she passes through Tekoa, joyfully looking up at the mountain from which the Savior ascended to the high throne of the Father, from which he governs the ages.

Long ago, it was customary for a red heifer to burn on this mountain; its ashes purified the people. When the cherubim moved into it, they left the heights of the Temple and established the firm foundations of the Church.

There, they say, the sacred remains of Jacob were hidden; he himself had placed in the Temple the venerable bones of the righteous, depositing beneath it the bones of Zechariah and Simeon.

From there, too, the report says that Pelagia, once submerged in pollution, after laying down the burden of the flesh, sought the heights of heaven. Her deeds, remembered and praised, provide a happy ending worthy of imitation.

[Col. 0527D] Paula sees the lodging of Martha and Mary, and Bethphage, retained under the authority of the priests. She also sees the place of the Lord, where the Gentile colt received the bridle, adorned with celebrated honor, and offered its gentle back to the seated one beneath the apostolic garment.

By this straight route she descends to Jericho. From the Gospel she remembers the man whom the savage weapons of robbers left half-dead and whom the severe-minded priests passed by; the Samaritan placed him upon his beast and mercifully brought him to the inn of the Church.

She also sees the tree of Zacchaeus, who, trampling underfoot what is harmful to life, saw the exalted Lord passing by from a lofty height.

Paula now looks upon the places of the blind, whose eyes, restored by the Lord, teach that the darkness of error must be driven from both peoples by the power of Christ.

[Col. 0528A] She enters Jericho and observes the tower of Achiel, which Abiram founded at the death of his firstborn and which, at the threshold, set its gates upon Segub’s lineage [Note: Joshua 6:26; 1 Kings 16:34].

She looks at Gilgal, with the foreskins of the camp—the old Israel leaving them behind while discerning the mystery of the repeated falling away of the flesh and recalling the purifications of the mind.

From there she sees the twelve stones brought up from the river’s depths, which established the foundations of apostolic authority.

She also sees the spring of the old Law, at times bitter and barren, which the wisdom of the great prophet transformed into sweetness, making it rich in flowing water.

Hardly had night passed with the lamp of returning light when she seeks the Jordan, meditating on how the priests once stood on dry ground in the middle of the receding river;

[Col. 0528B] and afterward, through Elijah’s power, how the water made a dry path at his command.

Thus the Lamb, white and without stain, consecrating the new baptism for souls, washed away the blemish in that river, cleansed our sins, and purified the polluted waters through his baptism from the slaughter of the human race.

She sees the valley of Achor, a place of troubles and tumult, where theft and condemned greed were found.

From there she goes to Bethel, the house of the Lord, where the poor man slept upon the bare ground, with a stone beneath his head. There she sees the seven-eyed Zechariah, the one Corner in whom both walls are joined.

She also sees the ladder of heaven reaching to the heights. Above it, the exalted ruler leans and extends his hand to those worthy to climb the stars by a proper ascent,

[Col. 0528C] while he hurls down the empty and malicious, dark with deceit.

Soon she venerates the tombs of Jesus and Eleazar and marvels that the censor himself had read of the ruggedness of the mountain, while he presented the remaining terrain as level and exceedingly fertile.

What shall I say of Shiloh, where the ruined altar of the ancient rites is revealed, where it is known that the tribe of Benjamin once preceded the Sabine women, seized without custom?

Crossing Shechem, which is called Neapolis, she enters the church on Mount Gerizim, raised along the mountain’s side. It looks toward the well that Jacob dug, beside which the Lord sat and asked for a cup, and where the Samaritan woman is satisfied with the water of faith.

She had five books of the Mosaic writings, and she passed beyond the error of Dositheus, the sixth man, and received the true Messiah and Savior.

[Col. 0528D] From there, departing, she observes the twelve tombs of the Fathers. She sees Samaria, called Sebaste in honor of Augustus, where the pious tombs of the prophets were kept: Obadiah, Elisha, and the great John the Baptist.

She trembled greatly on seeing many marvels. For she heard black troops rustling with their various wings at the tombs of the saints, howling like wolves, barking like dogs, and roaring with the growl of lions.

From there the lowing of bulls echoes, and the serpent hisses; some turn their heads backward, strike the ground with their crowns, while others she sees suspended in the air with their feet turned toward their faces, their garments not hanging downward.

[Col. 0529A] For these creatures she pours out tears and prays to Christ. Though weary, she rejoices in climbing the mountain on foot, in whose two caves it is said that, during the plague, Obadiah fed one hundred prophets.

From there, with pious steps, she visits Nazareth, the nursling of the Lord; then Cana and Capernaum, rich in Christ’s signs; and the Sea of Tiberias, crossed by boat and consecrated by the divine crossing.

Afterward she visits the vast place where the Lord satisfied five thousand people with five loaves, filling twelve sacred baskets with the surplus and storing up for the disciples the remains which the crowd could not contain in its belly.

Then she climbs Tabor, where it pleased the Lord to reveal his heavenly form, shining with light from above.

[Col. 0529B] Seeing Hermon and the Hermonites, and surveying the broad fields of Galilee where the ranks of Sisera were laid low by Barak’s victory, with the river Kishon cutting across the level places,

she then crosses Nain, bringing new joy to the widow. She intends to visit Egypt but pauses briefly at the spring that flows from a molar’s tooth and, like a torrent of Arcadia, refreshes its rushing depths.

She sees the tomb of Micah, diligently visiting the places of Moresheth, now a church, as it is said, in the fields of Canopus, to behold the broad and far-reaching deserts, fields fertile with the seed of miracles and virtues.

She traverses the five Pharian cities, speaking in the language of Chanaan: Goshen and Tahpanhes, the Nile-land of God, which Moses triumphs over by the splendor of the highest commands. Swiftly embracing the lofty columns

[Col. 0529C] of Christ’s Church, she falls at the feet of those who, exiles from the world, overcome the world’s heights.

The holy first priest Isidore meets her in the region of Nitria, a renowned confessor; with him come Macarius, Arsetes, and Serapion.

Seeing them, she believes that she truly sees the Lord, and rejoices that what she spends upon them she is paying to Christ.

She would have remained in this region to enjoy the honor of its solitude had not her vow of desire held her to the holy places. To these she returned swiftly, as though on swift avian wings.

She returns to sacred Bethlehem, intending to remain there forever:

[Col. 0530A] in lodging far too narrow she spends three years, until she carefully builds cells and monasteries suited to different purposes and constructs spacious dwellings for different pilgrims beside the road along which the heavenly Virgin, accompanying Joseph, once came and found no lodging.

For men she diligently establishes a hospice; she arranges choirs of virgins in companies and serves the monasteries whose final authority she held, so that one might see that she preferred to serve rather than to preside.

After her husband’s death she did not marry another, although she proved this virtue in the stronghold of holiness.

Nor was she refreshed after bathing by linen warmed in steam. She had no soft bed except when sick with fever; she lay upon sackcloth, and the harsh earth gave her sleep.

[Col. 0530B] By nights she also sought rest—if it may rightly be called rest—joining night and day to prayers and soaking her cradle with abundant tears of devotion.

She frequently combined fasting with pious vows. Giving everything to the poor, she became needy in earthly possessions but rich in the heavenly height of the gift.

Teachable, she carried the Scriptures in a remembering mind. Meditating upon them, she drew from them the instruments of the light of the New Testament and of the Old teaching itself.

Under the instruction of the celebrated teacher Jerome, she learned the Hebrew language and sang the psalms in Hebrew, resounding them in the genuine voice.

Her eloquence sounded in Latin like grass without restraint; she shone with the radiant light of various virtues.

She left her daughter Eustochium, whom she had enriched by that sole inheritance, and joyfully departed for her desired homeland.

When, as she was dying, she was asked whether she felt pain, she replied that she felt no distress: everything seemed quiet to her, everything already serene.

Thus she traced the cross upon her lips with the movement of her finger and released her soul, seeking the hidden places of heaven.

Carried on a bier borne by the hands of bishops, she was placed in the middle of the cave, within the Church of Christ. May we, together with Jerome, therefore proclaim her blessed and truly crowned with a long martyrdom.

## THE THIRD BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0529]

## CHAPTER I. On the holy martyrs Eusebius, Peleus, and Nilus

[Col. 0529D] Moreover, it is clear that many saints, overcoming fear, shone forth in triumphs in this land. A certain Eusebius, a devoted foster-child of the faith, was seized by the governor of Palestine for Christ’s name, first tortured on the rack, then beheaded; through the rich interest of the punishment of martyrdom he received the rewards of heaven.

[Col. 0530D] In the fifteenth year, as it is said, of Diocletian, while that emperor was torturing the devout in this country, the bishops of Christ, Peleus and Nilus, are reported to have sought heaven in a company of clergy through fire and to have offered themselves to the Lord as holocausts for the people.

## CHAPTER II. On Bishop Asclepius, and also the martyrs Eusebius, Nectarius, and Zeno

[Col. 0529]

[Col. 0529D] Asclepius of Gaza, driving off the enemies of the faith, is banished through envy; trusting in Roman rule, he seeks justice, which Julius, weighing with an even balance, restores to its see and ministry, blaming the perpetrators and restraining them with warnings and threats.

Here Eusebius, Nectarius, and Zeno, men of Gaza, triumph because impious shrines had been overthrown by their efforts. They are worn out with blows and chains; they are beaten with clubs, torn, burdened with stones, and deprived of their brains. Their remaining limbs are given to the flames, and their bones are scattered, mingled with the bones of beasts of burden. A woman, seeking and gathering them at a heavenly prompting, entrusts them to her nephew after their location has been disclosed by visions.

But Zeno, receiving the pledges of his beloved brothers, keeps them under the roof of his house, until, when a basilica had been built in the city and the bishop had been consecrated, he strives to associate Nestor with them,

[Col. 0532A] an outstanding companion in battle and partner in the crown. Sent while still breathing his last, for Zeno diligently attended to him, he shines forth as one who has completed his service and gains the honor of heaven.

Bishop Zeno too, a centenarian, unwearied in holy offices, regular and steadfast, is not seen to be lessened, nor does he grant rest from his observances. Thrice married by lawful marriage, father of three children, he excelled in the praise of a philosopher and adorned his soul with virtuous deeds.

## CHAPTER III. On Saint Hilarion

[Note: [Col. 0531D] See the Life of Saint Hilarion among the Works of Saint Jerome, at the beginning of vol. II, Patrology, vol. XXIII.]

[Col. 0531]

[Col. 0531A] Let us celebrate Palestine, made illustrious by Hilarion as her son, and follow Jerome, the guide of his life, in his account. He writes that Hilarion was first born in a village named Thavatha, near Gaza, five miles distant from the city walls,

[Col. 0531B] facing south.

As he unfolds the remaining contests of his life and virtues, this man rises like a fragrant rose among sharp thorns, born of cruel parents devoted to images. To be educated, he is sent to Alexandria and learns the art of grammar from shrewd teachers. Dear to all, he was fervent in study and character, applying himself with excellent discipline to the worship of Christ and meditating with pious affection upon the love of religion.

Hearing Antony’s name through renowned report, he eagerly seeks to see him and goes into the desert. Having settled there, for two months he changes his customary dress and lies close by him, marking the lofty pattern of chaste morals and the rule of discipline: how constant he was in prayer, humble in receiving visitors, vigorous in warning, and eager in exhorting; and what austerity he maintained in purpose and food.

After this, returning to his homeland when both father and mother had died, with some fellow monks he duly distributes the inheritance left to him: part to his brothers and part he gives to the needy, keeping nothing for himself. For fifteen years, naked and bearing Christ’s arms, he enters the desert, covered with the rough cloak of a countryman and wearing the garment of skins which Antony had given him when he had been equipped to bear the sweet yoke of Christ.

For the first fifteen years, three figs at night fed him when exhausted. For four years he kept off heat and rain in the corner of a narrow hut and tiny cottage, which he wove from soft rush and sharp sedge.

[Col. 0531D] Afterwards a cell is built, four feet broad and five feet high, lower than his stature, so that a humble visitor entering might be contained in it while his body rested. It was a little longer than it was wide; you might think it not a house but perhaps a tomb.

Only once a year, on the day of Easter, was he shorn. He did not change his tunic until the former one had wholly fallen into rags and been consumed by holy wear. A mat of rushes spread upon the bare ground was his bedding

[Col. 0532A] until the day of death. Nothing was ever more precious to him than the sack in which he had once been clothed; it was not washed in water, except in the fountain of tears poured out from his heart. He kept the Holy Scriptures in the treasury of his mind,

[Col. 0532B] and after prayers sang psalms to the Lord as though He were present.

[Note: [Col. 0531D] Jerome, in the Life of Malchus: “From his twenty-first [Col. 0532D] year until his twenty-seventh, for three years he ate half a sextarius of lentils soaked in cold water, and for another three,” etc.]

When he had passed his twentieth year, for three years he ate no food except lentils, softened with a little cold water. For another three he was refreshed with salt, bread, and water. For four years after that he used wild herbs for food, together with the roots of certain shrubs. Then for five years half a pound of barley bread and a little vegetable, cooked without oil, were his fare.

When he saw that his eyes were growing dim through toil and that his skin was being drawn tight by a kind of itch, he added oil as a remedy to the aforesaid food. In this regimen of diet he was nourished until the sixty-third year of his life was complete, adding thereafter nothing whatsoever to his sustenance.

[Col. 0532C] Thus unwearied, when he already perceived the goal of his contest approaching, he despises even a morsel of bread; and, despising it, he completes his eightieth year, burning with immense fervor as though he were a novice beginning combat at the very time when many are accustomed to lay down their arms. For his food is a little broth of flour and crushed herbs, and he drinks scarcely five ounces.

Thus he completed the course of his life, never breaking his fast before the setting sun plunged its rays into the waters, whether on feast days or when grievously ill.

Many battles assail the little band: outward conflicts crash without, civil wars murmur within. But taught by the heavenly breath, the pious man suppresses what is inward; calming the disturbances of his soul by serene restraint, he overcomes the wanton little ass by hardship, breaks and weakens it, and makes it fit for the uses of war.

[Col. 0532D] Accustomed to internal warfare, he goes forth stronger against barbarous foes. The hostile enemy, waging wars, provokes him with varied weapons, attacks him by a thousand tricks, and assails him in a thousand combats: a little boy cries, a little woman wails, an ox lows, a sheep bleats, a beast yelps; he sets before him portents and the sounds of things to be feared, and the din of armies. When he cannot move him by sound, he tries to terrify him with dreadful visions.

[Col. 0533A] He equips charioteers, brings yoked teams under the reins, sets chariots in motion, and deceitfully renews the saddle-horses. But Christ’s helmet and the breastplate of faith cover Hilarion; seeing the raging beasts rushing upon him, he cries out to Jesus, and the harmful procession is swallowed by an opening in the earth. He sings Christ’s bright triumphs, gives praise, and rejoices that he has conquered by a swift victory.

Thereafter many wars and attempts of deceit assail him. The crafty serpent displays naked female limbs to the man as he lies down, provides rich dishes to one who has no need of food, and itself, fierce, brings wild beasts against the unconquered man. It thrusts itself upon him as he prays, reproaches him, or wearies him with violence. Having conquered all these, the soldier persists in the contest.

The enemy heaps up ambushes and remakes his arms, or prepares greater ones, and sends robbers against the poor man.

[Col. 0533B] Roaming about all night, they cannot find his bed. At dawn they see him lying before them, safe and unconcerned, and ask what he himself did when he had been surrounded by night. “A naked man,” he says, “does not fear to be attacked by robbers.” “He can be killed,” they say. “He can,” he replies, “boy; yet I do not fear, for I am ready to die.”

Stupefied by his courage, confessing the darkness of night and the coverings of the shadows, they promise amendment of their lives. The serpent wastes away, seeing as many triumphs oppose it as it has brought on contests of war.

Thereafter many and frequent trophies and signs occur. A woman who had long been sterile dares to break through the barriers of his little dwelling; relieved through her vows, she departs, and after a year pays thanks for the child she has received.

[Col. 0533C] The Lord added to the marvels by which He exalted His servant. When another mother’s three children were drawing together their last breath under the danger of death, he restores them sound in a moment and carries off an Ethiopian demon.

A charioteer of Gaza, prepared to drive his chariot, while intent upon the practice of his art, is struck dumb; his limbs fail as though he had drawn back, and his sinews stiffen throughout his body. His hand cannot be fitted to the whip; he cannot draw tight the reins; now his neck remains unmoving, and the team, deprived of its driver, is borne along by no skill. At last the master, cast down from the useless pole, is lifted up and as a suppliant seeks the aid of the litter.

Thus, having approached the humble physician with bowed effort, he receives the joy of a remedy only on the condition that he submit his heart to the true healer and remain devoted, renouncing his guilty art.

[Col. 0533D] He vows his heart, receives the admonitions, and is healed in both respects, rejoicing that he has been restored in body and soul by a double healing.

Afterwards a man of Jerusalem, mighty in the proud strength of his body and able to overcome asses in carrying burdens, is blown upon by the dreadful guile of a savage demon and is led bound and laden with many chains of bronze. Often accustomed to break knots of steel, force locks, and sever the fetters on his legs, he had bitten the ears of some, cut off the noses of others, and crushed the legs, feet, and throats of others. The brothers are terrified at the sight of so black a tempest. But the Father, unmoved, orders the bonds to be loosened.

[Col. 0534A] Freed from the nooses, the man trembles and turns away his gaze, head lowered, fearing even to look opposite him. His madness laid aside, he longs to lick the Father’s feet and does not wish to move from the seat; at last, compelled and made to swear, the savage leader releases the one possessed.

Whom shall I recount—the man swollen with a dreadful legion? Eminent in rank and supported by the resources of wealth, as he excels many, he is pervaded by a multitude of enemies. Led to the healer with every limb burdened by iron, he is shaken free from his bonds; relying on his numerous soldiery, he presumes to enter the arena of the simple athlete. He seizes the fearless man, lifts him safely into the air, and, laughing, displays him to his released companions.

Hilarion strengthens his own men. Safely, he casts his hand back over shoulder and head with strength;

[Col. 0534B] catching him by the hair, he forces him down before his feet, binds both hands and feet, and tramples his feet on either side. “Twist him, black troop!” he repeatedly cries. The wretch howls with the lament of his madness. A thousand diverse tumults now flash from one mouth; from the breast of one man the wars of peoples resound.

But the pious victor does not allow the wretch to remain captive long in this condition. Rather, when he calls upon Jesus, he drives away every uproar of the crowds; the grim troop is expelled, his mind is restored to sense, and he is made whole again.

The cured man brings back many gifts as presents for his care. But the skilful healer rejects all of them entirely, and does not, even when urged, permit them to be given to the poor; while performing a kindness, he excuses himself from keeping his hands free of a gift.

[Col. 0534C] Not far from the cell, a certain man, while sweating at quarrying stones, has his limbs dissolved by illness. Intent upon the rocks, he becomes in body like the stones. There is now no movement in his limbs; he is wholly stone, alive only in heart and eyes, and otherwise dead. He is brought before the holy man; through him, strength restored, his limbs recover feeling and vigor enters his veins. The marrow frozen in his bones thaws from the cold. Thus put together again, he is soon restored to his former activities and returns, strong and rejoicing, to the work he had begun.

Thereafter he is frequently assailed by many people and heals many.

What shall I tell of the charioteer of the world, engaged in worldly affairs,

whom a rival, washed with chrism, was oppressing by pagan deceit? Seeing no more useful course against him, he sought Christ’s assistance through the prayers of Hilarion.

[Col. 0534D] Hilarion refused to expend prayers on empty trifles. At last, pressed by the brothers lest the foolish crowd mock the Church, he gave the man a tiny gift: an earthen cup, from which he had once been accustomed to draw water. As the man received it full, it supplied the needed aid.

Confident of victory, he went away, sprinkled the stable of the team, refreshed the recesses of the prison, and moistened the bars of the enclosure. He also sprinkled the charioteers, who laughed at the enemy prepared to publicize the holy object; but faithful hearts trusted and rejoiced in hope of future praise and honors. Once the signals were given, some flew forward while others were held back; the wheels of the former burned upon the axle, and scarcely could they see the backs of those ahead in the distance. A shout was raised to heaven.

[Col. 0535A] But the opposing side was not silent either, because the power of Marnas [Note: [Col. 0535D] The idol of Gaza] was to be subjected to Christ; and this victory, achieved with such speed, already shone forth as an occasion of faith for many.

Here he was draining the strength and art of the ancient serpent, and the monsters of the image could not stand before him. A young man burned with passion for a consecrated virgin; he had preferred amusements, but could not break her vows. He considered it no burden to travel to the city of Memphis and armed himself with deceits, so that he might prevail over Christ’s amulet. He spent the entire year in empty preparations. Then, returning equipped with the serpent’s cunning, and bearing the crime he had undertaken through the assault of his mind, he buried beneath the threshold a piece of bronze marked with certain signs, adding the savage mutterings of a magical spell.

Immediately the virgin began to rave: her head bare after tearing away her veil, she whirled about, her hair streaming, her teeth hissing, inflamed with burning passion, and called for the young man.

[Col. 0535B] The matter was reported to the old man. He exposed the hidden crime of the enchantment, while the virgin wailed and confessed the theft, saying that the Memphite had been summoned, dragged there by force, and was suffering torment, being burned in the fires of the cross.

“Force me to leave,” it said, “for the threshold which holds me has driven me in.”

“A great power,” said the old man, “when strips of metal bind you! Why did you not rather enter the one who was sending you against her?”

“Why,” it replied, “should I attack my colleague, whom the demon of love had ensnared? But I seized the seal so that the virgin would not destroy it.”

“You acted unwillingly, but go out,” he said. “You are accustomed to go forth to destroy, not to save.” And he drove out the savage spirit, without waiting for the young man, avoiding the traces of the deception; he rebuked the girl for not having guarded herself against the theft.

Not only had pious fame filled the neighboring cities,

[Col. 0535C] it had also stirred distant peoples throughout the world. Thus, from far away in our lands toward the eastern regions, an illustrious man whom the emperor of the Franks was pursuing with letters, an enlarged retinue, and honors, chose to seek the healing savior.

Possessed from childhood by a dark demon, he had been accustomed at night to grind his teeth, groan, and howl; carrying terrible scourges, he dragged his rest into torments. Many accompanied him out of love for his father. When the old man saw the crowd, he blessed them and ordered them to depart, while the young man and his own attendants were to remain, for he understood the reason for their coming from the young man’s own mouth.

Soon, when questioned, the man—scarcely able to touch the ground with his feet—spoke in the language of the Syrians, heard then for the first time, preserving the idioms of that tongue. He was no less proficient when questioned in Greek [the manuscript has *scitatus* for *citatus*].

Passing over the various arts with which he was endowed, Hilarion healed him by the name and command of Christ. Once freed, he flourished without the black plague; he brought out weights of pounds, simply supposing that they must be talents of gold. But he received barley bread from him, and at the same time heard this: “Let those who accept such things consider gold to be dung.”

He restored not only human beings, but also animals to health. Once a camel had been brought from the region of Bactra, led by thirty men who had harnessed themselves to its chest with ropes and presented it alive. When they were ordered to release the raging creature, they all fled, not daring to remain with their companions. The animal charged wildly.

[Col. 0536A] “Neither by your great bulk, devil,” he cried, “do you frighten me—whether in the great beast, the fox, or the camel!” He went on, stretching out his hand. While the troubled and monstrous creature advanced, roaring terribly, it slipped and pressed its head level with the ground.

Everyone marveled that one raging with such terror had so suddenly become gentle through such a remedy. The miracles of life performed through him could not be confined by number or restrained by chains.

No less powerful in speech, he filled the crowds who came, shining upon them, calling them to higher things and leading them toward the heights. He did not disdain to visit remote people, joyfully sowing the seeds of the Lord’s Word and beautifying the crop with heavenly rain; enlarging the fields broken open by his pious harrow,

[Col. 0536B] he increased God’s cultivated land, planting new seeds in the old soil.

Thus he opened up Elusa of the Hagarenes. Finding it formerly devoted to offering sacrifices at the festivals of Venus, he did not cease with tears and divine speech until, laying out the foundations for a church, he marked it with a bishop, crowned with sacred fillets like Adonis. (For after expelling the demon he had healed many of these people.) He marked him with the distinguished crown of Christ.

While emptying the mind of the fierce Alapion of his demonic breath and restoring him, he won him for Christ. As his kinsmen increased, Bethlehem was raised by the founder of the eternal name; and thus the village was filled with monasteries and halls.

Because he was watchful, he used to foresee many things concerning the brothers, skillfully guarding against future dangers and avoiding what was harmful. Once, for example, he warned his companions of the danger posed by an old miser and the disgraceful expulsion they suffered, when they compelled the hospitable father to inspect the lodging. His vineyard, surrounded by a wall and suffering from many reversals, produced less than usual and even that turned into dreadful vinegar after a month.

But the generous vineyard, which had refreshed the brothers with a cheerful gift and had been expected to produce a hundred jars, after three thousand of the common people had drunk from it, yielded three hundred within the space of twenty days, because Father Hilarion had blessed it with joyful speech.

When he allowed his own flocks to serve in their care, he taught them first to seek the lofty nourishment of the instructed mind. He urged that these things should constantly be sought and followed, not the things that continually waste away as the world passes.

[Col. 0536D] Whoever he knew to retain a monk’s concern for such matters, he could not tolerate the frenzy of that man’s greed. Therefore he had removed from the sight of his venerable face a certain anxious man, guardian of the poor man’s garden, who was accustomed to hoard money with a miserly heart.

Trying to appease the old man, the guardian arrived with a bundle of fresh chickpeas. Not daring to approach him openly, he secretly gave them to Hesychius to place among the dishes. But later, when the elder refused to inhale the smell of the food set before him, he declared that the greed of the chickpeas stank in their greenness.

“If you do not feel these dreadful vapors,” he said, “at least give them to the oxen. You will see even the animals flee from them.”

It was done, and the animals broke their bonds and fled.

[Col. 0537A] Such power did he possess that, if the breath of his spirit touched the body of someone afflicted, or if anyone touched a garment he had worn, the smell revealed whether the person was possessed by a demon, enslaved to vice, or burning with some corrupt condition.

Yet he wept, besieged on every side by numerous crowds and surrounded by a flock of brothers whom he had to care for. He suffered from the attentions and honors of those who came, longing for peace and quiet. He burned to escape these enclosing walls as though they were a prison; trampling underfoot the honors and insignia offered to him, he desired only the desert.

When he tried to enter it, hastening away on an ass already obtained, many thousands of the tearful populace came rushing after him, as though the destruction of their homeland and fire threatened them. They attempted to block his way and hold him fast with prayers.

[Col. 0537B] But he remained unconquered, turning these words over in his mind:

“I do not make the Lord false, nor can I watch churches collapse and blood poured out lie foul upon the ground. From this I have learned that dangers foreseen for my homeland have been granted to me.”

Yet they prevented him from going, and he himself testified that he would take neither food nor drink unless he were allowed to depart. After he had prolonged this fast for seven days, he was released and set out with a large company.

When he had dismissed many of them throughout their own lands, he chose forty to accompany him—men strong enough to endure the fasts—and proceeded toward the fields of Pelusium, visiting the servants of the Lord with a father’s love.

From there he sought the desert which another Antony had cultivated—for it had been revealed to him that he had ascended to the heights of heaven—and tried to console the brothers and inspect their dwellings.

[Col. 0537C] Choosing two companions equal to himself, he entered the vast desert. There he lived so abstinently and so silently that he then first professed that he had begun to serve God in the order of life according to Christ, to whom he had devoted so many years in a consecrated course.

The parched fields lay barren beneath excessive dust; thirst, boiling and deathlike, covered the countryside, and the torrid sky alone had deprived the enclosed land of water, since Antony had left it three years before, the elements themselves seeming to mourn his departure.

When flying rumor announced that Hilarion was present, the people came to him eagerly, led from every surrounding field, their faces laid low by the yellow wasting of hunger. The elder, overflowing with compassion, sympathized with the afflicted inhabitants. When he raised his hands toward heaven beneath the twin light, opening his mouth, he soon displayed abundant rains.

But as soon as the gravel was satisfied with the showers granted to it, suddenly the fields were filled with serpents that had appeared. Neither the fields were safe for farmers nor the pastures for cattle; nowhere was there rest for the land, and dangers were certain everywhere.

They did not know what healing care they might offer for the dying, unless they sought with certainty the known patron for aid—one who might lessen their grief and drive away what was harmful. Therefore the servants of God asked for protection against these things. Receiving from him trustworthy medicines of salvation, they soon drove away the accursed poisons with blessed oil.

The elder was burdened by the honors paid to him and, weary of the reverence of the country people, fled their pomp. He hastened to change his location, seeking no familiar region for his exile.

[Col. 0538A] In Bruchium, where the brothers rejoiced to receive so great a guest, and where night was already approaching, he prepared to travel along the route he had determined. His friends were disturbed and tried to hold him back, but he pressed on regardless.

As he began the journey, he declared that they should not be troubled by delay because of his hurried flight. “Later,” he said, “the reason will become clear why I have suddenly and swiftly withdrawn from you.”

Not long afterward, during the night, officers knocked at the hospitable doors, carrying the perverse edicts of the tyrant [Note: [Col. 0537D] Namely, Julian the Apostate], who, after destroying the monastery over which Hilarion had ruled his flock, had ordered him to be sought everywhere and consigned to death.

Their hopes frustrated, they said that he was a magician. It was commonly reported that he could know the future by magical arts.

[Col. 0538B] He explored the secrets of the desert and remained secluded there for almost a year, until, as rumor spread, his renown began to shine. Now deprived of concealment and well known throughout the eastern lands, he finally sought to shut himself away in the sands beside the sea.

Then the disciple Adrian arrived from the Palestinian coast and announced that the impious bearer of the royal scepter had perished and that a client of Christ ruled [Note: [Col. 0538D] Jovinian]. He urged Hilarion to reclaim the monastery.

Hilarion refused, fleeing distinction but not shrinking from conflict. He did not fear the ruler, whom he hated; entering remote places, he was carried by a hired camel through the wilderness to the city of Parethonium.

But Adrian, inflamed by honor and puffed up by the breath of high office, raged against his teacher through fury and deceit. He tore up the things Hilarion had said should be read, and, wretched man, departed, despising the old man’s face.

The royal official, whom illness soon forced toward death, joined the elder Zonanus. They boarded a fleet sailing toward Sicily. As they crossed the Adriatic after the ship had been split apart, the helmsman’s son was suddenly seized by a dark wind and, crying out, burned to reveal this:

“Why, Hilarion, servant of God, may I not be safe even amid the waves of the sea? Give me time to touch land, lest, driven away, I plunge into the lowest abyss.”

[Col. 0538C] Hilarion grieved that he had been exposed. “Remain here, my God, if he allows this companion,” he said. “But if he forbids him to stay, is it envy that makes you act against a sinful and idle man?”

When the father gave his word that the others should not believe the remaining crew, Hilarion cleansed the boy from his fault. Entering Pachynum (Pachynus), the only possession left to the poor man, he offered as fare the Gospel he had once written with his own hand, when his youth was still in its first flower.

The master of the vessel refused him unless he gave the book and his clothing. Seeing that they were destitute, Hilarion rejoiced to be poor and blessed in poverty. But to prevent the innermost parts of the book from being exposed, he went into the fields; cutting wood, he loaded it upon the shoulders of his disciple.

When the latter returned at day’s end, they obtained bread in exchange for the value of the load and prepared their sustenance through such labor.

Meanwhile, at the thresholds of Peter’s church in Rome, a certain soldier, seized by a demonic attack, cried out [Col. 0539A] that Hilarion had entered Sicily a few days before. “No one knows,” he said, “that he is hiding in secret; but I shall go and betray him along the roads.”

Soon seeking the harbor, he reached the winding shore of Pachymus [Pachynus], and, guided by his possessor [Note: [Col. 0539D] That is, by the demon], lay down before the old man’s hut.

Without delay, the demon departed, and the man wrote down the signs of his healing. Many came to Hilarion immediately and were relieved of diseases of body and mind.

Then one of the leading men, whose skin had been stretched by swelling water, came beneath the sun and soon returned free of his burden. When he offered the healer splendid rewards, he received this answer:

“You have received freely; give freely.”

Among these events, Hesychius, seeking his teacher throughout the world, surveyed the shores and penetrated the deserts, nurturing in his heart this consolation: that such a man could not remain hidden anywhere for long. He held to this hope for three years.

Then, from a Jew selling wares at Methone, he heard that in the Sicilian lands a new prophet of wondrous power had shone among Christian peoples, famous for so many signs and exalted by such great virtues that some thought him a prophet like those of old.

Soon he crossed to Trinacria by the Adriatic Sea. With a favorable oarsman leading the way, he learned from a single mouth the old man’s reputation—the harmonious proclamations of everyone, bright as a lamp:

how he shone, what he did, and what astounding signs he performed; how everyone marveled at the holy man’s mind, since, after such deeds, he accepted bread from no one as assistance.

At last the disciple, shedding tears of joy, watered with his own sweat the feet of the master he had found.
