[Col. 0539C] Scarcely had he risen and been refreshed for two or three days by sweet nourishment when he heard that Hilarion wished to leave these lands for foreign ones, unknown in name and appearance, where he could reside and devote himself peacefully to the Lord.

He was therefore carried away by ship to the fields of Epidaurus, where Hilarion did not remain concealed for long, though he lived hidden in a modest countryside.

For a great dragon was devastating the fields of Achaea—snakes which, in ordinary speech, people were accustomed to call “boas.” It devoured herds, flocks, and shepherds, drawing them in with a deadly breath.

Hilarion ordered a great pyre and funeral pile to be prepared for it, and commanded the summoned serpent to climb the structure [Note: [Col. 0539D] That is, a pile of wood], once the prayer had been offered. Compelled by the power above, the serpent obeyed.

[Col. 0539D] Hilarion burned the monstrous plague upon the fuel beneath it and gave the frightened crowd a spectacle worthy of wonder.

During this time an earthquake shook the land. The sea, driven beyond its boundaries and limits, poured out over the shores, as though another flood threatened mortals. Everyone feared the ancient chaos. From the high mountains they saw ships hanging as though suspended, and roaring waves of overflowing waters carried mountains toward the shores.

The people of Epidaurus trembled at the destruction of their city and sought the aid of the Father, whom they seized in hopeful expectation and brought to stand upon the shore.

Then, while he drew three signs of the cross in the sand with a plow, he stretched out his hands against the sea. Wonderful to tell: it rose as though growing and stood upon heaps of water; then, angry and roaring for a long time, as though turned back by a barrier, it gradually collapsed upon itself and, its waves receding, flowed backward.

Just as rocky mountains stood rigidly in the sea before the old man’s feet, on one side the waters flowed, while here they appeared like marble and there like liquid. The event was reported throughout the entire region, across fields and cities.

Everyone marveled at the greatness of the extraordinary sign. But Hilarion, grieved that he had been exposed, secretly withdrew by night in a small boat and escaped. Having boarded a ship, he encountered the waters of Malea [the manuscript has *Malta*] and Cythera.

While he was making his way across the deep, a pirate force was reported to be approaching. His companions trembled and called for weapons. They armed everyone [Note: [Col. 0540D] Perhaps read *contos*, “spears”], and repeated reports of the danger ran rapidly to the old man.

When he saw the hostile vessels from afar, he laughed. “Why,” he said, “are you trembling, my sons?

[Col. 0540B] O men of little faith! Do you see more numerous armies than Pharaoh’s forces, which were drowned in the midst of their triumphs?”

Meanwhile the foaming prows of the savage attackers drew near. They were as far away as a stone can travel when thrown. Hilarion raised his hand against them and spoke to those coming from the ships:

“It is enough to have come this far.”

Wonderful faith! The ships recoiled; the fleet of rowers turned back toward the sterns they had sought, against their will and in amazement, and were carried to the shore at a faster speed than that at which they had come, their effort having failed.

Thus the athlete of God, victor over the raiders without bloodshed, carried joyful trophies across the Cyclades. Amid various shores and lands raging with repeated dangers, he cut through the gentle waters safely, as one plows the calm surface of a peaceful pond.

Crowds from cities and villages everywhere ran together, and voices announced to their ears that people were possessed by demons.

Thus he reached Paphos and rested apart from the city.

But this did not last long. Scarcely twenty days had passed, for the fame of Hilarion was being proclaimed throughout all the cities of the island by the mouths of those who had been healed: the servant of God had arrived and must rightly be sought by them.

The Lapithae came, Salamis and other places echoed; people hastened from every city, driven on by the same affliction, and two hundred came together, distinguished by sex. Hilarion was grieved to have his quiet taken away. Seeking his familiar protection, he wearied the combatants with the fire of prayer, soon cast down some of them, and others after two or three days. When the week had ended, no one failed to depart rejoicing.

After he had spent two full years there, [Col. 0540D] the Egyptian exile considered going to the barbarous regions of Egypt. But Hesychius advised him to enter the retreats of Cyprus. He led him away by sea, between distant, shadowy mountains, climbing steep places on hands and knees where scarcely anyone could prevail.

Orchards planted there made the place beautiful, and streams flowed down from the summit. His honor was not diminished during the five years in which he is said to have remained there among the trees; he is said to have taken food from the fruit of none of them.

Nearby, the fallen walls of an ancient shrine lay exposed. Day and night, countless possessed people used to make them resound, like armies in battle.

[Col. 0541A] The elder rejoiced that he had there the weapons of combat, and that no one—or scarcely anyone—dared climb up to him.

Thus, while the Lord watched over his cherished quiet, one day he happened to see a paralytic lying before the doors. He asked who he was and what had brought him there.

As Hesychius explained, he learned that the man was the superintendent of the small estate and of the garden belonging to the village itself. Immediately weeping, he approached the helpless man’s need for healing and, with his right hand stretched over the man’s face as he lay, commanded:

“Rise, I tell you, and go in the name of Christ.”

Wonderful healing! The words were still turning upon the speaker’s lips, and he had not yet fully uttered them all, when swift health already strengthened the limbs and raised the man to stand.

When this became known, certain hope persuaded many to undertake an impassable journey and overcome the difficult approach.

[Col. 0541B] He preserved that place by traveling around the villages, secretly fleeing lest, through some misstep, he should encounter unknown people.

He was not, like the unstable moderns [the manuscript has *novos*, “new”], seeking money-pouches through fickleness; rather, he always fled honor and carried on an unknown and humble life.

When he felt that old age was carrying him toward his reward, he is said to have given Hesychius, who had always honored him with devotion, a small letter in place of a will. Written in his own hand, it entrusted to the faithful man, with due remembrance, all his poor possessions and wealth:

[Col. 0542A] the Gospel, a tunic with its covering, the dignity of a sackcloth garment and little cloak, and also the venerable hood.

Now the flame of warmth in his breast, glowing with a modest fire, had almost died; nothing human remained except his mind, which was vigorous in a living heart. With open sight he spoke:

“Why do you fear to go forth? Soul, why do you hesitate to depart? You have served Christ for almost seventy years, and now, sick, you fear death!”

He said this, and his breath, strengthened by great power, sought the upper air. Famous for pious miracles, he was scarcely then equal to anyone in merits.

Soon earth was added to earth, as the sick man had commanded, so that after his death it would not be delayed for even a short hour. When Hesychius heard this, he immediately sought the shore of Cyprus.

Here he portrayed himself as being exposed to many dangers and, ten months after the funeral, secretly took away the pledge. For he brought back a greater possession, accompanied by the joyful crowds of the people of Palestine and by companies of monks.

[Col. 0542B] When Constantine was granting civil laws, the place was called Constantia because of the dense fields of faith. He concealed the monk in the monastery according to the ancient discipline, preserving his tunic unharmed, together with the little cloak and hood.

The body was wholly intact, as though he were alive; and, as the crowd anointed the limbs with abundant spices, he who had spread the fragrance of holy power widely through the world also breathed forth a bodily scent.

CAPUT IV. On Mary of Egypt and Zosimas.

[Col. 0541]

[Col. 0541C] Palestine was inhabited by excellent men, lofty in virtue, who, following the narrow way, sought the sublime heights of exalted heaven. Some of them pleased God by pursuing the desert; others likewise lived gathered together in brotherly peace, dwelling in monasteries under the law of heaven.

Once a certain monastery stood on the bank of the Jordan. They say that it observed this rule: in each year, before the days when the customary fasts of Easter begin, each monk undertook his own discipline. Those who sought the vast wilderness there took up their contests; but when the paschal feast had come, they returned, so that together they might bless the Lord of peace.

Zosimas entered there, led by a heavenly ordinance, because he thought that in faithful warfare he had surpassed the rest with whom he had contended for Christ. Coming therefore to this place, he at last became a disciple of this discipline and resolved to adopt its rule.

[Col. 0541D] While, at the appointed time, he traversed the desert places of that region, striving to penetrate farther into their uncultivated tracts, he searched to see whether he might perhaps find here also some living person engaged in the pursuit of steadfast virtue, someone who could show him the practice of this warfare.

Given to these thoughts, once in the burning heat of midday, while he strove to send his prayers aloft, he saw a dark human form hastening from the rising of the sun and making for the lower ground, its hair white as wool with age down to the neck.

[Col. 0542C] Terrified by the sight, he fortified his face with the aid of the cross. But when he began to come face to face with the approaching figure, he saw it hastening in flight toward the secluded places. He followed, striving to overtake it in swift pursuit.

When he had now begun to draw near, he burst into these words and cried out with tears:

“Hey! Why, servant of God, do you flee and despise a feeble, decrepit old man? Wait, whoever you are. Wait for the sake of him in whose name you alone inhabit these lands. Wait; heed a worn-out man; stay your step, by the hope of the reward set before so great a labor. Bless the old man; stand, look back, turn toward us, for the sake of him who never rejects anyone.”

As he ran, repeating these words, weeping and entreating, they reached a place where the channel of a river had come to a stop, its course having departed and the torrent being dry.

[Col. 0542D] Crossing this too, the body that had fled from him stopped there and spoke thus to the weeping, importunate man:

“Abba Zosimas, forgive me, I beg you, for I cannot turn and reveal myself to you: I am a woman, and, as you see, naked, without even a bodily covering. But throw down your garment, if you wish to speak with this sinner, that, once clothed in it, I may turn around.”

When he heard his own name, Zosimas was shaken in mind and, overcome by excessive fear, stood aghast, perceiving that he was known to her by heavenly teaching. At last he threw down his little cloak and turned his face behind him. Receiving it, she modestly covered her flesh, turned about, and asked why so great an abba had come.

Both prostrated themselves upon the ground and begged one another’s blessing. She deferred to the priestly rank of Zosimas; he ascribed higher dignity to this mother because of God’s gifts. At last overcome by many prayers, she said:

[Col. 0543A] “Blessed be God, the support that heals souls.”

They rose, and she kindly asked the traveller how the state of the Church was and how the sacred order was arranged. He replied that peace was sustained through her support, and earnestly asked that she pray for the whole world. Nor did the mother cease to pour forth her prayers. Moving her lips but praying in a silent voice, with eyes and hands raised to the heights of heaven, she began; and she was lifted wholly from the earth, seeming to stand a cubit above the ground.

Then trembling seized Zosimas’s limbs and wavering his mind. He feared that perhaps he was being deceived by some empty breath; falling prone, he lay there, until the woman turned toward him, raised the monk, and banished his fear. She rebuked his error and, confessing human ashes with her mouth, showed that she had been washed in holy baptism; she made the signs of the cross upon her forehead, lips, and breast, and prayed that the Lord might deliver her from the snares of the enemy.

[Col. 0543B] He again prostrated himself, embraced her feet with lamentation, poured forth streams of tears, and begged her, swearing by the divine majesty of God and by Christ the Lord, who deigned to be born of a Virgin, not to conceal who she was, when, why, or whence she had come, nor what occasion had brought her to traverse so vast a wilderness. He testified that he believed himself sent to her for this very reason: that the deeds God had wrought in her might become manifest, and that it would be wrong to resist His judgments. Unless it had pleased Him that she should disclose her life, He would perhaps not have allowed her to be seen by him, nor granted her to endure so much labor and hasten over so long a road, though he stood there, as she could see, weak and broken by advanced old age.

Moved by these and other pious words, the woman raised him from the ground and began to speak:

“Abba, forgive me. I am ashamed to uncover the deeds of my vices and recount to you the filth of my acts. But because you have seen me naked and without a covering,

[Col. 0543D] I shall also uncover the shameful sins I have committed. You will be able to learn how great was my luxury, how foul and filthy the stain of my enormous crime. Not, as you yourself suppose, does any desire for glory make me strive disdainfully to recount these things to you; nor what boast remains for one so defiled, I who was chosen by the devil as a vessel of perdition?

“But I fear that, when I begin to uncover the disgrace of my crime to you, you may flee me as from a serpent, unwilling even to admit with your ears what I did shamefully in my body. Yet I shall tell it, and shall not conceal the deeds of my sins. First, however, I earnestly entreat from the depths of my heart that you not cease at last to ask Christ’s mercy for me, that it may profit me on the day of judgment.”

[Col. 0544A] The old man stood wet with tears, poured out in compassion. She began the course of her life in these words:

“I confess that Egypt was my country and that my parents were Egyptian. Despising their affection when I was only twelve years old, I hastened to the walls of the city of Alexandria. But I am ashamed to unfold the filth and recount the guilt by which my virginity abandoned me to wanton fornication, so that I lay defiled, subjected to the weapons of lust.

“For once an insatiable passion for this possessed me; for seventeen years, or even more, I raged in frenzied excess and became public property for the populace. Nor did I take from some men gifts that might have brought me shame, for I did not seek by payment to condemn the wanton; rather, I wished to ensnare more of them by yielding myself freely. Nor was it an abundance of wealth that compelled me to live so:

[Col. 0544B] I lived by begging and by spinning tow or thread, and considered seductive pleasure the highest good.

“While I was thus staining my life by disgraceful acts, I saw certain men of Egypt and Libya making for the deep sea, as if at harvest-time. I heard that they were hastening to worship the trophies of the cross, whose feast was soon to be celebrated at Jerusalem. Throwing down the distaff from my hands, I ran after them. Seeing sturdy young men suited to my desired uses, perhaps bathing on the shore, I came among them in an immodest guise and said: ‘Take me with you, men, as your companion, for I shall make myself not unwelcome to you.’ They laughed at these and other words in jest and received me into the little vessel that put out to sea.

[Col. 0544C] “Once the voyage had begun, how can I remember what disgraceful things were done? What tongue could speak them, what ear endure the sound of deeds so black—deeds in which I myself was the instigator, which I performed on ship and road, compelling the unwilling and adding incentives to the willing? Abba, forgive me: I am astonished that the sea did not swallow me, and that the open earth did not devour me, I who most wickedly cast so many into the snare of death. But I think that the Lord, who wishes none to perish and wills all to be saved, endured me patiently also, seeking to turn me and not preparing to condemn me.

“Finally arriving at Jerusalem, during the days I spent there before the feast, I committed every kind of wickedness. Nor did I think it enough to have joined the young men on the journey, but added the citizens of that place and those gathered from elsewhere.

[Col. 0544D] “When therefore the day came on which the Exaltation of the holy Wood is celebrated, I went before the youthful throng in sport, enticing souls into excess. I came before the doors of the blessed temple, attempting to enter the sacred building, but I was driven back by heavenly power. Again I mingled with the crowds; again I was repelled. Three and four times I stood striving while others entered, for I alone was kept outside by the force of heavenly majesty. Hardly then recognizing that I deserved this repulse, I began in silent reflections to consider that it happened through the dreadful weight of my sins. Thus grieving, looking about the courts, striking my breast and drawing sighs from the depths, I lifted my sorrowful eyes around the building.

[Col. 0545A] “I saw an image, painted upon the wall, of the Mother of Christ, made by the hand of art. Hastening nearer to look upon its form, I fixed my gaze upon it and uttered these words in a murmur:

“‘I see, Mother of God, that I am unworthy of your veneration, polluted by the act of so great a crime; you shine worthy of reverence, clean in soul and body, you who bore the Lord of the world in chaste flesh. I know that, being filthy, I am rightly abhorred by you; but I hear that Christ took holy flesh from your body to cleanse our sins. Therefore, I pray, bring help to one who has no comfort anywhere except in you and your Son. I ask you: command that the sacred doors be opened to me; allow me, O Lady of heaven, to see the royal signs of the holy cross on which He suffered in the body.

[Col. 0545B] “‘Receive me into your faith; once I have seen Christ’s sacred scepter, I shall be free of the filth of lust. Laying aside the excesses of this age and leaving its pomps, I shall go forth in haste wherever you, blessed one, summon me.’

“Having spoken thus, I hurried to the doors as though commanded, fired from my heart with the strong heat of faith and led, as it were, by the tenor of the Virgin’s commands. I entered among the crowds that were entering; no one forbade me, but, as though a path had been opened for me, I was received into the temple. I looked upon the precious wood of the blessed cross and stood trembling before the holy mysteries of heaven. I felt that the merciful Judge, whenever someone repents, is ready to open His bosom and forgive all our sins. Throwing myself upon the pavement, I pressed kisses upon it.

[Col. 0545C] “Coming out to where the image of the Virgin stood, I knelt, confident that I saw a true countenance, and added these words of prayer:

“‘Behold, Lady, how great is your mercy, in receiving the words of your unworthy servant. Glory has been shown to me which we, weighed down by the heavy burden of sins, had not been worthy to see. Supreme glory to God, who through you receives all whom true conversion leads into the way of life. But why say more? Now that the time has come to fulfill what I promised you, guide me where it pleases you; show me the way and go before me, mistress of salvation.’

“With these words I heard a voice giving this answer: ‘When you have crossed the Jordan, you will find blessed rest.’

[Col. 0545D] “Believing that this voice had been sent to me by heavenly power, and asking the Lady not to abandon me, I left the courts. Seeing me weep, a certain man gave me three coins; immediately I bought three loaves with them and departed. Having arranged my journey to the Jordan, I then entered the church of John the Baptist and received communion in the evening at the holy mysteries. Nourished by bread, at daybreak I tasted the waters of the Jordan, crossed it, and followed the vast wilderness, waiting upon the Lord who saves the needy.”

Here Zosimas learned the course of her life: how many years had passed since she had left the world and come there, what nourishment she had taken, and what harsh labors she had endured. She recalled that forty-seven winters had passed since she had left Jerusalem and begun to inhabit the desert.

[Col. 0546A] She said that her daily food had been the small fragments of loaves which she had carried away with her. “What more do you ask?” she said. “I fear that I may suffer again what I suffered for so long, if I try to recount the rest. Yet believe that in that time I endured trials more grievous in proportion to the depth in which I had lain submerged in the cesspool of lust. For seventeen years I waged a harsher struggle with the desires of the world, whose vain pleasure had long been familiar to me. The fish and meats of Egypt came into my mind; desiring wine, I could find not even water. At times the wanton songs which I had been accustomed to sing pleasantly returned to my mind.

[Col. 0546B] “Then I wept and struck my breast most forcefully with my hand. I called back to my heart the words I had once spoken before the Virgin’s image, placing myself in thought beneath her protection; I earnestly begged that she would make peace for me with God, until light coming from above might surround me and renew me, steadfast, gentle, and strong, for the contest.

“But with what words can I relate the flames of lust? A fierce fire burned my flesh from within; love seized and dragged me altogether too violently, driving me to the foul practices of shameful sin. Enduring this, I sought the earth and, watering it with my tears, I imagined by faith that the Virgin’s face stood before me. I reflected upon her threatening expression as she addressed me,

[Col. 0546C] terrifying me with a menacing countenance, displaying the punishments of avenged madness and the sword of the Judge’s wrath. Nor did I rise from the ground until that light of heavenly consolation, poured into me, had victoriously driven every frenzy from my troubled heart.

“For I always sought the aid of the Lady Virgin; she brought help, she herself contended with me, and she still directs me in all my actions.”

When Zosimas asked her concerning food and clothing, she said, remembering the years of her greater struggle, that she had lived for two and a half years on the two loaves which she had brought with her, and thereafter scarcely on such herbs as she found.

Having put on the garments which the passage of time had seized,

scorched excessively by the force of the sun and afflicted excessively by the force of the cold;

[Col. 0546D] but, by the power of God, she understood that in mind and body she was sheltered,

nourished and protected by the Lord’s safeguard and word,

since “man does not live by bread alone,

but by every word of the Lord that proceeds from his mouth,”

and that those stripped of vices are given the covering of the rock.

Having heard the titles of the sacred writings, the hero asks

whether the wise woman knows the letters of Scripture.

She denies this, and teaches that the living word of God

illumines the inner chambers of the heart and fills the understanding.

Then she begs Zosima to pray humbly for her,

and earnestly asks that, when she departs from the bonds of the flesh,

he not make her known publicly, but go away and return to visit her

at the same time in the coming year:

and, when the sacred fasts return in their customary season,

[Col. 0547A] that, returning to the wilderness of the Jordan, he should not let the year pass,

foretelling that, even if he should try to depart by any route,

he would not be able to do so, but should remain and await the blessed, venerable supper of Christ;

at evening he should rise and carry with him

the mysteries of the Lord’s body,

and he should wait for her on the bank of the Jordan with Christ’s gift,

so that, when she came, she might immediately receive communion from the holy things.

Then, indicating the monastery’s father by name,

she orders him to exhort him, to keep watch, to guard what has been entrusted to him,

and to attend to the flock, cutting away whatever wrong he should see.

He returns to the monastery; she to her retreat.

The abbot therefore kept silent for the entire year about what he had seen.

But when the sacred fasts were already approaching, he remained behind,

struck by fevers, while the others went out,

[Col. 0547B] just as the old woman had foretold to him with blessed lips.

When the brothers returned at evening for supper,

he, preparing to devote himself to the sweet instructions,

carried with him in a cup the sacraments of the divine body and blood

to the bank of the Jordan,

waiting for the holy woman’s arrival on the riverbank.

Long awaited, she came at nightfall,

crossed over by the cross prepared for her as a bridge,

and walked across the liquid waves with her solid body.

The old man, seeing this beneath the light of the moon, was amazed,

and perceived how unequal he was to the perfection of her struggle.

Then she asks that the Creed be said,

and that the Lord’s Prayer be added thereafter.

After she had received the mysteries of eternal life,

she immediately prayed that she might be dismissed in God’s peace.

[Col. 0547C] Yet, compelled by the man’s prayers, she brought to her lips

three grains of lentils carried by the old man in a basket.

Then she asks the elder to return again in the coming year

to the stream where they had spoken together before,

remembering that God had commanded that she be seen there.

Thus, asking that mutual consolations be carried to them,

they depart, pouring out devoted prayers on both sides.

Then, as the blessed old woman retraced her steps over the river’s waves,

[Col. 0548A] the joyful abbot returned to the enclosure of the monastery.

When the year had passed, he returned to the appointed place,

and, arriving, saw that the body had already been deprived of warmth,

with its hands composed and the corpse lying turned toward the rising of the sun.

The hero was drenched with tears,

and, while reciting prayers and psalms suitable for the rites,

performed the funeral ceremonies; but, ignorant of her name, he remained perplexed.

Looking down at the earth, he saw letters traced in the dust,

bearing the day of her death and her name.

He therefore concluded that she had departed during the night as Mary,

on the day of the preceding year when she had received communion with the saints,

and had returned to this place after the space of three hours,

the place to which he had scarcely come in twenty days.

The old man was distressed because he lacked the tools of labor

and the implements necessary for the burial.

[Col. 0548B] Seeing a small piece of wood lying nearby,

he seized it and, exerting himself, dug into the hardest earth,

rubbing his back, but making no progress and unequal to the work.

But, wet with the sweat of his labor, exhausted and panting,

he looked up and saw a huge lion standing nearby,

licking his hands and feet with a gentle tongue.

Terrified with fear, he armed himself with the sign of the cross.

Then, seeing the beast’s gentle movements, he reflected:

perhaps it had been sent to him as a companion for the task to be performed.

Trusting, he orders it to turn the clods,

and to prepare quickly a tomb for the holy limbs.

The beast obeyed the old man’s commands,

having received the soothing instruction.

At last its ferocity, forgetful of rage,

learned—though ignorant of service—to serve the holy labor.

Bearing a free heart, it performed servile acts.

[Col. 0548C] When the funeral duty had been completed in this unusual manner,

the companions returned, each going to a different destination.

One, following the desert, sought the hidden lairs of wild beasts;

the other, returning to the monastery, went to the company of the brothers,

and told them of the great things of Christ which he had been privileged to see.

The brothers resolved to celebrate a feast for the blessed woman,

and the aged old man Zosima rested in peace.

## CHAPTER V. On the holy martyr Fabius.

[Col. 0547]

[Col. 0547C] It is well known that Palestine was adorned with many trophies,

from the time when the illustrious standard-bearers of Christ,

menly in devotion, set forth and adorned the world with their triumphs.

They did not reject this land, though they found it lacking in palms,

while the Fathers of the old and the new Law shine here as victors.

I confess that I have celebrated only a few of them in a brief account,

neither polished with elegant brilliance;

for although ancient painters and poets once possessed

equal freedom to attempt whatever they wished,

I prefer to speak briefly but truthfully,

rather than follow falsehoods discovered in a long narrative.

Therefore I have not undertaken to sing of struggles

whose titles I found recorded in no region,

and whose triumphs are read as having occurred in an uncertain city.

For this reason Fabius’s radiant solemnity is commemorated, though we have not assigned to the city of Caesarea

his final suffering, when July scorches the earth

with the sun’s torch, because several cities were called Caesarea after Caesar,

and we have not read which of them he sanctified with his throat.

[Col. 0548C] Yet it is handed down that he bravely endured the contest of Christ.

Because he refused to take up the standards of the prefect,

the brave soldier is thrust into a loathsome prison.

After several days he is brought before the tribunal,

questioned once and again, and remains faithful.

Soon the furious judge orders him to be executed by the throat;

he is struck with a sword, compelled by the capital sentence.

Then, so that his body might not be given to the earth,

they guard it with a watchman and place it in a net

in the salty waters of the sea.

After three days, when both the body and the head have been sunk downward

in the net, the net is torn away by the Lord’s power,

and the blessed man’s limbs are restored to his sacred head.

[Col. 0548D] The neck is joined to the shoulders, with the stroke preserved as evidence,

and the whole body is brought back together on the sandy shore,

the kindly waves serving the burden,

and he is buried with the full honor of devout observance.

## CHAPTER VI. On the holy Theodosia.

[Col. 0549]

[Col. 0549A] We have not established that the virgin Theodosia belonged to this city,

for she is said to have been born beneath the stars of Cappadocia

at Caesarea. Yet, since they report that many of her deeds

belong to Caesarea of Palestine, I shall seem to have recalled her

at least at the end of the book.

She voluntarily joined herself to Christ’s confessors;

under the slaughter of Diocletian, while still unmarried and eighteen years old,

she was tested by the prefect Urbanus, beaten with blows,

hung upon the rack, tortured with cruel severity,

and bound in a dark prison, laden with chains.

[Col. 0550A] All these bonds were broken and fell away by God’s power,

but she herself remained guarded without fetters in her bonds.

Then she was plunged into the deep, with a great rock tied to her.

Soon the sea returned her unharmed to the dry sands.

She was then raised up before wild beasts, but emerged uninjured from them.

When neither the sea nor the beasts would accomplish what was required,

an attendant hastened with a deadly sword,

which she received gladly.

And, victorious and joyful, she completed the contest willingly,

hastening to bring her trophies before the Bridegroom’s throne.

[Col. 0549]

# ON THE TWO BOOKS OF THE DEEDS OF CHRIST’S TRIUMPHS AT ANTIOCH

## PREFACE TO THE FOLLOWING LITTLE WORK

[Col. 0549B] The leaders of ancient times had called Damascus

the summit of Syria and its capital,

and Damascus had been called the city of the father Abraham

through the offspring of Canaan.

But afterward, when a city had been built

by Seleucus in honor of the father Antiochus,

its founder preferred it to stand out above all Syria.

Recently the servants of Christ are said to have fled here,

terrified by the first persecution,

in which blessed Stephen is known to have been crushed

beneath a bloody hail.

Thereupon the faithful bearers brought to this city

the rays of blessed light,

sowing the fertile seeds of God’s

[Col. 0549C] word.

Here the light began, the darkness having been driven away,

to shine and glitter so splendidly

that this city gave the Christian name

its beginnings.

[Col. 0550B] Then the fruitful crop of the surpassing wheat arose,

and patiently, in the heaven-grown field,

returned a hundredfold fruit.

The Holy Spirit, radiant with light

and foreseeing the future hunger throughout the world,

strives to bring fertile sheaves

to the patrons of Solyma.

For she also received the gifts of prophecy

through the grace of the charism,

by which, once it had been given to the nations,

Judaea was deprived, with the fountain

of salvation denied to it.

In this city, where many contests

were fought through devout labor,

the faithful disciples of Christ

bring back the bright rewards of the kingdom.

Of these many, since here the fountain and origin

of the Christian name began,

I shall briefly touch upon a few

after the triumphs of Palestine.

# THE FIRST BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0549]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0549D] Antioch, a city that received its name from the name of its king,

equipped with great teachers of the apostolic office,

with the hierarch Peter seated here in the first chair,

and diligently carrying out the office of a worthy bishop,

and with Paul, a docile pupil of the heavenly school,

celebrates illustrious triumphs, Christ granting them.

After martyrs had been made, though not yet called by this name,

it reverently gives honor also to martyrdom,

[Col. 0550D] and commemorates the solemn rites of the Maccabean brothers.

While they bravely defend the testimony of the ancient Law,

with their blessed mother exhorting them,

they suffer their final torments for God the Lawgiver.

And because they are slain for the pure law of the commandment,

they are witnesses of Christ, who is held to be

the end of the old Law and the beginning of the new,

as the author proves for both.

While they strive not to renounce the sacred traditions of their fathers,

[Col. 0551A] they could neither be killed, seduced, nor conquered.

The boys’ hearts break the king’s terror,

and the machinery of torture does not break their observance of the Law.

The boys conquer the one who had conquered bearded enemies;

[Col. 0552A] the brothers’ endurance surpasses the victorious kings.

There is no doubt that those killed for God’s Law

will receive from the Lord of the Law the devout rewards of death,

receiving, through Christ’s gift, rose-colored crowns.

## CHAPTER II. On the prophet Agabus.

[Col. 0551]

[Col. 0551A] Here the holy monuments of the prophet Agabus possess power,

and, in the New Testament, in which the grace of the ancient prophets

shone forth, he sang clearly of what was to come.

Many days beforehand he had foretold the famine

that afflicted the whole world while Claudius ruled.

For, driven by the prophetic gift,

he came here from Judaea, revealing heavenly gifts,

[Col. 0552A] taken away from the Jews but handed over to the devout nation:

light expelled from the Hebrews, rising among the nations.

Here he sang to holy Paul that his bonds awaited him.

Seizing Paul’s belt, he bound his own hands and feet with it,

prophesying that the brother in Solyma would be bound in this way,

he whose belt it was.

## CHAPTER III. On Manaen, Prochorus, and Joanna.

[Col. 0551]

[Col. 0551B] Here also Manaen, who is recorded as Herod’s foster-brother,

teacher and prophet at once,

rests buried here in Christ in a glorious destiny.

Here, too, the festivals of Joanna are commemorated,

the wife of Chuza, who once served as Herod’s steward.

[Col. 0552B] Luke remembers that she followed the footsteps of the Lord Christ

and ministered to him and to his companions.

The deacon Prochorus also chose to dwell in this city;

distinguished by the merit of faith and by many virtues,

here he likewise completed his contest.

## CHAPTER IV. On the bishop Evodius.

[Col. 0551]

[Col. 0551B] Evodius was the city’s first bishop after Peter,

and, with Peter’s authorization, assumed the rights of the priesthood.

He was worthy for Peter to bestow such an honor upon him,

and to entrust him with the office of so great a shepherd.

Relying on strong courage for the flock committed to him,

he earned the crown of martyrdom by contending in this city.

His successor, worthy of his merits, praises him in worthy verses—

Ignatius, writing to the Church of Antioch,

[Col. 0552B] as he himself went to Rome to be handed over to the beasts.

“You are disciples,” he says, “called by Peter and Paul.

Guard the deposit left to you by them,

and remember the devout shepherd given to you by them.

Let us not, as pupils born from adulterated seed,

be put to shame.

Rather, by our gracious conduct,

let us become worthy of so gentle and holy a Father,

and of that Father who makes us chaste.”

## CHAPTER V. On the holy Ignatius.

[Col. 0551]

[Col. 0551C] For Ignatius shone while dwelling in this city.

After him, he gave this city the devout doctrines of the faith.

He triumphed over death, and, as he himself confesses having seen him,

he vigorously received what he had learned from the apostolic mouth.

When the senate heard of his celebrated reputation,

and the emperor Trajan was directing the fury of slaughter against our people,

it decided what might feed the beasts’ jaws

and provide spectacles for the insane Roman populace.

He is seized and, bound, voluntarily handed over to guards;

he is entrusted to ten soldiers to be taken to the City.

As he passed through the regions of Asia while traveling over the sea,

he gave the devout lands the revered seeds,

and taught the peoples of the churches to persevere

with their whole heart in holy faith,

to avoid the profane heresies that had then raised their heads

from the mouth of the serpent,

[Col. 0551D] exhorting them to cling with strong resolve

to the apostolic admonitions and to follow their commands.

Arriving at Smyrna, supported by Polycarp’s love,

he sent from there to Ephesus written consolations of the word.

From there he likewise instructed Magnesia, near the Maeander;

the seeds of life were also given to the Church of Tralles.

He sent devout writings to the Romans,

asking them not to grieve on his account,

nor to take away his hope of martyrdom;

let all affection of the flesh toward him now be absent,

for he would receive his punishments with a joyful heart.

“Behold,” he says, “I recognize the teeth of the beasts

as ready for me; let them come and consume these limbs.

I ask that they be permitted to prepare the dire things I desire,

and I beg that they not fear to touch our body,

as some are evidently accustomed to fear repeatedly.

Indeed, if they hesitate, I shall offer myself to them—grant me leave.

I know what is expedient for me: I have now begun to be a disciple of Christ [fore, for esse]; let no one begrudge me my attainment.

Let furnaces, fires, crosses, and beasts be prepared;

let my limbs be torn apart, and let my bones be exposed to the marrow.

Let all the forces of punishment be brought together against me,

so long as I may now succeed in grasping Christ Jesus.”

[Col. 0552D] Then, having given his writings, he entrusted Polycarp

with the care of the Church,

and, resuming his begun journey, entrusted the Antiochene Church to Polycarp’s care.

Coming to Rome, he stood before Trajan’s throne.

There, brought before him while the senate was also present,

and placing the worship of God above their terrors,

he first received blows from leaded scourges driven against his shoulders.

Then a claw tore both sides of his flanks,

and afterward rough, rigid pebbles rubbed them.

[Col. 0553A] Next the palms of his hands were filled with live coals,

and, oil being poured over them and flaming papyrus applied,

the grating of his ribs and the fat of his sides were burned.

Then the floor was strewn with a fire of embers,

and they forced the holy man’s feet to stand upon it.

Afterward a burning bed was granted to the righteous man for rest.

From it he was again dragged out to have his back torn apart,

the claw rending his flesh and penetrating to the bones.

Then his pain was tested while he endured such things,

and salt mixed with strong vinegar was beaten into his wounds.

Having suffered these things and remaining steadfast,

he wearied his torturers with horror,

tormenting, subduing, and breaking their whips.

Defeated by his punishments, the executioners prepared

to bind his blessed limbs in iron;

they thrust him into the deepest prison

and fastened his feet beneath the weight of a great piece of wood.

[Col. 0553B] After the athlete had remained for three days,

having taken no food

and no drink,

the indefatigable man was brought from Trajan’s proud residence

before the tribunal of the amphitheater.

With the whole Roman crowd hurrying there,

he was brought in chains and exposed to two lions.

When he had been handed over, and began to hear

the ravenous beasts’ roars from the cage,

he spoke these words, inflamed with the great love

of martyrdom and triumph:

“Take my words, Romans, whoever you are

watching our contest, and all you men, take them:

I do not suffer without reason, nor do I labor for empty things.

Devotion, not impiety, leads me to this;

I am slaughtered not for a crime, but for devotion.

I am Christ’s grain, I confess;

let me be ground by these beasts’ teeth,

so that I may be found to be pure bread.”

The lions came when they were permitted,

and, ordered to end the struggle, strangled the devout man.

They dared do nothing else;

they did not presume to touch the flesh

or violate the corpse by making it food.

The dead limbs keep the beasts away—beasts which a human being had torn apart.

[Col. 0554B] What had attacked living things with rational force,

the irrational thing preserves, though itself irrational,

and the intact remains are left to the Christians’ own church.

His companions carry them back invictoriously,

bearing the bones of the triumphant man,

which surpass the leaders of the world,

and place the devout relics outside the Daphne Gate,

so that the dead man might cover the living city

over which he had ruled.

## CHAPTER VI. On Heron and his successors.

[Col. 0553]

[Col. 0553B] This man had once looked upon angelic choirs,

and had seen the celestial citizens lift up a threefold splendor.

As the heavenly order sang hymns in melodious antiphons,

marking its proper rhythms, it taught the companies their instruments.

[Col. 0553C] From there the celebrated rite is spread through the regions of the world.

As he proceeded toward the contests, it is said to have been revealed to him

that Heron would afterward be bishop of this see.

He was then shining as a useful levite,

and, worthily undertaking the rank of this dignity,

he is regarded as its example and imitator,

and prostrates himself for the care of feeding Christ’s flock.

[Col. 0554B] After him, the bishop Cornelius instructed this city.

Then Heron, the fifth bishop after Peter, presided here.

The sixth was Theophilus, a wise and holy priest,

whose writings on Catholic doctrine are said to survive,

[Col. 0554C] learnedly contending against various sects,

and refuting Hermogenes and the other fools

who openly followed falsehood.

Most renowned for driving them far away with his learned tongue,

like a vigilant shepherd confronting with a cry

the jaws of beasts and the wolf lying in wait for Christ’s flock,

he strengthened those present, supplied weapons to those to come,

and adorned God’s Church by life and word.

## CHAPTER VII. On Maximinus and Serapion.

[Col. 0553]

[Col. 0553C] After the apostles, Maximinus is said to have rightly

ruled this city as its seventh bishop.

After him came Serapion, most distinguished in faith

and learned in authentic rules,

[Col. 0553D] by which he refuted the foolish songs of wicked men—

those who publicly boasted that they were prophets,

acting contrary to the holy prophets

and inserting filthy seeds among the pure,

while scattering tares among the wheat.

Here, exposing Maximilla’s lies,

while the ignorant honored her with the rank of a prophet,

he displayed her accursed seeds.

[Col. 0554C] Holy men—approved men, bishops, and martyrs—

subscribed to this man’s letters.

Writing to many with holy zeal,

he teaches the faithful and rebukes the faithless,

[Col. 0554D] protects the upright and corrects the deviating,

now confirming what is suitable, now rejecting what is unsuitable.

While censuring the doctrines of Marcian,

he shows that their adherents are themselves of one fellowship.

Marking out the followers whom they call Docetists,

he preserves the little fields from the evil seed,

among which benevolent grasses had been growing.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Asclepiades, Philetus, Zabennus, and Geminus.

[Col. 0553]

[Col. 0553D] When he withdrew to his heavenly homeland,

Asclepiades assumed the episcopate

of this city, illustrious and most courageous

among the devout soldiers through his confession.

[Col. 0554D] Alexander congratulated him,

the bishop whom we have recorded as appointed by God at Solyma.

In a letter consoling the city’s pupils, he says:

“Christ has lifted our bonds

[Col. 0555A] and widened this prison’s confinement.

I have learned that Asclepiades,

endowed with holiness and most worthy

of the honor of this dignity,

has taken up your governance.”

[Col. 0556A] After him came Philetus, then Zabennus;

Geminus, a priest, shines in this city’s senate,

famous for his charm and distinguished by knowledge,

as the monuments inserted in books proclaim.

## CHAPTER IX. On the holy Babylas and Theodore.

[Col. 0555]

[Col. 0555A] From this time Babylas, bishop of this city,

held first place through the dignity of his confession.

While he had often exalted Christ’s glory by his sufferings,

and had bravely endured the greatest scourges

from successive tormentors,

he reached the glorious end of life

within the bonds of a prison cavern.

With him, three little boys are said to have been killed:

Philidanus, Epolanus, and Urbanus,

who together followed this Father’s lofty path.

The mausoleum of this blessed martyr

shines at Daphne, in the suburb of the city.

When Julian, the pestilential apostate,

was worshiping the shrine of the Castalian spring

[Col. 0555B] and insolently sacrificing to wretched Apollo,

without obtaining any response,

and was asking the reason for this silence,

the demons finally brought back the answer

that they could not respond while the martyr Babylas’s tomb

was nearby.

Then he immediately ordered the Galileans to come—

for he was accustomed to call Christians by this name—

and to move the martyr’s tomb from there.

Then the Christians, endowed with Christ the King,

lifted the coffin and, singing the martyr’s praises

with jubilant hymns, made the following song resound,

striking the profane ruler’s ears for six thousand paces:

“O Christ, may all the pagans be confounded,

[Col. 0555C] those who, in supplication, worship vain carved images,

and those who glory in their own idols.”

The heavens echoed with lofty cries,

while the tyrant roared amid dark grief.

Then he ordered the Christians to be seized

and, thrust into the depths of the prison, to be punished.

[Col. 0556A] His prefect Sallustius carried this out.

First he seized any Christian who met him—

the man’s name was Theodore—

and tortured him from first light until evening,

with such savage cruelty, changing torturers at the scourges,

that no one had ever seen anything so atrocious.

Hanging on the rack, yet uttering nothing except devotion,

and driven from side to side by raging lashes,

he recited the hymn he had sung the day before.

When Sallustius considered that he had achieved nothing

by the savage severity of the sentence,

he received the young man into prison in astonishment,

and reported to the emperor what had happened.

He warned him not to presume to attempt anything like this again,

thereby preparing disgrace for himself

and glory for the Christians who resisted him.

Julian therefore threatens to take up Persian arms

against the Christians after victory,

and to devote all his strength to battle.

But divine majesty resists him,

sending into exile the wretched man who had endured the threat.

Indeed, struck down by a hidden enemy, he is overthrown,

and ends his life and his imperial office,

with Christ, son of the mighty architect,

building a dreadful little tomb for his burial.

But Theodore is said to have reported

that, though scarcely affected by the cruel sufferings,

he had been relieved by spiritual light,

and that a young man had stood beside him,

who wiped him with the whitest linen from his sweat,

frequently poured cold water over him,

and strengthened him beneath his labor.

Thus he grieved that his exhausted enemies spared him,

though he boasted that he enjoyed the light of Christ.

## CHAPTER X. On vengeance against the faithless and recompense for the faithful.

[Col. 0555]

[Col. 0555D] The shrine itself burns with heavenly lightning,

and the Pythian god hides amid the ashes.

The temple attendants, compelled by blows, proclaim this,

and the whole rural neighborhood reports it.

Another prefect, polluting the holy place with his urine

and considering Christ’s temple empty of divine power,

pays the rewards deserved for his presumption.

While, through the corrupted passages of his hidden organs,

he expels the filth of blasphemies,

he dies, aware of the savage plague.

The same official, adding insults to the royal treasury

and mocking it with derision,

does not escape the hand of the supreme judge.

He pours out the supports of his body

through the passage of his mouth,

and suddenly departs, emptied of blood.

Nooses are prepared to ensnare the innocent,

and he soils the springs of Daphne with contamination.

Here, foreign foods are soaked with defilement.

Some, groaning, judge that the clean belongs to the clean;

some, cursing, reject the filth.

They condemn the profane and meet death in praise of the light,

having gained the palms through the dignity of burial.

Some joyfully endure the seizure of their possessions,

as did the commander Valentinianus.

Indignant that the sacred object should be polluted by a drop,

he does not refuse imprisonment

[Note: [Col. 0555D] The passage is corrupt.]

with Laetus serving, nor the endurance of exile.

Having obtained the rank of centurion,

he soon afterward receives the imperial purple

from the military belt.

[Col. 0557A] The citizens, driven from this city’s merchandise,

reproach the madness of the city’s sluggishness,

because a bull-like upheaval had shaken the world.

[Col. 0558A] They resound with complaining curses,

and the lowest thread of the beard is twisted with ropes.

## CHAPTER XI. On Publia’s steadfastness.

[Col. 0557]

[Col. 0557A] A matron adorned with chastity and likewise with good conduct—

a beautiful shoot sprung from the earth,

where the flower John, a presbyter worthy of praise,

flourished, fleeing and often sought by the highest authorities—

[Col. 0558A] Publia laughs at the enemy marked out by the chorus.

Ordered to keep silent, she despises the frenzied man,

and, though struck, does not cease to sing against his error.

## CHAPTER XII. On Bishop Fabianus and his successors.

[Col. 0557]

[Col. 0557B] After the death of the holy and great Babylas,

Fabianus takes up the governance of the Church in this city.

To him the bishop Cornelius of the city of Rome

dedicated the decrees of his council for confirmation,

decrees directed against the heresy born from Novatus’s arrogance.

Dionysius of Alexandria writes many things to him,

pointing out how condemnable this doctrine is.

Demetrianus succeeded Fabianus in the chair.

Then Paul of Samosata, having assumed authority,

stained Christ’s flock with the leprosy of error,

speaking unsoundly about the Lord,

while teaching that he had been only of simple human nature,

and striving to empty him of divine majesty.

Therefore the leaders, manly in devotion,

and the good shepherds, drive away the beast

lying in wait for the sheepfold,

[Col. 0557C] pressing the lurking creature with a great uproar.

Among them were distinguished men, famous by reputation:

Firmilianus, then bishop of the Cappadocian people;

Gregory of Pontus and his brother Athenodorus;

Nichomas of Iconium; Helenus of Sardis;

and, foremost among them, Hymenaeus, bishop of Solyma,

and his neighbor Theotignus of Caesarea;

also Maximus, suitable for this synod of Bostra.

Along with these came many holy bishops,

levites, and presbyters from various parts of the world.

Stirred up for this purpose at Antioch,

they hurl the spears of reproach against the fleeing serpent.

While it escapes by many tricks, they strike it;

they assemble again and again, and again the serpent slips away.

They also rush together many times,

until, supported by divine power,

they finally crush the swollen dragon.

To pin down the monster’s winding coils,

[Col. 0557D] a certain prudent presbyter of the Church of Antioch

was especially effective.

[Col. 0558B] His name was Malchio:

a good man, adorned with merits and skilled in eloquence,

powerful in doctrine and deed, lofty in virtues.

It is said that, in his dispute with Paul of Samosata,

the entire council granted him sole authority,

and that his diligent proceedings, recorded by a scribe’s hand,

are preserved as something marvelous for every age.

For he alone was able to bind him with his own words

and publicly reveal Paul’s disguise;

he alone could drive the serpent from its inner caverns.

Caught, the water-serpent was condemned by a clear voice

and publicly shown to be condemnable throughout the world.

When this robber had been deposed,

the bishop Domnus was elevated.

After him, Timaeus assumed the rights of the bishop.

When he too had died, Cyril succeeded to the honor.

[Col. 0558C] Dorotheus followed him, distinguished by divine doctrine

and sufficiently attentive.

For this reason he is said to have learned to speak Hebrew

and to have been eloquent in Greek.

He is said to have been a eunuch from his mother’s womb,

and therefore also to have received earthly honor among kings,

and from the Lord a better portion among his pledges.

After his death Tyrannus was raised to the episcopate.

Under him the persecution of the Church grew fierce,

inflamed by the raging fury of Diocletian,

who chose to tear the holy people apart with every kind of punishment.

While he shook different cities in different ways,

the devout were burned on grates in this city.

Here two young men, twins in virtue though not in birth,

were seized and led to the altars to offer sacrifice to the gods.

They thrust their hands into the fire and said:

“Consider us to have offered sacrifice,

if by chance we withdraw our hands from the fire.”

The deed confirmed their words;

their palms were not removed from the fire

until all the flesh of their hands fell away into the flames.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the holy Julianus and Basilissa.

[Col. 0557]

[Col. 0557D] In this city the blessed Julianus shone,

of noble character and eminent in virtues,

with which he flourished devoutly from childhood,

and in which, as he grew, he completed

two times nine years of age,

laboring diligently day and night

in knowledge of God’s law.

But while he was the only joy of his parents,

they sought to bind him in a marriage union,

and, when he refused, admonished him

with the writings of the blessed apostle Paul.

[Col. 0558D] He asked for seven days’ delay,

supported by prayer and fasting,

and sought the will of the supreme Judge.

At last he received this oracle from him:

that he should fulfill his parents’ wishes by marriage,

and not shrink from the marital union,

by which the married man would not lose his chastity;

indeed, that he should take a companion in integrity.

Strengthened by this oracle, the modest man

reported that he would obey the command of his elders.

[Col. 0559A] His parents rejoiced and sought a noble,

well-born virgin to whom he might soon be joined.

With Christ’s favor, a suitable woman was found,

one who could fittingly be joined to a chaste man:

Basilissa, born of distinguished ancestry.

When the wedding day had been fixed,

abundant dishes were prepared and many guests summoned.

The bridal chamber was arranged;

a virgin led the virgin bride inside.

They entered the room and sensed a fragrance

as if there were an abundance of roses and lilies.

The bridegroom revealed that this scent had been sent from heaven:

there was neither the season for roses

nor had the room been scattered with flowers.

These were preliminary signs of the chastity

whose glory Christ commanded them to preserve,

so that the unmarried might attain the company of the angels.

The bride, filled with the sacred nectar of heaven,

rejoiced to be dedicated to the crown of modesty,

and gladly preferred celibacy to marriage.

[Col. 0559B] Thus their vows were strengthened by their union,

so that undefiled chastity might be nourished

within the marriage bond, while avoiding empty pleasures.

What are thought to be the bonds of the flesh

became the revenues of a blessed chaste life.

After this, when a brief period of time had passed,

and both their parents had died,

they lawfully took possession of their inheritances

and expressed their holy vows in worthy deeds.

For they gave away their earthly possessions,

and with those inheritances purchased heaven.

[Col. 0559C] They benevolently built monastic cells

and gathered together souls who loved Christ.

The man gathered an army of men

against the battalions fighting on behalf of demons;

the virgin gathered companies of virgins

to struggle against the dragon’s devices.

From these there grew a very great multitude,

abandoning the contagions of this world.

When the Evil One saw the heavenly gains increasing,

he was angered and tormented by dark envy,

and incited the emperor Diocletian

to send the prefect Marcianus there

to punish the ranks of the devout.

While he drove Christians toward the idols,

he learned of the faith of the blessed Julianus,

who was sustaining many ready to die.

He sent orders to Julianus from the emperor:

he should carry out the rulers’ decrees,

worship his own gods,

and urge the others to sacrifice with him.

The saint rejects the prefect’s commands

and exhorts Christ’s soldiers, strengthening them,

to fight against the servants of demons.

Thus the glorious ranks of the King were strengthened,

and they declared that they would not obey Marcianus.

These responses were reported to the prefect,

who immediately ordered a huge pyre to be prepared,

the saints gathered and thrown into the flames,

and Julianus alone brought before him.

The attendants went and fulfilled the ruler’s orders.

[Col. 0560A] They handed over to the pyre the attendants and priests,

and the entire clergy who, seeking consolation,

had come at that time to the blessed Julianus.

Christ’s soldiers were tested in the fire.

The gold was smelted in this splendid furnace,

and, before the throne of the high King,

the martyrs proceeded, shining more brightly

than golden light.

At their tombs many healings are performed,

and the hymns of the heavenly beings resound.

The blessed Julianus, however, was then

handed over to prison, to be brought before the prefect.

For the holy Basilissa had already departed

to the bright company of the angels,

surrounded by troops of white-robed virgins

and adorned with snow-white flowers of lilies.

[Col. 0560B] The strong athlete Julianus, brought before the prefect,

is challenged by the serpent’s hissing

to carry out the orders of earthly rulers

and obtain the favor of emperors.

He rejects Marcianus’s foolish words,

and proclaims that one must serve the true Lord,

who alone holds all kingdoms.

But those who shamelessly worship a carved image,

he calls blind and diseased through error.

When the illustrious man had spoken these things,

he is handed over to be savagely torn by hard clubs.

While his limbs are beaten by the cruel blows,

a blow raging about removes a soldier’s eye.

Marcianus prays to his molten gods

and asks that the lost light be restored to the soldier.

[Col. 0560C] Suddenly, while everything is being sacrificed,

the idols are shattered and scattered.

But when the blessed Julianus touches

the wounded soldier’s eyelids as he prays,

the man, having recovered his sight,

praises Christ.

The prefect kills him for confessing this name,

and the Redeemer, having washed him in a stream of blood,

consecrates him as a martyr.

Afterward the blessed Julianus is led

through the city streets as a spectacle.

The son of Marcianus sees a crown

being carried from heaven to Julianus by angels.

Seeing Julianus supported by heavenly honor,

he cast away all the books he had been studying,

and his father’s clothing.

Seeking Julianus’s garments,

he asks for them, kisses his wounds,

and confesses that Julianus alone is his father—and God.

The prefect hears this, and the entire city hears it.

The tyrant orders the son to be separated

from the embrace of the devout Father Julianus.

The attendants attempt it; their arms are drawn tight,

but they are unable to fulfill the prefect’s order.

They are led away together, since they cannot be separated.

The parents are astonished and claim

that this has been done by the art of magicians.

But they ask Julianus, undoing the magic,

to release their only son

and to go free, having received the rulers’ peace.

The eminent man despises these entreaties.

The boy rejects his parents:

rejoicing to have the Lord as his Father,

he scorns the whole world.

They despise private possessions,

so that the prison might guard them

and grim generosity might feed them.

Thus they are handed over to the depths

of the most dreadful prison,

the worst in darkness and filth.

Christ removes the foul stench from there,

granting the sweetest heavenly fragrance,

and displaying the brightest light to the saints.

The attendants who had led in the devout men

see the blessed men’s great radiance of light.

Refreshed by Christ with the sweetness of nectar,

they offer honor to the one who thus lifts up his own.

They reject returning from this light to the night,

having recognized the author of death, once the devout life was known.

The tyrant hears this and orders them shut up together,

[Col. 0561B] while he burns with fierce vengeance to slaughter them.

The blessed martyrs pray that Christ may bring salvation

to the confessors, confessing him.

There were seven brothers in the city, sons

of the city’s chief magistrate, a devout Christian who
The beloved had departed from the kings;

And they ordered his sons, princes in this calamity,

To live safely under the law already begun.

Antonius remained with them, a presbyter.

These men, driven by heavenly command,

Together with the priest, are ordered to visit the prison.

As they approach it, behold, they see before them

An angel of heavenly dignity,

Who, having scattered the prison doors of the dungeon,

Leads the young men, as they proceed toward heaven, inside.

[Col. 0561C] When the brothers see so blessed a light,

They rejoice willingly to cling to the confessors.

Thus the sacred vows of the martyrs are fulfilled,

And the soldiers are baptized;

The gracious Julian gives thanks to the Lord,

And these things are reported to the savage governor.

He orders the seven brothers to be brought out

And takes care to admonish them with gentle words.

The athletes despise the viper’s hisses;

They pass the words of deceit by deaf ears

And declare themselves ready for the arena.

The serpent is tortured, and gathering his poisons,

He sends them back to the closely guarded prison,

where those responsible for them are anxious for their safety.

Then he reports this slaughter to its instigators

[Col. 0561D] And accuses Julian, alleging the power of his art:

that he had shattered the polished idols,

recounting his other triumphs,

and asks what they decide should be decreed.

They order that for each man there be prepared a cauldron

Boiling with fat and liquid pitch,

So that, if by some chance they withdraw unharmed from the fire,

He may impose upon them whatever punishment he judges appropriate.

Soon the governor orders the blessed soldiers

To be brought from custody under chains.

He sets before them the permission granted to him;

And the holy men reveal to him the punishments

That will bind the impious, and they remain undaunted.

While these things are being discussed, behold, a dead body

[Col. 0562A] Is carried to the customary fires;

When Martianus sees it, he orders it to be set down

And commands Julian to restore it to life,

since Christ the master is proclaimed to have done this.

“Of what use,” said Julian, “is the sun to the blind,

When it illuminates the eyes of others?

But although your blindness does not deserve it,

Now it is time for Christ’s brightness to be revealed:

For his promise remains faithful,

So that our petition may not fall fruitlessly.”

He said this, and when he poured out a prayer to the Lord,

Life is immediately poured back into the restored limbs.

The man stands alive, snatched from the depths of Tartarus,

And praises Christ, whom previously he had not known.

He confesses that he was rescued from the most terrible

And impious giants,

[Col. 0562B] And from black punishments,

And that life was restored to him because of Julian.

The executioner, touched by grief, orders him

To be thrust back into the prison, adding him to the combatants.

But Julian causes him to be washed in baptism

And joins him to the company of the devout.

Meanwhile the ordered punishment is prepared:

Thirty-one cauldrons are appointed,

Filled with the fire’s prescribed fuel.

The saints are led to the prepared fires;

Everyone is summoned to that spectacle.

Martianus asks that his son be released

And promises that the saints will be returned free.

The blessed martyrs reject these offers,

And the boy refuses his father’s clemency,

[Col. 0562C] And asks his father, after he has overcome these torments,

To allow his mother to remain with him for three days.

The father returns home,

Providing a substitute to carry out these deeds,

For he cannot bear to see his son’s burning.

The gracious men are placed in the prepared cauldrons,

And a vast fire is heaped high around them.

The flames rise through the air;

The blessed sing psalms in a clear voice,

And by their exalted faith suppress the fires.

They emerge from the fire brighter than gold,

And with joyful hearts sing praises to God,

Bringing the citizens a great miracle.

But this charlatan attributes it to the power of magicians,

Turning darkness into day,

[Col. 0562D] Mixing left with right, bitter things with sweet.

When he had requested it, the son, having taken his mother,

Joyfully joins the blessed companions,

Whom the private chambers of the prison receive,

And which are filled with the fragrance of gracious nectar.

Captivated by their singing and dancing,

The woman, after experiencing such welcome sweetness,

Confesses Christ, her grief overcome.

Julian instructs her by the light of the Word,

and the son strengthens her with gentle love.

By a blessed birth, the offspring begets his mother.

The athletes rejoice with the citizens of heaven

That the sheep has been snatched from the wolves’ jaws.

[Col. 0663A] [Note: [Col. 0663] Migne printed 663 instead of 563.]

Martianus hears that his wife and companion

Has become a partner of the devout and an equal of his son.

He orders her to be brought secretly to the house,

Asking his son what had happened to her.

For the mother’s liberation,

The exalted man offers blessed thanks to Christ.

At home the tyrant orders his wife to be detained;

The servants who strive to obey are blinded;

The prison receives the devout woman.

On the following day Martianus beheads

Twenty gracious soldiers who, led by heavenly light,

Had abandoned vanity.

The seven brothers finish their combat in the fire;

They are restored like gleaming gold from a furnace,

Made splendid by the fire with shining light.

[Col. 0563B] After this the others are reported to the tyrant.

The profane man attempts to draw the martyrs away

From the law of Christ and subject them to an image.

He commands that the temple where the image sits

Be made more beautiful and secretly adorned with gleaming gold,

And that the saints be led there to sacrifice to the lost gods,

To appease the vain divinities whom they had offended.

The crowd of the little people proceeds to see this.

The blessed men are present, and mark the signs of Christ

On their foreheads, fortifying their consecrated bodies.

Strengthened by Christ’s gift, they enter the shrine,

Pray for his glory to be revealed,

So that the temple walls may collapse

And all the idols of the sanctuary be crushed.

The heavenly God hears the prayers of his servants.

[Col. 0563C] The shrine collapses; the baked bricks give way.

The attendants are crushed by the ruin of the temple,

And fire consumes everything as it demolishes it.

The gracious Julian mocks the governor.

The latter is pierced by the darts of his fury

And shuts the saints in the lowest depths of the dark prison.

There, while they offer praises to God during the night,

The blessed ones who had completed their triumph appear,

Companions of these men in their holy confession,

All clothed in exceedingly white garments

And sweetly singing “Alleluia.”

There the blessed virgin Basilissa leads a choir,

Rejoicing in her holy husband.

She announces to the saints that heaven’s kingdoms are open,

And promises that they themselves will be received on the day

[Col. 0563D] When Christ appeared as the world’s clear light,

So that they may appear with the citizens of heaven

And persevere in the heavenly dwellings.

After this the governor orders a tribunal

To be prepared and the martyrs brought before him in the forum.

There he exercises the fury of his cruelty

And orders oil-soaked lamp-wicks to be bound

By the hands to the fingers and by the feet to the toes.

When this has been done, papyrus is immediately set alight,

And the threads burn.

The men attached to them cannot be harmed;

Their limbs remain untouched by the burning lamps.

Then the savage man tears the scalp from blessed Julian

And from the holy boy,

And tears out the eyes of the priest Antonius,

[Col. 0564A] And of Anastasius, whom blessed Julian

Had restored to life by praying.

But when God sees that the boy’s mother, Martianilla,

Cannot endure the harsh torments,

He blinds all who had laid hands upon her.

He heals the wounded martyrs,

Gives them sight, and restores them whole.

The enemy is tormented in his heart,

Made more savage than fierce tigers

And more cruel than dreadful serpents.

He drives the saints into the amphitheater

And exposes them to wild beasts,

While he himself is fiercer than the beasts.

You would see the animals come and lick the feet

Of the devout, gentler than puppies.

Filled with furies and the fires of Gehenna,

Martianus orders the criminals to be sought.

[Col. 0564B] The guilty are dragged from the prisons

And mingled with the devout athletes.

A henchman is sent into the amphitheater for this purpose,

And the innocent are killed together with the guilty,

Following Christ’s example,

for he too, in his passion, was joined to thieves.

The earth is shaken, and the idols immediately collapse.

The air resounds with threatening thunder,

And great flashes of lightning terrify the wretched.

Martianus escapes from this half-alive.

But after a few days had passed,

He breathes his last, devoured by worms.

The Christians who remained during the night,

After the blessed martyrs ascend to the heavenly kingdoms,

Go to carry away the holy bodies of the devout.

[Col. 0564C] When they labor to separate them from the guilty,

They ask Christ in humble prayer

To reveal to them the remains of the devout.

And behold, they see what appear to be beautiful virgins

Sitting individually above their caskets.

When they see this sign, the limbs shine with light,

And nearby the congealed blood gleams.

From beneath the altar’s foundation, where they are buried,

A spring proceeds, flowing abundantly,

Filling the place with heavenly baptism.

Here Christ displays many benefits

And frequently grants comfort to the afflicted.

On the day of blessed Julian’s martyrdom,

Ten lepers are brought, hideous with decay,

Their flesh ulcerated and almost putrid.

[Col. 0564D] When they are washed in the waters of the bath,

They acquire the most beautiful appearance

And complete health.

A voice is said to have descended from heaven, saying:

“These things Julian, my dearest, his faith has earned;

It will earn greater things.”

Here also, and in the place where houses of prayer have been built

In honor

Of Basilissa and the gracious martyr Julian,

Abundant gifts of healing are granted,

And the beneficial prayers of the devout are fulfilled.

May their blessed spirits ask

That the knots of our sins be loosened

And that they grant us possession of heavenly joys.

# CHAPTER XIV. On Saint Romanus

[Col. 0565]

[Col. 0565A] Prudentius, with his golden eloquence,

Has sounded forth the struggle of Romanus;

Therefore it is enough to offer a taste of his triumphs.

At last the prefect Asclepiades is sent here,

And, plotting by dark deceit to break into the church,

He plans to destroy Christ’s gentle fold.

This is disclosed to the holy Romanus

By the heavenly King’s gift,

For he, distinguished by the discipline of a monk,

Strengthens the others with powerful support,

Exhorting them to stand and speak against the tyrant.

When the prefect hears this, he orders Romanus brought before him.

He is presented, accused, and found strong,

Fearless in the contest, steadfast, supported by love of the Lord.

He is shaken with whips and hung upon an instrument of torture;

He becomes more joyful, triumphing over the torments while tortured.

While being tortured, he reproaches and torments his tormentor,

and disregards the blows.

He sets the love of Christ before grievous trials;

And proclaims the servants of God better than kings.

Taken down, he is shaken by blows from balanced lead.

Then the honor of election is promised him;

He despises everything

And places every glory of the world after the honor of God.

Next he is beaten with wooden rods,

Stretched out by four lictors.

Then a sharp razor scrapes his cheeks,

So that pain might restrain the voice of his eloquent mouth.

The confessor, repressed by no device,

Speaks more readily and asks that any boy be admitted

And questioned about the true religion,

Whether he says that one god or several gods should be worshiped.

A boy is snatched up.

The martyr asks him to display Christ’s high power,

And, thus questioning the boy about the truth,

Orders him without deceit to confess what is proper concerning supreme worship.

[Col. 0565C] At once the boy declares that only the Lord of heaven and earth

Should be worshiped, not a worthless image.

The tyrant, stunned and clinging to these words, is distressed.

He asks who instructed the child in this.

The boy declares that he has a Christian mother

And that he learned Christ from her.

His mother is sent for and brought in.

The mother of the child is ordered to watch the torments.

After confessing that he is a Christian, the boy is suspended,

And tortured, while his pious mother strengthens him

And supplies him, thirsty, with the cups of the eternal fountain.

[Col. 0566A] Romanus is driven to the scourges together with the boy Barula,

A soldier with a recruit, a new recruit with a soldier.

They are shut together in the lowest recess of the prison,

Both tortured.

Meanwhile the serpent devises dreadful arts

And orders a pyre of wood to be set up outside the walls.

Afterward, when the darkness has been driven away,

Another light shone forth,

And the prefect went accompanied by a great crowd.

The saints too went, rejoicing to be tested by fire.

When Romanus saw the enormous pyre blazing,

He invoked the Most High, powerful over water and fire.

Behold, suddenly the shining sky is darkened by clouds;

With dense clouds the air is gathered into calm,

And a most abundant rain, descending from heaven,

Soaks and extinguishes the pyre

And removes all its heat.

Here the flame and fire accomplished nothing.

The people glorify Christ;

The savage enemy burns with rage

And, defeated, again thrusts the saints into prison.

[Col. 0566B] Then, when the following day’s light again spreads over the earth,

They are driven out and brought before the tribunal

Of the savage judge.

Grieving that he had not conquered them through fire,

He orders, inflamed with the torch and fire of Styx and Cocytus,

That the boy’s head immediately be cut from his tender neck,

And that Romanus, while praising God, have the tongue torn from his mouth.

Then the boy’s mother joyfully receives his limbs.

Next a physician is brought to Romanus to remove his speech.

He takes up the task and cuts away the root of his mouth.

The man, groaning and gazing toward heaven,

Strives to bless God with a clear voice—

God who gave him a voice without a tongue,

Speech without a voice,

Words without a blow.

The prefect threatens to torture the physician

[Col. 0566C] Because, by sparing him, he had not removed the honor

Of the unconquered mouth.

The physician openly shows that he had cut out

The tongue from the entire palate,

Declaring that no other animal could live

If cut away in this manner.

The prefect orders a pig to be brought.

When the surgeon cuts out its tongue with a similar stroke,

The pig collapses and dies together with its tongue.

The physician escapes.

The prefect reports these things to Maximian.

The latter secretly orders Romanus, shut in prison,

To be killed.

The cruel emperor’s order is carried out,
