And the martyr completes his glorious struggle

And receives from the King of heaven

An eternal crown.

# CHAPTER XV. On Saint Hesychius

[Col. 0565]

[Col. 0565C] At that time Hesychius happened to shine in the court of kings.

Therefore the nobles order all the palace people

Either to sacrifice to the gods or to lay aside their belts.

When he receives the order, he gladly strips himself voluntarily

[Col. 0565D] And departs, having cast aside his palace rank.

At this the savage emperor Maximian is indignant.

He orders Hesychius, dressed in a woman’s tunic,

To remain there shamefully

And, condemned, to perform women’s work.

Many watched him as he sat there,

Joyfully receiving from his mouth

Words of salvation,

And offering God’s servant the comfort of their love.

Maximian hears of this and orders Hesychius brought before him.

He is presented.

The emperor asks which he thinks would be better for him:

[Col. 0566C] Whether, resisting, he should be honored with the dignity of the palace,

Or whether he should wear the loose, disgraceful women’s clothing.

He replies that it is better to wear the women’s clothing

In Christ’s name,

While serving demons,

Than to serve the court.

Pressed by these words and by the force of the others,

[Col. 0566D] To whom he is indignant that the love of Christ is preferred,

The insane prince, driven by the furies of Avernus,

Orders Hesychius, bound to a stone,

To be thrown into the river.

But some kindly men, discovering his remains,

Collected them with reverence

And decently placed them beside the graves of the saints.

This storm crushed many there and everywhere—

Christians who followed the Lord with celebrated courage.

[Col. 0567A] During this storm Cyprian endured mighty struggles,

Having been converted from magic to the holy love of Christ

Through the merits of the virgin Justina.

For this distinguished virgin, born in this city

To illustrious parents,

Came to know Christ through a certain deacon.

She also won her parents,

Who were instructed in the sacred teachings;

The bishop Optatus baptized them in the waters

And taught them to preserve the way of salvation.

While the virgin Justina frequented God’s church,

Aglaidas [ms. 2: Acladius], a blind young man, was inflamed by desire.

He summoned many men and the girl’s mothers

And asked that she be joined to him by a firm marriage bond.

But she rejected all the words of the matchmakers

And announced that she was betrothed to the exalted King Christ,

[Col. 0567B] And affirmed that she would keep faith with her heavenly Bridegroom.

The suitor attempts to use force against the unwilling girl,

But is repulsed and yields through the power of the Lord above.

The less the young man achieves, the more he burns with love.

Seeing himself abandoned by human strength,

He dares to attempt demonic deceits

And dark magic.

He learns that Cyprian is skilled in magical incantations

And addresses him, asking by his art to break the girl’s chastity.

He promises to give him talents of gold

If perhaps he can kindle her with a fiery dart

And pierce her heart with Cupid’s arrow.

But Cyprian, cunningly exercising his accustomed arts,

Sees demonic phantoms present themselves before him.

To the demon he carries his command

And orders Justina to be afflicted

By the plague of madness,

So that she may be tortured by dreadful love.

[Col. 0567C] The phantom obeys and approaches the strong girl’s dwelling.

The virgin is thrown from her bed;

She senses the attempt at deception

And fortifies herself with the cross,

Asking for Christ’s protection.

When the serpent sees the sign of the cross,

Struck, he falls apart.

Seeing him defeated, the diviner seeks another.

He summons him and explains what his incantations demand.

The second demon flies out through the air

And swiftly glides through the aerial winds.

At midnight he seeks the virgin’s bed.

The virgin, sensing that she is being attacked

By the serpent’s swelling,

Seeks Christ’s protection, already known as her shelter.

Shielding her limbs with the banner of the cross,

She prays that Christ may deign to preserve her chastity unharmed,

So that the shining lamp may not be overcome and grow dark.

When he sees the revered trophies of the cross gleaming,

[Col. 0567D] He fails and withdraws,

Dissolved by heavenly honor.

Then the magician attempts greater efforts of his art

And summons a greater dragon by the deceit of Zoroaster.

The dragon, roaring proudly, boasts that he will inflict enormous labor,

Bind the defeated girl to the suitor,

And, by his deceits, draw a virginal body from the air.

Assuming the appearance of the virgin,

He presents himself to chaste eyes.

He pretends to love God

And falsely claims that he has been sent by God

As the companion of the chaste Justina.

He attempts to penetrate her heart with subtle deceits

And asks what rewards should be granted him

For such great labor.

The deceiver says that this labor is small,

though the rewards are great.

She replies in turn:

“Why did the Creator of all things not wish Adam,

The cultivator of paradise, to live alone,

But by divine law gave him a female companion in marriage,

Commanding them to increase,

Blessing and multiplying them,

So that the world might be filled through a lawful union?

Are divine laws to be despised through rigid chastity?”

[Col. 0568A] Struck by the venom of this savage serpent,

Justina is disturbed.

She rises, proceeds, is amazed, troubled, and hesitates.

The Lord looks upon her prostrate,

As he once did upon Peter, who denied the faith,

And does not permit the walls of the tower

To be seized while the enemy lies hidden.

For she recognizes these as the demon’s deceits.

She brings to mind the protections she knows in her heart,

Prays, and swiftly takes up the arms of the cross.

The fabricated apparition,

Terrified by the sign of the cross,

Dissolves and mingles with the empty air.

The serpent prepares to attack the virgin’s breast,

Supported by heavenly strength,

In many different ways,

Waging war through various deceits of dark magic.

He inflicts illnesses, noises, phantoms, and pains,

Caresses and riches, terrors, and harm to her parents,

Thefts, deceits, blandishments of food, and seditions—

Arguments by which walls securely defended

Might collapse.

But her mind, enclosed by Christ’s arms,

Remains unconquered, to be overcome by no contest,

Despising fortune’s gentler gifts

And at the same time overcoming its harshness.

[Col. 0568B] Seeing that his assaults upon the virgin—

those in which Cyprian had placed his greatest confidence—were broken,

the troubled demon comes.

Cyprian asks him to explain by what power

the tender girl has defeated them.

Fearing abandonment, the demon says:

“Swear that I shall not be forsaken through your deceit.”

Cyprian swears by the infernal powers.

“I am undone,” says the demon, “when I see the sign of the Crucified One;

[Col. 0568C] At the same sight I collapse,

And melt like wax before fire.”

“Is the Crucified One greater than you?” he asks.

“He is greater than all,” the other replies,

“And as avenger he will inflict punishments according to merit.”

“Then I must go,” he says,

“And seek the grace of the Crucified One,

So that I may not endure the punishments

With which he will rage against his enemies.”

Therefore, renouncing the powers that operated through deceit

And despising the authority of the conquerable serpent,

He falls at the feet of the bishop of the Church,

Asking that knowledge and the noble sign of Christ be given him.

While the bishop, fearing deception, sends the afflicted man away,

he tells how he recognized Satan’s arts as defeated.

The bishop gives thanks to God,

Catechizes him, nourishing him with the milk of holy faith,

Admonishes him to seek Christ in his church

And to attend frequently upon the clergy.

[Col. 0568D] Returning home, Cyprian immediately breaks to pieces

All the images with which he had been accustomed to serve

According to the established rite.

He throws away the vanities

And atones with tears for what he had done.

Returning to the church,

He asks that the signs of salvation be shown to him.

As he enters, he hears:

“May God make you safe, servant who hopes in him.”

Thus, as he draws each further lesson

Into his watchful ear,

He receives the instruction of saving eloquence.

He remains fixed inside as a catechumen,

While the others are ordered to hurry outside.

But when the levite tells him to leave,

He replies:

“I have become Christ’s servant,

And you drive me outside?”

“Not yet perfected as a servant of Christ,”

The anxious minister of the sacred rites replies.

“But Christ lives for me,” he says,

“Christ who confounded the works of the demon

And in his mercy took pity on me.

[Col. 0569A] I shall not leave here

Until I have become Christ’s complete servant.”

The deacon reports this to the bishop.

The bishop calls the new son,

Instructs him in gracious doctrine,

Makes him perfect by consecrating him in baptism,

And before long appoints him levite at the altar.

Moreover, grace given against the demon’s arts

Shone greatly upon him,

Granting many healings.

It is impossible to say how many cures it accomplished.

At last, ascending to the summit of priestly virtue

And shining through his teaching,

He received the honor of faith.

When the bishop from whom he had received the sacred washing died,

He obtained

The episcopal office

Through honorable merits.

He made Justina, God’s servant, a minister at the altar

And placed her before the choirs of virgins.

Then, while scattering Christ’s seeds in human hearts,

He remembered himself,

Making known the arts of Satan that he had conquered

And by which he had once languished,

Bound by alien powers.

As one accustomed to become his own accuser,

He accused himself,

Declaring that no one had been more wicked than he.

He recounted how his parents had devoted him to Phoebus

And how he had served Diana’s dragon on the mountain.

He did not conceal that he had served at the Olympian altars,

Where, advanced to sacrilegious honor as a priest,

He learned demonic powers,

The apparitions of the gods,

Aerial forces,

Insane words,

Wars, sounds, noises,

Herbs, lies, and deceits—

[Col. 0569B] Things by which various spirits hurry to seduce various peoples.

He told how afterward he had gone to Egypt

And to the fields of Chaldaea,

And had marked out astrology through the nighttime stars.

He explained that those demons assumed various shapes

And depicted their deeds and errors in magical books,

And that he had studied these things,

Imbued with their gloomy deceits.

He told how a demon, as an angel of Satan,

Appeared in the honor of light;

How the aerial prince had presented himself to him,

Deeming him worthy of his own conversation,

Greeting him,

Calling him a clever boy and an acceptable servant;

How, among his foremost servants,

He had deserved to be considered worthy of first place

And therefore to be called his son;

How he had asked that each thing promised to him be fulfilled

And that he be allowed to carry out whatever desire pleased him.

Surrounded in his service by the acquired bands

Of the shadows,

He rejoiced to see the nobles ready to serve him.

They marveled that such power had been given to him

And that his confidence before the king was so great.

[Col. 0569C] He continued by explaining what honors that king imagined for him,

What vanities he created,

And with what skill he prepared deceits;

What great and numerous deceits he had once hurled against Justina;

How he had sent the army of her parents against him;

And how long he himself, with the evil king’s army,

Had carried on that contest.

How at last, when he had been defeated,

He prayed the king to remove his love from him;

How he asked with many reproaches

For a remedy that the king was unable to provide,

And proved him worthless.

How, transformed into the likeness of Justina,

He had appeared before him;

How, when he assumed her name,

He had slipped away like a shadow.

How, by Zoroaster’s art,

He had taken on various shapes,

Becoming a woman or a bird;

How, having reached the threshold of the little door,

He had been released from the spell.

Cyprian himself, unwilling and horrified,

Seemed to see how Acladius,

Transformed by him into a sparrow,

Had flown over the girl’s high roof,

But, once he had settled there,

Had lost his feathers and wings,

And the unwilling young man had resumed his own limbs,

Having discarded the wings with which he had ascended.

He recounted the darts he had hurled

And the many evils he had prepared through deceits,

So that he might capture the strong girl.

But when he saw all his weapons emptied of Christ’s power,

Weapons directed against the virgin’s chastity,

He began to exalt Justina’s name

With frequent praises.

For this reason the spirits who had been granted to him fled,

Since they could not bear even to hear

The name of the distinguished girl resound;

[Col. 0570A] [Col. 0570B] He then began all the more to despise the powerless king’s vanities,

Reproaching and rejecting his futile scepters,

Renouncing the laws and arms of the wicked prince,

And magnifying Christ’s power, name, and glory.

When he repented of having been subjected

To so many disgraceful things,

The serpent sharpened his dreadful schemes

And attempted with excessive force to suffocate him.

He left him half-dead.

But when Christ’s name was spoken,

And the sign of the cross was made,

Cyprian escaped the fiery dragon’s mouth,

Rescued from the serpent’s savage jaws.

When the demon made many threats

And forced him to despair of salvation,

He nevertheless could not subjugate him.

Cyprian then asked the Christian friends

Whether Christ’s merciful compassion

Could embrace one so wretched,

Bound by the chains of so many crimes.

Then he reviewed his magic arts,

Deceits, deaths, adulteries, and sacrifices,

Vomiting forth many poisons

And cleansing his crimes with tears.

His friends, seeing him obscured by tears,

Comforted him with sweet words.

They brought forth examples of God’s holy goodness

And lifted the spirit that was staggering

Under so great a burden.

Above all, a certain Eusebius,

With polished and eloquent speech,

Encouraged him with words worthy of himself.

He was advanced toward the hope of the Lord

And raised by God’s mercy,

Receiving consolation,

As Eusebius eloquently made these things known,

Offering various proofs from holy Scripture

And showing what deeds God’s exalted right hand had changed—

How it had swiftly transformed the wicked

And raised up the gracious.

[Col. 0570D] Having been led into the church,

Cyprian received salvation there

And burned the books containing the fabrications of profane magic.

When Justina learned that this had happened,

She dedicated herself to Christ.

She sold the costly ornaments of feminine adornment

And distributed their price to the needy.

Afterward Cyprian became a teacher,

Knowing everything,

And taught people to avoid the weapons

Of the poisonous plague,

Pointing out the serpentine deceits,

Their winding paths, and their thefts.

But the venomous dragon,

Grieving that his crimes had been exposed

And that he saw the triumph of his former prey over him,

Sorrowing greatly,

Stirs the mind of the prince of the East

To Stygian anger,

so that he may seek Cyprian, the great teacher of this doctrine,

Who, together with a certain virgin,

Strengthens many to persevere in Christ’s faith

And not yield to the scourges.

[Col. 0571A] When Eutholimus, one of Satan’s servants, learns this,

He sends for the Father together with the virgin.

After ordering them to be bound in public custody, he says:

“Are you Cyprian, the teacher of magical art,

Who causes many to go astray under Christ’s name?”

“I was once learned in magical deceits,” he replies,

“A servant of lust and a fosterling of perdition,

Trapping many and handing over the lost to impiety.

But Christ saved me through this virgin’s

Battles, Justina’s,

Who conquered all the demons by Christ’s sign—

The demons whom I wickedly sent

To capture her and prepare her as my companion through deceit.

But she rejected all these things,

Conquered them all,

And rescued me myself,

Giving me knowledge of the Lord Christ.”

[Col. 0571B] Then the official orders Cyprian to be hung up

And torn with claws,

And orders Justina to be beaten with blows

And raw sinews.

While being scourged, she burns with love for God

And gives him praises beneath the blows.

Afterward they seek the holy bishop in the prison,

And seize Justina to be kept and guarded

At the house of Terentina.

By the light of Christ,

That house was illuminated through the merits of this virgin.

Then, after a short time had passed,

They are again led forth.

The strong soldiers stand before the judge’s tribunal,

Ready to endure even the final things

For Christ’s name.

Soon an iron frying pan is filled for them,

Boiling with a mixture of pitch, fat, and wax.

But when Cyprian enters,

He strengthens Christ’s lamb, Justina.

She, having received powerful strength,

Enters,

And they rejoice unharmed amid the fires,

[Col. 0571C] Glorifying God,

Through whom they triumph over the torments.

Athanasius, priest of the idols, sees these things.

Indignant, he says:

“Let your glory, prince, order me

To overcome the power of these men

Through the power of my gods.”

[Col. 0572A] With these words he hastens to display the gods’ power.

As he approaches, the leaping fire seizes him

and devours him.

Neither Jupiter nor Phoebus,

Nor the strongest Hercules,

Nor the whole crowd of gods,

Nor the Luperci protected them.

But when the official was terrified and amazed,

He reported Christ’s wonders to the emperor

And asked what he wished to be said to him about these events,

Reporting that the torments had been defeated and come to nothing.

But the prince, who at that time happened to be staying at Nicomedia,

Orders that Cyprian and the virgin be taken to him.

They are led forth after enduring various tortures.

Thinking it shameful to weary them again

With the same torments,

He orders them to be struck with the sword.

When Theoctistus sees them being led to their deaths,

He gives the victorious pair powerful kisses.

A certain relative of the king sees this

And orders him also to be killed.

Together they received the crown by the sword,

Leading a celebrated triumph

After overcoming their torturer.

Their bodies, cast out naked for wild beasts,

Lay there for six days,

But God’s protecting right hand preserved them.

Then Theoctistus’ fellow citizens,

Coming by night while the guards slept,

Take up the venerable bodies

And carry the saints’ bodies by ship to Rome.

The faithful matron Rufina receives them

And places them honorably in her little estate.

There, under their veneration,

Many healings are granted.

Moreover, many others,

Whose deeds we have not read,

Fought during this storm

Near the city of Antioch

And conquered the world through their triumphs.

[Col. 0572C] At that time forty struggles were completed together,

With virgins enduring various punishments

For the summit of the heavenly kingdom,

Whose beauty they deserved.

Many are joined to them, whose names we have not read,

But the heavenly writing has inscribed them in the lofty roll.

# THE SECOND BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0571]

## CHAPTER I. On Saint Theoderitus

[Col. 0571C] After this storm a clear light shone upon the churches.

The enemy of piety, attempting to obscure it

With black envy,

Orders the saints to sacrifice to profane gods

Or to be subdued by dreadful punishments.

Therefore the fierce prefect Julian,

This man’s uncle, is sent here.

When he arrives,

He savagely strips Christ’s fold

And scatters the sheep.

But the gracious presbyter Theoderitus,

Receiving help from heavenly protection,

Stands fearlessly,

Preserving the holy walls, *surmus* [sic; reading uncertain].

When the prefect discovers this,

He orders him to be held for scourging.

Then he assails him with various terrors

And savagely torments him,

Hanging him amid many tortures.

His sides are inflamed with applied lamps.

But when these are overcome by heavenly power,

The stunned attendants suddenly fall down

At the sight of the angel.

They shrink from carrying out their cruel service

And, devoting themselves to God,

Confess the true Christ with their mouths.

When the prefect orders them to be plunged into the deep,

[Col. 0572C] The holy martyr says:

“Brothers, go before me now to the Lord;

I shall soon follow you,

Having overcome the enemy.”

Thus persevering,

Strong in Christ’s love,

And also prophesying,

Full of the Holy Spirit,

That the destruction of the Persians

would be brought about among the *retrogradi* [reading uncertain],

He finally completed his struggle by the sword

And, worthy of heaven,

Received the honor earned by his merits.

The butcher is punished

By divine judgment.

Struck in the place where he had violated

The sacred treasures by his swollen pride,

His groin flows and melts in putrid decay.

Breathing worms consume him;

No ointments restrain the discharge,

And physicians labor in vain

With poultices.

[Col. 0572D] Nor is the punishment of the impious violator

Worn away only by this manifest penalty.

Rather, slanderers,

Watchmen and carriers of the sacred things,

Are thrust by a wretched death

Into the fires of Gehenna.

## CHAPTER II. On Licerius and Hippolytus

[Col. 0573]

[Col. 0573A] At various times and amid various disasters,

These athletes of Christ here

Conquered through many trophies.

Here the blessed levite Licerius

Bravely struck down the enemy,

Fighting for Christ’s name.

Tortured seven times

And enduring a long imprisonment,

He finally attained martyrdom

At the cost of his head.

Here Hippolytus also fought

To attain the heavenly kingdoms.

Once seized by a new schism,

He wandered along trackless paths;

But after triumphing first over himself,

He rose to other battles in faith.

A strong soldier,

Whether subdued by deceit,

Whom a savage hand had given into chains,

Freed once again from them,

Avoids the snares with great effort

And, instructed by every enemy’s ambush,

Takes care to atone for his lack of caution

With outstanding strength.

So too Hippolytus,

Freed by Christ’s intervention

And restored to the holy love of the Catholic faith,

Carefully avoids deceit

And teaches others to avoid it.

Fighting for the faith

In a strong and cautious contest,

He adorns martyrdom with glorious deeds,

Resisting to the end.

## CHAPTER III. On Saint Phocas, Peter, and the Others

[Col. 0573]

[Col. 0573A] Here the noble triumph of Phocas’s struggle is venerated.

After many contests for the Savior,

How he now triumphs over the ancient serpent,

And how he has triumphed for the peoples,

Is revealed here.

If a serpent should happen to strike anyone in that place,

Pouring deadly poison from its venomous tooth,

[Col. 0573B] As soon as the injured man reaches the doors

Of the martyr’s basilica,

He is freed from the poison’s power.

The levite Peter is venerated here,

And Hermogenes,

The bishop Demetrius,

And also the levite Anianus.

Eustosius likewise,

Together with twenty venerable companions,

Shines with them,

Having attained the heaven of light.

## CHAPTER IV. On Saints Cyricus and Julitta

[Col. 0573]

[Col. 0573B] Here the distinguished boy Cyricus

With his mother Julitta

Is said once to have conquered

Through wondrous trophies.

After the brave boy overcame the impious scourges,

He received mustard mixed with lime

In his biting mouth

And likewise overcame the dreadful mixture of vinegar.

Thus, nailed fast, they are thrust into prison

With their eyes torn out;

They are scalped and flayed.

Then, fastened to an iron bed,

They are roasted over embers.

At last, crushed by saws

And with their tongues cut out,

They consecrated the course of their martyrdom

By the splendor of their beheading.

Four hundred and four companions

Are counted with them,

Having suffered combats in Christ’s name.

## CHAPTER V. On Donatus and His Companions, and Saint Margaret

[Col. 0573]

[Col. 0573C] Here Donatus and Valerianus,

Together with Restituta, Fructuosa,

And the others,

Twelve in all,

Shine among their illustrious companions,

Having gained triumph in glorious battle.

Here the virgin Margaret is said

To have endured many torments

For the faith of truth.

Therefore she shines, crowned with the crown of glory.

Many martyrs here conquered the dragon,

Obtaining the lofty rewards

For worthy battles.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Saints Who Went Forth from Antioch

[Col. 0573]

[Col. 0573C] Many who went forth from this city

Illuminated numerous distant homelands.

From here the heavenly light of doctrine arose.

Luke carries the healing of faith to the nations.

Apollinaris, following the apostle from here,

Was the first to bring the words of life to Ravenna.

From there the gracious presbyter Lucianus went forth,

Preaching the world’s salvation in word and deed,

And gained trophies at Nicomedia.

[Col. 0573D] From these, Timotheus sought the walls of Rome

In the time of the blessed Melchiades,

While publicly preaching

The deeds of Christ.

He reveals it; he earns the crown of glory.

[Col. 0574C] Januarius, proceeding from this city, is said to have served as priest to the martyr Gordianus, in the place of a fellow soldier and patron whom, proven brave in the contest, he replaced.

From here also came John, born in Byzantium, a bishop who accompanies the world with eloquent teaching.

From here, it is said, Seraphia derived her lineage; under Hadrian she suffered death at Rome.

And many others, bright as the most luminous stars of heaven,

[Col. 0574D] shone forth from here throughout the regions of the world.

From here Erasmus, departing, illumines Campania with the splendor of his life; flashing with wondrous miracles, he conquers every torment.

## CHAPTER VII. On Bishop Eustachius and Euphronius

[Col. 0573]

[Col. 0573D] Many other patrons also shine forth from this city. While they often struck down the enemy through their triumphs,

[Col. 0574D] at last, perfected by their merits, they rested in peace.

There Father Eustachius, carried away from the altars of Beroea,

[Col. 0575A] poured forth streams of eloquence and faith, supplying nourishment to the Catholic peoples of the soul while the senate looked on; in the contest he struck down the blasphemous ranks with piety.

After his enemies had been received with generous hospitality and peace, he was driven out by the sharp quibbling of a false disputant, and by deceitful fraud was thrust down from the fortress entrusted to him.

[Col. 0576A] His successors too were entangled in swift disaster; the shifting woman, struck down, abandoned her deceits.

At last, after the savage fires of quarrels and turmoil, while Eusebius resisted, the summits of divided and improper pride, and the height of the allotted office contested, Euphronius, after a long retirement, was appointed to Reblatha.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the holy monk Simeon

[Col. 0575]

[Col. 0575A] Here the holy Simeon, near the city of Antioch, is celebrated with fitting honor, resplendent in his deeds.

When his thirteenth year was passing, he withdrew himself from the cares of the world and sought the secluded enclosures of a monastery. Proven strong and patient, he was received and adapted himself to the ways of the servants of God.

Ascending with vigour the narrow path of the highest life, abstinent and merciful to the poor, he brought them the food bestowed upon him; generous to the needy, he was severe and strict only toward himself.

In a short time he mastered the Psalter completely; ever watchful, he learned it and stored it in the treasury of his memory.

Striving bravely to restrain proud impulses, he bound his loins with a rope of palm-fibre, disciplining himself.

While worms, arising from the furrowed flesh, flowed back and forth, the brothers noticed them and brought word to the Father for investigation.

[Col. 0575B] He asked them to speak; the matter was concealed and suppressed. The wound was exposed when it was discovered: only the ends of the little cords were visible, and he was afflicted with great pain. While his companions struggled to apply a remedy, they finally drew the cord from his rotten entrails and, only after much time, managed to heal him.

Thereafter, fleeing to the depths of a high well, he shut himself in at the bottom. While he was exhausting himself there by prolonged fasting, the abbot Timotheus was shaken by a heavenly warning and a threatening vision: he was to seek the holy Simeon and restore him to his place, because he was holier than the abbot himself.

Terrified by this vision once and again, Timotheus ordered his men to go in search of him. When they returned unsuccessful, he hurried there himself, found him in the pit,

[Col. 0575C] drew him out against his will from the abyss, and brought him back to his cell.

After some years he left the monastery and sought the fields of the desert, desiring to dwell apart.

Here, out of love, he enclosed himself upon a raised column, burning with the contemplation of the divine vision, because he rose higher.

After three winters, as the fame of the blessed man increased, he extended the column’s height to thirty cubits. Standing upon it, he bestowed many blessings on the people: healing the sick, cleansing those possessed by demons, giving hearing to the deaf and sight to the blind, restoring hands to the maimed and speech to the mute; cleansing lepers and performing thousands of miracles. Whoever recounts all these things would also recount the stars of heaven.

From that time many peoples were ready to serve Christ: foreigners, Armenians, Persians, and scattered Agareni.

[Col. 0575D] He was struck by a widespread ulcer, that the nectar of his patience might be shed amid the burning fire of torment. When he saw worms swarming out, he picked up those that had fallen and put them back for their mother to nourish, ordering them to eat what the Lord provided.

Thus, supported on a single foot, he stood throughout a full year,

[Col. 0576A] and remained unconquered while the ulcer consumed his thigh, rising above bodily diseases and conquering his sufferings.

Basilicus, king of the Saracens, sought to visit the holy warrior and asked to be blessed by him. Seeing a worm falling from the consumed body, he received it and rejoiced that his eyes were touched by the corruption.

Then suddenly the decay shone like a sacred pearl, and the foul matter, transformed, assumed a distinguished beauty.

The worshiper of the Lord, who hated renown, attributed this not to his own merits but to the king’s affection.

The tyrant departed rejoicing, blessed by the holy man’s mouth: he had come rich and left far richer.

After the holy servant of the Lord had shut himself within this fortress, he took care neither to see nor to be seen by a woman’s eyes, fearing that, while striving toward the heights, he might withdraw in his heart from the Most High Lord.

Yet even when his mother came to him after a long time, he would not allow himself to see her, embracing God in place of his mother, as he sought higher things from the height of his virtues.

A column forty cubits high was then built for him. He remained fixed upon it, out of love for God, standing there for the rest of his life.

He restrained the rage of snakes and savage beasts. The eyes of the dragon that he healed testify to the mercy that shone forth in him from the beneficent nature of God.

A woman also came there, filled with a savage snake. At night, thirsty, she had drunk in the poison as though it were fuel. Having found the physicians’ remedies ineffective, she sought the comfort of a reliable physician.

The holy man supplied a fitting antidote, offering blessed water to the woman whose entrails had swallowed the accursed beast.

The deadly draught could no longer harm her once she had taken the drink imbued with the gift of life.

A drought occurred—the plague of a scorched region—and the fields lay parched beneath excessive dust.

Then the dense population of the district came to Simeon, who, from the lofty mountain, poured into devout hearts the river of compassion flowing from the eternal fountain of heavenly mercy, and gave their hearts joyful draughts.

The people sought their customary protection, asking for the lofty aid of God. Suddenly, when they asked, the earth opened and the abyss became visible, filled enormously with water.

Then Simeon ordered seven channels to be dug and made, through which the liquid would flow from there and fertilize the fields by inundating them.

[Col. 0576D] O virtue of the man worthy of celebration! His prayer, seeking heaven from his mouth, opened the abyss below.

By chance two men were resting beneath the shade of trees in this region, traveling beneath the sun that scorched the sky. Seeing a pregnant doe passing at a distance, they called upon Simeon to restrain it by his powerful virtue and allow it to be captured.

It stopped at the invocation of so great a name and, drawing back its foot, obeyed them with greater submission.

Wonderful is the man’s power: when his name was called, the wild animal, obedient even to the faithless, served them.

Here savagery passed from the beast to the human beings, leaving the animal behind: cruel and devoid of compassion, they did not reverence the words which the beast had revered.

They therefore attacked the prey, which had been seized by the power of another, and killed it, though it had been fixed there by divine power.

They ate and roasted it, yet did not eat the entrails that had not been given them for this. Soon a deserved punishment struck their bold minds: those who had been fierce men, deprived of reason, bore the sickness and the speechless breathing of the beast, subdued in punishment for their prey's piety.

Thus, having begun their journey with the hide torn away, they hurried and sought the venerable summit of the righteous man.

Nor was the presumption of the wild men hidden from the prophet, who prayed for heavenly aid and healing for them. But the wicked deed stood in the way of their rich prayers.

They were given something better than they had asked: they endured the punishment they had deserved for an appointed time, so that afterward they might not be tormented by eternal sufferings.

While they endured this, and while such presumption was removed from many others by a fitting scourge, the holy man, after two years endowed with great prayers, at last took pity on the exhausted sufferers and healed them.

A savage leopard once ravaged that region, driving away human beings and devouring sheep and beasts of burden.

The farmers sought the protection of the holy Father, asking how they might be defended from the raging enemy.

But he, knowing how to apply holy remedies to perverse things, blessed water and sent it to be carried through the places where the swift leopard usually passed.

The spotted and most cruel enemy, unwittingly setting a snare for the many hunters, hastened headlong over the fields sprinkled with the healing liquid; when the beast touched them, it fell and breathed its life out into the thin air.

It was unable to survive to bring death upon those whose lives the man of God strove to defend.

They therefore hung its hide beside the neighbouring path, and the traveller, confidently invoking the Lord of Simeon, set out without fear, asking that his journey be blessed.

[Col. 0577D] Yet Simeon in every way forbade honor to be offered to him, fleeing the gifts of boastful speech.

“Go home,” he said, giving each person healing. “Glorify God and honor him, for he healed you. Do not dare to declare that you were cured by Simeon’s powers, lest punishment befall you in reversed measure.

“Nor should you presume to swear by the name of the Most High God, knowing that this is a sin. Rather, swear by me, a poor man bound by vices and frail beneath the covering of flesh.”

O servant of Christ worthy of praise! While he strives to turn wandering souls back, he removes greater dangers, directing against himself the slippery arrows of tongues, so that sins committed against the Lord might not hold guilty those whom the Creator redeemed and saved with his own blood.

[Col. 0578A] Two companions completed their labor for a common reward, so that afterward what they were to receive might be divided by an equal balance.

They then hastened to be blessed by the holy man’s mouth. He looked at them and penetrated the secrets of their hearts—for one had deceived his companion by a crafty trick—and asked why they had come and who they were. He repeated the request, but they did not tell him everything.

“See whether a fraud has been committed.”

When they denied it, the blessed man, shrewdly, said, “Take off the shoe from your foot.” When he gave it to his companion, he added, “You are not guilty.”

After this, when the man who was taking off the sandal had done so, he ordered: “Divide it: take fifty solidi for yourself by right, knowing that as many are hidden in your companion’s matching shoe.”

Thus, after the balance of justice had been measured out, the colleagues departed, glorifying God and free of their perverse fraud.

God had granted such power to the prophet that, as he clung with all the strength of his virtue and was joined in mind to God, he was made one spirit with him by the gift of the Spirit, examining the blind recesses of the dark heart.

Thus, when a house belonging to an Antiochene citizen had burned, Simeon told a miser how much the man had lost and revealed how many talents of solidi he had hidden in various hiding places, and that he had accomplished no good with them in his old age.

For this reason he testified that the man had been plunged blind into the deepest bottom of the abyss, showing to one who was not unaware what he had done, while the Lord disclosed these judgments to his dear servant and to the man who doubted the decision of the impartial judge.

In addition, immense compassion flourished in Simeon, together with an eager and kindly desire to benefit everyone.

Thus, once, rescuing a robber from the jaws of death, he sent him swiftly to heaven with a saving remedy.

[Col. 0578C] After the robber had committed many evil deeds through deadly plunder, and was suffering the final punishments he had deserved in death, he approached the venerable column by a swift path.

No one was able to reach the man whom he sought with his eyes, nor did he dare extend his hand to seize him.

After he had mourned his deeds for seven days, the treacherous Honoratus at last learned to be faithful. Singing of the time of his grateful end, he climbed, washed clean by his tears, to the joys of paradise, and was carried by the merits of the blessed Simeon to the heights.

Thus the Lord followed the robber who confessed Christ’s glory in death and, snatched from the jaws of hell, led him into the pleasant beauty of paradise.

[Col. 0578D] This famous servant of the Lord obtained by his saving gift from the Master whatever he requested.

For a powerful queen, though barren by her husband, asked through ambassadors that the joys of motherhood be granted to her.

The venerable man, observing her faith, readily moved by compassion, promised aid; fulfilling his promise, he brought childbirth to the barren woman, not inferior to Elisha.

And so that the man’s virtue might shine more brightly through this celebrated deed, the queen gave birth to a boy who, after some time, was found unable to speak or to support himself on his feet.

She hastened to the borders near the summit of the servant of God, bringing her grieving husband with the wretched child. Simeon ordered them to wait while he sought the Lord’s help.

He sought it and received it: speech was given to the boy’s mouth, and his feet learned to walk.

[Col. 0579A] The pious elder became the boy’s guide and caretaker, providing service for his tongue and feet. His father had once been the man who obtained him.

The distinguished man, searching into closed secrets, saw that no woman was accustomed to enter his house.

There happened to be a certain woman who wished to visit the prophet. She saw soldiers seeking access to his dwelling and, seizing a disguise and changing herself into a man, entered beside the holy man’s doors accompanied by the soldiers.

Not daring to touch the forbidden threshold with her foot, she asked that the animals of her companions be kept safe. This was allowed. Her companions entered and were blessed by the holy man’s mouth.

Afterward he said: “Let each one remain outside the doors. Bring this message from me:

“‘Do not be troubled, nor direct your foot within, contrary to Christ’s ordinance. The Lord on high, seeing your faith, has shown mercy to his servant and puts it to the test.’”

The companions went out and revealed the truth of what had been requested. She disclosed that she was their companion, though they had previously supposed her to be a man, and added why she had dared to do this in the holy man’s mind.

Hearing these things and taking them into their astonished minds, they glorified the Lord and revered his gifts and his servant.

After the holy man’s death, a certain woman, seeking to violate the enclosure by a bold attempt, touched the forbidden threshold with her foot. She fell backward, struck down, and yielded to death.

Often a large crowd of people came seeking a blessing. While they waited through long delays for some time, Simeon drew them onward by his prayers.

The attendant, leaning on the steps, climbed to the upper part of the column, and, praying to console the people, received no answer.

At last, when the crowd persisted with repeated cries, the saint said:

“Dear brothers, I ask you not to trouble me because I delay you and bring you these little waits.

“A great ship was calling me while at sea. When a swollen storm arose to destroy it, the lives of nearly three hundred men were wavering.

“At the same time I understood that the Lord was asking me to ask for them. I approached the Almighty with prayers, and, taking pity on them, he immediately sent calm assistance upon the waters.”

He said this and, enriching them with his prayers, sent them away in peace.

O lofty mind of the man! Though enclosed beneath a narrow roof, he surveys in mind the waters of the sea and is present to those who are there, calming as present the swollen waves for those absent.

His spirit, rising above the flesh, transfers presence elsewhere; ready to be present to the troubled, it crosses the intervening ground.

Though burdened with flesh, he is already said to travel freely throughout the world.

Thus, when he refused them, he did not disdain those present: he had ears where he was not visibly present.

Clearly, joined to the Lord, he had transcended the depths.

Here the pious patron sustained this region, removing destructive diseases and driving away calamities.

For once an earthquake shook the fields and houses of the land, laying low both people and dwellings. Citizens and farmers alike, compelled by this disaster, sought the sublime protection of the blessed Father.

He made clear to the crowds coming from every side that God’s wrath was deserved by their merits, since among so great a people there was scarcely one who did good.

He urged the people to fall down with him in prayer.

Together, though not equal in merit, they struck heaven with one voice and prayed to Christ with humbled minds.

But who was praying to him worthily, and who with a pure heart? The Lord revealed this to his servant in a secret message.

Simeon disclosed to the people that, among so many thousands, the Lord had heard one man praying with him. He named the farmer, summoned him, and asked him to declare his way of life, so that the others might follow his conduct and merit.

The farmer persisted in saying that he was unworthy and a sinner, so that he might provide an example of virtue.

Lest a good deed useful to many remain hidden, he was compelled to reveal that he cultivated the fields. He separated his property into three parts: he gave one part to the poor, assigned one part to the treasury, and kept the rest for himself.

He strove to be content with his own possessions, rendering to God what belonged to God and to Caesar what belonged to Caesar; never laying snares for anyone, harming no one, and loving every brother in Christ as himself.

[Col. 0580B] When the citizens heard this, they revered the humble man, honored the countryman, and worshiped the merit of the pious Simeon.

Through these two men they had been snatched from imminent death, a deliverance that, it is said, nine men would not have been able to obtain for Sodom.

The Lord protected this dear servant from every enemy, declaring that whoever prepared to harm him would sin against the Lord, since in trying to touch one who shone before the Lord he would touch the pupil of the Most High’s eye.

A certain fierce man, urged on by a savage dragon,

[Col. 0580C] presumed to attack the beneficent man with dreadful words, calling him a seducer who deceived the crowds.

He sought from the military authorities a command for himself, so that he might go and harass Simeon and remove him from the height of his column.

He was permitted to proceed. He gathered companions and brought tall ladders. The wretched man tried to climb the steps, though his evil prayers denied him the ascent.

Having climbed three steps, suddenly, by supernatural force, the ladders gave way from the column.

The miserable man, hanging between heaven and earth and hated by the ground, dangled four cubits above the earth.

Then, raging and blinded in heart, he raised his fierce spirit, seized an arrow from his hanging quiver, and strained his crescent-shaped bow to pierce the holy limbs.

Heavenly anger struck his hand, and without delay he was punished: his hand dried up.

Then the savage man suffered contraction of the hand and was seized by gout, showing through the affliction of his hands and feet that he had sinned.

When he had attempted to overthrow Christ’s servant, he himself was overthrown, condemned by the heavenly right hand.

Long ago, the builder of the lofty tower that sought heaven separated the builders’ tongues, previously united in one language, and removed from the ascent of the sky those unworthy of it through their foolish ambition.

So he himself, removing the savage enemy, struck down the man who, in his presumption, was preparing to attack the lofty steps of the Lord and to disturb the servant who revered the secrets of heaven, though unworthy.

But after the holy servant of the Lord had stood fixed for many years upon the lofty fortress, out of love for God and without ever ceasing from prayer, at last, blessed, amid his words of prayer,

[Col. 0581A] he sought the secrets of heaven. He sent his soul, intent upon the heavens, to heavenly things, longing to see what he had desired for so long.

He placed it in the heavenly realm and satisfied it with the grace of the King; he placed it in the heavenly court among the assemblies above [Note: [Col. 0581D] So in both manuscripts.].

When the third day thereafter shone with light—the day on which Christ’s resurrection is celebrated with solemn worship—the gathered people waited a long time to receive a blessing.

The anxious Antoninus, concerned for the Father, climbed into the fortress. Thinking that Simeon was leaning upon his prayers, he stood attentive and at last called him, asking repeatedly and with many prayers.

When no answer was returned to the petitioner, and the attendant could not hear the familiar breathing, he bent down and applied his ear to the man’s mouth.

Instead of the breath of life, he sensed only fragrances and caught through his nostrils odors fragrant with nectar, breathing from the body and the breath of Christ. The famous scent spread widely through the air.

[Col. 0581B] Seeing that the man had left the depths of this world, the disciple drew out long sighs from his grieving heart, asking many questions and exhausting his soul with panting lamentation.

While he repeated his mourning, he was carried away in soothing sleep. Suddenly, while asleep, he received instructions by a hand through heavenly power.

Behold, he heard the Father begin to speak, giving him these commands:

“Do not fear; for I am not abandoning the beloved column, nor shall I leave the summit of the mountain where, striving, I obtained the light of life.

“Descend, and satisfy the people waiting for me. Carry this message into the city, secretly, lest the sorrowful crowd erupt in confusion:

[Col. 0581C] ‘For I have already rested in the end appointed by the Lord.’”

O soul full of virtue and unconquered even by death!

To relieve the servant, weary with grief and lamentation, he visited him in his inconsolable state, lest he abandon his disciple, and taught him how he himself should arrange the funeral.

Awakening, the man worshiped Christ in fear. As he tried to remove relics from the sacred body, he suddenly saw the cold corpse tremble and was completely terrified at having attempted it.

Abandoning the undertaking, he descended swiftly from the fortress. He then sent his brother to the bishop of Antioch, a man whom Simeon judged distinguished and who, illuminated from heaven, was accustomed to see him speaking many things in secret during his hours with Simeon, shining in a splendid garment, radiant and bright as a flash of light.

The next day dawned and washed the earth in rosy light. The bishop of Antioch, accompanied by three bishops, hastened there. Curtains were stretched around the fortress, more precious than gold ornaments.

When the body was brought near the adjoining altar, everything around it was filled with a dark cloud, so that the Lord might show that he was present—the Lord whom Moses sought while hidden in the darkness, and the cloud that had filled Solomon’s hall when the priests were placing the ark and the cherubim in their seats.

And, so that the presence of the Most High might be proved still more certainly, a heavenly brightness shone with radiant splendor, when he appeared to bear seven [the text is uncertain: possibly “elders”] hidden from sight.

The pope, wishing to pluck the hairs of the sacred beard and strip the Nazarene of the hairs consecrated to the Lord, raised his right hand toward the object of fear.

The hand immediately dried up and could no longer serve the wishes of the man who bore it. The bishop stood amazed, and wondered that the hand he knew was no longer his own. He prayed to the Lord, since the limb now seemed useless to him.

When he vowed, swearing that he would henceforth avoid such actions, and when he was supported by the great strength of the people’s prayers, he recovered the organs of his nerves, restored to him.

The palm, which had lost its function, grew warm again and regained its use. The rejoicing people therefore carried the venerable limbs, their powerful protection, toward the city.

As they proceeded with the pious funeral and entered a certain village, where the Almighty had chosen to glorify his servant, suddenly the sacred relic became immovable.

[Col. 0582B] The bearers set down the intolerable weight; they could not endure the force that had descended from heaven.

There was a man there who for nearly forty years had neither received speech through his ears nor expressed it through his mouth. Guided by divine power, he rushed before the bier, seeking with the feeling of his heart the help that he could not request with his voice.

Suddenly, in his amazement, he felt the aid of the divine summit come to him. Gradually he began to absorb sounds—a thing he had never done—and to receive words. Conceiving unfamiliar speech in his mind, he produced utterances with his mouth.

After remaining long silent, he cried out and spoke:

“Servant of God, you have come well. Your arrival has saved me. I shall serve you throughout my life, as long as the Spirit who gives life to these limbs of mine shall govern them.”

As he rose with this vow and seized the bier, the burden was lightened and suddenly became portable. Praising God, they carried the weight without difficulty.

There is no doubt that the Lord had preserved this man for that moment. Simeon’s power had already healed many sick people who had been brought from other regions.

Thus, by giving use to a living man who had been dead to life, the saint himself was proved to live happily in that region and to cling to the giver of the life of the living.

They were now approaching the city. Behold, the people came out from the walls, shouting psalms and singing hymns, glittering with lamps and torches and adorned with palm branches.

They hastened to meet the sacred limbs and to bring into their city the honorable burden of the triumphant man, the protection of the people and the fortress. Immediately they offered pious gifts to the great church.

[Col. 0582D] From that point the Lord revealed where he wished his beloved bones to be stored. They were carried to the hall designated for them.

To make clear to everyone that this was wholly accomplished by divine power, he sent down from the bright stars of heaven a man of noble appearance: shining with a golden staff, splendid to behold, clothed in a gleaming white garment.

He diligently attended to the task while the sealed doors of the tomb remained closed in silence. Then he departed and was never seen there again, nor had he appeared before.

Thus it became known that a inhabitant of heaven had come.

From that time, such extraordinary deeds are said to have been performed at the prophet’s tomb that he is thought not to have accomplished more while alive, when he stood upon the lofty column of the high fortress,

[Col. 0583A] so that it might be known that, joined to the Lord in the highest heaven, he nobly lives through the many signs by which he is seen to live on earth,

[Col. 0584A] his life not extinguished by death, but transferred by him to a better dwelling in heaven.

## CHAPTER IX. On the holy bishops Vitalis and Meletius

[Col. 0583]

[Col. 0583A] Vitalis restores and raises up the Church, worn down and overthrown by tyrants. He completes the kindly work of his predecessors, adding splendor through his own fervor, and reveals the pious zeal of Licinius’s time.

Meletius thunders divine teaching in pure utterances. After he had imbued the Armenian peoples with sacred doctrine, his voice could not be confined by a closed mouth; shining from afar, he inscribed heavenly things with his fingers.

He rejoices, though expelled, to preserve the balance of truth. Returning, he joins and arms his companions and acquires additional allies.

Apollo also mourns the plunder of the priest’s offspring, because a devoted woman offers to the saving Father the child stolen from a profane father.

Therefore, after the holy men had suffered their hands, feet, and backs to be scorched by fire and their father had been worn down in a celebrated contest,

[Col. 0583B] the pious king brings them out, unlocking the enclosures and bars, and restores the rescued girl to her mother, who had been concealed under the honor of caring for the soul.

From there he hastens to Palestine, accompanied by Cyril, who afterward begets a father from pious offspring.

The apostolic bishop gathers the synod, which had followed different paths, into the light of truth and calms it in harmonious peace.

He shows that God’s substance is simple, giving Jovianus a pure doctrine of faith to approve.

Avoiding divided disputes, he offers peace to everyone. He invites the wolf who carried off the sheep to join the sacred fellowship:

“Let him abandon his error, lay aside his savage crimes, cease to be a wolf, and appear as a gentle lamb.

“Let him pasture the flocks with me under equal protection. Let the word of God hold the see; let the leaders on both sides be joined; let the whole flock lie in one sheepfold.

“Let the one who prevails govern the common realms.”

But the savage beast does not know the covenants of peace.

Therefore the rights of the folds are entrusted to the pious shepherd. His honor grows through gentleness; kingdoms are governed according to peaceful prayers, and the scepters of empire are approved by virtue.

The bishops are added to the lofty insignia, with Theodosius prevailing over the barbarian hosts. Seeing himself adorned by the devout worship of the blessed men and entering into the splendor of the kingdom, he confirms the work he had seen, following their instruction.

When the prince first read the patron’s face with such splendor,

[Col. 0584B] he selected one man from among many. Recognizing him without anyone identifying him, he sought him and tested him.

Like a son, he embraced, welcomed, and honored him as a father. He gave kisses to his lips and eyes, to his breast and head, and also to his right hand, remembering that he had received his crown from it.

He honored it with his mouth, revealing what he had seen and recounting it. With Meletius himself he reviewed the rule of faith and the Fathers; the Fathers celebrated him and adorned him with fitting splendor.

Not long afterward the retired bishop sought heaven and was buried shining with the praise of noble proclamations, joined in the honor of the martyr’s shrine of Babylas.

## CHAPTER X. On the holy Flavianus and his friends and successors

[Col. 0583]

[Col. 0583C] With the Eastern Fathers and the whole senate in agreement, Flavianus was raised to the honor of the deserved episcopal chair and obtained the first seat of Peter’s governance.

The helmsman of that chair had long guided its boat amid the storms raging against the world. Through his counsels he prevented it from sinking in the raging sea; he worked with calm oars amid the storm and taught the King to be praised in ordered dances.

He gave the Church the Davidic song, so that the divine poems might resound and be composed for everlasting choirs.

Keeping watch over the Lamb, he gathered his ranks around himself, singing joyfully in harmonious praise of the Lord. He inspired terror in the wicked and gave joy to the righteous.

He did not abandon the pious doctrines through fear or ambush; he was neither captivated by high office nor compelled by threats to yield to wickedness.

[Col. 0583D] He defeated harmful men and gathered companions in the contest: Diodorus, under whose governance the Cilicians afterward were ruled; Acacius, who thereafter shone through his virtue at Beroea; Aphraates, renowned as an elder through divine light, who struck with the rays of truth the wicked ruler of the scepters and chastised the rigid minister with fiery heat.

Julianus too was summoned, great in rank, distinguished by the radiance of his virtues and faith. His absence was boasted of by the savage faction, but when he was present they lamented, oppressed by his lofty light,

[Col. 0584C] and bearing his great and wondrous deeds to the height of public renown.

Flavianus, a man eminent in these deeds and in birth, though not yet enjoying the episcopal seat, supported by his friends, set wars against the wolves, displaying the strength worthy of a shepherd and defending the sheepfolds against the beasts he had exposed.

He sharpened weapons, built quivers and fortifications, resisted enemies, and supplied protections for the flocks.

He restored combatants and provided counsel for battles; he strengthened bows and sent forth shining arrows.

He broke ambushes and tore apart the nets that sought to capture; he exposed the deceiving beasts beneath the lamb’s fleece and, once their fraud was dispersed, drew out the wolves that lay hidden.

He guarded the flocks and rescued them from black teeth. Through the skillful counsel of the shrewd man he separated the wasting disease, uncovered deceits, and drew out poison with honey.

Secretly forcing forth the hidden plague, he removed the shameful corruption of old age from the punished elder. Exposing the foul matter, he applied the art of healing to restore the corrupted flock, cleanse what had been polluted, bind what was broken, and lead back to the straight path those who had been misled.

He gathered the dispersed and returned them to Christ’s folds, collected the wanderers, and restored them to the one sheepfold.

If chance brought suffering, it was relieved by swiftly applied care,

[Col. 0585A] and the whole flock was covered by the shepherd’s peace and quiet.

Then, driven again by attacks, the patient and honorable bishop persisted, ready to endure everything dreadful.

Summoned before the rulers, he went; he did not flee his judges or his enemies. He did not reject those who opposed him, nor recoil from their grim faces.

He promised to yield and pledged to lay down the office; he was approved. He neither refused a successor nor feared anything further under an angry prince [ms. 2: “an admiring prince”].

He was worthy of the seat, since Augustus himself, asking him to assume both the cause and the accusation, dissolved errors and unraveled foolish quibbles.

He restored peace, joined together the disturbed heights, united peoples, and brought nations into treaties.

Illyrians, Egyptians, Asia, Thrace, and Pontus, together with the priests of the West, accepted the pious agreements.

The retired bishop also ascended to the heights of heaven.

[Col. 0586A] When Porphyrius had obtained Flavianus’s see by lot, the kindly Alexander succeeded him with fitting honor, frequently praised and enriched by the gift of integrity, distinguished in speech and still more distinguished in the conduct of his life.

He brought back to the sheepfold the flock that had long been absent. When he received the washed sheep with the refreshing river, he made the enemies lament while the citizens applauded, bringing joy to the city through the force of the restored stream.

Theodorus followed him in the keenness of his integrity and shone as a mirror of a chaste life and in piety.

He also returned what remained to the enclosures and the sheepfolds.

After him the great-hearted John assumed the sacred authority. He was appointed, and appointed Cyril with equal fervor; restoring him to the seat of Mark and also recovering the seat of Cephas, they removed disputes and adorned Christ’s hall with peace.

## CHAPTER XI. On the holy hermit Macedonius and Evagrius

[Note: [Col. 0585D] The Life of the monk Malchus occupies the principal place in this chapter; nevertheless, he is not mentioned in the title.]

[Col. 0585]

[Col. 0585A] Men fought around this city through their virtues, conquering together the raging world and the tyrant, protecting the citizens and sheltering the gentle camp.

At one time they guided the holy ranks by prayers, at another by admonitions; now through intercession, now through assistance, they brought fitting aid.

Macedonius, preparing to turn aside their cruel orders to slaughter at the throats [cod. 2: perhaps “of the condemned”], was brought from the high mountains to the trembling citizens. He attacked those carrying out deadly commands.

Clad in no bundles of rags, he was not afraid. Rather, by his approach he terrified the things that had been commanded to be read aloud by the threatening scepter-bearer.

He warned that such dominions and similar lots among brothers’ realms were transitory, and that it was not only imperial power that should be considered, but the equal offspring of all.

[Col. 0585C] “Let him not punish human beings made in the image of the Lord, provoking the Lord whose image is being punished.

“If he considers a cast bronze statue of his wife a serious matter when it is overturned, how much more should the Creator of all things be moved when an image is seized?

“Let him see how far sensible things differ from those devoid of sense, and let us recognize together that many of us possess worth through the honor of one.

“He cannot even restore a single hair once it has been cut.”

By restraining this raging lion—the chief man—through fear of guilt, he freed the people from danger, and his mind is said to have been carried into the king’s sanctuary, which was to be dissolved.

Here the holy and vigorous Evagrius, shining with the brightness of sacred light, gleamed as he handled divine matters with propriety.

Malchus, abandoning earthly things in this land for the worship of God and fleeing possessions and relatives by the law of chastity, preferred the contests of monastic life to the world’s allurements.

[Col. 0585D] In his actions he revealed the king whom he bears in his name [Note: [Col. 0586D] Jerome, Life of Malchus: “Malchus, whom we can render in Latin as ‘king.’”].

The crafty enemy, seeing him grow in the height of his virtues, spread dark snares around his heart:

“Restore your ancestral property, provide comfort to your widowed mother, and adapt your inheritance to sacred observances.”

The enemy did not desist, although Malchus had been warned by his guide, until he might drag him with hooks, drive him out into the waves, and cast him upon the sands of life.

Nor did the assaults of savage beasts fail the unprotected man.

[Col. 0586A] It was soon revealed that he had been attacked and carried off as booty by a band of Ishmaelites, while his companions were dispersed and driven into various disasters.

Thus, mounted high upon the humps of camels, he was carried through the vast desert. Raw flesh relieved his hunger, and he drank the wretched milk of a camel.

Bent beneath a barbarian mistress, he was ordered, without shame, to go about naked and learned to attend to the sheep.

The memory of the Fathers, held in respect, lightened his servitude.

The master demanded this monk, accustomed to prayers and psalms, and pressed him into service, delighting to see him subdued under the laws of servitude.

The enemy envied him and, laying snares in hidden places, urged the master to provide his servant with comfort. He saw that Malchus was an outstanding guardian of the folds.

The master decided to bind a wife to the servant as a companion in his chains. When Malchus refused to yield, he compelled him with a sword.

Malchus, detesting the marriage chamber, entered it with the virtue he hated to betray. He mourned instead of singing, uttered lamentation instead of dancing, wept for his chastity, and resolved to inflict death upon himself.

He sought an end and preferred modesty to life. He brandished the sword against himself, but his companion resisted his attempt.

She swore that he must refrain from a savage death, or that she herself would first descend to the Underworld. Their fierce struggle joined souls determined to set light after chastity.

But modesty itself pleased her: let him take as a companion of piety, an associate of purity, one whom the union of mind rather than of flesh might join to him.

Let God himself approve the splendor of their marriage chamber, and let their mutual love show them joined.

The astonished elder marveled that a woman could possess such manly virtue and easily withstand the allurements of sensuality.

He loved her, joined to him as a wife, with a deeper inward affection rather than sensual pleasure.

Nevertheless, he shrank from seeing or touching naked flesh,

fearing to lose in peace what he had labored to seek in war.

Such bonds render them more acceptable to their masters.

They feared no escape, while they traversed the vast wilderness,

with the flock led in greater freedom. The memory of their brothers

came back to their minds, and the kindly remembrance of their father.

Meanwhile, like an ant patiently wearing away what lay unused,

[Col. 0587A] a single companion stirred the dull grief that wandered in his mind,

and, with a troubled face, carried away the sorrow of his spirit.

She questioned the secret of his heart, and hidden things were disclosed.

She urged flight and strengthened the silence they had sought;

hope and fear revolved ceaselessly in whispers through concealment,

while provisions of goat-flesh were prudently prepared for the journey.

Late they undertook the road, carrying the meat and hides.

Leaning upon swift water-skins, they committed themselves to the rushing waters;

once across the river, uncertainly they ran through trackless places,

continually looking back over their shoulders.

Fearing ambushes by night, they covered the dry ground.

The third day had now passed, yet the same wandering vision

still urged them to turn back. Behold, two men came riding toward them

at a camel’s pace. The mind, presaging evil, drew back the thought

of their master and of death, and at the same time saw the sun grow black.

[Col. 0587B] “Look!” From far away, through the trembling of fear, a cave was revealed.

Yet no less did the terror of death and the poisonous pit within

forbid them to advance, and ordered those who had entered by the left-hand way

to remain there. With his servant accompanying him,

the master pursued them and reached the mouth of the cave.

Now the fear of a more terrible punishment of death seemed imminent:

terror had closed their mouths, and their tongues were bound by trembling,

when the master ordered the servant to bring out the wretched pair.

He himself, unsheathing his sword in order to kill them,

went in, leaving behind him those whom he had ordered to remain outside.

Seeing them, yet not being seen, he rebuked them with a harsh voice,

calling them “gallows-birds” and shouting that he would drag them out.

But the Almighty, mindful of his servants, stirred a lioness within,

carrying food for her cubs,

[Col. 0588A] and, attacking the savage enemy, seized him by the throat and tore it apart.

But the master himself, indignant that delay should postpone his vengeance

and unwilling to endure the other’s anger, rushed inward in fury;

and while raging against his sluggish servant with furious cries,

he encountered the savage jaws in the darkness.

Fury and terror shook the men who had been defending themselves.

A similar fear of death tortured their panting breasts.

Amid such dangers, the glory of the chastity they had preserved

alone lifted and comforted those in hiding.

Fear itself held them motionless, suspended as they were

upon the boundary of life, while the cautious beast seized

and left the pit, carrying her cub firmly in her biting mouth,

and yielded her refuge to those who were afraid.

Nor did they soon break out; trembling, they awaited

[Col. 0588B] the approach of their avenger, imagining it in their anxious hearts.

When the day had passed and the sun was already setting, they followed,

emerging from their hiding-place, and found the horses prepared for them,

led there under the protection of the Lord and brought through the enemy’s attack.

Thus, mounted and refreshed, they traversed the vast wilderness,

rejoicing. On the tenth day they reached the Roman camp,

and in due order disclosed what had happened to the tribune.

They left the animals with the commander as payment.

And so the returning company received the monk into the monastery;

joined with the chaste bands of his companions,

the beloved sister was supported, and it became clear that chastity,

even amid swords, wild beasts, and deserted places, had never been taken captive,

and that a servant joined to Christ could die, but could not be turned back.

# CHAPTER XII. On Saint Pelagia

[Col. 0587]

[Col. 0587C] We have learned that Pelagia was a daughter of this city,

whom, near the venerable heights of the Mount of Olives,

we have marked among the stars as having attained the summit of life by her merits.

Such was her passage from darkness to light, from the death of Gehenna

to the bright triumph of life through renowned devotion,

from stains to the sacred regions of heaven.

The bishop of this city once ordered certain people

from a neighboring district to hasten to him.

Among them was the holy man named Nonnus,

steadfast in justice and righteousness, remarkable in his conduct

and devout in goodness. On account of his virtuous behavior,

he was a venerable summit to all for his celibate life,

and, a beneficent monk, he shone as a beneficent bishop.

One chaste day, while he was scattering the seeds of the holy word

before the doors of the church, at the request of those companions themselves,

[Col. 0587D] he uttered, while all marveled, these words of the blessed old man,

so great to sow and so worthy to proclaim:

Behold, a glowing little actress passed by, blazing with shining gems,

seated upon a donkey adorned with the pomp of a prostitute.

Gold had covered her everywhere with its tawny, gleaming rays,

and she was laden with necklaces of brilliant beads.

A rejoicing, well-dressed crowd of boys accompanied her,

and a most splendid troop of girls, bright with gold;

all were distinguished by their clothing and adorned with collars.

Wherever she went, she scattered perfume upon the air,

filling the empty sky with anxious fragrances.

[Col. 0588C] At the sight of her, satiety fled from her lovers.

The foolish bishops, seeing her pass in such magnificence,

did not descend from their dignity in honor of God upon a donkey;

they exposed their shining hair from their bared heads,

and seemed, by their very gaze, to draw their faces back from a great stain.

But the excellent Nonnus, observing more attentively,

and watching her from farther away as she passed, remained fixed,

turning over in his astonished heart what the others did not know.

Then he inclined his head upon his knees, and soon filled

both his hands and his lap with the tears that had welled up.

Afterward, drawing deep sighs from the depths of his heart, he said:

‘Do you rightly approve, companions, of being delighted

by this woman and the pleasing adornment with which she has beautified herself?’

When they made no reply, he bent his face again toward his knees,

and joined sigh to sigh,

[Col. 0588D] striking his breast and filling his hair-shirt with tears,

the garment that subdued his flesh with the fierce heat of heaven.

Then he asked whether her lovely appearance had pleased his companions.

But even then they did not break the silence they had assumed.

He, skilled at plucking the rose from bristling thickets,

always calling them to the example of devotion

and removing the world’s sins from the hearts of his companions,

at last began to speak as if prophesying:

“Truly, I confess that the girl’s appearance delighted me;

her beauty and loveliness pleased me.

[Col. 0589A] But I confess that the lofty Judge will prefer her to us,
setting her before his dread tribunal,
so that he may judge our service and triumph over us.
How many brief hours, do you suppose, she has spent in her own chamber
adorning herself—washing, painting, and anointing herself with fragrant perfume,
and then diligently dressing herself before the mirror—
so that she may please the world, be desirable to all her lovers,
and seem unattractive to none who see her, though the coming day commonly overtakes them?

But we who worship the Father, who remains in heaven through eternal ages,

and rejoice in the Bridegroom who is not subject to death,

as he fittingly assigns riches shining without end to his servants—

does anyone estimate what the mind here has not conceived,

what the eye of flesh has not grasped,

what human ears have not heard, and what the heart cannot weigh,

[Col. 0589B] the things the Lord has prepared for his faithful and worthy children?

Moreover, holding fast the promises of the pledged covenant,

with the certainty that we shall behold the face of the heavenly Bridegroom

through the ages, at whom the cherubim themselves tremble

to fix their gaze—

do we not adorn ourselves, nor drive away the dark filth

and impurities branded upon fallen souls?

Rather, crushed and prostrate, we lie inactive,

although, following the example of the others,

we ought always to stand upon the lofty path

through the merits of the virtues.”

He spoke, and then withdrew into the inner rooms of the lodging.

Falling upon his face, he wet the ground behind him

with tears, praying in sorrowful words:

“Most high God, I beg you, spare our sins.

Forgive me, a sinner, for the adornments that this prostitute

customarily wore for a single day

[Col. 0589C] have surpassed everything in my life.

With what face shall I look upon you? Shall I be excused before you?

For I cannot hide from the eyes of the One who sees what is secret.

Woe to me, a sinner! I who stand before the altars

have performed, unworthy, no distinguished act

according to your will, O merciful one who created all things from nothing,

and who deigned to create me among them,

appointing me to offer you worthy service.

Do not reject me, wretched as I am, from the heavenly court,

nor, O revered one, let me be put to shame before your dreadful majesty

because of the dress of this prostitute,

who took pains to adorn herself proudly for earthly things,

to beautify herself with the greatest care for perishable objects.

But I, who resolved to please you by sacred right,

have ceased to fulfill the adornments required by the unconquered Lord.

[Col. 0589D] Why do I protect myself on earth while abandoning heaven,

and, needy in adornment, refuse to preserve for you my vows?

What she freely promised to mortals, she gives back in return;

therefore no hope now clings to my deeds.

My mind is suspended upon the heights of your compassion.

Your goodness, O immense and kindly Father, gives me confidence

in the many things you can do: save my soul by your gift.”

While he revolved such thoughts in sorrow,

night came down and covered the earth with black wings.

Sleep, descending, refreshed his limbs, wearied by labor.

Behold, the Lord, mindful of his troubled servant, revealed everything,

through signs foretelling the joyful blessings of the future.

For in his dream the bishop saw himself standing beside the altar,

and a dove, full of filth, flying around him,

[Col. 0590A] black with dreadful horror; he could not endure

its frightful, muddy, filthy stench.

It continued to fly around him until the order had sent outside

those hearers who had not yet been cleansed by baptism.

When they had gone out through the enclosure, the bird withdrew.

When the sacred rites were completed, it returned

and sought the one who was coming out.

Taking it, he saw it plunge itself before the doors of the church

into a basin; when its filth had been cleansed,

it rose high into heaven, white as snow,

ascending so far that it disappeared from his sight.

Stunned by this horror, the old man, when the clear, serene light

of the radiant day illuminated the earth with bright honor,

on the day when Christ’s resurrection is celebrated,

went to the church, where the sacred Mass was celebrated.

[Col. 0590B] When the rites had been completed, Nonnus was asked

to console the people by a sermon.

He began, speaking of heavenly things rather than earthly,

not polished by a rhetorician’s art,

but bringing forth things radiant with the light of heaven.

His speech was not noisy or boastful, but full of the Holy Spirit;

recalling the wandering, he opened the way to heavenly things,

and, recalling the merciful judgment, strengthened sinking souls
