with the warmth of heavenly hope.

When these exhortations struck the inmost parts of their minds,

the hearts of the men who received them were so pierced

that tears of devotion wet the pavement behind them.

The prostitute mentioned earlier stood there, led by the command of the Thunderer

to the sacred rites; although still a catechumen,

she had never been accustomed to approach this place,

buried beneath the heavy burden of her former life.

But the merciful compassion of Christ had led her

to his manger, where, among clean animals,

[Col. 0590C] he offered faithful servants heavenly food.

The fear of Christ now shook the girl’s dark heart.

When she heard the fear of the Lord from the servant’s mouth,

tears flowed abundantly from her crushed heart,

like streams from a spring, pouring forth in fear of the King,

whose dread scepters so resounded from the old man’s mouth.

Thus, returning and nourished by the living word of God,

she ordered the two servants to remain and see

where the shepherd had such an excellent lodging.

They stood and followed him, then reported everything to their mistress.

She wrote on wax tablets:

“Pelagia the prostitute to holy Nonnus, a worthy child of Christ;

Pelagia the harlot, the shameful child of the devil.

By hearing I have learned of the Lord whom you worship:

that once he bowed the heavens and sought the humility of earthly life,

[Col. 0590D] not because of the merits of the righteous, but to give sinners

the remedies of life, by which they might be healed.

The Holy One joined himself to shameful servants;

he, upon whose face the cherubim and seraphim tremble to gaze,

deigned to dwell with sinners, as you, holy Father,

proclaim in worthy words.

If you are truly known to be a disciple of this teacher,

do not despise me, but receive your servant,

who longs to find perpetual salvation.”

The holy old man wrote back the following:

“Whatever you are, you are shown to be manifest to our Lord.

I warn you only of this: do not attempt tender hearts

with the horror of a sordid man’s sins committed.

But if you desire to obtain true salvation,

and are able to see me, you shall observe me supported by companions,

for you alone shall never see me alone.”

As soon as she had read this, she hurried and ran,

sending a servant ahead.

The Father summoned his devout companions

and, with the sacred young woman under their very testimony,

at last ordered her to enter.

She went in and prostrated herself face-down upon the ground,

filling the house with bitter lamentation.

Adding an unusual veil of dust to her head,

she wet the bishop’s feet with a river of tears

and washed them with her weeping, wiping them with her loosened hair.

By these acts she imitated Mary in humble devotion,

to whom, because she loved much, much is said to have been given.

Since she could not embrace the Lord’s footsteps,

she reverently honored the worthy servant with a servant’s service,

[Col. 0591A] crying and saying:

“[Col. 0591B] Master, have mercy upon my sins,

and follow the holy teachings of your Lord Christ.

Pouring out upon me the entrails of holy compassion,

make me immediately a participant in that lofty name.

Indeed, I, Pelagia, am a sea of wicked pestilence,
boldly flooding with the foul waves of crimes.

I am a snare of the soul, an abyss of perdition.

With the torches of lust and the chasm of death

I have deceived many, myself previously deceived.

I shudder exceedingly at my deeds;

I curse myself, infected with such dark filth.

Therefore I beg to be washed in the holy fountain of baptism [Latin *lavacri*; the printed variant reads *lavari*, “to be washed”],

so that the deeds of my sins may perish there

and the filth of my soul may be cleansed and driven away.

I believe that, reborn through sanctifying baptism,

I shall flee from the hands of the wicked one who seduced me.”

[Col. 0591C] All the bishops and clergy marveled when they saw

so many tears and such faith, and such a sudden transformation

in the prostitute.

They marveled at the overflowing torrents of such abundant weeping;
no one declared that he had ever seen the like in anyone.

The joyful bishop scarcely persuaded her to rise from the ground.

Then, cautiously reconsidering the canon concerning this matter,

he declared that a prostitute ought not to be immersed in baptism

unless, after giving credible sponsors, she fortified her faith

by pledging never again to become involved in wicked deeds.

Hearing responses that delayed her against her will,

she again fell down and cast her body upon the ground,

striking it amid grief mingled with deep groaning:

“[Col. 0591D] You will be compelled to render an account for me

to the supreme Lord, and my evils will be charged to you by him,

if you delay washing me in the baptismal fountain.

For I fear that, while you sluggishly impose delays,

the enemy may again seize me in his dreadful chains,

from which I am hastening to escape by flight.

I know the snares and cunning thefts of the crafty one,

since I have been a trap through my disgrace

for the unwary.

May you find a share above the heavens with the saints

if you do not delay my salvation,

lest the savage boar tear me away with a cruel tooth

and, trusting in the interval, hurl me down into dark pits.

Therefore I beg you: wash me today in the sacred waters,

and offer pious gifts for me in God’s temples.”

When all heard this, they proclaimed Christ’s praises,

marveling that a prostitute burned with such a desire for salvation.

[Col. 0592A] Nonnus then sent the Levite Jacob to the bishop of the city,

so that he might disclose everything that had happened in due order.

The bishop gave thanks to God and rejoiced

that the gains of his fold were increasing;

he exalted Nonnus’s honor, and immediately ordered

the holy Roman mother to go,

so that she might hasten to become the mother of a new daughter through baptism.

When she arrived, she found Pelagia lying before Nonnus’s feet

in a flood of tears.

She rose, her face wet, and, ordered to confess her crimes,

lamented that they outnumbered the sands of the sea,

while, continuing the comparison, she declared them heavier than any burden.

Nevertheless, she trusted that through the Lord’s compassion

they would be forgiven and that pardon for all her crimes

would be granted her.

When the bishop properly asked her name for purification,

she said that her proper name was Pelagia,

but that, in Roman fashion, she should be called Margarita,

because of the necklace by which she had drawn souls captive.

[Col. 0592B] Then the old man exorcised the girl according to custom,

marked her with the name, and baptized her with holy baptism,

making her a participant in the divine altar’s gift.

The Roman woman lifted her from the sacred pool.

Then the bishop said:

“Let us rejoice with the citizens of the heavenly court,

and let us be merry with wine and oil

because of the victory of this sheep’s salvation, which must be celebrated.”

While the blessed Father was feasting with his company,

a demon was plainly seen, naked in form,
displaying the netted spoil that had been snatched from him.

With its hands bound around its head, it roared and howled

in a defiant voice:

“O violence of this deed!

What am I suffering? How greatly I am tortured by this old man!

[Col. 0592C] Were thirty thousand Saracens whom you violently captured

not enough for you, old man,

and whom, stealing them from me, you gave to Christ through baptism?

Was my Heliopolis not enough for you,

which the citizens, worshiping at its famous height,

consecrated to you?

Are not all the nations you have taken enough for you,

those who through you revere Christ’s scepters?

Were so many and such great robberies not enough for you?

In addition, my greatest hope of ample profit is taken away.

O violent falling robber, O wicked old age!

I can bear no more arguments of your savage deceit.

Alas, cursed be the day on which you were born against me!

For, driven to collapse, our house, wavering like a stream of tears,

has fallen from its badly secured foundation, torn away.”

[Col. 0592D] Thus livid, he continued with lamentation and roaring.

The other bishops listened to the voice of the wicked one,

and, with the venerable Roman mother, stood astonished.

He turned his words also toward the girl taken by Christ’s power:

“O Pelagia, what have you prepared for me—she who was dear to me?

You too seem to have followed my Judas.

He, crowned and bound with great honor,

having attained the apostolic summit among the twelve,

betrayed the teacher whose disciple he had been.

In the same way, since you had been mine,

you now reveal yourself to me through treachery.”

Then the Roman mother said:

“Daughter, fortify yourself with the protection of the cross,

renouncing the pomp of the black demon.”

When she made the sign of the cross and called upon Christ,

he fled beneath the air and vanished into the upper breezes.

[Col. 0593A] Thereafter, the deceiver, returning to his familiar arts,

added gentle flatteries to rigid terrors.

He approached her as she lay asleep and shook her with dreadful cunning;

he awakened her and tried to mingle bland words with his threats:

“Remembering evil, my Margarita, what have I ever done to you?

Did I not adorn you with jewels and costly hair?

Did I not fill you with silver and gold?

Tell me in what respect you think yourself slightly offended,

and I shall now make amends.

Only do not abandon me,

lest the worshipers of Christ torment me so shamefully.”

But the maidservant of God tried to defend herself with the sign of Christ,

and, blowing away the phantoms of the crafty monster, answered:

“[Col. 0593B] I renounce you and your pomp, savage one.

May the Lord Jesus oppose you, most evil demon,

who in his compassion has snatched me from your deep jaws

and led me into his bridal chamber and the court of heaven.”

Then, calling the Roman woman, she said:

“Venerable mother, pray to the Lord for me,

for Satan, like a roaring lion,

is preparing ambushes, both soothing and threatening.”

Then she replied:

“Do not fear the monster, daughter; it has already been defeated.

From now on, terrified, it will also flee from your shadow.”

On the third day after receiving the gift of baptism, she fought the cruel plague secretly and openly.

Now a woman made manly in heart and wary of the old enemy,

she hastened to conquer the snares of the greedy world

and to follow Christ, her leader, along the perfect path.

She summoned the servant who managed the household and ordered him

to transport everything listed among her possessions:

silver, clothing, gold, necklaces, and gems.

The servant hastened, fearing to delay her commands,

and brought all his mistress’s ornaments.

She immediately offered these through the mother to the Father’s administration,

declaring them to be the very wages of her dark crime,

by which the crafty enemy had deceived her.

She requested that they be expended according to holy judgment,

asserting that the gifts of the heavenly Bridegroom were sufficient for her.

At once she dismissed all her male and female servants,

and, by giving them freedom, comforted her dependents,

exhorting them to strive to loosen the bonds of sin

and preserve true freedom through devotion.

But Nonnus, the prudent merchant and faithful bearer,

called the church’s steward and, in the girl’s presence,

[Col. 0593C] handed over all the precious insignia of her adornment,

adjuring him by the one in whose honor they had been held in idleness

[Col. 0593D] not to defraud the poor of any portion of these resources,

and not to bring any of them into the bishop’s house,

or into the church, or into the hands of those who administered them.

Rather, everything was to be distributed among widows, orphans, and the poor,

so that the wealth accumulated by the blessed servant

might become relief for those in need.

It was done immediately; nothing remained undone.

Indeed, after the maidservant of God had become radiant

through the water of the font,

she took nothing from her own possessions for her own use,

receiving pious nourishment from the excellent mother,

and avoiding even touching anything acquired through dark vices.

[Col. 0594A] At daybreak it is customary to put white garments upon neophytes.

Before the day’s light had yet grown red,

she rose, removed the white baptismal robes,

and put on a coarse cloak and tunic.

Without anyone witnessing it, she put on the rough coverings of the Cinyphian goat,
and, taking a dove's wings, sought the heights.

Afterward she was never seen again in those places.

Because the Roman mother did not know this,

she feared that perhaps the love of the one who had been despised

had returned to evil,

and mourned as though Pelagia had again been caught in the snares laid for her.

But the excellent Father, conscious through the Holy Spirit

of Pelagia’s vow, consoled her:

“Daughter, do not weep, saying that your devout daughter is with the company of heaven.

Rather, rejoice cheerfully that she too, like that other Mary,

has found a share in the better leisure,

which can no longer be taken away from her.”

[Col. 0594B] When the whole city learned this, it gave thanks to the Lord,

and each person sought the prayers of the priests who were present.

Meanwhile the third year had passed in swift succession.

The Levite mentioned above made a vow,

and resolved to go and visit the holy places of Jerusalem.

He announced this to the holy Father and asked to be dismissed.

The bishop permitted him to go, and followed him with this advice:

“When, with God’s help, you have reached that place, brother,

and have properly venerated its consecrated sites,

take care to seek out a holy monk named Pelagius,

the only one who, since the time of the war,

lies hidden, shut up in a cell.

Take care to visit him, for he truly serves the Lord

and is proved to be a perfect monk.”

Thus he commended the holy girl under the honor of the male sex,

since she had conquered her sex and trampled underfoot

[Col. 0594C] all the vanities of the world with a manly heart.

Yet he did not reveal this more openly,

preserving the order that it should happen according to the divine will and command.

At last the deacon, reminded of these instructions,

went to the holy places.

He prostrated himself and worshiped the precious wood of the blessed cross,

then the places consecrated by the limbs of the buried King,

from whose conquered death Christ’s glory returned in triumph,

strengthened by the solid power of perpetual life.

When the next day was driving away the darkness of night,

the Levite hastened to seek the designated Pelagius.

Then, climbing the heights of the Mount of Olives,
where the Son sent his pious prayers to the Father’s ears,
and from which he bore his chief triumph above the stars,

claiming his proper right, he ascended into the heights of heaven.

There he heard that the man whom he sought with such zeal lived.

[Col. 0594D] Seeing a very small cell, closed on every side,

he searched with his eyes for the place where an entrance might be open.

He saw nothing there except a tiny window on one side.

When it was knocked upon, it opened, and the Levite was recognized. Unaware that the mother recognized him as he recognized her, he saw her little face withered and furrowed with wrinkles, her eyes sunken in their sockets and weighed down by wasting, her bones everywhere countable beneath her loosened skin, and her dried skin scarcely covering her bones. Asking to be blessed by her, he was blessed; she learned that he was a Levite serving the blessed pope and asked him, as he prayed, to return the favor for her. He marveled at the prophet’s disclosure of these secrets, but learned and said nothing further.

[Col. 0595A] Solemnly listening only to the praises

that she offered to the Lord when the third hour rose,

and thus blessing the Lord of heaven, he continued joyfully,

inflamed with an exceptional love of the holy places,

and wishing to be blessed by the lofty prayers of the holy ones.

Pelagius’s fame held powerful sway over him. When he approached that monk’s cell again, he heard nothing within.

He remained waiting through the daylight,

and, when night had already spread its black wings over the earth,

returned, ordering the day to pass, and came back again.

When the third light drove the blind hiding-places from the world,

he climbed up and, seeing the window closed,

ventured to open it.

Then, seeing the holy body lying in repose,

he quickly descended and announced to the city of Jerusalem

that Abbot Pelagius had sought the secrets of heaven.

[Col. 0595B] The communities of monks under both their rules

proclaimed this, and it was reported throughout the whole region:

the monks of the Jordan, of Jericho, and of Jerusalem.

The Fathers were already assembled in holy fervor.

Then the body was taken from the cell and placed upon a bier.

The priest of Jerusalem approached and, according to the customary rite,

arranged the limbs for the blessed funeral.

[Col. 0596A] Behold, suddenly they proved that the one whom they had thought a monk,

with a manly mind, had secretly been a nun.

They therefore glorified with a loud voice the kindly and wondrous God,

who guides many saints by hidden governance,

keeping the jewels known to himself.

The report flew abroad that a masculine mother had sought heaven,

and many took care to hasten to her funeral.

Holy companies of virgins flew about in joy.

While they treated the devout corpse with fitting honor

and committed it with solemn devotion to the grave,

the devout crowd shone with many lights,

and the people’s voice resounded everywhere with God’s praises.

Afterward Jacob, the minister sent there by Christ’s compassion,

returned and brought the news to the Father.

[Col. 0596B] From there he hastened to tell these things to the Antiochene mother,

and brought great joy to all the righteous there.

The people shed tears amid their joy,

praising the Lord, who by a divine gift grants

that he may take such fruits from them for himself,

and gladly store them, splendid, in the barns of heaven.

[Col. 0595]

# FOURTEEN BOOKS ON CHRIST’S TRIUMPHS IN ITALY

## THE PROEM OF THE FOLLOWING WORK BEGINS

[Col. 0595C] Rome, head of the world, renowned among powerful men

for scepters, consuls, Caesars, and Augustus,

famous for fathers and Quirites,

for arms, peace, and dominion—

but now brighter through the light of the Most High King,

noble among the princes of heaven,

lofty through Christ’s foremost companions,

you shine through martyrs and bishops,

you gleam with choirs of virgins,
who establish you, eternal in heaven above the stars,
through miracles, doctrine, battles, and victory-palms.

You surpass the ancient princes in majesty,

those powerful in wars by which they prepared kingdoms,

although they subjected the laws of the world to you.

Yet they blackened you with dreadful vices,

[Col. 0595D] polluted you with domestic arms,

often stained you with the blood of saints,

and filled you with every filth of crime.

Although they subjected kings and satraps,

[Col. 0596C] they nevertheless submitted their savage necks to a cruel yoke,

driven onward by crimes that pressed upon their weakened hearts,

to drive away the plagues of their feeble breasts.

Unless I am mistaken, these things resound through their own poets,
who water their decay from the Pegasean spring.

But Christ’s nobles, taught by lofty powers

to subject the proud princes,

to drive out the demons that rule the great,

trample the scepters that dominate through death,

breaking the darts of savage powers.

Those whom illustrious kings, with pitiful faces,

used to pray to while trembling, these men press beneath their feet,

overthrowing the divinities of the ancient age.

I do not undertake in my song to reveal matters

at which Maro would have been terrified as a theme,

[Col. 0596D] shuddering to weave the black threads of the toga;

rather, matters that, if Orpheus sang them,

would surpass Orpheus, the beautiful Linus,

and even father Apollo,

and that would surpass Arcadian Pan by their song.

## THE CHAPTERS OF BOOK ONE BEGIN

[Col. 0597]

I. On the contest of the holy apostle Peter with Simon Magus.  
II. On Saint Torpes.  
III. On the passion of the apostles Peter and Paul.  
IV. On Saints Processus and Martinianus and Lucina.  
V. On Saints Nazarius and Celsus.  
VI. On the vengeance of Nero’s persecution.  
VII. On the reign of Vespasian and Titus.  
VIII. On Saints Linus and Cletus.  
IX. On the other disciples of the apostles and Saint Apollinaris.

## BOOK ONE BEGINS

[Col. 0597]

### CHAPTER ONE. On the contest of the holy apostle Peter with Simon Magus

[Col. 0597A] At last, under the leadership of Peter, the excellent guide of Christ’s peoples, we have come to the Roman citadels, to unfold in verse the gracious trophies and pious triumphs of the cross, won in contests for the kingdoms of heaven and happily enlarged through the merits of the saints.

After his victories at Antioch, pursuing the pestilential enemy

of the divine light with the darts of the word,

he brought himself here, so that he might overthrow Simon,

who was fleeing far away upon the summit of the world,

and so that it might be clear to the whole world

that, from the head of the world, heavenly triumphs shone,

beneath which the wicked serpent groans, having been laid low before the Church.

Having sown himself widely through many kingdoms of the earth,

Peter thereafter scattered the richest seeds of the word.

Why should I recall the ancient frauds of the war from its beginning,

how Simon, [Col. 0597B] first attacking Christ’s flock with snares,

pretended to be an ally—and unwillingly taught the enemy—

when he saw that the companions of the one who possessed heavenly authority

were far stronger through their art than he,

and, astonished by the Philippian miracles and by the word,

received the strengthening of the life-saving bath,

hoping through an attractive endeavor to learn the wonders

that he knew in great number, accused as he was of Stygian frenzy?

Faith was as far removed from his mind as the sun—which abhors the darkness of the Rhipaean region—is from it when, on its fixed course, it travels around the world and irradiates earthly kingdoms with precious light.

The matter became clear: for when he saw no trace

of the fraud familiar to the arts of the blessed Church raging there,

[Col. 0597C] immediately, beneath his blind heart, astonished impulses

and a sickly envy, Gentile in spirit, raged against what was joyful.

He grieved that he himself could not attain

the power possessed by the ill-fated art throughout the world.

Turning over cherished deceits in his dark heart,

he brewed foul poisons and planned to press forward secretly.

Since he could not prevail to overcome the fortress of fraud by advancing,

he strove first to undermine the foundations of the structure,

so that he might be able to overthrow the whole mass of its building.

Seizing the weapons already long known to his father,

by which he had previously overthrown the earth-born first men,

he brought forward riches of gold,

thinking that he could purchase the gift of the lofty Spirit.

But Peter, instructed by the Lord himself

to cross through the foul snares,

seeing that this was an attempt against the sacred things,

pierced him with the strong point of the word,

whether he tried to buy or to take away by the monster’s contrivance,

and drove the wolf gently from the sheepfold.

[Col. 0597D] Then, like a wild beast driven by the shepherds’ shouts—

when it follows the prey suddenly snatched from the middle of the field,

while the shouting of the men and the swift mastiffs pursue it,

and, unable to endure them, it sends away its own comforts,

gathers greater anger in its thwarted desire,

and prefers to tear from hunger rather than think of eating—

it plots ambushes against the folds, secretly repeats its thefts,

and, wherever a path lies open, enters and tears the sheep,

now eager not merely to exist but to do harm:

so this wolf, a cruel beast of mind,

repulsed by the powerful voice of the shepherd Cephas,

unable to endure the pious burdens along a direct course,

laid them aside and, empty, was carried away in blazing anger.

Multiplying the weapons of harm that he had taken up,

he tested whatever sheepfolds of Christ he could by stealth,

preparing to attack the hearts of the flock with flattering snares,

bringing nothing common, propagating everything contrary.

When he learned that the sheep of Caesarea were gathered under Peter the shepherd,

he directed his hostile course here by deceit,

and stained with his savage tooth as many as he could.

Against this savage enemy of wicked contrivance,

the mighty warrior Cephas, strengthened by divine gift,

advanced and, vigorous in arms, took up the contest with his mouth.

The shadow was driven away; the brightness shone forth in holy light.

The disciples of the deceiver, whose minds were readier to perceive the truth,

penetrated the secret frauds of their dark master

and recoiled from the crime.

They were glad to lend their right hands to the truth

and joined themselves to the saints, prepared to receive the light.

Abandoned by his companions, the robber was consumed by dreadful anger,

[Col. 0598C] and secretly undertaking flight, made for the city of Antioch.

For he had heard that the strength of the faith had grown there so greatly

that they were taking their name from the name of Christ.

Burning fiercely with the torches of envy,

he strove to cast this out by hidden ambushes and deceits,

and labored to fight against the Lord of heaven.

But the wretched man, frustrated, was consumed by savage fire.

Driven away by Peter’s companions and cautious ministers,

he sought the protection of flight, and, seeing that all the kingdoms of Asia

had been denied him, chose to be carried across the seas.

[Col. 0598D] Learning that whatever he might undertake in Rome was false,

since it had been violated by the error of all the gods

and occupied by the foul domination of demons,

he trusted in them and, driven by them, came here as an exile.

[Col. 0599A] [Col. 0598A] Relying upon demonic aid, he cast many citizens into chains of error,

and increased his power through magic to such a degree

that he was regarded as a god by those same people

and was even honored with a statue,

which the Tiberian waters had washed between the twin bridges,

marked by an inscription.

But the divinity obtained by fraud did not last long.

The tender darkness was broken,

when Peter, the first leader and teacher of Christ’s army,

was immediately directed there like a commander.

Against the general enemy of the human race,

he was the first to bring the standards of the cross into this city,

after he had armed the Cappadocians, Galatians, Pontians, and Bithynians

with the faith, entrusting them with worthy duties.

[Col. 0599B] Strong in knowing how to fight divine contests,

he led the cohorts of virtues against crimes

and drove away the darkness of falsehood with the light of truth.

He was the first to open, with the keys of the word,

the court of the heavenly kingdom to the city’s citizens who ruled it.

The shadows were driven away by Christ’s gleaming rays.

The Gospel’s speech was already illuminating human minds

with peaceful sweetness.

No satiety held the hearers of the word;

seeing many miracles, they did not consider hearing enough,

but with a suppliant vow asked that the disciple

be commanded to set these things down in sacred writing.

He heard their prayers and received the Gospel of Peter

on writing tablets, to be preserved.

The old man too, full of the heavenly Spirit,

after the work had been completed,

received the faithful theft and, delighted by the acquisition,

confirmed and handed over to the Church for reading through the ages

[Col. 0599C] the teachings marked by Mark’s painted hand upon the page.

[Col. 0598B] The state quickly perceived, at the very threshold,

the brilliant aid of salvation brought by Cephas’s arrival.

For Claudius, fourth after Augustus,

having obtained the fasces of the world,

was preparing much against the consuls and senators.

A decree had indeed gone forth that all the nobles descended from Caesar

should be extinguished by them.

When Gaius had been destroyed,

that cruel friend of crimes,

the kingdoms were ordered to be driven from the yoke,

the scepters broken by being torn away,

the laws restored, and the old rights recovered.

But after Claudius secured the throne,

he extended the savage devices of cruel punishment against the judges.

Then, touched by divine will, he came to Peter’s aid, [lacuna]

[Col. 0599D] Lest the black storm harm the rising grasses while the new seeds, still split open, are being buried in the earth, he begins inwardly to consider in the recesses of his heart what devastation harsh vengeance would cause if it were begun; what famous and great men it would bring beneath the shadows; how it would leave the city desolate and bereft of its fathers. He reflects on these things, and the savage impulses of his spirit settle into the pleasing remedies of such fierce anger.

Just as the waters grow still after the wars of the winds, and at last the lingering breeze dies clinging to the sails, so he chooses voluntarily to relent from his savage purposes, retaining nothing of these matters in his fury; indeed, by word and deed he establishes forgiveness for all time, decreeing that no trace of the wicked deeds should recur in the light. Thus, through Cephas, famous Rome is refreshed by an amnesty,

[Col. 0600A] once issued by the Athenian censors. Cicero had indeed long before urged the senate, after Caesar’s slaughter, to introduce it among the peoples; but Antony, using ill-omened arms, forbade it, and Caesar Augustus, avenger of the secret murder, did likewise.

When Claudius, with Bar-Jonah at Rome as its leader, applied this amnesty, although the case called for a harsher vengeance in which the avenger might burn, he nevertheless voluntarily remitted the crime, though no one demanded it.

At this time another exceedingly remarkable event occurred, wrought by the grace of God while he ruled the lofty kingdoms. Furius Camillus, legate of Dalmatia, having devised a civil crime, had summoned the strong and fierce hands of the army to change their allegiance. On the appointed day, when a king was to be chosen by the entire army, the standards could not be moved by any means,

[Col. 0600B] as though they had been fastened by firm roots in the earth; nor could the eagles be fitted to their staffs, overcome by the power of Christ.

When the soldier saw these miracles, never previously witnessed, he repented of the undertaking, struck the tyrant with his hard sword, and judged that the army’s former loyalty must be preserved.

And what could be worse, what more destructive to the city, than Rome’s civil wars? The historian proceeds, properly denying that this was divinely checked in order to protect the tender lambs and lay firm foundations—Christ guarding what was fixed—if anyone can establish such earlier acts of restraining civil arms by the reasoning of example. [The transmitted syntax is difficult.]

For four years all battles were removed—those within and those without were restrained at the Lord’s command. At last the prince, complaining of the idleness of lethargy,

[Col. 0600C] sought hands for war everywhere and grieved that war had been denied him. He moved his standards without an enemy; he crossed the snowy Alps; seeing the peaceful Gallic fields, he passed on to the sea. Across the sea he discovered that some peoples were muttering rebellion; he went through their lands and suppressed their mild disturbances without bloodshed.

Thinking that he had accomplished nothing, he searched the sea to see whether he might encounter lands untouched by a Roman prince. Those which he could enter he subdued under rapid dominion. But when, returning at a swift pace, he came back in the sixth month and had set foot outside the open gates in search of war, he admitted the returning Quirites without loss into the folds where the Jordanian hero offers the holy pastures of life to washed sheep.

The devout rejoice in peace; they rejoice in the consolation of the word. The excellent father instructs the unlearned clients with his speech,

[Col. 0600D] and, as a pious guardian, defends them against the savage enemy. He points out and overcomes the robber, drives him from the city, and, while Claudius rules the world, sows the faith of Christ with his sacred mouth and increases it with accompanying signs.

But after the laws had yielded to shameful Nero, Simon, having heard that the disgraceful man was currying favor with the tyrant, voluntarily offered himself to him, worthy of such a patron, seeking to join teaching to outstanding conduct. A hateful alliance binds them together in dark friendship: the worst man is joined to the criminal friend in unspeakable wickedness.

The monstrous evil grows. The perverse man incites him to wicked arts; nothing disgraceful remains undone. The prudent king attempts everything through open crimes.

As this great evil grew, the Almighty provided Cephas with a strong and upright companion,

[Col. 0601A] granting Paul to come to his aid. Although Paul was intent on adorning the whole world with blessed teaching and extending its boundaries to the ends of the earth—after travelling from Jerusalem to the innermost villages, cities, and fortresses of the Illyrian countryside, filling everything with the doctrine of the sanctifying word—he was brought to see more conveniently the mistress of the world. For who, receiving the governing power of the world, could be permitted to ignore what Rome had approved?

Aristarchus, his fellow-prisoner, accompanies him as he goes, as does Luke the Antiochene, a physician of the body, but even more so of the mind. Paul travels with these companions through the greatest dangers; he is regarded as guardian of the guards and leader of the led.

At last he enters the city of the lofty summit,

[Col. 0601B] cleanses the stains of his chains, and is rescued from the lion’s mouth. Again he spreads the pious gifts of Christ.

But Nero, sated with the teaching of the Samaritan, gradually advanced toward greater crimes. After his unspeakable attempts against his wretched mother; his incest and the unmentionable assaults against his sister; after the burning of the City, the tyrant’s joyous spectacles, and the dreadful, disgraceful plundering of what the fire had left; after the throats of senators and the rich spoils of the senate; after the plunder of the forum’s loans; after the death of the equestrian order; after much bloodshed among kinsmen and associates—his brother, sister, wife, and wretched parent—he strove to increase this heap of crimes, seeking greater things, and was the first at Rome to undertake bloody warfare against heaven,

[Col. 0601C] the first there to torture, with punishments, throughout the fatherland, the saints who shone with the devotion of Christ. Preparing to eradicate entirely the holy name taken from the Lord’s name, he thrust the foremost fathers of this name into the Mamertine prison and savagely attacked the entire flock.

Although the lights of heaven may dwell hidden in the body, the heavenly radiance cannot be confined in an airy prison. Indeed, just as a lighthouse gives the shore to ships wandering over the sea, the holy men send forth splendid rays and provide a course for those seeking to enter the harbor through raging waves.

Wherever they see the tranquil brightness shining, they hurry there and leave the dark recesses of the men;

[Col. 0602A] they flee the shipwreck of the mind and seize the harbor.

The saints illuminate the peoples; burning with the warmth of the life-giving Spirit, they show that they can leave the vast darkness, recognize the true light, and lay aside the stains of the soul in divine waters.

The peoples rejoice to be watered by the heavenly fountain, and seek to have the contagions of their wounded souls cleansed. But the waters for cleansing are denied by the savage guardian.

The leading men, anxious to increase the profits of souls, approach the king and strive to address prayers to heaven.

But Christ, the giver of the water and of both laws, wishing to show himself the heir of the ancient law—he who gave the commandments to Moses and gave commandments to the fathers of the Church—who recently, in the dry countryside, brought water from a rock for the crowd needing the comfort of a drink,

[Col. 0602B] and removed their thirst, pours forth here also, for the parched people asking for the streams of heaven, abundant waters from the Tarpeian rock, so that those who do not doubt may know that God can do this also, producing hard, rushing springs from an unexpected source.

The fathers provide pious gifts to the children of the miracle. While they wash their bodies in waters bestowed by divine generosity, they cleanse their minds with sanctifying purification and enrich them with the fruitful pledge of the holy Spirit.

Processus is then washed together with Martinianus. They, teachers of the corruptly transmitted *animaelli principis*, go to the camp, beholding the miracles which the Lord Jesus performed there through the leading men, healing the sick and triumphing over the demon’s weapons.

But the savage man, who thought that the broad streams of God were closed off by the obstructed fountains,

[Col. 0602C] discovered that abundant rivers were flowing forth and that the sheep rejoiced in the health-giving water. Burning with envy of every goodness and of all justice, which cuts away vices with dreadful punishments, he saw holiness being born, virtue rising, and good fortune flourishing. Inflamed by black torches kindled in the burned-out Acheron, he raged to slaughter innocent flocks and overthrow companies everywhere; he massacred the guiltless.

Then, after forty-seven had been cleansed of their sins, with Peter as the guide of their virtues, he ordered these men likewise to be cut down. True confession joined them to the faith; the gifts of the bath joined them together; the honor of martyrdom and the glory of the palm united them.

## CHAPTER II. On Saint Torpes

[Col. 0601]

[Col. 0601C] Torpes shone with distinguished honor in the tyrant’s service. The divine hero Antonius instructed him, consecrating him in the holy fountain; Antonius, learned in the doctrine of the apostolic word as a presbyter, openly proclaimed Christ.

[Col. 0601D] When Nero learned that Torpes had embraced the sacred rites, he handed him over to a butcher to be forced to the profane temples. Since, fixed in faith, he could not be compelled to wickedness, Nero, furious unto death, ordered him, after a soldier’s resounding slap, to be bound to a huge and lofty column and assailed with repeated blows. As blood was drawn from his body in drops, a dreadful rain drenched the earth.

The cruel crime caused terror, and suddenly the column fell, crushing the savage censor and forty companions alike. Afterwards the father’s surviving son imposed revolving tortures upon the distinguished victor, contrived his death, and offered him to savage beasts. The fury abated beyond expectation: he was preserved by divine honor, and the beasts trembled to touch with their teeth the man whom a more savage human being had torn with a beast’s mouth.

[Col. 0602C] Seeing his virtue, Evellius, one of Nero’s advisers, despite the harsh law of the tyrant’s supporters, received the faith of Christ in his heart. Washed in baptism, he was crowned with the honor of light not long afterward, and later obtained heaven at Rome at the price of his neck.

But Silvius, the wicked heir of the father, ordered the Lord’s holy Torpes to be led outside the city of Pisa and commanded that he be struck with a dreadful sword. The martyr rejoiced that he had received a crown through his throat.

The savage lictor and the minister of crime placed the holy body in a boat worn out by decay and shipworm, together with a parricidal dog and a bird, giving it to be sunk beneath the swift river’s glassy waters.

[Col. 0604A] A resident of the heavenly court, the matron Celenina, was soon sent instructions to seek the pious limbs of the martyr, raise them, and lay them in their place. Celerina hastened to accomplish this: she entrusted the venerable body to a clean sarcophagus and arranged a basilica above it with pleasing adornment.

Felix of Nuceria and Constantia suffered at that time, along with many others in various regions of the world.

## CHAPTER III. On the Passion of the Apostles Peter and Paul

[Col. 0603]

[Col. 0603A] After many saints had been admitted to the joys of heaven, and companies stood ready to follow the royal standards, arranged in camps and accustomed to conquer wars; after battles had been fought everywhere with mighty labor; after the worthy insignia of the victorious and deserving palm; after peoples, cities, nations, and kingdoms had been subdued; after the yokes of the heavenly King had been placed upon the necks of nobles—the King himself called the leaders to their scepters and pressed the bold tyrant with the punishment he deserved.

At last the fathers were ordered to leave the prisons and, by an unjust command, to be led to the deadly walls, after Titan had nine times filled the bounds of the world, while they had remained at the threshold—[the transmitted reference to Paulinus is syntactically uncertain].

The guards, who, after seeing the wonders, had submitted their hearts to the holy faith, and all the companions, magnificently urged Peter to avoid death, preserve himself cautiously, and withdraw as a free man. They joined tears to their prayers and complained that the children would lose their father when he was killed, that the flocks would be scattered, and that the sheepfold would be left empty.

Overcome by these tears, the merciful shepherd was bent and yielded; compelled by compassion, he attempted escape. He had already stepped out at night through the open doors when, seeing Christ come toward him, he trembled and, recalling his courage, spoke in worship:

“Where are you going, Lord?”

“To Rome,” he replied, “to be crucified.”

“Again,” he said, “you will suffer the torments of the cross, Redeemer.”

“Again,” he answered, returning to his seat above the heavens.

Thus the old man, fixing his eyes in the world’s darkness, passed through the airy winds with his mind following after, and eagerly said: “I shall follow you, good shepherd.”

He returned and joyfully recounted everything in order. He comforted his companions; while all were mourning, he alone rejoiced, restoring his companions through the consolation of the word and strengthening them with a mighty defense in the faith of Christ.

While the pious shepherd provided pious pasture, he was snatched from the midst of the grieving band of companions, and with excessive groaning bearing witness to the sorrow of his heart. He was compelled, accused, and remained unconquerable—that father under whose rule they had happily rejoiced for twenty-five years.

[Col. 0603D] He exalted the honor of the cross, standing unmoved, like Olympus resisting every blast. The prince, whose honor is so greatly commended, was ordered to endure the punishment of the cross undefeated.

[Col. 0604A] He is led to the kingdom after he had utterly defeated and cast down into the depths of Phlegethon the enemy who threatened the lands and, by attempting heaven, enticed hearts, striking against his worn limbs and overthrowing him. By prayers and knees fixed upon the marble he cast him down from heaven; the mark of Peter’s body, pressed into the stone, is still visible in the open cave where he leaned.

The waters that fill it drive away diseases through their healing power and give the sick pleasant gifts of strength when they drink.

As the hero is led to follow Christ in death, he declares, with his spirit leaping up, that it is unworthy for him to be exalted in the same honor in which the Lord suffered—he who, coming from heaven, drew all things toward the heavenly realm, yet fashioned himself as an earthly nursling born of the earth alone.

[Col. 0604B] Therefore his cross should incline its head toward earthly things and show him to be earthly, revealing that heaven must be sought only with the neck subjected in this way.

Without delay the triumph of the cross is turned by the lictor. His feet are fixed above, seeking the path of heavenly light; and the palms, embracing the lowest and nearest parts of the earth, gather up earthly things to be carried above the stars.

From his punishment he addresses the crowds gathered around him. Cheerful while all weep, he comforts the panting; calm, he calls the sorrowful to divine joys. He renders outstanding thanks to Christ as a gift for the people, entrusting to him the sheep who offer their vows and asking that above the heavens he grant them pastures.

Then, amid admonitions, conversations of life, vows and prayers, and the most sacred words,

[Col. 0604C] he sends his soul, intent upon heaven, to the heavenly realms.

His pious disciples and fellow citizens, and the holy ministers—especially Marcellus, who was his faithful nursling—fulfill the duties of devotion after he was taken down from the cross. They arrange the funeral and honor him with abundant spices.

The most holy limbs of the Father, triumphant over all the kingdoms of the world, are buried together beside the triumphal road in the Vatican, with celebrated honor.

But the teacher, leader, and master of the Benjamites, after generously sprinkling the West with the discourse of faith and filling the East with teaching, is ordered by the butcher to be punished with his neck cut off. Offering his head for the divine King, he is beheaded in the world’s citadel for the holy light of the world, together with three soldiers who suffered their final fate alongside him.

[Col. 0604D] It is said that milk flowed from his severed throat—surely because he had nourished the lambs of faith with milk.

The veteran leaders are likewise raised from the world’s highest summit to the heights of the starry seat, and carry precious spoils before their King,

[Col. 0605A] from whom they receive the insignia of eternal glory.

It is reported that certain companions came from the Eastern region to Ausonia to bring back their dearest remains and provide appropriate care for their own tribesmen. While they were carrying the gifts, almost two thousand men seized them. But the boldness of the one who lingered beneath the path of the Catacombs demonstrated the lofty power of immense Christ, who was establishing the supreme city with its principal patrons so that from there they might bring consolation to the whole world, and so that the whole world might seek them in the world’s capital.

[Col. 0606A] Suddenly they were terrified by the force of thunder and the fire of lightning; they scattered and abandoned their attempt.

The citizens of Romulus, proved perhaps worthy, who had deserved to follow such splendor, raised up, embraced, and recovered the pledges that had been snatched away from them—the richest treasures of the entire world.

From that point they took possession of places in which they might be preserved as they wished, and from which they are reverently sought by the whole world. Joined to the Lord and seated above the stars of heaven, they arrange illustrious laws for the world laid beneath them.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Saints Processus, Martinianus, and Luciana

[Col. 0605]

[Col. 0605A] After the fathers had been driven away, the tyrant brandished his weapons throughout the flock of the children of God and labored to remove this race from its foundation, descended from the lofty origin of heaven, whose authority he saw spreading through himself and his followers. For a long time Paulinus, proud of empty nobility, had thrust Processus and Martinianus into chains.

When he heard them speaking the name of God with strength, he ordered their mouths, which proclaimed steadfast faith, to be crushed with stones. But they raised praises above the heavens.

A golden tripod belonging to Jupiter was brought before them; they spat upon the tripod and Jupiter with spittle. Suspended and stretched by their sinews, they were beaten with heavy clubs, while ravenous flames were kindled against their sides.

The renowned woman Lucina was present and urged the athletes, strong in battle, to persevere.

Afterward he again had them hung up and tore them apart, piercing their entrails with the sharp weapons of a scorpion. When they had again been thrust into prison, Lucina ministered to them.

[Col. 0605C] After three days Paulinus, dulled and seized by a demon, tortured and killed, was submerged in Lethean waters.

The prefect of the City reported this to the enemy of virtue. He ordered the saints of the clergy to be struck down with a dagger. Lucina received them, struck down by the sword upon the Via Aurelia.

The Almighty adorned their souls with the splendor of heaven; caring for their bodies in her own countryside and mixing in spices,

[Col. 0606A] Lucina received them and reverently honored them with pious worship.

The miracles performed for the buried testify to the glory that awaits them: the sick are freed from plague; the perjured are seized by demons; those bound by a savage enemy are released by the light of the saints.

[Col. 0606B] They reveal themselves in person to those who seek them in their circumstances, and sometimes appear visibly in the flesh.

A matron accustomed to visiting the holy tombs proves these words. Seeing monks attending in foreign attire, while she prepares to carry something, she herself receives relief. Confident in the promised help, she becomes more worthy through her deed.

To her it was granted to know that life would come rather than merely to believe it. With a thirsty heart she absorbed apostolic teachings, was instructed and consecrated in the holy bath, and burned to share in the righteous persons’ needy services, supplying support for their work. She gave relief to those suffering in chains and prisons, and lifted their torments.

With celebrated custom she devotedly tended the tombs. Therefore she deserved to be crowned, joined to the merits of the righteous, following the saints by a precious death. Confession of Christ and the outstanding work of faith, which she had joined to the Lord’s service, granted her entry into the kingdom.

A crypt, constructed to house the bodies of the blessed, received her funeral, arranged through her devoted care and joined to the sacred relics, adorning it with relics and uniting sacred pledges to sacred things.

## CHAPTER V. On the Saints Nazarius and Celsus

[Col. 0605]

[Col. 0605C] This madness is also said to have carried the Milanese saints—Nazarius, born to distinguished parents for Christ, and the boy Celsus, whom Nazarius himself worthily nurtured—from the savagery of death to the kingdoms of heaven.

Peter washed Nazarius’ mother Perpetua in the nourishing stream;

[Col. 0605D] holy Clement purified Nazarius in the fountain.

The savage Anolinus tortured Nazarius and afflicted him, together with the saint, his companion, with the long squalor of a dark prison; at last he slaughtered him with a cruel sword, though he had earned his rest.

Faithful men secretly carried away the devoted limbs and buried them outside the gate called the Roman Gate, in their own gardens, at the saints’ own direction. Acetarius, who was deemed worthy for this purpose, was illuminated by lofty visions, and his wife was Fortunata. The witnesses soon revealed to him the bodies of the slain and ordered him to lift them and hide them from the savage fury.

[Col. 0606C] Thus it was decided that they should remain hidden until, after the passing of many years, under Arcadius, the pious bishop Ambrose, to whom the Lord had revealed these things, lifted the holy gifts.

Then, after the long course of the sun had passed over Nazarius, when the tomb was finally exposed after the earth had been removed,

[Col. 0606D] the blood lay so tender and fresh with the body that it seemed to have been poured out on that very day when the sword opened the throat. The head was found unharmed and untouched by worms. The beard, combed after it had been raised, and the hair, washed and arranged, shone as though it had been set in order at that same moment.

A nectar-like fragrance exhaled so strongly that it surpassed the entire mass of an aromatic harvest heaped up with its buds. These signs revealed that he had borne the breath of Christ.

They also found the companion’s childish remains. They carried them on a bier and reverently placed them in a church dedicated under the ceremonial honor of apostolic law.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Vengeance of Nero’s Persecution

[Col. 0607]

[Col. 0607A] When the blood of the innocent saints had been unjustly shed, divine vengeance struck the guilty with a deserved judgment. It did not sit delayed, postponing matters for a long time, lest that savage wolf wound the tender lambs, and lest the dreadful destroyer tear up the plantings whose roots were not yet sufficiently strengthened.

While the saints were crowned with light, the wicked were condemned.

A plague arose everywhere, and vengeance wearied the City, carrying heavenly weapons. The clear air was corrupted; a pestilence arose unequalled even by the water-snakes, destroying bodies dissolved by slow poison. A pestilential breeze fell, and the fields and the lofty Cyclopean buildings were scorched beneath a covering of clouds.

The guilty souls perished; death overcame thirty thousand living persons. Libitina dedicated towns to herself. Some communities observing Roman laws were worn down by disasters and the excessive horror of slaughter.

The state lost the great native lands of Armenia. Roman legions sent beneath Parthian yokes were destroyed. An earthquake overthrew certain cities of Asia.

Nor did punishment pursue the tyrant with an especially slow step. Nero learned that Galba, in Spain, had assumed the royal diadem with the support of soldiers. He despised him and, dark in all his heart, turned toward Tartarus. While he revolved the incredible disaster of exile in relation to affairs and senators, he was convicted as an enemy of his country. The populace announced this and rejoiced that the senate had decreed it.

Terrified by fear, and having shamefully slipped away from the City, fleeing disgracefully with deep dishonor, while he feared confinement and payment of the punishments he deserved,

[Col. 0607C] he completed the remainder of his crimes and, hurrying beneath the shadows, pierced himself with a sword he had chosen for the purpose. As the origin of the Caesarean race slipped away, he himself tottered and fell.

Soon Galba arrived. When he learned of the wicked man’s death, he injured the Quirites through avarice and shameful sluggishness.

At last, after six months of rule, Galba was killed by Otho, with Piso—whom he had received as both heir to the throne and adopted son—also perishing. [The transmitted wording in this line is corrupt.] Rome paid for the impious slaughter of Christ’s leading servants through the deaths of its own nobles.

The city that had punished its foremost and most savage worshipers of the gods was itself punished through the slaughter of new kings. The weapons that, at Peter’s arrival, had been divinely rendered inert—those weapons threatening civil crime and held in check—were released, with the saints afflicted by punishment and the fathers murdered; their restraints were permitted to run loose in the open world, as winds stirred from different blows strike the air.

Indeed, Spain immediately produced Galba. When he was crushed, Otho rose and bloodied Rome. Vitellius emerged among the Germans and Gauls; Vespasian soon took up the scepters in Syria. All of them simultaneously raged through their commands and arms.

The blood of the saints was repaid by Roman blood, and the life-giving blood was cleansed by the advancing bloodshed.

[Col. 0608B] This had once been shown when Egypt was perishing: the waters were turned to blood when the first furious presumption against God was smitten upon the people by the first scourge.

But the Lord provided consolation for his servants, then struck by the whirlwind, pressing down so many wars of destruction. He did not allow these disturbances to wander for a long time through lands and waters; rather, he governed them so that they might easily be brought to an end in peace.

Otho brought his rule to an end in the third month. Refusing to be conquered, he pierced himself with his own sword.

Victorious, Vitellius resisted and entered the City. But when he grew weary of human lives through gluttony and his own excesses (sic), and learned that Vespasian was raising the fasces, he wished to lay down the reins of the authority he had assumed.

Thereupon, encouraged to this end, he burned and killed Sabinus, the brother of Vespasian, together with his companions in blood,

[Col. 0608C] whom he forced to burn in the Capitoline furnace.

Afterward, abandoned by the army and deserted by hope, he was dragged painfully from the confinement of his cell. Naked, with a rush of filth, he was hauled into the forum. After he had burdened the kingdom with his vices for eight months, he died beneath repeated blows, his flesh torn apart, and was dragged by a hook into the waters of the Tiber.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Rule of Vespasian and Titus

[Col. 0607]

Once the storm of the tyrants had been scattered like a cloud of tempest, under the mild prince Vespasian, the whirlwind calmed, and the world’s serenity returned.

The kingdom was quieted, and its enemies were punished. He who had dispersed the enemies of the heavenly power, and who wages war through the Son against the enemies of God’s Son, triumphs over kingdoms through the Lord’s Son together with his own son.

Although he did not know through whom such things were being given to him, he saw that such great deeds were being accomplished for him by a power from above,

[Col. 0607D] with his own Titus assisting—not Titus’ own battles, but battles which the Ruler of the world was waging through him against the wicked.

Thus, in triumph they attained the unprecedented honor that their triumph should be celebrated through all succeeding ages:

[Note: [Col. 0607D] After Jerusalem had been conquered, Vespasian and Titus celebrated a triumph, something previously unheard of.]

so that father and son might be carried in the same chariot

[Col. 0608C] and likewise be honored as triumphant throughout the world. In addition, honors were added to the lords.

[Note: [Col. 0608D] Thus both manuscripts.]

For two-faced Janus was shut up after the wars had been driven away, and thus peace was soon proclaimed throughout the whole world.

Thus the same honor might be reserved for Christ, vengeance having been taken on his enemies—an honor conferred on him long ago when he was born of the Virgin—and his kingdom grew immensely without the turmoil of war.

When Syria, Rhodes, Samos, all Achaea, Thrace, Commagene, and the lands of Byzantium had been subdued,

[Col. 0608D] they voluntarily accepted the Romans as their lords and their laws.

After Vespasian, his son Titus, peaceful, pious, and mild, ruled without bloodshed, and the world shone pacified through the virtues of Christ.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Linus and Cletus

[Col. 0609]

[Col. 0609A] After Peter, Linus arranged the great governance of the Church at Rome. The apostle Peter himself had consecrated him as pontiff, together with Cletus, by this authority, so that they might administer the sacred mysteries of the gift to the peoples.

Freed to devote himself lawfully to prayers and the word of salvation, he watched wholly over the increase of the pious people.

Here Linus enlightened the Church, following the examples of the excellent and blessed Father and teacher,

[Col. 0610A] and, crowned by martyrdom, departed above the stars.

The pious remains of Linus were joined to those of his pious teacher.

Thereafter Cletus, following him, governed Christ’s flock, solemnly presiding for twenty-two years after him, while Domitian, increasing the force of his crimes, moved the savage part of Nero against the Lord’s flock. Under him Cletus fulfilled his martyrdom and departed into heaven.

The blessed bones of Peter were placed together with his tomb.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Disciples of the Apostles and Saint Apollinaris

[Col. 0609]

[Col. 0609B] From this point, the blessed and glorious leaders are read to have appointed many bishops to proclaim the bright insignia of Christ, sending them to different regions of the world.

The following went forth to Gaul: Trophimus, Sabinianus, his companion Potentianus, Fronto with Georgius, Paulus, Martialis, and Valerius, as well as our Sixtus, Memmius, and Sinicius.

At the same time they were sent to Spain: Torquatus and Tesiphon, the second Esichius, Indalicius, Catilius, and Euphrasius.

Apollinaris, who had followed Peter from Antioch, was sent in this way to Ravenna. Coming from Troas, he stayed within the walls as the guest of the hospitable soldier Cyreneus.

His son, deprived of the honor of sight, he restored to vision through the sign of the cross, and consecrated the parents, washed in the holy fountain.

A certain matron, Thecla by name, the wife of a military tribune, had lain in extreme illness for many years. When the name of the healing Jesus was invoked, she was raised by his hand and restored to health.

Soon the tribune, his wife, and his children, and the entire household, were immersed in the waters of peace. In that house, divine baptisms were administered for twelve years with the faithful companions; Apollinaris washed the baptized and celebrated the sacred duties of the Mass.

[Col. 0609D] Then two noble men of equal rank were ordained there: Calocerus and Aderitus, both enriched by sacred rites and each made a presbyter of the divine court.

He appointed Martianus, most noble in the flesh, and Leucadius, distinguished in learning, as deacons of the heavenly altar, and fitted other men worthily to the clergy. With these men, singing by day and night, he resounded with hymns of heavenly glory.

This report disclosed him to an envious leading man, who seized him and assembled the pagan priests. The pious man was handed over to be sacrificed to savage powers; after being slaughtered, he was left half-alive and exposed as food for sea creatures and wild beasts.

The household members of the blessed school found him and did not delay to undertake care for their teacher.

[Col. 0610B] After six months had passed, at the house of the eminent and noble Bonifacius, whom a grievous illness had deprived of his charm, he came in order to restore speech; after driving a demon from a girl and loosening the hard bonds of her mute mouth, he prepared five hundred hearts for Christ on high.

After a short period he was seized by the pagans and long tormented with severe clubs. He stood naked with fire placed beneath his feet. But when he was conquered neither by fire nor by scourges, he triumphed over his punishments and was driven from the city as a victor.

Not far from the circuit of these walls, poor men possessed a hut of Christ.

[Col. 0610C] Here the holy man performs the divine mysteries, consecrating the vast blue waters in a holy washing for those who fear the pious Lord; in this place he is nourished by kindly consolation.

After remaining there for as many years as he wished, he continued to illuminate Emilia, relying upon the virtue of Christ and performing many signs.

Returning from there, he restored to life Rufus’ daughter, who had died, and then returned children to bereaved parents.

Showing himself a perfect foster-child of Truth, he raised many souls from death and made them children of God through consecration. For at that time he gave a heavenly father three hundred and four children of both sexes.

[Col. 0610D] Rufus, endowed with patrician dignity, he consecrated as a servant of Christ with a bowed heart, by whom wealthy Capua became richer through a martyr.

He washed the girl’s mother in the sacred fountain, and dedicated the girl herself, snatched from the jaws of monstrous Orcus, as a blessed virgin to Christ, strengthening her to remain steadfast.

The deeds of Rufus were reported to Caesar. But Caesar immediately appointed a successor for Apollinaris and wrote, ordering his deputy either to dissuade Apollinaris or to banish him far from the territory of Ravenna.

The deputy summoned the man appointed for this task, beat him with threats, and, seeing that he could not be moved, stripped him of his clothing and scourged him with a beating of rods.

[Col. 0611A] Groaning that the savage blows were being despised with a resolute mind, he drenched the wounds with boiling water.

Then, after tormenting him while suspended, lacerating his face with stone, and loading him with the heaviest iron weight, he shut him in the depths of the most terrible prison and tortured him stretched upon wood, according to the harsh law.

Abandoned here without human consolation, he was fed with the nourishment of angels. And lest he be thought worthless in the sight of the Ruler of the stars, he partook publicly of angelic food.

Brought out from the dark prison on the fourth day beneath the sun, bound in chains, he was sent into exile.

Three clerics, voluntarily embarking in a boat, provided him with the help of their kindly provisions.

The waters, angered by these events and bearing the man’s injury with distress, were disturbed,

[Col. 0611B] preparing to punish the injustice. The fierce sea rose with its crest toward the stars, and the deep opened its lowest chasm.

Now the lofty ship split the clouds upon the waves; now, falling headlong, it struck the lowest rocks. When the structure of the ship came apart, it received the harsh enemy, swallowing the salty waters.

Through every crack furious death entered, separating the savage men from the glory of the righteous. It utterly overthrew them in vengeance, so that while they attempted to keep the blessed Father from his homeland, they alone might be excluded from every homeland.

They were submerged and devoured by the waves; but the pious were preserved in kindly fields.

[Col. 0611C] The just Judge knows how to free the righteous, and just judgment knows how to destroy the wicked, just as once he freed his servants from the Egyptian yoke, providing salvation to the fugitives through the deep waters and overwhelming their pursuers.

Apollinaris, with his helpful ministers, safely reached the desired shore. At the same time he delivered two companions to safety, men whom he tore from the waves bringing death and washed with waters that bestow the kingdoms of life.

From there he went forth and traversed the lands of the Isthmus. Then, passing through Corinth into Moesia, he adorned the ugly skin of a leper, covered with foul blemishes, with beauty and restored him to health.

[Col. 0611D] Adding still greater aid to the man whom he had saved in body, he also saved him in mind, cleansing it from the filth of pagan impurity and washing his soul through the cleansing of the body.

Moving down to the bank of the Ister, he joined many to himself, strengthened in the nourishing faith. When unbelievers desired to kill him, he took possession of the regions of Thrace through preaching.

While he remained there, the demons were terrified. Serapis, in his presence, fell silent and could not give answers to those who asked.

At last the spirit, summoned for this purpose, roared:

“This disciple of Peter, the apostle of Christ, has come into these lands and binds me with chains. Unless you take care to drive him far away from here,

[Col. 0612A] we shall not be able to give you answers.”

The saint was sought out to be handed over to scourging; when found, he was beaten with harsh clubs.

But when Christ judged that he should return the man to the city assigned to him by the province’s authority, he was placed on a ship bound for Italy, with all his companions gathered around him.

Thus spreading the divine seeds everywhere, he returned to Ravenna in the third year.

A few days later, when a disturbance arose and the profane rushed forward violently, he was led in chains into the forum.

There he was beaten and suffered bloody wounds. He endured the proud priests of the Capitol urging him toward the sacrifices of Apollo.

[Col. 0612B] When he was brought there, he immediately raised his prayers. He destroyed the images of Phoebus as they stood, shattered the false divinity, and showed it to be nothing.

And lest this be considered too little, all the walls of the shrine collapsed from their foundations and were scattered.

Seeing these things, the fanatics raised an uproar, angrily calling the old man impious because of this destruction. They demanded that he be punished by a savage death and handed him over to Taurus—this was the judge’s name.

Taurus’ son, blind from his mother’s womb, received light when Apollinaris invoked the exalted name of Christ and poured it into him. Many, astonished and reflecting on this new event, submitted their hearts to the truth.

The blessed man remained on Taurus the governor’s estate,

[Col. 0612C] six miles from the City, teaching the sacred doctrines for four years.

From there Christians came and drank in serenity the teachings of life. His virtue, tested through such great sufferings, grew, like spices or medicinal remedies, according to its nature, so richly that whatever illness had overcome a person, once brought to him, he restored to health.

But a deceitful report, originating with his enemies, reached Caesar, carrying false accusations against the blessed bishop. Caesar rashly declared that the man who brought insult to the gods with his challenging speech should either make satisfaction or be expelled from the city.

[Col. 0612D] This order was conveyed to Demosthenes, who was called “Father” in honor by the citizens—[the supplied source ends here, with the sentence incomplete].

The persecutor of the gentle in his cruelty—

He orders Apollinaris to be brought before him. Sensing that he is firmly bound by love for Christ, and considering by what torment he might destroy him, he entrusts the faithful man to a guard. Not suspecting that he is a Christian, he permits him—or rather compels him—to go free in the silence of the deepest night, so that he might teach him the glorious deeds of Christ.

But while the soldier, reviewing the remaining battles, asks whether he should now complete his victories, he lingers, passing the hours in delay, lest he be thought to have fled from the fights. The pagans who are pursuing him catch the man as he delays and beat him, mangling him with blows.

Thinking him dead amid the harsh scourging, they leave him; secretly, the ministers gather him up and carry him to a certain estate. He survives for seven days, continually warning the faithful not to depart from the faith and instructing them with heavenly utterances. Thus, adorned with the glory and praise of Christ,

[Col. 0614A] and foretelling the battles and triumphs to come, Apollinaris completes his glorious course.

The blessed body is received by the earth and enclosed beneath a stone sarcophagus outside the walls of Ravenna—the city which, sent here from the city of Rome by the prince of the Apostles, the pontiff ruled.

After presiding for twice ten and four years, having suffered under King Vespasian, he ascends to heaven at last in praise of the truth.

## The Chapters of the Second Book Begin

[Col. 0613]

[Col. 0613A]

I. On Saint Clement.  
II. On Saint John the Apostle.  
III. On the confession of Christ’s relatives before Domitian.  
IV. On the vengeance of the second persecution.  
V. On the return of Saint John the Evangelist.  
VI. On the exile of the saints Nereus and Achilleus.  
VII. The account of Saint Marcellus concerning the miracles of Saint Peter.  
VIII. On Saint Petronilla.  
IX. On Saint Felicula.  
X. On Saint Nicomedes.  
XI. On the martyrdom of the saints Nereus and Achilleus.  
XII. On the saints Eutyches, Victorinus, and Severinus.  
XIII. On Saint Domitilla, and also on Marcellus and Apuleius, Sulpitius, and Servilianus.  
XIV. On the teaching, miracles, and passion of Saint Clement.

## The Second Book Begins

[Col. 0613]

### Chapter One: On Saint Clement

[Col. 0613B]

The heavenly gatekeeper, relying on divine governance, carefully laying the firm foundations of the lofty hall [Note: [Col. 0613] The codex of Sainte-Geneviève omits the following verses down to “I know that you are weary,” etc.], perceives that the appointed time is drawing near its limit, that the starry path is approaching, and that heaven is opening. Standing in the midst of the Church, with a crowd surrounding him, and holding Clement’s hand, he thus begins his speech:

> “My fellow servants and brothers, receive my words. Since I have been forewarned, and see that the time of my own reward is now at hand, Christ my teacher showing it to me, I hand over to you this Clement as supreme pontiff in due succession. He was present with me at the beginning of all my undertakings; he received my teachings exactly, readily obedient to what was good. Every trial recognized him as sharing my lot; I found him steadfast, faithful, and worshiping God,
>
> [Col. 0613C] more than the others loving his brothers through his devotion, eager to learn, chaste, pious, and restrained; upright in justice, knowing how to endure patiently the foolish chatter and empty babbling of foolish tongues, and able to compose the hearts of those who learn according to a worthy order.
>
> “To him I entrust the authority which he has shown to have been conferred by the Lord himself: to bind or to loose. May his steadfast judgment remain above the stars. For he will bind what ought to be bound, and at the same time absolve what ought rightly to be released, according to the Church’s clearly known rule.
>
> “Therefore, fearing to sin against Christ, obey him. Whoever is troublesome to the teacher loses life, because he provokes the Father of peace. But he should conduct himself in the place of a physician, not be moved against his subjects with the ferocity of a beast.”

[Col. 0614B]

Fearing such exalted footsteps, Clement approaches him, excusing himself from so great a burden of honor. The elder says to him:

> “Do not plead with me about these matters. Since they have been decreed in this way, you will rather appear worthy of the very thing you wish to avoid. For this chair does not seek someone who volunteers for it; it seeks one who follows the man withdrawing from it and is upright in character.
>
> “If someone better than you stood ready to take my place, if there were some assistant and minister equally diligent, if someone had mounted the summit of so lofty a doctrine and knew how to arrange the pattern of the Church in proper order, I would not force you to assume this office. For it is counted an empty concern to seek another when I have offered you to the Lord as the first-fruits of this people and this city.
>
> “Consider, moreover, that you who flee from taking the reins of the Church are like a ship facing high dangers. You may be sure that greater dangers of death stand before you: when the people of the Lord are placed, as it were, amid high waves, and you are able to help them, you flee, concerned only to seek your own advantage and refusing the common aid.
>
> [Col. 0614C] “If you are certain that great dangers await the people, do not hesitate to have me contend on your behalf in prayer. The more quickly you prepare to yield to me, the more quickly you will relieve me of such care and anguish.
>
> “I know that you are weary of enduring the proud insults of the unlearned crowd, the crude mouths of the untutored populace; nevertheless, I know that you endure them steadfastly and exceedingly well, seeing what rewards your patience holds for you.
>
> “But I want you to weigh with me, by a just reckoning, when Christ appears to need your labor more: now, while the enemy challenges his bride to battle, or when he has admitted her, victorious, to the lofty thrones, when every labor and every enemy will yield to the triumphant one. Who, possessing even the smallest measure of understanding, does not know that this is the time when the Lord requires holy struggles?
>
> “Therefore, embrace with your whole mind the battles that are arising, and undertake with utmost effort the serious tasks now before you. Strive to add ready assistance to those who are fighting, so that afterward, triumphing, you may receive great rewards after the battles.
>
> “Gladly, then, now undertake the office of the pontificate in my place, especially as one learned and the glory of this order, so that the salvation of the people may not waver through any fear, and so that through you the lambs whom we have won may be firmly established.”

He continues to set out the order by which the administration of the whole Church may be made clear and carefully observed: how the bishop should withdraw entirely from external affairs, giving himself wholly to the discipline of mind and to the word of salvation; what the presbyters should do, keeping watch with paternal love and striving to lead the people safely into heaven; what the rest of the clergy and the holy ministers should observe; what the laity should do; and what all should do in general.

When these arrangements had been made, he established Clement as a pontiff worthy of such governance, laying hands upon him and declaring him so. Before everyone, he put the redness of shame upon the face of the sacred man and compelled him to sit upon the apostolic chair. Then, with the people as witnesses, he entrusted and commended these matters to the pope. He sent the written account to James at Solima, asking him to reveal it after his own life had been surrendered, briefly indicating what sort of life Clement had received from his lips, who had been his companion, what teachings he had drawn from him, and what end had overtaken him there.

[Col. 0615C]

He affirmed that Clement would possess the greatest consolation of mind when he learned that a learned man, not lacking in holy law, had taken the place of the teacher and the chair of Peter.

Clement, obedient and fulfilling the teachings of the good master, delegated to the Lord’s brother the gracious commands which he had received from the magnificent Peter’s resounding mouth. Following the pattern of the learned and restrained Father, who wrote himself down as his companion and marked for heaven, he became all things to all people, so that he might save everyone.

He taught the Gentiles with clear reasoning how the deceptive error of the gods had crept into the people; from what source and by what deceit the human race had fallen; how, persuaded by a viper’s fraud, it clung to empty things. He testified that the people themselves could be freed through pardon and life if, abandoning idols, they prepared their hearts for Christ.

[Col. 0615D]
