He pleased the Jews by honoring the patriarchs, raising up the sacred law and the blessed fathers. He taught that they themselves, the race of the holy, would receive the first seats in heaven’s citadel, provided that they held fast to the sacred words of the prophets, completed in Christ.

He was especially beloved by Christians and in conduct was pleasing to everyone. He kept written lists of the needy and, as far as he could, provided them relief for life. He did not allow those who had been fed by Jewish or Gentile generosity to depart without food after seeking it through public streets.

[Col. 0616A]

He forbade those purified by the divine fountain to be stained by such things, and continually urged everyone to hasten to holy places. He formed those absent through his writings and those present through his speech.

Thus, supported by such teaching, he was pleasing to the people and to God. Yet the humble cannot cling to the proud, nor can the pious please the sacrilegious through sweetness.

Nevertheless, the courage of his mind remained undaunted, and with gentle devotion he repelled the terrors of the savage.

Therefore Clement placed the summit of the world beneath the honor of the Lord. He consecrated Domitilla, illustrious in her exalted blood, to Christ, taking her away from her bridegroom Aurelianus. For Nereus and Achilleus, eunuchs of the virgin, disciples of Peter and servants of Christ in every respect, approach Clement concerning these matters and speak as follows:

> “All the glory belongs to your mind, endowed by the Lord, because we learn that you rejoice not in the nobility of your parents but in descent from the heavenly Father.
>
> “Your own uncle Clement, although a consul in rank, was also your father’s brother by birth. His sister Plautilla purchased us when we were still small and tender in age, as the years passed.
>
> “When she eventually received the words that bestow life, she believed them from Peter’s mouth and was washed in the sacred bath. We too, together with her offspring Domitilla, were consecrated. This very year the lord Peter ascended to heaven as a martyr, and Plautilla piously departed from earthly life.
>
> “Domitilla, the bride of the illustrious Aurelianus, instructed by Cephas’s word through our mouth, heard salvation. Remaining a virgin through love of God, she deserves to attain the heavenly bridegroom, Christ, who rules forever,
>
> [Col. 0616C] and with whom she may enjoy delights and divine honor. Inspired by these and other words granted by God, she desires, through you, virgin, to receive the veil of her vow.”

Clement replies:

> “Behold, I see that the appointed time is approaching, since the call extends toward the martyr’s palm. Strive, Domitilla, to grasp this crown by this path.
>
> “But since by the Lord’s command we are bidden to despise those who kill us, let us despise those fierce in death, though lying under the same dominion of death as ourselves, ready to serve the King of everlasting life.”

Thus Clement, strong in mind and deed, betroths the bride of the first rank to the King as one destined to belong to him, consecrates her, and adorns her head, touched by piety, with a sacred garment.

The bridegroom, weighed down by love, asks for the virgin’s bridal chamber. She rejects his requests and remains firm in the strictness of her resolve.

[Col. 0616D]

He then attempts to harass the chaste girl through snares. Her nobility prevents him from using force; he then appeals to the emperor, but she cannot be overcome even through the emperor.

Domitianus decrees the virgin’s exile. Rejected by her, and especially abhorring her contempt for the sacred, he is believed to have thought that she could be recalled from her holy purpose only by exile. Pontia, the place assigned for her exile, is ennobled by this event. The distinguished eunuchs accompany their mistress as she departs.

### Chapter Two: On Saint John the Evangelist

[Col. 0615]

[Col. 0615D]

He also thrust many distinguished and famous men into various hidden places and killed them with the sword—this swollen prince, without any judge to restrain him.

[Col. 0616D]

Moreover, he undertakes Nero’s criminal beginnings: an unspeakable war against God, declaring battle against the Lord of heaven and slaughtering the saints. He searches for the protectors of the pious people, and, after learning that the governance of the faith remained with John, the wicked man seeks him alone as the pillar of the Church, so that he might destroy the great company of the prince’s companions.

John is therefore led from Ephesus to Rome and, while the Senate watches, is placed inside a full cauldron of boiling oil. But he emerges unharmed, already free from the fire, a witness of his integrity, showing how he shone in celibacy and freedom from every lust.

Having triumphed over the fire, he is driven into exile from the land. The island of Patmos receives him, cast upon its sandy shore.

Here the Author of the world does not abandon the exile from the world. He visits the banished man and discloses the secrets of heaven; in a glorious vision he consoles his stricken friend and, beneath an enigmatic covering, marks out the Church’s battles and the palms of its triumphs.

Afterward, in honor of the apostolic steadfastness of his faith, where he overcame the fires of the gleaming oil, the devout built a basilica before the Latin Gate. The generation of the Saint crowned it with a splendid work; from this event too a festival day is renewed with fitting honor.

### Chapter Three: On the Confession of Christ’s Relatives before Domitian

[Col. 0617]

[Col. 0617A]

The savage beast, meditating on raising himself beyond humanity, orders that Domitianus be worshiped as Lord and God. He rages with envy against Christ; believing the holy prophets, he fears that someone is still to be born from the Davidic line who will rule with scepters. He ruthlessly tracks David’s descendants and orders them to be sought out and killed amid impious tortures. The tyrant’s inquiry becomes cruel.

At that time certain descendants of Jude happened to remain. They too, being reported as related to Christ in the flesh, are brought before the king. He asks whether they are descended from David’s blood. They declare that they are. He asks how great their resources are.

[Col. 0618A]

They answer that they are poor. He asks: “How rich are Christ’s kingdoms?”

[Col. 0618B]

He himself asks who this Christ is, when he will come, and from where he will arise.

They explain that Christ’s kingdom does not consist of earthly heights to be seized for himself; rather, the heavenly scepters remain with God on high. Angelic ministers obey him. His kingdom is established at the threshold of the age, when he will come, supported by divine honor, to judge the living and those subjected to the law of death, repaying each according to his merits with what is fitting.

The swollen ruler despises them, since their persons are clothed in poverty. Not deigning to punish them, he allows them to depart.

Sent away, the courageous men proclaim the sublime message, and afterward live as leaders of the Church in peace.

### Chapter Four: On the Vengeance of the Second Persecution

[Col. 0617]

[Col. 0617C]

Domitianus, who had removed many Christians from their own lands, turns the cruel decrees of his judgment against their supporters. They are driven out by the very soldiers by whom the armies of heaven had been accustomed to be driven out.

They creep into and penetrate houses, assault their masters, and drive them from their own inner rooms. They are like the frogs of Egypt, which once, in the second plague, searched through the people’s houses in their devastation, driving out the insolent under the miserable law of vengeance.

Domitianus, the worst and most savage enemy of everyone, is killed by his own servants and faithful attendants. The cruel man is cruelly deprived of life; carried out on a bier by undertakers, he is shamefully thrown into a pit and sunk into a common burial urn.

### Chapter Five: On the Return of Saint John the Apostle

[Col. 0617]

[Col. 0617C]

After him, the aged Nerva adopts the chosen Trajan and makes him his associate in imperial honors. The acts of his predecessor are annulled, and the exiles are recalled. Thus John, released from exile by great mercy,

[Col. 0618C] returns and resumes the chair of teaching at Ephesus.

[Note: [Col. 0617D] The first hand of the codex reads *gentilium*; corrected to *ab exsilio* (“from exile”).]

### Chapter Six: On the Exile of the Saints Nereus and Achilleus

[Col. 0617]

[Col. 0617D]

The athletes of Christ, Domitilla’s instructors for the battle, are given hospitality by Pontia. While they seek to learn what sort of land it is, what faith it possesses, and what sort of inhabitants it has, they discover what battles the hospitable land bears for pious men.

For some pupils of Simon’s school are found there. By profane arts they have nearly overturned the native population, displaying false signs and figures through [an uncertain word: *atracias*], and deceiving them by representing their master as begotten by God the Father. Instead of the Son of God, they persuaded them to worship Simon.

While the saints refute them through their powerful virtue, they ask the people, supported by the assembled crowds:

> “Do you know Marcellus, born of Marcus, the prefect of the city?”

“Who here does not know him?” they reply.

> “Do you attribute greater faith to Peter or to Simon, according to their renown?”

“Only one exceedingly rigid would refuse to believe in a person so great and so distinguished by blood,” they answer.

The saints say:

> “At least do this much for your own salvation: until our letter is received and carried about, turn your minds away from the teaching of these men. First let our letter be read to you, so that each of you may carry it from here wherever you go. Let his counsels and yours be read aloud.”

Everyone approves this. The saints immediately write the following:

> “We, the servants of Christ Jesus, Nereus and Achilleus, send everlasting greetings to our fellow disciple Marcellus.
>
> “When Pontic prisons confined us as exiles, we rejoiced in the Lord’s name that we had suffered such things. But the joys of the disciples of Simon weary us: Furius and Priscus, exiles because of their teacher’s fraud, insist that Simon lived innocently and that Peter persecuted him with unjust hatred.
>
> [Col. 0620A] “Since we resisted them so that no one might believe them, we have established through certain reports that you are worthy to be informed about these matters. You can instruct them according to your own experience, once you yourself have examined his life more thoroughly, since you were his disciple and learned all his deeds.
>
> “We ask you not to be reluctant to write to them and bring forth the truth . . . so that the innocent may be freed from their errors.”

### Chapter Seven: Marcellus’s Account of the Miracles of Saint Peter

[Col. 0619]

[Col. 0619A]

The diligent Marcellus replies to these matters as follows:

> “May the pious grace of the life-giving Lord Jesus be with you.
>
> “Marcellus, servant of Christ through the merciful will of Christ, rejoices in reading your pious joys, Nereus and Achilleus, holy heralds, in your letters.
>
> [Col. 0619B] “I perceive that you are steadfast in body and speech, and that you are earnestly persisting in a good struggle for the truth. But because you describe Simon as perhaps innocent, I will confess something concerning him, at least in part, so that the wise may weigh the great matters from a few.
>
> “It once happened that I was his follower. But when I had proved him to be an impostor, a magician, wicked in every respect, and a murderer of children, I abandoned him and embraced Peter’s way, adhering to it.
>
> “While this Samaritan was calling Peter a Zoroastrian and kindling the people’s minds against him, behold, as the wicked man was pursuing his deceit, Peter was passing by, surrounded by a great crowd, and encountered a woman lamenting with bitter tears: her only son had died, leaving his mother a desolate widow, worn down by this double bereavement.
>
> “Cephas addresses the friends accustomed to Simon:
>
> > ‘Go, men, uncover the present corpse from the bier, and thus test the faith: whether death, ready to listen, will return its prey and send him back from the unwilling chambers.’
>
> “At these words the Magician rises, exceedingly proud, and says:
>
> > ‘If I release this man from the bonds of death, will you not kill this Peter of ours? At once,’ the crowd roars, ‘we will burn the living enemy in black flames.’
>
> “He invokes ministers skilled in deception, and, moved by [an uncertain word, *atracio*] service, shakes the limbs. At this sight the people begin to praise Simon and, in their foolish tumult, rage for Peter’s destruction.
>
> [Col. 0619D] “But the steadfast elder, when the crowd had scarcely been pacified, says:
>
> > ‘If he burns with renewed heat and is alive, let him speak, walk, eat, and return to his own home. But if he cannot do these things, recognize that you have been deceived by his art.’
>
> “The crowd applauds, its mind agreeing, and declares that otherwise Simon should be wearied by Peter’s torments.
>
> “The madman, pretending anger, looks for a way to hide. He withdraws in flight, is captured, and is held in disgrace. He remains terrified until Peter speaks these words, stretching his hands toward heaven:
>
> > ‘Lord Jesus, ruler, who gave these commands to us, your own disciples: in my name go forth; drive away Satan’s deceits; heal the sick; restore corpses to life. Return this boy to us, so that all this people may recognize that you alone are Lord and God,
>
> [Col. 0620A] > who, living with your Father and the holy [Spirit—printed *Fiamine*, uncertain], hold the kingdoms of life and reign throughout all ages.’
>
> “At these prayers the black one is brought back from the Stygian shadows. Rising, he worships Peter’s feet and says:
>
> > ‘I saw the Lord Jesus commanding his heavenly ministers concerning me and giving them these orders: for the prayers of Peter, our steadfast friend, let this only son be restored to his widowed mother.’
>
> “A sound of voices rises to heaven, with the men crying out:
>
> > ‘This is the only God whom Peter’s deeds proclaim.’
>
> “The informer is distressed, wearing a dog’s head [the text is uncertain], and seeks escape. The crowd follows with shouting, seizes him, and prepares fire as an avenger.
>
> “Cephas hurries to calm the fierce tumult, restraining it and soothing their minds with these words:
>
> > ‘Our teacher taught us to live patiently and not to repay evils with evils, but to return gentleness to the savage.’
>
> “Sprinkled with this salt, they pitied the dreadful dog. Freed by Peter’s goodness but bound by a demon, he attacks me, thinking that I do not know what had been revealed. He overcomes the huge dog, scarcely following in iron chains, at the entrance, saying:
>
> > ‘Let us see whether Peter, who is accustomed to summon you here, will be able to enter.’
>
> “But when Peter arrived, without delaying long, he released the iron bonds from the beast at the sign of the cross and imposed upon the dog commands to be carried to the dog’s master, so that, having been deprived of reason, he might rebuke him with the words he deserved.
>
> “Go willingly, and bring these words to the maddened Simon:
>
> > ‘Stop deceiving the people with demonic fraud, for whom the life-giving stream of Christ’s blood was given.’
>
> “Seeing such great miracles of God, I run and fall at Peter’s feet, rolling upon my knees. I receive Peter into my house and drive out the disgraceful monster.
>
> “But the dog, made exceedingly gentle toward everyone, pursues Simon alone and knocks him down beneath its feet.
>
> [Col. 0620D] “The holy apostle runs up and cries out:
>
> > ‘In the name of Christ I command you not to touch his entrails with your bite, nor to fasten your teeth into his limbs and tear them.’
>
> “Following the command and avoiding any attack upon his flesh, it tears his garment, allows no part of his skin to remain covered, and strips and exposes the robber.
>
> “The people and the servants of our household run through the streets with the dog, driving away the wonders of Satan and banishing the wolf of his mind from the walls of the city.
>
> “Unable to bear the weight of such disgrace, he hid himself and was nowhere seen for a whole year. Nevertheless he returned, insinuating himself to Nero and presenting himself to that wicked man. Fierce and criminal, he formed a friendship with him; a dreadful union bound the impious together.
>
> [Col. 0621A] “After this, the apostle was strengthened by the Lord through the following words in a vision:
>
> > ‘Nero and Simon, filled with defilement, are stirring up deceits against you, but let no fear seize you. I am with you as a strong shield of protection, and I give you the consolations of my servant Paul.
>
> > ‘Tomorrow he will enter Rome. You will see him, and together you will wage war against the black mockeries of the perverse Simon.
>
> > ‘After you have consigned him to the fires beneath Tartarus, you will ascend together as victors to me in heaven.’”
>
> “There was no delay: the following day made the words manifest by producing Paul. After you had seen each other, and after you had fought the robber in the arena, once you had endured what the seven courses of the sun had brought, it became clear that you had seen everything yourselves. I understood that it was useless to teach you matters so well known, since Linus, in the Greek language of the Eastern Church, has unfolded the conspicuous deeds of these battles.”

### Chapter Eight: On Saint Petronilla

[Col. 0621]

[Col. 0621A]

> “I shall briefly explain, as ordered, the struggle by which the labor of the blessed Petronilla, daughter of the lord Peter, reached its end. She became bedridden, as you know, according to the Father’s will. I remember that several of you were present when, at the customary meal of the disciples, we took food twice.
>
> “While we were eating, Titus began to address the elder:
>
> > ‘Since through you all those exhausted by illnesses are restored to health, why is Petronilla, who is paralyzed, neglected and left lying there?’
>
> “Peter answered:
>
> > ‘It is easy for her to be healed. But lest we seem to excuse an impossible cure with words, rise, Petronilla, and quickly undertake the duty of serving.’”

The virgin rises, unharmed and rejoicing, and serves. When her service has been completed, she is ordered to return to her own bed, so that, according to custom, she may again become burdened with her illness.

But after she began to be perfected in the fear of God, she remained entirely healthy and strong, indeed driving illness away from many.

Because she shone with an exceedingly beautiful face, the comes Flaccus attempts to take her by force as his wife. When he comes with soldiers and weapons, the virgin of God, warned by her father’s light, plays this stratagem against him:

> “Do you approach a girl’s dwelling with an armed troop? If you wish to join me to yourself in lawful marriage, after three days send matrons and girls distinguished by their virginity, with whom I may visit your house.”

[Col. 0622B]

Having obtained this interval, the virgin fortifies herself beforehand with the honor of virtue, adorns herself with chaste ornaments, and spends the intervening hours in continual prayer and fasting.

The illustrious Felicula, joined to her by the fear of the Lord, becomes her companion, a virgin as though her foster-sister.

The third day spread the earth with radiant light. Nicomedes, the presbyter, comes to Petronilla and celebrates Christ’s sacred mysteries according to the pious rite.

When the virgin has been nourished by the divine gift of heaven, she rejects the marriage bed and ascends into the starry heavens.

It happened, through the divine governance of the Lord, that the unmarried choir and the company of matrons were led by Flaccus to a wedding, but by Christ to a funeral, and celebrated the illustrious virgin’s funeral with honor.

### Chapter Nine: On Saint Felicula

[Col. 0621]

[Col. 0621C]

But the count, turning his attention elsewhere, seeks at least to possess the virgin’s consolation. “Felicula,” he says, “choose either of these two things: become my wife, or pour libations to the gods.”

She replies:

> “I shall not be your wife, because I am consecrated to the Thunderer; nor shall I pour libations to the gods, because I am Christ’s own servant.”

Flaccus hands her over to a cruel executioner to be tortured and orders her confined in the dark chambers of a bedroom.

She is left there for seven days without food. The wife of one of the guards speaks to her:

> “Alas! Why do you hasten to depart from life by a wretched death? Take a famous young husband, rich in possessions, handsome, powerful, and a friend of the king.”

She cares to answer nothing except this:

[Col. 0621D]

> “I am Christ’s virgin; I accept no one at all except him.”

Afterward she is taken to the Vestal Virgins to be kept there. Rejoicing to endure another week without food, she is not at all persuaded by their impure service to offer sacrifice or eat their food.

Therefore she is suspended upon the instruments of torture and cries out:

> “Only now have I begun to see Christ, the sober lover; he is my love, in whom I am fixed. But the hostile ministers rage and babble:
>
> > ‘Deny that you are a Christian woman, and you will go free.’
>
> “Happy that I am, I shall never deny my lover, even though I am seized on his account, though he was fed with gall, crowned with thorns, given vinegar to drink, and fastened to the cross.”

After these most holy words, she is thrown into the filth of a foul and vast sewer. There Felicula reaches the goal of heaven’s kingdom.

When he sees these events from the watchtower, Nicomedes comes silently by night, carries away the bones in his little chest, and transports them in a cart. He buries them on the Ardeatine road, about seven miles from the city.

There, in the course of time, her prayers bear fruit in response to the petitions of the faithful.

### Chapter Ten: On Saint Nicomedes

[Col. 0621]

[Col. 0621D]

Flaccus heard what had been accomplished by holy Nicomedes. He has him seized for sacrifice and orders him to offer at the altars.

The saint replies:

> “I sacrifice to the almighty Lord who rules in heaven. I shall not therefore pour libations upon stones that are shut up in temples as though in prisons and caves.”

After enduring these and many other things, he is beaten for a very long time with lead and flies away to the Lord. His holy limbs are carried to the Tiber.

His cleric, Justus by deeds and by name, rescues the body from the waters, transports it in a two-wheeled cart to his own garden, and buries it in a tomb near the walls.

[Col. 0624A]

He places the blessed bones on the Nomentan road. There, those who pray to God ask for what they rightly deserve through the intercession of the martyr, having suffered for the name of Christ, with the Father, who always reigns with the Holy Spirit [printed *Spiramine*], forever.

### Chapter Eleven: On the Martyrdom of the Saints Nereus and Achilleus

[Col. 0623]

[Col. 0623A]

When these matters had been completed, the following reply is sent:

> “Eutyches and Victorinus, servants of Marcus in every respect, send greetings.
>
> “The letters of the Lord Jesus that you sent to Marcellus, the holy writings, have reached us in this way. Thirty days had already passed since they attained the deserved crown.
>
> “Flavia, an illustrious virgin, most firmly bound to Christ, taught by the distinguished eunuchs Nereus and Achilleus to remain a virgin and to believe in Christ, the supreme God, is driven into exile by Aurelianus, the bridegroom whom she had rejected, on the charge of the name of Jesus.
>
> [Col. 0623B] “He then attempts through the pious eunuchs to test her mind, hoping through them to reconcile the girl’s affection to himself. The saints, rejecting his gifts, strive to strengthen the girl’s faith in Christ.
>
> “Therefore, after being savagely scourged by the bridegroom, they are taken away and handed over at Terracina to Rufus to be killed by punishments. Rufus [lacuna] with fire [Note: [Col. 0623] Codex 1 reads *Rufus [lacuna] igne*, leaving the space of one word vacant. Codex 2 reads *Rufus m mius igne*.]
>
> “He tortures them while they hang in the fire and attempts to compel them to sacrifice to the gods. While they confess that they have been washed in apostolic baptism and that they have never in any way sacrificed to images, they depart above the stars, punished by the penalty of death.
>
> “Auspicius, a fortunate disciple under whose instruction Flavia grew, secretly carried off their sacred bodies. Conveying them by boat, he brought them to Domitilla’s estate and placed them beside the tomb of holy Petronilla, about fifteen hundred paces from the city.
>
> “We received these events from Auspicius’s account.
>
> “May your loving care for us flourish. Hasten to send someone who may reveal your affairs to us, so that our brotherly greeting may illuminate both of us and our more joyful affection may shine with threefold light.”

### Chapter Twelve: On the Saints Eutyches, Victorinus, and Severinus

[Col. 0623]

[Col. 0623B]

After receiving this little letter, Marcellus sends to them a certain Germanus, who, having lived for a year with the confessors and the saints, returned and reported these events.

After the martyrdom of Nereus and his brother, Aurelianus sets about winning Domitilla’s assent. He heard that she was joining fellowship with the same holy men, whom she had once consecrated as her teachers, and he asked Emperor Nerva to hand them over to him if they refused to sacrifice to the sacred images.

While these men persevere with manly courage and trample the executioner’s threats beneath their faithful purpose, the savage ruler separates them and places them on distant estates:

Eutyches, sixteen miles from the city on the Nomentan road; Victorinus, sixty miles away at Salina; and Maro, one hundred and thirty miles from the walls.

Therefore the harsh overseer orders the saints to work with rakes throughout the day and provides [an uncertain word, *catabra*] in the evening.

[Col. 0623D]

But the good Lord does not abandon his own pupils, and grace is given to the righteous in foreign fields.

Eutyches drives out a demon from the child of the tenant of the little farm and restores the child to his father and to himself.

Victorinus, by prayer, restores to health the man who managed the estate in place of its master and who had spent three years confined to bed with paralyzed limbs; he raises him from his bed whole.

Maro frees the city’s curator from dropsy, a disease in which he had been swollen with watery fluid for seven years.

Finally, by chaste speech, they instruct the peoples and teach many the faith of Jesus who reigns. They are made presbyters and, increasing the people, bring them into being anew.

[Col. 0624B]

Therefore envy fills Aurelianus’s mind with hatred of their goodness. Anger raises his spirit and urges him to send torturers. Butchers are assigned to inflict various punishments.

Eutyches is beaten while the entire street watches.

As his mind, triumphing over the scourges, seeks a heavenly dwelling, the people, rescuing his devoted limbs from the executioner who despises what is worthy, hasten to heap honor upon him and prepare to erect a sacred temple over him in Christ.

Turgius, swollen with savage rage, is sent against Maro. When he cannot overcome the saint by terror, he attempts to strike him down with a stone. He orders a huge rock rolled upon him—a weight which seventy men could scarcely move with pulleys—and orders the saint to be burdened beneath it.

But the saint cheerfully bears it as though it were light straw for two thousand paces; at the very place where he was accustomed to pour out his prayers, he sets down the sarcophagus and remains unharmed beneath its weight.

The entire region is filled with the miraculous event. People hasten to have their souls purified, and, longing for holy baptism, destroy the altars of ghosts.

[Col. 0624D]

The judge announces the deeds of the pious man to Aurelianus, and the latter hastens to approach in order to slaughter the savage captive.

The believing people carry away the stone and the holy weight; in the same place they lay the saint’s bones in a hollowed tomb and bury them. Above, they build a lofty chamber of precious gifts, in which God’s gifts are bestowed upon his servants according to their merits.

There is a place that emits foul waters through sulfurous vapor. The ancients called these waters *cotillae*. There the tyrant orders Victorinus to be killed, with his head thrown backward, in the horrible stench.

After the martyr has endured this for three furious days, he is nourished by divine nectar and the pleasantness of heaven.

Aurelianus, still savage even after the martyr’s death,

[Col. 0625A]

prevents the body from being covered by earth and forbids earth to conceal the earth.

But when the limbs lie unburied beneath the advancing sun, the people of Amiternum approach, seize the bones of their blessed bishop, carry them back, and bury them reverently.

The brothers had indeed been joined by a twofold consolation. Victorinus had been especially strengthened by Severinus; after death they performed in turn the duties of parents, offering one another the support of a doubled care. They submitted themselves to one another in discipleship and exercised authority over one another by turns as teachers. They offered worthy gifts in rivalry of service.

A true affection had grown through their credible deeds. They had offered themselves to God as living sacrifices, and their brotherly virtue, seeking to attain perfection, pressed toward giving their possessions to those in need.

[Col. 0625B]

They were rich in the abundance of heaven, where Christ is all things. They possessed the same freedom, authority, and gracious service; they lacked nothing, since they possessed none of the pomp of the world.

But Victorinus, burning with hope of climbing higher and reflecting that it was imperfect to serve only in turn, and not enough that one should serve the other, considered whether either might accomplish something more outstanding for the other.

He entered the wilderness and sought the heights of a lofty crag. Beneath it he sat in a cave through which a river flowed, its course marked by the broken sides of the split rock on either side. The space was scarcely sufficient for one person to sleep while sitting.

If it received a companion, he would pray while standing awake. He made a little doorway, giving it strength with pliant wicker, and devoted himself continually to reading and ardently to prayers.

The envious enemy of piety could not bear to see this. He fabricated a deception and put on the face of a tender girl. Before the man’s door he repeated words of lament:

[Col. 0625C]

> “Alas for me!” he began. “Wretched that I am, wandering alone through the woods, error, and darkness, ignorant of this place and of the forbidden paths.
>
> “Whoever you are who dwell in this venerable wilderness, the heavens everywhere and the forests everywhere proclaim the fame of your virtues and your extraordinary work. Rescue me from the bristling boars, the savage wolves, and the gaping bears.
>
> “If I live, I shall be yours; if I finally die, that too will be yours. It will be enough for me to be sheltered beneath your roof or even at your threshold. I do not seek a long companionship; let me be a guest for one night only.”

Moved by pity, he opens the door and, sympathizing with the enemy, receives the terrible robber.

Scarcely an hour had passed when, amid frequent movements and gestures of the limbs,

[Col. 0625D]

the alluring figure touched the holy man’s foot, and soon pierced his heart with the arrow of desire.

Sweet words heap deception upon deception, and fiery speeches fan the flames;
Love burns the heart; lonely places counsel crime.

[Col. 0626A] But just as a mighty oak, surpassing all others in ancient strength and striking deep into the earth with firm roots, is found suitable for fire when the herdsman of the mountain pastures, having kindled his hearth, brings it to a cave, where its inner strength, consumed by the flames, is overcome: it falls and for a long time presses the sky upon the roofed fields.

The tall column collapses; blind passion accomplishes the crime. The enemy, now victorious, cries out openly:

“Hey! What are you doing, what are you doing, most perfect man? You, brother to the man for whom you had been a burden, are joining yourself to a stranger? Behold, you who hated the companionship of your own brother to endure . . .

“See what you are doing—you who, establishing a new doctrine among forests and crags, were teaching the rocks chaste disciplines? . . .”

While the devil hurled these insults with mocking speech,

[Col. 0626B] the devil vanished from the deceived man’s eyes like smoke into the air.

But the one who had fallen was silent, as though he had seen the Gorgon. When at last he recovered his limbs, bloodless and himself again, he emerged from the woods, seeking the comfort of his brother. Standing before him, and for a long time suppressing his voice out of shame, he finally disclosed the cause in halting order.

He himself imposed the punishment upon himself. For, splitting a tree, he thrust his hands into it and inserted them; wedges tightened the wound, and the wooden gashes closed all around. The brother revealed to the supreme Pontiff what had been done.

When the Pontiff came, he first tried to loosen the bond. But when he saw that the man resisted, he blessed him and, praying, pitied and comforted him; he strengthened and consoled him, then departed.

But the exceedingly strong man, fixed in so great a bondage, took only a little bread and a draught of water

[Col. 0626C] each week, compelled to do so by his brother, who lightened his own long fasts with similar nourishment and, for his brother’s fall, pressed himself beneath an equal cross.

While three severe winters passed under the weight of this ordeal, Victorinus’ endurance at last moved everyone. The bishop returned and scarcely succeeded in persuading him to allow the torments to be ended, once his flesh had been consumed—he who had himself remembered and trembled at the dread judgment.

How greatly he later shone as a saint, and how many wondrous deeds he powerfully accomplished, no human tongue can fully express. He was chosen by all the people of the city of Amiternum and raised as their bishop, a city flourishing through its martyr.

His brother Severinus also, his brother’s fellow soldier and discerning follower, after many wondrous manifestations of the virtues granted him, rested rich in holy devotion as a confessor. He is said to have served in the same office in which, living marvelously as a strict abstainer, he had led his life before being honorably chosen bishop. Campanian Naples commemorates him with devout observance.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Saint Domitilla, and also Marcellus and Apuleius, Sulpicius and Servilianus

[Col. 0625]

[Col. 0625D] When Aurelianus, with the virgin’s aid, had removed all the holy men, he released Domitilla from her long exile on Pontus and relegated her to Terracina. He asked that Sulpicius and Servilianus, reconciled with their illustrious fiancées, be sent to her, so that they might persuade her mind to turn toward marriage, since they were companions of the virgin and had been nourished by the same milk.

[Col. 0626D] The holy woman returning from the lands of Pontus is met in the fields. The celebrated women rejoice that they have seen their distinguished companion, and the distinguished companion rejoices that the celebrated women have come. They celebrate their joys together, though they do not enjoy them in the same manner: she is refreshed by the nourishment of the soul, while they are refreshed by that of the body. They recline at banquets, while Flavia observes a fast.

Her companions say to her: “[Col. 0627A] Since we dine and are joined in marriage to our husbands, how can we serve God while you practise such things?”

Flavia replied: “You shine as women properly betrothed to illustrious men. If some obscure persons wished to tear you away and bind you to themselves, would you consent or refuse?”

“May God turn such a thing away from our minds,” they replied.

Flavia continued: “And what of my mind, which rejoices in a Bridegroom—the King begotten of God, who came from heaven above and promised those who keep their hearts chaste that they would be his brides and that he would grant them eternal life? Surely, after the course of this present contest, he will lead them into bridal chambers beautiful with everlasting light, granting them continually to rejoice in angelic splendor and to bloom with the radiance of paradise’s flowers, so that at the end, without fear, they may feast forever in glory.

“While the Son of God made these promises, he saw scarcely anyone willing to believe and therefore did not delay to confirm faith by deeds: giving light to the blind, cleansing lepers by his word,

[Col. 0627B] and restoring bodies that had lost the functions of life. By these works he taught them to acknowledge and confess that he was Lord.”

Theodora said: “Herodes, my brother in Rome, is blind. He was deprived of his sight last year as a result of an illness. Restore it under the name of your Christ, if you have brought us true doctrines from him.”

Euphrosyna then said: “You admit that you left your brother blind in Rome; but here is my nurse’s mute daughter with me,” and she immediately ordered her to be brought forward.

Domitilla, prostrate, poured out prayers with prolonged weeping. Then she rose, stretched out her hands toward the stars, and said:

“Christ God, who promised always to be present with us to the end, prove that what I testify is true.”

With these words she added the sign of the cross to the mute girl’s mouth and said: “In the highest name of the Lord, in the name of Christ, speak.”

At once the mute girl burst forth, crying out these words: “Your God, Domitilla, is true; everything you have said is true.”

Then both women fell at her feet, believed, and were enrolled among the holy.

Theodora’s brother, brought along in blindness, was granted through Domitilla’s prayers the light of both body and soul, shining with radiance from above.

Then the gentiles who were present from Rome were renewed, believing in Christ through the clear water of baptism; and this same household shone as a holy church.

After the savage Aurelianus had killed the holy Marcellus and his companion Apuleius in each of their schools,

[Col. 0627D] he also sent many others, on account of the Lord’s heavenly citizen, to the celestial realms by a glorious death. He receives joyful instruments, while blessed Melicus leaps for joy, and the torches of the three virgins come forth to shine with the light of one day.

[Col. 0628A] But the devout Servilianus and Sulpicius, seeing the miracles worked by God and believing, submit their hearts to devout faith. While Aurelianus urged them to marry the women, they urged him to render honor to the Lord through them, since God’s manifest power had shone through their deeds.

He neither admitted this into his mind nor heeded their words. He ordered Domitilla to be enclosed in the secret chambers of a bedroom, and, hoping for more than his actions could achieve, took his delight as though he had already conquered the realm of chastity and had been given leave to insult modesty.

While he madly leaped about among the chambers, applauding, he twisted the gestures of his body in an evil manner. Unhappy man, ignorant that in seeking these forbidden things he was loosening the bonds of the life granted to him, he died suddenly, his soul already being summoned back to its blood-filled hiding places, and abandoned both life and his diversions.

When the companions saw this, they strove to give themselves to Christ.

Luxurius, the brother of that great tyrant, after these deeds returned to Trajan and demanded authority over them. Once he had obtained them, he slaughtered them together in different forms of execution.

He handed over the illustrious Sulpicius and Servilianus to the prefect Anianus, and unjustly accused them as servants of the Christian faith, reporting that they were to be killed.

Afterward, against the virgins bound together by a threefold grace, the gentile rites were set up to be mocked by them. Eager to remove the things suitable for earthly use, he threw fire upon them and burned the secret inner chamber that had sheltered the blessed maidens.

They prostrated themselves on their faces and, praying to the Lord amid their vows and supplications, raised their souls above the heavens.

The following dawn, rising amid the smoldering ashes, displayed the radiant triumph of the holy women. The deacon Caesarius approached the still-warm dwelling and found the blessed women untouched amid so great a blaze: the flame had dared nothing against them, nor had the garments been harmed by the fire.

Then, reverently arranging and burying the holy bodies in a new sarcophagus, he sealed them together and concealed them in the earth.

The prefect pressed Sulpicius and Servilianus to offer sacrifice to the gods. They declared that, having recently been cleansed in the renowned stream, they would not again be defiled with foul impurities. Since they could in no way be compelled to the dark rites, they were ordered to receive the sword with bowed necks.

The faithful laid their bodies in their own field,

[Col. 0628D] two thousand paces from the city on the Latin Way. From that place, through all the ages, their abundant power has overflowed at the site of their martyrdom.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the teaching, miracles, and passion of Saint Clement

Meanwhile Clement, sowing the seeds of the eternal word with the fervor of heavenly faith, unfolded many books, venerable volumes, instructing diverse peoples by divine light and summoning gentile hearts to the path of life, while exhorting the devout to persevere in steadfast faith. Hence they also received the name “Catholic” from his admonitions.

[Col. 0628D] Through him Rome instructs Corinth in religion. He decrees that the deeds of the regions be recorded in order by scribes who will strive to set forth the struggles of Christ’s soldiers. He also arranges the clergy according to the various ranks of dignity and consecrates five pontiffs, who are sent to the different parts of the world to bring the established ordinances of the law.

Here he orders the distinguished Dionysius to seek the savage peoples of Gaul;

[Col. 0629A] Sixtus to prepare the walls of Rheims for Christ; Memmius to acquire the city of Châlons; and Eutropius to sanctify the people of Saintes with his holy mouth.

Clement therefore devotes himself to heavenly teachings and does not cease to display the excellent path in the light. The ranks of the Roman people hasten to be instructed.

From this group came illustrious men, and from that one a distinguished company of women. Among them, when Theodora’s zeal was kindled, her husband Sisinnius pursued her and entered the holy church.

While the bishop of the Lord was celebrating the heavenly mysteries, the pagan, intent upon the rites with an inert mind, was struck in hearing and sight and deprived of both. He himself begged that he be restored and confessed that he was blind and deaf.

The servants, lifting him, were deceived by an empty circuit: they led the accused around in a blind whirl, unable to find the entrance of the house because darkness covered it.

[Col. 0629B] His anxious wife, hanging upon the guidance of the man, was astonished. When she learned through a boy whom she had sent what difficulty they were suffering, she threw herself down and, asking that the man be brought out, opened the way for him.

When the sacred rites were completed, she immediately embraced the lowest footprints of the bishop and begged pardon and the restoration of her husband’s senses, recounting the deed and the outcome of her marriage.

The bishop was moved by the tears and prayers of the woman who pleaded. On behalf of the man, he urged the people to pray for his health and, having sent up a prayer, entered the sick man’s house.

Finding him deprived of sight and empty of hearing, he restored both faculties with prayers poured out to the Lord.

When night had been driven away, day began to enter through the open windows. At the same time, a voice began to penetrate the hidden recesses of his head. When he saw Clement standing before his wife,

[Col. 0629C] he madly ordered his servants to bind him with ropes, claiming that Clement sought his wife through an illicit passion and that he had been deceived by him through the Thessalian art of sorcery.

The servants came, playing and hastening, and quickly threw bonds over the stones they had set down, thinking that they were binding Clement and the clergy together.

The bishop reproached him as one who bore a heart of stone, saying that, since he worshiped stones as gods, he deserved to be shown that stones could be rolled down. The man attacked him amid empty terrors; the bishop despised him and laughed at his fury.

Then, after pouring out a prayer, he blessed Theodora and departed, charging her to persist continually in prayer until the power of Christ should deign to visit the man’s heart.

While Theodora was praying, a venerable old man appeared openly before her as the stars were already hastening to dawn. Relieving her grief, he said:

“Through you Sisinnius will be saved, so that the words of Paul concerning his brother may be fulfilled: a faithful woman will make the unfaithful man holy.”

From this it is clear that the one who appeared to her was the apostle Peter. At his coming, the man’s diseased mind was restored. Touched in heart by God, he acquired human understanding and asked that his wife, summoned, pray to the Lord on his behalf.

Confessing his error and speaking of the clouds that he had endured, he asked that Clement be summoned and that the truth be delivered to him.

The woman summoned the holy man and related what had been reported to her. When the bishop arrived, he was honored with due respect and nourished the man with the milk of reason.

After receiving the nourishment of saving faith, Sisinnius embraced his teacher and fell at his knees, giving thanks to the Almighty for what had been granted him. He acknowledged that God had made him blind so that he might see truly and had taken away his hearing so that he might be able to hear the truth.

He accused the darkness and blessed the light that had been opened to him. He refuted the idols and proclaimed the praises of Christ. He pursued many other matters, while the holy company rejoiced and the name of the saints exulted, increased by this accession.

At the approaching celebration of Easter, he was purified in the font. At the same time, one hundred and twenty-four persons of different sex and unequal age were numbered among those reborn through the holy water and the nourishing Spirit. Through him, many distinguished persons also received the sacred gifts.

The enemy was distressed to see gains made through Christ’s powers. He grieved over the frequent losses of his captives and, seeking dark strategies for the conflict,

[Col. 0630B] stirred minds and raised them to savage anger. He urged wars to blaze and a foul tumult to seethe.

For these purposes he chose as a companion a man arrogant with ancient pride, bearing the old name of Tarquinius, to instigate the fury through the demonic goad of the crowd. He raged with a dreadful commission against the bishop’s name.

The peoples divided into different groups over this matter. Some defended the innocent and holy man, proclaiming the good he had accomplished and the gifts of salvation he had scattered, and following the broad consolations of his aid.

Others, with savage complaints and a mind maddened by rage, insisted that these things were being accomplished through subtle and wicked arts, so that he might overturn the worship of the gods descended from Aeneas. That man stripped divine honors from Jupiter, denounced the shameful image of Hercules, filled with an unclean demon, and censured the meretricious obscenities of Venus. He also accused Mercury, Mars, Saturn, and Minerva, along with Diana, and brought everything into disrepute.

The prefect, attempting to calm the people’s tumult, summoned Clement and, soothing him with gentle speech, pointed out that he was descended from noble ancestors and blood. He urged him to worship the gods, so that he might shine in their favor.

Clement, neither knowing how to yield to threats nor willing to be swayed by flattering words, worked to enlighten the prefect’s mind with blessed instructions and to shape the man through open reason. He explained where sedition takes its beginning and from what point the tumult of the crowd leaps forth, as one who loved reason in order to avoid folly and escape darkness while pursuing friendly light. He sowed many arguments, full of faith and rich in reason.

[Col. 0630D] The prefect disclosed the crime and the crowd to the emperor. Trajan inflamed Clement’s refusal to consent to the rites and ordered him either to go into exile on Pontus and enter the countryside of Chersonesus, or to endure the barren wilderness and unproductive soil.

The prefect announced these things to the holy man. But Clement strove to compose the man’s mind with the radiance of blessed teaching, fearing neither punishment nor the threat of Augustus. He turned the man and softened him with tears.

The prefect, seeking his welfare and providing everything suitable, assigned him a vessel and supplied what was appropriate for the ship. Many from the people and many from the ranks of the clergy embraced the distinguished Father and accompanied him as he departed.

[Col. 0631A] When the blessed man had been carried to the places assigned to him, he encountered exiles—many thousands of a devout people—who had been punished there by being ordered to cut stones.

When they all saw Clement, they were filled with tears and lamented that so great a pontiff had undergone such harsh treatment. He relieved their grief and, saying that he had been sent to them as a companion by the power of the Almighty, addressed them with soothing words, so that the glory shared by his passion might join and prepare him for them.

Thus, soothing the pain that had begun with a physician’s speech, he announced to the six thousand that water should be brought across the parched fields on the dry shoulders of the saints.

Then Clement said: “Let us all beseech the Lord Jesus, who drew flowing streams from dry marble in the deserts of Sinai, that he may now bring forth for the confessors here joyful veins leaping in a stream.”

[Col. 0631B] While the bishop looked around on every side after the prayers had been offered, behold, he saw the mountain of God standing above a lamb. With its right foot extended, it seemed to indicate that the place should be opened.

The saint did not doubt that he was seeing Christ. He went forward alone and said: “Under the Lord’s name, turn your plowshares here.”

They dug around the spot but did not know how to touch the soil that had been shown to the Pontiff by heavenly direction.

The Pope, lightly seizing an iron tool, struck the place. He brought forth a new spring by heavenly grace, which, gathering strength, poured out a happy river with force.

The people rejoiced, and Clement celebrated this event in song:

“The rushing stream gladdens the divine city.”

With the new spring sweeping swiftly across the earth, the fame of the river, leaping no less rapidly with its current, flew through the fields and filled the homeland with miracles.

[Col. 0631C] The people hastened to see Christ’s mighty works. They drank from the two-flowing stream and were renewed by the new river. More than five hundred souls were saved in a single day; they returned and hastened to be dedicated. In one year, more than seventy churches were built, after the shrines of the gods had been overturned and dismantled.

For three summers he had watered the hearts of the peoples with holy rain, when the jealous enemy of the light, brewing dark poisons, stirred empty minds to pursue the profane gains of heavenly light and to demand laws from Augustus against Clement, because he had driven innumerable peoples away from the altars of the gods above.

From Trajan, the savage Aufidianus was sent here to punish the worshipers of Christ or subject them to the rites of the gods.

Like a rabid wolf, inclined to break into the folds or scatter flocks spread widely through the pastures, he rushed to rage and tear apart the young sheep. Without delay, he received those who were burning with zeal and offering their necks to the sword.

He begrudged everyone’s death and refused to strike them. He demanded only that Clement enter the combat of God.

Testing him with various weapons through cunning attempts, he proved his exceptional and unconquerable strength. The contestant perceived that he could not be conquered by earthly means.

He ordered him to be driven into the sea under the weight of a stone. Thinking that the waters could be overcome by jumping into them, he commanded that an anchor be fastened to the limbs of the sinking man.

But Clement is said to have entered the realms of heaven from the waters, having long since become a citizen of the stars amid the waves.

His mind sought an ethereal seat from the depths of the sea toward the highest heaven; joyful, it flew through the waters and was not choked by them.

There were no funeral rites according to human custom, but service was supplied by divine grace. Human beings, who were absent from the funeral, performed the service; the inhabitants of heaven, who were present, took care of the funeral duties.

The anchor, bound to punishment, carried out its service as it was drawn along and brought the body into a constructed sepulchral chamber, built by angelic workmanship and furnished with divine preparation, where the saint’s limbs were placed by the hands of the stars.

The peoples, weeping on the shore’s sands, watched to see whether they might behold the body brought from anywhere. The disciples’ confidence that they would obtain the holy man’s body remained firmly rooted in their prayers.

[Col. 0632B] Together with Phoebus, Cornelius urged the people to beseech Christ with one accord, asking that he deign to unlock for them the remains of the spirit carried away upon the sea.

While they were free to beat upon the stars with continual prayers, the Spirit who once caused the waters of the Red Sea to dry forced the sea to retreat and loosened its long inlet. Extending a dry passage for three thousand paces to the people, it allowed them to see temples constructed by angelic workmanship from cut marble, raised in the heavenly court under the direction of the celestial craftsman.

A heavenly work and wondrous tomb were displayed: a stone chest enclosing the venerable relic of the martyr. Beside the martyr’s tomb the famous anchor remained as a witness.

As the eager disciples sought to transfer the holy body, the [uncertain: *Oroma*] of the divine sanctuary was disclosed,

[Col. 0632C] lest they should wish to empty the sacred walls of the bodies placed there. When they returned for the festivals, they again crossed the sea’s depths, marking the hidden places with their dry steps.

The words were fulfilled: the ranks of the peoples who had been placed there submitted themselves to the one highest and true Thunderer. The sea offered Clement a solemn path, and, as that unfamiliar sea opened a road of three thousand paces, those carried along amid diverse hardships were relieved of their distress.

It once happened that a mother, having set out with her little child, entered this place. After she had completed the solemn rites, she gave herself to the banquet and her child to sleep.

Meanwhile, when the sound of the returning sea shook the shores, the woman, frightened, withdrew with her companions. Following them headlong, she forgot the feelings of a parent.

Unmindful of the child she had lost beneath the vast chambers, she hastened ahead of the dreaded waves in rapid flight. At last, when her mind recovered itself in a safe station, she remembered the child left behind in the womb-like shelter of the place.

Uttering groans, she filled the harbor with her lamentation. Repeating her grief, she traversed the upper sands, asking whether anyone had seen the corpse of the child who had been carried away [Note: [Col. 0631C] The manuscript reads *enecti* (“of the slain”).].

Learning nothing from anyone, she returned beneath her mournful roof and prolonged the year with continual weeping.

When the sun returned along its accustomed course and the long-awaited festivals came back to the inhabitants, she returned as well and was soon the first among those who hurried back, if she could at least find the washed bones of her child.

[Col. 0633A] For when the sea uncovered the road, she first attacked the seaweed, outstripped everyone, and crossed the sands before them all. The wave followed and hung over the receding waters.

She reached the temple first, entered, and prostrated herself before the altar. After completing her prayers, she rose and turned away, wiping her face, drenched with the rain of grief, and drawing back her wet cheeks.

Then she saw the child in the place where he had been left in his cradle, not yet having broken the uninterrupted silence of sleep.

[Col. 0634A] Thinking him dead, she hurried to lift the body. Discovering that he breathed sleep, she quickly seized him and awakened him in her arms. She raised him unharmed and carried him back while the people watched.

When the mother asked where he had been throughout the long course of the year, he replied that he did not know how the revolving cycle of the world had passed. He explained that he had merely taken a pleasant sleep as though during a single night; and, presenting this spectacle to the astonished crowd, he doubled his mother’s blessed joy through everyone’s prayers.

VIII. On the saints Eleutherius and Ancia.  
IX. On the defense of Quadratus and Aristides, and the remission of the persecution.  
X. On Pope Telesphorus and Hyginus.  
XI. On Novatus and Pudens.  
XII. On the saints Praxedes and Potentiana.  
XIII. On Saint Alexander, bishop and martyr.  
XIV. On Saint Felicitas and her sons.  
XV. On Saint Concordius.  
XVI. On Saint Potentianus.  
XVII. On the vengeance of the fourth persecution.  
XVIII. On the rain and the victory granted to the soldiers through the invocation of Christ.

## HERE BEGINS THE THIRD BOOK

[Col. 0633]

## CHAPTER I. On Anacletus and Evaristus

[Col. 0633B] Clement had left Anacletus in charge of the Roman Church. Consecrated by Peter to the honor of the presbyterate, he adorned the apostolic sepulcher by his skill in construction, providing mausoleums in which the bodies of the pontiffs could be placed. Beside the great master he too received a tomb.

After him Evaristus obtained the chair of the Church. The walls of Rome, distinguished by the birth of God’s servant, gave him titles among the presbyters of the great city. He appointed seven ministers to serve the Pontiff while sowing the seeds of the rational word in the earth.

Crowned by martyrdom, the blessed man sought the stars, and his relics were joined to the apostolic tomb.

## CHAPTER II. On Saint Alexander the pope and his companions

[Col. 0633]

[Col. 0633B] After these men, Alexander, still immature in age but mature in mind, assumed the first seat.

With humble heart honoring the sacred mysteries of the Lord’s servants who had suffered, he ordered these to be inserted into the solemn rites. Not unlike Elisha, he commanded that the waters be sprinkled with salt, so that the blessed dwellings might be sprinkled with them.

Through the affection of the people, to whom the grace of Christ had been granted, he joined a company of senators to the Church and converted the prefect Hermes to the true King.

He baptized his wife, children, and sister at the same font, joining to them one thousand and two hundred servants; their wives and children were washed with them in the same baptism. Since he had previously granted them the joy of freedom, he allowed them to be consecrated on the day of Easter as a gift.

Swift rumor, winged with rapid feathers, announced these deeds to Trajan beneath the eastern sky. He hated the God whom he had known as Aurelianus, and when he read these things, he learned with rapid flight that Rome had been entangled in them.

He crossed land and sea, traversing everything in his precipitous course, and quickly entered Rome.

He was received in the city like an Augustus accompanied by Augustus. The furious pontiffs pursued him with mad lamentation, complaining that thousands had withdrawn from the sacred ranks of the Roman people and that Hermes and Alexander had been responsible for such daring.

They said that the gods had been worn down and that the shrines had been abandoned.

Alexander was overcome and imprisoned, and so was Hermes. Quirinus, a tribune who served as guardian and persuader, approached Hermes with honor and asked why he allowed himself to be deprived of so great an honor and why he considered it tolerable to endure such chains.

Hermes replied that he had changed his dignity, not lost it. An earthly height could be taken away because it was changeable; the divine heights, he said, could not be prevented from remaining forever.

The persuader called it foolishness to believe that life would exist after the ashes. Hermes said that this had once seemed true to him, but that Alexander had taught him to recognize it as true.

While their eager tongues exchanged these arguments, they came to the place where the statue had been approved by the prefect and the tribune, and a pact was concluded that Alexander himself should be joined to the statue’s threshold, triumphing over many bonds.

Hermes confirmed the agreement and departed. Quirinus came forth and, tripling the bonds around the Pontiff, guarded him with an increased watch.

The Pope prayed that the faith of the pact might be confirmed by this sign.

Their prayers sought heaven, and a star was sent down from the sky. For, while the stars painted the curved vault of heaven, behold, a little boy appeared. He illuminated the dark house with the radiance of a gleaming torch and ordered the Pontiff to follow him.

Fearing deception, Alexander said when he saw the boy and the torch: “I will not go with you unless you bend your knee with me and recite the prayer dictated and poured forth by Christ.”

The boy fulfilled his command. Seizing the bishop’s right hand, he drew him through the barriers as though opening doors and joined him to the prefect inside the enclosure of the locked chamber.

[Col. 0635B] Quirinus followed, broke open the barriers, and burst in. He found them together offering their prayers to the Lord—those whom he had thrust into caves and removed from their station by an increased guard.

He was astonished at the blazing torch and at these fearful events. When he was challenged to preserve his faith in the position he had adopted, the prefect, hesitating, answered with arguments drawn from the arts of Zoroaster:

“Have we ever read such things? Your choice is accomplished; now yield, prepared to believe. For the greatest gifts of our Lord are held by us: he gave hearing to the deaf and light to the blind, cleansing lepers, restoring paralyzed limbs, expelling demons, and returning bodies to souls.

“He even restored to the duties of life my son, who had died. When he was suffering from illness and had no interest in schools or studies, I carried him, seized by disease, to the lofty Capitols of the gods.

“While I wearied the deaf gods with heavy libations, prayed to their pontiffs, and stuffed them with empty gifts, I was bereaved, and my only child breathed out his soul before he had begun to live.

“Then his nurse burned me with these complaints:

“‘If, trusting in the holy Peter, you had brought him to his thresholds, you would rejoice in the prosperity gained by your child.’

“‘But if my sight is lost and has not been restored to light, how can you tell me that my son will be well on that account?’

“She replied: ‘You see that I am blind, but if I were willing to believe in Christ, I would already enjoy the light restored to me.

“‘Go, believe; and if Alexander can restore sight to you, I too shall believe that my child can be given back to me.’”

The third hour was blazing with the heat of day. She departed and returned at the sixth hour, rejoicing and seeing. Placing the cold child upon her shoulders, she ran, hastening so quickly that boys and young men could scarcely follow her.

When she saw the Pontiff, she said: “Christ, who rules Erebus, has released this boy by such a decree, so that the child may rise from the darkness of death and that the light once granted to you may remain open.”

Thus, after prayers had been poured out, she obtained the return of life to his limbs and came back to me with the sound pledge restored. When I saw him, I fell at his feet and begged to become immediately a servant of Christ.

From then on I clung to Christ. I appointed my son as his guardian, surrendered my mother’s patrimony, and gladly added some of my own possessions. I distributed the rest among the servants who had been renewed with me by the water,

[Col. 0636A] and I freed them all from slavery. Whatever remained afterward, I gave to the needy.

But now neither the confiscation of my property terrifies me nor does the fear of a dying man’s displeasure remain. I consider myself a participant with those who, having confessed the duties of Christ, deserved to receive the palm of martyrdom.”

The tribune replied to these words, compelled by his speech:

“May Christ gain me through you on this condition. I have a daughter of marriageable age whom I am considering giving to a husband. Exceptional grace adorns her beauty, but a shameful goiter burdens her neck.

“Redeem her with health, and, leaving all that is mine to her, I shall acknowledge Christ with an unfeigned mind.”

The bishop said: “Go quickly; take the *boia* (collar) from my neck and hasten to place it around your grown daughter’s neck; return tomorrow with the girl safe.”

[Col. 0636B]

He replied: “Let my household have you with it. Who will restore me to the house from the prison? Hurry, Pope, and return me there; for the one who brought me here will make me go back there.”

As he went, and the chambers were opened to him, the noblemen forced him, though unafraid, to be confined as usual. While he was saying farewell in prayer, behold, the boy bearing the torch stood beside him, opened the entrance, and brought the Pontiff back in a single instant; then he restored the bonds and departed.

After the passage of an hour, Quirinus arrived with his daughter. Seeing the guards whom he had left keeping watch, he approached the barriers, tested that they were fortified, and found that the seals remained intact.

He saw Alexander and, humbly prostrating himself at the opened entrance, asked pardon. The bishop said to him:

“Our Lord does not wish to destroy anyone, but rather to convert sinners. For, fixed upon the cross, he asked that the sins of those crucifying him be forgiven.”

Then, when Quirinus presented his daughter, the bishop ordered him to inquire how many prisoners were confined there and whether any were held for the name of Christ.

Twenty were reported. Among them were Eventius and Theodulus, whom the glory of the presbyterate had joined as friends.

He ordered them to be brought to him with due honor. Meanwhile he ordered his own *boia* (collar) to be transferred to the daughter.

The tribune immediately loosed every bond, kissed the bishop’s feet, and begged that the collar be placed upon his daughter.

It was placed upon her; he was urged to hurry, and the man carried out the command.

As he hastened, a boy flashed forth at once with the radiance of a torch and ordered that the girl be safe. He added:

“Remain always in your virginity, and I shall make you see in heaven your Bridegroom, who, out of love for you, poured out his own blood.”

After this Quirinus suddenly arrived, accompanied by the presbyters. When his daughter was found healed, he filled the place with his cry:

“Come forth from here, blessed Doctor Alexander,” he said, “lest, while you endure such unworthy treatment, an unjust thunderbolt sent from heaven burn me.”

The Pope impressed upon him what must rather be done, asking that all the persons confined in the prison be consecrated.

The guard complained, asking what benefit the holy man was to the wicked.

In reply, the bishop disclosed that God had come from heaven for the sake of sinners, born of a Virgin, to call all people to forgiveness and to the loosening of their sins.

Therefore Quirinus, instructed by this word, gathered everyone. All who desired to undergo Christ’s sacred rites hastened forward and, once baptized, went away free according to their wishes.

All hastened to submit themselves to the faith.

Alexander addressed them and proclaimed the mysteries of the heavenly Lord, who rules heaven and earth, who, in order to send his Son, begotten of a Virgin, into the world, called every human race. He strengthened his words with signs and taught that he had given life and afterward endured death, that, after trampling death down, he had risen and entered the heavens, granting those subject to him the power to perform wonders, and that he had declared he would come at the end of the age to give good things to the just and render fitting recompense to the unjust.”

All subjected their minds to these things, heard as teachings of salvation and faith. With the blessed presbyter’s hands laid upon them, they learned the beginnings of this life.

Quirinus was baptized together with his daughter Balbina; after all had been washed in the holy font, he gave the *vicus* [sic] as a church to those released from prison.

When Aurelianus learned these things, he became angry. He ordered Quirinus to be brought and set before him, and then addressed him, saying that Quirinus had been dear to him, yet had laughed at him.

Quirinus replied:

“Recognize that I have become a worshiper of Christ. You may kill me, lay me upon harsh wood, burn me in flames, or do anything else: I shall no longer be what I was.

“I presented to Christ all those bound in the prison and allowed his people to leave. But they attempted to go nowhere; they ask for combat and the crown of combat. Although they might perish after their crimes, they consider it better to pour out their souls for Christ.

[Col. 0637C] “Here are Hermes and Alexander, distinguished and devout, rejoicing in martyrdom as though they were prepared for banquets, and awaiting the radiance of heaven.”

When Aurelianus heard these words, his anger burned still more fiercely. Because Quirinus had not feared to speak so boldly before him, he ordered his tongue to be cut from his mouth and Quirinus to be hung up to weary the executioners and spectators.

But Quirinus continued to harass the tyrant with insults. The tyrant ordered his hands and feet also to be cut off with a sword, then commanded that his throat be filled with wounds and that he be left to be devoured by dogs.

The Appian Way, deprived of its victim, gave him a tomb.

While his holy daughter, shining in virginity, repeatedly pressed kisses upon the life-giving collar, the holy teacher Alexander said:

“Do not lick our bonds, which you seek again from the Lord, and cleanse the chains.”

Thus, undertaking this work with diligent and generous effort, he found these remains of the saint and delivered what he had found to his sister Theodora, who was to be honored for the integrity of Hermes.

She took care to give her beheaded brother burial and acquired a place not far from this city on the Salarian Way. There, after she herself had been martyred under the same judge, she deserved to be joined to her brother in bodily rest.

After the savage companion of Aurelianus had slain him, he ordered the remaining prisoners, washed in blind crimes, to be placed upon an ancient ship. With stones fastened around their necks, he ordered them all to be carried out and plunged into the deep sea.

After this, he ordered the blessed Pope Alexander to be brought and set before him, asking why he preferred to be killed rather than desist from what he had begun.

Alexander replied: “It is not permitted to give what is holy to dogs.”

At this the tyrant became furious and raged because he had been called a dog.

The bishop proved by his conduct that he was worse than a dog. The tyrant threatened him with lashes attached to divine objects. Alexander despised the threats of the man who boasted of them, rejected his honors, and preferred the pride and heights of those who were punished by him.

Fearlessly he cursed and despised the raging madman.

The savage man ordered the blessed prisoner to be hung up and tortured, scraped with claws, and burned with torches and lamps.

After the holy man had endured this for a long time without uttering a sound, the stern tyrant was astonished and demanded an explanation of the wondrous silence.

Alexander confessed that he was speaking to God in prayer. Then he rebuked the fool who asked for sacred words amid tortures:

[Col. 0638B] He admonished him that he was nearly thirty years old; the remainder, concerning the unconquered strength of mind, is corrupt. [Note: [Col. 0637D] The passage is corrupt, as are many others.]

With this blood, while the athlete sweats in the contest,

she declared that she was destined to be widowed by the dreadful death of her husband [Note: [Col. 0638D] Something is missing.],

like Pilate’s wife, once terrified by what she had seen;

and she sent word, urging that the brave athlete be released. But the savage man, scorning her words, orders Alexander’s companions to enter the contest; they joyfully retrace their steps,

already certain that they would reach the palms of the Father in the arena.

The unfortunate man, burning dreadfully in the Stygian fires,

when he reveals the invincible men, presses the furnace to burn;

then, as Alexander orders, and Eventius, who was eighty years old, their backs turned,

they are bound and burned in the glowing furnace.

Theodulus, standing by, is crushed beneath the horror of the punishments.

[Col. 0638C] But Alexander, exulting furiously in the furnace, says:

“Make haste, Theodulus, brother; hurry with us, and grow cold.

For let that fourth man who once appeared among the three Hebrew boys rejoice with us here.”

Theodulus bursts into the flame and cuts through the fires,

returning thanks and praises to God with his companions.

He sings:

“Behold, Father, you have tested us in the fire of this ordeal;

no evil adheres to us.”

The tyrant, raging in his mind, is inflamed when the fire is overcome;

he shouts, urges them on, and, wavering in uncertain guilt,

at last cuts off the presbyters’ necks with his sword.

Yet he does not allow the pope’s contest to end there.

He searches through all his entrails for the lofty soul,

piercing his mighty limbs with a many-pronged spear.

Thus the excellent man adorns the radiant flower

[Col. 0638D] which he has earned through so great an effort and seeks his deserved place in heaven.

While the bitter persecutor mocks him as he lies entangled,

behold, a young man appeared, carrying a burden of fire;

he brought rods of heated steel, and threw one before him,

adding these words at his feet:

“Receive your due, Aurelian,

for the black jaws of the Tartarean gate stand open to you,

while pleasant paradisal places are being prepared for those against whom you gnash your teeth.”

At these words he trembled, and fever was kindled by the fire.

His mind fled; he was carried away by madness and shaken by frenzy.

His tongue was thrust out, his life was snatched into the gloomy shades.

He proved true the prophetic words spoken beforehand to his wife Severina—but too late.

She, wounded by what had happened, seized the blessed limbs and carried them to her own estate.

[Col. 0639A] She buried them far from the City on the Nomentan Way,

seven miles away, where Pope Eventius also lay,

so that they might be entombed together in a single sarcophagus amid the flames.

Theodulus was received in a tomb apart, with his body alone;

but in spirit he was not separated from his companions in heaven.

Imma, the devoted buryer of the triumphant members,

[Col. 0640A] mortified her tender body with a garment of goat-hair cloth and lay prostrate before the tombs of the blessed.

While, through prayers to the holy bishop Sixtus, she obtained

that this place in the countryside should be consecrated as a church,

thereby later to render due honor to the martyrs,

the place thus became accustomed to having a bishop.

### Chapter III. The report of Pliny and the vengeance of the third persecution

[Col. 0639]

[Col. 0639A] At last, during this period, many earthly kingdoms in various parts of the world

were flourishing;

and Pliny, moved by their funerals, one of the destroyers of the Church,

brought the following report to the ruler Trajan:

“Most merciful among men, yet savage,

every day almost thousands of men were falling by the sword,

although they had done nothing against the laws and Roman justice,

nor committed any crime deserving the death of a condemned person,

except for the praise of Christ God and their orderly assemblies.”

Trajan replied:

“Let no judge investigate the Christians, but let him punish those who are arrested.”

Through this, as though half-asleep, the fire appeared more fiercely to burn;

the opportunity for the plots of enemies was not removed.

Indeed, by the deceits of robbers, the camp of the faithful was harassed.

But the watchful eye, the lover of Israel, does not, with its pupil obscured, favor the author of the unjust law;

rather, balancing everything on an equal shining scale,

the all-powerful Author overturned the work of this monstrous crime:

Nero’s golden house was struck

[Col. 0640A] by the flames of heaven, and its ashes settled in the lowest depths.

Soon three regions of the Roman world were utterly shattered by an earthquake;

the earth leveled four cities.

Greece lost two cities in the shock; Gaul lost two;

[Col. 0640B] and the greater part of the Syrian city of Antioch fell.

Nor did this vengeance strike human beings alone: it also struck the gods,

when the Pantheon at Rome, as though it were the common hall of all the gods,

was burned by divine fire.

Then, as once the gnats of Pelusium had emerged suddenly,

while the third plague shook the land,

living creatures arose from filth and squalor in foul places,

accustomed to burn every kind of human being and livestock with their bites,

and swarmed thickly against the savage inhabitants.
