Thus the Jews, scattered through various parts of the world and suddenly stirred up, harassed the peaceful inhabitants of Egypt, Libya, Cyprus, and other lands, and left the fields almost empty of cultivators.

### Chapter IV. Saint Pope Sixtus

[Col. 0639]

[Col. 0639C] Sixtus succeeded Alexander.

Having obtained the height of the apostolic see, he honorably arranged its administration,

assigning the sacred vessels of God to be handled only by ministers,

[Col. 0640C] and governing the insignia of this see and its subjects.

As a martyr, he entered heaven under the emperor Hadrian

and received the honor of burial beside the tomb of Peter.

### Chapter V. Saints Gaetulius, Amantius, and their companions

[Col. 0639]

[Col. 0639C] Many, under that emperor, attained the kingdom of heaven

through the reward of blood poured out,

while the cloud of the storm that had begun raged behind them.

Gaetulius then gained the stars through his flesh.

Because he was most firm in faith

and lived as a man most learned in discipline,

strengthening many in Christ’s law by speech and deeds,

Cerealis was sent to seize him.

His military colleague was Amantius,

[Col. 0639D] who was Gaetulius’ brother in the flesh and in faith.

Gaetulius, beloved by the emperor Hadrian,

was discovered teaching many people.

He disclosed that the tribune Amantius was his brother,

who, through fear of Hadrian, had been hiding in concealment.

When Cerealis unexpectedly saw him,

he became a companion filled with joy at his salvation

and took up life again at this discovery,

for these Fathers taught him carefully by the light of truth

and the worship of Christ.

They then went to Rome and soon presented Cerealis to Bishop Sixtus for baptism.

What had once happened to Saul happened again:

the man who had come to seize Christians

was himself seized; the man who had hastened to take away the blessings of salvation

now shone as one saved.

A certain superintendent of the imperial treasury, having discovered that Cerealis was a Christian, reported him to Hadrian. Hadrian sent Licinius, a consular official, to put Cerealis, his deputy, in chains.

With him the blessed Gaetulius,

and Primitivus together with Amantius,

were also bound.

[Col. 0640D] Then the former consul shouted at Cerealis:

“Has despair of life so affected you

that you brazenly despise the commands of the rulers

of the princes of the whole world?”

Cerealis answered:

“Moreover, by the full effort of my official inspection,

I have rendered the fleeting assessments

to the public treasury,

and I always promise that I will serve Christ.

I believe and desire to enjoy everlasting life.”

Then the former consul said:

“Tell me: do you wish to die, or do you wish to live?”

He replied:

“If I did not strive to enjoy the light of life,

I would not confess the heavenly glory of Christ.”

Stung by the martyr’s steadfastness, he turned to the renowned Gaetulius, a bulwark like a threatening rocky cliff, and ordered him to pour libations to Mars or Jupiter.

The blessed man laughed at the madness of the shattered man,

as at a storm raised by the Pharos of the raging sea.

When he could not injure his lofty heart,

he turned his weapons against the body.

He indecently tore away his garment of flesh

and shook the impregnable defenses of his mind.

When he recognized the martyrs’ firm strength,

defeated, he confined the men who had boasted,

where they remained for twenty-seven days.

Afterward they were reported to Hadrian still alive,

faithful to Christ, by whom they were ordered to be handed over to the flames.

The blessed Gaetulius triumphed alive at the pyre,

and, after his head had been battered with clubs,

he seized victory.

Thirteen miles from the City he placed the boundary of his faithful contest,

and from there entered heaven.

Symphorosa, his wife, taking him from the waters of the Tiber,

laid the remains brought back to her in her own estate.

Not long afterward, after her husband’s contest,

endowed with the companionship of her sons,

she too climbed to heaven’s heights as a martyr.

Having been struck with blows and hung by her hair,

she was lifted from the earth and brought near the heavens,

[Col. 0642A] and learned to walk the paths of heaven.

When her invincibility on earth was proved by her endurance,

she was bound to a stone and submerged beneath the river.

From there her spirit, triumphant, was received into heaven.

Eugenius, the chief official of Tibur and her brother,

carried away the body

and committed its limbs to the earth in an earthly burial.

As dawn leads Phoebus across the high eastern sky,

the emperor ordered seven stakes to be driven into the ground

and Symphorosa’s sons, bound to them,

to be burdened with as many agonizing tortures.

Stretched on the racks, Crescens was emptied of life through the throat;

Julianus was pierced deeply in the chest;

Nemesio was stabbed beneath the heart;

Primitivus was pierced through the navel;

[Col. 0642B] Justinus had all his stretched limbs torn apart,

and every restraint of life was driven from his flesh;

then Stacteus, pierced high by iron

amid a storm of spears, entered heaven.

Eugenius was split from chest to belly

and, stripped of his innermost limbs, was led to the stars.

On the following day, while the grieving spouses went forth,

at sunrise the enemies submerged their bodies,

torn by stabbing, in a deep sacred pit.

They called the place of the seven “Biothanatos,”

bright with the glorious victories of the faithful.

### Chapter VI. Saints Seraphia and Sabina

[Col. 0641]

[Col. 0641B] At this time the virgin Seraphia, having suffered,

shines forth; we have identified her by the blood of her Antiochene family.

While the renowned Sabina entertained her as a guest in her home—Sabina, wife of Valentinus and daughter of the illustrious Herod, a distinguished prince—the governor’s officials, alerted by report of Seraphia, seized her.

Brought before the governor, Seraphia was ordered to sacrifice to the gods.

She said:

“I fear God and worship the Lord, almighty over all,

the creator of heaven and earth.

For the false deities to whom you order me to offer sacrifice

are not gods but demons;

nor is it permitted for me to pray to them, since I serve Christ.”

While she raised up her lofty faith in clear words,

she was handed over to two lustful youths for sexual violation.

They shut her in the dark inner chambers of a shadowy bedroom.

When they sought to touch the chaste girl unlawfully,

the earth within the shaken chamber split open

and they fell lifeless, deprived of all strength.

But when dawn, returning to earth and to human beings,

brought the day on her purple face,

the governor’s ministers entered and found the holy woman

engaged in prayer, while the licentious men lay prostrate as dead.

[Col. 0641D] As many people hurried together from every side to see the heavenly deed,

amazed by it,

the governor ordered the victorious woman to be brought before the tribunal

and the men lying there in astonishment to be carried away.

The virgin touched them with abundant prayers and commanded:

“Rise, and stand upright in the name of Christ.”

At once, as though sleep had been shaken off and driven away,

they rose unharmed and rejoiced to stand upon their feet.

The judge asked the woman what had changed them,

whether she had made them mad or released them by her power.

They replied:

“Like the sun entering, a radiant light shone above,

and a wondrous young man, outstanding in appearance and beauty,

interposed himself between us and this girl.

By his splendor and trembling he shook us,

[Col. 0642C] weakened and terrified.”

The enraged judge ordered her to sacrifice to the gods

and threatened her with her father’s fate if she did not comply.

But she said:

“I will never fulfill the commands of your Satan.

Supported by the supreme name of Christ, I hurl them back.”

He ordered burning lamps to be placed on either side of her,

blazing beside her flanks.

The hurrying attendants fell backward, the brave girl overcoming their fury.

Raising her head again, she hissed at the serpent:

“Obey, woman doomed to a violent death (biothanata), and sorceress, so that by greater prudence you may escape the dark penalties of the law.”

She replied:

“Your being ‘Biothanatoi’—that is, dead by violence—is proved by you;

you are blackened by magic and deny the living and true one.

By worshiping ghosts, you yourselves will perish, clinging to them.

I offer sacrifice to the supreme Lord and God.

May he himself deem me worthy to receive me,

although I am a sinner; nevertheless, I am Christ’s servant.”

Then the sturdy virgin was beaten with hard clubs.

The ground trembled to its depths beneath the blows.

When the rod, terrified, was broken as it struck the pious girl,

it flew with a powerful force against the eye of the cruel governor.

His eye was crushed by grievous pain,

and with its extinguished light it marked him blind,

blind in heart as well.

Raging, and fiercely burning with anger at the loss of the lamp of his sight,

he declared that capital punishment should be imposed by law

on the woman who despised the nobles and public statutes,

attributing to magical figures what had been accomplished by God’s power.

The distinguished Sabina, now hastening toward the same goal,

followed her, bound by the faith of Christ through Seraphia herself.

The governor said to her:

“Why do you dishonor yourself and admit yourself to be vile

by binding yourself to these Christians in this worship,

forgetting the tokens and honor of marriage and your parents,

and scorning the gods whose wrath against you I dread?

Go back instead to your own house,

and leave the sorceress who, by her dark arts,

has removed many from the worship of the gods

and made them abandon them.”

The noble Sabina replied:

“If you could be persuaded, as I have been, by the arts of this girl whom you call wicked, you too would reject the impious images of foul gods and recognize the true God, who grants the rewards of eternal light to the just and Tartarus to the wicked.”

At these words the frightened governor allowed Sabina to leave.

She celebrated the pious virgin’s end and palm of triumph

with worthy rites and splendid honor.

Taking her relics as a precious gift,

she adorned the mausoleum’s enclosure prepared for herself according to ritual.

After some days she too was seized and brought before Elpidius,

who questioned her in these words:

“Are you the once-distinguished Sabina,

the wife of Valentinus and the illustrious offspring of Herod?”

She replied:

“I am she. I return thanks and praises to Christ,

who rescued me, a sinner, from dark filth.

While I strove to be his servant, Seraphia released me

from the bonds of phantoms and granted us knowledge of the true Lord.”

Incensed by these words, the judge pronounced sentence: because of her insults to the nobles and contempt for the gods, the steadfast Sabina was to be struck down by the sword, and her distinguished possessions added to the fiscal registers.

Her body, taken away because of her illustrious merit,

was placed among the men in the very tomb

where she had buried the bones of her venerable teacher

in faith and struggle, at the Arch of Faustinus,

in the precinct of Vindicianus’ Jupiter.

### Chapter VII. Saint Sophia and her daughters

[Col. 0643]

[Col. 0643B] Here virginly beauty, flashing with a threefold radiance,

earned the crown of martyrdom, bound by its root:

[Col. 0644B] Charity, Hope, and Faith, together with their mother Sophia.

### Chapter VIII. Saint Eustace

[Col. 0643]

[Col. 0643B] Eustace is said to have been called Placidus by name.

Together with his children, Agapius and Theopistus,

and with his wife,

he earned a triumphal splendor amid the storm.

Their deeds are read with amazement in wondrous fashion.

While the commander of the army was intent on bringing down a stag,

he became a follower of the Lord who was hunting him,

and lost the earthly gifts of wealth,

as well as his wife and children.

Poor, he lived in the countryside,

as a peasant earning his livelihood by labor.

How he was sought, and by what investigation he was found;

how he was restored to his former military honor;

how, when he was about to depart for war, he found his children and wife;

and how, after conquering the enemy, he returned with his sword victorious,

[Col. 0644C] scorning the gods and refusing to enter their temples;

how he was handed over to the wild beasts, which themselves departed after honoring him;

and how, shut up with his children and wife in the fire of Phalaris,

he reached the stars unharmed by the brazen instrument of torture—

all this is related.

### Chapter IX. Saint Eleutherius and Antia

[Col. 0643]

[Col. 0643C] Then Eleutherius, distinguished by virtue and blood,

governed celebrated Messana as its pious bishop.

Handsome in the fervor of God and in chaste beauty,

he gave himself, while capturing others, beneath Christ’s yoke.

For the praise of the Thunderer, he overcame

a fiery bed of steel,

[Col. 0644C] fires blazing with pitch, pine, and oil in a frying pan,

and defeated the coals of the grate with his powerful breast.

Exposed to wild beasts, he overcame the lions through his piety.

Thus, seizing the sword at his throat, he departed with his mother,

Antia, the blessed woman who rejoiced in her blessed pledge.

### Chapter X. The defense of Quadratus and Aristides, and the cessation of the persecution

[Col. 0643]

[Col. 0643D] While such legal violence raged everywhere through countryside and towns

against the saints,

men renowned for the teaching of the apostolic fountain remained.

Among these was the distinguished Quadratus, a servant,

a prophet supported by the doctrine and breath of faith

and radiant with heavenly inspiration.

By his writings and speech he defended the way.

Preparing an illustrious apologetic volume

in defense of the Christian religion,

he labored to offer it to Hadrian,

fortifying the truth with vigor.

Then the emperor received another outstanding work,

not unequal in reason,

which Aristides had sent beforehand,

fragrant with heavenly inspiration.

He received it in praise of our faith,

and, taking up the inquiries of the Greek governor Serenus

[cod. 2: *granu*],

he perceived that it was unjust to punish Christians for this matter

when no guilt impelled them.

Judging it unlawful that our people should be condemned without a crime,

he soon restrained the Jews, maddened by the torch of wickedness,

with slaughter.

He avenged the saints whom the Jews had tortured

because they would not join them in arms

against the Romans.

He excluded the Jews from Jerusalem and, restoring the city with walls,

yielded it to its pious worshippers. The following wording concerning the city’s designation and Augusta, the emperor’s wife, is textually corrupt: “and it lies open to these, called by the merits of the ancients without precedent, Augusta the wife, with the senate’s favor.”

But the victor arranged the matter according to equitable laws.

### Chapter XI. Telesphorus and Hyginus, popes

[Col. 0645]

[Col. 0645A] After Sixtus, Telesphorus adorned the Roman see.

Chosen as an anchorite for the apostolic office,

he had instructed peoples by an angelic life

through the vast fields over which he had travelled.

He, fervently teaching men to lay down the instruments of earthly warfare,

established the fasts which the holy Church maintains,

Easter,

and the celebration of the mysteries of Christ’s Nativity at night.

Nor was the third hour of the day to pass without brightness, the hour at which the heavenly splendor of the cross underwent its miracle.

He also commanded that an angelic hymn should resound amid the sacred rites.

Then, resisting as a martyr and triumphing gloriously at the end,

he was buried beside the sacred relics of holy Peter.

[Col. 0646A] His successor Hyginus arranged and adorned the clergy.

When he had completed this office and occupied the see for four years,

Pius, honoring his celebrated life with his name,

succeeded him.

Both were adorned with piety: Pius was the brother of Pastor.

During the episcopate of Pius, Hermes published a book.

Its commands are greeted by the first sheets of Paul,

revealing to himself the orders delivered through angelic admonitions.

The corrupt passage appears to say that, by a command of a heavenly being in a shepherd’s guise, the book received from the Lord its title, “Shepherd” (*Pastor*), and instructions concerning Easter.

The little book, which he was accustomed to read in Greek

in public churches,

is worthy of belief, as Jerome bears witness.

### Chapter XII. Novatus and Pudens

[Col. 0645]

[Col. 0645B] Under this bishop several distinguished men shone forth.

For the blessed Novatus, still surviving,

continued to flourish in the honor of apostolic light,

radiant with its splendor.

He was Timothy’s brother and the Lord’s minister to the end.

There was also Pudens, so called for his modesty,

[Col. 0646B] Paul’s disciple.

In honor of the holy name,

he built a title-church named for the Shepherd,

and preserved to the end, in apostolic teaching and baptismal worship,

the honorable purity of an innocent robe.

### Chapter XIII. Saints Praxedes and Potentiana

[Col. 0645]

[Col. 0645B] The daughters of this Pudens,

Praxedes and Potentiana,

were distinguished by his holiness.

He educated them in the light of the Word and in chastity

and appointed them as virgins to serve Christ.

After their father’s death,

they devoted themselves to prayer, praises, and fasts,

cultivating their life through kindly deeds

and spending all their inheritance

to support Christ’s poor.

They built a baptismal font in the royal residence

in their father’s name, that of the blessed Shepherd,

and constructed it so that their servants might shine there.

The pious Shepherd, radiant in the light of Easter,

consecrated there nineteen persons,

and six in the pool,

[Col. 0645C] all endowed with the splendor of freedom

and eager to follow Christ’s standards in battle.

These illustrious sisters, distinguished by such virtues,

after their father’s wealth had been poured through the bodies of the poor

into Christ,

and after many contests endured for the sake of chastity,

sought heaven,

to be rewarded with the prizes of their pious labor.

They were buried in the cemetery of the elevated Priscilla,

beside the bones of their father Pudens,

after striving to adorn many bodies of the faithful

with a glorious funeral.

Among these, Praxedes had prepared mausoleums

for the blessed martyr Symmetrius

and twenty-two companions,

whom Caesar Antoninus, with his impious sword,

caused to be buried beneath the slaughter

for the praise of Christ.

### Chapter XIV. Saint Alexander, bishop and martyr

[Col. 0645]

[Col. 0645C] After Nero, this savage emperor,

during the fourth persecution,

wearing down the Church by commands of fiery cruelty,

scattered the blood of the faithful

over many regions of the world in honor of the holy name.

This persecution gave the heavens the holy martyr Alexander,

most illustrious for the glory of his miracles.

When his reputation for virtues had spread widely,

at one time his parents brought to him a cold corpse

of someone who had died.

They declared that they would believe in Christ with steadfast faith

if he would restore life to the dead.

The blessed man devoted his prayers for life to the King,

then commanded the frozen corpse:

[Col. 0645D] “In the name of the Father, and of the only Son,

and of the Holy Spirit, rise.”

[Col. 0646C] Awakened by this lofty voice, the man began to say:

“Listen, parents, and all the assembled people.

I was led away by two most dreadful Egyptians

whose faces were dark,

and sent into a place like the darkest pit.

But when a splendid young man suddenly came,

the entire place was shaken and struck by trembling.

That most radiant young man cried out:

‘Release the boy immediately and without delay,

for Alexander, the servant of God, calls him.’

And behold, as you see, I have been restored to my body.

Now, lord Alexander, baptize me with holy water,

lest it appear that I have not been allowed to see him on this day.”

The name of the resurrected man was Luceius.

Together with him, one hundred and four neophytes

shone with heavenly radiance in the consecrated font.

[Col. 0646D] But while fame spread the saint everywhere,

Antoninus, moved by it, handed God’s chosen one

over to the prefect Cornelianus for custody.

The prefect seized him while he was celebrating and teaching the mysteries

at the command of the enraged emperor.

He brought him to Rome to be reported to Caesar

and presented the blessed man with his hands bound.

When questioned at length, he spoke with lofty eloquence

about faith in the heavenly truth of Christ.

He was ordered to be tortured on hard wood.

Then he was raised into a black prison.

As he was being led there with the guards,

he said:

“Caesar declares:

‘Four days of postponement are granted to you

for the sake of your worship.

Abandon your vanity and come over to us of your own accord.’”

[Col. 0647B] The martyr replied:

“Consider the days already past,

and today complete the sufferings you are postponing.”

Crescentianus, a presbyter, followed him,

together with Valerianus and Bonifatius.

When the blessed man was shut in the dreadful darkness of the prison,

one of them sat beneath a tree, lamenting.

After grief, he had grown heavy with sleep

when he saw an angel who knew his anxieties

and said:

“I have strengthened your bishop,

releasing his bonds by my visitation.

And now take care not to sit beneath the tree,

lest a messenger betray you to the tyrant.”

The bishop was then led out of custody

and displayed before the cruel prince to be tortured.

Hung on the rack, he was torn with claws,

[Col. 0647C] and lamps burned his sides with fire.

After triumphing over these torments, he was led to Apollo.

When he began to offer the lofty sacrifice of his vow beyond the stars,

part of the temple, struck by divine power, collapsed.

Caesar, attributing this to deceitful arts,

gave the saint to be devoured by savage teeth.

When none of the beasts touched him,

he ordered a furnace to burn with the greatest heat.

Clothed in glowing whiteness,

the saint, secure, poured out a prayer in the middle of the pyre.

No trace of the heat remained upon him;

the furnace’s fire was happily softened for the martyr.

The tyrant then ordered his head to be cut off.

One of the attendants, speaking from his heart,

whose name was Herculianus, cried out:

“Cruel Antoninus, tyrant whose senses are captive,

why do you stand so blind and deaf?

Behold the servant of Christ:

after sharp rods,

overcome racks,

blazing lamps,

the tearing of claws,

the fall of the idol and temple,

the troubled mouths of lions and bears being closed,

and the furnace’s blazing fire, which he survived,

he joyfully seeks the swords.

What fool would doubt that the true God exists,

who strengthens his own with such exalted power?”

Caesar, full of anger, wearied him with various tortures

and at last struck him with the sword.

But the bishop, about to be sacrificed,

asked a widow to lend him a handkerchief.

Taking it, and covering himself with the sign of the holy cross,

he uncovered his tunic, stood alone in a linen garment,

and covered his eyes with the borrowed cloth.

Kneeling, he received the stroke of death,

twenty miles distant from the City.

Soon the earth shook violently,

and destroyed the baths and all the buildings of the village.

The woman’s handkerchief, which the soldiers had displayed

as evidence of their wickedness,

was returned by a certain boy who carried it,

who was clearly a heavenly inhabitant.

Taking it back with amazement,

the woman confessed Christ and honored the martyr.

Crescentianus and the bishop’s companions,

having received the relics when the same boy revealed them,

placed them where the fiery furnace had pressed its heat.

They set up a marble bearing the blessed man’s name,

his dignity, and the boundary of the place.

Later Pope Damasus built a crypt there

and decently transferred the holy bones to it.

### Chapter XV. Saint Felicitas and her sons

[Col. 0647]

[Col. 0647D] Through this persecution Felicitas overcame,

beloved by Christ, who consecrated her pledges.

Afterward, by consecrating her children, she gave the most fruitful tree its happy fruits.

The prefect tried to turn her by his skill,

soothing her with calm words and threatening her with harsh ones.

Whether offering calm or savage threats,

he brought her sorrow.

She answered him:

“I cannot be loosened by gentleness,

nor can I be broken by the harshness of the raging man.

Nor will the heavenly Spirit allow me

to be caught in the nets of the lurking traitor.

Therefore I am confident that I shall conquer even beyond death: though I am butchered, I shall triumph over you completely.”

Then the prefect prepared a contest against the mother.

On the following day, the day of Mars, he sat in the forum

and ordered her to be brought before him,

accompanied by her seven children.

He warned her to yield to her sons.

The blessed Felicitas answered him:

“Your cruelty’s gentle exhortation

is an impious pity for this supposed affection.”

Then she turned to her beloved sons and addressed them:

“Look at heaven, my children, and gaze upon it.

Here Christ, in his goodness, supports you with his choir.

Fight for the salvation of your souls.

Open yourselves as faithful men to his love.”

At this, Publius ordered her to be shaken with blows

and, summoning her children, urged them to sacrifice.

Januarius said:

“You are urging this, fool that you are.

But the highest wisdom preserves me

and will grant that all your tortures be overcome.”

The judge hid him in prison, bound with scourges.

Felix followed:

“There is one whom we know,

to whom we pay the vows of pure service.

Do not believe that we can be separated from Christ

by affection for our family.

Let the blows rage;

our faith cannot be conquered or changed.”

Then Philippus said:

“Those whom you call gods

are neither powerful nor regarded as deities.

They are empty images, filthy and senseless.

Those who submit to them are destined to perish forever.”

Silvanus said:

“If you think that we fear these temporary tortures,

eternal torments will carry away those who are defeated.

For we know what rewards have been appointed for the just

and what due penalties have been established for the wicked.

Therefore we despise earthly laws

and strive to obey heavenly ones.”

“I am Alexander, servant of Christ, the God.

With my mouth I confess him,

believing with a steadfast heart.

I pray to him continually and humbly worship him.

You behold a frail age in the body, in which the white radiance of prudent wisdom glitters.”

Then Vitalis said:

“He lives who prays to the true God;

the one who prays to demons does not live.”

[Col. 0650A] Then Martialis said:

“Those who reject the true God

will burn in an inescapable flame of fire.”

Having continued in such words,

strong in conduct,

fervent in love and fear of the supreme King

and Judge of the world,

the censor reported their words to the emperor.

He handed them over to different judges

to be destroyed by discordant punishments.

After the savage scourging of Januarius,

he was struck with lead in prison.

Felix was killed with clubs, together with Philippus.

Silvanus was thrown down from a great height.

Martialis and Alexander,

together with Vitalis,

had their necks cut off

and descended to enter the glory of everlasting life.

[Col. 0650B] After all the sufferings that her pledges had endured,

the blessed mother was punished last.

Endowed with her children advancing to heaven,

she passed into the palaces of the heavenly King

to receive the certain joys of her rewards.

### Chapter XVI. Saint Concordius

[Col. 0649]

[Col. 0649B] Through this slaughter the city of Spoleto consecrated

the holy martyr Concordius to heaven.

He was born at Rome to his father Gordianus.

Once appointed subdeacon by the ordination of the bishop Pius,

he shone in office.

Later, raised to the title of presbyter of the Shepherd,

he lived nobly in heavenly service,

supported kindly by prayers and fasts.

By these he lived in the light;

by these he kept vigil in the darkness,

diligently attending to the needs of the poor with his household.

His father sent this willing son, who desired to climb to heaven,

to the blessed Eutyches, who was living

on his estate on the Salarian Way.

A certain count named Torquatus, remaining in the city of Spoleto

and envious of their praises,

called the blessed Concordius from the countryside

and asked him, inquisitively, what his name was.

He replied that he was a Christian (*fore*, for *esse*).

The count said:

“I am asking your name, not your Christ.”

“I am a Christian; I proclaim Christ.”

Firm in faith, he was pressed to profane acts.

He endured after his back had been beaten with harsh clubs.

Afterward the blessed Eutyches and the bishop

came and asked the judge for the martyr,

requesting that he be given to them for several days.

Perhaps through the count’s favor [cod. 2: *favorus*], Bishop Antimus granted their request and ordained Concordius presbyter. After the allotted days, once consecrated, Concordius was returned to the judge.

He was asked what he desired for his salvation.

But he said:

“Christ is my salvation.

To him I always offer the sacred gift of praise.”

The count, full of fury,

tortured him for a long time while he was suspended.

Then he sent him, loaded with iron, into prison,

where he was comforted by the solace of the heavenly ones.

After three nights spent in chains,

the enraged companion considered whether to overcome the mind through the body

and ordered the attendants either to kill him

if they found him sacrificing by the slaughter of his mind,

or to immolate him by the slaughter of his flesh

if they found him refusing.

The agents rushed in,

carrying a little statue of Jupiter.

They ordered him either to sacrifice to it

or to have his neck cut by the drawn sword.

He said:

“To you, Christ Jesus, I return thanks.”

Exalted in spirit, he spat in Jupiter’s face.

Relying on his confession of the highest name,

his head was cut off by the sword.

With his mind unshaken,

he sent his rejoicing spirit to the stars.

Two kindly clerics, gathering up the clod of earth

left with the relic,

laid it beside the walls,

still wet with blood.

At the same place, many streams of liquid

were brought forth from the fountain of the water of life.

### Chapter XVII. Saint Pontianus

[Col. 0649]

[Col. 0649D] Here Pontianus, triumphing over Fabianus

in the storm of this age,

became a sharer in the heavenly glory of Christ.

When asked what his name was, he replied:

“My parents named me Pontianus,

but ‘Christian’ is a greater name than that.”

[Col. 0650D] Enraged by his words,

Fabianus ordered Pontianus, stripped,

to be beaten with rods.

After he had been beaten and the ground was wet with the flow of blood,

he was ordered to tread barefoot upon burning coals.

The martyr said:

“I walk through this heat

by the power of my Christ.”

“Dip your hand in the name of Jupiter.”

When he resisted these words,

the judge ordered the suspended athlete

to be torn with iron hooks,

until the executioner was exhausted by the cruelty.

Then, thrust into the darkness of a prison,

he was strengthened by provisions granted by God.

Again led out for combat,

he was exposed, with the town watching,

to two lions.

Made gentle by faith in the martyr,

they avoided touching the blessed man’s limbs.

The crowd, seeing this, cried out loudly:

“The God of the Christians is great!”

Again the blessed man was sent back to prison.

For twelve days, covered in darkness,

people were forbidden to sustain him with their words.

[Col. 0651B] But the lofty love of the heavenly beings

[Col. 0652A] cannot be driven back by prison doors or restrained by bolts.

Rather, when earthly food was denied him,

the heavenly giver supplied him with a meal

through higher consolation

and strengthened him by heavenly nourishment.

When this period of days had passed,

and the executioners already thought him dead,

they entered the hiding place to remove the body.

Amazed, they heard him singing praises.

He was led out and placed upon an iron bed,

and his back was covered with burning lead.

The lofty warrior laughed at these things as worthless,

trampling torments under his exalted mind.

The fierce judge, confounded, brought the contest to an end with the sword.

Thus, with his head severed,

the martyr climbed to the kingdom of heavenly glory.

[Col. 0652B] His fellow soldiers rejoiced to receive the relic.

### Chapter XVIII. The vengeance of the fourth persecution

[Col. 0651]

[Col. 0651B] Here a divided, flying storm shook only Gaul

and Asia,

and crowned many saints,

who conquered earthly battles with a fierce executioner.

But a plague followed throughout the regions of the world,

infecting Roman bodies with a putrid disease,

and driving them toward worms,

just as once the kingdoms of Canopus were disgracefully corrupted

by worms, decay, and flies.

The pestilence soon slaughtered Italy itself,

which had been the head of wickedness,

with such a vast destruction:

[Col. 0652B] throughout it, without a peasant,

the countryside, towns, and villas became deserted,

the forests and great places were turned into ruins.

All the Roman battle lines and phalanxes,

which occupied distant winter quarters,

are said to have been destroyed far and wide,

consumed by the avenging force.

And when the Marcomannic wars arose and resounded,

they could be conducted only with a newly gathered levy,

which Marcus is said to have organized continuously for three years.

### Chapter XIX. The rain and victory granted to the soldiers through invocation of Christ

[Col. 0651]

[Col. 0651B] This power of Christ the Lord is shown to have been exercised

[Col. 0651C] not only among our own people, but also among outsiders, as the letter of the commander of the camp attests, setting forth how it occurred.

When the land had been scorched

and the thirsty troops were hemmed in on every side by the surrounding enemy,

with the barbarians closing in,

threatening death, and the sky offering no help,

certain Christian athletes, strong in piety,

fell on their knees and poured themselves out in public prayers.

Having obtained rain,

they calmed the heat beneath the clouds.

[Col. 0652B] They satisfied the troops with showers drawn down from heaven.

[Col. 0652C] They put the enemy to flight with frequent lightning

and heavenly fire.

From this the legion was afterward called “Thunderbolt,”

through which victory was indeed won by a few soldiers,

but attributed to Christ’s abundant goodness—

a deed not to be compared with any ancient trophy of the Romulids,

achieved by a cohort inexperienced in the laws of war,

but accomplished by the customary power of Christ’s majesty.

### Contents of Book Four

[Col. 0651]

CAP. I.—On Saint Apollonius. CAP. II.—On Saints Pontianus, Eusebius, and their companions. CAP. III.—On vengeance for the aforesaid cruelty. CAP. IV.—On Saint Pope Anicetus and the teacher Hegesippus. CAP. V.—On Saint Polycarp. CAP. VI.—On Saints Soter, Eleutherius, and Victor, popes. CAP. VII.—On vengeance for the fifth persecution. CAP. VIII.—On Pope Zephyrinus and Saint Callistus. CAP. IX.—On Saint Martina. CAP. X.—On Saint Pope Urban and Cecilia. CAP. XI.—On Saints Pope Pontianus and the presbyter Hippolytus. CAP. XII.—On Pope Anterus and vengeance for the sixth persecution. CAP. XIII.—On the two emperors named Philip, and on the martyr Pontius and Fabianus. CAP. XIV.—On Saints Pope Cornelius and the martyr Cyprian and their companions. CAP. XV.—On Saints Abdon and Sennen. CAP. XVI.—On Saints Parthenius and Calocerus. CAP. XVII.—On Saints Anatolia and Victoria. CAP. XVIII.—On Saints Pergentinus and Laurentinus.

# THE FOURTH BOOK BEGINS

## CHAPTER I. On Saint Apollonius

[Col. 0651C] The flame of war-bearing heat, briefly lulled,

tries to grow warm again against our world under Commodus,

[Col. 0652C] while he rules, when great men already embrace

the laws of the nurturing faith,

and they shine in the arms of Christ,

[Col. 0653A] among whom Apollonius was renowned for the power of his light—

a philosopher in the worship of Christ, and a senator of Rome.

He is accused of exalting Christ as his teacher.

He does not publicly refuse to proclaim the truth, setting forth

the words of the heavenly one above in faith,

while the senate listens,

and, when asked, commits them to a volume in polished speech.

And, as you may suppose, he deserved to plead before Getic bands,

for the sentence given against him orders that his head be cut off,

[Col. 0654A] since among them this old law had long been established:

that Christians once brought before them, unless they refuted the truth,

were in no way to be released unpunished.

What a welcome law! The just must die for the crime of truth;

liars live, and those who deny the truth flourish;

and, as one might approve, to condemn the truth and admit falsehood,

to destroy virtue, to raise crime without shame,

to call virtue vice,

and to defend crime as truth!

## CHAPTER II. On Saints Pontianus, Eusebius, and their companions

[Col. 0653]

[Col. 0653A] Then Pontianus, Eusebius, and their companions,

Vincentius and Peregrinus, high martyrs,

having been enriched by their gain, entered the stars;

they brought earthly things into heaven,

so that, freed first of all, they might take up heavenly things,

[Col. 0653B] and, so that they might devote their gains to heaven,

they diligently spend talents destined to be multiplied a hundredfold.

To these Julius the senator and his household are soon added,

won for the heavenly King; Rufinus the presbyter

consecrates them in the waters, and Julius, taught by pious teachers,

is himself made whole,

a soldier of the high King, a senator,

and a participant in the kingdom

which he had prepared with perishable resources,

bearing the burdens of the lofty path of instruction,

handing obstacles over to the needy,

giving earthly things and acquiring heavenly ones,

scattering what flees and gathering what is eternal.

When Commodus, taking up the matter with imperial authority,

heard of this, he angrily ordered him to be arrested

and handed over to the hearing of Vitellius,

[Col. 0653C] commander of the infantry,

so that he might demand his wealth and bend him to the shrines.

Vitellius gave him to the prison for three days;

afterward he ordered him to be brought forward in chains.

From that point, taking up a lofty, hard, vigorous beginning,

he had him beaten with savage rods for so long

until he sent his free spirit through the stars,

an elder dedicated to the heavenly senate.

Pious teachers gather his blessed body

and placed among the tombs of Calepodius.

Then, having been arrested by the judge Vitellius,

while they were suspended and weighed upon the distant rack,

their limbs stretched by powerful sinews,

cruelly tormented with rods,

and their sides set ablaze with dreadful flames,

[Col. 0653D] the executioner Antonius watches these things beneath the scaffold:

he sees a youth standing with a sponge,

healing and soothing the wounds of the pious.

[Col. 0654A] He cries out: “He is God—the Christ whom they preach.”

Then he secretly makes his escape;

Rufinus washes him in the sacred font when he confesses Christ.

Returning freely to the tyrant,

while he declares himself a Christian, he is punished,

[Col. 0654B] and by sentence his throat is cut and he is sent to the stars;

the broad Aurelia Road receives his limbs in the earth.

The fellowship stands unmoved in Christ’s praise,

whether suspended or released,

neither broken by harshness nor subdued by gentleness.

Therefore the maddened, savage judge orders

Eusebius’s instrument of blessed speech to be cut out;

but he cannot destroy the laws of Christ,

and the giver of the tongue supplies the mouth’s functions.

Without a tongue he produces the tongue’s words,

and, cut apart, he cries out with an unbroken voice:

“To you, Jesus Christ, be everlasting glory.”

Shut behind the prison gates after their struggle,

they resound with praises to the giver of victory.

[Col. 0654C] Thus, while days and nights echoed in succession,

a certain priest, Lappulus of the Capitol,

who had been afflicted with blindness for four years,

comes out of darkness and departs in light,

enlightened in heart and seeing in body.

Simplicius, seeing what had been accomplished in the prison,
renounces the altars of demons;
having received Christ and been cleansed in mind, he shines forth.

When the judge reports these deeds to Commodus,

he quickly orders that they be punished.

Afterward the martyrs are summoned to their crowns.

They are led to the rock of execution, where they seek their goal,

and there, their bodies struck with lead,

they leave behind their burdens and ascend, triumphantly joyful.

The holy Rufinus gathers their recovered bodies

and buries them [Col. 0654D] at the sixth milestone from the City.

At this same time, Faustinus, driven by the sword at Milan,

passes through blood to the stars.

## CHAPTER III. On vengeance for the aforesaid cruelty

[Col. 0653]

[Col. 0653D] The burning of the City followed as vengeance

for the king’s iniquity:

the renowned Capitol, struck by a divine, quivering thunderbolt,

blazed with fire;

the library, the splendor of the ancestors, was burned,

and the adjoining buildings, planted side by side, were consumed.

Then a more extensive fire followed,

[Col. 0654D] and, in the vast temple of Vesta and the noble palace,

is said to have overthrown a very large part of the City.

This Commodus, a nuisance to the City and the world,

judged a public enemy of humankind,

was laid low, strangled by the fury of the people.

## CHAPTER IV. On Saint Pope Anicetus and the teacher Hegesippus

[Col. 0655]

[Col. 0655A] After the pontiffs previously mentioned,

Anicetus was chosen to the heights of the Roman see;

he adorns its sacred laws,

forbidding the clergy long hair under the teaching of Paul,

and, crowned by martyrdom, blessed, he enters the stars.

In his time Hegesippus, an excellent teacher,

enters Rome, previously imbued with the commands

and sects of Plato and skilled in the sophistries of the age.

[Col. 0656A] When he sees that the worship of Christ surpasses all things,

as a critic of the sects he chooses the better way and follows it;

he shines in the doctrine of truth,

and, faithful in his deeds, is received as a witness.

Explaining the times of the pure beginning,

he follows the Gospel’s deeds without deceit,

and proclaims Christ in books and in actions.

## CHAPTER V. On Saint Polycarp

[Col. 0655]

[Col. 0655A] Then Polycarp, irradiated by the light of God

from the apostolic mouth,

John’s hearer and follower,

illumines the Roman citadels with divine light,

[Col. 0656A] recalling many through the lawful contest of faith,

and, watching the jester, marks him as an enemy,

with Satan as his father.

## CHAPTER VI. On Saints Soter, Eleutherius, and Victor, popes

[Col. 0655]

[Col. 0655B] Soter follows Anicetus;

he excludes the female sex from the altars,

though it possesses strength.

When he has been joined to the fathers, Eleutherius succeeds him.

Lucius, the British king, asks him by written petition

that he may deserve to become Christ’s pupil through the holy font.

He judges that no food should be considered unclean by Christians,

since human usage judges it clean.

After him Victor arranges the government of the Church,

and, together with the Eastern bishops,

confirms that holy Easter should be celebrated on the day

on which Christ’s sacred Resurrection took place. [Col. 0656B]

He also orders, if necessity should arise,

that a gentile who has confessed the mysteries of the faith of Christ

may be consecrated in whatever place,

whether on the wave or on land (*fluctuve solove*; ms. 2 reads *salove*, “or on the sea”).

From this he leaves behind little works written on parchment,

pure writings;

and he departs as a martyr while Severus persecutes Christ,

Severus, who, fifth after the dreadful commands of Nero,

scattered the saints to be killed in savage slaughter,

by which many in various regions prepared themselves for the stars.

## CHAPTER VII. On vengeance for the fifth persecution

[Col. 0655]

[Col. 0655B] Nor did vengeance remain long delayed,

for civil wars soon thunder,

three wars falling upon them,

and with threefold crash shaking the Romans’ great defensive strength,

[Col. 0655C] laying low the supports of the state,

no less than the plague once laid low beasts,

when the fifth plague of Egypt

[Col. 0656B] wore down the kingdoms that disturbed the people consecrated to Christ.

Although the storm was cut through by these evils

and not crushed,

while this whirlwind was completely stretched and driven on,

[Col. 0656C] Alexander reigns over the world

and raises many to heaven by the sword.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Pope Zephyrinus and Saint Callistus

[Col. 0655]

[Col. 0655C] Zephyrinus assumes the rights of Victor at Rome;

under his adornment the order of priests

and the mysteries of the sacred table shine.

Before him Proculus, a Cataphrygian, is said to have been defeated

by the law of Christ when the eloquent Gaius argued the case;

Zephyrinus himself was buried in his own tomb.

After him Callistus is raised to Peter’s seat,

a Roman by blood and a Ravennate by native region.

He establishes four sacred fasts each year,

to be observed in their seasons;

he orders murmuring among the people to be avoided,

and lesser persons to beware insults against the teacher and their elders;

he forbids fellowship with the condemned,

and insists that the decrees of the pious Fathers are not to be changed.

He also teaches that no one should attack the external duties of another,

being content with his own;

but permits sees to be changed according to law,

[Col. 0655D] and determines what is to be followed

concerning incest and other disgraceful offenses,

provided that the accusers can accuse properly

and their charges be proved by witnesses,

so that fallen priests may rise again from their guilt.

He founded a basilica for the people across the river Tiber,

and a burial place on the Appian Way,

where he gave rest to many sacred martyrs and bishops.

[Col. 0656C] He added praise to God, night and day.

While he persisted in prayers to the Lord

for the people’s deliverance,

and for the people to be pulled from the lake of death

and from dreadful darkness,

God reveals that He has heard the prayers of His devoted servant,

showing that the shrines must be overthrown

and that the human race, which wicked dominion had oppressed

under an unjust law,

must be snatched from savage hands.

Accordingly, among the rest, Jupiter’s chief temple was struck down;
its great collapse from the south made the truth manifest:
the true sun was admitted into the darkness, as one part received the light.

The hand of the wicked idol melted away,

proclaiming that the demon’s power was vanishing

and that all sacrilege was flowing away

before the face of the Lord, who crushes hostile kingdoms.

[Col. 0656D] The priests ask that offerings be brought to the altars of Jupiter,

and the frenzied crowd blindly orders the gods to be appeased.

Cattle are slaughtered; cakes fill the altars.

While they strive to soothe the shades with sacred pollution,

the clear sky suddenly hurls thunderbolts without warning.

[Col. 0657A] Four sacrificers collapse, killed by the sudden force of heavenly power,

before the very altars.

The altar of Jupiter himself is burned by the flames of heaven,

so that it may be clear that the heavenly weapons are not Jupiter’s:

that daylight grows dark, clouds cover the sky,

and everything threatens guilty mortals with present death;

the City itself, while heaven battles,

seems destined to depart in sudden ashes,

victorious over the world.

Fear urges the terrified to flee,

leaving the City behind.

While, warned by fear, they cross the waters of the Tiber,

they find Callistus secure in the Lord of all things,

giving his vows in praise

and occupied with joyful songs.

The consul Palmatius quickly reports this to Alexander,

who immediately assigns to him the task

of gathering the Christians to the altars

or subjecting them to punishment.

[Col. 0657B] He sends ten men from the army, ready to obey,

to bind the men, and to bring in the clergy

and Father Callistus.

But when they enter where the assembly was engaged in worship,

their faces reveal the darkness within their hearts.

Unable to see the sacred rites in a light they did not deserve,

deprived of sight by this justly deserved frustration,

they lose their sight.

Terrified by these events, the consul reveals what has happened to the king

and presents the men to him.

Recognizing them after careful examination,

Alexander assigns the deed to poisonous magic.

The consul replies:

“If these things are performed by magical arts,

where are the powers and divinities of our gods?

Why does your piety not order offerings to be brought to the gods,

lest the commonwealth be ruined by these men’s incantations?”

The Augustus advises that Mercury be invoked through sacred rites.

They appoint a day and order all Romans to be present,

with a herald revealing the gods’ secrets.

[Col. 0657C] While the blood of cattle is poured upon the polluted altars,

untamed calves fall here, pigs are slaughtered there;

there priests of Bacchus, mixed among the shrines,

are driven mad.

A girl is seized by the twisted god,

and cries aloud:

“Callistus’s God is living and true;

in his indignation at the pollution of these things,

he will destroy your power,

because you seek what is empty.”

Stunned by these events, Palmatius immediately approaches

the blessed pontiff of Peter,

prostrate, and clasps his feet:

“I have recognized,” he says,

“that Christ, whom the demons driven out today confessed,

is rightly worshiped as Lord and God.

Therefore, I beseech you by him:

rescue me from the worship of phantoms,

and wash me in the blessed bath,

by which you teach the righteous to shine.”

[Col. 0657D] When the bishop proves that he has spoken these things

from a pure heart,

he imposes the customary fasts and catechizes him.

When he has been washed and rises cleansed

from the life-giving waters, he cries out:

“Truly I have seen the manifest light, Jesus,

who has illumined me with heavenly honor.”

His children are reborn as children of the Church;

a wife is joined to him,

and the household of servants is washed clean,

a gracious company of fifty-two persons,

of each sex in distinct measure.

From then on he strives to spend his resources

on the holy and needy;

he supplies them with food and clothing.

After thirty days Caesar asks for him,

hears that he has become a Christian,

and orders that he be brought before him.

[Col. 0658A] Arrested by a certain tribune, Torquatus, who lay in ambush,

he is thrust into the darkness of the Mamertine prison.

Three days afterward he is brought in chains

before Alexander, who orders him to be released.

He is released but not disarmed.

Then the emperor says:

“Have you become so mad, poor Palmatius,

that, abandoning the gods,

you follow a buried man?”

The consul replies with a different answer:

“Once ignorant and wretched,

I wandered after empty things.

Now, recognizing the true Lord Christ,

I humbly seek him,

so that he may pardon my error,

driven by the darkness of stupidity.”

Laughing deceitfully, Alexander hands him over

to the illustrious senator Simplicius,

ordering him to recall the gods through gentle means

and compel him with persuasion,

while avoiding violent measures.

[Col. 0658B] Received with gentle and distinguished honor,

he spends his days in fasting,

accompanied by vigils and pious prayers,

praying with abundant tears to the supreme Father

and to the Begotten Son,

and seeking pardon for the paths of his former error.

Meanwhile Felix comes,

asking him on behalf of his wife Blanda,

who was sick and bedridden [Note: [Col. 0657D] *Clinica*: that is, lying in bed.]

and had endured a prolonged, almost lifeless death in body for four years.

He prostrates himself on the ground before Simplicius’s servants and wife,

and, drenched in a fountain of tears, prays:

“Almighty One,

who have irradiated your servant

with the light of pious illumination,

giving me Jesus as eternal light,

I ask you, while saving your servant,

to raise her gently from her bed,

so that you alone may be known

as the creator of all things.”

[Col. 0658C] At once Blanda joyfully hastens to his feet,

comes to Simplicius’s house,

and cries out and begs:

“Baptize me in the name of the Lord Jesus,

by whose hand I have been seized

and lifted from my bed.”

Felix, happy at seeing these deeds, and the senator Simplicius
begin to urge the blessed man Palmatius
that they themselves be purified.

Immediately he strives to summon Father Callistus.

When he comes, he consecrates them all

with Christ’s baptism:

Simplicius, Blanda and Felix, their children and servants,

sixty-eight souls in all.

The saints rejoice as they honor these venerable trophies;

they give praise to the Lord,

through whom comes the victory of the Most High.

When Alexander learns that many have been taken from the shrines

through baptism,

he directs weapons against them,

sending armed men against their bodies,

which he believes will not prepare to resist; [Col. 0658D]

he seizes what is light and earthly,

and judges that all must suffer the loss of their heads.

Raising the heads of the distinguished City on high,

he brings forth an example of death

and a triumph of faith.

He cruelly kills the presbyter Calepodius,

already aged and weakened in blood, but strong in spirit,

with a rigid sword.

He orders the old man’s bones to be dragged through Rome

and hides them in the Tiber.

But the good Father Callistus asks divers

to search for them.

When they find them,

they lift them from the winding currents of the river

and gladden the pope with joyful words of news.

With sweet hymns he returns pious songs to the Lord,

[Col. 0659A] receives the body,

and fills the holy funeral with abundant fragrance.

Covering the precious jewels with linen cloth,

he receives with powerful honor

the elder whom he himself had celebrated,

placing him in the tomb of Christ’s athletes.

A butcher, having cut down a dense mass of branches,

pursues the offspring of the noble tree.

Seizing Pope Callistus in raging fury,

he seeks to overcome him by hunger.

When the fifth day has passed,

and he hears that the weakened man

is growing stronger instead,

he increases the withering fasts

with powerful blows of rods.

Assailing him with wooden blows every day,

he beats the man savagely,

forbidding anyone to bring even the comfort

of visiting him by night;

whoever is found doing so

is to pay the penalty with his life.

While he shelters unfed for many days in the cave,

the sky offers him consolation.

[Col. 0659B] Calepodius is sent,

bringing these sweet words:

“Be firm, Father,

for your crown is now complete.

May you receive the abundant reward

of the eternal gift.”

Nor does the hidden guardian cease

to provide medicinal care.

There was a soldier named Privatus,

covered with ulcers;

constant pain tortured his breathless body.

Prostrate at the pope’s feet,

he devoutly begs in prayer

to be relieved of his disease.

The Father urges him to have faith

and encourages him to be cleansed in the bath; [Col. 0660A]

promising purity of soul and body.

When he confesses his belief

and receives both gifts without having purchased them,

he displays the honor of his mind

through the evidence of his body,

and extols the true God in joyful praises.

When the report of the deed strikes Alexander’s ears,

his fury is aroused.

He kills Privatus,

weakened and oppressed by his burden,

with the weight of lead,

and orders the pontiff to be driven from the church.

He has him thrown headfirst from a high window,

his neck weighed down by the stone,

and sunk into a well;

the abyss is filled with filth.

After seventeen days,

Asterius, together with the clergy,

cares for the sacred remains and raises them by night.

The Via Aurelia received them at the tomb of Calepodius.

But much later, by divine power,

they are transferred to Reims

and adorn the temple of God’s Mother.

[Col. 0660B] There, beside his companion, Nicasius,

near the steps of the palm,

they are placed.

The two lights of our city

adorn it and guard its walls,

which have been entrusted to the shield of prayers.

The presbyter Asterius,

guardian of his ancestral honor,

is arrested by Alexander,

who envies this glory of the tomb,

so that the man whom he had honored

might afterward himself be deprived of honor.

He orders him hurled from a high bridge

into the waters below;

nevertheless Ostia receives his limbs,

lifting them up.

## CHAPTER IX. On Saint Martina

[Col. 0659]

[Col. 0659B] In addition, this impious Caesar

kills many who have been subjected to various tortures,

under a capital sentence.

Under him a radiant virgin,

noble by birth and exalted in virtues,

Martina, adorned the lofty trophies of the cross.

[Col. 0659C] Rich in splendid wealth,

born of a father who was consul,

she generously supplied the needy Christians with food.

Seized by Alexander,

she is ordered to offer incense to Phoebus.

But as she pours out her prayers,

a tremor shakes the earth;

the City trembles;

part of the temple collapses and crushes the sacrificers,

while the statues, loosened from their foundations, crumble.

Enraged by these events,

Alexander orders the girl’s face to be struck with blows

and her eyelashes to be pierced with horrific hooks.

The executioners are ordered to persist in torturing the saint.

Overcome and stupefied,

they suddenly confess with a cry

that they see four men standing,

radiant with shining faces,

who strengthen her with joyful speech.

Yet they see the four men continue to inflict a deadly punishment upon themselves;

afterward, while the blessed woman is torn by fragments of pottery,

she steadfastly endures the executioners who perform these deeds,

[Col. 0659D] eight men ordered to administer the criminal punishments.

At last, clothed in divine goodness and standing in holy light,

they refuse the cruel service

and proclaim that they believe in Christ the true Lord.

Against them Caesar, inflamed with furious anger,

orders their entrails to be torn apart with hanging hooks.

They leave the world and the executioner behind,

their necks cut,

as martyrs,

and take possession of heaven’s blessed kingdoms.

Martina likewise is stripped of her garments

and struck with blows,

her entire body cut apart.

Then stretched upon four stakes

and beaten with clubs,

she laughs at all the dangers

received with steadfast courage.

Afterward, taken back into the black cavern

of the dark prison,

[Col. 0660B] her torn body is drenched with thick oil.

Again, in Alexander’s presence,

she is sentenced to be brought before the shrine.

But she directs a prayer to Christ as usual.

Fire is sent down from heaven,

[Col. 0660C] strikes the image,

and reduces it to a heap of ashes;

it burns the priests

and lays the people low.

Terrified and defeated by these events,

the ruler abandons that contest

and entrusts its prosecution to a certain prefect, Justinus.

He orders her stretched upon a stake

and cut with swords,

and her breasts to be handled with flesh torn out by claws.

When one hundred and eighteen wounds have been opened,

she remains victorious in the prison

and is shut again in the black darkness.

Afterward she is given to wild beasts

for the amphitheater’s entertainment.

She encounters a lion without fear.

Running at the virgin’s face,

it restrains its feet,

and, free of its natural savagery,

is held like a lamb.

But when it is withdrawn from her as she appeases it [Col. 0660D]

and recalled, unfed, to the cave,

it resumes the poisons of hunger,

opens its jaws toward the bodies before it,

and attacks the king’s kinsman

in a savage assault,

thereby avenging and killing him

for the pious girl.

Nor does it attack the king,

so that the virgin might not lack martyrdom

or suffer the savage tyrant unavenged.

The emperor’s orders once again close her in prison.

Two days later she is brought before the king

as he goes to offer sacrifice.

While she is shown to be steadfast for the Lord,

she is again weighed down by tortures

and again torn with claws.

When she overcomes everything,

she is judged victorious by magical art

and is said to hide her body beneath uncombed hair.

[Col. 0661A] Then they shave her and strip the holy woman,

as though restraining her by her hair,

just as the foreigners once bound the strong Samson.

But standing stronger through the power of her Christ,

she neither yields to savagery

nor breaks beneath the filthy assaults.

She is then shut, invincible and powerful in arms,

within Trivia’s shrine.

[Col. 0662A] Enclosed here for three nights and an equal number of days,

she drives the grim face of quiver-bearing Diana

into ashes.

Thus, overcoming the sacred rites and the nobles,

she is judged to have closed the final boundary

of her severe contest with the sword,

and by this triumphant leap

she seeks the heaven she has won.

## CHAPTER X. On Saint Pope Urban and Saint Cecilia

[Col. 0661]

[Col. 0661A] Urban, strong and steadfast,

takes up the laws of powerful Callistus

and vigilantly carries on the Lord’s battles.

He chooses faithful athletes for the divine camp;

he strengthens, trains, arranges, fortifies, and adorns them;

he instructs, arms, leads, and presses forward

the heavenly wars.

Nor does he merely compel men

to fill Christ’s battlements;

he also admits fighting maidens to arms.

Among them the illustrious deeds of Cecilia are related.

Noble in pious blood and nobler in conduct,

she adorns the nobility of the earth

with the nobility of heaven.

Night and day she revolved chaste sacred words in her mind

and constantly devoted herself to prayers

and to the Lord’s law.

While her parents were accustomed to adorn her

with golden garments,

according to the ancient custom of Ausonian brides,

[Col. 0661B] she disciplined her body with a covering of goats’ wool.

Betrothed to the distinguished Valerian,

she is pressed to obey the marital law

and enter the bridal chamber.

The suitor, overcome by love,

hastens the wedding torches,

inviting joyful dances to delight in feasts,

while the melody of the organ provides music for the festivity.

She sang her festivities to God

on the lyre of her mind,

asking that a pure heart be granted her

in a chaste body.

Meanwhile, while the heavens were being painted

with their frequent stars,

the bridegroom takes the bride

into their secret bedchamber.

But the virgin first, with great courage,

searches for the faithful friend

to whom she may reveal the innermost chambers of her heart.

He, strengthening her faith,

declares that he can in no way disclose

what is hidden,

for these things must be concealed in a faithful heart.

Then the chaste virgin reveals

the heavenly citizen whom she loves

[Col. 0661C] and who guards her,

watching over her with great ardor.

She says that he will avenge any impure touch upon her,

protected as she is by virginity.

Stunned by these words

and fixed by divine power,

the young man asks her to reveal

the heavenly being whom she calls her friend.

She kindly promises,

provided that he first allows himself to be purified.

When he asks who could cleanse him for this,

she introduces Urban,

a hero of venerable old age,

suited to this purpose

and instructed in the holy purification of God.

Thus the instructing woman indicates

through whom and where he should seek it.

The messenger, hastening,

finds the blessed pontiff,

who, as he had already confessed divine things

a second time before the rulers,

was hiding among the sacred tombs.

When the words sent by the virgin

are made known to him,

he draws great joy into his heart,

falls upon the ground on his knees,

[Col. 0661D] sheds tears of joy,

raises his hands to the stars,

and pours out thanks and prayers

to the king enthroned on high.

He then asks that his heart be opened

by these words.

While, as a suppliant,

he directs these vows to the ready heavens,

a heavenly face appears

under divine governance,

[Col. 0662A] and a tablet marked with stars and golden letters,

carried in by divine radiance, is proclaimed:

“One God is present, one faith, one baptism.”

At these words the bridegroom trembles,

believes, and adores prostrate.

He rises and declares his faith,

is consecrated in the flood,

sincerely instructed,

and restored to his blessed bride.

When he comes and finds her praying,

supported by a heavenly attendant,

the attendant displays the approaching rewards,

holding white lilies before roses.

Valerian had one brother, Tiburtius,

dear beyond all others. Valerian asks the angel

for his brother’s salvation; the angel promises it,

then, a citizen of heaven, returns to the stars.

Meanwhile, while the novice is being instructed

by these teachings,

Tiburtius, beloved in accordance with her prayers,

arrives and enters.

[Col. 0662B] He marvels that his nose has perceived

the fragrant breath of roses,

even though the year is barren of flowers,

and now remembers having been refreshed

by this sweet novelty.

The brother of faith continues,

striving to reveal the light

through alternating speech

and to disclose salvation.

The virgin assists him,

nor permits him to lack the marital gift;

she carefully instructs the pupil,

opening life, the course of life,

and the way.

She nourishes the twins

with the abundant milk of Wisdom.

Scarcely had the one wife been believed in that night—

for, thought to be marrying,

she herself gives birth to her husband—

when, lest this be thought a small pledge,

the offspring is increased:

behold, the heavenly one is born for the earth.

Thus Tiburtius is born through the faith of this mother,

and through the ministry of the pope

is brought forth from the waters,

a son of the Church,

growing in understanding and at the breast.

[Col. 0662C] After the milk, the pupils are nourished

with more substantial food.

The young men grow upward

to a splendid height;

now they yearn for the strength

of fully perfected virtue.

They raise up the needy

and carry the weary with consolation.

It remains only for them to provide, with manly and renowned devotion,

the burial gift for people who have been executed.

The turbulent prefect of Rome, Almachius,

was torturing the friends of the almighty Lord

with savage punishments.

Black with envy,

an enemy of holy sweetness,

he marks the acts of their gracious consolation

with the pestilence-smeared arrows of his arms.

Seized by death-dealing ministers

at the enemy’s instigation,

the righteous novices are driven before

the unjust judge.

He brings an accusation against them,

citing the title of their famous nobility:

they squander their patrimonies

according to the custom of empty superstition,

feeding dishonorable persons,

and, by giving them to death for a crime,

prepare honorable tombs,

thereby showing that they are bound to them

by such a pact.

[Col. 0662D] They wish to be servants of the friends

for whose sake they are accused.

Amid the spears of the heated struggle,

[Col. 0663A] the brothers are given victory

in a graceful contest.

But the judge, red-faced and torn apart

by mingled fury,

judging Valerian, outstanding in triumphal light,

worthy of disgrace,

orders him to be beaten with clubs.

But he rejoices

and warns his fellow citizens

not to be broken by his wound,

but to remain manly

through the strength of truth.

When the executioner grows weary of beating him,

he orders him to be struck with the sword,

unless both men willingly sacrifice

to the statue of Jupiter.

Maximus was present,

a cornicularius by office.

Weeping, he follows the joyful brothers to their death;

he weeps because they rejoice

at losing their present life.

They declare that another life,

everlasting and abiding,

is set before them.

They say that this present life

is to be rejected

and the other received,

just as the phoenix is renewed

through the ordeal of death.

At this, provided they prove the truth,

Maximus already wishes to rise.

[Col. 0663B] Fixed in the Lord,

they promise him signs:

at the hour when the Lord grants it,

they will be stripped of the body,

so that he may see with what splendor

the life to come is received,

and may testify that he has laid aside

his vain worship.

They order him, as one who swears,

to obtain a day’s delay.

When they are brought to his house at their request,

they instruct both its master and his household

according to divine precepts.

While the golden stars paint the night’s cloak,

behold, the priests accompany Cecilia

and arrive among them.

They provide baptism

for the new offspring.

As dawn uncovers the earth

and the shadows flee,

the guide of the starry battle addresses the camp:

she urges the blessed novices

to cast away the darkness of shadows

and take up the pious weapons

of shining light.

[Col. 0663C] The warriors hasten.

Cut down by the sword,

they are offered as sacrifices;

they lay aside the fragile garments of flesh

and seize the rewards of everlasting life.

The promises are fulfilled.

Maximus sees the gift of burial:

he sees heavenly ministers hasten from heaven,

take the maidens who have gone out from the body

into their embrace,

and carry virgin honor above through the air.

As he recounts these things

with tears poured out amid his joy,

many believers rejoice

that they have submitted themselves

to the heavenly King.

The lofty deeds are reported to Almachius:

Maximus and his household also follow the signs of Christ.

He, roaring with indignation

and displaying the dreadful weight of his fury,

has Maximus beaten with blows of lead.

But Maximus, light and joyful,

departs, now freed from the weight.

The noble virgin, teacher of this contest,

[Col. 0663D] places him beside the brothers

whom she had buried there herself.

Nor does she allow the proof

of the auspice and the faith

to remain hidden:

on the sarcophagus she depicts

the bird in which life was believed.

[Col. 0664A] After death, the light was revealed

through this example.

After sending the warriors to their rewards,

the female commander is summoned to battle

and called to the desired contest.

While the greedy judge seeks the brothers’ patrimonies,

he orders Cecilia to be confined

by this stratagem.

When he learns that these have been distributed

among the poor,

he orders her, as though she were about to burn incense

at the altars,

to be led to the raging ministers

in a furious contest.

But she turns the greedy ministers

toward true gain,

gaining those who sought gain

and storing up rich interest.

She leads the leaders of the crime

to the heights of piety

and joins them as participants in God,

with Urban consecrating them.

Within the walls of the house,

cleansing souls in the divine font

of the blessed virgin,

he produces a rich offspring

and adorns the chaste inner chambers

with the sacred things of the Church.

[Col. 0664B] Celebrating the holy mysteries

on festival days,

he prepared losses for the enemy

and pious gains for the Lord.

When the report of these deeds

strikes Almachius’s ears,

he orders that the girl be brought before him immediately,

terrified by the authority of his judgment.

She becomes greater as he questions her.

In reply she proves him foolish,

gives the empty glory of his rank to the wind,

charges him with ignorance and guilt,

and exposes him as an enemy of what has been proved.

She teaches that he has followed everything false,

and, in addition, shows him to be blind

and deserving of laughter.

Deeply grieved that she should be removed from his sight,

he orders the unconquered girl,

through the power of light,

to be burned in her own bathhouse.

The heat is stoked with abundant wood

around the enclosed woman.

But no heat produced by any device reaches the pious virgin.

[Col. 0664C] Rather, remaining lively all night and day,

unafraid amid the constant flames

of the piled-up wood,

she is marked by no sweat,

as though she were in a place of cold.

When the savage tyrant tries

to conceal the clear triumph

and extinguish it with a cruel sword,

he orders her to be offered there

by the harsh blade.

The dreadful attendant hastens

to complete the order.

But the iron force gives way

against the tender virgin’s throat.

Three times he swings it for the killing,

three times exhausting himself

against her gentle neck,

and he cannot tear the head

from the slender neck.

The virgin remains alive for three days,

in accordance with her wish,

and commends to the shepherd Urban

the sheep she had nourished as a mother.

Urban, who performs the burial

of the woman who had fulfilled her merits,

places her among his blessed colleagues

with funeral rites,

and joins the chaste pledge

to the chaste bishops.

Afterward, when the holy man has made

all the vessels of the sacred ministry from silver,

and sent many famous for martyrdom

to the stars,

the companion receives illustrious rewards.

## CHAPTER XI. On Saint Pope Pontianus and the presbyter Hippolytus

[Col. 0663]

[Col. 0663D] After this Pontianus fills the office of the government,

and, worthily conducting the wars

of the supreme ruler,

is handed over to Sardinia

by deceitful fraud.

There, with the father removed,

the people are exposed to brigands,

as a flock is exposed to wolves

and hidden thieves

when its shepherd is lost.

But so that he would not continue

without consolation,

this pope, far separated from his fellow citizens,

is joined in divine purpose, in that unfamiliar country,

[Col. 0664D] by Hippolytus, a suitable presbyter.

As a wealthy exile, he makes citizens of the barbarians,
multiplying spiritual profit
in their marketplaces.

When the hostile man, sick with rage,

kills the rich merchant with clubs,

he sends him to the lofty walls.

But the blessed bishop Fabianus

recovers his remains

and gives them burial among the pious tombs

of Callistus,

in a carefully arranged mausoleum.

## CHAPTER XII. On Pope Anterus and vengeance for the sixth persecution

[Col. 0665]

[Col. 0665A] Anterus takes up the lofty office

of this exile,

following in his footsteps.

He carefully records the worthy deeds of the martyrs:

the cause of the blessed Maximus’s holy death,

who is released from the flesh as both martyr and priest,

he investigates and stores in the sacred records.

For these records he earns his crown, when the emperor Maximinus,

after Nero, unleashes upon our people

by renewed law the storm of the sixth persecution—

a law issued from hatred for the preceding Caesar,

whose palace shone with the Christian name,

a faith his mother Mammaea ardently fostered.

[Col. 0666A] A dreadful persecution rages against the blessed bishops

and the lofty rulers of the sacred people,

the clergy;

it is closed within three years

by the king’s death.

The vengeance inflicted justly

upon the swollen rulers,

like the plague that struck the Egyptians,

lacerated with its blows the swelling of the sixth plague.

Indeed, after he was killed

by the spear of Pupienus,

the slayer himself,

ruling with his brother,

was killed.

As many of our bishops

were slain over the years,

so many rulers of the world

were given over to death.

Then Gordianus witnesses

prosperous wars.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the two emperors named Philip, and on the martyr Pontius and Saint Fabianus

[Col. 0665]

[Col. 0665B] After these events Philip shines forth

in distinguished peace,

adorned with the exalted title

of the higher law.

He makes his son Philip

a participant in his dignity.

Pontius, instructing these men

in Christ’s divine duties

through admonitions and prudent doctrine,

guides them onward.

But under Valerian he shines,

adorned with the palm.

Philip, the first of the Roman kings,

together with his son revering the divine Father and Son

with harmonious devotion,

rules the renowned scepters,

shining in fellowship with his son.

High in office but bowed before Christ’s mysteries,

when he asks that sacred rites

be brought to him during the vigils of Easter,

he is ordered to stand among those

who lament and weep over their sins,

and to confess and mourn his own offenses.

He receives the priest’s command

according to his vow,

stands with bowed breast,

and drives rank from his mind,

[Col. 0665C] while he recalls

the highest heights of the supreme kingdom.

But at last, sorrowful and having confessed his crimes,

[The supplied source ends here.]

Implores suppliantly the divine powers of the highest King,

And, drawing forth the holy fear of God to remain in his pious heart,

He receives the sacred rites he had sought with humble breast.

But the Lord takes care to raise him, bowed as usual;

He magnifies him with the fasces. To him alone, trembling before the holy laws,

This unique honor is conferred: that the king, in the higher order,

May shine as the thousandth year of the city’s populace,

Led forth under Augustus’s governance,

Is celebrated with the highest honor of exceptional worship—

That this glory should be borne to the supreme city amid its scepters,

The city long renowned for apostolic teaching,

Marked by the holy beauty of a pious divinity,

And, under this lofty Christ-worshiping prince, should flourish in such honor.

[Col. 0665D] But after the earth has seven times clothed itself in grass

And the smiling walls have been filled with sevenfold fruit,

While Philip rules the lands by divine gift

And proclaims shining laws to nations and peoples,

The ancient serpent seethes and gathers his strength,

Worn down and rubbed away so many times by so many triumphs.

He prepares ambushes to harass Christ’s ranks

And contrives for himself, by deceit, a suitable brigand—Decius.

[Col. 0666B] He equips him with the serpent’s livid poison of fraud,

Sharpens him with goads, and drives the madman to crime.

He, turning over his plots, attacks the righteous king

With an unexpected charge and kills him by a dark stratagem.

After the prince has been removed, the tyrant seizes the scepter;

With savage effort he takes care to extend what is his own,

Overthrows the son, and sets all his arms in motion throughout the army.

Then, seeking greater things, he strives to overturn the Lord’s camp;

Without delay he attacks the leader of this administration

And, under the law he has issued, slaughters Fabian.

This bishop had taken up command by celebrated authority

Over the holy troops whom the cruel Scythian ordered to be torn apart.

For, as the story goes, after leaving the countryside with his friends,
