He entered the church’s house, where the assembly of the people,

Divided in its aims, was disputing, and where the choice of a father was being made.

[Col. 0666C] He stood there, conscious of nothing that was about to befall the citadel,

Yet concerned to witness the outcome of so great a matter.

While this discordant gathering was loudly uttering divergent words,

The dove, preparing worthily to join what had been divided,

The friend of peace, came and commanded the gall of resentment to be absent from their hearts;

She caused all to feel as one.

Judging one from among the many and preferring him above all,

Seeking one head for all, she chose one man for everyone,

And joined them all, in agreement, to one father.

All cried out that he was worthy of the heavenly height

And elected as bishop the man known by divine authority;

Thus the governance of Peter’s chair was entrusted to Fabian.

And, so that he might preserve the deeds of the triumphant righteous,

He gathered pupils and resolved that they should devote themselves to this work;

He also taught the Church to shine through benevolent laws.

[Col. 0666D] But scarcely had he been joined to triumphal honor

When the sheep were scattered, torn apart, and thrust into prisons.

Their Moses, after enduring the long prison-houses,

Seeks the heights of heaven beyond the black bars.

The enemy wages different attacks against different brigands,

With weapons openly displayed and arms concealed within;

He chooses a new brigand, renewed for secret wars,

And attacks the holy camp with forked companies.

CHAPTER XIV. On Saint Pope Cornelius, the martyr Cyprian, and their companions.

[Col. 0665]

[Col. 0665D] Thereafter the Lord, in his gracious gift, provides an outstanding father

For the abandoned people: Cornelius is given to the city

[Col. 0666D] As bishop of the distinguished chair of Peter.

To him, as children hastening to the gentle consolation of a kindly father,

[Col. 0667A] The scattered sons come—those cut off by their lapse—

And Maximus and the others, faithful confessors.

They wage the celebrated battles of heaven under a faithful leader.

The heavenly Pancratius, it is said, was equipped by this teacher for the conduct of war,

With his blessed uncle directing him.

The impious man, horrified, grieves to see the holy forces assembling;

Preparing to disturb Christ’s massed cohorts,

He removes their leader from their midst and drives him into exile,

Sending him away to Centumcellae.

He cannot unite to himself the love of the military leaders.

Many hasten to visit the exiled pope

And to relieve him with pious consolation.

Then Cyprian, the light of Africa, rich in speech and faith,

Joins these rays by marking the blessed writings

With the deeds of Celerinus’s powerful arena:

[Col. 0667B] When the persecutor learns that many are bringing consolation to the pope,

He recalls the righteous man and falsely accuses him,

Claiming that, contrary to public laws, he had taken up pamphlets

And writings brought from a foreign shore.

“I received the writings of the Lord, with the crown above them,

Not anything against Roman affairs or the public interests.”

But when he hears the truth, his fury boils over,

And he strikes with lead those lips that confess so readily and purely,

Striving to crush the truth by blunt violence.

The bishop is then led away to sacrifice the rites of Mars;

If he refuses and rejects them, he is to be slaughtered at the bloody altars.

While he himself hurries to perform the sacrifice—he who ought rather to be sacrificed—

A certain Cerialis, pressed into this service, asks on behalf of his wife,

Who had lain sick for five years,

That he may rejoice to see her restored to health.

[Col. 0667C] But entering his house, the bishop raises her up, saying:

“Rise, and stand upon your feet in the name of Jesus.”

At once she rises joyfully, having received strength, and cries out

That Sallustia’s Christ is truly the Son of God.

She runs and fills a vessel with water, makes her vow and prayer,

And, carrying the washing herself, asks to be sprinkled with the sacred waters.

[Col. 0668A] Soon the prayers of all follow the vows of this woman.

The avenger who had been appointed to punish him and who throws himself at his feet

Asks to be permitted to carry out the office granted to him.

He is subjected, condemned, and thrown into confusion beneath the sentence.

But the bishop treats his persecutors in reversed order:

He captures those who had captured him and binds again those who had bound him;

He cleanses with water those preparing to defile themselves;

And those who had labored to associate him with profanities

He makes, through the holy mysteries, participants in Christ’s sacred rites.

He adds to the Church those who strive to join themselves to her shining masks,

And attaches to her those attempting to tear apart her bonds.

Decius, savage when he hears of this, sends for and arrests the white-robed men,

And orders them to sacrifice with the bishop;

If they then refuse to place incense on the altars, they are to be punished.

The inexperienced recruits go forth to divine warfare under their teacher’s leadership,

[Col. 0668B] Lest, if a troop should revolt from the prince,

It surrender its trophies to the enemy’s commands.

The bishop advances safely in heavenly armor.

The new troop rejoices to follow him;

They hasten to receive the palm, sprinkled with blood,

By taking it in the chapel amid spittle.

The crowned pope leads them upward to heaven.

But Lucina, a venerable woman of pious conduct,

Supported by God’s clergy and accompanied by a troop of servants,

Gathers the sacred bodies of the saints

And buries them in the cemetery of Callistus,

In a field made splendid by her devotion.

At this Lucina’s request, this Cornelius

Had transferred the bones of the holy leaders to the catacombs,

And had entrusted them to Peter’s church beneath Nero’s hill,

The golden church called the Vatican,

Where the bow-bearing Phoebus once had found temples and dwelt.

[Col. 0668C] He himself took the place beside the cross by which Cephas ascended to the stars,

Following the Lord through the heights of heaven.

At that time Hostiensis likewise took up Paul’s relics,

From the place where Paul, released from his body by decapitation,

Entered the honor he had sought, bound to Christ.

CHAPTER XV. On Saints Abdon and Sennen.

[Col. 0667]

[Col. 0667C] This mad fury did not rage only against the leaders,

But against the entire army as well.

It decreed that the righteous should be sought everywhere,

Raging against all their homelands,

Where the shameful power of Rome’s mistress held sway.

[Col. 0667D] It pursued the pious wherever the great world extended:

It shook the West, searched the wealthy East,

And this outrage struck the Persians, set far away.

The madness of Decius, driven onward by furies, wandered here and there,

And ordered the leading men of the nation, Sennen and Abdon,

To appear before him.

He reproached them for their noble worship,

So that, as men who despised the gods, they might rightly be subjected to the Romans;

Indeed, though conquered by the Romans, they confessed themselves victors through Christ,

The God through whom kingdoms triumph,

And praised for ever the summit of that faith.

While the strict guard received them in chains,

They glorified Christ, gratefully displaying that honor

Which they had always loved, with magnificent praise of him.

Thereafter others, detained on behalf of the heavenly law, were killed.

Twice four full circles had Cynthia completed

When the Caesar brought these men into the walls of Rome

[Col. 0668C] And prepared a celebrated triumph over the unconquered,

Presenting himself as victor, as though he had subdued enemies by the sword.

Since they persisted in the struggle by which they had been victors,

The descendant of Aeneas summoned them, honoring the great men with gold.

He displayed them adorned with beads and encircled with chains,

[Col. 0668D] Showing that he had overcome honor-bearing local rulers.

He sought to stir the people’s mouths to his own praises

And presented the savage enemies as friends of piety.

He boasted that the defeated men, guarding their hearts in freedom,

Had been given into his hands, and confessed that he was trampling on their scepters.

The stupefied senate admired the venerable faces

Of the holy men of Christ.

But while those men, fearless in his presence,

Uttered their heavenly proclamations with steadfastness,

They were handed over, Decius defeated, to Valerian.

If they did not burn incense, he would gather them as food for the beasts.

The savage man attacked the men and tore away strips of flesh,

And brought them, as though they were about to sacrifice, to the altars of Latona’s son.

When they spat in his face, declaring the confession of God accursed,

Men concealed behind them struck their backs with lead.

While the pious endured these things bravely, behold,

Assistance from beasts was demanded against them.

Two lions were given, and four bears, fearsome in their jaws,

Were brought with dreadful roaring all the way to the saints’ feet.

But here, as if by an astonishing agreement, they lay down like lambs,

So that you might judge that the beasts had come gently into obedience

To the warriors of Christ, whom they protected in peace.

The ferocity of the beasts passed into human breasts,

And men, with beastlike fury, were chosen to attack them,

While the beasts peacefully sought the men whom human law had demanded.

[Col. 0670A] Men were sent, roaring with frenzied minds,

And the gentle beasts, which had spared the saints, slaughtered them.

Thus, having completed their meritorious contest,

The athletes entered heaven from the conquered amphitheater.

Cyrinus, having obtained their sacred bodies by night,

Rescued them and carried them away,

Hiding them in a leaden chest,

Which, when Christ revealed it, later lay open in the light of peace.

CHAPTER XVI. On Saints Parthenius and Calocerius.

[Col. 0669]

[Col. 0669A] Parthenius and Calocerius, shining with strength,

Appointed to guard the imperial bedchamber,

Adorned their outstanding character with chaste bodies,

And were approved as men who rendered their duties both to Christ and to the king:

What belonged to the king, to the king; what belonged to Christ, to Christ.

[Col. 0669B] Anatolia, a virgin rich in wealth, was left to them

When her pious father, the consul Aemilianus, died.

[Col. 0670A] Their conduct taught her also to join wealth to Christ.

Because they refused to pray to vain images,

They were thrown into fires, yet safely overcame the flames;

Beaten with clubs, they joyfully climbed to heaven.

Their bodies were snatched away from the earth by a virginal theft,

[Col. 0670B] And their spirits were received into the starry kingdom of heaven.

CHAPTER XVII. On Saints Anatolia and Victoria.

[Col. 0669]

[Col. 0669B] The butcher’s dark attack against the men was not enough:

With the sword he also drives tender girls upward to the stars.

Among them Anatolia and Victoria overcome the law of the world.

Then, by seeking the vault of heaven,

The better one advanced their kingdoms to the heights;

She adorned the chaste girl with holy conduct,

And increased her, blooming, with shining virtues.

For Anatolia, betrothed to a savage man,

While she refused the torches of marriage and submission to profane laws,

[Col. 0669C] Victoria was sent to persuade her to accept lawful bonds—

She had been contracted to a pagan man,

Eugenius, and was soon to be married to him.

Victoria, hastening to persuade her, was instructed in this,

And, preparing to capture her, was herself captured;

While hunting, she was caught.

She rises to turn aside the work of the Almighty;

Seeking to make the path level, she becomes Christ’s venerable work:

“Listen to me, sister Anatolia [Note: [Col. 0669D] Victoria should apparently be read.],

I too am Christ’s servant, and I know that God does not condemn lawful bonds.

These bonds were entered into by holy prophets;

These bonds were entered into by the fathers, whose offspring was blessed.

Listen to me, and join yourself to a husband who will conceal as a friend

The secret of Christ’s companion and will not betray his foster daughter,

But will favor our cause as a gentle and loving husband.”

As she wove these words, Anatolia replied:

“Conquer, O Victoria, and for this purpose you may truly be Victoria.

Once, when the world was empty, the Almighty commanded mortals:

‘Increase and fill the world abundantly; fill the earth with much fruitfulness.’

Now it is full of human offspring, since Christ has descended from heaven.

‘Multiply faith; let love increase,’ he cries.

‘The kingdom is approaching; fill the heavens above.’”

After this she continued:

“I, who through Christ’s inward being have spread abroad the planted fruits

Of my virtues, see in the daytime a young man in dreams,

Adorned with the gold of a diadem,

Shining in a purple, jewel-encrusted garment.

Looking at me cheerfully, he speaks to me with gracious lips:

‘O holy virginity, which death does not know how to conquer,

Indeed, by death without end you carry off those who follow your law!

O good virginity, rejecting the works of darkness,

You dwell forever adorned with heavenly light!’”

When I heard these words, I awoke, drenched in tears,

And, prostrate on the floor, wearied the Lord with my prayers.

Then the sweetest one who had spoken these things to me

Repeated them again; thus, as I lay prostrate, that most gracious one continued:

“Virginity, blooming in the bright royal purple,

Is that by which the one who puts it on emerges superior to the rest.

Virginity is the precious jewel of the divine necklace.

Virginity is held to be the king’s unexpected gift.

Thieves lie hidden, setting ambushes for this treasure.

Guard it with watchful protection.

The more you know that you possess these riches,

The more carefully protect them, lest they waste away through dark deceit.”

Inspired by these and other pious beginnings of exhortation,

Victoria strips away all the splendor of varied adornment

And gives to the needy the treasure sought from God.

The betrothed men receive the tokens of their promised marriage.

But since they cannot ensnare Christ’s doves,

They hasten to drive them away.

With Decius’s permission, they barely carry across the fields

The small pieces of bread they gathered for themselves,

And only late and with difficulty;

Yet the fasts do not break those

[Col. 0670D] Whom Christ’s love strengthens.

No efforts succeed in bending them toward marriage-torches or altars.

After accomplishing many astonishing deeds, they remain unconquered,

Joining martyrdom to celebrated virginity.

From Christ they receive garlands mixed of lilies and roses;

The illustrious necklace of virgin flowers

Was joined together when Victoria received the sword in her heart.

Her executioner, Taliarchus, was struck by a plague-bearing disease;

After a brief illness—within six, specifically, circuits of the sun—

He breathed out his life, consumed by worms.

But the virgin’s pledge was healed by a worthy gift.

The gracious virgin Anatolia, strengthened by holy deeds,

After she had healed many afflicted people in Picenum,

[Col. 0671A] And those attacked by demons and trembling at the returning moon,

Is subjected to a varied contest after being brought to Tyre.

One whole night closed her in unharmed with a serpent.

Then in the morning she has the snake-charmer himself, the monster’s parent,

Carried off to be devoured,

And adorns him through the mercy of Christ God.

The man who openly confessed that he believed the Lord to be Christ

Was thrust into the prison’s caves amid this glorious praise.

While the holy virgin poured out her prayers with extended hands,

Her side was pierced by a sword,

So that, entering through the right side, the blade might pass through

And emerge from the left.

The spirit of the Most High ascended to the chamber of her beloved.

The Tyrians received the coffin pierced by the point of the spear.

The bold man, converted to Christ from his serpent-bearing deceit,

Was now mild and dragged from his confinement to the raging swords.

Soon his head was cut off, and he triumphed over death and serpents.

And since, honored by this, he was transferred from here to his eastern homeland—

CHAPTER XVIII. On Saints Pergentinus and Laurentinus.

[Col. 0671]

[Col. 0671A] Then the blessed Pergentinus and Laurentinus,

Twin boys of piety, triumphed at Arezzo beneath the whips,

Performing great miracles;

Then, wounded together by the sword, they entered the golden kingdoms.

[Col. 0671B] The walls bloom with their bodies, and heaven with their souls;

This city shines, rejoicing in the twin light of the righteous.

And when Decius prepares for many saints the joys of heavenly life,

Whom he sends from torments to the stars,

He proclaims a general seventh campaign

Against Christ’s people, after Nero’s earlier wars.

Amid barbarian wedges he paid for his deeds with blood.

He who, murdering the reigning Philip, father and son,

Overthrew by treachery that servant of God together with his child,

Receives the reward due to his deeds, with Christ and the Father as witnesses;

The king, carried far from the kingdom, is received with his son.

Yet it was not enough for blood to avenge what he had drenched every field with.

[Col. 0672A] Vengeance seeks the blood of the saints among the savage executioners,

The judges, informers, and those who had supported them by their approval.

Throughout the regions of Roman rule

Vengeance spreads everywhere as a plague.

The corrupted air pours harsh poisons through the limbs

[Col. 0672B] Of animals and human beings alike.

No region is free; no city remains untouched by the blood

Of the righteous.

It strikes every household,

And drains the life even from spectators,

For their guilt in the deeds that had been done.

And just as once hail, falling through the pestilential air,

By the divine scourge of the king of Pharos,

Crushed the fields, laying low cultivators,

Crops, beasts of burden, and pastures,

So the plague of the Aenead, coming with heavenly balance,

Under a fitting disaster for the tyrant,

Devastates cities, countrymen, livestock, and pastures.

HERE BEGINS BOOK FIVE

CHAPTER ONE. On Saint Pope Lucius and Stephen.

[Col. 0671B] Lucius follows the consecrated pontiffs,

Radiant in the splendor of their sacred office.

[Col. 0672B] He is stripped of the walls of his homeland and led away into exile.

The fugitive is preserved safely and restored to the city.

[Col. 0673A] He arranges the offices and governs the reins entrusted to him.

He judges that chosen ministers should stand beside the pontiff,

And that witnesses of his life should always be present.

The pontiffs themselves should preserve the bonds of peace

And observe the laws for restraining sacrilegious men.

While he directs God’s people with equitable governance,

Renowned for the brilliance of a shepherd under Valerian,

He is beheaded and seeks heaven as a martyr.

As he hastens to hand over his authority to his disciple,

He entrusts it to Stephen, the Church’s distinguished and highest minister.

Given as pope, Stephen is not inferior in virtue or speech.

He shines like his father, promulgates laws, and adorns the Church.

He decrees that sacred garments should be used only for sacred rites.

While Valerian, together with his companion, in his eighth god-fighting assault

Gives God’s flock to be torn apart,

[Col. 0673B] This strong leader leads the sheep amid the battles of lions.

He gathers, exhorts, and strengthens them to stand firm in combat,

And summons many outsiders to divine warfare.

Among these the tribune Nemesius hastens forward with distinction,

Together with the household throng and his daughter Lucilla.

Lucilla, long blind, is restored in both bodily eyes

And recalled from the darkness of her mind.

As this splendid lamp of Christ shines upon them,

Olympius, distinguished by equal authority, approaches,

Joined by his wife, his son, and an increased number of faithful servants.

They are proved by flames like gold and silver,

And, together with Symphronius, ascend brightly to the heights of heaven.

Nemesius is consecrated as Christ’s levite for the altars.

Without trial, the leaders order that he be punished

Wherever he is found.

Filled with heavenly virtue,

[Col. 0673C] He does not cease visiting the homes and hiding places of the righteous.

He seeks out those in hiding and comforts the poor with money.

Coming upon the road once called the Appian,

He discovers that Valerian is offering sacrifices to Mars.

Kneeling, he implores the Ruler of heaven and earth

To grant, under Christ’s name, salvation to the one

Whom he sent into the world,

And to frustrate this fraudulent plan,

So that the wretched might recover from Satan’s snares.

Maximus, who had been consul, was inside, possessed by a demon.

“Nemesius,” he suddenly cries, “has set me on fire,

And the prayer of this Christ-worshiper torments me cruelly.”

Some men, leaving the shrine, seized the blessed man.

While they were overwhelming him with insults, behold, Maximus breathed his last.

They brought Nemesius to Valerian.

[Col. 0673D] The emperor sought to flatter him and reviewed the honors of his former life,

Recalling what he had experienced and accomplished by his counsels.

He urged him to worship the gods to whom he had previously clung.

Then the deacon replied, drenched in tears:

“I was always miserable, foolishly fleeing the truth,

And, guilty, I poured out holy and innocent blood.

Burdened also by these crimes weighing down my neck,

Though late, I recognize the Maker in my own image.

Having received the saving pledge of Christ the Propitiator,

I fear him, venerate him, and am resolved to serve him.

I renounce and reject all images made by human hands.”

At these words the Caesar, enraged, imprisoned him in a cave.

When the third dawn thereafter brought back the work,

He was brought before the Caesars, accompanied by Lucilla.

[Col. 0674A] They had her put to death before her father’s eyes,

Thinking that the strong man might be subdued by this spectacle of slaughter.

But, more joyful beneath the destruction of his offspring and more ardent,

He became now an even more fervent herald of God.

When it was proved that he could not be bent

From the strong ardor of his faith in Christ,

He was ordered to be led before the shrine of Mars.

Having already triumphed in virtue,

He completed the arena with the sword,

And, once his head was cut off, sought the heavens in glory.

Stephen added his limbs to the earth, kindred earth,

And Sixtus later gathered and buried them more carefully.

After his death, his faithful disciple Symphronius

Was brought, bound, before the tyrant for the sake of the light of faith.

He was handed over to a tribune for torture,

And Olympius was ordered to investigate the possessions of Nemesius.

Receiving the orders, he reviewed them.

[Col. 0674B] Symphronius said:

“If you ordered me to seek the wealth of the Lord,

I have already reported that I am fit to serve Christ the King.

But if you order me to sacrifice, I willingly offer sacred rites—

Yet the honor of vows and praise belongs to the Lord Jesus,

To whom my master Nemesius offered himself as a sacrifice.”

At these words Olympius, filled with savage anger,

Ordered him stretched out on the rack to endure the rods.

After the blows, the golden Mars, brought on a tripod,

Melted like wax flowing from fire at the words of this man.

The judge, stupefied by these things, withdrew,

And recounted to his wife the deeds of the holy confessor,

Who had made the lips of the god of war melt.

He decided that pardon should be sought for the accused.

When this plan seemed useful to the minds of both,

They came together in the night,

With the son accompanying them,

Theodotus, the only child of both parents.

Thus they rejoice to prostrate themselves at his bound feet,

Praying to be saved and proving that they have repented.

The bishop, summoned by heavenly instructions,

Instructed them and perfected them so that they might shine

With the heavenly water of the rich rain of Christ’s grace.

When the leaders hear of this, their hearts inflamed,

They command that these saints be brought before them

With grim violence.

The white-robed men are snatched away by savage beasts:

Symphronius, pressed by the sword and bound with fetters,

Naked and exposed, is assigned to a glorious contest.

They tell the tribune to delay the punishments of Augustus,

As though these men, unquestionably divine,

Did not wish to abandon gods whom they had always worshiped,

And before whose shrines they had driven many to punishments,

Nor had poured out blood without purpose.

The impious man said this.

But he replied:

“I have not acted as Olympius did.

I repent of my crime and pour out tears to the Thunderer,

Whom I serve—the Father, the Son, and the holy Spirit.

May he deign to pardon the monstrous offenses

That I committed against the saints,

Whose blood has been poured across the fields by me.”

The sentence ordered them to be consumed together by flames.

Soon they were led before the face of Jupiter

And prepared as holocausts.

Applied to the fires, they sang pious songs to Christ.

Untouched by the flames, the vapors went ahead to the heights.

Thus the tireless hand received their released bodies,

While Stephen, together with the clergy and religious companions,

Accompanied them with abundant praises and hymns as customary.

These relics, later transferred under Sixtus’s care,

Gave the martyrs celebrated observance in December.

Tertullian follows them in the offices of the cross.

The holy Stephen had known him through the splendor of the font

And had soon consecrated him as a presbyter in generous kindness.

Amid chaste admonitions and words of salvation,

He ordered him to search for the bodies of Christ’s slain.

He had scarcely completed the rites owed to the sacred altars over two days

When he was seized and stood brought before Valerian by Marcus.

The latter handed him over, stretched out on the wood, to be slaughtered.

He was beaten while crying out:

“I give you thanks, gracious Jesus Christ God,

Because you do not separate me from your merciful ones,

So that Olympius, now my lord,

Who went before me through martyrdom to the heights,

May be joined to me, and I may follow him.”

While he proclaimed this, flames were ordered to be applied

To both sides of his body.

Steadfast and joyful, he said:

“Carry out what you are doing, wretched man, more swiftly,

So that by this heat you may release me more quickly,

A holocaust and incense for Christ,

Though weighed down by sins, yet supported by this auspice.”

The butcher envied him, delayed, snatched him from the flames,

And handed him over to the still more savage Sapricius.

The latter proved himself by his deeds:

He crushed his face against rocks,

And for a long time tortured him and burned him on the rack.

Safe amid the fires through divine honor,

He proclaimed that Christ was God above all things in heaven.

Unconquered by punishments, when he was brought to Valerian,

He was immediately ordered to be beheaded with a swift sword.

Released from torture, his severed throat sought heaven.

Bishop Stephen, with hymn-singing,

Placed his bones in the Latin cemetery,

Surrounded by bands of people, and buried them in the split sand.

The presbyters, here printed as “bonos” [Note: [Col. 0675] Thus both manuscripts. Perhaps “Bonosius”?], Faustus and Maurus, were received there.

[Col. 0675C] Then seven others, joined to them at that same time,

Entered the heavenly inner chambers beneath the laurel of martyrdom.

With these observances, he celebrated Masses for the burial places of the righteous

In the caves and gathered the sacred assemblies there.

The frenzied leaders sought Stephen for torture.

Seizing him with military force,

They held him together with several aged and faithful ministers from the clergy.

They ordered the bishop to enter the Caesar’s tribunal,

[Col. 0676A] But alone.

“Are you Stephen,” Valerian said to him,

“who strives to overturn the public laws of the kingdom

And by persuasive, wicked admonitions

Forces the people to depart from their ancestral worship of the gods?”

“No, emperor; I do not strive to overturn the affairs of the kingdom.

Rather, I urge those who worship demons in abandoned temples

To recognize the living and true Lord,

The Creator of heaven and earth,

Christ, who with the Father and by the power of the holy Spirit

Reigns forever,

So that they may not perish in eternal punishment with the demon.”

At this Valerian ordered him to be beheaded

At the temple of Mars unless he prayed to the image of the deity.

The blessed man, led to the temple of Mars,

Turned his eyes and heart toward heaven,

And asked the Thunderer:

“Almighty Lord, unique Father of Christ,

Who destroyed Babylon’s tower by various disasters,

Rubbing its face into the dust,

Destroy this temple too,

Where the souls of peoples are being lost through wicked worship.”

The Almighty nodded to his prayers.

Thunder answered the petitions, flashing from the highest cloud.

Lightning bolts burst apart,

And the temple of Mars, more powerful than Mars himself,

Was thrown to the ground.

Mavors, powerless for battle, said at this [Note: [Col. 0675] Here the manuscript of the Library of Sainte-Geneviève, Paris, ends.]:

“This is revealed as Christ’s thunderbolt;

These are not Jupiter’s thunderbolts, acting by his command.”

The executioners fled;

Confidence in Mars did not restrain them,

Nor did it protect his faithful followers.

But the free priest departed,

Rejoicing in offering sacred rites to God,

Singing of Christ,

With the crowd rejoicing with him.

He guided and consoled them by his deeds and words,

Strengthening them with great power.

While he joyfully celebrated the mysteries

Within the holy walls of Lucina,

That troubled man, Valerian,

Moved his troops and surrounded the sheepfold with a pack of wolves.

Although surrounded on every side,

He did not know how to make the great-hearted shepherd tremble

Before the fury of the raging men.

Fixed and intent upon the sacred rites,

Strong and fearless under the Lord’s auspices,

He continued to offer his own sacrifice.

He perceived neither the mad uproar

Nor relaxed his prayers.

Fearless and willing, the ram was slaughtered at the altar,

Following what had been begun.

The sacred hand, sprinkled with the blood of the blessed father,

Buried him in the same sanctuary.

CHAPTER II. On Saint Eugenia.

[Col. 0675]

[Col. 0675C] Now, with the sails swelling in the west winds,

It is pleasant to see the fields of Syene

And to touch the Pelusiac shore,

Then swiftly to return to the heights of Ausonia.

For we learn that in this season Eugenia

Bore the distinguished glory of martyrdom.

Her father was Philip,

[Col. 0675D] Prefect of the city of Alexandria and of the fields of Canopus;

Her mother Claudia, descended from the summit of the Aeneads,

Gave her to the world.

Shining with such distinction,

She chose to surpass them in character,

Exalted by the chaste honor of piety.

Although pagan, by the power of the chaste divinity she rejects

The bonds of the bridegroom,

While, burning with learned concerns,

She strove to pass through all things

And ascend, by the honor of her spirit,

To the heights of Paul.

She receives these teachings with such fervor

That her blessed mind already burns with love

For the highest King.

But because her father had driven Christ’s followers from the city,

She follows the high path with chaste companions and chaste associates,

Seeking the lofty road with Proto and Hyacinthus,

By which she might climb so great a mountain.

[Col. 0676D] With her mind inspired by heaven,

She asks to see the fields where her father is,

And asks that he permit her to inspect the estates,

So that her mind might return more joyfully from this pleasant survey

Of the region she had traversed.

Her father agrees to this

And orders faithful companions to remain with her,

To escort their mistress while preserving her modesty.

As she is carried into the fields, reading Paul’s writings,

She hears Christ-worshipers singing the psalm-writer’s praises

In melodious voices:

“All the gods of the nations are demons,

But the Lord made the sevenfold heavens.”

[Col. 0677A] She orders the carriage to stop,

And, secretly meeting her companions, says:

“It is clear that you are distinguished by learned doctrine.

Together with me you have spent yourselves studying many things

Worth discovering and unworthy things found through the tricks

And cunning of learned men:

The intricate sophistries of the learned Aristotle,

The Epicurean sect,

The strange inventions of Plato,

The teachings of Socrates,

And what Stoic voices read aloud;

What the wise have scattered

And what the poets have sung.

All this is driven away by the fragrance of Christ,

In which the congregation rejoices.

From the suitable answers of the saints

We learn that the gods are nothing

And that all deities are vain.

Therefore we must believe divine things

And hold fast to the truth,

Unless it pleases the mind more to perish through falsehood.

But it is proper for the wise man to act wisely:

Let him separate the impious from the holy

And hasten to distinguish the useless from the useful,

So that he may seek the summit of justice

By the path on which he must proceed.”

While she sows these words of reason in her companions’ fields,

The hearts of the three are prepared to take the lofty road.

The unmarried woman’s chaste resolve gives birth to the plan

That they should together seek the blessed dwelling of Helenus,

Whose outstanding deeds shone forth:

He restored sight to the blind

And sober hearts to those possessed by demons,

Applying many remedies to the afflicted.

Since no one was permitted to visit him

As he meditated on God’s sacred things,

Nor were girls allowed to enter the old man’s enclosure,

The virgin chose to mark her strong spirits

With male clothing.

She was carried in an empty litter,

So that the other disciples might accompany their mistress in faith.

But her honor was restored, and her clever plans were carried through.

The three companions carefully crossed the dangers of the world.

The bishop was present, surrounded by a resounding crowd of praises.

The road was made ready for the pious;

The entire journey of the saints was prepared.

The young men joyfully received divine oracles

And asked the people for the bishop’s blessing for their journey.

The men recognized the trophies of the one

Who, when still a child,

Had once been accustomed to carry fire in an unharmed bosom

And had brought forth a waxen magician, frozen amid the flames.

The virgin presented the three as brothers

Coming to Christ’s sacred rites.

She asked that this too be made known to the blessed man.

The father, forewarned in a dream, recognized that they had arrived.

Asking their family and name,

He received them as Roman citizens from the city.

The virgin gave the names of the two brothers from her household,

Calling herself Eugenius; they recognized that they had been received in secret.

Were ordered to remain under the superior,

Were consecrated,

And were joined to the monastery and its holy works.

They received consolation,

Having been taught by the saint everything that had to be undertaken in the contest.

[Col. 0677D] But as the empty wagon went away with its light driver,

The people lamented with such groaning

The parents who mourned,

Having lost a child so precious to them.

The region was searched:

Villages, groves, towns, and mountains.

The Delphic powers were questioned;

A vain soothsayer was consulted.

She was declared to have been carried off by the gods

And received into the distant heavens.

What was hidden was believed,

So that later it might be believed openly.

Her father had an image of the goddess made

And set it up for himself in gold,

Content to reckon his daughter’s worth

By this costly metal.

But her mother and brothers grieved

And did not believe what they had been told.

The gracious virgin, masculine in mind, dress, and conduct,

Undertook the work of the Lord

And meditated on Christ’s teachings.

Vigilant under the heavenly law,

She stored in her remembering mind

The two testaments of God within the twofold year.

She was not known merely as a woman;

Through those things proper to men,

She acted with distinction.

Led by humble love,

She carried herself to the heights through virginity and modesty,

Occupied with the praises of the Lord,

With prayers, and with piety.

Her former companions,

Following deeds worthy of the highest praise,

Strive in everything to obey their blessed mistress.

By this time a third summer was passing in these undertakings.

The accomplished father of the place departed to the high rewards,

And the whole community was pleased

To prefer to all else whatever was better in her.

They chose Eugenia,

Although she followed the lowest things

And fled with all her strength from assuming rank.

At last, instructed by evangelical sayings,

She humbly approached the summit,

Subdued to obedience to the admonitions.

[Col. 0678B] Subjected to the path of Christ,

She was placed in authority as though she were a little servant.

She did not rule;

Rather, she served everyone as one among them.

Though lowest, she shone above the ministers;

Subject to those beneath her,

She served those prepared to serve.

She strove to assist with inward and outward care.

She labored with her companions in every virtue,

Living always in the praises of the Lord

And in the commands from above.

She grew astonishing in spirit through former miracles.

She disturbed demons, driving them from their dwelling places by command.

She poured light into the opened eyes of the blind.

She performed many other deeds,

Spreading their fragrance far and wide.

Many came to be relieved of various illnesses.

A certain Melantia, long tormented by fevers, came

And soon departed unharmed,

The disease having been driven away.

But she prepared gifts to repay the medicine.

[Col. 0678C] She sent coarse cups filled with solid gold.

The saint, filled with prophetic inspiration,

Rejected these things

And ordered her to give them to the needy

And add them to the resources of the wasting poor.

But in opposition the savage serpent concocted foul poisons

Against these salutary remedies,

Rushing to destroy the mind

Of the woman whose body had been saved,

To obscure the kindly deed,

And refusing to reckon it among good things,

Although Christ is accustomed to turn evil into good.

For while she diligently visits the woman restored to health, the latter is seized by another illness—madness. Gazing upon his handsome appearance, she breathes forth a fitting young man for her lusts, and, most wretched, is consumed by a blind fire with which many have been oppressed. She offers a gift of precious weight, breathing lightly as though to bind his spirit with this chain, while, discerning that everything is sordid beside the higher power, she burns more fiercely and, driven by furies, gives vent to the passion she had perversely conceived and nourished in her mind.

[Col. 0678D] Unable to endure such great inward fires, she discloses what had been hidden in her breast and lays bare the conflagrations that ravage her clothing. The flames are revealed; the young man is judged to be wasting away through empty frugality of dress and vain emaciation, losing the flower of youthful beauty that he had received. It is as though God were displeased when the beloved reject joys, or gathered up those who hate delights, or were nourished by the torments of human beings, and as though tribute were made worthless to an ungrateful collector. Yet let him see and believe that a comfort has been granted him for his merits, rest and an end to labors, joined with joy and accompanied by prosperous circumstances:

“The Lord bestows riches and blood to adorn it.”

[Col. 0679A] Nor is it unjust that Christ should have taken the young man as his bride.

Here the devout virgin, suppressing the hissing of her serpent-like voice, faithfully conceals the beautiful summit of honorable dignity. Attempting to tear his soul away from death by her snares, she displays the world’s empty pleasures to the wretched man, so that, while they suddenly pretend to be capable of being held, they may offer sweetness but lead to bitter dangers; invite him by their adornments but accustom him to defilement; promise joys but deliver perpetual sorrows.

By these and other means she prepares to preserve the one subdued from death. She, filled with evils and covered by the darkness of death, whose ears the madness of an asp had blocked and crushed, passed through rocky places harder than marble caves. Sick with plotting, she deceitfully pretends that an external illness is worse than the inward plague by which she is lost.

[Col. 0679B] Meditating how to take away his salvation, she demands the physician’s aid, inviting him because she desires to destroy the remedy. The she-wolf seeks the lamb that has entered among obscene assaults; the dove escapes the hawk’s embrace as though from its talon.

She also adds, rebuking her:

“Melantia, worthy indeed of the name—black to you, since you are livid with the rust of treachery; you have built dwelling places for dark phantoms in your heart. Depart, impostor, seductive bitch; retreat! Beguiling serpent, depart from Christ’s lambs. The holy ranks of Jesus do not fight in this warfare by such means. In the name of the Lord we shall overcome this poison, and, triumphing, his lofty mercy will protect us.”

Struck by the grievous wound, she displays her shame. Piling wickedness upon her evil heart, the shameless woman goes to the prefect Philippus and, with complaining cries, demands that he be sought out—not by false charges, she fears, lest she herself be pursued and branded by truthful ones. She complains that she has suffered the young man’s crime, saying that, unless assistance had quickly come to her, he had nearly taken her captive through shame; she recalls that he was a Christian and that he had covered her shame.

[Col. 0679C] Inflamed by these words, the prefect orders the young man and his companions to be seized and bound, and, pressed into the iron prison, to be kept there while the mouths of lions are prepared by savage hunger. He orders that they be subdued, torn apart, and handed over to dreadful jaws; let the impure be terrified by what they hear.

The commands are obeyed. They are fastened with heavy bronze chains and judged deserving of the harshest form of death. The awaited day arrives, and the time of the arena. The lambs are led out, bound, to be exposed to bears and Libyan lions. A formal inquiry is made in turn. Eugenia’s battle is different, and victory is at hand; but devotion prevents her, and the dangers of others delay her, ordering the innocent woman to face the punishments of the guilty.

But from the right side arises a more just contest: it is unjust to crush the righteous, betray justice, join the criminal to the chaste, and, beyond this, darken Christ’s starry radiance.

The servants approach in sorrow, and the mistress’s attendants follow, adding to the crime. The crow is marked by whiteness: the splendid dove is stained with black dye. Although she longs for the inner chambers of the lofty nest and, shaken by martyrdom, desires to seize the peace of heaven, she draws back from suffering the indignity of a father’s death—one whom she might save—and from gaining her brothers and mother.

Yet she pities her enemy and asks that the offenses be forgiven.

[Col. 0680A] At last she reveals, by tearing open the covering, the plan that she had long concealed and conceived in her heavenly mind: that she bore masculine strength in a female body, and that a woman’s flesh shone with the courage of a man.

She reveals herself as Eugenia and acknowledges her father and mother. She recalls her brothers, Sergius and Avitus; she exposes the eunuchs and explains briefly the deed and its whole course. Her father himself recognizes his child and is astonished. He embraces her; her brothers rejoice with tears for their sister. The servants joyfully adore their mistress and hasten, vying with one another to be the first to bring this unexpected joy to her mother. Scarcely believing it, the mother rushes eagerly to behold the new joy.

Garments glittering with gold and gems are brought out. They hasten to adorn the girl, though she is unwilling. Freed from her chains, she is decked in golden clothing, lifted high, and carried before her father’s tribunal. With one voice all proclaim that Christ is the one God crowned with glory.

If any Christians had stood sorrowfully among the spectators, they now burst forth as joyful crowds, publicly glorifying the great works of the divine right hand.

[Col. 0680B] The Almighty also adds to the magnificence of this triumph. At God’s command, a lofty flame descends from the sky, consumes the deceiver’s house, and lays everything waste, leaving only the marks of ash from the ill-fated seductress.

New joys mingled with fear arise among the people. The hall set apart for sacred rites lies open to God; the scattered congregation is gathered into one, and the Church’s honor is restored. The prefect, his sons, and his wife are renewed.

[Col. 0680C] He restores the rights of the devout and grants peace to the nobles. In the insignia of the prefecture he is seen to shine as a bishop, and he is observed to weigh all things for the Church with gentle justice. Everywhere Christ’s churches rise toward lofty summits. The devout flourish in peace; the wicked are worn down by envy. They are tortured by the repose of the saints and burned by their honor; armed with savage fury, they rage with poisonous zeal.

They conspire to accuse Philippus, the holy prefect, before Rome. They consider it a light labor to endure so long a journey, and they disregard the threats and savage dangers of the Ionian Sea. With plaintive lamentations they urge the nobles to report that the prefect is a Christian and that he himself advises the cities to worship Christ in Egypt; that all the gods’ images now appear to the peoples as empty fabrications; that, with the shrines of the heavenly beings abandoned, they worship a human being who suffered death upon a cross.

[Col. 0680D] They complain that the ancient and public laws of the Roman people, the descendants of Aeneas, are despised, and that the Roman rites are being overthrown.

Moved by these accusations, the scepter-bearing authorities read out a decree to Philippus:

“Either let him pour the customary libations to the gods throughout their temples, or, cast down from his office, let him yield his honor to a subordinate.”

That shrewd man transfers the possessions of heaven into a citadel, so that he may laugh at the thieves and despise their threatening heights. He entrusts his increasing wealth and gifts to Christ.

Deprived of hope, his successor is swept into savage anger. He plans to put him to death, but is restrained by affection for the man’s adherents, whom the people’s flattering songs have bound to him.

Anxious, he turns over plots in his troubled mind and fabricates a crime. He arms and sends men whom he has found through deception. They pretend to be companions and clothe themselves in the sheep’s skin of a wolf. Having been given swift means of action, they reveal that they have come and, while the Father is occupied with prayers and vows, strike him as he follows the divine footsteps.

[Col. 0681A] But the people, instructed by his teachings and strengthened by his virtues—having seen him restore sight to the blind and drive away demons—seize the robbers and hand them over to a robber. He displays his customary character: just as he captures them as criminals, so he releases them as grateful friends.

The virgin daughter receives the martyr’s bones into the monastery that she had prepared for virgins. There her mother Claudia establishes a pious dwelling for the poor and way-worn; she assigns estates and adapts their resources to worthy uses.

When these matters have been arranged, she, strong in spirit, returns to Rome, her native kingdom, with her sons and virgin daughter.

[Col. 0681B] The senate applauds as it receives the prefect’s sons and honors them with increased distinction. Here too the masculine virgin never ceases to adorn God’s hall with white flowers gathered from every side. While she sows shining lilies into radiant garlands, Bassilla approaches, smiling in royal blood.

Sprinkled with the fruit of piety and fragrant with its sweetness, she began to burn with blessed beauty, lovely to behold. But a different profession of faith in Christ stands opposed. She asks to be instructed in a manner breathing forth so sweet a nectar. With the intervening attractions, the joyful masculine virgin, having begun to make her vows known, addresses her companions, orders them to prepare for the laws of battle, and entrusts them with the appointed duties: these gifts are to be offered by the illustrious girl to the Lord.

[Col. 0681C] Bassilla receives them as servants and venerates them as lofty messengers of the Lord. With them she devotes herself night and day to the sacred rites, and the worship of her household is adorned with the heights of beauty. When the pope has been summoned to the holy rites, the sacrament is completed, and the divine virgin is reborn in the water.

Already, more than once, white lilies had secretly been joined together. Eugenia is joined to Bassilla in beautiful splendor, destined rather to radiate eternal brilliance. She becomes the ornament of the illustrious assembly and hastens toward the lofty leader of the virginal choir. Their fragrance is scattered far and fills the highest palaces of heaven, from which it flashes and gleams with the golden brilliance of light.

The nourishing radiance penetrates the inmost being of the two leaders, and eternal honor grows in eternal light. A crown becomes the conspicuous mark of each companion.

[Col. 0681D] Meanwhile, while the noble daughters of Eugenia are watered with the dew of milk, Bassilla is nourished by compacted honey and nectar. The deeds are reported to her companion Pompeius. While he anxiously seeks an interview with the virgin, the denial of access makes him heavier in speech with the burden of passion, and he is kindled by a blind fire.

He gathers and enlists exceptional women, that, once approached, they might together overcome the hearts of those bound by their pledge. She, secure like a tower in steadfast strength, crushes the arrows that are shot and yields to no quiver. Indeed, she seizes the hostile bands, appeases them, and compels them to surrender. Once sprinkled with the sweetness of divine dew, they abandon their arms, renounce their wicked wars, and disdain to serve a barbarian leader in trivial matters.

[Col. 0682A] The young man is lifted into savage furies by resentment, and is not ashamed to pour out miserable complaints before the emperors. Bassilla is seen either finally to resume her betrothed, or, rejecting marriage, to pay the honor due to the law with her throat. Eugenia is ordered either to reveal sacred things to the gods, or to be subdued by punishments and perish by a cruel death.

Different blasts of wind rise against the tower, which rests upon a strong stone. Bassilla is attacked after the arguments have failed: different conditions, ages, sexes, and instruments of labor are employed. No machine prevails. Supported by Christ, she resists all things with an unshaken mind. She does not admit her betrothed even to her ear, but admits Christ alone, for whom she keeps her faithful heart.

But when she has proved invincible against so many clouds of darts, she is attacked by stealth. While the light of her birthday day bares the sword, within her household she gains her triumph by the sword and commits her glory to earth and heaven.

[Col. 0682B] Soon the holy companions of their worthy mistress are seized; the attendants are torn from their slaughtered lady and dragged in contempt to Jupiter’s shrines and altars.

Then, while open prayers are read to the heavenly King, the one who is commanded to be worshiped as a god by an unjust rite falls before their feet, struck down by heavenly power. He is reduced to ashes, and the dust is shown to be empty.

In his dark heart Nicetius attributes this to magical arts. He sends the victors, cut down by the sword, triumphantly from the contest to the heavenly kingdoms.

Then he summons Eugenia, binds her, and demands that she disclose the arts by which Christians rely upon magic. But she, tasting the mystical proclamations of the supreme God, declares them superior to the figures of the Zoroastrians.

[Col. 0682C] Stupefied and with his mind covered in black darkness, the prefect orders her to be led to the altar of the Huntress and either be beheaded or sacrifice to the goddess Diana.

While she directs her prayers to heaven before the shrine, the earth trembles beneath the temple, shaking its foundations. Unable to withstand the words of the venerable girl, the pagan shrine seems to dissolve like a shadow in radiance, and the Cyclopean structures collapse like ashes before the sun.

The people acclaim her as holy; the more wicked portion roars that she is a witch. Thus it is ordered that her neck, pressed beneath a stone, be given to the river. But she cannot be submerged in the waters or forced beneath the earth by the weight of the stone. The stone is released and torn away by the Savior’s heavenly power, and secretly, as a victorious divine vessel, she is guided across the waters.

The same hand that once guided Peter across the sea carries Eugenia, lest she be hidden in the swift depths.

The unconquered virgin is shut into fiery baths. But the flames flee, and all the heat is extinguished. Once the virgin has been admitted, the furnaces grow colder than if, fallen into the water of the northern stream, they had been pressed by snows.

When the fires have been consumed and the furnaces defeated, the victorious virgin, unharmed, receives the dark prison. Its light is shut away, and for many days she is given no food. But her bridegroom does not permit her, shining inwardly with the radiance of heaven, to lie hidden in external darkness. He refreshes her by sending forth the pleasant light of heaven.

Another day’s light is sent into the world. Christ visits and consoles his faithful beloved, feeds his cherished servant with heavenly bread, and reveals the bridal chamber above the stars where he will unite her to himself. He establishes the day on which, once born on earth, he came through a virgin to rejoice with his virginal bride.

[Col. 0683A] The king’s promise stands firm under immovable decrees. On the appointed day, the soldier approaches, dreadful with the ordered sword, and opens with steel the path to the girl’s kingdom. She seeks heaven amid the rejoicing spirits of the heavenly court. On that day, when pure light had once been sent down to earth, she shone with the splendor of her rising among the psalming ranks of heaven and was suffused with divine honor.

Her relatives seized the chest containing the distinguished virgin. Not far from the city, along the Via Latina, they placed it in the ground where she had prepared many tombs for the saints.

[Col. 0683B] While Claudia, her mother, mourns at the funeral, her daughter, accompanied by pious choirs, brings consolation. Adorned with garments embroidered with gold and radiant brilliance, she brings her mother joy and enduring gladness.

[Col. 0684A] At once she declares that she rejoices, having been received into the chambers of light, into the heavenly seats and everlasting summit with the Father of the saints’ senate. She indicates the day on which she will attain the heavens in holy peace, and commands them to preserve their heavenly glory and admonish the brothers whom they may have as companions.

The light accompanying the message shines with splendor, surpassing mortal bodies and dulling the eyes with its excessive brilliance. The heavenly beings are heard offering melodies to God in tuneful voices, voices not to be uttered by mortal mouths, which Christ alone and the gracious Spirit receive.

Claudia returns home and gives her sons the heavenly commands of their anxious sister. After revealing the appointed day, she departs to enjoy heaven. Her sons and daughters accompany her; the faithful observe the commands entrusted to them and live as those worthy of heaven’s gift. While caring to acquire rich gains for Christ, they prepare losses for Erebus and the densest revenues for heaven.

## CHAPTER III. On the holy Ruffina and Secunda

[Col. 0683]

[Col. 0683B] In this conflict we likewise take up Ruffina and Secunda, who overcame the kingdoms of men by the splendor of their pious triumph. Fear, their most evil counselor, compelled their betrothed to defect from Christ’s ranks amid doubtful circumstances.

Therefore, hostile in spirit, they despise the agreements of their engagements with degenerate men and choose to avoid shameful companions. Having approached a small estate as a solace for their vow, they decide to leave Rome—much nobler in their judgment—and to live as exalted women beneath a humble roof rather than remain beneath a gilded roof in the city.

[Col. 0683C] They investigate and disclose their flight to their companion Archesilaus, who, in the manner of a hawk following doves, pursues them and, carried along like a bird by swift horses, seizes the fleeing nest in a rapid assault. He brings them back and hands them over to the prefect of the City, Donatus, who shuts them in separate caves, although their hearts cling to one another so closely that no art can divide them.

After this, when the third light returns to the elements of their labors, he orders them to be brought before him. Receiving Ruffina first, he attacks her from within the inner chambers:

“Although you are noble by birth, why do you display yourself in this way? Why do you pursue servile labors, sitting captive in grievous bonds, when you could be free, flourishing in the happiness of a pleasing husband?”

The virgin replies:

“You urge two utterly foolish things. You promise one doubtful thing in every possible way, though you yourself are uncertain. You command me to sacrifice to sacred beings for whom I shall be punished by perpetual penalty. You offer me the honor of virginity’s destruction for love of a man, and you join lasting joys to such adverse pursuits, ignorant whether you will see tomorrow’s times.”

[Col. 0683D] At this the governor orders Secunda to be brought in and beaten. Seeing her sister lying beneath the lashes, she cries:

“What you are doing—she exclaimed—what you are doing, hater of the divine power! What is this? Why, while honoring my sister, do you begrudge me the same distinction and judge me unworthy of this height?”

The interrogator says:

“You are more insane than your sister.”

She replies:

“My sister is not insane, nor am I more insane. Rather, by the worship of Christ the Lord we are joined together. It is fitting that those whom the same fault binds should likewise be beaten together, so that together we may be adorned by Christ, whom together we confess as our life.”

Thus, while they readily proclaim their superior faith with glorious praise, the wicked exactor consigns them to darkness and supplies smoke and filth. But fragrances rise from the dung, and the place is filled with the breath of nectar-like perfume.

[Col. 0684C] The darkness is overcome by the flashing of radiant light.

Then, ordered to be dragged away and cast into blazing baths, they are thought to have been killed together by the heat. But those who come to remove their bodies see the fires subdued, and the sisters joyful amid God’s fire and gentle coolness.

The judge is astonished at this and decrees that the victorious women be covered by the Tiber, with stones fastened around their necks. They are hidden beneath the waves. They scarcely remain under the water for half an hour before they return joyfully, bearing their own weights. They had entered the river naked of clothing; they emerge from the water clothed in garments that have remained unharmed, praising Christ and singing a clear hymn.

The terrified judge confesses to the prefect, out of reverence, that he has been overcome by their magic or by some deception. He also returns the condemned women to punishment at the judgment of the judge himself, or permits them to go free.

[Col. 0684D] Archesilaus, not softened by the record of their deeds, orders them taken into the woods and, once killed, cast as food to woodland birds and wild beasts.

But the grace of the Lord does not leave the slain women hidden away. We learn of Plautilla, on whose country estate these things were done, a matron to whom they appeared seated in a prepared, jewel-encrusted chamber and gave the following commands:

“Cease from your crimes; stop, Plautilla, from your wickedness. Abandon your impious life in the worship of idols. Believe in Christ, go and see the property that belongs to you, and, when you find our bodies, place them there in tombs.”

[Col. 0685A] The woman rises and approaches to fulfill the command. Finding the gifts that had been given to her, she believes and worships, and richly adorns the venerable tombs with praises of God.

By this same fervor many everywhere ascend to heavenly things.

[Col. 0686A] By this same means Basileus and Jovinus together overcome the stars; slain, they seek the golden kingdoms by the Latin road, while the Lavican way produces a triumph of fifty.

## CHAPTER IV. On the holy Pope Sixtus and Laurence

[Col. 0685]

[Col. 0685A] After Stephen, Sixtus, worthy to guide the apostolic reins, governs the venerable rule of the world. He is said to have been renowned in learned Athens.

While he, gripped by dark fury, is driven into the shades, Laurence also seeks to enter the prison in order to struggle with him. Sixtus, having set his affairs in order, joyfully enters the Church’s contest and reveals the coming battles to his minister. Then, led to the shrine to sacrifice, he casts down part of the offering and offers his head to the Almighty.

The levite joined to him, the most blessed Agapitus, and four other companions are handed over; the fourth follows the venerable trophies.

Meanwhile Laurence is seized while bringing forth the sacred resources, at the same time showing himself ready to die. Indeed, he had distributed the wealth that had been given to him into the body of Christ. Visiting crypts and traversing the caves of the devout, he had cared for the needy, refreshing them with twofold nourishment.

He had freed Quiriaca, the widow of Quiriacus, from the fever of her head, relieving the grievous pains she had endured for a long time. By the sign of Christ he had restored the lost light of Crescentia, presenting these gains of radiant faith to the one who strove to see the athlete of heaven whom she desired.

The athlete, having exhausted his resources and seeking the swift palm through blood, is delayed. He is judged to be destined for a more important contest. He is ordered to reveal the father’s hidden talents while the savage interrogation proceeds.

[Col. 0685C] He is handed over to Hippolytus, who, bound in chains, carries light to the blind. He restores Lucillus in both respects, inwardly and outwardly, relieving him by the light that has been poured forth. Many pleasant heavenly lights rise together.

Hippolytus, with the people of his household, approaches the divine powers and shines with eternal brilliance.

After these events he is ordered to produce the one who gives light, and is asked to open the chests containing the hidden wealth. The wise steward of honorable bronze gives sweet gifts. Asking for an interval in which to bring the abundance of the presents, he obtains three full days, promising to provide them.

Soon he gathers a great crowd of the poor and a rich multitude of people. By adding the interest, he heaps up lofty treasures for Christ, gathers numerous companies as the Church’s adornment, and, with the wealth amassed, offers the tyrant fruitful gifts, presenting dense ranks of beggars as an assembly.

[Col. 0685D] The furious and savage interrogator—more savage than savage—comes out. He rages, angrily ordering that his avaricious hope be mocked.

He sharpens his weapons, preparing to rage with harsher fury against the prisoner, whom he subdues with rods and furrows with sharp instruments. While blades, a heated couch, and lead are prepared, while he reviews every kind of torture and death, seeking by some crime to drive him from life, he displays to the executioner instruments suitable for cruel death and gnashes out threats.

“These are the banquets beloved by the martyr,” he declares, and with his mighty strength he tires out the executioners. When the hot blade is tested against his burning faith, the leaden weights are overcome by his superior spirit.

He laughs at everything, exulting, strong in heaven’s armor. While he breaks the tortures of the rack in triumph, the hearts of those who were torturing him turn toward divine assistance.

A Roman soldier, a warrior moved by heavenly light at the blessed combatant’s struggle, declares that he sees the radiant faces of the heavenly beings and the faces of those contending, flashing with divine splendor. He asks for aid, lest he remain in such wickedness.

[Col. 0686B] The Almighty assents, wearying the torturer with anguish.

The soldier’s mind therefore seethes; he does not know by what stratagem to proceed. As his anger grows hotter and he desires to destroy the enemy, he orders the invincible man to be released and time to be granted, pretending that the victor should be relieved from the effort of handling and overcoming the conquered man. He thus seeks to show whom he will fight and whom he will withdraw from battle.

The Roman, seeing the favorable time, hastens and brings water in which he may shine. Supporting himself by prayers, he worships the victor’s feet, asking to be saved and cleansed in the sanctifying font.

The levite does not delay to wash his untutored companion. He baptizes him and gives him the victorious arms in shining whiteness.

[Col. 0686C] The new recruit, a novice, learns to fight beneath new weapons. He becomes accustomed to overcome even when driven by rigid clubs. Proving himself safe under an exceptional defense, he becomes a victor, and, tested by the sword, with his neck severed, he despises the earth and goes before his master into the stars.

Laurence likewise, beaten by punishments, remains joyful in lofty mind and countenance. Bruised in the face by stones, he persists exultantly and triumphs in praise of Christ. Bound, he is tortured by excessive suffering.

The torturer, grieving that all his weapons are being consumed in empty fury, envies him a swift stroke that would lift him above the heavens. He assails the invincible man with all his strength, and finally orders that the warrior be consumed by a slow fire, commanding that he not pass through the fierce flames too quickly. He orders him to be roasted over warm ashes beneath a gridiron.

[Col. 0686D] Once the fire has been supplied and the glowing coals increased, the heavenly martyr is placed upon the iron bed with his naked body. His face shines, and joy does not flee from the roasted man; his delight is not broken to satisfy the tyrant’s wishes.

The executioner’s weapons fall; the insignia of the sufferer rise. Joyfully he offers himself to Christ as a noble sacrifice. He gives thanks and praises to the Lord who consoles him. Amid songs of the heavenly gift he springs from the coals, flashing with the radiance of heaven, and as victor seeks the lofty palaces of Christ’s kingdoms, while the judge is confounded.

Hippolytus and the holy Justinus honorably care for the venerable relics of the martyr, and Laurence is buried in the field of Quiriaca.

Crescentia is joined to the holy triumphs by her slaughter. Claudius and Severus are then handed over to suffering.

The tomb of the levite is adorned with the honor of exceptional virtues. Shining with innumerable cures, it radiates ever more frequently through wondrous deeds; wherever the places of the blessed martyr are proclaimed, venerable memorials of salvation gleam.

Thus, while the fabric of his church at Brion is being rebuilt and the cut beams and timbers are being prepared, a short beam found there is lengthened through his merits. The tree that had seemed useless is seen to favor the vows. Stretched by the work and repeatedly repaid by various cures, it proves beneficial; it also benefits the construction as faith increases, and it benefits the needy by granting the pious gifts of strength.

[Col. 0688A] Nor did the virtue of the exceptional levite raise Milan less high. There a noble temple, named for the consecrated martyr who overcame the fire, preserves a crystal chalice with a beautiful setting.

The faithful drank divine blood from the shining vessel, which supplied heavenly things in the likeness of heaven. When the vessel fell from the hands of the minister who was lifting it to the sacred altar, it broke into fragments through the force of its fall.

Pallor and lifeless fear stained the minister’s face. Gathering the scattered fragments, he brought them to the martyr’s altar. Trusting in God’s power, he took up the weapons of faith. Keeping watch through the night in prayers and tears, he approached the altar in the morning and recovered the vessel unharmed by the damage.

He supported it with a steadfast heart made firm by faith and, by the fullness of his faith, completed the solemn vows.

## CHAPTER V. On the holy Hippolytus

[Col. 0687]

[Col. 0687B] After the martyr’s remains had been honored with celebrated ceremony, Hippolytus is seized because he had gathered the roasted limbs of his master. Discovered to be Christ’s servant, he is immediately shaken by blows. Proved faithful and strong, he is ordered to undergo the punishment of the earlier Hippolytus.

The servants of the Christ-speaking sect, marked by rumor, are led away, ready to serve the Lord unto death. Among them, the nurse of the confessor, Concordia, since she appears more fervent in faith than the others, is the first to ascend to the heights of heaven, driven there by leaden weights.

The rest of the strong company of servants follows soon afterward.

[Col. 0688B] They go before him to heaven in chariots, having lost their heads for their master, destined to measure out the lofty kingdoms for the Lord.

He follows after nineteen servants have been sent to the stars and, perfect in his integrity, completes the second series of his own company, carried through the rugged way to heaven.

Savage horses drag him heavenward with his feet fastened to them, show him the narrow path leading to the pole, and send him, worn down by thorns, slaughtered above the heavens.

Justinus gathers his mangled limbs after their various assaults and renders the pious honor owed to the meritorious martyr.

## CHAPTER VI. On the holy Herennius and Abundius

[Col. 0687]

[Col. 0687C] Then Herennius and Abundius, the companion of his fortunate service, who had been intercepted, enter heaven.

The same holy men, because they had removed from the foul sewer the body of Hippolytus’s nurse, are killed; their sacred relics are then honored with holy tombs.

[Col. 0688C] Not long afterward Tryphonia, once the wife of the ill-fated Decius, is buried by him. Cleansed in the divine font, she exchanges earthly kingdoms for heavenly ones with her daughter, and shines in true honor. Captured by a swift procession amid vows and prayers, she enters heaven.

## CHAPTER VII. On vengeance against Valerian and the Roman kingdom

[Col. 0687]

[Col. 0687C] After many thousands of saints among the descendants of Aeneas had been sent to the heavenly kingdoms through punishments, once this kingdom had been set aflame by the fury of the savage dragon,

[Col. 0687D] the author bears disgrace heavier than death and punishment. He who had driven many under a servile law is turned into a servile office and takes up a shameful servitude. The prince of Romulus’s descendants, captured by the ruler of Babylon, is forced, bent beneath the weight upon his back, to raise that ruler’s feet for mounting his horse.

Poor Valerian, with his eyes gouged out, grew old in chains, as though he had first been fixed there to prove that he had followed blindness, darkness, and black dangers.

But although so many thousands had already been slain, and although one head had been subdued for the crimes committed against the saints, since blood had been poured out in various regions of the world, a not insignificant quantity of blood was still demanded in vengeance against the savages.

New battles rise everywhere with loosened reins.

[Col. 0688C] Just as once locusts covered the fields of Pelusium, so barbarian peoples cover the Roman heights.

The Germans roam through Italy after the Rhaetian territories. Alamannian assaults pierce this land, and Gaul is worn down by whirlwinds. The Pontus and Macedonia are oppressed by the floods of the Getae, and Greece devastates Asia with this scourge.

Dacia is utterly taken away, as far as the Ister had separated it. The Sarmatian attack likewise lays Pannonia low. The Parthians, sent forth to plunder Media, the child of the rivers, and the Tigris, strip Syria as well. Spain yields to foreign Germans.

And lest secure peace within the body of the kingdom nourish those who are safe and be thought to shelter the unharmed, civil wars rage deep within, throughout all their hiding places. Everywhere a great abundance of Roman blood is poured out, as the very men who had scattered nourishing blood upon themselves persist in barbarity.

[Col. 0689A] But the peace granted to the just brings peace to the world. When the heat of savage wars has been put to rest, the peoples shine in peace, and Christ’s offices are honored.

[Col. 0690A] Once savage tyrants have been crushed everywhere by disgrace, the devout congregation, previously mournful, at last flourishes. It rejoices in God’s praises, struck by no attack.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the persecution of Claudius and the holy Lucius and Marcus, Peter and Theodosius

[Col. 0689]

[Col. 0689A] Claudius rekindles the extinguished fires of the flame, breathing upon and reviving the covered embers.

He executes Cyrilla, the child of Decius, purified by the holy Jordan, who despises threats and profane commands, with a cruel sword. He also confines many soldiers whom Dionysius, Sixtus’s successor, had renewed in the blessed font, and, while they laugh at the savage commands of his fury, he kills them.

[Col. 0690A] Among these four, Lucius, Marcus, Peter, and Theodosius, burning with the powerful heat of faith, soon behold the sword-bearing men hastening toward them. Eager to go to heaven at the first blows, they ask for it.

Justinus receives them in their tombs, as well as holy Cyrilla and many others gathered by devotion. A confessor who followed them is added as a companion in honor.

## CHAPTER IX. On two hundred and sixty martyrs together

[Col. 0689]

[Col. 0689B] It is said that two hundred and sixty martyrs were led out together to be excavating gravel.

At that time the king, after they had been worn out by heavy labor, assailed by troops, and wounded by arrows, raised them from earthly servitude to the kingdoms of heaven, their heads lifted by crowns.

The servants of heaven carried their bodies: Marius, accompanied by the devout and married Martha; and, joined in vows, Audifax and Abbacuc. Their names, suited to heaven, are recorded. For the sake of prayer they had come from Persia to the threshold of the apostles, supported by John, a most noble foreigner and presbyter worthy of honor.

Gathering the sacred bones with honorable care in purchased linen cloths, they buried them on the Salarian Way.

[Col. 0689C] At that time Quirinus too, strong in the love of Christ, had despised the enemy and won triumph after enduring proscription, lashes, chains, and deaths. While he was being held, they had sustained him in prison; they carried him back across the Tiber and placed him among the tombs of Pontianus, with the honor befitting a martyr.

After him, those seized with Valentinus remained voluntarily in the house where this blessed holy man, shut away in the glory of his noble confession, sanctified souls and performed splendid miracles.

Through these miracles Asterius, rescued from the darkness of blindness, rejoices in the beautiful light restored to the girl, whose sight had been recovered. By this light he leads many others out of darkness, including the girl herself, her father, her husband, and the members of her household.

[Col. 0690B] Then, beaten and not subdued by clubs, he is cut down by the sword and takes up the heavenly reward of his head, a royal prize that he had prepared.

After this, the most illustrious foreigners are brought forth. Driven by lashes and beaten across the back with force, they render vows of glory to the heavenly King.

Soon roasted by fire and pierced by an iron claw, they are hung upon the weighing rack. They offer thanks to God and joyfully cry aloud in the clear praise of Christ.

With their hands cut off and tied around their necks as an infamous disgrace, they are led through the City as a terrifying spectacle and give the Quirites a sorrowful display.

[Col. 0690C] Thus, with their necks severed, they ascend to the heavenly kingdoms. Martha rejoices to stain her head with blood. Having been immersed in water, she seeks heaven from the waves.

Nor does loving charity suffice for those who have been driven to such a slaughter unless it also provides them with tombs. Their bodies, offered to the pyres, were burned.

It is said that Felicitas snatched the half-burned bones from the savage fires, concealed them, and buried them in her own estate, after she had purely joined the heroic woman to her husband.

## CHAPTER X. On the holy martyr Caesarius

[Col. 0689]

[Col. 0689D] In this period, guided by divine power, Caesarius had come to the city of Terracina. While, with lofty mind, he rebuked those who worshiped stones, he was seized under the ruler Firminus, who protected the gods, and, shut in prison, was tormented with insults and blows.

After this Leontius took charge of the prisoner and, testing the invincible man in conversation, attacked him with savagery. For, proceeding in a chariot to Phoebus’s shrine, Leontius leads Caesarius there unclothed, with his hands bound behind his back.

When Caesarius arrives and pours forth pious vows to the Lord, refusing the commands of Latona’s son, the temple collapses to the ground, engulfing the pontiff Firminus in its ruins.
