[Col. 0690D] Lest the people crown the one who had triumphed in sacred matters with praise, the victor was soon shut away in black caves. There he is said to have remained joined to the Lord for nearly a year. Then, while Cynthia completed her full course, he was brought from there into the forum.

As he leapt toward the stars in prayer, he was suddenly surrounded by the brilliance of heavenly light. A broad light entered through his external eyes into the inner hearts of men. Leontius, strengthened by heavenly radiance,

[Col. 0691A] reveals that he believes and covers himself with his cloak, presenting spectacles to the crowd with his naked body.

Without delay, he is washed and reborn in the divine water. Receiving the sacred life of piety, with Julianus as donor, he soon seeks heaven in a swift leap after pouring forth his prayers.

The prince clothes the holy presbyter Julianus and the blessed minister Caesarius in the sackcloth of the city, as though they had deserved to receive a punishment for parricide. Taken into the bosom of the sea, they rise to the highest heaven, lest they drink the sea’s bitter waters as the waves whirl around them.

Immediately returning the chests to the shore’s sands, Eusebius, pious and good in monastic conduct, buried them there, giving earth to earth, near the city that bears his name.

[Col. 0691B] At their tombs, while offering prayers and fasts to the Lord, the fortunate presbyter converted many from the worship of empty things to the worship of the Almighty, renewing them in the heavenly font.

The savage Leontius, moved by an ambiguous semblance of piety, seizes both men and binds them to the father’s unshaken citadel. Led from there into the forum and subdued by no severity, they are then thrust into darkness because they refuse to offer sacrifices. They receive the swords and joyfully depart to the stars.

Their bodies, exposed to the waters of the river bath, are carried out toward the sea, for a faithful guardian—
Who might entrust themselves to one worthy of the gifts they seek:

A fourth priest, brought there from the city of Capua, lifts what had been entrusted to the shore and carries it off; having taken it away at a run to a hut, and seeking the heads, he finds them. They open themselves to him of their own accord, and he takes them, then stores them, separated from the bodies where those holy relics had been laid, in the honorable tombs of those who had been led away.

[Col. 0692B]

## THE SIXTH BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0691]

### CHAPTER ONE. On Saint Felix, Pope

[Col. 0691B]

Felix, succeeding to the chair of Peter with its governing authority, bears the burden well and administers the honor well. He decrees that mystical sacrifices be offered at the tombs of the victors, who triumph crowned and with blood poured out—the blood he orders to be shed, while he himself makes the martyred head a decoration.

Eutychianus, following him in office and faith, strives with no inferior love of piety to grow in honor toward those who have earned it. For they report that throughout various places he established three hundred and forty-two burial chambers for those crowned by slaughter; burying them with his own hands, he honored the martyrs with worship worthy of them and with honorable reverence.

Without delay, he joins himself among the victorious and, becoming a witness among witnesses, is increased in honor. Those whom he himself covered with pleasant cloth around their little coffins joyfully meet him as he seeks the golden kingdoms, and gladly lead him into the hall made radiant with light.

[Col. 0692C]

### CHAPTER TWO. On Saints Basilides, Mandalus, and Their Companions

[Col. 0691]

[Col. 0691C]

Then Emperor Aurelianus, stirred up by these events, harassed the camp of the heavenly King, forging the ninth edict, utterly disgraceful, and striving to provoke battles that had to be avoided.

[Col. 0692C]

The courage of Basilides, Mandalus, and at the same time twice ten companions is said to have won a triumph at Rome with a sudden assault; they are reported to have been received along the Via Aurelia.

### CHAPTER THREE. On Saint Agapitus

[Col. 0691]

[Col. 0691C]

Agapitus, amid that very fervor, illumines the Praenestine land with his virtue. After the blessed Porphyrius, a teacher renowned for piety, had completed his life, Agapitus, thirsting for him as for the clear water of a spring, burned in every fiber for the supreme honor of martyrdom.

Scarcely born, he had completed his fifteenth year when he was seized at the command of the scepter-bearing ruler, on account of the celebrated praises of Christ that he continually spread in his words. He was raised upon raw sinews and severe scourges. At last, tested by the exhausted executioner, he was handed over to the censor Antiochus to be brought to the altars.

Antiochus confined him for four days in filthy hiding places and a blackened cavern, keeping him unfed and without provisions. Afterwards he was brought before blazing coals piled upon the crown of his head. Exulting, he received them and returned thanks to the One who preserves everything and raises him for these battles.

Then he was beaten naked with scourges, hung with his head brought down toward the earth, and drenched with bitter smoke.

[Col. 0692C]

Meanwhile he said: “Your empty wisdom, governor, labors in vain in the smoke.”

Angered by these words, the governor tormented him again with raw scourges, while the executioner alternated the blows, and added four men to succeed one another in turn.

From there he poured hotter water over his belly. The ministers of Satan broke his jaws, but by no device could they break his praise of Christ, since he was protected by a greater power.

Yet, lest sacrilege should remain unpunished for long, the judge, confident in his ferocity, handed over Christ’s athlete. Suddenly a dark cloud surrounded him, and, falling back from the tribunal, the empty man learned that he had been overcome by the martyr’s strength. Seated upon his couch, he ended his life in this grim manner and sent forth his soul, full of gall, into the empty air.

[Col. 0692D]

While these deeds were immediately astonishing the ears of Caesar, the governor himself said that the victor of such great trophies of human fury ought to be devoured by lions.

The savage hearts of the beasts softened; they gladly laid aside their nature, and the tame animals rushed upon him while bound and licked his footprints.

Thus the perpetrators of the crime and accomplices in wickedness, grieving that he was safer among the beasts than among men raging with bestial savagery, carried the witness—proved by great virtue—away from the midst of the people. They led him far off; he willingly offered his neck, and they struck him with iron, raising him to the stars.

The faithful hasten by night and gather the sacred limbs. They carry them as protection for themselves and for their people, and immediately place the precious relics in a new coffin prepared by divine intention.

[Col. 0694A]

While he confessed God with joyful face amid the tortures by which Christ rules, one of those standing there, Anastasius, cried out: “Truly, God himself is great; there is none besides him.”

Astonished and maddened by these words, the governor reported to Augustus that Anastasius had been led astray by the martyr’s art. Augustus immediately ordered him to die. Thus a pious confession carried a pious witness to heaven.

### CHAPTER FOUR. On the Persecution of Claudius Being Suppressed

[Col. 0693]

[Col. 0693B]

The savage persecutor was not allowed long to disturb Christ’s ranks. As he was beginning his harsh-sounding war, dictating laws and reviewing his cruel decrees, a thunderbolt driven through black whirlwinds and clouds fell before the feet of the man sowing deadly ordinances, appearing to all who trembled as a source of dreadful fear.

It was no different from the way the inhabitants of Egypt, once oppressed by darkness, are said to have been stunned by the horror of night while obeying the cruel commands of the Pharaonic tyrant.

[Col. 0694B]

Without delay, Caesar perished while making his journey, struck down by the assault of the crowd. He had not been acting according to human will when he tested his scourges against Christ’s servants; rather, he was driven by a higher divine power.

Likewise Christ’s one bride rejoiced in clear peace. From then onward she openly feared death under no terror, until Diocletian, inflamed with madness and armed with the infernal Bellona, brought forth flames and poured Acheron over the world.

### CHAPTER FIVE. On Saints Chrysanthus and Daria

[Col. 0693]

[Col. 0693C]

Although King Numerianus is said to have raged against certain persons, he sent holy Chrysanthus, adorned with the lofty crown of many palms together with his companions, to the stars.

[Note: [Col. 0693] In the margin of manuscript 1, written by the same hand: “The ancient Romans call *mactum* ‘increased,’” and so forth. Scaliger, Book I, Letter 20.]

Chrysanthus was of illustrious earthly lineage through the ancestral pedigree of his forefathers. His father was the Alexandrian Polemius, who, allowing his son to devote himself to freer studies, trained him to know the sophistical deceptions concealed in obscure matters.

As Chrysanthus carefully reviewed the discoveries of many people, he finally climbed to the firm foundations of the evangelical harbor. Seeking an able teacher of the law and of the sect, he found Carpophorus, a priest living by chaste discipline, who avoided civic obligations and maintained a retreat in the forest caves.

Under this guide, after finding a path through the heavenly way in a short time, Chrysanthus advanced freely over its steep heights and openly confessed Christ in fearless speech.

[Col. 0693D]

This was reported to his father, who feared the authority of the nobles. He shut his son in a dark cavern of foul filth and, subjecting him to confinement, broke his fast with welcome food. The young man rejoiced that he had undergone what he had sought; he gave thanks, approved, leapt for joy, and embraced it. Thus he eagerly desired to train himself for a long time:

The father’s passion and the son’s delight were aroused—to hang upon the cross and joyfully undertake fasts, as the minds of Christ’s worshippers were accustomed to do, for whom glory and honor were thought to increase by this law.

Accordingly, it was urged upon the father that he should change his plan: such a man should not be oppressed by this treatment, but, abandoning and avoiding it, should instead be subdued by pleasures, provided with a distinguished marriage, bound by these ties, and drawn into such desires by this chain.

He willingly listened to this advice and carried out the commands. His father prepared the bridal chambers, furnished dining rooms, and immediately snatched his son from the grim prison and clothed him in richly adorned and precious garments.

He brought into the beautiful cell girls selected to soften his mind through charming games, attractive in face and dress; he ordered food to be stuffed in abundance and sumptuous tables to be set.

But Chrysanthus, enduring things more grievous than imprisonment, stood immovable, fixed like a strong man to a stone and clinging to Christ. He regarded filth as delicacies and the girls as serpents, and he scattered kisses and embraces as though they were arrows against a bronze shield, driving them away by the weapons and resistance of powerful faith. By wise song he laid the drowsing serpents low.

Defeated, nobler than the first through the sharpness of her reason, Daria came—more beautiful in face—as though she were to be joined in marriage to her companion. While she would return Chrysanthus, whom she had captured, to his father and to the gods, the contest already begun grew through her varied skill:

Nobility, beauty, and the grace of eloquent speech attacked the man who resisted everything with powerful determination.

Chrysanthus, whom grace, the honor of faith, and true wisdom had encircled, fought her with opposing weapons. She preferred the gods, who were to be worshipped by divine right; he taught that they were wretched and devoid of divine radiance, and proved it by explaining true and evident deeds.

At last the virgin, properly yielding to the sharpness of his reasoning, approached the yoke of Christ and submitted her neck. She approved the preservation of virginity and the assumption of the name of marriage, adorned by a great pledge.

The virgin wife was washed in sacred baptism. Thus joined as equals by the chaste bond of Christ, they never ceased to beget numerous children through heavenly increase. Chrysanthus gathered the holy camp of men, while Daria filled the female ranks.

[Col. 0695A]

When the enemy saw numerous companies assembling throughout the whole city under the leader’s sacred laws of Christ, and saw the old altars and yokes utterly rejected, he brandished livid weapons and roused the crowds with dreadful violence, stirring savage tumult against the pious.

At that time Celerinus governed the city. He handed these captives over to a certain tribune for scourging. His name was Claudius. Employing seventy torturers, he tried to bind Chrysanthus with harsh sinews, but suddenly, released by heavenly power, he stood free, and no yoke could hold his bonds together.

Then he was fastened with the knotted strength of a massive wooden frame. On the third attempt, when the bite of the frame spread his leg apart, the wood dissolved into fine ash and could impose neither force nor weight upon the saint.

[Col. 0695B]

The sweating executioners then tried to drive away the stench by washing it with urine, but it was changed into a nectar-like fragrance, and its warlike breath, exhaling joyfully, soothed them.

Next he was sewn inside the freshly removed hide of a calf and stretched beneath the blazing beam of Hyperion. But Phoebus ignored his own laws and laid aside his power; his heat merely warmed the outer covering, and the sun did not feel the need to burn the saint’s tender skin.

As the strength was removed from his limbs and remained on the outside of his body, the Cynthian heat, which had been drawing it away, withdrew from the saint.

Then they subdued his hands, feet, and neck with chains and threw him into the abyss of a prison and its blind hiding places. Immediately all the knots of his fetters were loosened, and light flashed, shining as though planted with countless lamps.

The makers of the punishments reported all this to the tribune.

[Col. 0695C]

He ordered Chrysanthus to be beaten with a woodland rod. But the rigidest branches of the attached forest feared to injure his limbs; they began to bend and wither in a slow collapse, and placed all their hardness in his hands.

Seeing this, Claudius ordered the saint to be raised from the ground and covered, and fell at his knees, praying that he and his household might be consecrated according to the holy law.

Soon he was catechized and received the divine waters. With several other couples and their companions, he rejoiced in the children born of their union: Maurus and Jason, together with seventy soldiers joined in marriage.

When Numerianus learned of these acts and of the many others who had been added to them, he ordered the tribune, who was enclosed in a great stone, to be submerged in a glassy body of water with fierce heat; then he ordered the heads of the seventy married couples, including Jason and Maurus, to be cut off by the sword.

[Col. 0695D]

There was an ancient tunnel hidden there, where the slain witnesses were placed. At night the worshippers of Christ lifted them from the filth and adorned them with many precious ornaments.

Hilaris gathered the limbs of the tribune’s parents after they had been given pious funeral rites. While he poured forth prayers and continued his petitions, he was forced to participate in profane acts.

As he was being dragged away, he asked that they allow him to complete his prayers. And so, while he took the mystical sign of Christ and, kneeling, stretched his palms toward the stars, he ascended to heaven with his prayers, and heaven received him as he prayed.

Then, suddenly astonished at the end of their plunder, the abductors abandoned the female servants who had accompanied them to the funeral. These women served their mistress with a final duty, buried her, and raised a basilica above her tomb, lifting its roof as far as they were able.

[Col. 0696A]

Meanwhile Augustus raged with still fiercer madness against the high-ranking standard-bearers. He thrust Chrysanthus into the foulness of an honorable prison, where flowing filth weakened the sewers; Daria was received into a prostitute’s enclosure.

But divine light was supplied to Chrysanthus in his confinement, and he is said likewise to have breathed forth fragrant balsam.

A bold lion was sent into Daria’s cage. It became the guardian of her purity, entered the cell, honored it, and watched over the praying woman, adorned with peaceful dignity. When many people reverently paid honor to Christ because of the miraculous sight, the terrified prefect ordered fire to be brought forth at the entrance of the brothel with a great quantity of wood.

The beast, frightened by the flames, disturbed the place with a hoarse roar. But the more courageous virgin said: “Go out safely, leaving without harming anyone. He sets you free, since you gently honor him in me.”

Afterwards Chrysanthus was brought before the prefect and stretched upon an equine torture device beneath an extended beam. But the machine recoiled, and he was carried into the winds; the pieces sprang apart into fragments, the bonds were scattered everywhere, and the lamps that had been attached were chilled when their heat was driven away.

Celerinus, shaken in his heart by this wonder, reported the events to his master. The latter, attributing them to magical frauds, ordered the chaste married couple to be buried beneath the sands of Grandia, which bears stones.

Following Stephen along the path into the heights of heaven, they earned twin crowns joined in a perpetual wreath of milk-white and rose-colored flowers.

While they spread gifts of salvation generously among the peoples, a crypt was built above their tombs with splendid honor.

[Col. 0696C]

When the vow-making crowd of the people often gathered there, the leader of the Aeneadae, savagely raging, ordered the entrance of the shrine to be closed by a wall raised above it while the mystical rites were being celebrated, and commanded the enclosed temple to be pressed down beneath a massive mound.

Thus it remained while harsh tribulation battered the pious, until the City was cleansed of its filth by the expulsion of the images, and the holy tombs of Christ were marked out when God revealed them.

Yet one window remained uncovered, through which the monuments of the saints could be inspected. Through it could be seen the silver that the people had formerly brought inside to offer libations of wine and that had remained enclosed in the chamber.

Someone, ordered by another to do so, crept into the inner sanctuary in hope of booty. He was seized, the plunderer being carried off by the plunder. Thus, when the thief who had been captured tried to creep out, he could not find the entrance by which he had entered.

He went around everywhere, struggling in a wandering circuit, but through the night he could not find a way out by which to leave the enclosure. When the appointed span of daylight had passed and the sky grew black, he sought the exit again and again, but it was again denied him. Once night had been marked out, the whole cataract of day withdrew.

Thus, deceived for three nights, he was worn down by anxious care and futile toil. On the third day light restored all things to the forum: boys to their rods, and the crowd to the streets; meanwhile the prison burned the accused with a different struggle.

On one side shame, on the other hunger, seized the man dragging out his uncertain existence; life weighed which he should place first. But when cruel hunger opened his mouth, his dignity perished.

[Col. 0697A]

At last, emerging while the people watched, he confessed his crime, oppressed by disgrace and not burdened by money.

[Col. 0698A]

When Damasus took up the event long afterward, he covered the entrance of the building and adorned the sacred threshold with verses.

### CHAPTER SIX. On Saint Gaius, Pope

[Col. 0697]

[Col. 0697A]

After Eutychianus, Gaius received the heights of the apostolic see and governed it with honorable authority. For he decreed that those who would climb by steps to the heights should approach them, and that no one should surpass the citadel of the Church by leaps, so that no one might seize primacy in Christ’s army unless he rose through each individual office by orderly advancement.

Relying on these and other directions of the saints, the sacred dove seeks the heights and is borne to the upper summits; it grows, is honored, flourishes, is fortified, and is loved; it expands its dominion, is adorned, and is magnified.

[Col. 0697B]

The livid serpent, rolling the ancient poison of its black gall in the savage ranks of its inexhaustible mind, suggests weapons through deceit and kindles hearts with the black torches of Cocytus. It persuades them to civil war, so that brother envies brother, attacks him while reproaching him, bites him, accuses him, and civil fury burns.

Thus, seeing more clearly that external dangers could produce gain after he had disturbed the inward organs, he aroused a strong enemy against the feeble populace, arming Diocletian with Tartarean flames. Diocletian stirred the whole world against Christ’s servants.

And because it was clear that some high officials were distinguished in military service, he judged that these should first be expelled or subdued by scourges; then he raged against the entire army.

He issued ordinances, recorded decrees, and published commands: the stones of the churches were to be overturned to their foundations, and the heavenly Scriptures burned in dreadful fire.

[Col. 0698B]

Anyone among us supported by distinguished honor, once his position had been removed, was to display an empty name. If any servant wished to serve Christ, he was to remain in this condition, wholly deprived of the hope of freedom.

Let these things be read first; afterwards even harsher orders were issued. The leaders of the churches were commanded to be reduced to chains and compelled by every kind of punishment to perform sacrifices.

### CHAPTER SEVEN. On Saints Marcellianus, Marcus, and Sebastian

[Col. 0697]

[Col. 0697B]

A savage flame followed these sparks, once they had been kindled throughout the world, through Christ’s fields. No land is believed to have been free from slaughter; still less did the walls of Rome fail to know the fires of war and the draught of blood.

[Col. 0697C]

Here the twin brothers, bright lights of their parents and Marcellianus and Marcus, were arrested and assigned to chains. They advanced the emblems of their noble lineage, exalted by a sufficiently distinguished ancestry.

Sebastianus, a man filled with God, was handed over together with their dependants. Although hidden beneath military dress, he was illustrious in honor and most welcome to kings. Every day he continually offered consolation, strengthening the counsels of living hearts, so that they might trample the blandishments and reject the harshness of the world—of the world’s flow, which decays as its dust slips away.

While these men strengthened the warmth of their minds with weapons and endured threats and scourges with steadfast hearts, they joyfully approached the sentence of death.

[Col. 0697D]

Their mother, wives, and children likewise followed them with an inseparable love.

As a result, they obtained a thirteen-day reprieve from Chromatius, the prefect of the City, so that they might be restored to the altars and joined to the laws.

They were therefore assailed by the blasts of many winds. A friendly crowd pressed upon them, asking why they persisted like stone and iron:

“Why should they renounce their father? Why should they prepare tortures for their mother? Why should they deprive themselves of their own possessions by rejecting pleasures? Why should they despise life, abandon glory, and pursue death with devotion to the temples?”

But the parents declared that they remembered their dear children, or [the text is uncertain: “even when summoned by blows”].

Soon the mother entered, crying out that she was a poor woman. She let down her white hair, uncovered her breast, and displayed her hanging breasts, while with tears she revealed the signs of her mourning. She lamented that she had been subjected to no suffering that could be compared with her present misery, since her children, who had willingly chosen to follow death, would be handed over to the barbarians, and she would boldly follow them through the hostile ranks.

She begged that a dagger be applied to them in a new kind of funeral; that, if the sword refused, force should be inflicted upon their dreadful death; and that their aged parents, surviving their children, should be forced to witness the voluntary death of their sons.

While these words were being sown, the old and feeble father was brought forward from the company of the servants. Soiling his swan-white head with dust, he filled the sickened air with words such as these:

[Col. 0698D]

“I am coming to bid farewell to my sons, who willingly approach death, bringing what I had prepared to offer at the funerals of my children.

And what sudden madness, my sons, has arisen in you, alas, to teach you to love death—those whom eminent knowledge instructed and the exceptional strength of your minds adorned?

What do you seek, if only prosperity, that orders you not to fear adversity at all?

Come, fathers; come and restrain such things, lest you ever suffer such things yourselves.

Young men, come and weep for those who are willingly lost. Let eyes washed with tears bring darkness before the old man, abandoned and hateful to himself, lest I see you, my leaders, struck by the sword—those whom I once could not bear to see beaten with rods and whom I dreaded to behold in tears.”

Their wives followed, carrying their sons, and thrust the beloved pledges before their eyes. They lamented that the men were abandoning them, and asked whether they thought they were losing conjugal love—men whom they had proved to be lords of households and children—so that they might rejoice to hand themselves willingly over to the executioner.

Amid these voices, the tears of the wives, and the sighs of the children they scarcely knew, the soldiers’ minds began to dissolve, drawing grief into their wounded breasts.

Their blessed protector Sebastianus, who had hidden himself in military guise, had judged it no empty matter to be present at this spectacle. Seeing the soldiers broken by the burden of the conflict, he burst through the hostile crowd, thrusting himself into the center of the tumult as a victor. Approaching the exhausted men, he addressed them in the language of the wrestling ground:

[Col. 0699C]

“O soldiers, already most courageous in virtue;

O men most fully equipped for heavenly battle;

O men, by the strength of your lofty minds, already near the palm of victory—

Is it now pleasing to set everlasting crowns aside for trivial nonsense and foolish chatter?

I ask you: let the courage of gentle souls be instructed through you in a faith better than all others, in weapons forged with iron hardness.

Do not release the necks of your conquered enemy. Trample the wars down, lest they rise again with renewed strength; and lest, once defeated, they raise themselves up as victors over you.

Although you have experienced this sharp and fierce battle, know that wounds become harder when repeated. Rather, raise the glorious heights of battle far above earthly love, and do not lower them because of the tears of little children.

For those whom you watch in mourning and anguish would stand rejoicing if they understood what you understand. They think that the only victory is to live in the world under temporal law, when, once that life ends, no life shines forth.

If they knew that death is secure and that immortality reigns there, with everlasting joys dwelling there, they would run with you to reach it.

They would consider this life worthless and desire that other life, in which perpetual rejoicing remains and knows no end.

Let them mourn, then, over the kind of life this is: how false, how deceitful, how swift, how ill-advised, crafty, wandering, and faithless; how it drives the wicked into dreadful crimes; where it leads those who love it; and what it prepares.

For everlasting death, brought forth from it, takes those who serve it by right and has driven the first parents into exile, deprived of the homeland of perpetual life.

[Col. 0700A]

This life deceives you, friends, and urges you to mock those who seek the life that remains, though you stop them.

It urges you, parents, to hold back your sons as they go toward heavenly beauty.

It forces you, wives, to take in mind the deadly cup of martyrdom under the bland appearance of honor; if you consented to them, the time would come when you would be separated forever, nor thereafter be permitted ever to see them amid eternal torments, where flame consumes the breasts of unbelievers, dragons devour the lips of blasphemers, serpents the entrails of the faithless, and wailing, discordant weeping, and groaning resound—punishments without any end, while one burnt and destined to burn is renewed a thousand times.

Therefore leave these things behind, and yourselves consider them carefully with cautious minds. Send these men on to the crowns appointed for them, and do not fear that they are being separated from you.

They are going to prepare homes in heaven, to dwell with you and live joyfully, where they will rejoice in everlasting glory.

If earthly homes are loved here, how much more should those homes be sought—built and roofed with refined gold, glittering brilliantly with shining gems—where beauty never withers in bloom, where the green grove never strips itself of its leafy crown, and where gentle streams water everything fittingly?

Here the pleasant meadows never lose their flowers; they breathe out a life everlasting in agreeable fragrance.

There is light without shadow, and night never ends the day. Clouds never darken the serenity; no evil breaks the security. No sadness interrupts the celebrated banquets.

[Col. 0700C]

Lament, mourning, wailing, and hissing are neither heard nor ever resound here. Nothing dreadful, hideous, filthy, or deformed is seen here. Beauty, pleasantness, serene brilliance, and shining loveliness always delight the eyes of those who behold them.

Nothing that could trouble the heart strikes the ears, where the joyful instruments of angels sing psalms.

Here no lightning, flash, or thunder ever struck the shining heavens.

No bitterness spoils the taste. The shrubs produce cinnamon and balsam, whose flavor comes with pleasing fragrance. No food produces excrement; refreshment with nectar entails no digestion.

As the ears are nourished by good news, the nostrils by fragrance, and the eyes by the most excellent sight, each person immediately receives what he longs to take. No one’s appetite is frustrated there.

There, whoever has resisted enticements and has left behind everything here for love of God will receive it a hundredfold.”

[Col. 0701A]

Explaining these matters, the teacher with his radiant eyes brought forth the clear truth: what life creates and what death places beside it; what sort of human being should fear the caverns of death; what kingdom of the future life should be sought; why bodily pleasure should be rejected here; and why the good things produced by the Creator should not be spurned.

He revealed the true riches and true joys: the path by which one passes from these things to those; what is prepared afterward for their friends; and how dreadful and cruel the torments are.

Let the blessed martyrs learn to avoid these things and patiently endure them for the sake of those other realities. Let tears be turned into tranquil joys. Let them now cease lamenting, since it will be clear that those men reign upon the lofty summit and, joined to Christ, receive the scepters of heaven.

Indeed, let them stir themselves to seek the crowns and understand that they have entered the pit prepared for the enemy.

While the blessed soldier of the Lamb—who spoke of the soldier of the world with his mouth—was explaining these things, the supreme Father was pleased to confirm his words by signs. A heavenly flash shone forth, illuminating his disputant. Soon, through a visitation of the heavenly citizens, a young man appeared, joyfully smiling, wearing a most splendid garment and shining brightly. He gave a kiss, promising the everlasting grace of his companionship.

Zoe, the wife of Nicostratus, in whose house these events were taking place, had remained silent for six years with her mouth closed, oppressed by the force of illness. Yet, retaining a sound mind and taking in what had been proclaimed, she beheld the majesty of the heavenly light. In astonishment she indicated with her hand that they should not fail to open their hearts to such manifest speech; prostrating herself, she asked by signs who could help her.

[Col. 0701C]

When Sebastianus understood the reason for her silence, he said: “If I prove that I am a true servant of the Thunderer, and if all these things I have related are true, and this woman has believed them, let him who releases her release her mouth as he released that of Zachariah.”

At these words Zoe cried out in joy, giving thanks and proclaiming her healer. She testified that she had seen an angel sent from above, who had brought a heavenly volume and illuminated the man with an open page.

Her husband, astonished at these things, sought pardon, prostrate at the feet of the gracious men, because he had burdened Christ’s servants with chains. Removing the fetters that bound their hands, he begged the saints to depart freely, offering himself to be made blessed and cleansed in their place, if he deserved to suffer their departure.

[Col. 0701D]

The martyrs, now released, said: “What will happen, they ask, if your faith has begun with such great perfection, and you wish to die for those who are to be killed? With what face, strengthened for so long by such great power, shall we offer you a draught of our own passion?

For Christ’s abundance is known to overflow, providing gifts better than those requested. He will add distinction to you who shine upon such a supreme summit of perfection.”

While the illustrious brothers were saying these and many other things, the parents and friends of their former wicked persuasion, weeping in repentance, began to draw themselves toward the party and yoke of Christ.

The chief secretary pressed them at once to have the sacred rites administered to them. Sebastianus ordered that those reduced to chains be gathered together so that they might receive the mysteries at the same time.

Nicostratus was amazed that men burdened by guilt could undertake sacred duties. He understood that he had presented himself to mortal eyes as a bishop of heavenly dignity, in order to free sinners from death, and that he had entrusted to believers the mystery by which the cords of crimes could be loosened.

The keeper of the accused obeyed, gathering them all together. The gracious soldier addressed them and found them ready for the service of the supreme ruler.

After this, the presbyter Polycarpus, summoned, rejoiced to watch over the gains of the divine granary. Exhorting the divided people, he imbued them with his words and prepared them for consecration by chaste fasting.

When Nicostratus reported all this to Claudius, the Commentariensis, the latter brought his sons, weakened by various diseases: one had a swollen belly from a discharge, while another had been made thoroughly leprous by a running ulcer.

He brought them forward, confessing that he held faith beneath his heart, and declaring that Christ, their glory, would restore them by returning health when the danger of death threatened.

While blessed Polycarpus immersed them in the sacred font, all traces of disease disappeared.

They were named Felix and Felicissimus, now happier than their parents. Afterwards Tranquillinus, infirm in his limbs, the father of the brothers Marcellianus and Marcus, was brought forward.

When he confessed that he believed with a pure heart and would not cease after baptism if he had to suffer, he was healed by the anointing of the sacred oil. Freed from gout of the feet and hands, he sprang into the waters as one released, invoking the true God whom the world does not know.

[Col. 0702D]

After him the friends of the children were washed: Crescentianus, Justus, Urbanus, Vitalis, Euthycianus, and Aristo, whose number had been increased; then Nicostratus and Castorius, followed by Claudius the Commentariensis.

Afterward Zoe, Symphorosa, and Martia, together with the crowd of the chief secretary’s household, were freed from the harshness of prison. All forty-seven were consecrated in the praises of Christ by the pious font.

Joining nights to days, they went about, eager to be consecrated by the sword to the heavenly court as soon as the appointed time of delay had passed.

Tranquillinus and Chromatius called them.

[Col. 0703A]

Giving thanks after his children had been restored—through whom he declared that he himself had been restored, and that they had been restored to him—the prefect rejoiced with them and ordered incense to be carried to the gods.

But when he heard the praises of Christ, he cried out that he had been overcome by the madness of his children and had not rescued himself from error.

The other man, explaining precisely what this error was and showing by the strongest reasoning how free our doctrine was from error, prayed with unconquerable logic.

But I must hurry to mark the triumphs I have destined to be carried in a swift chariot and rolled upon a fiery axle. I pass over these matters and many others.

The prefect requested that he be removed to the next hearing, so that he might be examined. At night he sent for him and summoned him more privately.

[Col. 0703B]

Offering him great weights of gold, he asked him to reveal by what medicines he himself possessed healing powers, so that he might recover from them the strength of health.

The other replied: “Know that they suffer the fury of God, those who think that Christ’s grace can be bought in the marketplace, when faith is able to prepare it—not gold.

Only believe that he is the ruler of health, the giver of life, and the director of well-being. He rejoices in those whom he can congratulate with complete joy for the health of both mind and body.”

The judge demanded that he explain by what force a Christian might rejoice in health.

He replied: “I myself could live as a Christian, so that he might announce the joys of health.”

Then, arranging the words and deeds of Polycarpus, he brought him before Chromatius. To him, the prefect offered the medium of good health as a gift, while the other rejected the filth, proclaiming that Christ must be worshipped and that health was to be given as the reward for this service.

He established the man as a supporter and ordered a fast. The latter was not slow to fulfill what he had been instructed to do, supported by the illustrious leader Sebastianus.

After they had consecrated three days by this discipline, they went to visit their new fellow soldier. While they greeted him as he persevered in his deeds, they learned from the depths of their hearts that his faith was already strong.

He asked that, as they had raised his father among the pious, they should loosen the stiffness of his limbs. They warned him that the everlasting pains were preferable to those unequal to the ending of cruelty, and that these pains were to be feared and guarded against.

The salvation of the graces was to be sought perpetually.

The prefect, as is customary for those being consecrated, gave his son Tiburtius a single name.

Sebastianus, skilled in administering the holy rites in a holy manner, warned him not to seek the sacred mysteries merely for the sake of bodily health. Rather, he should gather hope of everlasting life in his heart, and, if he loved salvation, raise his true mind toward the vision of truth.

He should prove by faith who the Creator of all things was and always rejoice in a sincere worshipper; reject the crowd of gods and goddesses; and shatter the images of baked clay that he had worshipped.

He could not be washed in the font of holiness in any other way unless he first renounced all the trifles of idols, by whose destruction the health of the wounded man had to be restored.

With Chromatius agreeing and ordering his household to do these things, the learned leaders did not allow an idle hand to be offered in this battle.

The heavenly princes, secure in their weapons, girded themselves for war. They attacked the empty images, ordered two hundred or more representations of the gods made as masks to be broken, and, once they had been shattered, gave thanks to God.

They urged that the matter be investigated with more diligent care and that the man be questioned and examined more closely: what he carried in his mind, whether any of the disorderly divinities’ images remained undamaged, and whether some scruple marked by a doubtful heart had been left behind.

He revealed a counterfeit mechanism: a glass chamber fashioned by heavenly art, giving signs through a portentous riddle.

[Col. 0704B]

His father displayed several further objects belonging to this construction, teaching that nothing in the house was more precious than the gold offered in sacrifice. They showed that this was a rival to health, that nothing in it was trustworthy or in harmony with truth, and that it revolved blind images through crafty nonsense.

They proved in the clear light of the divine gift that no truth was hidden in these adulterous objects, and that they produced neither purity nor help.

When the true light had been revealed, the sick man was astonished. He proclaimed that there was only one God of this law, who sent his servants forth in such serene light, and finally favored him in undergoing the losses inflicted by the broken deity. He confessed that he believed in the citadel of the twofold salvation that was to be sought in this way.

[Col. 0704C]

He therefore explained whether anything remained for decorating the house, whether any sign made of jewel or glass was left. While the emblems of the fragile metal were being crushed, the young man, presenting himself before the eyes of Chromatius, shone with a face bright as flame.

He declared that he had been sent from the heavenly seats by Christ the King to pour vigorous health back into the limbs of the sick believer.

At this, now healthy in every part of his body, the bold prefect ran after the healer.

[Col. 0704D]

He was forbidden to touch the heavenly body. But, holding fast to Sebastianus’ footsteps, he confessed that the heights of Christ were supreme. Tiburtius proclaimed that only Christ was to be worshipped, although shortly before he had been sending the saints to the furnaces.

Sebastianus chose to withdraw Chromatius from the world and nourish him under Christ’s protection. He gladly urged him to leave the business of the world after appointing a successor, and to seek from the civic magistrate the favor of being free to devote himself to God.

When asked about his faith, he freely declared that in his heart he abhorred idols. When questioned whether he was abandoning all sins, he replied that he could not disclose this earlier, asserting that the entanglements of his affairs had first to be dissolved, so that he might offer forgiveness to one who deserved anger and release what was owed to every debtor.

If he had seized anything through rampant greed, he would immediately restore it entirely and justly.

He freed himself from concubines and household slaves, wishing to renounce his disgraces.

Blessed and comely was the young Tiburtius:

“If, father, you demand that I renounce the affairs by which you insist that time must rightly be bound, I refuse the desire to be entangled in the undertaking of such acts. Let me be handed over, as an advocate of heavenly concerns rather than earthly ones, to the court of the inhabitants of heaven.”

While Sebastian bound him in embraces, Polycarpus moistened him with nourishing waters. The father, no longer delaying or drawing out the time, wholly renounced worldly affairs; stripping off the man of ancient, rusted metal, he put on the new man, blossoming in milk-white brightness. With him went forth, in honour of the blessed candidate of the sacred waters, one hundred and fourteen persons whom he had freed from the bonds of servitude.

Thus the holy Church of Christ, scourged by blows, grew amid the lashes of her persecutors; thus strong threshing filled the granaries. The fire of fury had burst forth fiercely, but the joyful shoots of Christ were sprouting.

The right of citizenship was denied to Christ’s citizens: the forum, the springs nearby, and the little markets where they might offer sacrifice; those who needed to leave this place went through countryside, cities, and islands. Every form of civic life had now been denied to the faithful.

Yet the illustrious Chromatius, as far as was fitting, cared for the whole flock entrusted to Christ, so that no bodily necessity might subject anyone to the dreadful rites of the pagans. But since light cannot be hidden in darkness, he sprinkled the fields situated farther from the city, so that Chromatius might preserve Christ’s tender sheep more safely through the broad green meadows. He considers visiting the Campanian estates, whether for rest or for the sake of healing.

The soldiers of old prepare for battle; they deem it shameful to leave the field of combat, where they know that the enemy, rushing upon their necks, can break every opposing weapon.

[Col. 0705D] But the kindly teacher and Peter’s deputy, Gaius, lest he send back the shepherdless flock, orders Polycarpus to go with the newly instructed young believers, to water the hearts of the little ones and receive the open crown already won. Bearing the permission of the Law, and mindful of it, he orders him to go with Chromatius to strengthen them, and joins to him a suitable companion, as a son.

But the brave young recruit himself, urged on by the Spirit, considers it disgraceful to leave the camp and cries out:

“I beg you, holy bishop of bishops, do not wish me to turn my back on the battles before us. It already stands as a very welcome thing if I were permitted to be beaten a thousand times and to die for the true God, so that from there I may attain life ignorant of its end.”

The pope rejoices with him, offers tears, and takes up [the prayer] and asks Christ to grant him victory.

Therefore the brave soldiers remain in the camp: Marcellianus, Marcus, and their father, Sebastian himself with Tiburtius, and the brothers Nicostratus and Castorius, together with Zoe, Victorinus, and Claudius, and with the children who had been freed from the jaws of death.

The pope, distributing sacred instructions among them, remained joined to them in the palace. Castulus, the guardian, cared for those whom he had sheltered in the house. There, in praise of Christ, they devoted themselves by day and night to tears and fasts, presenting to Jesus the pleasing gifts of prayer with assiduous devotion. They offered remedies to the sick afflicted by diseases, driving away apparitions and giving sight to the blind.

[Col. 0706B] While these things were taking place, the illustrious Tiburtius, crossing a certain street in the sunlight, found a young boy who had fallen from a height. His bones had been shattered into disjointed fragments, and his body and the crown of his head had been so broken apart in every limb that he seemed suitable only for burial.

Approaching him, he poured forth the Creed in prayer and joined to it extended prayers with heavenly speech. Soon, when his bones had been restored, the little boy rose again, joyful and vigorous, as though he had suffered no bruising at all.

The boy’s parents, who had been holding him as he went forth, offered the servant who had been restored, whether he should ask for anything more. Tiburtius took them aside from the crowds and clearly revealed the power of the supreme God. Seeing their hearts strengthened by fear of Christ, he offered them to Bishop Gaius.

Gaius received the one who was carried in, baptized him, and increased the glory of his parents. Gathering the first fruits of faith from the new tree, he enabled them to recognize the tree through the beauty of the fruits it had produced.

The furious enemy, grieving that such great profits of faith were increasing, attacked it openly and also assailed it by secret confrontation. Choosing a known accomplice in crime, he sent him to deceive the kindly man by pretending to be his companion and, joined to the father, to turn his dear pledges—or perhaps to ensnare them by disguises. He sought by hidden means the man whom Tiburtius frequently rebuked: because, by a barber’s art, he arranged his combed hair over his forehead, with which he smoothed his brow; because he devoted himself eagerly to the luxuries of banquets and willingly displayed himself to women’s eyes; because he withdrew from prayer and fasts; because he avoided remaining wakeful in Christ’s hymns.

[Col. 0706D] Deeply angered by these words, he covers his brow with a cloud and pretends that he has endured them with a simple mind. But, turning over the tricks of fraud in his deep heart, he renews the weapons of the treacherous; he betrays his rival in prayer and, in his mind, gives him over to heaven.

The lamb and the wolf are led together by an equal bond, though distant in spirit and unlike in thought.

Fabianus was the city’s presiding magistrate, serving to offer pious blood to the gods. He orders the man bound for the charge, who had been summoned beforehand, to declare his profession and name.

“I am called Torquatus, and I proclaim myself a Christian.”

The prefect then concealed the orders of the rulers. But Torquatus presents Tiburtius as his master, declaring that he must be followed and setting forth his deeds:

“Do you hear, judge, what this man asserts—this supposedly upright confessor who has long been deceitful? ‘He boasts that he is a Christian,’ says the traitor, ‘but this pretender is weighed down by the very behavior opposed to the name. He is offended even at being called by wicked men, although that name shines with heavenly virtue, the name by which Christ granted his followers the means to excel.

“Those who cultivate wisdom’s disciplines and wage war by crushing lusts are truly being refined. One cannot believe that this so-called Christian is one who softly nourishes the sinews of pimps, delights in the barber, sways with gestures, totters in the effort of his swollen steps, flees men, and entangles himself with women.

“Christ never gathered such plagues. For what sort of man he lived as before, see: he claims that he will follow our deeds, and in your presence his intentions will be proved.”

The censor urges him to look to his safety, to fulfill the rulers’ commands, and not to refuse.

“It is not for my safety that I will take better counsel,” says the martyr, “by rejecting the multitude of gods and worshiping and confessing the one Christ, ruler of the ages.”

Torquatus, unable any longer to conceal the force of the poison hidden in his silence, bursts forth with the beginnings of wicked speech:

“Cruel man! He is not merely a Christian; he persuades and deceives many, and busies himself with magical fraud. He infects his companions with criminal incantations.”

The Confessor says:

“Falsehood will not pass unchallenged. The eminent witness whom you see, now treacherously condemning the Christians, will not go unpunished. But he had no further connection with Christians except for the reproaches of his heart, under the name of holiness. While hiding himself, he would have been believed faithful, although he was treacherous, savagely playing with the faithful by dreadful arts.

“I rebuked his gigantic appetite, and his rule of chastity buried beneath wine. Like Antonianus, a habitual glutton, he ate, hungered, swallowed, and vomited; he burned with thirst and drank himself drunk. Now he blames, presses, and accuses the Christians, and rouses a quiet magistrate against us. He offers a cruel sword to the lingering judge and urges that holy necks be subjected to apparitions.

“Here are the vows fulfilled; here the hiding places of his heart are exposed—the fierce thirst for black blood. Begin to prepare the dreadful commands, executioner; bring out the racks, attach the Christians. You are treating us well: seize us, burn us, condemn us, strike us.

“Do you wish us thus to be exiled from our native city, the city of wisdom? You offer tortures and prison, and by these we escape from the flattering mouth by which we are separated from the Father. You threaten fires, but the flame of desire, conquered by us, has yielded freedom.

“Decide whatever you wish. A pure conscience despises every sorrow; all harsh things are worthless.”

Then the censor threatens him with darkness, suggesting a cup of death smeared with drops of honey. But the lofty soldier, suppressing the serpent’s words, boldly exposes the shameful thefts of the gods and proclaims Christ God with ready praise.

They order glowing coals to be spread before him, on which he must place incense or crush it with his feet, freeing them from their coverings.

Soon, strengthening himself with the sign of the cross, he enters the practiced fire with uncovered feet.

“Lay aside,” he says to the judge, “your treacherous mind. Learn that there is only this one who rules created things, whom we confess to be the God of all. For the soft little roses seem to be crushed by the power of the glorious name. Do you see how created things serve the Creator?”

“Who does not know that they have been equipped with magic by their master?” cries the executioner, stupefied at seeing this.

The blessed man says:

“Be silent, unhappy man, and do not bring these wicked words into my hearing, lest I endure you barking insults with your rabid mouth.”

The censor, inflamed by these deeds, orders—so the text reads [fumea, sic]—that his neck be severed by the avenging sword.

Thus, led through the crossroads of Lavican territory, he offers his neck and receives the dagger. With a single blow he reaches the air victorious, and in that same place he receives burial, enriched by his tomb.

Blessed Zoe, whose mouth faith had opened after it had long been denied, while she frequently visited the sacred halls of Peter and asked in mind and voice for heaven’s crown, is handed over to the naval arena of the district. Gladly she burns incense to Mars, her patron, despising the gods and mocking the sacred rites of the rulers.

Immediately she is shut up in the darkness of night; food and drink are taken from her, and thus she is left without light, a meal, or nourishment.

A weight is hung from her hair; then a dreadful horror assails the lofty rope. But confessing Christ the Creator, she ascends the vault of heaven to its high summit.

“Tell us now,” say the ministers of death, “what further task remains to be performed.” Victorious and exalted, she has departed. Should Christians consecrate her as a goddess to the heavenly powers? Or will she enter the deep waters?

[Col. 0709A] At this they bind a stone to her limbs and consign her to the glassy waters, throwing her into the channel of the Tiber.

The martyr cannot bear that these things done to his teacher should be concealed from Sebastian; he suddenly reports them.

When that holy man tells the story to his companions, he says:

“Why do we delay? Look! Women, calling us to crowns, go before us. They become married martyrs because we live.”

Therefore, inflamed, he visits the thresholds of the apostles, where his desired wife had received her reward. Praying at Paul’s manifest shrine, while the solemn rites of the fathers shine forth again, and suffering treachery, he follows Stephen’s path through a rain of stones and ascends the lofty heights.

Giving his limbs to the downward-flowing river, he allows the blue waters of the Tiber to wash his body.

Likewise Nicostratus, Claudius, Victorinus, and Castorius, together with Symphorianus, while they seek the martyrs’ bodies along the banks of the Tiber, earn the right to become martyrs among the waters. For they are captured and brought before the appointed judge, who urges them for ten days, through gentle and harsh measures, to offer incense to the gods; yet he cannot move them by any effort.

When his attempt is broken, he reveals these things to the rulers. Then, ordered to be torn by the torturers three times, they count their tortures as a game. After being beaten down upon the ground, they are assigned to the waters:

“It is pleasing to enclose the wrestling-ground within marble; it is pleasing to be carried through the clear streams into the air, and to be consecrated by the world’s waters and spring.”

After these men, driven from the stars by the treacherous, depart, Torquatus, through the fraud of the kindly assembly, leads them to seek their host. Castulus is seized; questioned three times, and three times placed upon the top of the rack, he is found steadfast while giving glory to God. Buried deep in a pit of gravel, confined beneath such a weight that only his body is enclosed, he is free in mind and ascends to the lofty stars.

Marcellianus and Marcus, then tested by the impious, are fastened by their feet to a pierced stake, following the Creator through the mark of suffering.

The brothers rejoice in enduring torments like those of Christ, giving divine instruments through their hymns. Already terrifying their executioners, they terrify them still more by their voices; rejoicing, they glory in standing fixed by the strongest power of love, and desire to depart furnished with this support.

Their prayers are heard; they persevere in praise. Thus night is joined to day in this arena, and, so that the duties of Christ’s cross may be fulfilled, each one’s side is pierced by a spear. Thus they too follow Christ into the golden kingdoms.

When these profits of victory have been returned to the King, Sebastian, freed and ready to follow, is brought before the ruler who holds the scepters in opposition to the gods.

[Col. 0710A] He stands summoned as an insult to the gods. He is blamed for having hidden himself from the rulers’ protection. But he confesses that he had diligently prayed for the rulers’ true glory: for the kindly Jesus, not for stone formulas, which it would be madness of mind to request.

The emperor, seized by the storm of a fiercer rage, says:

“Soldier, rush forth against the nobles who despise the kindly gods, lest they grant you a swift death by their heated sword. Let a dense column of the cohort attack him; let the point of frequent arrows be sewn into him; let a crown encircle his forehead, bound to the stake, and let him offer a target to the weapons rushing upon him.”

The troop of the turbulent soldiers goes forth obediently. In the open field they prepare what has been commanded, they fill their quivers with iron, and arrange the surrounding formation. The bows curve; the arrows are drawn out. So many reeds fly together from every side; they compete to inflict the more suitable wounds.

He receives all the weapons upon the surface of his skin, but no force can enter the seat of his mind. Alone, attacked by such a host of quivers, he stands among so many men as an impregnable fortress, protected and defended by Christ’s armor.

He becomes shaggy with bristles like a wild beast made secure by its covering. Those judging him, after so many signs of death, leave him, since the butcher’s method has proved unable to kill him, and they do not surround with the chambers of death the man whose body displays so many traces of burial.

[Col. 0710C] At night, Zetarius—[the text has “Zetarii,” perhaps a name in the genitive]—left behind the martyr, eagerly wishing to tend the body of the pierced man, brings back alive the one whom he had sought as dead.

The enemy, brought into a high house, recovers some health over a few days. Those urging him to flee strengthen him in the faith, now strengthened more by triumph. Revealing himself to the rulers, he makes himself known, charging them with the thefts of falsehood and rebuking the enemies with words of truth.

They marvel that the man whom they had killed is alive. To suppress their madness, he says that he has been restored in the very way by which they crush the blessed. Therefore he attacks the Viminosi, warning them.

[Note: [Col. 0709D] Are these the priests of Jupiter Viminius?]

[Col. 0710D] He is then ordered to be beaten with clubs until his spirit, set in motion, ascends to the stars.

The savage members of the sewer, envying this glory of the Christians, consign him to a filthy drain. But the Divinity prevents a body consecrated by so many past contests from being submerged in filth.

Lucina, a matron, devoted herself here to chaste deeds, full of the light of the holy Spirit.

Speaking to her through sleep from heaven, the martyr commands:

“Seek our hidden remains in the sewer of the Circus; you will lift the pledges that lie there, suspended by a [gumphus], that is, a nail [Note: [Col. 0710D] *Clavo*, ‘by a nail], and not covered with filth.

“When you have found them, you shall place these sacred relics at the blessed feet of the apostles’ king.”

She rises joyfully and breaks off sleep. With her household servants joined to her, on that same night she finds the gifts and, with the honor commanded, puts them away.

## Book Seven Begins

### Chapter One: On Saint Gabinius and Susanna

[Col. 0711A] Gabinius was Gaius’s brother. He was raising Susanna, a girl whom heavenly gold had adorned. Rumor, striking the ears of Diocletian, announced an exceptional girl in beauty and understanding.

He prepares a robe with which to clothe his son’s bride and sends a certain distinguished man, related to them by blood, who is skilled enough to sow these things and establish the whole marriage arrangement.

He therefore approaches the father. But the father and Susanna’s uncle find that Susanna is flourishing with deeply rooted firmness; the seeds they had planted feared no gusts of wind.

Claudius offers the highest honors of the empire, an illustrious royal offspring who would follow her father’s exalted position and rule lofty scepters with equal power, an outstanding young man, distinguished in splendor and strength.

But she, preserving faith in heavenly things, rejects earthly agreements; she places divine honor before human honor. In her heavenly pride, earthly summits are dishonored; before everlasting kingdoms, mortal rule is worthless.

While different vows are sown through alternating speech, the one who came to capture is captured, and the one laying the snare is held in it. He is instructed by the priests; he repents of his wicked deed. He is washed in divine waters and renewed in the heavenly stream.

The two lights of the twin household are also dipped: the children Quae[c]ivas and Alexander, and the wife Prepedigna.

While Claudius seeks to be a complete worshiper of God and to follow Christ, who calls him to heavenly scepters, he sells all his property and gives it to the poor. He visits each of the prison-workshops of the chained, prostrates himself at the feet of the saints, and strives to ease their chains with shelter or food, himself asking through them to be relieved by piety.

Augustus waits for him for many days, thinking that he is fulfilling the strongest bonds imposed by command. But when Cynthia does not restore her exhausted appearance and he does not return to the lofty house or to the festive theaters, he asks whether he has gone far away or whether something has hindered him on his return; he believes that illness has delayed him.

His brother was with him as his companion in the order of events. Maximus sends him to visit Claudius, to lighten the sick man’s bed, to sit beside him in his fever, to settle his agitation, to repel raw disgust, and in addition to inquire into the girl’s dowry and marriage agreement, to report what had happened, and to ask what gifts she might return.

Maximus, approaching with prayers, finds the brother engaged with the people in the Church. Stunned, he refuses to understand what business he is conducting for him. Claudius, amazed, brings him before the Fathers, who reveal the accessible path of righteousness and stir his mind toward the light [the reading *famulant* is uncertain].

[Col. 0712A] He believes, is filled with living waters that he has received, strives to reach the citadel of the highest summit, assigns his wealth to the public treasury, and offers it to the poor.

In this matter he uses his faithful companion Traso. Wearing the veil of his toga, Traso was warmed beneath Christ’s covering fire. Gaius is recorded to have consecrated him earlier with chrism.

At night he visited the neighborhoods and searched the prison-workshops, carrying food to the needy in honor of God. He recorded the deeds and honored the monuments with inscriptions.

But when the deeds are disclosed to the anxious tyrant, he sends men who will subdue the kindly ones with savage tortures. Julius, who had been sent into exile for this purpose, deported the brothers and Prepedigna, strengthened by her twin pledge.

Together they undergo holocausts through fire, impossible for heaven to conquer, shining with radiant brightness. The sea receives their remains when they have been gathered from the waters.

Gabinius, shut up with his child in black caves, where a long time is worn away by the continual filing of chains, springs free from his bonds and penetrates the heavens in liberty.

The fury of imperial power seethes and grows weary of allowing the pious and beautiful woman to go free. It orders that she be brought to its palace, invincible as a bride and companion in marriage.

The fool, unaware of her devotion to the heavenly King, thinks that Susanna can be bent to his commands.

But when she has spent the nights together with prayers and hymns, and has thus brought the days to an end in Christ’s praise, the father orders her, recalled to her paternal house, to be subdued by shame.

The young man rejoices and anticipates his hope. When she has been brought back, and night conceals the earth beneath its black covering, he approaches her. Entering the house, he sees it shining with brilliant splendor and sparkling with heavenly radiance.

Struck with terror by the dreadful light, he is stunned and pales, weak and lifeless, and returns empty-handed to the palace.

The traitor gives out that this was done by an Atracian serpent [the wording is uncertain] and sends him to the Numician [reading uncertain], who compels him to submit to the altars.

[Col. 0712D] Ordered to attempt to bend her, Macedonius does not spare her, though she is supported by divine strength; he shakes her pious entrails with cowardly clubs and lashes.

Glory resounds from the virgin’s heavenly mouth. As she continues the praises of God, she is struck down unconquered. Receiving the palm of triumph beneath the sword, she rises from her father’s house and crosses into the heavenly palace; she enters the bridal chambers of the eternal King, most worthy of him.

Serena gathers her limbs and gives them to the darkness. With abundant perfume she preserves them and wraps them promptly in shining cloths. Eagerly arranging the pious burial with her own hands, she places it beside the blessed bones of Alexander, her father.

She does not allow the holy blood to lie hidden in the earth. Searching out the cracks with linen, she takes it as an honored treasure, and, lifting it, covers the illustrious gifts with gleaming metal.

[Col. 0713A] She cherished these hidden things, preserving them within the palace, and secretly offered herself to the Lord upon the altar.

While she, raised up by these merits, is lifted to the stars, and while Gaius, having gained heaven through the blood of martyrdom, receives the heavenly kingdom with a crown that withstands opposition, Marcellinus succeeds him in the honor of the see. He follows him in deeds, and, beheaded under the same tyrant, gains heaven at the price of his neck.

[Col. 0714A] Antoninus, Claudius, and Cyrinus lie there with their naked limbs for thirty-five days. Later Marcellus gathers them with praise and hymns.

Savage persecution raged throughout these regions for an excessive period, within a single month of days, so that seven and ten thousand are said to have been slain then. For no short time heaven was filled everywhere with the deeds of the saints, but the Roman see remained vacant in the absence of its eminent bishop.

### Chapter Two: On the Saints Primus and Felicianus

[Col. 0713A] Then Primus and Felicianus, raised up to the golden city, reach heaven through slaughter.

While they shine in glorious exaltation and rejoice assiduously in Christ’s worship, the profane citizens of Romulus accuse them of living according to Christ’s law.

They are sought and both are brought before the rulers. Loaded with chains, they are thrust into prison. There, lifted up by heavenly consolation, they rejoice in receiving the message of the heavenly King.

Again brought before the rulers, they are ordered to be taken to the temple of Hercules. If they should dare to refuse to bring offerings there, they would be subjected to savage lashes and terrible tortures.

When the soldiers report that the torments have been overcome, the furious rulers hand them over to the governor Promotus to be killed by a cruel interrogation.

[Col. 0713C] Again they are consigned to the darkness of prison, and again they are strengthened by messages from heaven.

After many days have passed, the governor orders them to be brought before the tribunal presiding in the forum. They deliver answers with courageous hearts. He thinks that they ought to be separated by a cunning deception, believing that the strength they possess is fraternal, or that, once separated, they will suppress their struggle.

He therefore orders Felicianus to be beaten in the sight of the forum with the blows of crushing lead. Alternatively, he proposes that Felicianus choose to enjoy happy days, or compels him to be tormented by devices still to be devised.

But he says:

“I shall serve the one whose law I have chosen to serve. I have already completed eighty years—three times thirty [the text is inconsistent]—of the passage of time, and I have discovered the truth. In these years I have held nothing back from the trifles of the world, but I have preferred to serve the supreme Creator.”

[Col. 0713D] Thus, while he gloried, the governor, burning to conquer him, ordered him bound upright to a stake. He pierced his palms and feet with spikes, and, after torturing him for a long time, sustained him for three days without food or drink.

But the high hand of Christ nourishes him, lifting him up and protecting him. While he rejoices in remaining immovable in God’s praise, he is again ordered to be struck with lashes.

Not subdued even then, he is thrust into the caves, and holy Primus is brought forward to be torn apart. After being tormented with very savage clubs, he is lifted onto the rack in triumph. Burning lamps are placed around him.

Unconquered, while he smiles in the great battle, he is thrown down on the ground and attached to a bed. Felicianus is brought in to see the boiling lead being poured into his mouth.

The governor is distressed as he observes both of them remaining unmoved and glorifying Christ. Groaning in defeat, he orders them to be given to the amphitheater’s bestial fury, to complete what he could not accomplish with lashes, fire, or iron.

Lions are sent rushing at their feet, but, made lambs, they do not know the savage impulses of their hearts. Bears are driven upon them, and these too change their ferocity in their sober minds through the glory of the pious.

When the spectators behold this crown, and the hearts of those striving in wonder are touched, one thousand five hundred raise their right hands in faith.

The governor, surrounded on every side by dreadful anguish, orders them to be cut down with the sword, while they rejoice. Thus triumphing, they seek the crowns of the kingdom; thus they enter the glorious kingdoms of heaven.

The Nomentan embankment, with its pious turf, receives and buries the relics stolen by the Christians.

### Chapter Three: On Saint Pancratius

[Col. 0713D] The boy Pancratius triumphs beneath this slaughter of rulers and prepares an eternal crown at the price of his head.

Octavilla, carrying away his body in pious devotion, adorns it and covers it not far from the City, where worthy virtue condemns those who seek it and those who oppose the truth.

If anyone who comes there is caught uttering perjuries, he is either seized by a dreadful breath and carried away, or, having fallen to the ground, gives up the vital air.

[Col. 0714D] Hence many approach him, asking for certain dangers to be removed. His uncle Dionysius cherished him, gave him to be consecrated in the font of life, and kindled him with love for Christ. He strengthened him by pouring forth blood in radiant glory, and so, closing his day, rested in the peace of piety.

Then the illustrious virgin gained true salvation, receiving the palm in this storm through the attrition of her body, blessed in mind and body as a sacred offering to God the Savior [*Soteris*, uncertain].

### Chapter Four: On the Saints Claudius, Nicostratus, and Their Companions

[Col. 0715A] Claudius and Nicostratus, together with Symphorianus and Castorius, shone brightly. Skilled at cutting marble, they represented the faces of the ancients with exactness.

For the scepter-bearing they fashioned precious metals at command, and all the works they began proceeded according to their wishes, while they took care to fortify their undertakings with the sign of the cross.

A certain Simplicius, unequal to them in mind but their companion in craft, since he could not match the labor of his companions in skill, remained anxious and asked who their God was, in whose name such carefully finished and suitable works were produced.

Symphorianus, when he asked to know the secret, said to him:

“If you can believe, I will reveal the art, so that you may discover it and receive everlasting life without limit.”

Soon, having shown his faith, they strengthen him and entrust him to holy Cyril for consecration. The sacred water washes and forms him for the holy rites and reveals the mystical gifts.

Not long afterwards, when they had been brought before the authorities, they were required to contend in Christ’s service; because they would not carve the prescribed images of gods, they were examined at the order of the tribune Lampadius.

[Col. 0716A] The tribune Lampadius, after investigation, instructs them to worship Hyperion, so that they might turn aside the plan of their accusers.

They answer him steadfastly:

“Our Lord of heaven, who rules the world, the Son himself of the living God, who created all things—we pray to him, not to works made by hands.”

After he had spoken at length, and they had been pursued by various forms of deception, the public guard takes them while they remain strong. Once they have been proved incapable of being turned from Christ’s faith, they are stripped of their covering and cut with sharp lashes.

While Lampadius tears the holy men apart in a savage attack, seized by a demon, he is cast down into the foul Underworld.

When Augustus hears these things and is filled with fury, he orders that leaden coffins be made, that they be shut alive inside them, and that the coffins be covered by the waters of the river.

After twelve months’ worth of days [the text says “two times six months and days”], a certain faithful man named Nicodemus finds them and lifts them from the waters. He brings the precious relics home with the coffins and stores them there.

### Chapter Five: On Saint Severus and Severianus

[Col. 0715B] Severus and Severianus, together with Victorinus and their companion Carpophorus, are led to the sacred rites. No persuasion, threats, or deceptions can move them to bow their necks and offer sacrifice to the impious.

When these matters are reported to the turbulent ruler, he orders them brought before the shrine of Asclepius. If they do not pray there, they will fall beneath a slaughter of lead. He orders their bodies, when killed in the street, to be left to dogs or wild birds.

After they have lain exposed in this way for five days, the pious servants of Christ gather them and lift them away, placing the bodies beside the funeral offerings already prepared. There they rejoice in four crowns.

### Chapter Six: On Saint Genesius

[Col. 0715C] Genesius, leader of the mimes and of a graceful art, is turned and shaken by this threshing and is tested. Found upright and worthy, he climbs the heavenly granary [*horrea*, literally “granary”; the text is uncertain].

He was accustomed to soothe the prince’s savage spirits with jests and to calm his ferocious moods through play. He was devoted to presenting pleasing gestures to the persecutor, imitating a festive deception, and, in mockery, reproducing the playful rites directed against the cruel captor.

Therefore, one day, as he attempted to prepare a performance, the jester proposed the mysteries of Christ to the perverse spectator. In the middle of the theater he presented this little play: let a sick man lie down and ask to be washed for healing.

“Come, he says, my colleagues—here I am, heavy; I ask to be made light. Are we craftsmen? Will our file or our rasp make you light?”

The mad crowd of the people laughed. He continued:

“I wish to die as a worshiper of Christ.”

“Why?” they asked.

“Because,” he replied, “on the final day I shall be taken away as a deserter.”

An exorcist from the Church was summoned, a priest who sat beside the bed as though participating in the sick man’s games.

Suddenly, by God’s inspiration, the deception was driven away. When they asked why he had called them, he set aside all the thefts of his former trickery and, with a now-pure heart, confessed that he desired the gift of God with all his inmost being, so that, renewed by the waters, he might be snatched away from his wicked deeds.

When they had completed the mystical rites of Christ’s sacrament and clothed him in white garments, he was immediately seized by a soldier and brought forward, so that he might be questioned under the empty appearance of a game.

Placed before them, he approached the high seat and began to speak:

“Listen, Augustus, and let the people standing here, trained in jokes, listen; let the wise men of the prosperous city pay attention.
