I, who formerly hated even the name of a follower of Christ, insulted Christ’s servants and cursed the very parents of that name with a title suited to laughter. I thought that I could turn the mysteries into our game and, by provoking laughter, strive to defile the sacred things.

“But when I touched the waters and made the profession of faith, I saw a hand sent from heaven protecting my head from on high. I saw the shining inhabitants of heaven surrounding me and reading from a heavenly book the evils I had done from childhood; they erased that record in the laver in which, having been immersed, I stand white, and thereafter shine with a splendour whiter than snow.

“Now, illustrious prince, and you who follow the people, all who approve these mysteries that have been enacted with me, believe that Christ is the true God and also the Lord.

“Believe that he radiates pious light and that this is true devotion. Through him those who repent will receive forgiveness.”

The emperor, filled with bitter anger, had him tortured with clubs and severe, savage blows, and handed him over to the prefect Plutianus to force him to sacrifice through torture. A claw, tearing him apart, cuts through his appointed portion.

Burned by lamps, he perseveres in proclaiming the faith:

“Besides the one whom I saw and whom I worship, there is no king for whose sake I will die, even if I must remain here a thousand times. Since I have begun to speak of Christ, no one will snatch him from my mouth. Tortures will never drive Christ from my heart.

“But I repent exceedingly of the horror in which I mocked heavenly things, and of having approached the King so late, when I was still a proud novice.”

Persevering in these words and resounding in clear praise of God, he finally receives the eternal crown of martyrdom through the sword.

### Chapter Seven: On Saint Lucia

[Col. 0717A] The noble widow Lucia, in the severity of this slaughter, seeks the heights of heaven. For many years God’s right hand preserved the holy woman in heavenly honor.

[Col. 0717B] The Lord presents her to the servants, as he once foretold. She declares that she lives according to Christ’s law rather than that of the gods.

The tyrant orders her to be brought in and attacks her because she worships the one crucified and insults the shrines. If she wishes to live, she must approach and offer incense to the gods, so that they may be favorable to her through sacrificial offerings.

“They are favorable,” she says, “neither to me nor to their worshipers. My Lord has been accustomed to be favorable to me, and he will not abandon me to punishment. Whatever you inflict for his love, I am prepared to endure: bonds and fires alike.”

Taking courage from a woman and fearing to be defeated, the cunning serpent orders her to be hidden in the prison’s caves.

There, deprived of every human support, her King does not abandon her. He deigns to lift her with heavenly honor and, consoling her, raise her up with celestial splendor.

The savage lion turns and rages to seize the woman who despises the plunder. The blessed woman, brought back before him, is subjected to blows with rigid rods.

While she is long worn down, a sudden earthquake shakes the building, and the shrine of Jupiter collapses in a great fall, so that stone could no longer cling to stone in its walls.

But the executioner, made still more savage, cooks his dreadful rage more fiercely. He orders a large bronze vessel to be brought, commands it to be filled with lead and pitch, and orders all the surrounding sides to be cut down with gathered timber from one direction and the other. He orders the victorious woman to be plunged into the fire of Ammon.

While she joyfully sings her trophies for three days, the cruel man goes to see whether the enemy has completely subsided. He finds her safe, emerging with a cry from the ashes.

Nor does the butcher, struck by the summit of such virtue, lack ferocity or lay aside his agitated fury. In his madness he orders that the victorious woman, burdened with iron and lead, be dragged through the city streets.

[Col. 0717D] She goes adorned through the crossroads with heavy fetters [the transmitted word is uncertain]. At the door of a citizen named Geminianus she approaches. He, powerful in wealth, was accustomed to fumigate countless household shrines with incense and to worship them with foolish fire.

As the sheep destined for slaughter passes through the house of the Thunderer, suddenly a dove is seen to glide down from heaven and, tracing three bright signs of the cross upon Geminianus, settles upon his head.

He too, looking upward, sees the heights of heaven opened. He takes flight and swiftly reaches the field where the woman, by the strength of her spirit, is exhausting the torture and conducting a powerful battle through hard struggle.

Seeking the victor’s footsteps, he runs headlong to see what has been accomplished. He asks for the sacred gifts; the priest Protasius is ordered to come and cleanse the eager man in the divine laver. He carries out the command and consecrates the man, purified in the pure waters.

On the third day thereafter she renews her victorious battles with the joyful king of the Aeneads and with the newly converted recruit. He attacks them with newly devised torments and punishments and, in his fury, hands them over to a savage man whom the executioner judges to be even more cruel, so that he may supply whatever torture against the enemies is still lacking.

As he considers what more he might add to the torments already inflicted, he beats the necks of the victorious with hard wood and soon crushes the noble house by striking the ground and forcing it down.

Against the victors, Apophrasius [or “Apofrasius,” uncertain] takes up arms. Under him, five and seventy men who had submitted their necks to Christ’s yoke, moved by his virtues, are seized; God performed these wonders in his servants with marvelous honor.

After their funerals, the rejected judge is hurled into the waters. His horse, guided by the left-hand driver, shakes him, and he plunges from a high bridge into the lowest abyss, swallowed in body and mind by the Taenarian chasm. For his miserable remains were never seen afterward on any shore.

Then Megalesius, driven on by Stygian serpents, rises against the athletes, shining with monstrous trophies. He tests the unconquered and, unable to overcome them by any trick, attacks them with a sword, sending them through the heavens by the blade.

[Col. 0718D] A woman named Maxima carries away the illustrious bodies and, as befits victors, hides them with beautiful honor.

### Chapter Eight: On the Saints Marcellinus and Peter

[Col. 0717D] In this struggle Marcellinus and Peter triumph. Peter, the exorcist, wrestled through a many-sided contest, wearing down heavy chains while shut inside.

The jailer grieved that his daughter was bound under the siege of a demon. Peter urges him to believe that Christ is the Lord, begotten by the highest Thunderer, through whom he may rejoice in the salvation promised to his child.

“I am astonished at your counsel,” says the prudent Artemius.

Your God is unable to rescue you, and you worship him so that you may bear his wounds and bonds in his name.

[Col. 0719A] “Who will be able to save my child, if I lend assistance?”

“But,” he replied, “my God is able to rescue everyone from these punishments; yet it is better to fight bravely, so that I may be able to win an eternal triumph. If you wish to believe me, jailer, I shall double the chains and thrust you alone into the lowest darkness; I shall leave all the prison’s barriers secure, and I shall trust in everything if God rescues you from these things.”

Peter gives his assent and declares that he will come to his house—not, he says, at the whim of the trial, but so that this work of humanity may be done for the divine light of Jesus to be revealed to the darkness of men.

Shaking his head, the man says: “This fellow is delirious from excessive torments”; and he hastens, recounting the matter to his wife.

Suddenly, when the shadows had shut out the sun of night,

[Col. 0719B] Peter appears, carrying the venerable signs of the cross. The woman, prostrate at his feet, cries out that there is one supreme God and that Christ is the Lord without an image.

Soon the daughter, Paulina, receives complete healing, and those whom that household contained worship Christ. When the demon himself declares that he has been overcome by the power of the Lord, the news spreads among those standing around; a crowd of more than three hundred men rushes together, and an even larger number of women burst in, to see the glorious spectacle and offer praises to the supreme God.

Then, at their request to enter the sacred rites, Peter summons Marcellinus. The gracious presbyter washes all of them, joins the washed to the holy fold, and unites the consecrated offenders with those freed by the guardian—those released from bonds whom he delivers from dark vices.

[Col. 0719C] When the censor learns of this, he orders both men—the presbyter and the exorcist—to be brought before him. After the priest has spoken the truth, he is ordered, at the prompting of fury, to be beaten through the body by the savage fists of the executioners.

The slaughterers grow weary, but the holy man remains unconquered.

Then, separating Peter from him, the tyrant orders him to be spread naked upon a bed of sharpened glass, shut away in blind hiding places, deprived of the aid of light, and denied food. Peter groans that he has been separated from the savage tyrant and says:

“Though those subject to you call you serene, you are clouded throughout, dark in your purposes and deeds.”

He too is then bound, fitted with chains, and his feet are fastened in the cleft of crushing wood.

The heavenly disciple of the star-bearing one, desolate,

[Col. 0719D] is sent from the citadel of the supreme Thunderer to the presbyter. He raises him up from his wounds, wraps him in his own cloak, and carries him out of the stocks and irons in which Peter had been held.

[Col. 0720A] Having freed both men together, he leads them into the house where, only recently, they had joyfully spent their time in prayers and praise, strengthening the new lambs with heavenly teachings. He orders them afterward to approach the harsh censor.

As the sky grows pale and the dread darkness of night withdraws, the wrestlers are sought again in their hiding places. Since they cannot be found, Artemius himself is ordered to be bound and compelled to offer sacrifices to the gods. Standing steadfast in the honor of God with his daughter and wife, he is ordered to be shut away with their united affections. He himself is struck down by the sword at the threshold of the crypt; his daughter and mother, cast down and marked by stones, escape death and receive limitless life.

The leaders bring the slaughterers before them, intending to inspire terror, accompanied by a large crowd. But the executioners themselves are detained and intercepted, and they stand there while the priest completes the sacred rite.

The confessors, fearing that the crown they had earned might be delayed, order the people to withdraw, and voluntarily present themselves to chains and offer themselves to the swords.

Thus, like rabid dogs moved by no sweetness, once they have torn apart those brought before them and sharpened their fury, the executioners do not spare the noblemen, who seek eternal trophies. They attack them with chains, fasten them with knots to the trees, and hurry to ask the magistrate what death they should inflict.

He orders them to be led into the forest called the Black Forest, made white by the pious, and to be killed in its hidden groves.

Led into the dark woodland and beneath the lofty trees,

[Col. 0720C] they clear a space for the slaughter by tearing away the thorn bushes. In turn they kneel as suppliants, exchanging kisses of peace, offering vows with their knees placed on the ground but their hearts raised up, and readily receive the death-dealing sword at their necks.

Their virginal souls are seen adorned with jewels and gold, decked in heavenly beauty as they ascend to the lofty halls of heaven and penetrate the air of the sky.

It is said that the savage executioner was permitted to behold these things. While he reports what he had seen, and while he repents of his savage deeds, he—already an old man—earned the sacred gifts of life through the waters.

The blessed reveal their bodies to the worthy ground. Firmina and Lucilla, beautiful matrons and brighter in the light of their minds than in their blood, lift them up together. After being instructed, they place Tiburtius, who had been laid in the cave, in the sacred enclosure that flourishes with holy merits.

[Col. 0720D] Damasus once learned these things from the executioner and makes them known, although set forth in polished verse.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Two Holy Felixes

[Col. 0719]

[Col. 0719D] Two presbyters shone through divine rites, both named Felix, both happy in their deeds, brothers by the law of God and brothers by natural blood.

The elder, seized at the command of the nobles’ fury, is driven before the secret divinities of the judge Dracchus. The brazen Serapis, in Pelusium, was compelling the ancient Hebrew people, whom he had once subdued under Tricantes.

[Col. 0720D] When he breathes upon the suppliant mouths of the ancient fathers, the vast brazen images collapse like a leaf before the wind.

From there, led victoriously to other similar altars, he mocks Maia’s son, whose power has been broken. Nor is the huntress goddess, terrifying with bow and arrows, strong enough to resist the breath of the holy man’s mouth.

After his glorious trophies, he is brought back to the judge’s seat.

[Col. 0721A] He is raised up for torture, and the judge asks by what spell he had accomplished such terrible deeds and by what deceit he had overthrown the gods.

“Those are not evil deeds,” he replies, “but good deeds of the Thunderer. These things do not prevail through deceit, but through the praise of almighty God.”

The censor likewise orders the blessed man to be led to the temples for conversion. But lest he compel him to offer only the customary dry sacrifices, he orders him to pray to the leaves and branches of the tree that stands beside the shrine and thrives from its green root.

He pours out a prayer and declares that the tree should fall from its roots, overthrowing the temple roof that had stood for so long, so that those empty people might no longer be deceived by empty vanities. Seeking the depths, he prepares to uproot the tree and carries out the order. He strikes the nearby temples, shakes, destroys, and crushes them, then scatters the fragments and tears away what has been ground to pieces.

The judge, learning of this, orders him to be subjected to the avenging sword

[Col. 0721B] and given to the beasts, denying him the common rights.

He was climbing the appointed course toward the goal of his contest, joyful and hastening to rejoice in the crown he had won. But, so that his companion might shine more greatly, God brings forward another man.

[Col. 0722A] When this man hears the sentence and the order that the slaughter be carried out, he comes forward and offers himself for execution to the one who held the kingdoms, hastening to seize the palm:

“Even I,” he cries, “shall submit to the same law by which this elder shines, and I too worship Christ the Lord.”

At these words he is seized and, joined to Felix through holy kisses, is slaughtered with equal merits. Cut down together, he rises to the joys of heaven. Because they did not know the younger man’s name, they called him Adauctus—“Added”—in honor of the virtue bestowed upon him.

The righteous undertake their silent labor beneath the night, where the tree, torn up, had opened a vast hollow. They bury the bodies and conceal the pious trophies in the earth.

The wicked hand, wasting with black envy, attempts to tear from the countryside the treasures deposited there, marked by glory. Those who rush to the work are carried away by the furies of Hell, while the hall of peace is being built and raised up, adorned with the glorious shining trophies of the martyrs.

## CHAPTER X. On Saint Chrysogonus and Anastasia

[Col. 0721]

[Col. 0721B] Anastasia encouraged Chrysogonus in his chains.

She also brought him many consolations, for this man, kept in prison for two years, endured very many sufferings as a victor in Christ’s name. Moreover, he gained Rufus as his jailer and saved the households of the dependants whom he found; with them the Lord, made mighty in the contest, triumphantly conquers.

Anastasia’s husband, so that she could not visit those placed in prison whom she honored as members of Christ, shut her away alone in dark inner chambers.

Noble by birth and nobler in conduct, assigned to a savage husband but devoted in her vows to Christ, she clings in mind to the pious while imprisoned in blind hiding places.

Through an old pious woman who served as her messenger, she writes to Chrysogonus how her mother, radiant in divine religion, had ensured that she was consecrated in the waters while still a little girl.

After her mother’s rest, she takes upon herself the cruel yoke of her treacherous husband. Yet, pretending illness, she rejects the bonds, embracing day and night the footsteps of the Lord Jesus.

Her husband, ravaging her property with sacrilegious men, drives her into the darkness of his hidden chambers and thinks that she is now about to surrender her bodily life, though she would rejoice to lay it down for Christ.

But he grieves over her wealth, which she had vowed to heaven to the last coin, lest it serve the hated friends of crimes.

“Why, servant of God,” she says, “I beg you as a suppliant: pray earnestly to the Lord either that he himself subdue my husband’s heart, or, if he sees that he must be devoured by fire, command me to endure that place. For I believe it better that he should deny than that, by confessing, he should remain their lord and source.”

“Christ is my witness that, if I should live free, I shall cling to the feet of the saints and continue, with vigilant mind, the care of the pious labor that I have begun.”

The confessor replies to these prayers, poured forth:

“To you, wavering amid whirlwinds and the storms of the world, Christ will soon come, walking upon the waters. With one word of command he will restrain and shatter the savage blasts from the mouth of the warlike dragon.

“Therefore, as though in the middle of the sea, worship patiently and await the Lord with the holy prophet in your heart, crying: ‘Why are you troubled, my sick soul, and why do you afflict me? Hope in God: though hard pressed, I shall yet confess him. He is the glorious salvation of my countenance.’

“You will embrace a double gift of heavenly reward. When earthly things are restored to you, heavenly things will be bestowed; for this reason the Lord delays his high blessings for a long time, so that what he grants may not seem worthless or what is given quickly pass away.

“Do not be troubled that adversity once followed the pious. By these things you will not be deceived; rather, you will be proved steadfast.

“Secure defense does not stand by means of a human being. For cursed is the person who strives to place hope in another person, and blessed is the person who rejoices to fix hope in the Lord.

“Finally, beware all sins with a vigilant mind. You keep Christ’s commands; seek his consolations. In the time pleasing to him, he will soon look upon you turned toward him, as one who sees flowering lights after the darkness of night, and golden springs after winter’s ice and after the cold of the North Wind has been driven away.

“Then, while the south winds breathe, he will offer you his presence, pressed close beneath God’s love, and loosen the bonds of your chains with gentle consolation. You will receive starry gifts that have no end.”

These words raise the woman’s spirit, enclosed in darkness, so that the darkness cannot cloud her inward light.

She grows stronger under pressure and rejoices in the struggle. The unhappy husband is enraged and increases his fury. He crushes the imprisoned woman and denies her drink and food. He scarcely gives her water, so that, consumed by death, she may more freely surrender the wealth over which he could rule after she had abandoned it.

Now hoping to be received, she writes these words to her comforter:

“The end of my body is near.

[Col. 0723A] Remember us, that he himself, for whose love I suffer, may receive my soul as it leaves the darkness; continue the work of this old woman which you have begun by your exhortation.”

He replies:

“It is certain that light always advances through the shadows, and that the sick person may hope for healing; life follows death. Thus, in one conclusion, all the joys and hardships of the world’s course grow weary, so that there may be hope for the sorrowful and no arrogance for the joyful.

“Our boats, borne upon the same sea, are driven by one wind; so all hearts are carried forward by one oarsman. Here, certain vessels, joined by a firm framework of ribs and struck by the storm, cross the agitated waters of the sea. In some small boats, the beams are badly joined and the calm sea pours water through the cracks; these quickly perish while trying to seek the harbor.

[Col. 0723B] “But you, in spirit, adorn yourself with the trophies of God’s cross. Fit yourself to the Lord, so that, after you have fulfilled your vows, you may climb to him himself with the summit of the martyr’s palm.”

Without delay, Publius, sent from foreign shores, breathes his last, and his chilled body is brought back to the city, to his wife.

When the guards see this, they abandon the threshold and flee. Anastasia, now safe, seeks the virtuous prophet, telling him what had happened and mingling tears with joy, asking toward what end the holy prophecies had been fulfilled.

Thus, free from the chains of the imprisoned, the servant of Christ shines forth, tending the prisons and carrying out her vows.

The judge, this plague against the saints, was slaughtering the witnesses of the Lamb in the regions of the eagle. It was not enough for the executioner to be drenched in the blood of those present; he scatters Roman swords throughout the world.

He keeps in prison those whom the prefecture orders to be driven throughout the city by the dreadful sword. He orders holy Chrysogonus to be sent to him; Anastasia, heavy with devotion, follows according to her vow and offers abundant consolations to those in chains.

At last Chrysogonus is led into the presence of the advancing dragon. He is attacked with snares and shaken by renewed assaults. He is urged by the prefect or consul to worship the gods of Romulus and not to despise the sacred rites of his ancestors.

“I worship one God,” he replies. “With a suppliant heart I honor him and pursue him with sincere deeds. I despise and curse your gods’ images, which are proved vain, as demonic shrines.”

By his speech, revealing the unconquerable strength of his spirit, he completes the noble contest when his neck is severed.

[Col. 0723D] So that his limbs might not be honored by the peoples as belonging to a savior, they are washed, submerged in waters smooth as the sea.

But they are not swallowed by the Nereian abyss; they do not reach the harbor of the enemy or the joyless, inhospitable shores. They are carried to the happy groves of the holy sisters—Cyonia, Hyrene, and Agape—where the righteous old man Zoilus buried them for safekeeping in a chaste tomb.

Then it is revealed to the old man where the head had been carried over the sea. When it is found, as though freshly severed in the slaughter, it is bound up and placed upon its own body.

The martyr, enjoying peace and blessed in the light above, proves mindful of his guardian. Appearing to the old man, he announces the battles that the sisters named above must now undertake and teaches him to offer consolation to the pious disciple, telling him that she has been taken to the seat of rest appointed for the saints.

[Col. 0724A] Carrying the divine message to the holy sisters, he, after the thirteenth sun had completed its course, rises to the lofty inner chambers won by the martyr, receiving an extraordinary reward for the child entrusted to him.

From there, when the robber attacks the aforementioned sisters, the gracious servant does not abandon Anastasia’s companions, who have been thrust into prison, but supplies them with food through a double ministry of compassion.

She also adopts, under a starry name and in a mother’s embrace, those unworthy ones who had been rejected by their resources and by the courts. She carefully tends everything, asking that their possessions be stored in heaven, laboring through vows and deeds so that nothing she had vowed to the stars might remain hidden on earth.

For she follows the destroyer, who burns everywhere to pour out vast slaughter through the massacre of the pious,

[Col. 0724B] and, as though he could nowhere find those to kill wherever he went, strives to lead in chains those whom he discovers. Among these he leads captives to the cities called Macedonian in Germany. Undeterred by the roughness of the roads, she overcomes the journey with lofty courage; heavenly love bears her through hardships and steep places as she seeks fitting ministers for the horrors of Pharsalia.

The savage lion carries the victorious sisters here for punishment. The pious helper does not abandon them amid the fierce struggles and does not leave them behind after their glorious trophies.

Once they have attained the festive palaces of the eternal kingdoms, she adorns the treasuries of their merit with the ornament of honor.

While her property, entrusted to the heavenly powers over many years, now increases a hundredfold in lofty talents on earth, the lover of piety does not refuse to preserve this double lamp, joining Theodota to it as a light shining with equal brightness.

[Col. 0724C] Assigned to the enemies of the world, the wise woman strives to escape, seeking the stars by a leap from the snares of the net. Leaving to her jealous suitor the estates owed to her, she is bound by her zeal to serve her heavenly teacher, learning to devote to heaven whatever is suitable for the marketplace.

This is the whole concern of both women, this their single desire: like mothers to their children, to offer consolation to the saints, support to the needy, strength to the exhausted, protection to the fearful, and advocacy to the sorrowful; to lay up wealth in heaven and snatch the righteous away to the stars.

The mother, accustomed to inspect the prisons, while she confirms that Anastasia has departed after earning her reward,

[Col. 0724D] consoles herself in her desolation with tears and with her friends.

With her face wet and washed by weeping, she is discovered beside the caves. Because she confesses Christ with fearless effort while praying, she is handed over according to the legal authority of the Illyrian prefect.

Although he knows what has been given to him, he nevertheless accepts the exceptional strength beneath the tender breast. When he asks her lineage and her cause, she fearlessly declares them:

She declares that Jesus sits above the stars and brings present consolation to the saints on earth. Nor does she deny that she served as an anxious attendant to those whom they attacked: she strengthened the fearful, gave them weapons, showed them the way, and lightened their labor.

“She complains that she has suddenly been abandoned by them, yet she carries a heart emulous of their holy fervor and longs to follow them. Therefore, with open eyes, she waits for the rest that will follow when the appointed reckoning has been completed, so that she herself may follow the triumphant ones to heaven, even if late.”

When the governor learns that she is illustrious and descended from a family of the toga-bearing class, he considers it worthy of a king to preserve the captured offspring of such a distinguished house, seized in the powerful bond of the Christian sect and preferring to offer her throat in the name of Christ.

He orders her to be kept with every care, observing the commands and noting what the censor does and what gifts he offers.

The prefect investigates her wealth and demands her estates. Receiving the resources intended for heaven, he offers sacrifices.

He absorbs insults against the gods and considers the mad prophecies. He calls her insane, and she in turn proves him foolish and incapable of distinguishing falsehood from truth.

[Col. 0725B] The quaestor reports her words to the king. He rages, asking by what soldier he may overcome her and with what weapons he may fight. Having found an eminent devotee, free from a wife, he hands her over to him, either to be subjected to him, shrine, and marriage-bed, or, if she resists, to be forced to death by torture.

Rejoicing in the charge, the man leads her into various inner chambers and, showing her different objects, points out the diverse instruments of the struggle: here a sword, here gold, here gems, and there the racks; on one side silver couches gleam, spread with soft coverings; on the other, iron beds, scorched by savage fires, glisten; elsewhere a storeroom is filled with an abundance of food; elsewhere a cavern bristles with darkness and sharp stakes.

[Col. 0725C] The brave woman, bearing witness that these things are true dirt, considers the heaps of wealth she sees to be dung and regards iron chains as precious necklaces of heaven.

He, thinking that she could be turned from heaven toward earthly things, gives her three days and then sends ten women to overturn her heart and bind the unyielding dove with pitch or snares.

They assail her with various nets: gold, blazing gems, and perfumes brought from Parthia.

She fixes her eyes upon heaven and raises her palms. She stands clinging to prayer, turning neither heart nor mouth away, seeking neither food nor sleep, growing dull in none of her senses.

As the cries of crows fade before an eagle, so, while she stands unmoved, all their extended persuasions collapse.

After some time, when the womanly weapons have been shattered, the wicked champion of lust hears that she persists. Bursting into the sacred inner chamber already dedicated through vows, he attempts to force an embrace upon the heavenly girl.

Suddenly, darkness surrounds and encloses him in an unseen barrier. He circles the empty house, powerless to touch Christ’s servant, and calls upon deaf gods in the vacant air.

At last, deceived and compelled by the harshness of the disease, he calls out to those standing at the doors. When they admit him, he is carried away and brought for a long time to the adorned altars. He offers sacrifice and begs the leaders of death for life. He begins to endure punishments worthy of his mad attempts and is carried off beneath the Tartarean shadows by a Fury.

The liberated warrior visits her companion’s dwelling and tells Theodota, in order, what God has done for her. They add nights to days in the praises of God.

[Col. 0726A] Meanwhile, when the suitor arrives at Bebricia, he is unjustly relieved of the wealth of the righteous woman. He burns with idle passion to bind her to himself.

While he spends many days persisting in his empty assault, he finds another companion who can strengthen her by speech. A savage man seizes this woman and hands her over to the cruel censor, assigning Theodota to the first city.

While he strives to subject the pious woman to foul crime, and while he finds her fearless, he first sends Evodius, her son, to torture. The boy, speaking lofty words, he scourges, angrily assaulting him before his mother.

The mother strengthens him with manly speech, declaring through the blows that he takes joy in Christ.

The judge orders the honorable woman to be handed over to a filthy brothel and afterward to prostitutes.

[Col. 0726B] When an incestuous man attempts to violate the chaste woman, blood pours forcefully from his nostrils. The wicked man cries out that a young man, gleaming in a golden garment, had come to his mother’s aid and struck him on the nose with his fist.

The censor orders a great fire to be lit and the noble woman to be cast into it with her three children.

Giving thanks to the Lord, she joyfully blesses the name of the almighty master, whose mercy does not separate her from this age through her own pledge, nor permit the holy confession of Christ to be torn away, nor allow her to be abandoned in the struggle of martyrdom.

Thus the victorious guide ascends to heaven with her children.

The Illyrian prefect, gaping to fill his coffers with gifts, had occupied the matron’s revenues and shut up the Roman mother behind bolts, surrounded by a numerous guard. He tests her spirit, urging her, as one of the weaker sex but strong in heart, to fulfill the magistrate’s commands and easily release her wealth to him as a dowry.

He despises her as she despises gifts and imitates Christ:

“You command me to overturn the orders that Christ gives to the needy, while you, a rich man, beg to have them expended upon you, although the author has judged you unworthy of the table that he commanded to be set for the poor out of benevolent love.

“If our gifts help you, since you are shown to be in need, accept them, and grow rich in the generous talents of faith.”

While they exchange these words, the censor, failing in his calculations,

[Col. 0726D] shuts the victorious woman in dark caves. Attacking her with threats, he scarcely provides bread late in the day.

But the Lord does not abandon his beloved disciple in darkness. He restores to her the companion who had long ago obtained heavenly things, and does not allow her to be deserted without sweet consolation.

At night he sends Theodota, surrounded by a distinguished light, from her heavenly dwelling to the blind chambers. Since she was to be joined to her in heaven, as she had bound herself to her through holy action, Theodota sets out a table furnished with food and varied beauty. Raising prayers to the stars, she pours out upon her companion the consolation of heavenly love and bestows heavenly care upon her bodily needs, seeking the heavenly kingdom so that she may shine in heavenly light and rejoice to be fed with the divine nectar of heaven.

When thirty nights have been adorned with this light,

[Col. 0727A] and the enemy thinks that she has wasted away through hunger and dreadful horrors, he nevertheless investigates whether she has survived through some deception.

He finds her stronger and shining more brightly. The enemy, bearing his concern for the prisoner, removes her from every side; after changing the guards and sealing the cave, he plunges her into darkness, where she remains hidden for a second month.

Yet the customary consolations do not fail, nor does the beloved companion abandon her dear friend. Instead, she refreshes her as before and nourishes her with heavenly food. The woman shines more brightly, with a more joyful and august face, flourishing on starry food and divine nourishment.

The sluggish enemy melts away and collapses through his fruitless effort. Seeing himself defeated by this undertaking, he tries to discover whether he can hide the unconquered woman from the earth in the waters of the sea. Adding her to the condemned, he orders her to be cast into the waves of Thetis.

[Col. 0727B] A ship driven by the winds is carried across the vast sea. Stripped by savage waves, it is surrendered to the violence of the elements, loaded with one hundred and twenty companions to be hidden away.

As the wandering ship of death trembles amid the roar, everything threatens immediate death for those exposed.

But the Almighty, gathering souls from dreadful horror in order to lead them out, sends a companion to the servant in her fearful condition, to raise hearts shaken by the tumult.

Theodota hurries from the edge of heaven and settles upon the ship’s side. Strengthening the wavering spirits from the stern, she calms the swelling waters by a swift command. Consoling her companion, she calls the prisoners to the stars at the same time.

Among them Eutychianus flourished in serene devotion. Rejoicing to lose his fields and wealth, fixed in love of God, he despised the joys of the world.

[Col. 0727C] Whenever he had openly advanced the things he sought, he would say:

“Not even he who cuts off my head will take Christ from me!”

While the sisters honor him with celebrated reverence, one is enclosed by the murmuring of the wave-filled sea, while the other is free from the mad movement of the storms. Their hearts receive the presence of Christ, God; and, joyful in the middle of the sea, they rest in a calm station, as though in a harbor, joining day with night without a storm.

[Col. 0728A] The third light brings them to lands called by the name of palms. Some, driven there by various contests, rejoice to shine, and these pious women increase their number.

The serpent orders the sands where they are to be brought to be examined and seizes the fields they are to hold eagerly, so that they may be able to follow Christ in their hearts, whatever they do.

[Col. 0728B] Raging, he hastens to send savage ministers who might suppress the growing boldness by every effort. The furious executioners hurry to carry out the commands of the gladiator:

to soothe their minds with deceits, terrify them with scourges, entice them with gifts, and finally inflict harsh punishments.

But neither gold nor wounds break the noble ones; death itself does not break the brave hearts hastening toward funerals.

Two hundred men here ascended to the heavens by various paths, accompanied in the contest by seven hundred women.

But the strong leader, her hand trained for battle and her feet fastened to stakes, leaps into the midst of the flames, and, exulting, raises her soul to the radiant stars.

Apollonia, faithfully preserving her mother’s funeral, arranges that the body be buried with abundant spices. She beautifies it with the construction and distinguished ornament of a basilica, and Christ increases the honors of those who have earned them.

## BOOK EIGHT BEGINS

[Col. 0729]

## CHAPTER ONE. On the persecution of Maximian and Saint Marcellus, pope, and his companions

[Col. 0729A] Following the sacred footprints as we pursue the mother, we left the appointed city and went far beyond the fields of Ausonia.

But now that, under the guide of heaven, we have attained the sought-for seats, let us resume the proposed journey and return to the city. Let us see whom the madman burns here, what fires he stirs up, what uproar Maximian inflates, while his companion in madness tramples the eastern lands; let us see what slaughter he presses on with dreadful arms and what wars he wages.

Marcellus, having obtained the apostolic seat, vacant for a long time, guards the entrusted flock with vigilant care. He considers in what contest each person labors, what weapons he bears, and what struggles he undertakes.

From this watchtower he found Praso raising a camp and supporting the troops with human compassion.

[Col. 0729B] Sisinnius and Cyriacus were adding their assistance to him, together with Largus and Smaragdus—attentive, active servants moved by love of virtue.

The good leader encourages the nobles, and the serving hands of Sisinnius and Cyriacus are rightly consecrated at the altars, so that they may shine more worthily in their work and devote themselves more earnestly to their labor.

While they do not rest even at night from fulfilling their ministry, on the third day they penetrate the caves of the lictors’ treachery—the caves of darkness—from which the sands are given for examination.

[Col. 0730A] Clinging to their appointed work, they strive to lift foreign burdens, rejoicing and offering praises in songs to the gods and to the benevolent King and God.

When Caesar learns of this, he orders Sisinnius to appear and, when asked, to report his name and his song. He declares himself a servant of Christ and a lowly servant of the servants, raising his proclamation in praise of the creator of all.

“You will either render the honours due to Hercules’ serpent in sacrifice, or I shall consign your entrails to the deadly flames.”

To this he continually responds with devoted mind:

“These things will happen to me, if perhaps I am judged worthy to receive the crown of the honor I have long sought.”

Afterward he is handed over to Lauditio, the prefect, who besieges him with a harsh guard for seventeen days. Apronianus orders him to be brought before him.

[Col. 0730B] When the guard presents him, a heavenly radiance appears. Seeing him shining, the guard at once hears a voice from the heavens:

“Hasten, blessed sons; receive the kingdoms long ago prepared for you, from the beginning of the world.”

Terrified by this declaration, the guard approaches the martyr’s feet, begging to be washed at once in the clear cleansing water, so that he may attain the gifts of eternal glory.

The honor is not long delayed. When his vows are fulfilled, he shines with the sought-for crown, his throat cut.

[Col. 0731A] Thereafter Sisinnius began to keep the old Saturninus as his companion in the caves. The latter was refreshed by his affection, since he had recently comforted and supported him under a harsh burden.

Thus, with the prison-gates given to them, they freed many bands from the siege of Gehenna, those who sought the gifts of light. Purifying them from darkness by teaching and consecrating them by the font, they were permitted to remain hidden for fifty-two days.

Then, driven along with bare feet and bound in chains, they are brought before the prefect’s face and tribunal. A brazen tripod is brought forth, and they are ordered to sacrifice.

Then Saturninus says:

“May the Lord crush these wicked gods!”

At this word he shatters the tripod. As though driven by a storm, the high attendant trembles. He invokes the authority of Christ, the Lord and God; Papias and Maurus are stirred up. Soon, their mouths battered by wound-dealing hail,

[Col. 0731B] they are handed over to the cave of the prison. The leaders, their sinews stretched and their bodies hung upon the rack, are torn by scourges and burned in flames.

While they give thanks and do not cease to utter praises, they earn heaven with their necks struck off.

Traso buries the holy pledges with John alone, while Marcellus baptizes the cleansed confessors. The prefect brings to judgment those who confess the divine offices and reject the pagan rites, and orders them to be laid low in the open country. He crushes them with fire, though they say nothing with their mouths except the gifts of Christ. Having ground the timber of the wood, he attaches lead weights, so that the burdens of the contest may be weighed down. They rise to the heights of heaven.

John, the presbyter, in a venerable act carries their bodies to Peter’s springs, bringing there the heavenly gifts.

[Col. 0731C] Meanwhile, a long imprisonment surrounded the holy servant Cyriacus, who gave strength to the weary, a support to the oppressed, and light to those enclosed in darkness.

But a raging demon, with a mad and dreadful blast, had struck Artemia, offspring of the savage prince Diocletian, with a furious wound of the heart. The demon himself confessed that he would not depart except at Cyriacus’ commanding voice. Cyriacus is sent, released from his bonds, and asked to enter the bedroom.

He begins the struggle and fights the foul enemy. When the demon cries out and threatens much labor, Cyriacus drives it from the chambers of the invaded breast and expels it.

Nor does he allow the vessel to remain empty for the robber; rather, he makes the sacred vessel shine with faithful understanding and appoints it to be adorned in the heavenly court.

For these deeds he is released and receives the gift of freedom.

Not long afterward, an embassy from the eastern king, having crossed the long stretches of sea and land, seeks the Roman seat and the summit of the empire. It does not fear the terror of war, nor lack peace, nor come under compulsion by treaty or imperial majesty. It bears the mild petitions of the Chaldaean tyrant, seeking the presence of the Roman citizen Cyriacus with Sapor.

Not resplendent with sceptres, nor glittering with purple, gold, and jewels, but clad in the humble garments of a poor man, Cyriacus...

And content with a cloak, a devoted and humble servant,

let him drive away the enemy whom kings are unable to repel,

and release the king’s daughter, whom the serpent’s bond had bound.

[Col. 0732A] Though Augustus had been informed, matters were disclosed; but he himself ordered that the requested spouse be allowed to depart before the barbarian tribunal. [The syntax is corrupt.]

The Levite does not dread the journey, nor does he refuse the enemy; more ready, he is led along the long and burdensome road,

and reaches the East, while the queen provides post-horses,

with Largus accompanying him alone, and his companion Smaragdus.

Having pursued the enemy far into foreign lands,

he nevertheless does not permit himself to be carried by horse or assisted by chariots;

rather, content with a staff, he goes on and surpasses the mounted teams.

But when he had arrived at the radiant palace of the king,

the tyrant, adorned with gleaming gold,

humbled himself and worshiped the poor man, content with a cheap garment;

he invited him to enter the golden inner chambers,

where the captive woman, seated there, had been unable to redeem herself with much gold,

or to escape from the fetters and chains imposed upon her.

[Col. 0732B] As the saving minister entered the royal secrets,

the tormentor was tortured and the oppressor was conquered;

groaning and complaining greatly, he was finally compelled

to release the prey he had seized with grim violence.

And thus, filling the mind emptied by the demon with faith,

the triumphant man protects the limbs with heavenly water.

Nor was the benefit granted to the girl alone:

she was released from her bonds, manifestly freed from her madness,

and her father, liberated from his inward and invisible chain,

was restored, and dedicated his heart to Christ, purified from the enemy.

Nor did the king alone submit to the sacred rite; his friends accompanied him,

four hundred and twenty in number, consecrated by baptism.

The scepter-bearing man’s gifts the poor man disdained to touch,

considering faith a great reward, and using only bread and water.

With the glory of his triumph among the Persians, Cyriacus

[Col. 0732C] returned in splendor; illustrious Rome received her outstanding minister.

The tyrant was ashamed to make war upon him;

he consented to enjoy peace, unwillingly restraining his savage arms,

yet directed them against this man alone, because he had granted him the favour.

Meanwhile the son, burning to complete what his father had postponed,

and to exercise his father’s role,

proved himself truly his father’s offspring in cruelty; the impious heir raged

against the lovers of piety.

Burning to punish the merciful and the devout,

he ordered Cyriacus, stripped of his covering as a reproach to the others,

to proceed in an adorned chariot, bound with heavy chains and enclosed in fetters.

If his father had erred through excessive mildness, this man strove to atone for it,

and harassed the servants of God in their trial.

He handed Cyriacus over to be torn by the Carpasian scourge.

[Col. 0732D] In his fury, the one poured black pitch over the bound man’s head,

and drenched his head with the white-hot fire of the pitchy liquid.

The other, giving thanks, offered praises to Christ,

and, rejoicing together, his companions surrendered themselves as gifts to God.

One of these, Crescentianus, was lifted

high upon the scaffold; his torment increased,

and, stretched upon the rack, he was repeatedly beaten with a club,

while his limbs were cut open and his throat pierced,

as he proclaimed the glory above in a clear voice.

When the flames imposed upon him grew hot,

amid praises and amid the fires he released his spirit,

shining toward the stars in pure light.

After this had been accomplished, the guards shut up the companions.

After four days had passed, Cyriacus

was brought out from the prison and urged to sacrifice to the profane gods,

[Col. 0733A] but he offered libations to the one Lord, Christ:

stretched by cords and beaten with taut ropes,

he acclaimed King Jesus with praises and prayers,

and the endurance of the man fastened [to the torture-device] overcame the executioner.

The executioner, groaning with shame, hastened to report to the tyrant,

and announced to his master that the weapons had been defeated.

The tyrant, roaring in madness, ordered that all whom the prison held,

together with Cyriacus, should have their throats cut by the sword.

And thus twenty witnesses followed the illustrious minister above the stars,
shining with rosy radiance.

The elder John snatched up the relics and hid them,

and buried them in the earth.

Afterward Marcellus, with blessed Lucina accompanying him,

laid them out with celebrated honor:

she also received their companions Largus and Smaragdus,

whom Juliana and Menica received into their tomb.

[Col. 0733B] At that time Arthemia too experienced her brother’s affection,
receiving the heavenly kingdom through her brother’s sword.

Then Lucina provided all her possessions to the Church,

and handed over the house which, once duly consecrated,

the pope lawfully frequented for the celebration of the mysteries.

[Col. 0734A] When the enemy learned this, stirred in mind he reconsidered

what punishment he should impose, while reflecting on the public wars.

Therefore he turned the house into a stable,

and assigned the father as a servant to the beasts.

There, subdued with bowed heart,
he tended the wounds inflicted by the Lord upon the stricken man.

For a long time he supplied fodder according to a twofold routine,

and nourished the different animals with their divided food;

then, having completed his service, he was raised into the enclosures of paradise.

Covered from head to foot in a rough sack,

he devoted himself night and day to prayers and divine hymns.

The sacred John and Lucina concealed his limbs.

The house, by the gift of Cyriacus, yielded to the cruelty of Carpasianus.

He entered the fountain that the pope had consecrated

and polluted it with the filthy luxury of an obscene bath.

[Col. 0734B] While there he practiced theatrical and disgraceful revelry with the wicked,

he was suddenly snatched away by a grim procession of death,

and, joined to his accomplices, descended all the way to the depths.

Thus the holy house, closed against the cruel
but open to the kindly,
brings terror to the savage and consolation to the just.

## CHAPTER II. On Saint Lucina and her Companions

[Col. 0733]

[Col. 0733B] Blessed Lucina cherished many saints. Her husband Pinianus, leaving wealth and estates, [is linked by a corrupt construction with what follows]; Sisinnius likewise and Diocletianus, crushed beneath a hail of stones, and Florentius, rejoicing with the pious, received the tombs bestowed by him.

[Col. 0733C] These too shine with the honor of their merits.

A martyr, raised from the mouth of the sewer, instructed her that fasting should moderate her own strength.

With a body bearing a small basket filled with nuts,

she gave a little sip of wine as a remedy.

At her side, after the brothers had already been led out,

the nourishing Beatrix shone with Simplicius and Faustinus in twin light.

When these, through various trials, had attained the inner chambers of heaven,

their bodies, buried at the heights of the Tiber,

were restored, by God’s command, once the place had been opened.

Crispus and John raised them with celebrated honor,

and, together with their sister, paid the due offices to the slain soldiers.

[Col. 0734B] But a certain man, greedy to bring the neighboring fields of the pious

under his control and to join them to his own estates,

urged Beatrice toward the savage shrines—Lucretius.

She, horrified at the crime, cried:

“I do not offer sacrifice to the profane; I am a worshiper of the Lord Most High.”

[Col. 0734C] Thus thrust into prison,

while she was being held there she was secretly torn away from the hostile enemy:

she was strangled during the dark night in hidden caves.

Lucina received her beside the brothers who had been laid out.

The usurper entered the countryside and rejoiced,

believing that he had invaded what was not his and was enjoying banquets from plundered wealth.

While he reclined securely at lavish, ill-omened banquets,
a little boy, tearing himself away from his mother’s breast, cried aloud:

“Listen, Lucretius: after committing murder, you take possession of what you have invaded.

Unhappy man, you are being handed over to the enemy, having become property.”

Caught at the fierce voice in the noose of death,

he disturbed the meal, mixing dishes and cups,

and burst into Tartarus, driven on by avenging Furies.

## CHAPTER III. On Saint John and Crispus

[Col. 0733]

[Col. 0733C] John and Crispus, when they had honorably and resplendently

buried many relics of the just beneath their native covering,

were themselves, blessed for their merits, taken up into the stars,

those whose bodies they had entrusted to the pious earth.

The wealthy Thrason, who had also served the saints

by supplying many things,

[Col. 0734C] passed through the eye of a needle, his camel’s hump yielding,

and, having experienced a blessed contest,

departed joined to the martyrs and received the palm,

seeking the golden kingdoms with his companions in a twofold triumph.

## CHAPTER IV. On Saint Erasmus

[Col. 0733]

[Col. 0733C] Many indeed are the trophies celebrated in every place,

and they shine with this fervor.

How much more abundantly, we believe, did the fields

of Ausonia radiate with shining splendor,

when Campania revealed Erasmus, renowned in battle,

a worthy bishop, repeatedly tested in combat.

Diocletian, shaking him with a hail of lead,

found him strong and again subjected him

to a mighty beating, that he might be slain.

[Col. 0734C] He who had been crushed beneath the rigid timber of the forest,

unconquered, overcame the scourges of the conquered torturer.

The serpent was confined.

Planning to exercise the athlete in various contests,

he prepared various ointments through varied heating,

dissolving different substances together in swift fire:

resin, lead, wax, pitch, sulfur, and olive oil

were mixed together.

Having uncovered the limbs with such a liquid,

[Col. 0735A] he sprinkled them, though they did not yield to the separate heats.

The holy man stood there, offering a spectacle with an unharmed body,

and added faith in his protector to the hearts of those who marveled.

Enclosed in a great prison and afterward oppressed

by the great weight of iron,

he was held under a dreadful siege.

But a heavenly messenger was sent down from the highest heaven,

to give help to the witness engaged in holy warfare.

He dissolved the bonds, opened the doors,

brought him out, snatched from the darkness,

and gave him leave to depart free.

Thus, while he performed many deeds

that won the admiration of peoples,

he filled cities and countryside with illustrious miracles.

Winged Fame also marked his deeds

in the ears of the palace.

And now the triumphant man, superior in the virtue of his earlier deeds,

was ordered to enter the summit of another combat.

Challenged by praise, Maximian seized him

[Col. 0736A] and harassed him with various punishments,

exercising him in harsh combat;

he clothed him in a scorched cuirass of bronze.

But the martyr stood shining in a blazing tunic,

carrying fire upon his limbs,

and, scorning the heat, flashed with supernatural power.

The torments grew harsher.

The forms of heat that had previously been applied

flowed back into the cauldron,

and the soldier, mighty against fire,

was plunged into the flaming waves.

As though refreshed by lukewarm water

and rejoicing in a bath,

he overcame all the dreadful efforts at once in triumph,

and came forth exultant,

safe through divine aid.

He was brought out by a starry guide,

traversing the fields of Campania,

planting holy faith in the breasts of many,

and leading more people from darkness to the light of truth.

Thus, commanded by God,

he completed his celebrated contests.

## CHAPTER V. On Saints Sossius and Januarius

[Col. 0735]

[Col. 0735B] Under this tyranny, Misenum displayed Sossius,

a minister of the heavenly court,

who, through holiness and the gift of prudence,

vigorously protected youthful strength.

Therefore blessed Januarius,

who shone as bishop in the city of Benevento,

had often been accustomed to visit him

and strengthen him.

Accordingly, when he saw him summoned

to proclaim the clear doctrines of Christ beneath the Lord’s court,

he perceived a flame flowing from his head,

with its hair-like locks streaming.

And, shaken by such radiance alone,

he immediately foretold that he would soon become a martyr.

The prophecy was neither delayed nor prolonged.

A few days revolved after the prediction,

and behold, while the Levite was cherishing the stars,

[Col. 0735C] the prophet came, skilled at releasing bonds,

[Col. 0736B] and, having been seized, became a participant in the contest.

His excellent companions remained with him:

the deacon Festus, distinguished by honor,

and Desiderius, distinguished by learning.

After savage prison-houses,

these men were destined to undergo the penalty of decapitation.

But while they wore away the appointed day of death,

they were increased by an added rank of dignity.

For Proculus, a Levite from the city of Pozzuoli,

is said to have met two just men from the people—

Acutus and Eutices.

They asked why they should seek the death of the just,

when they had been proved to be nobles of the nourishing people.

At once they were ordered to perish with their necks cut.

Likewise, seven, struck down in the slaughter,

were carried away by the executioners,

while various citizens gave tombs to their fellow tribesmen.

## CHAPTER VI. On Saint Domninus

[Col. 0735]

[Col. 0735C] Julia, receiving Domninus,

the foremost nobleman and chief of the imperial bedchamber,

who avoided the savage companionship of the king,

in hospitable welcome,

soon rejoiced in his triumph.

[Col. 0736C] The rage of the bloody executioner pursued him,

snatched him away,

and raised him by the heavenly sword to the stars.

## CHAPTER VII. On Saint Barbara

[Col. 0735]

[Col. 0735C] At that time Tuscany saw the virgin Barbara engaged in combat;

she won illustrious trophies.

Her father Dioscorus, having worn her down

with a long confinement,

delivered her to the anger of the governor.

After she had been stripped,

she was cruelly torn by dark scourges.

[Col. 0735D] While she remained steadfast and laughed at the cords and bull-hide,
the wounds chafed by the goatskin cloak
grew raw again.

Then, received into a cave,

she was raised into heavenly light.

[Col. 0736C] A grating was applied to her ribs and set alight with the lamp’s flame;

a hammer was driven into her, aimed at the summit of her head;

her tender breasts were cut off by a dreadful executioner.

Then, with the marks of the cross exposed, she was led naked through the streets,

and, after a long and savage slaughter,

[Col. 0736D] she received the heights of heaven as the reward of her throat.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Saints Secundus and Alexander

[Col. 0735]

[Col. 0735D] They also searched the military camps,

to see whether any worshiper of Christ might be found in arms,

professing his name and law,

so that either by death or by sufficient incense

he might satisfy the emperor’s fury.

At that time Secundus, by chance among the lapsed nobles,

was seized by name.

The heavenly contest made him superior in virtue to the others; after bonds and darkness,

[Col. 0736D] beheaded by the sword, he became an enduring example.

The tyrant had heard that Alexander,

in the ranks of the legion,

had taken up the sacred rites of the starry contest.

With the ritual vessels set out, he sought to make him offer sacrifice to the profane gods.

Looking up at the vault of heaven, Alexander said:

“Would that such grace were granted to me, that, driving these vanities from your minds, I might be able to turn your hearts! Yet I behold a rotten, incurable wound. Spare your savage designs; persuaded by Satan, abandon your own ways, confess the evil deeds that you have done, and know the living God who made all things and calls all nations, myself included, to his gifts.”

Moved by these words, the emperor ordered weapons

to be brought against the man who refused,

and ordered him to be dragged unwillingly

and compelled to offer sacrifice.

Relying on faith and rejecting the serpent’s commands,

Alexander confounded the grim faces

with inward strength.

He kicked the table,

mixing with the earth the things placed upon it.

[Col. 0738A] Immediately the enraged fury handed him over

to be struck by the avenging sword.

The attendant stood trembling before the iron,

nodding and staggering.

The savage judge, rebuking him,

inflamed the inactive man.

“He says: ‘This man’s head is regarded as a great mountain for me;

hence the trembling in my limbs

and the horror driven into my senses.’”

The judge brought in others

and summoned many to cut off the face of one man.

The martyr hastened and rejoiced to be released.

Falling upon his knees and rolling down to the depths of the earth,

he sought the blade

and received it upon his bowed neck.

But after offering a prayer, and blessed,

he went to the lofty camps.

## CHAPTER IX. On Saint Theodore

[Col. 0737]

[Col. 0737B] When Theodore stood as a soldier in strong armor,

he steadfastly rendered his service to Christ Most High.

Seized on a charge, he was brought to the lofty tribunal.

Having confessed the laws of God,

he was ordered to change his mind.

Holding fast to eternal truth in his unyielding heart,

he was brought to be judged under the rule of the laws of the descendants of Aeneas.

Recognized as unrestrained,

he was confined in the caves of the prison.

The doors were sealed,

but divine consolations were not shut out by the prison.

Restored by lofty visions and judgments,

he was raised high upon a beam,

torn by hooks,

and cut with iron down to the bones.

The lattice of his ribs was exposed by the flesh being torn away.

From there, a sentence assigning him to the pyre

proclaimed him victorious.

Seizing the banners of the cross,

he went toward the fires he had won,

and ordered Cleonicus to follow his courageous footprints.

Glorifying God,

he sacrificed fire to the fires of his mind.

Eusebia devotedly took care of the burial.

## CHAPTER X. On Saints Victor, Felix, and Nabor

[Col. 0737]

[Col. 0737B] Victor shone with the beauty of old age and faith.

Of Moorish blood and faithful from his earliest years,

he adorned the imperial ranks with the honor of his spirit.

Felix was a citizen by birth, and so was Nabor;

Africa, where they had been slain,

gave them to the city of Milan.

[Col. 0738B] Compelled by the emperor to offer honor to the shrines,

Victor remained pious and overcame the savage timbers.

Long beaten with pieces of wood

and ignorant of pain,

he stood untouched by fire,

was drenched by waves of lead,

and thus, after the tortures, triumphed over the emperor’s swords.

## CHAPTER XI. On Saints Carpophorus and Abundantius

[Col. 0737]

[Col. 0737C] By this ardour of maturity Carpophorus received an abundance increased through Abundantius; the former a priest and the latter his subordinate minister, they adorned Spoleto with the glory of their contest.

For Christ’s glory they were first subdued by clubs,

then handed over to a foul prison,

with the consolation of drink and food denied them.

But afterward, led by a heavenly guide,

they were brought forth,

[Col. 0738C] and scattered the seed of the word into the fields of hearts.

Again, while their faces were held fast,

a stony hardness struck them.

From there they were lifted to the height of the rack.

While the brave men were tested by dreadful torture,

they were once more thrust into horrible darkness.

Worn down by these things

and prepared for the laurels,

at last they were slain by the sword

and climbed to the lofty stars.

## CHAPTER XII. On Saint Gregory the Martyr

[Col. 0737]

[Col. 0737D] Then blessed Gregory the presbyter

also subdued the fury of the livid serpent.

Flaccus said to him:

“Are you a rebel against the rulers,

a tempter of the sacred gods,

and still resisting their divinities?”

But he replied:

“If you wish to know my steadfastness:

I do not abandon my God,

who created me from clay,

from the beginning of my infancy.”

Thus persevering most bravely in faith,

he was torn apart,

his back worn down by clubs,

his belly pulled apart by twisted knots.

Then, bound upon a lattice,

with hands and feet,

he was confined beneath a fire

increased by added fuel.

But immediately an earthquake tore open the ground; where a part of the city collapsed, more than three hundred persons offering sacrifice in the shrines perished.

Loaded with iron and enclosed in prison,

he was lifted up,

sustained by heavenly consolation.

Then his knees were rubbed against iron thorns,

and each side of his body was scorched by the flame of lamps.

The holy witness said to the savage judge:

“Even if you destroy my entire body,

the gracious Mediator will not abandon me.

Christ kindly cherishes, heals,

and restores our inward parts.”

Then dragged through the amphitheater,

he scattered it with blood.

His neck cut off,

he rejoiced at the lofty height.

His body was exposed to savage beasts to devour,

[Col. 0739A] but remained undefiled by tooth and claw.

Then the devout woman Abundantia,

burning with piety,

claimed the blessed relic of the martyr.

[Col. 0740A] But because she could not obtain it for nothing,

she paid thirty-five gold pieces,

and buried it with the honor

that was fitting for a martyr.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Saint Sabinus the Bishop and his Companions

[Col. 0739]

[Col. 0739A] In this heat Sabinus triumphs, the bishop,

noble in heavenly disciplines,

pious in understanding,

most eloquent in speech.

He stands detained before the governor Venustianus,

together with Marcello and Exuperantius,

ministers of the sacred altar,

and many clerics.

The governor placed before him his golden Jupiter,

shining in a yellow garment,

for him to worship.

Taking it, Sabinus directed his vows to Christ,

struck the worn image against the earth,

and threw it down, shattered into pieces.

Thereupon Venustianus, burning with fury,

cut off the hands of the man who had overthrown the gods,

and attached his companions to the rack to be torn apart.

[Col. 0739B] When they had been cruelly tormented with harsh clubs,

he furiously furrowed them by cutting them with savage claws.

After they had been roasted in fire,

they confessed the glory of Christ

and sent their blessed spirits to the stars.

Their limbs were plunged into the waters.

A certain persecutor of living peoples,

together with the priest,

carried away the sacred gifts

and placed them beside the road,

having taken them from the waters.

The bishop Sabinus was thrust into prison.

Serena, devoted to him,

brought her nephew Priscianus,

whose blindness she mourned,

to be helped beneath his protection.

[Col. 0739C] But the bishop, with his arms,

joined over the blind eyes,

set the extinguished torches aflame,

pouring out light through clear prayer.

When the subordinate guards saw this miracle,

they followed the footsteps of the pious giver.

Soon eleven of them, washed in the font,

were consecrated.

When these things were reported and became known to the governor,

his eyes, which illness had made dim,

were so afflicted that neither food nor sleep

could be enjoyed by him.

He sent his wife with their two children,

asking that Sabinus come,

that he be brought from prison.

With pain and tears, he sought the severed hands, offering repentance.

His wife increased her lamentations,

and his sons asked to be dedicated

to the sacred waters.

[Col. 0740B] When the governor emerged from the basin

dipped in water and made white,

he felt no pain in his eyes.

These deeds were announced to the emperor.

Carried away by anger,

he handed Sabinus over to torture,

and ordered Venustianus to be punished by decapitation.

Lucius the tribune carried him away with his wife and children,

without waiting for the judge’s request.

He sent Sabinus to the city of Spoleto,

and struck down the blessed man

as he gave his spirit to the stars.

Serena embraced the body,

which her hands had embalmed with spices,

in a glass vessel,

and received it into her house,

placing it near the city walls.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Saints Felix and Fortunatus

[Col. 0739]

[Col. 0739C] In this fervor Aquileia saw

Felix and Fortunatus triumphing,

brothers in blood and grace,

whom it gave over to be bound to Christ’s proclamation by the sword.

They were brought here by the governor Eufimius,

to the place where they displayed

the strongest strength of Christ’s praise.

The fury of the maddened judge filled his breast;

he hurled cruel weapons at the witnesses,

applied them and fastened them to savage tortures.

Though lofty in mind,

they were raised upon the scaffold with honor.

Their sides were burned by lamps applied to them.

Yet, cooled by the divine hymn,

they overcame the lamps’ fire

with the fire of their burning spirit.

Their entrails were drenched and wet with the burning liquid,

[Col. 0739D] but with hymns they extinguished the flames,

and with the oil of heavenly anointing

they surpassed the fires of burning olive oil.

Remaining steadfast in praise of the Father without end,

they were led outside the city beside the city’s river.

From the multitude of their heads

they received the heavenly kingdoms,

and, released by the sword,

they entered the heights of heaven.

At night the pious men received their sacred limbs,

covered them with new curtains,

and embalmed them with spices.

Vicentia sent men to bring back the dear relics.

But Aquileia opposed the holy men’s efforts.

At last, shaken by pious disputes,

the conflict was quieted.

By a lawful agreement, Aquileia received the head of the saint,

and likewise received the bones of Felix and Fortunatus,

while Vicentia received Felix’s breast

and the head of his brother.

## CHAPTER XV. On Saint Afra

[Col. 0739]

[Col. 0739D] Afra, a worshiper of God,

is said to have endured the fury of the nobles in this madness,

and to have been snatched from the plunder of the Devil.

She was raised from the chamber of lust

by her host Narcissus,

and rescued from the filth of the mire

by heavenly light.

As dirty mud wastes away beneath the rays of the sun,

[Note: [Col. 0739D] Moisture of the earth.]

[Col. 0740D] so the holy man attacked her,

and drew her out from the snares of Hell.

He overturned the she-wolf’s den

and brought her forth into Christ’s court.

Nor did he tear her away alone:

her servant companions followed her.

Those whom they had followed in madness,

they followed in piety.

The worthy Eumenia also,

and Euprepia, having rejected luxury,

[Col. 0741A] followed the divine lamp

that surpasses the darkness of night.

While this lamp was illuminating her,
the mother Hilaria too was drawn along by her daughter.

She confessed the worship of the profane Cypris

and brought her daughter,

who was bound to her by that pollution.

Therefore the enemy groaned,

mourning that he was losing his prey.

He put on a sad appearance

and displayed a deeply troubled face,

blackened and roughened by the ulcer of an elephantine disease.

He complained that he was being subjected to force,

repeating the loss of his own rights,

and that his vessels could not be given to Christ.

Yet, unwillingly, he was compelled to confess Jesus,
and, constrained, to acknowledge
that the Lord had undergone the final suffering for sins.

He acknowledged that the possessed woman should follow the servant who sought her on behalf of her Guardian and Lord, who reclaims his own rights—the one who subdues the thief and brings back the captive talents.

Overwhelmed by these things

and subdued through the course of the battle,

[Col. 0741B] he turned the struggle of prayer

toward a deceitful stratagem,

being able to restore one soul,

or at least one caught in his nets.

The preliminary promises lifted their spirits

and comforted the needy man.

Already exalted by strength,

he exhausted his empty hope.

But the holy man, trampling down thefts and deceits,
bound the thief by his word. The thief swore by his own power that he would soon kill the captive prey unless Christ commanded him to enter the deepest abyss.

The bishop, cancelling the terms bargained with the bound one,
[Col. 0742A] handed the death-dealing serpent over to death’s jurisdiction.

By his authority he crushed it as it struggled, wrested the spring from the serpent, and turned the enemy’s weapons against the foe himself, into a dear friend. [The final phrasing is textually difficult.]

Cleansing the filth,

he purified the jewels that had been seized.

After holy fasts,

he sanctified the souls washed clean:

Hilaria and her daughter,

the serving girls,

and many other relatives and dear companions.

The Church was furnished,

the sacred order was assigned to the temple,

and Zosymus, Afra’s maternal uncle,

was consecrated as priest.

After arranging the clergy,

he is said to have sought Gerunda,

where the martyr triumphs together with Felix.

Blessed Afra, having distributed her wickedly acquired purses

to the poor,

securely followed the honor of the cross.

She remains steadfast though captured.

Neither despair nor force

can remove her from hope

or from heavenly praise.

[Col. 0742B] With bowed mind she seeks the torments

and embraces the fires.

She rejoices and offers thanks,

surrounded by flames.

She shines as a living offering to God,

and as an offering she emerges from the fires.

She becomes an offering,

yet such limbs are not proved purified by the pyres.

The mother and the blessed servant women,

having been received from the pyre,

placed her in the tomb,

and themselves merited to follow

the glorified Emerentiana.

Having entered heaven through the fires,

they are borne to the Lord as perfected holocausts.

## CHAPTER XVI. On Saint Eusebius

[Col. 0741]

[Col. 0741B] Eusebius succeeds Marcellus

in the sacred authority of the Roman city.

Adorning the holy rites of Christ,

he destroyed and suppressed heresies,

and brought back to what was right

perverse hearts wandering through crooked mazes.

Thus, shining in merits,

he was added to his blessed companions.

[Col. 0741C] Nor was there delay:

Melchiades followed,

and was proved a glory to the pious,

though he appeared fierce to the wicked in terror.

He exposed the perverse,

released fasts at the festivals,

and enriched the united Church with a sacred gift.

He did not allow what was bound together in Christ’s love

to be divided.

He strove to preserve the faithful mind

which, after the monuments,

[Col. 0742C] shines forth,

having completed its service

and received into the heavenly seat.

## CHAPTER XVII. On Saint Timothy

[Col. 0741]

[Col. 0741C] Timothy, coming to Rome from Antioch

under this pope,

proclaimed Christ along the streets and through the marketplaces.

The generous young man Silvester,

a lover of holy piety,

burned to raise him with praises.

After he had consecrated many hearts of the peoples,

Timothy confessed Christ continuously

for a year and a quarter.

Seized because of the praise of the cross,

he was handed over to the prefect of the city.

Cut by scourges,

worn down by the long squalor of chains,

and undefeated,

he underwent punishment three times before the judge,

strengthening his brave heart

three times through savage torments.

Following the Lord,

who was mingled with the cruel funeral,

he shone among the disgraced by a capital execution,

as a rose gleams among harsh thorns.

At the untimely end of night,

Silvester brought back the limbs to the house.

Calling together the pope and the clergy,

he dedicated the martyrdom with vigils

and with hymns to the saints.

The venerable Theon entrusted the body to the earth in his own garden, beside the illustrious relics of Paul; to Paul he added his namesake as a companion for the disciple,

and honored the venerable burial

in the house of the basilica.

The prefect, failing in his attack upon him, turned his weapons against the breast of the pious host, demanding back the money entrusted to him and threatening the chained man with harsher punishments. When he learned that not a single coin had been brought in the money-bags, he sat roaring with anger. He charged him with the hated offence of the Name, threatening that, unless he worshipped the shrines, he would breathe out his life amid tortures close to death.

Silvester said:

“Divine utterances declare that tonight your wavering soul will be torn by punishments from the seat of your foolish heart.

You will immediately enter the dangers of eternal punishment,

so that, seeing those whom you have slain rejoicing without end,

you may groan,

and may suffer without limit

the things you have inflicted in an instant.

Unhappy man, look upon those whom you punished as blessed.”

Tarquinius departed empty,

to be filled again with banquets.

Silvester hastened to be pressed beneath the honor of the sword.

Meanwhile, while the pious man asked

and the severe man dined,

a just judgment proceeded from the highest heaven,

and turned joys into punishment

and punishment into joys.

Finally, while the prefect strove with avid gaping

to stuff his belly with prepared delicacies,

he seized the mouth of a fish,

which he had incautiously taken,

and rolled it in his throat.

He tried to drag it out,

but achieved nothing by his effort.

He rose and pressed on with empty exertion.

At the command of his pain,

physicians of the methodical, empirical,

and logical schools were summoned.

They rejoiced in no method of treatment.

No incantations were effective;

no experience was of any benefit.

Tortured and driven by terrors until midnight,

[Col. 0743A] he sent his harsh soul down into the Tartarean shades,

to punishments after punishments,

to torments after torments,

compelled to darkness from the light of the world,

proud and exalted.

The just man was taken out of the darkness

and went forth into the light.

The former was led to the pyre

at the hour when he had vowed the scourges,

while a tumult mourned the Lord

of the private right.

The latter was led home

at the time when he had been thought destined

to undergo savage lashes,

while the entire senate of heaven applauded.

Even his bruises reverently honoured the victor.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On Saints Marinus and Almachius

[Col. 0743]

[Col. 0743A] We learn that this city has been adorned

with countless triumphs,

since Peter and Paul brought here

the lofty insignia of Christ,
