and, driving away the phantoms,

made the heavenly signs of the cross

shine upon the walls.

The ancient fathers did not raise Rome

to so great a height,

though they were fierce in conflict

and drenched in fraternal blood:

[Col. 0743B] neither Numa, nor the Decii, nor the Marii,

nor the Camilli,

nor the Brutuses, Scipios, Ciceros, or Catos;

neither kings, nobles,

nor those who bore annual offices;

nor those who possessed the world

through the splendor of the lord of the earth.

The more they had raised her

to the highest kingdoms,

the more they all subjected her

to harsh yokes.

Against these, the standard-bearers of the cross

and powerful athletes strive

to release her from her fetters

and join her to heaven,

shining under different leaders

and with great ardor.

Among them was Onesimus,

born under Paul’s chains,

Philemon’s household servant,

but a servant through Christ’s gift.

Once harsh toward his master,

afterward he became useful to him

and to many others.

The great Paul commends him

as worthy to be visited,

and, consecrating him as bishop,

appoints him to sow the seed of the word.

[Col. 0744A] Ignatius himself, remembering him

as pastor of Ephesus,

presents him as his beloved teacher and master,

and urges that the flocks be entrusted to his love.

He magnifies the Lord,

who granted such a leader

to retain and guard the folds.

When Rome summoned him,

a cloud of stones overwhelmed him

and buried him in the grave.

[Col. 0744B] Yet it did not hold him long:

he was restored to his seat and to his flock.

Here also appears the illustrious Marinus,

and the holy Almachius,

who, strong in mind,

rebuked the frenzies of the unteachable crowd

and its filthy altars.

On that day the people were accustomed

to rage with offerings and trifles

for more than the rest of the year.

While he strove to cut away the darkness

and to tear dreadful things from their foolish hearts,

on the very festival when the mystical circumcision

was given to Christ,

he turned the fury of the Bacchants upon himself.

Alone he opposed so many crowds,

one man against so many thousands,

resisting the fierce with reason

and the severe with piety.

Striving to turn them away

from their madness and grim minds,

he was attacked by flashing swords,

and, indignant at their filth,

went worthily to the heavenly realms.

## CHAPTER XIX. On Saint Agnes

[Col. 0743]

[Col. 0743C] Agnes’ fame ennobles the illustrious City,

the venerable virgin

who, while still tender in age,

won the glory of martyrdom

and trampled upon the swollen honors of the world.

While she consecrated her youthful years according to God’s law and devoted her mind to the highest pursuits, she wore down by her beauty the adolescent offspring of the prefect’s noble blood.

He sought to obtain her by gems, gold,

precious necklaces, wealth, splendor,

servants, fields, and houses;

he sought her from her parents

with dowry gifts, prayers, and presents.

But the virgin accounted these things dung; she regarded the suitor’s face as like the mouth of a serpent;

she preferred heaven to earth,

and, placing Christ’s insignia

before the ruler of the descendants of Aeneas,

she rejected gold, gems, necklaces, and garments

in honor of heaven.

She remembered herself adorned

with a jeweled radiance,

and to have entered the bridal chamber

of a better bridegroom,

whose nobility was preeminent,

whose power was superior,

whose appearance was more beautiful,

and whose grace was sweeter than nectar.

She added the treasures of an unexpected weight,

joining wealth and joys

that knew nothing of grief.

Music, gifts pressing honey from the sweetness of cares, splendour, strength, heights, and divinity—the heavenly Bridegroom places all these beneath himself; likewise the sun and stars, which he provides as good things and from which he prepares rewards.

The young man was seized by a fierce fire

and lay burning with disease,

unable to endure so great and unjust a burden.

The physicians reported to his savage father

that his son lay stricken.

The father repeated the message to the boy,

but in vain;

from the son it was sent back uselessly

and scattered into the air.

[Col. 0744C] She returned the bonds of the pact

that had been given to her unviolated,

declaring that her faith would endure

through eternal time.

The prefect marveled

that he was despised because of his noble blood,

and, searching, learned that she had undertaken

the lofty burdens of Christ.

But he, rejoicing, swelled with anger,

as though his commands had already been carried out.

He made a great uproar about bringing her before him,

and, alternately flattering and threatening,

shouted against her.

She, equal in spirit,

bore the swollen man and the pious man

with one expression,

and with equal firmness recoiled from both.

Harsh things did not break her steadfastness,

nor did gentle things deceive her.

Seeing his schemes slip away

through empty effort,

he finally seized open weapons

with more savage preparation.

Observing that she desired death,

summoned tortures,

and despised every harsh thing

in comparison with her heavenly vows,

he devised through cunning

what might horrify her more.

[Col. 0744D] He ordered her to be dragged naked

into a brothel,

and, to cause her still greater pain,

to be stripped through obscene mockery.

The gracious favor of Christ came to the struggling girl.

Coverings grew over her limbs

as her loosened hair increased.

The hair quickly thickened,
covering the exposed parts of her body;
poured out by Christ, it had not been produced by cosmetic ointment.

But when the virgin,

fighting against the obscenities,

entered the cave of lust,

she suddenly flashed with a brilliance of light.

The cavern shone,

illuminated by heavenly radiance.

A heavenly protector came,

as the contest grew more extraordinary

and the stars were struck with greater force.

For, borne from the highest heaven,

he brought suitable garments

for the girl prepared for battle.

She received a robe adorned

with heavenly light,

[Col. 0745A] unfamiliar with earth

and fitted to the virgin’s limbs.

With the holy heavenly guide,

she was clothed in this covering.

The cave of impurity became

a delightful temple of light.

Those who entered worshipped the divinity of the heavenly splendour, although they had been accustomed to go there to defile themselves in the world’s brothel.

But the wicked man,

still alive and pursuing the chaste beloved,

rushed in,

reproaching those who venerated

the holy light.

Scorning the fire of the divine fuel,

he broke into the midst

of the immense radiance.

But it was not granted to the unworthy

to touch the sacred beauty

with impure hands.

Instead, caught by a savage demon,

he was turned about,

and, his throat crushed,

he died.

After some time,

he was at last found,

his breath having been seized.

He was reported to his father.

The father mourned the consolation

of the one who had been taken away.

He redoubled his harsh request [the manuscript has the incomplete reading “crud.”],
[Col. 0745B] asking that the event be shown,

and that it be made clear

that she had not acted through magical fury,

but by a life-giving power.

She, uttering prayers to heaven, brought him back, black from Tartarus, by the gift of restoration.

She raised the stupefied father.

The shouting of those who raged in different directions increased,

and the tumult burned with varied fervor.

Some proclaimed her innocent;

many echoed that she was deceitful,

that through hidden frauds

she had extinguished the divine light.

The official, fleeing the crowd,

used substitute decrees.

A pyre was built,

blazing with human heat,

and Agnes was driven into its midst

amid the surging flames.

She rejoiced,

while the heat of the fire fled from her.

The heat departed;

the savage blaze was torn apart,

[Col. 0746A] and turned upon the madmen,

horrified to touch the holy limbs.

Alone, amid the vast expanse of fire,
the virgin put so many crowds to flight,

unmoved in the place

where she poured out her vows to God.

The ranks were blazing with flames

and roaring tumult.

She shone as she worshiped God

in the midst of the vapors.

She prayed,

untouched by the heat

of the entire trembling army,

asking to be received into heaven

and returning thanks

for the gift bestowed.

At her prayer,

all the summits of flame subsided,

and no vapor breathed forth.

Yet the fiery madness

did not know how to lay down its rage.

The fire, disarmed and subdued,

was turned into iron.

Thus freed from the earth,

the unmarried virgin sought the lofty bridal chambers,
Lilies mingled with roses, waving upon her shorn head,

She enters the lofty joys of the radiant bridal chamber of her chosen Bridegroom.

The praises of the victorious one resound above and below.

[Col. 0746B] Their parents, conducting the funeral rites, do not know how to weep,

But rejoice that they were deemed worthy to bring forth such a child,

Through whose merits and honor they trust that they themselves will be raised.

The devout people of Romulus throng the venerable tombs;

The livid enemy, burning with envy and with the fire of Lethe,

Brewing poisons and inflaming hostile hearts,

Stirs up plots against the devoted people;

They advance in arms, strong only through their piety,

And attack the devout bands with weapons and clubs.

## CHAPTER XX. On Saint Emerentiana

[Col. 0745]

[Col. 0745C] Here the virgin Emerentiana, companion of the virgin

Who had been martyred, and nourished at the same breast,

While bravely reproaching the dark tumult,

Resisting the fury of the wicked crowd,

Assailed by a cloud of stones at the martyr’s tomb,

She, a blessed martyr, sends her spirit to the stars.

Though not yet washed in Christ’s sacred font, yet believing,

She is preserved, stained with her own blood.

The elements are roused by savage deeds:

The earth threatens funeral destruction with trembling.

[Col. 0746C] Dense clouds seize the clear serenity of heaven;

The heights above crash with the force of the thunderclap;

Christ hurls weapons and fires against the enemies.

Some warlike men are struck down by the arms of the heavenly one;

Their ignorant minds’ merciful Creator taking pity on them,

They are saved according to the teaching of their Defender;

Thereupon the tumult ceases, and the turbulent

Rebellions in the sacred assemblies grow quiet.

Thus Agnes’s parents gather up her companion,

Giving her to the tomb in the fields of her foster-sister.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the Vision of Saint Agnes’s Parents

[Col. 0745]

[Col. 0745D] While they keep devout vigil for their child,

Before the tomb amid deathly silence in the middle of night,

When the turning world, by a lot assigned to weary labors,

Was shining with light, they see a radiant troop

Of virgins, gleaming in garments woven with gold;

Among them Agnes flashes with light,

Resplendent and most distinguished in the splendor of gold.

At the virgin’s right hand shines the Lamb,

Brighter than snow.

The astonished mortals stiffen beneath the heavenly light.

She bids her companions halt their steps for a little

And addresses her own: “Dear parents, rejoice!

Rejoice that your daughter has attained splendid seats,

And do not mourn her darkness: joined to the heavenly ones,

I rejoice, exulting in the Bridegroom’s bridal chamber,

Whom with all my heart I worshiped throughout the earth.”

She says this and withdraws to her blessed companions,

And departs with winged effort.

This story, flying from mouth to mouth, spreads widely,

Until at last it is handed down to a daughter of Augustus,

Who was flowing with the foulness of an ulcerous disease,

Yet strong in mind, still a pagan but believing in the truth.

Hastening to obtain the hoped-for healing,

She seeks the tomb by night to behold it and remains in prayer.

While she lingers, seized by the sweet repose of sleep,

She sees Agnes bringing her such consolation:

“Believe in God, Constantia, and act steadfastly in Christ,

Through whom you shall quickly obtain health for your limbs.”

The virgin awakens and rises healed; she is astonished

That no ulcer, nor any sign of an ulcer,

Has been left upon her unharmed limbs.

She brings joy to her father and bears glad tidings to her brothers;

[Col. 0747A] The city likewise rejoices; only the wicked are tortured.

She asks her father and brothers for the resisting virgin’s body

To be placed in her memorial shrine,

And then directs that she herself remain there, a virgin with the virgin.

The fame spreads; those seeking salvation run from everywhere

To receive gifts of healing. No one is deceived by empty hope.

The righteous rejoice to carry away the healing they have sought.

Her virginity also pleases the royal-born woman,

Who adorns and honors it to the end,

And, piling up distinguished gains,

[Col. 0748A] Strives to bring many more talents of companions to Christ.

In loving religious devotion she preserves sacred Agnes with her companions,

As the presence of a living teacher,

Whose example many follow in pursuing heavenly things.

These things I, though torn from shipwrecks and shuddering at grim dangers,

Wandering in a small boat upon the sea, yet following Ambrose’s sails,

Have read, venerating the necklaces bestowed upon the virgins.

By their prayers I ask to be cleansed from dark filth,

So that I may receive, through their merits, gifts of pardon

Which I cannot obtain by my own efforts.

# HERE BEGINS BOOK NINE

[Col. 0747]

## CHAPTER ONE. On Saint Valentine

[Col. 0747A] In the radiant light of heaven Valentine shone forth,

A bishop noble in doctrine, virtue, and beneficent goodness.

[Col. 0747B] To him Craton offers his son, raised in the nourishment of wisdom,

But oppressed by the heavy burden of an inward disease;

The boy, whose name is Cheremon, is offered to be freed from his misfortunes,

On the agreed condition that, once the boy is restored to health,

He will place his neck beneath Christ’s yoke

And that his household will follow the Lord.

The father’s mind, moved by his son’s restored bodily strength,

Is brought out of darkness; he fulfills his promises and is consecrated,

Together with his household. He does not long receive

The highest rewards of military service, but, while leaving the earthly realm as a martyr,

He gains the golden prizes of the starry life.

Valentine endures the scourges of rods and torments,

[Col. 0748A] Is thrust into prison, and joyfully tramples every hardship.

Remaining unconquered beneath the vast silence of night,

[Col. 0748B] He is led from his hiding place, beaten, and admitted among the stars.

The young disciples steal the martyr’s relics from the earth:

Proculus and Apollonius, beneath the darkness of night,

Carry them to their own church and cautiously render the final rites.

While they continually guard the sacred gifts,

They are seized, handed over to caves, and then sought out by the investigator.

Yet they do not yield, though offered flatteries and threats.

At last, unmoved, they are surrendered to be punished by decapitation,

And not far from the relics of their father they obtain the urn.

Domna and her companions shine here beneath a double honor of crowns.

## CHAPTER II. On Saints Anthimus and Maximus

[Col. 0747]

[Col. 0747B] They also beautify the Roman roads and the harbor

With glorious festivals; the trophies of heaven and Erebus blaze with weapons.

Through these the world, and the world’s power subdued to Christ, rejoice;

Thus the stores seasoned with your salt rejoice, holy

[Col. 0748B] Anthimus, illustrious in virtue and praise.

By deed and word you are borne above the flowing stars;

Safe, you are cast even into the storms of the Tiber.

## CHAPTER III. On the Seven Brothers

[Col. 0747]

[Col. 0747C] Tibur covers the ashes of the seven brothers with its mound;

The Appian Way adds one hundred and eight witnesses of Cecilia.

It also receives Trasitius beneath the tomb of Callistus.

While he was carrying out venerable duties as an attendant of the sacred rites,

And at a certain time was bearing the sacred mysteries of Christ,

He is seized amid a tumult after being discovered by a sacrilegious man,

Who demands that he reveal what secret object he is hiding.

[Col. 0748C] Unwilling to expose the gems to swine,

He is beaten by such a storm of sticks and stones

That he sends forth his mind, destined to be received by heaven and the stars.

Nor does this incorporeal treasure alone enter the sky:

The bodily mysteries of the bread, snatched away with him,

Are shaken from his garments, and the impious men search through his limbs,

But cannot discover the sacred things that have been denied to them.

## CHAPTER IV. On Saint Boniface

[Col. 0747]

[Col. 0747C] For his merits Boniface adorns the Latin church,

With the honor gained through the pious expenditure of his mistress.

[Col. 0747D] While they strive to wash away the adulteries of the bed by their own toil,

Moved by the governance of heaven,

They jointly decree that the noble Boniface, raised up,

Should hasten to honor the prostrate bodies of Christ.

If perhaps the saints’ services may be made favorable to their prayers,

He hastens as a spectator into battle and becomes a warrior of his own accord,

Magnifying Jesus by the praise of another’s battle,

So that he may prepare to be magnified by the assault of his own battle.

[Col. 0748C] He first kisses the bonds, then is suspended upon the bonds;

Arming the athletes, he is soon armed in the captured contest;

[Col. 0748D] Raising the wounds, he is torn by wounds down to the bones;

Encouraging those who are fastened up, reeds are driven into his nails;

Having gladly stirred himself to endure battles, he gladly endures them.

The heated lead cannot close his grateful mouth;

Nor does boiling pitch, into which he is immersed, know how to harm him.

The executioner, defeated, announces the final punishments.

But the earth trembles when he is beheaded, and the mountain trembles with it;

And, compelling belief, he composes proclamations of Christ.

[Col. 0749A] When his companions suppose that he, now rejoicing in the banquets of heaven,

Has been plunged into the filth of a tavern

And held by a prostitute, they find him enjoying heavenly sweetness.

He had sought to purchase the sacred things and, having received the price,

Is himself purchased, and is brought back for the payment.

Sprinkled with spices, he is honored according to his merit.

Aglae, a citizen of heaven, is recorded as the one who preceded this event.

She does not now meet a servant, but a faithful slave is said

To have gone out to meet her master; receiving the desired gift,

[Col. 0750A] She places it in the prepared resting place and beautifies the church with splendor.

Freed from the world’s yoke, she releases the necks of her slaves;

Renewing her household in freedom, she herself becomes truly free,

When by honorable deeds she reveals herself as Christ’s servant.

Stripping herself of the world’s adornments, she clothes herself with virtues;

Giving away earthly possessions, she grows rich in God,

In the lofty summit of virtues, and shines, sparkling with signs.

Successfully completing the course of her pious deeds,

She places the martyr’s bones in the house, while her mind is received into high heaven.

## CHAPTER V. On Saints Gorgonius and Dorotheus

[Col. 0749]

[Col. 0749B] Between these, this road earned twin laurel crowns

Through the companion Gorgonius and the honor of his comrade Dorotheus.

The companions had imbued one another with the strength of faith.

Therefore, before the tyrant who inflicts torments on Christ’s people,

They rebuke his servants and mark themselves as shining in this piety,

Burning with this devotion in heart and mouth,

And overcoming all their companions by this resolve.

When daylight was given, their entrails are torn from all their limbs,

Their skin is stripped away, and salt and vinegar are poured upon them.

After enduring these things bravely, they are ordered to be laid upon a gridiron,

To be heated by fire and warmed by a slow burning,

So that the conflagration may not carry off their desiring minds too quickly.

Thus, after the torturer has already been overcome, further fires

Are added,

To see whether perhaps their bones may be overcome by cooking

[Col. 0749C] Through the long heat roasting their marrow.

While it is shameful that faith has subdued the volcano by its heat,

[Col. 0750B] The executioner, warning that the half-roasted limbs must be removed,

Raises them upon the fortress of the cross,

Lifting them into the light of triumph;

And, led forth, they joyfully penetrate the heavens among the stars.

Snatched away and restored, under an angelic guide, to the accustomed altars,

He tends the buried talents; for that service he is crowned by beheading.

Maximus follows him; by his martyrdom he strengthens the hearts of the righteous,
and, powerful and eminent through slaughter, gains heaven.
His body alone remains at the place where he had been accustomed to offer vows.

Afterward Bassus appears, rejecting the sacred rites of Dionysus,

And tramples the grain with his breath, overthrowing the gods

With a slight breath; beaten, he seeks the heights of heaven.

Thus Fabius, worn down by long bonds and imprisonment,

At last ascends the stars, crowned at the summit as a holy man;

Victorious and having earned his reward, he ascends to heaven’s honor.

Twice one hundred, and sixty-two besides, also adorn this place:

Witnesses in relics whom this road hides beneath the sands,

And to whom the hill of the swollen gourd gives its name.

## CHAPTER VI. On Saints Luceia and Acceia

[Col. 0749]

[Col. 0749C] Then Luceia, accompanied by a saving company,

And the barbarian victory of Acceia accompanying the king,

Hasten to complete their course, with the ruler of heaven calling them.

[Col. 0750C] From the renowned Zeno flows an unbroken drop of sweat in the training ground,

Whom thirteen thousand two hundred followed.

## CHAPTER VII. On Saints Archelaus, Hippolytus, Vincentius, and Their Companions

[Col. 0749]

[Col. 0749C] The pious gifts of Archelaus, Hippolytus, and Vincentius

Also enrich the Roman harbor,

And, besides these, many others: Quiriacus and Herculianus.

Here the brave and worthy martyr Hyacinthus shines forth.

Immersed in fire, he joyfully overcomes the flames;

Then cast into the swift waters of a foaming river,

He is restored unharmed to the mound of the dry bank.

[Col. 0749D] Then Julia, attending him after he had been cut down by the sword,

[Col. 0750C] Lays him to rest with celebrated honor on her own estate.

There, in inscriptions shining with the law of Christ’s triumphs,

Are recorded the martyrs who came from elsewhere,

Together with Martialis, Aprilis, and their companions,

Felix and many others,

And, besides these, those known to the one God,

Who, around and beneath Rome,

[Col. 0750D] Crown the Roman city by carrying forth their standards, worthy of praise.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Saint Sylvester

[Col. 0749]

[Col. 0749D] Sylvester, having received the heights of Peter’s chair,

Proved himself the father of the people, great and small.

Calling back those who wandered, strengthening those who pursued heavenly things,

Governing clergy and people with careful rule,

The pious man weighed the affairs of the Church in a balanced scale:

The unworthy, the buildings of the temple, and the worthy ministers.

Appointing these also with prudent honor, he dedicated them,

Adorning them with holy conduct, heavenly salt, and vestments,

[Col. 0750D] And ordering them to devote an appointed time to God.

Besides this, he had a great struggle with the nations,

Refuting falsehood with arguments and defending the truth.

For the purpose of this he was given power to confront opposing hands.

He waged war against the dragon raging upon the Tarpeian hill,

Which, summoned by sacred song and profane ritual,

Was nevertheless gnawing the neighboring rock with dreadful fire,

[Col. 0751A] Afflicting the unwary people with the supreme plague.

He summons the fathers who deserve heavenly gifts,

And proclaims that fasts must be observed for three days.

Through chaste prayers and urgent vows he perseveres,

So that in this matter Christ’s manifest power may increase.

Then the shepherd Peter appears and brings consolation,

When, according to the order of the sacred clergy,

The elder Theodorus, Felicissimus,

And their third companion Dionysius, then ministers,

Together with Romanus and Honoratus, celebrate the mysteries.

After first relying upon these men, he then descends to the contest.

It is added what he has discovered and what gift he is to present,

By which he may subdue the dreadful enemy in combat.

He begins his approach while the hostile cohort terrifies him from afar.

Informed about the hiding place and fearless, he penetrates the abyss.

[Col. 0751B] At last he reaches the cavern of the raging serpent,

Forcing the enemy back; he makes the bronze doors his own,

Soon securing the rings and gates with a steel chain,

Shutting the plague behind iron and bronze and restraining it with a key.

Then, victorious and having fulfilled his vow, he returns to the spectacle.

The serpent-worshipers, at last approving the defeat of the portent,

Throw away the livid, feral skin they have cast off,

And rejoice to be clothed in the shining garments of the Lamb.

Nor does the horned serpent cease for long, once confined,

To drive the pious away and incite the profane to arms.

He spreads decrees that the worshipers of Christ should pray to the gods,

While those who shake the city with renewed fury are being torn apart.

The holy Father, increasingly attacked, leaves the city,

Enters the solitudes beneath Soracte, and, remaining in the countryside,

[Col. 0751C] Returns his vows to the Thunderer with the ranks of the clergy.

But the prince Constantine, driven by the error of one who had advised him toward danger,

Is struck in the body so that his mind may be healed.

His body is disfigured by a dreadful itching disease,

And he not only grieves that his face is defiled by unspeakable pustules,

But fears that he is hastening toward death through a fatal poison.

He seeks the haruspices; he seeks the aid of the gods;

With every kind of effort he investigates the laws of healing.

No hand is of help; no medical labor succeeds;

Useless art defeats all the practitioners.

But the inventors of crimes and ministers of shadows

Undertake a hateful and horrible remedy:

Bringing the gifts of unheard-of wickedness,

They assign the stains to be washed away with innocent blood,

And prescribe the deaths of many men as the prince’s cure.

[Col. 0751D] The fields are ordered to be trampled, and a company of servant-women is brought in.

Thousands of infants are seized, thousands of mothers;

The mothers carry their own children to the service of death,

Whom they nourish with milk, their blood now to be shed.

When the appointed hour of the crime had come,

The emperor was being dragged to the savage spectacle of slaughter.

As he approached the wicked bath with drawn swords,

A crowd rushed to meet him, the mothers’ breasts bared,

Their hair disheveled, preceding the savage death

With a river of tears, and confessing their grief

With heavy lamentation.

The emperor shudders at the crime; the shaken power trembles,

And tears restore the royal eyes.

He stands still, surrounded by a circle of nobles and fathers,

Touched in heart by pious integrity of mind, and speaks:

[Col. 0752A] He remembers that he was created a human being under the same condition

As servants, and that everyone rises from an equal origin.

There is no reason why so many thousands should be destroyed for his sake.

He remembers the proud enemies of the law whom he had preserved

And subjected to himself,

And he is ashamed to deny what had been granted:

To be a father to proud enemies, but a cruel enemy to citizens;

For victors to yield, defeated by the vices of their peoples,

And to be held guilty by their own laws while acting violently.

Thus it pleases him to tame savage character by virtue,

To conquer cruelty and be subdued by piety alone.

Piety rejects the counsel of the customary rites,

And the mothers’ children are ordered to be given back.

Astonishment strikes their hearts, and fear beats upon their inmost parts.

They are not easily persuaded to believe it.

Glad consolations are increased for the trembling,

Rewards on the road and aids for the journey;

Their joys grow amid their laments,

So that those who had been led weeping to the hated walls

Return happily to their own homes.

Thereupon the seeds of heavenly pity touch men’s hearts,

And lofty nobles withdraw from their seats among the gods,

While the taste of anguish hastens to quiet the tumult.

Two brilliant lights of the world are sent to the king:

The heavenly key-bearer Cephas, and the other,

Who cultivated the whole world of the nations through his word.

They declare the commands of God and announce that the fury has ended,

That the minds have been subdued,

And that the deeds of mercy have pleased the ruler of heaven.

They reveal that they have been sent to him

With counsels of salvation for his return.

He must listen and carry them out, and not resist the heavenly commands.

They identify Sylvester and his hiding place,

And order the king to seek the man

Who can provide him with the bath of salvation.

Then he should strive to render such a return to the Thunderer:

He should repair the wounds inflicted upon the Church through proper governance,

Restore the buildings,

Cleanse himself from demonic pollution,

Worship the one true God,

And strive with all his effort to follow his will.

When the two men had thereafter returned to the starry court,

The emperor, instructed by heavenly utterances,

Selects the holy and renowned physician and sends for him.

When Sylvester sees the emperor surrounded by a swift-moving military force,

He thinks that the time has come to win the palm through bloodshed.

He urges his companions to enter the contest with ready hearts

And seek the standards of the cross to be carried,

Calling them by his example to follow the Lord, who summons them to truth.

[Col. 0752D] Thus, committing himself to God, praying and carrying the cross,

He strengthens his subjects with kisses bestowed in peace.

The brave disciples accompany their father as he goes,

Rejoicing together that they are more able to endure torments,

Rather than, separated from their father, recline at perishable banquets.

But when they have reached the king’s anxious dwelling,

At last the joyful king rises and greets his astonished friend,

And the king who has been greeted in return leads him to the lofty seats.

He begins to recount the events and heavenly visions,

And asks repeatedly who the gods and divine powers were whom he saw—

Peter and Paul, bearing such commands.

“This is the one Father whom we worship with blessed rites:

The almighty Creator of heaven, earth, and sea;

He alone is God, who fills all things with his powers.

[Col. 0753A] Peter and Paul are known to be his disciples.

There they showed the divine things of God through Christ to the nations,

And adorn the world with pious splendor.

Thus they are the Lord’s witnesses and, first among those admitted

To the heavenly seat of the saints,

They are honored in the citadel of heaven,

Friends of the highest of the highest nobles of the Ruler of all.”

The Caesar then said: “Do any painted images of these men

Represent their appearance for you?”

He asks that proofs be shown to him.

The Caesar, examining the images shown by the pope, says:

“I have no doubt that these men truly gave me the commands:

That you should soon receive

Through our ministry the bath of salvation,

By which all your ulcers may dissolve.”

At this the emperor rejoices. The holy man brings the nourishment of faith to the king,

And urges him to grasp faith with a ready mind.

[Col. 0753B] He replies that he believes,

And that for this reason he summoned the patron of this law,

So that he might undertake the rite according to its proper rule.

Commands are soon dictated to the gentle tyrant:

To the novice, ready to submit his neck,

Dry fasts are given instead of sumptuous meals;

The purple garment blazing with the goat’s dye is exchanged for a humble cloak;

Instead of the broad and lascivious brilliance of the palate,

The inaccessible secrets of a strict chamber are prescribed;

Instead of pomp and cruel judgments,

Let the blessed confession of Christ resound from his triumphant mouth.

Let groans of lamentation atone for the sin of shed blood;

Let the shrines be closed; let offerings to the ghosts cease.

Let what is owed be given to the poor from the entire treasury;

Let the bonds throughout the city’s prisons be entirely unlocked.

Let those driven into exile and various tortures

Be comforted by pardon; let consolation be given to the weary.

Let ministers worthy to perform these things worthily be selected.

The emperor accepts this, and reviews it with faithful mind.

Professing Christ as the true Lord and God,

Rejecting the vain images, he receives the sign of the cross

And leaves, a distinguished catechumen, by the hand of the pontiff.

The pope, vigilant in sacred matters, joyfully leads the fasts,

And calls the Church to share in the devout labor.

When the rites have been completed through worthy solemn vows,

The blessed evening of the rising Christ draws near,

About to lead the highest scepters from the black darkness.

The perpetual fountain of water, through the lofty gift of its liquid,

Fills the font, not only extinguishing the plagues of the mind,

But also powerfully relieving the body’s dreadful diseases.

[Col. 0753D] The supreme bishop proceeds to consecrate the supreme ruler.

The latter, confessing the sovereign power of the most high God,

Renounces impure filth and savage altars.

He is immersed in the sacred waters with a threefold dipping,

And suddenly, in response to the prayers and words of the bishop,

A celebrated light radiates from heaven, surpassing the sun’s gleams.

Then the fountain’s crackling and the hissing foam resound.

The washed king rises, clean in mind and body,

And goes forth healed, confessing the face he has seen in Christ.

Pure in mind, he shines; serene, the childlike brightness flashes from his face.

His mind gleams within, and outwardly his flesh shines white.

He rejoices, endowed with an extraordinary healing in both respects.

Exulting, he takes up the white garments and extends beneficent laws:

He declares that throughout the world, wherever it reaches,

This one must be worshiped, because he had driven away fierce things

And bestowed the joys of salvation.

Whoever blasphemes him must receive worthy punishment.

Let the persecutor of Christ’s worshipers be oppressed by the fiscal exacter.

Let every bishop venerate the pope of the Romans.

If a guilty person seeks the Church, let him be shielded by the judge.

Let temples in the city be established only through the bishop’s support.

Let the imperial revenues be converted into holy tithes.

After laying aside the white garments, he resumes the glowing purple.

Pure and unharmed, visiting Peter’s mausoleum,

He prostrates himself face downward, having removed the diadem from his head,

And pours tears and Tyrian garments upon the ground.

Remembering himself guilty because of the blood that had been shed,

He arouses the people’s resounding weeping and groans,

Who, mingling grief with joy, celebrate the new happiness.

The king undertakes servile labor.

Rejecting the splendor of his purple cloak,

He takes up an unfamiliar tool, the mattock,

And turns the clods with lowered effort.

He opens the way for the foundations of the sacred temple,

Where the apostolic foundations are to be fixed.

As a mark of his bowed honor, after the foundation trench has been properly excavated,

He carries twelve baskets laden with earth upon his shoulders.

From there, seated in a carriage, he ascends to the palace with the bishop.

The following day was spreading a rose-colored garment over the earth.

The holy king rises to consecrate the palace of the Church,

The Lateran structure, and everywhere reveals

That he has bowed his neck beneath the Lord, the throne on high.

By law, if any poor person binds himself to submit to Christ,

Let him receive a garment shining with whiteness

And twenty solidi as an imperial gift.

[Col. 0754C] The harvest of the Lord increases,

And the people, shining with the sacred things of the Most High God,

Leave the criminal shrines.

Twelve thousand radiant men are counted,

Besides the weak multitude of infants and mothers,

Whose number is balanced by the measurer of heaven.

When the Roman fathers, fleeing faith, withdrew into the heights,

The gracious Father did not allow the emperor to be angered.

Seated upon the throne of the palace,

He raises the people and the fathers with words shining like heavenly light:

He declares that gods should neither be called nor worshiped—

Gods made by human hands, maintained by human action,

Whom they restore after they have been overthrown and need preservation.

They are unworthy to entrust themselves to divine mercy,

Which can repair what has been worn away and restore salvation.

What has been done in him stands proven in clear light:

Christ the Creator must be worshiped with an appropriate rite.

Therefore let superstitious gods now cease;

Let the one who alone can create all things alone be worshiped.

Let honor belong to the one who preserves,

Not to the one who is preserved.

Let sight be imposed upon the blind and hearing upon the deaf;

Let our wisdom desist from these things.

Let the churches of Christ be opened—

Those rights formerly preserved for profane priests

Are to be handed over to pious ministers.

Therefore we have begun the work of Christ,

So that our royal temple may shine,

And the Roman power may see everywhere

That no trace of doubt remains in our mind.

The fathers and brave Romans acclaim these words,

Exalting Christ and seeking that the shrines be closed,

That the temples of Christ, the true and only God, be opened.

[Col. 0755A] He granted Augustus sudden salvation beyond all expectation.

Let the profane be driven from the city, with Christ victorious.

At this the ruler explains with what mind the laws of God are to be honored:

They must burn in the heart and be sought voluntarily.

No one is to be unwillingly compelled;

No one is to be forced.

Let the mind judge freely and deliberate what is just.

Let each person, after balanced consideration, accept what he finds true.

All, even those compelled by necessity, praise this law,

Because it drives no one forward and repels no one.

The city is crowned; the light of Phoebus, with its many lamps,

Is surpassed, and rejoicing fills the Church.

The tombs of the saints are adorned with radiant splendor.

Those driven into exile are summoned with glorious honor,

And those joyfully received again in their homeland

Are honored as the king’s friends, admitted through his merits.

[Col. 0755B] Meanwhile Augustus’s mother, a woman who truly sought knowledge,

Helena, was examining the eastern regions,

Traversing the cities of the Bebrycians and the Greek kingdoms.

While she cautiously refuses to venerate the monstrous gods,

She chooses to serve the one ruler of the stars.

Therefore, favoring the ancient rites of Judea,

She judged that they should be followed and urged her son

To take up the Mosaic law by the path of the ancients.

She maintained that God ought not to be believed to have undergone torments;

But her son rejected these pleasing remedies of the gods.

In response, her son, carried forward by supreme moderation,

Advancing toward an outstanding summit,

Confesses that the divine surpasses the human mind,

As it surpasses heaven and earth.

He does not defend by divine power the worship that she had chosen,

Lest he presume to claim for himself the authority of so lofty a rite.

[Col. 0755C] But let teachers devoted to Christ and of the ancient people

Meet to contend with a weighing of the truth,

So that, by sacred law, books of worship, and divine doctrine,

They may reveal through alternating dispute

Which is preeminent,

And to whom the highest summit and the ages must submit.

From everywhere rabbis and friends of the carnal law are summoned,

And the enemies of the supreme Priest assemble.

Twelve leaders of the sectarians are selected,

And scribes polished in Roman, Greek, and Latin eloquence,

Who seem capable, are selected for the city.

From various seats, bishops distinguished by the piety of Christ

Are also summoned to this battle.

While servants of Christ are appointed to conduct the alternate dispute

And undertake its conclusion,

Sylvester, fixing his hope upon the one Lord,

Confronts the twelve alone.

[Col. 0755D] The opposing party, fearing to be overcome by its own weapons,

Forbids this matter to be touched.

The Caesar approves what is suited to triumph.

While the hostile party is overthrown by its own darts,

The heavenly contest rises and the duel is undertaken.

“The fools blaspheme by saying that we worship three Thunderers.”

The pope reveals from the ancient books

That the three are embraced in the supreme Godhead,

And that the One created everything in threefold form,

While receiving within himself nothing unequal, greater, or lesser.

When this point is overthrown, the twofold enemy is cast down.

They object that Jesus Christ underwent dangers,

And this argument, developed from the words of the ancients,

Is revealed to be fulfilled in Christ through all his deeds.

His coming and the reason for the labor imposed are brought forth,

And also how the Son of God assumed human limbs.

[Col. 0756A] As the holy man resolves these matters through divine reasoning,

The rival tumult yielded its neck to the truths.

Only one man remained, untouched by the conflicts of the battle:

Zambri, relying upon the effort of Zoroaster,

In whom lay the supreme confidence of sacrilegious triumph.

He reproaches the others for being defeated in a light contest,

And demands that he himself be brought into the arena by deeds, not words.

He asks that an untamed and savage bull be sought,

So that, through a powerful act of the supreme divine power,

He may reveal the virtue of his god;

And when the name is heard, the bull will fall.

For no living creature can endure the name,

Nor can the ears scarcely bear it or retain it.

After a bull has been brought forth through the great labor of young men,

Entangled by its legs and driven by bonds and ropes,

He relies on deception and insults the holder of the truth.

[Col. 0756B] He orders the holder of the true faith to prove his worship by death,

Or to have it disproved by death.

The righteous man, enduring the contest that has begun,

Dismisses the wicked man.

He whispers the dreadful name into the bull’s ear;

It falls and, pitifully bellowing, leaves the air,

Striking terror into the hearts of the men who watch its death.

A repeated cry rises from the confused crowd.

Like a lion, Sylvester stands fearless and confident,

Caring neither for the crowd’s uproar nor fearing its insults.

Steadfast, he prays for help from heaven with his whole mind.

Then he asks Augustus to impose silence, even if late.

When the commands suppress the voices,

The lofty priest ascends and raises the people toward the truth with pious words:

He proclaims to the ears of Ausonia

The one who is the author of life and the Lord of salvation,

Who restored sight to the blind and hearing to the deaf,

Speech to mute tongues,

[Col. 0756C] And restored hands to the maimed and footsteps to the lame.

By his word he drove away leprosy and every disease;

He also brought dead bodies back to the returning light.

He revealed himself as God through open signs.

But whoever strikes with death,

Unless he can restore life, is not the supreme God.

For it is clear that the fraud of death belongs to the power of the hostile demon,

Unless he can repay what has been taken away.

Abracius burns with anger, cut off in worship and heart.

Unable to endure this justice with his ears or accept it in his mind,

He barks that he has prevailed,

Demanding that silence be imposed upon the contender in the battle

And that the laws be abandoned.

The Father [the text reads *Pater*, perhaps for *patet*] does not consider this worthy.

The pope recalls that the ancient prophet prayed to the Lord,

The ruler of life and death,

That he who strikes with death and restores through his breath,

Who strikes and heals, the powerful ruler of both,

May afterward confer the righteous man upon the upper airs after death,

So that believing hearts may be properly prepared for him.

At this the cunning deceiver presses on,

Demanding that the power be displayed in solemn deeds.

He foolishly and thunderstruck resists the one who promises life.

But he is compelled to confess the true and supreme Lord,

Who can restore breath to the dead.

He declares and adds that he and his followers

Will follow the insignia of Christ’s worship

If Sylvester’s promise is brought to fulfillment.

The pope utters prayers, not deaf mutterings whispered under his breath,

But clear vows poured forth for all to hear.

He openly invokes Christ, the author and giver of life,

And the heavenly one.

As he asks that breath be restored to the bull,

He desires the divinity to be shown.

Approaching the beast, he proclaims the name Jesus.

Under that name he commands the restored bull to rise,

Releases it from its ropes,

And orders it to go on.

Immediately it leaps up, bringing miracles to the astonished crowd,

Joy to the righteous and grief to the wicked,

And returns to the pasture, now deprived of its herd.

The crowd falls prostrate at the victorious man’s feet,

Then turns to the opposing side,

Asking salvation from the victor.

The royal mother herself comes forth from the palace,

Her public curtains torn away,

And humbly begs that pardon be granted her.

Nor does the bull alone experience the aid, but the hostile powers do as well.

With Sylvester victorious, the black breaths crackle and declare

That they are leaving.

Captured, they are restored safe by the grace of heaven,

And the holy man washes many more in the heavenly waters.

[Col. 0757B] The dove betrothed to Christ grows and is adorned

With temples, gifts, and pleasant worship.

The enemy, stripped and crushed in his broken strength—

Egypt’s firstborn having been plunged beneath Tartarus—

And the Macedonian ranks roll in the depths of the sea;

The victorious eagles triumph under the leadership of Jesus.

Maxentius too felt it as he raged in civil war.

Trampling earthly and challenging divine laws,

The wicked man undergoes a death like Pharaoh’s in the waters,

Falling into the pit prepared for him by his own deceit in battle,

While the pious man rejoices and flashes forth in heavenly armor.

For him the standards of the cross shine forth from opened heaven;

For him the promised victory is confirmed by a heavenly voice.

His mother, Augustus’s mother, strengthened by these successful deeds

And made firm in faith, considers the labor of the journey

And hopes to continue it toward Jerusalem,

Rejoicing to touch the sacred places of God with her feet.

She expiates the crime committed by the malice of the eleventh Caesar,

Cleansing the holy lands from filthy shrines,

And adorning them with pious religion and sacred altars.

When Jerusalem is reached, she drinks in what she had begun to learn by reading,

Examining it with her eyes.

Among the remarkable things, she sits intent on searching out

The famous wood of the cross,

By which the whole world had paid the price of life.

Since no path lay open by which the hidden treasures might be reached,

She summoned experts under various conditions

And labored to learn the details of Golgotha’s punishment.

[Col. 0758A] When these had been revealed,

And men of both opposing sides had testified in agreement,

The queen undertook the task,

Taking divine hope into her heart,

And searched through the concealed pits.

Nor was the labor long; prayers favor the undertaking.

The treasure and its surrounding space offer themselves to eager eyes.

Long-hidden secrets appear to the faithful who had been unfaithful.

But uncertainty about the true object clouds the joy of discovery:

Three crosses have been found,

And doubt wavers over which was the cross on which the life-giving Vine had been raised.

But the supreme judge, intending to settle her anxious concerns,

Touches the queen’s mind with a heavenly sign.

She orders a recently dead, bloodless corpse to be brought in,

So that the gift may be tested by its power.

The corpse’s cold entrails are brought forth, stiff in their veins.

The crosses are applied.

The punitive wood of the robbers is rejected;

The life-giving wood reveals its powers.

The life of the risen one fills the tree of life with joy.

Feeding the spectators with the gift of restoration,

The man marvels at seeing himself walk again amid those who marvel.

Thus the cross, shining with divine beauty,

Is glorified, and, in obedience to the vows,

Is carried into the splendid palace.

There it radiates beneath richly adorned ceilings of gleaming gold.

A portion of the precious wood is also carried to the king.

The whole cross remains where it is,

Spreading its powers widely.

It suffers no loss while filling the world with its abundant gift,

Retaining its perpetual strength without diminution.

The nails, by whose points the divine treasure—the price of the world—

Was weighed, protect the royal crests once they have been fitted,

And are consecrated as the straps of the bridle.

Their outstanding power restrains the unbridled shadows.

This you proved by the merits of faith, Prince Justinus.

Nor does the sea fail to honor such power:

Its waves are calmed and its abyss obstructed.

The linens that had woven the cross do not remain without effect.

Once they have received its strength, they drive away diseases and chills,

Cast out demons, and restore sight to the blind.

Speech is given to the mute, and paralytic limbs are raised.

The great standard is transformed into the labarum of the cross.

It is set before the ranks and illuminates the battle lines with honor.

It protects the standard-bearers and their companions.

The bearer is not afflicted by disaster,

Nor can weapons harm the one who carries it.

The one who abandons the standards perishes;

The standard-bearer is preserved against the enemy.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Synod Held under Saint Sylvester

[Col. 0757]

[Col. 0757D] Under Sylvester’s authority the fathers assemble,

Reveal the lights of the Catholic faith,

And condemn the rebels.

They establish the strongest supports of the Church of light.

The pontifical summit is honored,

And the senate of the clergy is instructed by laws;

The laws of sacred matters are promulgated.

[Col. 0758D] The temples shine with their buildings;

Gifts are consecrated to the temples,

And the relics of apostolic honor are covered with abundant bronze.

Clear victory flashes forth over tyrants who have been crushed.

Lofty trophies shine over the nations that have been subdued.

## Source-adjudicated replacement readings

**Saved correction 4:** The event is announced beforehand to Aglae by a heavenly messenger;
no longer does she meet a servant, but she, a faithful handmaid,
goes out to meet her lord, receiving the desired gift,

**Saved correction 6:** The pious man weighed the Church’s affairs on a considered scale:
provision for the needy, the fabric of the church, and worthy ministers.

**Saved correction 7:** He spreads decrees that the worshipers of Christ should pray to the gods,
while they, in renewed fury, shake the riven city.

**Saved correction 8:** Thus, committing himself to God and praying,
he strengthens his followers with kisses bestowed as a peaceful pledge.

**Chapter II.** The bright Roman roads and harbor are adorned by festive trophies whose burning arms proclaim heaven and Erebus; by them the world and worldly power are subdued to Christ. The next compressed line is retained cautiously: *Hinc sale, sancte, tuo condita salaria gaudet, Anthime*—“Hence the *salaria*, seasoned or founded with your salt, rejoice, holy Anthimus.” *Salaria* may denote salt-works or things connected with salt; “stores seasoned with your salt” is not secure. Anthimus bears the insignia of virtues and praise, and, cast into the Tiber, passes safely above its storms.

**Chapter V.** In the damaged couplet *Raptus et angelico suetis duce redditus aris / Cessa talenta colit quo munere vertice plexus*, the martyr is “snatched up and, under an angelic guide, restored to the accustomed altars”; the remainder says approximately that he tends or honors “ceased/idle talents,” and is struck on the head through that office or gift. The exact construction is corrupt; it does not securely mean “buried talents.”

**Chapter VI.** Luceia is accompanied by the King’s saving company, and the barbarian victory of Acceia accompanies or crowns the company as they hasten to fulfill their course when called by heaven’s King. The continually flowing drop marks Zeno’s distinguished contest, followed by thirteen thousand two hundred people. The syntax linking Luceia, Acceia, the company, and victory remains compressed, so no extra agent is supplied.

**Constantine and the legal provisions.** In the damaged vision sequence, two splendid lights of the world are sent to the emperor: Peter, bearer of heaven’s keys, and Paul, who cultivated the world among the nations by his word. They report both their own and God’s commands, say that a limit must be put to fury, and direct Constantine to seek Sylvester and receive the saving bath. The legal lines require churches to be assigned in the city by the bishop’s effort; *si reus Ecclesiam petat, ut censore tegatur* says approximately that if an accused person seeks the Church he is protected “by the censor/judge,” whose precise office is unclear. *Caesareae fabricas decimae redigantur in almas* assigns an imperial tenth to pious building works, but its exact fiscal construction is compressed.

**Corrupt reading at Col. 0754D.** The source prints *Sit caecis visus ianime (sic) imperitetur / Auditus*. The secure frame is “Let sight be for the blind … let hearing be commanded/provided”; *ianime* is explicitly corrupt and is not silently normalized into a coherent conjunction.

**The Cross at Col. 0758B–C.** The divine talents weighed as the world’s price are the nails: fashioned from their points, they protect the summit of the royal helmet or crown, and the reins’ straps are consecrated. The following line says their eminent power scatters or breaks unbridled shadows. The source associates nails with the royal headgear and a bridle, but does not securely specify which individual nail became each object.

And when the darkness has been dispersed, joyful light adorns the pious.

## CHAPTER X. On Gallicanus and Constantia

[Col. 0757]

[Col. 0757D] Then Gallicanus, ennobled by the illustrious emperor and elevated by victorious insignia, while he is seen to be pleasing and dear to Augustus, asks that Constantia, dedicated to Christ and bound by perpetual law, be given to him in marriage.

[Col. 0758D] The emperor began to be troubled in his anxious mind, knowing that his daughter could be killed rather than violated. Seeking by this resolve to avert her father's wound, she then said: “Declare that I am to be married to Gallicanus, provided that he conquers the Scythians.

[Col. 0759A] Soon he will be both consul and royal son-in-law.”

Meanwhile, betrothal gifts are exchanged on both sides. The brothers John and Paul, guardians of the virgin’s lofty chastity, and the virgin herself retain Gallicanus’ two daughters, Attica and Artemia, whom she dedicates to Christ with her own lips and vows.

Then the suitor, alarmed by their terrifying multitude, fears to lead his small force against the Scythians, the people of Thrace. He heaps sacred offerings upon the Martial altars. The enemy grows in strength, and troubles gather force. The Romans abandon their standards and yield to the barbarians. The prince, anxiously considering the possibility of escape, receives from Constantia, through the satraps Paul and John, a harbor of salvation: she announces the vow that he should make to the God supreme, ruler of the heavens—that, rescued from danger through Christ, he would become a victor more glorious than he had been before.

When the word of the one making the vow resounds as approved, behold, a young man of imposing stature appears, ready to bear forward the standards of the cross upon his shoulder: “Follow me,” he says, “armed with the sword!”

Immediately following him, Gallicanus sees armed men prepared for battle on either side, strengthening themselves and offering assistance. They command him to enter the enemy camp safely; he fearlessly brandishes his unsheathed sword in every direction while he climbs toward the barbarian king’s secret quarters.

When the barbarian king sees these things, he falls at Gallicanus’ feet and lies prostrate, pouring out vows and begging for his life together with that of his people.

When these requests have been granted, he surrenders himself together with his children. Afterwards they declare that they will pay tribute, and, under the terms of the agreement, the Thracians are freed from the enemy.

From there, once he has returned as tribune, together with his soldiers, they prepare to serve Christ under his protection. The prince is consecrated and vows to remain abstinent from marriage; thus, as a triumphant man, he returns.

Nor does he enter Rome before advancing to the thresholds consecrated to Peter, directing his course there, and offering thanks to the giver of victory.

Augustus, accompanied by his offspring, comes to meet him. When he learns what has happened, he embraces him and announces that his daughters have been dedicated to Heaven.

[Col. 0759D] As the prince, supported by the king, approaches the palace, the holy queen, leaning upon her noble granddaughter, comes out to meet him and presents the pledges. Joys rich in tears pour forth.

He, now a private citizen, eagerly desires to go forth without the insignia of office, bearing before him the citadel of his lofty vocation.

He is nevertheless asked to appear from the palace as consul.

[Col. 0760A] Assuming the honors, he frees five thousand household slaves, removing the restraints of servitude; he enriches them with fields and assigned dwellings. The revenues collected in the marketplace, apart from those belonging to his daughters, he distributes among the needy.

Having become the companion of the holy Hilarinus, he undertakes lofty works of virtue, serving the poor. In his kindness he enlarges hospices, where his companions—those who had been fellow-slaves—remain together.

His lavish fame spreads throughout the whole world: people burn to see the eminent consul washing the feet of the poor as their servant.

In the city of Ostia he builds churches for Christ and appoints ministers to keep watch there.

The great deacon Laurence appeared to him and urged him to offer his house for worship. Fulfilling the command, he names it the Laurentian church.

The bishop is not favorably disposed toward those who make the request, but Gallicanus chooses that the church should shine with this distinction.

The distributor of gifts repays the favor and bestows so great a glory of splendor that those endowed with spiritual cunning may be cleansed when they are brought before him.

Thus, supported by a great grace of healings, he shines with an abundance of radiant holiness.

Then Julian, an enemy of innocence, having gained power in public affairs, constrains the Christians by deceitful statutes, so that they may possess nothing belonging to the needy.

At that time he approaches Gallicanus’ house, where the burdens of the poor are relieved, seeking to impose titles or to exact payments.

Seized by the avenging demon, he is torn apart; the tax-collector is driven into the pollution of leprosy.

When questioned, the spirits reveal that those who occupy his possessions cannot otherwise avoid these dangers unless Gallicanus offers sacrifices to the gods.

Yet no one dares to attack the holy man. Then the savage prefect of the palace appoints someone to read the orders: Gallicanus must offer sacrifices to the gods, submit to the Latin rites, or depart from the borders, abandoning his possessions.

He, trained in endurance, seeks the city of Alexandria and willingly joins the company of the confessors of Christ for a year.

Then he climbs into the desert by a difficult path. The savage enemy pursues the prince even there and orders the blessed man to burn incense to the impious gods. But, with his neck submitted, he takes the sword from the tempter and, rejoicing, reaches the stars.

His holy church is dedicated to his name, and gifts honoring the martyr of Christ shine there.

## CHAPTER XI. On the holy martyrs John and Paul

[Col. 0759]

[Col. 0759D] At the request of this teacher, the illustrious brothers John and Paul, Christ’s poor men and instructors of the virgin, having abandoned Constantia’s wealth, continually refresh the Christians.

[Col. 0760D] They are reported to the tyrant. He meets them with gentle words and asks them to remain attached to him:

[Col. 0761A] “Because of your injustice,” they say, “we are absent from public fellowship.

We shall no longer come out to greet you, for we live in the truth as disciples of Christ.”

“Consider,” replies the apostate, “that those who have been raised in the royal palace ought to be the first to attend the king in the royal court, so that I may honor the foremost men of the palace. But I am despised; I ask that I may not be despised.”

The brothers answer: “We would do you this injustice if we preferred a mortal man to you. We place before you the ruler of heaven, sea, and earth, who made everything that exists. Therefore we flee the glory of a temporal human being, mindful of the wrath of the heavenly King; and you should know that we shall no longer enter your palace even to greet you.”

The tyrant says: “For ten days I grant you freedom to reflect prudently, so that you may voluntarily make use of our fellowship; otherwise I shall punish you as public enemies.”

Then the blessed men summon faithful companions and arrange matters so that the rest may be provided for. Throughout the period of the truce, they distribute all their resources to the needy.

After this, Terentianus attacks them in their own house and finds them offering their vows. He confesses that a golden Jupiter has been sent by the king, before whom incense is to burn, and that they must sacrifice to him;

[Col. 0762A] otherwise the sword will pass through their necks, so that men unworthy of the king, though raised in the royal palace, may not be slaughtered before the eyes of the common people.

“If your master is Julian,” they say, “let him keep his peace with his prince. For us there will be no other Father except the one, and his only-begotten Son, and the Holy Spirit.”

He is not frightened by their refusal. Cast away from God’s sight, he prepares himself to make them companions in destruction. As an instigator, kneeling in the midst of the terrible struggle, he savagely opens the earth and prepares domestic tombs for those who are to come. Soon, after their necks have been cut, he plunges them into the trench, declaring—by the emperor’s command—that they have been exiled.

[Col. 0762B] After the storm has passed and calm has been restored, after the impious avenger has been overcome by the slaughter of many, demons confessing the struggle of the saints leave the vessels they possessed when touched at the threshold.

Terentianus’ son, seized by a spirit, cries out that he is being burned by the blessed brothers.

The father, driven by fear for his son, falls at their feet and proclaims his sins. He asks for baptism and gives tears to his grief. While the son is released at the tomb of the pious men, Terentianus, purging by tears of confession the dreadful acts he had committed in the persecution, sets them forth on trustworthy pages.

## CHAPTER XII. On the holy Januarius, Gordianus, and their companions

[Col. 0761]

[Col. 0761C] The apostate deserter consecrated many to Christ by a blessed death, while the fierce anger of the defeated foe increased against the public order. He assigns the pious men to custody.

Then he entrusts Januarius, seized under harsh authority, to Gordianus.

The pious priest, beloved by the impious king, is handed over to the wild beast in his place.

When Gordianus hears his words with a humble heart, he is filled with the Spirit of faith. His wife, Marina by name, joins him and is soon washed in the sacred font. Servants seeking the sacred rites, fifty in number, likewise follow their masters.

When these deeds are reported to the savage judge,

[Col. 0761D] he strikes both men with written accusations and, after appointing another judge, thrusts Gordianus back into the public dungeon.

He gives the chaste wife to the waters at the Salvian springs and orders her to serve the peasants.

Clementianus attaches Gordianus, bound in chains, to his dwelling. He, strong and immovable in the praise of Christ, is severely beaten with lead; yet he does not abandon his heavenly confession and, by his neck, gains the heavens.

When the worst judge has ordered the corpse to be cast to the dogs, the sleepless guardian covers it. The Christians carry it away at night, a mile from the city, and place it where the relics of the blessed martyr Epimachus had previously been gathered.

[Col. 0762D] One and the same day raises both martyrs with equal joyful festal observance.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Saint Pigmenius

[Col. 0761]

[Col. 0761D] This savage cruelty also stains itself with the blood of the teacher Pigmenius, a fosterling nourished under the law of God, the holy presbyter who held a titular church at Rome.

When he learns that the pious body of the pastor has been laid low by rage, he orders him to withdraw from the city, saying that he will restore his rewards because he is being sent into exile;

[Col. 0762D] for he is ashamed to strike down the one who has nourished him immediately at the first command.

Pigmenius seeks the land of the Persians. After remaining there for a time, he is deprived of bodily sight but remains strong in the light of his mind. He is ordered to return to Rome and to seek the cause of his martyr’s crown.

At last, with a boy guiding his steps, Pigmenius meets his persecutor, who comes exalted in a chariot and gold.

[Col. 0763A] Inflated with pompous arrogance, he gives thanks to the gods. Enflamed by the blazing fury of Acheron, he orders Pigmenius to be thrown headlong into the waters of the Tiber.

[Col. 0764A] Thus the pious soul returns to heaven, while his earthly remains find a tomb with Abdon and Sennen.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Saint Herculius, Hilarinus, and their companions

[Col. 0763]

[Col. 0763A] Donatus, a reader and companion in study and a fellow disciple under this holy father, flees when his father and mother are taken up by the savage sword, and, seeking Aricia, has made his way into the city.

While, joined to the pious Hilarinus, he reads vows to God night and day and practices frequent fasts, a pagan woman named Surana, covered in darkness in eyes and heart, bursts into the splendid cell with her son. She relates her faith to the bishop Satyrus.

Rejoicing at the sight of the light of dawning faith, and giving thanks to God, he commands fasts. He spreads ashes as a bed, gives her harsh haircloth as clothing, instructs and washes her. With her, her only son Herculius enters the waters.

Soon the woman’s darkened forehead recovers its light, and, recognizing her radiant offspring, she proclaims Christ true, powerful over life and light.

When Apronianus learns of this through reliable reports, he brings his own son, stunned by a dreadful spirit, to Donatus, Hilarinus, and the bishop. He persists in prayers; thus, when the spirit has been driven out by their vows, he restores the boy unharmed to his rejoicing father.

From this point his virtue and glory continually increased through successive stages.

A certain Eustasius joined him. After he had laid aside his fiscal office, his wife died.

Enduring the anger of a grim tax-collector, he sought Donatus’ aid with faithful heart. Taking refuge, he entered the cave of the heavenly fortress and, calling upon the name of the woman who had died through the powers of Christ, adjured her, adding the sign of the cross fixed in a staff, to say what had happened and where the money of the treasury had been taken.

Eufrasina’s words are reported from the depths of the tomb. The house is entered, and the hidden treasure is sought. The known bronze is brought out, and the man proceeds, relieved of his burden.

When Satyrus, summoned to the kingdoms by his worthy merits, had already departed, Donatus served at his sacred altars in his place.

One day, while he was celebrating the divine mysteries and, as a minister, giving the gifts of the heavenly blood to the people, he was driven forward by a pagan assault and smashed the consecrated chalice. The priest was troubled, and the people with him; but Christ’s right hand calmed the anguish.

The fragments were gathered and carried to the blessed man. Wet with tears, he took them up and, after pouring out his vows, restored them to their former shape by making the fragment whole.

[Col. 0764B] The barbarians, struck by the sight of this new deed, began with the singing crowd to praise God, and it is said that nearly eighty souls were converted.

Moreover, by many signs of divine power, God raised Donatus as a witness and honored him.

He was seized, and Hilarinus likewise; they were ordered to plead with incense. When the command was properly resisted, Donatus’ mouth was rubbed harshly with stones. Hilarinus, beaten with clubs, left the earth he had tested and received the ether he had sought. The prison gates take hold of his body, and Donatus is received within their enclosure.

Here too Christ, through him, performed many mighty works amid the applause of the people: he drew one whom a savage sword had cut down out of darkness and received him into the ether of true light.

## CHAPTER XV. On the holy Priscus, Priscillianus, and the others

[Col. 0763]

[Col. 0763C] Besides these, many others in this cloud seek heavenly honors by renouncing earthly ones.

The priest Priscus climbs to heaven by the sword. Priscillianus, a cleric who follows him, receives an equal crown by an equal lot.

A blessed chaste woman, following in their footsteps, enters the kingdoms of the righteous.

Faustus, triumphant, is joined to the king’s scepters. Dafrosa, after the glory of her marriage to Faustus, is separated from her denied homeland in exile and, driven from the earth by the sword, is received into heaven.

Faustus and Dafrosa flourish as the parents of their illustrious daughters Biviana and Demetria.

[Col. 0763D] When Demetria, led before the enemy,

[Col. 0764C] makes the glory of her confession shine forth, she places her mind among the heavenly stars.

The glorious presbyter John, when the twin sun gives a mournful spectacle, gathers the funeral remains from the forum by a praiseworthy theft and joins them in a tomb to his pious parents, to whom he had already joined the body of their sister.

Julian, who does not even consider him worthy of being heard, orders him to be beheaded at the Phoebean altar. Concordius, a priest shining with an equal lot and endowed with equal distinction, collects him, adorns him with the sacred honor due, and

[Col. 0764D] places the blessed martyr among the martyrs.

# THE TENTH BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0763]

## CHAPTER I. On the holy bishops Mark and Julius

[Col. 0763D] Having passed through the wars, let us return to the city, to see who followed Sylvester by succession in the seat of Peter.

Mark first undertakes the sacred office. Working in the world beneath the twofold sun, he prepares churches and adorns them with gifts and worship; he honors tombs and raises their steps with splendid distinction.

[Col. 0764D] He strengthens the absent through writings and the present through deeds, goes about on foot, and guards the Catholic faith against its savage enemy.

[Col. 0765A] Julius follows him. War is prepared against him by the enemy of Christ’s power. His tribulation tests, exercises, brings forth, and honors his virtue.

Glory brings him back from exile. Then he builds halls for the Ruler; then he prepares tombs for his pious friends. He establishes laws, sets the clergy’s dignities, settles disputes, provides memorials of faith, protects the innocent, restrains the unjustly guilty,

[Col. 0766A] and remains unmoved, persisting in honorable affairs.

After him Liberius is driven away by varied cunning: now because of the holy faith in the city, now because of the city’s adherence to the law, he is happily expelled from the divine chair. Yet he remains steadfast, fixed with firm strength.

He rebukes the king who had fallen into a second baptism, and because of this he is handed over to the swords and happily taken up among the stars.

But the palace he had built receives his remains after they have been recovered. Soon the harsh tribulation of the clergy exhausts many pious presbyters and others, and crowns them with death.

## CHAPTER II. On Saint Eusebius the bishop, and the presbyters Gregory and Orosius

[Col. 0765]

[Col. 0765A] The strong bishop Eusebius brandishes the weapons of faith and grieves that Liberius has yielded to a profane hand.

Therefore the enraged Constantius shuts him in a narrow cave,

[Col. 0765B] where he remains unconquered in friendly prayers, while the horns of the Titan fill the world seven times over.

From there he emerges from confinement and also enjoys peace far and wide.

The relics of the presbyter are carried away by Orosius and Gregory, who add them to Sixtus in the tomb of Callistus, and they place there for the man of God both title and honor.

When the tyrant receives these pious deeds as an act of devotion, he thrusts Gregory alive beneath the funerary urn. But Orosius carries him out while he is still breathing, and without delay joins the bones of the dead to the bones of the buried.

Driven from Cappadocia, Dionysius comes to the city.

[Col. 0766A] Here too, persisting bravely, he dies in exile, receiving the homeland he desired and the distinction of the seat.

When the great Basil restores the relics, blessed Ambrose receives them and deposits them with fitting honor.

[Col. 0766B] Eusebius then seeks the Scythian city of Basil. At last, returning from Vercellae and reclaiming his chair and the place of martyrdom, the pious man suffers the weapons of the furious.

After he had adorned the Psalter with the beginnings of his namesake, his mind receives the sought-for seat and his body receives the ether.

At that time the rhetorician Victorinus shone with eloquent light, illuminating Rome, which lay beneath him, with fluent teaching.

At last, as a veteran bearing his neck for the honor of faith, he attacks the serpent with salt and accompanies Paul with his light.

## CHAPTER III. On the holy Damasus, Jerome, and Siricius

[Col. 0765]

[Col. 0765B] From this point Damasus, after the men just mentioned, is regarded as the father of the City.

[Col. 0765C] Chosen by clergy and people with the senate’s approval, he beautifies the sacred churches of the martyrs, seeks their pious bodies, gathers them, raises them, honors them in measured verse, and publicly visits them on foot.

He is attacked by accusations but, with the approval of the synod, is purified. In words and writings he defends the honor of the faith.

He commands that psalmody sound forth day and night in praise; seeking a standard from Jerome, he receives and applies it.

By the law of the apostolic see he raises its summit, directing those beneath him while building them up with pure doctrine. He brings forth the heavenly lights of the ethereal Spirit,

[Col. 0766B] and, attacking the enemies with starry weapons, crushes them.

[Col. 0766C] As a victorious old man, he climbs the steep heights of heaven.

Against the wicked, Siricius sends decrees throughout the world. Removing those who follow perversity into exile, he purifies God’s flock and sets forth how carefully the rule of admission is to be observed and what strict measures are to be applied against the depraved.

He adorns the heavenly dove with divine law.

Anastasius rises after him and urges the people, together with the clergy, to rise toward the divine ones. With words from his mouth he drives away the profane, instructs the pious, prepares a temple, and receives the stars.

## CHAPTER IV. On the holy bishops Innocentius, Zosimus, and Boniface

[Col. 0765]

[Col. 0765C] After these, Innocentius condemns the guilty. Instructing the Church with statutes, he adorns the heavenly camp with worthy laws, and driving out the wicked, restores it pure from defilement.

Then he consecrates temples and dedicates gifts,

[Col. 0765D] appoints festivals for sacred rites and fasts on Saturdays, and, faithful in perseverance, seeks the lofty stars.

Zosimus does not grow weary of issuing statutes. He adorns the palace with ministers and the ministers with cloaks; he sets periods for seeking dignity and fixes salutary teachings, carefully transmitting doctrines,

[Col. 0766C] and confirms the rules that have been given by strict law.

Boniface, after rising above discordant controversy, then withdraws with a gentle spirit. He does not arrogantly claim the highest honors; once his rival has been expelled, he is received and strengthened.

[Col. 0766D] He contends that the chair should not be sought by intrigue. He judges that no woman should handle the sacred altar, nor should she seek decrees intended for lofty ministers; and that no cleric should be ordained under compulsion.

He adorns the temple where the burden of blessed Felicity rests with the pledges of that blessed woman.

## CHAPTER V. On the holy bishops Coelestinus and Sixtus

[Col. 0765]

[Col. 0765D] From this point Coelestinus administers heavenly rule and proclaims salvation to the upright and the wicked.

[Col. 0766D] He instructs the Church, appoints psalmody for the clergy, increases the work of religion, and beautifies the sacred sanctuary.

[Col. 0767A] He gives gifts to the temples of the Most High and adorns them with worship.

Sixtus follows him. He preserves the decrees of his predecessors and does not, when the sacred senate passes judgment, shrink from being judged by the censor. He purifies the stain and shows himself just.

The human enemy, worn down, is also punished by heavenly judgment. The pope, showing mercy to the profane man,

[Col. 0768A] preserves the heavenly commands amid the enemy’s funeral rites. He relieves the churches and enriches them with many gifts.
