With him clearly directing affairs, royal gifts shine forth. In sacred verse he honors the holy men and dedicates them in enduring bronze; joined with these men, he too is celebrated in remembered praise.

## CHAPTER VI. On the holy bishops Leo, Hilary, and Simplicius

[Col. 0767]

[Col. 0767A] From this point the deeds of the high-sounding Leo are woven into song.

By his pious authority he submits the decrees of Chalcedon for Augustus’ consideration and, through this undertaking, convenes the Fathers.

The union of the two natures, joined in one Christ, is expressed. Those who sever the bonds belonging to the persons are condemned, as are those who join together what must not be mingled.

He repeatedly strengthens the Fathers’ commands with rational doctrine. He increases their rights, admonishes kings, honors the Fathers according to due order, renovates and adorns temples, restores those worn down by wars,

[Col. 0767B] and polishes their inward and outward beauty through illustrious action.

Hilary follows him. He issues decrees, sends them throughout the world, urges that they be followed, and condemns their opposites.

[Col. 0768A] He makes the pious dove flourish through worship and edicts. He marks the triumphs of the saints in much bronze, adorns the golden wood of the cross with gems and gold, raises buildings, fashions precious ornaments, and gathers together the Fathers, books, and sacred ministers.

Through him Victorius shines in the paschal reckoning.

Then Simplicius ascends the heights of the lofty chair. In honor of his king, he dedicates adorned halls; he establishes offices, supports the afflicted with medicine, strengthens the sick, and strikes down the insolent with a drawn sword.

[Col. 0768B] He sows heavenly laws and accompanies sacred matters with a twofold gift.

## CHAPTER VII. On the holy bishops Felix and Anastasius

[Col. 0767]

[Col. 0767B] Afterwards Felix administers the governance of the Church. He overthrows heresies, adapts laws for those who return, examines frauds, and destroys guilt and what is harmful.

Gelasius, rightly following Felix’s rule, cuts apart errors, drives the profane from the city, burns crimes, releases the bonds of the wretched, enlarges the clergy, protects the needy common people, cultivates the Church, and saves Rome from danger.

[Col. 0767C] He establishes decrees for sacred matters and gives aid to those driven away by violence.

[Col. 0768B] By his virtue he strikes the difficult and brings back the compliant. Opening his breast to all, he shines through compassion.

He cleans, dedicates, and raises temples, establishes melodies, defends heavenly things, and shines with divine weapons.

After him Anastasius rises, giving strength to peace. As Christ’s legate, proud in the gift of peace, he moves the like-named Augustus and asks him to proclaim peace.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Saint Symmachus the pope and Paschasius the deacon

[Col. 0767]

[Col. 0767C] Symmachus, entering into varied conflict, grows in strength.

When the two parties, separated from one another, each seek the summit, they undergo the king’s judgment. The more equitable cause is evident on his side. The bishop sits and then judges that disagreements, swords, and unlawful favor must be avoided, and that honors worthy of so great a see must be bestowed.

His rival, having obtained rule over the people of Nuceria, feels his father’s compassionate affection flourishing

[Col. 0767D] and, ungrateful, takes pride in gifts freely given.

Then war rises again, and Laurentius reclaims the city. A wicked band, driven by envy, stirs up savage tumult. The just man is attacked with accusations and an unjust charge.

The king is persuaded to send a censor to Rome. After the Fathers have been summoned, the bishop clears himself of the insults. Both the censor and the invader are crushed by their presumptuous claim of authority; honor is restored, and glory added to the just man increases.

As bronze grows bright when fired in fierce furnaces, so wars against the pious increase, and insignia increase through wars. A reckless crowd rushes upon the quiet and cuts them down, but to these men the lofty laurel nevertheless grants the heavens.

The supporters, condemned by divine judgment, are punished and shown to have undergone a penalty corresponding to their merits.

Among them the radiant Paschasius, a deacon of the city,

[Col. 0768C] suffered the loss of the crown he was to receive, and, it is said, was assigned as a minister to the heat of the baths.

Nevertheless, he had shone through distinguished deeds and had grown in excellence. He despised himself, was notable for an upright life, and from childhood had been accompanied by compassion for the needy.

He had published teachings of truth, richly seasoned with wit, and in them, through the divine Spirit, he delivered mysteries worthy of the faith. From the edge of his garment we learn that he received salvation after it had escaped the black throngs;

[Col. 0768D] and he is judged to have deserved forgiveness through his pious deeds.

He appeared openly before Germanus. By his attendance he inspires fear, confesses his punishment and error, asks for help, and receives relief through prayers.

Once the owner of a small estate at Centumcellae, after death he was driven amid the fiery vapors of the waters and assigned to serve the presbyter John. He wavers beneath the double crown of that service, but rejoices that he has been rescued by the gift of having served at the baths.

Yet the blessed shepherd does not cease to preserve the flocks, drive out the profane, and put the wolves to flight.

He burns images and books, drives away the impious, and adorns Christ’s house with doctrine and worship. He sows many gifts in buildings, painting ceilings with gems; he restores new structures and repairs those that are collapsing.

No less persistently, he gives assistance to saints thrust into exile; he redeems them and grants them release from chains.

[Col. 0769A] He prepares heavenly kingdoms for those committed to him through his resources, by which he shines when admitted and elevated to the transferred height.

## CHAPTER IX. On the holy Pope Hormisdas and the bishops Germanus and Remigius

[Col. 0769]

[Col. 0769A] From this point Hormisdas cultivates the clergy, provides psalmody, raises temples, and labors to settle disputes through peace.

He strives to calm the arrogant disturbances of the Greeks. Although he is kept from the highest offices, he does not abandon his lofty undertaking; even when Augustus refuses, he does not delay in repeatedly sending kindly envoys.

The emperor, attempting to win him with gifts, accomplishes nothing either by force or payment. Moreover, he unworthily denies hospitality to those who have been expelled and proudly rejects the sacred rights.

Nor is there delay before he feels the anger of the neglected divine power: struck and overwhelmed by a heavenly weapon in his final hour, he reveals through his burial that royal scepters ought to submit to sacred authority.

After the unjust ruler has been punished, the righteous Justin gains the empire and seeks Peter’s see under the sign of peace,

[Col. 0769B] bringing treaties worthy of it after long admonitions and deeds.

The vows of the Father smile upon him. Sincere and faithful men, tested by their virtue, are chosen to establish peace. Capua gives Germanus, worthy of so great a gift.

Thus the lofty grace of Peter’s legates shines forth. Augustus, together with the princes and the holy throng, comes out from the royal city to meet him from afar and humbly receives the sacred limbs of the supreme head.

The wicked are terrified; the kindly rejoice in compassion. The heights of the heavenly Church are joined together in peace,

[Col. 0770A] and the guilty, rebels against light and peace, are condemned.

Impiety is overcome, the deadly ulcer is cut away, and, once the corruption has been removed, the limbs stand in joyful health.

The East rejoices in peace, and the South rejoices that it has been restored. Happy Africa rises to resume the rights that have been lifted up. Toward the setting sun, from the eastern region, the sacred children praise the Lord with the voice of their teacher, having been saved.

Gaul too does not remain without the summit of teaching. It exults in radiant Remigius, the star of heaven.

As a good tiller of the earth, he strives with the fruitful plow of faith to cleave the hearts of the barbarians, making the barbarian fields fruitful with divine seed. Through the honor of a new harvest, enriched by the abundance of grace, he strives with the first fruits to adorn the holy chair of Cephas.

[Col. 0770B] Meanwhile Clodoveus, king in Christ and his son, shining with the precious light of gold and gems, is the glory of Remigius through the governance of the kingdom he has obtained.

As an excellent parent and devoted pupil of his father, he sends pious gifts to the outstanding primate of Christ. He also sends the distinguished vestments that Greece has given for peace.

Augustus and the kings honor the city with adornments. While they read the illustrious lineage of the pious under Peter’s honor, the pope also prepares hearts and beautifies temples.

Thus he is given both in mind to heaven and in body to the temple.

## CHAPTER X. On Pope John, Symmachus, Patricius, and Boethius

[Col. 0769]

[Col. 0769C] Afterwards supreme grace grants John the rights of the first see and gives him the distinguished care of arranging matters, lest the sword devour Ausonia, where Greece is approached, and where the lofty legate of Peter receives those worthy of him.

As he travels, a horse is consecrated for him. The animal, accustomed to carrying a woman, then refuses the rider of the consecrated body; but it rejoices to serve the sacred man and to undertake doubled labor.

The summits of the lofty steps of honor come forward to meet the outstanding father. So that saving light may open to blind senses, he restores light to blinded eyes and the light returned enters gates long closed. Through his light-bearing hand, darkness flees the passages he has touched, and, while the people marvel, new lights shine openly.

The summit is brought low and immense pride is bent. The man who rules the world bows before the pupil of Cephas.

[Col. 0769D] The one who asks is entreated; he gives and obtains at once. He secures peace and bestows lofty honor. Savage fury is tortured beneath this honor of the pious.

He gives those who burn with light to the darkness, and burns those by whom darkness is kindled. Even the father himself is surrounded by the custody of the wicked.

He emerges from the cave, and neither royal barriers suffice to hold the blessed man nor can they deprive him of his heavenly lot.

He had adorned churches and restored the tombs of the Fathers. The worthy relics, recalled, regain the chair that had been given. Before long, torments seized the savage tyrant and consigned him to the perpetual flames due him.

[Col. 0770C] Yet the savage beast had already inflicted monstrous disasters, attacking in war the pious walls of peace through deceit.

The illustrious Symmachus, his son-in-law, and Boethius had suffered the gifts of the precious crown by the sword.

But Patricius, stripped of his belt, with bare feet and bound hands, is bound by Pope John and plunged into Vulcan's fire-vomiting cauldron.

Here the consul Symmachus raises his daughter Galla, named after him, in holy practices and pours forth pious lights.

Given to a marriage-bed and widowed in that very year, she arranges to serve God, caring nothing for the years of tender age, nor for the wealth or honors of the world. She does not fear the shame marked by the fire of her blood, nor the barbarity, nor does she preserve womanly hair.

[Col. 0770D] She considers nothing shameful in Christ except to deceive him, and gives herself with all her heart to the service of heaven.

She submits herself to chaste camps and, steadfast, continues for many years. With kindly hands and mind, she lavishly attends to the poor and persists in honorable vows.

While she is being called to the palm and the heavenly kingdoms, her body is shaken, but she is raised in heavenly peace.

She deserves Peter’s consolation, and to see his face and hear his words. She hears worthy pious sayings and returns her own voice; she is summoned to heaven and learns that her sins have been forgiven.

[Col. 0771A] She also hears the prayer that the company of her beloved sister should accompany her, and asks that the blessed companion of her request be permitted to follow.

After a month, she is to undertake the journey. She shines forth as she departs in fulfillment of her vow, and the promised consolations follow.

[Col. 0772A] Thus the words of the apostolic covenant are fulfilled.

## CHAPTER XI. On the holy bishops Felix, Boniface, and Mercurius

[Col. 0771]

[Col. 0771A] Felix happily exercises the honor of the Church. He dedicates statutes, raises pious buildings, restores those that have collapsed, lifts up the divine column, and beautifies sacred laws.

He judges that the mysteries should be celebrated only in chapels.

[Col. 0772A] Enjoying peace and shining in peace, he rests beneath peace.

Then Boniface follows in divine order and assists the clergy.

After him Mercurius relieves hunger and danger and fills the sacred places of the pious.

## CHAPTER XII. On the holy Agapitus, Cassiodorus, and Vigilius

[Col. 0771]

[Col. 0771B] From this point the pious Agapitus breaks the accumulated bonds, reconciles the flock, burns away the weight of chains, brings back the wandering sheep, and restores peace to the fold.

He also proceeds to the Greeks and brings peace to the kings. Received with pious honor, he performs divine works: he restores movement to the lame and gives speech to the mute.

He approaches Augustus and undertakes the duties of piety. He rebukes error, despises threatening kingdoms, cuts apart the clouds, and reveals the hidden things of deceit.

He also expels the serpent from the sacred places, exposes it lying in darkness, and cleanses the shrines of its deadly poison.

The purified people shine. Augustus, rejoicing, casts down his distinguished honor and, falling forward, adores the footsteps of the father. Thus the holy summit, freed from defilement, is consecrated.

The pope retains what he has sought; with affairs restored according to his vows,

[Col. 0771C] supreme peace chooses to settle the long-standing struggle, and they bring back to Rome victorious limbs in triumph.

Under this bishop’s splendor, the senator Cassiodorus submits himself to the service of the Lamb. Applying clear doctrines to the devout, he handles the songs of David, glorifying the poems that resound upon the heavenly lyre.

Illuminating the pious ranks with divine light, he raises both their minds and their bodies through a twofold nourishment.

Silverius assumes the lofty office in an unprecedented manner. When the clergy has been bound, fate soon seizes the tyrant. Wars wear down the homeland; Rome is burdened by siege. Savage famine rises, pestilence rages, and the sword,

after exacting enough slaughter, seeks vengeance upon the pope.

But already firm and strong in Peter’s seat, he receives the struggle and chooses to stand before Augustus’ face.

[Col. 0771D] Then he is driven from his own city, never to be restored to it; by deceitful power he is ensnared, deprived of his dignity, harassed unjustly, driven into exile, and crowned as a confessor.

At his tomb, when diseases and vices have been driven away, the glory given on earth reveals him as received into heaven.

Vigilius enters upon the governance and lot of the deposed man.

Peace smiles upon the West. With the enemy captured, the city triumphs. The deceit of Africa restores rule according to the ancient law.

Glory from the spoils is given as a gift to Peter the protector. Broad assistance and ready consolations are brought to the needy, and the servants of God are nourished by the gift of compassion.

The verses on apostolic struggle and triumph, inscribed by a radiant pen and adorned with shining brilliance,

[Col. 0772B] the author dedicates to this bishop with the Fathers’ favor.

The fury known to his predecessor also tears him away. By imperial command he is pressed to recall the chelydrus, a water-snake forbidden by the eminent Fathers to defile the sanctuary, and is asked to fulfill the pledges of a rash pronouncement.

He refuses, declares this foolish, and repents of what has been undertaken. He remembers that he holds the office and the chair of Peter, approves the laws of his ancestors, and strengthens their deeds.

A furious hand rises. Vengeance seeks the patron against the father. The author is accused of the crime of death, and he is ordered to be brought before the judge, unless Peter alone should keep his disciple.

He is found within Cecilia’s enclosure, giving gifts to the people. Seized and placed in a boat, he is driven upon the waters of the Tiber. From there he brings blessings to the people who continue to follow him.

[Col. 0772C] He receives curses amid insults; for the sake of peace he encounters a duel. He goes out through the howling perverse crowd. The lovers of the father accompany him as he cuts across the backwaters of the river.

Driven to the city of Catania, he rejoices to hand over his gifts to the subordinate clergy.

From there, after the guardians of the sacred palace have been bound, he enters the city against the threatening Fathers and flock.

The devoted people seize the father, while the nobles issue savage commands. A harsh inquiry ensues; the dispute is prolonged, and the quarrel consumes two such years.

The father denounces the impious scepters and endures savage, shameful lashes with a calm countenance, bearing insults with a gentle mind.

Then greater troubles follow: he is torn away from the pious altars. A rope binds his neck, providing a spectacle to all.

The city, struck with fear, is astonished that one accustomed to release others is bound. Refusing to release the robber, it binds him like a robber.

He is plunged into darkness and is said to receive only a little daily bread and water. He considers that he has undergone what he deserved and agrees that what is due should be repaid according to his deeds.

The clergy is worn down in exile, and the punishment of the guilty …

## Source-adjudicated readings for compressed and ambiguous passages

The following readings replace the corresponding over-smoothed sentences above. They retain the poem’s compressed syntax where the surviving Latin does not securely identify every relation.

### Chapter X

[Col. 0759B] [Col. 0759C] Gallicanus, raised by the renowned emperor and by the insignia of victory, asks for Constantia, who is dedicated to Christ by a perpetual bond, as his wife. The emperor is anxious because he knows that his daughter could be killed rather than violated. Constantia proposes the condition that Gallicanus first conquer the Scythians. During the Thracian campaign the prospective bridegroom, shut within a city and afraid to oppose his few standards to the Scythian multitude, offers sacrifices at the altars of Mars. As the enemy grows stronger and the Romans abandon their standards, he receives a harbor of salvation from Constantia’s attendants or officers, Paul and John: they advise him to declare a vow to God, through which he will be delivered by Christ and become more illustrious as victor. After the heavenly warrior carrying the cross leads him into the enemy camp, the barbarian king falls at Gallicanus’ feet and begs for his own life and his people’s blood to be spared; he and his children are granted this, and the Thracians are freed from their enemy under a promise of tribute.

[Col. 0760B] The tribune and the restored soldiers then prepare to perform Christ’s service. Gallicanus is consecrated, vows to abstain from marriage, and goes first to Peter’s sacred threshold before entering Rome. He exchanges the insignia of office for the higher citadel of his calling, frees five thousand household slaves, endows them with fields and dwellings, and serves the needy with Hilarinus. At Ostia he builds a church for Christ. Lawrence appears and urges him to establish a building for his cult; Gallicanus completes the command and calls it *Laurentia*. The following verses say, with compressed agents, that a bishop does not favor granting what petitioners ask but chooses one who may shine with this distinction, and that the distributor of gifts repays the service with such glorious power that those endowed with spiritual craft are cleansed at his appearances.

[Col. 0760C] When Julian takes public power, he forbids poor Christians to possess anything and seizes Gallicanus’ houses, which had relieved the needy. Anyone entering to post title or collect rent is seized by an avenging demon or afflicted with leprosy. The spirits say that the occupiers cannot escape unless Gallicanus sacrifices to the gods. Because no one dares test him, the savage court official carries the imperial order that he sacrifice, leave Italy, or depart its borders after surrendering his property. He goes to Alexandria, freely joins Christ’s confessors for a year, and then seeks the desert. Pursued there, he joyfully receives the sword after refusing incense to the gods. A church is dedicated to his name, where Christ’s gifts shine in the martyr’s honor.

### Chapter XI

[Col. 0761B] John and Paul answer Julian: “Let us not do you this injury, that we should prefer any mortal to you; we prefer to you the ruler of heaven, sea, and earth, who made everything that exists. Therefore, foreseeing the heavenly King’s anger, we flee the glory of a temporal man. Know that we shall no longer go to the palace to pay court by greeting you.” Julian grants ten days for them to disclose their decision and says that they must join his fellowship willingly or be punished as public enemies.

Terentianus finds them praying at home and says that the emperor has sent a golden image of Jupiter: they must burn incense or the sword will cross their necks, so that men reared in the palace will not be killed before the common people. After they refuse, he secretly beheads and buries them at home and spreads the claim that Caesar ordered them into exile. After Julian’s fall, Terentianus’ son, driven by a spirit, cries that he is being burned by the blessed brothers. The father falls on his face, proclaims his sins, seeks baptism, and weeps at their tomb until his son is released. Terentianus then makes known on trustworthy written pages both the acts of their passion and his own dreadful confession, cleansed by tears.

### Chapter XII

[Col. 0762C] The apostate deserter consecrates many to Christ by blessed death. As the defeated man’s savage anger grows against public affairs, he consigns the faithful to custody. Januarius, arrested under a dreadful law, is assigned to Gordianus: the gracious priest of the pious King is given to the savage deputy of the impious ruler. Gordianus receives his modest words, is filled with the Spirit of faith, and is baptized with his wife Marina; more than fifty servants follow their masters to the sacred font. When this reaches the savage judge, he strikes both men through written orders, appoints another judge over Gordianus, returns him to the public dungeon, and orders his chaste wife to serve peasants at Aquae Salviae. Clementianus brings out Gordianus in chains; after a beating with lead and an unbroken heavenly confession, he gains heaven by beheading. A sleepless guard protects the body exposed to dogs. Christians carry it away at night and place it at the first milestone, where the remains of Epimachus had already been gathered. One joyful feast day raises the two martyrs together with equal honor.

### Chapter XIII

The tyrant learns that Pigmenius, the presbyter of a Roman titular church, has buried the pious bodies laid low by the ruler’s fury. He orders Pigmenius to withdraw from Rome and promises to restore rewards because he is being sent into exile, ashamed to strike down his own foster-father at the first command. Pigmenius goes to Persia, where his bodily sight is taken from him although his mind’s light remains. He is directed to return to Rome and seek the cause of his palm. A boy guides his steps back. His former pupil meets him, riding high in a golden carriage and swollen with thanks to the gods, and in Acherontic fury orders him cast headlong into the Tiber. His soul returns to heaven; his earthly remains receive a tomb with Abdon and Sennen.

### Chapter XIV

[Col. 0763B] The syntax presents Surana, a pagan woman blinded in eyes and heart, breaking into the cell with her son. She is handed, now instructed in faith, to Bishop Satyrus; seeing the first light of her faith, he orders fasting, gives ashes for a bed and harsh sackcloth for clothing, instructs and baptizes her, and her only son Herculius enters the water with her. Her darkened brow at once recovers sight, and she recognizes her child. Apronianus then brings his son, stunned by a dreadful spirit, to Donatus; Donatus, joined by Hilarinus and the bishop, restores the boy through prayer.

Eustasius had hidden tax money in the earth, and his wife Eufrasina died. Under pressure from a grim collector, he seeks Donatus’ help. Donatus goes to the tomb, invokes the dead woman in Christ’s name, adds an adjuration by the one fixed to the cross, and asks what became of the stolen treasury money. Eufrasina answers from the grave: they go to the house indicated, question the “barking treasure” or guarded hoard in the poem’s compressed wording, bring out the known bronze, and Eustasius goes away freed from his burden. Later, when a pagan assault shatters the consecrated chalice during the mysteries, Donatus gathers the fragments, prays in tears, and restores it to its former whole form. Fewer than eighty souls are said to be converted by the sight. Donatus and Hilarinus are then ordered to offer incense to stones; Donatus’ face is battered with stones, Hilarinus is beaten with clubs and leaves the tested earth for the sought heaven, and Donatus is imprisoned and finally beheaded.

### Chapter XV

Priscus the priest and Priscillianus the cleric receive matching crowns, and Benedicta follows their path. Faustus joins the King’s scepters in triumph. Dafrosa, Faustus’ wife, is exiled after her husband’s glory, denied her homeland, and then taken from earth to heaven by the sword. Their daughters are Biviana and Demetria. Demetria, led before the enemy, makes the glory of her confession shine and places her mind among the heavenly stars. The presbyter John gathers her body from the forum in a praiseworthy theft at the mournful spectacle described as *sole bino*, “under a twin sun,” whose precise reference the poem does not explain, and joins it in burial to her pious parents, with whom he had already joined her sister’s remains. Julian orders John beheaded at Phoebus’ altar. Concordius, a priest adorned with an equal lot, gathers John’s body, honors it with due observance, and places the blessed martyr among the martyrs.

### Book X, Chapters I–VII

Mark is the first after Sylvester to undertake the sacred mysteries of office. The phrase *gemino quae solis in orbe* modifies the poem’s compressed account of that office and should not be expanded into a separate institutional claim. Mark builds and adorns churches, honors tombs, strengthens the absent by writings and those present by deeds, goes about on foot, and protects the Catholic faith from its savage enemy. Julius follows, suffers conflict and exile, builds churches and martyrs’ tombs, establishes laws and clerical ranks, settles disputes, protects the innocent, and restrains those guilty without right. Liberius is displaced by shifting stratagems, first from the city for holy faith and then, in the poem’s difficult wording, “from the city of law’s path,” but remains firm. He rebukes “the fallen king with a double baptism”; the source supplies no further theological explanation of *duplici baptismate*. He is taken by swords to the stars, and a harsh persecution then crowns presbyters and others with death.

Eusebius grieves that Liberius yielded to a profane hand. Constantius shuts him in a confined cave, where he persists for the seven circuits of the sun. Orosius and Gregory carry away his remains and add them to the tomb of Sixtus Callistus; when Gregory is buried alive under the same tomb, Orosius carries him out while he still breathes and after his death joins his bones to those already buried. The next relations remain compressed: Dionysius, driven out, goes to a city of the Cappadocians and dies in exile; Ambrose receives relics returned by Basil the Great and buries them honorably; Eusebius then seeks “the city of Basil of Scythia,” returns to Vercellae and his chair, and suffers the weapons of raging men after adorning a namesake’s Psalter with compositions. Victorinus teaches rhetoric at Rome, then as a veteran of the faith opposes the serpent with salt and accompanies Paul with light.

Damasus is chosen by clergy and people with the senate’s favor, honors martyrs and their bodies, is attacked by reproaches and cleared by a synod, defends the faith, orders psalmody by night and day, and adopts the norm at Jerome’s request and delivery. Siricius sends decrees against unspeakable offenders, exiles followers of error, and sets out both the cautious rule for reception and the strict rule for the perverse. Innocentius condemns offenders, establishes laws, dedicates churches and gifts, appoints feasts for sacred rites and Saturday fasts. Zosimus establishes provisions for the church, ministers, pallia, and the times for seeking office. Boniface rejects intrigue for the see, bars women from handling the sacred altar or seeking decrees for higher ministers, and forbids compelled clerical ordination.

In the difficult Sixtus passage, an enemy crushed by human judgment is also punished by divine judgment, while the pope pities the profane man’s penalty and keeps heaven’s commands amid his enemy’s death. Leo’s Chalcedonian statement expresses the bond of two natures joined in the one Christ and condemns both those who sever the bonds attached to persons and those who join what must not be mixed. Hilarus promulgates and defends decrees, adorns churches and the cross, gathers Fathers, books, and sacred ministers, and is associated with Victorius’ paschal order. Simplicius establishes offices, supports the injured and sick, strikes the obstinate, and joins sacred matters with a twofold gift. Felix combats heresy; Gelasius, who follows Felix in governance, disperses errors, drives the profane from the city, aids the needy, saves Rome from danger, and establishes decrees. Anastasius is presented as Christ’s envoy of peace seeking peace from his imperial namesake.

### Book X, Chapter VIII

Paschasius, one of the condemned supporters, was a brilliant Roman deacon who lost the crown he was to receive and, it is said, was assigned to serve in the heat of the baths. Yet he had shone in excellent deeds, mercy toward the needy, and writings full of truth. The poem says that “salvation snatched from the extremity of his garment” made the black companies flee as blessed spoils; it does not specify a fuller episode. He appears openly to Germanus, acknowledges his error and punishment, and asks help. Once the owner of an estate at Centumcellae, after death he was driven into the fiery vapors of the waters and assigned as a minister to the presbyter John; wavering under the double endowment of a crown, he rejoices, once rescued by that service, to have served at the baths. The remaining lines return to Symmachus’ pastoral acts: guarding flocks, expelling the profane and wolves, burning idols and books, adorning Christ’s house, repairing buildings, helping exiles, freeing captives, and using entrusted talents to prepare heavenly kingdoms.

### Book X, Chapter IX

Hormisdas repeatedly sends kindly admonitions in his effort to reconcile the Greeks. The emperor refuses the intermediaries, tries them with gifts, denies shelter to those unjustly driven out, and rejects sacred law. Struck by heavenly punishment, he reveals through his death that royal power must submit to sacred authority. Justin gains the empire after the just punishment of the unjust man and seeks Peter’s see under the omen of peace. Germanus of Capua is chosen as envoy; the emperor and clergy go out from the royal city and humbly receive the members of the supreme head. East and South rejoice in restored peace, Africa resumes rights that had been taken away, and from the eastern climate toward sunset the saved children praise the Lord in their sacred teacher’s words. Gaul too shines through Remigius: as a good cultivator he cleaves barbarian hearts with faith’s plough and offers the first fruits of a new harvest to Peter’s chair. Clodoveus is called “king in Christ” and Remigius’ son, a devoted pupil who sends gifts; the source does not make him Remigius’ biological son.

### Book X, Chapter X

John receives the rights of the first see and is sent so that the sword may not devour Italy where Greece is approached. A horse consecrated for his journey thereafter refuses a female rider. John restores sight to blind eyes by touch, humbles imperial pride, asks and is himself entreated, gives and obtains, and secures peace and honor. The compressed line *Dat tenebris qui luce nitent, quibus uritur urit* means approximately, “He consigns to darkness those who shine with light; he burns with the fires by which he is burned”; the shifting subject is not secure. The savage ruler’s custody surrounds John himself, but he comes forth from confinement, and royal barriers cannot deprive him of heaven. The relics he had worthily restored seek again the chair once given, while torment soon carries off the cruel tyrant to perpetual flames.

The “savage beast” had already killed Symmachus, his son-in-law, and Boethius by the sword. Patricius, stripped of his belt, barefoot and with hands bound, is bound by Pope John and plunged into Vulcan’s fire-vomiting cauldron. Symmachus’ daughter Galla, widowed in the year of her marriage, devotes herself to God despite youth, wealth, status, the mark of her fiery blood, barbarous circumstances, and the concern of a woman’s body hair. Peter appears, consoles her, tells her sins are forgiven, and calls her to heaven. She asks that her beloved sister be permitted to accompany her; she hears that the blessed sister will follow after one month. The wording concerns the sister’s companionship, not Peter’s sister.

### Book X, Chapters XI–XII

Felix limits celebration of the mysteries to consecrated chapels. Boniface aids the clergy against hunger and danger; Mercurius then supplies the sacred places of the faithful. Agapitus reconciles the flock, goes to the Greeks, confronts the emperor, exposes error and fraud, and purges the sanctuary; after his death the victorious remains are brought back to Rome. Cassiodorus, “a senator under the splendor of this bishop” in the poem’s compressed construction, submits to the Lamb’s service, treats David’s songs, and lifts minds and bodies by a twofold nourishment.

Silverius’ irregular elevation is followed by war, famine, plague, deposition, deceit, loss of dignity, exile, and a confessor’s crown. Vigilius succeeds to the lot and rule of the deposed man. The “ploughman” or poet (*arator*) dedicates the inscribed emblems of apostolic struggle and triumph to this bishop with the Fathers’ favor. Vigilius is ordered by the imperial ruler to recall the *chelydrus*, the “water-serpent,” forbidden by the distinguished Fathers to defile the sanctuary, and is asked to discharge the agreements of a headlong mouth. He refuses, calls himself foolish and repents of his words, remembers that he holds Peter’s place and chair, and confirms the laws and acts of his predecessors. In the next compressed clause, both a patron and an author of deadly crime are blamed “with lava-stones” (*lavicis*); the grammar does not warrant turning it into an accusation against an unspecified literary author.

[Col. 0772D] Vigilius is found giving gifts to the people in Saint Cecilia’s precinct, seized, put into a boat, and taken down the Tiber while blessing the following people. He reaches Catania and gives sacred gifts to its clergy. Back in the city he faces a long inquiry and conflict, is torn from the altars, bound by the neck, imprisoned in darkness, and allotted only a little daily bread and water. “Refusing to release the robber, he is bound like a robber” preserves the poem’s paradox. The supplied section ends with the incomplete clause: “The clergy is worn down by exile, and by the penalty of the guilty …”

It is afflicted. Soon an equal vengeance overtakes the savage people:

Hostile barbarism, rushing upon it with iron, besieges the city;  
famine shakes it with pestilence and constrains the pitiless to dreadful deeds.  
It also attacks the people deprived of private consolation,  
but reverence for Peter commands that they be spared.

The Fathers flee, and, desolate, duly seek the sister of their mother,  
and bring back the supports they had sought.  
A message is also sent to Rome; the Quirites are saved from the enemy,  
and, once saved, they ask that their father’s rule be restored to them.  
The glory of victory delights Augustus by these deeds,

[Col. 0773A] and, moved, he recalls the pope, who had been asking with prayers,  
restores to him what had been conferred, and strengthens him with the clergy’s support.

He then came with his companions to Syracuse,  
[Col. 0774A] but, arriving there, met the final destiny of death through a grave illness.  
Rome receives back the pledge that had been deposited.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the two Pelagiuses, and also on the bishops John and Benedict

[Col. 0773]

[Col. 0773A] Pelagius, while a modest senate of Fathers governed,  
was advanced to sacred office, though suspected by the pope of a crime deserving punishment.  
With the city compelled, he proved himself innocent,  
and warned and decreed that no one should seek the summit of the Church  
by means of a petty profit or grasp after honor.

Restoring the altars he adorned, he established foundations for the churches  
and undertook the shrine of Peter beneath the roof.  
John followed, restoring the tombs of the saints,  
which he cultivated with pure affection and venerated with honor;  
he adorned them at his own expense, consecrated them,  
and supplied what was incomplete.

[Col. 0773B] When the enemies had been crushed, peace was brought to the ungrateful homeland,  
which, puffed up, struggled to drive away its benefactor.  
[Col. 0774A] He, on the contrary, strove to retain the ruler, to protect the city,  
and to continue to the very end on behalf of holy peace.

Soon the times of Benedict were shaken by famine and the sword,  
and twofold punishment wore down Ausonia.  
But, through God’s mercy, the Nile brought relief.

Pelagius followed him and died “by the custom of the sea” [reading uncertain; the verse is corrupt].  
Indeed waves rose with excessive disasters.  
On one side the city was driven by savage swords, on the other by storms;  
a flood, and the dangers deemed those of the first age,  
which the nurturing power had been able to gather into beauty  
and had not ceased to adorn.

[Col. 0774B] Here the father surrounds the relics of Peter with silver and gold  
and prepares holy gifts for other churches.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Saint Gregory and his relatives

[Col. 0773]

[Col. 0773B] Here the renowned heights of Gregory rise:  
the ever-watchful guardian of the flock, attentive to the folds and the sentry-posts,  
he leads those whom he has fed by deeds and beginnings toward heaven.

Just from childhood, steadfast, and illustrious by blood:  
his great-grandfather Felix confirms this, as do his blessed aunts  
Tarsilla and Emiliana, sisters who, consecrated in mind,  
grew through pious increases in love of the Thunderer.

[Col. 0773C] While living in the body on earth, they had lifted their hearts to heaven.  
Of them, Tarsilla, whose name came first in the title,  
who was adorning the journey, was the first to receive a radiant heavenly home,  
when Felix called her by the heavenly light.  
Jesus, arbiter of the world, does not disdain to look upon her as she departs;  
she alone, receiving him, orders those standing by to withdraw,  
and, following him above the stars, passes beyond earthly bonds.

A nectarous fragrance bears witness that the bearer of the pious gifts had come,  
full of the gift of paradise, scattering the fragrant odor of a worthy work.  
The deeds themselves mark her body, with her elbows and knees uncovered.  
Inviting her sister to the feasts of light before long,  
he removes earthly cares, promises fellowship,  
and leads her into joyful choirs and the delights of heaven.

[Col. 0773D] Stenima, a descendant, adorned his lineage with noble character;  
he raised it by his abilities and fashioned it through excellent studies.

The young Gregory was nourished on maternal legumes,  
neither softened by the hearth nor merely scattered in liquid water.  
A man named Charaxas, pretending to be needy and pressed by shipwreck,  
approached him, seeking assistance.  
After Gregory had paid him eighteen coins from his purse,  
and after the man insistently complained that much had perished from him,  
he added his mother’s bowl and a basket of legumes.

Later, when he ordered that twelve dishes be brought to the poor who had been summoned,  
he saw that more people were sitting there than the number commanded.  
The servant could not ascertain the number of those who had been ordered,  
but Gregory alone was able to see the one guest who remained,  
changing his appearance in various ways at various hours.  
Gregory sent the others away and led him into a hidden place.

[Col. 0774B] He asked his appearance and name. The man refused to disclose  
any indication of his name, but revealed this remarkable fact:  
he had been brought out of shipwreck by him to whom Gregory had given  
the gifts contained in the vessel, which his mother Silvia had bequeathed to him.  
He declared with certainty that he would assume the seat and rule of Peter,  
as had been arranged by the highest governance.

[Col. 0774C] He also revealed himself as a heavenly being and declared the terror  
of the astonished man, explaining that he had been sent by him  
as guardian of his duties and as bearer of his prayers above the stars.

Thus, transcending the slippery joys of the world,  
he lifts his mind toward the highest rays, ready to despise all things,  
to burn for God alone, and to gain heaven by merits.  
When the reckoning of the matters that had been entrusted to him became clear,  
he announced what he carried in his mind and opened whatever had lain hidden in his heart.  
Whatever he possessed through vain piety he relinquished;  
he subjected it to worship and sacred observances, and gave it to the needy.  
Having himself become needy, he followed Christ in poverty.

Placing the ranks of the army in the fitting order of heaven,  
he arranges, cherishes, exercises, governs, and adorns them.  
Among the exposed and armed he brandishes the struggle;  
for, laying aside the covering of the military cloak and its flashing gems,

[Col. 0774D] he does not shrink from clothing that is dirty with poverty.  
Indeed, he himself, poor, ministers to Christ’s poor.

Rich in virtues, for whom wisdom is more precious than gold;  
the summits of virtue are more valuable to him than the gleam of stones;  
he possesses heavenly grace as wealth and conduct as adornment.  
All earthly things lie beneath him; only heavenly things shine in his mind.  
Among them he moves, passing through bodily light,  
aiming at the goal and seeking rewards;  
he fits nothing earthly to himself and no longer seeks anything carnal,  
neither possessing nor allowing anything to be possessed by those who inhabit his enclosures.

Hence, if anyone who preserves what belongs to him is found not to be free from this fault,  
the Just One teaches the matter by the example of the unjust,  
the careless guardian of a miser’s burden.

Gold brought him no profit, nor did great sums of money  
twist him through poisons thrust among medicines.

[Col. 0775A] His father, treating him with a harsh medicine,  
healed the mind of the one who tended bodies through the torments of the body.  
While striking him in death, he brought many back from death;  
while lifting him from death, he surrendered the life-giving gift.

Nor did the Lord permit so great a remedy to remain hidden,  
but, after Gregory had died, revealed its benefits to his brother who was still alive.

Nor did a brother who had given him three coins escape a similar punishment  
and the relief of assistance.  
The father of the monastery, betrayed by his speech, was bound;  
Gregory was carried away, still not freed from his bonds,  
and was seen promising the abbot that he had been shut up in prison,  
while a prayer given from the father’s lips was being poured out at the tomb.

The remaining matters are fitted to these, and the whole burden is likewise lightened.  
At the same time the father conducts the battle with a lawful army  
and sends many to the realms of heaven and to the crowns above.

[Col. 0775B] Some of them prophesy what is to come  
and know before death by what order they will receive their palms.

Gerontius sees these things and reports them with a truthful voice.  
Some, summoned, receive forgiveness for their sins  
and depart secure. Antonius confirms this by his deed;  
Merulus confirms it with tears. Both were accustomed to prayers.  
A flowered crown, fallen from heaven upon his head,  
leads him joyfully and safely to the heavenly realms.

The wondrous fragrance of the tomb also bears witness to those who saw it  
and comforts the young John, oppressed by illness.  
He is raised up and, ordered to prepare himself for his approaching fate,  
takes his meal, remembering the command.  
Within the second year he prepares his departure  
and, summoned, goes with certainty from the urn.

The excellent Father labors through exhortation and prayers,  
[Col. 0775C] striving to heap up the gains of his flock.  
He prepares their highest willing, helps them to desire it,  
bears their ability, and compels the rebellious.

Theodore experienced these gifts. He was a harsh boy, a mocker,  
and a hunter of the pious; yet, when he was dragging away his hand,  
he received sudden salvation while a dragon was swallowing him.  
He was snatched from its jaws, refusing and warding off the watersnake.  
Pious prayers drove it away, changed his mind and heart,  
established him in the worship of God, and sent him toward heaven.

Strong in these fruits, the good leader was soon seen to ascend this heaven  
by the rule of wings.  
He is drawn by the cord of ministry; the deacon is lifted up.  
The court receives a minister worthy in word and office,  
bearing the answers given to the Church and to the Father.

The brothers whose pleasant fellowship sustains them follow him,  
so that, safe from the world’s storm, he may avoid the errors of the sea  
and burn for heavenly things.

[Col. 0775D] When Maximianus returned and revisited the nurturing enclosures  
entrusted to him in proven faith and virtue of mind,  
and assigned to the guardianship of the excellent master,  
the Adriatic rose in terrors and savage anger.  
With furious winds it stirred up the wild waves  
and, with the sea lifted high, threatened a cruel death.

With the helmsman lost, the controls perished.  
The ship, driven into the waves by the wind-bearing host, fell;  
the sails, entangled with the shoals, followed the swollen waves.  
The vessel, its whole side overcome and loosened in its framework,  
admitted the swift enemy through the gaping cracks.  
The sea now carried the vessel, filled and submerged with the mass of its planks;  
it was carried by the sea, level upon the sea’s back.

[Col. 0776A] Near death no longer shakes their hearts; rather, its approach tears them away.  
They see nothing except the final thing; they exchange  
the kisses of supreme peace, receive the pious gifts as consolations for the journey,  
and entrust their souls to the One who confines their bodies in death.

The Almighty’s mercy is bent toward the trembling in their distress.  
Judging it extraordinary to save them from such danger,  
he approached them and shook their hearts with astonished fear.  
Thus, for eight full days, the boat, full of water and men, floats,  
completing its own course with God alone as its oarsman.

On the ninth day they are unharmed, while the shore of Cotronum receives  
the companions of Gregory. Maximianus follows them after leaving the small boat;  
it seeks the depths, now no longer able to bear the waves  
without the weight of the men whom it had carried,  
and the waves that it had carried by Gregory’s merits.

He nevertheless attributes this to Maximianus’s honor,  
while avoiding his own brothers’ praises.  
At their request, and for these and other reasons, under the pious love of Christ,  
he unravels and reveals the closed mysteries of the man  
who was unconquered in speech and tested through a thousand battles.  
He examines and clarifies the divine riddles, revealing them;  
he opens the sacraments and makes the hidden things that are to be revealed apparent,  
and encloses them in an excellent sequence through many volumes.

Then too he crushes the plague rising toward future light,  
buries it beneath the darts of truth in his speech,  
and completely sinks it while it is still at its first beginning.

Thus, returning triumphantly to the city,  
he restores the city laboring under disaster and deprived of consolation.  
He is chosen as shepherd after the shepherd has been snatched away.

[Col. 0776C] While he withdraws in simplicity, judging himself unworthy of so great a summit,  
and, humble, avoids weighing the height and attempts to free himself  
from the burden of carrying the scepter,  
he is perceived by the heavenly power.  
The empty votes and prayers are annulled; the acts of the people  
are carried into the court.

They delight the king beneath the grateful honor of his patron,  
and the joyful envoys bring back the gratifying commands.  
At the prince’s insistence, and at the request of the clergy and people,  
he is elected to the lofty summit under Christ’s governance.  
He considers what is advantageous to the people and what is suitable for himself,  
and, giving the suffering multitude the consolations of the word,  
he meditates exile from the summit and flight from honor.

But the watchmen’s guard keeps the doors shut,  
and it is not hidden from the citizens what the humble fugitive is planning.  
[Col. 0776D] Nevertheless, more watchful than all the sentries,  
he escapes through their midst while they are unaware and deceives those who see him.  
Surrounded by a vessel, he withdraws after obtaining a hiding place,  
and remains concealed until the fasting of the people  
and the prayers of the Romans earn new signs in heaven.

For once, a pillar, the very dark guide of the people,  
shining among the stars, bathes a pillar with light—  
the pillar of the Church—and brings forth the leader of the people,  
illuminating him with open rays.  
The citizens are seen approaching and returning  
through the bright paths of heaven.

Only one who happened to be worthy was able to perceive it:  
an inhabitant of the woods, removed from the crowd and the world,  
who recognized God’s roof, this temple, as his shelter.

At last, identified by these signs and by the heavenly light,  
the fugitive is seized, dragged to Peter’s threshold,

[Col. 0777A] clothed and adorned with a pious garment,  
raised to sacred office, and admitted to the divine altar.  
He is marked with the holy gift of heavenly grace  
and, suffused with the highest Spirit, by which he overflowed,  
is preferred in honor to the apostolic chair as bishop.

Worthy of the insignia, he worthily manages what has been entrusted to him.  
When he is reproached as idle, like John of Ravenna,  
for refusing what was so worthy of him,  
he gives a fitting answer, composing a work suitable for shepherds of the Church.  
He explains fittingly how a ruler ought to live,  
and how he ought to teach, preserve himself, and preserve his people—  
how cautiously, how discreetly, and how honorably he should live.

From then on he does not cease to teach through admonitions and writings.  
He calls those appointed and those set apart by voice and hand,  
leading them toward the heights of heaven by example and word.  
Arranging heavenly things through the hearts subject to him,  
he unravels the gold hidden in concealing cases.  
He marks virtues by their signs and displays the lives of those who came before.  
By training, he arms and adorns his ranks;  
filled by the holy Spirit received from the divine mouth,  
he gives pasture to the flocks.

The minister who served as scribe and recorder of his words bears witness.  
Compelled by the spite of his detractors, he reveals the secret things  
that Peter had written and approved after seeing them under heavenly inspiration,  
so that, once poured out, they would not be consumed by the death to come.  
He helped to disclose what he had seen, and, giving proof, revealed the secrets as he breathed his last.

After the Father’s death—though forbidden while he lived—he revealed  
that a dove, whiter than snow, rested upon his head,  
shown through a puncture made by a stylus in the veil,  
while the herald gathered the mystical instruments of heaven,  
drawing from his mouth the divine riddles of the heavenly beak  
and unlocking for them the hidden things of Ezekiel’s writings.

[Col. 0777C] Neither weakness, nor feverish heat lodged in him,  
nor pain that cut his entrails, nor anything clinging to his steps,  
nor anxiety for the city, nor concern for his beloved dependents  
drew him back from his undertakings. He cared for both hearts and bodies.

The fate of a poor man, believed to have perished through the horror of famine,  
moved him, as though he had killed one who had been extinguished by his own slaughter.  
Having gathered resources from every side, so that he might provide assistance,  
he once prepared fifty measures of grain.

He gave to everyone who asked; love held him back from retaining any wealth.  
The hermit-nourisher of Muricipus proves this, content with Gregory as his companion,  
and despising all the rest of the world.  
He prayed to know beforehand the lot of his reward,  
when, together with Gregory, whose glory he shared, he was chosen—  
not thinking it a great thing that one who had despised worldly prosperity  
should be equal to the world shining in splendor.

He accepts this one to handle the treasures’ talents more effectively,  
and to preserve the necessities of life for others rather than defend  
for himself a cat that offered him consolation.  
The man, giving thanks, asks that the promises be fulfilled  
and that, together with Gregory, he may be carried into the subdued light.

Nor did he nourish only those present; from afar he fed the needy as well—  
a fact known to the mountaineers remote in the crag of Sinai  
and to the Britons separated from the whole world by the Ocean.

[Col. 0778A] While he conceived of the English people as pasture for heaven,  
which, seen in the marketplace, might be woven into a form suitable for the kingdom,  
to be torn away from the shadows and consecrated by the light of day,  
to be led away from anger and summoned to heavenly piety,  
and made worthy to proclaim the praises of God in song,

the teacher and minister of the word hastened to direct his steps there,  
but was delayed because the people held him back.  
Unwilling to remain in his place, he learned from the leaping locust.

But when the mitre brought him the power to offer pious gifts,  
he selected beneficent cultivators to tend this untilled land,  
to clear it of wild beasts, and to enrich the new fields with thorns removed.  
He plowed the soil of the heart with the highly polished plowshare of the tongue  
and filled the countryside by heaping up the seed of the word.

He himself labored by exhortation and prayers  
to make what he sent capable of producing many sheaves in return.  
He assisted with gifts so that more miracles might be produced.  
He saved the people together with their ruler through his envoys,  
and did not care only for the salvation of a single kingdom.

Moreover, the peoples and neighboring kings increased.

[Col. 0778B] Barbarian hearts learned to lay aside their savage minds;  
barbarian mouths strove to proclaim the praises of God.  
The pride of the Ocean was laid low beneath pious feet.  
Those untamed by the sword were subdued by gentle speech.  
Fearless in war, they feared to be bound by words.  
They despised earthly things and burned in mind for heavenly things.

These are the works that shine through the merits of this Father,  
who rightly was appointed Apostle to that people.

Moreover, he bought back children of that same people,  
carried off into foreign regions, redeeming them at a price,  
and prepared them as lilies of heavenly faith and heavenly beauty.

When the country people of Sardinia wished also to remain entangled  
in their ancient error, he reproved the bishop’s sluggish speech,  
who proved by his prayers that he had yielded to the pious gifts of light.

Therefore, rescuing the Hebrews through gifts for heavenly things,  
and adorning their souls and clothing them in garments,  
he also took pains to extend the Father’s solicitude  
to the children whom dreadful heresy had fostered.

The land also felt the protection of the ruler of the West,  
and Roman power recovered the cities that had been taken away.

From this point, piling praise upon praise in the manner of a cento,  
and gathering songs together like a collection of divine books,  
he composes sacred volumes.  
By heaping up prayers so that sacred rites might be performed,  
he conveys them through a vow.  
He strikes the smiling faces of the mysteries  
and reveals the mysteries of blood to the eyes in red.  
He reports the fleshly rites to the carnal heart  
and teaches the wheat-flour to be changed into flesh  
and the wine created from wood to be converted into blood.

When, through these revelations of the flesh, he strengthens hearts and eyes,

[Col. 0778D] he restores the divine offerings to their ancient form.

No less remarkably, the altar-palls, revealed through their cloths,  
are secretly filled with sacred blood by its power,  
and he assigns them as a rich gift of the highest offering.  
He sends the bone relics of the saints to those who ask.  
When these had been rashly viewed, uncovered too unworthily,  
and treated as nothing, he patiently withdraws them,  
then, redoubling his prayers, reveals the astonishing secrets,  
and, while he cuts them with iron, gives forth wondrous streams of blood.

He amazes the envoys and casts the faithful prostrate in prayer.  
He makes those who had first been standing upright bend down to bless  
and to praise God, who grants such divine insignia.

He instructs that these coverings be placed among the sacred offerings on the altars,  
which, poured out in Christ’s name,  
[Col. 0779A] had thus drunk the holy blood by their power.

Filling these and others who saw them with the splendor of faith,  
he once more gives sure gifts, marking certain offerings for particular recipients.

While those who carry them proclaim the Lord’s great works,  
they bring joy. The one who receives gifts with reverence,  
in accordance with his desires, accompanies them, venerates them,  
and adorns them with love; great honor is given to these miracles of Christ.

Strong in these riches, the nurturing Father nourished the humble  
with examples, admonitions, and virtues,  
and prepared proud hearts, by wearing them down with his mouth,  
to prostrate themselves before the Lord.

The magicians experienced this. They saw the horse of the magnificent rider  
burning in Phlegethon, its goads of wickedness scorched.  
The light of the one who acts as light abandons them when they are obstructed,  
and they are attacked by their own fury.

The prudent judge drives them away, leaving the Father’s horse safe,  
and restores them once the ruin of their minds has been removed.  
But he orders them to remain dark forever,  
lest, having gained the light, they return to their accustomed darkness.  
For those purified in the pure spring,  
he decrees a twofold sustenance as a gift of piety.

It had indeed become the custom implanted in the pope’s nurturing mind  
to break the cruel and protect those who followed him readily.

A tyrant, raised up in savagery, confirms these words and deeds.  
He was trampling country people and fields that happened to be subject  
to Peter’s primate, and, despite the blessed Father’s admonitions  
and envoys, was striving to lay waste to the city.

The shepherd, who was running to preserve the sheep under his protection,  
met him and pressed him with terror; he struck him down by his speech.  
The man received strength from the holy Father’s pious words,

[Col. 0780A] changed his mind, and soon, now subject, prayed for pardon.  
He vowed to be an obedient servant and experienced the Father’s benign,  
honey-sweet goodness. Through the guardian’s prayers he earned time,  
though illness had bent him toward his final end.  
He returned to life and strength, and, advised how to preserve his life,  
lived better in all that followed.

Nor did only those who were present enjoy such great piety.  
Trajan too, tortured for a long time in Tartarean shadows,  
received—wonderful to tell—the extraordinary aid  
of the gentile patron whom his goodness had moved.  
Gregory redeemed him through prayers and drenched him in a flood of tears.  
He learned that his prayers had been received  
and thereafter heard that he should not presume such things  
in the face of the heavenly powers and the fates.

Fashioning renowned gifts for the case of the apostolic treasury,  
he raises them up, assigns them to sacred use, and adorns them with worship.  
Driving out heresies, he cleanses these places of their guilt,  
and rejoices to have seen the Suburra in triumph.

Nor does he silently and secretly leave the temple.  
As his spirit departs, a pig breaks through the assembled ranks;  
the sounds resound with a great crash, shaken by the loud tumult.  
The enemy unwillingly abandons the walls as he runs through them.

In honor of the Victor, the altar blooming divinely  
is covered in heaven by a veil of cloud.  
A nectarous fragrance fills the Church; terror keeps footsteps away.  
When fire is sent forth, the lamps shine with heavenly light,  
and the lights are renewed by a distinguished flame;  
the extinguished torches sparkle again with repeated light.

## CHAPTER XV. On the miracles of his monastery

[Col. 0779]

[Col. 0779C] Miracles are divinely performed in the likeness of this one,  
and at times a candle of heaven is lit by fire.

John, the superior of that monastery,  
while devoted to luxury and frequently practicing its cruel bonds,  
was struck by the sluggish illness of gout.  
Burned by the tormenting heat of the medicinal treatment,  
and despairing as the disease’s weight increased,  
he withdrew from filth and devoted himself to chaste honor;  
by the Lord’s mercy he was restored to the health prepared for him.

But, like an impure dog swallowing back its vomit,  
after some time he returned to the contemptible severity of the disease.  
He again practiced slippery, luxurious, and filthy crimes.

Soon a certain old man received a vision of Gregory.  
Approaching the relapse, he gave him this warning that very night:  
let him repent, and scatter the wealth acquired through shameful crime,  
for the third day’s light would soon carry him away.

[Col. 0779D] Then the foolish man, terrified by the commands of so great a Father, repented of his deed.  
As he strove to scatter his treasures,  
he was seized by illness on the day marked out in the vision.  
He burned in the violent fire of immense torment,  
and, thrusting out his tongue, dragged in his final breaths.  
Guards were assigned to attend the dying man,  
and the priests withdrew to offer vows to the Lord.

After the sacred rites they returned and were astonished  
to find that he had become more gentle.  
They called his name; he soon opened his eyes,  
and, smiling, asked what voices had disturbed him.  
He said that, from the first light of day,  
he had stood in judgment with the perpetual enemy of salvation.

[Col. 0780C] He was able to recount all the things that had been presented,  
and, having enjoyed Gregory’s assistance,  
he said that he had brought the measures of the monastery,  
its customary food and drink,  
and its usual lamps of piety before the footstool of the Most High.

He had been unable to cleanse only one of the accusations brought against him.  
Therefore, driven by shame and worn down by torment,  
he was ordered to disclose the matter.  
He said that he had appointed Gregory as his patron,  
but that he would not reveal anyone’s disgrace,  
whether of those who had performed the deeds or of their households.  
He relinquished the merit to those who had acted.

He said that he had heard the brothers’ detractors in everything,  
but, bound by judgment, had been unable to return any answer.  
He confessed that they should spare those who were dying  
and no longer bring forward the taunts that had been reported so often by the enemy  
against those hastening under such strict judgment to the judge’s presence.

[Col. 0780D] Finally, when the presbyter who had recorded the final matters  
asked him to disclose the crime of the supreme struggle,  
he turned his head away and exclaimed with breathless groaning:

> “Andrew, may you perish in this wretched year,  
> you who gave me counsel in such savage dangers.”

Then, rejecting the physician who promised him the gains of life,  
he asked the brothers to sing psalms, so that he might see  
the angelic ranks that he himself had seen before.  
He said that he was contemplating them, and, pale and trembling,  
made signs to the brothers as best he could;  
then he abandoned human things,  
leaving the monks overcome with great terror.

Andrew, the tenant of the Barbilian estate,  
at once, upon hearing the presbyter’s voice uttering curses,

[Col. 0781A] fell onto his bed and, released through a long illness,  
was stripped of his flesh. His wife, weighed down by the stench  
of her husband, consumed by decay but unable to breathe his last,  
urged him to reveal what deed had brought about such dreadful events  
and what fate of the superior he was dragging upon himself by his voice.

[Col. 0782A] When he confessed that he had taken certain documents  
and given them to the unworthy for a promised price,  
he soon revealed the matter in prison and covered it with his body,  
showing to everyone, through the struggle of his own punishment,  
what the slaughterer of Gregory’s laws deserved to suffer.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the minister who diminished his almsgiving

[Col. 0781]

[Col. 0781A] Here too, the man who is shown to have diminished  
the customary lavish expenditures of the Father for the consolation of the needy  
received the harsh commands of the blessed man through a herald sent beforehand:  
days were to be cut short for him in proportion to the piety he had taken away.

While he displayed less faith in the words for the appointed time,

[Col. 0782A] he suddenly saw the burning fire upon the wall alone.  
When he attempted to turn it aside with his hands, he himself was seized.  
He was consumed inwardly by burning and feverish heat  
and met the end of his life in a grievous blaze.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the monks of his monastery

[Col. 0781]

[Col. 0781B] In the church where Gregory used to pour out his prayers,  
an unclean hostile spirit is driven out by the virtue of the faith  
of a robust monk, although he was assailed by blows  
in the threatening visions of a sleepless delusion.

Afterward, when he seemed to be leading dangers from the jaws of death,  
he received in a vision the commands of the blessed Father:  
if he took care to live, he should reveal the fate of those who were dying.  
He promised to disclose it and took their names.  
He received the Father’s fingers in his mouth;  
when an ulcer burst, he excreted the pestilence born within him  
with dreadful corruption.

Soon health followed, keeping him from the jaws of death,  
and, contrary to everyone’s expectation, joined him to the hymn-singing company.

He disclosed the matter to the astonished.  
The order of those departing confirmed his words.  
When the bishop, the superior of the monastery, finally heard it,  
he too found himself counted among them.  
Compelled by the illness that followed,

[Col. 0781C] he resolved, terrified, to believe the matter concerning his own house.

[Col. 0782B] Then, entering the monastery, he was changed in status,  
assumed the monk’s habit, and renounced the world’s conduct.

At last, when blessed Andrew visited him  
and marked the hour of his death in his ancestral language,  
he died joyfully, asking that his funeral be performed at once,  
with broad lights and increased perfumes,  
so that the festival of Saint Fabian might be properly celebrated.

A monk prayed to Gregory for his brother, who was insane.  
While avoiding human company and traversing desolate places,  
he saw in a vision the Father offering consolation.  
When he saw this, he received his prayer with tears:  
he would restore his brother to health and bring him back with the light,  
while the presbyter, released by pardon, would depart from confinement.

The following day confirmed the promise. At the priest’s command,  
the pope was released, and the brother returned to his beloved.  
[Col. 0782C] He was restored unharmed and remained in faithful service.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the purification of the same estate

[Col. 0781]

[Col. 0781C] A hostile spirit ravaged the aforesaid Barbilian estate,  
disguised as a bull by its appearance.  
Harmful to the farmers, it pressed upon them and wearied them with its brow,  
and kept both the guards and the oxen away from their stalls.

After the others had been scattered, one oxherd, driven by terror,  
approached the monks in fear and wished to disclose the matter.  
While he was speaking, his speech broke off, and he withdrew,  
fleeing; he quickly departed, to the astonishment of his masters.

Returning in the morning, he said that he had been driven away  
by terror of the beast, which had harassed him throughout the night.  
He had endured the burning dangers until, refusing to plunge from a bridge,  
he fled and, amid the difficulties of pathless places,  
had protected himself behind the barred gates of the enclosure  
under the protection of a certain bishop.

Gregory himself, appearing to one of his people in a vision,  
commanded that blessed water be sprinkled through the countryside.  
After this had been done, the unseen stain withdrew.  
It was then seen circling the boundaries, but it did not dare to enter.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the vision of Bishop Tetgaud

[Col. 0781]

[Col. 0781D] A certain bishop, Tetgaudus, deprived of his honor,  
came to Rome and entered the monastery,  
which, at the pope’s arrangement, provided him lodging.

When he had slept only a little, the Father seemed to appear  
and utter threatening commands:

“Let him go out, and, hastening, leave his enclosures.”

He was shaken from his bed, prayed, and regarded the vision as a phantom;  
then he slept again. Once more the Father stood over him,  
this time in pontifical clothing:

“Did I not order you,” he said, “to leave our enclosure,  
which I consecrated to the Lord with the endowment of the prince,  
because I do not want the lodgings of Andrew?”

[Col. 0782D] Taking these rights of residence from the pontiff,  
he incurred a punishment under Christ’s own chastisement;  
both the one who had asked and the one who had granted it  
would suffer the penalty in that year.

Awakening in terror, he prayed and tried to return to sleep.  
Suddenly he heard a sound approaching the threshold.  
Very afraid, he pretended to be weighed down by sleep.  
Gregory entered in this way, holding Andrew by the right hand,  
and, approaching the bearer of the light, said:

“Correct the man lying prostrate.”

The man, however, corrected, sat up:

“Look at us,” said the saint in fear,  
“because, twice rejecting my commands, you compel me  
to lead away this nobleman of the Lord.  
Unless you leave today, you will be deprived of life  
when the week approaches, together with all your companions.

[Col. 0783A] But if you follow the commands and comply,  
you can now escape the sudden punishments.  
Yet neither you nor any of those living here with you  
will ever again see your ancestral fields.”

He immediately sprang from his bed and disclosed the vision.  
He went out from the enclosure; the words were fulfilled by events.  
For, deprived of the right of hospitality and going toward the Sabines,  
he was deprived of life within that year together with his entire company.

## CHAPTER XX. On the man who brought prostitutes into his monastery

[Col. 0783]

[Col. 0783A] Thus also that domestic servant, Suppo,  
who was not afraid to unlock the enclosures for prostitutes,  
deserved to experience his punishment.  
With his breath suspended in dreadful fashion, Gregory appeared to him:

“Do the other evils not suffice for you,  
enemy of God, which you have committed in great number  
within our enclosures?

[Col. 0783B] In addition, you have dared to bring prostitutes in there,  
whether for loose pleasures or for the amusement of the stage.  
Believe me: for that reason you will perish within the year.”

He promised that he would lay aside his criminal conduct;  
the voice from above ordered him to be taken down and returned to the ground.

But because he pretended to set his perverse thoughts in order,

[Col. 0784B] he proved by his own destruction that the prophet’s pronouncements were true.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the vision of Saint Andrew

[Col. 0783]

[Col. 0783B] Suppo’s dependent likewise experienced the death  
of the man whose suitable lodging-house had been seized.  
At night he saw an old man, who rebuked him while examining him  
and called him foolish. When he was lightly touched by the power of the rod,  
he was thrown down upon the lowest earth.

Soon a certain cleric, seeing the old man himself in dreams,  
heard that he should rise and reveal the matter to his companion;  
he should leave the enclosure and not provoke his anger,  
so that he might go away safely and recover the beaten servant.

When he asked who could be recognized under such an appearance,  
the cleric affirmed that, after seeing with the light he had received,  
he had discovered that Saint Andrew had given him the commands.  
Finding the proud man, marked by the appointed place,  
struck down by the avenger and half dead,  
he summoned everyone with cries.

Then, in the apostolic name, he proclaimed the words that had been poured out,  
and disclosed these commands together with the patron who had joined him.  
He called the monks and asked about the fault and the crime.  
At his urging he understood that the house had been shaken apart  
and, departing, ordered it to be restored.  
He did not presume to turn there again for lodging.

The destroyer of the house, however, fell forward into bitter death.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the man who polluted his fountain

[Col. 0783]

[Col. 0783C] That presbyter too, the superior of the same enclosure,  
who, uncovering the fountain, was not ashamed to make a pool for a prostitute  
and prepared a dark one, proved that he could not escape the avenging hand.

The ministers, speaking such things at the command of the Roman pontiff,  
drew the terrible man from the brothel.  
When the astonished man complained that the pope was not present,  
they disclosed that he was Gregory, whom he had injured  
by uncovering the fountain through shameful actions.

He heard the order that he himself was to be beaten a hundred times.  
Driven on by the harsh anguish of the blows  
and by the burning torment of fevers,

[Col. 0784C] he was placed upon a horse and returned, panting, to the enclosure.  
He disclosed what he had done and was mangled by the manifest punishment.  
Amid the torments of the persistent disease,  
when the sixth day had already come,  
the wretched man finally breathed his last.

Many proofs have shown that those overcome by the decay  
of polluted crime do not live long in these enclosures.

A measure and a scale of the blessed Father are still said to be kept there.  
If anyone attempts, using this, to prepare loaves for an outside purpose,  
he will not reach the customary number of serviceable loaves;  
the amount that ordinarily exceeds it astonishes the servant.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the vision of the deacon John

[Col. 0783]

[Col. 0783D] While the deacon John was sowing such things into his history,  
behold, in a dream he saw a certain priest standing and laughing,  
asking why he was writing the deeds of liberated men  
whose faces he had not seen.

John replied that he was more confidently speaking the truth:  
he had been moved neither by flattery nor by spite,  
but was describing as known through reading what was unknown by sight.

The other, growling and threatening what hostile power he possessed,  
extinguished the lamp obtained for John’s use  
and forced him into darkness and terror.

[Col. 0784D] With death placed in the balance and hanging uncertainly,  
Saint Gregory appeared, accompanied on both sides by the blessed:  
on his right, Pope Nicholas, and on his left, the kindly minister Peter,  
all radiant with much light.

He rebuked John:

“Why did you doubt, man of little faith?”

Pope Nicholas pointed out the exposed enemy with his finger.  
Gregory, accompanied by the broad flame of the minister,  
darkened him and declared that he had not merely blackened him  
but had shown him to be black.  
Then, lifting up the faithful man with consolation,  
he departed and left the place filled with great light.

[Col. 0785A] The seer awoke and summoned the boys lying before him,  
but could not raise them from their beds, though they began to speak of what had happened,

[Col. 0786A] until daylight, sent forth, returned to the heavenly air.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the vision of the Emperor Maurice

[Col. 0785]

[Col. 0785A] The Emperor Maurice, promulgating perverse laws  
and forbidding his soldiers—Christ’s athletes—to transfer their military service  
to Christ, opposed this with a proud mind.

Indignant that divine decrees threatened him,  
the king prepared to turn his fury against the pontiff.  
Suddenly a certain monk, venerable in his garment,  
appeared carrying an unsheathed sword,  
and Maurice was to perish by the sword.

The emperor, perceiving the portent,  
turned his terrors into prayers and asked that his evil deeds  
be repaid to him in the present age by a punishment
