through which he might escape future punishment without end.

He addressed many such prayers to Gregory and the Fathers,

[Col. 0785B] adding to his petitions abundant tears.

[Col. 0786A] Without delay he was shaken by the vision and, in the rigid bronze,  
was astonished to see a statue of Christ standing fixed before the doors.  
In response to the voice—“Give Maurice”—  
he heard, trembling, a crash in his ears.  
He was brought nearer and presented to the ministers;  
he was granted the choice to deliberate for himself  
and to set his crimes before him.

He chose that his evil deeds should be repaid  
in the present terror of the future.

Soon, ordered to be handed over with his children and wife to Phocas,  
from the military flock, he received the oracles of holy men.  
Although shipwreck and danger to life had marked out for him  
the pious gifts of salvation granted to him,  
he glorified the Lord. The tyrant, under a grateful law,

[Col. 0786B] underwent the punishment inflicted by divine power.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the humility of Saint Gregory himself

[Col. 0785]

[Col. 0785B] Here the Father declares himself unworthy of lofty visions  
and recalls that, casting himself down, he was overcome by one lesser in light.  
When John prostrated himself before him, Gregory himself lay face down  
until John arose.

He diminished his own words in comparison with the generous utterances  
of the Father, the great Augustine;  
he calls them cleansings of grain  
and forbids them to be read while he is present and living in the body.

Here he had received from a certain bishop Saint John’s garment,  
which had been offered by the highest gift,  
together with Paschasius’s dalmatic, which had been brought beneath the altar.

[Col. 0785C] It is preserved, and the desired rain too, once revealed, reveals itself;

[Col. 0786B] and at once the shaken [things] thicken, or restore the clear sky;

lamps, frequently kindled there by divine power;

and the increased olive oil reveals God’s heavenly gifts.

Amid these resources of piety, strengthened by the heavenly Spirit,

he seeks the realms above and receives the rewards he had sought,

exchanging his earthly eminence for the height of heaven.

The needy voices of those left without consolation cry out for

the kindly aid with which he had fostered his Roman children.

His successor’s deed, the pope’s firm rebuke,

and repeated correction prompted by harsh envy

[Col. 0786C] bring disgrace to an end and protect the complaining throng [the compressed syntax does not clearly distinguish the successor’s deed from the pope’s rebuke].

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the successors of blessed Gregory

[Col. 0785]

[Col. 0785C] Sabinianus’s death bears witness to the glory

by which Gregorian dignity flourished;

although he added fiery lights to the palace,

and supplied grain to the Forum in a time of famine.

Boniface succeeds him in eminence,

yielding no rights to favor that would overreach itself.

He maintains the high office and at the same time wins the prince’s favor;

he issues decrees to ensure a sacred choice for the episcopate.

His successor both in office and in name,

though troubled in his activity by various disasters,

labors to adorn the duties entrusted to him,

[Col. 0786C] and to proclaim the highest glory of Christ,

and to disperse the madness of the profane enemy.

Having taken possession of the shrine, which fools believed held
all the gods, he removes the monstrous images of the deities;
he consecrates the holy royal church

of the Mother and Virgin who bore the Ruler of heaven,

adding honor to all the witnesses of Christ.

From that time he establishes festivals and commands them to be observed;

the world follows him and adopts the rite.

Following Gregory in pious devotion, he

rejoices to dedicate a house of his own to the poor community,

enriching it with Christ’s abundant endowment.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the holy bishops Deusdedit, Boniface, and Honorius

[Col. 0785]

[Col. 0785D] From that point the holy Deusdedit assumes the authority

of the earlier Fathers, nourisher, restorer, and lover of sacred things and clergy,

dispenser [of their goods], at a time when peace blooms in Italy.

But lest sluggish leisure plunge them too deeply into security,

the land is terrified by the trembling of a quivering earthquake:

the populace is afflicted by disaster [the transmitted *affinitur ... vocatos* is syntactically uncertain].

[Col. 0786D] At the Father’s death, allowances are given to the clergy [*rogae*, distributions, is transmitted beside this clause; its connection is unclear].

Then the pious and gentle Boniface, marked by the praise of Moses,

is chosen prince of the sacred altars.

Guardian of wills and of those seeking sanctuary in churches,

he raises the saints’ relics and establishes the consecrated baptistery,

arranging its services with fitting honor.

[Col. 0787A] He adorns the tombs and pays the clergy a generous allowance;

punishment follows the wicked, victory the just.

Bishop Honorius, born of a father who was a consul, shines forth

in many illustrious deeds;

a kindly teacher, he resplends as the glory of the clergy

and restores and cultivates the dignity of the apostolic see.

He adorns the sacred buildings with silver,

raises the beams, and covers the temple with bronze obtained for the purpose.

[Col. 0788A] Moreover, he produces many works and steadies what is tottering;

in the name of the just he restores and rewards the churches;

he dedicates, heaps up, distributes, and offers rich gifts;

he sanctifies every Sabbath with prayer,

and extols it with song and praises.

From this he receives in heaven numerous blessings increased a hundredfold.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the holy Pope Severinus and his successors

[Col. 0787]

[Col. 0787A] Next Severinus, after the sun has completed its course through the signs,

after the Church’s losses and internal wars,

chosen for Peter’s see, renews the sacred things fallen into ruin,

gentle, merciful, and a kindly nourisher of the needy.

[Col. 0787B] He heaps gifts upon the pious clergy and gathers foster-children.

John, a redeemer of captives with compassionate heart,

also nourishes foreign peoples through his goodness:

Istria, which knew him through Abbot Martin as intermediary,

and Dalmatia too, protected by the pope’s clemency.

From there he receives the pious relics of the Fathers as a welcome reward;

he cultivates them with buildings, splendidly and with the gleam of metal,

and cherishes the ministers subject to him,

both while present and after his departure.

Then the pious Father Theodore, guardian of those who seek refuge,

amid civic tumult and private wars,

remains unmoved, steadfast, chaste, and faithful;

he spares the fallen and embraces those who follow what is right;

he conquers and condemns the savage and those who have fallen back into darkness;

he recalls the erring and restrains them with prayers and threats.

[Col. 0787C] He punishes contempt and chastises insolent necks;

he raises the holy relics and reverently brings them out from the sands;

he arranges them in the churches, adorns them with gold and silver,

raises them and dedicates them, and presents splendid buildings as gifts.

After him the vigorous witness of the truth, Martin,

fulfills the apostolic office and wages war with a worthy host,

tested by insults against the Lord,

and provoked by arrogant pride and swelling insolence,

through which the paternal decrees were torn away

and fury was turned against the sacred altars of Christ.

That fury destroys the kindly altars and overturns the holy peace.

[Col. 0788A] On these matters the Fathers are compelled to deliberate,

and the divine senate is consulted;

the truth is brought to light and the wicked are punished.

The world is defended against fires by its garrisons,

and with shields distributed throughout the regions of the earth

the battles of the opposing party now grow more intense.

[Col. 0788B] The ruler attacks the citadel of the sacred leader;

an exarch is sent to ensnare his faithful companions

and seize the Father.

But the concord of the brothers, their unanimity,

and the love of the people prevent this.

Then, even when assailed by deceit, the Father is protected,

hidden in the darkness of a sacred cloud:

the attendant can see the others, but cannot see

the distinguished man alone, whom he intends to kill with his sword.

The plots of murder frustrated, the author of the deception,

confounded by the exposure, is compelled to make peace.

After that man is brought down amid the whirlwind of war and death,

a more savage man is sent, openly fulfilling the commands of fury,

and he tramples upon the apostolic honor of the man.

Removing him from the altars, he leads him to Greek cities.

[Col. 0788C] He separates him from the city assigned to him,

but cannot separate him from his blessed mind.

He drives him from his throne, but cannot drive him from his resolve.

He remains the same arbiter in Rome and Constantinople.

Piously following the holy footsteps of Clement,

he enters exile at Chersonesus.

Once he had reached the stars, the rays of his many signs reveal

how faithful and how devout he proved in the harsh ordeal—

a confessor pleasing to Christ and steadfast to the end.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the holy Pope Eugenius

[Col. 0787]

[Col. 0787D] Eugenius, whom the cradle had destined for sacred things,

shines forth tranquil and gentle, kindly in disposition,

generous to the needy, holy in uprightness, and gracious.

[Col. 0788D] Nourisher of the clergy, cultivator of justice, lover of piety,

he always rebukes the deceivers amid the singing people.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the holy bishops Vitalianus and Adeodatus

[Col. 0787]

[Col. 0787D] Vitalianus, cultivator of the holy rule,

sending the see’s replies to the royal city,

restores the ancient privileges of sacred things,

and golden gifts are sent to Peter.

He leads the emperor, received at Rome, to the sacred rites;

flourishing through the worthy gift of holiness,

he ascends, enriched, to the clear heights above.

The holy Father Adeodatus succeeds him,

kind to all and gentle toward everyone.

[Col. 0788D] He cherishes the needy and is helpful and effective.

Under this bishop the wars that had begun are suppressed;

tyrants arise but are quickly overthrown;

a rebellious city is handed over to the barbarians.

He restores and dedicates buildings

laid low by ruin, assigns soldiers

to the camps of heaven, and provides the necessities.

At his death there arose whirlwinds,

crashes of heaven, and so many lightning bolts

[Col. 0789A] that the terrified multitude, astonished by things never before seen,

was struck with fear;

livestock perished in herds, and human bodies likewise fell.

While vengeance rests, they are gathered together again

in wondrous order through abundant prayers.

A shining star burns at the highest point,

[Col. 0790A] and afterward a plague carries many away in death,

while the house of choice presses for concord [*domus optionis ... foedere*, a defective or highly compressed expression in the supplied text].

He adorns the passageway of the church with marble,

lavishly restores the buildings,

increases the order of sacred things,

disperses the dark-hearted and wisely gathers the kindly together,

and brings Ravenna into unity.

# HERE BEGINS BOOK ELEVEN

[Col. 0791]

## CHAPTER ONE. On the holy bishops Agatho, Leo, and Benedict

[Col. 0791A] From this point the times of Father Agatho rise joyfully,

though saddened by the moon’s pallor and the Roman people’s deaths.

Yet the Church rejoices in peace and in the casting down of the savage.

While kings and Fathers seek fellowship with Peter’s see,

Rome, gladdening and instructing her sister through envoys,

and binds to herself those who share her lineage.

She rejects the deceiver and adorns Peter’s first chair with piety,

cleansing it of the webs that Arachne, swollen with a poisonous shower, had woven.

She removes the reprobate and cherishes the worthy in fitting order.

Then the younger Leo, adorned with Greek and Latin elegance

and accustomed to vocal choruses accompanied by instruments,

calls the people to lofty things,

scatters the talents entrusted to him for gain,

impoverished by generosity and most devoted nourisher of the needy.

[Col. 0792A] He approves the decrees of the Sixth Synod and condemns the rebels;

he restores his subjects and receives the pious rights of the see.

He dedicates churches to Paul and adorns them with gifts and worship.

The pope’s death follows an eclipse of the moon.

Benedict the Second, instructed in sacred matters,

takes up the sacred rights;

overflowing from the divine fountain of wisdom,

he fulfills, by mouth and hand, the office signified by his name,

and shines, worthy of rule, through generous goodness:

gentle, patient, and a lover of humble virtue.

He repairs the fallen temples, supplies vestments,

multiplies worship, and raises revenues by his gifts.

The Father and the city alike flourish through imperial favor;

signs gleam in the sky and the fires of Vesuvius blaze.

Strengthened by sacred honor, he seeks the summit of the kingdom.

## CHAPTER TWO. On the fifth John, Conon, and the others

[Col. 0791]

[Col. 0791B] Coming from Syrian stock, the fifth John of Rome

obtains the heights of the see.

Firm and learned under the bond of a universal vow,

he is serene with a disciplined mind.

He had exercised the offices of this see among the Greeks,

and in a council of the Fathers had piously joined the cities together.

Peace shines upon his fatherland:

while the Punic kingdoms are restored to their former lords [the supplied *Dominus* is grammatically defective],

the peoples remain in peace,

and the sacred decisions of the earlier Fathers are strengthened.

The companies of saints find consolation in his rich gift.

When he was taken away, the assembly split,

each part seeking a different course.

Neither part obeys the other, nor do they cease from warfare,

until the decrees of the clergy raise the angelic Conon

and choose a man approved in all things,

who had followed the work of religion with a perfected heart.

At once the Roman citizens assemble with the people

[Col. 0791C] worthily in his praise;

the worthy man ascends to the heights.

The pious head receives royal gifts and the favor of Augustus,

and although ill, he carries out his heavenly duties.

Nor is rest long granted to his meritorious labor:

the people are again divided into two,

and those of differing opinions cannot join hands,

until, through the mercy of the heavenly power,

Sergius is chosen after the weapons have been quieted.

The divided parties abandon their disputes and yield him their votes;

one man alone resists with a harsh and crafty mind,

causing harm through intrigues and secretly contriving losses.

The wretch overturns himself, bringing himself low by every deception;

afterward secret divinations and incantations carry him off.

[Col. 0792B] The bishop, who had grown through lofty zeal

in the service of the clergy and had been summoned through the ranks

to the highest office,

having advanced through each pledge of office amid the prayers of the devout,

now flourishes in virtue and eminence [*ad singula ... pignora* is compressed in the source].

He does not yield to scepters and does not fear profane commands.

Remaining steadfast and unmoved, he is ordered to be removed from the see.

But, strong through Peter’s aid and the love of the Roman people,

he is preserved for the chair,

and mercifully preserves the life of the hostile attendant,

who is driven from the city by his disgrace.

The king too is driven from his kingdom,

and thus the pious people obtain peace.

When the Lord reveals them, the divine gifts of the cross,

hidden in secret chests,

become visible to him and are venerated with honor;

then they are reverently and sacredly celebrated at the appointed time.

This Father renews and establishes distinguished buildings of excellent beauty;

he adorns the sacred buildings,

institutes forms of worship, and forges precious ornaments.

At the prompting of a warning he raises and elevates the bones of Father Leo;

he prepares worthy decorations and conducts the rites in due order;

he multiplies prayers, heaps them up, and appoints hymns.

He corrects the disorders of the people of Aquileia;

he absolves, heals, arranges, and reunites them;

he makes peace among the flocks and restores them to one fold.

He brings them to the supreme Shepherd,

and, as shepherd, shines conspicuously;

he adorns the cities with learned shepherds.

## CHAPTER THREE. On the sixth John and his successors

[Col. 0793]

[Col. 0793A] After him the sixth John, from the Greek people,

frees the exarch and places himself among the maddened troops;

he prevents and quiets the savage tumult.

Thereafter he drives away the barbarians,

and ransoms captives with generous gifts;

he restores them to the serenity of peace.

Piously he cultivates the venerable churches

and adorns the clergy in due order.

A priest of Greek stock, bearing his own name,

succeeds him;

learned and eloquent with polished wit,

[Col. 0794A] he renews the splendor of the walls,

beautifies the pious tombs,

ennobles them with forms,

and enriches the sacred places with vessels and gold.

He repairs the Church’s loss

and recovers what had been seized by force.

He makes the king repent of his error

and restores his dignity.

When this Father is taken away [*praecepto*, apparently defective here], Sisinnius is raised to the altars,

a man weighty in mind and afflicted in body,

zealous for the walls of the city.

Before long he lays down the burdens both of illness and of high office.

## CHAPTER FOUR. On Pope Constantine

[Col. 0793]

[Col. 0793B] Bearing a gentle heart, Constantine thereafter

attains the honor;

now he undergoes sorrow, now resumes joy.

The happy times cleanse the savage cruelty of famine.

The Father’s tempters are punished with many bitter penalties,

as the scorched, livid letter records.

The Father, obeying the commands of the ruler,

goes across the seas to the Attic walls,

accompanied by a company of saints.

When the Father enters Sicily, the illustrious Theodore meets him,

his sick limbs scarcely able to sustain their duties;

on seeing the prince of sacred things, he suddenly receives healing,

regains joyful strength, and rejoices.

From then on the foremost men of the Greeks

offer worthy expenditures to the pope;

the dignitaries of the palace rush to meet him.

They raise him up, receive him, rejoice, venerate, and honor him.

[Col. 0794B] The emperor himself, crowned with royal power,

worships the Father;

amid famous embraces, festive crowds applaud.

Honor is borne to heaven, and pious gifts are given to Christ.

Rights are restored and the guilt of wrongdoing is expiated.

Joyful and freed from anguish by heavenly consolation,

the bishop returns to the heights of the principal see.

Thereafter he does not heed impious written commands, bloody scepters,

or their admonitions, and disregards royal threats [the supplied *regna minnela* is defective].

He recalls the erring and gives peace to those who return.

He transfers the rule of the gentiles to the supreme Lord.

He strengthens his subjects and quiets civil wars.

He renews the dedicated vessels;

he is granted the news that the high offices have been restored;

he rejoices that rule of the empire has passed to peaceful men obedient to the Thunderer,

and that the upright have received honor.

[Col. 0793] [The following material, from here to the beginning of Book Thirteen, column 833, was published by Mabillon in *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti* III, 569.]

## CHAPTER FIVE. On the second Pope Gregory and Boniface, teacher and martyr

[Col. 0793C] After these events Gregory the Second assumes the sacred rights,

a celibate man, learned, eloquent in judgment and speech,

already known to the empire and already distinguished in doctrine,

wise with a pious heart, steadfast through strength of virtue,

an enemy of those who go astray and defender of those who follow what is right.

He studies the inner things but does not neglect the outward.

When he undertakes to repair the walls of the city,

he labors at the preparation of lime

and, having procured beams by labor

[Note: [Col. 0793] From Calabria. [Col. 0793] Through the printers’ carelessness, the marginal gloss that ought to have stood first bears the number 139.],

renews the basilica of Paul, restores its altar,

and adorns it with decoration.

He lifts up and prevents the ruin of many churches,

and restores their fallen honor.

He recalls companies of saints [Note: [Col. 0793] Congregations of religious.]

and gathers the hosts of heaven.

He calls the German peoples from darkness into the light.

For them the bishop and sower of the kindly word, Boniface,

is sent forth and dispels the shadow of death with a new sun.

[Col. 0793D] He beautifies the churches of the Gauls with the light of piety;

he adorns Rheims and those he judges worthy of the insignia

[Note: [Col. 0793] Trier and Rouen.]

He shines, enlarged by martyrdom, in the ordeal of virtue.

A prince sprung from the Germans, a first-fruit of that people,

[Note: [Col. 0793] Teuto, duke of the Bavarians.]

seeks the apostolic summit and the sacred threshold of Peter.

[Col. 0794C] At the supreme pontiff’s admonition, as he exhorts the tyrant

[Note: [Col. 0793] The king of the Lombards,]

the patrimonies of the first see are secured.

Civil disturbances and pressing foreign wars

are foreshadowed by Cynthia, stained with terrifying blood.

The empire is divided [Note: [Col. 0793] Between Anastasius and Theodore.];

the righteous is preferred to the wicked.

The sounder side emerges victorious,

the hostile army routed;

the venerable insignia of peace arise

[Note: [Col. 0793] Images,]

and the faith of the ancients is adorned with celebrated honor.

When the Tiber’s terrifying waters overflow its banks,

a savage rain occupies the fertile fields around,

and passes through roads, gardens, defenses, and farms.

It overturns huts, terrifies and drives away the peasants,

and carries off orchards and crops;

it seizes the walls of lofty Rome.

Then it reaches the rampart, crosses the walls,

and, with raging water, holds the very streets in a flood.

[Col. 0794D] In those days the farmers were not permitted to cultivate the fields.

The sorrowful throngs pass ill-omened days of enforced leisure

[Note: [Col. 0793] The periods of leisure.]

The pope, disturbed by the heavy murmuring of complaining voices,

persists in prayers and sends his vows up to the stars.

Nor does he let his spirit be defeated and turn away from what he has begun

until he compels the Tiber to return to its own boundaries.

He rebukes the Lombards [*Bardos*],

soothing their savage hearts with gifts and speech,

making them gentle through counsel,

and preserving them by prayer.

He instructs and builds; through his fitting efforts they recover what had been taken

[Note: [Col. 0795] The Romans recover a fortress seized by the Lombards.]

He removes the profit of those who act by stealth

[Note: [Col. 0795] That is, he frustrates the gain of the deceivers.];

fraud collapses through fraud.

The pope’s blessing, bestowed upon foreigners, also celebrates their triumphs

[Note: [Col. 0795] Bestowed.]

while the sponge makes the Franks victorious and protects them from the arms of the Hagarenes

[Note: [Col. 0795] The sponge with which the pope’s table was covered, sent to the Frankish duke as a blessing and distributed to the army that became victorious.]

They take part in the fighting and are not wounded by the sword or a blow,

while a few who lacked such protection are struck down.

This savage barbarian host abandons Constantinople, long burdened by its siege:

it is beaten back by war and famine,

its undertaking confounded by God’s opposition.

A cruel council grows hot;

a plot for the Father’s death

[Note: [Col. 0795] The pope’s.]

is forged.

Soon the towns of the empire yield to the enemies.

[Col. 0795B] The impiety is exposed;

those who took part in it are punished by the supreme divine power.

They are caught in their own nooses and in the pit they had prepared,

and their savagery is turned back upon the crown of the furious.

The pope’s protection prevents the Church from being stripped of its wealth.

Then again, when the pope is attacked by deceit on account of his primacy,

he is rescued, and Christ’s right hand keeps him unharmed.

Nor does defeated fraud remain silent for long.

Weapons are taken up against God himself,

and the images of the ancient adornment are ordered to be destroyed,

wherever painting marks the triumphs of Christ and the martyrs

[Note: [Col. 0795] Wherever it signifies the victories of Christ and the martyrs.]

The bishop is required to favor Augustus or lose favor and affection,

or to withdraw from his rank and high office [the middle clause is compressed in the source].

The priest rejects, overcomes, and despises these profane demands,

and remains fearless amid weapons blazing on every side.

The flock clings to the shepherd while rejecting the impious commands.

It fights bravely for the bishop’s life and safety.

[Col. 0795C] Error is condemned.

The pope forbids the removal of the king,

believing that shameful crimes may be changed by goodness.

The deceivers are struck down and the wicked driven away.

The deadly scheme, nullified by God’s governance,

is destroyed.

But the Father’s clemency protects the savage man

[Note: [Col. 0795] The patrician Eutychius.]

despite his deceit,

and support for the priest increases.

Rome joins the barbarian hand

[Note: [Col. 0795] That of the Lombards.]

to itself as an ally,

and through the Father’s help reveals the dangers threatening life.

But the distinguished bishop, seeking better relief,

lavishly distributes gifts to the poor, his patrons,

and diligently devotes himself to prayers and vows.

Nor is he harsh toward the people;

he gives thanks to their love

and urges the faithful to persist in pious undertakings.

Thus he preserved the hearts of his people

for himself and for the Lord.

[Col. 0795D] Then the fortress of Sutrium, captured in a treacherous snare,

is restored through the pope’s continual gentle admonitions and letters

and is offered to the honor of Peter and Paul.

We understand that Lucifer, the morning star, as a blazing comet signified the leaders’ dreadful treachery, joined in a pact of savagery

[Note: [Col. 0795] Because Lucifer has been turned into a comet; it is not proper for any particular star to be a comet, but different stars are accustomed to be transformed into comets. Thus the manuscript.].

A cruel plan is undertaken:

Rome and the leaders are to be subjected to barbarian power;

the just man is to be handed over to the wicked,

and the guilty are to attack the honor of the innocent.

[Col. 0796A] Part of the plan is fulfilled, and Rome remains to be captured,

while the sacred man offers himself alone for his fellow citizens.

Clinging to heavenly protection,

he seeks the hostile king

and presents himself to the man seeking his death.

Pressing him with pious words under Christ’s direction,

he softens the savage heart;

he prevails through vigorous and kindly piety,

and rejoices that the tyrant has approached the sacred footsteps

after laying aside the pride of his stern mind

[Note: [Col. 0795] That is, after falling at his feet.]

and has promised to inflict no harm upon the flock,

and has offered royal ornaments to Peter’s honor.

The king, having dismissed his diadem,

humbly begs forgiveness.

The king then obtains his request:

that the bishop’s enemy be received.

The Father receives the exarch

and protects the man who had been hostile.

He rescues him from his enemies,

comforts him with friendly supports,

preserves him through counsel,

and guides and adorns him with triumphs.

[Col. 0796B] The treacheries of the ungrateful emperor,

revealed at the pope’s death,

come into the open.

He strives to blacken or bury in dark fires

the standards [Note: [Col. 0795] Images.]

depicted with the palms [Note: [Col. 0795] Of victories.]

of Christ.

He punishes those who attempt to defend them.

He drives the pious pontiff Germanus from his sacred office

for refusing to join in assent

[Note: [Col. 0795] *Jugare*, “to join.”]

and installs an accomplice of his fury at the altars.

The apostolic bishop presses him with letters and accuses him.

Nor does the apostolic bishop cease to press the insolent man

[Note: [Col. 0795] He does not cease.],

insisting that, unless he returns, he must be expelled from office.

Nor is he silent before Augustus;

he urges him to abandon the crime.

Moreover, this Father’s renowned deeds

concern the temples of God and the worship and service of sacred things.

He restores the communities and rules left to the monasteries,

establishing new camps through his own provision

[Note: [Col. 0795] The monastery of Saint Agatha.]

He adapts his mother’s house to divine rites,

[Col. 0796C] and makes citizens of heaven heirs to its patrimonies.

He supplies adornments and decorates the sacred vessels with gems.

He distributes wealth to the poor.

Rich, he ascends to heaven;

leaving sorrow on earth, he gives joys to heaven.

## On Pope Gregory III

He is followed by the heir of virtue and of the name at the summit:

gentle, wise, and shining with divine law;

tested in praises and polished by the brilliance of understanding;

an exhorter and cultivator of goodness, guardian of the faith;

generous to the needy and a friend of poverty;

buyer of captives and kindly nourisher of orphans;

vigorous in love of religion and comforting pious hearts.

While attending to the Father’s funeral rites,

he is taken from the funeral

and called to the highest rule.

[Col. 0796D] He admonishes and rebukes kings concerning the signs

[Note: [Col. 0795] Images.]

of salvation.

He judges the fearful envoy hesitant to carry the admonition,

completes the work,

condemns wicked commands,

and rightly guards the Church’s ornaments,

which he orders to be restored for veneration

through written admonitions.

From there he reproves the nobles,

again and again warning them.

Nor can the sacred mind of the Father be turned aside

by the envoys’ imprisonment,

while his letters penetrate the palaces

and sternly admonish kings who are trying to seize rights

[Note: [Col. 0797] Usurp them.]

[Col. 0797A] He commands the Augusti and gives the insignia of Christ to the images.

He raises a splendid monument of the Church,

increases the splendor of its worship,

and receives relics of the just

[Note: [Col. 0797] Relics.]

sought from every part of the world.

He assigns them the honors they deserve

and orders continuous prayers and grateful praises to be poured out.

He gathers companies that fulfill the heavenly duties.

Restoring the shrines, he enriches them with shining gifts;

he adorns them through worship

and reforms very many things that had fallen.

Enlarging the buildings,

he enriches them with generous honor.

[Col. 0798A] He provides the citizens with the Lord’s help

and the support of the human king.

He calls upon the Frankish court,

restores the walls,

prepares defenses for the city,

and suppresses wars by calming the minds.

Through prayer and gifts he soothes them

and binds the tottering members to the structure of the Church.

Thus, with affairs properly arranged in a straight course,

and with internal and external matters ordered by his governance,

and with the camps of heaven

[Note: [Col. 0797] Monasteries.]

equipped and adorned with light,

he, having completed his service, seeks eternal rest after the wars.

## CHAPTER SIX. On Pope Zacharias

[Col. 0797]

[Col. 0797A] Holy Zacharias succeeds a holy man, a gentle man succeeds a kindly one,

a merciful man a merciful one: ready to spare, slow to anger,

accustomed to repay cruelty with kindness.

[Col. 0797B] Like a father embracing his children—the people and the clergy—

he does not hesitate to offer his life to the enemies.

He performs wonders before the crowds,

restrains the swords,

and recovers what has been seized.

Rescuing the defeated,

he brings the enemies [Note: [Col. 0797] The Lombards.]

to peace.

Receiving obedience from them and returning as victor,

he makes the people rejoice

and repays honor to Christ.

Then again, amid savage disturbances

and terrible fury,

when barbarian minds have fallen back into mournful wars,

the bishop too is sought,

as one skilled in running to preserve his children

[Note: [Col. 0797] Read *gnarus*, “skilled,” for *gnatos*, “sons.”]

Nor does he delay inertly.

Through envoys and gifts he seeks to procure peace.

When peace has not been obtained, he departs, leaving the city to Christ,

trusting as his country’s ambassador and nourisher.

He sends companions ahead,

and, following them by a swift road,

is received at the royal court with splendid ceremony.

Calming swollen hearts with divine grace,

he rejoices in what he has sought,

adorns religious life with light,

and returns to Christ the praises of the victory he has won.

[Col. 0797C] The Lord exalts the honor bestowed under the lofty glory of triumph

and removes the crafty enemy

[Note: [Col. 0797] Hilprand, nephew of King Liutprand.]

He brings forward the heir

and accumulates peace through the long years.

While peace flourishes through the years, the Father repairs the sacred buildings.

Enlarging the courts,

he fills the shrines with wealth.

He restores buildings,

adorns the temples with venerable images,

renews what is collapsing,

and increases their ancient honor.

He makes the apostolic columns flourish with hangings.

He fills the sacred cupboards with books devoted to God.

He enriches the sacred things

and cultivates the recesses of the separate chapels with lamps.

He clothes Peter’s altar with a garment heavy with gems and gold,

covers it with gilded veils and varied ornament,

and hangs upon it a rich crown gleaming with silver.

[Col. 0797D] As usual, he visits the royal city through envoys

[Note: [Col. 0797] Constantinople.]

illuminating it with the titles of faith

[Note: [Col. 0797] Synodal letters.]

and granting bonds of peace

[Note: [Col. 0797] Conditions.]

At their arrival, disturbance yields;

fraud is driven away;

crime, plots, and deceit, defeated, withdraw.

The city is restored to its former lord,

brought into subjection by victories.

When the deceptions have been dispelled,

the envoys are adorned with the honor of peace

[Note: [Col. 0797] The envoys.]

and, deserving it,

bring back to their patron what they had sought.

[Col. 0798A] Spurning the royal dignity of the Frankish king [*tempto* apparently stands for *contempto*, “spurned”],

his son [Note: [Col. 0797] Carloman.]

assigns himself and his gifts to Peter,

and accepts Christ’s yoke with bowed neck,

[Col. 0798B] so that, as a constant servant,

he may be free for the duties of heaven.

From master, a servant;

from king, a submissive minister,

so that he may be able to follow the footsteps of the supreme King.

This Father, moved by paternal piety

toward captives about to be sent away into profane kingdoms

[Note: [Col. 0797] Pagan.]

receives all who have been redeemed

at great expense.

He tears away their shackles

and grants them the enjoyment of freedom

and of their vows,

so that they may serve the Thunderer alone.

Again he moderates the barbarian disturbances

[Note: [Col. 0797] The Lombards.]

and their anger.

He softens their minds with gold

and with the gift of eloquence.

He redeems the cities and the fatherland

and removes the fury.

He changes the king,

making a giver from a plunderer,

a gentle lamb from a swift predator,

from a tiger’s offspring.

He captures the man who had sought to capture him

and leads the suppliant to Peter’s threshold.

He adds Christ’s heavenly yokes to the neck of the man fleeing pride and kingdoms,

[Col. 0798C] and rescues him from the mad passions of the raging world,

together with his wife and sons

[Note: [Col. 0797] With his wife and sons.]

He instructs him to serve God in peaceful worship.

He discovers a treasure of great and shining worth

[Note: [Col. 0797] *Talentum*, “a treasure.”]

in the holy cloisters

[Note: [Col. 0797] In the monastery.]:

the head of the illustrious martyr George,

by laying down which he once won the lofty kingdom of heaven

and a crown shining with perpetual light.

Golden veils lift up the treasure that has been found,

and it is placed in the hall,

while the people rejoice at what has been acquired.

There the pious Ruler

[Note: [Col. 0797] God.]

deigns to grant countless healings

through the lofty merits of the precious martyr.

The rich estates assigned to the sacred places are transferred.

The Father enlarges them with gifts and through a covenant of exchange;

he equips them with buildings and adorns them with the beauty of worship.

He subjects them to the churches of the saints

and dedicates them to the altars.

[Col. 0798D] He binds them with chains

[Note: [Col. 0797] Excommunications.]

and secures them by everlasting decrees.

Not forgetful of the poor,

while he cultivates the divine halls,

he directs and accumulates offerings

[Note: [Col. 0797] Allowances, distributions.]

and gives abundant care to the sick.

He establishes revenues that will bring a heavenly reward.

He renews the holy places of the just

and restores them to their ancient appearance.

He covers the altars with finely wrought canopies.

Cherishing the priests and clergy,

he protects his dependents,

[Col. 0799] and grants his people the joy of peaceful rest.

He skillfully sends the lights of Ausonia to the Greeks

[Note: [Col. 0799] The books of the *Dialogues*, translated by him into Greek.]

which had long been prepared in the distinguished eloquence of Gregory.

By giving worthy memorials to those below,

he wins memorials among those above.

## CHAPTER SEVEN. On the second Pope Stephen

[Col. 0799]

[Col. 0799A] The second Stephen undertakes the difficult sacred office of Peter,

after the one elected before him had been carried away

by the sudden violence of silent death

[Note: [Col. 0799] That is, after the man who had been elected before him had been removed and died.]

From childhood he had been accustomed to support good parents.

He had grown, assigned to each rank through the individual duties of the clergy.

While he shone in Levitical office,

he watched over the concerns of the Church

and guarded what had been decreed.

He was the helper and guardian of the poor,

the defender of the fold.

A steadfast herald of God,

restorer and promoter of the ancient protection extended to the needy,

he builds their dwellings,

renews those that have been overthrown,

and assigns and prepares gifts.

He cultivates and orders, with inward and outward honor

[Note: [Col. 0799] Spiritual and secular.]

the ministry obtained for him by divine power.

Peoples are driven into wars by evil counsels

[Note: [Col. 0799] The Lombards.]

He sends his brother

[Note: [Col. 0799] His deacon Paul.]

to restrain them and establish treaties of peace,

sending companions with him and entrusting gifts

[Note: [Col. 0799] To the same Paul.]

[Col. 0799B] They establish agreements, as though they were to be observed for many years,

but in truth they intend deceitfully to break them by an early act of wrongdoing.

Soon, when the moon had completed its fourth circuit

[Note: [Col. 0799] *Phoebes*, the moon.]

the tyrant

[Note: [Col. 0799] Aistulfus.]

bursts in and threatens the Father and the flock with fury.

Gentle men

[Note: [Col. 0799] Abbots.]

are sent to the raging bear in hope of a treaty.

The savage beast despises Christ’s peaceful lambs

and sends them away empty-handed.

But the bishop, entrusting his vows to the Lord,

sends them forth and sends his tears up to heaven.

Soon an imperial envoy arrives,

carrying commands to the raging king:

to recover his senses and return what he had seized.

The raider, admonished with gentle words,

returns empty and crafty replies

and, with savage effort, retains what he had seized.

While human assistance grows cold,

the Father judges it right to seek divine aid.

He gathers the ranks of his companions

and unites the Church.

[Col. 0799C] He urges them to implore the heavenly one—
and the merciful Father; he himself also persists with prayers and tears. He adds ashes and bares his feet; with importunate prayer they assault the lofty stars.

And so that prayers might worthily penetrate heaven and obtain a hearing, he commands his companions to persevere in holy works; he decrees that all things yield to pious prayers on the Sabbaths.

He himself, devoted to sacred things, adorns the altars with religious furnishings, enriches them with gifts, enlarges them with structures and buildings, and restores their roofs; nor does he cease from supplication.

Meanwhile he takes counsel to make known the cause to the king of the Franks, faithful to Christ and Peter. The pious Pippin receives it with compassion and, preparing to bring aid, promptly sends envoys to the City, asking only that he be deemed worthy to visit the Father.

[Col. 0799D] The shepherd, burning with love for his flock, leaves the fold and seeks peace for the sheep amid the troubled haunts of wild beasts.

Heavenly grace [Note: [Col. 0799] great serenity from heaven], the cherished comfort of the clergy, the commands of the imperial authority, and the leading citizens and [Col. 0800A] commanders of the Franks accompany the pope as he goes.

A heavenly fire shines brightly from the sky over the enemies of the Franks and threatens slaughter to the wicked, displaying beforehand the guiding signs of benevolent light.

The crafty wolf [Note: [Col. 0799] Aistulfus] strives to frighten him away from his righteous efforts; the undefeated leader persists on behalf of the flock.

He bears gifts and prayers to the enemy, but that man, with Pharaoh’s heart, refuses to release the captured sheep when admonished, nor does he admit the petitions of the grieving patron.

When the bishop sees that the iron hearts are in no way softened, he withdraws from the savage hyena. Where the most gentle piety of the excellent king calls him, he directs his journey, accompanied by a benevolent senate; passing over the deceits, he redoubles in praises the gifts offered to Christ the leader, and crosses the frozen Alps.

[Col. 0800B] The Frankish nobles hurry forward; thousands hasten to meet the pope. The king, together with his sons and wife, speeds to meet him, prostrates himself upon the ground, and adores the angelic Father who bears the laws of heaven.

He performs his duties humbly: he himself leads the blessed man, riding on horseback, and singing praises and songs; he receives him in the royal hall of the King of kings.

He sits beside him, watches him, accepts his devout prayers, willingly supports his petitions, declares himself ready to obey, and rejoices to serve Peter’s client.

While winter’s frost prevented his return [Note: [Col. 0799] Supply negatur (“is prevented”).—Anastasius omits this miracle; Stephen himself commemorates it in a letter, volume II of the Councils of Gaul.], he remains at the sacred threshold of your martyr, Dionysius.

Afflicted by severe illness, with the remedies of human medicine failing, he is thought to be approaching the extremity of death.

[Col. 0800C] Seeking better things and the strength of sure medicine, he asks the supreme physician, frequents the consecrated temples, and seeks the help of the pious Fathers.

Devoted to prayers in the shrine of the aforementioned martyr, he is visited by his own patrons, Peter and Paul.

With them Dionysius too stands present as a witness and is urged by the Fathers [Note: [Col. 0799] a Patribus, “by the Fathers”] to bring relief to the sick man.

Obeying the pious admonitions, he approaches with his companions the sick man, announces peace, removes fear from his heart, promises a joyful return to his own walls, and commands him, once restored to health, to rise, to dedicate an altar in the Lord’s name with apostolic authority, and to proclaim Christ’s praises.

Nourished by life-giving light and also by divine nectar, he leaps up, delivered from illness. Striving to perform the commanded duties, he is not considered to have lost his sound mind:

[Col. 0800D] until he reports what he saw and thus fulfills the martyr’s commands.

And, consecrating the father at the summit of the kingdom and his pledges [Note: [Col. 0799] Pippin and his sons] with sacred oil, he enriches him with munificent anointing, raises his future line to the heights, and adorns it with royal authority.

[Col. 0801A] He honors the place with dignity and enriches the altar with sacred furnishings.

Then the king, together with the nobles of the kingdom and the distinguished senate, taking counsel amid these dangerous circumstances to assist the pope, unanimously devote themselves to the service of Christ and Peter.

He cannot be turned aside by any deceits of the wicked serpent, nor by the crafty schemes of the brother who was sent; indeed, he places the dangers of the Church before those of his brother. Striving to stand firm in the settled conflict, he sends the bishop’s demands to the tyrant and, under the bond of peace, returns what had been taken from Cephas:

he repeats the same demand three times. Neither by gifts nor by persuasive words can he soften the frozen heart, nor does any moderation succeed in bending the rigid breast toward peace.

[Col. 0801B] Therefore, gathering the Frankish forces, he leads the army, intending himself to conduct the apostolic cause. He was traversing the road midway with the pope, striving to soften the defiant hearts and seeking to move the savage heart of the king also through messages, whenever he sent commands and prayers, entreating him to spare the bloodshed.

In reply, that man sends threats against the Father and the king.

But they, confident that they must entrust all hope to the Lord and that they are sheltered under the protection of Christ, for whom the wars are being waged, ask the prince for His aid. He brings the gifts promised to the arrogant man, to be given to the humble Father and his flock.

Thus, commending himself to a faithful leader and patron, he begins the journey already undertaken, sending some men ahead to guard the approaches and stand watch in the narrow passage.

When the enemy learned that the king was advancing ahead of the main force, he suddenly attacked these few men with united wedges, expecting them to lie overthrown; but he suffered the losses of slaughter instead.

Defeated by a few, while more of his own men were killed, he departs and relies on arms only as a means of escape; trembling, he shuts himself within the city’s covering.

But when the just men had turned the defenses of the wicked against them, they seized the plunder of the plunderers. After the avenging sword had brought slaughter, the king follows the Father and, supported by him, presses the walls that conceal the enemy. Meanwhile, by praying, the pope compelled the deceitful [Note: [Col. 0801] treacherous Aistulfus] to enter into a faithful [Note: [Col. 0801] Pippin] peace treaty, swearing that he would return what he had unjustly retained after seizing it.

Thus, recovering his own and the kingdoms of the Franks, the king gives the blessed Father faithful allies at the Roman walls.

Now, as he returns, crowds of peoples run out to meet the shepherd, bringing Christ exceptional thanks and praises.

[Col. 0801D] Bands of clergy and people receive the Father, bearing splendid trophies.

Here, striving to refresh the flock and restore its neglected duties, he renews the psalmody in nightly offices, increases songs worthy of choirs, and provides suitable comforts, so that the devout may vie with one another in living by psalms.

But the enemy, turning his accustomed deceits over in his heart, redoubles his crime and repeatedly commits his familiar perjuries.

[Col. 0802A] He refuses to let his burden [Note: [Col. 0801] sins] grow lighter and regards his deadly acts as nothing. Invading what had been left behind, he strives to heap wickedness upon wickedness, and drags the strength of his kingdom [Note: [Col. 0801] his own, toward destruction] with him beneath Tartarus.

He takes up arms, gathers his wedges and wretched forces, brings battle against the bulwark of the Church and against Peter, and surrounds the sacred walls with sacrilegious iron.

The bishop marks out for Pippin, the lover of Christ, the wicked deeds and actions of the fierce dragon against the pious camp [Note: [Col. 0801] the Romans].

Pippin deploys his forces and draws forth avenging arms, burning with the right of a just conflict against perjurers.

Resisting imperial messengers, envoys, and commands, he yields neither to prayers nor threats, nor is he overcome by gifts; he presents himself to the wicked in a fierce assault, terrible to behold.

He persists against the terrified enemy until [Note: [Col. 0801] donec, “until”] he forces the besieged enemy to restore the rights, and receives and returns to blessed Peter the towns that had been seized, restraining the swelling necks of the proud.

He governs the regions of Italy and brings peace and calm, while they rejoice to submit themselves to the apostolic reins.

The pope, giving thanks to God, raises a tower for the hall [Note: [Col. 0801] of Saint Peter] and clothes it with the gleam of silver and gold.

He raises bronze trumpets [Note: [Col. 0801] bells], cast from metal, by which he may urge the crowds of the people to offer praises and prayers to the Thunderer.

The All-Powerful increases prosperity and the enemy is removed; at the bishop’s command kings and kingdoms are governed; wars are lulled; public dignity rises in sacred order; the state grows; the shepherd enlarges the fold; he guards against deceitful plots and recovers what was taken away.

Bringing forth new columns in the splendor of Cephas, he builds churches for Peter, his brother, and his daughter [Note: [Col. 0801] Andrew and Petronilla].

He adorns them with structures and increases them with shining gifts; at the king’s instruction he beautifies Petronilla’s bones.

[Col. 0802C] Famous through these deeds and strengthened by the radiance of victory, he seeks lofty rewards, blessed under Peter’s guidance.

## On Pope Paul

[Note: [Col. 0801] The title is absent in the manuscript codex. In the margin, however, is written: “Paul.”]

Paul succeeds his brother Stephen in office; with him he had shone brightly in devoted piety and the light of wisdom; as an inseparable companion he had clung to him to the end, and soon the governance passed to him, like the dispersal of darkness before the sun.

[Col. 0802D] He, pious and gentle, strove to bring relief to the afflicted. Accustomed to visiting the sick and the pallets of the poor beneath the cover of silent night, he freed those bound in prisons and redeemed the oppressed from debts, being a father to orphans and widows.

A guardian of the Catholic faith, he admonishes, urges, asks, and insists that kings restore the images of the saints and the polished images of the Lord.

He honors the mausoleums of the righteous and advances them with urns; restoring the ashes to the city, he raises them into halls.

He strove to consecrate his own shrines beneath Christ’s roof with relics, adorning them in the name of the Fathers Silvester and Stephen, and further illuminating them with the splendor [Note: [Col. 0801] honor] of many holy men, supplementing them with abundant gifts,

[Col. 0803A] and dedicating them to endless dances of hymn-singing praise.

Here he built a basilica for the first Fathers [Note: [Col. 0803] Peter and Paul] of the city, where, with their knees pressed against the stone, the trophies were marked [Note: [Col. 0803] where they prayed, already about to suffer martyrdom, for the overthrow of Simon], while they poured forth their vows in anticipation of receiving martyrdom.

[Col. 0804A] He also built a suitable place for prayer, for laying his members to rest, and for preserving the site. He adorned the face of the church with various metals and enriched it with an image of the Mother of God.

There at last, having completed his service, he receives a tomb after death.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Pope Stephen III

[Col. 0803]

[Col. 0803A] From this point Stephen III, after the savagery had been removed from the sacred height he had occupied, assumes Paul’s dignity.

Energetic and learned, the benevolent pupil of his predecessors, he apprehends the thief, punishes the thieves by God’s judgment, and brings the leaders of so great a crime to trial. By the senate’s unanimous vote and equal favor, he is chosen chief of the clergy and of the city’s armies and treasures [Note: [Col. 0803] or, “by the favor of the senate”], and is consecrated bishop with worthy devotion.

As he disperses the clouds of error, bishops are summoned from every side, and, at his call, a council is gathered in Rome to defend the sacred rights of the Fathers.

The error is suppressed by decrees, and its author is punished. Those who had been unlawfully joined to sacred ministers repent.

The perverse burden is judged [Note: [Col. 0803] the burden of penance is imposed], the evil is cut away, the example of the crime is condemned, and divine laws are proclaimed.

[Col. 0804A] Once the terror has been driven from Rome, it next invades nearby Ravenna and is subdued by the bishop’s pious, fervent rigor, from which no wickedness turns him aside.

With the supreme power of the Teucrians [Note: [Col. 0803] Franks] employed, the force of the envoys drives the wolf from the Ravennate fold and opens the doors to the shepherd of pious governance.

He instructs this Church, entrusted to him, to be governed with prudent goodness; he reforms the honor of the clergy and arranges for Peter’s bishops to celebrate Masses properly at the altar on the day of light [Note: [Col. 0803] Sunday], and for the glory of heaven to be sung to the Lord each year in an angelic hymn.

He adorns the apostolic halls with silver furnishings and, preserving his own charges as far as he can, protects them. He strives to defend those deceived by an unpatriotic mind and to calm the plots of the savage with kindly efforts.

## CHAPTER IX. On Pope Adrian

[Col. 0803]

[Col. 0803A] Born from the outstanding blood of a noble family, steadfast Adrian next follows, firm in heart.

Defender of the faith, protector of his homeland and city, comforter and guardian of the poor, and interpreter of the canons, from childhood he restrained himself with a chaste body and subdued his limbs by wearing the sacred covering of a goat-hair garment [Note: [Col. 0803] a hair-shirt].

Free from worldly praise, he frequently practiced fasting for the Lord and diligently cared, as far as he could, for the needy.

Radiant through these deeds, he was joined to the bishop and clergy, and, strong in courage and advanced through the ranks, was instructed in the sacred order and consecrated a levite.

Thus shining more and more as his honor increased, he supplied the peoples with the nourishment of the word through the light of his works.

[Col. 0803C] Therefore, greatly loved by the citizens in pious affection, he is soon elected worthy to succeed the deceased bishop.

Without delay he restores to the city and their homes those who had been driven out, releases those thrust into prisons from darkness and chains, and, while all rejoice together, rises to the sacred heights, having thereby won exceptional honor through his merits.

Immediately, beset by the deceit of the crafty serpent, he cautiously speaks truths while tempering his response to falsehoods.

He does not refuse peace, while he avoids the crimes committed under the name of peace.

Nor is he swallowed in the waves by a faltering rush of words [Note: [Col. 0803] by verbosity]; rather, he judges that faith must be proved by deeds and circumstances.

Bardus does not endure the oracles of the venerable pope.

But, putting battles before any agreement, he rages and invades the cities, servants, places, and estates of Peter.

[Col. 0804A] Soon voices and tears of complaint are brought to the Father, as the dragon commits cruel plunderings against the shepherds.

He gives the savage thief letters demanding that he cease his plots and return what he has perversely invaded.

The other refuses to do what is requested unless he sees the bishop and receives a treaty from him, striving in the dispute to compel him to anoint the boys [Note: [Col. 0803] the sons of Carolomannus], fugitives from the kingdom, as heads of the Frankish nation, although their uncle held the sceptre as patrician of the city and friend of the Father and people.

The bishop, guarding against traps, is misled by no trick.

He commands the sower of hatred and maker of captures not to carry off the gentle lambs whom he had consecrated.

And the man who is proved a murderer and guilty of bloodshed—the envoy [Note: [Col. 0803] the legate]—while the bishop attempts to avenge the crime with gentle medicine, dies at the request of the Fathers and the people, with the pope forbidding the punishment and wishing to relieve his soul through perpetual penance and restore it renewed to heaven.

[Col. 0804C] Meanwhile the pestilent man does not spare Peter’s clients, but tears them apart with bloodshed, plunder, fires, and plots.

Often admonished concerning these matters by gentle exhortation, by sacred envoys, and by the distinguished senate, he returns nothing worthy of the silent prayers or of so great a patron; instead, he drives away Christ’s empty-handed servants and orders the blessed Father himself to come into his presence [Note: [Col. 0803] to his own presence].

The pope replies that he will go, provided the robber returns what he has taken.

Whatever he had ordered to be sent, he must recall after delaying it [Note: [Col. 0803] “recover what he had sent away”].

Otherwise he would not see the face of the pontiff.

[Col. 0805A] Such was the king’s message, and such the pope’s sacred embassy.

Nor did he admonish the tyrant once or only a single time, but repeatedly; indeed, he made every effort through Fathers sent from the sacred order.

In reply that man brings threats, terrors, wars, and plunder, and shakes Peter’s flocks in a raging whirlwind.

Moreover, adding his own fugitive soldiery to his forces, he hastens to bring violence against the benevolent Father.

But when gates were set against him and the walls strengthened, he withdrew, struck by a forceful anathema.

Confounded, he withdraws home, his wickedness turned against him.

The bishop had sent commands to the Sicambrian king, seeking his aid for this difficult undertaking.

Charles, learning everything more carefully from the envoys, urges the hostile enemy by peaceful prayers and persuasion,

[Col. 0805B] and also by gifts offered to dispel his savagery.

But even so, the heart harder than bronze cannot be softened.

Therefore, gathering a strong force with a wedge of troops, the stern judge departs while the petitioner himself is despised.

He approaches the fortified barriers [Note: [Col. 0805] the Alps] and again offers gifts, seeking arbiters of peace and war.

But even then he cannot calm the swelling, burning hearts of those who, closing the entrances to the kingdom with solid fortifications, kept the Franks from entering; repelled by the barriers, they were preparing to make a headlong return to their own kingdom.

By chance, only one night delayed their return.

Then suddenly, a terror sent by the heavenly ruler strikes the hearts of the rebellious men by the judgment of the savage one; panic, consuming their companions’ hearts, turns them to flight.

Soon, silently abandoning the camps during the night, with the supports of flight left behind and their possessions disregarded,

[Col. 0805C] they all together take up their march, with no pursuer following.

Seeing the descendants of Antenor [Note: [Col. 0805] the Franks] achieve victory without a struggle, those whom the divine hand had put to flight pursue the wicked and seize the plunder of the plunderers in a joyful assault.

The deceiver shuts himself in, seeking protection within the fortifications.

His terrified companions scatter, seeking different destinations.

Some, struck in their hearts, follow better counsels, and, placing their hair under apostolic authority [Note: [Col. 0805] laying aside their pride], surrender themselves and testify with eager vows that they will remain forever faithful to his service.

But, with Peter as his leader, the victorious king, pressing on in his footsteps, surrounds in the fields the wandering nobles and the fugitive king’s astonished troops, and encircles Pavia with iron.

He crosses the terrible Po and shakes Ducominuna by siege, capturing several cities at a distance.

He receives the devoted fugitives and, hastening to visit Cephas’s threshold, seeks to celebrate Easter in Rome.

[Col. 0805D] To meet him, the Father sends out crowds of people: grateful choirs and singing children, adorned with leaves, palms, and the green olive.

He displays standards and crosses. As the pious king sees them, he swiftly leaps down from the lofty horse on which he is riding and proceeds on foot with his nobles to the sought-for threshold.

Received with due honor by the sacred patron awaiting him,

[Col. 0806A] he humbly climbs the steps, giving a kiss to each [Note: [Col. 0805] read singlis, “to each,” for singulis], embraces the holy Father, takes his life-giving right hand, and ascends the celebrated hall of Peter.

The clergy and the Roman companions give high praises, crying: “Blessed is he who comes in Christ’s name.”

Thus the pious nobles, prostrate before Peter’s relics, joyfully pour forth their vows to the supreme Lord.

Entering the city, the prince seeks the intercession of the saints and visits the venerable temples.

Easter is celebrated with great and conspicuous honor by the princes [Note: [Col. 0805] by the pope and the king], according to the customary rite and at the appropriate stations.

The bishop orders the treaties and agreements with Peter to be renewed; the territories long since ceded [Note: [Col. 0805] concessa, “ceded,” for cessa] are restored to the jurisdiction of the apostolic see, and are recorded in written documents as enduring [Note: [Col. 0805] “inserted”].

Relying on these arrangements, the king hastens to bind the besieged robber,

[Col. 0806B] shaking the walls he had been given with a ready assault.

But within, a greater slaughter takes place: the pestilence, raging fiercely, inflicts more devastation than the hand of the fighting enemy.

At last justice captures the unjust; the wicked and foolish are subjected to the rods, while the wise man, having gained the scepters, leads Bardus, the tyrant, away into the kingdoms of the Franks.

But the Father of the Church, lover of Christ’s splendor, enjoying the light of peace and heir to Solomon’s devotion, honorably provides for the adornment of the Lord’s house.

Here he varies golden curtains with a pattern of gems, depicts Peter freed from his bonds with angelic design [Note: [Col. 0805] “paints what had been removed”], and lays down silver pavement for the floor.

He surrounds the house with curtains and much light.

Honoring it with porticoes, steps, and carved marble, renewing it with attached beams and brilliant images,

[Col. 0806C] he adorns the temples of the Nourisher with red-gold metal and irrigates Peter’s basilica, renewed with much labor, through channels of water, bringing the courts fresh streams again.

Covering the interior with gold, he fills it with rich vessels, and lavish images [Note: [Col. 0805] “figures”] are displayed in splendid signs.

He raises doors given in excellent bronze [Note: [Col. 0805] “made of bronze”] to a lofty height.

He builds a basilica on its own ground and adorns it with many relics and radiant splendor.

He restores the brilliance of its inscriptions, altars, and shrines, and illuminates Andrew’s hall with silver.

He adorns Paul’s urn and hangs numerous curtains; he paints the courts with marble brilliance.

He polishes the interior with forms fashioned in gold and silver, restores the roofs, surrounds the precincts with structures, and casts renowned vessels as gifts for the altar.

[Col. 0806D] He embroidered the Queen of Heaven with gems and gold at her departure [Note: [Col. 0805] assumption], by which she entered the thresholds of the heavenly kingdom; he multiplies the furnishings and binds coverings of woven bands.

Honoring the temples, he purifies, renews, and spaciously reshapes them; ennobling them, he inspects them and adorns them with lavish gifts.

He fits together the sections of the Basilica of the Savior, restores what was collapsing, and enlarges the fountains and vestibules.

He prepares golden vessels and necklaces for the sacred table.

Renewing the roofs of Stephen, he heaps adornments upon the halls with curtains.

[Col. 0807A] He repairs the timbers of Clement, already close to collapse.

Laurence receives the roofs with hangings in his halls.

For him new temples and pious communities are restored.

The images of the levites and the sacred vessels gleam with gold.

A portico of the Church is built at the city gate.

He makes the roof of the blessed Mark flourish through an equal work, and restores Silvester’s house with similar honor.

He builds silver arches and golden chalices for Mark.

He enlarges the church of Aedisius [Note: [Col. 0807] the name of a holy martyr], enriching the shrine with endowments.

He rebuilds the church of Cyriacus and the hall of Susanna.

Valentinus and Pancratius are honored in vestments; for the latter the venerable work of the temple is restored.

The house of Victor rises again through equal piety.

The broad avenue of apostolic splendor flourishes in the rebuilt temple, adorned with varied and abundant coverings,

[Col. 0807B] and the tombs of Peter and Marcellinus are restored.

The temples of Adrian shine with the brilliance of silver.

All the renewed buildings gleam and abound in the gifts of vessels.

The roofs of Sixtus, overthrown by ruin, are restored.

The churches of Agapitus, Eusebius, Rufina, and Secunda, together with those of Euplica, the prophet of Jerusalem, John,

and Felix, are raised and shine.

He restores the title of Pudens, the catacombs, and those of Leucius, Eugenia, Sophia, Praxedes, and Felicitas.

Epimachus, Zeno, Abdon, Boniface, Hermes,

and Marcellus, Saturninus, and the Jordanic relics [Note: [Col. 0807] the cemetery of the Jordani] shine with this adornment, as do the seven relics of Agnes.

Secundinus, Pammachius, and Agnes also shine,

together with Agnes’s nurse, Nicomedes, Hippolytus,

[Col. 0807C] the Four Crowned Martyrs, and Sabina’s temple.

Sergius and his companion grow splendid with their restored roof.

[Col. 0808A] He leads Anastasius’s hall forth from the fires in better condition.

Restoring the vessels for the services, the vestments, and the furnishings, he makes Martina gleam with silver and Serum [Note: [Col. 0807] Serum, the name of an Asian people, renowned for work in silk; so the manuscript] with a silken covering.

The title of Prisca is rebuilt, and its hanging cloth gleams.

Together with the remaining altars of Cosmas and Damian, many others are adorned with furnishings and restored to their ancient honor.

They are enriched with sacred vessels of refined gold.

Moreover, he brings golden gifts for repairing the walls [Note: [Col. 0807] of the city], restoring the fortifications at great expense in gold.

He arranges and restores the monastic regulations.

Assigning estates, olive groves, vineyards, and houses to the poor, he dedicates them to the eternal service and support of Christ’s people.

He cultivates this house through building works, as well as his fathers’ [Note: [Col. 0807] his predecessors’] house.

He multiplies and renews the various baths through his labor,

[Col. 0808B] and waters the form of the virgin people with streams.

He cares for the needy through services of consolation, establishes psalmody with various monastic choirs, restores and enriches the communities, and adorns them with leaders.

He also repairs the pious camps of virgins with choral communities, increasing their endowments and providing worthy services in return.

Thus, caring for internal matters, he does not cease adding concern for external affairs. At the emperor’s command [Note: [Col. 0807] the emperor’s palaces], he visits the palaces and, through envoys, governs them; he recovers the sacred signs [Note: [Col. 0807] images] that are to be preserved.

When the council of the earlier Fathers assembled in one place, they confirm the pious doctrine one hundred and fifty times over.

Rome, mournful and wet with the foam of the Tiber’s fury, seeks the help of her protector and the assistance of the Father.

He fights with prayers; when he calms the feverish waters, he settles affairs, transforms earthly things into heavenly, and enters the hall honored by his excellent merits.

## CHAPTER X. On Pope Leo III

[Col. 0807]

[Col. 0807C] Leo III soon succeeds him in dignity and conduct.

Strong in the Scriptures, radiant in integrity of character, undefeated in strength, eloquent in graceful speech, wise in the honor of his mind, and generous in the gift of piety,

he refreshes the sick and provides suitable comforts.

Relying on these resources, dear to both people and God, he is swiftly raised and climbs to the summit of the chair.

Here he is humble toward the gentle and stern toward the proud, generous in showing mercy to the lowly, and just toward the wicked.

He enlarges and increases the splendor of the clergy and the Church.

Multiplying golden gifts, gems, hangings, and crowns for Peter, he likewise renews the coverings of the hall, illuminating it with many lights and shining images.

With this splendor he makes Paul’s church radiant, and many other temples as well,

[Col. 0807D] striving through abundant endowments to equal the works of his patron [Note: [Col. 0807] predecessor], or even surpass them.

The raging water-snake [Note: [Col. 0807] demon] cannot bear to conceal its envy.

It prepares plots, supplying snares and weapons; it devises hidden deceptions under a disguised appearance,

[Col. 0808C] and attaches itself to acts of service previously prepared with the dragon’s gall.

They perform their service and color their poisons with honey.

Amid the solemn signs of prayers and praises, they draw their dreadful swords.

While the sheepish crowds are scattered against the shepherd of the flock, savage bears rage,

and wild beasts leap at the teacher’s ram-like face.

With claws stained by innocent blood, they burn to tear the sacred cheeks with savage hands,

to extinguish the twin lamps in his unbroken brow,

and to tear from his jaws the plectrum of sacred speech.

Nor is it enough to have once thrust the blade into his mouth.

The cruel hand keeps hold of the parts stripped of their functions [Note: [Col. 0807] the limbs deprived of the functions of speech by their wounds],

and, after he has been afflicted with various blows and sprinkled with much blood,

they seize him, drag him away, and thrust him back beneath a cave.

[Col. 0808D] They appoint guards to defend their mangled captive.

Though tested by blows, supreme compassion did not abandon the servant, nor did Peter reject his disciple.

His sight is restored by heaven and the light he had lost is poured back into him.

The returning light, blazing again, enters the corresponding windows in a wondrous manner.

Though deprived of speech, he speaks; the organs of his tongue return after being cut.

[Col. 0809A] Moreover, the Ruler adds blessings to the suffering man and allows faithful men to bring back the Father.

When they see Peter’s strongholds and hear the account of the one who speaks again,

the blessed and exalted man, performing miracles alone, is acclaimed by the people, who praise the one who brings promises.

In the man who trusts in Him, God becomes light and salvation, mouth and tongue; protecting him and strengthening him by divine power, He comforts the man and grants joyful happiness to the devout, while the savage beasts tremble at their dangers.

Yet they do not cease raging in their crime or completing their work.

They invade houses and revel in plunder and weapons.

But the Lord provides comfort for the servant who has been robbed:

He sends the duke of Spoleto, surrounded by the strength of his forces,

[Col. 0809B] to render aid, while he marvels at the gifts of heaven.

The citizens, sprinkled with these wonders, rush to visit the suffering man.

People of different ranks and ages, commoners and nobles, carry the marvelous trophies through the cities of Italy.

They also report these things across the Alps into the lands of Gaul, accompanying the Father as he shines with heavenly splendor.

They proclaim the divine greatness to the pious king [Note: [Col. 0809] Charles].

He orders his nobles and sons to go before him, and he himself swiftly follows, going out to meet the one who bears the most illustrious gifts of sacred virtue.

Everywhere praise resounds; everywhere glory thunders to Christ.

The king, mingling with his troops, frequently offers thanks and praises in hymns.

Tears flow back, shed amid joy.

Christ’s wondrous work is magnified among the peoples,

[Col. 0809C] the apostolic height of victory is carried above the heavens,

and Peter’s servant is celebrated with worthy honor.

But savage fury rages through the unprotected fields with sacrilegious extravagance and black fires.

Increasing the evil, it rages with thefts and plots; through deceptions it pursues the expelled enemy, tearing him apart with slanders [Note: [Col. 0809] defaming the pope].

Nor does the benevolent dignity remain long without battle in the enemy’s absence [Note: [Col. 0809] “without war”].

It does not permit the enemy to be shaken by a blind assault or stained with a dark crime; it renews the war, reclaims the field, and, coming forth, holds fast the city and the struggle that had been set in place.

When the leader’s arrival is known, the eager flock hastens in a body to meet the shepherd.

At the same time, the distinguished Fathers, the clergy, and illustrious crowds

[Col. 0809D] of both sexes, from diverse regions and lands,

raise the Father with praises and celebrate him with song [Note: [Col. 0809] singing].

They receive him at the summit and restore him to the highest seat.

Although powerful in office, he does not refuse to make amends for the charges brought against him.

He submits to examination and grants his enemies the opportunity to speak.

When they are unable to bring forward anything against him along the path of truth, they are finally sent to the king by the Frankish judges.

Charles also, acting as examiner, attacks the city,

[Col. 0810A] summons the leading men of the sacred order, and calls the nobles of Aeneas’s descendants, the Teucrians, and the lights of the kingdom.

Yet they judge no charge against Peter’s high seat.

This seat, free from every crime, clears itself of all accusations through the evidence brought forward.

The nobles bring joyful praises to Christ and celebrate the king of heaven’s birthday.

With exceptional praises and the honor of the highest splendor, the king receives the august crown from the apostolic see.

The honor of the Roman Fathers is proclaimed increased.

The scepters of the Frankish empire shine with dignity, and the king’s son rises to the kingdom after receiving sacred anointing.

The king offers tables gleaming with radiant silver,

adding golden vessels studded with sparkling gems,

a radiant altar with its bases, and a cross with an ornamented covering;

the Gospel also gleams with brilliant hyacinths.

[Col. 0810B] Through these gifts Christ, the Mother of God, and the nobles are honored.

The sacrilegious men are handed over to the executioner, and, by the senate’s judgment, are deprived of their lands, having confessed their reciprocal acts of atonement.

Enjoying peace, the bishop devotes himself to building and adornment.

With pious expenditures he does not cease beautifying the temples with gifts, hangings, altars, vessels, and baths.

He restores Paul’s buildings, which had suddenly collapsed in a tremor, to a better state and renews them with honorable adornment.

In addition, increasing these and many other things with numerous endowments,

he multiplies the laws of prayer and hands down the Gallican observances [Note: [Col. 0809] the petitions customarily celebrated by the Gauls before the Ascension], vows that precede the Lord’s ascent.

Thus, after he has assiduously propagated the Church’s glory through fervent effort and the gift of piety,

he, having completed his service, is received into the hall of heavenly splendor.

## On Stephen IV

[Note: [Col. 0809] The title is absent from the codex. “Stephen” is written in the margin of the text.]

[Col. 0810C] He had advanced Stephen through the ranks, recognizing in him a man of character and integrity, whose concern was to preserve in his conduct and life the useful things he sowed through the light of the word.

Therefore, suitable for sacred duties and approved by Peter, he is deemed worthy and placed over the divine citadel.

Striving to preserve peace and caring to strengthen the Church’s rights, he eagerly visits the illustrious kingdoms of the Franks.

Soon the lofty royal house serves him through pious acts of obedience and uses powerful gifts in his honor.

From there he exalts our Church to heaven—the Church through which the Frankish nation entered the light of the faith—adorning the church at Rheims with his services [Note: [Col. 0809] See Flodoard, book II, chapter 20].

He gives Louis the emblems of the kingdom and adds the imperial honors of august light, raising the pupils of Remigius’s dignity to a higher station.

He gladly obtains, according to his merits, what he asks of the emperor [Note: [Col. 0809] pro meritis, “according to his merits”]; moreover, distinguished gifts are added to the honored man [Note: [Col. 0809] the pope].

Indeed, he confers the seats and domestic rights as well, as partner of the Roman Empire and heir to its height, making Peter heir to estates in Frankish territory.

The pope, following the footsteps of the Redeemer, who loosens the sins of servants and restores kingdoms that have been taken away [Note: [Col. 0809] from the king of the Lombards],

brings the exiles back to their homeland with paternal piety.

[Col. 0811A] And as far as he is able, he adorns the Church with splendor, honoring vessels and crosses and producing sacred curtains [Note: [Col. 0811] hangings].

[Col. 0812A] He did not remain long on earth, burning with heavenly longing; he was taken from darkness and joined to the stars.

## CHAPTER XI. On Pope Paschal

[Col. 0811]

[Col. 0811A] Paschal, following swiftly upon the dignity he had undertaken, shines forth—chaste in his pursuits, pious, renowned, innocent,

great-hearted, generous, cheerful, devoted, honorable,
