and gentle; watchful in practicing prayers and fasts,

a receiver of strangers and a comforter of the needy.

Thus, having shone forth through his merits as abbot of the monks, he was given to the Church’s supreme authority.

Increasing in the radiance of his works, he is called to the highest jurisdiction as the hundredth pontiff, with the supreme patron [God] and the Roman senate joining in their prayers.

[Col. 0811B] Once installed, he firmly and skillfully holds the commands of the Fathers and the reins of the law.

As a celebrated governor, he promulgates decrees, a gentle friend of integrity, restorer and cultivator of sacred houses,

builder of holy houses, having received the pledges of the Passion.

He enlarges the alms of the clergy and brings gifts to heaven.

He draws those subdued in distant kingdoms out of their bonds and, with the weight of gold, removes the weight of their chains.

He brings back captives transported from Africa and returns those seized in Spain,

while each homeland rejoices to look upon its own children.

This pope solemnly adorns the shrine of the martyr Sixtus

and stores Peter’s relics in a hall flourishing through his merits.

He also transfers the ashes of the saints Processus and Martinianus [Note: [Col. 0811] transferring the relics] and treats them with worthy honor.

[Col. 0811C] Honoring the patron with gifts, he illuminates the shrine and gives pounds of silver and weights of gold for the images [Note: [Col. 0811] statues].

Preparing little vessels and hangings, he also fashions keys in gold.

It happened through the raging deceit of a fire-breathing dragon that foreign masses of flame were carried over the roofs.

After these had consumed everything, the heat, breathing into the Roman walls, had entered Peter’s porticoes.

Oppressed, their hearts poured forth a cup of forgetfulness [Note: [Col. 0811] sleep], while secret silence was broken by those who reported these things to the pope.

Trusting in faith, he swiftly flies toward the darkness, confronting the weapons of the triumphing battle against the raging fire.

He stands like a great mountain set against it; resisting the flames as the fire blazes back, he overthrows the conflagrations with prayers and, with Cephas as his protector, extinguishes the savage fumes.

Fighting through prayer, he does not leave the field of battle,

[Col. 0811D] until by his vows he overcomes the darkness and fires of night.

Grieving the losses of the needy, he restores what had been devastated, replacing for the afflicted what the guilty flame had devoured:

he brings golden gifts and restores clothing and provisions.

An abundance of timber is added to the buildings, so that they may be rebuilt as before.

And so that the hostile enemy might not rejoice either in the deceit he had perpetrated or in the Church’s loss,

the portico of Peter, seized by the fires, is repaired and enlarged,

[Col. 0812A] rising in better form and brought forth with greater splendor.

The bishop inserts the apostolic acts into the hall’s hangings

and adorns the façade of the temple with marvelous beauty.

Renewing the roofs of Praxedis and beautifying them with varied light, he raises a triumphal arch with radiant splendor.

Accepting many relics from worm-eaten tombs,  
he assigns the recovered remains of the righteous to the restored [Note: renovated.] church,  
and gathers together at once the blessed company of God’s servants,  
appointing praises to be sung in Greek melody,

[Col. 0812B] and grants fields suitable for the sacred uses of the servants.

Here, placing the ashes of Zeno, he builds shrines [Note: temples],  
accumulating splendor resplendent with silver and gold,  
and honoring them with histories and the palms [Note: victories] of gems and light.  
He restores and enlarges the walls  
of the luminous mistress, adorning them with gifts, hangings, and sacred furnishings.

Seeing Cecilia’s church burdened by misfortunes,  
he raises it to better things, rebuilding its enclosed upper structures.

The heavenly Virgin, who had appeared to him wearied by prayers  
and judged him worthy to address, nevertheless rebukes him: why  
had he abandoned the task he had begun of seeking the remains  
which the credulous populace believed had been lifted into the air?

After reporting how the matter stood, and recording the name  
for the one who asked, she urges him to persevere in his pious undertakings,

[Col. 0812C] until he rejoices in the relic that has been found. “For it pleases,” she says,  
“the eternal Lord, for love of whose splendor  
it is known that I suffered, that I, newly found by him,  
should be enclosed by you within the protection of the temple you have built.”

After these words she swiftly returns to heaven.

The pope, rejoicing at so clear a revelation of the light,  
searches for the treasures and counts the talents granted to him [Note: entrusted to him];  
he discovers precious necklaces of extraordinary gems.

[Note: [Col. 0811D] Frod., Book II, chapter 19.] Here he dispatches our Ebo to the Northmen,  
as a minister of light and life to the barbarian people.

Golden coverings concealed the maidenly relic:  
the linens of martyrdom gleamed with illustrious blood.

The life-giving Father, handling these holy gifts with devoted hands,  
gathers them and brings the instruments of salvation into the city,  
placing the shining remains in a splendid chamber [Note: mausoleum].

[Col. 0812D] At the same time the lover of virtue, the bridegroom [Note: cf. Valerianus],  
is brought in, having obtained the agreement made with his chaste brother [Note: chaste ones].  
Maximus, Urbanus, and also Lucius, his companion at the altar,  
are deposited there. The companies [Note: congregations], radiant in piety, receive them,  
and he supports the hymn-singing choirs with worthy assistance.  
He brings in more than a thousand pounds of silver,  
relieving them with vineyards, fields, houses, and servants;  
and with an increased endowment of many suitable vestments [Note: ornaments].

[Col. 0813A] Renewing the virginal bands, the bishop restores them  
to their ancient splendor, adding things suitable for their uses;  
and he increases the honors of the various halls in different ways.

Bringing golden gifts for vessels, images, and altars,  
and honoring the bodies, altars, and basins with silver;  
he piles up marble splendor and the ornaments of the Seres.

Heaven receives these things, sown on earth, multiplied a hundredfold.

## CHAPTER XII. On Saint Eugenius II, Valentinus, Gregory IV, and Pope Sergius

[Col. 0813]

[Col. 0813A] Eugenius the Second undertakes the office entrusted by lot,  
pious in heart, learned in understanding, eloquent in speech;  
cheerful, generous, a diligent thinker on holy goodness [Note: holiness],  
just, a despiser of avarice, and a hater of strife.

Under him the world, shining with peace and overflowing with abundance,  
dances, adorning its rule as much as is granted.

This Father once adorns the church of Sabina  
with the splendor of the rite granted to him [Note: granted to him before he became pope],  
and enriches it with abundant gifts.

Receiving with fatherly compassion the citizens  
who had long been expelled and returning them,  
he enriches them with accumulated gifts.

He sends back the commands previously given to our pontiff [Note: Ebo],  
so that he may cultivate barbarian hearts with admonitions  
and strengthen them by his deeds.

While these things are happening, he is swiftly carried above the stars,  
and Valentinus follows him on a shorter course.  
Rome is then illumined under the name of Gregory IV.

Although he resisted, he was nevertheless seen by all in due order  
to be carried away as a worthy man and placed upon the highest throne.

For a long time he had scattered everywhere the fragrance of virtue,  
renowned, diligent, filled with integrity,  
adorned with understanding, and modest with witty charm,  
Catholic in doctrine and just in moderate government;  
a cultivator of the heavenly law, a watchman of the sheepfold;  
a father to the poor and widows, compassionate and their advocate.

Despising earthly things and seeking heavenly things through merit,  
illustrious by birth, but more illustrious in holy conduct,  
he was diligent in handling sacred laws, prayers, and fasts.

These are the wings of virtue that carry him to the heights.

He does not cease to adorn them also with lofty splendor,  
while enlarging the beauty, worship, and radiance of the churches,  
restoring and adorning the sacred buildings with ornaments.

He transfers Gregory and brings forth illustrious witnesses [Note: into more suitable places],  
and beautifies them with gifts, altars, and springs.

Renewing the basilica of Mark, he greatly increases its honor,  
adorning it now with endowments, as he had previously cultivated it with prayers.

Enriching this and many other churches with abundant resources,  
he repairs the water conduits and prepares their nourishment,  
so that the house of Peter may once again be supplied with water in the ancient manner.

Seeing the church of the holy Mother  
shining with the light of virtues,

[Col. 0813D] he raises it with devoted honor.

He brings in and establishes companies equipped with praises,  
and fortifies the church, filling it with abundant gifts.

Arranging the altar, he draws together the tombs of the saints.

He restores various buildings, cells, steps,  
courtyards, paintings, apses, cloisters, and baths.

Moreover, turning over in his heart plans for warding off enemies,  
he resolves to restore the city with new walls [Note: he presses on with the work].

Having founded it, he persists in raising it with strong walls  
and calls it by his own name [Note: the Gregorian city],  
the place once called Hostia by the ancient settlers.

[Col. 0814A] He then builds for himself and for Rome’s future companions  
a house of hospitality; enriching and adorning  
the halls dedicated to the heavenly ones, he is raised to heaven’s hall.

From here Sergius, once the empty cloud of turmoil had been dispersed,  
obtains the chair, the celebrated senate judging him  
worthy of the throne’s lofty majesty and rule:

pious from childhood, nourished on pure teachings [Note: supports],  
trained in the arts and shining among illustrious Fathers.

[Col. 0814B] A suitable and powerful alumnus after those who had gone before,  
shining in lineage, pure in the integrity of faith,  
sent by Christ, supreme among the peoples in virtue;  
expressing his heart with a lively mouth and kindly mind,  
a vigorous ruler, defender, and nourisher of the Church,  
guardian of the unworthy assembly and of the flock entrusted to him.

Gathering the scattered through piety and preserving those gathered,  
a tester of unstable things [Note: things that pass away], a strong lover of Wisdom.

Calm, patient, generous in forgiving faults,  
by vengeance he removes the enemy hostile to his high office.

Thus, while all rejoice together, he climbs the heights.

When the Frankish Emperor hears that he has attained this eminence,  
he sends his son to the walls of Rome,  
while his allies are ravaging certain cities of Hesperia.

Suddenly the cloud-filled sky is covered with springlike clouds;  
fiery weapons flash, and strike the hearts of the fierce young men with fear,  
pressing some beneath death.

The bishop receives the offspring of Augustus with distinguished honor.

Meanwhile, seeing that one of the men surrounding him  
has been seized by a demon, and touched by the highest inspiration,  
the pope orders the doors and bars of the church to be closed.

Turning to the prince, he is said to have addressed him with these admonitions:

“If you come with a sincere mind and a kindly heart,  
if you come for the safety of the Church, the kingdom, and the city,  
then enter these sacred thresholds at last by our command.

If otherwise, our authority will not open these doors to you.”

After the prince had testified that he was plotting no deceitful schemes,  
the Father’s bolts are reported to have been withdrawn at his command.

When they entered the hall, the Antenorids [Note: Franks and Romans] and the descendants of Aeneas  
offered praises and vows to the Thunderer, singing heavenly songs.

The pope, watching over the city’s safety and crowning the king,  
disposes the scepters and grants the rule to Augustus’s offspring.

He passes by the pontiffs and companions who oppose him,  
with lofty eloquence, striking them with the force of shining truth  
and taming their swollen minds by the strength of piety.

Nor does he permit Peter’s own clients [Note: Romans]  
to serve the boy under imperial authority. Rather, while preserving the throne,  
he grants pardon to the condemned and bestows honor upon the censors;  
and he is prayed to [Note: worshiped] with the necks of the nobles bowed low,

[Col. 0815A] revered by the whole people as the teacher of peace.

Reflecting these things to God, he adorns the altars and churches  
with beautiful structures, gives them coverings with decorated fabrics,  
enriches them with gifts, gathers the relics of the saints,  
and dedicates the erected church, enriching it with endowments.

He gathers and strengthens the flocks seeking eternity,  
and restores the school resounding with divine praise.

When all things have been properly ordered, he ascends to heaven from the chair.

But the ancient enemy, wasting away with envy  
of the repose of light [Note: honor] and of the Church, brandishes cruel weapons  
and incites robbers from the race of the Hagarenes.

They cross the sea and scour the innermost regions of Ausonia,  
and, roaming as far as Rome—an atrocious crime!—dare  
with blind, sacrilegious fury to profane the sacred churches  
of Peter and Paul, the patrons,

[Col. 0816A] and to plunder them with savage hands, stripping away  
the splendor of their gifts and rejoicing in the success of their expedition.

While they hasten toward their unexpected joy,  
exulting as they carry it across the waters to the Punic kingdoms,  
they are drowned in the reversed order of triumph:  
sunk and swallowed by the waves, they are devoured in the avenging abyss.

And, as in the ancient triumph over the Red Sea,  
the powerful heights of the apostolic see flourish.

# HERE BEGINS THE TWELFTH BOOK

[Col. 0815]

## CHAPTER I. On Pope Leo IV and his deeds, and on Saint Pope Benedict

[Col. 0815B] The Lord multiplies consolations for the sorrowful people,  
inclining their minds to request that the laws of the venerable Leo  
be placed first, and adorning him with this fourth name.

This man, renowned for apostolic deeds, shone  
as gentle, patient, generous, pious, and kind;  
innocent, a cultivator of justice, a governor of the people,  
a searcher of the law, watchful and accustomed to prayer;  
preserving the serpent’s eye and the dove’s mind;  
shining in and loving religion, prevailing through piety,  
supporting the needy and despising both himself and earthly gains.

Freely devoted to study, he advanced from boyhood  
all the way to the perfect man. Among approved monks  
he lived as an upright monk, supreme in integrity,  
and, as the least among them, was carried upward

[Col. 0815C] through the steps of virtue, shining with the honor of the rite.

Shining with these merits, he is carried by the Fathers to the heights.

Remaining joined to his illustrious virtue and to those who had gone before [Note: predecessors],  
he assumes the distinguished tribunal, compelled by the Church.

From here, radiant with signs, he shines like a lofty lamp,  
illuminating souls and the see with brightness.

Adorning the halls with gifts and the throne with virtues;  
restoring what was hanging and protecting what was standing;  
establishing provisions and beautifying them with buildings and honor;  
he orders evening praises to be sung to Peter,  
openly adorning the feast of the departing day with praise.

The earth terrifies the trembling hearts of men when shaken.

But the life-giving Father, intent upon devoted prayers in his heart,  
moves whatever he sees must be removed; he arranges honors  
and gathers the sacred steps of the mixed throng of the people.

[Col. 0815D] [Note: Frod., Book III, chapter 10.] Twice he sends pallia to our pontiff Hincmar,  
giving the first for the feasts and the second in response to diligent requests—  
something he testifies that he had never granted to any of the Fathers.

Whatever the barbarian plunderer had dared to tear away with violent hands,  
he strives to restore with worthy splendor:  
in buildings, vessels, hangings, crosses, and crowns.

[Col. 0816B] Meanwhile, in dark caverns behind, a deadly serpent  
rises amid horror; the fierce basilisk, king of the cold poison,  
brandishing swift death, prowls through hiding places,  
breathing upon those approaching death,  
and powerful even by its deadly gaze to strike down those it sees.

The people, terrified by the monstrous plague,  
announce to the Father that the enemy cannot be approached.

Seeking the customary aid, he joins fasting to unceasing prayers.

At last the bright day, queen of the heavens, the Assumption  
of the Queen-Mother, arrives. The dreadful road led through caves  
to the Virgin’s temple. The pope, proceeding with a melodious company,  
approaches the darkness of the horrible lair.

While all are afraid, he alone advances  
and treads upon the savage threshold of the cave.

Raising his mind, his hands, and his eyes toward heaven,

[Col. 0816C] he called upon Christ with poured-out tears and prayers.

Having protected the people by prayer, he went on to the sacred place,  
performed the rites owed, and conquered death by the sacrificial offering [Note: the sacrifice offered].

By prayer he compelled the plague to vanish completely,  
destroying the disaster when he poured out his holy supplications.

Driven from these caverns, the savage dragon rolls the fiery poisons  
in his heart and, with flames, seeks again [Note: repeats]  
to seize the district once before taken from him under Peter’s protection,  
which had become famous through the endowment restored by Paschal  
and through the merits of Gregory, inhabited by a people [Note: of Angles].

Increasing its strength, the fire flies across the walls,  
devouring everything nearby. The masses of the people  
try in frenzied effort to break the heat opposing them.

But when the fires, driven upward by savage blasts,  
have consumed the buildings, they dare to attack the halls of Cephas.

[Col. 0816D] Struck to the heart by the dreadful report,  
the bishop hastens to meet it and is carried into battle against the flames.

Opposing them, he divides the combat by standing in their way;  
and, displaying the signs of the unconquered cross with his fingers,  
he crushes with prayer and the cross the savage vapors  
of the fire breathing upward.

[Col. 0817A] Unable to bear the standards of the standard-bearer,  
the heat, colliding with itself, sinks into the lowest ashes.

The Father restores what has been overturned, fills the empty roofs,  
restores the companies with gifts, increases their honors with donations,  
confirms what has been established, and strengthens their acts.

He establishes the celebration of the octave of the blessed feast  
of the Queen, the Mother of the heavenly King, without alteration.

He adorns the devoted people with generous giving  
and decorates the churches with pious splendors provided for them.

The gifts offered throughout the sacred buildings exceed counting.

Restoring the walls with their ancient defenses,  
he rebuilds them and their gates, and governs them with barriers and locks;  
raising towers, he adapts them with lofty structures.

Moreover, he undertakes to fortify the harbor with marvelous equipment,

[Col. 0817B] and completes a work both extraordinary and fitting,  
so that it may serve those present and those yet to come.

Here he constructs a roadway, so that the enemy may not be able  
to invade the city from that direction while intent upon attack,  
and he drives naval raids far away.

Finding everywhere the neglected relics of many holy men,  
he raises them up and stores them with kindly devotion.

He places many of these in the church which the king had once ruled  
and adds the ancient honor of the four crowned ones to the basilica,  
increasing its splendor and multiplying its patrons;  
he multiplies the rites at the altars and the rich gifts.

While he brings many things to this and to numerous other halls,  
the hostile people again attempt [Note: repeat] the strait and unjust plunder,  
where they had brought death, eager to carry off spoils to sate their dreadful greed.

Burning with this desire,

[Col. 0817C] he strives to pass through the Italian fields.

God provides unexpected aid for his servants  
and brings peoples who inhabit the hidden regions of the sea  
to fight against the hostile ranks.

The Father receives those who have come, proved by their effort to help,  
and refreshes, blesses, and arms them for the sacred cause;  
he follows them with tears, protects them by prayers, and strengthens them.

When they have prostrated themselves before the pope  
with humble supplication, they bravely meet the enemies.

The eternal Power, wishing to display greater triumphs of heaven,  
summons contrary winds against the hostile ships.

They rise to drive away the boats drawn up against the shores,  
and lift toward the sky both the raiders and their ships.

Snatched away by the waves, they are overturned upon the submerged sands;  
swallowed by the shoals, while heaven and sea fight against them,  
they perceive the divine hand preventing their attempt  
to reach the shores they sought; fallen, they perish by sword and hunger.

Some are preserved by the piety commanded by the descendants of Aeneas,  
and rejoice to serve the pious in servile condition.

Anticipating the blind actions of the enemy’s soldiers,  
the wise pope, while adorning the halls with sacred furnishings,  
undertakes to fortify Peter’s tomb with walls,  
following the efforts of his namesake predecessor.

Completing this work swiftly by the Lord’s command  
and with the help of the Frankish king, he gathers the sacred companies.

And, after sprinkling them with ashes, he leads them barefoot  
around the walls—the rejoicing companies and the leaders of the people.

[Col. 0818A] Having completed the prayers, he fortifies the fortress with their protection,  
asking that it remain unharmed and quiet from the enemy,  
or requesting that it be blessed with the gift of triumphs.

Thus, returning thanks to God, adorning Peter’s chair  
with life-giving praises and beautifying it with gifts,  
he gives joy to the Fathers and to the entire people.

Renewing another defense, he receives Corsica,  
the peoples whom Cephas sends.

With these matters well arranged—the harbor, city, and land  
of Ausonia made secure—he receives a worthy reward.

The orphaned people, stricken with grief at the Father’s departure,  
mourning themselves, together with the illustrious Fathers and the army,  
seek Jesus with bowed hearts, asking to be consoled  
by a bishop worthy of them.

Nor is the Lord slow to receive the groans of his servants,  
while he breathes into their minds the single request  
that all together, with one voice, ask for Father Benedict,

[Col. 0818B] who, rich in heavenly dew, seemed from childhood  
to grow through the fruitful gift of study.

Able to carry [Note: drink] the waters of light and faithfully retain them,  
wise in proclaiming them, an upright follower of peace,  
compassionate toward commands, humbly and kindly obedient,  
he had trampled the flesh far beneath him and conquered the tricks of darkness.

Radiant with these merits, he receives the laws  
in the holy and illustrious senate,  
joined to the Fathers in the venerable light of wisdom,  
and avoids the snares of the flattering world.

Skilled at giving wealth to the needy, fasting, praise,  
and vows, he meditates with burning love upon Christ.

When he had reached the highest and difficult summit,  
he was chosen and called.

He opposed the prayers with tears,

[Col. 0818C] begging that he not be weighed down by so great an honor.

But the pious people, inflamed by God, persisted in their undertaking,  
used force against the man, and hastened competitively to carry him away.

Raising him to the lofty sanctuary, they brought hymns and sacred songs  
with joyful voices.

The whole exultant city thronged the celebration with radiant joy.

Thus, with all things flourishing together, suitable decrees are issued,  
recorded in books and marked by the celebrated signature of the Fathers,  
so that they may properly be presented to the favor of the nobles [Note: Emperors].

The crafty serpent rises and ensnares those carrying them,  
binding the messengers of the throne [Note: the pontificate] with condemned iron.

Sending those entangled by deceit to the Frankish kingdom,  
he persuades the Roman leaders, heated by fraud,  
to hasten to the Frankish strongholds with the highest offices.

He also binds certain men from the city and takes them along.

[Col. 0818D] The chosen men violate the sacred right of envoys  
even among savage peoples, sending some and detaining their guardians.

Moreover, by crafty darkness, they induce the people—  
ordered to leave the walls—to enter the city of Peter  
flashing with weapons; in a wicked procession they enter the church.

They trample the heavenly signs [Note: images], burn them in savage fires,  
and devastate the heavenly figures while the people lament.

These things are not enough for the invader. Once the city is subdued,  
he climbs with grim assault to the Lateran see.

Removed from his own position, he seeks another’s height;  
he casts down the one he had enticed in the customary manner  
and, repelled, takes his seat.

The see ought not to be handled in so cruel a plight.  

[Col. 0819A] Stripped of the garment of his mind and bound by a loathsome serpent,  
he strips the man radiant with the light of virtues of his sacred furnishings,  
and, inflicting blows, subjects him to dark guards,  
a condemned man condemned to act through condemned ministers.

The city, roaring with groans and weeping, resounds everywhere with wailing.  
The pious order fills the sanctuary with mourning.  
The priests, drawing deep sighs from their hearts,  
pour tears over the blackened and filthy altars,  
lying prostrate and begging that such wickedness be redeemed.

The blessed day worthy of consecrating the throne had arrived.  
But honor is sought through dishonorable acts by the unworthy.

For the envoys, raging in the arrogance of the nobles,  
leap into the council of the Fathers, threatening to punish  
those who resisted with swords and to strike down the upright with clubs.

But the mind of the pontiffs, like a mountain, stands unmoved,

[Col. 0819B] fixed by the Spirit of God: they will not consent to profanity,  
will not yield to punishments, and will not fear terror or death.

Seeing minds supported by divine strength,  
the enemies turn over various plans.

Now they strive to ensnare the men with blandishments,  
now to break them by harsh measures,  
now threatening to overcome the pious through death.

They prefer to surrender themselves, limb by limb, to be slaughtered  
rather than be struck down by a dreadful anathema.  

Giving themselves thus [Note: perhaps *fantes*, “speaking,” for *dantes*], they rebuke the enraged men  
and disclose the divine pronouncements concerning matters  
which it is not lawful to oppose.

Meanwhile, the swelling subsides, the fury of the action diminishes,  
and furious pride is seen to be broken in their hearts.

Wickedness is dissolved, and the assemblies are released from the threshold.

On the returning third day, the Roman ranks return to the churches

[Col. 0819C] and all seek to approach Father Benedict.

With resounding voices they echo that he alone is suitable.

The hostile parties marvel even more at the concord of their hearts.  
Secretly, the leaders of the people stir themselves  
and renew their blind conflicts and struggles.

When they have been examined by the light of truth,  
they recognize the invincible men [Note: or, “these men”],  
yield, and resolve to abandon their wicked efforts;  
they decide that the deposed offender should be driven out of the captured fortress.

[Col. 0820A] The usurper is rejected with a shameful repulse and insults.

The joyful people triumph in grateful choirs and song.  
They recover their chosen glory with becoming [Note: decently] splendor;  
they raise him up upon a suitable horse,  
carrying him to the ancient shrine of the divine manger,  
crowned in the bright light of the people shining with joy.

They press him with prayers and celebrate splendid fasts;  
tears flow, drawn forth amid their rejoicing.

Then the enemies, radiant with the light above, approach,  
their hearts pierced by trembling fear,  
seeking the worthy footprints of the chosen leader.

They confess that they had erred and, having been overcome,  
ask for the Father’s goodness.

But he receives them into his motherly bosom,  
and, kindly, gives them pure-hearted kisses  
and embraces them with gentle arms.

He consoles their fear and orders them to rejoice  
that the Church, cut apart, has come together again  
and has been reunited by the power of Christ.

The imperial envoys hasten forward, joining the bishops,  
the clergy, and the gathered people.

With hymn-singing voices, they restore him to the seat  
sought in the honor of virtue, surrounding the rejoicing flock.

Thus, when the day has returned, adorned with divine radiance,  
he is offered to Peter’s throne and dedicated to the sacred rites,  
endowed with apostolic authority and the highest summit.

As heavenly light shines after the storm has been overcome,  
he grants the hall of Christ the radiance of worthy splendors.

Shining with light from above and endowed with lofty learning,  
he cultivates the inner things but does not reject the outward.

[Col. 0820C] He illumines the façades of the churches with precious gifts and images,  
adorns them with varied splendors,  
fills them with vestments, histories, vessels, books, and crowns,  
renews what has fallen and restores what had long been lost.

Leaving altars enriched as much by his own gifts  
as by those of kings, he hastens to shine with the honor of heaven.

## CHAPTER II. On Saint Pope Nicholas, Pope Benedict, and John of Ravenna

[Col. 0819]

[Col. 0819C] After the shepherd had been taken away, the Fathers and the Roman people  
devote themselves to sorrowful tears and resume their groans.

[Col. 0819D] They apply themselves to the fervor of prayer and practice fasting.

They persist in vigils, asking who is worthy to succeed,  
requesting that the blessed man be shown  
and that a Father be placed first.

Illumined by heavenly radiance [Note: enlightened],  
they unanimously judge that Nicholas must properly be sought,  
as one who had shone as holy from his earliest character:

despising amusements and rejecting dishonorable things from his mind,  
sighing for sober conduct and patiently considering serious matters.

Sincere, humble, a chaste student of learning,  
shining in conduct and powerful in the sweetness of his spirit,  
he, radiant in his studies, bore clear signs  
that he would one day ascend the lofty steps of the throne.

By the encouragement of the Fathers he entered the fellowship of the clergy  
and advanced in the cultivation of virtues and the honor of wisdom.

From there he shone as the equal of the Fathers,  
suited to his predecessors,

[Col. 0820C] and, joined to them, served with devoted honor.

He shines more dearly and more brightly as his renown grows,

[Col. 0820D] and, entrusted with counsels, he alone surpasses Benedict.

The bishop had chosen him from a thousand followers  
to be his constant companion. Having served with him in holy deeds,  
he receives the final draught of the desired cup [Note: of death].

Carried on his shoulders and placed in the tomb,  
he rejoices that his companion flourishes in the chair.

Drawn from Peter’s buildings and its fearful hiding places,  
he is raised to the throne, resisting and protesting humbly  
that he is unworthy to flourish in so great an honor.

But he resists without effect. For soon, surrounded and carried away  
by the flock, the people, and the senate,  
he is consecrated in the presence of Caesar,  
and, with Augustus standing by, receives the sacred honors.

As a holy man, bearing life-giving purity, he crowns the city,  
makes the king glad, shares his table,  
reveals the hidden lights of his heart,  
and binds the king’s affection to himself.

[Col. 0821A] He accompanies him with the gentle goodness of a modest mind;  
each of the nobles adorns himself with generous honors.

The bishop is honored with gifts and compelled to serve Augustus.  
He instructs the king with imperial words,  
and the two, returning to their respective seats,  
give each other kisses of peace and depart joined in heart.

Living by life-giving morals and distinguished in doctrine,  
the pope is clever with charm and lofty in vows and deeds;  
generous to the needy and kind to widows and the wretched,  
a protector of the people, he becomes dear to the whole city.

He diligently strives to enrich the churches with varied radiance,  
bringing vessels containing splendid talents of gold and silver.

He accompanies the vestments with histories and beautifies them with gems.

He renews the city’s appearance, secretly supplied by a spring,  
and adorns it by founding and restoring the buildings of the pontiffs.

[Col. 0821B] He receives the embassies and gifts of the Greek king.

Having investigated the venerable responses that bring messages to the city,  
he directs them; he disperses the corrupted Aeolians through a blind gift,  
investigates the matter, and cancels the guilty charges.

He restores the man wrongly removed from the seat of judgment,  
deposes those who dared to violate the sacred laws,  
and arranges pious justice with direct authority.

With gentle reasoning he addresses John of Ravenna,  
exhorting the citizens to grow mild after laying aside their dispute,  
to yield in their disorder and attend to difficult concerns.

When he cannot bend his harsh mind by entreaty,  
and when he also refuses to submit to the council calling him [Note: to present himself],  
he is deprived of the sacred office by the judgment of the holy senate.

Following his arrogance and setting himself against the heights of the world,  
he troubles the authorities, inflated by the honor of the envoys,

[Col. 0821C] and advances toward Rome with the army accompanying  
the scepter-bearing ruler.

Admitted by the merciful, he withdraws with his lot empty.

From here the Father is sought to restore the divided people of Ravenna  
by the healing method of a surgeon.

Fearing the shepherd, the ravager of the flock returns to the imperial court;  
but he is rejected by the cautious flock and the devoted Caesar,  
and is ordered to lay aside his pride and submit to the Father’s commands.

Repulsed, he rushes to solicit patrons with importunate prayers.

Agents are also sent against the hard man. When he is ruined  
and attacks the city, he encounters Pope Sixtus,  
who bears the rule with his customary balance,  
maintains an unmoved scale, is equipped with laws,  
and wisely sows decrees.

When he sees the invincible strength of the assembled Fathers,

[Col. 0821D] he lowers his neck and constrains himself to lamentation.

Through the envoys, with tears, he sent the sighs of his miserable heart  
to the Father in mournful, breathless groaning.

The censor, compassionate and imbued with love of the Lord,  
seeks the sheep that had strayed through trackless places  
and calls it back to life.

He receives the one who has gone astray, weeping over his dangers,  
praying amid his grief, confessing that he will keep the laws,  
purging his crimes, and promising the rights of service.

He frees him from the bonds [Note: excommunication]  
and restores him to his former honor.

The pope approves the decrees and decisions of the senate.

[Col. 0822A] With the storm calmed, he grants access to sacred worship,  
and makes the place shine with pious gifts and flourish with images.

He properly restores the minister of the Lamb,  
cast down by envy, anxious that the beauty of the bride  
should shine—he, the renowned paranymph of the Church—  
which he burned to carry to the Bridegroom without wrinkle or stain.

He persists in the chaste studies of guiding the rule entrusted to him,  
and in cleansing whatever might be foul with rotten defilement.

He examines by what right the king of the Sicambrian people  
punishes adultery, cutting down its supporters with a diseased sword,  
and heals the plague with the piety of prayer.

He directs the abolition of envoys’ wrongdoing  
and the restoration of peace by the dove sent across the Gallic fields.

When the light is seen from afar, shining with divine radiance,  
the peoples pray competitively to be illumined by its rays.

[Col. 0822B] From there a frequent embassy seeks Rome from the heavenly regions,  
more frequent than usual, and asks for nourishment from heaven.

The pope receives them and satisfies those whom he desires with food;  
he waters their thirsty hearts with paradisiacal streams  
and also pours out rivers for the Bulgarian people,  
granting the North to flourish with southern beauty.

Thus, finding the southern father [Note: the southern father] growing cold in the north,  
he takes care to kindle him with flames  
sent from the fire of heavenly ardor,  
so that the pious may shine with the powerful light  
of the fiery Fathers and the enemies of the light may be consumed.

Of this wondrous Father, whose name is Eleemosyna,  
the inseparable companion of John’s life and deeds,  
he causes the ears of the Latins to hear the material  
from the Greek archive,  
with Anastasius, acting at his father’s command, as translator.

After the bishops have been restored and the invader driven out, Piacenza shines;  
with its shepherd, Soissons flourishes.

The savage emperor, rival of Peter’s church, is punished.

The condemned pope, condemned by the adulterous judge [Note: Lotharius], is also punished.

The royal city of the Greeks rejoices after receiving back its Father.

Here the Father restores the insignia of the ancient Fathers,  
renews the structures of the churches, the dining halls, and the cells,  
and, raising the tombs of the saints, adorns them with splendors.

Taking up and fostering the blessed companies with a double allowance [Note: communities of monks],  
he presents himself as a father to the afflicted with a tender heart,  
refreshes their hardships, and prepares what is useful for their healing.

With the water conduits restored, he waters Peter’s halls,  
restoring with strong support the fortress established by Gregory.

He supports it with great strength and fortifies it with walls and soldiers,  

[Col. 0822D] so that, leading the people of the Lord into the camps of heaven,  
he may carry them forward with skillful rule and just balance.

He was a sign of the world’s decree spread across its broad regions.

He had heavenly concerns fixed in his pious mind:  
vigils, continual prayers, and fasts joined to vows.

Fertility and abundance of possessions smiled upon him,  
raised him up, showed him generous, and taught him kindness.

Thus, when he departed, the elements are said to have mourned.  
Yet he rejoices in his departure, and the allied companies of heaven rejoice with him.

## CHAPTER III. On Pope Hadrian II, our bishop Hincmar, and King Charles

[Col. 0823]

[Col. 0823A] Here the sacred authority of Hadrian II succeeds.

He is praised as pious and gentle, distinguished in rank,  
generous to the poor and kind to the wealthy;  
moderate toward all, to be regarded as dear by everyone.

Compassionate toward the afflicted and patiently preserving the wicked,  
bearing the cause of the suffering, he traverses distant kingdoms  
through letters, admonishing the rigid, restoring the broken,  
and opening the way of justice with just authority.

And, as the heavenly Fathers [Note: predecessors] do,  
he restrains the pride and arrogance of the king.

He strives to cleanse the bed [Note: of Lotharius] of dark stains,  
now by gentle admonition, now by severity.

[Col. 0823D] [Note: Flod., Book III, chapter 20.] He takes our pontiff, our king, and their companions—  
Hincmar and Charles—as allies,  
and adopts them as companions in his labor.

Thus together he strives to protect the scepters from crime.

In many matters governed by divine law,

[Col. 0823B] he takes this Father of ours as his brother in the struggle.

### On Pope John VIII and his successor Marinus [Note: The heading is absent in the manuscript.]

When this man is carried away, John VIII takes up the portions  
of the distinguished throne.

He is said to have shone with blessed conduct,  
adorned with learning and deeds,  
a guardian of judgment and a lover of upright piety.

Frequently driving tares from Christ’s harvest  
and scattering pious seeds through rational fields,

[Col. 0824A] he is eloquent in teaching, prudent, and skilled in understanding,  
and showed himself solicitous in feeding the flocks.

When Marinus, a diligent man, joined the Fathers,  
he quickly assumed the lofty rule.

He is pleasing to the Lord and regarded as the world’s glory,  
dear to the Augusti and a worthy lover of the peoples.

Shining in doctrine and pouring sacred, divine seeds  
into human hearts throughout the regions of the world,  
he surpassed the Greeks, drove away errors,  
restored the Church to unity, and compelled the divided flock together.

[Note: [Col. 0824D] Flod., Book IV, chapter 1.] Here, adorning our pontiff Folco with the insignia,  
he instructs him by word and hand to adorn the rights of a shepherd,  
and readily rejoices in his love of justice.

Outstanding in giving support against the wicked,  
he presents himself as an assistant, threatening the proud with many penalties.

[Col. 0824B] Embracing this brother as though he were his own,  
he reveals his hardships [Note: perhaps “tears them away”],  
and urges him to show his faith and reveal it in writing.

At his command he returns the Fathers’ instructions,  
and orders strength to be exercised against the contemptuous.

Taking care to yield to this man’s prayers,  
he urges him to retain the Frankish king’s paternal affection,  
consoling him and providing help through his vows.

## CHAPTER IV. On Pope Hadrian III, our bishop Fulco, Emperor Charles, and Stephen V

[Col. 0823]

[Col. 0823B] [Note: [Col. 0824D] The same, in the same place.] Hadrian III, following those sent before him in honor,  
is prepared through the efforts of the already mentioned bishop Folco

[Col. 0823C] as Father, protector, and nourisher of the Church of Reims.

He strengthens the rights of honor belonging to himself,  
so that he may reinforce what is fitting,  
provide due consolation against opponents,  
and adopt our king with a father’s affection.

He properly shows himself a kindly father to the bishops.

When he is soon carried away, Stephen V, by that name,  
is raised to the highest insignia.

In paternal writings of consolation he judges our previously mentioned pontiff  
worthy of the title of brother and worthy of the name of friend,  
and declares himself ready to confirm whatever he properly requests from him.

Yet the latter chooses rather to make himself the lowest servant,  
raises up the Father, and offers him the honor of the Lord.

And, begging that those who petition on behalf of his dignity  
be brought forth into the light, he burns to go and see him,  
unless barbarian forces should obstruct the vows of those prepared.

[Col. 0823D] Therefore, by the protection of his prayers, he asks  
that the kingdom be redeemed from the cruel danger of so savage a plague.

He also strives with all his strength to resist  
those who seek to darken his apostolic splendor.

Whatever he hears has been done for the noble kinsman Widon,  
he accepts as though it had been done for himself.

[Col. 0824B] He asks that what Rome has granted to the see  
of the Church of Reims be preserved with inviolate and perpetual honor:

[Col. 0824C] for he knows it to be faithful in every respect  
to apostolic authority, and to contend for him  
against all hostile forces.

It was handed over to the poor and dedicated to sacred ministers,  
but was seized by savage and raging bears.

May it help to tear the broken ones away from their dark jaws.

The supreme bishop rejoices and returns consolations,  
and proves that he remains devoted to his brother’s rights.

He also cherishes this man and his son under a father’s love,  
grieves over the harmful blows he suffers as though they were his own,  
and prays continually for his peace.

He orders the bishops to compel the plunderer  
to restore what he has seized,  
and, if he does not restore the stolen property, to exclude him from sacred fellowship.

Writing to Augustus concerning Charles, he renders praises to Christ  
for the Emperor’s holy love.

[Col. 0824D] Since, burning with zeal, he had restored under the supreme name  
to our holy see the patrimonies long ago taken away,  
he urges him to complete what still remains to be done here,  
so that he may fully receive the honor of his reward.

He also gratifies Folco, offering him consolation,

[Col. 0825A] and affectionately urging him to persist in his vows  
toward the Roman citadel of supreme governance.  
He gathers the assistance of those who complain of suffering undeservedly,  
and commands that it be carried to this Father’s aid.  
Thus, for love and in the name of Peter,  
he asks that he receive, cherish, protect, and honor them as pilgrims.  
He returns thanks for the peace of the laboring whole kingdom  
and urges him earnestly to promote its growth.

He entrusts to him the complaints of the city of Langres:  
that the people are oppressed contrary to the wishes of their shepherds  
and cannot obtain a Father chosen by worthy effort.  
He signifies that he has given instructions to the bishop of Lyon  
that he should consecrate the desired man with equal honor.  
When that bishop refused, and after the vacant church  
had long been subjected to labor, he consecrated as bishop  
the man who had been chosen by the petitioner.

[Col. 0825B] Therefore, hastening, let him supply what the city lacks,  
appoint the rule of a duly consecrated rector,  
and disclose to the other bishops the pope’s decrees.

The other, ready for these things, unfolds the Fathers’ instructions.  
He records the king’s commands, explaining that the king remains delayed  
because he forbids it, until he sends to Rome and receives again  
certain information. After that, he will not be compelled in any way  
by apostolic commands, nor even by the torment of death.  
Moreover, he asks to be instructed in the doctrines of the Fathers by right,  
so that he may worthily preserve the holy authority of the pope.

[Col. 0826A] The apostolic bishop, strengthening this government as well,  
confirms the gifts granted to our Church,  
and the rights conceded to the ancient nobles in their full splendor.  
Let no one of them unjustly usurp anything by diminishing it,  
and let no bishop be appointed unless he is sought according to the law of the canons.  
If anyone violates these things, striving to profane the statutes,  
let him be oppressed by a fitting penalty, imposed by the see of Peter,  
which dictates many things worthily;  
while preserving what has been promulgated, let him deserve to receive blessing.

[Note: [Col. 0826D] The same source.]

To this pope he delegates the holding of a synod  
with the Fathers of certain regions,  
and with the leaders between Agrippina and the peoples beyond the Rhine,  
to hear causes that must be made equal by just regulation.  
Afterward, if he is able, let him come in person  
and handle these matters, together with many others requiring action.

[Col. 0826B] He further warns him that the other Gallic Fathers  
are also being subjected to unjust treatment in the city of Bourges,  
which complains that its rights are being claimed by another;  
let them compassionate it. He rebukes them, asking  
why they do not disclose what they have presumed while remaining silent,  
since they ought to oppose themselves like a wall against hostile forces.  
Therefore let them arm themselves with zeal for justice;  
having entered the contest of the Lord,  
let them compel the usurper to return to his own see.  
The pope’s mercy extends to him only so far;  
if he despises it, let him know that he is wholly deprived  
of every honor of sacred office.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning Stephen and Formosus, and also the translation of Saint Callistus to our city

[Col. 0825]

[Col. 0825C] [Note: [Col. 0825D] Flodoard, Book IV, chapter 1.]

Formosus follows Stephen; to him our priest,  
often exposed above, directs letters,  
rejoicing that he has assumed the duties of Peter’s rule.  
May he carry the see toward better things, consoling him,  
in speech and action alike, so that he may fittingly fulfill them.  
He testifies that God is favorable to the Church,  
as is shown by the fact that this office is being handled so honorably.

Submitting himself to him, he promises that all his service  
will honor him, and excuses himself for not hastening to visit him.  
He gives thanks that he has sent him something begun for his consolation,  
indicating that he wishes to see him,  
and marking that he will go to meet him,  
offering to grant him increases of useful distinction  
and, at Stephen’s direction, to *sese edere* (“present himself”; editorial reading *exsequi*, “carry out”) what has been ordered.

[Col. 0825D] He asks that the Church’s scattered possessions, sought with strength,  
be fortified, lest at some time they be taken away  
from the sacred Church, driven by greedy plunderers.  
Certain men were striving to tear away  
the relics of the great pontiff of Christ and witness, Callistus,  
which had been given to him through signs by Abbot Rodulf,  
together with the property attached to the saint.

[Note: [Col. 0825] Granted.]

He asks counsel concerning these matters,  
and seeks help by which the wicked may be restrained according to law.  
Since he had learned that the supreme see was being disturbed  
by some kind of assault, he grieves for the head as for the limbs.  
Under the way of peace, he advises him not to show unworthy favor  
to subject bishops who demand what is not owed.

[Col. 0826C] In reply, the other says that they should strive  
to exalt the government of the supreme ruler alike in words and deeds,  
according to the grace granted to each of them,  
lest they be accused of being held empty-handed beneath it.  
Rather, let them labor to bring forth suitable fruits through it.  
Let them forbid what is unlawful, tear out shameful growths,  
and offer assistance to all servants of Christ.

He wishes to know the care taken for this purpose,  
lamenting the wretched disasters and labors of humankind,  
and the nets of the ancient enemy’s deceit,  
with which he ensnares the human race by cruel craft.  
Hence he stirs up heresies, hence wars, rejoicing in crime,  
boiling with blood and burning with quarrels of hatred,  
and breaking the Eastern peoples through the schism of heresies.

[Col. 0826D] Therefore he admonishes the priests by persuasion  
to take up arms and raise the ark from the savage danger.  
Let them therefore come together to seek Christ as their mediator,  
who may give counsel, offer help, and bring salvation.  
For this reason he asks our pontiff to strive,  
to gird himself, hasten, break through every delay,  
and bring aid to a world collapsing beneath its evils.

Christ is the way, Christ the guide, Christ the victory.

[Col. 0827A] Nor is it enough to have admonished him once;  
he is not reluctant to repeat his fatherly warnings:  
to come to the aid of the Mother,  
to arrange for a synod to be held under universal law,  
and to hasten to it without being detained by any burden of idleness.  
At the same time let them discuss more fully all matters  
that ought to be discussed, and publish the oracles more clearly.

He grieves greatly that the kingdoms of the Franks  
are being disturbed by the storms of barbarian peoples,  
and asks the assistance of Christ’s nobles  
so that the supreme right hand may suppress them.  
He teaches that the rights claimed for the Church of Rheims  
are to be retained under the protection of its own law,  
and forbids wrongdoing, lest anyone unjustly presume  
to touch its sacred possessions or remove *cassa* (“empty things”; editorial reading *concessa*, “things granted”).

Let no authority of pontiffs, kings, or counts  
unlawfully usurp these things or bend them to private use,

[Col. 0827B] so that no one may invade the Church  
when it happens to be vacant of a bishop,  
or attempt a violent undertaking.  
Nor should a bishop be appointed except with fitting honor.  
Pontiffs, kings, the clergy, and the subject peoples  
should see to it, with God’s help, that what has been rightly entrusted  
is preserved, enlarged, adorned, and advanced toward heavenly reward.

Once a bishop has been duly appointed,  
let no one enter upon the task of mutilating his dignity  
or altering it. Rather, let the Church’s possessions remain intact  
and devoted to the uses of Christ’s servants,  
to be administered by worthy ministers under the pontiff.

Whoever presumes to act against these things  
should know that he is condemned to punishment by anathema.  
May he deserve to receive everlasting life from the Savior.

Regarding the property of Avignon, and the rights of the blessed Callistus,  
he likewise advanced decrees supported by equal authority.

[Col. 0827C] Moreover, he had learned that certain pontiffs  
were being led along crooked paths,  
giving the peoples examples of ruin,  
and, when rebuked, returning responses unworthy of them;  
indeed, that they were following even worse courses  
and failing to avoid dreadful things.  
He confesses that he cannot endure this without deep grief.

Inviting them to peace, he seeks to extinguish scandals,  
because Christ is despised through the dreadful pride of pontiffs.  
Our bishop grieves, accuses, rebukes, and afflicts them.

Therefore he warns and commands that the assembled Fathers compel this man,  
and summon other upright men,  
to disclose the decrees of the divine law  
and celebrate a synod with the strength

[Col. 0827D] supported by the protection of apostolic authority—printed *cesso* (perhaps “I yield”), with the editorial reading *concesso* (“granted”).

Let them uproot what is harmful from the flocks  
and sow what is profitable.  
But if any perverse dispute should arise,  
let it be reserved for the judgment of the outstanding bishop,  
so that, God granting it, they may bring it to a worthy conclusion.  
Let no one attempt to withdraw from this council,  
whoever desires to share in apostolic favor.

Restraining the movements of war throughout the Frankish kingdoms,  
he urges the primates of the Church to contend through their labor,  
lest the realms entrusted to their care be drenched in blood,  
or Christian kings arm themselves for unjust wars.  
Let them cease touching what belongs to others and invading it.  
Let wars be put to sleep; let savage disturbance be suppressed.  
While Folco returns from Rome, let peace govern the scepters.

Writing the same exhortation to peace to Odo,  
he asks that no unjust war be stirred against Charles,

[Col. 0828A] and that he not enter forbidden boundaries,  
striving to invade what belongs to another’s jurisdiction.  
Let him abstain from greed and avoid crossing the straight paths.  
Let him reconsider carefully what pleases the Lord,  
setting His fear before his eyes beneath the love of Him.

Rejoicing in the acts of the bishop who labors for peace,  
he warns Folco to persist in these matters with cautious effort,  
lest peace, sought without prudence, be driven away,  
or the spark of royal and exalted lineage be worn down.  
The crimes of the scepter-bearer must be restrained by prudent medicine,  
lest the worst scandals rise under the government of the kingdom.

With his exhortation he consoles and gladly honors Charles,  
rejoicing that he has been raised to the summit of his fatherland’s see,  
and asking Christ that for long ages he may grow  
in justice, piety, and the light of wisdom.

[Col. 0828B] He also warns him to set the Lord before his heart’s light,  
clinging to His commands with all his efforts.  
Let him love and preserve whatever he has judged just and right;  
let him lend his ear to the just and turn away from the wicked.  
Let him be superior in strength of soul to the use of the flesh,  
so that he may overthrow the enemies of body and mind.

He promises that he too will provide whatever increase he can.  
Let him send the blessed bread as a welcome gift,  
which the king had sought as an endowment of twofold salvation.

He commands that the benefits be dealt with attentively;  
indeed, he should send the priest Folco for such matters,  
so that by his counsels the most useful things,  
suitable to honor and to the king’s exaltation,  
may be brought forth.

Assailed by the excessive complaints of certain people,  
he complains that the city is suffering undeservedly  
and that his dependents are being frightened.

[Col. 0828C] He asks that Folco present himself for their calming.

At last, having learned through the bishop’s administration of truth  
how faithful he is to apostolic things  
and how ardent in obeying commands,  
he rejoices to obey the heavenly directives and returns thanks,  
promising to show himself gracious wherever expedient.  
He says that at this man’s request he had suppressed the kings’ conflict,  
and had therefore given instructions to the bishops and the king,  
so that he himself might more safely visit Peter’s see.

Honoring him also with a brother’s honor,  
he sends special gifts to his dear friends,  
and asks that the honor of protection be maintained,  
that scandals be destroyed, and the bonds of peace joined:  
to restrain the implacable and compel them toward holy peace.  
He trusts that this has been granted to him as a broad gift from Peter.

Lambert the Emperor, related to him by blood through Folco,

[Col. 0828D] he declares that he protects him as his own son with consolation,  
and sets forth the most welcome vows of our bishop,  
by which he venerates Peter’s see with honor.

He reports that certain sacrilegious, black assailants  
of the consecrated summit, who had dared to defile  
the brightest members of the supreme head,  
had been cut off by the sword of anathema.  
He warns him to add the bonds of a fitting penalty  
and to strive for the exaltation of his scepter-bearing kinsman.

Thus, when he sends these instructions to the Parisian patron

[Note: [Col. 0827] Bishop.]

he tells Anscheric that these men must be avoided entirely,  
as must the dreadful companionship of dark madness.

Comforting the Church of Sens, which groans while its pastor is consigned to hiding because of a criminal and condemnable undertaking,

[Note: [Col. 0827] Deserving condemnation.]

[Col. 0829A] he urges it to hope in the Lord  
and patiently to endure bitter things, through hope  
and by the strength of the Thunderer, for the sake of heavenly glory.

He says that he trusts it will be comforted  
when he sees its own bishop.  
He declares that he has condemned the savage men  
and marked them for destruction by the Fathers and the divine Spirit,  
so that no one may attempt such things afterward.

He will send legates when a suitable time presents itself,  
by whom the storms of this matter may be calmed.

To the savage usurper of the bishop of Langres  
he directs the beginnings of a letter,  
so that at last he may come to his senses concerning his bitter deeds,  
restore the pontiff, and condemn the dreadful things he has perpetrated.  
If he does otherwise, he will be punished with eternal torment.

Concerning these sacrilegious men he delegates to Odo,  
the scepter-bearing man, paternal warnings,  
so that he may know that they have been bound by anathema:  
he should neither receive them nor join conversation with them,  
and should avoid staining himself with their crime.

[Col. 0829B] Indeed, he should offer outstanding consolation  
to the exhausted Church and protect it,  
extending aid whenever he sees it to be appropriate.  
He rereads these same instructions to Charles for observance.

He rebukes Walter of Sens, who was violating the oracles of the laws,  
asking why he had imposed upon the city of Troyes  
the government of a bishop who had not been chosen,  
and had accepted one from another Church  
contrary to the paternal decrees.

Removing him, he appoints the chosen man

[Note: [Col. 0829] Elected.]

and entrusts the administration to him;  
he grants sacred honor to the consecrated Ricveus.  
Let no one resist: the decrees accompany him as he goes.

To this Father, Formosus, Charles sends a letter,  
committing to him the rights of himself and his dignity for protection.  
He returns extraordinary thanks under the honor of favor,  
because the bishop had judged him and his family worthy of praise,  
and had considered his advancement agreeable to him.

[Col. 0829C] Let him therefore know that he has in the king  
a faithful man according to his knowledge,  
a devoted servant ready to obey his commands.  
Let him be permitted to trust in his protection,  
provided only that the enemy cannot turn aside the apostolic mind.

Let him win the Emperor’s favor and pray to Christ  
for himself and for the government of the kingdom entrusted to him.  
He asks that the Emperor judge him worthy of entering into his affairs,

[Col. 0830A] so that by his presence and speech he may be comforted.

Meanwhile, let him send blessed bread as a gift,  
and favor no enemy or assent to any hostile person.  
Rather, let him suppress opposing forces by sacred effort and right,  
so that the kingdom may grow through his protection.

The bishop Folco also, summoned from the see, returns thanks,  
and asks Peter’s assistance for the king.  
He expresses gratitude that the matter undertaken for the king  
is being treated kindly, that the scepters are being cherished  
with ancestral splendor, and that the pope is concerned  
for the royal line.

[Note: [Col. 0829] Let him be concerned.]

Therefore, while asking him not to favor the enemy’s party,  
he suggests that he strengthen it further, exalt it, and increase its power;  
let him heap up prayers and send vows to the stars.  
He adds that he is being attacked on every side by scattered enemies.  
He asks that they be kept away and the invaders repelled,

[Col. 0830B] that plunderers be restrained by the governance of the gracious ruler,  
lest civil war arise among Christians,  
lest a fierce rival rejoice in the shipwreck of the Church,  
or those subject to him attempt unlawful acts there.

He asks what remedy he should apply.

To Lambert the Emperor, related to him by blood,  
he acknowledges that the pope is showing multifaceted care;  
he rejoices and asks that such affection remain.  
He declares that Lambert, although related to him, is not to be honored by him on any legal claim unless he is known to have been strengthened by the Father’s friendship.

But he asks King Charles that Lambert be joined to him  
under a covenant, and that both kings’ comfort  
be extended to the royal offspring.  
If anything can be added as a remedy for the condemned men,  
and if he knows in what way or by what medicine he can heal them,  
he asks that it be disclosed to him, ready to serve.

[Col. 0830C] This outstanding bishop Formosus is raised up in lofty praises:  
chaste, frugal toward himself, generous to the needy.  
He scattered the seeds of faith among the Bulgarian people.  
He destroyed shrines, instructed the people with heavenly weapons,  
and, ready for action, endured many dangers.  
He gave an example that adversity must be endured  
and that no misfortune need be feared by one who lives well.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning Pope Boniface and Stephen VI, and also Pope Theodore

[Col. 0829]

[Col. 0829D] From here the blessed poet Boniface briefly enters.  
He completed three times five days of honor in the citadel.  
Soon changing his lofty office, he surpassed the high summits,  
climbing in a short space the heights he had sought,  
and was enrolled among the nobles of the apostolic white-robed company.

Then Stephen the Sixth took up the sacred government of the see,  
harsh toward our people, and harsher still toward his predecessors.  
He reads out savage things against the living,  
and more savage ones against the buried.  
He shakes Folco with threats and Formosus with legal acts.  
He gathers an ill-fated council over which he presides cruelly,  
rejecting his predecessor and setting himself in his place.

He seemed thereafter to have incurred a downfall worthy of his deeds.  
He too was seized, cast out of the sacred see,  
thrown into the darkness of prison, and bound with black chains;  
[Col. 0830D] then vengeance crushed him with a cruel death by suffocation.

After him, within a short time, Roman rulers of the see arose.  
The next man governed the summit for not quite four months;  
he was received into heaven after obtaining deserved honors.

After his brief removal, the beloved Theodore,  
a friend of peace, ascended the heights by lot.  
He governed the Roman rights for *bissenos* [or *bis denos*: twice ten] days,

sober and chaste, filled with native goodness,  
living as a lover and nourisher of the poor,  
lavishing himself upon them.  
He taught the people to join the bonds of peace.  
When he had united the priests in harmonious honor,  
and was recalling those divided from their proper sees,  
he was himself happily taken away,  
to be placed in the appointed see.

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning Saints John, Sergius, Benedict, Leo, and Christopher

[Col. 0831]

[Col. 0831A] John next assumes the office, shining as the ninth in order.  
By him Sergius, elected in his native city, is driven out,  
and some relate that certain Roman flocks were carried away.

Nevertheless, he is said to have taught saving doctrine  
in three councils, to have abolished the novelty of evils,  
and to have strengthened the faith handed down  
by the teachings of the Fathers.

Then the sacred government of Benedict IV rises,  
the great pontiff who shone by merit worthy of that name,  
generous and kind toward all.  
A rich splendor of lineage and piety adorns all his work;  
he meditates upon the commands of the Thunderer.  
He preferred the common good to private profit.  
He cherished neglected widows, the needy,  
and those without patrons, as though they were his own children,  
with constant generosity.  
Having purchased heaven, he poured out all he had upon the needy.

[Col. 0831B] After him Leo ascends the lofty rights of office,  
the fifth in name.  
He departs before the moon has twice completed its circle.

Christopher next receives the administration of the see  
and dispenses it for a little more than half a year.

Concerning Sergius and the others up to Leo VII

[Note: [Col. 0831D] The title is lacking in the manuscript.]

Sergius returns, who had earlier been elected  
to the citadel of the high office  
but had been driven into exile and rejected.  
There he remained in hiding for seven revolving years.

Then, returning at the people’s prayers,  
he is consecrated with the honor formerly assigned to him;  
under that name he emerges as the third pontiff.  
With the outstanding bishop received into Peter’s see,  
the world rejoices for more than seven years.

Favoring the clergy, he strikes down the invaders  
with the sickle of his judgment, after they have seized the height.  
When he has been taken away from human affairs,  
the sacred court sings of Anastasius,

[Col. 0831C] the third pontiff of that name to shine in Rome,  
ruler of the apostolic see with gentle governance,  
so that he may feel Christ gentle toward him  
through the gift of forgiveness.

When he afterward ascends to Peter’s supreme see,  
he holds it for six months and ten days.  
Having fulfilled his term, he follows the fate  
of the earlier Fathers.

From here the tenth John rises, ascending the sacred rights.  
He had governed the people of Ravenna.  
Then summoned to this office, he adorns the Roman citadel,  
in which he shone for fourteen years and a little more.

To our pontiff he sends sections to Seulf,

[Col. 0831D] and adorns the sacred hall with munificent ornaments.

[Col. 0832A] While he shines in peace, deceived by patrician injustice,  
he is thrown into prison and confined in dark chambers.  
But his spirit cannot be held in savage caves;  
rather, he bursts forth into heaven and ascends  
to the decreed seats.

In his place Leo VI assumes Peter’s lofty government.  
He preserves it for seven months and five days,  
then seeks the company of his predecessor-poets.

From here Stephen VII shines for two years,  
with one month added beyond the two full years.  
After that period, the arranged see is occupied.

Then the sacred office passes to John, born of a patrician woman,  
the eleventh who is raised to Peter’s see by that name.  
He is without strength, lacking splendor,  
and now performs only sacred ministries.

His brother, the patrician

[Note: [Col. 0831] Alberic.]

having seized control of affairs,

[Col. 0832B] confined John X, whose incestuous mother had attempted to surrender the heights of power [*rerum*: of affairs; f. *imperii*: of empire]

to her adulterer,

[Note: [Col. 0831] King Hugh of the Lombards.]

and whom she had handed over to the vigilant guard and keeper of the prison.

Under him our Artoldus assumes the sacred vestments,  
and the pope dies, having borne that name for nearly a year.

Leo VII rises next. Yet he does not ponder such things,  
nor care for the world’s summit, nor seek high office.  
He turns with an eager heart only to the things of God,  
avoiding high positions and unwilling to undertake  
what is offered to him.

Yet he is carried up and judged worthy of distinction,  
and is placed in the outstanding government  
and in Peter’s see.  
But he by no means abandons his accustomed care for adornment.  
Devoted to constant prayers and lofty in contemplation,  
joyful in speech, wise, and serene in countenance,

[Col. 0832C] when I visited the holy threshold of heavenly Peter,  
he received me joyfully, with a kindly spirit;  
he admitted me graciously and favored me modestly.  
Sowing agreeable words, he refreshed us both  
with banquets for body and soul.  
He blessed me, and, giving and renewing kisses,  
he increased the gift of his gracious favor;  
then he dismissed me, joyful, with an honored embrace.

May the omnipotent Father raise him up,  
lively and beautiful in worship,  
and preserve him long, adorning him with worthy deeds.  
And with the holy bishops, whose company  
he has deserved, may He grant him a seat  
above the heavens, among the blessed.  
With them may he remain illustrious forever.

[Note: [Col. 0831D] 1. Baronius and others assign only three years and four months to Sergius III; Frodoard assigns seven years. — 2. Baronius assigns two years and twenty months to Anastasius; Frodoard assigns six months and ten days. — 3. Frodoard omits Landon, whom others call Bando. — 4. He assigns to John X not quite fifteen complete years. — 5. To Leo VI, however, he assigns seven months and five days, whereas more recent writers assign him only six months and fifteen days.]

[Col. 0832D] (Up to this point, Mabillon.)

# THE THIRTEENTH BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0833]

## CHAPTER I. Concerning Saints Theodore, Acontius, Servulus, and Januarius

[Col. 0833A] Who could count the triumphs by which Rome,  
made radiant by Christ, shines,  
when even Gregory, admitting that he was unable  
to encompass within one work the mighty deeds of Peter,  
or to depart from the whole undertaking,  
would deny that anyone could complete what he refused?

Was Theodore alone worthy to see the face  
of the Lord visiting and the voice of Him speaking,  
to follow it with his ear—  
he whose presence Peter showed openly  
by his service?

Or had Acontius alone lived so devoted  
to the service of his Church  
that he should be judged worthy to reveal signs through him  
and raise up paralyzed limbs?

Or was it only this girl,  
who was seen to be worthy of salvation,  
who knew how to endure patiently  
the labor of sickness within the walls  
or in the apostolic places?

[Col. 0834A] Was Servulus alone, poor in worldly possessions  
but rich in the gift of merits,  
generous though needy, manly in piety alone,  
and strong in devotion,  
watching to praise the Lord while covered in suffering—  
he whose patience makes the heavens rejoice,  
while his holy mind, devoted to seeking the stars,  
scatters heavenly fragrance over the roofs  
as it rises, having drawn it from the nectar of paradise?

Or was the martyr Januarius alone  
who forbade the temples to be polluted by a criminal burial,  
accustomed to change the coverings by their colors,  
so that, while the fierce spirit cried out,  
he would be driven most miserably from the sacred places?

## CHAPTER II. Concerning Saints Deusdedit, Victorinus, Anastasius, Redempta, Galla, Romula, and Mosa

[Col. 0833]

[Col. 0833B] Was this commendable work of religion accomplished only at Rome—  
by that Deusdedit, the shoemaker whom Ezekiel and Daniel  
are said to visit and make known? The printed syntax is compressed,  
but it says that on the Sabbaths alone he built and extended a house  
whose workmanship and adornment matched his worthy deeds.

Or did Victorinus alone wash away his crimes well  
with tears, so that, having completed what he had committed  
with pious consolation, he might rejoice that they had been loosened for him,  
struck by the radiance through which it was shown  
that he had been freed from darkness by his merits?

Or is the labor of only one soldier  
praised within the Roman camp,  
so that he deserved to see peaceful dwellings  
and alone to report the splendor he had seen?

Or was it Galla alone, beautiful though she resisted  
her patrician father,  
yet led by Peter and more beautiful  
because of her exalted Bridegroom?

[Col. 0833C] Or was it the boy devoted to simplicity in tending flocks,  
whom an all-powerful will granted to heaven  
and sent back to earth?  
[Col. 0834B] The gifts of languages proved him a disciple of heaven,  
and soon words followed the death that had been foretold.

Was Anastasius alone found energetic  
in setting aside the affairs of the flattering world,  
the sole man in the Roman citadels  
who abandoned the records and chose the monastic camp,  
and, having completed his course, was summoned to heaven,  
called from the rock?

Soon the brothers who would follow  
are recited in order,  
and a friend is obtained through prayers,  
though he is not marked by his voice.

Or did Redempta alone, with her disciples,  
live in Rome a life worthy of the blessed herald Gregory,  
shining in honor of mind  
and worthy of the swallow as teacher?

Was Romula alone raised up by the consolation of the heavenly beings,  
purified by light, nourished with heavenly nectar,  
and granted heavenly funeral rites and supernal light?

Or was Mosa, the sister of Probus, alone suited  
[Col. 0834C] to be admitted to the dances above,  
called and instructed by the visit of the Mother of God,  
and released when the Mother herself requested it?

## CHAPTER III. Concerning the saints of various places in Italy, namely Honoratus, Libertinus, and the others

[Col. 0833]

[Col. 0833C] While I attempt to close within verses  
and bind with poetic measures  
the material spread out through Gregory’s venerable narrative,  
having undertaken so lofty a path  
and striving to reach such heights,  
I fear to touch the steep slope of the vaulted hill,  
like a filthy man trembling to enter  
the blessed meadows and the flowers  
given through renowned fields  
by way of polluted streams.

But if the fallen waters run  
with the breath of God blowing through them,  
they will be able to cleanse what is unclean  
with their sweet-flowing heavenly current,  
and the very drops will be adorned  
with little golden sands.

Yet, as I seek access to these flourishing delights,  
shall I search through the countryside and towns  
of Ausonia, reaching unknown folds  
with a wavering turn?

Or, following the pure footprints  
of so great a father,  
shall I briefly recall, by touching on them,  
the matters reported at length,  
bringing back to mind what is known  
rather than revealing what is hidden?

[Col. 0833D] Who could be so capable  
of deriving the channels of such an immense river?  
And lest he blame me for denying too much  
to my undertaking,

[Col. 0834C] I shall gladly touch briefly upon the richest matters.

We shall leave aside Honoratus,  
learned through divine inspiration,  
to whom heavenly love gave heavenly counsel,  
and for whom Samnite fare was prepared  
on a sea-like rock.

He was the father of many blessed men.  
When he saw a mass broken from a rocky side  
sliding down a steep slope,  
he fixed it in place and suspended it  
in the name of Christ,  
rescuing the cell and preserving the brothers  
from the onset of death.

Shall I be silent about Libertinus,  
who, as Honoratus’s disciple,  
himself shone blessed through his teacher’s merits,  
and, distinguished by miracles, was once thrown from his horse  
while piously administering lashes, yet by heavenly power  
opened an easy channel. After the plunderers’ maddened horses  
had been beaten, he set down his own horse  
and caused all the others likewise to be set down.

[Col. 0834D] The next compressed verses—*dum recipit recipi,  
mulctata sedilia praestat, pauperis et votum ligat, absolvitque phalanges*—  
say, with uncertain syntax, that while receiving one who was received,  
he provided penal seats, bound the poor man’s vow,  
and released the companies.

So also, when the Franks raged  
with the heat of plunder,

[Col. 0835A] did he envelop them in darkness  
and hide the present from their eyes?

What of the boy taken away from the light,  
with his mother lamenting,  
restored and brought back to life  
through the touch of the teacher’s sandal,  
which bore a broad imprint?

Shall we attribute this to Honoratus or Libertinus,  
each relying on the merits of faith  
but on the mother’s faith in both cases?

The lofty patience of this man  
is displayed through great signs,  
a teacher of the corrector  
and a teacher of his teacher,  
leaving behind disciples renowned  
for marvelous deeds.

[Col. 0836A] Many venerable works of the devout remain hidden,  
and the silence of the outstanding leader  
has kept them from us.  
But the thefts of vegetables are not forgotten;  
when revealed, they shine with remembered praise,  
having been nobly performed under God’s honor:  
the grass saved, the snake seized,
