the robber protected,  
the enemy released after worthy punishments,  
the anxious comforted with gentle hopes,  
and the needy warmed by a gift.

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning Saints Equitius, Constantius, Marcellinus, Nonnosus, and Boniface

[Col. 0835]

[Col. 0835A] What shall I say of Equitius,  
whom a heavenly surgeon made a eunuch,  
a guide for chaste men and for maidens themselves,  
and an extraordinary teacher of the holy way,  
lowering himself to the depths  
while raising minds to the heights?

[Col. 0835B] While he strives to carry sheep  
to the upper fold,  
he receives many.  
When he sees one whose heart is full of the demon,  
he calls him Satan and prepares to take him in.

To test the work, he takes a robber inside the enclosure,  
while the sheep’s mind is troubled  
by the wolf’s assault.  
When the robber is expelled,  
the lamb is pulled away from the snares.

Nor is it long before the thief, seized by the fire  
of his zeal for the faith, is caught:  
he had often reported to Equitius  
that he had hung himself in the cell by magical means  
and had been able to harm no one.

No less does he extract the succulent lettuce swallowed in the serpent’s fiery throat—  
the printed *fruit* is corrupt; the editorial reading *eximit* means “draws out.”

When, rebuking [editorial reading: petitioning], he asks the reason for their coming  
and by God’s word terrifies those who bring terror, he is commanded to hasten  
and water the thirsty hearts of the people with saving rain.

[Col. 0835C] Laden with the armor of piety, he strives to win souls for the Lord,  
traveling through villages and camps, lowly in bodily appearance  
but beautiful in mind. He is reported to the pope as a preacher  
who must be constrained by canonical discipline and checked in such bold acts,  
and a summons is sent for him. Those who had sought him change their minds:  
the presence of so great a man frightens their uncultivated hearts.  
The pontiff is rebuked and shaken by a terrifying vision asking why he vexes  
the Lord’s servant. A letter then speeds forth to forbid the journey,  
fulfilling the prophet’s words after he had urged the unwilling, exhausted man to hurry.

The miracles of his burial  
testify to what sort of man he was in life.  
Sitting upon the farmer’s chest,  
he is driven by the force of a whirlwind  
and then thrown far away.

Thus, when assailed by a complaining voice  
[Col. 0835D] as he grinds down his enemies,  
he covers the servants with a hostile company  
and, bringing protection, preserves many  
under his guardianship.

At the same time, Narcissus shines  
with constant light,  
illuminating the temples like oil  
with his blazing waves.

[Col. 0836A] You too, tester of your own testers,  
and a gracious friend,  
great, yet greater still in gentleness—  
what praises shall I bring to you, Marcellinus, bishop,

[Col. 0836B] who, though sitting in sickness,  
performed manly deeds of strength,  
while, broken by gout,  
you broke the strength of the flames?

How shall I calmly explain Nonnosus,  
who equals the deeds of former Fathers  
in his titles and accomplishments?

He prepares a garden  
on a mass of rock far away,  
follows the holy Greek Gregory,  
solidifies a glass lamp,  
and, having given it, replenishes the vessels  
of the entire monastery with a small quantity of oil,  
returning everything in the sign of Elisha.

Nor does Boniface shine with a different kind of deed. At Ferentum,  
amid poverty and hardships, he raised up a fruitful spirit  
and knew how to return thanks to the Lord for losses.  
With scant drops he filled the storehouse and jars; vessels barely touched  
with wine poured it out by that gift alone, a gift which [Col. 0836C]  
the guardian of his soul forbade to be disclosed while he remained in the body.

He likewise caused wine to increase in a small vessel for barbarian men,  
producing a drink for their use. A man who struck cymbals and forestalled  
the praises from the blessed man’s mouth, and was liable to punishment  
before Christ the supreme judge, was foretold; humbled, he obtained  
the consolation he sought.

When his nephew accused him over a loss of gold, Boniface returned  
golden profit and foretold grave loss for the nephew, who was removed  
from the honor of high office because of his desire for gold.

Indeed, compelling irrational creatures to obey him,  
he frees the garden, under oath, from caterpillars.

Nor is it so astonishing what this priest,  
worthy of honor, accomplished,  
if his deeds are weighed with a child’s mind:  
he adorned the needy,  
often stripping himself,  
and, after giving grain to the saints,  
left his own granaries emptied by plunder.

[Col. 0836D] Moved by his mother’s tears,  
he restores what was lacking through fruitful prayer;  
by that same prayer he rescues the hens  
from the thief and the enemy.  
The fox that had stolen the prey  
is punished as the thief,  
while God does not disdain to hear  
His servant even in the smallest matters.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning Saint Fortunatus, bishop

[Col. 0835]

[Col. 0835D] Nor should the deeds of Fortunatus of Todi  
be left unmentioned,  
a bishop shining with the distinguished light of virtues.  
Supported by prayer, he often drove away  
hostile armies of spirits,  
expelling their terrifying battalions  
from their habitations.

A married woman experienced his assistance  
when, overcoming carnal desire in a single night,  
she forbade herself from living in seclusion  
and from withdrawing from the marriage chamber.

[Col. 0836D] When she dared to break into the temple  
to be consecrated to the Lord,  
the arrival of the martyr restrained her  
with severe vengeance.

When the protector tried to conceal her,  
he was carried away by a snake.  
A legion of chelydri—serpents associated with Thessalian sorcery—attacked her; raging fiercely,  
it was inflamed with excessive heat.

[Col. 0837A] At last her parents confessed the crimes of their guilt  
and presented her to the pontiff.  
He lifted her through his zealous labor,  
and not long afterward they brought her back  
safe and clean.

He deprived a parent of his child  
when a treacherous host, treating his guest badly,  
openly marked him as unworthy of admission  
and drove him away under this judge’s sentence.

Here the pope restored light  
to eyes condemned to darkness.  
He also rescued beasts of burden  
after their madness had been driven away,  
and whatever he sought was accompanied  
by an accomplished deed.

He approves the fall of the Goth,  
who, having despised his father,

[Col. 0838A] suffered the crushing of his hardened heart  
after his thigh had been bruised;  
the binding of the body brought gentleness  
to the hard mind;  
the command of patronage brought swift healing  
to the limb;  
and soon health followed,  
with healing after the pain.

Marcellus too, restored from death,  
when he left the appointed seats  
at Fortunatus’s arrival,  
returned with a gentle voice, saying:  
“What power his prayers possessed!”

Fortunatus, as though still living in the body,  
had been accustomed to cure the sick,  
release those bound, and drive away destruction;  
nor did he cease to do so after death.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning Saints Martyrius and Severus

[Col. 0837]

[Col. 0837A] Venerable Valeria also raised up  
the holy Father Martyrius,  
who marked bread covered with coals and ashes  
with the sign of faith,  
without touching it with his hand.

[Col. 0837B] In this region we understand the priest Severus  
to have excelled in good deeds  
and acts of wondrous piety.  
Forbidden to visit a sick man,  
he delayed until the end of his work  
and found that the man had died.

[Col. 0838A] He mourns the guilt of the death,  
and thus receives back with tears  
the man who had been given over  
and redeemed by dreadful punishments.  
While Christ does not allow him  
to be saddened for even a brief hour,

[Col. 0838B] He grants, at the patron’s request,  
that he weep over the man’s passing,  
and thus joyfully leave earthly things,  
washed in his own tears  
and in Severus’s lamentation.

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning the priest who bound a thief in the tomb after his death

[Col. 0837]

[Col. 0837B] How vigorous he was,  
how exalted by bright deeds,  
how rich in praise,  
this priest who flourished in the Lord  
in this region—  
he who, dead and buried,  
bound a thief as he passed by.

His companions rejoice to marvel  
at the splendor of their teacher,  
who, while living, teaches the good,  
and, when dead, restrains theft.

The thief, fearing that he will be seen by the living,  
is bound and wastes away. He can neither lay down the booty  
nor carry off what he has retained. While a dead man’s bond  
is imposed upon the stupefied living,  
it is uncertain whether he is bringing it  
or stealing it, burdened by its weight.

When he confesses the crime,  
he is granted release through prayers.  
[Col. 0838B] The man who is bound by an unseen law  
while carrying what was stolen  
is allowed to go free  
once the bundle has been set down openly.

Thus also, in the Prenestine mountains,  
the outstanding Father shows, after death,  
how he lived.

His sons marvel at the agreements  
made with the buried man:  
whatever he promises while drawing breath,  
he fulfills once buried.  
Having been laid down,  
he yields the places by laying them down [the surviving source ends in this syntactically incomplete phrase].

[The supplied source ends here.]
to a friend,
Admitting a dear companion, once obtained through slaughter,

At the voice of the complainant, while his loosened limbs prepare themselves.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Saint Benedict and his many miracles

[Col. 0837]

[Col. 0837C] Worthy of heaven’s praise, renowned above the ether for his merits,

Adorned by Gregory’s elegant style and pleasing volume,

With what praise shall we celebrate the famous Benedict, foolish as we are?

Venerable throughout the world’s regions to the whole earth,

He, shining, sends Christ’s battalions [Note: [Col. 0837] companies of monks.] toward the stars.

As a boy, reading lofty things, he conquered disgrace with an aged heart;

While trampling the flowers of the world, dry as dust,

He scorned the splendor of an arrogant lineage together with the brightness of charm,

And, wisely unpolished, abandoning cultivated things,

He sought the heights of heaven, having sent worldly concerns and pursuits away.

[Note: [Col. 0837] See Saint Gregory, *Dialogues*, Book II, chapters 1 and following.] And the deed proved what his spirit, with what devout mind [Note: [Col. 0837] namely, “he sought the heights.”] had undertaken,

As did at once the signs that preceded his deeds:

The solidified broken vessel, the flight of the windy report, and the nurse who was abandoned,

The retreat into the wilderness, and the cave inhabited alone for three years,

The Roman bread suspended by a cord [Note: [Col. 0837] rope];

The priest warned to bring the Easter meal;

[Col. 0838C] The shepherds transformed into sheep, their hearts formerly savage;

Yet even then the tempter was not absent, and he harassed the fugitive,

Preparing to burn with the torches of lust the limbs mortified by the shameful assault,

Casting out snares for the dove that had crossed the heights

And fallen back from the worldly citadel:

The wicked black bird, with its blazing [Note: [Col. 0837] perhaps “tail”] tail, attacks the gentle bird,

And with its dark wings injects black poisons into the soul;

But at the sign of the cross it departs into the empty air.

Flung darts weary his breast, unaccustomed to flames,

And fiery force besieges his mind;

Stealing into its innermost chambers, it can scarcely be shut within his breast,

[Col. 0838D] And, growing, had consumed the innermost treasure [Note: [Col. 0837] riches of grace],

Had not the guardian of the heavenly resources [Note: [Col. 0837] virtues] of those seeking the secrets of heaven

Given counsel and brought his right hand to him in the struggle.

While the weapons of fury are checked by the goads of the thorns,

The fire of Venus is driven away by the fire of nettles,

And pleasure, transformed by pain, yields and flees.

[Col. 0839A] Having triumphed over the enemy, leader of his brother’s struggle,

Ruler and protector, after the vices had been expelled,

He emerges from his vessels [Note: [Col. 0839] people], nourisher and teacher of salvation.

Flying Fame carried his name through men’s mouths as she celebrated it,

Exalting his work and the renowned arena of virtue.

Dense crowds rejoice to approach the devout master,

To leave the shipwreck of the world, to gain a station

In the saving harbor, and to entrust themselves to secure camps.

There the excellent leader governs them with pure reins,

Cutting off unlawful deeds and leading the battalions,

Balanced to right and left, along a straight path.

Strong cohorts of the soldiery gather and persist,

Loving to follow the precepts of salvation along the right road;

They dread pursuing the slippery windings of luxury,

And eagerly undertake the rule and balance of the just scale.

[Col. 0839B] Certain men, brewing black poisons,

Secretly plan the death of their innocent father through deceit,

Preparing for themselves rather a joyful disgrace:

What [Note: [Col. 0839] disgrace.] they undergo through their own fault, and they lose their protector,

When the vessel is broken and the poison poured out under the sign of the cross.

The father, dismissing the faithless, ascends to the heights known to him,

Where, with virtue increasing, he produces abundant fruits,

Establishing twelve camps [Note: [Col. 0839] monasteries], each to contain twelve

Soldiers, apart from [Note: [Col. 0839] except those whom he was raising with himself] those whom he was nourishing with milk;

Opening to all the narrow thresholds of the heavenly road,

Leading both illustrious and poor toward the heights,

Arranging, adorning, and governing the battalions of the holy war,

Shining upon the ready and compelling the slow to strenuous effort.

He strengthens those who struggle, surrounding them with heavenly protection;

He drives away ambushes and terrifies thieves with his light.

Following the blind guidance of the Ethiopian boy,

The monk consents; having endured the father’s pious blows,

He is rescued by the blow and, after the thief has been struck, is recovered.

The leader adds resources to the athletes and gives provisions to the camps:

From a high mountain, from a lofty cliff,

He pours abundant streams by prayer for the thirsty soldiers.

From the dwelling of the good prince waters flow to the known streams,

And continually water the slopes of the summit in their descent.

Nor was he inferior in merits to Elisha, when by his deeds he instructed

And trained a novice [Note: [Col. 0839] Zalla], relieving the sorrowful through deliverance,

And caused the backward-flowing water to overcome the weight of iron.

Conscious of the danger of the boy carried away by the water,

He ordered the rescued servant [Note: [Col. 0839] Maurus] to hurry swiftly

Along the unusual path, and, with his limbs gliding through the water,

[Col. 0839D] To follow the footsteps of the great Peter;

He recalled the client [Note: [Col. 0839] Placidus], swallowed by the cruel throat,

As the companion served as witness to the father’s aid [Note: [Col. 0839] who had seen Benedict’s *melote*—his sheepskin garment].

So too, while Christ conquered hostile rages,

He often resisted them, overcoming them through continual triumphs;

He knew how to endure envy and avoid pain,

Recognizing as the only grief of enemies their ruin.

Concealing the serpent beneath the dove’s [Note: [Col. 0839] simplicity] innocence,

He removed the venomous gall by means of the wavering raven’s service;

The victorious weapons of the warriors, overcome,

[Col. 0840A] The girls’ weapons, the gentle departure of the father,

The enemy’s death, and the warning of the rejoicing disciple

Reveal the safest hearts of an unconquered mind.

The famous strength of his warlike triumphs over the enemy

Shows how temples collapse, how conquered Apollo

Complains openly that his servants have been snatched away to heaven,

That he himself is driven out and overcome, and that his rights are torn from him.

Then a stone, pressed down, was raised at Benedict’s prayer;

An image dug out of the earth, in the dining hall,

Deceives the soldiers, who pretend that there is a fire;

But at the leader’s command these things collapse, emptied of their deceit.

The more that deceiver struggles to mock the holy man,

The more, defeated in that struggle, he provides the means of victory.

For once, as he hurried to visit the working brothers,

While he overturned a construction of stones, crushing the bones of a boy in the collapse,

[Col. 0840B] He drove the forewarned men into grief and sorrow over the death;

He himself was granted the pious consolation

And restored the boy to life, to the joy of the devoted pupils [Note: [Col. 0839] disciples].

Soon the wicked enemy groaned over the work restored.

The father’s breast is filled with heavenly light.

Concerned for the sons entrusted to him by divine gift,

Though absent, he sees their deeds and duties as though present.

He rebukes errors, reveals food that had been presumed consumed,

Counting the cups and pointing out the lodging places.

He corrects the astonished pupils and, while sparing them, reforms them.

Thus, as usual, reproaching himself to his fasting stomach,

He broke his vow at the urging of a companion,

While the stupid man marveled at the red liquid dissolved into lamentation.

The servant of Totila, who had tested the heavenly gifts,

Thus confused, departed, having been ordered to lay aside his royal dress.

[Col. 0840C] But the barbarian king himself, praying humbly to the father,

Heard from him what had been done and what he himself must do, or even what fate awaited him;

He departed gentler and afterward became less wicked in his restrained fury.

Then, comforting fearful Rome, the friend [Note: [Col. 0839] Sabinus, bishop of Canusium] testifies

That she will not perish through the nations, but will at last be brought low

By whirlwinds, earthquakes, and frequent flashes of lightning.

A cleric, rescued from serpents’ throats,

Was forbidden to attempt the holy steps [Note: [Col. 0839] orders]; while he obeyed the command,

He remained unharmed. When he abandoned the warning, he was handed over to the enemy,

Went mad, and suffered the pains foretold,

Which the man of God had described after searching the hidden places within.

Learning by revelation from the Lord that the monastery was to be plundered

By a savage robber, and that everything suitable for use was at risk,

He protected the souls taken away by many prayers and tears,

[Col. 0840D] As he confessed, drenched in grief, to his faithful friend.

While revealing the hidden thefts of the faithless wine-bearer,

He protects him from the serpent of death and makes the evil of the deceit tremble [Note: [Col. 0839] protects him from it].

Thus also, rebuking a client for having secretly thrust gifts into his bosom,

He proves that he is present to servants who are absent,

And that he partakes of the actions of his own.

And even now, united with the Lord as one spirit,

He understands the words of the heart and guards the secrets conceived within;

While warning that the hearts of the minister exalted by the cross must be humbled,

He instructs one boy, removed from office and table,

[Col. 0841A] While preserving the hearts of the others.

Strengthening the fainthearted with his speech and raising up those who fear,

He promises abundant bread to the needy;

He prepares the promised grain through hidden consolation,

And returns the foretold relief in a plentiful bundle.

Also, as though freed from a prison intended for confinement,

His spirit flies into the camp [Note: [Col. 0841] the monastery at Terracina];

He repays the promises, measuring out suitable places

For the brothers warned by a vision,

And fulfilling, without a body, the duties of the assigned journey.

Moreover, he had received the power, through easy speech, to bind the guilty

Or to release souls through lofty merits.

He marks for complaining virgins the punishment inflicted for threats,

The rejection shown when the sacred rites were also to be tasted,

The father’s pious participation restored to the dead,

With the dowry offered through the sacraments for the peace of these women.

[Col. 0841B] Likewise, a boy raised in chaste integrity

Dared to visit the holy man’s carnal parents without his favor,

And was soon condemned to death and laid in the earth.

After the night, he was found above the ground and buried again;

And again cast out, when he sought to bring the sacraments

To the tomb, he made the buried man stand upright.

Though dismissed against the will of his protector to depart,

He returned, compelled by the dragon, the guide of the crooked road.

And the one whom he followed, concealed in darkness,

Had gone out through the father’s favor; when he saw the ambusher revealed,

He sought safety as the enemy pressed him.

A boy brought in, flowing with elephantine disease and corruption,

He gave speedy healing, driving away the sickness.

He was asked to bring comfort to the distress of a poor man

Bound by debt and lacking the money to repay it;

While pitying him and prepared, with fatherly concern, to provide help,

He had no funds at hand; yet, by repeatedly seeking the familiar aid,

He obtained the gifts requested through accustomed prayer.

Moreover, the generous right hand of the giver made up for the delay,

Relieving poverty and paying what was owed [Note: [Col. 0841] settling the debt].

At his touch diseases flee; the plague, driven away, withdraws;

The man’s own complexion is cleared of the spots that had been removed.

Astonished, he marveled that he had received such swift healing

And had returned to his own skin. His limbs,

Though the poisons could not drive out his soul,

Had defiled them with shameful whiteness and the yellow face of leprosy;

Under the holy man’s care they recover their lost beauty.

His ready hand had distributed provisions until everything was consumed.

Hardly a little oil remained beneath a glass vessel;

He ordered it to be given for the needs of his pressing friend,

[Col. 0841D] Preparing to retain nothing while seeking to increase his wealth in heaven.

When he discovered that the fainthearted minister had transgressed the command

Through extravagance, he ordered the flask, held back in the tent,

To be thrown headlong out of the high window.

Safe, however, as it fell upon the stones lying below, it settled [Note: [Col. 0841] came to rest];

It did not feel the hardness natural to stones,

Nor did it suffer the loss of the liquid as it tilted.

When it was brought out unharmed [Note: [Col. 0841] completely unharmed] and lifted for the petitioner,

[Col. 0842A] The miser was rebuked, while the others were consoled.

Loans are taken up, poured out through heavenly power;

Through the father’s prayer and devotion, the empty barrel is filled

And, overflowing, pours forth heavenly gifts.

Nor did he perform such wonders only through customary prayers;

Sometimes he brought them forth merely by a glance or a nod.

This is learned from a monk subdued by a pretended deception

And from the applause and slap of the hand of a mule-doctor [Note: [Col. 0841D] From this it is clearly confirmed that the reading we defended in chapter 30 of the *Life of Saint Benedict* is *mulomedici*, a compound word not to be divided into two expressions.].

That rustic too, driven by the torturer’s straps,

Indicates that, having been looked upon, he was freed by sheer power.

And the Goth [Note: [Col. 0841] Geta, a Goth], becoming gentle, abandoned his anger and prostrated himself.

There are also celebrated deeds accomplished through humble prayer,

As when a farmer, carrying the pitiable corpse of his son in his arms,

Compelled him, with importunate prayers,

[Col. 0842B] repeatedly to demand the return of the child snatched away by death;

While, with knees bent, he obtained life for him through prayer,

Restoring fiery nourishment to his cold marrow.

But once he was overcome by a nod of affectionate kindness,

And the prayers of his devout sister [Note: [Col. 0841] Scholastica], though he refused them,

Surpassed his own: she prolonged through the night the delay of her thirsty brother,

Until he was satisfied from her honey-sweet mouth with the nectar of the life above.

With prayers she darkened heaven and melted the air into clouds;

The maiden thunders with silent murmur,

And, compelled by tears, condensing the clouds, poured down rains through her weeping.

She halted his departure through the storm that served her;

Scholastica delayed and held her unwilling brother beneath the sky,

And, rejoicing, triumphed that a great prize had yielded to her.

Having obtained comfort for her soul after a night of vigil,

She returned joyfully and exchanged earthly things for heaven,

[Col. 0842C] Seeking the heights of heaven; her brother, fixed in the ether,

Saw her seeking the lofty summit of the stars

And surpassing the stars with a dove-like flight.

Rejoicing with her at the summit [Note: [Col. 0841] at his sister’s honor],

He strove in worthy measures to render thanks,

Composed praises to Christ and directed them to him,

And, recalling, received the members of his fellowship,

Which he buried for himself with sepulchral honor:

So that the tomb might unite those whom heavenly love had united [Note: [Col. 0841] affection].

Nor is it so astonishing that, while entering the heavenly realms,

He saw the soul of his sister, to whom the whole structure of the world

Lies open before her eyes, with the radiant brilliance

Of heavenly light, through which the entire world is seen;

The fiery celestial sphere, supporting Germanus with its heavenly company,

Shone back, and what she saw brought beauty [Note: [Col. 0841] glory].

Summoned by the sight, he hastens to behold it,

And the deacon Servandus, a witness to the miracle,

Seizes a share of the radiance.

The rest of the father’s deeds, which we ought to follow,

The silences of the leader [Note: [Col. 0841] Gregory] have suppressed for us,

As he pursued the struggles [Note: [Col. 0841] contests] of the others.

He flourished in doctrine; he composed the rule of the monks.

Since he had foreknowledge of the day of his death, he was worthy of this privilege.

When he himself revealed it, the way laid out in beauty

Was disclosed to the disciples and flashed with the honor of splendor.

[Col. 0843A] He is shown ascending by it toward the heavenly heights, the righteous man

Shining with uplifted hands and nourished by sacred food,

Giving up his final breath through words of prayer,

Renowned, stretching from the house of prayer toward the temples of heaven.

The idols given to the shrine, by which Apollo was driven away,

Bring forth an excellent triumph through their celebrated conqueror.

Aigulf and Mummolus, warned by this event,

Who were sent for this matter, while eager to preserve

The honor of the light above, obtain, through the dark silence of night,

The gifts long sought with labor.

They snatch them away and raise them,

And entrust the sister’s relics [Note: [Col. 0843] of the sister] to their united accomplices;

At the same time, sent by the saint’s command for these duties,

They hurry and make for the furthest lands

Of Ausonia, while, persuaded to recall the pope,

The battalions follow, under Christ’s leadership, the talents that had been carried off.

[Col. 0844A] He who shelters the servants blinds the bitterly raging men,

So that they cannot see the things they seek placed before them [Note: [Col. 0843] desired].

He orders the treasures, taken under his protection, to be carried away quickly,

And allows the enemy to be seen without allowing himself to be seen by the enemy.

Thus protected by divine power, they joyfully carry away the rewards given to them,

Which, after the ruins foretold and carried off by God’s judgment,

Shine forth when revealed to the Franks, together with the sister’s bones,

Adorning the cities of Gaul with frequent signs.

Yet the father does not appear to have abandoned the cultivated places;

Rather, when asked, he is present and even freely bestows rewards.

A woman experienced this: wandering through [Note: [Col. 0843] or “for a long time”] thickets and pathless places,

She entered the chamber of a cave,

Where she had first been trained by a man in the struggle of her novitiate.

When she emerged with understanding and preserved the strength given to her,

She did not reveal the former dangers to her uninjured mind.

## CHAPTER IX. On Saint Paulinus

[Note: [Col. 0843] On this saint and the others celebrated by Flodoard in chapters 10–25, compare Saint Gregory the Great, *Dialogues*, Book III, chapter [number uncertain] and following.]

[Col. 0843]

[Col. 0843B] With what praise shall we celebrate the work of Paulinus’ immense devotion,

Who followed Christ along the steep footsteps of God,

By a scarcely trodden path, yet with wondrous virtue,

Shining in doctrine and strong against hostile weapons?

The prince of the Church devotes himself to the needy widow:

He gives himself willingly as a servant, so that the servant may lay down his chains;

He presses his neck beneath the yoke, so that he may loosen the servant’s neck;

He binds himself as a captive, so that the captor may release his captive;

He attends upon kings as a servant, yet balances royal power;

He submits himself to the Lord, yet grants honor to the tyrant;

He arranges the heights, serves, and at the same time commands;

A cultivator of gardens, he is appointed ruler by royal order,

And, as a tender of vegetables, he undertakes the management of kings.

While governing peoples, he ensures that he himself is bent

[Col. 0844B] By the cultivation of the grass assigned to him,

And that he escape the savage blow by the judgment of the servant

Who governs the scepters of his masters.

He is raised up by the hoes and led away from the cultivated gardens;

He is honored by kings, and the servant is asked to offer prayers.

Putting souls before gold, he asks for those captured on behalf of the flock;

The scattered are gathered together, increased by the gift,

And sent back to their father, while ships and provisions are brought.

The shepherd returns joyfully, surrounded by a flock of sheep.

And he who had submitted himself for the sake of one servant,

After rescuing many, returns free with the people—

Redeeming many through the servitude that one man had assumed.

His wondrous life, illumined by divine light,

Is proved by his precious death,

By the trembling of the cell,

And by the honey brought near John’s lips as he was departing.

## CHAPTER X. On Saint Datius, bishop

[Col. 0843]

[Col. 0843C] Datius of Milan, supported by what strength,

Shone forth; Corinth felt glad at his faith,

When, at the expulsion of the complaining spirit,

The household gods were restored,

After the demon, formerly held by monstrous savagery,

Was driven away at the host’s command through dreadful wickedness.

By the light with which his mind flourished, by the radiance with which he shone,

The already milk-white old man [or “white-haired elder”] shone upon the city of Canusium;

Blind in face, indeed, but radiant in heart, the Sabine,

He shines when the barbarian Totila tests him through his servant.

While compelling and restraining the bearer of death,

Condemning the revealed aconite of death,

He drinks the pressed potion under the sign of the cross,

And triumphs over the prostrate giver.

How brightly Cassius of Narni shines with venerable voice,

The cruel king sees in advance by experience;

He leaves aside his armed escort and receives the man,

Whose merit is preeminent.

Accustomed to be present on so many days at the sacred mysteries,

He sacrifices himself amid abundant secret tears,

[Col. 0844C] A living victim slaughtered to God upon the altar.

Nor is the labor of the devoted old man proved fruitless:

Although worn out by the admonition,

He postpones the rest owed to his duties,

While, receiving the promise that his rewards will be returned to him

At the apostolic festival,

He is delayed seven years;

At last, given to the lofty stars, the priest shines forth.

Andreas, bishop of Fundi, of blessed life,

Follows the slippery corrector, black with corrected [or “corrupting”] deeds,

Trained by dreadful warnings;

He rescues the man removed from his masters,

Who warned him to beware the snares,

And tears him from the snares.

The renowned cedar of paradise,

Crushed by Tartarean deceits, while it changes, clings fast;

He strengthens the leafy summits of the eternal grove.

The dying seer Constantius, beginning at Aquinum,

Cries out that these things must be endured;

They mark, after the false mule-driver [reading uncertain],

The loss of rule and the vacancy of the sacred and widowed see.

## CHAPTER XI. On Saint Frigdianus

[Col. 0845]

[Col. 0845A] The sanctity of Frigdianus, of what power,

Flourished and shone beneath the rule of Lucca,

Proclaims the river, whose channel had left its course,

Following the rake that he ordered to proceed,

As it was accustomed to spare the scattered estates.

[Col. 0846A] Nor is Piacenza accompanied by lesser brilliance,

When he restrains the swollen waters of the Po,

The river having been calmed by the letters of Sabinus,

At the command of the father, through the episcopal stream.

## CHAPTER XII. On Saint Populonius

[Note: [Col. 0845] So the manuscript; but it should be read “on Cerbonius, bishop of Populonia, and Fulgentius of Utricoli.”]

[Col. 0845]

[Col. 0845A] How renowned once was Populonius as a host,

How outstanding in lofty merits was the bishop Cerbonius!

When the Gothic king tested him, he was protected by the bear’s display,

And celebrated the man blessed by such a teacher,

Whom the savage king had judged worthy of being devoured by the beast’s throat.

His holy spirit restores the funeral rites,

Ordered to be recalled before the urn already prepared was carried away:

Surrounded by rains, yet carried beneath a dry covering,

He was brought before the enemies and, when ordered, carried back by the bearers.

Nor did Fulgentius of Utricoli shine less,

Through a similar miracle, though he still bore mortal flesh.

[Col. 0846A] Distinguished amid the trembling danger of imminent death,

Shut within the compass of the sky,

In the burning heat of the starry sphere,

He was suddenly covered by a flashing cloud,

Which, terrible to the wild beasts and protecting the gentle client,

Drove away the bonds and drove off the thunderbolts that formed the crown.

When the wolves had been driven away, the ram stood with a dry fleece,

[Col. 0846B] While everything was drenched by whirlwinds,

While the savage host, overcome by heaven, gave way;

The shepherd, safe beneath whose rule,

Drives back the enemies and overcomes the strength of the victors,

Overthrows their heights, breaks and subdues the tyrant,

Making gentle the fierce lion beneath the threatening sky.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Saint Herculanus

[Col. 0845]

[Col. 0845B] At whose roar Perugia trembles,

Herculanus, the bishop struck down amid murmuring,

Admiring that the severed neck of the martyr who had died

Was again made firm and joined to the body,

And that the entrails, cut apart by the straps,

Had blossomed again with their pleasing flesh;

[Col. 0846B] At the same time, when the corpse of the boy,

Its body loosened and teeming with the decay of worms,

Was buried;

And when the old man’s limbs, after ten days had passed,

Were restored as though on the first day of his death, they shone.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Saint Isaac the monk

[Col. 0845]

[Col. 0845C] What kind of guest Isaac the All-Good was,

Brought from Syria to Spoleto,

The virgin Gregory discovered.

Protected by him, she fled from wanton marriages,

She who is joined to the earthly king of the attempted assault of heaven.

The sacristan too, hostile to his abundant prayers, perceives this;

Soon the avenger restrained him with the blows of his palm,

The betrayer of the athlete’s lofty virtue,

Immediately revealing that he must be expelled,

Having tested himself against the soldier.

While honor is carried to him in competition,

While he flees all the gifts offered by the countryside,

The man friendly to poverty leaves the city dwellers

And chooses the hidden lairs of wild beasts.

Here too, when the disciples following the narrow path

Urged him to take the little fields allotted for food,

He avoided poverty, fearing that he might lose the good;

He declared that the person who seeks earthly things is not heavenly.

[Col. 0845D] And the more he rejected perishable things,

The more he seized what endures.

He performs miracles and, strong in divine inspiration, shines.

Once, when thieves of vegetables tested him with zeal,

They changed their occupation and labored with the hoes—

Those who had sought theft turned toward its opposite;

They subjected themselves to the work they had acquired,

Forgetting their own wishes and following secret commands,

Despising crimes and performing duties of devotion.

What they had sought as a disgrace they brought back as an honorable reward,

Rejoicing that they had completed an unexpected task.

So too, the apparently poor, seeking what belonged to another,

Take up their own things, covered by shame.

Thus the faithless carrier is rescued,

Bound by a salutary blush and protected from a dreadful death.

The riches of virtue, which sometimes concealed invincible joys,

Kept his mind ready for battle through their goads.

## CHAPTER XV. On Saints Florentius and Eutychius

[Col. 0845]

[Col. 0845D] By what merits Florentius, the brother, flourished!

The bear’s obedience proves it, as do the comforts supplied by the untamed beast.

An inexperienced shepherd, he learned to serve flocks of two-year-old sheep,

To obey commands, to endure fasts,

To preserve the food that was present,

And to add rules to the evening meal.

At the dim light, the hand that destroyed the sign and killed the servant

[Col. 0846D] Of the innocent man—his master’s vengeance following the pain—

He sees the streams given to vengeance and groans through punishment,

While the envious Levite, preserved as a lover,

Finds his dwelling surrounded by a poisonous host.

At the voice of the fearless guest,

The heights of heaven resound,

And the ether, strengthening, serves him;

[Col. 0847A] He strikes down and destroys the venom-bearing crown.

When he seeks further assistance, reliable aid is prepared for him:

Suddenly a succession of feathered troops is brought,

Lifting the dreadful corpses and cleansing the courtyards from their sadness.

Eutychius, his companion on the road that seeks heaven,

The leader and instructor of pious companies,

By what righteousness, governing souls, did he call them to the heights?

[Col. 0848A] This is revealed after the contest has been completed through distinguished signs.

The garment itself also, a witness to divine favor,

Comes forward, accustomed to turn away the avenger’s anger,

When the fields were blazing with the heat of the sun,

While, brought forth, it filled the thirsty countryside with moisture

And enriched the fertile estates of Nursia with rain clouds.

## CHAPTER XVI. On Saint Martin

[Col. 0847]

[Col. 0847A] The hills of Marsica deserved to see Martin’s triumphs

Often enacted:

The dark dragon’s necks were subdued,

And he drove away the column striving with outstanding strength

To shine from its lofty seat with the ruddy splendor of heavenly life.

Indeed, penetrating safely through the frequent hiding place,

He joins himself to the one prostrate in prayer,

And, striving to cast trembling upon the suppliant,

He offers the theme of victory [Note: [Col. 0847D] The words are corrupt];

[Col. 0847B] Nor can he pierce the uncovered flesh of the one who despises him.

But when the sun completes three circuits of emptiness,

Inflamed by the heat of Phlegethon’s fury,

He vomits horrific flames through the slopes and trackless ways,

Throwing himself headlong and burning the scattered groves with fire.

[Col. 0848A] Thus, overcome by his own furies, the victor’s glory shines.

For him Christ, bearing water from the cliff as an ancient gift,

Teaches with what beloved affection he embraces his servant.

And the woman’s sudden death

Makes known that she had offended God by harming his disciple.

Nor is the account of the fallen boy less astonishing:

Falling safely over the rough cliffs,

Down the steep face of the rock,

And over the roofs lying below the broken cliff,

He was driven into the father’s cave, lest he be harmed by the impact.

The chain itself, loosening the foot at Benedict’s command,

Often gave strength to what was collapsing,

And gave the cord the power of iron.

## CHAPTER XVII. On a monk named Quadragesimus

[Col. 0847]

[Col. 0847B] What a man of such great merit was Quadragesimus,

The venerable monk who fled honors,

[Col. 0848B] His face rubbed with life-giving dust proves it:

Hardly snatched from death through prayers,

He was restored to life and light.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the monk Benedict and Menas

[Col. 0847]

[Col. 0847B] How brilliantly the Campanian Benedict shone from the fire,

Immune from the crime!

The hostile fire reveals it,

[Col. 0847C] While the flame, prevailing, consumed all else.

The indication is strengthened by the furnace testing the work of unconquered integrity:

The more he is assailed by the burning heat of the furies,

The more brilliantly he shines with the honor of gold,

Since the pyre dares not burn even the outermost garment.

Menas, whom Samnium honored as holy,

[Col. 0848B] The bees declare to have been protected;

The invader, overcome by punishment and compelled by words,

[Col. 0848C] Submits his savage hand meekly;

The fierce enemy is subjected,

And the bears, groaning beneath the rod and blows,

Flee the honey from the gentle lashes of the slayer.

The adulterer, trembling at the illicit gift of hidden slaughter,

Caught by the light of the judgment of his crime,

Was exposed;

And through this rebuke many were saved from the crime.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the forty peasants and those who refused to worship the goat’s head

[Col. 0847]

[Col. 0847C] How firmly the pious hearts of the men of Ausonia stood,

The strength of the country folk proves,

When forty brave men, seized and tested,

[Col. 0847D] Could be torn from Christ neither by a barbarian hand threatening with the sword,

Nor by the horror of death,

[Col. 0848C] Nor by the harshness of execution.

Here too, those who laughed at the rites of the slaughtered little goat,

While shuddering at the mad worship of the goat’s severed head,

[Col. 0848D] obtained the splendor of the kingdom as the reward for their heads.

## CHAPTER XX. On Saints Amantius and Floridus

[Col. 0847]

[Col. 0847D] How strongly the elder Amantius, by the deed of his virtue,

Shone forth, excelling in simplicity as he relieved diseased limbs

By the touch of his hand, lofty in apostolic honor!

How powerfully Floridus extinguished poisonous things

[Col. 0848D] at the sign of the cross,

Gregory the bishop relates: frequently fed with the splendid abundance

Of a multiplied meal and filled to satiety,

He, the father and lover of true brightness, proves this

When food set before him is received without harm.

## CHAPTER XXI. On Sanctulus

[Col. 0847]

[Col. 0847D] Sanctulus flourished with what righteousness, bright with the light of devotion,

The neighboring people bear witness and relate.

[Col. 0848D] He himself, even when tested, declares the outcome of his prayers.

For, when he sought oil, though the press refused its liquid,

[Col. 0849A] And, persistent, pressed on amid the surrounding barbarians,

He received what he requested and conferred what he appeared to seek.

Calm, he softened the hostile;

Joyful, he cheered the raging,

And, sowing water, gathered cheerful ointments.

He who once fed thousands with a few loaves

Restored many by feeding them with bread through one servant,

Given by divine goodness and found for the exhausted

Workers who were repairing the burned church.

What could have been sufficient for a few, even for one day,

Was enough for many at ten meals,

As the bread increased on the tables through the accumulated fragments.

This man, outstanding and exalted in his love of God,

Did not hesitate to surrender his own life for his brother,

Compelling him to accept assistance in flight.

[Col. 0850A] He himself hastened to offer his neck in place of the one to be killed;

And, submitting himself, restrained the arm of the striking sword.

Freezing the raised weapon, he softened the hearts of the enraged;

With bent knee he bent the hearts of the savage men;

He made the cruel gentle and subdued the fierce enemies.

Releasing the guilty man who had dared to violate the holy things,

He ordered the innocent to be dismissed and allowed to depart free.

While offering himself to death for the neck of one man,

He himself, a free man, released many from the loss of life.

This deadly evil of swift fury against the sacred vessels,

This savage pit and Charybdis of blood,

Eutychius, a martyr and bishop, bore before the Redeemer;

And thus at Ferentum, as his end drew near,

The consecrated man learned that human flesh

Is borne onward to its final end.

## CHAPTER XXII. On Saints Speciosus and Gregory, brothers, and Saint Spes

[Col. 0849]

[Col. 0849B] How holily and devoutly the brothers Speciosus,

Purified by the doctrine of the father Benedict and united in mind,

And Gregory, carried the treasures of heaven into its secrets,

The departure of the former and the vision of the latter reveal.

How Spes, patient and long-suffering beneath Christ’s scourge,

Stood firm, blind in face but radiant in heart,

Lacking outward sight but not inward brilliance,

He himself declares, after a long period,

When sight was restored to him.

After four times ten circuits of the years had finally passed,

[Col. 0850B] The end of his labor was made known to him,

When the Lord revealed it,

And he was ordered, having received bodily light,

To sprinkle light upon the hearts of the blind.

After completing his service, he returned and revisited his station;

He sought the sacred place and stood in the midst of the summoned brothers.

He sang divine songs and composed the beginnings of hymns;

Intent upon prayers, he ascended to the stars with his vows.

He was revealed to be seeking the heavens in a dove-like flight,

At the point where his simple contest had reached its end.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On a certain presbyter of Nursia, Bishop Probus, and Abbot Stephen

[Col. 0849]

[Col. 0849B] That old man of Nursia, who drives away his companion at the threshold,

Although bound by death,

Fearing the straw as though it were fire,

Prevents it from being kindled against his loosened limbs.

How well and chastely he preserved the entrusted fold,

The arrival of Peter and Paul and their grace proclaim:

The repeated joy of the old man drawing his final breaths,

And his departure, freed from black fear.

But neither does the death of Probus, the bishop flourishing at the height of life,

In the Reatine city,

Though weighed down by illness, lack the light above,

When, trembling at the brilliance of Juvenal and Eleutherius,

The attendant cannot bear the beauty of those who come to see him.

Accompanied by them, the bishop joyfully approaches heavenly things.

[Col. 0850B] In contrast, Stephen, shining with inward virtues,

The despiser of the world,

Ruled this city with firm strength of spirit,

Excelling in patient endurance of the heavenly camp.

[Col. 0850C] His end, full of distinguished signs, reveals the completion of his contest.

It is seen in his deeds, words, and love for those who do harm:

He abandons the harvest, scorched with tranquil mind,

And grieves for its author, rejecting his own losses,

Mourning the crime whose honor is adorned by him.

His departure, whose angelic presence

Mortal sight cannot endure,

Nor can it bear heavenly things,

While the venerable father ascends to grasp

[Note: [Col. 0849D] The verse is halting.]

The rewards of the perpetual crown in the kingdoms of heaven.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On two monks of Abbot Valentio, Saint Surannus, and a certain deacon

[Col. 0849]

[Col. 0849D] Those whom the holy Valentio had imbued with virtuous goodness,

The brothers, reveal by their barbarian hands’ savage treatment of their sturdy bodies,

While, having completed their task, they alternately resound their hymns.

Even amid their astonished wounds, with clear voice they confess

How truly the servants of the Lord live after death.

The mountain too, shorn when Surannus’s head was cut off,

And receiving his breast with trembling motion,

Speaks this, shuddering at the dreadful dangers of savage crime,

And trembling to bear such great burdens of devotion.

He too, the executioner of the Marsican minister beneath the sacred rites,

Reveals the matter through its outcome:

After his deserving and dear client was beheaded,

He was handed over to the Lord’s cruel enemy.

## CHAPTER XXV. On Saints Mellitus, Theophanius, and Peter

[Col. 0849]

[Col. 0849D] How simple and pure Mellitus shone in his devout deeds,

The visions and golden letters also indicate.

By these, marked out by what consolation he relied upon,

He declares that he is now happily departing from human affairs

[Col. 0850D] And in venerable speech declares that they will soon follow him.

Thus Theophanius, of Centumcellae,

Ruled the reins of the city with vigor, mercy, and fitness;

His end reveals it,

When it becomes clear that, after following his devout destiny,

He passed through the storm into serene light.

The soundness of his limbs, formerly flowing with disease and corruption,

And the fragrant odor of his flesh when it had decayed, prove it.

The monk Peter undergoes death,

So that, lost, he may not perish by a second death;

For he had seen the fiery Gehenna

And was about to be plunged into fire.

But when the inhabitant of heaven called him back,

He returned,

And, warned, restrained himself through honorable deeds,

Striving by his life to declare that he had seen Tartarus,

His tongue bearing witness whither he was going,

What certain end he was pursuing,

And what terrors, now familiar, it feared.

At the same time, these things are confirmed by his stainless deeds.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On Saints Severus and Egistius and the other martyrs of Ravenna

[Col. 0851]

[Col. 0851A] We have said that Ravenna, dedicated to the laws of Christ,

Received the command through the client of Cephas,

Who gives the order,

So that Severus, their martyr and bishop,

Might strive to bear worthy pledges to heaven.

His companion Egistius purifies her with blood,

Together with Victor the liberator and Valentinus.

Here, when Ursicinus, already wavering beneath the burden

Of the arena after the fiercest struggles,

Was hanging in the horror of death beneath the shadow of the palm,

[Col. 0851B] Vitalis, the gracious father of a blessed offspring,

Who begot Gervasius and his brother for heaven,

Strengthens Ursicinus, the physician, by urging blessed steadfastness,

Reviving him with a perpetual remedy.

He makes him firm to bear the yoke of the kingdom’s gift,

And the honor of death crowns him with final distinction.

He himself, having gained the cup of salvation,

Drinks it after openly invoking the name of Jesus.

[Col. 0852A] Held fast, he is tortured by the torment of the horse;

Then, resisting the commander's order to endure the company of his fellow soldiers,

He is plunged headfirst into a deep pit;

Pressed down by stones and covered by earth, he is hidden,

And is joined to Ursicinus in the hall of light.

The martyr’s wife, Valeria,

Having returned from Milan while seeking comfort,

Encounters country folk offering sacrifice to the rustic god Silvanus,

Performing rites more foolish than foolishness itself.

[Col. 0852B] With a horse fastened below, they demand that she lie down

Upon polluted dishes.

She refuses, avoiding the unspeakable meals,

And publicly declares herself Christian;

Therefore, struck, she is beaten with many blows;

and, still breathing, is borne to the destined walls;

scarcely half-alive, she is restored to her abode,

and, after remaining for two days, climbs the heights prepared for her.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On Saint Germanus, Bishop of Auxerre

[Col. 0851]

[Col. 0851B] Germanus himself, bishop of a Gallic city,

a teacher flashing with the brilliance of wisdom,

after many marvels of illustrious strength,

and after twice bringing back from death

[Col. 0851C] Britons who had been snatched away,

is brought here for the sake of securing peace,

and is gloriously received into the palace.

Here, amid the lofty lights of holiness,

[Col. 0852B] he draws a young man from death

—the young dependant of the noble Volusianus—

and, when the Lord visits him, abandoning earthly things,

he climbs the heights above, blessed with light;

[Col. 0852C] among which he shines, exalted amid the stars,

with royal kindness toward the faithful people.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On Saints Theodosius, Donatus, Secundianus, and Romulus

[Col. 0851]

[Col. 0851C] Thus once, along that road of red marble,

the lofty glory of the governor is prepared,

under the guidance of the traveller, through the fearful signs

of the heavenly shepherd’s mouth, which were uttered amid the surging waters.

[Col. 0851D] While the earth was dry, the soldiers, by the feet of Theodosius,

cross the marsh with dry feet—

a passage which had been thought incapable

[Col. 0852C] of ever providing a route, under the oppressive tyrant,

by an immeasurable path.

The faithful leader joyfully carries the sacred cry,

giving worthy praises to the giver of the palm,

and, sending forth the festivals of worldly glory,

[Col. 0852D] persists in bearing continual thanks day after day.

Donatus, Secundianus, and Romulus,

and their companions, illuminate the harmony of the contest.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On Saints Hermagoras and Fortunatus

[Col. 0851]

[Col. 0851D] Aquileia shines, radiant through Mark's disciple Hermagoras,

as he drinks from the stream of Peter.

After the bright miracles of saving light,

he undertakes with fervent zeal the labor of doctrine,

[Col. 0852D] brings forth the harvest of peoples nourished by faith,

and steadfastly overcomes very many torments of punishment.

Together with Fortunatus, his first minister in the holy rites,

he compensates the loss of his head with the honor of heaven.

## CHAPTER XXX. On Saints Cantius, Cantianus, Cantianilla, and Probus

[Col. 0851]

[Col. 0851D] This city is adorned by brothers noble in flesh

and illustrious in blood, heavenly lights of the Anician family:

[Col. 0852D] Cantianus and Cantius beautify it,

together with their sister Cantianilla, in due order.

[Col. 0853A] Drawn there from the City by love of glory,

with their tutor as their leading guide,

and with Probus [Proto], their teacher, through whom they flourished in faith,

[Col. 0854A] they climb to the stars with their necks cut by the sword,

shining with a rosy and milky radiance.

# THE FOURTEENTH BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0853]

## CHAPTER I. On Saint Michael the Archangel

[Col. 0853A] Campania raises up, at the Garganian boundary, a hill

which Michael the archangel adorns

with heavenly light and frequent brilliance,

and with the structure of a temple.

He declares that he inhabits it,

appearing with the frequent splendor

of the virtues bestowed for the illumination of the human race.

This is proved by the bull which he follows,

a bull dwelling in the lofty forests and fleeing the herds,

after the weapon, turned in the opposite direction,

which he had fixed there by the force of his high thrust.

The citizens also prove it when he commands them to fast

and teaches them, through omens, to seek the divine will.

The supreme messenger now makes himself known to him,

revealing the deed he wishes to disclose:

he will preserve the mountain,

and will cherish the one mountain chosen above the others.

[Col. 0853B] They therefore become accustomed to summon the minister

of the ethereal light by their prayers.

Not daring to enter the temple,

they offer their devotions before the doors

and persist in their praises.

Then, attacked by enemies, they ask for the aid

of angelic protection and offer fasts to the Lord.

Only night intervening divided the battle.

While the archangel assists the bishop, distressed by uncertainty,

revealing to heaven the prayers that had been offered,

he appoints the time for battle

and promises that he will be present.

He gladdens the pope with the gift of the promised victory.

Trusting in these promises,

and already carrying their vows, as it were, in their bosoms,

they bring forward signs against signs

and burn with the struggle.

One could see the slope trembling with a great shaking,

frequent flashes flying,

the summit encircled by darkness,

and the heavenly ministers glowing above in fiery flame.

[Col. 0853C] The peoples are terrified,

and, fearing the heavenly weapons, flee in every direction;

they are struck by missiles from above.

Having fallen into Naples, they enter its trembling walls,

recount the event, and handle the thunderbolts they have experienced.

They recite the downfall of the defeated,

compose praises of Christ,

magnify the divine power,

and rejoice to submit their necks.

Then the people of Sipontum, wishing to offer thanks and vows,

seek the lofty heights and, examining the discovered walls of the temple,

see footprints impressed upon the rocks.

They proclaim the heavenly champion,

whose presence is made clear by this sign,

[Col. 0853D] and adorn the marble with a vaulted roof.

[Col. 0854A] They ennoble the altar and embellish it with the name bestowed upon it;

they add sacred buildings.

They fear to touch the divine inner chambers with their feet

and are afraid to cross the threshold.

They choose someone to inquire of the sacred pope

and to ask whether the place itself needs to be consecrated by sacred rites.

The father gives an informed reply

and returns instructions worthy of the matter.

Thus the will of so lofty a guardian must be sought concerning the precincts of so sacred a temple, for the healing of humankind.

On the day when the victory shone forth with particular brilliance,

let prayers be offered with humble devotion;

let both sides, through fasts, bring their certainty before God,

so that Christ, having accepted his gifts,

may carry them to completion.

Night had brought back its shadow to the earth

and the stars to the heavens,

when the prince of the heavenly army came,

about to reveal, from the highest stars, what was uncertain.

[Col. 0854B] He disclosed to the priest the undertaking

which had long been requested and commanded:

“Your temple does not need to be consecrated by us,” he said.

“I myself am both recognized as its founder

and am myself its consecrator.

You need only enter,

and, with the people standing by,

frequently offer appropriate prayers and utter praises.

When gifts have been given,

let the people share in the altars,

and it will be made clear that I have consecrated

the place prepared for me.”

The citizens hasten joyfully

to proclaim the new happiness.

They enter the basilica,

frequent the divine offices,

and marvel at the house shining with angelic power,

adorned with a red altar-cloth,

with no human work or human hand discernible.

[Col. 0854C] Holy joys fill the hearts of the people.

A blessed order of ministers is appointed

to continue praises and divine songs throughout the day,

for at night no one dares to keep watch

or bring a foot inside the sanctuary.

A drop flows from the stone

by which the building is sheltered;

clear, it falls drop by drop into a glass vessel.

When drunk, it is sweet

and medicinal against diseases.

After the rites of God,

the faithful are accustomed to taste it.

It drives away fevers

and heals the sick who gasp for breath.

Here very many gifts of salvation

are bestowed upon the devout

through the angelic assistance

given by the goodness of the Thunderer.

## CHAPTER II. On Saints Aristo, Justus, and Their Companions

[Col. 0853]

[Col. 0853D] Many martyrs beautifully adorn Campania,

flashing with illustrious triumphs.

Among them are Aristo, Justus, and their companions,

Crescentianus together with Felicissimus,

Urbanus, Vitalis, and Felix,

[Col. 0854D] together with Martiana and Symphorosa, who go before them.

Antonius, stained with blood,

flourishes here, broken into pieces,

and consecrates the river with them—

the river in which they are washed,

which takes the place of a tomb.

## CHAPTER III. On Saints Priscus, Antoninus, Aristeus, and Paulinus

[Col. 0855]

[Col. 0855A] Priscus raises up Capua,

handing on new teachings,

a pupil of ancient Christian devotion,

shining with its radiance.

Together with Antoninus,

whose childish limbs he consecrated,

the bishop Aristeus honors this place with the palm of martyrdom.

Paulinus adorns the struggles of Felix with his pen,

the gracious Nolanean,

who was pleased to touch upon them briefly.

The presbyter, driven before Dravus’s eyes,

teaches that the wonders of the gods are nothing but fabrications.

He is also compelled to pour libations to sacrilegious images:

“You are enemies,” he says,

“of your own gods.

By this service you will suffer what befell those

whom you grieve to have displayed

as Felix’s brother.

But if it is in your heart to seek the divine powers of my Lord,

let Jupiter, as ruler, fall,

and let me be led to the Capitol.”

The judge orders his ears to be crushed

[Col. 0855B] and a lofty platform to be prepared and fitted for him.

From there he is thrust into the blind abyss

and the dry darkness,

bound with chains.

Sharp fragments of pottery are spread across his back,

and the jagged edges of broken shells arm his bed,

making sleep lie upon their rough fleece.

The powers above visit him,

and he is relieved by divine brightness.

In the middle of the night,

the wheel which had pressed upon both his legs,

stretched out upon its loosened axle,

splits apart with a broken beam.

Then, with his bonds broken,

he is entrusted to the presbyter,

and, leaving, is ordered to seek his own bishop,

to find him,

to lead him cautiously out to the city and his household,

and to restore him under a roof

until the storm should subside.

The old man, unable to endure the torments,

had been sheltering in the lairs of wild beasts,

dragging out the last of his life,

worn down by cold and suffering the dangers of hunger.

[Col. 0855C] After Felix had traversed the thickets many times,

he found his father lying there,

already rigid, motionless,

and a cold corpse.

He was distressed about how to revive his father

and care for him as he breathed his last.

And—O marvelous faith!—

he saw a grape hanging from the thorn bushes.

Behold, the berries lying there,

pressed into the old man’s mouth,

renewed his spirit

and raised up his restored strength.

The harsh forest offered an unfamiliar sweetness,

and the thorn bush gave the joy of unmixed wine.

Felix approached,

carried his father back in his arms and on his shoulders,

and concealed him in a rural hut

under its roof of thatch.

He nourished him in secret

and cautiously supplied him with food.

The martyr, likewise captured,

is given over as an exile at Circeii

[Col. 0855D] to cut stones at the summit,

a companion in the life imposed upon the condemned.

[Col. 0856A] The punished man expiates the punishment imposed upon him;

and, driven away,

he brings back to the harbor those who had suffered

the losses of the raging sea.

After a shipwreck,

he rescues Probus, his son, and his wife,

and their demonic offspring,

who had been seized by a delirious disease,

and offers them, together with many others rescued,

to Christ.

When he returns to his household

and properly attends to what is fitting,

he is again attacked by a serpent

raging with savage venom.

The terrible robber is darkened;

the wicked plunderer is blinded.

The investigator, overcome by darkness,

asks for an opening.

He searches and addresses him;

he sees him and prays that he may emerge for him.

Looking upon the man who is present,

he seeks him with an absent mind,

and gropes in the darkness

as though in the pure brightness of day.

With the madman deceived,

Felix enters the innermost recesses of the hiding place.

Before long he returns,

turning over in his heart the face of the foolish captor.

But the spider, obeying the command,

swiftly closes the entrance with webs drawn across it,

and protects the devout man.

It mocks the savage with its veil

and separates the robber from his prey

by a slight but decisive distinction.

When the frustrated wolf withdraws,

the lamb seeks the sheepfold,

and, without delay,

obtains the care of the nourishing ewe.

By her support he is fed

and carefully watches over his mouth.

He takes in infant’s milk

and preserves a man’s proper balance.

Thus, while three courses of the moon were passing,

he persuaded the bishop, who wore the mask,

to believe in Christ.

He also rescued the temple

which had been transformed by divine power,

where Apollo gave his responses,

as the god fled and withdrew.

Renowned through these deeds

and adorned with the honor of virtue,

while the entire people sought him with fervent enthusiasm,

he refused to choose another

to be raised to the pontifical throne.

[Col. 0856C] From then on he proceeded peacefully

through twelve courses of the sun.

Then, rich in great virtues,

he departed from the human scene,

as though prostrating himself in prayer

before the blessed altars.

After celebrating the sacred mysteries of Christ by day,

Felix, having given peace to all,

entered the heavenly realms.

After completing the triumphs of the cross

through many struggles,

he happily received the titles

of Felix’s victorious palm.

Under the care of the presbyter Helpidius,

he was given a tomb,

and the fertile ground,

enriched with incense,

shone with his virtue.

This same presbyter Helpidius

placed in the Nolanean church

the blessed bishop Felix,

who had received the light,

who had fittingly attained the summit

from childhood amid many wonders,

and who was joined to his companions in martyrdom

by a thirtyfold crown.

## CHAPTER IV. On Saint Juliana

[Col. 0855]

[Col. 0855D] The brave heroine Juliana

sheds radiance upon Cumae.

After crushing the head

of the wicked enemy in battle,

she bore blessed limbs

tested by various combats.

Her father drove her to these sufferings

under the pretext of a contest,

and, having worn her down with blows,

tore her with bitter zeal.

Then, after she had wearied the prefect and her betrothed

with her torments,

she was furrowed with rods,

shaken while suspended by her hair,

and drenched from the crown of her head

with molten lead.

Having been received into the cavern of the prison,

into the blind abyss,

[Col. 0856D] she found there an enemy more savage

than all terrors,

one who stirred up internal and external wars against her.

Knowing that she was unconquerable inwardly,

he openly revealed his terrifying face

and the marks of his wretched appearance.

Yet the virgin stood fearlessly

and remained undaunted.

She did not tremble when shaken

or grow afraid when abandoned.

Fighting openly,

she shone with the splendor of victory.

Nicomedia, astonished by her waging war,

saw her contend;

Campania joyfully received her

as she triumphed over kingdoms.

## CHAPTER V. On the Church of Saint Paul at Spoleto

[Col. 0857]

[Col. 0857A] We have placed Spoleto first,

adorned by the shining splendor of the Fathers,

bright, lofty, and devoted to holy contests.

The powerful Church of Paul also purifies it.

By the palm of faith

it illuminates the darkness of the enemy:

closed against the fury of the wolf,

but open to the triumphs of the lamb,

[Col. 0858A] blinded by threats,

yet illumined by trophies.

The one who approaches to break through the closed entrance

is forbidden to enter the open one.

When the light approaches it,

the swollen darkness is subdued.

Once the thief has been blinded

and the radiance of faith is blazing,

the enemies of the light

are driven back from the Church’s assault.

## CHAPTER VI. On Saint Eleutherius the Martyr

[Col. 0857]

[Col. 0857A] Here the illustrious goodness of Father Eleutherius shines forth.

The blessed Gregory declares, through his companions as witnesses,

that Eleutherius restored a corpse to life.

Nor does he keep silent about the gifts of strength

which he himself obtained through him:

he was enabled properly to bear the burden

of a strengthened stomach through fasting,

and also to overcome an imposed weight.

Yet while he performed great deeds,

he himself was still weighed down,

under the governance of the divine hand.

Having received a boy and taken him to himself,

he cleanses him of black pollution.

His holy companions release him from savage bonds,

and report that he spent his nights in an unusual peace.

The father, rejoicing and boastfully displaying his gifts,

is nevertheless deprived of his thoughtless joy

when the boy falls back into his former condition.

At last the tears and fasts of the brothers redeem him,

and he remains thereafter completely free,

living in freedom.

Here he had brought up his illustrious brother John,

famous for his goodness,

whose glory at the foreknown end of his holy life

he had anticipated.

[Col. 0858A] Marking the day and rejoicing,

John is carried toward the rewards.

He asks for a mystical song,

joyfully offers hymns,

and, summoning his companion,

admonishes the brothers to proceed to the high kingdoms:

“Ursus, come!” he cries.

His companions neither grasp his words in their minds

nor understand whom he has named.

Later it becomes known

that their father had died,

removed from them by a long journey,

at the very moment when Eleutherius

stood at the end of his life,

summoned by that final voice.

Here the father adorns the virgin mind

with gifts.

They consider her,

who had died to Christ,

who had renounced the world and her father,

and who regarded golden gifts as clay,

to be a bride of the bridegroom’s splendor.

Thus she is received as worthy,

and as pleasing above to the king.

When the countryman receives a rebuke

and the robber is driven away,

no worldly thing possesses any right

to the purity of the gift

or can violate the harbor granted to the virgin.

## CHAPTER VII. On Saint John the Confessor

[Col. 0857]

[Col. 0857B] John, leaving Syria,

rich in the summit of virtue,

and making for Ausonia,

illuminates the city of Penara.

[Col. 0857C] Seeking a place and a small plot

for a secure dwelling,

he first carried a broad psalter,

but soon brought it back for his vows.

Having received a sign,

he chooses the dwelling assigned to him.

Immediately he hears, through an angelic utterance,

the assurance that this place

is rightly prepared for him by the Lord:

a harbor for living,

and relief from the course of his journey and his road.

The icy winter was singing;

the entire grove was stiff,

bare of foliage,

and written over with frost.

He lived beneath the shelter

of a roofless structure of wood.

After long traverses of the forest,

hunters, exhausted from the chase,

while seeking the familiar comforts

of their long wandering,

saw oak branches

flourishing unusually

and clothed with a garment

given to them out of season.

[Col. 0858B] They asked who he was,

where he came from,

and by what right or custom he dwelt in the house.

He confessed that he had come

for the service of Christ alone,

and that by this right,

under this star,

he dwelt in those rural places.

[Col. 0858C] They reported what they had seen to the people.

Dense groups came in crowds

to see the marvel.

They set up camps on the ground,

content with the bare earth and the sky.

An overseer of the contest

was appointed over those about to compete.

He gathered and governed the crowds

under the Lord’s direction.

Thus, powerful in virtues,

after forty-four years,

he was taken from this world

and shines here with the honor of rest.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Saint Cassian the Martyr

[Col. 0857]

[Col. 0857D] Cassian glorifies the Forum of Sulla

with renown.

Aurelius Clemens, recounting the arena

in his ringing poem,

learns of him through a painter's art

and through his host.

Appointed instructor over a band of schoolchildren,

and refusing to pray to sacred formulas,

he is ordered to teach the unformed crowd

and to provide the schoolchildren with his death—

those whom he had offended

by suppressing them with serious instruction.

[Col. 0858D] Given over to savage little boys

to be torn apart,

he receives a thousand severe wounds

while bound.

As the executioner grows exhausted

with the punishment,

and the boys play upon their teacher’s skin

with the points which the stern teacher himself

had once used to mark them,

God, pitying the lingering delays

of the spirit that had long struggled,

finally commands it to be released

from the hiding places of the soul,

lifting it from that bloody crowd of tormentors

to the gentle heights of the angels.

## CHAPTER IX. On Saints Syrus and Hivent(i)us, Martyrs

[Col. 0859]

[Col. 0859A] In the Genoese city,

the church of the martyr Syrus shines,

rejecting what is sordid

and receiving what is venerable and chaste.

It refuses to be defiled by foul things.

There, a corpse from Milan

shines forth after a harsh rejection:

a defender of the Church

had been dragged away by a savage crowd,

while Syrus drove away from him

the spirit of black demons,

and the man lamented loudly

with a terrifying and violent cry of disgrace.

Moved by this,

and rebuffed by the savage faces,

they search the little chapel for the vessel

after these dreadful events.

[Col. 0860A] They find the corpse,

cast out from the tomb and the temple.

Syrus and Hiventius adorn Ticinum as bishops.

Through Hermagoras, who handed on the teaching,

they were given to impart the doctrines of Christ

in these regions,

as ministers of the Gospel and of Mark.

Consecrating this city also

with their first holy devotion,

they illuminate it with signs of virtues

and enrich it with their gift.

Lights are scattered far and wide;

Verona, Brescia,

and Lodi are purified

and honored by sacred radiance.

## CHAPTER X. On Saints Martin and Augustine, Bishops

[Col. 0859]

[Col. 0859B] This city [Note: [Col. 0859D] Pavia.] nourished Martin,

a pupil of the heavenly light,

the glory of the Church

and the crown of Christ,

who shines illustriously

with the radiance of a heavenly jewel.

Here the pious remains

of the outstanding and blessed teacher Augustine

are brought,

through the devotion of Leutbrant,

to the Catholic faith,

the four-square light of the world,

whose speech purified the city

with the flowing stream of Christ.

With this treasure enclosed,

he triumphs over swollen and empty honors,

having been rescued from darkness by Ambrose

to give the gifts of light.

Nor does he remain silent in word or deed,

leaving hope and a resource to the devout.

He follows the King of heaven

through the heights of the world.

Naked, he follows the naked cross

and despises earthly things.

He persists in excellent deeds,

turns over the sacred laws,

and day and night composes

the commandments and utterances of God.

By speech he admonishes those present,

and by his pen those who are far away.

Raised to the priesthood,

he chooses for himself the lofty things

that he seeks,

joined to Christ’s poor companions.

Chosen bishop by his predecessor

for the sacred altars,

with a pious mind

he sows heavenly seed

through a learned mouth.

Strong and unharmed for nearly forty years,

he proclaims the heavenly laws without interruption.

When he seeks the final kingdoms,

his old age having fulfilled its course,

he joyfully climbs the stars,

leaving the stars to those who follow him.

## CHAPTER XI. On the Church of Saint Zeno at Verona

[Col. 0859]

[Col. 0859C] At Verona, the Church of the martyr Zeno

is illuminated by divine miracles,

as Gregory bears witness.

The Adige, raging with the swelling of its waters,

washes around it.

Although its waters had entered

with an accumulated and unusual force,

it holds itself back in an unfamiliar manner

and refuses to remain open.

[Col. 0860C] It closes the doors

with its surging barrier,

does not enter through the waves,

turns aside from the entrances open to the current,

and, although it offers itself to be drained,

does not dare to penetrate.

It stands ready to help,

and, while the current spares it,

flees from doing harm.

## CHAPTER XII. On Saint Christina

[Col. 0859]

[Col. 0859C] Christina adorns Italy,

Tyre,

and the shores of Bolsena

with the triumph of many contests.

While still flourishing in tender youth,

she undertakes manly struggles.

The strong girl attacks her father’s gods,

overturns them,

shatters them,

and distributes them to the needy,

strengthened by God

and by a manly love for the divine.

Her father afflicts her,

striking her cheeks

and beating her body.

After she has been scourged,

he orders her to be bound with iron in prison.

Having experienced her father’s affections

and her parent’s madness,

while her flesh flows away

under a long and savage tearing,

she scatters it into her father’s face,

returns the entrails to their source,

and balances her mind

on the heavenly sower.

Then they fasten her to a wheel,

which blazes with torments,

and roll her, attached to the fires

and drenched with rich oil.

[Col. 0859D] But when the fire flees from Christ’s consecrated limbs

and bursts forth,

the flame, stirred into fury by the oil,

rages in globes and whirlwinds,

enveloping the savage spectators

and the cruel crowds,

killing them with its heat

and burning them in its embrace.

Then, received into the prison’s bridal chamber

and its harsh bed,

[Col. 0860C] she enjoys heavenly nourishment

through its splendor and healing power.

God acts as physician,

and she is healed,

making use of the divine deed.

Safe and discovered

to be exalting the praises of Christ,

she is pressed beneath the heavy weight

of a vast and burdensome stone

and plunged into the deepest recesses

of the lake’s waters.

But, rescued by angelic assistance

and heavenly strength,

she overcomes the cruel efforts of her father.

After this another man undertakes

to conquer the brave girl,

the leader of Tartarean warfare

and of a dreadful arena,

seeking through many torments

an unconquerable glory.

He orders her to pray to Phoebus,

whose images she suddenly turns into ashes

while passing through the stars in prayer.

Astonished at these trophies,

many thousands immediately praise Christ as God,

bow their necks in submission,

and abandon their empty images.

[Col. 0860D] After the father has been overthrown,
