the tyrant’s third successor undertakes the battle

and tries to extinguish flame with flame,

approaching the furnaces

with the terror of Vulcan.

The unconquered heroine is shut

inside a burning furnace.

Thus, after five days,

she is given over to become entirely ash.

[Col. 0861A] Yet the black vapor of the fires,

immune to the flames,

kills the guilty,

while the victim of Christ remains victorious,

having subdued the furnaces.

What the kilns cannot accomplish,

the serpents are given to complete.

Yet they wither

through the power of her heavenly triumph.

[Col. 0862A] The sword of words and the plectrum

are cut away from her mouth,

but the inner tongue,

full and undiminished,

sows praises.

She, adorned with so many wounds,

is attacked by savage arrows;

her militant mind,

driven back by the darts,

flashes toward the stars.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Saint Ambrose

[Col. 0861]

[Col. 0861A] The city of Milan is adorned

by the merits of Ambrose.

It honors him through his deeds

and adorns him through his virtues and speech.

You unfold these things, Paulinus, at Augustine's prompting.

When his father marvels at the infant,

invaded in his cradle by a swarm of bees

which soon flies toward the stars,

he foresees that the child will one day give

heavenly honey.

But the boy,

showing that he was to be honored

in a sacred manner,

held out his right hand in play

to be revered as a virgin.

While prophesying,

he recalled that he had been given

according to the order of the prophets.

Educated under the rods

and shining with the radiance of wisdom,

he is summoned to the ears of the leading men

to record their deliberations.

He himself also is summoned

as a leading man and teacher of the laws.

He protects his fatherland,

governs peoples,

and orders cities.

By this power he strives, with Milan laid open before him,

to restore the torn portions

of Christ's garment (core, sic).

[Col. 0861B] With what zeal he enters the temple

and prepares to reconcile

the divided factions,

while vows are being offered in greater numbers.

The voice of the child gives Ambrose

the honor of being consecrated.

Through it,

the men who had turned aside

and been carried in different directions

come together in agreement.

One mind is placed in them all,

and all alike proclaim in concert

that Ambrose must be consecrated for them

by sacred right.

He, planning flight,

orders the savage tribunal to be restored

and turns the torments over to the condemned

who have been brought forward.

Nor can he remove the people

or lead them away from their purpose,

as they cry:

“Let your crimes be added to ours!”

He is recalled

when he reads the burden of wisdom.

He brings prostitutes to his own consecration,

without turning aside the vows

of those who see these sins

and ask for iron against themselves.

[Col. 0861C] With these efforts frustrated,

he seeks a time for flight.

He leaves the city

under the vast silence of night,

thinking to make his way directly

to Ticinum.

In the morning he is found

at the gate of the city of Milan.

Astonished at what has happened,

they seize the ram of the Lord

who is to be brought into the sheepfold.

Found, captured, and held,

he is compelled and bound.

He rejoices to be dragged

to the sacred rites.

Caesar rejoices, and the things previously foretold

are fulfilled in his companion,

whereby the bishop proceeds

as though commanded to give laws.

From there he escapes again,

seeking secret dwellings.

Fearing to enter the heights,

he is betrayed as a lamb

by a threatening judge.

He is examined

and washed in pure waters.

[Col. 0861D] He places beneath them

the shining fleece of sincere faith.

[Col. 0862A] He undertakes each duty

of the sacred service.

To the joy of all,

he advances to the highest honor.

Made bishop,

he administers the holy things

in holiness,

shining in the Lord’s deeds

and flashing with radiance.

A paralytic woman,

touching his garment,

joyfully confirms this.

She returns,

bound by another’s guidance,

to her own strength.

Another woman,

unworthy of the favor,

strives to reach the bright lamp.

Grasping the fleece of the candlestick,

the foolish woman draws death upon herself

by the garment

and blunts the rash weapon.

Here too he found,

burning with the spirit of Elijah,

the raging fury of Jezebel,

black with venom.

Through this woman,

the serpent plots fraud against

the enemy who stands openly.

She seeks hatred,

prepares exile,

and incites the leading men with gold,

[Col. 0862B] and, through promises,

their spirits toward the weapons of rage.

Yet Jesus does not abandon

the athlete who governs his camp.

As a powerful helper,

he drives the enemy away

from the hearts of those who bear arms

and preserves his servant

from ambushes.

The robber learned this,

as did the plotter of the hidden snare,

who presented himself as a neighbor of the Church

and claimed that he was raising up a captive,

so that he might easily remove its authority

through the crime [Note: [Col. 0861] Another hand wrote the words “authority through the crime” [facilis crimine culmen], but they make no sense.].

The attempts directed against him

turned back upon their own course.

The man who thought he was carrying him away

was himself carried away.

On the day when he thought

the father had to be carried into exile,

he departed as an exile,

the fraud turned back upon his own head.

Yet the bishop knew,

by the Lord’s admonitions,

that he ought to love the enemy.

He raised up the proscribed man

and gave him comfort through his resources,

although the man himself claimed

that he had been punished by an impartial judge.

Nevertheless, the dark hand

did not fear to add weapons to its frauds,

while the fierce woman gave

fighting men orders

to close the gates of the Church

and repel the sacred people.

But the Lord,

who is accustomed to provide trophies

from an enemy,

changes the savage hearts of warriors,

so that they preserve those whom they had found

and admit the faithful through the threshold.

And this was not enough:

they also poured out their vows with the people,

and the attendant raised up God

together with the people.

The lion, the ox, the wolf,

the lamb, and the kid

were fed together.

Nor does the bishop,

ungrateful for such great honors,

remain silent.

He adorns their insignia

by bringing forth grateful praises,

and entrusts Christ’s triumphal songs to measured music,

so that they may resound

in hymn-singing choirs,

from the time when the blessed western boundary

has been accustomed to sing songs without limit.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Saints Gervasius and Protasius

[Col. 0861]

[Col. 0861D] God adds to the glorification of the man

who glorifies him,

revealing the precious talents

that had long been hidden.

When the witnesses of the Lord,

Gervasius and his inseparable brother Protasius,

appear to him,

they mark him out

for the reproaches of his adversaries

and for the honor of the prophet,

[Col. 0862D] flashing with heavenly light

and shining with signs.

Having been summoned by the bishop’s prayers,

through the praise of Christ

and the light of the servants,

the young men,

radiant with brightness,

appeared openly beside him

as he lay weighed down by sleep.

They stood in heaven

with their hands spread out,

as though presenting vows.

[Col. 0863A] The holy man is troubled and uncertain

when the visions withdraw.

He asks that they be repeated if true,

or, if false,

that they depart on the winds.

His devotion grows through restraint.

The visions return.

When the third crowing of the cock

restores the voice of the fading night,

the young men return

and reveal themselves to him,

who is sleepless,

astonished,

and empty as an exhausted body.

A third figure leads them—

Paul,

whose form represents this event.

He records their companions

and reveals that they had followed his commands:

they opposed the pageants of the age,

followed the footsteps of the lofty Lord,

despised the summit of what is perishable,

and, shut away for twice ten years,

devoted themselves to the service of God

and to divine wisdom,

until they were proven

to flourish in a worthy martyrdom.

He reveals the casket

in which their bodies lie,

where vows may discover them,

a chest to be celebrated

and a famous temple to be prepared.

He takes up the book,

after learning the names,

and goes to read in it

their names,

their merits,

and the crowns they received.

He calls the brothers of the earth,

and, first in order,

opens the ground by digging.

For a long time the hidden gifts are revealed,

neither corrupted by decay

nor dissolved by rot,

but, as though long placed there,

sprinkled with fragrant nectar.

At last the awaited book lies open,

revealing the promises.

It states that Philip had hidden

these relics when his son accompanied him,

and that Valeria had borne the twins

by their father Vitalis.

[Col. 0864A] Soon it records their names and deeds,

all their estates,

the payments due to the forum,

and what was to be carried to the needy servants

once they had been freed.

Thus, for ten years,

they were to devote themselves

to prayers and reading,

so that it might be made known

by what contest they would climb to the palm.

When they were brought before the priests,

they refused to give answers.

When they were detained in the temples,

they were urged to offer sacrifices to the gods.

The first, teaching that the images were empty fabrications,

is ordered to send a man forth by blasts of lead.

The other is urged toward the darkness.

He too, exposing the miserable and trembling persuader,

is beaten with clubs

and raised to greater struggles.

Compassionate toward the enemy,

he is taught by the example of Christ.

Thus, given over to the swords,

he is summoned to the stars together with his brother.

When their relics are lifted

from the worn tomb,

many insignia of salvation,

provided for the weary,

are revealed,

with a title of honor

for the martyrs.

Through the devotion of the blessed bishop,

the veils of the martyrs

are touched in an act of faith.

A blind man is restored to the light (luce; the source reads “Lucc”), as Severus shines forth.

Many possessed by black breath

are cured.

Those who return

gratefully increase through the power of the light

and diminish the wicked forces

of the Church’s fury.

The savage crowds

begin gradually to grow sparse,

and the arrows aroused against

the priest of Christ

are shattered.

## CHAPTER XV. On the Miracles of Saint Ambrose

[Col. 0863]

[Col. 0863C] Although black mutterings murmur

within whatever savage palace,

those who were preparing to attack

nevertheless fall back in confusion.

When a certain man,

seized by their master, the Devil,

gives unwilling testimony to the truth,

he raises the enemy by his praise,

disturbs his companions,

and, unaware of piety,

proclaims it.

The fierce gods add companions

and destroy their associate.

They heap upon themselves

the disgrace hateful to the truthful,

while the worthy bishop bears

all honor to Christ.

Christ grants these heavenly gifts

to his servant.

While he protects the people standing above

with heavenly speech,

an ethereal citizen is seen

standing close by,

bringing to the people

the laws that ought to be sown.

The jealous enemy sees these things,

burning with hostility and rage.

Although he is thought invincible

because of his deceitful speech,

he, despising all the efforts

of the dark fraud,

begins to reveal the light

that he had concealed.

This happened to the man

who guarded the oracles

with a watchful mind.

But at other times,

while the ears of the royal chamber’s guardians

forbade the proud promises,

the words were truly directed outward

[Note: [Col. 0863D] Compare Paulinus’s Life of Saint Ambrose, his annotation, §18. A speech is understood, except for these corrupted words [Col. 0864D] “horia vere,” which, if they are absolutely necessary, might perhaps be restored as “obvia veri,” “meeting the truth.”]

with ready mouth,

when the inquiries of the assenters fled.

Soon, however,

after the bishop had dealt with them

and they had fallen

and been brought back by the sword-hilt,

they could not hear him—

those who had despised the instruments of faith

in proud arrogance.

Christ himself,

the protector and avenger of the priest,

himself watching over his servant,

preserved him from every deceit.

Nor does the enemy remain silent

about the punishments of the flesh

which he suffered,

burned by the fire

of the prophet’s infernal vengeance,

while the blessed man was being protected

by an angelic guardian.

What was the man,

his heart inflamed

with Zoroastrian fury,

persuaded to do?

In the fierce heat of his anger

he stretched out snares

against the teacher who bore the scepter,

turned his forces against the Church,

and strove to climb

the heights of the sanctuary.

Under the dark silence of night,

he had prepared to offer sacrifice

on the summits

and stir up quarrels.

But when his vows were reversed,

and hatred had been sought in place of slaughter,

holy love for the Father

burned in the hearts of his sons.

He revealed that he had assigned

savage ministers

to extinguish the life

hated by the wicked.

Yet they had not even been able

to approach the enclosure

of the house,

fortified on every side

by the invincible heat of fire,

while the just man was defended

and the savage enemy inflamed.

Through these encounters

the black arts lay defeated.

Open battles rise up

and fall, shattered.

[Col. 0864D] For a certain attendant,

ordered to slaughter an innocent man,

entered the chaste chamber

with a drawn sword.

While he balanced the weapon

to drive it into the sacred throat,

the joint of his arm stiffened,

his sinews dried up in astonishment,

and he could not control

the raised arm in its movements.

At last, confessing the crime

and the fury of his mistress,

he who had approached

to deliver the man to death

was restored by the father

to salvation.

Nor did this father,

fearful or hesitant,

dread approaching kings.

When the king had been killed,

the tyrant raged;

admonished by sacred warnings

and removed from the altars,

he was made to regret

that he had shed innocent blood.

But because he despised

the salutary counsels of the prophet,

he not only set aside

the honors of the stars,

but even those below.

And he who despised

the bishop bearing kindly commands,

broken by womanly fear,

wasted away.

But Theodosius was seized differently

and, reproved by harsh words,

was said to have listened to the bishop.

Declared unworthy of the Lord

and ordered to hear the admonisher,

he was commanded to revoke the decree

and tear up the laws he had issued,

while he was granting pious victories

to the savage armies of Christ.

He calmly accepted the admonitions

and the harsh commands; persuaded to obey them

under faith's title alone,

he obtained, with assent,

permission to approach the holy bishop.

Thus once,

because of errors committed

through guilty offenses,

after much innocent blood

had been unjustly shed,

he was removed from the temples

and repelled from the altars.

While the bishop looked only

toward heavenly beauty,

he did not shrink from

a lowly rejection shown in humble devotion,

nor did he rejoice in pardon

until the due penalty for his sorrow

had been discharged.

[Col. 0865B] There was also a written law,

approved by the holy lawgiver,

which could restrain the sudden fury

of decrees,

when imperial scepters

submitted to sacred admonitions.

A second victory was won

with the enemy thrown down.

Above all others,

the king honored Ambrose alone.

Above all others,

he approved him as strict

in the divine laws.

Just as he reconciled to the Lord

the pious man,

rightly struck by the blow of punishment,

so the enemy was regarded

as sacrilegious.

He did not fear,

while avoiding the wicked,

to speak to the tyrant.

He rebuked the crime

with the severe hem of a written page.

Presenting the One who sees all crimes,

he condemned everything,

and declared himself free

from the savage treachery,

rejecting gifts

and even peace when it was refused in prayer,

as he opposed

the assailant of peace

and the enemy of quiet.

Stirred up by these things,

the treacherous leading men,

roaring savagely,

threatened to make the Church

a resting-place for beasts of burden,

after they had promised themselves

a palm through infernal pollution.

But the just Lord

distributes the lots

with an even balance.

He does not allow scepters

to prevail by lot over justice,

lest the right hand

be carried toward the wicked.

He gives victories

to justice

and to the worthy devout.

Thus the devoted king

prostrated himself at the feet

of the blessed protector,

the faithful servant of Christ in all things.

He regarded the sacrilegious enemy

who had thrown him down

as something to be trampled underfoot,

and, trusting in his merits

and protected by his prayer,

he sought safety.

Soon they obtained pardon for the deed

through an easy grant.

This was the one favor

which led the king

to the pious father.

How great his goodness was,

and how kindly his heart,

the prisoners’ chains,

often released,

testify.

[Col. 0865D] A delegation fervent in its efforts,
The road itself is also the labor of a long journey, and the nobles who had been summoned,

the wild beasts, aroused by grief, weeping at the father’s shameful joy,

the joy of those rejoicing at the rescue of the guilty man,

the avenging punishment springing forth, Stilicho’s surrender in supplication,

the man restored from exile and subjected to the supreme wrath.

Through him many others, likewise sent away, rejoice under that judge.

These things, their hearts entangled in gall, they report even to the harsh praetorian judge,

the threshold of whose gates was barred,

and they recount the prophecies of the grieving seer pronounced against him,

the hope of men which that man had placed in empty arrogance,

while, fleeing, he was unable to enter the open Church.

Here this eminent father, exalted to the summit of piety,

how powerful he was in virtue, his wondrous deeds confess;

and the frequent, renowned expulsion of dark spirits

[Col. 0866A] Pansophius, himself a boy, later records, after he had been torn from the bloody robber’s

nets and snatched from the jaws of death.

How piously this man’s presence could be borne by the enemy

is shown when the boy Probus was captured by a dreadful guest,

sent to the bishop, with none of his property burdening him in the city,

and, once he had left the walls, received back by his savage possessor.

The robber reveals under oath that he had feared Ambrose

and that, for this reason, he had waited near the city for a post-horse.

What Nicentius, renowned in due order, was able to reveal,

he himself perceives, receiving healing in his anguish:

he rejoices that he will be saved when the foot has been trampled,

through the touch of the heel and the gift of healing that followed.

What honor of speech, what eloquence filled with power,

astonished the servant when Stilicho’s breath had been snatched away,

before the speech of his cruel judgment had even been completed;

[Col. 0866B] through this father’s many deceitful documents, many men’s sufferings

were exposed—men who had endured them without following conduct worthy of fetters.

He too, warning that whoever easily laughs at another’s misfortune

is admonished to observe his own,

proves by his own fall that his words were not empty.

His successor, Simplicianus, likewise,

reported in a subdued voice, senses the power of the word,

and astonishment seizes the mouths of those who repeat it from afar.

Even barbarian tongues speak of the bishop’s virtue:

the triumph of the Frankish leader, achieved through the enemy’s defeat,

is acknowledged by fame to have been won through this man’s friendship—

he who, powerful in imperial authority, could pin down the moving sun.

How learned he was, how full of exalted inspiration!

Dense seeds mark out the earth, living creatures the sky;

rumor fills the kingdoms, and fame, once the truth is known,

[Col. 0866C] makes the leaders of the Persians renowned for their wise splendor.

Exhausted by the long road and by the desire to see him,

they come to the eloquent man known in the eastern city through his radiance;

seeking those things that, flashing with divine light,

might be scattered abroad, when the light of day has driven away

the darkness at the turning-point of night.

That Symmachus too, whose whole labor was in speech,

thinking that he had surpassed kings in the splendor of his charm,

was repeating sacrilegious rites and impious libations.

He receives a volume as the worship of piety’s honor,

filled with heavenly light and divine savor,

and thereafter does not dare to answer the bishop in words.

The queen of the Marcomanni proves this: having abandoned

the darkness of errors, she learns solely through the report of the blessed man

and, having understood, seeks what is spread abroad by the higher light.

[Col. 0866D] She asks that this light be seasoned for her ambassadors with nourishing salt;

and, receiving the bishop’s catechism, [she receives] the light of the little book.

Having been persuaded, she stands intent on urging that peace be joined,

and subdues the savage tyrant together with the Romulid people.

With what splendor of God shining, with what inspiration endowed,

you earned the right, blessed Pauline, to see these things,

having striven through writings, astonished by your fortunate vision,

and to see the just man crowned by the radiant benevolence

of the kindly and protecting will, as though beneath the covering of a shield;

and you see him enter the virtuous dwelling-places of the gods,

while the seer examines God’s laws and handles heavenly matters.

How fervently he clung to God, how firmly—

pastoral love, ever watchful, and care reveal—

he protected the flock’s safe pasture and drove away the wolves’ madness;

his willing poverty, and the resources devoted to Christ;

[Col. 0867A] the extensive estates, spread out for the blessed poor;

the lands possessed under the law of the Church;

his vigorous interventions, his arduous acts of aid;

his constant, watchful concern for the whole people of God;

his frugal piety; fasts continued through almost every day;

watchfulness in chaste prayers;

and the holy work likewise bears witness: the labor of his hands,

the books dictated and written, the level field of the word ploughed;

his generous hands giving gifts to the needy and the captive;

and the love of brotherly devotion that remained without end.

Service faithfully rendered in sacred matters—

[Col. 0868A] scarcely five years later requiring a pastor to undertake it—

reveals, weighed and tested, the holy grief of his heart,

and his goodness, weeping over the sins of others who had fallen.

The sad sighs uttered at the sight of disgrace,

the tears so often poured out for cities deprived of their inhabitants,

and shed always from a heart thirsting for God!

He is not shaken by death; through his goodness he confesses himself

to be a burning servant, according to the fire with which God yearns,

and he shines clearly in the light with which he illuminates the summit of miracles.

This too, the holy relics long concealed through the ages,

revealed themselves to this worthy man, worthily disclosed.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the holy martyrs Nazarius and Celsus, Vitalis and Agricola

[Col. 0867]

[Col. 0867B] Nazarius and Celsus, raised up in radiance,

we have set forth, the blessed man’s mind irradiated by divine light;

were ordered to be kept by the tenants in place of treasure.

They did not dare to leave the garden entrusted to them,

while the holy man carried away treasures unknown to their guardians,

so that, placed with deserved splendor in a fitting location,

he might fill the grateful assemblies with divine light,

while the citizens of the Church above applauded throughout the city.

The savage enemy groans, complaining that he is tormented by the father,

Ambrose, who was ordered to silence the sound of his voice.

He silences it, and declares that Ambrose does not know how to be puffed up:

rather, the lofty faith and sacred fire torment him,

and he grieves that earth-born men should ascend to heaven,

[Col. 0868B] from which he himself, falling, is whirled into the depths.

The blessed man also gives a temple to Vitalis and Agricola

in the city of Florence, whom generous Bologna sends:

after enduring many torments from the savage scourge,

they obtain the highest honor, fixed upon the cross.

Their relics, mingled among Jewish hiding-places,

lie unknown to mortals for several years,

until, revealing themselves to the bishop in divine light,

they rejoice under this worthy father to retain their fitting honor

and to be separated from black sands like gold’s radiance.

The altar receives them together amid the joy of the people

and the sufferings of the dark throng,

displaying the saints’ lights and the love of divine goodness

around the servant.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the passing of Saint Ambrose

[Col. 0867]

[Col. 0867C] That, in the hope in which he had placed his trust, he did not fear death

is shown by his blessed passing and happy end—

the palm of a worthy military service and of a renowned contest,

foreknown by the heavenly power and reported to his companions.

There was also that laughter radiating from the saint’s face,

when he saw the Lord Jesus smiling upon him,

as he poured out his prayers to him together with the bishop of Lodi,

and gentle grace already revealed the prayers that had been heard.

With his mind always fixed on these things, he does not withdraw even in death;

while, stretched out with arms extended toward heaven in the form of a cross,

he bears forth his blessed soul accompanied by its vows.

The bishop of Vercelli is present, summoned by a heavenly voice,

having learned in dreams, through messages that disclosed it,

that Ambrose would soon depart and withdraw.

He hands over the mysteries of the divine light;

[Col. 0867D] and when Ambrose receives the supreme offering of the holy sacrament,

he joyfully begins life anew and, nourished, rises into heaven.

This passing shines with the celebrated splendor of Easter,

on the night when Israel leaves the darkness of Egypt.

The citizens of heaven joyfully welcome the citizen and inhabitant

of paradise’s realms, washed in the river with lambs

at the spring of living water.

The glory of the blessed seer is revealed,

and they behold him approach the throne, saying with their finger

that the father, shining with illustrious radiance, has taken his seat.

A shining star appears to the others to illuminate the funeral.

When the Ambrosian church receives this to be sown in the earth,

the black throng, groaning, declares the cause of its torment.

[Col. 0868C] The kindly spirits gather to serve Ambrose’s splendor;

thousands of children run to heavenly duties,

and fervent companies of various orders crowd around,

striving to touch the bier, or at least to draw near it.

Nor are absent beloved ones hidden from him, nor does he abandon those who love him,

for the letter sent to the men of the East declares

that he has appeared standing beside those who pray,

laying on hands and pouring forth prayers together with them.

Bringing relief to Zenobius and to the Florentines,

he often appears when summoned, frees the city from danger,

restores the exhausted, and afterward renews their hope of salvation.

By his prayers he wins relief for Mascezel, who was despairing

in the savagery of danger; and, marking the palm with a sign,

he indicates three times, with his staff, the time and the place of his arrival.

To a blind man seeking the place of the treasures and the light,

[Col. 0868D] appearing in the illustrious honor of a company of white-robed men,

he orders him to meet his companions at Milan,

so that he may rejoice in the light he has sought.

The man obeys, rejoicing; by touch he follows a path

whose walls he had not previously seen,

and, greeting the city according to the bishop’s words,

he himself meets the patrons as they enter the city by daylight—

Sisinnius, Alexander, and Martyrius.

Soon he receives the promised gifts when he touches the shrine.

[Col. 0869A] Those whom, holy bishop, you order to illuminate with the manly light of the word

the city of Trent and the fields of Anaunia:

while they water them with sacred dew, an unworthy hostile crowd,

burning with envy, rages and provokes conflict;

with black complaints it stirs them up, adorning dark divinities with mourning,

and strives to defile the captured holy men with filth,

beating them almost to death with scourges as they resist.

Only night remains, covering the lands pressed down by darkness;

when it uncovers them and the sun restores color to things,

they win the crowns offered them in a glorious contest.

Sisinnius, an old man from the race of the Cappadocians,

first in shining honor, struck on the head by a bronze club,

pierced through, and with his limbs hewn by axes, departs this life,

ascends from the threshold of the Church to heaven’s heights.

Martyrius, held fast and unable to move, gives thanks

to the saving Lord; pierced with sharp stakes,

he continues to satisfy the double axes with wounds to his head,

and, while dripping with blood, is driven to offer a libation to profane things,

[Col. 0869B] taking another path, he flies to the stars, released from his executioner.

The revelers insult the slain, bind the martyr’s hanging face

around their necks, clattering with ringing and shouting,

and cry out that Christ the avenger should vindicate those who have been struck down.

Among the dead, Alexander too is noticed, breathing;

he endures every harsh thing while they drag him,

and, when they have come to the pyre’s burning tomb,

they place the raw bodies there, ordering the living man

either to offer a libation or to burn in the fire.

He tramples their threats and seizes the crown at the highest end.

Nor does the vengeance that has been aroused conceal itself,

nor does it delay the fitting punishment.

Yet a shadow snatches away the sky, near to earthly things,

blinding the lands with a veil;

it casts darkness over the blinded peoples, while the air flashes with fires.

Frequent thunderbolts fly; the sky threatens death to trembling mortals.

The liars are compelled to speak the truth,

[Col. 0869C] confessing that these things happen through the saints’ power.

These men are Ambrose’s companions; through them the blind receive light.

The savage are blinded; the kindly shine with radiance.

[Col. 0870A] The hosts of heaven applaud Ambrose’s merits;

the just rejoice together, while the wicked are worn down by envy.

Those who, with poisonous mouths, had attempted to tear apart the seer’s reputation

are suddenly seized and torn away by the avenger.

And in the eyes of those whose minds they seek to tear away,

through love of the father, they are dragged off and punished.

But he himself flourishes through the merits of his merits

and through the light of the offspring produced by them.

Among these is Paulinus, who, through the honor

of his outstanding rank and the tasteful splendor of his elegant charm,

adorns Italy and carries its light across the sea.

Augustine too, the illustrious glory of the Church and teacher of the whole world,

the banisher of hostile deceit,

who fills everything with kindly light and sows the world with seed;

and Martin, the model, leader, and nourisher of the Gauls,

[Col. 0870B] the pious shepherd of shining lambs, the pillar of the holy,

the jewel of bishops and powerful protection of the devout.

By divine power he transfers Ambrose, the father, to his funeral,

yet he is not separated from his station.

He stands beside the western Gauls and tends the funeral rites;

he presides over the altars at Milan and the tombs at Tours.

He performs the service of the urn and does not abandon the holy offerings;

he is present to the people in body and serves the beloved in spirit.

And who could prevail to recount all the distinguished deeds

of so great a father, the one who knows their whole sum

and, knowing it, understands everything?

For although many more things may be added to what has been said,

the greatest part of his sacred deeds still remains untouched.

For by devotion, learning, and the summit of his life,

as he rescued Italy from darkness and turned it toward doctrine,

giving light to the whole world of the Catholic faith,

[Col. 0870C] may he also snatch us from the perpetual whirlwind of death

and carry us by his aid to the eternal joys of light!

[Col. 0869] The chapters that follow, 19 and 20, were published by Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, vol. II, pp. 20 ff.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On Saint Columbanus

[Col. 0869]

[Col. 0869C] The various lands of the West shine with radiant glory,

and the West itself is likewise illumined by various enemies.

The renowned seer, Columbanus, born of the race and blood of the Scots,

seeks the illustrious city distinguished by Ambrose. [Note: That is, Milan.]

He lived piously and wondrously from childhood throughout his life,

establishing Christ’s camps [Note: Monasteries.]

and filling them with a numerous soldiery.

Following eagerly by scent the boundaries of this purpose’s virtue,

I may seem to have exceeded what is appropriate.

But since Italy bestowed upon him the end of his contest [Note: Life],

it pleased us at last to join him to the triumphs of the Ausonians.

While his mother carried him in her womb,

she was granted, as she looked upon the rising sun in her lap,

to foresee the light of her offspring,

the light that would scatter over the lands.

Instructed in distinguished arts, and excellently supported by the lessons

of the heavenly arena,

he approaches the fields of Gaul, bearing divine seeds there,

calling everyone by mouth and hand toward heaven’s heights.

Seeking lofty places by steps, he searches out the secrets of the wilderness,

and, ascending on dove-like wings, enters the heights.

Nor is the servant frustrated by the comfort of divine aid. [Note: Divine.]

Relying on the commands, he despises the conveniences of tomorrow.

God grants consolation to the sick brother,

relieving his distress and sending a man to carry the desired provisions

to the exhausted; nor does he allow the messenger to depart empty-handed

[Col. 0870D] or without payment for his journey. [Note: *Iter, itineris*, as also *itiner, itineris*, is not uncommon among ancient writers. See the note to Bede’s metrical *Life of Saint Cuthbert* under the year 687.]

The helper of the sick man asks remedies for his wife,

receives assistance, and brings back the requested gifts;

at the father’s prayer he finds that his spouse has recovered.

Then the abbot Carantocus, warned by secret visions

[Col. 0871A] to provide aid for the saint’s labor,

summons his servant and unfolds the heavenly command:

“Let him fulfill what has been ordered.” Marculfus hastens,

loads the horses with what has been brought, [Note: Brought.]

but is ignorant and unaware by what route he should go

or where the inhabitant whom he must seek resides.

And while, with wavering heart, he considers what to do,

a plan is placed in his mind:

he should assign the animals the task of traveling,

so that they may lead the way and the action may follow.

Divine power guides the animals along the straight road

and leads them into the presence of the desired father,

with the driver following.

Thus, when the animals have guided him to God’s servant,

he presents the work.

Thanks are given to the Thunderer from both sides;

the prophet’s blessing enriches him,

and he sends back the bearer, sowing worthy praises. [Note: “Leads him back to his own people.”]

From then on, many visit the man who had withdrawn from the world,

[Col. 0871B] and the peoples honor him, seeking through the reverence of piety

to be enriched, refreshed by his word, and relieved by his prayers.

He favors their vows, heals breathless diseases,

works miracles, drives away wild beasts, and keeps enemies far off.

Surrounded by them, he remains unharmed amid lupine savagery,

daring to calm the fierce and to soothe their rage with gentle peace.

Having driven away the bear, he chooses the dark cleft of a threatening rock;

he lives there alone, with a boy serving as his attendant.

Wild vegetables sustain him, and water provides his drink.

When the boy himself seeks water from far away

and complains of the long labor,

he is ordered to search the rock’s back.

While heaven’s secrets are sought through the father’s prayers,

the deed is accomplished, and with the vows abundant waters are poured out.

A spring rises from the mountain rock,

flowing continually from that point,

already watering the slopes and offering welcome gifts.

[Col. 0871C] Crowds hasten from every direction to fill God’s camp.

The surveyor, gathering the troops, provides suitable places;

he distributes the assemblies, striving to display the contest beforehand;

arranging duties, he gives laws and handles legal matters.

These written rules show what kind of author shone forth.

He himself traverses the wilderness accompanied by two pupils.

Lacking food, he orders his companions to go and seek it,

and marks the place where they should bring back whatever provisions they find.

They hurry, enter the appointed places,

and see river gifts lying upon the earth,

not spread there by the land’s own element.

They take three salmon out of five [Note: Salmon.]

and carry them off for dinner.

They are rebuked as ungrateful because they reject

the father’s freely offered gifts;

they return as they were sent and bring back what they had scorned.

He likewise orders a companion [Note: A Gaul.]

to persist in fishing,

and marks the place where he should spread the loosened nets.

The man, having seen other things, does not trouble the blue water [Note: That is, the river.]

as ordered; and, seeking the prey granted to him,

he marvels that the fish, driven together and pressing upon one another,

cannot be caught in the folds [Note: The folds of the nets.]

He watches them struck by the meshes but removes none from the water.

After the day has been consumed in fruitless labor and sweat,

the contemptuous pupil returns empty-handed.

He is accused of having rejected the commands through a vain effort,

and at last is ordered to enter the appointed waters.

Thereafter the dependent obeys, loosening the capacious linen nets,

[Col. 0872A] and can scarcely draw them back, stuffed with the weight of the catch. [Note: Filled.]

Thus rejoicing, he finds the father and returns the gifts he has received.

Once, while he himself was living farther away in the bear’s cave,

he learns through the words of the sick brothers

that the attendants assigned to serve the ill are the only ones remaining.

Moved by pity for them, he goes to the camp at Lussovia

to drive away the plague.

He orders the exhausted to rise and attend to their service,

to apply themselves to the threshing-floor, which must be worn down

by fervent labor.

They rise at his command, accustomed to rejoice in their father’s orders;

they obey his instructions and strive to work at threshing.

The force of the disease flees before their humble virtue,

and, their weakness expelled, their limbs are filled with strength.

The father rejoices in their obedience.

Seeing that they can now restore the labor,

he joyfully renews the tables

[Col. 0872B] and adorns them with rich foods.

They celebrate their joy, with no one remaining in pain,

except those alone who had delayed to follow the commands in disbelief.

Their idleness is reproved, their sloth marked,

and the languor of their souls is atoned for by the languor of their bodies.

A delay of the plague is foretold [Note: Predicted.],

and a long anxiety, revolving in its course,

continues until the year closes the threshold.

Once the stalks had dried at harvest time,

the rains rise and prevent the annual gifts from being gathered. [Note: Collected.]

The rains persist; the very hope of reaping is taken away

from the minds of the terrified,

lest the new shoots rise again on the fruitful stalks

and the grains fall into the dangers of famine.

At this the father entrusts his vows to the kindly Lord,

and, balancing his hope upon Christ,

orders his companions to take up their weapons [Note: Sickles.],

to enter the harvest and attack the fields with curved sickles.

His companions marvel, but no one dares to speak against it.

Rather, they approve the commands and, carrying rural weapons,

approach the grain.

He distributes guards throughout the edges of the fields,

men whom a higher life adorns,

receiving four: Coniminus, Eunocus, Econamus,

of Scottish blood, and Gurganus, of British stock.

With these arrangements made, the abbot works with the brothers.

O wondrous faith! Dew pours down around them from the whole sky;

the crop falls upon the dry field,

and, scorched by the astonishing heat, is all gathered in. [Note: Dry.]

The sterile first parents perceive the virtue of this poor man,

approach him, and receive the desired joys of offspring;

they rejoice in the celebrated honor of parenthood.

[Col. 0872D] Wandalenus, rejoicing, flourishes in the name and deed of Donatus,

while the holy father purifies him with water

and nourishes the one entrusted to him with heavenly milk.

Later he is raised by Vesontio to the episcopal rank;

establishing for Christ a monastery under the rule and patronage [Note: Columbanus.] of its founder,

he organizes its communities in holy rivalry.

The father and guardian receives, as the increase of his children,

the reward for the pledge entrusted to him. [Note: Conferred.]

The parents themselves bind themselves to the Lord;

the mother gathers a holy company,

rejoicing to be a companion among those chaste companions.

Cramelenus succeeds the father,

and he too, devoted through love to the splendor of the blessed abbot,

establishes a community governed by this father’s rule.

This illustrious father, endowed with the gift of goodness,

lived how rich in works, how abundant in light!

His frequent comforts, bestowed upon the afflicted, demonstrate it.

Theudegisolus, having cut off a finger with his own sickle,

learned it by experience [Note: “Experienced it.”]:

he received sudden healing through the father’s mouth,

when saliva was poured over the open wound.

Stronger, he resumed the work he had begun without defect,

believing that the limb he had thought lost had been restored.

Nor was he less distinguished in the honor of an excellent cure.

Seeking swift aid and relief from his injury,

the elderly Winocus, who had pursued rustic leisure,

while he marvels at the work of the fathers engaged in earthly tasks

and is astonished that the men of the heavenly service labor with the farmer,

is struck in his exposed forehead by a leaping wedge;

he groans and is drenched in blood.

But the father, pitying his anguish and hastening to help,

leans over him in prayer and quickly cleanses him with saliva.

He restores the face sprinkled by his mouth,

and, soothing the savage wound, spreads a gentle ointment upon it.

He heals it, scarcely leaving any trace of the scars.

The man follows this saving father by a worthy path.

The brothers grieve that the grain is failing. [Note: Or “are discouraged.”]

The father raises their anxious companion with trustworthy words:

“The just man will not be abandoned, nor will he seek bread for his offspring.”

[Col. 0873C] His words make the prayers credible:

the empty granaries are filled

by God, the generous giver, through an effortless miracle.

Night came upon everything, with no transporter found—

except the immeasurable Creator, alone giving generously to all.

Thus once, standing beside men who were breaking the clods with a rake,

he orders sixty measures of double loaves

to be carried, together with whatever small amount of drink was available.

The countrymen marvel that the food increased as they ate;

and the servant is astonished to find twice as much,

having gathered it, [Note: Collected.]

for the guests, now satisfied,

both food and the proceeds of drink.

The merciful man thus preserves not only his own pupils;

he also comes to the aid of outsiders and releases their bonds.

The iron fetters, crushed by the servant’s touch,

fall apart at the father’s command.

Crimes are removed from those confessing them,

who now willingly promise to purify themselves with tears.

Once drawn out from their bonds [Note: Or “those drawn out.”],

he washes them and wipes away their traces.

Having washed them, he leads them into the church;

but, with the threshold closed, entry is not open to the frightened,

for the band of guards is already approaching to drag the rescued back to their torments.

He who opens the threshold by commands and prayers

unbars the bolts with the sick men’s wavering vows,

and, once they have entered together, builds the doors

with their accustomed barriers.

Seeing these enemies and the doorkeeper fortified by his power,

they fear to attack those protected by divine authority

or to subject to human laws those who have been compelled to act.

[Col. 0874A] Even toward adversaries he is good, and toward the savage kindly.

He receives the man who had struck him, bound in inward fetters,

his right hand cast down and numbed by the iron.

Pitying him as he lay at his feet,

the father restores his mind, taken away by demonic force and furious madness.

Two men once full of savage darkness

brought their faces into his presence;

soon he redeemed them through prayer.

Thus five men afflicted by raging madness come to him,

and immediately he grants them salvation after the plague has been driven away.

In this way, by prayers, he restores to the father

a young man driven twenty thousand paces

with the swift power of a flying serpent. [Note: A serpent or demon.]

He has been made steadfast and recovered through vows.

A mother likewise rushes in, filled with this disease together with her child,

and without delay this father sends them back, cleansed alike.

Thus, while a man raves at the threshold of the Parisian gate,

[Col. 0874B] he cries in mournful tones that the enemy [Note: Columbanus.] has come here,

and identifies the servant of God

by his commonly known name.

While he resists with strong commands and dreadful powers,

the demon seizes his innocent hand with its mouth;

and, its tongue restrained by the life-giving man’s fingers,

it is ordered to depart, leaving the afflicted and mangled man behind

with the stench of Aetnean sulphur.

After a long time deprived of Phoebus’s gift,

he recovers the shining gift of light from his illustrious host.

Defeated, he rejoices when his light has been restored,

as the foreigner himself captures a foreigner through the light.

This exceedingly powerful man, the radiant Columbanus of Christ,

how bright he shone in light and how he flashed with heavenly brilliance,

the shining summits of his innumerable gifts of virtue reveal.

Birds and wild beasts speak of them,

[Col. 0874C] summoned from the glades [Note: From the glades or forests.]

and received with flattering submission.

Did not the raven proclaim these things [Note: Miracles.]

when it returned from its theft,

and, trembling, appear to terrify it with the power of its mighty command,

until, ordered to go after returning what it had taken,

it dared no further?

Or does not the bear roar these things with unusual fear,

driven away by a word from the food already tasted,

preserving unharmed the back of the deer it had seized,

and serving the saints according to the commands

issued for the saints’ benefit?

Nor is the bear alone a witness to these things. [Note: The bear.]

Various animals are reported to have been drawn here

by foul-smelling things [Note: That is, by meats giving off an odor.],

with keen nostrils;

at the father’s gestures they are driven away,

while, their hides torn off, the stripped carcass

is allowed to provide food.

Nor is the parent, who has learned through his disciple

to refrain from the apples that have been cut off,

governed by a different discipline.

He knows to spare what has been forbidden

and ceases to gape after stolen things:

he lives according to what has been decreed [Note: Permitted.]

and abstains from the foods set before him. [Note: Present.]

How outstanding this father was in the virtue of the word,

how eminent in rank,

his commands and deeds alike reveal.

The service of his chaste pupil also discloses this:

once, a liquid poured out by an attendant

did not remain spilled.

It passed through the enclosure of the vessel’s rim

and, instead of spreading over the ground,

sought heaven in an unusual rush. [Note: Impetus.]

It was lifted into the air and doubled the height of the vessel,

[Col. 0875A] adorning the father’s command

and beautifying the servant’s accomplishment.

Thus a single measure of meal remains for all uses,

while, at the same time, it is carried by an unworthy person

who gives the order.

Acra, rich in possessions [Note: The manuscript reads *Aëra*. It is a proper name, as is Doda below; these names are lacking in Jona.],

obeys the heavenly instructions.

On the third day, as light returns to those awaiting it in hunger,

it supplies four hundred portions of drink and food,

a complete support beyond hope and faith.

And grace increases and multiplies,

while Doda supplies three hundred.

Once, when the needy lacked food,

nourishment is carried from heaven:

he sends food to those praying by a great multitude of birds.

The feathered procession does not flee;

without labor they bring the food,

making the rich tables seethe with feasts

and surpassing, in the sight of the palace, royal delicacies in sweetness.

For three days this abundant food remains upon the earth,

while on the fourth day an abundance of grain is added,

by heavenly prompting, when the bishop [Note: Namely, the bishop of Mainz, called Leonisius. This event and the following one are reported by anticipation.]

[Col. 0875B] dwelling in the neighboring region orders provisions to be given to the saint.

Thus, when his friends’ companions lack consolation,

he himself, confident in spirit, seeks a faithful friend [Note: Christ.].

Approaching the church, he asks that it be opened

through the Lord’s gift and right hand.

Nor does the friend delay his vows:

he sends a bishop filled with eagerness to carry

whatever may delight the seer,

asking him to accept what has been freely given.

The man gives thanks to the good Lord with bowed heart

and devoutly receives what has been offered,

summoning his own companions.

From there, following the streams of the Rhine,

he visits barbarian lands.

He approaches the Sarmatian region,

where the fierce Suebi [Note: Read “Suebi,” not “Saevos.”] are accustomed to dwell.

As he proceeds, he encounters empty-handed priests

offering the libations of eternal light—

[Note: The printed form *lyphantia* is probably corrupt; perhaps *lymphatica*.]

There was a great vessel, capacious in its sacred interior,

holding the turbid offering of foul beer.

[Col. 0875C] The soldier of the Lord bursts it with a gentle breath;

at once both the crash and the liquid burst forth.

You could see the dreadful spirits [Note: Demons.]

fleeing from the saint’s breath.

The barbarian people, struck with fear, marvel;

and, abandoning their falsehoods,

a considerable part of them receives the gentle yoke

of the true God.

Those weak in faith are made firm by being strengthened.

Meanwhile he considers visiting the borders of the Slavs,

to illuminate with holy light souls blind from their origin.

But an angel, standing near him after seeing this,

depicts the deserted world in the form of a globe,

under a delicate image,

so that he may choose whether to seek the right or the left

and undertake the fruits acquired by labor.

Filled with holy inspiration,

he discerns that the time has not yet come

when the nation’s bonds may be loosed for the Lord,

and he rests.

[Col. 0875D] What sort of person, and how great, he was judged to be by the citizens of heaven,

the guardian of his namesake [Note: Another Columbanus.]

reveals through a fruitless attempt.

To the man desiring the palm and goal of his military service,

praying for the labor he had sought,

he reveals himself in golden light:

“Not in body alone,” he says,

“can I lead you onward, since Father Columbanus asks for you,”

and, weeping, he is refused.

[Col. 0876A] At once, grieving, he orders the servant to hasten,

to run quickly and summon the father,

to visit the man who was wasting away.

Found weeping in the holy church,

he is asked to approach;

he comes and asks the reason and the man’s vows.

“Ingrate”—that is, unwilling—[Note: Against his will.]

he complains that he is being held fast by prayers,

that the guide is being obstructed by tears,

and asks that the restraints be loosened.

“Now let the heavenly entrance open the realms

for the one thirsting for heaven.”

Struck with fear, he summons the brothers sent for by messenger,

and provides provisions for the one departing.

He offers kisses and completes the funeral rites

of his kinsman [Note: Countryman.] and friend.

Now the kings themselves do not refuse to submit their necks

to this father’s commands.

Thus the hostile, driven by the goads of envy,

renews his familiar schemes,

filling the heart of the scepter-bearing queen [Note: Brunhild.]

and of the king’s mother.

And because the man of God refuses to bless the king’s offspring [Note: Theodoric.],

born in sin, declaring that he will not receive the royal scepters,

[Col. 0876B] the queen, in savage fury, persecutes him,

preventing pious gifts from being carried,

his companions from being received as guests or aided with a grant,

and the wearied monitor from reproving or restraining

the movements of the angry king.

The unwearied admonisher does not cease to reprove and restrain the angry king;

he accepts no hospitality

and receives no gifts from kings.

He rejects the wicked presents,

breaks the little vessels offered at a gesture,

and by the power of his gaze pours out the food and drink.

When the tyrant hears this, he is stunned with trembling horror,

hurries forward in supplication, asks pardon for his crime,

vows to correct what he has done,

promises anxiously to restrain the stain,

and appeases the father through this pact.

But as soon as the father returns to his camp [Note: Monastery.],

the agreements are broken;

they heap crime upon crime and resume their customary offenses.

[Col. 0876C] In response, the giver of nourishment returns blows of words;

he sends letters [Note: Letters.] full of threats

and sharp denunciation,

by which the woman, filled with the fury of ancient poison,

stirs up the king and the palace officials,

and her own grandson, the king,

so that he may drive away the man who dwells in the monastery

and compel the one burning with zeal to submit to public law.

Spurred on by these goads, the provincial governor attempts

to violate the laws.

Against him the invincible, pious inhabitant stands firm,

prophesying that the whole family would be sacrificed [Note: Cut off.]

for the sake of the wilderness.

Terrified by this speech, the king quickly leaves

the sacred places against which he had acted in violation,

and declares that, by pursuing this man, he himself

would not attain the crown of martyrdom.

Rather, let him go and leave behind the troops

that he had offended by his rite;

let him return to his native soil by the road on which he came.

[Col. 0876D] He refuses of his own accord to abandon Christ’s camp.

The departing king appoints for this task a savage minister whom he knows.

He captures the father, driven from Vesontio.

Yet, performing these marvels by his word,

he loosens the bonds of the condemned [Note: Or “of the guilty.”],

opens the doors of the church by prayer,

fortifies those left open,

frees the rescued,

and turns and governs those whom he has redeemed.

[Col. 0877A] The citizens themselves, watching and resisting the superior power,

judge that they should restrain themselves from his injury. [Note: Injustice.]

Seeing that he is troubled by no guard,

he seeks to return to the camp he had been given

and goes back at midday,

passing through the middle of the city in full view of the people.

Without delay the nobles, receiving this news,

are shaken into savage anger

and everywhere urge that the fury already begun be increased.

A frenzied cohort, accompanied by a tribune,

is chosen to tear away the leader

and bring him back under the penalty of exile.

The brutal band approaches and is blinded as one man [Note: In Columbanus.]

while it sees everything else;

it searches for and surrounds the man who is present.

They kick at him and touch his clothing with their garments;

they see him seeing, yet are unable to see themselves.

He sits in triumph amid the anxious gusts of the trembling tumult.

But the leader, who had come by chance, reluctant and unwilling,

is granted this sight:

alone, he sees the man seated and reading in the midst of the wandering crowd,

joyful beneath his covering [Note: His face.].

He recalls them and orders them to go back,

reporting to the king that they had vainly harassed a man

sheltered by divine protection.

When the tyrant hears this, he roars;

his fury increased, he heaps crime upon crime [lacuna],

[Col. 0877B] assigning cruel servants tasks to be carried out.

They find him singing psalms, surrounded by a melodious assembly,

and indicate that he must leave,

telling him by what road he should go.

He refuses to leave his dear flocks and beloved children.

Fear and horror disturb the lictors on both sides:

here is the king’s fury; there, reverence for so great a father.

The pious, merciful protector, sympathizing with their danger,

leaves the enclosure.

The pupils accompany him, lamenting;

some, torn away, are held back by grief too powerful to bear.

[Col. 0877C] Yet he entrusts these to the Lord as their comforter and protector,

and urges them to praise the Thunderer without end,

so that they may be able to have him as a nourishing father and creator.

He is led into exile.

When attacked with an ineffectual sword,

he is shielded by heavenly power;

he rescues the enemy from his torturers [Note: By demons.],

and restores him, together with many others, to their former health.

He also addresses the leader,

saying that he should quickly have as ruler

one whom he had despised as a master,

and gives up the time,

so that Lotharius may be without beloved lords under the prince.

At last he is driven to enter the waters of the Loire by boat,

intending to pass across the ocean’s plains.

While the brothers, unwillingly, board the boat with slow effort,

one of the guards, exceedingly audacious,

strikes with an oar Luam,

the holy man’s distinguished companion by name.

[Col. 0877D] The leader [Note: Columbanus.] rebukes him for the crime,

pronouncing that he would pay a penalty to Christ as avenger.

The broad prophecy is followed by certain vengeance and proves it:

soon the insolent man, returning to the harbor,

is swallowed by the wave.

But the pious man, scraping along the river’s back with the keel,

wherever he marks the way,

carries light to the blind who bow before him

[Col. 0878A] and drives away the dreadful black monsters of the spirits.

Cutting through the waves, he descends to the shores of Tours.

Wishing to visit the holy shrine of Martin,

he turns aside there.

With grief he groans and obtains the harbor through his deepest prayers.

Guiding the boat with eager oars, he holds it back against the current;

Triumphing over the weapons of the helmsmen and disregarding the pilot,

He makes for the shore of his own accord, carrying [him] to the lands against his unwilling master’s will.

The pious newcomer gives thanks to the heavenly guide,

Enters the desired temples, and keeps vigil through the night at the holy altars,

Entrusting himself and his companions to God through the favor of Martin,

And, invited by Pope Leuparius [Note: [Col. 0877] Thus, even in the tenth century bishops were still called popes; likewise, at least those supreme pontiffs who were metropolitans, as is clear from Odo, abbot of Glanfeuil, in the History of the Translation of Saint Maurus, abbot.], agrees to share a meal.

He complies with his companions, taking care to relieve their grief,

And, while they prepare to dine, confirms the oracles he had uttered,

The words with which he had already struck at the enemy:

He recalls that, before three circuits of Hyperion [Note: [Col. 0877] the sun.],

[Col. 0878B] Theoderic would fall together with his offspring.

Returning from there to the ship, he finds the brothers held in anguish,

And learns that they had suffered the theft during the darkness [Note: [Col. 0877] the night.].

Without delay, lamenting Martin’s loss, he returns to the urn

And confesses that he had not kept watch there,

Lest he allow his companions to endure such losses.

Soon the thief is shaken by a severe, striking scourge,

And openly cries out where he has hidden the coined money.

The companions, seeing this, run up, recover what was taken,

Ask that the crime be pardoned, and tremble with horror.

They are truly afraid to handle the matter as the Father’s sacred property.

Everything is given to the poor, and food is prepared for the needy;

Heavenly gifts are carried to the one who is ready to bear them,

And the grateful recipient accepts them, while he drives away plagues and livid demons [Note: [Col. 0877] demons.].

At last carried to the banks of the Loire,

[Col. 0878C] He is ordered to return to his homeland and cross the Ocean.

A Scottish ship appears; it takes aboard the companions and their goods,

Who wish to revisit the native fields abandoned by the Father.

Driven, therefore, by favorable oars and west winds,

It cleaves the sea’s surface and strives against the high waves.

Suddenly the man perceives that the sea refuses to carry him,

And, leaping up from the depths, opposes him with savage force;

Driving the vessel back through the waves, it returns it to the sands.

Drawing back its blue waters, it exposes and dries the keel,

Then rests, having gathered itself within its appointed boundaries.

Thus it compels the boat to remain for three days without the deep water,

While the helmsman observes by what circumstance the divine powers

[Col. 0878D] Have exhausted the Father’s resources, and sends the companions away from the ship.

Soon the waters return, and they hasten to recover the small vessel,

And carry it over the smooth, flowing surface with the desired winds,

All praising the decision of the Thunderer to give precedence to his will,

Marveling at the deed by which he wished his prophet to depart,

Sending him away of his own accord and relieving him with resources and service.

He is sent to Lotharius’ devoted court,

Where the king joyfully receives him as though he were a heavenly gift.

[Col. 0879A] He asks him to remain and provides dwellings for his stay.

Fearing to increase disputes among kings, he refuses;

He rebukes the error and skillfully governs the king by his direction.

Meanwhile, while the two tyrants are contemplating war,

He is summoned by each of them and ordered to obey neither.

The king is told, at the Father’s command [Note: [Col. 0879] supply *ac*, “and”], that the scepters of both will be subjected to his rule within three periods.

The prince obeys the instructions, and, faithful in his trust,

Awaits the promises with a steadfast mind; his hope is fixed on heaven,

And he patiently keeps watch until he receives the kingdoms that were granted.

Joining the prophet’s companions, he brings consolation to those beginning the journey,

Who wish to cross the frozen Alps.

Wherever the illustrious Father comes, he shines with virtue;

He drives away horrors and establishes gentleness through consecration.

Chagnericus, from the city of Meaux,

[Col. 0879B] Offers himself voluntarily as his companion, and asks that he pronounce a blessing over his daughter, Burgundo-Fara, who is joined to Christ in character.

When the father, attempting to tear her away by an unfaithful effort,

Sees her struck in the eyes and dragging out her final days through fever,

He groans and asks Eustasius, this Father’s disciple,

To receive her as a guest and heal her by removing the disease.

The latter repeats the request, asking that it be granted, and from there brings healing;

As he proceeds, she chooses death rather than breaking the agreement.

While she is carrying out her promise, while she seeks the sacred veil,

She establishes the shining camp [Note: [Col. 0879] the monastery of Evoriaca], where the Lamb’s bride may serve,

And where the flourishing hosts of the starry kingdom may assemble.

Columba himself, advancing, received the matron with honor [Note: [Col. 0879] or, “was received”];

[Col. 0879C] She is honored through the gift of Autharius, her devoted friend.

While her mother bore this offspring, shining with a double splendor,

He consecrated her and blessed her with the honor of faith.

Accepted by kings and distinguished by royal gifts,

Aspiring thereafter to heavenly things and burning for Christ,

Avoiding the dangers of pleasures, they seek heaven

In mind and summon the heavenly hosts.

They establish blessed camps and till the groves of Juranus [Note: [Col. 0879] perhaps, “of the other”];

The other, on the bank of the Briegensis stream at Resbaca.

Thus, whoever is fortified by this Father’s abundant blessing,

The best end [Note: [Col. 0879] perhaps, “the Most Good”] raises to the heights of heaven.

All who, favorably disposed, did not refuse

To obey this king’s counsels rejoice that prosperity is being brought to them.

But those who set aside the counsels of the paternal heart,

Having failed in their hopes, wept in empty grief:

[Col. 0879D] As did that king, the brother of the one who rejected [Note: [Col. 0879] Theodebertus] the gracious Father,

Who, while avoiding obedience to the Father, was subjected to the enemy

By the saving service he had voluntarily undertaken for Christ.

Nor was the matter long delayed: wars are stirred up on both sides,

And peoples of different kinds come together in battle.

The man of God alone, accompanied by his servant,

Had at that time entered a vast wilderness; as he sat and read,

He was suddenly overtaken by sleep, under the Lord’s direction,

And saw the kings among whom the wars were growing hot.

Awakened, he revealed the blazing weapons to the servant standing nearby,

[Col. 0880A] And sighed that too much blood was being poured out on both sides.

The servant advised him to pray against the one who was striking [Note: [Col. 0879] Theoderic.].

The Father marked the advice as foolish, declaring it wicked,

Since he should rather love the enemy’s salvation,

And pray to God, by whose power these wars are balanced,

Who arranges a just battle on the scales of his divine will.

Now the man who had refused to serve benevolent counsels

Offers his back to his brother, and, captured and subdued by his grandmother,

Lays down his gem-studded hair beneath a woman’s shears;

And what he had refused to take for the love of Christ,

He displays in ridicule as the marks of a crown.

Without delay, torn apart by the hyena’s [Note: [Col. 0879] Bruneschildis’s] rage, he is slaughtered;

His brother [Note: [Col. 0879] Theodoricus], struck by heavenly fire, is consumed.

And so Lotharius, seeing the scepters prepared for him,

Submits to the holy Columbanus’ command, takes up arms,

[Col. 0880B] And hastens with his troops to seize the kingdoms owed to him.

With an easy march he captures and kills the offspring born of the king’s adultery, together with the instigator of the crimes. He takes from the court the woman who had fostered the crime, mounts her on a camel, binds her to untamed horses, and wears her away in their rushing charge.

Thus, thus the sayings of the truthful prophet are fulfilled.

Therefore Columbanus, on the wings and with the spirit of a dove,

Seeking the kingdoms above, flies across the Alps of Gaul,

Enters Italy, and is honorably received by King Agilulf.

Entering the pious walls, he dwells in Milan,

Purges heresies, and, supplying arms to the Church,

Meditates the doctrines of the path of righteousness.

Hearing [perhaps: “receiving”] of the mountain-ridge’s being broken by vinegar [Note: [Col. 0879] perhaps *acuta*, “sharp”], through the wondrous radiance of Peter, both companion and worshipper [the corrupt wording is uncertain],

He quickly surmounts these things and seeks the heights in eager flight.

[Col. 0880C] Finding the palace half-ruined through the neglect of the mountaineers,

He hastens to restore it to its ancient beauty.

Carrying cut beams over the rough paths of the hill,

He bore loads weighing forty men across the level ground,

With three or two disciples, without a pole.

Nor did they seem to be carrying the weight; rather, they were carried by the weight.

Thus strengthening the brothers’ minds with pious encouragement,

He urged them with joyful prayers to persist in the work they had begun,

So that they might grasp the will of God through his manifest support.

He quickly restores the roofs, repairs the ruins,

And establishes the monastery’s various dwellings.

When Lotharius sees that the prophet’s predictions have been fulfilled,

He sends Eustasius, governing the camp at Luxeuil,

To follow the sacred footprints of his beneficent master,

With the king’s broad and urgent prayer,

[Col. 0880D] So that he may return, live according to his wishes, and receive what he seeks.

He rejoices at the arrival of his son and urges him to remain

For some time with him, a disciple of illustrious piety,

For the rest of the companions and for the direction of the brothers;

But he refuses to turn back and declines to return.

He then bids a message go to the gracious king, instructing him to correct his own life by the regulation of his conduct, support the companions dwelling at Luxeuil, protect them with safeguards, and honor them with royal gifts.

[Col. 0881A] The joyful king adorns the pleasing treaties with honor,

Supports the heavenly camp, sustains the assigned troops,

Fills it with resources, and enlarges the boundaries of its rule.

But Father Columbanus himself, when the year is ending,

Dwells according to the commands [Note: [Col. 0881] or, “rules”] in the newly enclosed cell at Bobbio.

[Col. 0882A] From there he brings his soul, released from the bonds of flesh and darkness,

To heaven, adorned with beneficent splendor.

The relics restored by him are placed in the temple building.

What a lofty life deserved, the signs that were given proclaim;

His teaching declares the excellence of his spirit.

## CHAPTER XIX. On Saint Attala

[Col. 0881]

[Col. 0881A] A great disciple succeeds the illustrious Father [Note: [Col. 0881] Columbanus]:

Attala, to whom Burgundy gave a noble lineage.

His father presents him to the bishop to be reared [Note: [Col. 0881] “to be instructed”];

He burns to climb the ever-narrower path.

[Col. 0881B] Thus advancing secretly, he passes through the camps of monks,

Burning with desire for better things [Note: [Col. 0881] “desiring them”],

Offers his neck to the patron at his command,

And hands himself over to Columbanus to be guided by his light.

The latter binds him to himself and kindles him with the light he has sought,

Until, by his virtue, he is sought to take the master’s place.

Worthy to exercise battle brilliantly for the holy camps,

He wages the wars of the raging, deceitful serpent [Note: [Col. 0881] “the devil”].

Austere toward the lukewarm and stern toward the lax, he is assailed by a savage tongue;

The fierce tongue tears away the tender companions [Note: [Col. 0881] “the imperfect”] from his side,

Carries them off, and drags them through the hidden byways of the wilderness.

The instigator and teacher of evil burns in a savage fire [Note: [Col. 0881] fever],

Crying out that he is paying the deserved penalty.

Nor is he able easily to approach the Father while seeking a remedy;

Rather, he is seized and, voiceless, gives up his soul to the air.

Many terrified companions return to the Father’s halls,

[Col. 0881C] And are caught like sheep in a wolf-worn throat.

But those who, in arrogant pride, despised their protector,

Consume their boldness, shaken by various disasters.

Some, bound by iron, some, swallowed by swift waves,

Find pious healing, as many as return.

The prayers of this powerful Father are fulfilled;

By his commands they become renowned, and by his prayers they obtain what is worthy.

The Bobbio river, once swollen by violent rains,

Pouring over its banks and rolling with surging water,

Proves this: ordered to remove its fury from the sacred place,

It is forbidden to disturb the mill’s grain-bearing machinery,

And, when the staff is set down, the law is established;

At the sign of the cross the stream obeys his commands,

And, once the difficult path has been undertaken, it flees into an easy channel.

Sinoaldus returns to report the seen trophies to the Father.

[Col. 0881D] He also proves the virtue of the illustrious master,

While a countryman is at work and repairing the plow-handle [Note: [Col. 0881] *stivae*, “handles of the plow”], his left thumb is severed by his unfortunate right hand.

Already given over to the earth, while the deed is being reported to the Father,

He is ordered to be brought out of the grave and carried a thousand paces.

Having been anointed with sacred saliva under the physician’s direction,

And with the healer bringing life to what had been buried,

The severed thumb is joined to the bereft palm by a single unifying bond,

And he is instructed to handle silently the health that has been granted.

Thus, once, when asked to look upon and aid with consolations and prayers

A boy thought to be breathing his last,

[Col. 0882A] He gave him, at his arrival, safety, and sent him away vigorous through his prayers.

Later, amid many other deeds of pious virtue,

God, judging that he should be released from his breathless troubles,

[Col. 0882B] To be purified by the light of peace and nourished by rest,

Marks the appointed time of the journey he must soon undertake.

And although it is not openly stated in the instructions

What day he is to depart after fifty days,

He nevertheless prepares what is suitable for those who will remain,

And, for the one who is migrating, thickens and repairs the monastery’s enclosing coverings,

Taking care that nothing damaged or fallen should remain.

He strengthens and repairs the books and binds those that have come loose.

Devoting himself to vigils and prayers, he prolongs his fasts,

Afflicts his body, and prepares his soul for heavenly things.

After nine renewals of the harvest, he orders the disciple [Note: [Col. 0881] Jonas] to go and see his parents, who were longing to see him,

And to return without any delay hindering him.

Following the road between two guards and strengthened by them,

He is allowed to embrace his mother in the light of day.

[Col. 0882C] Night, however, urges him to return, and pressing fever

Compels him to cry out that he is burning with complaints about the Father,

And that he will be carried to destruction if delay keeps him from returning.

As soon as day returns, he again takes the road and hastens toward his desire;

He is saved on his return, and the force of the fever leaves him as he goes.

He finds the Father drawing his final breath.

His arrival nevertheless brings joy,

And the paternal funeral sees its own torment—that is, the cause of torment [Note: [Col. 0881] namely, the cause of torment, and so forth]—in his swift return.

But the Father, composing and marking his final instructions,

Fortifies himself with the cross, bows down, and worships the exalted cross,

And, raising the cross, adorns it with tears and praises.

Then, seeking private matters, he asks that the ancient sins

Be wiped away, and cleanses them with tears that pour forth.

Thus, amid the groans of an exhausted body and the sighs of his heart,

[Col. 0882D] Raising his eyes, he sees heaven opened for him.

Glorifying God, he offers thanks and hymns.

A witness had secretly remained there to report what he saw,

And to disclose the divine consolations received through the voice.

The next day was already bringing heavenly gifts to the earth.

Calling the brothers and giving them a final farewell, he adds,

Exhorting them to remain in their undertakings and pursue better things.

Thus comforting those born through his word, he is released from this world

And carries the breath of his pious, starward mind into heaven.

## CHAPTER XX. On Saints Bertulf and Eustasius

[Col. 0883]

[Col. 0883A] This man [Note: [Col. 0883] Attala] is followed by another burning with love of religion,

Born of Frankish stock and of lofty blood,

Bertulf, connected by lineage with the renowned Bishop Arnulf,

Whom he sees possessing lofty heights of mind

And despising them for heavenly things.

He follows him, and, scorning the high summits of the world,

Seizes the exalted trophies of the cross.

Seeking Eustasius, who governs according to the rule of Luxeuil

The camp of Columbanus, he is raised by beneficent instructions,

And, pleasing to all, lives fitly according to virtue.

But when the company seeks the Gauls [Note: [Col. 0883] “Gaul”], Luxeuil,

With the shared piety of both Fathers [Note: [Col. 0883] Eustasius and Attala] favoring him,

He also gives himself over to the Italian struggles

And remains faithful.

After the Father [Note: [Col. 0883] Attala] departs to the stars,

He is chosen master by the common fervor [Note: [Col. 0883] “desire”] of the brothers,

[Col. 0883B] And cherishes and governs those entrusted to him with divine guidance.

A serpent, brewing dark poisons, drives the hearts of relatives

Toward evil, persuading them to subject this man [Note: [Col. 0883] Bertulf]

To themselves, and not to cease seeking what had been granted to them [Note: [Col. 0883] *concessa*, “granted”].

He approaches the nobles, then the king, and does not abandon his requests;

He does not recoil from his undertaking.

Compelled by this pressure, the blessed Father approaches the Roman pope to seek redress.

When summoned, he recites the rule and restores the precepts.

Bishop Honorius rejoices at the suitable instructions,

Embraces the man, encourages him, venerates and honors him,

Grants him rights and strengthens the laws and governance,

And, unwillingly, allows him to return.

He was treading the Tuscan fields

[Col. 0884A] With a faltering step; illness weighed upon the Father,

And anguish upon the disciples who clung to him,

Since they had no hope of his return.

The night brings a sound vigil of strength [lacuna].

The sick Father arranges the observance of apostolic law
