And orders the solemn rites to be performed in the customary manner,

Prescribing for himself and his companions that they should keep vigil.

Night suppresses their cares; deep sleep overwhelms everyone,

And even the guards are laid low by deathlike forgetfulness.

Abandoned by his disciples [Note: [Col. 0883] “left by his disciples”], he is raised up by Christ his guardian,

The abbot is comforted by the visitation of Peter [Note: [Col. 0883] “by Peter”], the prince. He is ordered to rise and return safely, and learns that Peter had offered himself as the patron sought.

Astonished, he asks the awakened attendant to disclose what he has seen.

The attendant, denying that he himself had been illumined by the desired light,

[Col. 0884B] Asks that this light be revealed, and extracts it through fervent prayers,

Then marks what he has discovered and approaches as a bold witness.

The Father himself goes on in strength and enables others to go on in strength;

He drives away demonic plagues and purifies minds through prayer.

Victorinus, having experienced this and being sent to meet the beneficent man,

Is promptly healed and, restored to health, strives to give thanks.

Thus a boy, oppressed and devoured by a savage robber,

Returns from the dark throat into which he had been received, at the abbot’s command.

He also drives away the wasting disease of leprosy through heavenly honor,

And, after pious prayers and fasting,

Makes safe through sacred oil one whom the physicians had despaired of saving.

Thus he cleanses the skin of its defilement and the entrails of their corruption, so that afterward no trace of disease remains to mar the beauty [Note: [Col. 0883] namely, of health].

## CHAPTER XXI. On Saints Blidulf and Meroveus the Monk

[Col. 0883]

[Col. 0883C] These renowned signs of the life-giving grove

Shine forth in joyful fruits and breathe the nectar of life,

While they produce devoted pledges to God.

Blidulf, persisting in solid honor,

As defender of the persecuted Godhead before the tyrant,

Praising and teaching its indivisible beauty,

Kindles the furies of the wicked one at the heavenly summit.

Secret weapons are prepared against his life;

Hidden treachery is organized and deadly war is stirred up.

The herald of truth is attacked by treachery and, overcome by blows,

Is beaten with repeated clubs,

Until it is clear that his senses have abandoned the slaughtered man.

Thus, sought out by a faithful host, he is found insensible beneath the lashes,

But, roused as though from gentle sleep,

He declares that he is standing free from his wound,

More peacefully than he had ever slept.

[Col. 0883D] Although his limbs bear the marks of a slight welt,

He does not know the anguish and does not remember the dreadful battle.

Nevertheless, punishment does not fail, after a long time,

To visit Bardo the aggressor;

Rather, seized by a demon, it compels him to cry out

That he suffers punishments worthy of his crime,

Confessing that he had dared to inflict such fires upon the just man,

[Col. 0884C] And that whoever favors a similar fire against sacrilegious people should melt in the same flames.

But the leader of the evil, fearing for himself when he sees such things

Inflicted according to his deserts, assigns the wretched man

To the beneficent camps as a gift.

The illustrious Father Attala rejects the faithless man’s gift,

Runs to help the tortured man,

And demands that the brothers redeem him while he burns in the dreadful fire;

Let them labor in prayers and protect the breathless man with their vows.

Released from his bonds, he is enabled to go away safe.

Yet he does not long live in a manner worthy of forgiveness.

He chooses to squander in trivialities the time granted to repentance

Rather than preserve it with tears.

Boasting and laughing that he had treated his vows as a disgrace,

He is soon driven by fevers;

His flesh grows hot with the fire of death,

And, shouting and raging, he is snatched away to the punishments of Gehenna; the tomb, raised upon its mound, displays how dreadful were the deeds he committed.

[Col. 0884D] Nor do they note any lesser excess in those who had offended God;

They impose punishment and declare their offense,

As they pressed Meroveus into a spring.

When, sent by his abbot to Dertona, he strives to bring down a dark shrine in a dense grove, he is struck by *fameolis* [reading and meaning uncertain] and plunged into the stream’s waters.

Nor is he allowed to be subdued by the waters; rather, he is loaded with their hostile force.

[Col. 0885A] Cast beneath the forest’s weight and apparently buried,

He rises unharmed from the river and revisits the brothers.

Swift punishment strikes the sacrilegious,

Afflicting those overcome by blows in various ways:

It deprives some of the light of their eyes,

Burns others with fires,

And torments others with the bonds of their sinews.

Some of these, afterward brought to the Bobbian fathers,

Escape their torments through tears;

Others pay for their crimes with deserved punishments

And restrain their offenses through scourges.

[Col. 0886A] Here a brother, once joined as a companion to Leupardus,

While, at the Father’s command, they were thickening the defenses of the vineyard,

Which many could not raise by united effort,

Carried a wooden column strengthened by divine power.

A little fox, attempting to drink the forbidden clusters

Of this Leupardus, and holding them in its mouth after taking them,

By the death that followed revealed the crime in its danger.

## CHAPTER XXII. On Baudacarius and Certain Other Holy Monks

[Col. 0885]

[Col. 0885A] Bertulf, with Baudacarius appointed as his overseer,

Takes charge of those sent under restraint and gives them consolation.

While he supplies the small amount of bread that is available and a duck,

[Col. 0885B] He cheers thirty men with scant provision but great generosity of spirit,

And fills the brothers with rich food as well.

These athletes, radiant in the rays of the fathers

And shining with piety, enter heaven eagerly in an ordered company.

Among them, Tedoaldus, shining in a joyful mind and deep within,

While lying on his bed and traversing heavenly things in his mind,

Calls the companions and, bidding them farewell with a joyful face,

Addresses them gently, asks for the final provisions for his journey,

And, marking his end, adorns it with a beautiful poem.

Beginning a melody and ascending through the virtue of the blessed

To the heights of virtues, he will be seen as the nourisher of the saints:

“Now God places the soul in Zion among the shining stars.”

When Sicagibodus, among these ready fathers,

Had pursued the lofty path, pure, gentle, and upright,

He carries out the obligations of obedience at the friendly prayers.

[Col. 0885C] While he lies there, drawing breath with his final effort,

He sees the sun shining with heavenly brilliance

And Phoebus’ rays darkened by our splendor.

He sees heavenly men standing there,

And, marveling, learns that he himself is immediately about to enter

That radiance by which he will be joined to the exalted assemblies.

He merits learning that, beyond this light,

He will shine among his companions with equal brilliance.

[Col. 0886A] But he returns and gives a final farewell to those present,

And without delay, returning, joins the pleasant ranks.

To the astonished brothers, coming back, he adds his final instructions;

He reports the vision when asked,

Announces the consolations he received,

Receives the mystical sacraments,

Gives kisses with bonds of affection,

Asks that he be cared for at his funeral,

And ascends to heavenly things.

By his blessed death he leaves shining footprints,

Showing that those who follow a similar path in the light

Are blessed with the splendor of the same perpetual light.

May all these fathers, resplendent in heavenly peace—whose magnificent triumphs we pursue, though with the humblest praise—and those who likewise rejoice in heaven, obtain for us certain release from guilt, the divine governance of life, and the remedy of conduct: that we may avoid crimes and lighten what we have committed with tears,

To offer fruitful mourning with groans that shake us,

So that, cleansed of the world’s filth, we may be made radiant by the light,

Fitted for the heavenly assemblies,

Blessed without end,

And worthy throughout the ages to behold the saving face.

[Col. 0885] Here ends.

The epitaph of Flodoard follows in the codex; we have already given it in the Prefaces.

# In the Year of the Lord 968. Saint Mathildis, Queen

[Col. 0885]

## Preliminary Observations

[Col. 0885C] To the distinguished women by whom the Ludolfing family had been renowned in the ninth century, there was added in the tenth century Mathildis, wife of King Heinricus and mother of Otto I, Duke Heinricus, Archbishop Bruno, Queen Gerberga, and Duchess Hathwidis [Col. 0886C]. The fame of her virtues spread widely while she was still alive; at her death it was celebrated by Widukind [Note: [Col. 0885C] III, 74]. Afterward, among her sons and grandsons, and in the monasteries founded by her—Quedlinburg [Col. 0887A] [Note: [Col. 0887D] Compare the Quedlinburg Annals, year 936], Northhausen, Pöhlde, and Enger—the memory of her flourished in writings and among people until, about forty years after her death [Note: [Col. 0887D] For the author wrote under King Heinricus, therefore after 1002 and before 1012, by which time Thietmar had already used our Life], at the command of King Heinricus II, her great-grandson, the Life that we present here was written.

The author appears to have been a cleric or monk from among those whose talent and wisdom commended them to the king and who enjoyed his familiarity, but who wished to keep his name hidden [Note: [Col. 0887D] He seems to have known Ruotger’s Life of Bruno; see chapter 30]. He seems to have relied on earlier writings [Note: [Col. 0887D] The reference was identified as Godehard, then abbot of Altaha, through whose intervention Heinricus in 1017 confirmed the village of Gamin to the monastery of Northhausen; see the distinguished E. G. Foerstemann, vice-principal of the Northhausen gymnasium, in his commentary on the Life of Mathildis, published on 9 August 1838. But I cannot safely attribute the book to that man—whose learning, habits, and relationship with the king would make him very suitable—because Godehard’s Life is silent about the matter, and it is clear that several other men of the same standing existed at that time] and on the accounts of the queen’s household, perhaps Richburga, abbess of Northhausen.

Certainly, he was well informed about the events he narrates, although he related some things less accurately: the duel of Widukind with Charlemagne [Note: [Col. 0887D] Chapter 1], Widukind’s baptism by Archbishop Boniface [Note: [Col. 0887D] Ibid.], and the uncertain manner of the succession of Heinricus I [Note: [Col. 0887D] Chapter 4]. Indeed, in matters concerning Mathildis’s final years, he writes that King Berengarius was entrusted as a captive to Duke Heinricus, Mathildis’s son [Note: [Col. 0887D] Chapter 15], and that Otto II went to Italy together with his father [Note: [Col. 0887D] Chapter 22]. These points do not prevent us from generally trusting the author and rejoicing that he teaches us many otherwise unknown things about the life and deeds of the excellent queen and of her sons and grandsons.

The book, written for the use of Heinricus II, celebrates the virtues of his great-grandmother, by which she equaled the saints, but does not conceal the error of the mother who preferred her son Heinricus to Otto.

The author, whoever he may be, read the Latin poets, especially Virgil, and displays a poetic vein in prose whose members correspond with one another in rhythm and sound [Note: [Col. 0887D]

For example, in chapter 23:

“But when she had traveled through the cities of the region of Saxony and had provided each monastery with whatever was necessary, she again visited the city of Northhausen, which she loved very much, in order to see Richburga, whom she had recently appointed abbess. As soon as she arrived, she ordered her to be summoned to her.”]

This style was also common among several other writers of this age [Col. 0887C]; in our author, however, it prevails so strongly that almost his entire work could be broken into sentences resembling verse. This was demonstrated by the distinguished Foerstemann in his 1838 commentary on the Life of Mathildis, and any reader can easily understand that the same is true in every part of the book. Just as this practice is foreign to Roman usage, so too the author’s distinctive use of the word *nihilominus*, which in his writing means anything but what it means in good Latin, departs from sound Latin usage.

As soon as the book appeared, it was known to Thietmar [Note: [Col. 0888D] I, 11, from chapters 6, 10, and 17; II, 12, from chapter 25], who adapted it for his own purposes. At the beginning of the twelfth century it was abridged by Ekkehard, abbot of Uraugia [Note: [Col. 0888D] He did this in the same manner in which he abridged the histories of Alexander, the Goths, the Franks, the Lombards, and the Saxons from the works of Alexander, Jordanes, the Deeds of the Frankish Kings, Paul the Deacon, and Widukind; namely, by inserting into the Life also the things he had read about Queen Mathildis in Widukind. See *Archiv*, vol. VII, 486–493]. Shortly afterward it was copied by the Saxon Annalist [Note: [Col. 0888D] For the years 911, 921, 936, 946, and 968]. At the beginning of the fifteenth century it was transcribed in full at Cologne in the monastery of Saint Pantaleon.

All editions that have appeared—the Bollandists’ [Note: [Col. 0888D] *Acta Sanctorum*, March II, p. 358], Leibniz’s [Note: [Col. 0888D] *Scriptores rerum Brunsvicensium* I, 192], Erath’s [Note: [Col. 0888D] *Codex diplomaticus Quedlinburgensis*, p. 925 ff.], and ours—depend on that fifteenth-century codex.

It is preserved today:

1. In Brussels, in the Burgundian Royal Library, numbered 329–341, beautifully written in two columns and here and there decorated with pictures in the margin. We have reproduced the whole book, which Bethmann transcribed for our use, correcting only the fifteenth-century spelling and emending several passages. In this work we were assisted by:

2. Ekkehard of Uraugia’s abridgment of the Life of Queen Mathildis [Col. 0888B], often contracted from our text in the same words but frequently moving sentences from their proper places. For this reason I judged that some passages which seemed to have fallen out of the Brussels manuscript could not safely be restored from Ekkehard. Nevertheless, I used the Vatican–Wolfenbüttel manuscript [Note: [Col. 0888D] On this I reported in our *Annals*, vol. V, 158–161] of the twelfth century, whose readings, insofar as they are preserved in the Wolfenbüttel portion, had already been published by Leibniz, vol. III, 655 ff.; the Würzburg manuscript [Note: [Col. 0888D] Ibid., vol. VII, 489] of the twelfth century; and the Klosterneuburg manuscript transcribed by D. Goldhann [Note: [Col. 0888D] Ibid.]. I discussed other manuscripts of the same abridgment—the Munich manuscripts of the twelfth and fifteenth centuries, the manuscript of Heiligenkreuz in Austria from the twelfth century, and the paper manuscript of Homburg—in our *Annals* [Note: [Col. 0888D] Vol. VII, 487–488, and VI, 184, 239].

3. The Paris Royal Manuscript among the books of Saint-Germain [Col. 0888C], no. 440, parchment, from the twelfth century, containing the Saxon Annalist. Its text, insofar as it derives from the Life of Mathildis, agrees almost word for word with ours.

4. Finally, we mention the last part of the Brussels Royal Manuscript no. 3202. According to Bethmann, it was copied from the manuscript of the Carthusian monastery at Cologne; one folio from the seventeenth century contains only the beginning of the Life of Mathildis, excerpted word for word from ours, beginning as follows: “Saint Mathildis the queen, from the lineage …,” and so forth.

[Col. 0889]

# LIFE OF SAINT MATHILDIS

*(In Pertz, Monumenta Germaniae historica, Scriptores, vol. IV, p. 282.)*

## Here begins the Preface to the Life of the Glorious Queen Mathildis

[Note: [Col. 0889] *Mathildis* in manuscript 1; but in the excerpts of Ekkehard of Uraugia written at the beginning of the twelfth century, the older and genuine form *Mahthildis* is consistently used.]

[Col. 0889A] To Heinricus, a king most worthy of supreme veneration, the expounder of this work wishes an increase of spiritual gifts, an abundance of virtues, and prosperity in temporal affairs.

Since it is known to many that you are endowed with knowledge and training in various arts, and that you have read through many volumes containing the lives of the holy Fathers, by whose examples your venerable conduct can rightly be formed and raised to higher things, it is no small virtue for you to inquire into the pious deeds of your preceding relatives, and especially of your illustrious great-grandmother, Queen Mahthildis. Her radiant life is rightly to be imitated, and her virtue is the more praiseworthy because her sex is the weaker.

We give thanks to your beneficence that you have been pleased to have this work recited by us. It is a great and exceedingly fearful task for our ignorance, since many men superior to us in talent and wisdom are subject to your rule, men who can penetrate the depths with the ray of their language [Col. 0889B]. At your command that this work be begun, the task seemed most difficult to our littleness; yet it would have been the height of presumption for us to resist your command.

We have fulfilled your order beyond the measure of our strength. We do not doubt, however, that the efforts of envious people will be present, who wish to criticize what we have done. Therefore we beseech you, glorious king—and, if it is permitted to say so, sweetest king—not from rash boldness but from necessity: do not bring this [Col. 0890A] little handbook into public view for the wise to mock before your own skill has discerned what in it displeases your piety and those things that do not seem correct to your wisdom have been mercifully corrected.

For it is fitting that the one who ordered this writing should also be its emendator and defender, lest what has been foolishly published by us [Note: [Col. 0889] Erath reads *vobis*; manuscript L. 1?] be pierced by the tongues of the envious.

In this volume you have a few deeds of your forefathers, from which you can learn what it is useful for you to do and what to avoid. May the Ruler of the whole world, who, visiting their hearts, granted them to recognize what was just and fulfill it in their works, grant you to do what is right and to admonish others to do the same; may he grant you invincible weapons [Col. 0890B] by which the savagery of your enemies may be overcome.

May his grace also be your firm helper and constant companion, and may it make you an example and model of justice, so that you may faithfully govern and rule the Church; and, having become a suitable watchman, may you be a man of great counsel, industry, and discipline.

May the Lord order all your ways so that you may live without reproach in all his commandments, attain the prize of the heavenly calling, and there receive the crown of justice and the gifts of the treasures of heaven.

If anything in this little work pleases anyone, the praise will belong to its instructor.

## Here ends the Preface to the Life of Queen Mathildis

[Note: [Col. 0889] One word is missing in the manuscript at *in v.*]

## Here begins the Praiseworthy Life of the Glorious Queen Mathildis

[Col. 0889]

[Col. 0889C] 1. (A.D. 912.) In the time of Conrad, the glorious king of the Franks, there was in the regions of Germany a certain duke named Otto, distinguished for the integrity of his character and prudent in deciding matters, renowned for the nobility of his lineage and famous for his triumphs in war. Hathuwic, a venerable matron, was joined to him in the bond of marriage. Two sons were born to them, adorned with a lordly appearance; they raised them with the greatest diligence, as the honor of their nobility required. The elder was called Thancmar, and the other Heinricus. Although he was the younger, he nevertheless shone more brightly in moral excellence, and from his earliest years devoted himself to good works, following the footsteps of humility, by which one most certainly reaches the summit of the virtues [Note: c. v. 1.].

He loved all with whom he associated no less than himself; he preferred himself to no one, nor did he oppress anyone by force. When this boy of remarkable distinction and lovable character reached the flourishing years of youth, his parents began to discuss among themselves arranging a marriage for him with a maiden not inferior to him in birth, whose generous character would be very like that of the distinguished young man.

Meanwhile they heard that an exceptional girl named Mahthilda was residing in the monastery of Herivord, noble by birth, desirable in appearance, and distinguished in character, where, together with her grandmother, the abbess, she was learning the psalter and the skills of handiwork. This virgin too derived her eminent lineage from the venerable man Witikin, who had been a glorious duke in the western region, rich in possessions and surpassing many in the honor of his rank. Alas! [Note: “proch” in 1.] But, taken captive by error, he worshiped idols made by the hands of craftsmen and inflicted various torments upon those who worshiped Christ, because there were no preachers to proclaim Christ and convert unbelievers to the faith.

King Karolus, a most Christian man and benevolent toward the worshipers of God, held the stronghold of sovereignty at that time. When he learned of the unbelief of the aforementioned duke, he grieved deeply; and, gathering his entire army, he went to war against Witikin, in order to defend the faith and convert the wanderer to the way of salvation. When they had met and the soldiers of both sides had fought one another for a long time, and the strength for battle had already failed on either side, the leaders agreed that the king should engage Witikin in single combat, and that the one to whom Christ granted victory should rule with his entire army.

When they engaged, they long and fiercely pressed the battle with struggling strength. At last the Lord, moved by the tears of the Christians, granted His champion triumph over the enemy; thus the faith received what it deserved.

2. On the conversion of the duke Witikin. Then, by God’s gift, Witikin cast away the weapons of unbelief and took up the shield of Christian faith, burning with a new zeal to lay aside the old man in the mystery of the sacred font and put on the new man in Christ. The most Christian king received him kindly and ordered him to be baptized by the venerable bishop Boniface; he himself raised him from the sacred font. Thereafter, united by kinship in the faith, they were harmonious friends.

After Witikin had been baptized, he was immediately transformed entirely, in a wondrous manner, toward the work of God. Then his whole army, subject to him, confessed this same belief in the faith, and, devoutly imitating their prince, was immersed in the sacred font of baptism. When these things had been accomplished and a treaty of peace had been established between them, King Karolus returned joyfully in victory.

Duke Witikin returned to his own homeland, enlightened by the grace of the Holy Spirit. Just as previously he had persecuted those who called upon Christ, so afterward he drew into the faith of Christ those who had gone astray; and just as he had formerly been a persecutor of the good, so then he appeared a most vigilant defender of the sacred faith. He now desired to rebuild the churches that he had previously destroyed in his unbelief, and where he had set up idols, there he now placed shrines of the saints.

From the descendants, therefore, of this same Witikin, the outstanding duke, came the stock of the blessed Mahthildis. Her father, named Thietricus, had been a glorious count in the western region [Note: He lived at the estate of Enger, near Herford; see below, chapter 11], and had taken as his wife the venerable Reinhilda, born of Danish and Frisian stock [Note: That is, with a Danish father and a Frisian mother], commendable in character. By God’s gift he was worthy to beget a child lovable to humanity.

O happy birth of this child, to whom royal dignity later fell by the grace of Christ! For she became the glory of her parents, the joy of her relatives, the hope of the inheritance, and the adornment of all her future offspring—lovable at birth and more lovable as she was raised. What more need be said? At that time a child such as this was rarely seen.

When the illustrious little girl had been weaned, the abbess Mahthild, the mother of Count Thietricus, who held the abbey at Herivord, desired to receive the aforementioned girl for upbringing. Her parents, consenting to the abbess’s request, entrusted her to her care, so that she might teach her sacred readings and the work of her hands.

3. On the betrothal of Mahthildis. The distinguished girl therefore advanced wonderfully in every respect: young in age but mature in moral excellence, capable in the study of literary discipline and skilled in practical works. When her praiseworthy virtue was being proclaimed everywhere, it also reached the ears of the distinguished Duke Otto, who immediately sent his count Thietmar to investigate the matter (A.D. 909).

Obeying the duke’s command, Thietmar hastened eagerly to the monastery mentioned above. He immediately approached the women’s quarters, where the girl served at the abbess’s order, and, secretly entering the monastery with their assistance, carefully observed the maiden’s noble and most admirable appearance. After silently investigating and cautiously considering everything he wished to know, he happily reported to his lord all that he had seen.

On the following day Duke Otto arranged for his son Heinricus to go to the aforementioned monastery together with Count Thietmar, his tutor, so that they might carefully determine whether the girl’s appearance and character suited him. He therefore chose not a few young men, elegant in birth and appearance, to accompany the young Heinricus, so that he might proceed more ostentatiously to the appointed place.

As they approached the monastery, they pitched their camp in a field. A few of them entered the oratory, ostensibly for prayer, and saw the virgin sitting inside [Col. 0892C] and holding a psalter in her hand, most proper in dress and exceedingly reverent in bearing. Heinricus, inflamed with love for the exceptional virgin, forbade his companions to tell anyone why they had come here; then he immediately returned to the camp where the rest of the young men were staying.

Putting on noble attire, he entered the church again with a large retinue and asked that he be granted an opportunity to speak with the abbess. She came out and joyfully received him and all his attendants. After they had exchanged words of greeting, she led the young Heinricus, together with Count Thietmar, into her chamber and prolonged a familiar conversation with them.

Meanwhile the distinguished young man, taking courage, gradually began to speak about the virgin, asking how advanced she was in age and what her stature was; finally, he also requested permission to see her. When she was summoned [Note: 1 has *Que*] at the abbess’s command, there appeared in her the bearing of a virgin and the demeanor of true modesty. Her brow was serene [Note: Thus in 1; corresponding to the following “face.”], and her beautiful face was lovely to behold: in its whiteness it was very like lilies, while in its vivid color it resembled rose petals.

When the distinguished young man saw her beauty of such magnitude, he could no longer conceal the love in his heart and earnestly requested that the virgin be betrothed to him. At this the abbess lowered her eyes and hesitated for a long time in her response, her mind uncertain. But when the young man persisted more and more in his request, the lady finally answered him in these words:

“It is not ours to give her in marriage to anyone without the counsel and consent of her parents. It is right that she should be restored to them by us with complete fidelity, since she was entrusted to our care by them. Moreover, we are uncertain whether they have decided to give her to another man in marriage, for many men distinguished in birth and appearance desired her. Although it is unknown to us which of these they wish to choose as their son-in-law [Note: “hiis” in 1], we shall nevertheless fulfill your wish; and, if it is God’s will, we shall not delay the marriage on our part, because the excellence of your lineage has often resounded in our ears, and this is no small part of the alliance: that you yourself have directed your journey to us [Note: Thus in 1 and 3; in the latter, however, the word was later erased and “ipsi” was written].”

Without delay, suitable ornaments having been honorably prepared for the virgin’s betrothal, Heinricus took the venerable virgin with him the following day into Saxony. Then Count Thietmar and the other soldiers escorted her through the cities [Note: Thus in 3; 1 has *ciuitas* without *per*] of the distinguished Duke Otto, until a wedding feast was prepared at Walohusun [Note: Walhausen in Thuringia, on the Helme, near Rosla and Sangershausen] with great honor, as befitted those who would later rule many peoples. There they enjoyed their marriage and the lawful bond of love.

Heinricus gave his venerable bride as her dowry everything pertaining to that city, with the consent of his father [Note: Compare the charter of King Heinricus I, dated September 16, [Col. 0894D] A.D. 919]. The venerable Duke Otto himself raised her as a daughter until the end of his life.

Three years after these events, the venerable man suffered temporal death (A.D. 912), and by God’s ordinance Heinricus received the honor of the dukedom. Having ascended the step of dignity, he displayed such humility toward his subjects that, if it could have happened, they would even have desired him already to possess the royal throne.

4. On the death of King Conrad. Meanwhile, while these things were taking place, a cruel illness attacked King Conrad, and a still more cruel death followed (A.D. 918). Then, by God’s arrangement, Heinricus succeeded to the royal throne (A.D. 919, April). Whether this came about by war or peace is uncertain, but there can be no doubt that it did not happen without God’s disposition [Note: “vocem inserui”: I have inserted the word].

When these matters had thus been arranged, with Christ’s help he performed many good works with watchful diligence, giving thanks to God the giver for his worldly dignity. He proved himself a most ready consoler of the poor and widows. As the praiseworthy prince advanced wonderfully, Christ increased still further the honor of his dignity, subjecting many nations to his rule: the Danes, Slavs, Bohemians, Bavarians, and very many other kingdoms that had not been subject to his predecessors.

5. On the piety of Mahthildis. Much is omitted here concerning the praises of King Heinricus, because one must hasten to the life and character of the illustrious Queen Mahthildis, who advanced from day to day by Christ’s grace in every good work, so that her grandchildren and descendants might have joy of heart as often as they found the merits of so holy a mother worthy of reading. Whatever honor and dignity may come to her future offspring is reckoned to her virtue and merits.

When the venerable queen had ascended the royal throne, illustrious in her husband’s power and still more illustrious in divine religion, she remained chaste within the bond of marriage, and nevertheless did not lack a reward close to that of virginity [Note: 1 has *nichilominus*; that is, “not at all.”] [Note: I punctuate thus; the edition places the break after *palma*]. In this way she reached toward glory through humility, so that by God’s gift she might later deserve to be welcomed into the heavenly homeland.

For the greater the power that came to her, the more devoutly she humbled herself [Note: 2 adds *jam*, “now”]; and, something that very rarely occurs, she possessed worldly dignity without pride. In public she appeared adorned with gems and silk, but inwardly she wore a more precious ornament: a heart acceptable to God. She displayed such humility toward her subjects and such charity in the manner of a mother that she was loved and honored by all.

At night she would secretly withdraw from the king’s side, leaving the royal bedchamber as though he did not know, and would enter the church near the palace [Note: Ekkehard appears to have read this thus: “As though he were unaware, she rose and entered the church near the palace”]. There she devoted herself to prayer, seeking to reconcile herself with the God whom she loved with chaste affection and served with undivided faith.

Who could doubt that the chosen servant of Christ could do such things without the king’s knowledge? He understood everything very well, but pretended not to know, because he truly knew that all her works were good and beneficial to both of them. Therefore he readily granted her consent in everything she desired. For her will began with God and brought to completion in God what it had begun.

Almost everything the world found delightful she despised for the love of Christ. She did not desire riches and did not fear poverty; her hand was always generous toward the poor, and it was rarely found empty when alms were to be distributed. No one ever approached her in sorrow without departing in joy, and whoever came to her in need obtained what he wanted.

But if she learned that someone was being oppressed by force, or imprisoned for a criminal offense, or condemned to death by popular judgment, she had no cheerfulness until she had reconciled the king’s anger. If at any time she withdrew without being heard because a popular judgment required it [Note: 2 reads *id dictante populari*, “with popular opinion so dictating”], the king silently groaned to himself that, by not fulfilling the petitioner’s wish, he had disturbed her. Often he withdrew from the judgment [Note: 2 and 3 have *egressus*, “having gone out”; 1 has *regressus*, “having returned”], as though soothing her, and left to the assessors whatever matters were legally to be punished; then, entering a church or occupied with some good work, he fulfilled in an attentive spirit the Gospel saying which the servant of Christ diligently impressed upon his ears:

“Do not judge, so that you may not be judged; for with whatever judgment you judge, you will be judged, and with whatever measure you measure, it will be measured back to you” (Matthew 7:1–2).

6. On the begetting of their children. Almighty God, who never abandons those serving Him, mercifully regarded the good works of King Heinricus and the most blessed Mahthildis, and multiplied for them the excellence of a most noble offspring.

Blessed was their offspring, which shone most beautifully in both sexes; it is neither described in detail nor wholly passed over in silence. The illustrious Otto, begotten before his father’s royal dignity, was the eldest in age, distinguished in appearance and illustrious in character. Heinricus, born after his father had assumed the royal throne, was younger in years but not inferior in the excellence of his virtue.

He possessed such great beauty that at that time he could scarcely be compared with any man. In skill, arms, and appearance he resembled his father [Note: I correct thus. 1 and the edition read “in fiducia”; Ekkehard, from whom this passage is taken, has: “In skill, courage, and appearance he resembled his father”]. In every endurance of adversity he carefully followed the renowned footsteps of his mother. For these qualities he was especially loved by the holy servant of God, as though he were her only child; cherishing him with every delight, she preferred him in affection to her other sons and desired him to possess the kingdom after the death of the illustrious King Heinricus, if God’s permission allowed her wish to be fulfilled.

From this arose the boy’s first stain of evil, and for this reason the distinguished Otto was somewhat angered against his brother; in this way envy and continual quarrelling grew between them.

Bruno, however, youngest in age but not least in moral excellence, devoted to scholarly discipline during his boyhood, labored day and night in the service of God. But the distinguished glory of their parents in their sons now forbids a lengthy discourse, because we must return to the life of King Heinricus and the most blessed Queen Mahthildis.

Their virtue cannot be enumerated as it deserves. Both were fortunate and worthy of praise; for their virtue had earned whatever good now shines forth in their grandchildren. Blessed were they, who were united not only in the flesh but also in one mind and spirit, ready for every good work! They possessed one love in Christ, equal union in goodness, a will pleasing to God, and the ability to perform what was right; equal love toward their neighbors and equal compassion toward their subjects.

O blessed man, diligent in the worship of divine service, and distinguished woman, who loved Christ the King with all her inmost being! There is therefore no doubt that they have now received a reward close to that of virginity, because conjugal chastity reigned in them, yet praiseworthy continence was not absent.

In all their actions the virtue of moderation shone forth. They rightly became rulers of the kingdom, rewarded by God with such virtues. They are blessed and will possess the rest of eternal blessedness; the alms themselves plead for them, which they distributed with generous hand to the needy while they remained in mortal life.

What more need be said? The higher the rank of dignity they had ascended, the more devoutly they rendered service to Christ.

7. On the intention to build monasteries. While they continued in great prosperity and peace, they desired, by the inspiration of almighty God, to build monasteries and to provide those dwelling there with support from the royal resources, so that the memory of themselves, their parents, and their grandchildren might be firmly preserved there forever.

Therefore, while they were considering where to lay the foundation of so great a work, they summoned the leading men of the people together (A.D. 935) and asked their advice about the region in which this could suitably be accomplished. The leaders replied that at Winithehusum [Note: 3 has *winethusum*] there were nuns lacking regular discipline, who could not remain there longer unless they were supported by royal assistance; and they advised transferring them to Quitilingoburc.

Both approved this advice and agreed to carry it out. Afterward King Heinricus went to Batfelthun, where he very often practiced the hunt. There, after a few days had passed, he was seized by illness and suffered greatly from the force of the fevers. When the pain of the illness had somewhat subsided, he set out from there for Erpesvort [Note: “erpesford” in 3], and ordered all the leaders of the kingdom to assemble there, so that they might join together and choose which of his sons they wished to possess the royal throne (A.D. 936).

Diemoth [Note: Thus in 2; 1 has “dietmoet,” Cl. “diemut,” 3 “demot”], abbess of Winethehusum [Note: “winethesusinensis” in 1], also came, summoned by the king’s command. Not forgetting her earlier desire, she asked that he consent to having the nuns subject to her transferred to Quitilingoburc. She gladly received the king’s request and willingly consented to it.

8. On the death of King Heinricus. When these matters had been arranged, King Heinricus proceeded to Imilebun [Note: 1 has “unilebun,” 2 “imileba,” 3 “imilebi”], accompanied by only a few men. There his illness returned, and not long afterward the severity of death followed (July 2).

When he felt the dissolution of his body approaching, he summoned the queen to him, discussed many private matters with her, and finally concluded his speech with these words:

“O you who have always been most faithful to us and deservedly most beloved, we give thanks to Christ that we are leaving you as our survivor. No one has taken [Note: 2 has *conjunxit*, “joined”] a wife more faithful or more praiseworthy in every good quality. Therefore give thanks that you diligently appeased us when we were angry, gave us useful counsel in every matter, often recalled us from wickedness to justice, and diligently urged us to show mercy to the oppressed by force. Now we commend you and our sons to almighty God and to the prayers of God’s elect, together with the soul that is now about to depart from the body!”

When he had said this, and the queen had likewise given him thanks [Note: 2 reads: “she gave him thanks for all the good things he had kindly bestowed upon her”], she entered the church full of sorrow and commended herself and all that was hers to God, as she had always been accustomed to do.

Meanwhile the king’s soul departed from the prison of the flesh. When the holy woman perceived from the lamentation of the people of God that the illustrious man had departed from human affairs, she prostrated herself in prayer and commended his soul to the faith of Christ.

Afterward she rose and asked whether anyone was still fasting who could sing a Mass for the soul of her lord. The priest Adeldach [Note: Thus in 2; 1 has “adeldac”], hearing this, quickly replied:

“Lady, we have not yet tasted anything.”

The venerable queen had once put on two armlets, beautifully ornamented by skilled workmanship, which had been fastened so firmly around her arms that they could not possibly be removed without a smith’s assistance. Then, touching them only with her little finger, she shook them off faster than speech, and said to the priest:

“Take this gold for yourself and sing a Mass for the souls.”

For as long as the venerable lady lived afterward, she showed that priest great favor, never forgetting that he had sung the first Mass for the soul of King Heinricus. In memory of this deed she obtained for him the episcopal dignity [Note: 2 adds: “at Bremen”] from her son Otto [Note: At the end of A.D. 936].

When the Mass for the souls had been completed, the queen entered the chamber weeping, where the dead body lay. Inside she found the royal sons weeping greatly, together with all the leading soldiers. When the illustrious queen saw this, her beautiful cheeks were covered with tears, and she fell at the feet of the lifeless body and wept most bitterly, as the venerable king had deserved from her.

But God had granted her such great grace and such praiseworthy self-control that she did not offend him through impatience, yet mourned the king’s death as befitted her. Then she called her sons to her and admonished them in these words:

“O dearest sons, diligently impress this upon your minds [Note: “Remember,” she says, “how a certain wise man exhorts us, saying: ‘At all times remember your last things, and you will never sin.’ But fear and honor Him who is always King and Lord, who formed us from the earth and makes us return to the earth, who rules in the kingdom of humanity and gives it to whomever He wishes, and sets the lowliest man over it. Do not contend, and so forth.’ Thus certain material has been omitted here]. Fear God [Note: 1 has *timere*, “to fear”] and always honor Him in all things [Note: 1 has *honorare*, “to honor”], for He is powerful enough to do such things. He is rightly called King and Lord, who displays such power over the poor and the rich.

“Cease now contending for transitory dignity; every worldly glory comes to such an end. Blessed is the one who prepares for himself things eternal and everlasting. Nor should your spirit be saddened by one of you being placed before the other. Remember well what is said in the Gospel from the mouth of Truth: ‘Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted’” (Luke 14:11).

After everything necessary for the funeral had been properly prepared, they transported the body to Quitilingoburc with the greatest honor, for he had decided to rest there; and there they solemnly committed him to burial.

Then the venerable queen summoned again to her the aforementioned abbess of the Winithehusum monastery [Note: 1 omits this phrase] and urged her to transfer the congregation subject to her there. The abbess initially refused, but afterward, when her son Otto ordered it, she consented.

9. On the election of King Otto. After the death of the illustrious King Heinricus, the leading commanders assembled and deliberated about the condition of the kingdom. Many judged that Heinricus should possess the kingdom because he had been born in the royal palace; others desired Otto to hold the honor of rule because he was older in age and more prudent in counsel.

What more need be said? By the arrangement of God’s providence, the scepter of rule passed to Otto (August 8). From that time discord, which had existed between the brothers from childhood, grew stronger and stronger. They quarreled continually and spoke nothing peaceful to one another.

Then the royal youth Heinricus endured many adversities, which his illustrious mother softened by salutary instruction. She diligently reminded him of the Scripture that says: “For whom the Lord loves, He chastises, and, as a father with his son, He takes pleasure in him” (Proverbs 3:12).

Much concerning his distresses is omitted here, because, if each matter were narrated in turn, it would seem lengthy both to those recounting it and to those reading it. At last Christ Jesus the mediator, unwilling that the brothers should remain at odds any longer, reconciled them into one through the merits of their holy mother (A.D. 939–941).

After this King Otto appointed his brother Heinricus duke over the Bavarian people (A.D. 946). Saint Bruno, the youngest in age, was still living under the discipline of literary study and, with a joyful disposition, advanced from day to day in the service of Christ.

When he had advanced in age and wisdom, the king joined him to himself through fraternal affection in the office of archchaplain. Meanwhile the venerable man Wigfridus died, he who had held the archiepiscopal see of Cologne; and, by the appointment of the heavenly Dispenser, the episcopal honor of that dignity passed to Bruno (A.D. 953).

Having ascended so great a height of power [Note: 1 has *accenso*], he did not thereby acquire any swelling of pride; [Note: Compare Ruotger, *Life of Bruno*, ch. 30; chapter 5 of the other Life is copied from our text.] rather, the holy mind of the bishop inclined itself to humility, remembering what Scripture admonishes: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclesiasticus 3:20).

His wisdom was ever watchful and his gentleness exceedingly conciliatory. He guarded the serpent’s cunning together with the law and did not lose the simple spirit of the dove. He loved the flock entrusted to him and, by the staff of discipline, rescued many from error. Some he led to better things through the conferences of constant disputation; others he filled with the desire for holy conduct through the maturity of peaceful teaching.

In speech he was gentle, in teaching humble, a most vigorous destroyer of evil and a devoted defender of truth; gracious toward the humble and severe toward the proud. Receiving some within the folds of the flock, he made sheep out of wolves; he nourished others outside the folds. Whatever he taught others, he first fulfilled himself.

In that same city he also built very many monasteries. In everything he proved a strong athlete of God and defender of the Christian faith. What wonder that sons should advance in goodness when their mother never ceased to serve God?

10. How she lived after her husband’s death. Who could comprehend in writing, or what tongue could explain, how gloriously the love of Christ began to burn in the mind of the illustrious Queen Mahthildis after the death of King Heinricus?

She remained steadfast in faith and humble in the fear of God. She remembered every discipline and retained justice together with religious devotion; she was strong for every endurance and gentle in bearing injury, ready to show mercy, and maintained fraternal peace [Note: 2 adds: “She was gentle and affable. She was rarely seen angry or disturbed; no one saw her grieving or laughing beyond measure; she condemned no one and repaid evil to no one for evil.”]. In all her actions and conversations, a praiseworthy gravity and admirable dignity appeared. She displayed herself as so honorable in modesty that many would have thought her a virgin, had they not seen [Note: 2 reads “unless they saw”] the extraordinary fruitfulness of her offspring [Note: 2 adds: “Those who saw her thought so”].

O what reverence for the fear of God! She was always devoted to prayer, and how resolutely she prepared herself to resist the devil [Note: 1 has *quam*; L has *perquam*, “very”], confidently bearing the shield of strength to fight against the sea of worldly temptation. Not entangled in transitory affairs, she followed Christ alone.

At night [Note: Widukind III, 74], when it is customary for everyone to rest, she lay down in bed as though intending to sleep, concealing in this way the purpose of her good work. She yielded briefly to sleep so that she might rather be strengthened [Col. 0899D] for serving God.

When she perceived that everyone sleeping in the chamber with her had fallen asleep, she despised the shining bed, rose secretly, and quietly awakened the chambermaid. Then she left the chamber with measured steps [Note: Thus corrected from *ingressa* in the manuscript and *ingressu* in L.] and entered the church amid the sacred celebration of hymns. She was not surrounded by the services of crowds but proceeded without human favor, while Christ’s grace accompanied her; throughout the night she did not cease serving God in prayer.

Whenever she entered the church, she never approached the altar empty-handed, neither while the king was alive nor during her widowhood. O how happily she completed the length of the night in every zeal for good works! How familiarly she cried out to God and asked forgiveness for sins! What friendship she deserved to have with the holy souls, for whom she implored eternal rest from Christ!

Before cockcrow she had completed the entire psalter, unless the shortness of the night prevented her. When she perceived the time approaching at which the nocturnal praises ought to be celebrated [Note: 1 has the plural *conveniebant*], she silently withdrew to the chamber and, without anyone knowing, lay down in bed as though she had spent the whole night sleeping there and had not moved her foot from the place.

When the signal was given for Matins, she rose without delay and hurried once more into the church, listening to the divine praises and laboring with attentive heart in the urgency of prayer. After Matins, when everyone else had gone out, she remained inside with the doors closed. Directing her eyes and hands toward heaven, she did not relax her unconquered spirit from prayer until the dawn of light had driven away the shadow of night.

Afterward she entered the chamber and reclined for a short while to rest, so that she might refresh her weary limbs and not fail in the service of Christ [Note: 2 adds: “Then, rising, she visited the sick wherever she heard of them nearby and supplied what they needed.”].

Meanwhile a multitude of poor people gathered to receive food and clothing from her hand. As soon as she perceived their cries, she rose eagerly from sleep [Note: 1 has “more often from sleep”]. Mercifully feeding the hungry and clothing the naked, she did not hesitate to clothe the members of Christ beneath the garments of the needy.

When they had been refreshed and abundantly supplied with what they needed, she put on clothing appropriate to widowhood and entered the church reverently. No one could adequately say with what devotion she was accustomed to hear Mass: meanwhile she uttered no word, but in action and dress alike she directed herself toward God.

What more need be said? From the morning hour until evening no one saw her idle from good works.

Nor should the most blessed queen’s moderation be passed over in silence, which she praiseworthily preserved in all things. She indulged neither in food nor in sleep beyond what the necessity of nature demanded.

O blessed woman, who was free from deceit and in whom piety appeared! Gentle and peaceful, most ready to show mercy to all, judging no one, condemning no one, returning evil to no one for evil, she did nothing according to her own judgment but directed everything toward the command and will of God.

All who acted wickedly hated her, while those who lived rightly loved her. She assumed great [Note: 1 has *magnas*] patience toward every injury, and although she was an eminent queen, she endured many adversities for God’s sake.

She was rarely seen angry or even disturbed; no one saw her grieving or laughing beyond measure [Note: 2 adds: “She was rarely seen angry or disturbed; no one saw her grieving or laughing beyond measure, and she condemned no one or returned evil for evil”].

She shone with the wondrous splendor of charity, was an extraordinary lover of moderation and a peaceful follower of humility. She was generally more severe toward herself but more merciful toward others, and to all she was an example of complete goodness: giving generously, showing compassion, and converting those who had gone astray.

Whenever taxes were paid to her from the revenues, she gave a tenth of them to the poor and to those serving Christ; and where she could not go on foot, she visited by sending a gift.

For the things she did are not so slight that they can all be contained in writing. If anyone had wished to count them all, he would have produced for readers a volume of immense size.

## 11. On the tribulation that Queen Mahthild endured from her sons

Then the devil’s cunning deceit, always envious of one who does good, strove by its most crafty temptation to hinder the queen beloved of God from the service of Christ. It stirred up against the venerable handmaid of Christ certain perverse men, envious of her life and virtues, who spread among her sons that she had amassed innumerable sums of money and had utterly squandered the wealth of the royal revenues.

[Note: [Col. 0901] *imperaliter* (“imperiously”) in one witness.]

[Note: [Col. 0901] *regales* (“royal”) in one witness.]

[Note: [Col. 0901] “As though she were wasting the revenues of the state, she was ruining everything,” in another witness.]

When these and similar reports were spread before King Otto, he was deeply angered and demanded back, in an imperious manner, everything that the holy woman distributed to the poor. He sent investigators everywhere, who robbed her messengers as they carried gifts to the needy and sent them back after subjecting them to abuse.

[Col. 0901C]

Although Christ’s handmaid endured these things and others like them undeservedly, what seemed more grievous to her was that Heinricus, whom she had placed above all her sons with extraordinary affection, inflicted no less serious an injury upon her. Finally, they compelled her to leave her dotal lands and to take the sacred veil.

O blessed woman, who, tested in many ways, nevertheless did not succumb, defeated by temptation! What grief must we believe was within her while she was beset on every side by such a force of tribulation? She would have borne it less painfully if Heinricus, whom she had loved exceedingly, had not agreed with his brother. Thus impious discord, which had existed between them from childhood, then united in wrongdoing those whom it had previously prevented from maintaining fraternal peace.

[Note: [Col. 0901] *gerens* (“maintaining”) in one witness.]

[Col. 0901D]

Against all these things the venerable queen displayed extraordinary patience and steadfast courage in adversity. She guarded her mouth, lest she utter anything improper, and devoted herself diligently to continual prayer, so that she might overcome the schemes of her adversaries—or rather, the injury inflicted upon her made her more steadfast. She did not forget the psalmist’s verse:

> “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man can do to me” (Psalm 117:6).

She considered lightly whatever she had to endure, provided only that she did not become worthless in Christ’s eyes. She cursed no one, but attributed to their own merits whatever distress she suffered from her hostile sons, always remembering what she had learned in Sacred Scripture:

> “Through many tribulations and afflictions we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:21).

If anyone, in her presence, lamented the calumny that she was suffering, as though wishing to ease her grief, she is said to have replied in these words:

> “King Otto calumniates us because our merits demand it. But may God know him who has stirred up against us our beloved son Heinricus, whose comfort led us to hope that we would rise above whatever sadness befell us.

[Note: [Col. 0901] *excitaverunt* (“they stirred up”) in one witness; *excitavit* (“he stirred up”) in another.] Now he opposes us, though he ought to have been our consoler. Nevertheless, we cannot endure hearing anything harsher said about him, for he is now loved by us from the depths of our hearts, although he is thought to be our enemy. What pierces us deeply is the recollection that he, once so sweet to us, is now so bitter toward us. Yet he would accomplish nothing if the king’s aid were lacking. May God spare him, lest he receive vengeance from God himself. Would that, by God’s gift and without danger to either of them, such a firm unity of peace could be established between them on our account that they might never again enter into hostility!”

[Col. 0902C]

When the holy woman saw that her sons’ grievances against her were not diminishing but increasing day by day, she abandoned whatever King Heinricus had given her as a dower and went to Enger in the western region,

[Note: [Col. 0901] “Thus she withdrew into the western regions,” in one witness.]

[Note: [Col. 0901D] Enger was therefore her ancestral home; see above, chapter 3.]

desiring to spare her hostile sons, lest they incur the anger of divine vengeance. There, with God’s cooperation, she practiced every good work no less than she had been accustomed to do.

After this, by divine dispensation, innumerable scourges came upon the king, with the triumphs of his victories reversed (944), together with other circumstances that were no less favorable.

[Note: [Col. 0901D] The author seems to allude to the illness of Liudgard, Otto’s daughter, on account of which the king granted the estate of Kinling to the monastery of Quedlinburg; 30 September 944, at Thornburg.]

[Note: [Col. 0901D] That is, “nothing less than favorable.”]

Heinricus, however, was seized by the heaviness of an illness, which also purified him from his offense. Yet heavenly mercy spared him while striking him, as though Christ were answering the prayer of his mother, who by persistent supplication entreated him for forgiveness and remission.

## 12. How she was brought back

When King Otto saw that he was prospering no more as before, he became afraid and was saddened almost to death. Then priests and the other princes, whose hearts God had enlightened, entered to the venerable Queen Edith and urged her to admonish the king to recall his mother honorably to the kingdom.

She immediately went to the king and said:

> “Let not our lord be saddened, though he has been chastised by divine scourges. Let your most holy mother be recalled, and let her possess the kingdom first, as is fitting. As we hope, all your affairs will prosper and be restored to their former condition.”

[Note: [Col. 0903] “are restored,” in one witness.]

The king, pierced by repentance and not forgetful of the guilt he had committed, recognized, by God’s inspiration, that he had sinned against his holy mother. Without delay he sent bishops, dukes, counts, and all the wisest of his soldiers, ordering that his mother be recalled with honor. He had the following letter delivered to Christ’s handmaid:

> “O venerable lady, we have already, and more than sufficiently, provoked God’s anger against us by persecuting you. We confess that we have sinned and acted unjustly against you. For God’s sake, forgive us and implore from Christ the forgiveness of remission. We willingly endure any punishment, provided only that we may enjoy your favor. We ask you, moreover, to direct your journey to us. We submit ourselves and all that is ours to your authority, and we shall also restore whatever we unjustly took from you. Nothing will bring us joy until we have been permitted to see you.”

The most blessed queen received her son’s request with a joyful heart. She consigned everything adverse that she had endured to complete oblivion, delayed no longer, and hastening her journey, arrived at Gruona.

[Note: [Col. 0903] “She hastened cheerfully to Gruona,” in one witness.]

## 13. On the reconciliation of Otto and his mother (October)

When the arrival of the venerable Queen Mahthild was announced to King Otto, he went out to meet her with a large retinue, accompanied by Queen Edith. As soon as he saw the beloved of God approaching, he leapt down from his horse, drew near, bent his knee to the ground, and asked forgiveness, saying:

> “O complete ornament of our dignity and consolation in every labor—to whose merits shall we attribute the kingdom that we possess? Inflict upon us whatever punishment you wish, provided only that we may return to the grace of reconciliation. We have already sufficiently atoned for whatever we did against you. For from the time when you departed from your dotal region, all our prosperity in war was reversed, our strength was broken, and our enemies repeatedly prevailed against us.”

In response, the venerable mother, her beautiful eyes filled with tears, immediately offered her son the kiss of peace, as though she had suffered no adversity from him at all. She consoled the suppliant’s spirit with these words:

> “My son, do not be saddened. We hope that you will obtain forgiveness from the Lord. For if the merits of our sins had not demanded it, no adversity would have confronted us from your side. May God grant you indulgence through his ineffable mercy. He is ready to have mercy on every penitent who has perfectly mourned his offenses and afterward has not committed them again.”

## 14. On the reconciliation of Heinricus

When Heinricus, a handsome young man and greatly beloved of his excellent mother, learned that his brother King Otto had reconciled their illustrious mother to himself through such satisfaction, he too was deeply pierced by repentance. He set out and, when he found the holy woman, addressed her in these words:

> “O venerable lady—and, if I may say so, dearest mother—we confess that we have grievously sinned against your maternal tenderness. Yet now we ask forgiveness, though we do not deserve it. Nevertheless, we beseech you by the soul and name of our father to permit us to return to the former state of your favor. We do not doubt that we shall obtain forgiveness from Christ if you forgive us wholeheartedly, for ever since we provoked your goodness to anger, we have been placed in the greatest danger by the heaviness of illness.”

[Col. 0904B]

When the venerable lady saw him weeping and humbly begging forgiveness, she could not bear to endure it longer, but quickly burst forth with these words:

> “My son Heinrice, do not weep; stop, my son, stop! Your mother cannot bear to hear these pleading words from you. Come nearer and give your mother a kiss. May the faithful God be reconciled to you. We love you as before, for we do not fail to recognize that the persuasion of your enemies stirred you against us.”

[Note: [Col. 0903] “Having received such satisfaction,” in one witness.]

Without delay, after receiving this satisfaction, King Otto and Duke Heinricus brought the holy woman back into her dotal lands.

[Note: [Col. 0903] “*deest*” (“is lacking”) in one witness, but present in another.]

They restored her to the first place, as was fitting. After this there was wonderful peace and tranquility between the mother and her sons, and united goodwill toward every good work. They were of one mind in consoling the poor and concordant in constructing churches and monasteries. The mother displayed extraordinary love toward her sons, and holy humility obeyed in the sons. To conclude briefly, they persevered in the stability of peace until the end of their lives, trampling down through love the devil who had recently sown the tinder of strife among them.

## 15. On the death of Queen Edith

Meanwhile it happened that the pious Queen Edith, destined to live forever, lost her present life (946, January 26). King Otto, now advanced in age,

[Note: [Col. 0903D] The king was only thirty-four years old; therefore these words should probably be referred to Mahthild, or attributed to an error by the author.]

together with his mother, built churches and monasteries. Bringing peace and judging rightly, he imitated his father’s piety in all things.

[Note: [Col. 0903D] The author appears to have assigned Edith’s death to the year 917.]

After the death of the illustrious Queen Edith, he spent three years in widowhood. He devoted himself diligently to every good work and read sacred lessons attentively. He had already shown to many, by the chastity of his widowhood and the constancy of his prayers, that he intended thereafter to abstain from marital companionship.

Then the most blessed Queen Mahthild built a monastery at Palidi,

[Note: [Col. 0904D] Pölde, near Herzberg, at the foot of the Hercynian Forest.]

gathering there a multitude of clerics,

[Note: [Col. 0905] So the manuscript; three thousand according to the *Acta Sanctorum* and Leibniz.]

for whom she generously supplied whatever was necessary.

[Note: [Col. 0905D] Compare the spurious diploma in Mader, *Antiquitates Brunsvicenses*, p. 107.]

Meanwhile Lotharius, an eminent prince of the Latins, died (950). Queen Adelheid had been married to him; she excelled in uprightness of character and nobility of lineage. A certain wicked man named Berengarius

[Note: [Col. 0905] “Berngarius,” in one witness.]

harassed her with many injuries, so that, having obtained her as his wife, he might likewise usurp dominion over the kingdom of the Latins.

When this came to the ears of the illustrious King Otto, he summoned his brother Heinricus and all the princes of the army and ordered arms to be prepared for war. He said that he intended to visit the Roman region, resist the arrogant Berengarius, and aid the oppressed widow.

Why say more? When the preparations had properly been made, they reached Italy in a prosperous campaign (951), and by God’s grace victory fell to King Otto in the defeat of King Berengarius and the rescue of Adelheid. Having accomplished these things, the king offered a sacrifice of praise to Christ with his army, for Christ had fulfilled his desire in all things and strengthened his hand against his enemies.

Afterward the king entrusted Berengarius to his brother, Duke Heinricus, to be guarded,

[Note: [Col. 0905D] Berengarius was indeed defeated in the first expedition, but was left in the kingdom; when he was captured afterward, Heinricus had already died. Leibniz.]

ordering that he be sent to the region of the Bavarians and confined there under strict guard. There he also ended his present life (964).

The king gladly took the aforesaid lady Adelheid with him through the cities of the Latins. When he saw that she was remarkably prudent and of a commendable life, he yielded his heart to love for her and joined her to himself in marriage. They remained in Italy for some time, and not long afterward departed for the region of the Saxons (951–952).

After possessing the royal throne for a long time, they were blessed by God with royal offspring. First they produced a girl, named after the illustrious Queen Mahthild. King Otto placed her in the community of nuns at Quitilingoburc, according to his mother’s wish. Afterward they produced a boy, named after his father. After his father’s death, by God’s ordinance, royal dignity came to him (955).

Whenever the most blessed lady Mahthild learned of the birth of one of her offspring, she gave thanks to Christ, to whose mercy she attributed whatever good and joy came to her.

## 16. On the illness and death of Duke Heinricus, Mahthild’s son

The venerable queen had therefore become very joyful because her sons had returned safely from the borders of Italy and the offspring of her lineage had multiplied gloriously in both sexes. But unexpectedly a great sorrow arose, which completely consumed this joy in grief, and which she did not consign to oblivion for as long as she drew the breath of mortal life.

Heinricus, the distinguished duke of the Bavarians, was seized by a severe illness. When he perceived that the heaviness of his illness was not diminishing but increasing more and more, he hastened to Palidi to see his pious mother. There he saw the holy woman for the last time and asked permission to depart for his own region.

The queen kept her sick son with her for a few days and applied every care and remedy to his illness. As the day approached on which he had decided to leave, the holy mother foretold many things to him and finally admonished him with these salutary words:

> “My dearest son, heed carefully the words of your mother and do penance for your sins, so that you may obtain forgiveness from God. For it is uncertain what this illness signifies; and, as we fear, we shall not see your desirable face again.”

[Note: [Col. 0905] “The final words of your mother to you, dear son,” in one witness.]

Besides this, she foretold many things to him through the spirit of prophecy, which subsequent events confirmed. Afterward they embraced one another and exchanged kisses, weeping profusely.

Why say more? Heinricus went to the region of the Bavarians and there suffered from illness for many days, until, at God’s command, his soul departed from his body and, as is hoped, entered the gate of paradise (955, November 1). When these things had happened, the body of the illustrious duke was buried in the city of Regensburg.

Then the venerable lady Judit, joined in lawful marriage to an illustrious man, sent messengers to announce the grievous news to the pious mother. When they came by a direct route to Quitilingoburc and announced the duke’s sad death to the nobles, everyone remained uncertain throughout the day as to how this should be peacefully reported to the holy woman.

The next day, after she had heard Mass, when she had taken a book of dialogue in her hand and was attentively engaged in reading it, Richburch, her faithful attendant, entered and reported that messengers had come from the region of the Bavarians.

She was immediately shaken by grief, as though already aware of the evil that had occurred, and said:

> “Order them to be summoned, so that we may learn how the illness of our son is faring.”

When they had entered and permission had been given for them to speak openly (Virgil, *Aeneid* I.520), they greeted the queen but still said nothing sad. She asked them many questions about her son, her heart anxious, whether his illness had become milder or how his affairs were prospering.

The envoys, however, answering little about these matters, presented very sorrowful letters containing the cause for which they had come to report. When the glorious queen learned from the letters that her beloved son had departed this life, pallor appeared on her face, a cold tremor ran through all her limbs, and the book she held in her hands fell and received her face as it fell.

When the sharpness of her grief had somewhat cooled, she immediately burst into tears and spent the entire day weeping. Because of the bitterness of her sorrow, she tasted no food that day.

Then she summoned the nuns to the church and exhorted them to implore the Lord’s mercy for the deceased. She herself first bent her knees and poured out this prayer for the soul of her dear son:

> “O Lord God almighty, have mercy on the soul of your servant, whom you have commanded to depart from this world. We beseech you, remember that he lived joyfully only very rarely and spent almost all the time of his mortal life in distress.”

After this she rose from prayer and proceeded at a measured pace to the tomb of King Heinricus. Bending her head over it, she spoke through tears:

> “O our lord, how much happier you have been than we, since you did not await this bitter sorrow in the course of mortal life! Now, as we hope, you rejoice in rest and care nothing for our disturbance. Whenever we brought the bitter day of your death to mind, we breathed again through this one consolation: that the life of our dearest son still survived, for in face, name, and appearance he resembled you most closely.”

[Note: [Col. 0907] *quod* (“that”) in one witness; *quid* (“what”) in another.]

[Note: [Col. 0907] *ore* (“in face”) in the text; *voce* (“in voice”) in another witness.]

[Note: [Col. 0907] “What hope and consolation do we have now, except in God?” is added in one witness.]

On this same day she laid aside her courtly garments, which she had worn as an adornment during her widowhood. After the death of the memorable King Heinricus, she had regularly worn scarlet

[Note: [Col. 0907D] Ekkehardus writes that she wore a scarlet garment. Widukind III.74 shows that *coccinum* (“scarlet”) should be understood in this sense, where he says that Mahthild diminished nothing of her royal dignity.]

of a single color, not in public but beneath a linen garment, and for the beauty of her adornment she wore a small amount of gold before her. She laid all this aside then and afterward appeared dressed in mourning garments.

From that time on she wished to hear no one singing secular songs or to see anyone engaged in games. She heard only sacred songs taken from the Gospels or other holy writings, and she took special delight in having songs sung to her about the life or passion of the saints.

[Note: [Col. 0907] One witness adds: “singing secular songs.”]

She rejected the other delights of the world and devoted herself with complete attention solely to divine service.

[Note: [Col. 0907] *oblectamenta* (“pleasures”) in another witness.]

[Note: [Col. 0907] The text reads *tota* (“complete”); one witness has *tuta* (“safe, secure”).] She loved God in all things and above all things, placing nothing before his love.

[Note: [Col. 0907] One witness reads: “Indeed, loving God from her very cradle.”]

[Note: [Col. 0907] One witness reads *nil* (“nothing”) instead of *nihil* (“nothing”).]

[Note: [Col. 0907] One witness adds an interpretation that may be inferred from the wise praises of her virtues: “For, as blessed Gregory says: ‘The love of God is never idle; for if it exists, it performs great things. But if it refuses to act, it is not love.’”]

In her shone the gold of justice, the jewel of mercy, lovable dignity, admirable honesty, and speech that was restrained and suitably uttered at the proper time. She never kept silent about anything that was fitting for her to say. She cared for foreigners, widows, and orphans as a mother does for her children. In everything she did, the moderation proper to justice was not lacking.

## 17. With what care she bestowed alms upon the needy

It is difficult to enumerate how devoted the venerable queen was to the generosity of almsgiving. Twice each day she refreshed the needy with every kind of exquisite food.

[Note: [Col. 0907] *accederet* (“approached”) in the text; *accideret* (“happened”) in Erath.]

Moreover, whenever she approached the royal table, she ordered foreigners and the needy to be summoned and devoutly distributed to them the finest food that was set before her, believing that she was feeding Christ under the appearance of the poor.

If a monastery was present, she sent three portions from the table to those serving Christ and lying sick.

[Note: [Col. 0907] One witness reads *rex* (“king”); Leibniz reads *ter* (“three times”); another witness reads *tres superpositiones* (“three additional servings”).]

[Col. 0908A]

If no monastery was present, she offered these same portions to other needy people.

What wonder is it that she was generous and kind toward human beings, when every day she provided for the rooster that announces the light of day and rouses all the faithful to Christ’s service? Nor did she forget the birds that resound in the trees during summer. She ordered her servants to throw crumbs of bread beneath the trees, so that if any bird were sitting above, it might find nourishment there in the name of the Creator.

Wherever she traveled, she ordered candles to be carried beside her carriage, so that they might be distributed to individual oratories, along with food with which the poor encountered on the road might be refreshed.

If she was occupied with reading or chanting psalms, so that she herself could not see those passing by, or if she had inclined her head in sleep—for she was accustomed to pass the night wakeful in good works—she instructed the nun Richburga, who served her, to watch carefully that no poor person passed by without being greeted or without being refreshed by her generosity.

[Note: [Col. 0907] One witness lacks “without.”]

If, through her negligence, some needy person passed by without receiving food, the queen immediately raised her head from sleep, as though filled with the spirit of prophecy, ordered the carriage to stop and the needy person who had passed to be called back, and gave him food or whatever else was necessary.

Afterward, somewhat moved, she admonished the nun with salutary words to observe more carefully in the future whatever had been entrusted to her charge. The voice of the needy never sounded vainly in her presence, nor did she pass by deaf to it.

[Note: [Col. 0907] Another witness adds: “but she gave the person whatever was necessary.”]

The practice of mercy was no less abundant than the crowd from the common people. There was never a lack of those who asked, nor did what she could give run out.

In whatever city she wintered,

[Note: [Col. 0907] Another witness reads: “In whatever place.”]

fire burned throughout the entire night in every dwelling that was there, and also beneath the open sky,

[Note: [Col. 0907] “under the heavens,” in another witness.]

so that anyone in need might warm himself there, or so that anyone who wandered in the darkness of night might see the light and not stumble.

In addition to her daily generosity in almsgiving, she celebrated Saturday with exceptional honor. From the first hour, indeed from the very dawn of light, she was never free from good works. In the morning she ordered a bath to be prepared and ordered the poor and foreigners to be washed.
