Sometimes, when she could withdraw from the crowds of the people, she herself entered secretly and with her own hands washed the dirt from each person. The queen, who commanded many people, served the poor there as though she were a servant.

If she was prevented from entering because the crowds surrounded her, she sent in her attendants whom she knew to be especially trustworthy in their fidelity, so that they might supply the needy with what was necessary and serve them humbly in her place.

When they came out of the bath, she brought them all into a room, giving food to the hungry and clothing to the naked, for she did not doubt that the members of Christ were being clothed beneath the garment bestowed upon the needy.

To those suffering from illness who could not come to her, she sent fruits and whatever seemed best among the royal foods. It often happened, by God’s grace, that someone who had tasted no food for ten days received both nourishment and health through her merits.

Nor do I think that it should be left unsaid why she guarded Saturday with such reverence. First, because of the vigil of the Lord’s resurrection, which is celebrated on that day throughout the world; and then because the soul of the venerable King Heinricus was released from the body on that same day and, as is hoped, entered the gate of paradise.

As long as the holy woman lived, she diligently observed the eighth, thirtieth, and anniversary day of the illustrious king. Let no one doubt that her good works, which she performed on Saturday with such devotion, were pleasing to God; for she too departed from this world on that same day and passed from labor to rest.

## 18. That she never indulged in idleness; and concerning the bread thrown from the mountain to a poor man

On feast days, when it is not permitted to engage in manual labor, she read or listened attentively to those reading, and she retained in memory whatever Sacred Scripture commanded.

[Note: [Col. 0909] Ekkehardus, following Widukind III.74, reports that she taught her attendants letters and continues: “For she herself also knew letters, which, while still a young girl in the monastery of Hervord, she had learned from her grandmother, the mother of Theodericus, abbess of that place.” as was stated above, chapter 2.]

On ordinary days she devoted herself to psalmody and divine reading, and no less diligently to manual work. If she was ever prevented by the varied speech of the people from carrying out her customary devotion to divine work, at least at the hour of refreshment, standing before the table, she tasted no food until she had done some work, remembering what the Apostle says:

> “If anyone will not work, neither let him eat” (2 Thessalonians 3:10).

But the mercy of almighty God, unwilling to allow the merit of the venerable queen to remain hidden any longer, worked miracles through her, so that it might become plainly known to all how pleasing to him was the life of one who served him.

Once, while she was celebrating the anniversary of King Heinricus at Quitilingoburc with great ceremony, as she was always accustomed to do, such a multitude of poor people gathered that they could not be counted.

The queen rejoiced at their arrival and ordered some to be stationed on the summit of the mountain and the others at the bottom of the valley. She herself served those eating on the mountain and entrusted the others to her stewards.

When she had distributed all the royal food and abundantly supplied everything necessary with a generous hand, those sitting in the valley had still not received twisted bread.

[Note: [Col. 0909] “The twisted loaves that she used to give,” in another witness.]

Standing at the top of the mountain, she suddenly seized a loaf, made the sign of the cross over it, invoked Christ’s name, and threw it from the lofty summit. Rolling from place to place among the dense rocks and hedges, it arrived intact in the lap of a certain poor man, to whom she had intended it to be given, in the presence of a great multitude of people who had witnessed the same miracle.

For this the most blessed queen humbly gave thanks to Christ, knowing that it had occurred by his gift and power. But she was also made known by another miracle in the same city.

[Note: [Col. 0909] “In the same castle,” in another witness.]

## 19. On the hind that had swallowed a flask

It had been the custom of the holy lady every day to present to the priest at Mass an offering of bread and wine for the welfare and benefit of the whole holy Church.

One day, after Mass had ended, a golden flask was carelessly lost. In it the holy woman had offered wine for the sacrifice. Her attendant Richburc and the other women serving her were greatly frightened and searched everywhere, but they could not find it.

The following day, while Mass was being sung, Christ’s handmaid asked the aforesaid nun for the customary flask. She, flushed with shame, said that it had been taken away by theft.

After Mass the queen left the church somewhat troubled. Immediately she encountered a certain young hind, tamed within the monastery enclosure.

[Note: [Col. 0909] “A fawn,” in another witness.]

When she saw it, she called it to her with a gentle gesture and adjured it by the name of Christ to return to her the vessel that it had swallowed.

The beast obeyed the power of the one commanding it and, quicker than words can say, vomited up the flask. It rightly obeyed her command, since she had always been obedient to God.

All who were present gave thanks to God because the queen received the vessel unharmed from the brute animal, although she had neither seen it swallowed nor heard of it from anyone.

## 20. On the prophecy of the holy woman of God

She was not lacking the gift of prophecy, which shone forth through the efficacy of signs.

At one time the royal offspring gathered at Fraso.

[Note: [Col. 0909D] Frose on the Elbe.]

The royal boys came together: namely, Otto, the son of the emperor Otto, and Heinricus, the son of Duke Heinricus of the Bavarians. Just as the venerable queen had loved this Heinricus more than her other children, so she placed his son Heinricus, her little grandson, before her other grandsons in affection.

Mahthild the venerable was sitting at the royal table for a meal, together with Queen Adelheid,

[Note: [Col. 0909] “Adilheida,” in one witness.]

while the boys stood nearby, playing children’s games. Then Heinricus, who was dearer to the holy woman, came closer to the table. Gazing attentively at his excellent grandmother, he familiarly leaned against her lap, as though desiring a kiss from her.

The venerable queen gladly received him, embraced him in her arms, and said:

> “O Lord God almighty, we give thanks and praise to your goodness, who have preserved this little grandson for us unharmed, although a dark day of death took away his father. But we give you thanks because you did not wish this name to be erased from our family. We beseech you, preserve him safely for us as long as you wish to keep us in mortal life, so that at least in name and voice he may imitate our beloved son Heinricus.”

Then the venerable Queen Adelheid also said:

> “How desirable is this boy’s appearance, and how beautiful his face to behold! Where, then, shall a maiden be found who suits him in beauty and character? We have a little daughter named Hemma. Let us reserve her for him, if it pleases God and you, so that this desirable son-in-law may be joined to us.”

[Note: [Col. 0911D] She married King Lotharius of the Gauls in 966.]

Christ’s handmaid, however, remained silent and hesitated for a long time before answering. After drawing long sighs, she gave this reply:

> “May such sadness never come upon you from our side. It is better for your daughter to join herself to a more fortunate man. This name possessed honor only as long as our lord Heinricus lived. But after it passed to his descendants, it was never free from misfortune. Why should we speak of the hardships and tribulations endured by his father? Yet what must happen to this boy still lies in the disposition of God. We hope, however, that this name will not disappear from our family before a little grandson is born from this boy’s seed, one who will be raised to royal dignity.”

[Col. 0911B]

Who, then, could doubt that the prophecy of Christ’s chosen handmaid has now been fulfilled in the most Christian King Heinricus? He received the summit of rule without force or arms and now holds the honor of his dignity in the tranquility of peace.

O King Heinrice, rightly worthy of praise, bring again and again to your mind the prophecy of the distinguished queen, and recognize that you have ascended the throne of such dignity through her intercession and merit.

May the Lord God almighty, who chose you and granted you the summit of honor without force, give you an abundance of his blessing and crown you with the crown of justice. May he make you gentle toward the just and terrifying to the impious, so that you may strengthen those who pursue justice through the meekness of gentleness and frighten the erring through the severity of justice.

May the angel of the Lord always go before you, accompany you, and follow after you; may he direct all your acts and crush all your enemies beneath your feet, so that you may live for a long time for the advancement of holy Church and afterward receive life without end.

The author of this discourse would not fail to wish for you, glorious king, still more perpetual happiness and worldly prosperity, if he did not fear that the envious would attribute it more to the reproach of flattery than to the love of truth.

Many more things remain to be said about you in praise, but these must be omitted, so that the mouths of the envious may be closed.

[Note: [Col. 0911] One witness continues: “Who would doubt that this prophecy was fulfilled in Heinricus of Babenberg, the later son of this boy, who, after administering the duchy of Bavaria most successfully, when Emperor Otto III, the great-grandson of this same Mahthild, had died, himself, likewise her great-grandson, received the imperial crown? Moreover, the same handmaid of God …”]

## 21. On the anointing of King Otto

We must return to what came before, so that what has been begun may be brought to completion. When the innumerable virtues of Queen Mahthildis were being proclaimed far and wide, her son King Otto was summoned to the kingdom of Rome by the bishop of the Apostolic See, amid extraordinary renown for his glory, so that he might receive the glory of the imperial crown and rule the Romans (961).

Then, commending the kingdom and his little son Otto to his pious mother and to Archbishop Wilhelm, he took with him the courageous hearts of his men and, with Christ as his leader, hastened toward Rome, as the pope had commanded; Queen Adelheid accompanied him. When he had arrived at the chair of Saint Peter, he received the imperial crown together with his wife, as a gift from Christ, and the entire Roman people voluntarily subjected themselves to his rule. They paid tribute to him and, after him, to his other descendants (962, February 2).

Meanwhile the venerable queen was distressed between hope and fear, uncertain whether prosperity or adversity had befallen her son; for his safety she continually offered sacrifice to God through persevering prayer and generous almsgiving. At that time she also built a monastery in the city of Northusun [Note: Witness 1 consistently reads “Northusanensis”; witness 2, “in the fortress of Northusun”], with the consent of her little grandson Otto, for the soul of King Heinric and of her dearest son, whom she had named after his father and whom she had borne in the aforesaid city. There she gathered a little band (*turmula*) of sisters serving God and the blessed Virgin Mary [Note: Witness 2 has the same reading].

Meanwhile it was reported to the Emperor Otto at Rome that his most devoted mother was exceedingly saddened by his absence. Inflamed by wondrous love and desiring to see the woman beloved by Christ, he immediately left Rome and arrived at the city of Cologne, where his brother Bruno held the archiepiscopal office (965, May–June).

There the holy and venerable queen came to meet her son, together with her little grandson, whom Otto had entrusted to her when he was departing for Rome; she was also accompanied by the noble boy Heinric, whom she loved in place of a son after her own son, the duke of Bavaria, had departed this life. Queen Gerbirc also came, a daughter of the holy God.

There the royal assembly exchanged their final embraces, and there they received the last words of their conversation from one another, by the disposition of divine mercy. For afterward they did not see one another again in this mortal body, but, as we hope, they now rejoice together in eternal rest.

## 22. How she kissed the footprints of her son Otto

Thus the illustrious queen was first honorably received by the emperor, by her son Archbishop Bruno, and by the others who had gathered there. She rejoiced that she had seen her sons and grandsons, and she offered praise and thanks to Christ for the safety of them all.

After they had greeted one another, they entered a chamber and engaged in intimate conversation. Meanwhile Bishop Balderic entered [Note: Bishop of Utrecht, not, as Ekkehard maintains, of Liège]—he had been the tutor of Archbishop Bruno during the reign of King Heinric—and, bowing his head to everyone, blessed the royal assembly.

Afterward he addressed the holy lady Mahthildis in particular:

> “Rejoice, venerable queen, honored by God with such gifts. Now you see your sons and their sons! Truly fulfilled in you is the verse of the psalmist who says: ‘And may you see the sons of your sons’ (Psalm 127:6).”

The queen, for her part, gave thanks to God, as she had always been accustomed to do. [Note: One witness adds: “because the Lord blessed her so greatly from Zion.”]

Then she spoke to her sons and grandsons about the construction of the monastery at Northusun, and about the fear that troubled her [Note: Witness 1 reads “as though”]: that she might not be able to complete the work she had begun. At last, bathed in tears, she said:

> “This monastery, which we are building, is, as we believe, our final work. Our age is frail for labor; moreover, we have distributed possessions and material resources among the other monasteries. Therefore we commend to all of you that you complete the work we have begun, because we began it for the soul of our lord and dearest son Heinric, as well as for the stability of the kingdom and the safety of all of you.” [Note: One witness reads “of the men” instead of “of all of you.”]

To this Emperor Otto replied before them all:

> “May God prosper your undertakings. Our assistance will not be lacking. Indeed, we exhort our son Otto and our other grandsons to provide it with support for as long as they live.”

Afterward they proceeded together to the city of Northusun to see the community itself. Then the queen, beloved of God, summoned the nuns [Note: This is the editor's correction; witness 1 reads “ordered [them] to be summoned”] and commended them all to the emperor. He received them all with a calm spirit and cheerful countenance and commended them to God, saying:

> “May the holy Virgin Mary, Mother of God, heavenly queen [Note: Witness 2 reads “queen of heaven”], receive them mercifully and always preserve them through the love of her Son, so that they may love God above all things and serve him with their whole mind—not out of a desire for human praise, but solely from the desire for eternal reward.” [Note: Another witness reads “these servants of hers” and adds “of our Lord Jesus Christ”; another reads “retribution” instead of “reward.”]
>
> “We also ask that our sons and grandsons be moved by such mercy toward these nuns that, as long as even one spark of our offspring remains, they may never lack the support of consolation.”

Then, for the salvation of himself and of his parents and nephews, he repeatedly confirmed all these things which the holy woman had previously granted with the consent of her grandson; moreover, he added what his mother desired. [Note: Witness 2 reads: “Immediately he confirms with his own hand what …”] They then remained in the same city for seven days. The holy queen commended many things to her son, as though she would not see him again in this mortal body. [Note: One witness reads “months” instead of “seven days.”]

When the day dawned on which the king had decided to depart, they rose in the morning and prolonged their conversation, weeping greatly. Afterward they entered the church together to hear Mass, and the venerable queen feigned cheerfulness in her face, while suppressing great sorrow in her heart.

When Mass had ended, she again addressed her son in these words:

> “My dearest son, diligently bring to mind everything that in this place we have entrusted to your keeping. [Note: Witness 2 reads “of” instead of “in.”] We often lived here happily, and God rescued us from the danger of childbirth. In this city we bore your brother Heinric, whom we loved exceedingly because he bore his father’s name; your sister Gerbirg was also born here.
>
> “Therefore, because through the intercession of the holy Virgin Mary we twice passed safely through the dangers of childbirth in this place, we laid the foundation of this monastery in her honor [the words ‘in her honor’ are absent in one witness], especially for the soul of your father and brother and for your safety, as we mentioned above. Therefore, whenever you remember these things [Note: Witness 1 reads “whenever you remember whom”], it is fitting that you show greater compassion for those who dwell in this place on our account.
>
> “Moreover, as we believe, here we are receiving the final words of our conversation with one another. What more is there to say? Let this final sight of your mother be a reminder of this monastery.” [Note: One witness reads: “Let this monastery be a frequent reminder.”]

Then the emperor, moved in his heart, promised to fulfill everything she had requested. Afterward they left the church together and stopped before the door. They embraced one another, and the tears of both drenched their faces.

After they had exchanged kisses, everyone who was present began to shed tears. The queen, standing in the very doorway, watched her departing son go to his horse with a clear gaze. Then she entered the church and hurried to the place where the emperor had stood during Mass. Bending her knees, she kissed in tears the footprints of her departing son.

When Count Witigo and the other soldiers who had remained there saw this, they were overcome with groaning and went out, reporting it to the emperor. He immediately leapt down from his horse and returned to the church, groaning. When he entered, he found her still praying and weeping bitterly in the same place. He at once fell prostrate on the ground and said:

> “O venerable lady, by what service can we repay you for these tears?”

They approached one another again and said very little in tearful voices. Finally the venerable queen spoke as follows:

> “What benefit is there in remaining longer? Although unwilling, we are nevertheless compelled to be separated from one another; and by looking at one another we shall not lessen our grief but rather increase it. [Note: Witness 1 reads “you” for “we.”] Go now in the peace of Christ. You will no longer see my face in mortal flesh.
>
> “As we believe, we have omitted nothing, but have entrusted to your keeping everything that we carried in our minds. Grant only this gift to my soul: diligently bring this place to your remembrance.”

The emperor then departed and traveled through other cities of the region of Thuringia (966). Later he went again to Rome, accompanied by his son (967).

## 22–23. On Mahthildis’s illness

Now the mournful hour was approaching in which God willed to release the soul of the illustrious queen from the prison of the flesh, so that she might receive the reward of her labor and the glory of eternal recompense. [Note: Witness 2 adds: “Thus blessed M., now worn out by old age—for she was no less than seventy years old, etc.” Certainly, having married in 909, she was at least seventy-five years old in 968.]

For an entire year she suffered from a serious illness, yet she continued to visit the royal residences, although the strength of her body was failing. When she had traveled through the cities of Saxony and had supplied each monastery with whatever was necessary, she returned to the city of Northusun, which she loved exceedingly, in order to see Richburg [Note: Witness 1 reads “Rigburg”], whom she had recently appointed abbess. As soon as she arrived, she ordered her to be summoned and asked many questions about the community entrusted to her.

Afterward she herself entered the monastery and carefully investigated with what zeal each sister had been trained in discipline. For from the time she had built her first monastery, she had always maintained this custom: she herself entered the school and attentively examined the studies of each person. It had been especially pleasing to her to see or hear of anyone’s progress. [Note: One witness reads “of each man” instead of “of each person.”]

She remained in the same city from the time of autumn [Note: Witness 1 spells it *autumpni*] until the feast of Christ’s Nativity. After the solemnity of the holy apostle Thomas (December 21), she again summoned the abbess and held this conversation with her:

> “O you who have always been faithful to us and especially knowledgeable about our labors! We now recognize, from the frequency of our illness, that the day of our dissolution is approaching. Therefore it is necessary for us to hasten from here, lest the final day of this present life overtake us here.”

The abbess, overcome by sobbing and tears, was initially silent. A little later she said:

> “O beloved lady, what does this prophecy mean? Why do you foretell such a sorrowful misfortune to us poor women, or to whom are you leaving us desolate? For we hope that, with God’s favor, nothing of this kind will yet occur.
>
> “But because it is uncertain in what direction this illness of yours will turn, we humbly ask you to remain here for some time, until we see whether, by God’s gift, your illness is eased. If grave misfortune should occur—if death, hostile to our salvation, should deprive us of your life—at least we may draw breath from this consolation: that your beloved body may rest here with us.”

Then the queen, beloved of God, gave this answer:

> “We had already considered these things long ago. How pleasing it would have been to us for our body to be buried in this place, if it had been predestined by God, so that our sons Otto and our other grandsons might show you greater care!
>
> “But we fear that this cannot be allowed, because our lord Heinric rests at Quitilingoburc; beside him we ought to be committed to burial and await the final day. If our death should occur in this place, your spirit would be constricted even more severely, and you would incur the charge of contempt if our dead body were taken away from you while you were still alive.
>
> “These reasons therefore urge us to hasten from here. What more is there to say? Always love God, and admit no other beloved besides him; devote yourselves continually to his service. Be watchful in prayer and persevere in your holy purpose.
>
> “Remember the souls for whom we founded this monastery, as well as our grandsons who are still living in mortal life, and remember us also; for you will see no one more favorably disposed toward you. [Note: Witness 2 reads: “For you will be able to find no better concern for the salvation of our souls.”]
>
> “We commend you to God, the Father of orphans, and to the holy Virgin Mary, and to the intercession of the saints whose relics we have placed here. Let not your heart be troubled, but hope in God. Although we shall be absent from you in body, we shall always be present to you in love.”

## 24. On the queen’s anointing

The queen, beloved of God, therefore departed from the city of Northusun on the eleventh day before the Kalends of January (December 22), leaving the nuns who remained there in the deepest sorrow. She had always loved them with a mother’s affection, and because of their grief they would not see her again in this mortal body—she who had been their honor, joy, glory, and adornment.

She then hastened to Quitilingoburc, where God had foreordained that her holy soul should be released from the prison of the flesh. There she was seized by an extremely serious illness and remained sick until the day of her death (968).

As the day of her dissolution approached, she ordered the aforementioned abbess Richburg to be summoned. Since all her secrets were then known to Richburg, the queen asked her to await the day of her death there and, at the end, to minister faithfully to her as before.

When the holy lady perceived that her final day had arrived, she distributed to bishops and priests all the revenue that she had not yet devoted to the needs of the poor, and with a generous hand divided it among the monasteries. She kept in mind what the Gospel Scripture commands [Note: So also Widukind, III.74]:

> “Sell everything that you have and give to the poor” (Matthew 19:21).

Since an innumerable multitude was flocking to visit the sick queen, Wilhelm [Note: Witness 1 reads *Wilhelmus*, here and below], archbishop of the See of Mainz, also came. Although, by God’s command, he was destined to die first, he approached the holy woman to offer words of consolation: the man about to die visited the woman about to die, and, unaware of his own death, consoled one who would live only a little longer than he.

When the blessed queen saw the bishop, she received him with a cheerful countenance and very familiar speech:

> “We do not doubt that God’s will has directed you to us now, for no one could be more familiar to us or more acceptable for this task. [Note: Witness 1 reads “to be” for “was.”] Our hope has been taken away that our beloved son Bruno might remain alive until he saw our final moments and committed our body to the earth.
>
> “Now first hear our confession and grant us absolution, by the authority that has been handed down to you by God and by Saint Peter, chief of the apostles. Then enter the church and celebrate Mass for our sins and negligences, for the soul of our lord King Heinric, and for all Christ’s faithful, living and dead.” [Note: One witness lacks the word “faithful.”]

When her confession had been completed, the bishop entered the church and fulfilled everything the queen had requested. After Mass, he entered the chamber again and, repeating the rite, granted her remission of sins. Then he anointed her with sacred oil and refreshed her with the most holy mystery of the body and blood of Christ.

He remained there for three days, because he believed that her death was imminent. On the fourth day, when he understood that the day of her dissolution had not yet arrived, he approached the sick queen and asked permission to leave, weeping with inconsolable grief because he perceived that her illness was not being eased. Yet if the severity of his sorrow allowed his spirit any respite, he ought not to grieve but rather to rejoice, because the soul of God’s holy woman was about to depart from the body and, as it was believed, pass from labor into rest.

The holy lady and the bishop spoke together at length about many matters, which would take too long to enumerate. Meanwhile the queen summoned Abbess Richburg and asked whether anything remained that she could give to the bishop.

Richburg replied:

> “What could remain for you, most beloved of God? Everything you possessed has been distributed for the needs of the poor.”

But the queen said:

> “Where are the cloaks that we ordered to be hidden for our burial? Let them be brought to us, so that they may be given to our nephew as a pledge of love. For he needs them before we do, as we think, since he is about to undertake a very difficult journey.
>
> “The condition of unstable fortune is always uncertain: it is unknown where it may turn or into what hardships it may drag wretched human beings. When our death occurs, this proverb may be fulfilled in us, which is commonly spoken by the people: ‘Relatives often find both a wedding garment and a mourning garment.’”

While the queen was saying this, the abbess arrived carrying the cloaks. The queen took them and gave them to the bishop, saying:

> “Let these gifts of ours be memorials.” [Note: One witness reads: “Let them be defenses”; another: “May this gift of charity from me be a reminder to you.”]

When the bishop had received them, he gave thanks, blessed her, and departed. Turning silently to those standing around him, he said:

> “From here we are going to Radulveroth, and we are leaving one of our clerics here. If our lady should die, let him quickly return to us and announce it, so that we may come again and commit her body to the earth with fitting honor.” [Note: One witness reads “from here” instead of “here.”]

The queen raised her head and, as though the bishop had said these things directly to her, replied:

> “There is no need for him to be left here. Let him depart with you; you need him more in the company of your journey. Go in the peace of Christ, wherever his will shall ordain.”

## 25. On the death of the bishop

The bishop then departed for Radulveroth and, after receiving a medicinal potion there, died suddenly (March 2). Messengers went to Quitilingoburc and reported this.

Everyone was uncertain how the news should be communicated to the queen, lest the severity of her illness be increased. But the venerable servant of Christ, as though illumined by the spirit of prophecy, smiled through her tears and said:

> “Why are you murmuring among yourselves? Why do you wish to conceal this sorrowful misfortune from us? We know that Bishop Willehelm has departed from this world, and this is a great addition to our illness. Order the church bells to be rung and the poor to be gathered, so that they may receive alms which will intercede with God for his soul.”

After this, she lived for twelve more days.

## 26. How she consoled her people

On Holy Saturday (March 14), the day on which the servant of Christ was to depart from the world, as soon as she perceived that dawn was breaking, she instructed everyone staying with her in the chamber to rise from sleep, summon the priests and nuns, and carry out whatever needed to be done.

When an innumerable multitude of both sexes had gathered, the holy woman of God ordered that no one be prevented from entering. Once everyone had come in, she instructed them with salutary admonitions, saying:

> “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice before him with trembling; embrace discipline, lest the Lord become angry and you perish from the righteous way” (Psalm 2:11–12).
>
> “Turn away from evil and do good, so that at your final hour your souls may be rescued from the devil’s snares and eternal rewards may be granted to you by God.”

After this she ordered everyone to depart in the peace of Christ except those who were needed to minister to her.

Then she summoned her granddaughter, Abbess Mahthildis, daughter of Emperor Otto, and gave her salutary admonitions: that she should be devout and humble, prudent and watchful; that she should guard the flock entrusted to her; and that she should rarely leave the monastery, lest, becoming devoted to worldly affairs, she be hindered from Christ’s service.

She also placed in her hand a register in which the names of deceased nobles had been written. She commended to her the soul of her lord King Heinric, and commended her own soul and those of all the faithful whose memory she recalled.

Finally Abbess Richburg came forward in sorrow. Bending her knee to the ground, she embraced the queen’s feet with tears and said:

> “My dearest lady, to whom are you leaving this desolate community, over which you appointed me, unworthy as I am, abbess? It is difficult for me to guard the flock entrusted to me, because your support will be absent.”

The holy queen, deeply moved by these words, said:

> “We commend you to the supreme Defender. We are not leaving you to strangers, but to our son Otto and our other grandsons.”

Richburg replied:

> “Our minds are uncertain, my lady, as to where their disposition will turn.”

When the abbess wept bitterly and sought words of consolation, the queen, wishing to ease her sorrow, said:

> “Where should our hope be directed, where should our spirit be guided, except toward God? ‘Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you’ (Luke 12:31).
>
> “We believe that our son Otto, mindful of his earlier promise, will provide you consolation. But whoever, on our behalf, tears away or diminishes by unjust despoiling any ecclesiastical possession entrusted to you for your needs should consider what answer he will give to God. On the other hand, whoever fortifies or increases it will receive from God, the faithful rewarder, a worthy recompense.”

## 27. How she died

After these words she ordered the priests and nuns to come nearer, so that they might hear her confession and ask remission from God on her behalf. When this had been done, she ordered Mass to be celebrated and Christ’s body to be brought to her, so that through communion in the sacred mystery she might more securely escape the injury of the crafty enemy.

When all these things had been duly performed, she instructed those standing beside her to chant the psalms vigilantly and read the Gospel until her soul should depart from the body at God’s command.

After this she spoke no word. With her eyes open and her hands raised, she directed her mind and spirit toward heaven. As the ninth hour approached, she ordered a hair shirt to be placed on the ground and her dying body to be laid upon it. With her own hands she placed ashes on her head, saying:

> “It is not fitting for a Christian to die except in haircloth and ashes.”

Then, fortifying herself with the sign of the holy cross, she fell asleep in the Lord in peace and rest, on the second day before the Ides of March (March 14).

As could be established with complete accuracy, the soul of God’s holy woman departed from the body at that very hour of the day in which she had always been accustomed, during the days of Lent, to refresh the poor in the name of the Lord. [Note: One witness adds: “that is, at the ninth hour.”]

When they had washed the body and carried it to the church, messengers from Queen Gerburg, the daughter of the venerable lady Mahthildis, arrived, bringing a pall embroidered with gold, suitable for covering the bier.

Thus the prophecy of Christ’s chosen servant was fulfilled in every respect, both concerning the departure of Archbishop Willehelm and concerning the mourning garment.

## 28. On her burial

They therefore buried her body in the basilica of Saint Servatius, beside the tomb of King Heinric [Note: The tomb is still visible], with great honor. She herself had decreed that she should rest there and await the day of judgment.

Thus she departed from the body, noble by birth and nobler in character and holiness, aged and full of days, leaving a good example to all her descendants.

She had lived her present life with honor, and with honor she departed from the world. Whatever time she had lived, she brought to completion in good works. She should not be considered dead, for, as we hope, the crown of righteousness has been given back to her. While living in this world, she desired everyone to be saved and no one from Christ’s flock to perish. She rejoiced at each person’s progress and was deeply sorrowful at adversity. She was devout and compassionate toward everyone, except toward vices, which deserve not compassion but rectitude.

The festivals of many saints are celebrated in the Church. We hope that she is not inferior to them in merit and that she will not be separated from their company in eternal blessedness.

Truly she had been a worthy temple in which the Lord had dwelt: disciplined by fasts, refreshed by prayers, [Note: One witness adds “and cleansed, adorned with purity”] and cleansed by purity.

But what can worthily be said in her praise? Let the Lord be praised in her, and she in the Lord; for he is her praise, whose praise never departed from her mouth. To him belong honor and glory, splendor and dominion, forever and ever. Amen.

**The life of the glorious Queen Mahthildis ends here.**

---

## Within the years 967–985: Gumpold, Bishop of Mantua

# Gumpold’s Life of Venceslav, Duke of Bohemia

(Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae historica*, *Scriptores*, volume IV, page 211.)

## Preliminary observations

When some time had passed after the murder of Duke Venceslav, and the fame of the miracles performed through his power had crossed the borders of Bohemia [Note: Widukind I.35], and plans were already being made to establish the bishopric of Prague and to remove Bohemia from the authority of the bishops of Regensburg, the Emperor Otto II commissioned Gumpold, bishop of Mantua, to write the Life of Venceslav. [Note: Nothing further is known about Gumpold himself; he must have occupied the see between 967 and 985.]

Gumpold collected whatever he could discover, after so long an interval, through the testimony of truthful men [Note: See chapters 21, 22, 23, and 25], and explained it in an expansive, convoluted, and often obscure style.

The book was written between 968 [Note: Otto had already become emperor on December 25, 967, but Bohemia had not yet been removed from the diocese of Regensburg; see chapter 15] and 973. As the late Joseph Dobrowsky taught [Note: In the book *Critical Attempts to Purify the Earlier History of Bohemia from Later Fictions*, fascicles I–III, Prague, 1803, 1807, and 1819], it appears to have immediately become the root and foundation of almost everything that was later published concerning the life of Venceslav [Note: Except, naturally, the Life of Venceslav by Laurentius of Monte Cassino]. For it was excerpted more than once in the tenth century for use in the breviary [Note: See Dobrowsky, *Legends B, C, D*, fascicle I, page 8 and following; fascicle III, pages 20 and following. I have seen the manuscript of Legend D, written as early as the tenth century, in the Royal Library at Munich, among the Benedictbeuern manuscripts, numbered 105. Compare our *Annals* VII, 387, and below], became known at the beginning of the eleventh century to the author of the Life of Bishop Adalbert [Note: Compare chapter 1, the description of Bohemia], and in subsequent centuries was copied not only by Sigebert of Gembloux [Note: Under the year 921] and Cosmas [Note: Under the years 894, 929, and 932], but also by the other authors of legends of Saint Venceslav, among whom Emperor Charles IV particularly distinguished himself [Note: See *Acta Sanctorum*, September VII, 837–839]. [Note: See Dobrowsky, cited work, III, 25–52.]

Setting these aside [Note: Balbinus printed a legend in his *Epitome of the History of Bohemia*, and from there it was again printed in *Acta Sanctorum*, September VII, 825 and following. They pretend that it was written by Christian, son of Boleslav I. It derives chiefly from Gumpold and from the legend of the Munich manuscript], we present only Gumpold’s work. It is certainly far from free of errors, since it rests only on hearsay, but it comes closest to the time of Venceslav.

We propose to publish Gumpold’s book, which the eminent Dobrowsky had copied in 1819 from a fourteenth-century manuscript of the Metropolitan Library of Prague—neither complete nor preserving a good text, and without the author’s name [Note: Cited work, III, pages 53–119]—with the aid of excellent manuscripts, one of which I examined in 1823 in the ducal library at Wolfenbüttel and the other in 1826 in the Royal Library at Brussels.

### 1. The Wolfenbüttel manuscript

Manuscript C, among the Augustean manuscripts, quarto no. 11, 2, consists of several codices; the second of these, on folios 18–37, contains Gumpold’s book. It was written in a beautiful hand at the end of the eleventh or the beginning of the twelfth century. The beginnings of the chapters are marked with gold letters.

The first page (18 recto) [Note: Its outer page, left blank by the scribe, received the conclusion of the Life of Saint Aegidius at the end of the thirteenth century; a whole page before it has been cut out] displays an image painted on purple parchment with gold and various colors: Emma, princess of the land, prostrate on the ground and embracing the feet of Duke Venceslav. Christ, holding the book of life in his left hand, places on the duke’s head with his right hand a triple crown, the reward of martyrdom. The following inscription is added in golden letters:

> “The venerable princess Emma ordered this little book to be made for the salvation of her soul in honor of the blessed martyr Venceslav.”

The duke wears a green garment decorated with a gold border, red leggings, gold bands, and gold spurs. He holds a lance in his left hand and raises his right hand, with which he adores Christ, to whom Emma had offered Gumpold’s book. Emma wears a violet garment sprinkled with gold, together with a gold border and gold cloak.

On the second folio (19), likewise adorned with purple and gold, the beginning of the preface is read; the initial letter S is decorated in red, green, and gold. On folio 20 verso, after the preface has ended, there is a scene of the banquet at which Venceslav offers a cup to his brother and the other guests. On folio 21 are the duke’s murder near the church and the beginning of the Passion, written in gold letters on purple parchment.

The text ends on folio 37; the verso of folio 37 was left blank.

Since the book cannot, on account of the forms of its letters, be assigned to the tenth century or the beginning of the eleventh, I would believe that it was produced at the command not of Emma, the wife of Boleslav II, who died in 1006, but either of some other Emma [Note: Our late colleague Ebert identified her with the Emma mentioned by Adam of Bremen, book II, chapter 49; but the designation “princess” seems to indicate that she was a duchess of Bohemia], or that it was copied from an older manuscript at the command of that Emma.

In any event, it must be highly valued. Although the text is quite often corrupted through the copyist’s incompetence, it nevertheless comes closest to Gumpold’s autograph; therefore we have departed from it only rarely, and only when the sense clearly required it.

### 2. The royal Brussels manuscript

Manuscript C of the Royal Library at Brussels, now numbered 9289 and formerly belonging to Saint Lawrence at Liège, is a parchment manuscript from the beginning of the twelfth century. Besides Gumpold’s book, it contains the Lives of Saints Trudo, Pigmenius, and the two Ewalds.

Bethmann collated it for our purposes. It presents a generally good text, though one that has clearly been corrected and emended according to the standards of its time. We have unmistakable evidence of this in chapter 15, where it omits the words proclaiming that Bohemia was subject to the see of Regensburg. In this respect, as in many others, it agrees with the manuscript just described.

### 3. The Prague manuscript

Manuscript C of the Metropolitan Library of Prague, from the fourteenth century, is the form in which we read the text printed by Dobrowsky. At the end, however, it adds from the Chronicle of Cosmas a miracle that occurred in 1091 or 1092.

### 4. The Aachen manuscript

A manuscript formerly belonging to Saint Adalbert of Aachen is now lost. The Bollandists report in *Acta Sanctorum*, September VII, 771, that they possessed a copy of it.

### 5. The Brno manuscript

A book formerly existed in a manuscript of the Brno Library in Moravia. Bonaventura Pitter reported it to Dobner as having been written between 1100 and 1130.

Its text nevertheless ended with the death of the saint, at the end of chapter 19, with only the formula “through the Lord, etc., unto the ages of ages. Amen” added, as an ancient reading for use in the Breviary [Note: Dobrowsky, cited work, I, 7–8]. The later history of this manuscript is unknown.

It will be useful to append to Gumpold’s text some material derived from a legend dating from the end of the tenth century, which the distinguished Föringer, keeper of the Royal Library, copied from manuscript M, a royal Munich codex among the Benedictbeuern manuscripts, numbered 105. Although it is not of great importance, it shows how the same event was narrated a second time within the space of a few years.

The book of Laurentius, a monk of Monte Cassino, compiled during the final years of the eleventh century from the reports of a certain Bohemian and of “Lord Benedict the Saxon, a monk of Monte Cassino,” and making use of the Life of Saint Adalbert, is omitted here because it is full of errors. Whatever in it could have been of any importance has already been extracted and inserted into our *Annals* sixteen years ago [Note: Volume V, pages 136–143].

# Here begins the prologue of Gumpold, Bishop of Mantua

[Note: The initials “G. M. E.” are absent from manuscripts 2 and 3.]

[Col. 0923B] The various kinds of study commonly impose upon mortals’ minds diverse concerns, in which that kind excels above all others which, through the power of inward imagination, by nature and also by diligence, rejoices to discern intellectually things presented to the senses in whatever manner, and to refashion them according to human wishes for agreeable uses. One person, disciplined in mind and despising the sport of transient things, directs his attention to what is above; another, burning with an ardent thirst for fleeting things, desires honors built on high. Youth often draws one unlawfully toward forbidden things, while the mature longevity of cold old age adapts another to strict and salutary customs. For one, the bold prudence of military skill earns the desirable glory of praise; for another, the labor of skilled craftsmanship in diverse works removes idleness and draws out the mind’s natural subtlety.

Some, however, fixed upon the contemplation of literary profundity and devoted, in liberal leisure, with remarkable clarity to the beauties of eloquence, labor through the scrupulous investigations of the arts to discover by constant reflection in what order the movements and immovable fixity of the stars are arranged; what measure, or of what kind, by some hidden principle, constrains the compass of the earth’s magnitude through geometrical formulas to a definite grasp of measurement; by what reckoning the whole sum of quantity and solidity proceeds; by what proportions of consonances natural song is attuned; or through what image of opinions, amid the proposition and difficult mixture of truth and falsehood, so profound a disputation of eloquent speakers insinuates itself.

Others, stirred by the study of verse and occupied with poetic play, turn their lofty minds toward the chatter of dirges. Yet, delighted by fables, they do not fear to suppress, through deadly negligence, the fame of truth concerning the memorable deeds of God’s saints, so often displayed to mortal eyes by heavenly benevolence. Nor is it surprising that such wise men, raising grand questions and questions belonging to philosophy, have drawn them away from the simple sequence of compositions, since many of them, clinging more ardently to the writings of the pagans, have not merely set aside what in sacred deeds ought to be brought forward for divine praise and disseminated to posterity through written testimony, but have utterly rejected, as though devoid of usefulness, whatever appears divine and most gentle to a devout mind when presented simply and without perplexity.

Finally, as many think, while human affairs are being turned by this fortune and the discernment of lofty rhetoricians looks toward ever higher things, we who are very far removed from such wisdom and learned loquacity are nevertheless preceded by the unusual text of a brief little note—although corruptly expressed—which the sacred command of the most victorious and august emperor Otto II imposed upon our rusticity. It will shortly disclose the name and distinguished deeds of a memorable man and precede the rarity of the text that follows. Whatever the fault of a writer who wrote defectively detracts from it, the lofty dignity of the saint adorns it all the more, since sacred authority indicates the subject and cause of the work.

[Notes: *Praestantissimum* (“most excellent”) is written *prestantissimum* in witness 1. *Mente* (“in mind”) is written *mentem* (“the mind”) in witness 1. *Speculatione* (“contemplation”) is written *speculationi* (“to contemplation”) in witness 2. *Frequentissima reputacione* (“by very frequent consideration”) is written *disputatione* (“by disputation”) in witness 2. *Terrenae* (“of the earth”) is written *tenere* in witness 1, probably corrupt. *Ambitum* (“compass” or “circumference”) is written *hambitum* in witness 1. *Asstringat* (“constrains”) is written *astringat* in witnesses 2 and 3. *Dictu* (“by reckoning,” literally “by saying”) is written *dicto* (“by a reckoning”) in witness 2. *Quantitatis soliditatisque* (“of quantity and solidity”) appears in witness 1 as *decer quantitatis solidatis*, an evidently corrupt form. *Desudant* (“they labor”) is written *desiderant* (“they desire”) in witness 2. *Transduxerint* (“they have drawn away”) is read as *transduxerunt* in witness 1 and *traduxerint* in witness 2. *Non* (“not”) is followed in witness 1 by the notation “to be noted.” *Postposuerint* (“they have set aside”) is read as *postposuerunt* in witness 2. *Mitissimum* (“most gentle”) is represented in witness 2 by *menti d.*, apparently an abbreviated or corrupt reading involving “to the devout mind.” *Abjecerint* (“they have rejected”) is read as *abjecerunt* in witness 2. *Rhetorum* (“of rhetoricians”) is written *rethorum* in witness 2. *Nobisque* (“and to us”) is corrected in witness 2 to *nobis itaque* (“and therefore to us”); witness 3 has *nobis*. *Sapientum* (“of the wise”) is corrected to *sapientium* (“of the wise”) in witnesses 2 and 3. *Seriola* (“little note”) is absent from witnesses 2 and 3; witness 2 has a marginal subnotation represented in the source by dots, apparently resulting from correction. *Corrupte* (“corruptly”) is the reading of witness 1. *Raritatem* (“rarity”) is written *raritem* in witness 1. *Designantis* (“indicating”) is written *designantes* in witness 1.]

[Col. 0923] **THE PROLOGUE ENDS**

[Note: In witness 1 the ending of the prologue is absent. In that witness pictures of the banquet and the murder of Wenceslav follow; then comes “The Passion,” and so forth.]

**THE PASSION OF SAINT WENCESLAV, MARTYR, BEGINS**

[Col. 0923]

[Col. 0923D] **1.** Thus, when the poisonous growth of heresy had been torn away by the ancient and authoritative opposition of Catholics concerning the indivisible mystery of the Trinity, the life-giving splendor of doctrine, radiating in its diffusion, divinely restored to serenity the world darkened by the gloom of error. But although we know very well that the salutary advances of faith, from what first beginning of strength they took their origin, have been sufficiently established by the diligence of earlier theologians, whose beneficial studies shone forth more widely in ecclesiastical writings and were inscribed in books and more securely marked out for believing posterity, nevertheless not all the nations of the world, though predestined, received this gift of grace at the same time. Certain peoples, after a long and wandering detour through tortuous paths, were brought back by sacred illumination to the straightness of the proper road; but, as heavenly majesty ordained, the process advanced more successfully by regions, as though the losses inflicted by the devil were gradually being overcome.

We undertake to express in the simplicity of the present style one of these regions, inhabited by the Sclavonic peoples. The northern district, harsher than the others and slower to faith, yields to our purpose. The grace of the Holy Spirit itself has deemed it worthy to be established, though late, in the worship of the Christian confession through a blessed conversion.

[Notes: *Idoneoque* (“and authoritative”) appears as *idoneque* in witness 1 and as *i. c.* in witness 2. *Refragatu* (“opposition”) is written *refugatu* in witness 1. *Eorum* (“of them”) is printed in witness 1 at [Col. 0925], where the context requires *errorum* (“of errors”). *Ecclesiastici* (“ecclesiastical”) is read as *ecclesiasticum* in witness 2. *Priore* (“earlier”) is read as *priorum* (“of the earlier [theologians]”) in witness 2. *Anfractuum* (“tortuous paths”) is abbreviated as *amfr.* in witness 2. *Sclavanicis* (“Sclavonic”) is read as *germanicis* (“Germanic”) in witness 3. *Aggredimur* (“we undertake”) is absent from witness 1. *Aquilonalis* (“northern”) is written *aquilonaris* in witness 2. *Prostratur* (“yields” or “is laid low”) is read as *protestatur* (“protests”) in witness 2 and *protestat* (“protests”) in witness 3. *Pneumatis* (“of the Spirit”) is read as *pneumati* (“to the Spirit”) in witness 1.]

**2.** The name Bohemia, they say, was imposed upon the region by the inhabitants of the land themselves. While the most illustrious King Henry, of blessed memory, was reigning there, a certain man named Zpuytignev, distinguished by the nobility of his lineage and eminent in power among his fellow citizens, held the governance of the principality under the king’s authority. Touched by the sweet desire for divine worship and greatly longing to be regenerated through the mystery of the sacred font, he was cleansed in baptism. Burning with a new zeal, he built houses of God in memorable veneration of Mary, the most blessed Mother of God, and of Saint Peter, chief of the apostles. In them, with divine assistance, innumerable miracles later shone forth each year.

[Notes: *Vocabulum* (“name”) is written *vocablum* in witness 1. *Jam* (“already”) is corrected from *etiam* (“also”) in witness 1. The name appears as *Zyptineus* in witness 2, *Spitigueu* in witness 3, and *zpitigneus* in manuscript M. Compare the Fulda Annals, year 895; he already appears to have been a Christian at that time. At [Col. 0925D] the reference reads: “At Prague, in the city of Prague.” For Saint Peter’s church the reference reads: “At Budec, where Wenceslav attended school.” *Miracula* (“miracles”) is written *milacula* in witness 1.]

**3.** Meanwhile, during the days of this man’s praiseworthy life, when the law of nature had closed the path of honorable deeds, his younger brother Wratizlav succeeded him in the principality, with the public consent of the people. He himself also embraced the Christian religion and, believing in Christian truth, erected a basilica to be dedicated to God in honor of the victorious athlete of God, the blessed martyr George.

When, after the slow passage of time, he too naturally departed from human life, he left surviving him, to be praised by mortals with profound admiration, his son Wenceslav, beloved of God, the elder of his sons both in age and in conduct, and much more ardent in heavenly things.

[Notes: *Aetate* (“in age”) has *post* supplied in witness 1. The name appears as *Wratyzlaus* in witness 2, *Wratislaw* in witness 3, *wirizlaum* in manuscript M, and *bratesclabus* in Laurentius of Cassino. *Ipse* (“he himself”) is absent from witnesses 2 and 3; *assecutus* (“having embraced”) is written *assectutus* in witness 1; and *Dei* (“of God”) is absent from witnesses 2 and 3. At [Col. 0925D] the reference reads: “In the Prague fortress.” *Eunte* (“departing”) is written *eunte* in witness 1. *Ammiracione* (“admiration”) is written *amiracione* in witness 1. *Wencezlaum* (“Wenceslav”) is written *Wencezlaum* in witness 2 and manuscript M.]

**4.** When this boy of wondrous brilliance and lovable character had first reached the flowering age of youth, while his father was still alive, he desired to be assigned to the exercises of learning. By repeated entreaty he bent his father’s will, and through his father’s arrangement he was sent to the city of Bunsza to learn letters. His swift intellect had been divinely endowed with receptive capacity; within a short period he learned the psalter and many other divine writings from a venerable priest named Uceno, and joined them more firmly to his inward memory.

Meanwhile, as has already been said, after his father had entered the way of all flesh, the young man, displaying through his deeds the examples of old age, was chosen—with the favorable consent of the peoples and against his own strong resistance—to succeed to his father’s duchy under the shining power of the most serene King Otto. He was raised to the seat of princely dignity.

[Notes: *Indolis* (“character”) is read as *i. puer* (“the boy’s [character]”) in witness 3. *Exercitia* (“exercises”) is corrected from *exertia* to *exerticia* in witness 1. *Transmissu* (“through [his father’s] arrangement”) is written *transmissum* in witness 1. The place-name appears as *Budec* in witness 2 and *Budess* in witness 3, and as *Budêea* in manuscript M. *Spalmodialem* (“psalm-book”) is read as *psalmodialem* in witness 2. Manuscript M adds that he learned from “a certain venerable priest named Uceno.” *Universae carnis viam ingresso* (“having entered the way of all flesh”) is abbreviated in witness 2. At [Col. 0925D] the reference identifies Henry as the king who later attacked Wenceslav in war.]

**5.** It is not surprising that the kindness of the young prince, having undertaken earthly authority, was inwardly distressed by the many varieties of serious trouble that disturbed him, since, looking with a devout mind toward heavenly things above all else, he resolved that although he was bound to provide for the public good, he would nevertheless devote his first years to the exceedingly sweet service of God and would not reject it by despising secular exaltation.

Fearing that he would have to atone for the crime of the people entrusted to him if he did not impose the appropriate rule of civic discipline, he did not long leave this matter in uncertainty. He wisely seized a path by which he would neither omit what had to be done in worldly affairs nor thereafter fear that, in striving toward heavenly things, he had neglected this duty. Finally, while seated in the exercise of the most kind and highly discerning rule, he strove by princely command to regulate the decrees of the laws for the common benefit of citizens and the army.

Prudent in judgment and ready to show mercy to anyone, he was easily persuaded to lessen the punishment deserved by the wretched faults of the accused; in his judgments he was alien to punishments of every kind. In domestic conduct he was simple, transparent in the chastity of his morals, not slow to promise benefits to the powerful, and equally devoted to fulfilling those promises. He often preferred the rusticity of the poor inhabitants to their superiors in the practice of love. He always shone with a wondrous splendor of charity as a consoler and fatherly protector of those deprived of parents or material support, as well as of those exiled from their homeland.

Modest in all his actions, and memorable as a lover of patience, he was a prudent moderator amid every adversity. He was a most generous distributor of possessions to the tearful needs of the poor, a peaceful practitioner of the gentlest humility, usually stricter toward himself and everywhere more merciful toward others. By giving to all, showing mercy, reforming the ignorant, and strengthening the instructed, he shone forth as an example for eternity.

[Notes: *Gravibus* (“serious”) is written *gradibus* (“steps”) in witness 1. *Debitor* (“bound”) is written *debita* (“owed”) in witness 1. *Praedulci obsequio* (“exceedingly sweet service”) appears in witness 2 as *D. t. predulce obsequium*. *Despecto* (“despising”) is written *d. de s.* in witness 1. *Communes* (“common”) is written *comunes* in witness 1. *Dominio* (“rule”) appears as *domiolio* in witness 1 and *domicilio* in witnesses 2 and 3. *Decernendo* (“in judging”) is written *decerno* in witness 1. *Praeferens* (“preferring”) is written *proferens* (“bringing forward”) in witness 1. *Exulantibus* (“exiled”) is written *exultantibus* (“rejoicing”) in witness 1. *In* (“in”) is read as *inter* (“amid”) in witness 2. *Placidi* (“peaceful”) is written *placidissimus* (“most peaceful”) in witness 2, which omits *mansuetissimae* (“of the gentlest”). *Plerumque* (“usually”) is represented in witness 3 by *ipse* (“himself”), with an additional abbreviated reading. *Inscientes* (“the ignorant”) is read as *in socios* (“into companions”) in witness 1. *Edoctos* (“the instructed”) is read as *et doctos* (“and the instructed”) in witness 3. *Perluxit* (“shone forth”) is written *perduxit* (“led through”) in witness 1.]

**6.** Adorned with these shining jewels of virtue, the conduct of the blessed young man became so deeply devoted to this pursuit of piety that whenever, after arrangements had been made for public necessities, proclamations concerning discussions or hearings had been issued among the ordered benches of judges and common people, and he had learned the details of the cases in court with still greater distinction, if someone held by a crime and condemned by a mortal sentence, though deservedly, had been brought into his presence from the condemnatory judgment of his accusers, he would leave by his intervention exempt from punishment.

If, however, that merciful prince, neither the necessity of the law having been changed nor the judges having been in any way persuaded by him to release the man, recognized that the accused could not be rescued from the dreadful law, then, wishing to withdraw himself and not stain his sacred eyes with bloodshed, he left the assembly and judgment after offering whatever excuse could be made acceptable. In this way he was a wise imitator of the salutary command of the Gospel in which it is prescribed: “Do not judge, and you will not be judged; and do not condemn, and you will not be condemned” (Luke 6:37).

[Notes: The clause “he would leave exempt from punishment through his intervention” is absent from witnesses 1 and 2. *Adductus* (“brought”) is read as *addictus* (“assigned” or “condemned”) in witness 3. *Accumine* (“sharpness”) is written *accumine* in witness 1.]

**7.** Loving this command more perfectly, the young man, filled with God, and foreseeing that no mortal could safely fail to follow it, most kindly spared the condemned whose crimes had been marked out for destruction. But lest the detestable memorials of torture grow any longer, he ordered all the gallows erected in many places of his kingdom for the hanging of men to be completely demolished, and thereafter did not permit them to be rebuilt.

With the happiest progress in his actions, increasing day by day the accumulation of an already proven goodness by adorning it further, he received clerics arriving from every part of the earth with joyful generosity, graciously taking them into his presence with every provision their needs required. Keeping before his eyes the divine love by which one must serve one’s neighbor, he treated with reverent charity those who willingly remained with him, carefully and kindly. His chaste mind, instructed from heaven by their frequent and sacred teachings, was cultivated more abundantly through learning and advanced to a wondrous capacity for Scripture.

Whatever the zeal of his teachers had foreshadowed in him, he himself fulfilled through honorable deeds. For he sympathized with everyone’s distress, visited some who were weakened by infirmity with charitable comfort, and buried those entangled in the law of death, often neglected by less religious citizens, through the office of funeral service.

But when he saw the peoples subject to his rule by ancient law and custom, still wavering in the teaching of an immature faith, frequently rushing during the year through the impious houses of entrances and frenzied altars—and even the nobles themselves coming there to sacrifice to foreign gods—this young man of noble character, though often invited to share in that wicked communion of eating sacrificial victims, hungering above all for the banquets of the heavenly table, not only refused the unlawful feasts but also energetically avoided the profane company of the banqueters polluted by demonic filth.

Nevertheless, deeply concerned for those weighed down by this pestilential error, he repeatedly turned over the Scripture in which, through the apostle’s words, it is commanded: “Bear one another’s burdens” (Galatians 6:2). He never ceased to exhort with the gentleness of persuasion those who were somewhat more pliable toward the path of the true highest good, promising them the immeasurable rewards of heaven if, despising the images of idols by which they had been deceived, they inclined their minds and desires with faith toward the true and immutable essence of the Godhead, which cannot increase or diminish but always remains.

Others, less capable through lack of knowledge of this saving teaching, harder of heart and more sluggish in understanding the truth, he catechized at suitable and unsuitable times according to the apostolic admonition, reproving them, and designating the reward appropriate to either way. Striving with all his strength, he hastened to join as many as he could, through both willing and even compelled invitation, to the banquet of the master of the household, richly supplied with every resource and, having driven away hunger, providing the joys of eternal satisfaction.

[Notes: Manuscript M adds: “He also destroyed the prisons and cut down all the gallows.” Witness 2 omits the clause concerning the gallows not being rebuilt. *Servando* (“serving”) is read as *servandum* (“to be served”) in witnesses 2 and 3. *Eorumque* (“and their”) was corrected from *erumque* in witness 1. *Quicquid* (“whatever”) is preceded by *nam* (“for”) in witnesses 2 and 3. *Illaqueatos* (“entangled”) is written *illaquaetos* in witness 1. *Funebris* (“funeral”) is read as *funeribus* (“with funerals”) in witness 1; *obsequii* (“service”) has been supplied. *Consuetudinem* (“custom”) appears as *v. c.* in witnesses 2 and 3. *Aspexisset* (“had seen”) is written *aspexisset* in witness 2. Manuscript M expands the passage as follows: “Those wicked men mentioned above went to sacrifice lambs and piglets to demons so that they might eat of these most impious offerings; but he, looking for an opportunity, withdrew from them. He constantly nourished those established in the bosom of holy Mother Church with divine food; but if he found them drinking in taverns and departing from instruction, he immediately bound them prone to the table and beat them severely with many blows.”]

**8.** Amid these remarkable deeds, shining with fasts and almsgiving, he was accustomed to add this outstanding example to his most modest way of life: namely, having perceived more deeply through divine prompting and the insight of a sacred mind that God is read to approve obedience more than sacrifice, he strove to adorn his pious and reverent conduct to the fullest.

When the yearly fast of arduous observance returned, the sacred young man, although he was often interrupted by secular affairs because of his governance, nevertheless brought each day to completion through tireless works of prayer and through gifts that flew generously among the poor.

At night he devoted himself to the most serene vigil, gentle and forgetful of sleep. At the first silence of the night’s rest, despising the shining bed of his chamber, he secretly rose from his couch and silently awakened the chamber servant. He seized a little book worn smooth by frequent handling, left the palace without the knowledge of the guards, and with only one servant as his companion traversed the rugged peaks of the mountains, the deadly precipices of the valleys, and the stony or ice-covered roads and paths between the towns, barefoot, continually reciting psalms and other prayers, visiting the churches one by one.

He endured such affliction of the flesh that, when the tender soles of his feet had been torn, flowing blood marked his tracks here and there. Returning home, he concealed what he had done inwardly; seated on the throne, he put on the princely garments of his ornaments, but beneath them his most pure flesh was furrowed by the sharpness of a hair-shirt.

When the summer heat announced the harvest, during the safe silence of night he himself cut sheaves in a wheat field with a small sickle, carried them on his own shoulders in a heavy bundle, and hid them in a secluded corner of the house. There he threshed them; after breaking the grain among stones and carefully sifting it with his holy hands until it was clean of field refuse, he drew water from the spring, accompanied only by the servant-boy carrying a pitcher, and marked it by invoking the true Trinity. With this water he prepared the little quantity of flour, gathered into a natural mass, to be baked into sacrificial loaves and offered by the hands of priests.

Nor did he yet consider that he had satisfied the solemnities of the Mass. Rather, delighted by the taste of obedience, which he had already learned from God to be praised above sacrifices, he continued his practice. When the vintage arrived in its annual course, he secretly summoned the servant of excessive fidelity already mentioned, crossed the enclosure of the vineyards by night, and filled baskets hanging from both their backs with heavy clusters. In this praiseworthy theft he returned to the cell farther removed from the palace and so dear to him.

Meanwhile, after carefully securing the doors of the little dwelling on every side with bolts, he crushed the grapes of the small vintage in a suitable vessel with a pestle. Having pressed out the tender liquid of the must through the clean fineness of a linen bag, with the most diligent pressure of his chaste hands, he strained it. He poured it into a two-handled vessel, with only the servant aware, and stored it more secretly. When the proper opportunity came, he distributed it among the neighboring clerics together with the offerings that he himself prepared for the celebration of the Mass, amid the wondrous communion of divine things.

O indissoluble bond of inviolate faith around a most chaste breast! O most devoted follower of praiseworthy obedience! O wondrous humility of a prince who was not ashamed, moved by divine love, to undertake the duties of servants! Gazing through the lofty contemplation of his mind upon the heavenly mysteries that he held in his heart, he venerated and loved the reverent and salutary giving of the Lord’s body and blood with such devotion that, in the worship of the heavenly offering that cleanses the contagion of sins, he not only served with the steadfastness of faith but also himself obtained, through the outward labor of a rustic servant at the purest spring and through pious generosity, a place among the religious service of priests.

[Notes: *Dominum* (“the Lord”) is written *dominum* in witness 1; witness 2 has the corrupt reading *D. t. predulce obsequium*. *Sollempniis* (“solemnities”) is abbreviated as *s. a.* in witness 2. *Adveniente* (“arriving”) is written *adventante* in witnesses 2 and 3. The overly faithful servant is written *sequace* (“follower”) in witnesses 2 and 3. Manuscript M adds: “He hastened into his vineyard with his faithful servant.” *Repagulis* (“bolts”) is written *repaculorum* in witness 2. *Castarum* (“chaste”) is written *castrarum* in witness 1. *Celebritati* (“celebration”) is written *celebritate* (“with celebration”) in witness 1. *Communione* (“communion”) is corrected by the editor to *communicatione* (“communication” or “communion”) in witnesses 1–3. *Servulorum* (“of servants”) is read as *servorum* (“of servants”) in witness 2. *Libaminis* (“of the offering”) has a corrupt or abbreviated reading in witnesses 1 and 2.]

**9.** We consider it useful not to conceal the benevolent intention of lovers of truth, since, according to the honorable report of certain people, we have learned that the young man, already taught from heaven, foresaw with certainty future events amid the frequent happenings of human affairs and often foreshadowed them to the faith of his household through new and terrifying circumstances. The writer’s most humble devotion does not remain silent about the glorious mention of this memorable gift amid so many proclamations of miracles. For, through a vision divinely opened in the silence of night, the courtyard of a certain priest Paul appeared to him—surrounded by the pleasant and spacious boundaries of buildings—utterly deserted of all the adornment of walls and entirely alien to human habitation, under the clear gaze of the holy and God-filled Wenceslav.

The young man, awakened from the heaviness of bodily sleep and roused by the watchful contemplation of his heart, made known in prudent speech what he had seen. Then, explaining prophetically what he had already declared would more truly come to pass, he addressed those summoned in these words:

[Notes: *Praescisse* (“to have foreseen”) is absent from witness 2. *Eventibus* (“events”) is read as *evenientibus* (“happenings”) in witness 2. The phrase concerning the frequent miracles is absent from witness 2. *Experti sumus* (“we have experienced this”) is absent from witness 1. Witness 2 calls the priest “Paul the presbyter.” *Habitacione* (“habitation”) is absent from witness 2, which has *possessionis* (“of possession”) or a related reading. *Pervigilis* (“watchful”) is written *pervigili* in witnesses 2 and 3. *Quisdam* (“certain”) is written *quibusdam* (“certain things”) in witnesses 2 and 3. *Quid* (“what”) is read as *quod* (“that which”) in witnesses 2 and 3. *Prophetanti* (“prophetically”) is written *prophetandi* (“of prophesying”) in witness 1.]

**10.** “As I lay upon my bed, a grave and profound vision lifted me up in the silence of night, sweet friends and familiar servants. For I saw the portico of the priest Paul, with all the grandeur of its buildings and human adornment, utterly desolate. At this sight I was cast down in grief and overwhelmed by the distress of inward concern for God’s faithful.

“Yet, because I am transferred by the immense mercy of the knower of all things into the hope in which the believer has been promised that all things are possible, I undertake to explain, through the interpretation of a clear solution, the truth of this dream, which is already to be understood through the impending event, so as to establish with certainty what has happened.”

[Notes: *Cuncta* (“all things”) is written *cunta* in witness 1. *Imminente jam casu* (“through the impending event”) appears in witness 1 in the corrupt form *supernoscendam praeposito casu*. *Interpretamento* (“interpretation”) is written *interpretamenta* in witness 1. *Excurs­sionem* (“investigation” or “establishment”) is written *excessionem* in witnesses 1 and 3.]

**11.** “The destruction of the houses that was seen portends the blessed death of my grandmother Liudmila, a holy and venerable matron. She will shortly suffer a cruel bodily passion for the profession of the Christian name and faith; my mother, a gentile both by birth and by the defilement of her deeds, will conspire with several servants equally prepared for crime, and the weapons of the wicked will secretly burst in upon her.

“The breadth of the portico, deserted of its peoples, as the vision testifies, foreshadows the pitiable expulsion of our clergy, included within its protection, from the kingdom, and the unjust loss of all their possessions. For my mother, of accursed memory, bitterly envious of the living sect—which I strive with all my power to confess, worship, follow in my heart, and love, and shall hereafter strive unchangeably to follow elsewhere—plots to have those same clerics of various orders, who do not deny that they agree with me, deprived of earthly assistance and expelled more harshly from the kingdom.”

[Notes: *Aviae* (“grandmother”) is absent from witnesses 1 and 2. The name is written *Iudmillae* in witness 3. *Sanctae* (“holy”) is absent from witness 2. *Corporis* (“of the body”) is read as *corporis sui* (“of her own body”) in witness 2. *Visio* (“vision”) is written *viso* (“at the sight”) in witness 1. *Populis* (“of peoples”) is read as *populi* (“of the people”) in witness 2. *Incluso* (“included”) is written *inclusi* (“of the included clergy”) in witnesses 2 and 3. *Clericos* (“clerics”) is abbreviated in witness 2 as *o. c.* In *ejectum iri molitur*, *iri* forms the future passive infinitive: the mother “plots for the clerics to be expelled”; witness 2 instead reads *ire*.]

**12.** Finally, the mind conscious of truth in this shrewd conjecture and foreknowledge was not deceived. Rather, just as the signs of the fitting interpretation resounded, so it was soon established that everything had been fulfilled in unbroken order: the destruction of the matron already mentioned, and the savage expulsion of the clergy from the wide regions that lay around them, which had readily yielded themselves to his rule—or rather to his most gentle generosity.

With this significant foreknowledge of spiritual grace shining in the innermost heart of the chosen young man, his envious mother and brother (identified by DOBR.), greatly shaken, continually attempted, by secret conversations and the counsels of attendants placed near him, to draw the steadfast lover of Christ away from the purpose by which he had resolved to apply himself more devotedly to attaining heavenly things, on the pretext of public needs to be provided for by him.

Strengthened by the protection of heavenly armor, he sometimes openly lent his sacred ears to such songs of familiar suggestions before the nobles of the kingdom, as though consenting; but inwardly, in the consideration of his heart, he refused consent in his actions. For although he pretended to yield under the appearance of human fear, and attended the temples of God somewhat less frequently than usual at public gatherings, he manifested through the wondrous constancy of his works what he loved in the depths of his mind.

He had carefully and secretly retained with him in a small book a continuous sequence of divine prayers. Setting aside secular business for the time being, he read it through to the end twelve times or more—although sometimes he could find a place for prayer only in the more secluded silence of a chamber or of his own bedchamber—praising Christ with chaste intention at fixed intervals of night and day.
