[Notes: *Familiarum* (“of households” or “of families”) is written *familiarum* in witness 1, where the context may suggest *familiarium* (“of familiar attendants”). *Applicabat* (“he applied”) is written *applicat* (“he applies”) in witnesses 2 and 3. *Humani* (“human”) is written *huni* in witness 1. *Occultiusque* (“more secretly”) is written *occultusque* (“and hidden”) in witness 1. *Depositis* (“having set aside”) is written *repositis* (“having put back”) in witness 1.]

**13.** Meanwhile, when the years of his youth had passed in such a fortunate age, the duke himself had ascended more deeply into the strength of a manly spirit. Gradually and manfully rejecting the vain counsels of his followers, and detesting their wandering ignorance of the truth, one day, when an assembly of soldiers and friends had been held in the palace, he rebuked them in this speech:

“O friends and faithful ones—if only faithful to Christ! When, once upon a time, under the care of my parents, I eagerly absorbed the teachings entrusted to me through literary study, among the other sayings of my teachers I learned a certain passage of the apostle, in which he says: ‘When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child; but when I became a man, I put away the things that belonged to a child’ (1 Corinthians 13:11).

“By this sentence, looking now at myself, I recognize that, when I was first approaching childhood, I was a worthless creation who desired more ardently to know the maker of all things and to devote myself to his service. But while still a child, succeeding to the principality after my father’s death as the eldest among my brothers, I regulated the state through the measured reins of the laws, with God arranging it, and defended my homeland to the best of my ability against the mass of its attackers.

“But you, because you are sluggish in heart to contemplate the highest truth and remain unequal to me in faith, have until now caused me considerable injury through counsels pleasing to your perversity but utterly unlike uprightness. If life and the kingdom remain safe, I shall henceforth be released from this discipline and shall have leisure. Having become a man, according to the Scripture, after leaving behind my youth, I shall put away the things that belong to a child. Strengthened by heavenly mercy, I shall devote myself to the acts commanded by the Lord and shall no longer obey your wickedness.

“Therefore let your conspiracy against me in whispered counsel vanish; let the savage plans that you form among yourselves at public gatherings cease. Let love of peace burn in the kingdom, at home and abroad. Let no business of whatever usefulness be condemned through the overthrow of the judges. Let no one henceforth presume to commit the crimes of parricide by which you are accustomed to pollute yourselves. If you do not abandon these defilements of the law through fear of the highest King, our anger, kindled in zeal for God against the wicked, will behead any culprit of this kind.”

When this excellent command had ended, the participants in the wicked conspiracy returned home in fear. Having received the powerful strength of the sacred duke, they were compelled to lay aside the proud heights of their minds, and, at least for a short time, ceased to devise their customary plots against the man of wondrous holiness.

At that time, with God bringing serenity, barbarous disturbances were somewhat suppressed under his authority; the joyful growth of the Catholic religion, however, arose. Temples dedicated to divine worship, which shortly before had been falling through the neglect of unbelievers, were founded anew on stable foundations. Clerics deprived of their homeland and possessions were recalled through his kindly generosity. At once, their substance was not only restored but enriched by the holy man’s many gifts, and throughout these regions the whole Church rejoiced, exalted under such a prince.

[Notes: Manuscript M adds: “At that time many priests from the province of the Bavarians and from Swabia, hearing his fame, flocked to him with relics of the saints and books. To all of them he cheerfully provided an abundance of gold and silver, furs, servants, and clothing, according as each had need. All these teachers also marveled at his learning. For he could have been an imitator of the psalmist, who said in the Spirit: ‘I have more understanding than all who teach me, because your testimonies are my meditation.’ In his mind alone shone the brightness of the precious pearl, and the Lord deemed him worthy to confer such grace upon him that he was also victorious in battles. His face was tall, his body chaste, so that, as a celibate, he willingly desired to end his life. He had gentle speech with the meek; but those whom he knew to be harsh and aimless he avoided with all his heart.”]

[Additional textual notes: *Transcursa* (“having passed”) is followed in manuscript M by: “When he had become a man, he summoned all his men and his mother and reproached them,” and so forth. *Felici aetate* (“fortunate age”) is written *felicitate* (“fortune”) in witness 1 and *felicium* (“of the fortunate”) in witness 3. *Conscenderat* (“had ascended”) is written *conscederat* in witness 1. *Contione* (“assembly”) is written *contentione* (“dispute”) in witnesses 1 and 3. *In* (“in”) is absent from witness 1. *Injunctus* (“entrusted”) is written *injunctas* (“entrusted,” feminine plural) in witness 2. *Quoniam* (“since”) is corrected in witness 2 to *deum* (“God”), producing a different reading. *Implicari* (“to devote myself”) is written *implicare* (“to involve”) in witness 2. *Patri* (“to my father”) is written *patre* (“with my father”) in witness 2. *Praestruente* (“arranging” or “providing in advance”) is written *praestante* (“providing”) in witnesses 2 and 3. *Mihi manetis dispares* (“you remain unequal to me”) is represented in witness 2 by a corruptly expanded reading. *Rectitudini* (“to uprightness”) is followed in witness 3 by *valde amabiles* (“very pleasing”), a different reading. *Injuriosos* (“injurious”) is written *injuriosus hactanus* in witness 1. *Jam* (“already”) is absent from witness 2. *Retromissa* (“left behind”) is written *etro missa* in witness 1. *Effectus* (“having become”) is written *efectus* in witness 1. *Damnentur* (“let them be condemned”) is written *damnetur* (“let it be condemned”) in witness 1. *Metu* (“through fear”) is followed in witness 1 by the corrupt phrase *metum non desideretis* (“if you do not desire fear”). *Finito* (“having ended”) is written *inito* (“having begun”) in witness 1; witnesses 2 and 3 have *finito itaque* (“therefore, when it had ended”). *Motiones* (“disturbances”) is corrected from *nationes* (“nations”) in witness 1. The final clause concerning the growth of the Church is expanded in manuscript M by the account translated above.]

- **N192 · Col. 0933 · after `has partes tali sub principe elata congaudet aecclesia`:** source note: In tempore autem illo multi sacerdotes de provincia Bauuariorum et de Sueuia, audientes famam de eo, confluebant cum reliquiis sanctorum et libris ad eum, quibus omnibus habunde aurum et argentum, crusinas et mancipia atque uestimenta hilariter prout unicuique opus erat prestabat. Hii quoque omnes magistri mirabantur in doctrina ejus. Poterat namque imitator fore psalmistae qui in spiritu dixit: Super omnes potentes me intellexi, quia testimonia tua meditacio mea est. In cujus etiam mente sola preciosae margaritae claritas fulgebat, cuique dominus tantam graciam conferre dignatus est, ut et preliis victor existeret. Uultu autem fuit procerus, corpore castus, ita ut celebs libenti animo optaret uitam finire. Blandum habebat cum mitibus eloquium, quos autem sciebat inmites et uagantes sine causa, toto animo uitabat. addit M. — Manuscript M adds that many priests from Bavaria and Swabia came to him with relics and books; he generously gave each gold, silver, vessels, servants, and clothing as needed. They admired his learning. Like the Psalmist he understood beyond the mighty because he meditated on God’s testimonies. The precious pearl alone shone in his mind; God gave him grace to prevail in battles. He was tall, chaste, and willingly desired to end life celibate; gentle with the gentle, he wholly avoided those he knew to be cruel and to wander without cause.

[Col. 0933B] **14.** Then, as the glory of his virtues shone more brightly throughout the world, the interests of the commonwealth were diligently advanced under the careful governance of the duke, armed from heaven [Note: [Col. 0933] *reguntur* (“are governed”) in 3.]. But whatever is first established as needing to be done through the vigor of heavenly love is neglected all the less through the watchful diligence of the prince: for although the frequent bustle of the palace retinue habitually surrounds him on both sides, nevertheless, as a constant and prudent intercessor for himself and for the unbelieving people, the readiest patron of the poor, the kind consoler of those oppressed by grief, and the compassionate helper of those suddenly robbed, he perseveres without interruption or delay caused by worldly affairs.

**15.** But while the deceitful machination of the most impure enemy, cunningly seeking, if ever it could, to destroy the zeal for works of this kind, caused only the slightest delay, his brother Bolezlav [Note: [Col. 0933] *Bolezlaus* in 2.]—younger in age, but execrable in perversity of mind and in the quality of his actions, stirred by diabolical touch [Note: [Col. 0933] *tactus instinctu* (“stirred by touch”) in 2.] and savagely armed with the wickedness of fury against the man of God, eager to seize the kingdom with fraternal violence—tried with every effort, together with the criminal audacity of his servants, to set deadly snares for him [Note: [Col. 0933] *mortalis* (“mortal”) in 2 and 3.]. Yet it is certain that, by divine predestination, what was later to happen had at that time been delayed.

After a short interval, the man beloved by God bound himself by a saving vow: with God’s permission he would build, through a noble work of craftsmanship, a church to be dedicated to Christ and to his victorious athlete, the blessed martyr Vitus. Without delay, eager in deed and fervent in purpose, he sent envoys to the royal see of Ratispona [Note: [Col. 0933] *Ratisponae sedis* in 2 and 3; *radaspone* in M.], and by humble petition implored Bishop Tuton [Note: [Col. 0933] “He held the see from 894 to 942.”], a man of complete integrity, whose diocese entirely enclosed Bohemia [Note: [Col. 0933] *c. d. t. s. b.* is absent in 2 and 3.], asking that the work, which was to be consecrated to God, might be carried out with his permission and consent [Note: [Col. 0933] *legaturus*, supplied in 1.].

**16.** When the bishop had granted permission in accordance with the blessed duke’s desire, and the messengers had returned with expressions of affection, he summoned craftsmen by a swift command. The work was in full activity; impatient labor shone forth; the church was brought to the final touch of perfect adornment and was embellished with the marvelous gleam of metals. After the bishop just mentioned had been invited, it was consecrated in honor [Note: [Col. 0933] *honore* in 2 and 3.] of the holy martyr Vitus [Note: [Col. 0933] “Bishop Tutus spread out his hands, rejoicing and giving thanks to the Lord, and said: ‘Go and tell my son Wenceslaus: “Your church now stands most beautifully constructed before the Lord God.”’ When they had reported this according to the bishop’s command, he rejoiced greatly, and, summoning everyone, he himself began, with God’s help, to found the church in marvelous order in the name of Saint Vitus. M.]. [Note: [Col. 0933] Cosmas reports that the church was consecrated by Tuton’s successor, Bishop Michael.] There, too, signs of the many miracles performed among mortals by divine power continue to shine forth to the present day [Col. 0934B].

Yet the depth of the thirsting heart’s desire for God’s justice had not been filled. The chosen servant of God, Wenceslaus, a man of immeasurable merits, thought of laying aside the earthly fasces of honor, which he knew by experience to be frail, and of voluntarily transferring the reins of principality to his brother’s authority. He also longed, in the ardor of his inward desire, to go to Rome to visit the thresholds of the apostles for the sake of prayer, to renounce secular affairs under the sacred authority of the apostolic lord, to be clothed in the monastic habit, and in that manner of life to behold the end of his temporal existence. But the providence of the most generous rewarder, who always glorifies as worthy those whom it deems deserving through an equitable recompense of merits, deigned to reserve greater contests of heaven for this companion of the heavenly realm [Note: [Col. 0933] *glorificans*; *huic coelestis consortii* in 2 and 3.], so that, after these noble triumphs, he might seize nobler rewards [Col. 0934C].

**17** [Note: [Col. 0933] The division into chapters has been introduced here.]. Because the insane desire of his brother Bolezlav to acquire the kingdom by whatever means possible [Note: [Col. 0933] *vel invidia* (“or envy”) in 3.] was inflamed against God’s saint through manifold cunning plots, the journey to Rome was intercepted [Note: [Col. 0933] *inter* in 1.], and the daily conspiracy of the profane people [Note: [Col. 0933] Absent in 2.] was secretly thickened in the hiding places of their dwellings; while the envy [Note: [Col. 0933] *nequitia* (“wickedness”) in 3.] of the brother himself, with the devil supplying fuel, grew ever more fiercely inflamed.

Nevertheless, the savagery of all the conspirators was unable, before God’s foreknowledge, to hasten the blessed day of triumph by the secret murder of the most holy man [Col. 0935A]. But his brother, impatient enough to carry out the crime against him, decided that the other plots against his life should no longer be pursued, and instead chose to bring to maturity one wicked plan, more suitable than the others, which he had cautiously devised [Note: [Col. 0935] *persecuturum* (“to pursue”) in 3; *ac* for *a se* in 1.]. For, with weapons of every kind deceitfully hidden beneath their clothing and peace feigned, affection was fabricated under a brotherly appearance as though it were genuine; yet this showed that an opportunity for doing greater harm was being sought [Note: [Col. 0935] *praemonstratur* (“is shown beforehand”) in 2.].

**18.** On the joyful beginning of a certain festive day, that wretched ally of fraud carefully made his own house—at Boleslav’s, today Bunzlau; called *Uollesclabus* in the book of Lawrence of Monte Cassino [Note: [Col. 0935] *Bolislawiae, hodie Bunzlau; in Laurentii Casinensis libro Uollesclabus vocatur*]—splendid with every abundance of ornament that this people had ever been accustomed to possess [Note: [Col. 0935] *habendam* in 1.]. He ordered his servants to prepare a banquet more lavish than usual, invited friends under the appearance of merriment, and, entering the palace of the prince himself as a suppliant [Note: [Col. 0935] *suplex* in 1.], first of all begged him to honor the fraternal banquets with his presence.

The God-worthy Wenceslaus, greatly rejoicing in his gentleness, although it was false, entered the house joyfully with him, their hands clasped together [Note: [Col. 0935] *super lineam* (“above the line”) is added in 2.]. They reclined at the feast. After some of the fierce banqueters had been sated with wine [Note: [Col. 0935] *quibusdam* in 2 and 3.], the fraud, long contrived but unable to remain hidden, aroused them as though with one accord to murder the holy man. These malicious men, their daggers already concealed beneath their clothing, rose three times, and three times again, as though exhausted, bent themselves toward their seats [Note: [Col. 0935] *acclinantes* in 2 and 3.]. Their strength at least [Note: [Col. 0935] *saltem* in 2; *saepius*] and courage were entirely softened, however, because the hour of his passion appointed by God had not yet arrived, and they left him unharmed.

He himself was either unaware of this or, being unafraid of danger and strengthened by confidence in divine protection, was not shaken, although the caution of a certain retainer whispering in his ear had warned him how they had plotted against him [Note: [Col. 0935] *ut* in 1; *ad* in 3.]. Yet he was not moved from his seat [Note: [Col. 0935] *sed eo* in 2 and 3.] and kindly urged his brother and the others reclining with him [Note: [Col. 0935] *confidentes* in 1 and 2.] to be cheerful, as if he were acting as a gracious host [Note: [Col. 0935] *ospitis* in 1.].

A little later he rose after the table had been removed. Filling a cup with wine and speaking to everyone in a gentle word of greeting, he addressed them sweetly:

> “May Christ, the salvation of all, greet you! Let none of us hesitate to drink the cup that I hold in my hand in honor of the holy archangel Michael, venerating, as far as we can, the height of his spiritual love [Note: [Col. 0935] *spiritatis*, corrected to *spiritalitis* in 2.]. Let us pray from the depths of our hearts that, whenever the law of nature leads us to our final end, he may graciously deign to become the ready receiver of our souls and the kind guide into the delights of paradise” [Col. 0935D–0936A].

Immediately after speaking he drank cheerfully, and one by one, with the same love, offered each of them cups to drink, sealing them with a most affectionate kiss [Note: [Col. 0935] *singilatim* in 1; *cyphos* in 1.]. Fearless, having taken such honorable refreshment, and leaving the matter to be deferred according to God’s command, he returned home unharmed.

**19.** During the course of the following night [Note: [Col. 0935] *frequentis* in 1; *frequenti* in 2.], he passed the night in devotion, laboring with the most earnest persistence in prayers and almsgiving, conscious of what was to come and devoted to suffering the rights of death for Christ [Note: [Col. 0935] *futurae* in 2 and 3.].

When the hour of morning returned after the cockcrow office, the signal was struck. Rising promptly from his bed, as was already his custom, he hurried into the church and listened with modest attention to the nocturnal chant and the morning praises. After many prayers, he withdrew home to restore his weary limbs with a little sleep [Note: [Col. 0935] *somnio* in 1; in 2, *aliquanto* appears, with *somno* absent].

When dawn first began to redden [Note: [Col. 0935] *autem* in 2 and 3.], the execrable Bolezlaus [Note: [Col. 0935] *belezlaus* in 1.], brother of the holy man and author of perversity, mindful of the weapons that he had earlier secretly stirred against the innocent man [Note: [Col. 0935] *c. l.* in 2.], rushed like a wolf from the cave where he had lain hidden, falling upon the lamb whom he was secretly to tear apart. He advanced furiously with several followers suited to this crime, girded with a sword, and stood in the middle of the road to confront the simple man.

The saint himself, greeting him with the mildest kindness [Note: [Col. 0935] *salutandum* in 3; *benignitate* in 1.], addressed him thus [Note: [Col. 0935] *ita* is absent in 1.]:

> “Hail, beloved brother! Let immense thanks for your affection be rendered to you by us, because yesterday you served us well and pleasantly at the banquet you had honorably arranged [Note: [Col. 0935] *deposito* in 1; *abunde* in 3.].”

The wicked man did not answer this sweet address [Col. 0936C]. Instead, he quickly drew his sword and struck the crown of the saint’s head as forcefully as he could, saying:

> “Today I shall prepare a better banquet for you!” [Note: [Col. 0935] *praeparo* in 2 and 3.]

But the iron rebounded without even leaving a wound, and the blow was repeated [Note: [Col. 0935] “And scarcely did blood flow, because he was powerless through terrible fear; and blessed Wenceslaus could easily have overcome him, for he even took the sword from his hand, but did not wish to defile himself. But the man shouted: ‘Where are you? Help me!’ Then all the malicious men rushed from their hiding places with swords and spears, tore him with many wounds, and killed him. M.]. When he wished to strike a third time, the sword fell from the frightened soldier’s hand together with the extended blow [Note: [Col. 0935] *m. t.* in 2.].

The holy Wenceslaus immediately seized it by the hilt [Note: [Col. 0935] *capulam* in 1.] and, holding it above the already unarmed criminal’s head [Note: [Col. 0935] *vibrans* in 2 and 3.], said:

> “Do you see, wretched man? The destruction of your cruelty could be turned against you. Behold what prevents me from becoming a shedder of fraternal blood! But I do not wish, O brother, that your blood should be demanded from me at the final judgment [Note: [Col. 0935] *tuus o f. s.* in 2.]. Take back the sword; hasten your punishment. Do not delay what must be done!”

The impious brother took up the weapon again and, shouting loudly as though afraid of being overcome, called his companions to his aid [Note: [Col. 0937] *s. in a sui* in 2.]. He pretended that he was compelled to resist and had first been wounded by his brother’s attack. At once his associates, summoned by the great shouting, came running. As though unaware of the cause of the crime [Note: [Col. 0937] *s. q.*], they asked about the tumult and perceived their lord’s heated anger.

Then the author of the crime himself shattered the sacred head with a fourth blow, at least to some extent; all of them rushed upon him together, and in rivalry pierced his limbs with spears and swords. The wounded body fell half alive upon the ground. The savage blows of swords grew more frequent again and again; innocent blood was poured out; the body, free from stain, was torn to pieces as though by dogs [Note: [Col. 0937] *minuatim* in 1.].

The most sacred soul, released from the torments of so many wounds and from the fleshly enclosure of its dwelling [Col. 0937B], was carried by angelic hands in noble triumph to behold with joy the face of the supreme rewarder and to sit forever among the glorious ranks of martyrs. On the fourth day before the Kalends of October [Note: [Col. 0937] “The third day before the Kalends of October. M.”] it entered the companionship of the heavenly kingdom, rejoicing forever.

**20.** The few believers who were present reverently placed the sacred body in a sarcophagus [Note: [Col. 0937] *sarchofago* in 2; *constanter* (“steadfastly”).]. After the clergy had celebrated the funeral rites, they buried it outside the church, near the place of the combat.

After Bolezlav, a duke of excessive perversity, succeeded to the kingdom, and his savagery raged against the bands of the faithful [Note: [Col. 0937] *f. c.* in 2 and 3.], not long after the holy man’s death [Note: [Col. 0937] Absent in 1.], while he was still alive, he condemned the clerics and friends, as well as those familiarly attached to his service, to sudden death [Note: [Col. 0937] “They too, perhaps, coming swiftly into the city of Prague, killed all his friends and persecuted his clerics. M.”].

[Col. 0937C] **21.** After the venerable passion of the most steadfast athlete of God [Note: [Col. 0937] *atletae* in 1.] had been accomplished, certain servants, ordered to wash with water the blood that appeared scattered across the church’s boards at the very hour of the martyrdom [Note: [Col. 0937] *apparuit* in 2.], completely wiped it away. The next day they came there and saw that the blood had spread in the same place no less than when it had first adhered to the wall [Note: [Col. 0937] *dilatam* in 1.]. Terrified at this sight [Note: [Col. 0937] *ipso hoc viso* is absent in 2.], they brought water again and tried much more diligently to wash it away [Note: [Col. 0937] *multa* in 1.]. On the following day they returned to test whether they had again been deceived, and recognized that the wall was no less stained with blood, although it seemed to have been washed three times. They marveled greatly at this and thereafter ceased the labor of washing it; to this day the wall itself shines as a venerable sign, marked by the same blood.

[Col. 0937D] **22.** As has often been disclosed to us by the report of truthful witnesses, after the triumph of the steadfast athlete [Note: [Col. 0937] *ath. tropheum* in 2.], all those who had shed the innocent blood were struck by heavenly fury or seized by demonic power. Thereafter they either did not appear again among human beings, or, their nature being changed because of their vices, they used the barking of dogs in place of speech and imitated canine bites with the gnashing of their teeth [Note: [Col. 0937] *canu* in 1; *imitantur* in 1.], or, dried up by the miserable wasting of their bodies and continually deprived of hearing, they brought their lives to an end that was hateful even to themselves.

**23.** While the venerable body rested there for a period of three years, it appeared one night to certain faithful people that, with God revealing the matter, it ought to be transferred from there to the church of the holy martyr Vitus, which he himself had built, so that it might be buried in a more reverent tomb. Awakened from sleep and believing what they had seen, although they feared the prince’s tyranny, they nevertheless, in the dead silence of midnight, cautiously opened the tomb. They placed the precious relic of the martyr, without opening the sarcophagus, upon a vehicle, securely bound [Note: [Col. 0937] *vegiculo*, corrected to *vehiculo* in 1.], and set out along the road toward which their steps were directed.

They came to a stream [Note: [Col. 0937] Dobrowsky notes from Cosmas and Christian that the stream was called Rokytnicza.], which the animals drawing the cart could not cross because it was excessively deep, and which had neither boats nor a landing on either side [Note: [Col. 0937] *utrimque* in 1.]. They stood looking around. The bridge had already been broken apart and scattered by the rushing water, and no timber could be found for its repair. What were they to do? [Note: [Col. 0937] *q. f.* is absent in 2.]

While they were caught in this difficulty, they suddenly raised their eyes and—behold!—through the miraculous presence of God’s power, the cart stood on the opposite bank, untouched on every side by the moisture of the water [Note: [Col. 0937] *stat a.* in 2 and 3; *secus* absent in 2; *humiditatem* in 1.]. Astonished for a while at the miracle, they swam the horses across the stream, followed the vehicle laden with the sacred burden, and quickly reached the appointed place. Praising God, they entered the church with the sarcophagus, carefully closed the doors, and poured out sincere prayers. Then they opened the sarcophagus, and behold: the body was still whole in its fleshly substance and sound throughout all the wounds. Only the marks of the injuries were visible, except for the wound inflicted by the brother’s sword, which appeared to gape and pour out blood [Note: [Col. 0937] *aparentibus* in 1.].

They enclosed it again beneath the entrance to the altar, with a crowd of the faithful accompanying it and the hymns of the clergy sounding around them, and buried the precious body in a place to be revered in solemn memory. There, as divine omnipotence repeatedly shone forth, the joyful celebration of the faithful and the terror of unbelievers frequently became manifest through countless signs of miracles worked by the merits of so great a man.

The date of this translation is recorded for celebration by mortals as the fourth day before the Nones of March [Note: [Col. 0937] “The third day before the Kalends. M.”]. It seems fitting to insert, in the course of our account, a brief mention of the miracles that divine piety afterward deigned to perform through his merits, as his glory shone throughout the world [Col. 0938D].

[Col. 0939A] **24.** Certain men seized on a judicial charge [Note: [Col. 0939] *judicario capiti* in 1.], brought into the palace in chains, were shut up in prison at the prince’s command and bound below with tighter restraints around their hands and feet under cruel custody [Note: [Col. 0939] “After this, many men lay in prison enclosed in wood; each had an iron collar around his neck, and all of them, in their distress, prayed to the almighty Lord, saying: ‘Lord God, through the merits and prayers of blessed Wenceslaus, help us.’ During the following night something like a little bell sounded in their ears, and light shone in the prison; the wood bent like a bow, and they pulled their feet out of the wood. Then they all cried out together: ‘Lord God, have mercy on us.’ At once the power of Christ was present, and each one’s collar broke and fell from his neck to the ground. M.”].

At midnight, as necessity required, they remained awake, miserably crushed by the tightness of their fetters and handcuffs. Striking their hearts with bitter groans, while the guard slept a little, they all burst into these words of prayer, weeping [Note: [Col. 0939] Absent in 2 and 3.]:

> “O God, supreme consoler of those who groan, wondrous creator of heaven and earth, look upon us, destined for the power of death. Through the intercession of your beloved soldier Wenceslaus, who, while still living in the world, always showed himself a kind defender of the wretched for your name’s sake, deign to draw us, most miserable men, out of the condemnation now threatening us.”

After the prayer, half the prison, where the guards stood watch, was suddenly completely darkened as though by a very dense mist [Note: [Col. 0939] *denso* in 2.]. The burning lamps of the guards within were extinguished, while the other part, where the prisoners lay, became bright as though beneath the clearest sun. And behold, a sudden voice—truly, as must be believed, sent from heaven [Note: [Col. 0939] *u. v. c. c.* is absent in 2.]—thundered into the ears of the prisoners [Note: [Col. 0939] *intonat* in 2 and 3.] and commanded them to rise.

Stunned by both fear and joy [Note: [Col. 0939] *et* in 1.], they silently moved their limbs. Immediately the chains broke apart and fell; their hands and feet were freed. When the prison door had been opened by divine power, they joyfully leaped out. Thus released by God’s will, they proclaimed praises to Christ and to his holy martyr Wenceslaus among the peoples, and strove with unwavering faith and wonder to spread the immense marvels of his virtues.

**25.** Among them was a certain gentile who had not yet been cleansed by the grace of baptism [Col. 0939C]. When he realized that he had been freed from death through the merits of Wenceslaus, he devotedly turned to true recognition of the Catholic faith, was cleansed in the saving bath, and, with his faith strengthened [Note: [Col. 0939] *firmitaque fidei* in 1.], fixed in himself by the love of God [Note: [Col. 0939] *a. c.* in 2; *gnatum*, corrected to *natum* in 1.], promised that he would give to the service of God at the church of the holy martyr his only son, whom he loved as dearly as his own life, for the clerical office.

When he later fulfilled this promise, he himself continued to believe and serve God and lived to a sufficiently advanced age [Col. 0940A].

[Note: [Col. 0939] “At once a pagan who was being held in the same place made a vow to the Lord, saying: ‘If God helps me through the merits of blessed Wenceslaus, I believe in Christ, and I shall give my son to him in service.’ Immediately all the iron bonds fell from him. They enclosed him again and again, even more tightly, and once more the fetters fell from him as before. He was immediately released, instructed in the holy faith, and baptized; afterward he lived for many years. M.”]

**26.** Another miracle no less remarkable followed this one [Note: [Col. 0939] What is read in this chapter is not found in M.; *Quicquid* in 1; *H. quoque* in 2 and 3.]. A certain young chamberlain named Podhiwen [Note: [Col. 0939] *Podhivuen*, written in another ink but by the same hand in a blank space in 1, where *h* is superscript; the name and *n.* are absent in 2 and 3.], more faithful than the other servants [Note: [Col. 0939] *s. f.* in 2.] and better suited to his secrets, had been greatly loved by the holy man while he was still living in the world; the earlier writing also mentions him. Deprived of his beloved master [Note: [Col. 0939] *vi* in 1.], he repeatedly mourned sadly for many days and enlarged among many people, by praising them, numerous examples of his master’s deeds, of which he himself had knowledge.

When the mad duke learned of this, inflamed by furious anger [Note: [Col. 0939] *rabid.* in 3.], he immediately ordered him to die by hanging [Note: [Col. 0939] *enim* in 1.]. After he had been hanged, as the true testimony of good men confirms, two years later his head appeared to grow and whiten with flourishing gray hair, just as the living and healthy heads of human beings ordinarily do [Col. 0940B].

**27.** In the meantime, a certain man seized by the severe sentence of a judge was thrust into a similar punishment of prison custody, to be killed the following day [Note: [Col. 0939] *includitur* in 2 and 3.]. After his earlier restraints had been removed, he was bound much more tightly. Weeping most bitterly, he called upon God’s holy Wenceslaus from the depths of his heart for help, saying:

> “Holy martyr of God, if you possess such influence with the most high God as people say, intervene for me, who am about to die, so that, freed through your merits, I, wretched man, may remain alive for a little longer in order to cleanse the crimes I have committed.”

As soon as he had prayed [Note: [Col. 0939] *oratus* in 1.], his bonds broke with great force, and by God’s grace he was released from the prison without the guards knowing. But outside, pagan robbers were standing; they captured him again and bound him exceedingly tightly. As he was carried farther under restraint, to be exchanged for whatever price might be paid for him, he repeated his earlier prayer. The hearts of the gentiles were softened, and they voluntarily released and dismissed him. Thus freed once again, he magnified the praises of God and of the blessed duke as he journeyed through the lands [Note: [Col. 0939] *Et* in 2 and 3.].

[Note: [Col. 0939] “Afterward the prince ordered another man to be shut up in prison. He frequently called upon the Lord with sighs, saying: ‘Lord God, through the merits of blessed Wenceslaus, help me.’ While he slept, he suddenly awoke and saw himself standing outside the prison in the streets; there were no fetters on his feet, no handcuffs on his hands, and no collar around his neck. He returned to the vicar and related how, by God’s miraculous power, he had been snatched from the prison; they immediately released him. Added in M.”]

**28.** It is said that a certain woman remained in the same city where the holy body rests. She had been deprived of sight and, from the very beginning of her life, had contracted hands bent backward in a crooked curvature, so that she lacked every use naturally granted to the hands [Note: [Col. 0941] *visu* in 1.].

When the yearly festival day returned [Note: [Col. 0941] *festo* in 2.], she entered the church of the holy martyr Vitus and was led to the tomb of blessed Wenceslaus, where she desired to go. Prostrate in prayer, she continued mourning and praying until, in the sight of everyone, the merits of the holy man restored her sight and renewed the soundness of her hands.

**29.** Later, a certain man was seized by those to whom he owed a small sum of money under an agreement of loan [Note: [Col. 0941] *accomm.* in 1.]. He was long tormented under the harshness of chains until he should pay the debt. But, because other business was pressing, those who were wandering about the city left him meanwhile under guard, lying bound on the public road outside the church [Note: [Col. 0941] *cum* in 1.].

Caught in the midst of his distress, he raised his hands toward the church door and prayed in these words:

> “O most gentle duke and most holy martyr, since your holiness has already rescued many from the hands of the impious by interceding with the great God, I, wretched man, beg you not to forget me in my bonds, but by your customary compassion to have me released from here” [Note: [Col. 0941] *absolutum* in 2.].

As God’s mercy quickly appeared [Note: [Col. 0941] *Crescente* in 1.], the chains were suddenly severed as though cut by an iron blade through the prayers of the blessed martyr [Note: [Col. 0941] *c. a.* in 2.]. He entered God’s temple, giving thanks, offered prayers to God and the holy martyrs, and returned home free.

**30.** In the province of the Franks there was a certain man who had been deprived of the use of his feet from infancy [Col. 0941C] [Note: [Col. 0941] Absent in 1.]. His nature was impaired: he could not walk but moved by dragging himself across the ground like a crawling creature [Note: [Col. 0941] “A lame man. M.”].

One night, while sleeping, he trembled at a vision. A man of extraordinary beauty, clothed in white garments [Note: [Col. 0941] *alis* (“wings”) in 2.], stood beside his bed, awakened the lame man, and showed him the way to salvation, saying:

> “However you may be able, poor man, rise and go to Prague, the city of Bohemia [Note: [Col. 0941] *boemiae*, corrected from *boemaniae* in 1.]. Even if you must spend all your substance on whatever vehicle will carry you, go there; and when you have arrived, enter the church of the holy martyr Vitus, where the body of the holy martyr Wenceslaus rests. After praying there, you will unquestionably regain the health of your feet.”

When he awoke, he disregarded the command [Note: [Col. 0941] *visa somni n. se d. esse c.* in 2.], believing that the dream had deceived him, and entirely postponed the journey imposed upon him.

The following night, while the poor man was resting in bed, he again saw the same elder of such great radiance standing beside his bed [Note: [Col. 0941] Absent in 1.]. Rebuking him in these words, the elder said:

> “Dear poor man, awaken from sleep and recognize the truth of this vision. Why has negligence arisen in your wretched heart concerning the healing of your infirm body? Why have you postponed the journey to your own salvation, recently commanded to you by my vision?” [Note: [Col. 0941] *certum* in 2; *ita* in 2.]

Awakened by the harshness of the rebuke, the lame man, having no further doubt about what he had heard, replied:

> “I shall not delay departing, pious and venerable elder!”

When morning came, a vehicle was prepared as quickly as possible. He paid an agreed fare to merchants traveling along the same road and, guided swiftly by them, reached the place already appointed [Note: [Col. 0941] *designatum* in 2.]. In accordance with the earlier admonition of the man who had appeared to him in sleep [Note: [Col. 0941] *ammonitionem* in 2.], he was carried by others into the church of the holy martyr Vitus, where the blessed body rests, since he was powerless through the loss of the use of his feet [Note: [Col. 0941] *ab horum* in 2; *in s. a.* is absent in 2.].

Prostrate alone before the altar, he prayed inwardly to God and the saints. The aid of divine power did not delay [Note: [Col. 0941] *d. v.* in 2.]. Through the wondrous merits of the blessed martyr Wenceslaus [Note: [Col. 0941] Absent in 2.], the tendons of his feet, previously contracted, were stretched out as though with a crack [Note: [Col. 0941] *dist.* in 2.]; his legs and soles were strengthened. He rose healthy by God’s grace and, having rendered thanks [Note: [Col. 0941] *elataque* in 1.], went out powerfully, without anyone’s support, with his walking restored in health and strength. Rejoicing and proclaiming God’s miracles more widely, he returned to his homeland [Note: [Col. 0941] “Here ends the passion of Saint Wenceslaus. 2.”].

**In the year of the Lord 971. Heraclius, bishop of Liège.**

[Col. 0943]

# HISTORICAL NOTICE

*(Gallia Christiana.)*

[Col. 0943A] Heraclius, also called Euracius and Everaclus, and named Euracrus by Fulcuin, was highly distinguished by the nobility of his Saxon lineage, his exceptional wisdom, and his rare learning. Educated at Cologne, he made such progress in sacred letters and conceived such zeal for extending them that, after becoming dean or provost of Bonn, he was made bishop of Liège around the year 960. He inspired the entire Church of Liège—or rather the whole province, which until then had been enlightened by no letters—to the pursuit of learning; gathered skilled clerics from every direction; generously supported them from his own resources while appointing them teachers; and established schools throughout the cloisters of both the secular and regular clergy, says Giles.

He considered it in no way unworthy of his dignity to attend these schools. He encouraged the minds of beginners and proposed the most difficult questions for the wiser men to solve; if they were unable, he himself unraveled them. When he was traveling, there were always people with him with whom he could discuss Scripture. When absent, he urged by frequent letters those whom he had left as teachers of the schools to devote themselves to study. Through this distinguished diligence he advanced many men to an exceptional knowledge of human and divine affairs, so that the schools of Liège soon became famous throughout the neighboring kingdoms.

His wisdom was so great that many of the princes of the world held him in high esteem and summoned him even to affairs of the kingdom. Thus, at the command of Otto Augustus, he accompanied Bruno of Cologne to France, where Bruno had been sent to bring assistance to his nephew, King Lothair. While passing through Troyes, Bruno obtained the body of Saint Patroclus from the bishop [Col. 0943C]; but, compelled by urgent business to return, he entrusted the entire matter to Heraclius. Heraclius diligently completed it and carried the sacred relic to Cologne.

He followed the emperor, or his namesake son [sic], into Italy and witnessed the victory won in Apulia and Calabria against the treacherous Greek emperor. Indeed, he roused an army made illustrious by so many victories but terrified by an eclipse of the sun and almost driven to collapse. He taught them that their fear was empty and childish and restored them to their former courage.

He loved the beauty of churches so greatly that he founded two basilicas at Liège, dedicating one under the name of blessed Paul and the other under that of Saint Martin, and assigning thirty canons to each. He established three courts and built parish churches: that of Saint Mary Magdalene in the middle of the city, and those of Saint Severinus and Saint Margaret in the suburbs.

He also showed his zeal for monastic affairs by appointing a suitable pastor, Lord Aletramnus, to the monastery of Lobbes, and afterward Fulcuin; he helped them greatly, restoring three estates that had previously been alienated, says Fulcuin in chapter 27. Toward the end of his life he undertook to build the monastery of Saint Lawrence. When the walls had risen from the foundations, fearing that—as happened—his life might fail him before the work was completed, he wished to endow the nascent church. Before the greater altar was finished, he consecrated a smaller altar in honor of Saint Sixtus, martyr and Roman pontiff.

There he received Leo, a most noble man among the Greeks, whom the emperor Otto had brought into these regions because he suspected him. Heraclius welcomed him as an exile, assigned him a dwelling, and arranged that he and his companions should receive stipends from the goods which he had assigned there. Leo was also given burial there after his death [Col. 0944B].

He possessed such faith that he himself experienced a notable miracle. At the beginning of his episcopate, a dreadful disease, which physicians call lupus, attacked him and consumed his limbs so severely that it consumed two chickens applied to them every morning and two every evening, yet even then it did not spare the sick man’s flesh.

After every medical art and power had been overcome, he finally sought divine aid. He hoped to obtain it through the merits of blessed Martin, who, after the incursions of the Normans, had been carried back from Auxerre to Tours and was shining forth through wondrous miracles. He therefore went to Tours and celebrated the saint’s birthday. He arranged to spend eight continuous days at his tomb. At last, on the seventh night, carried away in ecstasy, he saw Saint Martin impress the sign of the cross upon his body, and he was immediately healed of the disease.

When morning came, the clergy of that church made him a canon, and he performed the sacred rite with more solemn ceremony. Not forgetting the benefit, as soon as he returned to his own see he offered his gracious physician precious ornaments of every kind and sent special gifts to each of the canons. At Liège, on the descent of the public hill, he built a church under the saint’s name and endowed it with such revenues that they abundantly sufficed for thirty canons and the other ministers [Col. 0945A]. Finally, concerning so great an event, he composed a charter in his own hand and, as long as he was able, went to Tours every year to give thanks to his benefactor.

The body of Saint Evermarus, long hidden in an obscure place but revealed through divine revelation, he raised from the earth and brought into a church dedicated to Saint Martin. He gave his people an example of patience: although provoked by their injuries, he did not even consider taking revenge. At length, renowned for his virtues, he exchanged this fleeting life for eternal life in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 971, on the sixth day before the Kalends of November, [Col. 0946A] in the twelfth year of his pontificate and the thirty-fourth year of Otto I’s reign and empire, says Giles, who also reports his letter to Ratherius. In it he calls himself his son and thanks him for the embassy sent to him from the city of Verona with balsam; finally, he expands upon his praises, which we have given above. The Magdeburg and Liège Chronicles likewise place his death in the year 971. He was buried in the basilica of Saint Martin on the mount. He attended the Council of Ravenna, where, by his subscription, he also confirmed the establishment of the archbishopric of Magdeburg, around the year 967.

[Col. 0945]

## LETTER OF ERACLIUS TO BISHOP RATHERIUS

*(Chappeaville, Gesta Pontificum Leodiensium, pp. 191–192.)*

[Col. 0945B]

To the lord and father, thrice-blessed bishop Ratherius, a man of distinguished reputation and proven character: Everaclus, servant of the servants of Christ, unworthy though he may be called his son—whatever is more fortunate in Christ Jesus.

Setting aside inversion and circumlocution, I am glad to describe in plain and open speech how great a part of my soul is yours; if I cannot do so scholastically, then, I hope, at least rustically, though not falsely, because with a pure voice I draw forth what lies hidden in an inward, not unspeakable, fiber. I wish to record how deeply I have fixed you in my winding heart. You know the comic saying: “I am Davus, not Oedipus,” so that I may not deceive my hearers with embellished words. But enough of this.

When I heard and more attentively received your honeyed embassy, although I had not yet seen or received the balsam that, moved by pious affection, [Col. 0945C] you sent, and although your letter had not yet been read, the undiminished affection of so great and illustrious a man toward me, whom I came to know, added no small joy to me, so insignificant a person. The precious liquid, of which I was almost destitute, greatly brightened my face when it was given. Finally, when I heard an epithet unsuited to my name, which your affection bestowed upon me without any commendation of my deeds, it gladdened my heart beyond belief.

Therefore, a hundred times bending my knees toward Verona, as though kissing your footprints, I return you a thousand thousand thanks.

If any image of virtue should appear in me—though none at all shines before me—it will nowhere be far removed from you, if you desire to learn by experience.

I often place before my eyes the sweetness of former days, and I gladly repeat it in frequent conversations: how, if not in the morning, then after meals while drinking, you cherished me, passing food into my mouth to be chewed, just as nurses put food into the mouths of little infants who cannot yet eat.

What should I recall, before or after, in return for so great a benefit? I am uncultivated and ignorant. For who is superior to you in wisdom, integrity, devotion to the best arts, innocence, or any other kind of praise? The Ciceronian voice speaks: “There is no such river of genius, no such power of speaking or writing, no such abundance, which could—not merely adorn, but even recount—the praises of your virtues.” If patience is mentioned—if I may say so without offending God, while preserving faith—you are patience itself. You did not swallow or sip saliva [the text is uncertain here: “mercurialem”], and you were able to pass beyond the number fixed in mud. Let us leave aside the satirical and comic writers; let us return to the simple and [Col. 0946C] holy.

You not only did not seize what belonged to others, but did not even desire it; you gave away what was your own, grieving over the miseries of others and not envying their prosperity. You became all things to all people, so that you might win them all. Your native land stretches out supplicating hands to you and invites you to return. All who belong to either order, clerical or military, cry out in mind, will, devotion, gesture, and voice that you should come; they long to see you. In the service we shall render you, we set no number or limit. Everything we possess will be in your hands, according to what has taken root in your heart, beloved Ratherius. Foresee, arrange, establish everything, and act in all matters as you wish. Under your skilled and masterly thumb, I shall not be ashamed to withdraw my hand from the schoolmaster’s rod. Farewell; rejoice; and may the grace of our Lord continually protect you from every evil attack.

[Col. 0947]

## ACCOUNT OF THE MIRACLE OF SAINT MARTIN

Eraclius describes in his own hand his miraculous healing, as well as his second vision.

[Col. 0947A]

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity.

In the second year after the return of blessed Martin from exile—namely, from the city of Auxerre—through God’s providence and the assistance of Ingelger, count of Château-Gontier, kinsman of Hugh, the illustrious duke of Burgundy, with vigilant care, remarkable solicitude, and a great multitude of armed men, he was honorably and fittingly restored to the place where he had previously been venerated. I, Eraclius, by the patience of God humble bishop of the Church of Liège, having heard of the miraculous powers that, by God’s grace and through the merits of blessed Martin, were continually performed there, came as quickly as possible, devotedly, to Tours with clerics and soldiers, bound by a vow in hope of recovering my health. I was grievously afflicted by the disease called lupus and had been brought almost to death.

[Col. 0947B]

While in the church of the most glorious confessor mentioned above I persevered day and night with an outpouring of tears and groans, vigils, fasts, and prayers, imploring God’s mercy and his intercession, on the seventh night blessed Martin appeared to me, together with Saint Brictius, while I was lying, as though in an ecstasy, from exhaustion. He said to him as follows:

“Brother Brictius, what do you think of our brother, the bishop of Liège, who has come here from distant regions and so devotedly seeks God’s help and ours?”

Saint Brictius replied to him as follows:

“Most merciful lord, if it pleases God and your goodness, it is right that he should be healed, since he is a man of great holiness and belongs to our order, whose life does not dishonor that order.”

Immediately, approaching nearer and touching the place of the disease with the point of his staff, he said:

“Brother Eraclius, our Lord Jesus Christ heals you and restores you to health through his mercy.”

[Col. 0947C]

“Therefore, joyful, healthy, and restored, reveal God’s manifest power to our brother canons, and command them in his name and ours to offer immense praises to their Savior together with the devout people, and to receive you permanently as a canon by right. Today you shall celebrate a great Mass in praise of God, so that those who had previously seen you as virtually condemned to death may place greater confidence in the aid of their patron.”

When this had been done and these words spoken, he disappeared from my sight. Both were clothed in episcopal vestments. I rose joyfully. My clerics and soldiers, together with the servants, were summoned and came, as did the entire venerable assembly of the canons. The place of the disease, which I had suffered on my buttocks, was no longer found; nevertheless, as a sign of the scar, a certain reddish line remained visible. For this glorious and evident miracle, the clergy sang the *Te Deum laudamus*, and the voices of the devout people were raised on high with praises.

[Col. 0947D]

When morning came, the canons assembled in chapter and received me as a brother and canon with unanimous will and desire. When the hour of the great Mass arrived, I celebrated the divine service according to blessed Martin’s command. After bestowing many gifts upon the church and the brothers, I returned joyfully and healed to my own country.

[Col. 0948A]

After a short time had passed, not forgetting so great a benefit bestowed upon me by God and blessed Martin, I founded, built at my own expense, dedicated, and most richly endowed a church in the city of Liège, on the public mount, for the praise of God and the honor of my healer. In it I established thirty canons, together with servants and other personnel, instructing them in reading and singing and in the other ecclesiastical customs according to the practice of the Church of Tours. As I had been accustomed to do every year, I went to Tours with great devotion and considered it my duty to make manifest to my brothers what had been done by God’s preceding grace.

While I was spending a certain Sunday night there and invoking God’s clemency, blessed Martin appeared to me again in a vision, together with the blessed Brictius and Eustachius, saying:

“Tell your brothers to receive into their brotherhood, under the form of a pious agreement and by perpetual right, the canons whom you established at Liège to serve God and me, and likewise all your successors in the bishopric of Liège.

“This shall be the form of their mutual brotherhood: Whenever they are able and a suitable occasion arises, they shall visit one another, have a stall in the choir, and receive a daily [Col. 0948C] allowance.”

This was carried out with the greatest devotion, holiness, and solemnity. In the tenth year after blessed Martin’s return, it was celebrated and confirmed by the authority of almighty God, and forbidden under anathema, so that no one might dare neglect or violate what divine authority and the will of blessed Martin had established and strengthened.

Moreover, it was added that the names of the dead should be solemnly commemorated by each side in turn, for the redemption of sins, and that divine services should be celebrated with the ringing of the brothers’ bells.

The same bishop also miraculously built another church at Liège, on the island, in honor of Saint Paul, up to the level of the windows, and assigned thirty canons to it.

[Col. 0948D]

For it is said that he prayed to the Lord to deign to show him the length and breadth for the construction of that basilica. When morning came, although snow had covered all the surrounding places, it did not touch the site of the future church at all.

Among other disciplinary institutions, he also decreed [Col. 0949A] that during Advent and from Septuagesima until Easter the clergy should be clothed in dark garments, namely black capes, because the color black is more appropriate to penitence and affliction than white.

[Col. 0950A]

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 973. POPE JOHN XIII

[Col. 0949]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

*(In Mansi, Councils, vol. XIX.)*

[Col. 0949B]

John, bishop of Narni, became pontiff after the death of Leo, the false pope—whether Benedict V was alive or dead is uncertain—in the year of the Lord 965, during the reigns of the emperors Otto and Nicephorus Phocas. Since at the beginning of his pontificate he pursued the Roman nobles, perhaps more harshly than was appropriate, he was captured at their instigation by the prefect of the City and exiled to Campania.

But when these events became known to the emperor Otto, he himself set out for Italy to avenge the injury inflicted upon the pontiff. After restoring John, he took revenge upon his enemies: he had the living prefect of the City stripped naked, placed him on a donkey and bound with a wineskin, and led around as an object of ridicule, flogged him, and finally committed him to prison. He ordered the corpse of the deceased prefect, [Col. 0949C] by whom Pope John had been expelled from the City, to be dragged from its tomb and scattered in various places. *(Regino.)*

For the conversion of the Poles he sent Giles of Tusculum, bishop and legate *a latere*, granting him authority to establish King Mieszko—who had been converted through his marriage to the Christian wife Dąbrówka, daughter of the first duke of Bohemia—in the faith together with his people, to establish bishoprics, and to undertake whatever seemed to pertain to the conversion of the entire kingdom and the instruction of its people.

For the conversion of the Vandals he likewise sent Willibald, Prochorus, and other highly learned men:

“They washed Mieszko the monarch”—I quote the words of Stanislaus Orichovius in Sander, *On Visible Monarchy*, no. 695—“and our nation subject to him, in the waters of sacred baptism, cleansing them from original sin; and, washed and purified from the city of the devil, they transferred them into the city of God and dedicated them to the Church of Christ. This was indeed done. For those most holy men entered Vandalia—or, if you prefer, Poland—and preached Christ to us and celebrated his grace, by which God had called us into communion with his people. They baptized crowds of people flocking to the rivers and expelled idols from Vandalia.”

He crowned the younger Otto, son of the great Otto, as emperor. He traveled from Rome to Capua with the emperor. Because the Church of Capua had honorably received him when he had been driven from Rome and had faithfully guarded him from the plots of Pandulf, prince of Capua, he honored it with the dignity of an archbishopric in gratitude.

After these events, when he had returned to the City, the principal bell of the Lateran church, newly cast and of extraordinary size, was raised onto the bell tower. The pontiff immediately consecrated it to God with sacred rites and gave it the name of John the Baptist, without doubt because that church was dedicated to him.

The heretical innovators acknowledge and condemn this, as though by his example he had led all later pontiffs and bishops into the error of believing and teaching that the sacrament of baptism ought to be administered to bells. But the ignorant are mistaken: bells are not so much baptized as, by a preceding blessing and sacred rites, dedicated and consecrated to divine worship, just like other sacred vessels. In that consecration names are given to them, as though to distinguish them from other bells—or at least, which would contribute more to piety, so that the people may be said to be summoned to church by the voice of some saint.

He sent an embassy to Theophanu, daughter of the eastern emperor Nicephorus, to arrange her betrothal to the younger Emperor Otto; the mission was undertaken by Liudprand, bishop of Cremona. But since Nicephorus, deeply angered by the coronation of the two Ottos, granted nothing to this embassy, he nevertheless, in Greek bad faith, himself sent an embassy to Otto under the false pretext of arranging the marriage, announcing that he should prepare the wedding and that he would soon arrive with his daughter.

While Otto’s army was occupied on this pretext with preparing the wedding, the eastern forces unexpectedly attacked the emperor’s troops and put them to flight with great slaughter. But when, elated by that victory, they attacked the same army a second time, an innumerable multitude of the enemy was killed. For this reason Nicephorus was killed, and a certain John, surnamed Zimisces, was elevated to the empire.

Not long after he had become emperor, he sent the daughter of the slain Emperor Nicephorus to Otto. Otto himself, as Witichind says, immediately handed her over to his son; and, after the wedding had been magnificently celebrated, he made all Italy—and Germany even more—rejoice at the event. Sigebert testifies that she was crowned empress by Pope John.

[Col. 0951A]

By means of a chain of Saint Peter, placed around the neck of a possessed man, he expelled the demon. In the city of Magdeburg, recently founded by Otto, he appointed Adalbert as the first bishop. After holding the apostolic see for six years, eleven months, and twenty-five days, he died on the eighth day before the Ides of September. He was buried in the basilica of Saint Peter, as may be seen from his epitaph:

Here lie enclosed the remains of the supreme pontiff John,

Who, a wise shepherd, paying the debt of death,

Forewarned at his death that his members should be placed here;

So that, released by God’s mercy from dark bonds,

He might ascend into heaven through the merits of the eminent Paul,

And, among the apostles, reap the joys of heaven,

And rejoice and exult, joined to blessed choirs.

All of you who read these verses, say with devout heart:

Have mercy, Christ, on your servant; cleanse his sins,

You who redeemed the world from guilt with holy blood.

[Col. 0951]

## LETTERS AND DECREES OF POPE JOHN XIII

### I. JOHN XIII CONFIRMS THE IMMUNITY OF THE CANONS OF BOLOGNA

*(Year 967.)*

*[Mansi, Councils, XVIII, 509.]*

[Col. 0951B]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

When I, John, thirteenth pope of the holy and apostolic Roman Church, was residing in the city of Ravenna together with my bishops and the Italian bishops, devout priests and deacons of the holy Church of Bologna appeared before us. Prostrating themselves on the ground on behalf of the entire clergy of the canonical congregation and kissing our feet, they presented a letter of protection from the holy memory of Pope Leo V, so that they should not be required to make any donation or public payment.

[Col. 0951C]

Moved by this, we lent our attention to their petition through divine mercy. Therefore, from this tenth indiction onward, we wish it to be known to all dukes, marquises, counts, judges, and to the entire people, from the greatest to the least, residing in the town of Bologna, our beloved faithful: all the sons of the Church of Bologna—that is, priests, levites, and the whole clergy—have represented to our apostolate that they suffer force and violence with respect to their goods, possessions, and property, and that public services are exacted from them both in their ecclesiastical assets and in their movable and immovable goods. This was clearly contrary to all the statutes of the holy Fathers and to canonical authority.

[Col. 0951D]

Therefore, sympathizing with their calamities, by these letters of ours we entirely forbid and prohibit anything whatsoever from being exacted from them or their successors by any person, great or small—anything that is known, or is to be read as belonging, to them by right and law [the reading is uncertain: *compertum* or *competunt*].

Moreover, we prohibit the imposition of portage dues, riverbank dues, tolls, lodging dues, military provisioning, or the oath—an exaction whose very name is shameful. Rather, without disturbance or harassment from any persons conducting public business, let them remain secure and peaceful, suffering no violence with regard to their property or any of their possessions, movable or immovable, whether their own or ecclesiastical. Let them continue peacefully and quietly in God’s service and praises, so that they may pray daily to the Lord securely on behalf of us and the entire Christian people.

[Col. 0952B]

Given on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the second year of our pontificate, the sixth year of Emperor Otto, in the aforesaid indiction.

### II. BULL OF POPE JOHN XIII FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF THE ARCHBISHOPRIC OF MAGDEBURG

*[Note: [Col. 0951D] The work of establishing the archbishopric of Magdeburg was begun under John XII but had not yet been completed; it was finally carried out in the two Councils of Ravenna. One of these councils was held in April of the year 967, and Pope John attended it together with Otto I, by whom the following bull for that establishment was issued. The conciliar decree—or, more properly, the agreement stipulated between the bishop of Halberstadt and those concerned with the establishment of the archbishopric—belongs to the second Council of Ravenna, held in 968.]*

*(Year 967.)*

*[Mansi, Councils, vol. VIII, col. 509.]*

[Col. 0952C]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, bishop of the city of Rome, to archbishops, bishops, all who fear God, and every assembly of Christians.

We wish it to be known how, through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit and through the merits of the chief of the apostles Peter, of the most holy Paul, the chosen vessel, and of thousands upon thousands of Christ’s martyrs, Rome, the head of the whole world, and the universal Church, after being utterly brought low by the wicked, was raised up by the Lord Otto Augustus, emperor, Caesar crowned by God, great and thrice-blessed, in the second year of our apostolate and the sixth year of the most holy empire of that aforementioned spiritual son of ours, and restored with every mark of reverence to its former honor.

[Col. 0952D]

In that same year, with the invincible emperor mentioned above favoring and consenting with us, a great synod was held at Ravenna on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May. Archbishops and bishops from throughout Italy assembled, while we were residing in the church of the blessed confessor of Christ, Severus. After all ecclesiastical matters had there been regulated according to the canons and the decrees of our predecessors, that most holy emperor began, with the most ardent love, to seek how, by our apostolic authority, the name of Christianity might be extended from its beginnings into the northern regions.

We, marveling that his mind was so wonderfully devoted to God’s service, deemed it right to consent to him. Therefore, with the holy synod and the emperor present and consenting, we decreed that Magdeburg, situated beside the river Elbe, where that God-blessed emperor had placed the body of Saint Maurice together with many martyrs and had built a church of extraordinary size, should henceforth be a metropolis and be so called, by the authority of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, and with the same authority by which our predecessors established Constantinople.

[Col. 0953A]

Because our son, the often-mentioned Otto, most august of all the Augusti, third after Constantine, has exalted the Roman Church above all others, we have granted that Magdeburg shall not be inferior to the other metropolitan cities, but shall remain first among the first and ancient among the ancient, firm and unshaken.

As suffragans of that metropolitan see we have unanimously appointed the bishops of Brandenburg and Havelberg; and we decree that the archbishop be consecrated in the city of Magdeburg by all those whom the emperor has wished.

[Col. 0953B]

Thereafter, that archbishop and his successors shall have authority to ordain bishops in suitable places wherever Christianity has grown through their preaching. At the present time, specifically, we perpetually confirm Merseburg, Zeitz, and Meissen, beginning with this tenth indiction.

By apostolic censure, under threat of divine judgment and the prohibitions of anathema, we decree that none of our successors or pontiffs, nor any other person whatsoever, may overturn or disturb these provisions, established by us with pious intention; rather, they shall remain firm, stable, and unshaken.

If anyone should presume, as we do not believe will happen, to act rashly against this apostolic decree of ours, let him know that he is bound by the chains of anathema, alienated from the kingdom of God, and condemned with the impious to eternal punishment. But whoever proves to be a pious observer of this privilege of ours shall deserve to obtain the blessing of our most merciful Lord God, become a participant in eternal life, and rejoice without end with all the saints.

[Col. 0953C]

Written by the hand of Stephen, notary, regional officer [*regionarius*], and archivist of the holy Roman Church, in the month of April and the tenth indiction. I, John, bishop and prelate of the holy catholic and apostolic Roman Church, have subscribed this decree made by us as confirmation.

[Col. 0954A]

The sign of the lord Otto, most devout emperor.

I, Rudoald, patriarch of the holy Church of Aquileia, was present, consented, and subscribed.

### III. DOCUMENT OF POPE JOHN XIII AT THE COUNCIL OF RAVENNA

*[Note: [Col. 0953D] This synod is mentioned by the continuator of Regino in these words: “In the year 967 of the Lord’s Incarnation, Emperor Otto celebrated Christmas. Except for the prefect of the City, who had fled, he ordered thirteen of the leading Romans, who had been responsible for the expulsion of Pope John, to die by hanging. Proceeding from there through Spoleto, he went to Ravenna. There, celebrating Easter with Lord Pope John, he assembled many bishops from Italy and Romania; and, after holding a synod, he devised many measures for the benefit of the holy Church. He restored to the apostolic John the city and territory of Ravenna and many other things that had been taken from the Roman pontiffs over a long period—or rather, he confirmed a restoration already made—and then sent him back to Rome with great joy.”]*

### ISSUED WHEN HE DEPOSED AND EXCOMMUNICATED HEROLD, ARCHBISHOP OF SALZBURG, AND CREATED FREDERICK ARCHBISHOP IN HIS PLACE

*(Year 967.)*

*[Mansi, Councils, vol. XVIII, col. 499.]*

John, prelate of the holy Roman and apostolic Church, to all archbishops and bishops, our beloved brothers in Christ assembled with us at the holy synod of Ravenna: the joys of eternal blessedness.

We wish it to be known to your holiness and charity that Herold, formerly archbishop of the Church of Salzburg, appears, contrary to canonical and apostolic authority, to have presumed wickedly to celebrate the sacred mystery after the loss of his eyes and, what is ridiculous, to wear the pallium solemnly.

[Col. 0954B]

This amounts to no small madness of heresy and ought to appear detestable to us and to the judgment of all orthodox brothers, especially since he was blinded because of his guilt and the rashness of his treachery: he had despoiled the churches of God, given their treasure to pagans, joined himself to them for the killing and plundering of Christians, and, as a rebel and traitor, had stood against his lord and most pious senior emperor. Accordingly, our predecessors, pontiffs of holy memory, had often forbidden him every priestly function.

[Col. 0954C]

Moreover, at the election and petition of nearly all the nobles—namely, the Bavarian clergy and laity—the holy Roman Mother Church, by the privilege of her authority, had decreed that Frederick, a venerable and universally praiseworthy man, should be made and should be archbishop in place of the same Herold.

Therefore, following the authority of our predecessors and strengthened by the assent of all your brotherhood, in the name of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, we now and henceforth condemn and utterly reject the heretical and presumptuous depravity of Herold, as well as all those who follow his blindness of body and mind in such presumption. Those who communicate with him we excommunicate and anathematize until complete correction.

[Col. 0954D]

Furthermore, by the authority of the apostolic see, we confirm and strengthen for the aforesaid Frederick, most worthy archbishop, the honor and dignity of the archbishopric of Salzburg. We bless and approve as Catholics all who submit themselves to his authority. Therefore, we ask and exhort your holiness and brotherhood to agree with us in this matter and to provide your confirmation of this apostolic sanction of ours.

*[Note: [Col. 0955D] The subscriptions are extremely corrupt.]*

I, John, bishop of the holy catholic and apostolic Roman Church, have subscribed this sanction issued by me in the synod at Ravenna.

The sign of the lord Otto, most serene emperor.

I, Rodoald, patriarch of the Church of Aquileia, was present and subscribed.

Peter, archbishop of the holy Church of Ravenna.

Walpert, archbishop of the holy Church of Milan.

Lanward, bishop of the holy Church of Minden.

Otker, bishop of the holy Church of Speyer.

John, bishop of the holy Church of Rimini.

Hubert [Adalbert], bishop of the holy Church of Luni.

Honestus, bishop of the holy Church of Perugia.

Peter, of the holy Church of Camerino.

Ingizo, bishop of the holy Church of Assisi.

Leo, bishop of the Church of Assisi.

John, bishop of the holy Church of Cagli.

Erfemarius, bishop of the Church of Ancona.

Attingus, bishop of the Church of Osimo.

Benedict, bishop of the Church of Humana.

Eberardus, bishop of the Church of Jesi [*Esinatae*; variant *Aesinatae*].

Benedict, bishop of the Church of Foligno.

Julianus, bishop of the Church of Lucera.

Gregory, bishop of the Church of Comacchio.

Ruodo, bishop of the holy Church of Cesena.

Arnaldus, bishop of Populonia.

Rihelardus, bishop of the Church of Fano, subscribed.

Done at Ravenna on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, by the hand of Stephen, archivist of the holy Roman Church, in the month of April and the tenth indiction, in the presence of all the holy bishops.

### IV. PRIVILEGE OF POPE JOHN XIII FOR THE CHURCH OF FERRARA

*(Year 967.)*

*[Mansi, Councils, vol. XIX, p. 1.]*

In the name of the Lord, John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the faithful of God and of the holy Church.

Declaring, we command as follows: after the just and lawful election and consecration of Martin, bishop of Ferrara, performed by us in the holy Roman Church, we came with that venerable bishop Martin to the city of Ravenna, together with many other Romans from our city. At the general assembly with Lord Emperor Otto, various cases and disputes were examined and deliberated; and with us, both the resident and attending multitude of peoples—clerics and laymen, bishops and abbots from many regions—was summoned within the basilica of blessed Apollinaris.

There the aforesaid Martin, bishop of Ferrara, presented a new petition, begging and asking us to confirm by this our decree everything that had previously been granted, delivered, and confirmed through ancient privileges by Pope Vitellianus, Adrian, and Leo, our predecessors and pontiffs of the holy Roman Church, in the time of Constantine and Emperor Charles. Moved by his prayers and petitions, and by those of all the princes, bishops, abbots, and other clerics and laymen, out of fear of God and for the sake of that venerable brother of ours, Bishop Martin, we have learned that everything which our holy predecessors, the pontiffs of the Roman See, granted to the holy Ferrara church of blessed George through ancient privileges—read aloud by Urso, judge of Ferrara, in the time of Martin, Andrew, and John, the predecessors of the aforesaid Martin—we likewise confirm by this decree, on behalf of the holy Roman Church of the apostle blessed Peter, to the aforesaid holy Ferrara church of blessed George, likewise in the presence and sight of all who were standing by.

Specifically, the Babylonian estate called Ferrara, in which that holy church of blessed George is situated and consecrated, together with its twelve farms; and to it we subject, with every obedience and security, all the other smaller estates situated within our duchy and county of Ferrara: namely, the estate and bank of Pullariolus, with its twelve farms; the estate of Constantiacus, with its twelve farms; the Quartisian estate, with its twelve farms; the estate of Doncro, with its twelve farms; likewise the estate of Petriculus, with its twelve farms; the estate of Popularis, with its twelve farms; likewise the estate of Curulus; the estate of Salecta, with its twenty-four farms; the Senetica estate; Castilio, with all its farms; and likewise the Firmian estate, with all its farms and appurtenances.

All these estates, with all their rights, just as we have learned that they were granted by our aforesaid holy predecessors to the aforementioned holy Ferrara church of blessed George, we likewise, by this decree of ours, as stated above, grant and confirm to our holy church, and to you, the aforesaid brother and our bishop Martin, and to your successors, throughout our entire duchy, county, and bishopric of Ferrara: in each of the estates, to ordain and consecrate churches, clerics, priests, and deacons.

Moreover, we wish it to be known to all, both present and absent, that throughout the aforesaid bishopric of Ferrara and the church of Saint George, and for you, Bishop Martin, and your future successors, bishops, the two parishes shall remain perpetually as our aforesaid predecessors possessed and held them in their dominion. Thus we too, by right, dominion, and privilege of our holy Roman Church of the apostle blessed Peter—and of ourselves and our successors—shall always hold them. They shall remain perpetually subject to our election, ordination, investiture, consecration, and jurisdiction.

No future successor of yours, when bishops are to be elected in that episcopate, may ever go for anyone’s election, investiture, or consecration except to our most holy Roman and apostolic See of the apostle blessed Peter and to our successors. Nor may any of our successors, or any great person of the kingdom—whether king or duke, bishop or archbishop—separate the aforesaid bishop and the church of Saint George, or its bishops, from the dominion, right, election, ordination, investiture, consecration, and jurisdiction of the holy Roman Church of the apostle blessed Peter.

But if any person of this kingdom of ours, whether king or duke, small or great, separates or alienates the aforesaid holy Ferrara church of blessed George from the right, dominion, and power of its bishops, and from the election, consecration, and investiture of the holy Church and Roman See of the apostle blessed Peter; or if that person should ever attempt, by any means or device, to diminish or molest in any way anything that has been given and delivered to it by the holy Roman Church, we bind that person perpetually with the bond of anathema, on behalf of almighty God, the blessed virgin Mary, the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, all the saints, and ourselves.
