[Col. 0984C]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable bishops Guisadus of Urgell, Peter of Barcelona, and Soniarius of Elne: greetings in the Lord.

Let your fraternity know that we have assigned the Church of Tarragona—which, because of the continual incursions of the pagans, has been reduced to nothing through the lack of a shepherd—to the Church of Ausona, and have made one Church out of the two. In it we ordained our brother Atto as archbishop, giving him the pallium, just as there formerly was one at Tarragona [Col. 0984D]. By the authority of the apostolic see we command and admonish you to render him the obedience which your predecessors once rendered to the archbishops of the Church of Tarragona, and that whether he himself or whoever shall in due course be archbishop in the Church of Ausona shall hold your sees subject to him and, after you, ordain and consecrate bishops in them.

## XXI. John XIII Undertakes the Protection of the Monastery of Saint Mary of Glastonbury (970)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XIX, 23.]

Let it be known to all the faithful that I, [Col. 0985A] John XIII, by the mercy of the Creator the unworthy pope of the holy Roman see, have been earnestly approached by the supplication of the glorious Edgar, king of the English, and of Dunstan, archbishop of the holy Church of Canterbury, concerning the monastery of Saint Mary, namely Glastonbury. They had enriched it, moved by love of the heavenly King, with many great possessions, increased the body of monks there, and established it by royal decree; and I shall not delay to do the same.

Assenting to their gracious petition, I receive that place into the bosom of the Roman Church and under the protection of the blessed apostles, and I establish and strengthen it by privileges, so that it may remain until the end in the monastic order in which it now flourishes. The monks themselves shall appoint a shepherd for themselves. The appointment of both monks [Col. 0985B] and clerics shall be at the discretion of the abbot and the community.

We also decree that absolutely no one may enter that island in order to conduct litigation, investigate anything, or carry out correction. If anyone should attempt to oppose this, or to take away, retain, diminish, or harass through rash attacks the possessions of that Church, let him, by the authority of God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, of holy Mary, the Mother of God, of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and of all the saints, be condemned to perpetual malediction unless he repents.

But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who preserve what is just for that place, amen; and let our stipulation remain unshaken.

Enacted in the time of Aelfard, abbot of the same monastery.

## XXII. Letter of Pope John XIII to Edgar, King of the English (971)

On expelling the clerics and introducing monks into the bishopric of Winchester.

[Col. 0985C]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Edgar, most excellent king, and to all the bishops, dukes, counts, abbots, and the entire faithful people of the English nation: Christian greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since whatever is sought through reasonable desires must always be granted, the zeal of your pious petition ought not to be offended in the privileges that are to be bestowed [Col. 0985D]. For we know, glorious son, that the dignity of your rule is everywhere so fortified by zeal for divine law that you constantly consider the stability of venerable places, so that, through the reward arising from your labor, the school of the Lord’s service may multiply and abundant fruits in the thousandfold may be returned to God, the giver of all things.

Therefore, illustrious king and most beloved son, whatever your excellence requests through our brother and fellow bishop Dunstan from this apostolic see, over which we preside, although unworthy, we grant in every respect. By apostolic authority we decree that from the monastery built in the city of Winchester in honor of the holy Trinity and the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul—the old monastery, so called to distinguish it from the new monastery nearby—the canons, who are hateful to the lord bishop and to all worshipers of the Catholic faith because of the manifest shamefulness of their faults and who persist shamelessly in them according to their impenitent hearts, shall be expelled, together with their provost, as vessels of the devil [Col. 0986A].

As your Sublimity desires, our most beloved brother and fellow bishop Ethelwold, thoroughly trained in regular discipline, shall nourish there a flock of monks living according to the precepts of the rule and establish for them a permanent dwelling. He shall adorn their life with such holy conduct that, when their shepherd is called to the reward of his labor, another shall succeed to the office of governance from that same congregation and from nowhere else.

But if, because of sins—which God forbid—it should happen that no one suitable for this pontifical office can be found within the same congregation [Col. 0986B], we command, by the authority of Peter, prince of the apostles, to whom our Lord and Savior granted the power of binding and loosing, that no one from the clerical order be promoted to govern this Church. Rather, a monk found worthy shall be taken from another congregation and placed over this Church.

If meanwhile anyone—which we do not believe—should presume to invalidate these decrees of the apostolic see or defile what has been piously granted to us, let him know, by the authority of that same heavenly key-bearer Peter and of all his successors, that he is bound by the bond of anathema and shall be eternally condemned on the day of that great judgment.

Farewell in Christ, lord son.

## XXIII. Privilege of Pope John XIII for the Monastery of Saint Mary of Thangmarsfeld (971)

[In Eckart, *Historia genealogica principum Saxoniae superioris*, 145.]

[Col. 0986C]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

We are impelled by the care and ardor of entrusted oversight to consider the establishment of venerable places and the security of those who serve God, and to undertake this pious labor for the soul: so that souls devoted to Christ, which have decided to serve him during their days, may persevere undisturbed, and so that the things acquired by Christians in the praise of God may remain firm until the end [Col. 0986D].

Our beloved and spiritual son Gero, archbishop of the holy Church of Cologne, visiting the thresholds of the apostles with worthy devotion and discussing many matters with us concerning the state of religion, reported that he and his brother Thietmar, margrave, prompted by the love of Christ, had restored a certain place in honor of holy Mary ever-virgin and had established there the duties of monks observing the rule of Saint Benedict.

He requested that the stability of this place and its religious life be made secure through our support and privilege. Assenting to his petition, by apostolic authority we decree that the place and the community of brothers may devote themselves to divine service without the power of anyone else interfering.

Nor shall bishops or their authority be permitted in any way to interrupt or draw back what is theirs [Col. 0987A]. Rather, their abbot, together with the monks, shall arrange and establish the things which they now have or shall have in the future. They shall owe no service of any kind to anyone except divine prayer for Christians.

Let them call upon the emperor as defender, and entrust the administration to an abbot piously chosen from among themselves. Let them ask bishops, if necessary, only about the state of religion. If the place should happen to falter, let the bishop assist in correcting it. In every other respect, let him leave the place free from any service.

Let them choose an advocate from that same lineage, if they should favor the good. But if they attempt to inflict force or harm, let them safely seek wherever they please a person who fears God and favors stability.

If anyone should attempt to violate this our authority, bound by the bond of anathema, he shall sorrowfully suffer the torments of Gehenna without end [Col. 0987B].

Written by the hand of Stephen, scribe of the holy Roman Church, in the month of January, in the fifteenth indiction.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, by the hand of Witlo, bishop and librarian of the holy apostolic see, in the seventh year of the pontificate of our most holy lord Pope John XIII, in the tenth year of the empire of Otto the elder and the fourth of the younger, in the fifteenth indiction.

## XXIV. Rescript of Pope John XIII for the Excommunication of the Invaders of the Possessions of the Monastery of Saint Symphorian in the Diocese of Autun (971)

[In Mansi, *Concilia*, vol. XVIII, col. 450.]

[Col. 0987C] In the name of God, I, John, pope and apostolic of the apostolic see and of the city of Rome, by the gift of divine mercy, wish it to be known to all how a certain bishop came from the regions of Gaul, named Girardus, the eminent prelate of the city of Autun. Also out of love for the king and in the service of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, he sought Rome and honorably approached our presence.

Since he was pleasing, acceptable, and dear to us because of his ability and the magnificence of his dignity, and while we were discussing many matters together, he humbly revealed to me, making complaint, that certain men appeared presumptuously and violently to hold land belonging to his bishopric. Moreover, he begged us to excommunicate them and condemn them with the dart of malediction.

Receiving his petition favorably, I, Pope John, servant of the servants of God, ordered such excommunication and malediction to be made, written by the hand of our archbishop Benedict. The land lies in the territory called Provence, belonging to the abbey of Saint Symphorian.

Therefore, whoever holds that land of Saint Symphorian, or anything from the land of Saint Nazarius, without the consent of Girardus, bishop of that city, by the authority of God the almighty Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and of all God’s saints; and furthermore by the power of blessed Peter, our lord, together with the other apostles to whom the power of binding and loosing was given; and through our ministry—let them be excommunicated and anathematized [Col. 0988A], and excluded from the thresholds of the holy Church of God, unless they turn and come to make satisfaction.

Let all the curses written in the Old and New Testaments come upon them unless they come to correction. Let them be accursed in cities, villages, fields, roads, fortresses, forests, and every place. Let them be blotted from the book of the living and not be written with the just, unless they repent and come to make satisfaction and correction.

Let it be so.

## XXV. Letter of Pope John XIII to the Most Glorious [Count of Barcelona?] (971)

He appoints the prelate Atto as governor of the diocese of Girona.

[In Flórez, *España Sagrada*, vol. XXVIII, p. 252.]

[Col. 0988B]

John, servant of the servants of God, [lacuna] to the most glorious [lacuna], [lacuna] and most beloved greeting to [lacuna].

We have learned how in your regions [lacuna] suddenly become priests, which ought to be the gravest and most detestable thing of all among Christ’s faithful. Therefore, because concern for all God’s Churches constrains us, we strive to eradicate such a pestilence completely from [lacuna] your realm and from all Catholic Christians, supported by [lacuna] the authority of the holy Fathers, especially that of the most blessed Pope Gregory, who, among other things, writing to the bishop of Autun, says [Col. 0988C]:

> [lacuna] “We have also learned that something not unlike this, and worthy of detestation, has come to our attention: certain men, inflated by a desire for honor, are tonsured after the death of bishops and suddenly become priests [lacuna], and shamelessly seize the leadership of a religious calling, although they have not yet learned even to be soldiers.
>
> What, we ask, do such men think they will provide for those subject to them, when, before reaching the threshold of discipleship, they do not fear to take the place of a teacher? Therefore it is necessary that, even if someone is of blameless merit, he should first be exercised through the distinct offices of the ecclesiastical order; he should see what he is to imitate, learn what he is to teach, and be instructed in what he is to hold, so that [lacuna] err, and [lacuna] may demonstrate [lacuna].”

[Col. 0988D] Let him therefore be refined for a long time by religious meditation, so that [lacuna], and thus shine like a lamp placed upon a lampstand, so that when the force of opposing winds strikes, it may not extinguish the flame of instruction he has kindled but increase it.

For since it is written that a person must first be tested and then minister, much more must the one who is appointed an intercessor for the people be tested beforehand, lest bad priests become causes of ruin to the people. There can therefore be no excuse or defense against this, because it is plainly known to all how diligent the holy and eminent teacher was in this matter, forbidding a neophyte to ascend to the sacred orders.

Just as at that time a neophyte was called one who had been planted in the instruction of the holy faith at its beginning, so now a neophyte must be considered one who, suddenly planted in the religious habit, has crept in to seek sacred honors [Col. 0989A].

One must therefore ascend to the orders in due sequence. For [lacuna] seeks to climb to the highest heights of a position by steep paths, setting aside the steps. And because we have heard that a neophyte was consecrated bishop of the Church of Girona without the election of the clergy and people, since no principle permits one to be counted among the bishops who was neither duly elected by the clergy nor sought by the people, we wholly will and command—and establish Atto, a venerable man, archbishop and our brother, as administrator and governor of the same Church of Girona, to preside over that Church in all things.

Let him rule the people and congregation entrusted to him justly and canonically, so that concerning [lacuna] he may render an account to [lacuna], the Judge [lacuna].

## XXVI. Letter of Pope John XIII to All the Bishops of Lesser Britain (972)

[Martène, *Thesaurus anecdotorum*, III, 868.]

He forbids them to resist the archbishop of Tours until he himself has rendered judgment concerning their dispute.

[Col. 0989B]

John, servant of the servants of God, bishop of the city of Rome, to all the bishops of Lesser Britain, our brothers in Christ: greetings in Christ and visitation.

Since, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and by the favor of the Lord God, we have undertaken the care of all the Churches, we must everywhere observe with severity the concern that each person’s faith be preserved whole in the same Lord, without which no one can please him [Col. 0989C].

Therefore let it be known to you that our most beloved brother Arduinus, archbishop of the holy Church of Tours, came to Rome to pray at the thresholds of the apostles and appealed to us that the rights of his archbishopric—which from ancient times had been granted and confirmed to his predecessors by the decrees of the holy pontiffs of the holy Roman mother Church—appear to have been taken away by your archbishop and his predecessors through violence and through the opposition of the pagan Normans.

Therefore, by apostolic authority, know that it has been forbidden to you [Note: [Col. 0989D] The editors add *esse*] henceforth to resist his right in any way concerning everything which the aforesaid archbishop confirms ought to belong to his archbishopric [Col. 0989D], until that archbishop of yours, or one of you with Archbishop Arduinus, whether with his suffragan or with another faithful messenger, comes to our holy mother Church, so that, after the causes between you and him have first been examined there, whatever we establish as equitable may be defined to the praise of God and our Lord Jesus Christ.

But if you do otherwise than we command, against his will, know that you yourselves are excommunicated from every ecclesiastical office by God and blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, through the command of our humility and by our authority.

[Here the Tours manuscript ends; what follows is added in the printed editions.]

But if you are willing to observe due reverence toward the aforesaid brother of ours [Col. 0990A], according to the decree of justice established by the holy Roman Church, may you remain, with God’s blessing, in the unity of our Catholic communion.

Meanwhile, let the people of your kingdom, especially the nobles—namely Berengarius, his son Conatus, and Hoel with his brother Guerech, together with the other leading men—know that if they are disobedient to this our command contrary to justice, and prove hostile or rebellious toward our aforesaid brother, the bishop of Tours, they too shall be excommunicated and deprived of our apostolic blessing.

## XXVII. Privilege of Pope John XIII for the Monastery of Cluny (965–972)

He commends Maiolus, abbot of Cluny, and his monasteries to Hicterius of Arles, Amblardus of Lyon, Theutbaldus of Vienne, Stephanus of Clermont, Aimo of Valence, and others.

[*Bullarium Cluniacense*, 5.]

[Col. 0990B]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the brothers and fellow bishops residing and presiding in the cities of Gaul—namely Hicterius of Arles, Amblardus of Lyon, Theutbaldus of Vienne, Stephanus of Clermont, Aimo of Valence, Wido of Besançon, Ado of Mâcon, Frotgarius of Chalon, Wido of Velay, Londricus of Avignon, Geraldus of Geneva, Magnerius of Lausanne, Luboinus of Lurs, and Rostagnus of Viviers—apostolic grace of blessing and the glory of eternal blessedness.

[Col. 0990C] We rejoice greatly in the Lord and exult because the love of God and charity toward one’s neighbor—which, as we have heard from the reports of many, you diligently preserve—make you eagerly hasten along the Lord’s ways and commandments, so that the prudent governance of your pontificate may provide necessary relief to many sons of the holy Church. We desire and piously admonish you always to demonstrate this by clear proofs, so that, flying heavenward on the wings of the virtues, you may be able to draw many peoples after you to Christ.

For it is our duty to exhort you not to disregard or neglect the discipline of the Lord, through which one arrives at glory. For you are, as the Lord says, “the light of the world and the salt [Col. 0990D] of the earth,” to whom the Lord Jesus Christ entrusted the governance of his Church, which he acquired with his blood.

Therefore, most beloved, we inform you that our special charity toward the monastery of Cluny is broader and greater than toward others. Our most beloved son, Lord Maiolus the abbot—whom, as we believe, you know well, since he is a religious man—presides over it wisely and blessedly. We commend him to you with particular attention and diligence, together with all the monasteries subject to his governance. We beg your Blessedness that, for the love of God and in veneration of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and also out of affection for us, you may be protectors of the monasteries entrusted to him.

Moreover, strengthened and confirmed by our authority and that of blessed Peter, and by the ordering grace of almighty God, I admonish you that, whenever any powerful person or anyone of notable rank should attempt with wicked audacity to invade the property or possessions of the aforementioned places, as soon as you learn of it, he is irrevocably and most severely to incur the strictest censure of your excommunication and to be separated from the assembly of the faithful. Through your sufficiently fearsome testimony, he is likewise to know himself bound by the chain of our excommunication until he comes to his senses through suitable satisfaction and humbly presents himself to Father Maiolus of the aforesaid monastery, seeking and obtaining pardon.

Finally, under invocation of the most holy and undivided Trinity, I adjure you, earnestly command you by apostolic authority, and beg you as beloved brothers not [Col. 0991B] to pass over this burden of our command. Its fulfillment brings both exaltation to the holy Church and advancement for you toward eternal goods.

To you also, brother and fellow bishop Stephen, I speak in the Lord: because of the innate goodness in you, compel your faithful Amblard to restore to the monastery of Celsinianum the land belonging to it, which until now he has withheld from that monastery, [restitute], so that, corrected by your judgment, he may escape the terrible bonds of excommunication and the penalties of eternal damnation. For if he does not come to his senses, he will be struck with an unending anathema.

Circumstances also require that we say something to you, most beloved brother and dear Lord Ado, bishop, whom, although we have not seen, we know by name to possess every spiritual goodness. We therefore implore the most kindly sweetness of your fatherhood: since you appear to be nearer to the school of the aforesaid monastery, may you, through your protection, come as swiftly as you can to the needs of the brothers. They love you out of an abundant charity, embrace you most perfectly with the arms of complete affection, and desire to hold you close.

Therefore, always be the protector of the monastery of Cluny, just as you are a faithful lover of blessed Peter.

## XXVIII. PRIVILEGE OF POPE JOHN XIII GRANTED TO ADALBERO, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS

*(Year 972.)* He confirms the decree of Adalbero, who had installed monks in the monastery of Mouzon in place of canons.

*[Mansi, Councils, vol. XIX, col. 31.]*

[Col. 0991D]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved brother in the Lord, Adalbero, most worthy archbishop of the holy Church of Rheims: perpetual salvation in the Lord.

If we recognize that churches spread far and wide are growing in holy religion by divine providence, we ought to exult in praises and render continual thanks to almighty God. Accordingly, we have learned that through your diligence a monastery of monks has been established at the fortress of Mouzon, which lies upon the River Meuse, in honor of Mary, Mother of God; that it has been adorned with religious observance [or: decorated; the reading is uncertain, perhaps *deculatum* for *decoratum*, or a form derived from *decus*], endowed from your own properties and those of your church with lands and churches; and that, under the charter of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, you have received our decree at your request.

Moreover, you transferred to the same monastery of Mouzon a small estate which had been established by Stephen, an illustrious man, and his wife Freduida, under the name “Tin,” and had been placed under Saint Remigius. Since it could not stand on its own because of the smallness of its resources, you gave it to the monastery of Mouzon, with property transferred in compensation to blessed Remigius, with the consent of the brothers.

So that the universal Church may know that we unanimously assent, by the decree of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and by our own decree, we confirm all that has been or will be granted by you or by anyone else—cultivated and uncultivated lands, vineyards, meadows, churches, male and female slaves, waters and watercourses, and everything belonging to the aforesaid monastery—so that, without the hostility of detractors, that place may always remain peaceful and inviolable.

Meanwhile, if anyone—which we do not believe—should attempt with rash audacity to act against what has been piously and firmly established by this authority of ours through this privilege, or to break or in any way violate what we have decreed for the praise of God and the stability of the aforesaid monastery, let him know that, by the authority of blessed Peter, whose vicars we are, although unworthy, he is bound by the chain of anathema and destined to be consumed in eternal fire with the devil and Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ.

But whoever proves in all things to be an observant guardian with pious intent, preserving the command established by our apostolic decree for the worship of God, let him obtain the grace of blessing and pardon for his sins and become a sharer in eternal life.

Written by the hand of Stephen, notary of the holy [Col. 0992C] Roman Church, in the month of April. Given through the hands of Andrew, bishop, on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, in the seventh year of the pontificate of our most holy lord John, thirteenth pope; and in the eleventh year of the empire of the elder Augustus, Lord Otto, the second of the younger, on the fifth [year], in the month of April, indiction 15.

## XXIX. LETTER OF POPE JOHN XIII TO ADALBERO, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS

*(Year 972.)* Privilege of the monastery of Saint Remigius.

*[Mansi, Councils, XVIII, 485.]*

[Col. 0992D]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved brother in the Lord, Adalbero, most worthy archbishop of the holy Church of Rheims: perpetual salvation.

It is fitting that our apostolate should take care, on behalf of all the Churches of God, that they not suffer the loss of their property but rather always increase and grow for the better. Therefore, since your brotherly affection requested that we fortify with the privilege of our holy apostolic see the monastery made illustrious by the body of blessed Remigius—so that, for the praise of almighty God and the honor of that same blessed Remigius, it might in no way be violated or diminished by the greed and rashness of any person, but rather increase and grow—we hereby, at the intervention of your affection, confirm and strengthen by this privilege of our authority, for the arch-monastery situated in France not far from the city of Rheims, over which you appear to preside, [Col. 0993A] all its possessions and all its movable and immovable property that can be listed and named: lands, vineyards, male and female servants, male and female tenants, buildings and dwellings, treasures, ornaments, and every kind of money.

We establish, under the solemn appeal of divine judgment and by firm prohibitions of anathema, that no king, nor any archbishop or bishop, nor any person whatsoever, great or small, may ever presume to impose harm or disturbance upon that arch-monastery, or to take away or alienate any of its property and possessions.

By the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we further promulgate through the constitution of this our apostolic privilege that everything donated to that arch-monastery by you or by any of the faithful of Christ, or that may hereafter be donated, shall remain permanently and securely under its right and ownership. No one shall have the license either to transfer or to alienate anything belonging to it, except for strengthening the common good through a just exchange and the grace of an appropriate compensation.

Moreover, let the abbot of the monastery provide the abbey of Saint Timothy—which your diligence has given to that same Saint Remigius for the use of hospitality—so that, for both your needs and those of your successors and the monks, benevolence toward the necessities of guests may not fail, and let him distribute it for the common benefit, provided only that archiepiscopal abundance does not exceed what the place can properly sustain.

But if anyone—which we do not wish—with full knowledge should presume to act with wicked audacity against the charter of this our apostolic privilege, let him know that by the judgment of God, of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and of our humility, he is excommunicated, indeed anathematized, with the devil and all the impious, for whom eternal punishment has been prepared.

Whoever, however, strives with pious intent to observe and preserve this privilege, may deserve to obtain from our most merciful Lord God the grace of blessing and the glory of eternal life among the saints and the elect.

Written by the hand of Stephen, notary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of April, indiction 15. Given through the hand of Andrew, bishop, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, in the eighth year of the pontificate of our most holy lord John, thirteenth pope; and in the eleventh year of the empire of the elder Augustus, Lord Otto, and the fifth of the younger, in the fourth month, indiction 15.

## XXX. PRIVILEGE OF POPE JOHN XIII FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT SAVIOR AT PAVIA

*(Year 972.)*

1. He declares that the monastery of Saint Savior at Pavia is exempt from every ecclesiastical or secular jurisdiction and is to remain under the protection and patronage of the holy Roman Church.  
2. He permits baptism to be administered in the monastery’s churches and grants permission to receive chrism and holy orders from any bishop.  
3. He decrees that the abbot is to be elected by the monks from within the monastery and consecrated by any bishop.  
4. He forbids anyone to exact tithes from the monastery’s goods.  
5. He promulgates excommunication against those who plunder or disturb its property.  
6. He bestows blessing upon its benefactors.

*[Margarini, Cassinese Bullary, p. 45.]*

[Col. 0994A]

Peace of God.—John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to my beloved daughter in spiritual matters, the lady Adelaide, most serene empress.

Since those things which are recognized as belonging to reasonable desires ought to be granted, the authority of our apostolate must by no means be withheld in granting privileges to strengthen the pious devotion of those who build holy places.

1. Therefore, your Excellency’s praiseworthy gentleness requested that the monastery of God and of our Lord Savior, situated not far from the city of Pavia, which you appear recently to have built, renewed, and [Col. 0994B] erected to the praise and glory of his name, and to have adorned with the gathering of religious monks under the regular discipline of a venerable abbot, as well as enriched from your own possessions, should in every way be honored with the privileges of the holy Roman and apostolic see, so that, established under the patronage and protection of our holy Church, which by God’s authority we serve, it might be subject to the jurisdiction and authority of no church.

Therefore, favoring your pious desires, by this apostolic authority of ours we decree that the aforesaid monastery of our Lord Savior, from now and unto the end of the age, shall belong, together with everything pertaining to it, under the patronage and protection of the holy Roman Church and of the apostolic mother Church.

For we establish, under the solemn appeal of divine judgment and the prohibition of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of our humility, that no emperor, king, bishop, duke, marquis, count, viscount, gastald, or any person established in any order or office may ever dare to impose disturbance upon that monastery, or presume in any manner to take away or alienate its property and possessions, its utensils and ornaments which appear to belong to it. Nor may anyone attempt to inflict any malice or harm upon it, whether in time of peace or of war.

Indeed, as stated above, we decree, confirm, and grant that it shall always remain with firm stability under the patronage and protection of our holy Roman mother Church.

2. By apostolic authority we also freely permit baptism to be administered in the churches belonging to the monastery; as for chrism or anything pertaining to holy orders, let them receive it from whichever church they choose, by our authority.

3. After the death of the abbot, let no one appoint an abbot there except one whom the agreement and common will of the brothers have elected from within the congregation itself. Once an abbot has been elected, he shall always have the power to choose a bishop who, with the fear of God and the consent of the entire congregation, may confer upon him and the other brothers the insignia of consecration wherever they wish, by the privilege of this authority of ours, without any pretext or withholding [the printed text has *datione*, “by giving,” apparently corrupt].

4. By a similar determination, according to your desire, most excellent daughter, we decree that the tithes [Col. 0995A] of the revenues of the aforesaid monastery of our Lord Savior, founded by you, shall not be exacted by any prelate of any church, by any device whatsoever.

5. We promulgate and decree, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, before God and the terrifying future judgment, through the constitution of this our apostolic privilege, that everything donated and granted by us to the aforesaid monastery, whether movable or immovable, as well as the possessions granted by kings, princes, and any of the faithful of Christ, or to be granted in the future, shall remain permanently and securely under its right and ownership throughout all ages.

Nor shall any person, great or small, have permission to plunder or take away anything belonging to the said holy monastery, so that it may remain secure and peaceful, well endowed and to be endowed still more abundantly, in accordance with the protection by which we have decreed that it is fortified under the patronage and protection of the holy apostolic see, for the praise of God.

But if anyone—which we do not wish—should presume with wicked audacity to violate what we have established for the honor of the Lord our God and Savior and for the stability of that monastery, let him know that he is bound by the chain of anathema and excommunication and assigned, with the devil and all the impious, to the most dreadful punishment of eternal fire.

6. But whoever proves to be a pious guardian and observer of these provisions may deserve to obtain from our most merciful Lord, throughout the ages of ages, the grace of every blessing, the absolution and forgiveness of all his sins, and the blessedness of heavenly life with the saints and elect. [Col. 0995C] Amen.

Written by the hand of Stephen, notary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of April, in the aforementioned indiction 15.

Farewell. Peace.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of May through the hand of Bishop Wido, librarian of the holy apostolic see, in the year of the pontificate of our most holy and most religious lord John, thirteenth pope; and in the eleventh year of the empire of the elder Lord Otto, and the fifth of the younger, in the month and indiction 15 mentioned above.

## XXXI. LETTER OF POPE JOHN XIII TO PETER, BISHOP OF PAVIA

*[Year 972.]* He entrusts the monastery of Saint Savior, erected and endowed by the empress Adelaide, to the bishop’s protection but not to his jurisdiction.

*[Margarini, Cassinese Bullary II, 47.]*

[Col. 0995D]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Peter, venerable bishop of the holy Church of Pavia: greetings.

Since the desire of a pious will and the intention of praiseworthy devotion must always be assisted by priestly diligence, care must be taken that what has been ordained for the peace of a religious congregation be neither neglected through indifference nor disturbed by presumption. Just as what reason’s usefulness requires ought to be defined, so what has been defined must not be violated.

Since our most excellent daughter, Adelaide Augusta, inflamed by the fervor of divine love, established a monastery on her own property not far from the walls of the city of Pavia, and took care to gather there holy and venerable monks from wherever she could, who, living under an abbot according to the regular rule of the most blessed Benedict and persevering in the purpose of holy conduct, might continually entreat the Lord of majesty both for the repose of her former husband, King Lothar, of glorious memory, and for the welfare of our most merciful son, the invincible Augustus Otto the emperor, as well as for the reward of our common son and of their souls and of our own Augustus Otto; and since she generously endowed the aforesaid monastery with possessions and increased all necessary provisions, as she piously judged appropriate, for the support of its inhabitants, your most reverend holiness should know that she asked that her will never be frustrated, that what had been arranged for the peace of the monks not be disturbed, and that what she had contributed to the monastery be confirmed by apostolic authority.

She added to her petition that we should likewise grant the monastery certain privileges both in the disposition of its property and in the appointment of its abbot. For she knew that the faithful show such reverence to the apostolic see that whatever has been established by its decree cannot afterward be shaken by anyone’s usurpation.

Therefore, since both the imperial will and such pious concern for the peace of God’s servants demanded fulfillment, in accordance with the petition of that most excellent daughter of ours, Augusta, we gladly grant apostolic privileges to the aforesaid monastery established in honor of our Lord Savior. There, everything that the devotion of her embracing will requested has been strengthened by the support of apostolic authority.

Among other provisions, we decree that no bishop of neighboring churches, nor any priest whatsoever, may in any way claim or defend ecclesiastical jurisdiction over that monastery, unless perhaps he has been invited by the monastery’s side—that is, by the brothers—for some ecclesiastical matter.

And since, most beloved brother, the place where the aforesaid monastery has been built is known formerly to have belonged to the diocese of the holy Church of Pavia, over which your fraternity presides by God’s authority, we absolutely forbid you, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of our humility, ever to presume on this occasion to usurp any prerogative of power in that monastery.

If requested by the monastery, namely by the brothers, piously offer them your visitation out of regard for divine love. But if you have not been requested, do not presume in any way to enter the monastery’s secluded places, lest through your arrival a public disturbance be offered in the retreats of God’s servants.

Let all these matters, which we now forbid you concerning the aforesaid monastery, and which are likewise eternally forbidden to all who succeed you in the order and place you occupy, be known to them under threat of divine judgment and by the authority of blessed Peter the apostle and of our humility.

You, brother, preserve inviolate what we have established, with the priestly diligence that is fitting, and do not allow it to be violated in any respect. In guarding these provisions, let your fraternity always show itself diligent and devoted, so that it may exclude every occasion of disturbance from the venerable place and persuade others to act similarly. May you long and carefully, as is proper, display your concern and devotion in preserving our will.

We have decreed that a record of this injunction be written in duplicate, establishing that one copy be kept among the archives of your church and the other by the abbot of the monastery.

Written by the hand of Stephen, notary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of April, indiction 15, [Col. 0997B] in the year of the Lord 972.

## XXXII. LETTERS OF POPE JOHN XIII CONCERNING THE ESTABLISHMENT OF THE BISHOPRIC OF PRAGUE

[Note: [Col. 0997D] In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 967, on the Ides of July, the duke of Bohemia, Boleslaus, whose byname was “the Savage,” having wickedly purchased the duchy with his brother’s blood, namely that of the blessed martyr Wenceslaus, lost both his life and the dukedom of Bohemia. His son, bearing the same name, succeeded him in the principate, differing greatly from his father in good character and spiritual conduct. For he was a most Christian man, Catholic in faith, father of orphans, defender of widows, clerics, and pilgrims, and an outstanding founder of churches. For, as we read in the privilege of the church of Saint George in Prague, he erected twenty churches and endowed them abundantly with every ecclesiastical resource.

His sister was named Mlada, a consecrated virgin learned in letters. When she came to Rome for the sake of prayer, she was kindly received there by Pope John XIII. Remaining there for some time, she was instructed in monastic disciplines. Then the pope, with the advice of the cardinals—or rather, wishing to assist the new Church—consecrated her abbess, changing her name to Mary, and gave her the Rule of Saint Benedict and an abbatial staff. Returning to Prague and being received by her brother, she presented him with the apostolic letters, whose formula you have above.]

*(Year 972.)*

*[In Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, fifth age, p. 833.]*

John, servant of the servants of God, to Boleslaus, foster-son of the Catholic faith: apostolic blessing.

It is right to lend favorable ears to just petitions, because God is justice, and those who love God will be justified; and, “All things work together for good for those who love God.” Our daughter, your sister, among other petitions not to be refused, brought sweet prayers to our heart on your behalf, namely, that with our consent it might be permitted for a bishopric to be established in your principate, for the praise and glory of God’s Church.

We received this with a joyful heart and gave thanks to God, who always and everywhere expands and magnifies his Church among all nations. Therefore, by apostolic authority and the power of Saint Peter, whose vicars we are, although unworthy, we assent, approve, and canonically establish that the church of Saints Vitus and Wenceslaus, the martyrs, shall become an episcopal see; and that in the church of Saint George the martyr, under the Rule of Saint Benedict and the obedience of our daughter Mary, your sister, a community of nuns shall be established.

Nevertheless, do not choose for this work anyone according to the rite or sect of the Bulgarian people, or of the Rus’, or of the Slavic language, [Col. 0997D] but rather, following the apostolic constitutions and decrees, choose for this work one eminent cleric, thoroughly learned in Latin letters, to the satisfaction of the whole Church, [Col. 0998A] who may be able, like a plowman, to cut the fallow ground of the hearts of the gentiles, sow the wheat of good works, and bring back to Christ sheaves of the harvest of your righteousness.

Farewell.

## XXXIII. PRIVILEGE OF POPE JOHN XIII FOR THE CHURCH OF ARLES

*(Year 965–972.)*

*[Bouche, History of Provence, II, 36.]*

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, by the will of divine mercy the humble pope of the apostolic see, wishes perpetual salvation and blessing to Yterius, a worthy brother and archbishop of the metropolitan Church of Arles, and to Thetbaldo, archbishop of the Church of Vienne, with all his suffragans; to Aymericus, venerable archbishop of the first Church of Narbonne, with his subjects; and to Sylvester, worthy archbishop of the second Church of Narbonne, with those subject to him—namely Laudericus, Theodericus, Ayrandus, Honoratus, Pontius, and Humbertus, most worthy pastors of their respective churches—and to all a common and perpetual glory of eternity.

Know that you are rulers and that God has granted you the keys of the heavenly gate, with the power to bind and loose, and so forth.

I therefore grieve and am exceedingly distressed over the cause of so great a crime, which is repeatedly reported to our presence by the mouths of many: the primate of Arles, who holds primacy and is the head of the other Churches, second only to the Roman [Col. 0998C] see, lies disemboweled by manifold wounds, and we have heard that he has been trampled underfoot. In it has been fulfilled the prophet’s sentence: “The mistress of the nations sits in sorrow.”

Therefore, in our own letters, we wish to point out to you and to all the faithful of God’s Churches the complaint concerning so great a sacrilege: why the prelate of that same Church is wickedly subjected to continual injury.

You should know that those aids which are due from the benefactors of our Church are always to be granted by us with the utmost fullness. Therefore, by the authority of the key-bearer of the heavenly kingdom, the author of our illustrious power, and by our own providence—which has also compelled him to yield—we grant him complete license and power to condemn and to strike with the sword of excommunication those who oppose him. We truly cannot deny this, as is known to all.

For this reason we command you with entreaty and earnestly ask you fraternally to ensure that all who, with rash audacity, dare to touch the land of the sanctuary, harm it in any way, or inflict injuries upon him, without regard for any person, are made to render the fullest amends in every respect [the printed reading *legere* is uncertain]; and, in accordance with the prescriptions of the sacred canons, correct them severely.

Finally, if necessity should require it, at the time and hour when he himself admonishes you by entreaty, strike them together with him with the sword of excommunication. The tenor of our excommunication is as follows, and we wish you to strengthen and confirm it:

By the authority of the holy and ineffable Trinity—that is, of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—let them be excommunicated. Let them have their portion with Dathan and Abiram, whom the earth swallowed alive; with Judas also, who betrayed the Lord, let them be consumed in eternal fires. Let their houses be laid waste, and let them be with the devil in the fire whose flame does not die and with the worms that do not die.

In this present age let them experience the same punishment suffered by Herod, who expired consumed by worms. May the Lord add pestilence to them until they perish from the earth and from the things that are in it. May the Lord strike them with poverty, fever, cold, burning, and scorching heat; and may all these evils pursue them until they are torn from the dwellings of paradise.

May the Lord also strike them with a sore, including the part of the body through which excrement is discharged; with scabies and itching, so that they cannot be cured. May they be struck by the Lord with madness and blindness. Let them also share the lot of Arius, whose intestines passed out into the privy.

With perpetual malediction may the eternal Father curse them unless they prepare themselves for correction. Let them be barred from the thresholds of the holy Church of God, separated from the fellowship of all faithful Christians, and furthermore bound by everlasting chains of anathema, so that they cannot be released until they have attained suitable correction.

Cursed be they sleeping, and cursed be they waking; cursed be they going out, and cursed be they returning; cursed be they eating and drinking, and cursed be they hungry and thirsty. Cursed be they working, and cursed be they ceasing from work; cursed be they in the house, cursed be they outside the house; cursed be they in the city, cursed be they outside the city; cursed be they in the villages, cursed be they on the mountains; cursed be they in the valleys, cursed be they in the forests; cursed be they in the meadows; cursed be they in the waters; cursed be they [Col. 1000B] in every place, unless they correct themselves.

Let them be removed from the merits of holy Mary, Mother of God, and of all the other saints; and let them be shut up in the abyss of hell.

Finally, with the perpetual sword of our excommunication and that of the Roman Church, we strike them, slaughter them with all the curses contained in the Old and New Testaments, and deliver them to be consumed in the everlasting fire of Gehenna, unless they attain satisfaction.

We wish those who hear these words to follow them by saying: “Let it be done, let it be done, let it be done.” Whoever refuses to obey this sentence of ours, whatever his order may be, let him be anathema, *maranatha*. For it is likewise said: “Let destruction be theirs at the coming of the Lord.” Amen.

# In the Year of the Lord 973. Saint Ulrich, Bishop of Augsburg.

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON SAINT ULRICH

Ulrich, bishop of Augsburg, the second of this name—for our Fabricius has already discussed the first above, book VIII, p. 305 and following—governed his Church from 924 to 973. His life is presented by an Anonymous author, published by Velser in his works, p. 515; by Surius, 4 July; by Mabillon, Benedictine fifth age, p. 415; and in the *Acts of the Saints*, vol. II, July, p. 97, edited with a preliminary commentary by Jean Pinius, pp. 73 and 97. Also by Benedict Gullmann of Augsburg, in a dissertation delivered at Leipzig in 1693 under the presidency of M. Gottfried Ludovici.

A synodal sermon, to be proclaimed to parish priests at synods, is attributed to him; it was first published in vol. IX of Binius’s *Councils*, second edition, p. 803.

## LIFE OF SAINT ULRICH

By Gerard the priest, his companion.

*[In Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, fifth age, p. 415, from Velser’s edition and manuscript codices.]*

# PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS

[Col. 1001A]

1. There are found altogether three ancient authors—for the more recent ones we leave aside for the moment—who transmitted the deeds of Saint Ulrich, bishop of Augsburg, to posterity. All were printed by Marcus Velser, a most distinguished member of the government of Augsburg. The first appears under the title of Anonymous; the second is Gebehard, the fourth successor of Ulrich in the same see; the third is Berno, abbot of Reichenau. Ekkehard the Younger praises them without naming them in book 5 of his *On the Misfortunes of the Monastery of Saint Gall*, where he reports certain matters omitted by them.

Besides these authors, Ditmar, the *Augsburg Chronicle*, and other historians of German and Alemannic affairs speak honorably of Ulrich; among more recent writers, the most illustrious is Cardinal Baronius. But here we must speak chiefly about the earliest writers of his life.

[Col. 1001B]

2. The first person to commit Ulrich’s acts to writing, called Anonymous by Velser and the others, indicates in several places that he was Ulrich’s contemporary and companion, as in section 18: “It is not fitting to omit entirely the things we saw.” And in section 54: “I learned these things not from anyone’s report, but I observed them being accomplished with my own eyes in very many cases.”

Some have thought that he was Udalscalc, but they do not adequately explain who this Udalscalc was. There was one monk of that name at Augsburg, at Saint Afra—or at Saint Ulrich—who wrote an outstanding book about the dispute that arose between Bishop Henry and Abbot Eginon, published in volume II of Henry Canisius. There he records certain miracles of Saint Ulrich. He later became abbot of that same place, from 1126 to 1148.

Another Udalscalc was bishop of Augsburg after the middle of the twelfth century; but both men lived long after the time of our Anonymous author.

That the author was a canon of the cathedral church is clear from the book on the Miracles appended to this Life, which I consider to be by one and the same author. For in chapter 28, after recounting a miracle performed at Saint Ulrich’s tomb in the church of Saint Afra, he adds that from there the people proceeded in a throng to the principal, or episcopal, church of Saint Mary. [Col. 1001D] “From there,” he says, “coming into the city to the church of Saint Mary, [Col. 1002A] they announced these things to us.”

The second writer of the Life, Gebehard, appears to have been unaware of the name of the first author. In his prologue he says that the first work on the deeds of Saint Ulrich was “composed by a certain illustrious man.” But at last, during our German journey, we learned the name of this Anonymous author from an ancient codex of the monastery of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg, written five hundred years ago. In it this first Life appears under the following title, after the chapter headings:

“In the name of the Lord begins the Life of Saint Ulrich, bishop and confessor of Christ, written by Gerard, who was ordained priest by him.”

Henceforth, then, we may call the Anonymous author Gerard. I do not know whether he is the same Gerard as Ulrich’s chaplain, mentioned in section [Col. 1002B] 63, or as the provost mentioned in section 70, or as the priest mentioned in section 83.

3. When Bishop Gebehard had read Gerard’s two books on the Life and Miracles of Ulrich, written in a plain style, he undertook to polish them in a new manner of expression, as he himself testifies in his prologue. But, overtaken by death, he could not complete the work.

He was the fourth bishop of Augsburg after Ulrich: after Henry, Ulrich’s successor, died in 982, and Ethic died in 988, Gebehard succeeded Liutolf after seven years of Liutolf’s rule; Gebehard himself departed this life in the second year after 1000. His unfinished work ends with praise of Ulrich’s active and contemplative life, beginning from the start of his episcopate.

[Col. 1002C] **4.** Shortly afterward Berno, at the request of Fridebald, fourth abbot of the monastery of Saint Afra at Augsburg, undertook to embellish the anonymous author’s work in another form, and in fact completed it before the year 1030, which was the last year of Abbot Fridebald’s life. Hermann speaks of Berno under the year 1008:

“In that same year King Henry, having at last learned, after two years, of Immo’s cruelty, removed him and appointed Berno, a learned man and formerly a monk of Prüm, [Col. 1002D] abbot of Reichenau. [Col. 1003A] Gladly received, he gathered the scattered brothers together again and, consecrated by Lambert, bishop of Constance, as the twenty-ninth abbot of that place, governed it with great distinction for forty years in learning and piety.”

He died in 1048. God willing, we shall give his eulogy elsewhere. Of these three authors we present here one, Gerard, because from the others there is scarcely anything worth knowing that they did not receive from him. The work of the anonymous author—that is, Gerard—was first printed and furnished with notes by the distinguished Marcus Welser at Augsburg in 1595; from that edition we have prepared the following text.

**5.** But before presenting it, it is useful to put forward certain matters for its elucidation. First, it must be investigated whether [Col. 1003B] Udalricus—whom some call Vodalricus or Othalricus, and others Wolricus—was a monk. The authors of the *Life of Saint Wiborada*, the recluse at Saint Gall, deny that he was a monk before becoming bishop. When he had disclosed to her his intention of entering the monastic profession, she indicated that God had appointed something else for him: namely, that he would become bishop of the Church of Augsburg, as is related above in her Acts under the year 925. Yet Ekkehard the Younger, in the passage cited shortly afterward, testifies that he had previously been a canon of that church.

Although Udalricus was not permitted to be a monk, as bishop he nevertheless wore monastic clothing and, insofar as episcopal dignity allowed, adhered to the Rule of Saint Benedict, whose elementary principles he had learned while being educated at the monastery of Saint Gall. Thus Gerard says in chapter 17:

“Always placing a woolen garment next to his skin, and following the rule of the monks.” [Col. 1003C]

Berno adds that he likewise abstained from meat. Since Saint Benedict prescribes strict silence for his monks at night, Udalricus resolved to observe it especially during Lent. During that season he “entirely avoided all conversation, except with God and the saints, until the first hour of the following day had been completed.”

Finally, when toward the end of his life he intended to transfer the burden of the episcopal office to his nephew Adalbero, “the bishop clothed himself in a garment fashioned according to the manner of monks, whose rule he had formerly been accustomed to follow through many virtues,” as Gerard says in chapter 62.

At the Synod of Ingelheim he also ordered his chaplain Gerard to explain his intention of abandoning the world [Col. 1003D]. Gerard did so in these words:

“Most excellent emperors and most devout bishops, it is my lord’s desire to abandon the world, to enter upon a holy life according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, and to await the day of his death in the contemplative life. You can certainly recognize his inward intention from the outward appearance of his clothing.”

Thus Gerard in chapter 63. The Fathers did not consider that Udalricus was permitted to do this; nevertheless, we may rightly affirm that he died in the habit he had once assumed, and therefore we do not without justification count him among our own. Trithemius, in his *History of Hirsau*, asserts that before his death he became a monk in the monastery of Saint Afra, which he himself had built.

[Col. 1004A] **6.** Udalricus performed certain acts before his episcopate which have been omitted by the three authors; these must be prefixed here from Ekkehard, chapter 5:

“But concerning Saint Udalricus, how he conducted himself among us, we heard certain things from the statements of the Fathers which we have not found recorded in his Life, although it has already been written for the third time. For he was born of noble parents, as has also been said by others, and was brought up and educated among our people. Here he learned to fly along the road by which he flew to heaven; here he began those virtues which he now practices. For he chose our saints Gallus and Otmar as fathers while still a little boy, joining himself to the monks; with the saints he entered as the most holy, and with the elect as the most chosen.

He drank deeply, before all others, from the divine Spirit, having first tasted it through the teaching of the younger Hartmann. In the refectory, before the Fathers, where to sin even in the smallest matter was a capital offense, he was frequently an unimpeachable reader, although he was a canon. This, however, was granted him by the favor of his ancestors.

When his contemporaries had been given permission to prepare themselves for games, he was accustomed on feast days to visit Wiborada [Col. 1004B] the recluse secretly. From time to time he was instructed by her in divine words and examples. For one day, when she saw him standing before the little window of the enclosure, girded with a very light belt, she offered him one prepared by herself and said:

‘My son, receive from God this woolen belt of mine as a girdle of chastity, and remember that from this day forward you are girded by your Wiborada with the belt of continence—that is, with a virgin’s girdle. But beware: since I bring you a command from my Lord, do not henceforth engage in idle conversations with women. If, as [Col. 1004C] most easily happens, you should be inflamed by some fire of the flesh, change the place where you are and immediately sing, “O God, come to my assistance; O Lord, make haste to help me.” But if, because of some other lapse of yours, preventing peace, you still do not have it, seek a burning brand or candle, as though you were doing something else, and lightly burn your finger; after reciting the same verse, you will be secure.’

Thus, as he himself used to relate to the Fathers, that hardened teacher had hardened her most holy future disciple against fire by means of fire. He had told the Fathers many things about the teaching of his nurse—for even when he was old he used to call her so—but because they may seem harsh and impossible to the saints of this age, we pass over them lest anything improper be detected in them.

From the hair shirt which she herself wore, the roughness of which [Col. 1004D] we now shudder to contemplate because we possess it as a relic, she had sewn a little cushion for her son—as she herself called him—to use on days of abstinence. He used to carry it in his bosom during the day, and at night he would fit it beneath his cheeks, placing a stone underneath. With such a bed, as though it were a luxury, he would wait for the sound of the night offices, either before the church doors on a seat, or indeed upon the bare ground.

Because he accustomed himself to such things and others like them from childhood, and had fled both women’s conversations and the customary amusements of his companions, they soon began mockingly to call him ‘the little saint’ [lacuna]. He frequently used figurative expressions, sometimes even expressions that provoked laughter, though they were neither false nor empty [lacuna]. The same privilege was also granted him out of respect for himself, namely that, as a canon [Col. 1005A], he should read the Gospel to us. For at that time this enrolled brother possessed the gift of a most beautiful voice.”

Indeed, among the enrolled brothers of Saint Gall, in Goldast, volume II, page 185, there is recorded “Oadalricus, bishop.”

Ekkehard adds:

“He had remained longer than the rest of his contemporaries devoted to Wiborada and her schools. At last, however, he left them and, once he had come into possession of his own property at Augsburg, where he had been a canon from infancy, he was most distinguished in examples of virtue. He frequently visited his Gallus, and, himself acting as minister, fed his enrolled brothers three times a year.”

He then relates a miracle concerning a wine vessel which remained intact after the vehicle carrying it had fallen from a bridge.

“On one occasion he had spent a day at the place of Saint Magnus, a day which was always dear to him; and, as is our custom, wearing that eagle-bearing cloak, he himself carried the relics of the saint home in the evening of the feast day. Since he was ill at the time, as indeed he often was, a certain paralytic, with the help of his attendants, had thrown himself down [Col. 1005B] in the road so that he might walk over him. But when he approached the man, as though annoyed by the obstacle, he said, ‘Rise, for I too am unable to proceed over you on my infirm feet.’

At these words, as though rebuked, the man rose with great speed and went away healed. He followed the brothers without anyone’s assistance and entered the church of Saint Magnus with the others in good health.

The bishop, having placed the hood of his cloak upon his head, stood panting and weary from the journey. When he heard of the man’s recovery, he vehemently attacked those who were telling him and at last leaned upon the railings. Disavowing so manifest a sign as having come from himself, he declared to those standing nearby that the power was Saint Magnus’s [Col. 1005C], whose relics he was carrying in his hands. Even so, he could not persuade them in any way not to believe that the man had been healed by him.”

We have written these things, among many others that he did while living at Saint Gall, without prejudicing the three writers of his Life. We are not surprised that those who lived with him in the world, knowing less about what he did with spiritual persons, failed to write these things down. But we are surprised that they concealed many more things commonly composed and sung about him, while magnifying certain very lowly matters concerning him.

After some further remarks about Udalricus’s witty sayings and the siege of Augsburg by the Hungarians—which latter matter we shall report in the notes—Ekkehard adds the following:

“A certain Hugo, a prominent man of royal lineage, had insolently become the enemy of the man of God because he had committed incest with the latter’s sister, a consecrated virgin, and had often been humbled by him. One day he encountered him while the bishop was being carried in a cart, as was required by his infirmity [Col. 1005D].

When the bishop’s soldiers warned him beforehand not to meet Hugo, Hugo said, ‘I shall never turn aside from my route for that cart-rider.’ When the bishop later heard this from those who told him, he said, ‘Know, my sons, that he will need the wagon more than I do.’

Not long afterward, one night, when he had surrendered himself to sleep and awoke, he suffered the most severe pain in his loins, with which he had sinned. From that night onward his lower body [Col. 1006A] had wasted away so completely that nothing remained but skin and slender bones. Thus he passed through many years, never able to be compelled to seek peace from the man of God.

That very religious woman afterward appeared as a holy woman; for while he lived, her brother annually punished her with new sentences. When he learned that the Hungarians, departing from him, intended to invade Buchow, where that sister was, and our own region, where he knew that Wiborada, his mother, was, he is said to have prayed:

‘My Lord, grant me this aged [read: servant] woman still unpunished, so that she may not perish by the sword; but strengthen and fortify her, ever prepared for the sword, so that she may deserve the martyr’s palm. Preserve also, in your piety and mercy, the cell of your Gallus intact, together with those serving there.’

And so God granted fulfillment to his holy prayers on every side.”

Thus far from Ekkehard.

**7.** Augsburg, situated on the river Lech (the Lech) [Col. 1006B], was governed by several bishops from among our own people, whom it is not easy to identify here with certainty because suitable evidence is lacking. We have already praised Simpert in the preceding volume, page 553. King Charlemagne, according to Ermenricus, a ninth-century monk of Ellwangen, “appointed him bishop in the city itself,” and “restored everything that had previously been transferred there by his predecessor Pippin, adding many things besides. After receiving the episcopate, Simpert went to Augsburg and governed those monasteries themselves for nearly thirty years”—namely, Kempten, Saint Gall, and the cell of Saint Afra—“building the basilica of Saint Afra and restoring the monastery of Saint Magnus,” namely that of Füssen (see chapter 46 of this Life), concerning which we treated in the second [Col. 1006C] century, under Saint Magnus.

“After Simpert’s death, Hanto”—so it should be read, not Lanto, as will be clear later—“assumed the episcopate; he himself had been born in Bavaria. Seven years after he received the episcopate, the first of his successors appointed in that Church, Nitkarius, began to build the church of Saint Magnus from its foundations; the other bishops, following him, built it similarly as far as they were able. Nevertheless, the hall of the basilica was not brought to completion until, with the Lord’s favor, Lanto obtained that holy see from the most glorious King Louis, son of the illustrious Emperor Louis.”

Brusch’s catalogue must therefore be corrected. It places Walther after Hanto, Adelger in second place, and Neodegarius only in third, whereas [Col. 1006D] Ermenricus, an author of that period, places Nitkarius immediately after Hanto; Nitkarius is the same person as Neodegarius. Ermenricus is supported by an ancient list of the bishops of Augsburg, published at the end of this Life, in which the bishops are listed in this order:

Simpertus, Hanto, Nidger, Odalman, Wigger, Lanto, Adalpero, Hiltine, Oudalricus.

Lanto “completed the basilica of Saint Magnus in the fifth year of his episcopate,” and transferred the body of the same Saint Magnus to a more suitable place, “after taking counsel with Otgar, archbishop of the Church of Mainz, and his other suffragan bishops.” Hermenricus, who was present, describes these matters at length in Goldast, volume I of *Rerum Alamannicarum*, page 315 [Col. 1007A]. From him we extracted the more important points in the *Eulogy of Saint Magnus*.

Brusch records Lanto’s death under the year 877, in which year he gives Udelmann as his successor. Udelmann is said to have been succeeded in 888 by “Widgarius or Widogerus, abbot of the monastery of Ottobeuren, exceptionally learned and most humane.” We have seen that distinguished monastery of the Augsburg diocese, situated in a pleasant place on the river Günz, furnished with elegant buildings. Its basilica is dedicated to the holy martyrs Alexander and Theodore, whose relics are kept there.

The first abbot of the place was Totto, whom they regard as a saint, although they celebrate his anniversary annually. Concerning him, the Ottobeuren Calendar says:

“Thirteen days before the Kalends of December: our abbot Totto, who brought the body of Saint Alexander here, and [Col. 1007B] whose parents founded this place.”

And in a short chronicle arranged according to the Paschal cycles:

“In the year 1163 Totto is buried”—that is, transferred—“and the high altar is dedicated.”

The monastery was founded in the year 764. Udalricus restored its freedom, as appears from chapter 25 of the following Life.

To return to the subject: Brusch notes that in 898 Widgarius preached Christian truth to the Helvetians, who were still infected with paganism, and that for this reason he was called “the Apostle of the Helvetians.” In 902 Widgarius was succeeded by Adalbero, whom Brusch testifies to have been a monk of Ellwangen and simultaneously abbot of that place and bishop.

“He was,” says the same author, “a man exceptionally learned, an outstanding musician, a most generous benefactor [Col. 1007C] of the monastery of Saint Gall, and a pupil and instructor of Saint Ulric or Udalricus.”

Ekkehard, chapter 5, records that Adalbero was an exceedingly generous enrolled brother of Saint Gall. This is confirmed by the booklet *On the Enrolled Brothers*, in Goldast, volume II, page 181, where Adalbero is said to have come to Saint Gall in 908, on the vigil of the saint himself, “accompanied by the very gentle bishop Meginbert of the Church of Säben”—which others call Sabionensis [Säben] (see *Metropolis Salzburgensis*, p. 439), now Brixen—and to have enriched the place with various gifts.

While Adalbero held the see, Udalricus set out for Rome in 909 and learned of Adalbero’s death from the pope. Since Udalricus could not be persuaded by the pope to accept the episcopate, Hiltinus was appointed in the meantime. When Hiltinus died in 924, Udalricus finally succeeded him; he is the man [Col. 1007D] whose Life we now have before us.

If Udalricus suffered anything human in his devotion to his nephew Adalbero, whom he had designated as his successor, he unquestionably expiated it before his death, when he turned the premature death of that same nephew into a means of penitence.

**8.** Moreover, Udalricus was deservedly called and believed to be a saint immediately after his death. Besides the writers of his Life, Hartmannus, an author of the same period, calls him Saint Udalricus in the Acts of Saint Wiborada cited above. Ditmarus, who died in 1018, calls him “holy father Othalricus” in Book I, and in Book III calls Othelricus “a gem among priests.”

This is hardly surprising, since in 993—that is, in the twentieth year after his death—he was enrolled among the saints by Pope John XV. We shall report that pope’s letter on this matter after the Life and Miracles [Col. 1008A].

Bishop Liudolf, who at the pope’s command raised the body of Saint Udalricus from the tomb, built an oratory in his honor, according to the Magdeburg Chronicler. This honor deserves all the more consideration because the solemn rite of canonization, as it is called, appears to have begun with Saint Udalricus, as we explained in the preface to this volume, after an inquiry had first been made into his life and miracles, which are set forth in the two following books.

It is also worthy of note that Pope Gregory VII granted the use of the pallium to Henry, bishop of Aquileia, who had formerly been a canon of Augsburg, among other occasions, “on the feasts of blessed Udalricus, confessor and bishop of Christ, and of blessed Afra, martyr,” as is read in Book VI, letter 38 [Col. 1008B].

Udalricus’s name became so celebrated that it first bestowed its name and title upon the highly distinguished church and monastery of Saint Afra at Augsburg. That place is now called Saint Udalricus and Saint Afra (Saint Ulric), because of his burial and veneration there.

Bishop Bruno of Augsburg granted the place to Benedictine monks in 1012, with Reginbald as its first abbot. Bernard Hertfelder, prior of the monastery, calls Reginbald a saint in his *Basilica of Saints Udalricus and Afra*, and says that he was descended from the counts of Kyburg—that is, from Udalricus’s family.

Reginbald was succeeded by Dego in 1015. After three years Dego was succeeded by Godesgenus, and after two years by Frideboldus, who died in 1030. At Frideboldus’s request Berno undertook the third writing about Saint Udalricus [Col. 1008C].

The relics of Saint Udalricus are preserved in the same basilica, most of them placed beneath his altar, at which we were granted the privilege of celebrating the sacred mysteries. The head and certain other relics are enclosed in separate reliquaries, whose reproductions Hertfelder presents, as he does those of the chalice, chasuble, stole, maniple, and dalmatic used by the holy man.

His stole and certain relics are likewise preserved in the monastery of Muri. His discovery will be discussed after the Book of Miracles.

**9.** There are extremely doubtful and uncertain conjectures concerning certain writings attributed to Udalricus. Among them is a “synodal sermon to be proclaimed to parish priests at synods.” Marcus Welser thought that it belonged to Udalricus because most of the questions which Udalricus was accustomed to put to priests at such synods, according to Gerard in chapter 6 of the following book, correspond to the questions in the aforesaid sermon, which was published in Labbe’s volume IX of the Councils, column 803 [Col. 1008D].

It may be said, however, that Udalricus took this sort of question from the common formula of a sermon customarily delivered at such synods. Certainly the same sermon, with a few changes, is attributed to Pope Leo IV in volume VIII of the Councils, column 35. Ratherius’s synodal sermon in volume II of the *Spicilegium*, page 256, is also similar.

Another sermon of Udalricus addressed to the people is reported in chapter 9 of the following Life.

In addition, during the previous century a letter to Pope Nicholas was circulated under Udalricus’s name. Innovators attempted to lend it authority from Aeneas Sylvius’s *Apology to Mayer*, where he says that the pope was reproved by Udalricus for keeping concubines [Col. 1009A].

Welser regards it as pure invention: first, because during the whole period of Udalricus’s life no Pope Nicholas governed the Roman Church; second, because these words of Aeneas do not occur in certain manuscripts and are absent from the Roman edition of 1584; and finally because Gerard makes no mention of this reproof.

Nevertheless, it may reasonably be said that the matter could apply to John XII, who was given over to disgraceful acts and whom Otto the Great had deposed in a large synod, since he refused to repent after being frequently admonished.

**10.** But at last the work of the anonymous author, or Gerard, must be presented. Baronius rightly preferred it to the others because of its simplicity, which is more consonant with truth. He praises Marcus Welser, a man of great renown among the citizens of Augsburg, who “brought this writing back to life, already buried in oblivion, by printing it and illuminating it with notes.” Thus that most distinguished man under the year 924.

[Col. 1009]

# LIFE OF SAINT UDALRICUS, BISHOP OF AUGSBURG  
## By Gerard the Priest

*(In Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, fifth century, p. 117.)*

## [Life of Saint Udalricus]

[Col. 1009B] Since the ears of many people were constantly being struck by the report of the miracles of Christ which, through his servant Saint Udalricus, he permitted to be performed in honor of his most holy mother Mary, while doubt still occupied their minds, they sent messengers to me wishing to learn the truth of these matters from my answers. They asked me to make clear to them, in lucid description, those things which I could know with certainty.

And since so great a multitude of questioners surrounded me on every side with their inquiries that I thought I could not give written answers to each one individually, I began silently to consider within myself how, by inwardly investigating the origin of his birth, I might, after describing his birth, make his subsequent life and death known in a truthful account to all who were asking and wishing to read it [Col. 1009C].

I did not rely upon my preceding merits or upon the acuity of my own mind, but hoped in the mercy of almighty God, who said, “Open your mouth, and I will fill it.” May he deign, through the merits of the aforesaid bishop, by the watering of the Holy Spirit and the fervor of divine fire, to direct my understanding, so that he may not withhold the strength to complete what he inspired me to conceive, unless he permits me to publish it according to the suitable measure predestined in my mind [Col. 1010B]. Thus may those who love God be presented with examples for their edification, while those who despise God’s commandments may receive an increase either of benefit for their conversion or of warning of condemnation.

We are confident that, for those who read these things in the love of Christ, the help of almighty God will be present, so that through his servant they may be protected in this world and, with his assistance, may be brought to eternal joys.

First of all, with the help of the Holy Spirit, we must not conceal the interpretation of the name of so great and eminent a man. In the Teutonic language, therefore, an inheritance handed down from one’s ancestors is called *Altuodal*; *Ric* means “riches.” Thus Vodalricus may not incongruously be interpreted as “rich through his paternal inheritance,” for he flourished enriched by the inheritance of the eternal Father, of whom we say daily in our prayer, “Our Father, who art in heaven,” and so forth [Col. 1010C].

To the possession of this inheritance Saint Paul consoles those who persevere in God’s will, saying: “Heirs indeed of God, and joint-heirs with Christ” (Romans 8; 1 Corinthians 2). Concerning this inheritance it is also written: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2).

While living in this pilgrimage, he not only enjoyed the benefit of this inheritance himself, but also drew many people toward it through manifold consolations of benefactions [Col. 1011A]. By many kinds of assistance and continual miracles he will lead them into it, as is found in what follows.

## I

Thus, Saint Udalricus, of blessed memory, was born of the distinguished lineage of the Alamanni, from religious and noble parents—namely, his father Hupaldus [Note: [Col. 1011D] Alternatively, Hucpaldus.] and his mother, called Thetpirga [Note: [Col. 1011D] Diepirch.].
