Nursed in the customary manner and raised with the greatest care, although his little body was handsome in stature, he was nevertheless so weakened by emaciation that his nurses would have been ashamed if any stranger had looked upon his face.

His father and mother wondered why he was afflicted with such extreme thinness and deformity of body, and they often pondered the matter. Meanwhile, in the twelfth week after his birth, an unknown cleric happened to arrive and begged to be received by them as a guest for a few days. He was kindly welcomed and, sitting with them in the courtyard of their house at the hour of refreshment, heard the infant crying in the bedroom. He asked who the child was and whose child he might be. But, out of embarrassment at the child’s emaciation, they were unwilling to say. Then he said:

> “If you want him to remain alive, wean him quickly.”

They paid little attention to his words and did not withdraw the child from the breast. On the next day, hearing him again, he said:

> “Why did you not follow my advice?”

Still disregarding his advice, they did not believe him. On the third day, hearing the child’s cry weaker than before, he said to them:

> “Through your negligence this little child is being delivered over to death. Know for certain that, if he is not withdrawn from the breast, he will die this very night; but if he is withdrawn, he will be saved. In the future, something great will be manifested in him by the Lord.”

Only then did they obey him and begin to sustain the child with other foods. He was immediately restored, grew stronger day by day, and acquired such beauty of body that his parents themselves gazed upon him with delight and showed him to others. Praising the Lord day and night for the child’s recovery, they also gave thanks that He had sent them such a guest, who understood and had made known to them the proper discernment in this matter.

Believing, therefore, from what had happened previously that something awaited him in the future, they considered where they might find a life of the greatest religious devotion and the greatest zeal for learning and teaching. Having taken counsel, they entrusted him to the monastery of Saint Gall, because at that time there was found there a multitude of noble servants of God, together with religious devotion and zeal for learning and teaching.

He was entrusted to a certain religious man named Waning, learned in the art of grammar [Col. 1011D], who cared for him well. From him Udalricus received daily instruction in religion and reading and planted it deep within his heart, so that little by little the brothers perceived that the fruitfulness of his learning was making great progress in him. For this reason they sought, by repeated requests, to bring him into the fellowship of their brotherhood.

Often urged by their petitions, he asked for time to give his answer. He then went to a certain recluse living there, named Wiberat [Note: [Col. 1011D] The recluse Wiberata.], seeking her advice. She replied:

> “Come back to me after three days, if it pleases God, and you will be able to learn my counsel.”

After he had departed, she earnestly besought the Lord in devout prayer that, on the appointed day, He might reveal to her the indication of a certain and truthful counsel. When Udalricus came to receive her answer, she said to him:

> “Let no further hesitation occupy your mind, for you will by no means be appointed by God to govern as the spiritual father of this monastery. Rather, in the eastern region, where a certain river divides two territories [Note: [Col. 1011D] The Lech separates Swabia and Bavaria.], you will in the future serve God in the episcopal ministry. In that same place you will have to endure many such hardships as your predecessors have never before suffered from pagans and evil Christians. Nevertheless, with God’s help, you will overcome all these things most honorably at the end.”

He reported what he had heard to the most trusted brothers and softened their persuasion through gentle conversation. He abandoned in his mind all hope of his former appointment. Yet he did not on that account abandon his zeal for learning, but conducted himself charitably with everyone there. At the proper time, filled with the double nourishment of knowledge and religion, consoled by the common prayer of all and relying on the love of the brotherhood, he was affectionately dismissed and returned to visit his parents.

They then, having taken wise counsel, placed him under the authority of Adalbero, bishop of the Church of Augsburg [Note: [Col. 1011D] He was commended to Adalbero, bishop of Augsburg.]. They recognized him as a man filled with great wisdom for that time, especially accomplished in the art of music, and arranging nearly all the affairs of the kingdom together with the king [Note: [Col. 1011D] King Louis IV.].

Adalbero himself, receiving Udalricus gladly because of his parents’ nobility, his good character, and his handsome appearance, entrusted to him the office of chamberlain [Note: [Col. 1011D] Onulphus, *On Obscure Ecclesiastical Terms*, interprets *camerarius* as “one who takes care of money,” whereas Welser understands it here as “chamberlain.”]. Having accepted this office, and other benefits appropriate to his rank, he prospered and advanced from day to day, for he was precocious in everything.

Meanwhile, he desired to visit the thresholds of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul. When he arrived there, he was kindly received by the venerable Pope Marinus [Note: [Col. 1012D] Welser thinks that Marinus is called pope by anticipation; Baronius holds the same view under the year 924.]. The pope asked him from what province or city he came. He replied:

> “I come from the province of Alamannia and from the city of Augsburg, and I serve Adalbero, the bishop of that city.”

> “Do not be troubled in spirit, brother,” he replied [Note: [Col. 1012D] If Marinus had been pope, he would not have called Udalricus “brother” rather than “son.”]. “Adalbero, your master, of whom you have spoken to me, has departed from this world. By God’s command, it is fitting that you become shepherd of the same ecclesiastical see [Note: [Col. 1012D] The cathedral church].”

When Udalricus refused, he continued:

> “Why do you resist God’s appointment? If you now refuse to accept an undisturbed and unravaged church in peace, later you will receive it devastated and plundered amid turmoil, and you will govern and rebuild it with toil.”

On the following day, without the pope’s permission, both because of grief for his deceased lord and because he did not want the pope to bind him further with words, Udalricus left Rome and returned to Augsburg. He found everything just as the pope had foretold.

Hiltine [Note: [Col. 1013D] Hiltinus, Hiltenius.] had become Adalbero’s successor. Yet he was not of such eminence that he wished to attach himself to Udalricus’s service. Meanwhile Udalricus’s father died, and Udalricus returned and took responsibility for his mother, remembering the Lord’s command:

> “Honor your father and your mother” (Exod. 20), etc.

He guarded and arranged for her and all her affairs with such diligence as the strength granted him by the Lord allowed.

After fifteen years, Bishop Hiltine died. Through the machinations of his nephew, Duke Burchard, and his other relatives, Udalricus was presented to King Henry [Note: [Col. 1013D] Henry the Fowler.]. They informed the king of the bishop’s death and begged that episcopal authority be granted by him to the aforementioned lord Udalricus.

The king observed his lordly bearing and learned of his knowledge and education. Granting their request, he received him into his hands according to royal custom and honored him with the office of bishop. When these matters had been completed, they returned from the king with joyful hearts and, arriving at Augsburg, completed his investiture in the bishopric with authoritative hand, according to the king’s decree.

As the season of the Lord’s Nativity approached, on the day of the feast of the Holy Innocents [Note: [Col. 1013D] Evidently at the beginning of the twenty-fourth year.], his ordination was carried out according to the customary rite [Col. 1013C].

Returning home successfully, he saw that the church walls had everywhere been thrown down and that all the buildings had fallen into serious ruin, just as they had been consumed by fire under the former bishop. Greatly distressed in mind, he considered how he might most suitably rebuild what had been so completely destroyed. Most of the household had been killed by pagans, the fortified settlements had been burned and plundered, and the portion of the household that remained was suffering under the heavy burden of poverty.

Nevertheless, after obtaining architects and gathering a large number of members of the household, he began skillfully to restore the ruins and to arrange everything with sound judgment. With great fervor of spirit, he labored not to abandon what he had begun.

Although he was burdened by limited resources, this man of great gentleness, relying on divine assistance, ardently completed the work he had begun. He strove to adorn every interior part of the church with every kind of decoration, insofar as he was able. He also frequently surveyed the arrangement of the church, inside and outside, with the keen discernment of his eyes. He complained that the smallness of the poorly illuminated crypt and its meanness displeased him greatly, and declared that, if God granted it, he would construct it more suitably and more beautifully.

When the work that had been begun seemed to be making considerable progress, a certain brother named Rambertus, in an ecstasy of mind, seemed to himself to be chanting psalms with Udalricus as he usually did. Meanwhile, he saw Bishop Adalbero appearing to him in the northern part of the crypt, dressed in the vestments for Mass and beckoning him to come to him.

But Rambertus, seized by anxious fear of both his living and his dead lord, began to look at him fearfully. Adalbero asked him why he was directing his eyes toward him in this way. He replied:

> “Look: I see my master Adalbero, dressed as a bishop for Mass, calling me to him.”

Udalricus said:

> “Hasten to fulfill his command.”

When Rambertus came to him, Adalbero said:

> “Rambertus, tell your bishop, your lord, that he will receive a reward from the Lord for the prayers and alms that he faithfully sent to me. Tell him this sign as well: Fortunatus [Note: [Col. 1014D] Welser understands this to mean Fortunatus, bishop of Poitiers.] and I will sanctify the chrism with him at the next Lord’s Supper, if the Lord permits. Also tell him that the work on this crypt will collapse. Nevertheless, he must not abandon his efforts, but should strive to make it stable in the future.

> “Also warn the brothers to remember that they promised to labor for me without compulsion and of their own accord, through diligent and continual prayer; they did not do so, and if they do not correct this, let them know that they will have to render an account of it in the Lord’s presence. And you shall sing one psalm for me every day, without negligence; I warn you to amend this.”

Meanwhile, the bishop, occupied with royal duties, set out for the royal court. There he was retained for a long time by the courtiers with due honor. At last, having obtained the salutary permission he had requested, he returned home. The work whose completion he had hoped to see he found completely collapsed and overturned, exactly as Rambertus had foretold.

Then he laid stronger foundations and completed it securely.

On another occasion, when he was in the town called Waringa and had undertaken, early in the morning and according to custom, to complete the chanting of the psalms with the same Rambertus, the brother began timidly to move his eyes, turning them aside.

Questioned by Udalricus, he replied:

> “Look: I see my master Adalbero, just as I saw him before, ordering me to minister to him at Mass.”

Udalricus immediately rose, withdrew the doors, and left the church until the vision had ended.

We must not consign to oblivion another vision, which we have learned from many brothers who truthfully reported that it occurred. When a religious man was diligently striving to perform the sacramental ministry on Easter Day, a multitude of clerics arrived, with a certain priest named Heilricus serving as cantor [Note: [Col. 1014D] Henry.]. A right hand appeared, sanctifying the sacraments together with the bishop’s right hand.

When the Mass had been completed, the aforementioned Heilricus followed Udalricus into his chamber and fell at his feet. More carelessly than he should have done, he explained this vision in the presence of laymen. Udalricus replied:

> “It would have been more useful for you to keep this silent than to speak of it.”

Astonished by this reply, Heilricus withdrew from him and sat down in the dining room situated before the bishop’s chamber. Immediately his eyes began to pour forth tears in great abundance, and they continued to do so until he was completely deprived of his present sight.

## II

At another time, on the night before the holy day of the Lord’s Supper, he heard, as though in a dream, a voice speaking to him:

> “Bishop Udalricus, know that today you will receive guests.”

Awakened by the voice, he began to consider who those guests might be. When he had fallen asleep again, he heard the speaker’s words:

> “The eyes of the Lord have seen your prayers and your alms. Therefore you have been commended to your two predecessors, Fortunatus and Adalbero [Note: [Col. 1015D] This expression seems to have to be understood broadly, since no Fortunatus who was bishop of Augsburg is found.], so that today, and thereafter during these sacred solemnities, they may assist you as you celebrate the sacred mysteries and bless them together with you.”

When morning came, after he had completed the other rites as was customary, and while the ranks of ministers stood around him, he consecrated the sacraments. He himself and some of the more devout bystanders saw the Lord’s right hand consecrating the sacraments with him and imposing the sign of the cross.

Because Udalricus knew through the Spirit that they had seen this, when they approached to receive viaticum from him, he placed his finger over his mouth so that they would remain silent about the vision. Later, when he had summoned them to himself, he secretly told them what had been said to him during the night and ordered them, if they wished to continue living this present life, not to reveal to anyone, while he was alive, either what they had seen or what they had secretly heard from him.

I do not think that the miracles revealed to him in an even greater vision should be buried in silence. One night, after he had placed his body on his bed to sleep, he saw Saint Afra in great beauty, dressed in and girded with a beautiful tunic, standing before him and saying:

> “Rise and follow me.”

As she said this, she led him out into the plain commonly called Lechfeld. There he found Saint Peter, chief of the apostles, with a great multitude of bishops and other saints, as well as others whom he had not previously seen but whom, by God’s sign, he now recognized well. Saint Peter was holding a synodal conference with them and making great and innumerable arrangements.

He was also lawfully judging Duke Arnulf of Bavaria, who was still alive, accused of the destruction of many monasteries that he had divided as benefices among laymen. Saint Peter showed Udalricus two very lordly swords, one with a hilt and the other without a hilt, and spoke as follows:

> “Tell King Henry that the sword without a hilt signifies the king who will hold the kingdom without pontifical blessing; the sword with a hilt signifies the one who will hold the government of the kingdom with divine blessing.”

When that synod had ended, the martyr of God showed him the locations of the camps where Otto, then still king, would later hold a royal assembly with peoples from various provinces. There King Berengar of Lombardy [Note: [Col. 1015D] Others call him king of Italy.] and his son Adalbert appeared with many bishops and submitted themselves to Otto’s authority [Note: [Col. 1015D] King Berengar, together with his son, surrendered himself to Otto at Augsburg in the year 951. See the *Chronicle of the Monk of Weingarten*, the *Chronicle of Marianus*, [Col. 1016D] and others.].

The martyr of God also announced to Udalricus the coming invasion of the Hungarians and the places where the battle would occur. He told him that, although with difficulty, victory would be granted to the Christians.

When this vision was completed, he led Udalricus back and left him lying on his bed. Coming to himself, Udalricus reverently called to mind the words of the illustrious preacher who had been caught up into the secrets of the third heaven:

> “Whether in the body or outside the body” (2 Cor. 12), etc.

He revealed this vision only to a few prudent men who were close to him.

Later he went to the king’s court and, as usual, placed himself at the king’s service, until King Henry ended his present life [Note: [Col. 1016D] In the year 936.]. When Henry’s son Otto had been raised to the kingship, Udalricus strove to render him the same diligence in service and steadfastness of loyalty that he had given his father in all things.

At that time Bishop Udalricus had a nephew, the son of his sister Luitgard, a young man of good character named Adalbero. He had entrusted him to a very learned master, the monk Benedict, to be educated in the knowledge of the art of grammar and of other books.

When Adalbero had been instructed and trained by Benedict in every kind of progress in sound learning and discipline and had reached manhood, he was immediately taken from the school. His uncle, the bishop, presented him to the emperor and commended him into the emperor’s merciful hands. Adalbero devoted himself so diligently and becomingly to royal service that his ministry in ecclesiastical and secular matters pleased the emperor greatly.

Because of the manifest diligence of his daily service, permission was granted to his uncle, Saint Bishop Udalricus, for the aforementioned Adalbero, in his place, to undertake military expeditions with the episcopal forces at the emperor’s command and to remain at the emperor’s court in his stead through constant service. This was done so that the bishop might be free to devote himself, according to his desire, to the service of God, to the guardianship of the flock entrusted to him, to the needs of the church, to prayers, and to alms.

The more he perceived himself to be freed from secular cares, the more he strove to bind himself to the will of God.

Whenever other obligations allowed him to remain at home, he carefully observed the daily office in the choir of the same cathedral church with the *matricularii* [Note: [Col. 1016D] *Matricularii*: clerics of the mother church.]. In addition, he was accustomed every day to complete one office in honor of Saint Mary, Mother of God, another of the holy cross, a third of all the saints, and many other psalms, indeed the entire Psalter, unless some unavoidable necessity prevented him.

He also did not cease to celebrate three, two, or one Mass each day, according to the time available, unless bodily illness or some good undertaking prevented him [Col. 1017A].

## III

For many periods he abstained from meat, but he nevertheless gave it abundantly to others who ate with him.

At the daily meals, whenever he sat at table with his household, the first serving of bread and food was for the most part distributed to the poor by a cleric appointed for this duty. The exceptions were those crippled and infirm people who, walking with the aid of little beds, couches, and stools, and in beds fitted with small supports, received their daily food in his presence—food and drink of the best quality.

No one else who took food in his presence, whether known or unknown, ever departed hungry or thirsty, unless at times this happened through the negligence or stinginess of the servants, contrary to the bishop’s will [Note: [Col. 1017D] Also.].

When guests came to him, they were received with rejoicing and with such great cheerfulness of face and spirit, and were provided for in every way, as was most suitable for them. He knew that in them he had received Christ, who said:

> “I was a guest, and you received me” (Matt. 25).

The emperor’s vassals, whether departing from him or returning to him [Note: [Col. 1017D] Another reading has: “His vassals, in their own [Col. 1018D] … from him.”], were received with the greatest honor and feasted so generously that neither they nor their animals were wearied by any want. They received with them the provisions necessary for their journey and returned from him joyfully.

He loved monks, clerics, and nuns who visited him as sons. He abundantly refreshed them with spiritual and bodily food, allowed them to remain with him for as long as they wished, and, at the appropriate time, dismissed them to depart with every sign of joy.

He ordered that his own household clerics, whether humble freemen or men of higher birth, be raised and taught with the greatest care. Whoever among them he recognized as worthy of honor, he enriched with offices and suitable benefits.

The laymen subject to his rule always lived with him in honor and joy. They feared no fraud or deception from him, but firmly believed—and knew for certain—that whatever he promised them, he promptly fulfilled with the Lord’s approval.

Whenever anyone from the household entrusted to him came before him, crying out that he had been unjustly oppressed, despoiled, or injured in some way by his own lord, to whom he had been granted as a benefice, or by one of that lord’s fellow servants, or by anyone else, Udalricus listened carefully to his case. When he learned that an injustice had been committed against him, he immediately and firmly ordered that the wrong done to him be corrected, and he did not cease until it had been accomplished.

He allowed the entire household to retain firmly the lawful right which it had enjoyed under his predecessors, and he did not permit any powerful person living under his rule to take it away.

He never allowed his mind to submit to empty idleness unless he was devising or carrying out something useful—whether concerning the church, which he had found ruined on every side; its adornment; the equipment of the altars and the clerics; the discipline of the canons and the school; the support and preservation of the household; or the means by which he might surround the city with walls. He had found the city enclosed by unsuitable ditches and rotten timber, at a time when the ferocity of the Hungarians was raging through these provinces like that of demons.

While he considered all these matters externally with the counsel of his faithful men, he was inwardly inflamed by the heat of divine love and hastened with the greatest zeal to unite himself to God through vigils, prayers, fasts, and alms. He always wore a woolen garment next to his skin and followed the rule of the monks.

After Compline, he never, in response to any person’s request, took food or drink by indulging the pleasure of his body.

He did not sleep in the softness of a feather mattress, but rested on a *psiathus*—Greek *ψίαθος*, “a mat or covering”—with a cloak or rugs placed beneath him [Note: [Col. 1018D] *ψίαθος*, a mat or covering.].

At the first sounding of the bell during the night, he rose and completed the offices mentioned above with the greatest care.

IV. How devotedly he observed the season of Lent, my speech is not sufficient to relate; nevertheless, it would not be proper for us to omit entirely what we saw. For after completing the morning praises, at the first light of dawn, and after completing his other prayers, he began to chant the Psalter. When it was completed, and the litany had been completed, he persisted firmly in other prayers until the signal for the office of the vigils for the dead sounded. Upon hearing it, he immediately rose and celebrated the Vigil and Prime with the brothers. When Prime had been completed, while the brothers customarily carried the cross, he remained in the church and meanwhile recited a shortened little book of psalms together with other prayers, until the brothers returned with the cross and began to celebrate the sacrifice of the Mass. He first devoutly offered the sacrifice to God, humbly kissing the priest’s hand.

When the Mass had been completed, he completed Terce with the brothers. While the brothers proceeded to the chapter meeting, he remained in the church in his usual manner until the signal for Sext sounded. After Sext had been completed, he went around the altars asking pardon, singing “Have mercy on me, O God” and “Out of the depths.” Only then did he return to his chamber to wash his face and prepare himself for Mass.

When the celebrations of the Masses had been completed and Vespers had been sung, he reached the hospice of the poor, washed the feet of twelve poor men, and gave each of them from the alms-fund the value of one denarius. Returning from there, he sat down at table to dine. There was no lack of reading, nor of the aforementioned poor, present in great number. He joyfully ate what was set before him and distributed it with the greatest cheerfulness among those staying with him, remembering the Apostle’s words: “For God loves a cheerful giver” (II Corinthians IX). He gave each person whatever he thought he would most gladly eat.

When the meal had been consumed and all who dwelt with him had been made cheerful, at the proper time he recited Compline. After completing his other prayers, he returned silently to the privacy of his chamber and wholly avoided every conversation—except with God and his saints—until Prime of the following day had been completed.

In this manner he completed the days of Lent, up to the day of indulgence which they call Palm Sunday. On that day, early in the morning, he went to Saint Afra—unless he had remained there during the preceding night—celebrated Mass of the Holy Trinity, and blessed palm branches and branches of various kinds.

[Note: The church of Saint Afra—now commonly called the monastery of Saints Ulrich and Afra—then lay outside the city.] With the Gospel book, crosses, and banners,

[Note: Banners, *fanones*.]

and with an image of the seated Lord upon an ass; with the clergy and a multitude of people carrying palm branches in their hands; with chants composed in honor of that day; and with great splendor, he proceeded as far as the hill called Perleich. There the choir of canons came to meet him in great beauty, together with the citizens who had remained in the city and those from the surrounding settlements who had wished to join them, there imitating the humility of the children and the other peoples who spread palm branches and their garments upon the road.

When these things had been completed, the holy man delivered to everyone a most fitting exhortation concerning the Lord’s Passion. He spoke so movingly that he himself wept, and by his weeping caused many others to weep. After the exhortation, all together praising God, they reached the mother church, where they celebrated Mass with him; from there they all returned to their own homes.

Afterward, during the three immediately following days, he was accustomed to hold a synodal assembly, because the canons prescribe that councils of bishops be held twice each year: one on the fifteenth day of October, and the other in the fourth week after Easter. He resolved to complete this one at that time, lest any obstacle thereafter prevent him from completing it, and so that on Maundy Thursday the chrism and oil might be consecrated more fully and honorably, with the same multitude of clergy and people.

[Note: Distinction 18, chapter 4: “The first after the third week of Easter, so that it may be completed in the fourth; the second on the Ides of October.” It therefore appears that here *XV Kal. Oct.* has been taken to mean the fifteenth day of October; this phrase, although scarcely Latin, is also to be observed in other writers.]

On that day, at the third hour, all the clergy, dressed in the most solemn vestments, came to the church. He too, prepared in his customary and most glorious manner for the service of God, began with them to perform the sacred rite with the greatest devotion. After the Gospel had been read, an exhortation had been given to the people, and the people’s confession had been received, he humbly granted them absolution. While the entire synod offered the oblation, he completed the rite with the greatest care, up to the blessing of the chrism and oil.

He arranged for these to be brought to him with great reverence: with crosses; with boys carrying them concealed beneath a small pall; with candles; with verses composed for this ministry and sung most beautifully; and with a procession of twelve priests, who were to remain in their ministry with him until the end of the Mass. When they had been properly brought to him, he received them with the greatest humility and asked the entire synod that, when he made the sign of the cross over them in blessing, they too, together with the same priests who were in the procession and assisting him, should not cease to bless them. He also asked the rest of the people to sing the Lord’s Prayer with great humility.

After the chrism had been blessed, the people refreshed with the sacred viaticum, and Vespers completed, he went to the sacristy to distribute the chrism and oil to the clergy. After distributing them, he went to the hospice of the poor and ministered to them in his customary manner.

From there he walked into the church and came before the sacristy. When the chamberlain had brought new clothing, he clothed twelve poor men and distributed a heap of alms to others. On that day he allowed no one to depart from him empty-handed, although a great multitude of them was present.

Afterward he went to eat. When all who were staying with him had eaten, he began, following the Lord’s example, to wash the feet of his disciples. When the washing had been most properly completed with suitable antiphons, verses, and readings, with great charity and humility he generously supplied the finest cups stored in his cellars. After completing Compline, he entrusted his limbs, wearied in the service of God, to the rest of his little bed.

On Good Friday, after carefully completing the appointed hours in their proper order, and omitting the other offices except those pertaining to that day, as on Maundy Thursday he hastened early in the morning to complete the Psalter. When the sacred mystery of God had been performed, the people had been nourished with the body of Christ, and, according to custom, what remained had been buried, he again completed the Psalter by walking and singing among the churches. In the evening, without a table or table companions, he began to refresh himself in his chamber with bread and beer, and ordered that bread and beer be provided according to the will of each person who was with him.

On the most holy day of the Sabbath, after completing the nocturnal offices and reading through the beloved Psalter, he entered the bath prepared for him. He never used it at that season except on the Saturday before Lent, in the middle of Lent, and on that day. After washing his body and putting on his prepared clothing, he solemnly prepared himself for the sacred office. He directed that the entire clergy be ready with him at the ninth hour.

Immediately, after the triple litany had been read, the candle had been sanctified, and the readings and tracts had been completed, he proceeded to the church of Saint John the Baptist with the quintuple litany and every honor, in order to consecrate the baptismal font. After baptizing three boys there, he returned with the septuple litany to the sacristy to prepare himself for Mass, while the clergy meanwhile sang in the choir.

After the solemn rites of the Mass had been solemnly completed together with Vespers, the body of Christ had been distributed, and the sacred vestments had been removed, he sat down that day at a table prepared for a meal with a great multitude. When all had been abundantly refreshed, he gladly allowed them to return to their little dwellings.

When the most desired and most holy day of Easter arrived, after Prime he entered the church of Saint Ambrose. There, on Good Friday, he had placed the body of Christ beneath a stone.

[Note: No memory of this church survives, but Welser notes that it stood near the cathedral.]

There, with a few clergy, he completed Mass of the Holy Trinity. After the Mass had been completed, he preceded the clergy, who had meanwhile assembled in the portico beside the same church, dressed in the most solemn vestments. Carrying with him the body of Christ, the Gospel book, candles, and incense, and proceeding through the atrium with an appropriate salutation sung in verses by boys, he went to the church of Saint John the Baptist. There he sang Terce and from there proceeded, with antiphons most suitably composed in honor of that day, to the *tuomum* in a most beautiful procession, with the people walking two by two in proper order, to celebrate Mass.

[Note: The superscript read: *ad summum*, evidently referring to the German name of the cathedral church, *Thuom*.]

When the Mass had been sung with the greatest devotion and reverence, and all had received the sacraments of Christ and returned to their homes, he went to eat. There he found three tables prepared with every adornment: one at which he usually sat with those who were able to sit with him; another for the cathedral clergy;

[Note: *Matriculariis*, that is, the clergy of the cathedral church.]

and a third for the congregation of Saint Afra.

[Note: At that time regular clergy occupied the church of Saint Afra, now Saint Ulrich.]

After sanctifying the food, he distributed to everyone pieces of lamb and bacon that had been blessed during the solemn rites of the Mass, and only then joyfully ate with them.

At the appointed time the musicians came. Their multitude was so great that they almost filled the length of the hall, standing in order, and they performed three musical modes. When these festivities had thus been multiplied, the canons, at the bishop’s command, received the “charity” and, while asking for it, sang a responsory about the Lord’s resurrection. When this charity had been completed, the congregation of Saint Afra did likewise at the second table.

As evening approached, he ordered cups to be cheerfully offered to himself and those sitting with him, and asked everyone to drink the third charity charitably. After they had received that charity, the entire clergy together joyfully sang the third responsory. When it had been sung, the canons rose while singing a hymn, so that, suitably prepared, they could proceed to Vespers.

After Vespers had been completed, the bishop returned to his own residence with the guests and soldiers, to cheer them all.

On the morning that is Monday, the entire clergy assembled at Saint Afra, so that they might honorably receive the arriving bishop, dressed in the most beautiful vestments. For it was his custom on that day to serve God there in the solemn rites of the Mass, and, after the solemn rites of the Mass had been completed, to confirm with the sacred chrism the multitude of people assembled there. When these things had been completed, he returned to the city and there most devoutly celebrated the entire Easter week.

V. When the Easter solemnity had ended, if some necessity arose that allowed him lawfully to travel to other places or monasteries belonging to the bishopric, he would sit on a seat arranged upon a cart, suspended by iron from the shafts of a wagon, and would travel to Wthinuvanc,

[Note: Also called Staphense, Wisintessteigia, Houvibach, Fauces, Suichuvac, or Fuich-Wanc. Other forms are Scaphense, Unisintessbela, Houivibach, Fauces, and Sinchuvanc.]

Staphense, Fauces, Wissintesteiga, and Heuvibach. He never granted these monasteries as benefices to laymen, except that he granted some of the outer lands belonging to them to a person from the district in which his monastery was situated, so that he might have an advocate for the monastery there to defend its ecclesiastical property. But he retained the best properties under his own authority, specifically so that he would have the means to visit them, remain there, and correct what required correction.

With him there was one cleric from among his chaplains, who sang psalms with him throughout the entire day. He did not begin traveling in this manner at first because he was unable to ride a horse,

[Note: *Nisi* is used in place of *quod non*.]

but so that he might be separated from the crowds and not be hindered from singing the psalms by their foolish conversations.

He always ordered some of his most prudent priests to accompany him, and only enough of his chaplains to enable him to complete the service of God properly each day. Likewise, he always wished to have some of his wisest vassals with him, in case any matter concerning ecclesiastical or secular affairs came before him for discussion, so that he might always be prepared to deliberate and govern it prudently on their advice.

Chosen members of his household also served as drivers, walking with the oxen that pulled the vehicle, and carefully watching over him in front, behind, on the right, and on the left. Each day he caused such an abundance of grain to be given to them personally and through his ministers in his presence that it could have sufficed for three times their number.

A very dear company of the poor always traveled with him among his estates. Those who were able to ride travelled on the safest mounts. The others traveled in the vehicles in which they were accustomed to go, together with the carts carrying the episcopal equipment.

He carefully arranged each day, through one of his faithful men, their little dwellings and all their provisions.

[Note: *Quorum* is superfluous here.]

He never remained idle in any of the aforementioned monasteries, unless he had worked on buildings of the church, the cloisters, or other structures or walls that had previously been prepared, and had gathered furnishings and equipment.

He diligently regulated and arranged the life and stipends of the monks or canons serving God in that monastery, and absolutely did not permit the rights of the household to be dissolved. Nor did he fail to impart the gifts of the Holy Spirit wherever there was need, through confirmation with chrism.

VI. When he had decided, in a manner grateful and necessary to the people, to visit the diocese entrusted to him every fourth year, according to the constitution of the canons, in order to fulfill his ministry of governing, preaching, and confirming, he sat in the same manner as we described above, upon a seat placed on a cart, and sang psalms in his customary way. He imitated the eunuch who, while reading the prophet Isaiah, sat upon his chariot and traveled along the road; Philip was sent to him by the command of the Holy Spirit, and, after being preached to and baptized by him, he received the faith of the Holy Trinity. The bishop considered with certainty that the more he withdrew himself from human conversations, the more he could draw near to divine things.

When he reached those places where his assemblies had been announced, he was received with the Gospel book, blessed water, ringing bells, and as much honor as the strength of those gathered there could provide. Immediately after Mass had been celebrated, he sat down in the assembly and had the people summoned before him. He ordered the more prudent and truthful men to be questioned under oath about what in that parish deserved correction and about sins committed against the laws of Christianity, so that the facts might become known to him through a truthful report.

Whenever he heard from them of matters that exceeded the rule of righteousness, he hastened, without regard to persons and according to the judgment of the clergy, to draw them back to the path of righteousness as far as he could with the help of almighty God. With the sickle of God’s word he most diligently cut away the shoots of vices that had grown up badly, lest the thickets of evil buds be allowed to choke the harvest of Christ entrusted to him. He applied remedies of correction most suitable for the diseases of vice, yet in accordance with the word of God that says: “Reprove, entreat, rebuke, with all patience and doctrine” (II Timothy IV).

When he learned from them of matters difficult or impossible for his ministers to settle, he strove to bring them to completion in his presence, with the assistance of all who were staying with him, through extremely careful direction. Whatever he perceived could be brought back to a state of righteousness by them without complaint against others, he firmly entrusted to their governance for completion.

Following the rule of his ministry, he strove to impose the gift of the Holy Spirit—the confirmation of sacred anointing—upon the people gathered for this purpose. If, while these matters were still unfinished, night came upon them as usual, he struggled to complete what had been begun in the name of the Lord by lighting lamps, lest any portion of the sheep entrusted to him suffer the loss of the heavenly gift.

Sometimes, when such great conflict arose with those who resisted justice that, as the day departed, the darkness of night was poured out upon the world, he ordered the canonical rules to be read by lamplight, lest the councils held there on his behalf remain uncorrected. Thus the mouths of those resisting justice might be stopped by the bars of justice, and everything might be brought to completion through just judgments in accordance with God’s will.

When he returned to his little dwelling after completing the assembly or the confirmation, he did not taste lunch to refresh his body until alms had been distributed to the poor by the cleric entrusted with that duty. He ordered that an abundant meal be set before the weak who arrived with him, seating them in his presence.

On certain days he arranged to hold chapter meetings with the clergy in places where the archpriests thought this could most suitably be done, and where they judged that he would be freer from other worldly assemblies. After assembling the clergy before him, he carefully questioned the archpriests, deans, and the best men he could find among them about how they fulfilled the daily service of God, and how the people subject to them were governed by them in the pursuit of preaching and teaching; how carefully infants were baptized, the sick visited and anointed, and the bodies of the dead delivered to burial with compassion;

how the poor and weak were refreshed from the tithes and offerings of the faithful, and widows and orphans assisted in all their needs; with how much diligence they ministered to Christ in guests and strangers; whether they kept women living with them under the same roof and thereby incurred suspicion of crime; whether they went hunting with dogs or hawks; whether they entered taverns for the sake of eating or drinking; whether they were accustomed to engage in shameful jokes; whether they loved drunkenness and excessive feasting; whether they devoted themselves to quarrels, disputes, and rivalries; whether they attended secular weddings; or whether any of them habitually performed unbecoming ministries;

whether on the Kalends, following the custom of their predecessors, they gathered at appointed places, completed the customary prayers there, and revisited their churches at the proper time; whether they had shown obedience to their superiors and striven to remain devout and capable throughout their entire ministry.

When they had answered the questions and he had learned the truth of the matter, he rewarded those who stood in righteousness with the grace of the sweetest consolation. He admonished them in gentle conversation not to depart from the standard of justice thereafter. But he terrified the brothers who walked along crooked paths with deserved corrections and ordered them afterward to abandon their customary vices.

VII. Among those who possessed estates in his bishopric, whenever one of the religious wished, for the love of Christ, to establish a church, and, with permission granted by the same holy bishop, had built it and requested that he consecrate it at a suitable time, he most readily consented to each person’s request—provided that the man did not delay immediately to give the consecrated church its lawful endowment in lands and bondservants into the hand of his highness, in the presence of his fellow citizens and truthful witnesses, so that the truth of the transaction might not later be obscured. This was also done so that the rights of the other surrounding churches might in no respect be diminished on account of that new church.

After the consecration had been completed and the endowment had been formally transferred, he approved the priest there and entrusted the care of the altar to him. He firmly entrusted the advocacy of the church to the rightful heir by placing the cloth upon him.

[Note: Observe the rite of transferring the advocacy of a church.]

He did not demand an offering of any gift, unless the priest of that church, out of respect and goodwill toward him, voluntarily persuaded him to accept something.

VIII. At a certain time, while obeying Jesus’ commands, when he had decided to fulfill the duty of his ministry in a district called Aldegowe,

[Note: Commonly Algua or Algare.]

some men from that district came to him lamenting and saying:

“Our fathers, on the estate they left to us, built a little chapel of stones, mortar, and wood. They wished it to be dedicated to God and his saints, and desired to deserve to hear the celebration of the sacred offices there, since this place lies in a great wilderness. But, because of the difficulty of the road and the poverty of their resources, they were never able to bring a bishop to consecrate the aforesaid chapel.”

When the servant of God heard this, he said with a cheerful face: “Can you now, for the time being, acquire what is necessary for the consecration of the church?” Relying on the consolations of their friends, they replied: “We can.”

Then he said to them: “Leave Canto, my guide for the road, with me; go ahead and put in order what must be arranged. Behold, I will arrive there to assist your need, and, with God’s help, I will consecrate the church.”

On the following day, after the consecration had been completed, the citizens themselves came before him offering gifts according to their means. When he saw them, he said with a smile:

“I did not come here for love of any gift, but to attend to your need and to increase the service of God in this place. Keep these things offered to us for your benefit, grow in the service of God, and remain in peace.”

After saying this, he departed, and made no complaint about the difficulty of the road except as though rejoicing.

## IX

Persisting in these pursuits of good works, he spiritually refreshed all who lived with him by the gentlest exhortation, teaching them not only in words but also by his actions that each person should love the Lord perfectly with all his strength, prefer nothing to his love, love his neighbor as himself, and honor father and mother. Moreover, he taught that every person of good will, of whom the angelic multitude sings, saying, “And on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2), should [Col. 1025D] resist the wicked in all their evil deeds, according to the holy prophet David, who says: “The wicked is brought to nothing in his sight, but he glorifies those who fear the Lord” (Psalm 14). Each person should not do to another what he would not wish done to himself. They should frequently visit the churches of God with devoted minds, humility, and offerings, and there earnestly implore God, with an outpouring of tears, both for the remission of their sins and for all their own just needs.

He also urged them to ask pardon from their enemies, according to the Lord’s Prayer: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our [Col. 1026A] debtors” (Matthew 6); and according to the Gospel: “So also my heavenly Father will do to you, if each of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts” (Matthew 18); and again: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke 6).

They should hasten, with great care, to offer the tithes of all their labor to the Lord and his saints, and to the churches to which they were assigned, lest they incur the guilt of Cain, the murderer of his brother. He urged them to venerate Sundays and the other annual solemnities, not only by abstaining from servile labor but also from every vice. Each person should receive the Eucharist frequently, strive to present himself purified before receiving it, and preserve himself clean after receiving it.

[Col. 1026B] He urged everyone to observe with complete devotion the days of Lent and the other fasts established in ancient times, as well as those newly instituted with common agreement; to practice self-denial and follow Christ’s footsteps; to discipline the body and not love luxuries; to refresh the hungry and thirsty with food and drink; to provide clothing for the naked; to visit the sick and those in distress; to offer lodging to the needy and homeless; and to provide whatever was necessary for Christ’s love. They should visit orphans and widows in their tribulations and assist them in all their needs; retain no malice in their hearts; provoke no one to anger by their words; lay aside anger and leave vengeance to the Lord; repay no one evil for evil, nor embitter anyone by any injury; not return curses upon those who curse them, but rather bless them; and endure persecution for righteousness.

[Col. 1026C] They should recall those who were divided and hostile to one another to harmony and unity; resist those who resisted God; offer assistance to those who fought faithfully for him; and allow themselves to be ensnared by none of the eight principal vices that afflict every class of human beings.

When people asked what the eight principal vices were, he answered not only them but also those who still remained uncertain, saying [Note: [Col. 1026D] This division of the principal vices was also approved by Cassian and certain others.]:

The first is *gastrimargia*, that is, gluttony of the belly, with its offspring: feasting and drunkenness.

The second is fornication, with its offspring: obscene speech, buffoonery, frivolity, which are also foolish talk.

[Col. 1026D] The third is *philargyria*, that is, avarice or love of money, with its offspring: lying, fraud, theft, perjury, the pursuit of shameful profit, false testimony, violence, inhumanity, greed, and rapacity.

The fourth is anger, with its offspring: murder, shouting, and indignation.

The fifth is sadness, with its offspring: resentment, faintheartedness, bitterness, and despair.

The sixth is acedia, with its offspring: idleness, sleepiness, importunity, restlessness, wandering, instability of mind and body, talkativeness, and curiosity.

The seventh is *cenodoxia*, that is, vainglory, with its offspring: contentiousness, heresy, boasting, and presumption concerning novelties.

The eighth is pride, with its offspring: contempt, envy, disobedience, blasphemy, murmuring, detraction, and hostility.

[Col. 1027A] He called blessed the person who did not stumble into the snares of these vices.

He urged them carefully to receive with the ears of their hearts the eight most famous beatitudes enumerated by God in the Gospel and to implant them firmly in their innermost thoughts, so that, when temptation came, power would not be granted to evil spirits to tear them out, but that each person might be lifted by their consolations toward the hope of heavenly desires.

He also urged them always, day and night, to offer abundant praises and thanks with all their desires and strength to Christ, the Lamb of almighty God who takes away the sins of the world, because by his incarnation, birth, baptism, crucifixion, burial, resurrection, and ascension he is worthy to loose the seven seals of the sealed book shown in a vision to the holy apostle John on the island of Patmos.

[Col. 1027B] Earnestly and humbly he asked the goodwill of everyone in common: if anyone felt that a crop of some virtues had grown within him [the manuscript’s *victutum* is probably an OCR error for *virtutum*, “virtues”], he should attribute it not to his own merits but to the mercy of almighty God, lest it suddenly be destroyed in him by the hailstorm of boasting, but, ripening at the proper time under the protection of the Holy Spirit, be stored in Christ’s granaries.

They should guard their mouths from evil or corrupt speech; willingly hear holy readings; confess their past sins to God every day in prayer with groaning and tears, and thereafter correct them; not fulfill the desires of the flesh; break their own will; obey the commands of priests, even if—God forbid—they themselves act otherwise, imitating those of whom the Lord says: “For they say, and do not do” (Matthew 23).

[Col. 1027C] He urged them to love chastity; hate no one; harbor neither envy nor jealousy; not cultivate disputes; hate arrogance; honor elders; love the young; keep the fear of the Lord continually in heart and mind; and believe that the Lord’s eyes see everything and his ears hear everything, as the Psalmist says: “Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are toward their prayers; but the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth” (Psalm 33).

[Col. 1027D] They should always hold before their eyes with apprehension and fear the day of their death and the day of the final judgment, when the Lord will say to those who hasten daily to feed, clothe, and visit him in his poor—those who will not fear the evil report—“Come, blessed of my Father” (Matthew 25), and so forth; but to those who neglect these things and do not minister to God in his members: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid.).

They should frequently contemplate with the eyes of their mind the punishments prepared for the accursed: that dreadful place, forever without refreshment, light, or sweetness, and which will be without end; where their worm does not die and the fire is not extinguished; where weeping and gnashing of teeth are heard continually without interruption; where the devouring flame is constantly renewed by the devil’s devices; where there is absolutely no hope of consolation, but sadness increases from hour to hour, because they cannot find an end to their dwelling there, and they remain forever in distress with those whom they served in this world.

[Col. 1028A] But they should always consider, as far as human minds can, how great are the joys and rejoicings awaiting God’s blessed, placed at his right hand, of whom it is written: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2).

There the hymn-singing choirs of angels will shine with indescribable brightness; there the exalted company of patriarchs, rewarded with fitting honor, will rejoice; there the truthful order of prophets, having fulfilled their prophecies in every respect, will never cease giving thanks to God; there the judging choir of apostles, having received the reward promised beforehand, will rejoice forever; there the martyrs, crowned with the palm of their martyrdom, will enjoy eternal consolation; there confessors, their rewards multiplied, will persevere in the praises of God; there virgins will abound in the recompense of the hundredfold fruit, and widows will be honored with the restoration of the sixtyfold fruit; there monks, having renounced all worldly things, will be satisfied with those who hunger and thirst for God’s righteousness, their desires fulfilled, and will never cease devoting themselves to God’s praises.

[Col. 1028B] There penitents, having laid aside the burdens of their sins, will rejoice together, praising God without end; there children, following the Lamb in white garments and joining the angels beneath the throne, will never cease praising God in song; there the most glorious virgin Mary, Mother of God, exalted above the choirs of angels, will be seen gladdening everyone with immeasurable brightness and beauty; there the righteous will shine like the sun, and all the saints will see face to face, rejoicing, their Creator and that of all creatures in his glory, who will remove from them every fear, grief, sorrow, and adversity.

[Col. 1028C] In that kingdom the light of the sun, moon, and stars will not be needed; hunger and thirst will harm no one; cold and heat will weary no one; sickness and pain will come to no one; and the misery of approaching old age will not be feared. Rather, just as on the day of judgment the bodies of the dead will rise in the measure of the fullness of Christ’s stature, so they will remain in that same freedom from suffering and beauty.

No weddings will be celebrated there, and the human race will not afterward increase in number; but the full number of the righteous will neither diminish nor perish, but will be preserved forever in joy. They will no longer fear the devil’s snares and will no longer need the forgiveness of sins. Just as the angels will remain in the freedom from suffering of their original condition, so human beings, after the resurrection, equal to the angels, will persevere in sobriety and unchangeableness in the city of our God, built upon his holy mountain.

[Col. 1028D] This city is said to be adorned and founded upon twelve precious stones, whose names and order the holy apostle and evangelist John enumerates in the Apocalypse:

- Jasper is placed in the first foundation; they say that it drives away every phantom, and in it the greenness of faith is signified.
- Sapphire is in the second, signifying hope of heavenly blessedness.
- Chalcedony is in the third, representing the flame of inward charity.
- Emerald is in the fourth, representing the strong confession of that same faith amid adversity.
- [Col. 1029A] Sardonyx is in the fifth, signifying the humility of the saints among the virtues.
- Sardius is in the sixth, expressing the blood of the holy martyrs.
- Chrysolite is in the seventh, signifying spiritual preaching amid miracles.
- Beryl is in the eighth, signifying the perfect action of preachers.
- Topaz is in the ninth, displaying their ardent contemplation.
- Chrysoprase is in the tenth, signifying both the work and the reward of the blessed martyrs.
- Hyacinth is in the eleventh, representing heavenly elevation toward higher things and, because of humility, descent toward human things.
- Amethyst is in the twelfth, signifying the perpetual remembrance of the heavenly kingdom in the minds of the humble.

This arrangement of the twelve stones signifies the firmness of the apostles, who were placed as the foundation of the Church, just as the Savior of the world said to blessed Peter: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16).

[Col. 1029B] By saying this to Peter, he made known to all the apostles that his Church would be built upon them—those whose sound has gone out into all the earth and whose words have reached the ends of the world. If the apostles are the foundation of God’s house, and all Christianity is the building of that same temple, then we must remain steadfast, as the Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple, and you are God’s building,” and so forth (1 Corinthians 3).

[Col. 1029C] Let us all strive with all our strength to join ourselves to our Builder and Dweller, so that, with our teachers placed in the foundation, we may, by his gift, deserve to be built upon them; so that, placed among the chosen stones and joined to the orders mentioned above, we may be seen to belong to them; and so that, seeing face to face our Creator and Redeemer, the judge of the living and the dead, we may deserve to praise him with them through endless ages of ages. Amen.

## X

As the fame of his goodness spread far and wide, and the devil saw him standing at this summit of virtues, he tried by every kind of stratagem of his malice to plunge him into some abyss of difficulty and hinder him from the good works he had begun.

At this time Liutolf, son of the glorious King Otto, was duke of the Alamanni. His father had previously subjected all the peoples of the regions under his rule to Liutolf by an oath, to take effect after his own death. Liutolf’s uncle, Henry, the king’s brother, was duke of the Norici. [Note: [Col. 1029D] This is superfluous.] Because of the boundaries between their regions, and at the persuasion of evil men, they began to engage in quarrels and disputes with one another. When the king could in no way recall them to harmony and peace, he set himself against his son and turned to assist his brother.

When his son tried to resist him with all whom he had been able to gather, and attempted to drive him from royal power, Henry, the aforementioned duke, entrusted the city of Regensburg and the whole region of the Norici to Count Arnulf the Palatine and to his other faithful men, and went to the king. While he remained there, the aforementioned Arnulf, with a multitude of people, fraudulently brought Regensburg under his control, together with the other cities, their inhabitants, and everything he could obtain, under Liutolf’s authority.

[Col. 1030A] When the king learned this, he invaded Bavaria with his brother Henry in a hostile manner, in order to restore him to the dignity of his former power. The aforementioned bishop Udalric, whose steadfast loyalty had never been separated from assistance to the king, learned of this. He left part of his vassals in the city of Augsburg and placed his other affairs in order; then, with as many men as he could gather, abandoning the wagon and riding on horseback in the king’s service, he came shrewdly into the region of the Norici. Because the journey had been extended, he could not conveniently retain the means of returning.

Meanwhile, the aforementioned Arnulf gathered a multitude, went to Augsburg, stripped it of all the goods he could carry away, and took certain of the bishop’s soldiers captive with him back to Bavaria.

[Col. 1030B] When the king had returned from the region of Bavaria, and the bishop wished to return to his own city, he did not think that he could defend himself in Augsburg with a small force, because nearly the whole bishopric was being divided by Liutolf and his followers as benefices for outsiders. Some of the bishop’s soldiers had been captured, some had been separated from him by wicked persuasion, and some had been reduced to poverty by plundering, so that they could not assist him according to his wishes.

Those who remained with him, strengthened by his conversations, adopted a prudent plan: they would leave Augsburg, build a fortress called Menichingen, and strive to defend themselves there against their adversaries.

[Col. 1030C] Thus he remained shut up in Augsburg for only one night. The next day he immediately went to the aforementioned fortress, which was deserted both inside and outside, without any buildings at all. Although the winter had certainly been harsh, they nevertheless waited in that place, in tents and huts hastily assembled, until the gathered household surrounded the fortress with a wooden enclosure and constructed suitable buildings inside, as far as their ability allowed.

When Arnulf and all who were with him learned this, they opposed the royal authority on every side and sent messengers, saying that, if the bishop wished to preserve his own safety and that of his people, he should without delay submit himself to Liutolf’s authority and abandon the attempt to complete the aforementioned fortress with his men. At that time, they claimed, no one in the whole region of Swabia remained in assistance of the king except Count Adalpert with his subjects, Theodpaldus, the brother of the devout bishop, and a few others; therefore, they thought that the bishop could in no way acquire the strength to resist by their decision.

[Col. 1030D] Using wise counsel with his men, the bishop by various promises and most humble replies, and sometimes by giving hostages and then receiving them back, entirely calmed their anger and sieges, until, after the fortress had been built and its ditches renewed, he believed that he could defend himself and his men from their violence within that stronghold.

When the truces could no longer be prolonged by arguments and replies, he openly confessed that he wished to remain in the king’s will, as he had begun.

Then the aforementioned Arnulf, son of Duke Arnulf, gathered a multitude of those accursed men who had previously plundered Augsburg, together with others whose assistance he then trusted. [Col. 1031A] He wished, by besieging the fortress, to force the venerable bishop and his men under Liutolf’s authority.

When the bishop learned this, he sent messengers, promised a large sum of money, and begged that, when they returned, he might be allowed to remain in peace. But if they refused to return after peace had been rejected, he ordered the same messengers to bind his parishioners under the ban of Christianity, so that they would not dare invade the lands of Saint Mary situated within his bishopric.

They, however, despite the money offered and disregarding the Christian ban, did not wish to abandon the evil undertaking they had begun. To their own destruction, on that Sunday [Note: [Col. 1031D] Commonly called Quinquagesima.], on which it is customary for clerics to eat meat before Lent and thereafter abstain until the holy season of Easter, they invaded the estate of Saint Mary in a hostile manner and besieged the bishop.

[Col. 1031B] The bishop, however, remaining diligently in God’s service day and night, casting away fear and trusting in God, regarded their sieges as nothing and remained firm in the purpose he had undertaken.

When this siege became known to Count Adalpert and Theodpaldo, the bishop’s brother, they gathered a troop of people and, on the first day of the Lenten season—that is, Monday—invaded the enemy camp at daybreak.

Those men, who had not thought this could happen so soon, were found unprepared for battle. Struck by sudden fear, they abandoned their plunder and tried to escape their enemies by flight. The pursuers captured Hermann, Arnulf’s brother; struck down some in the camp; and killed others as they pursued them farther.

[Col. 1031C] After most of them had been killed and the rest put to flight, none of them dared hope to defend himself except one named Egilolf. While fleeing, he inflicted a slight wound on Count Adalpert’s arm, and Adalpert also died from that wound. Egilolf, the man who wounded him, was immediately killed by Liutpert, a vassal of Adalpert.

Very few of the enemy, bruised by blows and wounded in various ways, nevertheless escaped the danger of death that day, carried away by their horses. Some of them, miserably stiffened by frost, returned naked to their own huts in despair of life.

The venerable bishop carried Adalpert’s body, slain according to God’s will, to Augsburg, commended his soul honorably to God, and buried him in the church of Saint Mary.

[Col. 1031D] None of those who had previously claimed the plunder of Augsburg for themselves in opposition to holy Mary, Mother of God, escaped unpunished, except those who did not delay redeeming themselves by means of their own possessions, with the pardon of the venerable bishop.

## XI

One of these men tore at his own hands and, while his neighbors truthfully declared that he had lost his senses, breathed out his spirit.

Another, having taken a book from Augsburg, bought a horse he liked very much and brought it home with him. He showed it to his wife and said: “I would rather have this handsome horse than leave behind in Augsburg the book with which I bought it.”

[Col. 1032A] His wife answered him: “It might have been useful to you if your hand had not touched that book unjustly.”

Meanwhile, as he stroked the horse with his hand and touched its hindquarters, the horse immediately struck him, and he died.

When the multitude of people learned of these new and unexpected disasters, and of many other frightening events that had befallen the guilty, great fear seized those who knew themselves guilty of the aforementioned plundering of Augsburg—not only those who had gone there, but also those who had received anything from the goods unjustly acquired by them.

[Col. 1032B] Therefore they turned to penitence and lamentation and, by worthy amendment and restoration of the things that had been taken, together with earnest pleas for the bishop’s pardon, strove to reconcile themselves with Christ and with holy Mary, his mother.

Not long afterward, the aforementioned Arnulf, who had dared to invade Saint Mary’s possessions in a hostile manner and had persisted uncorrected without repentance, went out ready for battle when the city of Regensburg was besieged and was immediately killed in the midst of the tumult.

A certain man from the bishopric called Eichstätt carried away to his own property a piece of a very cheap tablecloth. Immediately possessed by a demon, he could find no place to hide from it, neither inside nor outside a church, nor even when sprinkled with holy water; the demon always seemed to remain beside him. [Col. 1032C] At last he returned to Augsburg and brought back what he had unjustly carried away. He asked the bishop, for Christ’s sake, to impose a scourging on him with brooms, and further begged him to pardon and forgive the aforementioned offense. Thus, freed from the demon and saved, he departed.

## XII

Lest I withdraw for too long from the account I began, I would like to draw my pen back from enumerating the cities besieged on both sides, the battles raging everywhere, and the succession of various stratagems [Note: [Col. 1031D] *stromatum* is printed here for *stratagematum*; [Col. 1032] Migne printed (24) instead of (42).]. Rather, I wish to recount how almighty God deigned through the merits of his servants to free his people, lest the devil’s machinations bring them to destruction.

[Col. 1032D] When King Otto was in Alamannia with his army, because of those who wished to resist the authority of his royal power together with his son Liutolf, he was staying near the river called the Hilara, in the field of a town called Tussa [Note: Tussen.]. There his aforementioned son Liutolf came against him with another army, prepared to fight. They were so closely joined that, unless battle were begun by one side or the other, no uncertainty could remain concerning the multitude of either party.

At that moment Udalric, beloved of God, placing all his trust in God, took with him Hartbert, the devout bishop of the Church of Chur, and began to act as mediator between them. He pleaded for agreement in peace, lest the people entrusted to them by God to govern should, on account of their guilt, be led to destruction.

[Col. 1033A] With God’s consent, the minds of both men—the father Otto and his son Liutolf—were softened by the useful admonition and teaching of the venerable bishops. They agreed upon a pact of peace between themselves, and, the storm of war having been calmed, they returned peacefully to their own places.

After they had overcome such great hardships of tumult, they thought that they could rest in peace for some time. But immediately in the following year, that is, in the year of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 965, such a multitude of Hungarians burst forth as no living person of that time professed ever to have seen before in any region.

[Col. 1033B] They devastated and occupied the region of the Norici [Note: Bavaria is meant here], from the Danube River to the Black Forest, which extends toward the mountains. When they crossed the Lech and occupied Alamannia, they burned the church of Saint Afra, plundered the whole province from the Danube to the forest, and burned a very large part of it as far as the river Hilara.

They besieged the city of Augsburg, which at that time, surrounded only by low walls without towers, was not strong in itself. But the holy bishop had stationed inside the city’s enclosure a very large number of excellent soldiers. Through their agility and courage, and with God’s help, the city stood strongly fortified.

When they saw the Hungarian army surrounding the city to attack it, they wished to go out against them. The bishop, however, did not consent and ordered them firmly to close the gate where the greatest access for entering remained.

[Col. 1033C] The eastern gate [Note: The gate we call Jacob’s Gate], from which one goes toward the water, was so occupied by the dense mass of Hungarians that they thought they could enter immediately. The bishop’s soldiers fought manfully before the gate and resisted them until one of the Hungarians, who surpassed the others in fighting and whose leadership and advance gave them their greatest confidence in battle at that hour, was killed and fell.

When the others saw him fall dead to the ground, they seized him amid loud shouting and lamentation and returned to their camp.

[Col. 1033D] During the battle the bishop sat on his horse, wearing a stole but protected by neither shield nor breastplate nor helmet. Javelins and stones flew all around him, yet he remained untouched and unharmed.

When the battle was over, he returned and went around the city. He ordered houses suitable for war to be placed around the city, to be built throughout the night, and the ditches to be renewed as far as the time allowed.

He himself spent the entire night in prayer and roused the religious women gathered in the city: one group was to go around inside it with crosses, devoutly crying out to the Lord, while the other group was to prostrate itself on the pavement and earnestly implore the mercy of holy Mary, Mother of God, for the people’s defense and the city’s deliverance.

He allowed his body only a very short portion of the night’s rest before Matins, so that, after Matins and Lauds had been completed, he might offer the saving sacrifice to God at the first breaking of dawn.

[Col. 1034A] After the sacred ministry had been completed, he refreshed everyone with the sacred Viaticum and, with humble admonition, persuaded them not to doubt that, remaining steadfast in the true faith, they should place their hope in the Lord. He promised them every kind of consolation and announced to them the words of the psalm-writing David: “Though I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me” (Psalm 22).

When the bishop’s saving admonition had been completed and the radiance of the shining sun first illuminated the breadth of the earth, the Hungarian army, innumerable beyond description, surrounded the city on every side to attack it, bringing various instruments for bringing down the walls.

[Col. 1034B] When they were prepared for battle on every side and all the city’s battlements were filled with defenders, some Hungarians forced others into battle by threatening them with whips. But when they saw so great a multitude of defenders on the battlements, they were so terrified that they did not dare approach the walls.

While they were prepared for battle inside and outside, Berchtolf, son of Arnulf, came from the fortress called Risinesburch to the Hungarian king and announced the arrival of the glorious King Otto.

When the Hungarian king heard this, he ordered the signal known to the whole army to be sounded. At its sound the entire army abandoned the attack on the city and hastened to join their king for a conference.

After he had conferred with them [the Latin *autumatione* is uncertain], he ceased, by God’s gift, from attacking the city and began to go to meet the glorious king. His intention was that, once Otto had been overcome together with his men, he could return victorious and freely possess the city and the entire kingdom.

[Col. 1034C] As King Otto approached, Count Dietpald, the bishop’s brother, went out at night with the others who were in the city and came to meet him.

When the king saw such a great Hungarian army, he thought that it could not be defeated by human beings unless almighty God deigned to destroy them. Trusting in God’s help and strengthened by the encouragement of his princes, he began to fight them manfully.

After both sides had fallen in mutual slaughter, and those whom God had predestined for death had been killed, God—before whom nothing is impossible—gave the glorious King Otto victory. The Hungarian army was routed and no longer possessed the strength to fight.

[Col. 1034D] Although an incredible number of them had been killed, so large a force still remained that those watching from the battlements of Augsburg thought they were returning without having been challenged in battle. Only when they saw them pass beyond the city and hasten toward the farther banks of the Lech did they understand what had happened.

The king followed them with his men, killing as many as he could overtake. In the evening he reached Augsburg, where he spent that night with the bishop and gave him great consolation concerning his brother Dietbald, who had been killed in the battle, and concerning his other relatives who had been killed there.

[Col. 1035A] He honored Rihgwin, the son of Dietpald, with his father’s countship, and, in faithful assistance to the bishop, restored a worthy reward to him in every matter where he recognized the bishop’s desire.

At dawn, he returned to the region of Bavaria [Note: [Col. 1035D] Alternatively, “of the Bavarians.”] in pursuit of the fleeing barbarian forces. Sending messengers quickly, he ordered them to watch all the river crossings and fords in order to kill the fugitives—and so it happened.

When the Hungarians came there by night, some were drowned in the rivers by those who were in boats; some were killed; and those who reached the bank were slain by those watching the shores. They could find no route or byway by which the Lord’s vengeance did not remain manifestly upon them.

[Col. 1035B] Indeed, not many days later their kings and princes were captured and brought to Regensburg. To the disgrace of their nation, they were hanged on the gallows together with many others of their countrymen.

### XIII

King Otto, holding his power in God, confirmed his brother Henry in the kingdom with the authority of his own hand, and himself returned victorious to Saxony, as he was accustomed to do. The venerable Bishop Udalric, when the king departed from Augsburg, went to the places where the battle had been fought, seeking his aforementioned brother Dietbald and the noble Reginbold, his sister’s son [Note: [Col. 1035D] Luitgard.].
