Finding them, he brought them to Augsburg and faithfully buried both in the church of Saint Mary, before the altar of Saint Walburga the virgin, in one tomb [Note: [Col. 1036D] Sepulchre.].

When these matters had been completed as described, the bishop, although wearied by many adversities [Col. 1035C], took up the task of good consolation, as is most fitting for anyone who hopes in God, and began to consider with his people how he might most effectively overcome the impending losses. First, he considered how he might sustain the plundered community of clerics so that they could fulfill the daily ministry of God’s service in the church. For he knew that they had no food. Therefore, from what he himself, though plundered, had been able to retain, and from what benevolent people sent and offered to him, he continually had them eat and drink in his presence according to his means, and strengthened them with every kind of assistance, until they themselves alleviated the misery of the plundering and their own lands, through renewed labor, brought them the means of sustenance [Col. 1035D]. Their own dwellings had been burned by fire, their crops consumed, and the places reduced to desolation; so he ordered them to be restored through diligent labor in the fields and buildings. The vigor of the household, obeying his command, began this work and, at the proper time, restored the places to useful service insofar as their ability allowed.

The church of Saint Afra, which had been burned by the pagans, had not yet been rebuilt. A hut roofed with shingles [Note: [Col. 1036D] For *scandulae*, shingles.] protected the altars from rain and bad weather; but the tomb of Bishop Simpert, situated in the choir beside the steps, still remained without a roof. Having been warned in a vision about covering it, he roofed it with pieces of wood joined together by craftsmanship in the manner of a lid [Col. 1036A]. Not long afterward, he was again warned not to delay rebuilding the church of Saint Afra. He very often considered how its restoration could most suitably be carried out and how, by placing a crypt beneath it, the eastern part of the church could be adorned most appropriately. Since no firm solution entered his mind, he began, with continuous prayers and fasts, together with his household and devout priests, to beseech God’s mercy most earnestly and secretly, asking that the place where Saint Afra’s body had been laid might be shown to him, and whether it remained lawful to construct a crypt in the place that pleased her will.

To make it clear that his prayer and fasting had reached the ears of the Lord, in accordance with the song of Saint David the prophet [Col. 1036B]: “Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are attentive to their prayers” (Psalm 33), Saint Afra appeared to him one night in a vision and showed him the place where her body had been laid, as it is written in the account of her passion: at the second milestone from the city of Augsburg, in the church. But she forbade a crypt to be made in the appointed place, because the relics of the saints there ought to await the day of judgment in rest.

Fully instructed by this revelation about what he should do, he had the walls, which the fires had brought down for the most part, rebuilt with great haste. He added one cubit to their former height, and adorned the western part of the church with a suitable crypt. He ordered the building materials, carefully measured in his presence, to be cut and brought [Col. 1036C] with the utmost diligence, and did not delay until he had covered the whole church with roof tiles. Inside, he clothed the church with a coffered ceiling, adorned it with bright paintings, and had the church ornaments that had been carried into the city because of the barbarians and preserved in the mother church restored to their places.

### XIV

That this eastern part of the church always remains under God’s special protection has been manifested by certain signs; it seems appropriate to insert one of them here. A gardener named Adelpoldus, while walking there among the grass, discovered a grotto. Entering it, he saw beneath the earth a beautiful little chapel built of masonry. He came and reported this to the bishop, saying: “In this place I can store my vegetables and other necessities [Col. 1036D].” The bishop answered him with a warning: “If you do this, there is no doubt that you will lose the use and health of your limbs.”

But the gardener did not believe the bishop’s words. Without his permission, he began gathering the aforementioned things in that same grotto. In doing so, he lost his senses, together with his hearing and sight. When this was reported to the bishop, he ordered the gardener to be brought before him and said: “Why did you wish to occupy that holy place, disregarding my command?” Although he was deprived of his senses, the man replied: “I do not deny it. I know that I have incurred this affliction because of that offense, because I did not obey your commands.”

The benevolent bishop pitied his affliction and, granting him forgiveness together with a blessing [Col. 1037A], restored him to health by God’s permission. Wonderful to relate: afterward that gardener could in no way find the grotto.

Then the bishop summoned undertakers and ordered them to dig a tomb for him on the southern side of the church’s exterior wall, to enclose it with an outer wall, and, after breaking through the church wall, to arch a masonry vault over it. He also ordered a suitable coffin to be made to cover the body in the tomb, and a thick wooden covering, joined with careful workmanship and durable against decay for a long time, to be placed above it.

After completing these preparations for his burial, he became accustomed thereafter to visit that place every Friday and offer sacrifices there, unless some other occupation or absence prevented him [Col. 1037B]. Meanwhile, by God’s merciful gift, peace was illuminating these regions, and the multitude of persecutions was no longer preventing benevolent minds from serving God. Therefore he decided to travel to Rome, and arrived there safely. With devoted zeal he humbly visited the thresholds of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul. There, after pouring out abundant prayers and distributing generous alms to the poor, he was honorably received by Alberic, prince of the Romans. Laden with frequent services and offerings, he remained there for several days.

While staying there, he indicated that he wished to acquire relics of the saints. A certain cleric came to him and, in the silence of night, led him to a church where the head of Saint Abundus the martyr was kept enclosed in an altar. Showing him the account of the martyr’s passion and presenting the head, the cleric confirmed by oath that the relics brought by the bishop with him included the head of that same Abundus whose passion had just been read aloud.

When the bishop heard that the oath had been completed, he gave the cleric a suitable reward. Receiving Saint Abundus’s head, he carried it back with him to Augsburg and there honorably enclosed it for the consolation of many [Col. 1037C].

He also regularly visited the monastery of Saint Gall, where he had been thoroughly instructed in literary studies. There he gave a feast to the monks serving God, and from there proceeded to the cell of Saint Meginard, to see God’s servant Saint Eberhard and to assist him and the monks subject to him in whatever needs he was able to learn they had [Col. 1037D].

On the final occasion, while Eberhard was still alive, when he had to depart from there, after completing a long and affectionate conversation and receiving permission to leave the church with prayers, he went out to the vehicle that was to carry him away. When he was ready to depart, and did not think he would see Saint Eberhard again that day, Eberhard suddenly came after him, as though hurrying, and, repeating the kisses of affection, said with tearful eyes: “From this hour onward you will not see me again, until, released from our bodies, we may be deemed worthy to see one another in the presence of God.”

The bishop replied to his words: “Most beloved Father, do you now know for certain that I am soon to depart from this world?” He answered: “The end of your life is not yet near; but do not doubt that the words I have now spoken to you are true” [Col. 1038A]. After these words had been completed, the bishop returned. Before he visited that same cell again, Eberhard happily departed from this world.

### XV

At another time he also went to the region of Burgundy and visited, with great humility, the place of Agaunum, where Saint Maurice and his companions suffered martyrdom for the name of the Lord. Earlier, he had received a promise from the king of Burgundy that, through the king’s gift and assistance, he might be worthy to bring one of the holy martyrs from there back to Augsburg.

When he arrived there on Saturday, he found the monastery newly burned by the Saracens and saw none of its inhabitants except one caretaker of the building [al. an aged man], who was guarding the burned monastery. He spent the holy night there in the praises of God. In the morning, when the rays of the sun first spread light over the breadth of the earth, he celebrated Mass of the Holy Trinity. After it was completed, he immediately began to celebrate another Mass appropriate to the veneration of the Lord’s Day. Twelve clerics arrived with a multitude of people and, hearing the celebration of his ministry, remained there.

When this had been completed, the holy bishop greeted those brothers and honored them with gifts, and made known why he had come there. Perceiving the sweetness of his cheerfulness and the piety of his holiness, they did not wish him to depart deprived of his delightful desire. They opened the saints’ burial grotto, cut into the rock, and gladdened him by giving him a considerable portion of the holy relics [Col. 1038B].

When he returned from there with the desired permission of the clerics and the most loving farewell of the people [Col. 1038C], he visited the city of Constance for the sake of prayer. From there he came to the island of Reichenau, where Abbot Aleuwicus received him affectionately and provided him with every kind of comfort. As they conversed in friendly exchange, he told him everything that had happened to him on the journey.

When the abbot heard that he had gone forth out of love for the holy relics, he satisfied his desire. Giving him a considerable portion of the body of Saint Maurice and relics of many other saints, he allowed him to depart joyfully.

As he approached the city of Augsburg, he sent messengers ahead and instructed them that, for the much-desired gift [pro: the much-desired gift] of the holy relics that he had brought with him, the clerics and people should come out honorably to meet him with crosses, incense of perfumes [Col. 1038D], and holy water, and should solemnly receive the relics with praises and fitting melodies and escort them honorably with him into the church consecrated in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God.

When they had been brought there, the relics were carefully placed by the bishop in a chest covered with gold and silver, for the praise of almighty God and for the aid of the people who would come, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and glory throughout infinite ages of ages. Amen.

### XVI

Always serving God’s will through such pursuits and others like them, he strove to raise the bishopric that he had undertaken to govern to every kind of honor. He labored tirelessly to increase the service of God and of holy Mary, Mother of God [Col. 1039A]. Therefore, preceded everywhere by God’s grace, as it is found written in the Psalms: “He will fulfill the desire of those who fear him, and he will hear their prayer and save them” (Psalm 144); and according to the Apostle’s saying: “We know that for those who love God all things work together for good,” and so forth (Romans 8), he was honored by many manifestations of God’s greatness and strengthened by firm faith.

Receiving the desires of his will, he benefited many in their necessities, while humbly concealing the power of his ability as much as he could. For many who were afflicted by a falling sickness were restored to health after receiving his blessing, provided that they did not disclose for what reason they had sought the blessing. But when people openly announced the affliction of their need [Col. 1039B], he withheld the blessing and allowed them to depart out of humility, saying: “I am not worthy to be able to free you from this illness.”

The consecrated oil that he prepared on the day of the Lord’s Supper became so health-giving that many who were ill, after being anointed by him, were quickly restored to health. Many who suffered from dimness of the eyes and thought themselves deprived in this world of the gift of present light were again granted the use of clear sight through contact with this oil.

I learned these things without anyone telling me, for I saw them performed with my own eyes in very many cases.

Nor should we remain silent about the bishop’s own recovery. Once, when he had decided to return from the monastery of Saint Gall to the city of Augsburg, he came to Kempten and was seized by such a serious illness [Col. 1039C] that he could not walk by himself without the assistance of others, and lacked sufficient strength to take food for the refreshment of his body.

He sent messengers swiftly to the city of Augsburg and ordered them to bring back to him from there the oil he had consecrated. When the messengers returned on the vigil of Pentecost at the ninth hour, the community of monks was still attending the solemn office of Mass, while he had heard the sacred mystery within his chamber. When the oil was presented to him and the sacred mystery had been completed, the monks were brought in to him, together with the clerics who had come there with him. After they had sung seven psalms for his illness and devoutly completed the litany, the brothers, returning to the cloister, left behind a certain holy monk named Hiltine [Col. 1039D] to anoint him with the holy oil, together with his two priests.

When the anointing had been completed, the bishop said to the provost, according to the teaching of the apostle James: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the presbyter of the Church,” and so forth (James 5): “Provide suitable service in my place for these men who have anointed me, together with my other companions, with the good things that God has granted us today.”

When they had sat down at table to eat, and the meal had not yet been completed, a messenger came from the bishop saying: “Be joyful and refresh yourselves with gladness, because our lord the bishop, although during the past week he had not been able to take even a morsel of bread for nourishment [Col. 1040A], is now, by God’s gift, taking refreshment and has improved, his health having returned.”

When they heard this welcome message, they all became joyful, praising God together and giving thanks to him. When evening arrived and the evening signal had first sounded, he immediately rose and walked to the church. There he remained tireless in the praises of God until the evening praise had been completed at length by the brothers according to the monastic course. Thereafter, strengthened from day to day, he was quickly restored completely to his former health.

O how great is the multitude of God’s sweetness, who granted him so swiftly as a remedy what he had prepared for others as medicine and for the remission of sins, so that, through his perfect faith, the faith of very many others might be strengthened!

### XVII

Here I must also relate another account concerning him, which I learned from the words of his chaplain Herewigus. One day, when he had to ride across a river called the Vindix [al. Vindomen; al. Vindonem, commonly Werten] for some useful purpose, the river had been raised by flooding. All the bishop’s companions avoided the proper ford and looked for other, more suitable fords. The aforementioned Herewigus alone remained with him [Note: [Col. 1039D] He crossed the flooding river without getting wet.].

The bishop himself crossed without fear the ford that the others had avoided, wearing socks made from a cloak (*sagum*) because of the cold, for it was winter. But after Herewigus had crossed the river, he became wet from his belt downward, although he was riding a taller horse than the bishop. He looked at the bishop’s clothing to see whether water had soaked it, but he did not see even a single wet hair on the bishop’s socks. He said to the bishop: “I am drenched with wetness, while not a hair on your lofty person’s socks has become wet.”

The bishop answered him: “You must not presume to tell anyone, while I am alive, what you have seen.”

At another time, when he had decided to travel by ship along the Danube to the city of Regensburg for a meeting with Emperor Otto, the sailors one day were looking carelessly ahead, and the ship struck awkwardly against a piece of wood. It filled with water and threatened everyone with sinking. All were disturbed and terrified, and they hurried with great effort to bring the ship to shore.

After the ship had been brought onto dry land, they carried to the shore those who were inside it, but forgot the bishop, who was sitting at the ship’s stern [Col. 1040D]. One of the clerics, named Mesi, struck with great amazement, said: “Alas for us wretched men, because we have not helped our lord in this danger!”

With these words he ran through the depth of water that had collected in the ship, took the bishop by the arms, lifted him onto his shoulders, and carried him out of the ship. Once everyone had been brought out and he had been the last to leave, the ship sank in its rear section into the depths.

Why is it surprising that the ship, with him sitting in it, could not sink, but remained upon the water at the command of him who, by his own will, strengthened the waves of the sea so that the blessed apostle Peter could walk upon them? Thus, not by its own nature but through the merits of the one sitting in it, the ship was compelled meanwhile to float upon the waters [Col. 1041A] until it had been relieved of all its equipment and burdens; afterward, it was reported to have sunk.

### XVIII

When he once ardently desired to visit Rome and came to a river named the Taro [Note: [Col. 1041D] The Taro according to Pliny, a river in Cisalpine Italy.], he found it made so dangerous by the flooding waters that no one arriving from either bank hoped to be able to cross it that day or the next.

The holy bishop, trusting in God, hastened to put on the vestments for Mass. On the bank of the river he devoutly celebrated Mass with his companions. After Mass, he crossed the aforementioned river with such ease that none of his companions suffered any adversity. All went on their way safe and unharmed, praising God with joy.

### XIX

[Col. 1041B] As he fervently devoted himself to the services of Christ in many ways and strove to increase them everywhere, by God’s gift he conceived the plan—on account of the religious devotion of a certain nun named Emoza—to establish a community of nuns at the church of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, subject it to the rule of holiness, and unite women betrothed to Christ God under the holy veil.

When this had been done, a certain woman, despising marriage with her husband by mutual consent, joined that community, professing obedience for the sake of the reward of future blessedness. She had not been trained to perfection in knowledge of letters, but she possessed great energy for the practical tasks of necessity. Therefore the other nuns wished to make her cellarer.

When she refused, the matter was reported to the bishop, and he was asked to entrust her with the office of cellarer by his authority [Col. 1041C]. The bishop consented to the request and ordered that the aforementioned nun be cellarer. But she did not obey the bishop’s command and attempted to persist in her former resistance.

The following night, in a dream, she heard a voice saying to her: “Because you did not obey the bishop’s command, you will therefore be deprived of the use of your legs until he releases you.” When she awoke, she perceived that her limbs were so disabled that she could not walk at all.

Bound by this illness, she anxiously awaited the bishop’s arrival. Meanwhile the time for the synodal conference was approaching, and the bishop was returning to Augsburg. When the sick nun heard this, she asked to be carried into the church of Saint Mary and brought before him [Col. 1041D]. When she came into his presence, she began to implore his mercy, asking that she might deserve to be freed by him from the bonds of illness that afflicted her.

After hearing her prayer, the bishop rebuked her for her disobedience and dismissed her, granting her both the gift of his blessing and forgiveness. When the bishop was returning from her, she was immediately restored to health. She ran ahead of the bishop before he had walked through the church, then prostrated herself before his lofty presence. Praising God for the health that had been restored, she promised that she would amend her disobedience in the future, and returned joyfully to her own little dwelling.

### XX

[Col. 1042A] The holy bishop, singing hymns to the Lord, later began at a suitable time to build a church in the cemetery of Saint Mary in the form of a cross. When the building had been completed and five altars had been set up in it, he dedicated it in honor of Saint John the Baptist. He had a stone baptismal basin cut out and installed there, and, after providing it with a lawful endowment, entrusted it to a priest to oversee the divine offices.

He ordered the matricularii to visit it reverently every Saturday and on the other solemn feasts, with the Gospel, crosses, and candles, accompanied by the praises of God. During Easter week, which they call “within the White Robes,” because it is then customary to sing three psalms at Vespers, they were to sing the remaining two as they walked there, with an antiphon and tone in beautiful melody [Col. 1042B]. He himself was also accustomed very often to offer saving sacrifices to God there.

### XXI

Desiring to save his life (*zoa*) [Note: [Col. 1041D] He used *zoa* for “life,” and “life” for “soul.”] in his final days, he resolved, although he felt his bodily strength diminishing from day to day, to labor devotedly to visit the thresholds of the apostles Peter and Paul.

After he had traveled some distance in a cart and reached more difficult roads, he could not continue the journey. Before proceeding, he was placed on a bed and carried upon horses. Thus he continued onward. Although the journey seemed dangerous to his companions everywhere, with God’s help and that of the holy apostle Peter he reached Rome without danger.

There, after devoutly fulfilling the vows and promises previously made, and receiving the gifts of highly welcome benefits and indulgences [Col. 1042C], and after receiving a salutary permission [Note: [Col. 1042D] Permission: *Urtaub*.] from Saint Peter and his vicar the pontiff, as well as from the others serving God there under Saint Peter, he honorably set out on his fortunate return. He decided to visit Ravenna.

As he approached it, he learned that the glorious Emperor Otto was staying there with the empress Adalhaida. He sent a messenger ahead to announce his arrival, and then, following the messenger, came immediately to the door of the emperor’s chamber. When the emperor learned that he was staying so near, he hurried affectionately to receive him, out of humility and fervent divine love, with one foot shod and the other still unshod.

When the empress had been summoned into the chamber, they enjoyed pleasant conversation and brought their exchanges about the outcomes of various matters to an end [Col. 1042D]. Then the holy man began to urge the emperor, with the empress’s assistance, faithfully and firmly to entrust to Adalbero, his sister’s son, the administration of his bishopric, the governance of the household, and all the secular affairs belonging to it. He also asked to receive from the height of the emperor’s imperial power a promise of consolation: that after his departure the emperor would grant Adalbero the episcopal see, so that he might be given greater leisure for prayer, ecclesiastical governance, and the strengthening of Christianity.

The glorious and benevolent emperor consented to his request. He entrusted the conduct of secular affairs to Adalbero and promised that, after the bishop’s lifetime, if God willed, he would grant him the honor of the episcopal see. In addition, he generously gave the bishop many pounds of gold and allowed him to depart affectionately. He carefully arranged for the bishop’s lodgings and other necessary service, together with his faithful men, as far as the end of that province [Col. 1043A].

### XXII

When the bishop and the aforementioned Adalbero returned joyfully to the city, they were received honorably, as was fitting. All who were found there rejoiced greatly when they learned of their prosperous return and of the honor the emperor had shown them.

Then the aforementioned Adalbero gathered the bishop’s soldiers and desired that they swear oaths of fidelity to him. They did so in the bishop’s presence [Col. 1043B]. The household throughout the entire bishopric did likewise.

The bishop wore clothing fashioned in the manner of monks; earlier he had been accustomed to follow their rule through many virtues. While these things were taking place, because of the rivalry of certain clerics who thought that, after the holy bishop’s death, they might acquire the bishopric with the emperor’s permission, Adalbero dared to carry the episcopal staff publicly, so that their entire hope of acquiring the bishopric might be removed.

### XXIII

Afterward, when the emperors—namely the father and his son—were returning from Italy to Francia, a synod was held at a place called Ingelheim [Note: [Col. 1043D] The Synod of Ingelheim in the case of Adalbero, in the year 972.]. The archbishops, together with their other suffragans, honorably invited Saint Udalric with his legates [Col. 1043C], and decided that his nephew Adalbero should come with him.

When they arrived there and the bishops gathered in that place learned that Adalbero was publicly carrying the episcopal staff, they became angry with him. They said that he had fallen into heresy against the rule of canonical rectitude, and that, while the bishop was alive, he was claiming for himself more than was just of the honor of pontifical dignity. Therefore, they said, it was no longer proper for him to be ordained bishop.

When he heard this, Adalbero avoided entering the synodal conference on the first day and remained in another house with the bishop’s other clerics. The bishop entered the synod with a few of his chaplains.

When the bishops began to confer among themselves, they wished each person’s case to be concluded in Latin speech. When the case of Saint Udalric was to be discussed, and he was unable, because of his infirmity [Note: [Col. 1044D] He was in his eighty-second year.], to present his case in a voice loud enough for the whole synod to hear, one of his clerics, named Gerhard, was summoned. He had remained outside the synod with Adalbero, so that he might explain his lord’s desire in Latin.

With difficulty, because of the density of the crowd, he stood in the presence of the emperors and bishops. He was asked what his lord desired. After these questions had been repeated several times, he said: “I ought not to answer your questions on behalf of my lord unless he commands me.”

The bishop said to him: “Brother, my desire is well known to you. Explain it, and ask that, with God’s help, it be fulfilled through their counsel and permission.”

Then the aforementioned cleric Gerhard said in the presence of all: “Most excellent emperors and most religious bishops, my lord’s desire is to leave the world, enter a holy life according to the rule of Saint Benedict, and await the day of his death in the contemplative life. In the outward clothing of his habit, you can certainly recognize the will of his inner mind.”

After he had brought these and other arguments concerning his lord’s will to their conclusion, he fell face down at the feet of the emperors and bishops, entreating them not to disdain fulfilling his lord’s petition according to God’s will.

They jointly requested a delay in giving their answer until the following day [Col. 1044B], and afterward considered among themselves how Adalbero’s case should be settled. Some of the bishops, however, supported Adalbero, so that he would not be entirely excluded from hope of episcopal ordination after his uncle’s lifetime.

While they were discussing these matters, they finally reached a common decision and all together established that, unless Adalbero cleared himself by oath, declaring that he did not know that seizing episcopal authority with the staff constituted heresy, he could in no way thereafter lawfully become a bishop.

On the following day Adalbero also attended the synodal conference with the bishop. When the aforementioned charge was brought against him, he decided, with the support of his allies, to defend himself against it through many objections and exchanges of argument.

When the united body of all the bishops did not accept this, he completed the oath according to the bishops’ aforementioned determination, swearing by the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit over the four Gospels [Col. 1044C].

Then Bishop Udalric again sought, through the aforementioned cleric, the answer to his petition, which had been postponed the previous day. He wished his aforementioned nephew to be ordained bishop and, according to the rule of Saint Benedict, to deserve to serve in a monastery with their consent.

Although the bishops were not entirely pleased by this, they did not wish to oppose his petition openly in the synod. Instead, the wisest among them, with the counsel of the others, asked him to walk outside the synod with them. There they held a private conversation with him and with his wisest clerics [Col. 1044D], saying:

“Reverend Father, to whom the rule of all ecclesiastical books is known, who have always walked the path of rectitude without straying, it is not fitting that you now abandon the way you have always followed and provide the seed for such an error: that another should be ordained in your place while you are alive. For if such a custom begins with you, many adversities will grow in the future for many venerable and good bishops, when their nephews and clerics desire such things.

“It is better for you to remain serving God in the ministry in which you began than, by following your own will, to cause scandal to many others [Col. 1045A]. For through you, canons, monks, nuns, and the other Christians ought to be constrained toward a state of rectitude, since they hasten of their own accord to fall throughout the world. Those who have fallen by walking carelessly are to hope that through you, with God’s help, they may be raised up.

“Regarding your nephew Adalbero, to satisfy your will we jointly establish that, after your departure, no one other than he shall be ordained by us to that place where you are shepherd, so long as he is alive.”

The holy Bishop Udalric consented to this counsel. As he returned with them into the synod, he then, with the agreement of the other bishops, had Adalbero commended to the emperor in their presence, so that he might hold the administration of his see under him and faithfully carry out the careful governance of the entire bishopric in all matters [Col. 1045B].

When these matters had thus been settled and the synod had ended, the bishop and Adalbero returned to Augsburg with their companions [Note: [Col. 1045] A certain miracle in another example followed here; since it is repeated below, it seemed best to omit it.]

## XXIV

The aforesaid synod was held in the autumn; and when Eastertime came the following year, after Holy Week had ended, the bishop and Adalbero, at the affectionate invitation of Count Rinuvinus [Richuvinus], the son of Dietpald, the bishop’s brother, came to a castle called Dilinga, so that they might remain there for several days as guests with him and with his wife, named Hiltegart.

After a few days had passed, Adalbero had blood reduced by a phlebotomist who performed bloodletting on him. He then sat down to supper with the bishop, and, rising from supper, lay down in bed to rest. When each person had withdrawn to his own lodging, Adalbero died suddenly that same night, in the year 973.

His presbyter Herewingus entered the bishop’s chamber to announce this to him. Before he could speak, the bishop said to him: “Behold, Adalbero has died.” He replied: “That is why I came here, to announce this to you. No one else preceded me in coming to you; how could you have known this?” The bishop answered him: “Go and rouse Riuvinus and all who are with us, so that they may quickly prepare a conveyance by which we can take his body to the city of Augusta.”

The bishop sent messengers to Augusta and ordered that his grave be prepared in the church of Saint Afra beside the bishop’s own grave. This was done. He placed the body on a cart with those who were with him, and, with horses harnessed before it, conveyed it to Augusta amid a great crowd of people.

The matricularii, carrying crosses, holy water, candles, and incense, together with a great multitude of members of the household and the other people, went out to meet the approaching procession. Receiving it honorably, they escorted it with fitting prayers and chants to the place of the grave. There, after the vigils had been completed and saving offerings had been presented to God for his soul, the bishop commended his soul to almighty God, and they buried the body with the utmost devotion.

When the commendation of the body had been completed and the bishop had returned in sorrow, everyone went back to his own lodging amid weeping, lamentation, and great grief. They mourned because they had lost so quickly a man who was born of noble lineage, handsome, well trained in the grammatical arts, devoted to the service of God, energetic in good works, prudent in eloquence of a sweet tone, generous in giving, sorrowful in the adversities of others, enriched with an abundance of many virtues, prompt in aiding the needy, and adorned with manifold benevolence.

## XXV

The religious bishop sent a messenger to announce to the emperor the death of his aforesaid nephew, and asked that the abbey called Utenbura, which had been granted to him by the emperor’s authority, be given to him—not out of avarice, but with the intention that he might restore to the monks serving God there the freedom which he had earlier obtained from that same emperor for them, written and sealed, and which he had secured for them as a grant.

The emperor granted the abbey through the same messenger and sent back a great and manifold consolation and every good wish. When the messenger returned, he found the bishop at a place called Staphense and related all these matters to him.

A few days later, while the bishop was still staying in the same place, a messenger came seeking the support of prayers for the emperor’s soul and announced his death to him.

As the bishop was returning from there to Augusta, his nephews came to him: Count Riuvinus, the son of his brother Dietpald, and Count Hupaldus, the son of his brother Manegold. They asked him to go to the settlement called Witeselinga and show them how to arrange the church located there, where the bodies of their parents had been committed to the earth, and how large it ought to be made. He had often warned them beforehand to improve it and to enclose the bodies within it, so that they would no longer be drenched by rain falling through the roof.

Although the holy bishop knew with absolute certainty that the separation of his own body and soul was near, he nevertheless went there out of divine love and affection for them. With prudent planning he instructed them to enlarge that same church over the bodies mentioned above. He remained there with his nephews for several days, and from there proceeded to a castle called Sunnemotinga [or Sunnennotinga], at the request of Manegold, the brother of the aforementioned Adalbero.

While they were on the road, before they reached that place, they had made camp in a field because of the grass, near a village called Gerilehona. As the sun began to insert the rays of its light into the west—that is, as it began to set—a certain man came and said that Bishop Chunradus had certainly died. He named the day of his death and the day on which his body had been placed in the grave.

When they heard this report, the clerics and his other companions were struck with amazement. They immediately decided to send a messenger to Augusta, so that the customary prayers might be completed for the bishop’s soul.

The holy bishop, knowing the truth of the matter with complete certainty, addressed them in a gentle tone: “Do not yet send a messenger. At daybreak tomorrow you will learn what the situation concerning the bishop really is.”

The next day at dawn, a certain man came from Constance and truthfully contradicted the report of the bishop’s death; he announced that the bishop was still alive and in his usual condition.

The holy bishop Udalricus continued the journey he had begun. At the place to which he had been invited, as though to a banquet, after completing the saving offering which he strove daily to offer to God by himself, although he was greatly deprived of bodily strength, he sat daily at table with the diners. He offered no food to his body except that he put crumbs of bread soaked in water into his mouth; he very often expelled them from his mouth after the water had been drained away. At times he refreshed his body with draughts of water while he was still sitting at table.

When he had completed the matters for which he had been summoned there, he began to leave. On the following day he arrived at a place called Utiuntiga.

**[Note: [Col. 1047D] Also, Ottinga.]**

There he summoned to himself the monks from the monastery called Utenbura and, together with them and his faithful men, began prudently to consider how he might restore to them the freedom which, as I have said, he had earlier obtained for them from the emperor. He said to them:

“Choose one of yourselves as abbot, someone who will be useful in God’s service and can be found attentive to your needs. If you choose the man whom I favor for this purpose, I shall entrust the abbey to him until the presence of my lord the emperor. But if you choose someone other than the man who pleases me, I shall not entrust it to him.”

They replied: “Let your holiness name for us the man whom your lordship favors for the election through which we shall be united.”

Then he said to them: “I shall name your brother Rudungus for this office.”

**[Note: [Col. 1048D] Also, Ruodungus.]**

When they heard this, the brothers asked for time, until they could all discuss whether this election could be carried out with the consent of all the brothers.

When the brothers had gathered at the appointed place and began to confer among themselves about the aforesaid election, some of them approved it and some disapproved. Nevertheless, strengthened by the counsel of their friends, submitting to the bishop’s will, they came together and elected Rudungus as abbot. Returning with him to the bishop, they announced to him their unanimous election.

When he heard this, the bishop took up his staff and entrusted the abbey to the aforesaid Rudungus until the presence of the emperor, who had then succeeded his father and namesake in the imperial office. He commended Rudungus to his nephews and to his other faithful men, so that they might present him to the emperor’s majesty and, with their faithful assistance, obtain confirmation of these arrangements from him.

When all this had been completed, he returned to the proper seat of his bishopric.

## XXVI

After entering the walls of the city of Augusta, he was surrounded by great sorrow because of the death of his nephew Adalbero and the death of the emperor, to whom he had always preserved faith in every matter and whose love had been firmly joined to his heart.

For the repose of the souls of both men, he distributed many alms to the poor and daily poured out many prayers and supplications to the Lord, asking that he might deign to have mercy on them. He did not cease celebrating the offices of the Mass every day, until his bodily strength failed so completely that he could no longer stand by himself.

He sat at table and held a meal with those sitting there with him, while he himself withdrew as though fasting. Afterwards, in the church or in his chamber, he was refreshed by the sweet chanting of psalms or by listening to sacred readings.

When his bodily strength had failed him so far that he could no longer sing Mass by himself, he was brought into the church every day and did not cease listening to it with the greatest devotion and meanwhile persisting attentively in prayer.

Indeed, after Mass had been completed and he entered his chamber, he did not entrust himself to the rest of a bed before the hour of Vespers. Instead, he sat shod upon his own seat, sometimes reclining to the right upon a cushion, sometimes to the left, and sometimes, while seated, leaning backward against the rear part of the seat on which he sat.

After the completion of the office and of the entire Psalter, he listened to sacred readings from books as Gerhardus the provost read them **[perhaps of the cathedral church]**. At times he also enjoyed sweet conversation with him on the subject.

When a certain conversation between them had ended, the aforesaid cleric asked him: “Lord, do you have hope concerning this illness, or do you believe that your death is approaching?”

He answered him as though rebuking him: “Why did you say that? I do not hope it; rather, I know with absolute certainty that the day of my death will come to me within not many days.”

The presbyter was saddened by this and asked pardon. He said to him: “Lord, which of the bishops do you order us to summon for the commendation of your body?”

He replied: “At the time when my soul is about to leave this body, you will not be able to summon any of them here. My fellow-provincial, Bishop Chunradus, is held by such a serious illness that he cannot come here, while the Bavarian bishops have gathered in Francia for a royal council.”

The other said: “Lord, what must we do then?”

The holy bishop said: “Do you know how to commit a man’s body to the earth?”

He answered: “If such a person were present, over whom our commendation ought to be performed, we would have no fear concerning it.”

The bishop said: “When the time comes, do what you can as well as possible in this matter. The Lord will provide someone to commend my body.”

After saying this, the aforesaid presbyter again took up the reading and continued in it, as was his custom, until the hour of evening praise was announced by the sounding of the bell.

The readings were from the Lives of the Fathers of the Saints and from the book of Saint Gregory which they call the Dialogues. Its final book discusses at length those who, having been snatched from the body in spirit, saw many things and then returned again to the body.

Thus conducting himself, he awaited the day of his death with the greatest beauty of conduct. At times he saw very many things in the spirit, of which he related a few to those who were with him.

Meanwhile, when Abbot Werinharius of the monastery called Vulta [Fulda] came to him on a visit, he said to him among other things:

“After me you ought to become bishop here. Everyone chose you except two; but if those two had agreed with the others, your election would undoubtedly have been completed.”

After saying this, he clasped the hands of Attelinus, then vicedominus,

**[Note: [Col. 1049D] Vincentius of Borgo San Lorenzo observed that before the year 1000 vicedomini were generally drawn from the clergy, and that afterward this dignity passed to laymen. Onuphrius, in his *On Obscure Ecclesiastical Terms*, says that they were also called household stewards. But in Distinction 89, chapter *Volumus*, Gregory distinguishes the vicedominus from the household steward; there the gloss interprets him as the steward of the household or estate. [Col. 1050D]]**

and the hands of Hiltinus the chamberlain, commended him to their fidelity, and charitably allowed him to depart.

## XXVII

On another occasion, one day, as though awakened from a deep sleep, he said while those seated beside him listened:

“Alas, alas, that I ever saw my nephew Adalbero! Because I consented to him according to his desire, they do not wish to receive me unpunished into his company!”

After saying this, he immediately fell silent.

The strength of his body declined from day to day and failed to such an extent that he could not enter the church unless supported by two men.

When he was brought into the church on the feast day of Saints Mark and Marcellianus, which is the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July, so that he might hear Mass, after Mass had been completed he ordered a carpet to be laid down for him before the holy cross, and prostrated himself upon it.

After lying there for about half an hour, he rose and summoned to himself the presbyter Liutpaldus, the chamberlain. He ordered him to bring before him all the goods which he possessed in his office and to place them before the altar, except for one set of household and table furnishings and one marten-fur coverlet, which he left for the service of his successor.

When these things had been placed before him and he had looked at them, he said: “What need had I of all these things now?”

Although they appeared to him to be many, their number amounted to no more than a few shirts, seven or eight tablecloths, two towels, and ten silver solidi. These he immediately entrusted to the provost Gerhardus to distribute to the poor.

He arranged for all the rest to be divided among the clerics of that place.

From his garments he sent some to the venerable man Antonius,

**[Note: [Col. 1050D] Also, Hatto; Welserus supports this reading.]**

whom he had earlier enclosed at Utenbura in the name of God.

He also sent garments to a certain Ruozonus, who was incapable of moving his limbs except upward from the arms. His dwelling had been built in the cemetery of the monastery of Campido, raised above the ground like a little bed, so that whatever he discharged would fall to the ground and be kept separate from the dwelling.

When the bishop had previously stayed in that same monastery, he often visited this poor man in person and gladly listened to the sweetness of his speech, because that same poor man always remained behind a closed door, day and night, in the praises of God and in prayers.

O what tongue could recount a man of such kindness, who, at his end, did not fail to clothe Christ despite such a great distance intervening! Certainly, the one who wished his limbs to be clothed by him was always present with him.

After these things had been distributed as described, he ordered the vicedominus and his other faithful men and ministers whom he chose that, in every place belonging to his service, everything found there should be divided into three parts, and that one third should immediately, while he was still alive, be given through prudent distribution to the presbyters and the poor.

This was done.

Certainly, although his body was held by a grave illness, his understanding, spirit, and will could not be occupied except with—and only with—devout purposes.

## XXVIII

On the holy day of the nativity of Saint John the Baptist, at the first hour of the day, blessed Udalricus was suddenly awakened, as though from sleep, and said to his chamberlains:

“Put my clothes and shoes on me.”

They hesitated because of his great weakness, wondering whether he was giving them this command in a mental trance or in a loss of awareness. Nevertheless, they fulfilled his command and clothed him in his garments and shoes.

Immediately he ordered himself to be clothed in the vestments for Mass. When he had been vested, he walked through the principal church and reached the church of Saint John the Baptist, which he himself had earlier built and consecrated in his honor.

There he powerfully and carefully completed the Mass which he was accustomed to sing at dawn on the morning of its annual solemnity.

**[Note: [Col. 1050D] In ancient times three Masses were celebrated on the feast of Saint John the Baptist: one, namely, on the vigil, and the other two on the day itself. See Albinus and Amalarius, book III, chapter 38.]**

When it had ended, he immediately began the public Mass and, with God’s help, performed it with the greatest devotion.

When he had brought both Masses properly to their conclusion with their blessings, standing without assistance from others, he sat down and said to the clerics standing beside him:

“I did not undertake these mysteries which, by God’s gift, I have now completed from the capacity of my body, but by command. Today, when I was lying in bed as though sunk in sleep, two young men of exceedingly beautiful appearance stood before my bed. One of them said to me: ‘Why do you not rise? Today you must celebrate Mass at Saint John the Baptist.’

“The other replied to him: ‘How can this happen? Because of the incapacity of his body, he has not yet completed Prime.’

“But the one who had spoken to me first said: ‘Rise, and hasten, according to my words, to fulfill God’s mystery in the aforesaid church, because today no one other than you will sing Mass there.’”

After saying these things, he returned to his chamber.

He awaited the day of his death with a devout mind and joyful spirit, according to the words of the psalmist David: “As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God” (Psalm 41). Although he did not express it in words, he showed by his actions that he thought he would depart from this world on the vigil of the apostles Peter and Paul.

On that same day, before evening praise began, while all the bells were being set in motion by their keepers so that they might sound, he had himself bathed and clothed in the vestments which he had kept for his death, and lay down as though he were about to die.

When evening praise had ended, he raised himself from the ground with the assistance of others and said almost privately:

“O Saint Peter, you have not acted now as I expected!”

He remained somewhat troubled in mind because of this.

The aforesaid presbyter Gerhardus said to him:

“Lord, do not be saddened, but remember that the same thing happened to other holy bishops. To one of them it was said: ‘Around the feast of the apostles you will be led from this world to rest.’ When he expected to die on the feast of the apostles, his reprieve was prolonged until the eighth day, and then he died.

“To Bishop Cassius of Narni, through a certain presbyter who had been scourged by an angel, it was said: ‘Let neither your hand nor your foot cease. Do what you are doing; perform what you are performing. At the feast of the apostles you will come to me.’”

The bishop, believing that his death was approaching on the solemnity of the apostles, which was then near, strove to prepare himself in every way he could for the laying down of his body.

When the solemnity arrived, however, he remained healthy and unharmed. He remained so until the course of seven years had passed, and then, on that same day, as had been told him, after many good works had preceded it and the sacred ministry had been completed, he happily departed from this world.

When he heard this, the holy bishop remembered that it was true and replied to him:

“You have spoken well, brother.”

His mind was restored, and he remained in good spirits. He showed himself gentle and agreeable to those who stayed with him. No one heard him rebuke or reproach anyone, be angry with anyone, trouble anyone, or act hostilely toward anyone. No word of lamentation was heard from him; rather, he did every good thing he could at that time for those present and absent. He refused pardon to no one and marked everyone with the grace of his blessing.

The aforesaid Count Richwinus, his nephew, had still not returned from the royal conference. From time to time he said:

“O Richwinus, if only you would come while I am alive, so that I might see you!”

That year the solemnity of the apostles Peter and Paul fell on a Sunday. As I have said, he awaited it with the most exemplary conduct until the day of Thursday had passed.

During that night, before the dawn of Friday could be clearly perceived, he had himself laid down after being sprinkled with ashes in the form of a cross and sprinkled with holy water, and he remained lying there until dawn illuminated the whole breadth of the world.

Then Richwinus, returning from the palace, entered and recited the emperor’s message in the bishop’s hearing. When he saw him and heard the message, the bishop raised his eyes and, according to his ability, gave thanks to almighty God, who, according to the words of the prophet David, “will fulfill the desire of those who fear him,” and so forth (Psalm 144).

When Richwinus departed, at that very hour the bishop commended his soul to God while the clerics devoutly sang the litany. In the year of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 973, at the age of eighty-three, in the fiftieth year of his ordination, on the fourth day of July, the fourth day before the Nones of that month, a Friday, he was lulled as if by a sweet sleep in a happy death, released from the prison of the body, and departed to rest.

When the holy body was stripped for washing according to custom, the fragrance of a sweet odor filled the nostrils of everyone present there. It remained until the body had been washed, clothed in the appointed garments, placed on a bier, and carried into the church.

When the clergy heard that the Bavarian bishops were returning to their province from the aforesaid conference, they sent a messenger and wished to summon Archbishop Frederic for the commendation of the sacred body. When the messenger came to him, he found him held by such a serious fever that he could not come in any way.

The messenger returned from there in sorrow and then heard that the venerable Bishop Wolfgangus wished to come to a place called Nordilingga. He hastened to meet him.

When he reached him, Wolfgangus greeted him and heard that he wished to travel to the city of Augusta to visit Udalricus, the holy servant of God, who was held by illness.

The messenger replied:

“The Lord commanded your holiness to visit him, and I have come for this purpose: to tell you that he has died and to ask you on behalf of the entire congregation serving God there to come quickly and commend the holy body to God.”

When he heard this, the holy bishop was overwhelmed by great sorrow. He rose at dawn that same night and began to travel to Augusta.

On the road, however, when he realized that he would not be able to arrive there at the appropriate time, he sent the same messenger ahead to announce his arrival.

Meanwhile, the congregation guarded the body carefully and devoutly in the church of Saint Mary, day and night, with prayers and celebrations of Mass, until Sunday.

On Sunday, after the first Mass had been celebrated for his soul, the clergy assembled, the congregation of holy women arrived, and a great multitude of people came from the provinces. The presbyters lifted the body and began to carry it to Saint Afra, where his grave had earlier been prepared.

When they reached the hill called Pereleich [or Perelich], the aforesaid messenger arrived and announced the arrival of Bishop Wolfgangus.

They brought the body into the church of Saint Afra and again celebrated a sacrificial Mass with complete devotion for the repose of his soul.

The bishop had still not arrived, and the hour of the day was advancing. The time for celebrating the public service of God was approaching, and the congregation of clerics was completing it with complete devotion. Then the aforesaid bishop arrived. After he had been honorably received and had completed his prayer, he greeted the brothers and said:

“What seems best to you? Shall we commend the sacred body today, or postpone it until another day?”

The brothers replied:

“If it pleases your holiness, it seems good to us that all who are now present here should be informed, so that they may assemble here tomorrow at a suitable hour for the commendation of the sacred body, and that the gift of the saving sacrifice may be offered to God by you, while we sacrifice, for the repose of his soul. The suitable hour has already passed, and you are surrounded by great weariness.”

When he heard this, the bishop most willingly agreed with their counsel and awaited the following day.

That night Hiltegart, the wife of the aforesaid Count Richwinus, although married, was nevertheless sufficiently religious. She came and brought a shirt soaked in wax. She asked the highest-ranking clerics to wrap it carefully and secretly around the sacred body, so that the priestly vestments in which he was clothed would not quickly be consumed by the earth.

For while he was still alive, he had ordered that they not place a wooden board beneath his body, but lay it upon the bare earth and cover it with a wooden lid.

According to her request, they wrapped the shirt around the sacred body.

When morning came, a great multitude of people arrived. The clerics and holy women serving God there assembled, together with many others from the provinces who joined them in the sacred offices.

The bishop, while all were offering sacrifices for his soul, offered the saving host to God with great contrition of heart and humility. After also completing the public Mass, he exhorted everyone together in sober and careful speech to pray devotedly for that holy soul with the deepest intention of heart, so that, freed by God’s gift from every bond of sins, it might deserve to enjoy everlasting joy forever with the saints and elect of God.

After everyone had completed the prayer according to his word, the bishop buried the body and commended the soul to almighty God with the greatest devotion and tears.

The ministers, as was stated above, covered the body with a wooden lid. Above this they placed a thick wooden plankwork, built into the steps of the tomb, and at the surface of the earth they firmly closed it with stones joined together.

When these things had been completed, the bishop went to Augusta for the sake of prayer.

After completing many prayers, he was asked by the brothers out of affection to accept the vestments for Mass which had belonged to Saint Udalricus and with which he had abounded during his lifetime. Because of the saint’s holiness, he accepted them.

After being honorably dismissed, as he was fully worthy to be, he returned to his own home with God as his companion.

XXVIII. After the death of Saint Udalric, bishop, Heinricus, son of Count Purchard, became his successor—not entering the sheepfold lawfully, but climbing in by another way. For Duke Purchard of the Alamanni, who had married the daughter of Heinricus’s maternal aunt, together with many others, including certain soldiers who cunningly desired to have their benefices increased by him, began to consider by subtle counsel how he might usurp the aforesaid office for himself. Although it came to his knowledge that Abbot Werinharius, in an invisible assembly inaccessible to bodily eyes, where Saint Udalric, joined in an ecstasy of mind, had heard, “If two should agree with the others, he would have been appointed from that whole assembly to this ministry, so that he might become his successor, just as I foretold earlier.”

Certain clerics, accompanied by the advocate and several soldiers from the same bishopric, began traveling to the emperor’s court, carrying the episcopal staff. When they came to the city of Worms, to the monastery of Saint Cyriacus, they found Duke Purchard there with his wife, both afflicted by illness. When they explained the purpose of their journey, they were deceived by him through various contrivances and cunning reasoning. He told them that the emperor was staying in those days near the remotest borders of his kingdom, and that along the road they would have to travel everything was exceedingly expensive, and forage everywhere was kept under restriction, so that they could not obtain provisions for themselves or their horses.

“Our emperor wishes within a few days to hold a royal assembly at a place called Erinstein. You can easily go there; therefore return now, and when my trustworthy messenger comes to announce to you the day of the aforesaid assembly, do not hesitate to come there. You will find me there, a firm helper to you, and in the episcopal election know that I shall agree with you without hesitation.”

Hearing these words, and believing them to be true, they accepted his advice and turned back. Not long afterward, however, the duke’s messenger came and announced that the royal assembly would be held at the aforesaid place, urging them to come there. They immediately took other brothers with them and hastened toward the place. When they had approached a location called Balneos, a messenger who met them said: “Heinricus, son of Purchard, whom the emperor with his faithful men, and Duke Purchard, have decided should be bishop of Augsburg, will now quickly meet you.”

When the brothers heard this, they were saddened because they were to be deprived of the aforesaid episcopal election. They went no farther, but turned back and waited at a suitable place until they could accompany the aforesaid Heinricus from there. On that very day, when the soldiers who had come with Heinricus from Duke Purchard arrived at the camp, they began asking the clerics who had joined them to approve Heinricus as their common bishop in that place.

The clerics requested a delay until all the brothers at home could gather together in a common chapter. When the soldiers rejected this and they argued at length among themselves, they returned to Heinricus and, together with certain clerics, elected him as their bishop. Others, however, refusing to elect him, reached Augsburg and joined the remaining brothers.

When they arrived at Augsburg, divided in this way over his election, a certain count named Wolveradus came with several other men, as though carrying a legation from the emperor to the assembly, saying: “The emperor has asked you for grace, mercy, and every good thing, and has requested that you also, out of love for him, not refuse unanimously to elect as your bishop this lord Heinricus, whom he and his faithful men have decided should be pastor in this place.”

This embassy, however, had been contrived through a fraudulent plan. They answered him: “Let him come with you into our chapter to hear our reply.” When they had scarcely obtained permission to enter the chapter, the canonical readings concerning the election of bishops were read. When the aforesaid Heinricus heard from the readings recited in their presence that it lay within the power of the canons either to elect or reject him, he humbly asked their pardon and requested that they not disdain to elect him bishop. He promised them that, if they consented to his petition, he would thereafter provide benefits of every kind.

Some believed his promises; some acted willingly; others sought to avoid disagreements. Nevertheless, all together decided that he should be bishop. When this election had become known in the church to the soldiers and household, it was confirmed by everyone with the ringing of bells.

Then at last the aforesaid Heinricus, taking certain canons with him, went to the emperor and, strengthened by the testimony of others in his presence, announced his election. He humbly asked that the episcopal office named above be granted to him by the height of the emperor’s authority. The emperor did not oppose his request, but neither did he fulfill it immediately; instead, he promised that after five days, on the feast of Saint Maurice, he would grant his petition, as he indeed did.

Afterward, at the appointed time, Heinricus came to Mainz and received episcopal blessing from Archbishop Rudpertus and his suffragans.

At this time Otto, son of Luitolf, son of Emperor Otto, was duke of the Alamanni, while Heinricus, son of the brother of that same emperor, was duke of Bavaria. Although their close kinship ought to have united them in affection, through the plotting of Satan, the author of evil counsel, they began to exercise envy and discord against one another.

Accordingly, Bishop Heinricus remained more favorably disposed in every respect toward his namesake, the duke, and agreed more readily with his counsels than with those of Duke Otto, although the city of Augsburg remained situated within Otto’s duchy. For this reason Duke Otto began to be angry with him and to consult with his followers about opposing him wherever he could; and this he did.

Moreover, the bishop wished to take away the benefices of certain soldiers, the nephews of Saint Udalric—Manegold and Hulpald—because of the counsels of certain people, though they themselves were not at fault. While Saint Bishop Udalric was still alive, they had often come at his summons with a great company of soldiers to assist the emperor, and had remained in his service, diligently fulfilling his wishes in every respect, until they were dismissed and returned, honored with gifts by his favor.

The queen also declared that she was their kinswoman. Therefore they opposed the bishop concerning the benefices they had received and, against his will, retained them under their own control. Thus the bishop, wearied by these and many other adversities, became sorrowful.

Once, when Emperor Otto wished to invade the people of the Slavs with an army, Otto—who at that time was duke of the Alamanni and Bavarians, after Heinricus had been deposed—was prepared to come to his assistance with the Alamanni and Norici. Bishop Heinricus promised that he too would go with him. He waited with his soldiers until the army had departed and then, as they had previously plotted, occupied with his soldiers whatever cities he could and entered Nuwingburg.

Heinricus, who had previously been duke, entered the city of Pazova, intending that, once Otto had departed with the army, he might bring the province under his control with the assistance of his nephew, the bishop. When this plan became known to Duke Otto, he returned with the army of both provinces and besieged him in the aforesaid city of Pazova.

Emperor Otto, having been delivered from the Slavs by God’s mercy, afterward came to the same city to join the siege. When the siege had ended and the conflict had been calmed, the emperor returned to Saxony. Later, at the appointed time, Heinricus, son of Heinricus, and his namesake, son of Perhtolf, were summoned to the emperor’s assembly. Bishop Heinricus also came to the emperor with them, to defend himself concerning the aforesaid offense, hoping that, restored to the emperor’s favor, he might be permitted to return to his own place.

When the assembly had been completed, Heinricus and his namesake were sent into exile. Bishop Heinricus, however, was entrusted for custody to the abbot at Werden, where Saint Liudger rests. When he had been guarded there with great care from Easter until after the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, an imperial assembly took place in a town called Trulmanna.

Two priests from Augsburg, Gerhardus and Anamotus, came there and, through the intervention of Duke Otto and the bishops who were present, pleaded not only on their own behalf but also on behalf of all the clerics and laymen living in that bishopric, asking that they not long remain deprived of their bishop.

The emperor, satisfying the petition of Duke Otto and of his other faithful men, as well as of the aforesaid clerics, ordered that the bishop be brought back from exile. In his presence, after repeating his oath of loyalty, Heinricus was permitted to return to his bishopric with the emperor’s favor.

Restored to his position, the bishop began to consider in his mind for what offenses such varied adversities had so frequently befallen him: how the duke had injured him in many ways, more than his predecessors had been injured; how the leading soldiers presumed to retain their benefices against his will; and how the most distinguished ministers of his father’s household had suddenly perished in various ways.

He secretly asked the familiar clerics whether Saint Udalric had spoken concerning Abbot Werenharius, saying that he ought to become his successor, just as had previously been told him. When he discovered that this was truly so, although previously he had refused to believe it, he was exceedingly terrified, but did not reveal this publicly. He was all the more afraid because at that time great and wondrous signs were frequently occurring, by God’s permission, at the tomb of Saint Udalric, bishop.

At last, changed in many ways for the better, he attempted to reconcile himself with God. He ordered that the cathedral church be covered with a new roof, and built a bridge over the river Lech at Saint Afra. He also ordered that no member of his household receive toll or any other payment from the bridge, but that anyone who wished might cross it freely, without contradiction or obstruction, as an act of almsgiving.

Afterward he visited Rome and the thresholds of the holy apostles Peter and Paul for the remission of his sins. Before he began his journey there, he transferred to Saint Mary, upon her altar in the city of Augsburg, the property which his father Purchard was known to possess at Geisinhausa and which, under witnesses, he had assigned to his faithful man Eticho, on the condition that Eticho should firmly transfer it to wherever his son Heinricus, the bishop, should ask him.

Then, at the bishop’s definite request, Ethich lawfully conveyed the aforesaid property with the bishop’s hand, according to the law of the Norici, to Saint Mary, upon her altar situated in the city of Augsburg and upon the gilded reliquary adorned with inlaid stones. The property included the church and all its buildings, fields, meadows, pastures, mills, waters and watercourses, roads and trackless places, settlements, forests, cut and uncut timber, things acquired and still to be acquired, the household, and everything legally belonging to that same property—except that he withheld twenty hides from the transfer.

He assigned these to the service of Saint Magnus at Fauces. He also agreed with the canons that they should have the power, if they wished, to exchange those twenty hides for ten hides situated in a good place in this province, into the hand of Werinharius the advocate and the hand of Gerhardus the provost, for the remedy of his soul, and of the souls of his father and mother, his maternal aunt, and his other kinsmen and relatives.

The agreement was that the property should remain perpetually in the right and power of the canons as an offering, while their daily allowance should remain secure in every respect. They were also to celebrate, for the repose of his soul, a full vigil every year on the evening before his anniversary, and on the anniversary itself to complete another vigil. After the Mass of the altar had been celebrated, they were all together to offer the oblation of the host to God. In addition, they were to provide sufficient food and drink for one hundred poor people, and clothe twelve of them: in one year with woolen garments, and in the next year with woolen clothing, together with leggings and shoes.

But if any successor of his as bishop—[another reading: “my successor,” and so afterward]—should attempt to violate this agreement, and should try in any way to take the aforesaid property from the canons and turn it to his own advantage, and, once the matter had been brought to his attention, should not immediately restore it, his legitimate heirs should have the free power to place three denarii upon the altar, redeem the same property from there, and possess it as their own right through all future generations.

Done at Augsburg, in the church of Saint Mary, Mother of God, before the altar, Bishop Heinricus carrying out the transaction, in the presence of the canons, before a great gathering of the people, and before the witnesses listed below.

The sign of Etih, who made this transfer. The sign of Adalbero. The sign of Jagob. The sign of Marahnurat. The sign of Willehalm. The sign of Hunurid. The sign of Engilmar. The sign of Wezzi. The sign of Pilgirim. The sign of Gundachar. The sign of Cadolt. These men are from the province of the Norici.

[Note: Another copy has these names: Etich, Adalbero, Jacob, Marahunart, Wilichalm, Hunfrid, Engilmar, Wezzi, Pilegrim, Gundechar, Cadolt, Weinhere; Gerhardi, Hittebold, Gotebold, Reginhar, Suidger, Arebo, Vrolf. The day and year are not written. Moreover, these designations are reversed: these belong to the province of the Alamanni, while those belong to the Norici.]

These, however, are from the province of the Alamanni. The sign of Werenhere the advocate, who received this transfer with the hand of Gerhardus the provost. The sign of Histipold. The sign of Gotebold. The sign of Reginhar. The sign of Suidger. The sign of Aribo. The sign of Vrolf.

In the year of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 980, in the eighth indiction, on the fourth day before the Nones of October, and on Thursday the twentieth [Note: “and twentieth” appears to be deleted]. I therefore, Gerhardus, an unworthy priest, recorded the day and year.

When these matters had been completed, as I have related, he went to Rome, fulfilled his vows, and returned safely to his own place. Yet great anguish of mind still troubled him inwardly, because, although he and Duke Otto had been reconciled outwardly, he was compelled to render the duke more service from the possessions of Saint Mary than his predecessors had rendered; and because certain soldiers possessed, against his will, ecclesiastical benefices that legally belonged to his authority.

Since he was born of noble parents and possessed great knowledge of grammar and other books, and since he excelled greatly in gracious conversation and well-sounding speech, he was diligent in the sacred solemnities, in the service of God, and in preaching. He used the service of his household at his table, and offered abundant food and drink to those who lived with him, with a cheerful face and a peaceful mind.

Toward his household, however, he was harsher than was just, taking away their rights and creating a new census in certain places. At last he understood that he could not overcome the adversities mentioned above except with God’s help and through the working of the imperial majesty’s favor. With all his strength he therefore strove to bind himself to the emperor’s service, so that, by obtaining his favor, all the opposition threatening him everywhere from others might be alleviated through the emperor’s presence and commands.

For this reason he visited the emperor frequently with imperial gifts and attempted to please his own *drudes* [other readings: “friends”; “counselors”] with suitable presents. He also undertook hostile expeditions with him, conducting himself in the manner he judged would please him best.

In the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 983, the emperor entered the province of Calabria with an army. Bishop Heinricus also arrived there with him. When a battle was fought there against the Saracens, with many men killed on both sides—alas for the grief!—whether captured or killed, he too remained there.

His loss is to be mourned beyond measure, because his place cannot be found and visited by his clerics, relatives, kinsmen, and friends. It is exceedingly dangerous to overstep God’s decree revealed through his saints and to despise prophecies, as Scripture says: “Do not extinguish the Spirit; do not despise prophecies” (1 Thess. 5).

Later, when Werrenharius was asked by the emperor whether he wished to accept the bishopric, as Saint Udalric had previously decreed, he replied that he no longer wished to accept that bishopric. After he had refused the bishopric, as I learned from his ministers, he began to fall ill a few hours later and ended his life at Lugga. His body was carried as far as Saint Domnus and honorably buried.

Duke Otto also died at Lugga. His men carried him over the mountains and brought him as far as Aschaffenburg, where he was committed to the earth with great honor and excessive mourning.

# Miracles of Saint Udalric

## I

After the precious treasure of the holy body of Udalric had been entrusted to the tomb, a carpet was placed over the sepulcher and a continual light was set beside it, burning without interruption.

One of the custodians carelessly placed a burning candle near the tomb. When he went away, the candle fell sideways upon the covering of the sepulcher and continued burning until the part of the candle lying upon the carpet was consumed by the fire. As it burned together with the front part of the carpet projecting beyond the tomb and sent its flame upward through the carpet, the custodian arrived.

Seeing this, he stood trembling in astonishment. In fear, he removed what remained of the candle and carefully examined the carpet to see whether anything had been damaged by the fire. He found traces of fire from tiny particles of candle wax, but he could not find a single hair burned on the surface or side of the tomb-covering.

When he announced this miracle to his master and brothers, showed them the trace of the candle, and nevertheless displayed the carpet unharmed, they were filled with wonder and joy, and all glorified God and Saint Udalric.

## II

Although no miracle was yet clearly known to have occurred there, a multitude of members of the household of both sexes continually lay prostrate on the pavement beside the place where the holy body had been laid, praying for assistance in their necessities. Discovering that many kinds of help and benefit came to them from there, they began to visit the place more frequently.

Thus, as the Lord permitted that place to be commended by the constant visits of many people, a man from the province of the Norici named Reginwalech came there. He had been afflicted by fever for a full year and had been reduced to extreme weakness. He went to Wicfredus, the provost of that place, and asked whether he could indicate some remedy for his recovery.

Wicfredus answered: “Go and obtain a staff for yourself, and carry it to the tomb of my lord Saint Udalric for your recovery.”

The man went away, cut himself a staff from the wood of the *bidulla* tree, and carried it to the aforesaid provost. The provost went with him to the holy tomb and showed him that he should place the staff upon it.
