Trusting in the prayers of the clerics and strengthened in faith by their instruction, he was freed from the fever at that very hour and clearly restored to health.

At that same time an incredible multitude of people in these regions was being afflicted by fevers. When they heard that the aforesaid man had been freed at the holy tomb, as I have related, some hurried there with staffs, while others added further offerings, seeking health by visiting the holy tomb. All of them, from wherever they came, were quickly restored to health.

## III

A member of Saint Mary’s household named Hisenhart [another reading: Isenhart] took one of the staffs that sick people carried to the tomb. Carrying it in his hand, he began to walk away with it. When he reached a hill called Perileich, he began to be violently afflicted by fever.

Then, realizing for what offense the illness had been granted to him, he returned to the tomb, restored the staff to the place from which he had taken it, and made a vow that he would never again presume to remove anything from there. After fulfilling his vow, he was released from the fever.

## IV

A priest from the congregation of Saint Afra named Adelger took two attractive little staffs from the tomb, pleasing to look at and suitable for carrying in the hands. Forgetting himself, he carried them to his house. After he had sat down there, he was seized by frequent yawning and an extreme bristling of the skin, and all his limbs were overcome by distress, so that he could not properly sit, walk, or even lie down.

He began to consider within himself why he was being afflicted by such a sudden weakening of his limbs. He rose, went to Wicfredus the provost, and reported what had happened.

Wicfredus said to him: “Did you take those little staffs from the holy tomb?”

He replied: “I did.”

“Hurry,” said Wicfredus, “and put them back in their place.”

When this had been done, every bodily affliction fled, and the priest was immediately restored to his former health.

## V

Whenever any of the multitude of common people took in their hands staffs that had been brought there, intending to lean upon them during the sacred mysteries and to await the end of the service more easily, they were suddenly shaken by an attack of fever. Once the cause of what had happened was discovered, they were freed at that very hour when the staffs had been cast aside.

## VI

When these events had been reported and brought to everyone’s knowledge everywhere, no one dared remove even the smallest staff without permission. As a result, such a multitude of staffs accumulated that they could not easily be counted or placed without obstruction in the corners of the church.

It therefore happened that they were placed upon the beams of the same church, where the tomb was situated. The custodians, at the command of their master, frequently carry them to the fire and, when they are burning, melt them into wax for making additional candles for the service of God.

Nevertheless, many always remain upon the beams, and those who see them do not think that their number has been reduced in any way. Numerous crutches belonging to people who, by God’s grace and through the merits of Saint Udalric, were healed there of various illnesses hang there. Many other likenesses, fashioned according to the different limbs of the sick, can also be seen there.

The vehicles of those who had come there lying upon carts, crippled by various bodily weaknesses, and who were granted perfect health in all their limbs, can also be seen before the church doors. They left their carts and huts there and returned joyfully on foot.

## VII

The daughter of a certain woman in the village of Geltenstein had become completely disabled in one arm. One night the woman was told in a dream: “Why do you not bring your daughter with a lamp to the tomb of Saint Udalric for her recovery?”

When she awoke, she reported the dream to her daughter and, as quickly as she could, led her there with a candle. The daughter was restored to perfect health, and the mother brought her back joyfully to their own dwelling.

## VIII

From the same district, from a small town called Toningewe, a man was brought by his brothers to the tomb of Saint Udalric. His ears were closed, so that he could hear nothing, and his tongue was bound, so that he could never utter a word.

There he lay prostrate for a long time, shedding tears. His brothers lifted him and carried him around the altars. When he began to walk and reached the altar of Saint Donatus, situated on the western side of the church, he heard the sound of the clerics singing in the choir. Still with a weak voice, he said to his brothers: “Behold, I hear and I can speak.”

When, after the service of God had been completed, they announced these things to the clerics, and the clerics recognized that they were truly so, they ordered the bells to be rung and began together to praise God. When the praise had ended, the sick man, endowed with perfect speech and complete hearing, was able to depart.

## IX

A certain man from Bishop Heinricus’s household, named Luitnotus, lost his lord’s favor through his own fault because he had carelessly scattered grain entrusted to him in various places belonging to the bishop.

When the bishop’s ministers had greatly frightened him and he had fallen into extreme fear, he went barefoot to the tomb of Saint Udalric for deliverance from the impending distress. There he long sought his assistance with tears.

When he returned from there, after a few days had passed, he regained his lord’s favor more easily than he could have believed. Thereafter, firmly trusting everywhere in the saint’s help, he frequently drank during his recreation out of love for him and was accustomed to ask others to drink as well.

## X

One day the same Luitnotus came to the house of Razo [another reading: Raso], who was then a powerful minister of the bishop, in the town called Pobingga, and ate lunch there with him.

When he wished to leave after being satisfied, the aforesaid Razo compelled him to drink more. Luitnotus did not dare refuse his request, but accepted the vessel offered to him, saying: “I wish to drink this beer out of love for Saint Udalric, through whose help I was freed from the greatest distress.”

When he had drained the cup and turned the vessel downward in his hand, he said: “Having been marked with this act of charity, I am certain that no evil of adversity can harm me today, nor can a sword wound my body.”

Razo said to him: “Give me your finger, so that I may see whether my little knife can wound your limb.”

Luitnotus immediately offered him his finger in great faith. Razo seized it and, with his other hand, tried to draw a knife from its sheath in order to wound the aforesaid baker’s finger. Instead, he inflicted a great wound upon his own hand with the same knife. He quickly let go both of the finger he had grasped and of the knife, and began lamenting his wounded hand. The baker, strengthened in faith, departed unharmed.

## XI

Another member of the household, named Adelhardus [another reading: Adalhardus], wished to travel from the city of Augsburg to his dwelling, situated in a town called Eitingen. Before the city gate, a certain man invited him to drink with others.

When they had begun drinking, one of those who lived there asked them to accept a drink out of love for Saint Udalric. The aforesaid Adelhardus uttered a filthy word from his mouth and refused to accept the drink offered as an act of charity.

When he had gone a little way from there, his horse fell on the level road, and his leg was broken. He was laboriously carried to his house and remained disabled for a long time.

Afterward he made a vow to the tomb of Saint Udalric and, by God’s gift, was restored to health. Thereafter he frequently asked others to drink the charity he had previously despised.

## XII

One day in the aforesaid village of Eitingen, when many members of the household had gathered together to drink, one of them named Walterich, a disciple of Wicfredus, the provost of Saint Afra, heard someone asking for the charity of Saint Bishop Udalric.

With profane lips, as though raving, he spoke most foolishly: “What benefit is the charity of that bishop to me, since he cannot perform signs any more than a dog?”

When he had uttered these words, he was handed over to the devil and lost human speech. Like a dog, he began to make sounds in fury; after a short time, whining and barking, alas, he miserably ended his life.

## XIII

In the city of Augsburg there was a smith named Herevuns who had long been held by a severe illness affecting his entire body. He could not walk except with the help of others and sometimes had to be supported by two crutches. With his head bent almost to the ground, he could scarcely reach the places necessary for bodily needs.

When he heard that many sick people were often healed at the holy tomb, he began to crawl there beyond his strength. At daybreak he would leave his dwelling and scarcely reach the tomb before the third hour.

After he had done this frequently, one time during Lent, on a Friday, he came to the gate above which the chapel of Saint Michael is situated. Excessively tired and deprived of all strength, he stopped and said:

“Lord God, almighty Father, deign to recognize with what great infirmity I have now approached this place; and through the merits of your confessor Saint Udalric, have mercy on me.”

After resting a little, he crawled as far as the tomb. When he had completed his prayer there and wished to rise with the help of his companion and the crutches he had taken, one crutch slipped on the pavement, and he was again thrown to the ground.

As he fell, his knees, pulled backward by the contraction of the sinews, made a sound like broken hammers, and his legs stretched out across the pavement. When his companion wished to lift him as usual, he said: “Wait a little. It seems to me that I can rise and walk by myself.”

Having said this, he left the crutches on the pavement, rose, and walked. Immediately, taking up a cross, he walked powerfully without a staff to Saint Mary in the city of Augsburg, accompanied by clerics and the other citizens. There, after they had together completed praises of God, he returned at that very hour to Saint Afra carrying the cross.

## XIV

A poor native from the town called Messlinga [another reading: Messinga], named Hiltibaldus, was struck blind and remained in that blindness for two years.

In the third year, certain men from the same district decided to go to the city of Augsburg for the sake of prayer. On the road they found him seeking food through the towns with his guide, and they said to him: “Come with us to the city of Augsburg and to the tomb of Saint Udalric; perhaps there you will be able to obtain mercy.”

He answered them: “I have neither provisions for myself and my guide nor offerings to carry to those holy places.”

They replied: “If you go with us, we shall help you as much as we can.”

Agreeing to their persuasion, he went with them to Augsburg. That same night he waited outside the church beside the holy tomb for the coming of day.

When morning came, he was led inside the church to the tomb and prayed devoutly. By God’s grace, he received again the light of his eyes, which he had previously lost. Then, taking up a cross and accompanied by a great multitude of people, he reached Saint Mary and recounted to his fellow citizens how he had been given sight.

## XV

[Note: This miracle is also related in one copy near the end of chapter 23 of the Life of Saint Udalric. Moreover, Saint Udalric attended at least two synods at Ingelheim; the later one, held in the year 972, is mentioned in chapter 23 of the Life. Frodoardus mentions the earlier one under the year 948, on the seventh day before the Ides of June.]

Once, when the holy bishop was traveling to the synod of Emperor Otto convened at Ingelheim, a poor man from the town of Affelterbach, named Rudpret [another reading: Rutpertus], joined him beside the road. He was carrying his intestines, which had fallen from his abdomen at the place of the navel, in his lap.

When he showed them to the bishop with his lap opened, the bishop ordered a denarius to be given to him and said: “Go in the peace of God.”

Not long afterward he began to improve day by day and, his abdomen healed, was freed from the aforesaid illness.

Later the same man became lame, so that he could not walk unless supported by crutches. He was also entirely deprived of the use of his right hand in its joints. After he had remained afflicted by this illness for four years, he desired to come to the tomb of Saint Udalric and obtained wax to carry with him to the tomb.

Once the wax had been obtained, the power to walk with the support of staffs was granted to him, and he abandoned the crutches. When he arrived there in this manner, his hands and knees were restored to health and resumed their functions, so that the same man returned upright, walking without support and leaping for joy.

## XVI

From the kingdom of Lothair there was also a certain Lutericus [another reading: Luitharius], who had long been deprived of the light of his eyes. He came to the holy tomb and, after completing his prayers, received clear sight.

## XVII

A certain cleric, who often stayed among the students in the city of Augsburg for the sake of study, became mute when he returned to his relatives.

When they had led him to the holy tomb, he released two denarii from his mouth upon the tomb and received back the speech he had lost.

## XVIII

A certain blind man attempted to travel to the holy place in winter with a very small guide. When they were crossing the river Smuttura and came to a long stream, gathered from small springs and running across the road, his guide could not offer him assistance. His strength failing from cold and weariness, the guide fell.

When his guide had fallen, the blind man, with great care and sadness, walked along the course of the stream, feeling his way everywhere with his staff. In a loud voice he called upon Saint Mary, Saint Afra, and Saint Udalric, the holy servant of God, earnestly asking that help and mercy be granted to him.

As he felt his way and cried out, and had nearly reached the end of the stream, by God’s merciful gift his eyes suddenly opened and he saw the light. He turned back, lifted his guide, and carried him as far as the holy tomb, praising almighty God and his saints. There he openly recounted to the clerics and all those present everything that had happened to him on the road.

## XIX

There was a certain matron in the land of the Franks, exceedingly wealthy and noble, who was violently afflicted after being seized by the devil. Five bishops, together with many others, assembled for her deliverance. When they constrained the devil with prayers and adjurations to release the possessed body, he cried out and wailed:

“Unless something belonging to Bishop Udalric comes here, I will not release the vessel I possess, despite your command.”

When he repeated the same answers again and again, they began to consider sending messengers to Augsburg to obtain something belonging to Bishop Udalric. While they were deliberating among themselves, however, the devil cried out through the matron’s mouth:

“Woe is me! Woe is me! Nearby there is a priest who has a shoulder-cloth that belonged to the aforesaid bishop!”

Although unwillingly, but at God’s command, he named the priest and the place where he lived. When the priest was summoned and came with the shoulder-cloth, before he entered the house the demon said:

“Woe! Woe! Now the bishop’s shoulder-cloth has come.”

After saying this, he departed from the matron’s body, crying out and lamenting, leaving it utterly exhausted.

When the priest was asked where the shoulder-cloth had come from, he replied:

“Once, when the bishop was going to a royal assembly, he came to our church and asked us to sing Mass for him. When he saw that we were putting on our albs without shoulder-cloths, he said: ‘Where is your shoulder-cloth?’ I answered him: ‘I do not have a shoulder-cloth.’ Then he ordered this shoulder-cloth to be given to me.”

The matron, freed from the demon and restored to her senses and health, sent all the clothing she had been wearing that day, together with her stockings and shoes, by messengers to the tomb of Saint Udalric. She also instructed them to report there how, by the Lord’s grant, she had been delivered through his merits. Wicfredus, provost of that place and also at that time guardian of the church, had a dalmatic made from the matron’s cloak; he arranged her other garments, as was suitable, for the service of God, so that this sign of God’s mercy might remain more frequently in the memory of later generations.

## XX

In the land of the Slavs, the son of Duke Wolezlavus [another reading: Woleslaus] fell ill and was brought into such grave sickness that his father and mother, together with the other friends present, despaired that he could continue to live. While the father was in this distress, he was reminded by the boy’s mother and by others who knew how many people had been freed from various troubles through the merits of Saint Udalric. He immediately made a vow that, if his son returned to life, he would send messengers with offerings to visit the tomb of Saint Udalric.

On that very day the duke’s son returned to life and brought no small consolation to his father. Recognizing God’s mercy toward his son, the father immediately hastened to send messengers and fulfill his vow. They came to the tomb and offered five pounds of silver, very many gold pieces, and as much wax as one strong pack animal could carry. The boy’s mother separately sent a considerable quantity of gold coins for her son.

The messengers also devoutly visited the altar of Saint Mary with gold and other offerings, as they had been instructed, and likewise the altar of Saint Afra. They explained why they had been sent, saying that before they themselves left their province, they had left their lord’s son walking and in good health.

## XXI

At another time a certain duke of the Vandals [Note: Poles are meant], named Misicho, was wounded in the arm by a poisoned arrow. When he realized that he had been struck by a harmful poison and thought that death threatened him at that very hour, he made a vow with great faith and steadfastness that, as soon as he could, he would not delay sending a silver arm with a hand to Saint Udalric.

Immediately after making the vow he was relieved of the danger and returned to his home. He ordered an arm to be fashioned according to his vow. When the smiths began to make the arm and formed a hand upon it, the duke immediately rose, freed from the danger that threatened him, praising God, who through the merits of his holy bishop had delivered him from the peril of death. He fulfilled his vow by sending the arm with the hand to the holy man’s tomb.

## XXII

A certain woman from Curia in Rhaetia, having left her own husband, was joined in marriage to a man from the district of Albegewe named Durinc. After she had lived with him for some time, she was possessed by a demon and grievously tormented by it.

She sought help for her deliverance at many holy places but found none. She received the advice to go to the tomb of the holy bishop Udalric, and she did so. When she was approaching the city of Augsburg and could clearly see the church of Saint Afra, she fell to the ground, crying out and raging, and became as if dead.

The aforesaid Durinc, with those accompanying him, tried to lift her. Once she had been raised, her senses returned, and she was freed from the demon.

## XXIII

A certain almswoman of Abraham, bishop of the city of Freising, from a village called Camera, had her jaw inserted into her chest and had been entirely deprived of speech. Her hands were also bent back against her arms and fused together, so that the shapes of her fingers could scarcely be recognized.

When she came to the holy tomb and, returning from there, walked across the bridge of the river Lech, a certain man met her and asked where she was going. She could not answer him, but turned and inclined herself toward the church of Saint Afra to show him where she was going. When she turned toward it, her jaw came loose from her chest, and speech was granted to her so that she could answer.

## XXIV

A certain blind man, when he reached the river called the Vindex with his guide, asked him whether he could still see the city and the monastery. When he heard that the holy place was nearby, he had his stockings and shoes removed so that he might reach it barefoot. His guide, however, seized his shoes and other belongings and secretly withdrew, while the blind man assumed that he had entered the nearby town for some necessary reason and would soon return to help him.

After waiting for a long time, he began calling out his guide’s name and asking him to come. Meanwhile, he searched for his bags and shoes but did not find them. Then he realized that his guide had stripped him of his possessions. Weeping and praying, he began to cry out to Saint Mary, the Mother of the Lord, to Saint Afra, and to Saint Udalric, asking that some consolation and relief might come to him.

While he was laboring under this prolonged affliction and tribulation, he suddenly perceived an unfamiliar light with his eyes. At once a little cross made of twigs pointed out the same place to him. Then, rejoicing, he visited the places he had intended to visit, giving thanks to almighty God and his saints for the restoration of his sight. The citizens of Hovarchusa later placed a larger cross as a sign at the very spot where they found the little cross that had been shown.

## XXV

At a certain time, when people were flocking from every direction to Augsburg on the eve of the Nativity of Saint Mary to celebrate the holy day there solemnly, a certain woman among them resolved to come there with her little child, so that she might have him weighed at the tomb of Saint Udalric with offerings for his safety.

When she wished to convey the child, placed in a wagon along with other belongings, across the bridge of the Vindex, the wagon tilted because of the unevenness of the bridge, and the child fell into the stream. The river had risen violently because of excessive flooding and threatened death to everyone crossing it.

When the mother, in the deepest grief, wished to throw herself into the stream after her child and could scarcely be restrained by those standing nearby, the people on both banks of the river hurried to help the infant. Since none of them could rescue him, he was submerged in the river and disappeared from everyone’s sight.

The mother was forcibly led away from the river and, as far as possible, comforted. Weeping and lamenting, she first sought the help of the most holy Mother of God, Mary. Then she went to the tomb of Saint Udalric with the offerings she had previously intended to bring there for her son’s safety, and devoutly gave them for the repose of the child’s soul.

On the following night, while sleep overcame the woman’s sorrowful body, a very venerable old man in episcopal clothing appeared to her and said:

“Are you not deeply grieved, woman, for your little child?”

She answered:

“Yes, lord.”

He said to her:

“Rise at dawn and go to the river. At the place where he was last seen in the water, search for him on the riverbank among the bushes.”

Awakened, and scarcely able to wait for the coming day, she went with those assisting her to the riverbank. According to the holy man’s word, she found her child safe and unharmed. Then she returned joyfully, praising God, and recounted what had happened in the city and everywhere.

## XXVI

At the same time, a certain man near the Danube, while all the people were spontaneously celebrating the feast of Saint Udalric with solemn observance, gathered hay with rakes into heaps, scorning the holy day.

When he came the next day with wagons to carry it to his hay-barn, he found it beautiful on the outside. But when he probed the inside with a wooden drinking vessel, he found that it had all been changed into ashes. The holy day, which he had previously refused to celebrate, he afterward did not dare to despise through fear.

## XXVII

At the same time, the servant-girl of a certain matron named Gerbirc [another reading: Gerbirch], while she was working at weaving, was suddenly seized by a pain that contracted her hands. When she told the others about it with lamentation, they answered:

“Lay down the weaving iron, because this suffering has come upon you as punishment for today’s work.”

Hardly freed from the iron, she entered her bed. Since she found no rest there because of the contraction of her hands, her fellow servants informed their mistress. The mistress ordered that at dawn she should be taken to the tomb of Saint Udalric for her deliverance.

When, weary from the journey, they sat down around the ninth hour in the plain of the Lechfeld to refresh their bodies, the pain began to diminish in the hands of the afflicted woman, so that before they rose from that very place her hands were restored to their former usefulness and straightness.

They then reached the appointed place joyfully, and from there went into the city to the church of Saint Mary, Mother of God. Arriving after Vespers, they reported to us what had happened, just as it had occurred, and returned joyfully to their homes.

## XXVIII

A certain noble matron from the land of the Burgundians, when she had decided to go to the city of Augsburg for prayer, ordered a certain lame almsman to accompany her. She entrusted his horse to two of her servants and instructed them to shoe its feet with iron, as is customary for animals used by travelers.

They treacherously wounded the horse’s feet with nails, so that their informer would not remain with them on the journey to report their actions out of loyalty to his mistress, as he usually did. They said to the lame man:

“Your horse is lame, and therefore you must remain here.”

The lame man answered them:

“Although the horse is lame, I nevertheless do not agree to remain here. Almighty God, who can do all things, is also able, as it pleases him, to bring me to the places appointed for me.”

When he began traveling with the others, he reached Augsburg on a sound and suitable horse. While he prolonged his devout prayer at the tomb of Saint Udalric and with firm faith implored God’s mercy for his safety, he was restored to health in the presence of many people.

When the aforesaid men who had tried to prevent his journey by disabling his horse saw this, they fell to the ground. They confessed their offenses to the clergy and to the others who were present, asking pardon because they had tried to hinder the lame man from reaching the place where the Lord, through the merits of Saint Udalric, had deigned to heal him.

After receiving a penance, they followed the healed lame man, who carried a cross. Each of them carried a stone as large as he could lift, all the way to the church of Saint Mary, Mother of God, which stands in the city. There they lamented their sins at length, asking forgiveness with tears.

When this sign had been recounted in the presence of everyone, the clergy sang *Te Deum laudamus*, and the people, singing *Kyrie eleison*, gave thanks and praise to God.

## XXIX

A certain young man, the son of a count, was held by such a severe illness that he could not turn onto his other side in bed unless supported by others. For a long time he could not take food unless he was revived by being offered small amounts.

When he was exhausted by immense suffering, his faithful attendants carried him in bed to the tomb of Saint Udalric. After offerings had been presented, he tearfully prayed there for mercy.

When they began carrying him in his bed to Saint Mary, halfway along the road he began asking those carrying him to put him down so that he might walk. Since they did not believe that he could walk, they refused to put him down.

At the city gate he again asked to be put down, saying that he could walk. Again they did not consent. When he reached the steps of the church’s courtyard, he earnestly begged them all together, in the name of almighty God, to set down the bed and allow him to walk. But they, wavering in faith, did not grant his request.

When he realized that the illness had left him and that strength had been granted by God’s command, he leapt from the bed, reached the church with a vigorous stride, and returned home in good health.

# EPILOGUE

[Col. 1069]

[Col. 1069A] These few miracles, offered here in advance, should suffice as good examples for diligent readers, so that they may not cause excessive nausea even to the slow and indolent [*nimii nausii*, for *nauseae*, “of excessive nausea”].

For if I were to begin enumerating one by one all the benefits granted by God to those going to the tomb of Saint Udalric and returning from it, or to the sick and weak near the tomb, I could complete the task only with the help of God alone, who can do all things.

They are so numerous and varied that human perception and agility cannot count them. For some, after devoutly fulfilling their vows to come there with offerings, received the gift immediately in their own homes. Others received it while still far away on the journey; others as they approached the place; others when they arrived; and others as they returned from it—each received the benefit in a shortened manner.

The report of these things flew, with good renown, not only through neighboring regions but also through lands far away. The frequent and repeated arrival of peoples from every direction most clearly demonstrates this, showing that many great works of God have been accomplished in their own regions through the merits of Saint Udalric. Knowledge of these things impelled us, because of our own needs, to come to these places.

Having heard this, why do we not awaken, we who are residents of this church, who have so often seen the face of so great a patron, so often received his teaching and blessing, and observed in him the finest examples, and who now, in return for his good works, see and hear continual miracles and various signs in the deliverance of many? Why do we not lay aside the weariness of our desire?

Let us imitate him, as far as God grants us the ability, and with his help enter upon the path of righteousness, by which we may deserve to reach him who, one in divinity and equal in three Persons, remains forever and throughout the ages the unchangeable and almighty God. Amen.

[Col. 1069]

# THE SYNODAL SERMON OF SAINT UDALRIC, BISHOP OF AUGSBURG

From a manuscript codex of the monastery of Neresheim, written in the year of Christ 1009, as may be inferred from these words:

“From the beginning of the world until the coming of the Lord, according to the Hebrew truth, there are 3,956 years; according to the interpreters, however, 5,699 years. All the years from the creation of the first man to the seventh year of Emperor Henry are reckoned as 4,965 according to the Hebrew truth, but 6,708 according to the interpreters.”

(*Labbé, Councils*, IX, 803.)

# MARCUS VELSER’S CONJECTURE REGARDING THE AUTHOR OF THE FOLLOWING SERMON

[Col. 1069]

Since the Neresheim codex in the diocese of Augsburg was written in the year of Christ 1009—that is, thirty-six years after the death of Saint Udalric—it seems likely that these synodal constitutions flowed from Saint Udalric. The bishops who followed him, as the inscription suggests, repeatedly used and proposed them.

That Saint Udalric was their original author is strongly confirmed by a passage of an ancient writer in his *Life*, chapter 6:

“On certain days he resolved to hold chapters with the clergy, in those places where the archpriests thought they could most suitably be held and where they judged that he would be freer from other worldly councils. After summoning the clergy before him, he carefully questioned the archpriests, deans, and the best men he could find among them about how they fulfilled the daily service of God; how the people subject to them were governed in the work of preaching and teaching; with what care infants were baptized, the sick visited and anointed, and the bodies of the dead committed to burial with compassion; how the poor were refreshed from tithes and the offerings of the faithful; how widows and orphans were assisted in all their needs; and with what diligence they served Christ in guests and strangers.

“He also asked whether they kept women introduced into their households and thereby incurred suspicion of wrongdoing; whether they pursued hunting with dogs or hawks; whether they entered taverns for eating or drinking; whether they indulged in shameful jokes; whether they loved drunkenness and banquets beyond measure; whether they devoted themselves to quarrels, disputes, and rivalries; whether they attended secular weddings; whether any of them habitually performed unbecoming services; whether at the Kalends they gathered at appointed places according to the custom of their predecessors and completed the customary prayers there; whether they revisited their churches at the proper time; whether they showed obedience to their superiors; and whether they strove to remain devout and suitable in their entire ministry.”

Since most of these questions correspond to the constitutions, and the time and place also agree, nothing certainly prevents us from attributing both the constitutions and the questions to the same Saint Udalric.

# SEVERINUS BINUS’S NOTICE

[Col. 1069]

Dear reader, after the first edition, the most distinguished Lord Marcus Velser, of revered memory, formerly one of the two chief magistrates of the illustrious Republic of Augsburg, sent me this synodal sermon to be included in the second edition of the councils, together with the following monument of antiquity and his conjecture concerning its author.

I thought I would do something worthwhile by bringing this sermon, hidden in darkness but exceedingly useful for all pastoral synods, into the light. May this prove auspicious for ecclesiastical discipline. I hope it will, if those who have been enrolled into the lot and ministry of the Lord will sink these salutary instructions into their inmost marrow and strive to conform their lives, morals, and actions to their prescription.

Since it is uncertain in what year it was delivered by Udalric, I judged that the year prefixed at the beginning of the written book should be retained.

## [SERMON]

[Col. 1071A]

Brother priests and priests of the Lord, you are fellow workers in our order. We, although unworthy, occupy the place of Aaron; you occupy the place of Eleazar and Ithamar. We act in the place of the twelve apostles; you are patterned after the seventy disciples. We are your shepherds; you are shepherds of the souls entrusted to you.

We will have to render an account of you to the supreme shepherd, the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will have to render an account of the peoples entrusted to you. Therefore, beloved, consider your danger. We admonish and entreat your fraternity: thinking carefully about your common salvation, listen attentively to our admonition; commit to memory what we suggest to you, and strive to carry it out in practice.

First of all, we admonish you that your life and conduct be irreproachable. Your cell should be beside the church, and you should not have women in it. Rise every night for the night offices. Sing your course at the appointed hours. Perform the celebrations of Mass reverently. Receive the body and blood with fear and reverence. Wash and wipe the sacred vessels with your own hands.

No one should sing Mass unless he is fasting. No one should sing who does not communicate. No one should sing without an amice, alb, stole, maniple, and chasuble. These vestments should be clean and should not be used for any other purpose. No one should presume to sing Mass in the alb that he uses for his ordinary purposes.

No woman should approach the Lord’s altar or touch the Lord’s chalice. The corporal should be perfectly clean, and the altar covered with clean linens. Nothing should be placed upon the altar except reliquaries and relics, or perhaps the four Gospels and a pyx containing the Lord’s body for the sick. Everything else should be stored in a clean place.

Every church should have a complete Missal, a Lectionary, and an Antiphonary. A place should be prepared in the sacristy or beside the altar where water may be poured out when the sacred vessels are washed; a clean vessel containing water should hang there, and the priest should wash his hands there after Communion.

Churches should be well covered and vaulted, and the churchyard should often be fortified. No one should sing Mass outside the church, in houses, or in places without a vaulted roof. Every priest should have a cleric or a student who can read the Epistle or the lesson, answer at Mass, and sing psalms with him. No one should sing Mass alone.

No one should sing Mass wearing spurs—which country people call *sporones*—with little knives hanging outside, because this is unbecoming and contrary to ecclesiastical rule.

Sign the chalice and the offering with a straight cross—that is, not in a circle or with a movement of the fingers, as many of you do, but with two fingers held together and the thumb enclosed within them, through which the Trinity is signified. Strive to make this sign + correctly, for otherwise you cannot bless anything.

Visit the sick, reconcile them, and, according to the Apostle (James 5), anoint them with holy oil. Give them Communion with your own hand. No one should presume to entrust Communion to a layman or woman to carry to a sick person.

None of you should demand a reward or gift for baptizing infants, reconciling the sick, or burying the dead. Take care that through your negligence no infant dies without baptism. None of you should be a drunkard or quarrelsome, because a servant of the Lord must not quarrel. None of you should carry weapons in a disturbance, because your weapons ought to be spiritual. None of you should devote yourselves to the amusements of dogs or birds.

No one should drink in taverns. Let each of you, according to his understanding, proclaim to his people something from the Gospel or the Apostle on Sunday or on feast days. You must preach the word of the Lord. Care for the poor, pilgrims, and orphans; invite them to your little meals. Be hospitable, so that others may take a good example from you.

Every Sunday before Mass, make holy water with which the people may be sprinkled, and keep one vessel solely for this purpose. Do not pawn sacred vessels or priestly vestments to a merchant or tavernkeeper. None of you should exact interest or become a lender at interest.

Know that the property and possessions you acquire after the day of your ordination belong to the church. No one should acquire a church without our knowledge and consent. No one should obtain a church through secular power. No one should leave the church to which he has been appointed and move to another for the sake of profit. No one should hold several churches without the assistance of other priests. Under no circumstances should one church be divided among several men.

No one should receive another priest’s parishioner for Mass except while traveling and when it has been agreed. No one should sing Mass in another’s parish. No one should invite a penitent to eat meat or drink wine unless he has first given alms for him in the present circumstance.

No one should presume to baptize except at the vigils of Easter and Pentecost, unless there is danger of death. Let each of you have a baptismal font; if he cannot have a stone one, let him have another vessel prepared for this purpose, in which nothing else is done.

See that you teach all your parishioners the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer. In every way instruct your congregations to observe the fasts of the Four Seasons, the Rogations, and the Greater Litanies. On the Wednesday before Lent, invite the people to confession and impose penance upon them according to the nature of their offense—not according to your own judgment, but as it is written in the Penitential.

Four times a year—that is, at the Nativity of the Lord, the Lord’s Supper, Easter, and Pentecost—admonish all the faithful to approach Communion of the Lord’s body and blood. At the appointed times exhort married people to abstain from their wives. Distribute *eulogiae* to the people after Mass on feast days. No one should wear lay clothing. No one should presume to sell, exchange, or alienate by any means any object, possession, or serf belonging to the church.

Teach that Sunday and the other feasts are to be celebrated without servile work from evening to evening. Prohibit women’s songs and dances in the churchyard. Under adjuration of almighty God, forbid the demonic songs that the common people customarily perform over the dead during the night, as well as the loud laughter in which they indulge.

Do not associate with the excommunicated. No one should presume to sing Mass for them, and you must also announce this to your congregations. None of you should attend weddings. Announce to all that no one should take a wife except at a wedding publicly celebrated.

Prohibit abduction in every way. Let no one approach a close blood relative, and let no one take another man’s betrothed. Make swineherds and other herdsmen come to Mass on Sunday. Let godparents teach their godchildren the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer, or have them taught.

Let the chrism always be kept under wax with a seal [perhaps: under lock and seal], because of certain unfaithful people.

We also take care to admonish you concerning the ministry entrusted to you: let each of you, if possible, keep written with him an exposition of the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer according to the tradition of the orthodox, and understand it fully. From it, if he knows it, let him diligently instruct the people entrusted to him by preaching; if not, let him at least retain or believe it.

He should also understand well the prayers of the Mass and the Canon; if not, he should at least be able to recite them from memory and distinctly. He should be able to read the Epistle and Gospel well—and would that he could explain their meaning word for word. He should know how to recite the words and divisions of the Psalms regularly from memory together with the customary canticles.

Let him know by heart, as we said above, the sermon of Bishop Athanasius on faith in the Trinity, which begins, “Whoever wishes”—*Quicumque vult*. Let him be able to recite clearly, in the plural and singular forms, the exorcisms and prayers for making a catechumen, for consecrating a font, and the remaining prayers over a male and a female.

Likewise, he should at least know how to read well the order and prayers for baptizing, for assisting the sick, for reconciliation according to the canonical rite preserved for him, and for anointing the sick, together with the prayers appropriate to the same need.

Likewise, he should know the order and prayers for conducting the funeral rites of the dead. Likewise, he should retain by heart the exorcisms and blessings of salt and water. He should know the night and day chant.

If possible, he should understand the lesser computation—that is, the epacts, the regular concurrent days, the paschal term, and the rest. He should have a Martyrology and a Penitential, and the other books.

We wish, beloved brothers, that you strive to fulfill in good works what you have received through our instruction, insofar as human weakness permits, with the assistance of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# CHARTER OF UDALRIC, BISHOP OF AUGSBURG

By which he restored to the monastery of Kempten the freedom to elect its abbot.

[Col. 1073C] Let it be known to all who possess the hope of life and to those yet to be born in the future that, while Otto the First was administering the government of the kingdom, Udalric, bishop of the city of Augsburg, of most holy memory, received the flock of the monastery of Kempten from the hand of the aforesaid ruler. He governed it with paternal foresight, not out of greed or severity, but for the advancement of the service of Saint Mary.

At that time, entrusting the burden of his labor to two chosen brothers serving in the same monastery, the venerable man imitated Moses the lawgiving prophet, who, wearied by the multitude of the people, was supported by the help of Aaron and Hur.

On that occasion Saint Udalric designated one of them, named Liuterich, to become dean and master within the cloister of the brothers serving God. He ordered the other, named Irminhart, to labor in the provostship of secular affairs.

Irminhart, who conducted himself wisely in external matters and earned a good reputation in the neighboring regions and at the king’s court through his worthy merits, decided to prepare some remedy for his soul and to build a basilica from the foundations in honor of God. As he had resolved in his mind, he completed it with God’s help and the counsel of the excellent bishop.

The worthy Bishop Vodalric dedicated this very church, honorably built in the brothers’ outer precinct, in honor of the Holy Cross, Saint Erasmus, and Saint Nicholas the Confessor on the seventh day before the Ides of May. In the presence of a multitude of clergy and people, by episcopal decree he determined that one of the brothers who was worthy in regular life and excellence of conduct should provide daily service to that same church and should receive every day, fully, his bishop’s allowance from the brothers’ storeroom.

After dedicating the altar, the holy man, surrounded by every form of piety, gave as its lawful endowment one estate at Ivoningewe, half an estate at Lietenbere, and a third part at Heimirtingen. Still believing that the church could not be maintained from such scant resources, he added a serf named Madelbreth, together with the newly cultivated land that Madelbreth had first reclaimed from the green forest on Mount Chnieboz, and placed it upon this altar with the consent of Salecho the advocate.

Then, clothed in priestly vestments, he said publicly before the people:

“If anyone removes from this church or altar anything of what we have given, may he not be permitted to enter the gate of eternal life, and may he be separated from this light, which every righteous person joyfully beholds in the sight of God.”

[Note: Compare what is said about the bishops of Augsburg both in the preliminary observations, no. 7, and in the *Life*, chapter 1. Velser removes Dionysius from the catalogue of the bishops of Augsburg in his notes on the conversion of Saint Afra, near the end.]
