# APPENDIX

# THE OFFICE OF SAINT UDALRIC

(Dom Gerbert, *Ecclesiastical Writers on Music*, II, 117.)

[Col. 1075D] **Antiphon at the Magnificat.** The solemn feast of the venerable father Wodalric presents joys of great delight; they are received by the vow of clergy and people and celebrated with rejoicing. Let the earth rejoice, adorned with such a bishop. Let heaven exult, enriched by so great a companion. Let the devil alone groan, for at his tomb he continually loses his dominion. Hail, now, crown of martyrs. Hail, glory of confessors. Ornament of all the saints as well, commend us to Christ forever.

[Col. 1076D] **Invitatory.** Let us adore Christ the King and Lord, who today brought Saint Wodalric to the kingdoms of heaven.

**Antiphons of the Nocturns**

1. Blessed Wodalric, from noble and devout parents, was born, God predestining him for the salvation of many.

*Blessed is the man.*

2. His devout parents entrusted him to the monastery of Saint Gall, to be instructed in the sacred studies of letters.

*Why have they raged?*

3. Among the distinguished teachers of regular discipline, he daily gathered the sweetest fruits of contemplation.

*Lord, why have they increased?*

4. Therefore, after the holy youth had been led forward according to the rule of sacred instruction, he was raised to the episcopal chair.

*When I called.*
5. In a vision a voice said to the blessed man: “Bishop Wodalric, know that today you will receive guests.”

“My words.”

6. Among the other notable signs of his miracles, the man of God was very often deemed worthy to enjoy a heavenly vision.

[Col. 1077B] “Lord, our Lord.”

(Three responsories of the first nocturn.)

(R. 1.) As we commemorate the natal feast of the most blessed pontiff Wodalric, who caused him to shine with such great virtues, let us venerate Christ with worthy praises. * (V.) He who, among the other benefits of his favor, granted us the protection of this Saint. Christ.

(R. 2.) The renowned child of God, Wodalric, when he was not yet twelve weeks old, was ordered by divine admonition to be withheld from his mother’s milk. * (V.) So that, strengthened by solid food, he might be prefigured as an outstanding dispenser of the heavenly word. From divine [admonition].

(R. 3.) When the period of infancy had passed and he had become a boy of good character, he was entrusted to the monastery of Saint Gall, * to be instructed in the sacred studies of letters. [Col. 1077C] (V.) There, destined by God’s favor to become the teacher of many, he diligently applied himself. Sacred.

7. (Antiphons of the second nocturn.) When the holy priest was once celebrating the divine mysteries, the right hand of God visibly appeared above the sacred elements.

“Lord, who shall dwell?”

8. One night, Saint Afra appeared to him in a vision and showed him the place in the church where her own body had been laid.

“Lord, in your strength.”

9. He went to the holy place of Agaunum for the sake of prayer, where, by God’s gift, he acquired the relics of the martyrs of the Theban Legion.

“The earth is the Lord’s.”

10. He brought them to Augusta with the greatest honor [Col. 1077D] and devoutly placed them, with hymns and psalmody, in the oratory of the Mother of God.

“I will bless.”

11. Through the oil which the holy Pontiff consecrated on Maundy Thursday, he bestowed, by the grace of Christ, very many benefits of healing upon the sick.

“It is fitting for you.”

12. After celebrating the solemnities of the Masses, he crossed a certain river, swollen by a dangerous flooding of its waters, together with his people, and did so safely.

“It is good.”

(Three responsories of the second nocturn.)

(R. 4.) The one beloved by God, as he had been taught in childhood through a divine oracle, * was adorned with the sacerdotal mitre in the city of Augusta. [Col. 1078A] (V.) This occurred when the grace of God went before him and the vote of the entire people converged as one. In the city.

(R. 5.) “Your prayers and almsgiving, Wodalric, are pleasing to God; he commended you to your two predecessors, * so that they might assist you as you celebrated the sacred mysteries and bless them together with you.” (V.) “Bishop Wodalric, know that today you will receive guests.” So that they might.

(R. 6.) While the man full of God was offering the saving sacrifice, and himself making the sign of the cross according to custom, the holy right hand of God visibly appeared, * and from heaven consecrated the sacred mysteries of the Lord’s sacrament. (V.) Truly blessed and holy was he to whom, at the hour [Col. 1078B] of the holy sacrifice, the right hand of God appeared as he ministered. It consecrated the sacred.

(Antiphon at the Canticles.) “Rise, Wodalric, and hasten to fulfill the divine ministry in the church today according to my word.”

(Three responsories of the third nocturn.)

(R. 7.) A certain man, refusing to obey the words of the man of God, lost both his understanding and his sight and hearing; but, soon brought to him, * he was restored to his former health. (V.) When the most gentle man, sympathizing with his afflictions, granted him pardon and a blessing. To his former.

(R. 8.) After a religious woman had been healed through the prayer of the holy pontiff, she immediately ran ahead of him, * praising and blessing the Lord. (V.) Prostrate at his feet, she devoutly offered thanksgiving. Praising.

(R. 9.) “Holy Woldaric, full of the grace of virtues, hope of the wretched, glory of the churches, * heed the prayers of the supplicant people, that you may obtain pardon for their sins.” (V.) “Because you have been faithful over little, you have been set over much; enter into the joy of your God.” Heed.

1. (Antiphons at Lauds and the Hours.) The Lord Jesus Christ mercifully looked down from heaven upon the earth when he destined Saint Vuodalric to become pontiff of the Catholic Church.

2. The outstanding worshiper of God, raised to the summit of the pontificate by divine election, scattered everywhere the seeds of the heavenly word through the hearts of the faithful.

3. The saving teachings of this most holy man were always accompanied from heaven by the effective power of divine signs. [Col. 1078D]

4. With Saint Afra the martyr once providing the man of God with guidance through a vision, he was deemed worthy to be happily associated with the assembly of the citizens above.

5. In the midst of this sacred gathering he saw the prince of the apostles together with others whom he had either known previously in the flesh or then recognized for the first time in spirit.

(At the Benedictus.) O blessed man, worthy of a heavenly vision, who, among the other secrets of divine revelation, also learned of the war that the Pannonian people would bring and of the triumph granted from heaven to the Christian side.

(At the Magnificat in Second Vespers.) When Wodalric, the priest of God, had been raised from the prison of the flesh to the heavens, such a fragrance of the sweetest odor flowed from his lifeless body that it filled the nostrils and breasts of all who stood there. In his honor let us say: Glory to you, O Lord.

(Collect at Mass.) O God, who have made the day of today’s festival glorious through the passing of your blessed confessor and pontiff Wodalric: mercifully grant that we may venerate on earth the merits of so great a patron and teacher in such a way that we may experience his protection with you in heaven. Through.

(Secret.) May the offering of our devotion, placed upon the sacred altar, be made acceptable to you, Lord our God, through the devout supplication of the blessed Wodalric; and may it purify the hearts of all of us to receive it. Through.

[Col. 1079B] (Preface.) It is right and salutary. Indeed, it is right to proclaim you wonderful in your saints, since whatever sounds wonderful in their words or shines forth as outstanding in their virtues is always the gift of your freely given grace. Therefore, as we celebrate the solemnity of your blessed confessor and pontiff Woldaric from among their company, we ask to be marked for eternity by that same most sacred right hand of your Son, our Lord Jesus Christ—the hand by which you willed the unique sacrifice of our redemption to be visibly blessed while the priest himself stood beside the sacred altar. Through the same Christ our Lord, through whom they praise your majesty.

(Postcommunion.) Having become partakers of the heavenly sacraments, we beseech you, Lord our God: through the intercession of your blessed confessor and pontiff Wodalric, may we be found worthy to obtain both the forgiveness of our sins [Col. 1080B] and eternal life. Through.

ANNO DOMINI DCCCCLXXIV. BENEDICTUS VI PAPA.

[Col. 1079]

HISTORICAL NOTICE.

(MANSI, General Councils, vol. XIX, col. 37.)

[Col. 1079C] Benedict, a Roman by origin and son of Hildebrand, was substituted in Donus’s place after his death, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the year 972 of the Redeemer. During his pontificate, the emperor Otto the Great, after the funerals of his mother and of William, bishop of Mainz, died in Saxony in the twelfth year of his reign. Adelaida, the surviving wife, followed the soul of her deceased husband Otto with those acts of piety which are described by Widukind at the end of Book III.

After the death of his father, Otto II began to rule alone; he had begun the sixth year of his reign together with his father. Benedict was captured and thrown into prison by Boniface, a Roman Frank, son of Ferentius, a cardinal-deacon and a most wicked man, and was strangled by him in the year of Christ 974, after he had occupied the see for one year, three months, [Col. 1080C] and several days.

But the sacrilegious murderer Boniface, who is elsewhere found designated as the seventh of that name, violently invaded the Apostolic See, left vacant by the sacrilegious murder of the excellent pontiff, and held it for one year and one month. Following the older writers, I have judged that he ought not to be counted among the true and legitimate pontiffs, since he entered the Apostolic See disgracefully and abandoned it even more disgracefully. For after the wicked man had stripped the Vatican basilica of all its ornaments, along with many other crimes and scandals, Benedict, relying on the support and assistance of the Alberici, whose family he belonged to, harassed him so severely that, abandoning Rome, he was forced to go to Constantinople. When and on what occasion he returned to Rome, I shall relate below in the life of John XIV.

[Col. 1079]

DIPLOMATIC NOTICE.

(JAFFÉ, Regesta Pontificum Romanorum, 331.)

+ The bulls of Benedict VI were written by the hand of

Stephen, regional notary and scrivener of the Holy Apostolic See (2, 4, [lacuna] Benedict, scrivener of the Holy Supreme and Apostolic See (3).

Issued by the hand of

Wido, bishop and librarian of the Holy Apostolic See (2); John, beloved of God, primicerius of the Holy Apostolic See (3); John, bishop and librarian of the Holy Apostolic See (4).

+ That Donus—whom some judge to have been substituted in the place of John XIII, and others in that of Benedict VI—ought to be removed from the series of popes, whether his name was Donus, Domnus, or Bonum, has been conclusively demonstrated by W. Giesebrecht, *Jahrbücher des deutschen Reichs unter Otto II*, p. 141.

For from the records and other trustworthy indications on whose authority the chronology of these pontiffs has been established, it is sufficiently clear that the interval of one year and six months attributed to Donus in more recent catalogues existed neither between the pontificates of John XIII and Benedict VI nor between those of Benedict VI and Benedict VII. Moreover, it is established that, while Benedict VI was still alive, the antipope Boniface VII had already invaded the Church; thus Donus could by no means have succeeded Benedict.

Finally, it is especially noteworthy that the oldest and best catalogues say nothing about Donus. Thus, in them, the following account is found concerning Benedict VI:

In the Estense manuscript, in Muratori III, II, 332, note o, p.:

“Benedict VI, a deacon from Region VIII below the Capitol, son of Ildebrand, a monk, entered [the office] on January 19. He was elected in the fifth year of King Otto, in the first indiction. Domnus held [the see] for one year and six months. This man was strangled.”

In the Vatican manuscript, in Muratori III, II, 332:

“Benedict VI, Roman by nation, son of Hildibrand, held the see for one year and six months. This man was seized by a certain C[res]cencius, son of Theodora, and confined in the Castel Sant’Angelo, where he was strangled because of the deacon Boniface, whom they sent while he, the pope, was still alive.”

In the catalogue of popes in Eccard, *Corpus historiae*, II, 1640:

“John—or Benedict—VI, Roman by birth, son of Hildebrand, held the see for one year and six months and was strangled in the Castel Sant’Angelo on the advice of Maliface.”

From these three catalogues, which clearly derived from a common source, one—the Estense manuscript—contains the word “Domnus.” Since this word is frequently used in those catalogues in place of “pope,” and since in this passage it can refer only to Benedict VI himself, anyone will readily agree that, through the false interpretation of copyists, that Donus, together with a pontificate of one year and six months—the length we know to have belonged to Benedict VI—entered the later catalogues.

[Col. 1081]

LETTERS AND PRIVILEGES OF POPE BENEDICT VI.

I. Letter of Pope Benedict VI to Frederick, bishop of Salzburg, and his comprovincials. He grants him and his successors apostolic authority in Noricum and Pannonia. (Year 973.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XIX, 38.]

[Col. 1081A]

BENEDICT, by the favor of divine grace and by the election of the entire Roman people apostolic, to FRIDERIC, archbishop of the Church of Salzburg, together with his brothers, namely the bishops of the province of Noricum, lasting happiness in Christ.

When the first parent of the human race and his offspring fell, through the serpent’s persuasion, into a twofold death, God, moved by mercy, sent many remedies into this world: namely, righteous patriarchs, truthful prophets, and the lawgiver together with the law. When all these were unable to save the world, at last he graciously sent his Son, clothed in human flesh, into the world for the redemption of the human race.

While he therefore lived among human beings, he chose twelve apostles and sent them throughout the whole world to sow the word of God in the hearts of the faithful. He established the holy Peter as their prince and as prince of the whole Church, entrusting the ecclesiastical flock to him and saying to him a third time: “Feed my sheep” (John XXI). He also gave him the power of binding and loosing, saying: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven; whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew XVI).

This power was granted not only to the holy Peter, but also to his successors, who hold his place in the Church; from God they too received the same power of binding and loosing. The successors of the holy apostle Peter therefore appointed archbishops in various places, wherever it was necessary and appropriate, to hold their place in the churches, since they themselves could not govern all the churches.

We too, holding the place of the blessed apostle Peter in the Church, insofar as is possible for the people of this age, gladly desire to confirm, [Col. 1081C] as far as we can, the enactments of those who preceded us.

Therefore we grant apostolic authority to Frederick, bishop of the Church of Salzburg, and to his successors, throughout the whole province of Noricum and throughout all Pannonia, both Upper and Lower, in the same manner as his predecessors received that authority from our predecessors: namely, that no one may presume in the aforesaid provinces to assume the pallium for himself, ordain bishops, or perform any office that ought to belong to an archbishop, except the aforesaid archbishop and his successors.

Whoever should oppose or contest this decree, which we, acting in the place of the blessed apostle Peter, have issued with the consent of our bishops and of all the clergy of the Roman Church, should know that he is opposed to Saint Peter and his vicar and will be anathema until he gives satisfaction—whether he be a bishop, priest, cleric of whatever order, or layman of whatever dignity. For we neither wish nor are able to undo the holy enactments of our predecessors.

But just as they established these things with the consent of their bishops and of all the clergy, so let them be made firm and perpetual by their decree together with ours. Furthermore, if any bishops have ever sought, or should seek, through friends or secretly by some fraud, a privilege of the same dignity, we suspend them from that dignity. For we judge it unlawful for any bishop, without the consent of his entire province and his suffragans, to presume to obtain from the Roman pontiff the pallium or any privilege of an archbishopric.

II. Privilege of Pope Benedict, granted to Theoderic, bishop of Trier. (Year 973.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XIX, 45.]

BENEDICT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most beloved brothers in Christ, all bishops, and to Catholic men of every dignity and order, [Col. 1083A] both present and future, perpetual salvation.

Although unworthy, yet by the disposition of divine favor we have assumed the most sacred See of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and the universal teaching office throughout the whole world. It is therefore necessary that we continually exercise the most diligent care for all the churches, so that their rights, inviolably established and confirmed by the authority of that same prince of the apostles and of his other venerable successors, may not be diminished or perish in our time, but rather, strengthened, may fittingly increase and advance.

Therefore we wish your holiness to know that, when our most beloved brother Theoderic, archbishop of the Church of Trier, sent a legate to Rome, we learned—as we had previously discovered by hearing and indeed by reading—that this Church, above the other churches of Gaul, received the beginning of the Catholic religion and the first foundations of the Christian religion and Catholic faith through the evangelical teaching of the holy men Eucharius, Valerius, Maternus, and the others whom the aforesaid most blessed apostle Peter in his own time ordained and instructed and also sent there to preach.

Therefore, with the counsel of the entire order of our Apostolic See and by our freely given consent, we have judged it fitting to reconfirm, strengthen anew, and restore in every way to the Church of Trier and to our aforesaid brother Theoderic—and through him to all his successors—the rights of the privileges authentically granted from the beginning until now by the holy Roman Mother Church to the aforesaid saints and to their remaining successors, namely Agritius, Maximinus, Paulinus, and Severus, those beneficent and apostolic men. This includes the privileges which are acknowledged to have been destroyed in the ruin, fire, or some other disaster of that city.

We decree, therefore, that the bishop of Trier shall hold the first place among the other pontiffs after any ordinary legate of the Apostolic See sent to Gaul or Germany. If no such envoy of the Roman Church is present, he shall likewise have primacy after the emperor or king in sitting, giving judgments, and canonically promulgating synodal decisions, since he is rightly constituted vicar of our Apostolic See in those regions.

For it is not fitting that the bishop of that Church should at any time be regarded as inferior to the others, since the honor of that Church in those regions was primordial under the very prince of the apostles.

In the same way we decree that all who live in his parishes, or who receive from that bishop the ordination and promotion of any ecclesiastical rank, ought canonically to submit to and obey that mother Church and its bishop. For the decree of the blessed Pope Clement appears to have provided as follows on this matter (Epistle 3, to Rufinus of Torana): “If the bishops do not obey you, and all the priests, deacons, subdeacons, and the remaining clergy, and all princes both of higher and lower rank, and the rest of the peoples, tribes, and languages do not obey, they shall be excluded from the boundaries of the holy Church of God,” since the Lord says: “Whoever despises you despises me” (Luke X, 16).

Among all these things, whatever appears to belong to the aforesaid Church of Trier within and outside the city—that is, churches with all their appurtenances, and monasteries both of monks and of virgins, which by royal or imperial grants or written instruments, or by the authority of their founders, belong and ought to belong to it, and whatever that same Church possesses or ought to possess everywhere and by any title—we generally and specifically grant and restore to the aforesaid brother and fellow bishop Theoderic and to his successors, for the perpetual lordship and jurisdiction of the holy Church of Trier, by the text of this command of our Apostolic See, which is to remain valid in this present first indiction and until the end of the age.

If anyone should presume to act against it or attempt in any way to violate what has been justly and canonically decreed by us, let him know that, by the authority of Almighty God, of the aforesaid most blessed prince of the apostles, and of all the saints, and then by our authority, he is to be condemned and anathematized and assigned, together with all the impious, to eternal punishments.

But whoever faithfully determines to observe this privilege of ours may effectively obtain from the Lord God the grace of blessing and the fullness of mercy in the heavenly camps, among the number of the elect.

Written by the hand of Stephen, notary and scrivener of the Holy Apostolic See, in the month of January, in the first indiction. [Col. 1084C]

Issued on the sixth day before the Kalends of February by the hand of Wido, bishop and librarian of the Holy Apostolic See, in the first year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of Lord Benedict, the most holy supreme pontiff and universal pope, Benedict VI; and in the twelfth year of the reign of Lord Otto the Great and the sixth of Otto the Younger.

III. Benedict . . . . . [VI], pope, confirms to Peter, the most reverend abbot of the monastery of Saint Benedict and Saint Scholastica, all its possessions, including the house and church of Saint Vitus in Rome, in Region VII; the monastery of Saint Erasmus; and the monastery of Saints Cosmas and Damian, with its houses and court, situated in Rome beside the Via Lata, together with the larger court and the church within it, which is dedicated to Saint Benedict and Saint Scholastica. This property formerly belonged to John the priest, duke of the Alban castle, and was situated in the third region of Rome, in the place called Massa Juliana. (Year 973.)

[MURATORI, *Italian Antiquities*, V, 774.]

[Col. 1084D]

. . . Written by the hand of Benedict, scrivener of the Holy Supreme and Apostolic See, in the month of November, in the second indiction. Farewell. Issued on the sixth day before the Kalends of December by the hand of John, beloved of God, primicerius of the Supreme Apostolic See, in the first year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of Lord Benedict, supreme pontiff and sixth pope, in the most sacred See of blessed Peter the apostle; while Lord Otto, most pious perpetual Augustus, crowned by God and peaceful emperor, was reigning.

IV. Privilege of Benedict VI for the monastery of Vézelay. (Year 973.)

[D’ACHERY, *Spicilegium*, II, 504.]

[Col. 1085A]

BENEDICT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to ELDRAD, the religious abbot of the holy monastery of Vézelay, and to the entire congregation of that monastery, forever.

Whenever those things are requested from us which unquestionably conform to reason, we ought to grant them with a willing mind and to offer fitting assistance to the desires of those who ask. Therefore, since you requested that we should make an apostolic privilege for the monastery of Vézelay, over which you are known to preside—a monastery established long ago by Gerard, a most noble and Christian man, and by his wife Berta, in honor of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ and in veneration of the most blessed ever-virgin Mary, mother of that same Lord Jesus Christ, in the kingdom of Burgundy, in the county of Avalois, and granted by the aforesaid founders to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, through pious devotion and by a testamentary document—we have willingly decided, moved by your prayers, that this should be done.

Therefore we establish and decree by apostolic authority, and by this apostolic privilege confirm, that no king or pontiff, abbot or count, or any person whatsoever, great or small, seized by greed or deceived by diabolical suggestion, shall dare or presume to rise up in any way against your honor, O venerable [Col. 1085C] Abbot Eldrad, during your lifetime, or to inflict upon you any injury concerning your office, or to inflict any invasion, plunder, or violence upon any of the monastery’s possessions which have been granted and confirmed to you and your predecessors by us and our predecessors through the text of a privilege.

No one may do so, on pain of being separated, by the authority of God, Saint Peter, and our Apostolic See, from the body and blood of the Lord Jesus Christ and from entry into the church.

We also add the following provision to this present chapter, so that we may exclude the occasion for greed: no king, bishop, priest, or any of the faithful may himself, or through an intermediary, dare to accept anything under any guise as a gift in return for the appointment of the same abbot or of clerics or priests, for the distribution of chrism, for the consecration of the basilica, or for any other matter belonging to the same monastery. Nor may the same abbot presume to give anything for his appointment, lest on this pretext the offerings made by the faithful to the holy place be consumed.

Nor may the bishop of that city or diocese celebrate public Masses there unless invited by the abbot of the monastery; nor may he announce stations in the same monastery, lest the repose of the servants of God be disturbed in any way by a popular gathering; nor may he presume to demand provisions or lodging dues from it.

As for the reception of the faithful and of religious men, and the beneficence which the Apostle commands to be shown to all according to the means of the place and its resources, we not only do not forbid it to be practiced there, but even commend it. Nevertheless, the number of the congregation should be kept within such bounds that neither an excess should bring poverty nor a deficiency of inhabitants cause the place to be abandoned.

Furthermore, we wish it to be known that a petitioning letter from Gerard, bishop of the Church of Autun, has reached us concerning the tithes of four churches—namely, of Saint Peter, Saint Christopher, Saint Germanus, and Saint Leodegarius—which the aforesaid abbot had obtained from that bishop, just as his predecessors are known to have obtained them from the bishops successively appointed to that see. We have confirmed this under the protection of our privilege [Col. 1086B], decreeing under excommunication that no bishop of the Church of Autun, either personally or through an agent sent by him, may bring any charge against the abbot of that place or its monks concerning those churches or their tithes, diminish them, or transfer them to another parish.

If any king, bishop, priest, abbot, judge, count, or secular person should attempt to act against this charter of our institution, struck by apostolic anathema, let him lose the dignity of his power or rank, recognize himself as guilty before the divine judgment, and, unless he removes what he has wrongly done, be separated from the most sacred body of our Lord Jesus Christ and subjected to the strict vengeance of the eternal tribunal.

But let the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all who observe what is just toward this place, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace.

Written by the hand of Stephen Nicolanus, bishop [read: Stephen, regional notary] and scrivener of the Holy Roman See. And in the month of November, in the second indiction. Issued on the fourth day before the Kalends of December by the hand of John, bishop [he is the librarian of the Apostolic See], in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Benedict, the most holy pope Benedict VI, while Lord Otto, crowned by God, was reigning as great emperor, in the sixth year, second indiction.

V. Pope Benedict VI confirms the privileges of the monastery of Saint Peter of Rodes. (Year 974.)

[DOM BOUQUET, *Collection*, IX, 242.]

[Col. 1086D]

BENEDICT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to HILDESIND, the religious abbot of the venerable monastery of the apostle Saint Peter, founded in the county of Peralada, on the mountain called Rodes, below the castle of Verdera, and through you to the abbots who will succeed you in that venerable monastery, forever.

Since those things which are known to belong to reasonable desires ought to be granted, the authority of our apostolate, for the strengthening of the pious devotion of the faithful, should in no way refuse to bestow privileges. Therefore, since your excellent and praiseworthy gentleness requested that by apostolic authority we grant and confirm to you [Col. 1087A] and to your successors forever the aforesaid monastery, with all its adjacent and dependent possessions and with its boundaries and limits, we, favoring your pious desires, decree by our apostolic authority that the aforesaid monastery of the apostle Saint Peter, with all its possessions, shall henceforth and until the end of the age remain perpetually under the protection and defense of the holy Roman Apostolic Mother Church, and be established under the guardianship of our holy Church, which by God’s authority we serve. It shall be subject to no other jurisdiction or power except yours and that of your successors forever.

For we confirm to you and to your successors the aforesaid monastery, with its boundaries and adjacent possessions and with all that is set out below: [Col. 1087B] namely, from the boundary-marker which is below the harbor of Fraxani and from that cleared area as far as the place called the Three Brothers; from the eastern side, that is, as far as the middle of the sea. From there it goes to the place called the Mill of Balascho, and from there reaches the Tamarit; then it proceeds as far as Petrafita, and along the ridge as far as Fitorio of Mount Pininello. It ascends to the stronghold of that mountain and, descending, proceeds along the road as far as the place called Sorberelo; descending, it reaches the Clusa and the farmstead of Friulano.

From there it ascends along the aforesaid road to the farmstead of Salvatore, then to the pass of Trederic of Vinea Vitula, and reaches the summit of the mountain [Col. 1087C] that is there. From there it goes along the ridge to the pass of Hermeneard, reaches the spring or pass of Filmera, and from there the pass of Saint Genesius. Thus, ascending and descending, it follows the summit of the ridge called Calmi and reaches below the castle called Pinna Nigra, as far as the vineyards belonging to Palatro.

It goes below the forest south of the castle of Verdera, as far as below the crag called Fitorio, and ascends to the valley of Fulcimania; then it reaches below the springs of Bevotis in the valley of Frinone. From there it goes along the crags to Mount Infesta and descends on the western side along the public road [Col. 1087D] as far as the crag of Ventosa and to the place called the valley of Budiga. It ascends to the cross and then descends along the road from that cross, through the valley, as far as the stream of Budiga.

From there it descends to the pass of Terrario and reaches the summit of the mountain called Rocha Morena. Then, descending and ascending on the northern side, it reaches the summit of Wardia Maurisca and proceeds along the crest of the ridge as far as the clearing of Durando. It reaches along the crest of the ridge the boundary-marker of Saint Genesius. It ascends along the crest of the ridge to the hill above Rovescarium and descends along the ridge to the aforesaid boundary-marker, which lies within the sea.

Moreover, within these boundaries we confirm to you [Col. 1088A] and to your successors the church of the Holy Cross with its tithes and firstfruits; Saint John’s with its tithes, firstfruits, and offerings, together with the lands belonging to those churches; the church of Saint Baudilius in the valley of Tabellaria; the church of Saint Stephen in the valley of Subiradellos; the church of Saint Fructuosus; the church of Saint Vincent in the valley of Lanciani, with its tithes and firstfruits; the church of Saint Genesius; the church of Saint Peter with the castle of Miralias; and the castle of Verdera with its fortified settlement, Fitorio, and Pinna Nigra, together with all the crags, lands, and forests within these boundaries, except the forest of Saint Romanus, as is set out in the charter made for the aforesaid monastery by Count Gausfred and Bishop Suniarius.

Moreover, we confirm permanently to the aforesaid monastery the pond of Castiglione, together with its access to the sea and its islands, as is set forth in the privilege of King Louis, or in the charter which Count Gauzfredus and Bishop Suniarius made for the aforesaid monastery; and whatever that monastery possesses in the villa of Castellione and in the villa of Palatioli, which they call Upper Furtianum and Lower Furtianellum; and the villar of Ildesindus, with its ponds and fisheries; and everything it possesses in the territory of Faro, and in the villas of Saccari and Nova, and in the villar of Stagniolo, with its ponds and small dependent villars; and whatever it possesses in the villa of Petralta, [Col. 1088C] in the villa of Oleastrum, in the villa of Saint Clement, in the villar of Dodolfus, and in the county of Impuritanum; and whatever it possesses in the villa of Militiano, which they call Saint Peter; and in the villa of Armentaria, with the church of Saint Martin; and in the villa of Mucroni, in the villa of Columbus, in the villa of Chaniano with the church of Saint Martin, in the villa of Suntrana, in the villa of Dalmalia, in the villa of Torricella, and in the villa of Rinbeuri mortui.

And in the county of Bisuldunum, whatever it possesses in the villa of Lertium, or in the mills, or in the Tapiola estates which they call Figarias. And in the county of Gerona, the very estate which lies within the walls of that city; and the villa of Palatioli with the church of Saint Genesius; and the church of Saint Mary in Blandas; and the church of Saint Julian; and the church of Saint Gauginus; and the villa of Felgari with the church of Saint [Col. 1088D] Cyprian; and the church of Saint Justa, with the tithes, firstfruits, and offerings belonging to those churches; and the pine tree which belonged to Borellus; and the allods of Soccoronio.

And in the county of Barcelona, and in Vallès, on Mount Signius, and in the valley of Jordaria, whatever it possesses there; and in the villa of Larona, in Agello, and in the territory of Olerdula in Penedès, the allod which belonged to Guilisclus. And in the county of Ausona, whatever it possesses in the villa of Berga, with the church of Saint Cecilia and its allod; and the allod which it possesses in the territory of the castle of Cardona; and in Correzano, the church of Saint Mary and Saint Peter with its allod.

And in the county of Pallars, near the city of Liminiana, the church of Saint Andrew and everything it possesses in that county. And in the county of Cerdanya, [Col. 1089A] in the villa of Atzela, the church of Saint Peter and Saint Columba, with the tithes and firstfruits, and the allods and offerings belonging to it; and whatever it possesses in the villa of Exi; and the villa of Villella in Conflent, with its boundaries.

And in the county of Fenouillèdes, the church of Saint Andrew in the valley of Poziliano, and whatever it possesses there. And near the walls of Narbonne, one estate. And in the county of Roussillon, the church of the Holy Savior with the villar of Milianus; and the villa of Lupianus; and the church of Saint Columba with its tithes and firstfruits; and the villa of Conjuncta with its mills; and the villa of Pollestris with the church of Saint Martin, with tithes, firstfruits, and allods; and the villa of Torrilias with the church of Saint Peter, with firstfruits and offerings.

And in the county of Vallespir, the allod of Campellos and [Col. 1089B] of the valley of Crosa; and the villa of the Nugarius river with the church of Saint Michael, with tithes and firstfruits.

The tithes, firstfruits, and offerings of the aforesaid churches, and the monastery mentioned above, together with the estates and allods, with all their boundaries, limits, territories, and appurtenances, whatever that monastery today possesses within the counties written above, and whatever, with God’s help, it shall acquire in the future, we establish as belonging to the jurisdiction of the holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve.

From this present second indiction, by the text of this privilege, we establish forever the aforesaid monastery, its villas, allods, and churches, with all their appurtenances, as described above, for you and your successors to hold, and to govern and administer with fear of God, so that no king, no bishop, and no person whatsoever, established in any order or office, may ever dare to interfere vexatiously in the affairs of that monastery.

And, decreeing by apostolic censure, under invocation of the divine judgment and the prohibition of anathema, we ordain that all these things, as we have commanded above, remain forever; and that none of our successors in the pontificate may ever presume to inflict any force or invasion upon the possessions of that monastery.

After the death of the abbot, no one shall appoint an abbot there except one whom the agreement and common will of the brothers from that congregation shall have chosen according to God and the Rule of Saint Benedict; and no one shall seek to receive any reward or gift for his consecration. If the bishop of whose diocese the place belongs is unwilling to ordain him freely, he shall be freely ordained, by our authority, either by our Roman mother Church or by whatever bishop he wishes.

But if anyone—which we do not wish—should presume by criminal audacity to violate these provisions established by us for the honor of our Lord Jesus Christ and for the stability of the aforesaid monastery, let him know that he is bound by the chain of anathema and assigned, together with the devil and all the impious, to the most terrible punishment of eternal fire.

But may he who, with pious regard, has proved himself their guardian and observer deserve to obtain from our most merciful Lord God, forever and ever, the grace of every blessing, the absolution of all his sins, and the blessedness of heavenly life with the saints and elect. Amen.

Written by the hand of Stephen, regional notary and archivist of our apostolic mother Church, in the month of April and in the second indiction. Farewell.

## VI [Note: [Col. 1089D] Doubtful.]

Pope Benedict VI confirms the privileges of the monastery of Saint Cecilia of Montserrat. (Year 972.)

[Dom Bouquet, *Collection*, IX, 241.]

Benedict, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Caesarius, abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Cecilia of Montserrat, and to your entire congregation and your successors, perpetual greeting in the Lord.

Since those things which are recognized as pertaining to reasonable desires ought to be granted, our apostolic authority, in providing privileges to strengthen the pious devotion of the faithful, must by no means be denied. Therefore your Excellence and praiseworthy gentleness requested from us that, by apostolic authority, through this privilege, we should grant and confirm to you and your successors forever the aforesaid monastery, with all its appurtenances and dependencies, and with its boundaries and territories.

And therefore, favoring your pious desires, by our apostolic authority we decree concerning the aforesaid monastery of Saint Cecilia, with its territories and appurtenances, and with everything contained below:

No king, archbishop, bishop, count, viscount, [Col. 1090C] or any person, great or small, shall dare to place the aforesaid monastery under his jurisdiction and dominion, nor shall anyone have the power or permission to alienate that place or subject it to the dominion of another monastery. Rather, you shall always retain it free and secure under your authority and that of the Roman Church.

No mortal shall presume to invade or usurp anything which is now there or shall be there in the future, or to disturb the brothers serving there. Thus no king, no bishop, and no person whatsoever, established in any order or office, shall ever dare to interfere vexatiously in the affairs of that monastery, or to constrain its people for any reason.

And the monastery itself, its villas and allods, its tithes and firstfruits, which it formerly possessed and shall acquire thereafter, and its churches [Col. 1090D] with all their appurtenances, as described above, we establish forever by the text of this privilege for you and your successors to hold, and to govern and administer with trembling before God. And we decree that all these things, as we have commanded above, remain wholly and forever.

By apostolic censure, under invocation of the divine judgment and the prohibition of anathema, we ordain that none of our successors in the pontificate may ever presume to inflict any force or invasion upon the possessions of that monastery.

After the death of the abbot, no one shall appoint an abbot there except one whom the agreement and common will of the brothers from that congregation shall have chosen in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Saint [Col. 1091A] Benedict, if a suitable man is found there; and no one shall seek to receive any reward or gift for his consecration.

If the bishop of whose diocese the place belongs is unwilling to ordain him freely, he shall be freely ordained, by our authority, either by our Roman mother Church or by whatever bishop he wishes.

Whoever proves himself the guardian and observer of this privilege of ours shall, by our blessing, enjoy a share in the grace of almighty God and of the apostles Peter and Paul.

But whoever—which we do not wish—is a despiser and transgressor of this privilege of ours shall incur the wrath of almighty God, become alien from the body and blood [Col. 1092A] of Christ, and, by our apostolic authority, remain excommunicated until he has made worthy satisfaction, separated from the fellowship of holy Church and joined to those who said to the Lord God: “Depart from us; we do not desire the knowledge of your ways” (Job 21:14). Bound by the chain of anathema, let him be assigned, together with the devil and all the impious, to the abyss of eternal fire.

Written by the hand of Peter, deacon of the holy Roman Church and chancellor of the sacred palace, in the month of December, on the sixteenth day, in the fifteenth indiction.
